We construct a sliceness obstruction invariant for virtual knots that detects the $\Delta$-move, which functions when the $\Z_{2}\oplus \Z_{2}$-index of chords is available.

Utilizing Floer theoretic conditions, we derive quantitative bounds regarding the proximity—measured via Hausdorff distance, flat norm, or F-metric—of two Lagrangians, contingent upon the magnitude of their Lagrangian angles. Notable applications encompass a strong-weak uniqueness theorem for special Lagrangians and a characterization of varifold convergence to special Lagrangians based on Lagrangian angles.

Lattice paths serve as functional constructs for modeling efficient navigation within discrete or grid-based maps. This study introduces a novel method to generate collision-free lattice paths with maximum efficiency by leveraging the bijective relationship between these paths and rooted ordered trees, thereby reducing the challenge to a one-dimensional search problem. Computational experiments utilizing ten advanced, nature-inspired swarm heuristics across navigation scenarios featuring convex and non-convex obstacles demonstrate the practical viability and efficiency of producing collision-free paths. We posit that this approach holds promise for developing rapid algorithms for planning and combinatorial optimization in discrete map environments.

The infrared solar spectrum offers abundant physical insights into the Sun, which are currently being investigated using advanced ground-based telescopes and modern detection technologies. Among these is the Cryogenic Near-IR Spectro-Polarimeter for the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST), an instrument designed to capture sensitive images of faint infrared solar coronal spectra across all Stokes I, Q, U, and V polarization states. Magnetic dipole emission lines from highly ionized species have been detected in both galaxies and the solar corona. Achieving precise spectral inversion demands accurate spectroscopic calibration of observations. Therefore, carefully analyzing spectral regions surrounding prominent magnetic dipole lines is crucial for deriving physical parameters, especially for off-limb coronal observations from DKIST. This study analyzes the infrared coronal emission lines of Fe XIII at 1074.68 nm and 1079.79 nm, Si X at 1430.10 nm, and Si IX at 3934.34 nm, with the objective of identifying solar photospheric and telluric lines to support reliable data inversion and product generation for four sets of coronal observations. The resulting outputs will be incorporated into the processing pipeline to create Level-2 science-ready data for DKIST users.

Although the hacktivist threat actor known as Phineas Fisher appears frequently in risk decision documents, their specific tactics and techniques often remain obscure. We have developed a MITRE ATT&CK model for this well-known group, mapping their activities against critical infrastructure. This analysis synthesizes data from hacker manifestos, journalistic reports, and official government records to address gaps in existing threat models and better define the skills and methods employed by determined hackers. Additionally, the paper outlines seven essential mitigations that critical infrastructure operators and asset owners can implement to prevent hacktivist intrusions. We are currently in the process of submitting this threat actor to the ATT&CK knowledge base.

The significance of Smart Healthcare in recent years is undeniable. This study aims to advance the field by integrating solutions for Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD), specifically through identifying OCD via oxidative stress biomarkers (OSBs) using machine learning. This process entails gathering OCD class labels from hospitals and matching OSBs from biochemical labs, creating an integrated and labeled dataset, applying appropriate machine learning algorithms to build a prediction model, and deploying these models for predicting OCD in unlabeled OSBs across various laboratories. Additionally, as labeled data volumes grow significantly over time, the prediction models must be periodically redesigned for continued utility. This workflow necessitates distributed data collection, data integration, coordination between hospitals and labs, dynamic design of OCD prediction models using suitable algorithms, and the availability of these models for laboratory use. Considering these requirements, Accu-Help—a fully automated, smart, and accurate conceptual model for OCD detection—is proposed to assist biochemical laboratories in efficiently identifying OCD from OSBs. OSBs are categorized into three classes: Healthy Individual (HI), OCD Affected Individual (OAI), and Genetically Affected Individual (GAI). The core of this proposed framework is the design of a machine learning OCD prediction model. Within Accu-Help, a neural network-based approach is introduced, achieving an OCD prediction accuracy of 86 percent.

Real-Time Magnetic Resonance Imaging (rtMRI) of the midsagittal oral cavity is a significant area of study for speech production research. This work addresses the estimation of utterance-level rtMRI videos based on spoken phoneme sequences. By extracting time-aligned phonemes through forced alignment, we create frame-level phoneme sequences synchronized with rtMRI frames. We introduce a sequence-to-sequence learning model comprising a transformer-based phoneme encoder and a convolutional frame decoder. To enhance this model, we incorporate intermediary features sampled from a pretrained phoneme-conditioned variational autoencoder (CVAE). The model is trained in a subject-specific manner using data from eight participants, with performance evaluated via a subjective test. Additionally, an auxiliary task involving air-tissue boundary (ATB) segmentation is employed to generate objective performance metrics. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method successfully generates realistic rtMRI videos for unseen utterances, and the integration of the CVAE proves particularly beneficial for learning the sequence-to-sequence mapping in subjects where such mapping is challenging.

Artificial learning agents are poised to become ubiquitous in our society, interacting with both humans and other agents within complex environments, including social dilemmas. This study addresses how an external agent can foster cooperation among artificial learners by strategically distributing rewards and punishments based on observed behaviors. We introduce a mechanism for automatically deriving appropriate incentives by analyzing the players' expected parameter updates. Applying this learning rule successfully promotes cooperation and achieves high social welfare in matrix games where agents would typically default to defection. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the resulting cooperative state remains stable in specific games even after the planning agent ceases operation after a set number of episodes, whereas other scenarios require continuous intervention to sustain mutual cooperation. Notably, even in these latter cases, the magnitude of required additional incentives diminishes over time.

Very recently, Foroghi et al. (2022) introduced the extended fractional cumulative residual entropy (EFCRE). This paper presents the extended fractional cumulative past entropy (EFCPE), a dual concept to EFCRE. The new measure relies on the logarithm of the fractional order and the cumulative distribution function (CDF). We investigate various properties of EFCPE, extend it to a bivariate framework, and examine its conditional form along with specific characteristics. Additionally, we propose an EFCPE for inactivity time and introduce the extended fractional cumulative paired phi-entropy for study. The EFCPE is estimated using the empirical CDF, and its behavior within coherent systems is analyzed. Validation of the proposed measure is demonstrated via the logistic map, followed by a reported application.

The entropic uncertainty relation (EUR) is fundamental to quantum information theory, as it characterizes nature's intrinsic uncertainty through an information-theoretic lens. Achieving a tighter lower bound for these relations enhances the precision of predicting measurement results and strengthens quantum information processing capabilities. Despite this, identifying meaningful EURs for multipartite scenarios has remained elusive. This study introduces a generalized EUR (GEUR) applicable to measuring multiple observables within arbitrary many-body systems. When applied to a tripartite scenario, the derived GEUR bound surpasses the bound established by Renes, Boileau, and colleagues. We experimentally validated the GEUR using a four-photon entangled state on an optical platform. Our results demonstrate that the GEUR yields a tighter lower bound for the quantum-secret-key rate, thereby accelerating practical quantum key distribution protocols. By offering deeper insight into the nature of uncertainty, these findings hold broad potential for enhancing security analyses in quantum cryptography.

Excess quasiparticles are vital for superconducting quantum technologies, including qubits and quantum sensors. This study investigates their behavior in phase-biased, finite-length weak links featuring multiple Andreev subgap states, utilizing coupling to a microwave resonator for parity (even/odd) readout. Our theoretical findings demonstrate that near-perfect dynamical polarization within a specific parity sector can be achieved by applying a microwave pulse that resonates with a transition in the opposite parity sector. These results offer a qualitative explanation for recent experiments on hybrid semiconducting nanowire Josephson junctions and provide strategies for the efficient control of parity states in Andreev qubits.

Comparing various dark matter (DM) experiments demands models that adhere to fundamental consistency conditions, such as gauge invariance and perturbative unitarity. Using the two-mediator DM (2MDM) framework as a representative case, we analyze a scenario grounded in a spontaneously broken $U(1)'$ gauge symmetry, featuring a Majorana DM candidate and two $s$-channel mediators: a vector boson ($Z'$) and a scalar (dark Higgs). We conduct a comprehensive parameter scan under the assumption of thermal freeze-out, subjecting the model to extensive constraints from direct and indirect detection, collider searches (monojet, dijet, dilepton), Higgs properties, electroweak precision data, and unitarity bounds. Our results indicate that thermal DM is viable only near an $s$-channel resonance or when at least one mediator is lighter than the DM particle, allowing for thermal abundance even with minute Standard Model couplings. Notably, we observe that vector-mediated DM-nucleon scattering imposes significant limits despite velocity suppression, and indirect detection remains crucial when DM annihilation into both mediators is kinematically permitted.

Using the stellar evolutionary code MESA, we analyzed six exoplanetary systems to determine that their planets will likely spin up the envelopes of their host stars during the red giant branch (RGB) or asymptotic giant branch (AGB) phases sufficiently to induce non-spherical mass loss. We selected these six observed systems, characterized by semi-major axes of approximately 1–2 AU, and simulated their evolution using MESA's binary mode. In four systems, the star engulfs the planet during the RGB phase, while in two, this occurs on the AGB, triggering common envelope evolution (CEE). For the two systems with exoplanet masses around 10 Jupiter masses ($M_J$), the planets spin up the envelope to roughly 10% of the break-up velocity, creating conditions likely to result in significant non-spherical mass loss geometry. Conversely, in the four systems with masses near 1 $M_J$, the envelope reaches only ~1–2% of the break-up velocity; however, magnetic activity influencing dust formation could still cause minor deviations from spherical symmetry. In the two cases involving CEE on the AGB, the planets deposit energy into the envelope exceeding 10% of its binding energy. We anticipate that this energy injection will drive non-spherical mass loss, ultimately shaping elliptical planetary nebulae in each instance.

This paper introduces a fresh proof of the Pythagorean Theorem based on George Birkhoff's axiomatization of Euclidean geometry, which integrates the field of real numbers. Furthermore, the proof's methodology is extended to derive new characterizations of real finite-dimensional unital associative algebras; these characterizations, supported by an associated functor, are also detailed and demonstrated.

This study employs machine learning techniques to automatically classify experimental two-time correlation functions from XPCS measurements of arrested liquid-liquid phase separation in protein solutions. By coupling simulations grounded in the Cahn-Hilliard equation with a glass transition framework, we automatically categorize measured correlation maps based on quench depth and critical concentration at the glass/gel transition. We introduce an automated classification methodology utilizing an autoencoder network alongside a differential evolution algorithm. This approach serves as an initial step toward managing the vast dynamic datasets generated by high-brilliance synchrotron and X-ray free-electron laser sources, thereby enabling rapid comparison with phase field models of phase separation.

This study presents an analytical examination of the insulator/superconductor phase transition within a 5-dimensional $AdS$ soliton background, utilizing both the matching method and thermodynamic geometry. Initially, the matching method was applied to determine the critical chemical potential. Subsequently, the model's free energy and thermodynamic geometry in 3+1 dimensions were explored; specifically, the divergence of the scalar curvature in the thermodynamic geometry approach yielded the system's critical chemical potential. The critical chemical potential values ($\mu_{c}$) derived from these two distinct methods in $d=5$ dimensions were then compared. Additionally, an expression for the condensation operator was derived using the matching method. Our results align closely with existing numerical findings in the literature.

This work examines two categories of operator algebras linked to a unital subsemigroup $P$ within a discrete group $G$: those grounded in universal structures and those based on co-universal structures. Initially, we establish relationships among universal C*-algebras derived from isometric representations of $P$ corresponding to the space $\mathcal{J}$ of constructible right ideals, as well as those arising from associated Fell bundles and induced partial actions. These connections include links between specific quotients and the strong covariance relations defined by Sehnem. Subsequently, we analyze the reduced representation $\mathrm{C}^*_\lambda(P)$ and the boundary quotient $\partial \mathrm{C}^*_\lambda(P)$, which corresponds to the minimal boundary space. We demonstrate that $\partial \mathrm{C}^*_\lambda(P)$ serves as a co-universal object in two distinct contexts: (a) regarding equivariant constructible isometric representations of $P$, and (b) concerning equivariant C*-covers of the reduced nonselfadjoint semigroup algebra $\mathcal{A}(P)$. Under the conditions that $P$ is an Ore semigroup or that $G$ acts topologically freely on the minimal boundary space, $\partial \mathrm{C}^*_\lambda(P)$ aligns with the standard C*-envelope $\mathrm{C}^*_{\text{env}}(\mathcal{A}(P))$ as defined by Arveson. This framework encompasses total orders, finite type and right-angled Artin monoids, the Thompson monoid, multiplicative semigroups of nonzero algebraic integers, and $ax+b$-semigroups over integral domains excluding fields. Specifically, we prove that $P$ is an Ore semigroup if and only if a canonical $*$-isomorphism exists between $\partial \mathrm{C}^*_\lambda(P)$ (or $\mathrm{C}^*_{\text{env}}(\mathcal{A}(P))$) and $\mathrm{C}^*_\lambda(G)$. Furthermore, whenever these conditions are met, $\mathcal{A}(P)$ is established to be hyperrigid.

We conducted a search for transit signals across all known pulsating {\delta} Sct variables (with effective temperatures between 6500 K and 10,000 K) within long-cadence Kepler data by removing the pulsation signal via an automated process. To accomplish this, we developed a straightforward and computationally efficient technique to differentiate low-frequency pulsations from transits in light curves. Our analysis identified three new candidate transit events previously obscured by pulsations, though we note these are likely false positives. Additionally, by reviewing the Kepler Objects of Interest catalog, we pinpointed 13 more host stars exhibiting {\delta} Sct pulsations. For every star in our sample, the absence of pulsation timing variations for a known transiting planet allowed us to derive both an upper mass limit for the planet and the anticipated radial velocity semi-amplitude of its host. Simple injection tests indicate our pipeline achieves 100% recovery for planets with masses of 0.5 RJup or more. Based on the extrapolated number of Kepler {\delta} Sct stars, we anticipate 12 detectable planets above 0.5 RJup in the TESS mission. Our dataset includes some of the hottest known transiting planets orbiting evolved stars and represents the first complete sample of transits around {\delta} Sct variables. We have made our code and pulsation-subtracted light curves publicly available to support further research.

We examine the nonlinear Schrödinger equation featuring a repulsive Dirac delta potential within one-dimensional Euclidean space. Furthermore, we categorize the global dynamics of even solutions that possess the same action as the high-frequency ground state standing wave solutions.

We present a new training strategy for federated learning involving heterogeneous networks, where individual devices may utilize distinct architectures. Our method incorporates a side objective for more complex devices to enable the joint training of diverse architectures within a federated environment. Empirical results demonstrate that this approach enhances performance across various architectures and achieves significant communication efficiency improvements compared to current state-of-the-art techniques.

Most DNA sequencing methods follow the shotgun paradigm, where numerous short reads are generated from random, unknown positions within the DNA. A key issue, explored in arXiv:1203.6233, concerns the necessary read length and coverage depth to ensure reliable sequence reconstruction. Driven by the potential for DNA-based storage, we investigate a coded variant of this problem, where the DNA molecule represents a codeword from a specific codebook. Our primary contribution is an exact characterization of the capacity of this shotgun sequencing channel as it depends on read length and coverage depth. Specifically, our findings demonstrate that whereas the uncoded scenario requires $O(n)$ reads exceeding $2\log{n}$ in length to reliably reconstruct a binary sequence of length $n$, the coded approach achieves a capacity arbitrarily close to 1 with only $O(n/\log{n})$ reads of length greater than $\log{n}$.

Vector boson scattering (VBS) involving two-to-three final states serves as a complementary method for probing Higgs self-couplings within both the Standard Model (SM) and the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) at collider facilities. This work presents the first extensive investigation of the primary $2\rightarrow 3$ VBS processes at high-energy muon colliders, incorporating a detailed analysis of backgrounds. The dominant processes identified are $W^+W^-\rightarrow W^+W^-h$, $ZZh$, and $hhh$. We derive constraints on the Wilson coefficients $c_6$ and $c_{\Phi_1}$, which correspond to dimension-6 operators governing Higgs self-couplings in the SMEFT. At center-of-mass energies of 10 TeV and 30 TeV, our analysis indicates that the expected sensitivity to the coefficients $c_6/\Lambda^2$ and $c_{\Phi_1}/\Lambda^2$ can achieve a precision of approximately $0.01 \text{ TeV}^{-2}$. While the $hhh$ channel yields the most stringent limits, those from the $WWh$ channel are similarly competitive. These findings are critically reliant on the selection of longitudinal polarizations for the final-state $W$ and $Z$ bosons. Furthermore, we examine the impact of varying the efficiency of longitudinal polarization tagging on sensitivity, observing that the statistical significance remains robustly high across different efficiencies.

Using proton-proton collision data from the LHCb experiment at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV and an integrated luminosity of 1.0 fb$^{-1}$, the ratios of the branching fractions for the decays $\Lambda_{c}^{+} \rightarrow p \pi^{-} \pi^{+}$, $\Lambda_{c}^{+} \rightarrow p K^{-} K^{+}$, and $\Lambda_{c}^{+} \rightarrow p \pi^{-} K^{+}$ relative to the Cabibbo-favoured $\Lambda_{c}^{+} \rightarrow p K^{-} \pi^{+}$ mode have been determined. The results are:
\begin{align*} \frac{\mathcal{B}(\Lambda_{c}^{+} \rightarrow p \pi^{-} \pi^{+})}{\mathcal{B}(\Lambda_{c}^{+} \rightarrow p K^{-} \pi^{+})} & = (7.44 \pm 0.08 \pm 0.18)\,\%, \frac{\mathcal{B}(\Lambda_{c}^{+} \rightarrow p K^{-} K^{+})}{\mathcal{B}(\Lambda_{c}^{+} \rightarrow p K^{-} \pi^{+})} &= (1.70 \pm 0.03 \pm 0.03)\,\%, \frac{\mathcal{B}(\Lambda_{c}^{+} \rightarrow p \pi^{-} K^{+})}{\mathcal{B}(\Lambda_{c}^{+} \rightarrow p K^{-} \pi^{+})} & = (0.165 \pm 0.015 \pm 0.005 )\,\%, \end{align*} where the uncertainties represent statistical and systematic errors, respectively. These findings represent the most precise measurements of these quantities available to date. By multiplying these ratios by the world-average branching fraction for $\mathcal{B}(\Lambda_{c}^{+} \rightarrow p K^{-} \pi^{+})$, the absolute branching fractions are derived as:
\begin{align*} \mathcal{B}(\Lambda_{c}^{+} \rightarrow p \pi^{-} \pi^{+}) &= (4.72 \pm 0.05 \pm 0.11 \pm 0.25) \times 10^{-3}, \mathcal{B}(\Lambda_{c}^{+} \rightarrow p K^{-} K^{+}) &= (1.08 \pm 0.02 \pm 0.02 \pm 0.06) \times 10^{-3}, \mathcal{B}(\Lambda_{c}^{+} \rightarrow p \pi^{-} K^{+}) &= (1.04 \pm 0.09 \pm 0.03 \pm 0.05) \times 10^{-4}, \end{align*} where the last uncertainty in each case arises from the uncertainty in $\mathcal{B}(\Lambda_{c}^{+} \rightarrow p K^{-} \pi^{+})$.

To capitalize on the extensive redundancies within video streams and minimize computational overhead, we introduce Skip-Convolutions. Videos are modeled as sequences of frame-to-frame changes and network activation shifts, referred to as residuals. We redefine standard convolution to operate efficiently on these residuals by associating each layer with a binary gate. This gate determines whether a residual is critical for the model's prediction, such as foreground areas, or can be discarded, such as background areas. These gates may function as a jointly trained efficient network alongside convolution kernels or simply filter residuals based on their magnitude. Furthermore, gating mechanisms can enforce block-wise sparsity to optimize performance on specific hardware. By substituting all standard convolutions with Skip-Convolutions in two leading architectures, EfficientDet and HRNet, we achieve a consistent 3 to 4x reduction in computational cost across two distinct tasks without compromising accuracy. Comprehensive evaluations against existing model compression techniques and video efficiency methods confirm that Skip-Convolutions establish a new state-of-the-art by effectively harnessing temporal redundancies in video data.

Seismic data processing utilizes various techniques to mitigate unwanted phenomena arising during acquisition and pre-processing. These challenges primarily include coherent artifacts like multiples, non-coherent signals such as electrical noise, and receiver-related signal loss that results in incomplete traces. Over recent years, machine-learning-based approaches have significantly advanced in addressing these problems. Specifically, deep-learning experts have predominantly adopted heavily fine-tuned, customized discriminative algorithms. While these methods deliver robust outcomes, they often lack a semantic understanding of the underlying data. Driven by this constraint, this study employs a generative approach, which can explicitly model complex data distributions to facilitate superior decision-making. We specifically introduce diffusion models applied to three seismic tasks: demultiple, denoising, and interpolation. Experiments were conducted on both synthetic and real datasets, with diffusion performance benchmarked against standard algorithms. We contend that this pioneering research not only validates the efficacy of diffusion models but also paves the way for future integration of generative models into seismic workflows.

To optimally design materials, it is essential to comprehend structure-property relationships by examining how microstructural parameters influence macroscopic behavior. Computational homogenization achieves this by explicitly modeling the microstructure within the macrostructure, resulting in a coupled two-scale framework. However, the prohibitive computational expense of these multiscale simulations often makes solving design, optimization, or inverse problems impractical. To overcome this limitation, this study introduces a non-intrusive reduced basis method that generates cost-effective surrogates for parametrized microscale issues. This approach is particularly advantageous for multiscale simulations because it decouples the coupled process into two distinct tasks: (1) solving the microscopic problem across various loading or material parameters to train a surrogate model, and (2) solving the macroscopic problem using the derived material model. The proposed method offers three primary benefits. First, it enables the complete recovery of the microscopic stress field. Second, it accurately predicts stress fields across a broad spectrum of material parameters; additionally, it provides derivatives of the effective stress with respect to these parameters, facilitating optimization tasks. Third, it exhibits superior data efficiency, requiring less training data than direct regression on effective stress. In two test cases, the mean approximation error for effective stress was as low as 0.1% despite using a relatively small training set. When integrated into the macroscopic problem, this reduced-order model achieves an online speedup of approximately three orders of magnitude while maintaining high accuracy relative to the FE$^2$ solver.

We examine the spectral decomposition of hypergeometric differential operators defined on the line $\mathrm{Re}\, z=1/2$. These operators emerge in the context of decomposing tensor products of unitary representations for the universal covering of $SL(2\,{\mathbb R})$. Our primary objective is to identify natural bases within the generalized eigenspaces and to derive corresponding inversion formulas.

We present the exceptional topological insulator (ETI), a novel non-Hermitian state of matter defined by unique surface states that are exclusively supported by a three-dimensional topological bulk. This phase emerges from Weyl semimetals or Hermitian three-dimensional topological insulators near criticality, specifically when quasiparticles possess a finite lifetime. Unlike other phases, the ETI does not rely on symmetry for stabilization; instead, it is defined by a bulk energy point gap and displays robust surface states that span the bulk gap as either a single sheet of complex eigenvalues or a single exceptional point. Furthermore, the ETI can be universally induced in gapless solid-state systems, establishing a new framework for understanding non-Hermitian topological matter.

This study introduces a new total Lagrangian, cell-centered finite volume approach for geometrically exact beams featuring arbitrary initial curvatures that experience large displacements and finite rotations. Key aspects, including the selection of rotation parametrization, the mathematical definition of beam kinematics, conjugate strain measures, and the linearization of the governing equations' strong form, are detailed. The paper outlines the finite volume discretization of the computational domain and the specific equations for each volume. A block-coupled Newton-Raphson method is employed to solve the discretized integral equilibrium equations. The proposed methodology's effectiveness is demonstrated by comparing numerical simulations with established benchmark cases from existing literature. Additionally, the study examines the objectivity of the strain measures and conducts mesh convergence analyses for both initially straight and curved beam configurations.

We introduce a framework for computing a "scaling constant" for neural network layers and weights, linking this constant to two key metrics that determine network optimizability. We argue that preconditioning a network through scaling—ensuring all weights share an identical scaling constant—facilitates training. This scaling calculus yields several implications, notably that the geometric mean of fan-in and fan-out, rather than the arithmetic mean or individual fan values, should govern the initialization of weight variance. Consequently, our system enables the off-line design and engineering of ReLU networks, potentially replacing reliance on blind experimentation.

Utilizing holography, we calculate the precise retarded Green's functions for thermal conformal field theories (CFTs) that possess chemical potential and angular momentum. By analyzing the field equations governing quasi-normal modes within charged and rotating black holes in Anti-de Sitter (AdS) spacetime, we transform these equations into Heun equations through suitable variable substitutions. Leveraging the AGT correspondence, we derive connection formulae linking the solutions of these Heun equations across various singularities by employing the crossing symmetries of five-point correlators in Liouville CFT. Ultimately, applying the boundary conditions from the bulk field equations to these connection formulae yields the exact thermal correlators for the boundary CFT.

This paper presents a distributionally robust chance-constrained formulation for the Optimal Power Flow (OPF) problem, enabling system operators to utilize contextual data. We employ an ambiguity set constructed via probability trimmings and optimal transport to safeguard the dispatch solution against uncertainties regarding the relationship between OPF variables and context, derived from a sample of their joint probability distribution. We offer a tractable reformulation of this robust chance-constrained OPF problem using the widely adopted conditional-value-at-risk approximation. Numerical experiments on a modified IEEE-118 bus network with wind uncertainty demonstrate that accounting for the statistical dependence between wind power point forecasts and their prediction errors significantly benefits the power system. Additionally, our experiments indicate that the distributional robustness provided by our probability-trimming approach outperforms alternative methods in terms of both expected cost and system reliability.

This study investigates the dynamics of multi-charged ions released from aluminum plasma generated by a Q-switched Nd:YAG laser. Using time-of-flight (TOF) measurements derived from Langmuir Probe (LP) and spectroscopy (STOF) within an argon ambient at 0.02 mbar, the research systematically analyzes the temporal evolution of multi-charged ions, background neutrals, and ions across varying laser intensities. Results reveal that all species exhibit a double-peak structure regardless of the laser intensity used; the fast peak remains sharp while the slow peak is broad, consistent with prior findings. Furthermore, higher-charged ions demonstrate greater velocities, suggesting acceleration by a transient electric field established during the initial stages of plasma expansion. Notably, as laser intensity increases, the fast peak is delayed while the slow peak advances in time—a phenomenon not previously documented. These observations suggest that ambipolar electric fields play a significant role in the unexpected behavior observed in the TOF profiles.

Addressing the difficulty of leveraging temporal redundancy for inter-predictive coding in point cloud compression due to irregular geometry, this paper introduces an efficient block-based inter-coding method for color attributes. The approach employs integer-precision motion estimation alongside an adaptive graph-based in-loop filtering mechanism to enhance attribute prediction. Specifically, the motion estimation process features an initial search utilizing both geometric and color data, followed by a refinement stage focused solely on minimizing color prediction error. Additionally, a vertex-domain low-pass graph filtering technique is proposed to adaptively suppress noise in predictors derived from motion estimation of varying accuracy. Experimental results indicate that this method achieves substantial coding gains compared to current state-of-the-art techniques.

This study presents a measurement of prompt $J/\psi$ meson production in association with a $W^\pm$ boson, where the $W^\pm$ decays into $\mu\nu$ and the $J/\psi$ decays into $\mu^+ \mu^-$. The analysis covers $J/\psi$ transverse momenta between 8.5 and 150 GeV and rapidities within $|y_{J/\psi}|<2.1$, utilizing ATLAS data from 2012 LHC proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}$ = 8 TeV, with an integrated luminosity of 20.3 fb$^{-1}$. The ratio of the prompt $J/\psi$ plus $W^{\pm}$ cross-section to the inclusive $W^{\pm}$ cross-section is reported as a differential measurement across various $J/\psi$ transverse momenta and is compared against theoretical predictions employing different double-parton-scattering cross-sections.

We investigated a system of polar self-propelled particles (SPPs) within a thin rectangular channel structured into three distinct zones: order-disorder-order. This configuration is defined by the noise levels experienced by the SPPs in each region; the two wider outer regions exhibit noise levels below the critical threshold for order-disorder transitions, whereas the central region or interface features noise exceeding this critical value. This setup renders the system's arrangement analogous to a Josephson Junction (JJ) in solid-state physics. By keeping all other parameters constant, we examined the characteristics of moving flocks both within the bulk and along the interface for varying junction widths ($d$). As the junction width increases, the system undergoes an order-to-disorder transition, shifting from coherent motion of SPPs throughout the entire system to an interrupted current flow at large interface widths. Notably, for intermediate interface widths, we observed a current reversal within the interface itself. This reversal is attributed to the high randomness inside the interface, which causes the interface walls to act as reflecting barriers. This phenomenon mirrors the current reversal seen in JJ systems. Consequently, our study reveals novel collective properties of SPPs at interfaces, offering potential applications in designing devices such as switches utilizing active agents.

Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) offer a promising solution for manipulating and controlling wireless electromagnetic signals, with the potential to significantly enhance network performance. Achieving this requires adjusting the reflection coefficients of unit cells, a process that often results in complex and costly hardware. To mitigate these expenses, system resources can be shared across multiple transmitters and receivers. This paper introduces an efficient reconfiguration technique capable of independently controlling multiple beams. Unlike traditional optimization methods that are computationally intensive, our proposed analytical strategy configures the surface for multi-beam radiation with ease, effectiveness, and efficiency by requiring only phase adjustments. We evaluate performance in both indoor and outdoor broadcast modes, which represent some of the most challenging conditions for wireless networks. Our results demonstrate that the proposed technique yields substantial improvements in channel capacity when receivers are positioned near the surface in an indoor office setting, and it achieves a significant boost in system throughput in outdoor environments.

This paper introduces a fully conservative, positivity-preserving, and entropy-bounded discontinuous Galerkin scheme designed for simulating compressible Euler equations with complex thermodynamics and chemical reactions. Building upon the high-order conservative method by Johnson and Kercher [J. Comput. Phys., 423 (2020), 109826], which ensures pressure equilibrium between neighboring elements, our approach extends this framework. As the first installment of a two-part study, we concentrate on one-dimensional scenarios. Our methodology relies on the minimum entropy principle applicable to entropy solutions of multicomponent, compressible Euler equations, a concept originally proven by Gouasmi et al. [ESAIM: Math. Model. Numer. Anal., 54 (2020), 373--389] for nonreacting flows. We demonstrate that this principle also applies to reacting flows. Subsequently, we detail the components necessary to ensure nonnegative species concentrations, positive density, positive pressure, and bounded entropy, while also maintaining the capability to preserve inter-element pressure equilibrium. To manage stiff chemical reactions, we utilize operator splitting. Specifically, to satisfy the minimum entropy principle during the reaction phase, we construct an entropy-stable discontinuous Galerkin method employing diagonal-norm summation-by-parts operators for solving ordinary differential equations. The proposed formulation is applied to canonical one-dimensional test cases, including thermal-bubble advection, multicomponent shock-tube flows, and a moving hydrogen-oxygen detonation wave featuring detailed chemistry. Our results indicate that enforcing an entropy bound significantly mitigates large-scale nonlinear instabilities arising from merely enforcing positivity, yielding improvements even greater than those observed in monocomponent, calorically perfect cases.

This paper outlines the application of Green functions in solving electrostatic problems. We begin by deriving the electric potential as a function of the charge distribution and the Green function. Subsequently, we present various example problems within spherical, Cartesian, and cylindrical coordinate systems. For each coordinate system, we derive the appropriate Green function for specific geometries and then introduce an arbitrary charge distribution to calculate the resulting electric potential.

Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate that 2D Euler turbulence asymptotic states develop large-scale flow structures resulting from nonzero energy transfers between small wavenumber modes. These initial-condition-dependent states are out of equilibrium and diverge from the predictions of both Onsager and Kraichnan. We introduce "hydrodynamic entropy" as a metric for quantifying order in 2D Euler turbulence, showing that it decreases over time despite the system being isolated, devoid of dissipation, and uncoupled from any heat bath.

We present Tuna, a static analysis technique designed to optimize deep neural network programs. Enhancing the performance of these networks hinges on optimizing tensor operations like convolutions and matrix multiplications. While current optimization strategies often rely on dynamic analysis—using experimental execution on target devices to create data-driven cost models—this approach demands access to specific hardware during compilation and consumes substantial machine resources. In contrast, Tuna profiles programs by constructing features based on target hardware characteristics and employs static analysis to evaluate the relative performance of tensor operations for optimization. Experimental results demonstrate that our method can deliver up to 11x better performance compared to dynamic profiling-based approaches while maintaining equivalent compilation times.

In numerous correlated electron systems, including high-temperature superconductors, competing and intertwined orders manifest as inhomogeneous spin and charge patterns. Utilizing an advanced constrained-path auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) technique, we investigate the interaction between thermal and quantum fluctuations within the two-dimensional Hubbard model. Our analysis provides a precise and systematic description of how spin and charge correlations evolve with temperature $T$ and relate to the ground state across three specific doping concentrations: $\delta = 1/5$, $1/8$, and $1/10$. We observe that lowering the temperature strengthens short-range commensurate antiferromagnetic correlations. Once the correlation length becomes sufficiently large, a modulated spin-density-wave (SDW) emerges. At $\delta = 1/5$, this SDW saturates and stays short-ranged even as $T$ approaches zero; however, at $\delta = 1/8$ and $1/10$, it develops into a ground-state stripe phase. Furthermore, we examine the connection between spin and charge orders, concluding that charge order formation is driven by spin order. We also identify a finite-temperature phase transition below which charge ordering occurs and explore the implications of these findings regarding the nature of this transition.

This study establishes and verifies the equivalence between the joint distributions of first-letter and descent statistics across six classes of permutations that avoid specific patterns of length four. We further demonstrate that these distributions match those found on a restricted set of inversion sequences, where the statistics track the final letter and the count of distinct positive letters, thereby confirming a recent conjecture by Lin and Kim. Both the permutation avoidance classes and the corresponding inversion sequences are enumerated by the $n$-th large Schröder number, yielding a novel bivariate refinement of these numbers. Our proofs rely on auxiliary combinatorial statistics, specialized generating functions tailored to each class, and the kernel method. Additionally, in certain instances, we creatively apply the conjecture itself to facilitate the resolution of the functional equations governing the associated generating functions.

Floquet engineering offers a suite of tools to generate new quantum phases that lack static equivalents, typically requiring intricate manipulation of temporal dynamics. In this work, we introduce a systematic and high-precision method to achieve unconventional Floquet topological phases by designing local band structures within specific momentum regions known as band inversion surfaces (BISs). This approach relies on a novel bulk-boundary correspondence applicable to generic $d$-dimensional periodically driven systems, where the local topological configuration of each BIS uniquely dictates the characteristics of gapless boundary modes. By tailoring the BIS arrangement, we present a highly efficient strategy for realizing, controlling, and detecting new Floquet topological phases. Specifically, we predict a two-dimensional (2D) anomalous Floquet valley-Hall phase; although it possesses trivial global bulk topological invariants, it exhibits protected counter-propagating edge states within every quasienergy gap. The distinctive nature of this 2D phase is further highlighted through analyses of edge geometry dependence and its resilience against disorder scattering. Additionally, we explore and predict anomalous chiral topological phases with valley protection in higher dimensions. Our comprehensive and practically feasible framework establishes a new pathway for realizing and engineering unconventional Floquet topological phases using ultracold atoms and other quantum simulators.

In the animal kingdom, control and communication rely on spikes and rhythms rather than the bits and clocks characteristic of digital technology. Because spikes are countable continuous-time signals, they possess a hybrid nature. This paper examines current initiatives to formulate a control theory for spiking systems. The core argument posits that this hybrid nature stems from a mixed feedback principle, which can be established using the operator theoretic framework of maximal monotonicity. Serving as a nonlinear extension of passivity, maximal monotonicity simultaneously captures the physics of electrical circuits, the computational efficiency of convex optimization, and the feedback control mechanisms of incremental passivity. Finally, we explore the significance of spiking control system theory within the context of the rising era of event-based technology.

We offer initial insights into the far-infrared characteristics of a sample of Lyman Break Galaxies (LBGs) at z ~ 3, identified via IRAC and MIPS-24um detections. These observations, conducted with the PACS instrument on the Herschel Space Observatory in the northern field of the Great Observatories Origins Deep Survey (GOODS-N), yield no individual detections. However, utilizing a stacking method, we construct the average spectral energy distribution (SED) for infrared-luminous LBGs spanning from UV to radio wavelengths for the first time. Our analysis reveals a median infrared luminosity of L_IR = 1.6 x 10^12 L_sun, categorizing this population as ultra-luminous infrared galaxies (ULIRGs). By integrating our findings with existing multi-wavelength data, we constrain the dust temperature, determining that MIPS-detected LBGs are warmer than submillimeter-luminous galaxies for their respective L_IR values, yet they align with the L_IR-T_d relation observed in local ULIRGs. Consequently, our results, supported by average SED estimates, explain the marginal detection rates of LBGs in current sub-mm surveys. This suggests a bias in these studies toward detecting colder ULIRGs at high redshifts, while overlooking high-z ULIRGs possessing warmer dust.

By integrating transport measurements with angle-resolved photoemission and scanning tunneling spectroscopy, we examine various low-energy effects of Hund's coupling within the canonical FeSC family, Li(Fe,Co)As. We establish how doping influences the coherent-incoherent crossover temperature and the quasi-particle effective mass enhancement in the normal state. Furthermore, our tunneling spectroscopy findings in the superconducting regime support the hypothesis that superconductivity arising from a Hund's metal state exhibits a universal maximum superconducting gap relative to the transition temperature ($2\Delta_{max}/k_{B}T_{c}$), a ratio that remains constant regardless of doping concentration or $T_{c}$.

Surgery represents a high-risk field where practitioners must carefully maneuver around critical anatomical structures to prevent complications while completing their primary objectives. This activity significantly influences long-term patient results, yet the underlying mechanics remain largely unexplored for most procedures. To address this gap, we posit that the fundamental components of surgery must be quantified reliably, objectively, and at scale. Establishing such quantification is essential for delivering surgical feedback and optimizing surgeon performance to enhance patient care. To achieve a comprehensive quantification of surgical acts, we introduce Roboformer, a unified deep learning framework that analyzes intraoperative video footage to independently perform multiple functions: identifying surgical phases (the "what") and classifying gestures and assessing skills (the "how"). We validated this framework using four video-based datasets covering two prevalent steps—dissection and suturing—in minimally invasive robotic surgery. Our results demonstrate that Roboformer generalizes effectively across unseen videos, surgeons, medical centers, and procedures. Furthermore, the framework's inherent capacity for explainable findings allows it to pinpoint relevant information for specific tasks. These capabilities are expected to build surgeon confidence in the system's behavior, thereby accelerating clinical adoption and enabling more targeted feedback.

The numerical evaluation of a discrete-time channel model derived from regular perturbation for unamplified links reveals that analyzing the separation between discrete nonlinear interference points allows for the estimation of effective channel memory.

Drawing inspiration from elliptic complex geometry, we investigate M-theory compactifications on real toric fibrations. Specifically, we examine real toric equations instead of the complex equations utilized in F-theory and associated dual frameworks. These geometries are constructed by sweeping real circles across real bases. By analyzing topological transformations, we reveal specific data linked to gauge sectors that depend on affine Lie symmetries.

This study investigates lepton dipole moments within an extension of the Standard Model featuring vector-like leptons that interact exclusively with second-generation Standard Model leptons. This framework naturally generates significant contributions to both the muon $g-2$ and the muon electric dipole moment (EDM). Notably, the presence of these new vector-like leptons in loop diagrams also induces a substantial electron EDM at the two-loop level. We identify viable parameter spaces that resolve the muon $g-2$ anomaly while remaining compatible with current experimental limits on the electron EDM and Higgs decay $h\rightarrow \mu^{+}\mu^{-}$. The resulting EDMs could reach magnitudes of $O(10^{-22})~e \cdot \mathrm{cm}$ for the muon and $O(10^{-30})~e \cdot \mathrm{cm}$ for the electron, making them accessible to detection in upcoming EDM experiments.

Unsupervised multi-object representation learning relies on inductive biases to identify object-centric representations that generalize effectively. However, existing methods often face impracticality due to extensive training durations and high memory usage, or they neglect essential inductive biases. To address this, we present EfficientMORL, a streamlined framework for unsupervised object-centric representation learning. We demonstrate that the optimization hurdles associated with enforcing both symmetry and disentanglement can be overcome by minimizing reliance on costly iterative amortized inference. Our two-stage inference process first employs a hierarchical variational autoencoder to extract symmetric and disentangled features via bottom-up inference, followed by a lightweight network that refines these representations through top-down feedback. By implementing a curriculum that reduces the number of refinement steps during training, the model achieves 99.1% of the refined decomposition performance at test time with zero steps. We validate the framework's superior object decomposition and disentanglement capabilities on standard multi-object benchmarks, delivering nearly an order of magnitude faster training and inference compared to the previous state-of-the-art.

This study addresses a multiblock nonsmooth nonconvex optimization problem featuring nonlinear coupling constraints. Drawing inspiration from the information zone and adaptive regime concepts introduced by Bolte, Sabach, and Teboulle (2018), we introduce a multiblock alternating direction method of multipliers designed to solve this class of problems. The updates for primal variables are determined through a majorization minimization procedure applied within each block. We provide an independent convergence analysis demonstrating that the generated sequence converges subsequentially and globally to a critical point of the augmented Lagrangian. Furthermore, we derive the iteration complexity and present initial numerical results validating the proposed algorithm.

Audio effects whose parameters change periodically over time are commonly known as time-varying or modulation-based audio processors. While most current approaches for modeling these units are tailored to specific circuits and lack the efficiency to generalize across different time-varying effects, we introduce a deep learning architecture grounded in convolutional and recurrent neural networks. This framework is designed for the generic black-box modeling of audio processors capable of long-term memory. We investigate the ability of deep neural networks to capture these extended temporal dependencies and demonstrate their efficacy in modeling a range of linear and nonlinear, both time-varying and time-invariant audio effects. To evaluate the model's performance, we propose an objective metric rooted in the psychoacoustics of modulation frequency perception. Furthermore, we analyze the internal mechanisms of the model to understand what it learns and how it executes the modeling task.

The classical maximum force limit in general relativity (GR) is established between black holes with merging horizons. This study extends the maximum force conjecture to the Kiselev solution, where black holes are enveloped by quintessential matter with an equation of state $w=-2/3$. We demonstrate that within this framework, the maximum force bound remains independent of the black holes' masses, and we show that for black holes surrounded by static quintessence, the maximum inter-black-hole force can approach zero. Furthermore, we investigate the maximum force bound for 4D Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet (4D-EGB) black holes, finding that a maximum force exists in this theory and exceeds the GR limit. Finally, examining the Barrow entropy within entropic force theories, we conclude that the maximum force principle is valid only when the entropy correction exponent $\Delta$ equals zero; for other values of $\Delta$, the principle fails, and the resulting mass dependence in the force bound could lead to the formation of naked singularities.

Wannier functions serve as real-space equivalents of Bloch orbitals, offering a localized perspective on single-particle wave functions and a valuable framework for understanding chemical bonding. While constructing these functions from Bloch orbitals involves a degree of unitary freedom, this flexibility allows for the selection of Wannier functions with desirable characteristics. A common approach exploits this freedom by minimizing spatial variance to generate maximally localized Wannier functions. In this study, we minimize a weighted combination of spatial and energy variances to produce what we term "dually localized Wannier functions." By localizing in the energy domain, these functions become associated with specific energy levels, enabling the simultaneous inclusion of both occupied and unoccupied states. This capability permits the formation of fractionally occupied Wannier functions, a crucial feature for addressing delocalization errors in density functional approximations. We demonstrate how this dual localization generates bonding and antibonding functions for occupied and unoccupied regions, respectively, around the frontier energy in silicon's diamond lattice and molecular ethylene. Consequently, dually localized Wannier functions provide a pertinent description of chemical bonding and are ideally suited for orbital-dependent methods that link Wannier functions to specific energy ranges without necessitating the separate treatment of occupied and unoccupied spaces.

This paper utilizes the sharpened Helgason-Johnson bound to categorize every irreducible unitary representation of $E_{7(-5)}$ possessing non-zero Dirac cohomology. As a practical application, we demonstrate that the cancellation phenomenon between the even and odd components of the Dirac cohomology persists for specific unitary representations of $E_{7(-5)}$. Furthermore, under the assumption of an integral infinitesimal character, we refine the Helgason-Johnson bound for this group, which should facilitate a better understanding of (a portion of) its unitary dual.

Crespo, Hajto, and van der Put demonstrated that for a linear differential equation over a formally real differential field $K$ with real closed constants $k$, there exists a unique formally real Picard-Vessiot extension up to $K$-differential automorphism. Nevertheless, such equations can possess Picard-Vessiot extensions that are not formally real. In these cases, the differential Galois group of a Picard-Vessiot extension forms a linear algebraic group over $k$ and represents a $k$-form of the group $H$, which is the differential Galois group over $K(i)$ (where $i$ is a square root of $-1$ in the algebraic closure of $k$). These observations motivate two inquiries: counting the $K$-differential isomorphism classes of Picard-Vessiot extensions and characterizing the variation of the differential Galois group across the set of $k$-forms of $H$. We examine these questions for instances where $H$ is a special linear, special orthogonal, or symplectic linear algebraic group, concluding that no uniform behavior exists.

In classical metrology, shot noise imposes a fundamental barrier to measurement precision. Recent breakthroughs in quantum devices and algorithms leveraging interference offer promising pathways to surpass this noise-induced limitation. Nevertheless, progress remains hindered by the inability of current algorithms to adequately address the decoherence inherent in experimental setups. By employing a systematic evaluation of metrological effectiveness, we develop the Linear Ascending Metrological Algorithm (LAMA), which significantly enhances precision when measuring continuously distributed variables using a decohering quantum system. We present this protocol within the framework of magnetic field sensing, utilizing superconducting transmon devices in a qudit configuration. Our results demonstrate a quantum metrological method capable of counteracting harmful dephasing and relaxation effects.

This study introduces a novel three-dimensional diffuse interface finite volume method designed to simulate multiple solid and fluid components undergoing large deformations, sliding, and void formation. By extending an existing reduced-equation approach with new flux-modifiers and interface seeding techniques, the method supports various material boundary conditions. It facilitates slip across solid boundaries, interactions between materials and voids, and interface separation. Engineered for ease of implementation, low computational cost, and high parallelizability, the method is well-suited for large-scale, multi-dimensional simulations involving complex material interactions across multiple levels of adaptive mesh refinement. Additionally, the method conservatively generates new interfaces, naturally accommodating high-strain-rate fracture simulations. The governing model has been enhanced to include ductile damage, enabling validation against rigorous physical experiments. Results demonstrate excellent agreement with both experimental data and established Eulerian interface tracking algorithms utilizing sharp interface methods.

Ensuring the safety of autonomous systems operating in unstructured environments requires robust verification algorithms, a task often hindered by factors such as opaque control software components or dynamics that are difficult to model. We introduce a new verification framework capable of analyzing unknown dynamical systems using only a collection of noisy observational data. By training Gaussian processes on this dataset, the framework represents the system as an uncertain Markov process with discrete states constrained within the safe set. Transition probabilities for this abstraction are calculated based on the probabilistic error margins between the regression model and the actual system. Leveraging an established method for verifying safety in uncertain Markov processes, we derive formal safety guarantees. The framework's adaptability is illustrated through various examples, including both switched and nonlinear systems.

We demonstrate that the natural conjugation-invariant cone structure on the linear symplectic group $\mathrm{Sp}(2n)$ exhibits global hyperbolicity within the positively elliptic region $\mathrm{Sp}_{\mathrm{ell}}^{+}(2n)$. This finding resolves a query posed by Abbondandolo, Benedetti, and Polterovich and provides an explicit formula for the bi-invariant Lorentzian distance function defined by these authors for elements in this domain. Furthermore, we characterize both the positively elliptic region and the element $-id \in\mathrm{Sp}(2n)$ based on the causality properties of this cone structure.

This study introduces a content-based recommendation strategy designed to enhance the visibility of opposing beliefs and opinions. Our objective is to equip users with a broader range of perspectives on issues debated within partisan communities. Given that the backfire effect causes individuals to reinforce their original convictions when confronted with contradictory evidence, it is crucial to present counterarguments at opportune moments. The work presented here marks our initial step toward this goal, using political discourse on Twitter surrounding Donald Trump's presidency as a case study.

This study introduces a novel generalized two-dimensional learning method tailored for particle swarm optimization (PSO) in feature selection. The central concept involves enhancing the velocity dimension to incorporate subset cardinality information within the learning framework. Although this added dimension expands the model, the 2D-learning structure preserves all essential characteristics of the original PSO. Consequently, numerous popular PSO variants can be readily integrated into this framework for feature selection tasks. The proposed method's effectiveness was assessed using various benchmark datasets alongside two induction algorithms: Naive-Bayes and k-Nearest Neighbor. Comparative analysis, which included time-complexity evaluations against Genetic Algorithms (GA), Ant Colony Optimization (ACO), and five other PSO variants, demonstrates that the 2D-learning approach yields feature subsets with reduced cardinality, superior classification accuracy, and faster execution times.

This study presents the first experimental visualization of domain structures in Cu$_{0,47}$Ni$_{0,53}$ films, a weakly ferromagnetic alloy with varying thicknesses, at liquid helium temperatures. An enhanced high-resolution Bitter decoration method was employed to map magnetic contrast on the film surfaces well below the Curie temperature ($\sim$ 60 K). Unlike magnetic force microscopy, this approach enabled the observation of domain patterns without disturbing the sample, while also allowing for the examination of larger areas. The results revealed maze-like domain patterns characteristic of perpendicular magnetic anisotropy, with an average domain width of approximately 100 nm.

In our recent work, we introduced a general model describing the light curves of chromospherically active stars as the interference of two real, constant-period signals from long-lived starspots. In this initial paper, we address six specific challenges to this model, which conflict with established views on stellar differential rotation and spot behavior; our goal is to resolve these issues. We provide evidence that the long-lived starspots inherent in our model have already been identified in prior surface imaging research. Furthermore, analyzing both simulated and actual data for FK Com using the Lomb-Scargle power spectrum reveals that this technique fails to detect the two constant-period light curves predicted by our model. If our model holds true, the method yields incompatible estimates for period, amplitude, and minimum epoch, rendering them useless for determining the true characteristics of the underlying light curves. This implication suggests that all previous one-dimensional period analyses of such stars, accepted uncritically since starspots were discovered in 1947, have produced spurious results. However, we reach an impasse as we cannot solve the real light curves of FK Com using current methods. Consequently, our second paper will introduce a novel two-dimensional period-finding technique to solve these real light curves, validate our general model, and answer all six questions raised here.

Remote state estimation, which involves numerous sensors transmitting measurements of distributed dynamic systems to a remote estimator via shared wireless channels, is vital for mission-critical Industry 4.0 applications. While most prior research on remote state estimation relies on orthogonal multiple access (OMA), the associated dynamic radio resource allocation algorithms are limited to very small-scale environments. This study addresses a remote estimation framework utilizing non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA). We formulate a new dynamic resource allocation problem aimed at minimizing the overall long-term average estimation mean-square error. Decision-making at each time step incorporates both the estimation quality state and the channel quality state. Given the problem's large hybrid action space, which involves joint channel assignment and power allocation, we introduce a novel action-space compression technique and develop an advanced deep reinforcement learning algorithm to resolve it. Numerical results demonstrate that our algorithm effectively solves the resource allocation issue, exhibits superior scalability compared to existing literature, and delivers significant performance improvements over various benchmarks.

Stochastic control problems involving delays are notoriously difficult because their path-dependent nature results in inherently high-dimensional systems. This paper introduces and rigorously evaluates algorithms based on deep neural networks designed to address such delayed stochastic control problems. Specifically, we utilize neural networks for sequence modeling—such as recurrent neural networks including long short-term memory—to parameterize policies and optimize the objective function. We validate these algorithms using three benchmark scenarios: a linear-quadratic problem, optimal consumption with a fixed finite delay, and portfolio optimization featuring complete memory. Notably, we observe that the architecture of recurrent neural networks inherently captures path-dependent features with significant flexibility, delivering superior performance alongside more efficient and stable training compared to feedforward networks. This advantage is particularly pronounced in portfolio optimization with complete memory, which involves infinite delay.

Efficient information retrieval (IR) relies heavily on document indexing. Following preprocessing like stop-word removal and stemming, indexes typically retain term frequencies (tf), which indicate a term's importance within a specific document. Conventional IR models augment tf with term discrimination values (TDVs), such as inverse document frequency (idf), to prioritize more distinctive terms. This study introduces a method to learn TDVs using shallow neural networks that approximate classic IR ranking functions like TF-IDF and BM25. The proposed approach surpasses traditional methods in both nDCG and recall, even when trained on a limited set of positively labeled query-document pairs. Furthermore, utilizing these learned TDVs to eliminate vocabulary terms with zero discrimination significantly reduces the inverted index's memory usage and accelerates retrieval—speeding up BM25 by up to three times—without compromising retrieval quality.

This study employs Hamiltonian reduction to streamline Falqui and Mencattini's recent demonstration of Sklyanin's formula for the spectral Darboux coordinates within the rational Calogero-Moser system. By adopting this perspective, we not only confirm a conjecture proposed by Falqui and Mencattini but also derive Sklyanin's formula as a direct consequence.

COVID-19 has impacted over 223 nations globally, creating an urgent demand for affordable, non-invasive, and scalable detection methods, particularly in resource-limited regions where PCR testing is scarce. This study aims to create a deep learning model capable of identifying COVID-19 through voice recordings and brief questionnaires voluntarily submitted by the general public via personal devices. The primary innovation lies in utilizing voice data to distinguish infected individuals. For the methods, we employed the Cambridge University dataset, comprising 893 audio samples from 4,352 participants who utilized the "COVID-19 Sounds" application. We extracted voice features using Mel-spectrogram analysis and developed deep learning classifiers, specifically Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models, to detect positive cases. These were benchmarked against baseline models, including Logistic Regression and Support Vector Machines. The results indicate that an LSTM model using Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCC) features achieved the highest accuracy at 89%, with both sensitivity and specificity also reaching 89%. These findings suggest a significant enhancement in diagnostic prediction accuracy compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches. In conclusion, deep learning demonstrates the ability to detect subtle vocal alterations in COVID-19 patients, offering a promising complementary tool for healthcare professionals to facilitate rapid diagnosis and case tracing through simple voice analysis.

Neuroscience models typically possess a vast number of degrees of freedom, meaning that only narrow regions within their parameter space generate the desired dynamics. Consequently, creating tools and strategies to efficiently locate these critical areas is essential for advancing brain research. Over recent years, numerical simulations have been a standard method for exploring this high-dimensional parameter space across various fields of computational neuroscience. Today, high-performance computing (HPC) offers a robust infrastructure capable of accelerating these explorations, thereby enhancing our comprehension of model behaviors within practical timeframes.

Model misspecification poses a significant challenge across various domains of theoretical and empirical economics. Specifically within misspecified Markov Decision Processes, Esponda and Pouzo (2021) introduced the concept of the Berk-Nash equilibrium and proved its existence for finite state and action spaces. Nevertheless, numerous practical applications—such as the two motivating examples from Esponda and Pouzo, along with Gaussian and log-normal distributions, and CARA, CRRA, and mean-variance preferences—feature continuous state or action spaces, rendering them ineligible under the Esponda-Pouzo existence theorem. This paper extends the existence of the Berk-Nash equilibrium to compact action spaces and sigma-compact state spaces, accommodating potentially unbounded payoff functions. A key difficulty emerges because the Berk-Nash equilibrium relies heavily on Radon-Nikodym derivatives, which are inherently bounded in finite settings but often unbounded in continuous misspecified models. The proofs utilize nonstandard analysis and, distinguishing them from prior economic applications of this method, incorporate innovative arguments derived from the second author's work on nonstandard representations of Markov processes.

We present a new approach for mechanistically studying solid-solid phase transitions, termed \textit{metashooting}. By integrating transition path sampling molecular dynamics with metadynamics, this method enables both comprehensive mechanistic analysis and precise mapping of the free energy landscape. This capability is demonstrated through \textit{metashooting} simulations of the pressure-induced B4/B3 $\rightarrow$ B1 phase transition in ZnO. The resulting free energy map elucidates the function of intermediate configurations within this activated process and highlights the competition among different mechanistic regimes with enhanced accuracy. We contend that \textit{metashooting} is efficiently applicable to a wider range of activated processes.

We present a general theory derived from first principles that addresses both linear and Kerr nonlinear couplings among modes in dielectric optical resonators. Because this approach is independent of specific geometries or mode bases, it serves as a versatile foundation for analyzing phenomena arising from any mix of linear coupling, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity. These include losses due to bending and surface roughness, geometric backscattering, self- and cross-phase modulation, four-wave mixing, third-harmonic generation, and Kerr frequency comb generation. The framework is subsequently applied to a translationally symmetric waveguide to compute the evanescent coupling strength between the waveguide and a nearby microresonator, as well as the Kerr self- and cross-phase modulation terms within the resonator. Finally, this enables the derivation of a dimensionless equation governing the symmetry-breaking dynamics of two counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator, demonstrating that cross-phase modulation is precisely twice as strong as self-phase modulation only when the two counterpropagating modes are otherwise identical.

While numerous researchers have extensively explored learning word embeddings through distributional information, comparatively fewer studies address multilingual contexts. The proposed approach aims to create a unified representation for language pairs where semantically similar words are positioned closely together regardless of their original language. Consequently, this enables the use of classifiers from one language to compensate for missing data in another.

We present a convenient set of analytical tools (the Gaussian formalism) and diagrams (symplectic circuits) for studying multi-mode scattering in analog gravity, specifically pair creation akin to Hawking radiation at black hole and white hole analog event horizons. These diagrams serve as effective ansätze for scattering dynamics, particularly in scenarios where direct analytic solutions are elusive and numerical simulations are required. Applying these tools, we explore entanglement generation in single- and multi-horizon contexts, focusing on cases where the Hawking process is stimulated by classical (e.g., thermal noise) and non-classical (e.g., single-mode squeezed vacuum) inputs. We demonstrate, for example, that initial squeezing can boost entanglement production and mitigate the negative impact of initial thermal fluctuations on output correlations. To address practical considerations, we also analyze how attenuation degrades quantum correlations between Hawking pairs. The methods developed are broadly applicable to analog gravity systems involving Gaussian bosonic quantum systems, such as optical analogs and Bose-Einstein condensates, offering significant utility in these fields. We validate these techniques by applying them to an optical system featuring a white-black hole analog pair, thereby extending our earlier analysis published in Phys. Rev. Lett. 128, 091301 (2022).

In numerous practical scenarios, it is essential for the underlying graph to be as evenly colored as feasible. A coloring is defined as equitable when the count of vertices assigned to each color varies by no more than one; the minimum number of colors required to achieve such a coloring is termed the equitable chromatic number. This paper presents a novel integer linear programming framework for analyzing the equitable chromatic number of a graph and demonstrates its utility in enhancing lower bounds for this parameter. The proposed two-stage methodology involves either determining or upper-bounding the maximum size of an equitable color class within a valid equitable coloring, followed by the sequential refinement of the lower bound for the equitable chromatic number. Computational experiments were conducted using DIMACS graphs and additional datasets drawn from existing literature.

As machine learning systems become increasingly popular, there has been a significant surge in research dedicated to explainability, ensuring that these models remain reliable, fair, and accountable for their decisions. While Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is commonly used to debug black-box models on tabular, text, and image data, explainability within time series remains relatively underexplored. This study aimed to develop and assess model-agnostic explainability specifically for time series forecasting. The project addressed a challenge for a digital consultancy firm seeking a data-driven method to analyze how their sales activities influence closed deals. By framing the issue as a time series forecasting task to predict sales outcomes, the research utilized two novel model-agnostic techniques: Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). These methods were validated through human evaluation. The findings demonstrate that explanations generated by both LIME and SHAP significantly aided humans in comprehending the machine learning model's predictions. Furthermore, this approach is readily adaptable to various other time series applications.

This study introduces the application of meta-learning to low-resource automatic speech recognition (ASR). By treating ASR across various languages as distinct tasks, we utilized the recently developed model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) algorithm to learn initialization parameters from multiple pretraining languages, enabling rapid adaptation to unseen target languages. Our evaluation involved six languages as pretraining tasks and four as target tasks. Preliminary findings indicate that our proposed method, MetaASR, significantly surpasses state-of-the-art multitask pretraining approaches across all target languages and pretraining combinations. Furthermore, leveraging MAML's model-agnostic nature, this work paves the way for applying meta-learning to a broader range of speech-related applications.

Photon pairs created via spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) exhibit robust correlations in their transverse position and momentum. For these pairs, the transverse position correlation length is determined by the crystal's thickness and the pump's wavelength, while the transverse momentum correlation length relies on the pump's beam waist and spatial coherence. By manipulating these factors, one can engineer spatial entanglement. In this study, we exploit the circular asymmetry of the pump by employing an elliptical-Gaussian beam to modulate the entanglement across different transverse axes, a phenomenon termed anisotropic entanglement. We demonstrate the relationship between the level of anisotropic entanglement and the asymmetry of the beam width. Furthermore, we show that with a highly asymmetric pump beam, entanglement along the y-axis disappears entirely, while entanglement along the x-axis persists.

Fake news poses a significant challenge on social media platforms. This paper introduces an empirical investigation into visual, textual, and multimodal models designed for claim verification, assessing claim-worthiness, and conspiracy detection—all key aspects of fake news identification.
