While recent studies indicate that images often exert a stronger influence than text and frequently accompany deceptive content, several recent multimodal approaches have leveraged this combination to detect fake news on sites like Twitter. Despite these advances, the specific impact of images on claim detection remains unclear, particularly within transformer-based textual and multimodal frameworks. Consequently, we evaluate state-of-the-art models utilizing visual, textual, and multimodal data across four datasets in two languages to elucidate the function of images in claim and conspiracy detection tasks.

Reducing inference complexity is crucial when learning Bayesian networks with bounded treewidth. We introduce a new anytime algorithm called k-MAX for this purpose, capable of scaling to thousands of variables. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms competitors in generating higher-scoring structures on complete datasets. We then address structure learning from incomplete data, a challenge typically handled by structurally demanding Structural EM. To mitigate this, we integrate the k-MAX algorithm into the maximization step of Structural EM, enabling efficient calculation of expected sufficient statistics. When tested on data imputation against a state-of-the-art random forest approach, our method matches their accuracy while running approximately ten times faster. Additionally, we confirm that the algorithm features linear worst-case complexity relative to input size and is highly parallelizable.

Dask is a prominent parallel and distributed computing framework that competes with Apache Spark for scalable, task-based big data processing. Built upon the Dask Distributed library, which supports the addition of various communication backends, the system currently utilizes two: TCP and a high-speed network option via UCX-Py, a Cython wrapper for UCX. This paper introduces MPI4Dask, a new communication backend designed specifically for modern GPU-equipped High-Performance Computing (HPC) clusters. MPI4Dask leverages mpi4py over MVAPICH2-GDR, a GPU-aware implementation of the Message Passing Interface (MPI) standard. It implements point-to-point asynchronous I/O communication using non-blocking coroutines defined with Python's asyncio `async/await` syntax. Performance evaluations indicate that MPI4Dask outperforms UCX by 6x for 1-byte messages and 4x for large messages (2 MB and above). Additionally, comparative benchmarks using two applications—a sum of a cuPy array and its transpose, and a cuDF merge—demonstrate that MPI4Dask reduces execution time by an average of 3.47x and 3.11x, respectively, on an internal cluster featuring NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPUs with 1 to 6 Dask workers. Scalability analysis on TACC's Frontera system, utilizing up to 32 Dask workers across 32 NVIDIA Quadro RTX 5000 GPUs and 256 CPU cores, shows MPI4Dask achieves average speedups of 1.71x for cuPy and 2.91x for cuDF applications.

Addressing the persistent challenge of lattice regularization for chiral fermions, this study employs the Density Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG) to simulate the 3-4-5-0 model of (1+1)D chiral fermions. This model features an anomaly-free chiral U(1) symmetry, comprising two left-moving and two right-moving fermions with respective U(1) charges of 3, 4, 5, and 0. Building on the Wang-Wen framework, we implement chiral fermions alongside their mirror partners on opposing boundaries of a thin strip within a (2+1)D multi-layer Chern insulator lattice; the strip's finite width effectively reduces the system to (1+1)D. By introducing two specific sets of six-fermion local interactions exclusively to the mirror sector, we demonstrate that these mirror fermions can be gapped out through the symmetric mass generation (SMG) mechanism without violating the chiral U(1) symmetry, provided the interaction strength exceeds a critical threshold. Our analysis indicates that this interaction-driven gapping transition belongs to the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) universality class. We tracked the evolution of Luttinger parameters prior to the transition, confirming that it occurs precisely when the interaction term becomes marginal. Following the transition, with the mirror sector gapped, we verified that the fermions in the light chiral sector remain gapless, thereby achieving the desired lattice regularization of chiral fermions.

Recent research has increasingly focused on online image hashing, a technique that processes large-scale data in a streaming manner to update hash functions dynamically. However, most existing approaches rely on a supervised setting that uses class labels to enhance performance, yet they suffer from significant limitations in adaptivity and efficiency. First, the requirement for extensive training batches to learn current hash functions results in poor online adaptivity. Second, the time-consuming nature of this training contradicts the fundamental requirements of online learning. To overcome these challenges, this paper introduces Fast Class-wise Updating for Online Hashing (FCOH), a novel supervised online hashing scheme that employs a new and efficient inner product operation. To ensure rapid online adaptivity, a class-wise updating method decomposes binary code learning, allowing hash functions to be refreshed independently for each class; this approach significantly reduces the burden of processing large training batches and achieves at least a 75% reduction in storage. Furthermore, to improve online efficiency, we propose a semi-relaxation optimization that accelerates training by handling binary constraints independently. This method significantly lowers time complexity without introducing additional constraints or variables, while also effectively preserving historical information during updates. Extensive experiments on three widely-used datasets demonstrate that the combination of class-wise updating and semi-relaxation optimization yields superior performance compared to various state-of-the-art methods.

Extending the concept of Brownian motion (BM), fractional Brownian motion (FBM) serves as a standard self-similar framework for anomalous diffusion. By adjusting its Hurst exponent, FBM encompasses sub-diffusion, regular diffusion, and super-diffusion. Like BM, FBM is a symmetric, Gaussian process featuring continuous paths and stationary velocity; however, unlike BM, FBM lacks Markov and martingale properties, and its velocity exhibits correlations. Drawing from recent research on self-similar Ito diffusions, we investigate an alternative self-similar model for anomalous diffusion termed fractional Ito motion (FIM). FIM mirrors FBM's Hurst-exponent dynamics and maintains symmetry with continuous trajectories. In stark contrast to FBM, FIM is demonstrated to be non-Gaussian, a Markov process, and a martingale, while possessing non-stationary, uncorrelated velocity. While FBM presents challenges in simulation, has limited analytic tractability, and produces only Gaussian dissipation, FIM is straightforward to simulate, analytically tractable, and generates non-Gaussian dissipation patterns. Furthermore, we establish that FIM is intrinsically linked to diffusion within a logarithmic potential. Given these advantageous characteristics, FIM provides researchers and practitioners with a highly practical analytic model for anomalous diffusion.

This study addresses Model Inversion (MI) attacks within Split Federated Learning (SFL), a distributed training approach where clients transmit intermediate activations rather than raw data to a central server. Although this method lowers client-side computational demands, it exposes the system to data reconstruction risks by the server. Current protection mechanisms for SFL focus solely on inference, leaving training-phase attacks unaddressed. To resolve this, we introduce ResSFL, an MI-resistant SFL framework designed specifically for the training stage. This framework employs attacker-aware training to derive a resilient feature extractor, which initializes the client-side model before standard SFL training commences. This strategy reduces computational complexity by leveraging a potent inversion model for adversarial training and mitigating vulnerabilities prevalent in early training epochs. Evaluated on the CIFAR-100 dataset, ResSFL effectively counters MI attacks on a VGG-11 model, achieving a high reconstruction Mean-Square-Error of 0.050 compared to the baseline's 0.005. Furthermore, the framework maintains 67.5% accuracy (a mere 1% drop) with minimal computational overhead. The source code is available at: https://github.com/zlijingtao/ResSFL.

This study improves the established fifth-order WENO shock-capturing scheme by integrating deep learning. Specifically, we fine-tune the existing algorithm by training a compact neural network to adjust the smoothness indicators within the WENO framework, thereby enhancing numerical accuracy, particularly at discontinuities. Our approach eliminates the need for additional post-processing to maintain method consistency, which streamlines the procedure and amplifies the neural network's impact. Furthermore, the convergence of the proposed scheme is theoretically guaranteed. We validate our results using the inviscid Burgers' equation, the Buckley-Leverett equation, and the 1-D Euler equations, examining both the Sod and Lax problems. Our findings demonstrate that the novel method surpasses classical fifth-order WENO schemes in simulations where standard solutions suffer from excessive diffusion or overshoot at shock fronts.

A straightforward and budget-friendly laser interlock system is introduced, functioning through software commands sent by an ESP32 microcontroller. The device's design guarantees that the laser beam is immediately terminated if the interlock signal line within the enclosure experiences an open circuit or if the system loses power. To prevent accidental exposure, the system overrides local controls, such as a keypad, requiring the enclosure to be re-secured and active user intervention before operation resumes. Specifically, this device is engineered to mechanically close the shutter of a Spectra-Physics Millennia Pro pump laser while the internal laser continues to run. Furthermore, the accompanying hardware and code are adaptable, allowing deployment on any instrument capable of receiving software instructions via a serial interface.

This work introduces a fractional time-derivative modification to the Drude dispersive model. Both analytical calculations and numerical simulations of the dielectric susceptibility demonstrate strong alignment between the theoretical framework and computational results. In the frequency domain, the absorption coefficient and wave vector—which are essential for characterizing wave propagation in such media—are observed to adhere to a power law, a behavior frequently seen in practical applications. Furthermore, the inclusion of two distinct parameters renders this model more versatile than many existing approaches and facilitates efficient numerical implementation.

The swift expansion of electric vehicles (EVs) heralds a next-generation transportation ecosystem characterized by lower carbon emissions. This rapid advancement, alongside the proliferation of charging infrastructure, is catalyzing the transition from the Internet of Vehicles (IoV) to the Internet of Electric Vehicles (IoEV). By leveraging smart grid and Internet of Things (IoT) technologies, IoEV enables sophisticated bi-directional charging and real-time data analytics. However, controlling IoEV charging faces significant design hurdles due to the stochastic nature of charging events and vehicle mobility. This article offers a comprehensive review of advanced bi-directional EV charging control algorithms. Specifically, for Grid-to-Vehicle (G2V) interactions, we examine charging control strategies in two contexts: the operation of a solitary charging station and the coordination of multiple stations within coupled transportation and power networks. Regarding Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G), we explore how EVs can engage in energy trading within electricity markets and supply ancillary services to the grid. Additionally, a case study demonstrates the economic advantages of jointly optimizing routing and charging schedules for multiple EVs in the IoEV environment. Finally, we identify key open challenges and propose future research directions for IoEV charging scheduling.

We build supersymmetric gravitational soliton solutions that are asymptotically AdS$_5$ within five-dimensional gauged supergravity coupled to an arbitrary number of vector multiplets. These solutions extend the previously known supersymmetric solitons of $U(1)^3$ gauged supergravity established by Chong, Cvetic, Lu, and Pope. We demonstrate that these solitons possess evanescent ergosurfaces and provide reasoning suggesting they are likely nonlinearly unstable.

This study proposes a Lie symmetry analysis for space-time convection-diffusion fractional differential equations involving the Riemann-Liouville derivative, defined by three independent variables and one dependent variable. By utilizing the similarity solutions derived from the Lie symmetry, we derive a reduction form of the governing fractional differential equation. Additionally, we identify a one-dimensional optimal system of Lie symmetry algebras. Finally, we introduce a computational approach employing the spectral method with Bernstein's operational matrices to solve the two-dimensional fractional heat equation under specific initial conditions.

Data from various sources can be represented as multimodal time-series events characterized by diverse sampling rates, data compositions, temporal relationships, and specific attributes. These events exhibit complex nonlinear interactions and occur at irregular intervals. Consequently, both traditional Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and advanced Transformer models struggle to effectively handle these characteristics. This paper introduces a feature fusion framework for multimodal irregular time-series events built upon Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. The approach first extracts intricate features aligned with the irregular patterns of distinct events. Next, it captures and fuses the nonlinear correlations and complex temporal dependencies among these features into a tensor. Finally, feature gates regulate the access frequency of different tensors. Extensive evaluations on the MIMIC-III dataset show that the proposed framework significantly surpasses existing methods in both AUC (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve) and AP (Average Precision) metrics.

This study introduces continuous dynamic average consensus (DAC) algorithms enabling a network of agents to collaboratively estimate the average of their time-varying reference signals. The proposed consensus protocols are designed to remain robust against agents joining or leaving the network, eliminate chattering phenomena, and ensure zero steady-state consensus error. These edge-based protocols utilize smooth internal functions to prevent chattering. Additionally, each agent is restricted to local computations and communication solely with its immediate neighbors. For a balanced and strongly connected communication graph, we offer convergence analysis to identify design parameters that ensure the agents' estimates asymptotically converge to the average of their time-varying reference signals. Finally, simulation results are presented to validate the proposed algorithms and compare their performance against existing methods in the literature.

We execute a Carlotto-Schoen-type gluing procedure featuring interpolating scalar curvature on cone-like structures or their deformations, within the framework of smooth Riemannian asymptotically Euclidean metrics.

Knowledge graph (KG) link prediction is a core challenge in artificial intelligence, finding utility in domains such as biomedicine, information retrieval, and natural language processing. Recent advancements have utilized cross-modal information by ensembling knowledge graph embeddings (KGEs) with contextual language models (LMs). However, current ensemble methods suffer from either inconsistent improvements in ranking accuracy or significant inefficiency on large datasets due to the combinatorial explosion inherent in pairwise ranking with deep LMs. To address these issues, we introduce CascadER, a novel tiered ranking architecture that preserves the accuracy of full ensembling while drastically enhancing efficiency. CascadER employs LMs to rerank outputs from more efficient base KGEs, utilizing an adaptive subset selection strategy that minimizes LM invocations while maximizing accuracy gains. Extensive experiments show that CascadER boosts MRR by up to 9 points over KGE baselines, establishing new state-of-the-art results on four benchmarks and improving efficiency by one to several orders of magnitude compared to competitive cross-modal approaches. Our analysis indicates that the effectiveness of CascadER stems from cross-modal model diversity and the preservation of individual model confidence signals, offering insights for future cascaded architectures. The code and pretrained models are accessible at https://github.com/tsafavi/cascader.

Observations of early rebrightenings occurring 10^2 to 10^4 seconds after a burst have been detected in the afterglows of certain gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). Unlike typical X-ray flares, these events tend to persist for extended durations. While continuous energy injection typically yields a plateau in the light curve rather than a rebrightening, and sudden energy injection creates rebrightenings that are too rapid, this study proposes that ring-shaped jets can account for these phenomena. In this model, the GRB outflow forms a centrally hollowed ring rather than a solid cone. By assuming the observer's line of sight aligns with the central symmetry axis of this hollow structure, we simulated the dynamical evolution of the outflows and derived the corresponding multiband afterglow light curves. The results indicate that this framework successfully explains the early rebrightenings seen in several GRBs, including 051016B, 060109, 070103, and 070208. Consequently, it is suggested that these long-duration early rebrightenings in GRB afterglows originate from ring-shaped jets.

This study examines the tunneling radiation of fermions with spins $1/2$ and $3/2$ originating from a non-stationary Kerr black hole. Initially, we construct the relevant gamma matrices and derive the Hamilton-Jacobi equations for these fermions using the Dirac equation for spin $1/2$ and the Rarita-Schwinger equation for spin $3/2$. Subsequently, the tunneling dynamics of the fermions at the event horizon are analyzed. Ultimately, the thermodynamic characteristics of the non-stationary Kerr black hole are determined. The findings indicate that the tunneling radiation rate, surface gravity, and temperature are all dependent on ${\dot r_H}$ and ${r'_H}$.

This note demonstrates that for two biorthogonal Riesz-Fischer sequences within a separable Hilbert space $H$, if one sequence is complete, then both constitute Riesz bases for $H$. This finding extends a recent result by D. T. Stoeva, which establishes the same conclusion under the condition that the sequences are Bessel sequences rather than Riesz-Fischer sequences.

This paper investigates the long-time dynamics of strong solutions within the 2-D compressible finite extensible nonlinear elastic (FENE) dumbbell model. Applying the Fourier splitting method, we establish an $L^2$ decay rate of $\ln^{-l}(e+t)$ for any $l\in\mathbb{N}$. Leveraging time-weighted energy estimates, this rate is refined to $(1+t)^{-\frac{1}{4}}$. Furthermore, under a low-frequency constraint and utilizing Littlewood-Paley theory, we demonstrate that the solutions reside in a Besov space with a negative index, thereby deriving the optimal $L^2$ decay rate.

Current image deblurring techniques often rely on overly simplified image formation models, rendering them vulnerable to realistic degradations. We introduce a new variational framework that explicitly accounts for pixel saturation, noise, quantization, and non-linear camera response functions (such as those caused by gamma correction). Our findings demonstrate that accurately modeling a more realistic image acquisition pipeline yields substantial improvements in both image quality and PSNR. Additionally, we show that integrating the non-linear response into both the data and regularization components of our energy function produces more detailed restorations compared to naive inversion of the non-linear curve. The proposed energy is minimized using stochastic optimization, and a dataset of realistically degraded images has been generated to evaluate the method's performance.

A low-energy magnetic dipole (M1) spin-scissors resonance (SSR), predicted to lie just beneath the standard orbital scissors resonance (OSR) in deformed nuclei using the Wigner Function Moments (WFM) framework, has been re-examined via fully self-consistent Skyrme Quasiparticle Random Phase Approximation (QRPA). Employing Skyrme interactions SkM*, SVbas, and SG2, we investigated SSR and OSR characteristics in $^{160,162,164}$Dy and $^{232}$Th. The validity of the QRPA approach is confirmed by its accurate reproduction of the M1 spin-flip giant resonance. Results indicate that $^{160,162,164}$Dy possess $I^{\pi}K=1^+1$ states within the 1.5–2.4 MeV range (below the OSR), characterized by substantial $M1$ spin strength, where $K$ denotes the projection of the total nuclear angular momentum onto the symmetry axis. These states are predominantly exhausted by $pp[411\uparrow, 411\downarrow]$ and $nn[521\uparrow, 521\downarrow]$ spin-flip configurations, which map to $pp[2d_{3/2}, 2d_{5/2}]$ and $nn[2f_{5/2}, 2f_{7/2}]$ structures in the spherical limit. Consequently, the anticipated SSR essentially corresponds to low-orbital ($l=2,3$) spin-flip excitations. Contrary to the WFM spin-scissors model, our analysis concludes that nuclear deformation is not the primary driver of low-energy spin $M1$ states but merely influences their properties; instead, spin and orbital strengths are generally mixed and exhibit interference, with weak destructive effects in the SSR region and strong constructive effects in the OSR region. In $^{232}$Th, the $M1$ spin strength is negligible. The experimentally observed groups of $I^{\pi}=1^+$ states at 2.4–4 MeV in the Dysprosium isotopes and 2–4 MeV in $^{232}$Th are primarily attributed to the fragmentation of orbital strength. Furthermore, the distributions of nuclear currents in the QRPA states align partially with isovector orbital-scissors flow but fail to match the spin-scissors pattern.

Accurate depth perception is essential for robots to comprehend their surroundings. From a cognitive neuroscience perspective, visual depth perception is classified into three types: binocular, active, and pictorial. While the former two have been extensively researched for decades, investigations into pictorial depth perception remain in their early stages, gaining significant traction recently through the application of deep learning. Neuroscience indicates that pictorial depth perception relies on the recognition of visible objects. Building on this insight, this thesis explores the connection between object perception and depth estimation within convolutional neural networks (CNNs). To this end, we designed new network architectures based on a basic single-image depth estimation model. Unlike the original model, our proposed structures accept both an image and its corresponding semantic label as inputs, utilizing the semantic labels as the output of the object perception module. Comparative performance results demonstrate that these novel architectures enhance depth estimation accuracy, reducing the relative distance error by 52% across tested scenarios. Most experiments utilized synthetic datasets generated by game engines to ensure a fair performance comparison by eliminating the inaccuracies inherent in depth and semantic labels found in real-world data. These findings suggest that specific synthetic datasets are viable for training depth networks when appropriate real-world data is unavailable. Furthermore, we established that incorporating semantic labels increases the network's robustness against domain shift when transitioning from synthetic training data to non-synthetic test data.

Let $(f,\mathcal{X},\mu)$ denote a measure-preserving dynamical system and let $\phi \colon \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a measurable function. We examine the maximum process $M_n:=\max\{X_1, \ldots, X_n\}$, where $X_i=\phi\circ f^{i-1}$ represents a sequence of observations. Given a non-decreasing sequence of real numbers $(u_n)$ such that $\mu(X_1>u_n)\to 0$, we establish a zero-one law for the event $\mu(M_n\leq u_n\,\textrm{i.o.})$ for specific systems, such as piecewise expanding interval maps like the Gauss map. For the wider category of non-uniformly hyperbolic dynamical systems, we significantly refine existing characterizations of the admissible sequences $u_n$. These findings align with the optimal sequence and series criteria derived by Klass (1985) for independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) processes. Furthermore, we introduce novel series criteria for cases where i.i.d. theory is no longer applicable. Our investigation is closely linked to problems concerning eventual hitting time statistics and extreme value theory.

The dissipative quantum Rabi system, defined as a finite-component setup involving a two-level atom coupled to an optical cavity mode, undergoes a quantum phase transition that significantly boosts the precision of estimating unitary parameters like frequency and coupling strength. Employing the quantum Langevin equation alongside standard mean field theory and adiabatic elimination, this study explores quantum thermometry of a surrounding thermal bath using quantum optical probes. As the atom-cavity coupling strength increases, two distinct singularities emerge: an exceptional point (EP) within the anti-parity-time (anti-$\mathcal{PT}$) symmetrical cavity field, and a critical point (CP) marking the transition from the normal to the superradiant phase. The results indicate that optimal measurement precision is achieved at the CP rather than the EP, with direct photon detection serving as an effective proxy for this optimal state. Furthermore, when the target thermal bath is independent of the additional bath interacting with the cavity, temperature estimation precision consistently improves with higher coupling strength. Conversely, if the target bath is in equilibrium with the extra cavity-interacting bath, increasing the coupling strength introduces noise that degrades temperature information, except when the system is near the CP.

Synthetic data generation offers significant benefits across various domains, including application testing, benchmarking, and privacy protection. A critical component of this process involves generating links between relations while adhering to cardinality constraints (CCs) and integrity constraints (ICs). Specifically, we address the challenge of imputing missing foreign key ($FK$) values in a relation that depends on another via a foreign key, ensuring that both join-view CCs and table-level ICs are satisfied. We introduce a novel framework based on declarative CCs and ICs, demonstrating that the problem is NP-hard. Our proposed two-phase solution guarantees IC satisfaction: Phase I produces an intermediate solution for CCs alone using a hybrid method tailored to different CC types, modeling some as Integer Linear Programs while solving others efficiently. Phase II enhances this by incorporating ICs, utilizing a conflict hypergraph coloring approach to infer the missing $FK$ values. Extensive experiments confirm that our method scales effectively with increasing data and constraint counts while maintaining low error rates for CCs.

Surface buoyancy gradients in a quasigeostrophic fluid allow for surface-trapped Rossby waves. The interaction between these waves and surface quasigeostrophic turbulence creates latitudinally varying mixing, which, under specific conditions, develops into a surface buoyancy staircase. This structure features a meridional buoyancy profile with mixed layers separated by sharp gradients, characterized by eastward jets at the gradients and weaker westward flows in between. This study explores the emergence of this buoyancy staircase limit in surface quasigeostrophic turbulence and analyzes how the resulting dynamics depend on vertical stratification.

Under decreasing stratification [$\mathrm{d}N(z)/\mathrm{d}z\leq0$, where $N(z)$ denotes the buoyancy frequency], the resulting flows exhibit a longer interaction range compared to uniform stratification, along with highly dispersive Rossby waves. In the staircase regime, these flows consist of straight jets perturbed by eastward-propagating along-jet waves, resembling two-dimensional barotropic $\beta$-plane turbulence. Conversely, under increasing stratification [$\mathrm{d}N(z)/\mathrm{d}z\geq0$], the flows display a shorter interaction range and weakly dispersive Rossby waves. In this scenario, the staircase limit yields sinuous jets with significant latitudinal meanders; their shape evolves over time due to the westward propagation of these weakly dispersive along-jet waves. These along-jet waves possess larger amplitudes under increasing stratification than under decreasing stratification. Consequently, the ratio of domain-averaged zonal to meridional speeds is two to three times lower under increasing stratification compared to decreasing stratification. Finally, for a fixed Rhines wavenumber, jets under increasing stratification are spaced more closely together than those under decreasing stratification.

A linearly polarized Laguerre-Gaussian (LP-LG) laser beam with a twist index of $l = -1$ possesses a field structure fundamentally distinct from that of a standard linearly polarized Gaussian beam. Near the beam axis, the longitudinal electric and magnetic components dominate the transverse ones, creating a promising environment for vacuum electron acceleration. Three-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations demonstrate that this configuration can be achieved by reflecting an LP-LG laser off a plasma featuring a sharp density gradient. These simulations reveal that a 600~TW LP-LG beam effectively injects electrons into the beam upon reflection. Electrons injected near the axis undergo sustained longitudinal acceleration driven by the laser's longitudinal electric field. This process yields distinct monoenergetic bunches with minimal divergence. The most energetic bunch reaches an energy of 0.29 GeV, carries a charge of 6~pC, and has a duration of approximately 270~as, with a divergence angle of only $\dg{0.57}$ (10~mrad). Employing a linearly polarized beam rather than a circularly polarized one facilitates the experimental demonstration of this electron acceleration scheme at high-power laser facilities.

We show that numerous Naturalness tests for particle theories found in existing literature can be recast as simple algorithmic evaluations of fine-tuning when matching Wilsonian effective theories across particle mass thresholds. We explore the consequences of this EFT-based definition of Wilsonian Naturalness for various frameworks, including the Standard Model, heavy singlet scalar models, supersymmetry, Grand Unified Theories, twin Higgs scenarios, and extra-dimensional theories. Furthermore, we contend that the Wilsonian Naturalness algorithm introduced here offers a clear, prior, and significant criterion that the Standard Model satisfies and that the next promising theory of particle physics will almost certainly also meet.

We present a new phase transition in black hole physics by examining the thermodynamics of charged dilaton black holes within an extended phase space, treating the black hole's charge as constant. Beyond the standard first-order and critical (second-order) transitions known in charged black holes, we identify a finite jump in Gibbs free energy driven by the dilaton-electromagnetic coupling constant, $\alpha$, across a specific pressure range. This phenomenon signifies a small/large black hole \emph{zeroth-order} phase transition, characterized by divergent thermodynamic response functions such as isothermal compressibility. This zeroth-order transition lies between the typical critical point and the standard first-order transition curve. We demonstrate that raising the dilaton parameter ($\alpha$) expands the zeroth-order segment of the transition curve. Furthermore, while the exponents for the second-order (critical) phase transition remain independent of the dilaton parameter, the requirement for a positive critical temperature imposes an upper limit on $\alpha$ (specifically, $\alpha<1$).

Utilizing the Nambu-Jona-Lasinio (NJL) model, we construct a framework to compute the spin alignment of vector mesons, specifically applying it to $\phi$ mesons within a magnetic field. Our calculations of the $\phi$ meson mass spectra reveal a splitting between longitudinally and transversely polarized states. In a thermal equilibrium system, the $\phi$ meson favors the $\lambda=0$ spin state over the $\lambda=\pm1$ states due to lower energy levels. Consequently, measurements along the magnetic field direction should yield a spin alignment greater than 1/3, a finding that qualitatively matches recent STAR experimental data. Near the critical temperature of $T_{C}=150$ MeV, the positive deviation from 1/3 scales with the square of the magnetic field strength, aligning with predictions from the non-relativistic coalescence model. Furthermore, incorporating anomalous quark magnetic moments alters quark dynamical masses, thereby affecting both the mass spectra and spin alignment of $\phi$ mesons. Ultimately, investigating spin alignment within the NJL framework may enhance our understanding of hadron spin structure formation during the chiral phase transition.

This study identifies the primary challenge in image aesthetics assessment (IAA) as the abstract nature of aesthetic labels, where diverse image contents map to identical aesthetic categories. Consequently, IAA models face a dilemma: during inference, they must associate varied distinct contents with a single aesthetic label, yet during training, they struggle to differentiate these contents based solely on abstract aesthetic supervision that lacks direct content-specific information. To resolve this, we propose distilling semantic pattern knowledge from multiple pre-trained object classification (POC) models into an IAA model. By leveraging the comprehensive content knowledge provided by combining multiple POC models, the IAA model can more effectively relate diverse images to a limited set of aesthetic labels. Supervising an end-to-end single-backbone IAA model with this distilled knowledge significantly enhances performance, yielding a 4.8% increase in SRCC compared to models trained exclusively on ground-truth aesthetic labels. For specific image categories, the SRCC improvement reaches up to 7.2%. Furthermore, comparative analysis demonstrates that our method surpasses ten prior IAA approaches.

Adjoint-based optimization is highly desirable for aerodynamic shape design because its computational expense remains constant regardless of input dimensionality, and it provides high-fidelity gradients essential for gradient-based optimizers. These advantages make it ideal for optimizing complex, highly parameterized geometries, such as aircraft wings, using high-fidelity simulations. However, developing adjoint solvers demands rigorous mathematical handling and extensive software engineering. Additionally, their cost can become prohibitive when solving multiple optimization problems that require numerous restarts to escape local optima. This study introduces a machine learning-driven, surrogate-based framework that substitutes the costly adjoint solver without sacrificing predictive accuracy. Specifically, we train a deep neural network (DNN) on data derived from high-fidelity simulations across a model-agnostic design of experiments covering geometry parameters. The optimal shape is then determined using a gradient-based optimizer paired with the trained DNN. Furthermore, we apply gradient-free Bayesian optimization, utilizing the DNN as the prior mean. Our results indicate that this DNN-Bayesian optimization (DNN-BO) approach outperforms DNN-only optimization at the same computational expense. Overall, the framework achieves high accuracy in predicting the true optimum while requiring significantly fewer high-fidelity function evaluations than traditional adjoint methods. Additionally, we demonstrate that multiple optimization problems can be efficiently solved using the same pre-trained model, thereby amortizing the offline costs of model construction.

As the most widely used operating system globally, Android has become a primary target for diverse malware. In response, the security community tirelessly develops detection mechanisms, with machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) approaches being among the most prevalent. However, sophisticated adversaries have created extensive evasion strategies to bypass these systems by subtly altering malware samples. This survey specifically examines "problem-space" evasion attacks within the Android ecosystem, where attackers modify the actual APK files instead of manipulating extracted feature vectors. We aim to investigate this often-overlooked area, which is frequently neglected due to limited domain knowledge or an overemphasis on general mathematical, feature-space attacks. Furthermore, we present a novel taxonomy of problem-space evasion attacks, analyzing critical components such as the attacker's model, operational methods, and the functional evaluation of the compromised applications post-attack.

We demonstrate the derivation of the tightest possible upper and lower bounds for the median of a gamma distribution across all shape parameters $k > 0$, utilizing the form $2^{-1/k} (A + Bk)$ with closed-form constants $A$ and $B$. The optimal lower bound of this type, which performs best at high $k$, remains within the 48th to 50th percentile, whereas the uniquely superior upper bound stays between the 50th and 55th percentile. We further illustrate how interpolating between these limits produces even tighter, closed-form expressions for the median. Additionally, we identify high-quality closed-form approximations within these bounds, including one that is exact at $k = 1$ and consistently falls between the 49.97th and 50.03rd percentiles.

Diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) represent a severe complication for individuals with diabetes. Patient care can be significantly enhanced through self-management strategies aimed at early detection, ulcer prevention, and the management of complications in existing wounds. This study examines two categories of image-to-image translation techniques (ItITT) to support decision-making and monitoring in DFU cases: noise reduction and super-resolution. In the first scenario, we assessed the noise removal capabilities of convolutional neural network stacked-autoencoders (CNN-SAE) using RGB images corrupted with Gaussian noise. The second scenario involved deploying four distinct deep learning models for super-resolution. Performance across both scenarios was evaluated based on execution time and perceived quality. The results demonstrate that these techniques offer a viable and easily implementable alternative that should be integrated into any system designed for DFU monitoring.

Although deep learning models demonstrate impressive performance across various learning tasks, it remains uncertain whether they can robustly handle reasoning tasks. This is often because models may succeed by exploiting spurious statistical correlations rather than by learning the actual underlying reasoning processes required. Measuring reasoning robustness is particularly challenging, as it demands tasks that resist shortcuts based on data correlations while involving complex objects and constraints. To address this, we introduce ChemAlgebra, a benchmark designed to evaluate the reasoning capabilities of deep learning models through the prediction of stoichiometrically balanced chemical reactions. This task requires manipulating complex discrete objects—molecules represented as formulas or graphs—under algebraic constraints such as the principle of mass conservation. We believe ChemAlgebra will serve as a valuable testbed for next-generation machine reasoning models and help advance their development.

This study generalizes established connections among global asymptotic controllability, sample stabilizability, and the existence of a control Lyapunov function to a broad spectrum of control systems featuring unbounded inputs, notably encompassing control-polynomial systems. Specifically, we examine open-loop controls and discontinuous stabilizing feedbacks that can become unbounded near the target, potentially inducing chattering in the resulting trajectories. A central contribution of our findings is demonstrating the equivalence of global asymptotic controllability, sample stabilizability, and the existence of a control Lyapunov function for these systems—or their impulsive extensions.

This study advances the decomposition of camouflaged regions in images into significant components, specifically camouflaged instances. To advance the emerging task of camouflaged instance segmentation for in-the-wild imagery, we introduce CAMO++, a dataset that expands upon our preliminary CAMO dataset by offering greater quantity and diversity. CAMO++ notably increases the volume of images annotated with hierarchical pixel-wise ground truths. Additionally, we establish a benchmark suite for camouflaged instance segmentation, featuring a comprehensive evaluation of current state-of-the-art instance segmentation methods across various scenarios. Furthermore, we propose a Camouflage Fusion Learning (CFL) framework designed to enhance the performance of these advanced methods. The dataset, model, evaluation suite, and benchmark will be publicly accessible via our project page: https://sites.google.com/view/ltnghia/research/camo_plus_plus

Business Process Simulation (BPS) is a widely used method for evaluating the effects of changes in business processes, such as determining how increased trace volume impacts cycle time. The foundation of BPS is a business process model enriched with simulation parameters. While various studies have developed methods to automatically generate these models from enterprise information system logs using process mining, these approaches typically estimate activity durations based on recorded start and end timestamps. In practice, however, recorded start times often fail to accurately represent the true onset of an activity; for instance, a resource may begin work before their interaction with the system is logged. Without correction, this discrepancy creates artificial waiting periods where the resource appears idle despite being occupied. To resolve this, the article introduces a technique to detect and correct the actual processing time preceding each activity instance. The core concept is that, for simulation purposes, an activity begins when it is enabled and the necessary resource is available. Consequently, the proposed method estimates both the enablement moment and resource availability using event log data, thereby adjusting the start time to account for unrecorded processing durations. An empirical study utilizing eight real-world event logs demonstrates that this approach produces BPS models that accurately mirror the process's temporal dynamics.

I demonstrate that quantum corrections arising from a massive particle introduce a non-local term in the gravitational effective action at zeroth order in the derivative expansion, analogous to the cosmological constant. This term features a fixed coefficient that is significantly larger than the cosmological constant and is not subject to fine-tuning. The interaction operates at energy scales exceeding the particle's mass. The specific form is given by $m^4 (\frac1{\Box}R)_x "<x|\log (\Box +m^2)|y >" (\frac1{\Box}R)_y$, and I examine the interpretation of the kernel $"<x|\log (\Box +m^2)|y >$" along with other relevant aspects.

We present a deep convolutional neural network (DCNN) framework designed for model-free prediction of extreme events in two-dimensional nonlinear physical systems, determining both the timing ("when") and location ("where") of such occurrences. Input data consists of two-dimensional snapshots or images. To facilitate training and temporal prediction, an appropriate labeling scheme is established for a specific prediction horizon. Once an event is identified as likely within this timeframe, a spatial labeling approach is employed to estimate the event's location with a defined resolution. We validate and demonstrate this machine-learning framework using synthetic data derived from the 2D complex Ginzburg-Landau equation alongside empirical wind speed records from the North Atlantic Ocean. The analysis illustrates the trade-offs between prediction horizon, spatial resolution, and accuracy, while also addressing how spatial biases in extreme event occurrence impact predictive performance. Ultimately, the proposed deep learning framework proves viable for forecasting real-world extreme events.

Neutron star (NS) mergers provide a promising environment for synthesizing heavy r-process elements with mass numbers A > 140, a process stabilized by the robust mechanism of fission recycling against various astrophysical uncertainties. This study presents enhancements to the SPY scission-point model, specifically designed to calculate fission fragment distributions for neutron-rich nuclei critical to r-process simulations. These updates involve adjusting the scission distance phenomenologically and applying a smoothing technique to the distribution, resulting in significantly improved alignment with experimental fission yields. Utilizing these refined yields, we estimate neutron emission from excited fragments using distinct evaporation models. The new results are rigorously compared against predictions from the GEF model, and the influence of fission on r-process nucleosynthesis in binary neutron star mergers is re-evaluated. Two specific scenarios are examined: one characterized by a low initial electron fraction subject to strong fission recycling, and another incorporating weak interactions on nucleons. The analysis discusses nuclear chart regions driving fission recycling both during neutron irradiation and post-freeze-out. Furthermore, the impact of fission on the final abundance distribution is investigated using newly established quantitative metrics for fission recycling, seeds, and progenitors, enabling estimates of fission contributions from specific heavy nuclei. Finally, calculations employing SPY and GEF fission fragment distributions are contrasted across both r-process scenarios.

The current atmospheres of gas giants serve as remnants of their formation and evolution, making the measurement of their elemental makeup a critical avenue for addressing longstanding questions about planet origins. However, obtaining precise observational data on the elemental inventories of giant exoplanets has been difficult due to the restricted simultaneous wavelength coverage of existing space-based instruments. In this study, we report thermal emission observations of the non-transiting hot Jupiter $\tau$ Boo b using the SPIRou spectrograph, which offers new wide wavelength coverage (0.95–2.50 $\mu$m) and high spectral resolution ($R=70,000$). By integrating 20 hours of SPIRou data collected over five nights within a comprehensive atmospheric retrieval framework tailored for high-resolution datasets, we determined the abundances of all major oxygen- and carbon-bearing molecules. Additionally, we reconstructed a non-inverted temperature structure using an innovative free-shape, nonparametric TP profile retrieval method. Our results indicate a volume mixing ratio of log(CO) = $-2.46_{-0.29}^{+0.25}$ and a significantly depleted water abundance, less than 0.007 times the solar envelope value. When combined with upper limits for CH$_4$, CO$_2$, HCN, TiO, and C$_2$H$_2$, these findings yield a gas-phase C/H ratio of $5.85_{-2.82}^{+4.44}\times$ solar—consistent with Jupiter's value—and an envelope C/O ratio robustly exceeding 0.60, even when accounting for oxygen potentially sequestered from the gas phase. Collectively, the inferred super-solar C/H, O/H, and C/O ratios in $\tau$ Boo b support a formation scenario beyond the water snowline within a CO-enriched disk driven by pebble drift.

Heterogeneous networks, linking text-rich nodes via diverse edge types, are standard tools for managing information across numerous real-world domains. While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and their hyperbolic counterparts offer effective methods for embedding these networks into low-dimensional latent spaces through neighborhood aggregation and hierarchical feature extraction, they often overlook metapath structures and existing semantic data. Additionally, these methods struggle with noise in training datasets. To address these shortcomings, we introduce the Text Enriched Sparse Hyperbolic Graph Convolution Network (TESH-GCN). This model leverages semantic signals to capture metapath structures and enhances prediction accuracy in large-scale heterogeneous graphs. Specifically, TESH-GCN extracts semantic node information to serve as a connection signal, identifying relevant local neighborhoods and graph-level metapath features from a sparse adjacency tensor within a redefined hyperbolic graph convolution layer. These features, combined with robust semantic inputs from language models, are utilized for downstream tasks. Experimental results on multiple heterogeneous graph datasets demonstrate that TESH-GCN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in link prediction. Moreover, our reformulated hyperbolic graph convolution reduces both training time and model parameters compared to existing hyperbolic approaches. Finally, we validate the model's robustness against varying levels of simulated noise in both graph structures and text, and we provide a mechanism to interpret TESH-GCN's predictions by analyzing the extracted metapaths.

This work examines bivariate stochastic recurrence equations featuring triangular matrix coefficients and determines the tail behavior of their stationary solutions, ${\bf W} = (W_1, W_2)$. Recent findings indicate that $W_1$ and $W_2$ can display regularly varying tails with distinct indices, a phenomenon that contradicts established Kesten-type results. Although only partial results existed previously, we provide a complete characterization of the tail behavior for both components under standard "Kesten-Goldie" and "Grey" conditions. Furthermore, the derived tail asymptotics represent a novel observation within the context of stochastic recurrence equations.

Kernel density estimation (KDE) is a highly prevalent nonparametric technique for density estimation. However, its reliance on the complete training dataset for predictions renders it impractical for many modern big data scenarios. To address these efficiency challenges, various approaches, including tree-based and hashing-based estimators, have been developed. The proposed Density Matrix Kernel Density Estimation (DMKDE) method leverages density matrices from quantum mechanics and random Fourier features for explicit kernel approximation to generate density estimates. Rooted in traditional KDE, DMKDE functions as an approximation method that eliminates the inherent memory constraints of the original approach. This paper presents a systematic evaluation of the DMKDE algorithm, benchmarking it against other state-of-the-art fast approximation techniques across diverse synthetic datasets. Experimental findings indicate that DMKDE performs comparably to its competitors in general density estimation but demonstrates superior advantages specifically in high-dimensional contexts. Additionally, all implementation code has been released as open-source software.

Measuring the universe's expansion rate via cosmic chronometers offers a fresh perspective on cosmic history, yet this method, which directly determines Hubble parameters across various redshifts, is hindered by inherent systematic uncertainties. This study examines recent cosmic chronometer data both with and without these uncertainties to assess their impact on outcomes. To mitigate potential model bias, the analysis employs both model-dependent and model-independent frameworks. The model-dependent approach evaluates the $\Lambda$CDM, wCDM, and CPL models, whereas the model-independent analysis utilizes Gaussian processes, a technique uniquely suited for handling data with non-diagonal covariance matrices.

This research investigates massless 1-dimensional Dirac-Coulomb Hamiltonians, defined as operators on the half-line with the matrix form $D_{\omega,\lambda}:=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{\lambda+\omega}{x}&-\partial_x \\ \partial_x & -\frac{\lambda-\omega}{x}\end{bmatrix}$. We characterize their closed realizations within the Hilbert space $L^2(\mathbb R_+,\mathbb C^2)$, accommodating complex values for the parameters $\lambda$ and $\omega$. In physical contexts, $\lambda$ corresponds to the electric charge, while $\omega$ relates to angular momentum. Our analysis focuses on realizations of $D_{\omega,\lambda}$ that are homogeneous of degree $-1$, which can be arranged into a unified holomorphic family of closed operators indexed by a specific 2-dimensional complex manifold. We detail the spectrum and numerical range of these operators and provide an explicit expression for the integral kernel of their resolvent using Whittaker functions. Additionally, we outline their stationary scattering theory, offering formulas for a natural set of diagonalizing operators and the scattering operator. It is established that $D_{\omega,\lambda}$ emerges from the separation of variables in the 3-dimensional Dirac-Coulomb operator; we present a straightforward argument demonstrating this holds in arbitrary dimensions. We also elucidate the connection between spherically symmetric Dirac operators and the Dirac operator on the sphere, including its associated eigenproblem. Motivated by extensive literature on distinguished self-adjoint realizations of Dirac-Coulomb Hamiltonians, we demonstrate that these realizations arise naturally when holomorphy serves as the guiding principle and represent infrared attractive fixed points under scaling actions. Beyond applications in relativistic quantum mechanics, we argue that Dirac-Coulomb Hamiltonians offer a natural framework for studying Whittaker (or equivalently, confluent hypergeometric) functions.

This study explores the application of discrete-time survival techniques for predicting continuous-time survival. To achieve this, a discretization scheme based on quantiles of the estimated event-time distribution is proposed, which outperforms the standard equidistant approach for smaller datasets. Additionally, two interpolation methods for continuous-time survival estimates are examined, both demonstrating superior performance relative to discrete-time estimates. The underlying survival methods utilize likelihoods for right-censored data and employ neural networks to parameterize either the probability mass function (PMF) or the discrete-time hazard rate. Simulation studies and real-world data analysis indicate that parameterizing the hazard rate yields slightly better results than parameterizing the PMF. Building on these findings, a new continuous-time method named PC-Hazard is introduced, assuming a piecewise constant continuous-time hazard rate. PC-Hazard proves to be highly competitive, performing comparably to the previously discussed methods as well as other established survival prediction techniques in the literature.

This study examines the application of Bayesian optimization (BO) to fine-tune support vector machine (SVM) hyperparameters for facies classification based on elastic properties derived from well data within the East Central Graben of the UKCS. Field dataset cross-plots demonstrate successful classification using non-linear boundaries. While the BO framework requires predefining certain parameters, such as the number of iterations to balance prediction accuracy against computational expense, it effectively minimizes human subjectivity regarding SVM architecture. Consequently, the proposed workflow offers significant potential benefits for resource exploration and development by facilitating objective technical subsurface evaluations.

This two-paper series addresses topological invariants in interacting topological insulators. The initial paper (I) establishes an efficient numerical framework for evaluating these invariants, clarifying the methods used to compute the Z2 invariant and spin Chern number through zero-frequency single-particle Green's functions within quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations. By introducing a periodization technique to address common finite-size effects, we ensure the spin Chern number yields ideally quantized results. Furthermore, we demonstrate that leveraging the symmetry properties of the systems significantly lowers computational costs. To validate this approach, particularly the periodization method, we apply it to two distinct two-dimensional models of interacting topological insulators. The follow-up paper (II) extends this scheme to broader classes of interacting topological insulator models, highlighting specific limitations encountered when constructing topological invariants via single-particle Green's functions.

This study establishes the theoretical basis for sensitivity and stability analysis, with a primary focus on constrained systems. We examine general models defined by multifunctions mapping between Banach spaces, concentrating on characterizing their well-posedness through Lipschitzian stability, metric regularity, and linear openness relative to specific sets. Unlike standard approaches, these enhanced relative well-posedness concepts enable the inclusion of diverse classes of constrained systems. Utilizing tools from variational analysis and generalized differentiation, we define new relative coderivatives and establish fundamental calculus rules for them. This advanced variational framework facilitates complete characterizations of relative well-posedness, with applications extending to the stability of affine variational inequalities. Furthermore, most of the derived results, which hold in general infinite-dimensional contexts, represent novel findings even within finite-dimensional spaces.

The muon collider stands out as a distinctive accelerator in the post-LHC era, offering the capacity for extremely high-energy leptonic collisions and enabling access to a largely uncharted physics landscape. Nevertheless, this immense scientific promise is offset by extraordinary technological hurdles, primarily because muons are unstable. Their decay generates a powerful flux of background particles that interact with machine components, potentially compromising detector performance. This paper introduces technologies capable of meeting the stringent requirements of a muon collider detector and proposes a strategic roadmap for future research and development.

Pre-built map-based localization systems struggle with long-term scene changes. This paper introduces a LiDAR-based approach designed to maintain robust localization despite such variations. The method initiates a temporary mapping process whenever global alignment with the pre-built map becomes unreliable; this temporary map is subsequently merged into the main map once reliable matching is restored. Additionally, we incorporate LiDAR inertial odometry (LIO) to deliver motion-compensated scans and a trustworthy initial pose estimate for the global matching module. To ensure a smooth, real-time trajectory for navigation, we fuse odometry and global matching poses through pose graph optimization. Extensive experiments on the NCLT dataset, covering diverse indoor and outdoor environments with significant changes over a year, demonstrate the system's robust and accurate performance. The code is available on GitHub.

This study systematically investigates the half-lives of proton radioactivity for 33 spherical nuclei by examining the connection between Skyrme parameters and macroscopic properties of nuclear matter. Employing the two-potential approach within the spherical Skyrme-Hartree-Fock framework, we analyzed the correlation between proton decay half-lives and these macroscopic quantities. Additionally, a novel Skyrme parameter set was derived by fitting the two most significant macroscopic quantities. When compared to the MSL0 Skyrme parameters and the UDLP theoretical model for proton radioactivity, the half-lives calculated using this new parameter set demonstrate a superior ability to reproduce experimental data.

Integrated Access and Backhaul (IAB), which utilizes wireless links for both access and backhaul, is considered a promising method for creating flexible and dense networks. Furthermore, Mobile IAB (mIAB) offers a potential solution to enhance connectivity for User Equipments (UEs) that move in groups. Distinct from other literature, this work provides a comprehensive overview of mIAB deployment foundations by addressing: 1) the current state of IAB standardization within 5G New Radio (NR); 2) a novel taxonomy for state-of-the-art research on both fixed IAB and mIAB; 3) an in-depth performance analysis of mIAB derived from simulations; and 4) existing challenges and future opportunities for mIAB. The proposed taxonomy classifies IAB studies across various dimensions and specifically categorizes mIAB research based on mobility types, detailing key topics for each. In terms of performance evaluation, the study examines an urban macro scenario where mIAB nodes are installed on buses to boost passenger connectivity. Results indicate that, relative to other network architectures, deploying mIAB nodes significantly enhances passenger throughput and reduces latency in both uplink and downlink directions.

Creating accompaniment arrangements is a complex music generation challenge that requires balancing intertwined constraints such as melody, harmony, texture, and overall musical structure. Current models struggle to effectively capture all these elements, particularly in the context of long-term generation. To overcome this limitation, we introduce AccoMontage, a system designed to generate accompaniments for entire musical pieces by unifying phrase selection with neural style transfer. Specifically, our approach focuses on creating piano accompaniments for folk or pop songs derived from lead sheets (which contain melody and chord progressions). The process begins by retrieving phrase montages from a database and recombining them structurally using dynamic programming. Next, the chords within these retrieved phrases are adjusted via style transfer to align with the target lead sheet. Finally, the system provides users with controls over the generation workflow. Unlike purely learning-based methods, AccoMontage employs a novel hybrid framework that leverages both rule-based optimization and deep learning to complement one another, ensuring high-quality output. Experimental results demonstrate that our model produces well-structured accompaniments with delicate textures, significantly outperforming existing baselines.

Deep learning is rapidly advancing within seismic processing and interpretation; however, most current methods limit computational demands by subsampling data and constraining model architecture. These strategies pose significant risks: subsampling may discard crucial spatio-temporal details essential for training, while restricting model size can degrade performance or make complex tasks like segmentation unfeasible. This paper addresses the primary hurdles in training large neural networks—memory constraints and prohibitively long training durations. Since seismic datasets are typically four times larger than those in standard image processing (utilizing float32 instead of uint8), preloading data into memory is particularly challenging. Using a microseismic case study, we demonstrate how a data generator approach, which retains only the necessary batch in memory, enables the training on over 750GB of data. Additionally, we showcase efficient training for large-scale models by implementing a 7-layer UNet with 4096x4096 input dimensions. By employing a distributed training method with batch splitting, we achieved a fourfold reduction in training time. Combining data generators with distributed training eliminates the need for data subsampling or model size restrictions, thereby facilitating the use of larger networks, higher-resolution inputs, and the transition from 2D to 3D problem spaces.

We present Balboa, a link obfuscation framework designed for censorship circumvention. Balboa offers a general solution for tunneling data through existing applications by operating between the application and the operating system. It intercepts outgoing network traffic and rewrites it to embed hidden data. To ensure no distinguishable divergence from normal application behavior, Balboa only modifies traffic that aligns with an externally defined \emph{traffic model} pre-shared between the communicating parties. This model represents a specific subset of network traffic (e.g., a portion of audio streamed by a server). The sender replaces outgoing data with a pointer to the corresponding location in the model, utilizing the freed space to embed the actual data. The receiver then retrieves this data, substituting the pointer with the original content from the model before forwarding it to the application. When utilizing TLS, this method ensures that application behavior with Balboa is \emph{equivalent}, aside from minor protocol-dependent timing variations, to running the application without Balboa. Balboa distinguishes itself from previous approaches by (1) providing a framework for tunneling data through arbitrary (TLS-protected) protocols and applications, and (2) executing unmodified application binaries with standard inputs, whereas most prior tunneling methods run applications on non-standard—and thus potentially detectable—inputs. We demonstrate two instantiations of Balboa: one for audio streaming and another for web browsing, illustrating the challenge of detecting Balboa using machine learning classifiers.

Investigating IO performance irregularities is essential across diverse computing settings, from massive cloud infrastructures to standard desktop environments. Yet, the intricate architecture of modern OS IO stacks hampers the ability of current tools to diagnose these issues. Kernel IO operations are often disrupted by internal kernel processes, necessitating an advanced profiling tool capable of filtering out such noise. Additionally, complex interactions among concurrent IO requests generate various sources of tail latency within the kernel stack. Consequently, developers require fine-grained latency profiles for individual IO requests across different layers. To address these needs, this paper introduces ReLayTracer, a profiler that tracks every request and layer. ReLayTracer facilitates comprehensive root-cause analysis by delivering per-layer latency distributions for each request, monitoring hardware performance, and measuring time consumed by kernel activities like interrupts.

We present a new viewpoint on ${\cal N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills (SYM) theory utilizing the Nicolai map, a transformation of bosonic fields that enables the calculation of quantum correlators via a free, purely bosonic functional measure. Typically, a Nicolai map is derived from the path-ordered exponential of the coupling flow operator. This operator can be canonically built in any gauge using an ${\cal N}=1$ off-shell superfield formulation of ${\cal N}=4$ SYM, or alternatively by dimensionally reducing ${\cal N}=1$ $D=10$ SYM, which requires fixing the Landau gauge. We propose a comprehensive theory of the ${\cal N}=4$ coupling flow operator, suggesting it possesses an ambiguity corresponding to R-symmetry freedom within the $\mathfrak{su}(4)$ Lie algebra. This framework treats our two construction methods as specific instances within $\mathfrak{su}(4)$ and establishes a wide range of Nicolai maps for ${\cal N}=4$ SYM.
A variant of Williamson's product theorem, specifically applicable to Williamson matrices of even order, is introduced.

Urban patterns exhibit multifractal scaling, yet the specific data required to represent these patterns and their scaling remains a critical question. This study computed Renyi's generalized dimension (RGD) spectra using four distinct urban modalities: land cover, impervious surfaces, population density, and street intersection points. Based on circa 2010 data, RGD spectra were analyzed across six urbanized regions in the United States. Unlike traditional methods relying on statistical moments, we employed Hill's numbers to calculate these spectra, which facilitates a clearer interpretation of generalized dimensions and enables the spatial visualization of multifractality. The findings indicate that within a single urbanized area, different modalities possess distinct RGD spectra and consequently display unique morphologies. Specifically, among the six case studies, land cover and impervious surface patterns generally exhibited monofractal characteristics, street intersection points showed moderate multifractality, and population density patterns demonstrated strong multifractality. These numerical results are supported by spatial visualizations. Therefore, selecting an appropriate modality is essential when investigating urban multifractality, as areas may appear morphologically similar under one metric but dissimilar under another. Our analysis revealed that only two of the six urban areas shared similar morphologies across all four modalities.

Within the framework of heavy-meson chiral perturbation theory, the vector form factor $f_+(q^2)$ governing the exclusive semi-leptonic decay $B\to \pi \ell \nu$ is intimately linked to the strong coupling $g_{B^* B\pi}$ (or its normalized counterpart $\hat g$) in the soft-pion regime, where $q^{2} \sim (m_B-m_{\pi})^2$. By integrating the precisely recorded $q^2$ spectrum from BaBar and Belle with various $f_+(q^2)$ parametrizations, we determine these couplings via the form factor's residue at the $B^*$ pole. This determination necessitates extrapolating the form factor from the physical semi-leptonic domain to the unphysical point $q^2=m_{B^*}^2$. Comparing these extracted values against other experimental and theoretical benchmarks allows us to evaluate the distinct parametrizations, which vary based on the extent of physical information they incorporate. The analysis reveals that results derived using the BK, BZ, and BCL parametrizations are mutually consistent and broadly align with other theoretical and lattice predictions; in contrast, the BGL ansatz, which introduces an artificial pole at the cut threshold, yields a significantly higher value.

As Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) become more complex, mapping them to tile-based neuromorphic hardware grows increasingly difficult due to the limited synaptic storage on each crossbar tile, which restricts the number of pre-synaptic connections per neuron. Consequently, complex models often require pruning connections to fit these constraints, resulting in degraded model performance. This study introduces a novel unrolling method that breaks down neurons with numerous inputs into a series of homogeneous units, each handling only two pre-synaptic connections. By spatially decomposing the neuron function in this manner, the approach maximizes crossbar efficiency and preserves all connections, thereby eliminating accuracy loss from pruning. Integrated into an existing SNN mapping framework, this technique was evaluated on the DYNAP-SE neuromorphic processor using various machine learning tasks. The results show a 60% reduction in crossbar requirements, a ninefold increase in synapse utilization, a 62% decrease in wasted energy, and an improvement in model quality ranging from 0.8% to 4.6%.

Autocomplete, also known as Query Auto-Completion (AC), generates complete search queries based on a user's input prefix and serves as a fundamental component of commercial search engines. This paper introduces DeepPLTR, a novel context-aware neural network-based pairwise ranker designed to enhance AC performance. DeepPLTR utilizes contextual and behavioral features to optimize query ranking by minimizing pairwise loss through a fully-connected neural network architecture. In offline evaluations, DeepPLTR outperforms the LambdaMART ranker with a +3.90% improvement in Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR). Furthermore, an online A/B test at Amazon demonstrated a statistically significant (+0.06%, p < 0.1) increase in Gross Merchandise Value (GMV).

This study introduces mlreflect, a Python package designed to automate the analysis of reflectometry data through an optimized machine learning pipeline. By integrating various training and data processing methods explored in prior research, the package utilizes a neural network that generates accurate and robust predictions. These predictions serve as excellent initial parameters for an optional subsequent least mean squares (LMS) fitting procedure. Testing on a substantial dataset comprising 242 reflectivity curves from thin films on silicon substrates reveals that the pipeline reliably identifies an LMS minimum nearly identical to one derived by a human expert utilizing physical insights and specific boundary conditions. The work also examines discrepancies between simulated and experimental data and their impact on neural network training and performance. Additionally, the experimental test set was employed to establish the optimal noise level for training. Finally, the neural network's exceptionally rapid prediction speeds are utilized to mitigate systematic errors by sampling minor data variations.

Flow-based models serve as robust instruments for constructing probabilistic models with manageable densities. This work presents Convex Potential Flows (CP-Flow), an efficient and intuitive parameterization of invertible models rooted in optimal transport (OT) theory. Defined as the gradient map of a strongly convex neural potential, CP-Flows leverage their convexity to guarantee invertibility and facilitate efficient inversion through convex optimization of the convex conjugate. To support maximum likelihood training, we introduce a novel gradient estimator for the log-determinant of the Jacobian, which computes an inverse-Hessian vector product via the conjugate gradient method. This estimator maintains constant memory usage and achieves effective unbiasedness by tightening the error tolerance within the convex optimization routine. Theoretically, we demonstrate that CP-Flows function as universal density approximators and are optimal within the OT framework. Empirical evaluations indicate that CP-Flow yields competitive performance on standard benchmarks for density estimation and variational inference.

Let $A$ be a subset of the positive integers, where an $A$-partition of $n$ represents $n$ as a sum of elements from $A$. For given $i, n\in\N$, the quantity $c_{A}(i,n)$ denotes the count of $A$-partitions of $n$ consisting of exactly $i$ parts. This paper presents several findings regarding the sign behavior of the sequence defined by $S_{A,k}(n)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}(-1)^{i}i^{k}c_{A}(i,n)$, with $k\in\N$ held constant. Specifically, we demonstrate that for a wide class $\cal{A}$ of subsets of $\N_{+}$, every $A\in \cal{A}$ satisfies the condition $(-1)^{n}S_{A,k}(n)\geq 0$ for all $n, k\in\N$.

High-energy photons originating from astrophysical sources serve as distinctive probes for testing specific predictions of candidate Quantum Gravity (QG) theories. Specifically, Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov Telescopes (IACTs) are specialized instruments designed for astronomical observations within the energy spectrum ranging from tens of GeV to approximately 100 TeV, rendering them ideal for detecting QG effects. This article reviews QG phenomena amenable to testing via IACTs, with a primary focus on Lorentz invariance violation and its implications. These effects are frequently modeled by modifying the photon dispersion relation to include energy-dependent terms. We will outline the analytical techniques used across various studies, facilitating a detailed comparison and discussion of IACT results spanning over twenty years. Adhering loosely to the field's historical progression, we will examine how analysis methodologies have been refined and enhanced over time, investigating why certain studies achieved greater sensitivity than others. Finally, we will address the future of this domain by proposing strategies to boost analysis sensitivity and identifying potential directions for future research.

Low-surface-brightness galaxies (LSBGs) offer promising targets for detecting dark matter emission because of their minimal baryonic content; however, estimating their expected dark matter emissivity remains challenging due to difficulties in measuring their distances. This study introduces a stacking technique that utilizes catalogs of LSBGs alongside unresolved gamma-ray maps from the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope. We demonstrate that for sufficiently large samples, precise individual distance measurements are unnecessary, as the aggregate distance distribution of the population is adequate to constrain dark matter properties. Additionally, we show that covariance effects between closely spaced galaxies—separated by an angular distance similar to the Fermi point spread function—are negligible. As an application, we processed a sample of 800 faint LSBGs identified by Hyper Suprime-Cam, finding that the 95% confidence level upper limits on the dark matter annihilation cross-section scale inversely with the number of galaxies. Given this linear relationship with object count, we argue that applying this methodology to the over 100,000 LSBGs available in the Legacy Survey of Space and Time could yield extremely stringent constraints.

Amidst rising population and roadway congestion, vehicle collisions have become a primary cause of global fatalities. Consequently, the automotive sector is driven to employ sensors and computer vision advancements to create systems for detecting and preventing accidents, thereby aiding drivers. This article introduces a deep learning model built on the ResNext architecture enhanced with SENet blocks. Its performance is evaluated against established models such as VGG16, VGG19, ResNet50, and standalone ResNext. The proposed model surpasses these baselines, achieving a ROC-AUC of 0.91 while utilizing a substantially smaller fraction of GTACrash synthetic training data, which significantly lowers computational demands.
