To address the domain gap between synthetic and real composites, we also collected 100 real composite videos using copy-and-paste techniques. The datasets can be accessed at https://github.com/bcmi/Video-Harmonization-Dataset-HYouTube.

Relational Quantum Mechanics (RQM), also known as the relational interpretation, addresses the measurement problem by positing an ontology composed of sparse relative events, termed "facts." These facts emerge from interactions between any two physical systems and are inherently relative to them. The theoretical foundation of RQM rests on the insight that quantum transition amplitudes yield physical probabilities exclusively when their arguments constitute facts relative to the same system. In scenarios where decoherence suppresses interference, the relativity of these facts can be disregarded, rendering them approximately stable.

The worldwide Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic presents a severe risk to both public health and the economy. Consequently, swift and precise diagnosis is essential to curb transmission and lower mortality rates. While Chest Computed Tomography (CT) is a powerful modality for early detection of lung conditions such as pneumonia, identifying COVID-19 in CT scans remains challenging and susceptible to human error, particularly because early-stage cases may yield negative imaging results. Although recent deep learning approaches have demonstrated remarkable efficacy in this domain, many fail to fully leverage the rich spatial information inherent in 3D structures or are prone to error propagation. To overcome these limitations, we introduce the Dual-Attention Residual Network (DARNet), designed to automatically distinguish COVID-19 from common pneumonia (CP) and healthy individuals using 3D chest CT scans. Our approach incorporates a dual-attention module that combines channel-wise and depth-wise attention mechanisms; the former enhances channel independence, while the latter recalibrates depth-level features. By integrating these components, the network effectively extracts and refines features across various levels, thereby boosting diagnostic accuracy. Evaluated on a substantial public CT dataset, DARNet achieves superior performance. Furthermore, ablation studies and visualization analyses confirm both the effectiveness and interpretability of the proposed method.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have made it possible to reconstruct 3D human bodies from single images, opening up wide-ranging applications across various fields. This paper introduces SHARP (SHape Aware Reconstruction of People in loose clothing), a novel end-to-end trainable network designed to accurately recover both the 3D geometry and appearance of individuals wearing loose garments from a monocular image. SHARP employs a sparse and efficient fusion mechanism that integrates a parametric body prior with a non-parametric 2D representation of clothed humans. The parametric prior ensures geometric consistency for body shape and pose, while the non-parametric representation effectively models loose clothing and manages self-occlusions. Additionally, we exploit the sparsity of the non-parametric representation to accelerate network training using losses applied to 2D maps. A major contribution is 3DHumans, a new dataset featuring life-like 3D human body scans with rich geometric and textural details. We evaluate SHARP on 3DHumans and other public datasets, demonstrating superior qualitative and quantitative performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

Recent years have seen extensive research into optimal locally repairable codes (LRCs) that meet the Singleton-type bound. This paper introduces novel bounds and constructions for Singleton-optimal LRCs characterized by specific parameters: minimum distance $d=6$ with locality $r=3$, and minimum distance $d=7$ with locality $r=2$. First, we demonstrate an equivalence between the existence of these two LRC families and the existence of specific subsets of lines within projective space possessing particular attributes. Subsequently, utilizing the line-point incidence matrix and Johnson bounds for constant weight codes, we derive enhanced upper limits on code length that surpass existing results. Finally, leveraging techniques from finite fields and finite geometry, we present new constructions of Singleton-optimal LRCs that achieve greater lengths than previously known solutions.

This paper introduces a streaming end-to-end speech recognition system built on Monotonic Chunkwise Attention (MoCha) and trained jointly with enhancement layers. While MoCha allows for streaming recognition with accuracy rivaling full attention methods, training this architecture is highly sensitive to factors like data difficulty and hyperparameters. Consequently, applying multi-style training to MoCha models often causes a significant drop in performance on clean speech. Drawing inspiration from Curriculum Learning [1], we propose two strategies: Gradual Application of Enhanced Features (GAEF) and Gradual Reduction of Enhanced Loss (GREL). Under GAEF, training begins with clean features, with the contribution of enhancement layer outputs increasing over time. GREL gradually decreases the Mean Squared Error (MSE) weight assigned to enhanced outputs as training progresses. Experiments on the LibriSpeech corpus and noisy far-field datasets demonstrate that our model, utilizing the combined GAEF and GREL strategies, achieves substantially better results than standard multi-style training.

This study introduces L-DQN, a distributed limited-memory quasi-Newton algorithm designed for empirical risk minimization within a master/worker framework. L-DQN facilitates asynchronous computations across worker nodes while maintaining efficiency in both storage and communication overhead. Specifically, each iteration involves the exchange of $O(d)$-sized vectors between the master and workers, where $d$ represents the decision variable dimension, and requires $O(md)$ memory per node, with $m$ being a tunable parameter. To our knowledge, L-DQN represents the inaugural distributed quasi-Newton approach to offer provable global linear convergence guarantees in an asynchronous environment characterized by inter-node delays. Numerical experiments are included to demonstrate both the theoretical validity and practical efficacy of the proposed method.

This study expands upon Gu & Chen's 1D perpendicular isothermal C-shock linear analysis of drag instability by applying it to both perpendicular and oblique 2D C-shocks within star-forming cloud environments. We derive simplified dispersion relations for these unstable modes and observe that their characteristics primarily depend on the ratio of transverse (normal to the flow) to longitudinal (along the flow) wavenumbers. For large-scale transverse modes, the growth rate and wave frequency in 2D shocks mirror those found in 1D shocks. Conversely, small-scale transverse modes involve an unstable mode coupled with an acoustic mode propagating mainly in the transverse direction. In perpendicular or slightly oblique shocks, a slowly propagating mode exists that can evolve into a nonlinear regime and drive the maximum instability growth; however, this mode vanishes in more oblique shocks, shifting the maximum growth contribution to the transversely large-scale (nearly 1D) mode. Across all scenarios, density perturbations significantly exceed those of velocity and magnetic fields, indicating that density enhancement dominates the dynamics during the linear phase. Finally, we briefly address remaining questions in the linear analysis and potential astrophysical implications.

This study examines the Fourier coefficients $b_k(T)$ associated with the net baryon number density in strongly interacting matter under conditions of non-zero temperature and density. The asymptotic behavior of these coefficients at high $k$ values is governed by the singularities of the partition function within the complex chemical potential plane. Using a QCD-inspired effective chiral model, we demonstrate that the chiral and deconfinement characteristics at finite baryon chemical potential manifest as distinct dependencies on $k$ and $T$ in the Fourier coefficients. Additionally, we analyze the impact of the Roberge-Weiss transition on these coefficients. Our findings suggest that the Fourier expansion method offers valuable insights into the critical behavior of QCD matter.

This paper investigates the emergent dynamics of the Kuramoto model with frustration on a general directed graph that includes a spanning tree. We establish a sufficient condition for asymptotic synchronization when the initial data lies within a half-circle. Addressing the absence of uniform coercivity in such graphs, we employ the node decomposition criteria from \cite{H-L-Z20} to reveal a distinct hierarchical structure. This approach effectively demonstrates the dissipation of the phase diameter and the formation of a small invariant set within finite time. Consequently, the frequency diameter dissipates, ultimately resulting in synchronization.

This paper establishes a lemma regarding the logarithmic derivative for holomorphic curves mapping annuli into compact Kähler manifolds. As an application, we present a second main theorem concerning holomorphic curves from annuli into semi-abelian varieties that intersect a single divisor.

Building upon the method introduced in \cite{Popov:2019nkr} for neutrino oscillations within a magnetic field, we extend the approach to encompass three neutrino generations. We establish a theoretical framework capable of calculating probabilities for Dirac neutrino oscillations involving spin, flavor, and combined spin-flavor transitions in the presence of a magnetic field. Our analysis demonstrates an inherent entanglement between flavor and spin oscillations, indicating that these phenomena generally cannot be treated independently. We derive closed analytic expressions for these oscillation probabilities, incorporating both normal and inverted mass hierarchies as well as potential CP violation effects. Specifically, we find that conversion probabilities without flavor change ($

u_e^L$ and $

u_e^R$) remain independent of the CP phase, whereas other conversion channels are influenced by it. Overall, the oscillation probabilities reflect a complex interaction between magnetic ($\mu_{
u} B$) and vacuum oscillation frequencies. These findings are particularly relevant for applications involving extreme astrophysical environments, such as magnetars and supernovae, and for investigating neutrino propagation through interstellar magnetic fields.

Conventional sound diffusers consist of quasi-random phase gratings mounted on reflective surfaces, designed to enhance the spatiotemporal incoherence of scattered acoustic fields. By periodically tiling unit cells across extensive reflective areas, these systems mitigate undesirable specular reflections from incident plane waves. However, the inherent periodicity of these unit cells generates coherent constructive and destructive interference in specific directions, undermining acoustic diffusivity. Consequently, the spatial uniformity of scattered energy remains a fundamental constraint of this traditional method, particularly when covering large surfaces. This study explores spatiotemporal modulation of surface acoustic admittance as an innovative solution to enhance sound diffusion. We developed a semi-analytical model utilizing Fourier series expansion to calculate the scattered sound field from a surface admittance based on a quadratic residue diffuser (QRD) design, where individual well admittances are modulated by a traveling wave. This modulation features a frequency ($\omega_{\mrm{m}}$), amplitude ($Y_\mrm{m}$), and wavenumber aligned with the unit cell length ($\Lambda$). Our findings indicate a substantial improvement in diffusion performance, attributed to the generation of additional frequency-wavenumber pairs corresponding to harmonics of the modulation frequency and their diffraction orders. The results from the semi-analytical model were validated using time-domain finite element modeling.

Subset sum is a foundational and longstanding challenge in theoretical computer science. Given $n$ items with weights $w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_n$, the objective is to determine whether a subset exists whose total weight equals a target value $t$. Although the problem is generally NP-hard, it admits a pseudo-polynomial time solution of $\widetilde O(n+t)$ when weights are non-negative integers. This work addresses the dynamic version of subset sum, where an upper bound $\tmax$ is fixed beforehand. In each step, the system either inserts a new item or, for any query $t \leq \tmax$, must decide if a subset sums to $t$. Regrettably, current subset sum algorithms cannot handle these operations in truly sublinear time with respect to $\tmax$. We present an algorithm achieving truly sublinear amortized processing time per operation—defined as $n^{1-\Omega(1)}$—provided the total number of operations reaches $\tmax^{2/3+\Omega(1)}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that if both insertions and deletions are permitted, no algorithm can achieve an average operation time of $\tmax^{1-\Omega(1)}$ unless the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH) is false.

This work investigates the overparameterization thresholds necessary for the global convergence of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on one-hidden-layer feed-forward neural networks, covering a broad range of practical activation functions such as ReLU. We enhance current state-of-the-art findings by reducing the required width of the hidden layer. Our approach introduces a novel proof methodology that merges nonlinear analysis with the characteristics of random network initializations. Initially, we demonstrate the global convergence of continuous solutions to a differential inclusion, which serves as a nonsmooth counterpart to gradient flow for mean squared error loss. Subsequently, we present a technical lemma applicable to general approximators that links solutions of this differential inclusion to discrete SGD sequences, thereby proving linear convergence to zero loss for the SGD iterations.

This study investigates how hydrogen (H) and its various bonding arrangements influence defect state density and orbital localization within hydrogenated amorphous silicon (a-Si:H)/crystalline silicon (c-Si) heterostructures. Employing density functional theory (DFT), we analyzed model interfaces between amorphous silicon (a-Si) and a-Si:H on c-Si substrates. To replicate the atomic structure of a-Si on c-Si, we utilized classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations involving melting and quenching processes. Subsequently, we introduced varying hydrogen concentrations in diverse bonding configurations into the a-Si, followed by DFT relaxation to generate stable a-Si:H structures representative of hydrogenated a-Si on crystalline silicon surfaces. Unlike crystalline heterojunctions, where interface defect density peaks at the junction, our findings indicate that in the most energetically favorable hydrogen configurations, defect state density remains relatively low at the interface and instead reaches its maximum within the center of the a-Si layer. Structural analysis reveals that in these stable states, hydrogen atoms do not always bond to dangling bonds or interface atoms; yet, they significantly alter the heterostructure's atomic architecture. This modification reduces defect state density and orbital localization throughout the a-Si layer and, even more notably, at the a-Si/c-Si interface. Overall, the modeled defect distribution highlights the passivating capability of a-Si:H layers on c-Si substrates.

In the general Two-Higgs Doublet Model (THDM), it has been demonstrated that the Higgs potential can be formulated using gauge-independent variables. Specifically, this approach offers a concise framework for understanding stability, electroweak symmetry breaking, and CP symmetry, effectively bypassing unphysical gauge degrees of freedom. This study completes that initiative by demonstrating how all physical parameters—including scalar masses, trilinear and quartic interactions, gauge-boson-Higgs couplings, and Yukawa interactions within the general THDM—can be expressed in a gauge-invariant manner.

Recent studies have established that the kinematic viscosity of liquids at its minimum ($\nu_m$) can be derived from fundamental physical constants, resulting in a value approximately $10^{-7}~{\rm m^2/s}$. In this work, we demonstrate that quark-gluon plasma (QGP) exhibits a comparable kinematic viscosity, a conclusion supported by both experimental observations and theoretical calculations. This resemblance is remarkable considering that QGP's dynamic viscosity and density are roughly 16 orders of magnitude greater than those of liquids, despite the two systems being governed by vastly different interactions and underlying theories. We explore the consequences of this finding for QGP physics, highlighting the parallels in flow and particle dynamics at the viscosity minimum, the linked dynamical crossover, and the universality of shear diffusivity.

Ensuring service reliability remains a primary challenge for cloud providers, as unplanned outages can trigger severe cascading failures in dependent services, ultimately harming customer satisfaction. Accurately and efficiently forecasting these cascading effects is vital for cloud system operations and maintenance. While current methods use distributed tracing to determine if a dependency exists between services, no prior research has focused on quantifying the degree of that dependency. This paper investigates outage patterns and failure diagnosis procedures from two cloud providers to motivate the concept of dependency intensity. We define dependency intensity as the extent to which the state of a callee service affects its caller. Subsequently, we introduce AID, the first approach designed to predict this intensity. AID begins by generating candidate dependency pairs from trace spans. It then represents each service's status using a multivariate time series derived from these spans. By calculating the similarity between the statuses of callers and callees for each candidate pair, AID aggregates these similarities into a single metric representing the dependency intensity. We evaluated AID using data from an open-source microservice benchmark and a live cloud system, demonstrating that it can accurately and efficiently predict dependency intensity. Furthermore, we validated the method's practical utility within a large-scale commercial cloud environment.

Forecasting significant wave height represents a critical challenge within ocean data analytics. Accurate prediction of these heights is essential for calculating potential wave energy generation, while timely forecasts of extreme waves are vital for maritime safety, such as guiding vessel navigation. We formulate the prediction of extreme significant wave heights as an exceedance probability forecasting task, aiming to determine the likelihood that wave heights will surpass a specific threshold. While this is typically addressed using probabilistic binary classification, we introduce a novel methodology based on forecasting models. Our approach utilizes forecasts of future observations to estimate exceedance probabilities via the cumulative distribution function. Experiments conducted using data from a buoy off the coast of Halifax, Canada, indicate that this proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques for exceedance probability forecasting.

Zadeh [1] established the concept of a fuzzy set as a generalization of a crisp set, thereby extending classical set theory through fuzzification. This paper aims to broaden the notion of fuzzy endomorphism to encompass fuzzy automorphism. Furthermore, it introduces the concepts of fuzzy inner automorphism and fuzzy inner automorphism induced by a fuzzy subgroup. Ultimately, fuzzy analogues of established results from classical group theory are derived.
We derive a criterion for divergence operators that depend on both the gradient and the function itself to satisfy the S+ property. This finding is supported by multiple examples and an application.

Improving the generalization of deep neural networks to unseen domains is vital for safety-critical real-world applications like autonomous driving. To tackle this challenge, we introduce a novel instance-selective whitening loss designed to enhance the robustness of segmentation networks against unseen domains. Our method disentangles domain-specific style from domain-invariant content within the higher-order statistics (specifically feature covariance) of feature representations, selectively eliminating only the style components responsible for domain shifts. As illustrated in Fig. 1, our approach yields reasonable predictions for (a) low-illumination, (b) rainy, and (c) unseen structural scenarios—conditions absent from the training data where baseline methods suffer significant performance degradation. Despite its simplicity and effectiveness, our technique boosts the robustness of various backbone networks without incurring additional computational overhead. Extensive experiments on urban-scene segmentation demonstrate the superiority of our method over existing approaches. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/shachoi/RobustNet.

The general approximate Carathéodory problem involves determining, for two symmetric convex bodies $P, Q \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$, a parameter $k \in \mathbb{N}$, and a point $\mathbf{z} \in \textrm{conv}(X)$ where $X \subseteq P$, a set of vectors $\mathbf{v}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{v}_k \in X$ that minimizes the $Q$-norm distance $\|\mathbf{z} - \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^k \mathbf{v}_i\|_Q$. While Maurey established that an error of $O(\sqrt{p/k})$ is achievable when both $P$ and $Q$ correspond to $\| \cdot \|_p$-balls, we demonstrate a reduction to the vector balancing constant from discrepancy theory, yielding tight bounds for most general instances of $P$ and $Q$. Specifically, when $P$ and $Q$ are $\| \cdot \|_p$-balls, we derive an upper bound of $\sqrt{ \frac{\min\{ p, \log (\frac{2m}{k}) \}}{k}}$. Notably, this result cannot be achieved through independent random sampling; instead, we employ the Lovett-Meka random walk. Furthermore, we extend these findings to the scenario where $P$ and $Q$ are $\|\cdot \|_p$ and $\| \cdot \|_q$-balls, respectively, satisfying $2 \leq p \leq q \leq \infty$.

This study presents fluid dynamics simulations investigating melting and crater formation on a copper cathode subjected to high plasma heat fluxes and pressure gradients. The simulated free surface deformations and internal temperature evolution are validated against previously published simulation data. Even though the physical model relies solely on hydrodynamics and neglects various plasma-surface interaction mechanisms, the outcomes align remarkably well with both advanced model predictions and experimental observations. These findings establish a robust foundation for applying similar models to future research on transient surface melting and droplet ejection from metallic plasma-facing components following disruptions.

Although factor models featuring sparse loading matrices are widely used, there has been minimal formal investigation into their identifiability beyond conventional rotation-based constraints, such as imposing a positive lower triangular structure. To address this limitation, we introduce a counting rule for nonzero factor loadings that guarantees generic uniqueness in the variance decomposition of the factor representation. This approach is formalized within sparse matrix spaces, incorporating key concepts from graph and network theory. Additionally, we develop a computationally efficient tool to validate this counting rule. We demonstrate the utility of our methodology by applying it to real-world data for post-processing posterior draws in Bayesian sparse factor analysis.

Non-local quantum computation involves executing a unitary operation on $n$ qubits across two parties within a single communication round, ideally requiring minimal pre-shared entanglement. We present a novel protocol that leverages the efficiency of port-based teleportation when applied sequentially to small subsets of qubits. Unlike prior methods where entanglement costs were either independent of the unitary or scaled with its complexity, our approach scales according to the unitary's non-locality. Specifically, the entanglement requirement is approximately $\sim n^{4V}$, where $V$ represents the maximum volume of a past light cone in a circuit realizing the unitary. This allows for the implementation of unitary circuits with $V\sim O(1)$ using polynomial entanglement and those with $V\sim \mathrm{polylog}(n)$ using quasi-polynomial entanglement. For a general unitary circuit composed of $d$ layers of $k$-qubit gates, $V$ is bounded by $k^d$, though imposing geometric locality restricts it to be at most polynomial in $d$. We explicitly demonstrate a class of unitaries for which our protocol achieves lower entanglement costs than any existing method. Furthermore, we show that the protocol's entanglement cost remains largely unaffected by several extensions, including arbitrary local pre- and post-processing, global Clifford pre- and post-processing, and the inclusion of a polynomial number of auxiliary systems.

In 1946, J. Rosenbaum introduced a series of problems concerning the minimum number of power points required to guarantee that the boundary $c$ of a specific convex body is a disk. This paper demonstrates, utilizing Riordan matrices, that when the curve $c$ is analytic, a single exterior power point is adequate to ensure this condition.

Conditional waveform synthesis models generate audio waveforms based on inputs like text, mel-spectrograms, or MIDI, utilizing deep generative approaches that sample sequentially (autoregressive) or in parallel (non-autoregressive). While Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are frequently used for non-autoregressive synthesis, current state-of-the-art GAN-based systems often produce artifacts during mel-spectrogram inversion. This paper argues that such artifacts stem from the generator's failure to accurately capture pitch and periodicity. We demonstrate that simply conditioning on pitch and periodicity does not reduce this error as effectively as autoregression. We further explore the inductive bias inherent in autoregression for modeling the link between instantaneous frequency and phase, noting that this advantage persists even when large waveform segments are sampled autoregressively per forward pass. Compared to prior top-performing GAN models, our proposed Chunked Autoregressive GAN (CARGAN) lowers pitch error by 40-60%, cuts training time by 58%, sustains rapid generation speeds ideal for real-time or interactive use, and preserves or enhances subjective audio quality.

This study examines the Nambu--Jona-Lasinio model's ability to replicate fundamental Quantum Chromodynamics vacuum properties, specifically the hadronic spectrum. In this approach, mesons are treated as quark-antiquark bound states using the random phase approximation of the Bethe-Salpeter equation, whereas baryons are modeled as quark-diquark bound states under the static approximation of the Fadeev equation. By employing a Bayesian framework, we restrict the model using established phenomenological data to analyze the effects on its parameters and vacuum predictions, along with the correlations between them. Our results indicate that the framework successfully reproduces the vacuum masses of both mesons and baryons. However, accurately matching the baryon octet masses requires scalar diquarks to be significantly more bound, necessitating scalar diquark coupling values that exceed those predicted by canonical Fierz transformations. These insights may significantly influence our understanding of strongly-interacting matter under high temperature and density conditions, as well as the physics of compact stars.

Accurately determining the Hubble parameter, $H_0$, requires isolating recession velocity from the influence of peculiar velocities. This study examines various peculiar velocity models within the local Universe, specifically comparing those derived from density reconstruction in galaxy redshift surveys against adaptive kernel smoothing of peculiar velocity data. The density reconstruction utilizes the 2M++ galaxy redshift compilation and is evaluated against two kernel-smoothed velocity fields: one based on the 6dF Fundamental Plane sample and another generated from a Tully-Fisher catalogue combining SFI++ and 2MTF data. We emphasize that smoothed velocity fields must be rescaled to yield unbiased estimates. By comparing these models against observational test sets from the Second Amendment Supernovae catalogue and various Tully-Fisher catalogues, we determine that the 2M++ reconstruction offers a superior representation of local peculiar velocities compared to kernel-smoothed models. Furthermore, we investigate how peculiar velocities affect $H_0$ measurements from gravitational waves and megamasers, introducing a probabilistic framework to marginalize over line-of-sight velocity corrections. Using the 2M++ velocity field, we derive an $H_0$ value of $69^{+2.9}_{-2.8}$ km s^{-1} Mpc^{-1} for megamasers. Finally, we analyze the peculiar velocity of the galaxy NGC1052-DF2, concluding that a distance of approximately 13 Mpc is unlikely to account for its anomalously low dark matter fraction.

This study examines the impact of Lorentz violation on superconductivity. By developing a Lorentz-violating Ginzburg-Landau framework, we analyze how the Lorentz-violating tensors $\hat{k}_{c}^{ij}$ and $\hat{k}_a^i$ affect the London penetration depth, coherence length, and critical magnetic field.

Accurate segmentation and morphological evaluation of the left ventricle are critical for advancing cardiomyopathy diagnosis and understanding, ultimately helping to reduce myocardial infarction risks. However, Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) approaches for segmenting cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) images typically require pixel-level annotations, often struggle to generalize across different domains, and remain sensitive to variations in imaging protocols and acquisition methods. Given that annotating multi-sequence CMR images is labor-intensive and prone to observer variability, there is significant interest in developing methods capable of automatic domain adaptation. This paper introduces a transfer learning approach for multi-sequence CMR segmentation that integrates information from multiple sources. We initially train an encoder-decoder CNN using pixel-annotated T2-weighted and balanced-Steady State Free Precession (bSSFP) images, then fine-tune the network with a small set of Late Gadolinium Enhanced (LGE-MR) subjects to adapt domain features. The adapted model, trained on only four LGE-MR samples, achieved an average Dice score of approximately 85.0% on a test set of 40 LGE-MR subjects, significantly outperforming a non-adapted network trained from scratch on the same limited LGE-MR data.

Service-Oriented Computing utilizes services as fundamental components for constructing distributed applications. Historically, the drive to orchestrate services in the cloud stemmed from distributed business processes, which catalyzed the standardization of Business Process Execution Language (BPEL) and established the core concept that a service equates to a business process. Recently, however, motivations for cloud service orchestration have shifted toward alternatives such as XaaS and RMAD. While theoretically feasible to convert all such services into WSDL/SOAP formats, doing so would be prohibitively complex and expensive for widespread industry adoption, rendering the traditional definition of a service as a business process too limiting. Consequently, we redefine a service as a technology-neutral, loosely coupled, and location-transparent procedure. Guided by this perspective, we present Ozy, a novel general-purpose orchestration container. By framing this approach within existing technologies, we demonstrate that the Ozy container alleviates many conventional constraints, enabling the creation of simpler yet more feature-rich applications.

The primary goal of this paper is to introduce the theory of embeddings within the manifold Osc²M. Initially, we define the 2-osculator bundle. The second section focuses on submanifolds of the total space of this bundle, Osc²M, and constructs a moving frame. The third and fourth sections examine the induced N-linear connections and relative covariant derivatives. Finally, the last section presents the Ricci identities associated with the Liouville d-vector fields.

Open clusters (OCs) serve as essential tools for testing stellar evolution theories and validating stellar models. This study introduces a robust methodology for identifying OCs. Initially, a hybrid technique combining pyUPMASK and Random Forest (RF) algorithms is employed to filter out field stars and pinpoint reliable members. Subsequently, an identification model constructed using the RF algorithm, trained on 3,714 OC samples from Gaia DR2 and EDR3, is utilized to select OC candidates. These candidates undergo rigorous validation through isochrone fitting, advanced stellar population synthesis (ASPS) model fitting, and visual inspection. Applying this approach, we re-examined 868 candidates and initially grouped them using the friends-of-friends algorithm within Gaia EDR3. After excluding previously reported clusters, our focus shifted to 300 unknown candidates. These unrevealed clusters were categorized into Class A (59), Class B (21), and Class C (220) based on descending fitting quality. Ultimately, visual inspection confirmed 46 new, reliable open cluster candidates from Classes A and B.

Real-world time series data frequently arise from multiple sources of variation. Capturing the factors driving this variability through learned representations facilitates a deeper understanding of the underlying generative mechanisms and enhances performance on subsequent machine learning tasks. This study introduces a new generative framework designed to learn representations for both global and local variation factors in time series. Specifically, the local representation of each sample utilizes a stochastic process prior to model temporal non-stationarity, while the global representation encodes time-invariant characteristics. To promote decoupling between these two representations, we implement counterfactual regularization that minimizes their mutual information. Experimental results on simulated data confirm the successful recovery of true local and global variability factors, and applications to real-world datasets demonstrate that the representations learned via this method outperform existing approaches on downstream tasks. We contend that this proposed definition of representations offers significant benefits for data modeling and provides superior insights into the complexity inherent in real-world data.

This work presents the inaugural calculation of two-gluon production at mid-rapidity within ultra-peripheral collisions using the Color Glass Condensate framework. To address systematic uncertainties stemming from the poorly understood wave function of nearly real photons, we evaluate two contrasting models: the dilute quark-antiquark dipole approximation and a vector meson model where color charge density follows the McLerran-Venugopalan description. Within the experimentally relevant range, the target nucleus can be accurately modeled as a highly saturated state. This simplification facilitates efficient numerical simulations, allowing for the extraction of two-gluon correlation functions and their corresponding azimuthal harmonics.

Accurate channel parameter estimation poses significant challenges for wideband millimeter-wave (mmWave) large-scale hybrid arrays, primarily due to beam squint and the constraint of having far fewer radio frequency (RF) chains than antennas. This study introduces a novel joint delay and angle estimation method tailored for wideband mmWave fully-connected hybrid uniform cylindrical arrays. Initially, we propose a new hybrid beamformer that leverages Bessel function convergence to reduce the dimensionality of received signals on the horizontal plane and employs preselection to minimize active beams vertically. Crucially, this design preserves the essential recurrence relationships required for subspace-based angle and delay estimation, even when the number of RF chains is substantially lower than the number of antennas. Subsequently, we generalize linear interpolation to reconstruct hybrid beamformer signals, enabling coherent combination across the entire bandwidth to mitigate beam squint. Consequently, efficient subspace-based algorithms can be developed to estimate the angles and delays of multipath components. Furthermore, to ensure the estimated delays and angles are correctly matched and associated with distinct paths despite non-negligible noise, we introduce perturbation operations. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves performance near the Cramér-Rao lower bound (CRLB) with significantly reduced computational complexity compared to existing techniques.

Euler's totient function, $\varphi(n)$, determines the count of integers in the range $0, 1, \dots, n-1$ that are coprime to $n$ and possesses an explicit asymptotic lower bound of $n/\log \log n$, up to a constant factor. This note extends the concept of $\varphi$ by defining an arithmetic function $\varphi_P(n)$ for any irreducible integer polynomial $P$. This function counts how many values within the sequence $P(0), P(1), \dots, P(n-1)$ share no common factors with $n$. Furthermore, we establish an asymptotic lower bound for $\varphi_P(n)$.

The inherent security vulnerabilities of IoT devices facilitate attacker exploitation, allowing compromised devices to be recruited into botnets. When hundreds of thousands of such devices join a botnet, attackers leverage them to execute large-scale, complex Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks, rendering target websites or services unable to respond to legitimate users. Although numerous botnet detection techniques have been developed, their effectiveness is often restricted to the specific datasets used for training. This limitation arises because machine learning models trained on features from one botnet dataset struggle to perform well on others due to the diversity of attack patterns. Consequently, this paper introduces a universal feature set designed to enhance botnet detection regardless of the underlying dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed feature set yields superior performance when evaluating trained machine learning models across three distinct botnet attack datasets.

A primary obstacle in training Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) arises because target outputs, such as classification labels or generative images, are naturally represented signals that must be converted into spikes. This conversion typically relies on manually designed target spiking signals, which inadvertently constrain the decoding mechanism—often limiting it to rate decoding. Such arbitrary choices regarding both the target signals and the decoding rule generally hinder the SNN's ability to leverage spike timing for information encoding and processing. To overcome this limitation, this study proposes a hybrid variational autoencoder framework comprising an encoding SNN and a decoding Artificial Neural Network (ANN). The decoding ANN is tasked with learning the optimal method to transform the SNN's spiking outputs back into natural signals. Furthermore, we introduce a novel end-to-end learning rule that optimizes a directed information bottleneck criterion using surrogate gradients. The efficacy of this approach is validated across various tasks, including experiments on real-world datasets.

Stellar population synthesis (SPS) models serve as the essential bridge between a galaxy's physical characteristics and its spectral energy distribution (SED). This paper introduces DSPS, a Python-based SPS package where all functionality is natively built on the JAX library for automatic differentiation. Consequently, DSPS generates fully differentiable galaxy photometry predictions, leveraging JAX's performance advantages, such as GPU portability. The package also features novel capabilities: i) a flexible empirical framework for stellar metallicity that accounts for correlations with age, and ii) integration with the diffstar model, which establishes a physically grounded link between a galaxy's star formation history and the mass assembly of its dark matter halo. We outline theoretical methods for utilizing autodiff to compute gradients of galaxy SED predictions with respect to various SPS parameters, including star formation history, metallicity, nebular emission, and dust attenuation. Our forward modeling of synthetic galaxy populations demonstrates that DSPS achieves a 20-fold speedup over conventional SPS codes on CPUs and over 1,000-fold acceleration on modern GPUs. When combined with gradient-based optimization and inference techniques, DSPS renders large-scale likelihood analyses of galaxy–halo connection models practical, enabling full forward modeling of galaxy spectra and photometry.

This paper presents the fourth edition of the MediaEval 2021 Predicting Media Memorability task, addressing the ongoing challenge of forecasting both short-term and long-term video memorability. The evaluation utilizes two distinct video datasets: a subset of the TRECVid 2019 Video-to-Text collection and the Memento10K dataset, the latter being included to facilitate research into cross-dataset generalization. Furthermore, the study introduces a pilot subtask focused on prediction based on Electroencephalography (EEG) data. The authors provide an overview of the task's core components, detailing the datasets, evaluation metrics, and submission requirements for participants.

A significant obstacle in investigating the structure of the three-dimensional homology cobordism group lies in comprehending the relationship between hyperbolic geometry and homology cobordism. In this work, for a hyperbolic homology sphere $Y$, we establish explicit bounds on the relative grading between irreducible and reducible solutions to the Seiberg-Witten equations, expressed through the spectral and Riemannian properties of $Y$. Leveraging these results, we determine explicit bounds for specific numerical invariants found in monopole Floer homology (including its $\mathrm{Pin}(2)$-equivariant variant). Finally, we utilize these findings to examine subgroups of the homology cobordism group formed by hyperbolic homology spheres that meet particular geometric criteria.

We demonstrate that the universal theory of the hyperfinite II$_1$ factor is undecidable. This conclusion relies on the recent finding that MIP*=RE, which, when integrated with a prior insight from the authors, provides a resolution to the Connes Embedding Problem that circumvents the standard equivalences linking it to Kirchberg's QWEP Conjecture and Tsirelson's Problem.

We calculate the cooling rate, coefficient of performance, and their respective variances for a quantum Otto engine operating within a finite-time cycle. This engine features two driven strokes, during which an isolated system undergoes finite-time unitary transformations, and two isochoric steps where finite-time system-bath interactions drive the system away from equilibrium at the end of each stage. We explicitly determine the statistical distributions of the cooling rate and coefficient of performance for a machine utilizing an analytically solvable two-level system. Our analysis clarifies how the finite-time durations of the four processes influence the engine's performance. Furthermore, we demonstrate a trade-off between the performance parameter and its associated variance, indicating that while the cooling rate or coefficient of performance can be increased, this enhancement comes at the expense of greater fluctuations.

We demonstrate that neural quantum states utilizing extremely deep neural networks (ranging from 4 to 16 layers) surpass current variational methods when applied to highly frustrated quantum magnets, such as quantum-spin-liquid candidates. Our approach centers on group convolutional neural networks (GCNNs), which enable the enforcement of space-group symmetries within our ansätze. This method yields state-of-the-art ground-state energies for the $J_1-J_2$ Heisenberg models on both square and triangular lattices, covering both ordered and spin-liquid phases, while also exploring techniques to identify low-lying excited states in nontrivial symmetry sectors. Furthermore, we calculate spin and dimer correlation functions for the quantum paramagnetic phase on the triangular lattice, revealing no evidence of either conventional or valence-bond ordering.

Intrinsic Image Decomposition (IID) is inherently under-constrained, prompting traditional methods to rely on manually crafted priors; however, these are often insufficient for complex scenes. While deep learning approaches implicitly learn these constraints from data, they frequently struggle with dataset biases that fail to encompass all imaging conditions. This paper proposes a hybrid strategy that leverages component-specific priors, such as semantics and invariant features, to ensure semantically and physically plausible reflectance transitions. These transitions guide a progressive CNN equipped with implicit homogeneity constraints to separate reflectance and shading maps. An ablation study confirms that combining these priors with the progressive CNN enhances IID performance. The method achieves state-of-the-art results on both our proposed dataset and the standard real-world IIW dataset. The source code is available at https://github.com/Morpheus3000/SIGNet.

Contrastive learning plays a pivotal role in recommendation systems, making the selection of representative and informative negative samples essential. While current approaches predominantly rely on centralized data—where access to plentiful, high-quality negatives is straightforward—this model raises privacy concerns and faces limitations due to data sparsity and bias in decentralized client-side environments. To address these issues, we introduce FedCL, a federated contrastive learning framework designed for privacy-preserving recommendations that leverages high-quality negative samples without compromising user privacy. Our approach begins by deriving user embeddings from local data via client-side models, which are then perturbed using local differential privacy (LDP) before transmission to a central server for hard negative sampling. To counteract the significant noise introduced by LDP in individual embeddings, we implement server-side clustering to reduce noise impact, utilizing cluster centroids to retrieve hard negatives from the item pool. These selected hard negatives are sent back to clients, where they are combined with locally observed negatives and in-batch negatives derived from positive samples to facilitate federated model training. Comprehensive experiments across four benchmark datasets demonstrate that FedCL effectively enhances various recommendation methods while maintaining strict privacy safeguards.

By applying the string/gauge duality to a deformed AdS$_5$ background, we investigated deep inelastic scattering involving unpolarized spin-1/2 fermions within the large Bjorken $x$ regime. Our analysis incorporated the anomalous dimension of the boundary operator representing these fermions. Consequently, we calculated the resulting structure functions, which depend on both $x$ and the photon virtuality $q$. These findings align with experimental observations.

Nanomechanics has introduced mesoscopic physics to the realm of vibrations. Due to the diminutive scale of nanomechanical systems, fluctuations are pronounced, causing vibrations to exhibit nonlinearity even at relatively low amplitudes, while introducing novel dissipation mechanisms. Simultaneously, the precise controllability of these systems establishes them as an ideal platform for investigating diverse classical and quantum physics problems far from thermal equilibrium within a well-defined context. This review conceptually outlines fundamental theoretical concepts and illustrative experiments concerning the mesoscopic physics of nanomechanical systems, while also summarizing major scientific and technological applications. It examines a wide spectrum of phenomena involving both conservative and dissipative nonlinearity and fluctuations through a unified framework. Topics include the linear response of individual and coupled vibrational modes, as well as nonlinear effects arising from periodic driving. Such driving disrupts continuous time-translation symmetry and detailed balance, leading to significant impacts on fluctuations, especially when driving-induced bi- and multistability are present. Mathematical methods are detailed in the appendices to facilitate reading and serve as an introduction to the underlying theory. The objective of this review is to highlight the richness of the physics involved. Given the ongoing theoretical and experimental progress, nanomechanical systems remain a dynamic field of research filled with numerous new phenomena awaiting discovery.

Dynamic movement primitives (DMPs) are extensively utilized for acquiring skills demonstrated by humans or controllers. Although their straightforward formulation and generalization abilities are highly attractive, they lack robust guarantees for meeting operational safety constraints. This paper introduces Constrained Dynamic Movement Primitives (CDMPs), enabling constraint satisfaction within the robot's workspace. We propose a non-linear optimization framework that perturbs the DMP forcing weights—initially regressed via locally-weighted regression—to incorporate a Zeroing Barrier Function (ZBF), thereby certifying adherence to workspace constraints. The efficacy of the proposed CDMP is demonstrated through various end-effector constraints, including obstacle avoidance and workspace limitations, on a physical robot. A video illustrating the algorithm's implementation across different manipulators and environments is available at https://youtu.be/hJegJJkJfys.

Our primary result demonstrates that the conical sandpile monoid $M = SP(G)$ associated with any directed sandpile graph $G$ can be realized as the $\mathcal{V}$-monoid of a weighted Leavitt path algebra $L_K(E,w)$, thereby allowing the sandpile group to be represented as the Grothendieck group $K_0(L_K(E,w))$. We provide an explicit method for constructing the pair $(E,w)$ from $G$. Furthermore, we characterize those conical sandpile monoids that emerge as the $\mathcal{V}$-monoid of a standard (unweighted) Leavitt path algebra.

Infographics frequently serve as a vital element in scientific literature, simplifying the understanding of complex qualitative and quantitative data. Nevertheless, interpreting these visuals remains difficult for blind, low-vision, and other print-impaired (BLV) individuals. To address this, we introduce ChartParser, a fully automated workflow that combines deep learning, OCR, and image processing to extract figures from research papers, categorize them into types such as bar and line charts, and extract specific data from bar charts (including horizontal, vertical, stacked horizontal, and stacked vertical variants), which present unique challenges. The extracted information is then displayed in a screen-reader-friendly tabular format, ensuring accessibility for BLV users. We validate our method through a comprehensive evaluation using our pipeline on real-world, annotated bar charts from research publications.

Exploring molecular heterogeneity offers critical insights into tumor origins and metabolomics. As data volumes grow, manual analysis becomes impractical, necessitating the use of automated unsupervised learning methods to identify heterogeneity. However, these methods typically demand significant expertise in hyperparameter tuning and prior knowledge regarding the number of expected substructures. Additionally, processing numerous measured molecules often requires an extra feature engineering step to yield meaningful results. This study introduces DiviK, a scalable, stepwise algorithm featuring local data-driven feature space adaptation designed for segmenting high-dimensional datasets. The quality of the unsupervised analyses in 3D space is evaluated using three metrics: the Dice Index, Rand Index, and EXIMS score. DiviK was validated on two distinct high-throughput Mass Spectrometry Imaging datasets, both in 2D and 3D. It emerges as a strong candidate for the initial exploration of Mass Spectrometry Imaging data, offering a balance between detecting absolute heterogeneity and identifying biologically plausible structures without requiring the user to pre-specify the number of expected structures. Its unique local feature space adaptation ensures robustness against dominant global patterns when analyzing details. Furthermore, due to its simplicity, DiviK is easily adaptable to a flexible framework applicable to other '-omics' data or general tabular data, including medical images with appropriate embedding. A generic implementation is freely available under the Apache 2.0 license at https://github.com/gmrukwa/divik.

An L-sequence in a graph $G$ is defined as a collection of unique vertices $S = \{v_1, \dots, v_k\}$ where, for each $i$, the set $N[v_i] \setminus \cup_{j=1}^{i-1} N(v_j)$ is non-empty. The maximum length of such a sequence is referred to as the L-Grundy domination number, symbolized by $\gamma_{gr}^L(G)$. This paper establishes the inequality $\gamma_{gr}^L(G) \leq n(G) - \delta(G) + 1$, a conjecture previously proposed by Bre{\v{s}}ar, Gologranc, Henning, and Kos. Furthermore, we demonstrate several preliminary findings regarding $n$-vertex graphs where $\gamma_{gr}^L(G) = n$, along with bounds on how the L-Grundy number shifts following various graph operations.

This paper presents a generalized topological quantum field theory rooted in a symmetric monoidal category termed causal network condensation. This framework extends the constructions of Baez's spin networks, the Turaev-Viro model, and causal set theory. We define several novel concepts, namely the causal network category, causal network diagrams, and their associated gauge transformations. Leveraging these definitions, we introduce the nerve functor for the symmetric monoidal category, which serves as a generalization of the nerve functor applied to simplicial categories.

The WL-dimension of a graph $X$ is defined as the minimum positive integer $m$ for which the $m$-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm can accurately determine isomorphism between $X$ and any other graph. It has been demonstrated that for any circulant graph with an order that is a prime power, the WL-dimension is no greater than 3, and this upper limit is tight. This result relies on the application of coherent configuration theories and Cayley schemes defined over cyclic groups.

Modern software development, characterized by contemporary methodologies and source control systems, is frequently cited as a prime example of self-organization. In this model, code evolves organically without relying on centralized authority, leadership, or top-down directives. However, verifying these claims is difficult because self-organization cannot be directly observed; instead, it must be inferred by analyzing system metrics for specific indicators, such as power laws governing features like the magnitude of changes over time. This paper addresses the challenge of establishing a rigorous methodology to mathematically validate whether such power laws hold true for a previously measured set of repositories. Although power laws are widely discussed in software engineering literature, they are often more elusive than they appear. Consequently, we introduce a suite of statistically robust tests designed to determine, based on repository evolution patterns, whether the distribution of commit sizes in 16 open-source Git repositories truly follows a power law. Such a fit would suggest the presence of a state achieved through self-organization. Furthermore, we revisit a seminal paper on this topic to reevaluate its findings and compare them against the current state of the analyzed repositories, aiming to clarify whether the presence of a power law has changed over time.

A Weyl semimetal (WSM) represents a three-dimensional topological state characterized by pairs of nondegenerate bands intersecting at isolated points in the Brillouin zone known as Weyl nodes. In the vicinity of these nodes, the electronic dispersion remains gapless and linear. Applying a magnetic field $B$ transforms this dispersion into a series of Landau levels that are dispersive solely along the field's direction. The $n=0$ Landau level is distinct due to its linear, unidirectional dispersion, a feature that differentiates Weyl fermions from Schrödinger fermions. This paper investigates the quantum oscillations of orbital magnetization and magnetic susceptibility within Weyl semimetals. Building upon prior research \cite{Mikitik2019} regarding De Haas-Van Alphen oscillations, we extend the analysis to include the effects of tilted Weyl nodes. We examine how the tilt vector $\mathbf{t}$, in terms of both magnitude and orientation, alters the fundamental period of oscillations in the low-$B$ regime and the critical field strength $B_{1}$ needed to achieve the quantum limit. Our findings indicate that the magnetization arising from a single node remains finite as $B \rightarrow 0$, with its sign determined by the product of the node's chirality and the tilt component parallel to the magnetic field. Furthermore, we analyze oscillations from a pair of nodes with opposite chirality, considering scenarios where their tilts are either identical or opposite; our calculations reveal significantly different magnetization behaviors in both small and large $B$ limits for these cases. Finally, we explore the impact of an energy shift $\pm \Delta_{0}$ on a node pair on magnetic oscillations, assuming a constant carrier density that establishes a shared Fermi level for both nodes. This framework is readily adaptable to WSMs containing any number of Weyl node pairs.

Quantum circuit mapping is a critical component of the software stack for Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices, significantly influencing the reliability of computational tasks. To enhance the fidelity of physical circuits, we introduce a multi-agent cooperative quantum circuit mapping approach. This method accounts for the spatio-temporal fluctuations in quantum operation quality during the insertion of ancillary operations. The framework comprises two primary modules: a qubit placement algorithm and a qubit routing method. The placement algorithm utilizes an iterated local search framework to determine an optimal initial mapping for the reduced symmetric form of the original circuit. The routing method constructs the physical circuit through multi-agent communication and collaboration, where each agent independently inserts ancillary gates based on its local environmental state. The evolution of physical circuit quality is driven by an information-exchange mechanism between agents that integrates both local and global search strategies. To evaluate the approach on benchmark circuits containing hundreds of gates—exceeding the capacity of current NISQ hardware—we developed a noisy simulator with a gate error rate ten times lower than that of the latest IBM NISQ device. Experimental results validate the method's ability to improve circuit fidelity, demonstrating an average success rate increase of 25.86% and a maximum improvement of 95.42% compared to state-of-the-art techniques.

Confounding significantly hinders our capacity to infer causal relationships from observational data. It occurs when a statistical link exists between two variables because they share a common cause, the confounder. For instance, if $Z$ influences both $Y$ and $X$, then $X$ and $Y$ will appear statistically dependent even without a direct causal link between them. Various methods exist to mitigate confounding by eliminating or diminishing this induced association, such as stratifying the analysis by the confounder or incorporating it as a covariate in regression models. However, most adjustment strategies depend on the assumption that the causal impacts of a confounder on different variables remain independent across observational units. If the effect of $Z$ on $X$ and the effect of $Z$ on $Y$ vary together, residual confounding persists despite adjusting for $Z$. This paper focuses on the phenomenon of causal-effect covariability and its implications. First, we clarify this concept using structural causal models, demonstrating that such covariability typically generates confounding that standard adjustment techniques cannot resolve. Furthermore, empirical evidence suggests that confounding arising from causal-effect covariability is a genuine issue in practical applications.

Login notifications serve to alert users about recent sign-in activities and assist in safeguarding their accounts against unauthorized access. These alerts are typically triggered when a login originates from a new device or location, suggesting potential malicious intent. The notifications generally include details regarding the device, date, time, and geographic location of the sign-in. Users are prompted to verify if they recognize the activity—whether it was performed by themselves or an acquaintance—or to secure their accounts immediately by changing their passwords. Through two user studies, we investigated users' understanding, reactions, and expectations concerning these alerts. We employed two experimental treatments to assess user behavior in response to notifications for both self-initiated logins and those simulating malicious actors using statistical sign-in data. While users generally feel confident distinguishing legitimate logins, they exhibit various risky and insecure behaviors when faced with simulated malicious sign-ins. We analyze these identified issues and offer recommendations to service providers to ensure that login systems remain both usable and secure for all users.

We investigate Bayesian optimization applied to networks of functions where each node's input depends on its parents, and where evaluation is computationally expensive. These scenarios are common in fields like reinforcement learning, engineering design, and manufacturing. Unlike standard approaches that only observe the final result, our method improves query efficiency by utilizing intermediate outputs typically ignored. We achieve this by modeling network nodes with Gaussian processes and selecting evaluation points based on the expected improvement calculated from the resulting posterior distribution over the objective. While the non-Gaussian nature of this posterior prevents a closed-form solution for the acquisition function, we demonstrate that it can be efficiently optimized using sample average approximation. Furthermore, we establish that the method is asymptotically consistent, guaranteeing convergence to a global optimum as evaluations increase, thereby extending known convergence properties of expected improvement. Significantly, this holds even when the method does not densely explore the domain, instead relying on problem structure to skip unproductive regions. Finally, empirical results on both synthetic and real-world tasks show that our approach significantly outperforms standard Bayesian optimization techniques.

Density tracking by quadrature (DTQ) serves as a numerical method for solving Fokker-Planck equations, which model probability densities for stochastic differential equations (SDEs). This paper expands on current tensorized DTQ methods by employing a versatile quadrature rule capable of handling unstructured, adaptive meshes. We outline the procedure for $N$-dimensions and show that this adaptive strategy yields substantially greater efficiency compared to traditional tensorized approaches. While our illustrative examples are confined to two dimensions, the computational framework is fully scalable to higher-dimensional problems.

Achieving human-like dexterity in robot manipulation requires replicating the human sense of touch, a goal that necessitates an integrated approach combining soft robotics, biomimetics, and the high-resolution sensing provided by optical tactile sensors. This specific integration is defined here as a SoftBOT (Soft Biomimetic Optical Tactile) sensor, with the BRL TacTip serving as a representative example in this review. The discussion covers the connection between artificial skin morphology and human touch transduction mechanisms, the significance of tactile shear sensing, the role of 3D printing in fabricating and integrating these sensors into robotic hands, the application of artificial intelligence to tactile perception and control, and the transformative impact of deep learning on current capabilities. By consolidating advancements from the last decade, this article outlines a trajectory for robots to attain dexterity comparable to that of humans.

High-energy jets traversing the quark-gluon plasma formed in heavy-ion collisions act as ideal probes for investigating this novel, deconfined state of QCD matter. Currently, however, interpreting the growing array of jet observables measured experimentally with precision is limited by selection biases. This study aims to reduce biases related to the modification of the quark-to-gluon jet fraction to isolate and evaluate other medium-induced phenomena, specifically color decoherence, by analyzing the rapidity dependence of jet substructure. Previous measurements at mid-rapidity indicate that heavy-ion jets are narrower than those in a vacuum. We demonstrate through both analytical methods and Monte Carlo simulations that if this narrowing persists at forward rapidities—where the fraction of quark-initiated jets is significantly higher—it would provide a clear experimental signature of color decoherence dynamics in heavy-ion collisions.

This study examines a wireless powered communication network (WPCN) operating under a harvest-then-transmit protocol. In this setup, a hybrid access point with a constant power source replenishes passive user nodes via downlink wireless power transfer, followed by each user node transmitting independent data to the hybrid access point in the uplink using time division multiple access (TDMA). The paper addresses both sum-throughput and min-throughput maximization problems. For the sum-throughput maximization, an optimal time allocation strategy is proposed utilizing Jensen's inequality, offering deeper insights into WPCN design. Additionally, a low-complexity fixed-point iteration algorithm is developed for the min-throughput maximization problem, which achieves significantly lower computational complexity compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Simulation results validate the efficacy of the proposed algorithm.

The issue of separating spin and orbital angular momentum (AM) has become a prominent topic of discussion. Current debates regarding the gauge-invariant separation of spin AM from orbital AM rely on the assumption that the gluon field can be decomposed into additive physical and pure gauge components ($A_\mu = A_\mu^{\text{phys}}+A_\mu^{\text{pure}}$). This paper demonstrates that within non-Abelian gauge theory, this decomposition finds strong mathematical justification through the contour gauge framework. Specifically, we elevate the decomposition ansatz to a formal theorem and prove it using the contour gauge. Furthermore, for the first time, we establish that the contour gauge features a unique residual gauge symmetry tied to boundary field configurations and expressed via pure gauge fields. Consequently, trivial boundary conditions imply that the decomposition consists solely of physical gluon configurations when the contour gauge condition is applied.

GeoChemFoam is an open-source numerical modeling suite built on OpenFOAM, featuring custom packages designed to handle intricate flow phenomena such as multiphase transport with interfacial transfer, single-phase flow within multiscale porous media, and reactive transport involving mineral dissolution. This paper introduces a new numerical model within GeoChemFoam specifically for simulating conjugate heat transfer in micro-CT scans of porous media. The model employs a micro-continuum approach, defining the fluid-solid interface via the volume fraction of each phase within every computational cell. Velocity fields are resolved using Brinkman's equation, where permeability is derived from the Kozeny-Carman equation, yielding near-zero permeability in solid regions. Conjugate heat transfer is subsequently modeled with heat convection occurring where velocity is non-zero, utilizing a thermal conductivity calculated as the harmonic average of phase conductivities weighted by their respective volume fractions. The model's validity is confirmed by comparing results against the standard two-medium approach for a basic 2D geometry. Furthermore, the authors simulate conjugate heat transfer to determine heat transfer coefficients across various flow regimes and injected fluids, analogous to geothermal reservoir injection scenarios using a micro-CT image of Bentheimer sandstone. Finally, a sensitivity analysis is conducted on a porous heat exchanger featuring random sphere packing.

This study introduces a unified framework for user profiling designed to detect hate speech disseminators across multiple languages by analyzing their tweets. The approach utilizes sentence transformers to encode tweet data and employs an attention mechanism to isolate significant tweets for constructing user profiles. Additionally, the attention layer facilitates interpretability by generating attention weights at both the token and post levels, thereby elucidating the reasons behind a user's classification as a hate speech spreader. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model surpasses existing state-of-the-art multilingual transformer models in performance.

Although machine reading comprehension has been extensively researched, understanding spoken content remains a less explored challenge. This paper introduces the Open-Domain Spoken Question Answering Dataset (ODSQA), which comprises over three thousand questions and represents, to our knowledge, the largest real-world spoken question answering dataset. Our analysis on this dataset reveals that automatic speech recognition (ASR) errors have a devastating effect on spoken question answering. To counteract this, we incorporated subword units, resulting in consistent performance gains across all models. Additionally, we discovered that augmenting text-based question answering training data can enhance spoken question answering capabilities.

Integral transforms serve as effective tools for simplifying differential equation calculations. This study systematically examines integral transforms within the framework of $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric Hamiltonians. Initially, we derive a closed analytical expression for the exponential Fourier transform of these Hamiltonians. Subsequently, utilizing the Segal-Bargmann transform, we analyze how the Fourier transform influences the eigenfunctions of the original Hamiltonian. Furthermore, we discuss the holomorphic representation of non-Hermitian spin chains, where the Hamiltonian operator is expressed via analytical phase-space coordinates and their partial derivatives in Bargmann space, contrasting this with matrix representations in complex Hilbert space. Focusing specifically on non-Hermitian $XX$ spin chains, we numerically solve the quantum master equation to demonstrate the system's transition from dynamical to static behavior as the coupling constant increases from weak to strong. Finally, we resolve the Swanson Hamiltonian and evaluate its properties under integral transformations.

Strong invariance principles characterize the error term arising from Brownian approximations of partial sums within stochastic processes. Although these robust approximation results are widely applicable, their extension to continuous-time environments has historically been constrained. This paper establishes strong invariance principles for a wide range of ergodic Markov processes. These principles offer a cohesive framework for examining frequently employed estimators of asymptotic variance in contexts featuring dependence structures. We illustrate this utility by analyzing the batch means method for simulation outputs generated by Piecewise Deterministic Monte Carlo samplers. Furthermore, leveraging our strong approximation findings, we derive a fluctuation result concerning additive functionals of ergodic diffusions.

We introduce a straightforward, highly parallel technique for re-indexing "indexed" datasets, such as triangle meshes or unstructured mesh collections, which facilitates tasks like eliminating redundant or unused vertices and merging distinct meshes. Specifically, our approach is optimized for GPUs because every step is either inherently parallel or relies on GPU-native primitives like sorting and prefix-sums, rendering it ideal for execution on highly parallel architectures.

Let $d$ denote a square-free integer and define $L_d$ as the field extension $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{8},\sqrt{d})$. This study identifies every such field $L_d$ for which the $2$-class group, $\mathrm{Cl}_2(L_d)$, exhibits a structure of type $(2,4)$ or $(2,2,2)$.

The integration of density functional theory and dynamical mean-field theory (DFT+DMFT) has emerged as a potent first-principles method for investigating strongly correlated materials within condensed matter physics. The widespread adoption of this technique depends on robust and user-friendly implementations; expanding its presence across various numerical frameworks will both broaden its applicability and enable cross-validation of results. In this study, we establish a formalism based on the linear combination of numerical atomic orbitals (NAO) that facilitates the coupling of NAO-based DFT codes with DMFT quantum impurity solvers. This framework is realized by interfacing two NAO-based DFT packages with three distinct DMFT impurity solvers, with its accuracy confirmed through benchmark calculations across a diverse array of strongly correlated systems, including 3d transition metal compounds, lanthanides, and actinides. Our contribution not only allows for DFT+DMFT computations using popular and rapidly evolving NAO-based code suites but also streamlines the integration of advanced post-DFT methods available in these codes with DMFT capabilities.

The oscillation continuum observed in the bound-free transitions $c^3\Sigma^+ \to a^3\Sigma^+$ and (4)$^1\Sigma^+ \to X^1\Sigma^+$ of the KCs molecule, recorded via a Fourier-transform spectrometer, was modeled using the adiabatic approximation. Within the regularization direct-potential-fit framework, the interatomic potentials for the ground $a^3\Sigma^+$ and $X^1\Sigma^+$ states were reconstructed as analytical Chebyshev polynomial expansions. This approach integrated experimental line positions from [R. Ferber et al, Phys. Rev. A, \textbf{80}, 062501 (2009)] with current \emph{ab initio} calculations of short-range repulsive potentials. The study demonstrates that the repulsive portion of the derived $a^3\Sigma^+$ potential above the dissociation limit yields superior agreement with experimental data compared to existing literature potentials. Furthermore, it is established that all available empirical and semi-empirical potentials for the $X^1\Sigma^+$ state describe the bound-free (4)$^1\Sigma^+ \to X^1\Sigma^+$ spectrum with equivalent accuracy within the observed range.

This paper introduces an analytical approach to performing tractable approximate Gaussian inference (TAGI) within Bayesian neural networks. The proposed technique allows for the analytical derivation of the posterior mean vector and diagonal covariance matrix for both weights and biases. With a computational complexity of $\mathcal{O}(n)$ relative to the parameter count $n$, evaluations on regression and classification benchmarks demonstrate that, for identical network architectures, this method achieves performance comparable to existing techniques based on gradient backpropagation.

This work examines polynomials of bi-degree $(n,1)$ defined over the quaternion skew field, assuming that the variables commute both with one another and with all coefficients. Such polynomials typically lack factorizations. We revisit a necessary and sufficient condition for factorization into univariate linear factors, originally established by Skopenkov and Krasauskas. While known results indicate that such factorizations are generally non-unique for univariate quaternionic polynomials, we identify bivariate polynomials exhibiting non-unique factorizations that cannot be attributed to this standard cause, providing both geometric and algebraic characterizations for them. The existence of factorizations corresponds to the presence of special rulings of two distinct types (left or right) on the ruled surface parameterized by the bivariate polynomial within the projective space over quaternions. This specific type of non-uniqueness can be explained algebraically through the commutation properties of factors in appropriate factorizations. A requisite geometric condition for this phenomenon is the degeneration of at least one of the left or right rulings into a single point.

This project developed a DC motor speed control system utilizing a PID controller with gains ($K_P$, $K_I$, $K_D$) automatically adjusted via Fuzzy Logic. To ensure system robustness, a Fuzzy Logic Controller (FLC) was constructed using 25 specific rules for the auto-tuning of each PID parameter. The FLC operates with two inputs: the speed error (the difference between the reference setpoint and actual motor speed) and the rate of change of this error. Consequently, the FLC's output determines the PID parameters necessary to regulate the motor's speed. By combining the precision of PID controllers with the adaptability of fuzzy logic, this fuzzy self-tuning approach successfully controlled the DC motor, enhancing both its dynamic and static responses. Simulation results from MATLAB/SIMULINK compared conventional and fuzzy self-tuning performances, demonstrating that the adaptive controller delivers superior dynamic behavior, including rapid rise and settling times, zero overshoot, and zero steady-state error. Finally, a practical experiment was conducted using simple code on the Arduino IDE to model the fuzzy PID system, thereby validating the theoretical findings.

Probabilistic numerical solvers for ordinary differential equations generate posterior distributions over initial value problem solutions through Bayesian inference.
