Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method is both efficient and achieves state-of-the-art results in both transductive and inductive reasoning settings, attributable to the enhanced depth of propagation.

This study examines bias within historical corpora by analyzing diachronic distributional semantic models, with a specific focus on political (anti-communism) and racist (antisemitism) biases. Our analysis utilizes a newly developed corpus of German parliamentary debates, DeuPARL, covering the years 1867 to 2020. We enhance the evaluation of historical biases in evolving word embeddings by introducing a novel metric based on term co-occurrences and graph-based label propagation. Our findings confirm that these bias measurements correspond with established historical patterns of antisemitic and anti-communist sentiments in German politics across various eras, thereby demonstrating the effectiveness of using semantic spaces derived from historical corpora to track bias trends over time.

Silicon nanoparticles hold the potential to exceed the theoretical efficiency limits of single-junction silicon photovoltaics by inducing a "phonon bottleneck." This phenomenon involves a theorized delay in the cooling of hot optical phonons, which subsequently slows the relaxation of hot carriers. Verifying this bottleneck in silicon nanoparticles necessitates the simultaneous observation of electronic and structural dynamics at ultrafast timescales. This study employs extreme ultraviolet transient absorption spectroscopy to monitor excited-state electronic and lattice dynamics in polycrystalline silicon nanoparticles after 800 nm photoexcitation, which injects carriers with an excess energy of $0.35 \pm 0.03$ eV above the ${\Delta}_1$ conduction band minimum. The samples consist of nanoparticles with nominal 100 nm diameters and crystalline grains approximately 16 nm in size. The extracted carrier-phonon and phonon-phonon relaxation times for these nanoparticles were compared against those of a silicon (100) single-crystal thin film at comparable carrier densities ($2 \times 10^{19} cm^{-3}$ for the nanoparticles and $6 \times 10^{19} cm^{-3}$ for the thin film). The measured carrier-phonon and phonon-phonon scattering lifetimes for the polycrystalline nanoparticles were $870 \pm 40$ fs and $17.5 \pm 0.3$ ps, respectively, compared to $195 \pm 20$ fs and $8.1 \pm 0.2$ ps for the silicon thin film. These reduced scattering rates in the nanoparticles align with the phonon bottleneck hypothesis.

The variational derivative of a Lagrangian with respect to the metric tensor serves to define Hilbert's energy-momentum tensor for matter fields in classical field theories. In solid-state physics, diverse models address the constitutive relationships among fundamental field variables; within this framework, higher-order constitutive tensors supplant the second-order metric tensor. Recently, a similar premetric approach featuring a linear constitutive relation has been proposed for classical field models of gravity and electrodynamics. This paper investigates extending the Hilbert definition of the energy-momentum tensor to models governed by general linear constitutive laws. To ensure a covariant treatment of integrals on differential manifolds, differential forms are employed. Specifically, the Lagrangian, electromagnetic current, and energy-momentum current are formulated as twisted 4-forms, 3-forms, and vector-valued 3-forms, respectively. We derive a commutative variation identity for any arbitrary linear map on forms, enabling direct variation procedures without addressing individual components. By restricting the linear map to the generalized Hodge dual map, Maxwell-type Lagrangians can be handled in any dimension. The Hilbert energy-momentum current is derived in differential form as the variation derivative of the Lagrangian with respect to a coframe field. We demonstrate a close connection between this commutative variation identity and the explicit expression of the energy-momentum current. Finally, this construction is applied to various field models characterized by general linear constitutive laws.

Measuring how much a probability distribution deviates becomes difficult when the target density involves an intractable normalizing constant. The Kernel Stein Discrepancy (KSD) was introduced to solve this issue and is now used for tasks such as evaluating approximate MCMC samplers and performing goodness-of-fit tests on unnormalized models. This paper examines a convergence control characteristic of the Diffusion Kernel Stein Discrepancy (DKSD), a specific form of KSD developed by Barp et al. (2019). Building on Gorham and Mackey's (2017) finding that KSD bounds the bounded-Lipschitz metric, we extend this result to functions exhibiting polynomial growth. Specifically, we demonstrate that DKSD governs an integral probability metric defined by pseudo-Lipschitz functions, which represent a polynomial extension of standard Lipschitz functions. Furthermore, we establish practical sufficient conditions regarding the reproducing kernel required for this property to be valid. Notably, we show that DKSD can identify non-convergence in moments when paired with a suitable kernel.

This research introduces a deep learning framework utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to recover high-resolution turbulent velocity fields from extremely low-resolution inputs across various Reynolds numbers. The study employs a Multiscale Enhanced Super-Resolution GAN (MS-ESRGAN) for reconstruction and evaluates its performance using direct numerical simulation (DNS) data from turbulent channel flows featuring large longitudinal ribs at different Reynolds numbers. Results indicate that the model successfully and accurately reproduces high-resolution velocity fields, including velocity magnitudes and turbulent statistics, from two distinct low-resolution data levels. Furthermore, the findings demonstrate the model's capability to reconstruct velocity fields at Reynolds numbers that were not included during the training phase.

The Linear Threshold Model is a prevalent framework for describing information diffusion within social networks, positing that an individual adopts an idea once a specific proportion of their neighbors have done so. Conventional applications of this model typically assume uniform thresholds across all nodes or randomly distributed ones, often overlooking variations in individual susceptibility to peer influence. To account for these individual-level differences, we propose causal inference techniques designed to estimate unique thresholds, thereby improving the accuracy of predictions regarding when and if individuals will be influenced by their peers. We introduce the notion of heterogeneous peer effects and construct a Structural Causal Model aligned with the Linear Threshold Model, which facilitates the identification and estimation of these varying effects. Furthermore, we present two algorithms for threshold estimation: one utilizing causal trees and another employing causal meta-learners. Empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our proposed models outperform existing approaches in predicting individual thresholds, leading to more precise forecasts of node activation over time.

Constant mean curvature (CMC) spacelike hypersurfaces are well-established as crucial for addressing the Einstein equations, encompassing both constraint and evolution components. This paper reviews the CMC existence theorem derived by the authors in [10] and examines additional existence findings inspired by a conjecture proposed by Dilts and Holst [8]. Furthermore, we discuss several aspects related to the conformal structure of cosmological spacetimes.

Lately, predictor-based methods have arisen as a compelling solution for Neural Architecture Search (NAS). Traditional NAS requires evaluating the validation accuracy of countless Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), a process that is highly computationally demanding. Predictor-based NAS tackles this issue by training a proxy model to estimate a DNN's validation accuracy directly from its architecture. During the optimization phase, this proxy helps reduce the number of architectures requiring actual accuracy computation, thereby enhancing sample efficiency. Typically, the proxy is evaluated across the entire search space, and architectures maximizing the proxy are selected as candidates. However, this approach is often impractical because search spaces can be enormous, containing billions of possible networks. This paper presents three main contributions: first, we introduce a metric to quantify sample efficiency gains among various predictor-based NAS algorithms; second, experiments on the NASBench-101 dataset reveal that sample efficiency drops significantly if the proxy is only computed for a subset of the search space; and third, we demonstrate that intelligently selecting the subset for proxy evaluation can restore the sample efficiency of the original algorithm with full-space access. This advancement is crucial for making predictor-based NAS practical in real-world applications.

Magnetotransport measurements were conducted on SnTe/PbTe heterojunctions fabricated using molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) on undoped (001) CdTe substrates. At low magnetic fields, quantum corrections to conductivity indicated topological states at the interface. For the 5 nm SnTe sample, analysis revealed that midgap states are gapped; conversely, phase coherence in 10 nm and 20 nm samples is consistent with gapless Dirac cones. High-field magnetotransport was analyzed using mobility spectrum analysis (MSA). We show that simultaneous electron- and hole-like peaks across all samples arise from the concave and convex regions of the topological energy isosurface, rather than from quasiparticles with opposite charges. This conclusion is backed by numerical calculations of the conductivity tensor for gapless (100) Dirac cones using a classical Boltzmann transport model. Our findings demonstrate the viability of applying MSA to magnetotransport studies of topological materials.

This study examines the irreducible representations $\phi_n^1$ and $\phi_n^2$ of the symplectic group $G_n=Sp_{2n}(P)$ defined over an algebraically closed field $P$ with characteristic $p>2$, which possess highest weights $\omega_{n-1}+\frac{p-3}{2}\omega_n$ and $\frac{p-1}{2}\omega_n$, respectively. The analysis establishes that the dimension of each representation $\phi_n^i$ (for $i=1,2$) is given by $(p^n+(-1)^i )/2$, with all weight multiplicities equal to $1$. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that their restrictions to the naturally embedded subgroup $G_k$ are completely reducible, consisting solely of the irreducible components $\phi_k^1$ and $\phi_k^2$. Finally, the restrictions of these representations to $Sp_{2n}(p)$ are shown to arise from reducing modulo $p$ specific complex irreducible representations of the group $Sp_{2n}(p)$.

Software bugs substantially drive up development costs and elevate the likelihood of system failures. While numerous automated program repair methods have been introduced in recent years to correct undesirable behaviors, challenges persist, particularly regarding bugs addressed via partial fixes. A partial fix represents a programmer's unsuccessful initial attempt to resolve a known issue; although it does not fully succeed, it provides valuable insights, including the location of the problematic code and the nature of the bug. Rather than proposing a new repair technique for partial fixes, this study addresses a foundational question: are partial fixes frequent enough to be significant for automated program repair research? By crawling 1,500 open-source C repositories on GitHub, we identified a dataset comprising 2,204 benchmark tasks tailored for automated program repair based on partial fixes. This benchmark set is publicly available, open-source, and welcomes further contributions and enhancements.

This work clarifies arguments regarding Jefimenko's equations to construct solutions to Maxwell's equations for charge and current distributions that satisfy the continuity equation. We then identify a condition for non-radiation that holds across all inertial frames, a requirement that is intuitively necessary for the stability of atomic systems, and demonstrate its equivalence to specific relations between charge and current, including the wave equation. Finally, we establish that under these relations, electromagnetic field energy becomes quantized and exhibits characteristics consistent with the Balmer series.

Let $k$ be a field, and let $A$ and $B$ denote polynomial rings over $k$, with $S = A \otimes_k B$. Given monomial ideals $I \subseteq A$ and $J \subseteq B$, we derive a binomial expansion for the rational powers of the sum $I+J$ within $S$, expressed through the rational powers of $I$ and $J$ individually. We identify a sufficient condition under which this formula applies to the integral closures of powers of $I+J$. When this condition is met, we present exact formulas for the depth and regularity of these integral closures. Our approach relies on linear algebra, specifically utilizing the characterization of rational powers of monomial ideals as optimal solutions to linear programming problems.

Solving distribution-level optimal power flow (D-OPF) using nonlinear programming (NLP) often leads to convergence difficulties and poor scalability within unbalanced distribution systems. Current scalable D-OPF methods either rely on approximations unsuitable for unbalanced networks or utilize relaxation techniques on nonlinear power flow equations that fail to ensure feasible solutions. This paper introduces scalable D-OPF algorithms capable of delivering both optimal and feasible results by iteratively solving low-complexity, approximate or relaxed D-OPF subproblems. The first approach employs successive linearization of the nonlinear power flow equations around the current operating point, deriving the D-OPF solution through multiple iterations of linear programming (LP). The second approach relaxes nonlinear power flow equations into conic constraints alongside directional constraints, achieving optimality and feasibility via repeated iterations of second-order cone programming (SOCP). Results demonstrate that these proposed algorithms attain optimal and feasible solutions while drastically cutting computation time compared to equivalent NLP D-OPF models for the same distribution system.

This work investigates the Higgs mode within a Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) superconductor. Driven by the finding that the U(1) symmetry of the BCS Hamiltonian is not a prerequisite for the Higgs mode, we analyze an Ising-like Hamiltonian expressed in the pseudospin representation. We demonstrate that the Higgs mode arises as the ground state's first excitation, resulting from the spontaneous breaking of $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry under the time-reversal operation $\mathcal T$ in pseudospin space. Additionally, we forecast the presence of multiple Higgs modes possessing quantized energies given by $2(n+1)\Delta_0$, where $\Delta_0$ denotes the superconducting gap, $n$ is an integer, and $N_{k_F}$ represents the number of states at the Fermi surface.

We investigate evolutionary games featuring a continuous trait space, where replicator dynamics are confined to the manifold of multidimensional Gaussian distributions. We show that these replicator equations function as a natural gradient flow designed to maximize mean fitness. Our results broaden earlier findings concerning the information-geometric properties of evolutionary games with finite strategy sets. Throughout this work, we utilize the information-geometric framework and explore the connection between evolutionary dynamics and Natural Evolution Strategies, a concept originating from black-box optimization. This relationship offers fresh insight into replicator dynamics, characterizing them as a balance between maximizing mean fitness and maintaining population diversity.

We introduce a high-precision thermometry system designed to monitor room-temperature components in radio-astronomy telescopes, specifically for cosmic microwave background (CMB) observations. This system achieves a precision of 1 mK$\sqrt{s}$ over a 20-second interval at 300 K. Such high accuracy is attained by measuring only relative fluctuations and integrating thermistors with a low-noise measurement apparatus. We outline the necessary precision standards for CMB temperature monitoring and demonstrate our system's performance. This advanced room-temperature monitoring capability allows for the reduction of low-frequency noise across a broad spectrum of radio-astronomical detector signals, thereby enabling large detector arrays to operate at their intended high sensitivity.

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) typically encode valuable dataset information within their architecture and weights. To safeguard this data upon publication, one approach involves applying secure multi-party computation (MPC) to interfere with the network. This paper proposes converting deep neural networks into polynomials, which are more amenable to efficient MPC processing. We demonstrate a method for translating entire networks into a single polynomial and executing calculations using an efficient, information-secure MPC algorithm. Notably, the computation proceeds without intermediate communication between participating parties, offering distinct advantages as detailed in the study.

Most Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) based super-resolution (SR) techniques presuppose known degradation processes, such as bicubic interpolation, causing significant performance declines when faced with differing degradation types. Consequently, some strategies train SR networks using complex combinations of multiple degradations to encompass the realistic degradation spectrum. To better adapt to unknown degradations, integrating an explicit degradation estimator can enhance SR performance; however, prior methods typically rely on ground-truth blur kernels to supervise Gaussian blur predictions, where estimation errors often result in SR failure. Therefore, a method capable of extracting implicit, discriminative degradation representations is required. In response, we introduce the Meta-Learning based Region Degradation Aware SR Network (MRDA), comprising a Meta-Learning Network (MLN), a Degradation Extraction Network (DEN), and a Region Degradation Aware SR Network (RDAN). To address the absence of ground-truth degradation data, the MLN rapidly adapts to specific complex degradations over several iterations to extract implicit degradation information. A teacher network, MRDA$_{T}$, is then designed to leverage this extracted information for SR. Since the MLN necessitates paired low-resolution (LR) and high-resolution (HR) images for iteration—data unavailable during inference—we employ knowledge distillation (KD) to enable the student network to directly learn the same implicit degradation representation (IDR) from LR images as the teacher.

The Posner-Robinson Theorem asserts that for any reals $Z$ and $A$ satisfying $Z \oplus 0' \leq_\mathrm{T} A$ and $0 <_\mathrm{T} Z$, there is a $B$ such that $A \equiv_\mathrm{T} B' \equiv_\mathrm{T} B \oplus Z \equiv_\mathrm{T} B \oplus 0'$. This implies that every nonzero Turing degree $\operatorname{deg}_\mathrm{T}(Z)$ is a Turing jump of some $B$. In this work, we establish a hyperarithmetical counterpart, relying on an unpublished proof by Slaman: for any reals $Z$ and $A$ where $Z \oplus \mathcal{O} \leq_\mathrm{T} A$ and $0 <_\mathrm{HYP} Z$, there exists a $B$ such that $A \equiv_\mathrm{T} \mathcal{O}^B \equiv_\mathrm{T} B \oplus Z \equiv_\mathrm{T} B \oplus \mathcal{O}$. Consequently, any nonhyperarithmetical Turing degree $\operatorname{deg}_\mathrm{T}(Z)$ is a hyperjump relative to some $B$.

Natural Language Inference (NLI) involves identifying the semantic connection between a premise and a hypothesis. This paper specifically addresses the {\em generation} of hypotheses from premises within a multimodal context, where the objective is to produce a sentence (hypothesis) based on an image and/or its textual description (premise). The primary objectives are (a) to assess the validity of framing NLI as a generative task and (b) to evaluate how beneficial it is to ground textual premises in visual data for generation purposes. By comparing various neural architectures and utilizing both automatic and human evaluations, we demonstrate that entailments can indeed be successfully generated. Furthermore, our results indicate that multimodal models slightly outperform unimodal models in this specific task.

Recent thermal Hall conductivity measurements, which detected a successful probing of neutral Majorana modes, supported the particle-hole symmetric Pfaffian (PH-Pf) topological order, distinguishing it from theoretical predictions of Pfaffian or anti-Pfaffian phases. In this study, we report a reentrant anomalous quantized phase that remains gapped in the thermodynamic limit and is distinct from conventional Pfaffian, anti-Pfaffian, or PH-Pf phases, occurring at intermediate Landau level mixing strengths. Our proposed wave function, which aligns with the PH-Pf shift in spherical geometry, accurately captures this phase's topological order due to its high overlap with the exact ground state and its reproduction of low-lying entanglement spectra. This phase exhibits a unique topological order independent of flux shifts, a finding that may corroborate the experimentally observed topological order.

LTE-Licensed Assisted Access (LAA) networks are increasingly being deployed across major US metropolitan areas within the unlicensed 5 GHz spectrum, a band already saturated with dense Wi-Fi infrastructure. This environment offers a practical setting to investigate hidden-node conflicts between LAA and Wi-Fi. While the hidden-node issue is well-documented among overlapping Wi-Fi access points, its presence alongside LAA is intensified because LAA lacks the ability to utilize the Request-to-Send/Clear-to-Send (RTS/CTS) handshake to manage contentions, leading to significant Wi-Fi throughput degradation. This paper details experimental measurements and findings from the University of Chicago campus, which presents an ideal hidden-node scenario: Wi-Fi access points managed by the authors and an AT&T-deployed LAA base station are mutually hidden, yet their respective clients are not. We conducted rigorous experiments across three distinct zones within the coexistence area: (i) clients positioned midway between the LAA and Wi-Fi systems, (ii) clients located near the Wi-Fi AP, and (iii) clients situated close to the LAA base station. Our data indicates that when LAA aggregates three unlicensed channels (60 MHz bandwidth) overlapping with an 80 MHz Wi-Fi transmission, Wi-Fi client throughput suffers substantially. Overall, the hidden-node problem impacts Wi-Fi performance far more severely than LAA; under optimal outdoor conditions, coexistence reduces Wi-Fi throughput by 97% and LAA throughput by 35% compared to scenarios where the other system is absent. Additionally, we conclude that when both systems utilize multiple 20 MHz channels and multiple Wi-Fi APs share the same spectrum as LAA, the selection of the Wi-Fi primary channel can significantly influence LAA throughput.

Testing physical theories against subsets of the Gaia catalogue without correcting for the biased sampling process risks leading to erroneous scientific conclusions. To address this, we generate selection functions for three specific Gaia science samples, allowing the community to account for these biases. We calculate the probability that a source in Gaia EDR3 possesses: i) reported parallax and proper motion, ii) an astrometric renormalised unit weight error under 1.4, or iii) a reported radial velocity. These selection functions are modeled as a function of $G$-band apparent magnitude and sky position, with the latter two also depending on the $G-G_\mathrm{RP}$ colour. The resulting non-trivial dependencies on these observables highlight the necessity of empirically deriving selection functions. Additionally, we provide a straightforward estimate for the selection function of the complete Gaia EDR3 source catalogue to complement the subset-specific functions. All selection functions are made readily available via the GitHub repository \textsc{selectionfunctions}.

Cosmic Birefringence (CB) refers to the in-vacuo rotation of photon linear polarization directions as they propagate, resulting from parity-violating extensions to Maxwell's electromagnetism. Utilizing Planck Legacy and NPIPE data, we have constructed low-resolution maps of the CB angle and, for the first time, derived estimates for the cross-correlation spectra $C_L^{\alpha E}$ and $C_L^{\alpha B}$ between the CB field and CMB polarization. We also present updated auto-correlation spectra $C_L^{\alpha\alpha}$ and the cross-correlation $C_L^{\alpha T}$ with the CMB temperature field. By defining scale-invariant amplitudes $A^{\alpha X} \equiv L(L + 1)C_L^{\alpha X}/2\pi$ (where $X = \alpha, T, E, B$), we report constraints that reveal no evidence for CB. Specifically, at 68% confidence level, we find $A^{\alpha E} = (-7.8 \pm 5.6)$ nK deg and $A^{\alpha B} = (0.3 \pm 4.0)$ nK deg.

The formation of subduction zones, whether occurring spontaneously or through induction, involves a phase of strain localization characterized by the emergence of lithospheric-scale shear bands. This study utilizes a solid-mechanical constitutive framework applicable to oceanic lithosphere to examine factors that either facilitate or hinder deformation localization within brittle and ductile regimes during convergence-driven numerical simulations. Employing the Drucker-Prager yield criterion alongside a non-associative flow rule, we permit viscoplastic deformation to occur independently of the yield surface's preferred orientation. We provide a detailed, step-by-step exposition of the constitutive law and the consistent algorithmic tangent modulus. The simulation domain features an initial weak zone where localization may nucleate. In addressing energy conservation, we integrate a heat source term derived from mechanical deformation, representing irreversible plastic work; this term links the energy equation to the constitutive description and stress balance through the evolving temperature field. We begin with isothermal benchmark tests at the sample scale and subsequently investigate behaviors involving shear heating and volumetric work, both individually and combined, to evaluate their respective significance. Our findings indicate that dilatational effects generally enhance both shear band formation and shear heating. Furthermore, we observe that elevated temperatures promote shear band development while high confining pressure suppresses it, suggesting that the interplay between these factors primarily dictates the depth within the lithosphere where shear bands nucleate.

We report the derivation of optical potentials via the double-folding method, utilizing chiral effective field theory nucleon-nucleon interactions at next-to-next-to-leading order and employing dispersion relations to limit the imaginary component. Validated against $^{16}$O--$^{16}$O collisions, this methodology is further applied to $^{12}$C--$^{12}$C and $^{12}$C--$^{16}$O systems. The resulting predictions are evaluated against experimental data for elastic scattering up to 1000 MeV and low-energy fusion. Remarkably, these potentials yield excellent agreement with experimental results without any parameter adjustment. Additionally, we investigate the sensitivity of the associated cross sections to variations in the underlying nucleon-nucleon interactions and nuclear densities.

Current gait recognition techniques predominantly rely on appearance cues, utilizing silhouettes derived from video footage of human movement. In contrast, skeleton-based approaches, which have received less attention, directly model gait dynamics from 2D or 3D skeletal sequences; theoretically, these offer greater robustness against appearance variations caused by factors such as clothing, hairstyles, and carried items. Despite these advantages, skeleton-based methods currently lag significantly behind appearance-based ones in performance. This study seeks to bridge this gap by introducing GaitMixer, a novel network designed to extract highly discriminative features from skeletal data. Specifically, GaitMixer employs a heterogeneous multi-axial mixer architecture that combines a spatial self-attention mixer with a temporal large-kernel convolution mixer to capture rich multi-frequency signals within gait feature maps. Evaluations on the standard CASIA-B dataset show that GaitMixer substantially outperforms existing state-of-the-art skeleton-based methods and achieves results comparable to leading appearance-based solutions. The code is accessible at https://github.com/exitudio/gaitmixer.

For a poset $P$, the collection $\Gamma(P)$ of all Scott closed sets, ordered by inclusion, constitutes a complete lattice. A subcategory $\mathbf{C}$ of $\mathbf{Pos}_d$ (the category of posets and Scott-continuous maps) is defined as $\Gamma$-faithful if, for any $P, Q \in \mathbf{C}$, the isomorphism $\Gamma(P) \cong \Gamma(Q)$ guarantees that $P \cong Q$. While the categories of continuous dcpos and bounded complete dcpos are established as $\Gamma$-faithful, $\mathbf{Pos}_d$ is not. In 2009, Ho and Zhao posed the question of whether the category $\mathbf{DCPO}$ of dcpos possesses this property. This paper provides a negative answer by presenting a counterexample. To accomplish this, we define a novel subcategory of dcpos that is $\Gamma$-faithful and encompasses all previously identified $\Gamma$-faithful subcategories. Leveraging this new concept, we construct the required counterexample, which depends significantly on Johnstone's renowned non-sober dcpo under its Scott topology.

We establish sufficient conditions guaranteeing solutions for systems of polynomial equations defined over general real or complex algebras, thereby extending established results regarding quaternions, octonions, and matrix algebras. Furthermore, we extend the fundamental theorem of algebra for quaternions to polynomials featuring two monomials in their leading form, while demonstrating that this extension does not hold when three monomials are involved.

To address the demanding radiation requirements of future high-energy physics detectors, a new 3D 4H-SiC detector was examined. Due to its superior thermal conductivity and high atomic displacement threshold energy, SiC detectors are well-suited for operation in harsh radiation environments at room temperature. The 3D architecture, which separates detector thickness from electrode spacing, further enhances both timing performance and radiation hardness. We created a simulation tool called RASER (RAdiation SEmiconductoR) to model the time resolution of planar and 3D 4H-SiC detectors across various parameters and structures; the software's reliability was confirmed by comparing simulated results with experimental data. Based on these simulations, an approximate time resolution for the 3D 4H-SiC detector was estimated, and the derived parameters can serve as a guide for designing and optimizing future 3D 4H-SiC detectors.

We examine how diquark fluctuations, which organize into robust collective modes near the critical temperature of color superconductivity, alter the dilepton production rate. By analyzing the photon self-energy via the Aslamasov-Larkin, Maki-Thompson, and density of states terms from metallic superconductivity theory, we demonstrate that these diquark channel collective modes significantly impact the photon self-energy. Consequently, this interaction leads to an anomalous enhancement of the dilepton production rate within the low invariant-mass region.

Ground truth labels are frequently unavailable across many domains. Although crowdsourced labeling has been investigated, current models often struggle with sparse, unreliable, or conflicting annotations. Co-teaching has demonstrated significant improvements for computer vision tasks involving noisy labels by utilizing two classifiers that train on each other's high-confidence samples within each batch. Drawing inspiration from the separation of confident and uncertain data during training, we adapt this concept for crowdsourcing scenarios. Our proposed model, CrowdTeacher, leverages input space perturbation to enhance classifier robustness against noisy labels. We treat crowdsourced annotations as a noisy source and perturb samples according to the certainty derived from aggregated labels. These perturbed inputs are then processed by a Co-teaching algorithm adapted for smaller tabular datasets. We demonstrate the increased predictive performance of CrowdTeacher on both synthetic and real datasets under various label density conditions. Experimental results indicate that our approach outperforms baselines that model individual annotations separately before combining them, methods that simultaneously learn classifiers and infer true labels, and the standard Co-teaching algorithm using aggregated labels via common truth inference techniques.

The proliferation of the Internet of Things underscores the necessity of robust strategies for processing big data to uncover meaningful insights. Time series data generated by interconnected devices often reveals valuable underlying patterns, which recent research has leveraged from spatio-temporal datasets to facilitate tasks such as road network generation and activity recognition. In these applications, the speed and precision of geometry reconstruction are critical. While existing approaches like kernel density estimation (KDE) are commonly employed, they frequently incur high computational costs. We propose enhancing edge quadtrees by exploiting their inherent hierarchical structure. Our modification employs a novel trajectory count function for density estimation, which ensures the stability of counts through invariance to local perturbations. We evaluate the method's efficacy in extracting underlying geometry and representative subsample points. To verify performance, we compare our approach against a KDE variant for recovering the shape of noisy synthetic trajectories and against current methods for map extraction from GPS traces. Our results demonstrate significantly improved runtime while achieving superior or comparable geometry extraction. Furthermore, comparisons with maxmin subsampling on an activity recognition dataset reveal substantial runtime gains with equivalent performance.

Automated decision systems are increasingly employed for high-stakes choices for various reasons. These systems frequently depend on complex yet opaque models that make it difficult or impossible to comprehend the reasoning behind specific decisions. This lack of transparency poses significant legal challenges and increases the risk of undesirable, such as unfair, outcomes, as the validity of such systems is hard to evaluate and adjust. This research evaluates various explanation methods for these systems to determine their impact on human perceptions of fairness and trust regarding the underlying mechanisms. An initial pilot study uncovered surprising qualitative findings and preliminary significant effects that require verification, expansion, and detailed discussion within the comprehensive main study.

Orbital angular momentum (OAM) of light is considered a significant asset in quantum technology, particularly for applications in communication and sensing. However, the stability of OAM states is compromised by adverse experimental factors, such as varying propagation distances and phase distortions, which currently limits the practical deployment of these technologies. This paper demonstrates the use of an advanced deep learning neural network to classify distinct OAM modes across multiple distances despite phase distortions. Specifically, our trained model accurately determines both the vortex beam's topological charge and its propagation distance with 97% precision. This approach holds substantial promise for enhancing OAM-based communication and sensing protocols.

This study introduces a predictor-corrector numerical scheme designed to solve nonlinear fractional initial value problems using the Atangana-Baleanu derivative in the Caputo sense (ABC). The method approximates the nonlinearity within the resulting Volterra integral—derived by converting the fractional differential equation via ABC properties—using Lagrangian quadratic polynomials. This approach yields a high-accuracy, implicit corrector formula paired with an explicit predictor formula of identical precision order. Notably, the memory term is calculated only once for both phases, ensuring computational efficiency. The paper also establishes an error bound for the scheme and presents numerical experiments on two differential equations to validate its accuracy. Additionally, a case study applies the proposed method to an ABC-fractional generalized susceptible-infectious (SI) epidemic model, demonstrating its effectiveness in analyzing system dynamics and solving real-world problems.

Space debris density poses a growing environmental threat, which can be mitigated through three strategies: collision avoidance, debris removal, and debris mitigation. This study focuses on collision avoidance by presenting a method designed to significantly enhance orbit prediction accuracy. We apply batch least-squares differential correction to the public Two-Line Element (TLE) catalog, utilizing a high-precision numerical propagator to fit orbits based on successive TLE-derived state vectors. These fitted orbits are then propagated forward in time and compared against precision ephemeris data from the International Laser Ranging Service (ILRS) for various satellites, particularly those in the congested sun-synchronous orbital region. The results demonstrate that the method achieves a range error growth rate of approximately 100 meters per day, representing a tenfold improvement over TLEs propagated using the standard SGP4 analytic propagator. Such enhancements for debris trajectories could yield initial conjunction analysis precise enough for operationally viable collision avoidance systems. Additionally, we examine computational requirements and optimization strategies for applying all-on-all conjunction analysis to the entire current and future TLE catalog. Finally, we propose a framework for debris-debris collision avoidance that may become feasible as these advancements mature.

Building upon our recent establishment of $l^2$ bijectivity for defocusing Ablowitz-Ladik systems within the discrete Sobolev space $l^{2,1}$ via the inverse spectral method, this paper aims to analyze the long-time asymptotic behavior of the initial-value problem for these systems under initial potentials of lower regularity. Our approach involves executing specific deformations and analyses of the corresponding Riemann-Hilbert problem, utilizing the unit circle as the jump contour $\Sigma$. Consequently, we demonstrate that when $|\frac{n}{2t}|\le 1<1$, the solution follows a Zakharov-Manakov type formula, whereas when $|\frac{n}{2t}|\ge 1>1$, the solution decays rapidly toward zero.

In crowded electromagnetic settings, cognitive radios must identify other emitters to refine their dynamic spectrum access strategies. While deep learning classifiers offer high accuracy in recognizing wireless signal standards, they are constrained to categorizing only those classes present in their training data. This limitation hampers field deployment, as these models fail to accurately identify signals from unknown classes. This paper introduces a convolutional neural network-based open-set classifier capable of flagging signals that do not belong to known classes by applying a threshold to the sigmoid activation output. The model was trained on 4G LTE, 5G NR, IEEE 802.11ax, Bluetooth Low Energy 5.0, and Narrowband IoT signals degraded by Rayleigh or Rician fading, AWGN, frequency offsets, and IQ imbalances. Subsequently, it was evaluated on OFDM, SC-FDMA, SC, AM, and FM signals absent from the training set. The closed-set classifier attained 94.5% average accuracy for known signals at SNRs above 0 dB but, by design, achieved 0% accuracy for unknown classes. Conversely, the open-set classifier maintained 86% accuracy for known signal classes while successfully detecting 95.5% of unknown signal classes at SNRs exceeding 0 dB.

Recent advancements in hyperspectral image (HSI) classification have increasingly relied on deep network models, with graph convolutional network (GCN) architectures demonstrating notable performance. Nevertheless, these deep learning frameworks, which depend on point estimation, struggle with limited generalization and an inability to measure classification uncertainty. Conversely, applying Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) based on distribution estimation to HSI classification often fails to deliver high accuracy due to the excessive number of parameters. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a Bayesian layer utilizing Bayesian principles as an insertion module within point estimation-based neural networks, resulting in a Bayesian Layer Graph Convolutional Network (BLGCN). By integrating graph convolution operations, this model effectively extracts graph information and estimates classification uncertainty. Additionally, a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) is employed to mitigate sample imbalance in HSI datasets. Furthermore, a dynamic control training strategy is designed based on classification confidence intervals, allowing for early termination once the interval reaches a predefined threshold. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that the proposed model successfully balances high classification accuracy with robust generalization while quantifying classification uncertainty.

Calculating shortest path distances is fundamental to numerous graph algorithms and applications. However, conventional exact approaches like breadth-first-search (BFS) fail to scale effectively on today's massive, rapidly growing networks, necessitating approximation techniques to achieve scalable graph processing with substantial performance gains. This paper leverages vector embeddings derived from deep learning to estimate shortest path distances in large-scale graphs. We demonstrate that a feedforward neural network utilizing these embeddings can approximate distances with relatively low distortion error. The proposed approach is assessed across the Facebook, BlogCatalog, YouTube, and Flickr social networks.

Over the past few years, telecommunication (Telco) technologies have rapidly evolved from 2G to the forthcoming 5G era. Precise outdoor localization is crucial for Telco operators to effectively manage, operate, and optimize their networks. Distinct from GPS, Telco localization enables operators to determine the positions of outdoor mobile devices by utilizing measurement report (MR) data. However, when MR samples include noisy signals—often due to interference or signal attenuation—Telco localization frequently results in significant errors. Consequently, this paper focuses on enhancing Telco localization accuracy by employing algorithms to identify and correct outlier positions with high error rates. Specifically, we introduce RLoc, a context-aware Telco localization method comprising three core components: a machine-learning-based localization algorithm, a detection mechanism to identify flawed samples, and a repair algorithm to substitute outlier results with superior estimates (ideally ground truth positions). Unlike prior works that detect and repair each flawed MR sample independently, our approach leverages the spatio-temporal locality of MR locations and utilizes trajectory context to detect and rectify erroneous positions. Experimental validation using real MR datasets from 2G GSM and 4G LTE networks demonstrates that RLoc significantly improves Telco location accuracy. For instance, when applied to a large 4G MR dataset, RLoc achieves a median error of 32.2 meters, representing an improvement of approximately 17.4% over state-of-the-art methods.

Direct flow simulation offers the most precise permeability estimates for complex porous materials but is computationally prohibitive, especially as domains become more heterogeneous or constricted. While semi-analytical models utilizing averaged properties like porosity and tortuosity exist, their reliance on summary statistics limits their applicability. Conversely, data-driven machine learning methods hold significant potential by capturing the spatial arrangement of solid boundaries; however, existing Convolutional Neural Network (ConvNet) approaches, adapted from 2D image recognition, fail to scale to the large 3D domains necessary for Representative Elementary Volume (REV) analysis. Consequently, previous studies largely restricted themselves to homogeneous samples where small REV sizes allowed the neglect of global fluid flow dynamics, thereby bypassing the memory constraints of 3D ConvNets. This limitation prevented the effective modeling of critical geometries such as fractures and vuggy domains. This study overcomes these barriers with a general multiscale deep learning framework trained on porous media simulation data. By employing a coupled neural network architecture that analyzes the domain across multiple scales, the model can process large images in approximately one second on a single GPU. This architecture enables the modeling of domain sizes that remain infeasible for traditional direct simulation tools on standard desktop hardware.

Cluster analysis, which emphasizes the grouping and classification of similar items, is extensively utilized across many research domains. Recently, a new and efficient clustering technique known as the fission clustering algorithm has been introduced. This article presents a robust fission clustering (RFC) algorithm alongside a self-adaptive noise identification method. By integrating RFC with the noise identification technique, we developed the self-adaptive robust fission clustering (SARFC) algorithm. The performance of this proposed approach was evaluated using several common datasets and compared against other existing algorithms. Comprehensive results demonstrate that the proposed method offers significant advantages over other standard techniques.

We demonstrate a quantitative form of the strong almost reducibility result for $\mathrm{sl}(2,\mathbb{R})$ quasi-periodic cocycles that are close to a constant within the Gevrey class. Specifically, for quasi-periodic Schrödinger operators featuring small Gevrey potentials, we show that the lengths of spectral gaps decrease sub-exponentially relative to their indices. Furthermore, the long-range duality operator exhibits a pure point spectrum with eigenfunctions that decay sub-exponentially for almost all phases, and the spectrum forms an interval for discrete Schrödinger operators on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ with small separable potentials. These findings rely on an enhanced KAM scheme and are consequently perturbative in nature.

Data hiding serves as a prevalent method for safeguarding authentication and ownership, yet most multimedia files, such as images and videos, are stored or transmitted in compressed formats. Lossy compression techniques like JPEG can corrupt embedded data, necessitating robust data hiding solutions. Achieving data hiding resilience against such compression remains an unresolved challenge. Although deep learning has recently achieved significant success in this domain, the non-differentiability of JPEG algorithms complicates the training of deep pipelines designed to enhance robustness against lossy compression. Current state-of-the-art methods circumvent this issue by substituting non-differentiable components with differentiable modules that mimic similar operations; however, these approaches suffer from several drawbacks: (a) substantial engineering overhead, (b) the need for white-box knowledge of compression attacks, and (c) limited applicability to simple compression schemes like JPEG. This paper introduces a straightforward yet effective solution that simultaneously addresses all these limitations. Furthermore, the proposed method extends beyond JPEG, demonstrating improved robustness against a variety of image and video lossy compression algorithms.

This work examines history-deterministic one-counter nets (OCNs). History-determinism permits a specific form of non-determinism that can be resolved dynamically during execution. While token games have characterized this property across various models, they also do so for OCNs. By reducing 1-token games to simulation games, we demonstrate that verifying history-determinism in OCNs is decidable. Specifically, this problem is PSPACE-complete under unary transition encoding and EXPSPACE-complete under binary encoding.

Furthermore, we analyze the language properties of history-deterministic OCNs. We establish that the mechanisms resolving non-determinism in these systems are eventually periodic. Consequently, for any given history-deterministic OCN, we construct an equivalent deterministic one-counter automaton. Additionally, we prove that comparing languages of history-deterministic OCNs—including tasks like language inclusion and universality—is decidable.

We build and examine a phase diagram for a self-interacting matrix field coupled to the curvature of a non-commutative truncated Heisenberg space. This model converges to the renormalizable Grosse-Wulkenhaar model as the matrix size approaches infinity and displays a phase characterized by purely non-commutative, non-uniform ordering. Special emphasis is placed on the scaling behavior of the model's parameters, and we also derive the infinite matrix size limit for the boundary between the disordered and ordered phases.

Deep learning models are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where negligible, imperceptible input modifications cause incorrect predictions. Although most existing detection methods target image processing systems—often analyzing embedding feature spaces—current state-of-the-art approaches in Natural Language Processing (NLP) rely exclusively on input text features, ignoring model embeddings. This study investigates the efficacy of transferring image-based detection strategies to NLP, finding that they perform poorly. This failure is anticipated due to fundamental input differences: NLP deals with discrete, sequential data, unlike the continuous, fixed-size inputs of images. Consequently, this work introduces a novel, model-centric NLP detector based on sentence-embedding "residue." Across various tasks, this approach surpasses both adapted image-domain detectors and recent NLP-specific state-of-the-art methods.

Ultracold CH radicals offer a promising platform for investigating quantum-state-controlled organic chemistry. In this study, we computed vibrational and rotational branching ratios, incorporating ground-state mixing, to guide optical cycling strategies and evaluate two potential radiative cooling methods based on the $X^{2}\Pi \leftarrow A^{2}\Delta$ and $X^{2}\Pi \leftarrow B^{2}\Sigma^{-}$ transitions. As an initial step toward laser cooling CH, we characterized effective buffer gas cooling, generating approximately $5\times10^{10}$ CH molecules per pulse with a rotational temperature of 2(1) K and a translational temperature of 7(2) K. Additionally, we measured the CH-helium collisional cross section as $2.4(8)\times10^{-14}$ cm$^{2}$, a critical parameter for accurately determining in-cell CH density and accounting for collisional broadening. These ultracold CH molecules represent an optimal foundation for upcoming laser cooling, trapping, and cold organic chemistry experiments.

This paper proposes a sound field estimation approach utilizing a physics-informed convolutional neural network (PICNN) enhanced with spline interpolation. While conventional methods typically employ wavefunction expansion to ensure estimated functions adhere to the Helmholtz equation, their reliance solely on physical principles leads to substantial accuracy degradation when measurement data is scarce. Conversely, recent neural network-based techniques excel at handling sparse measurements provided sufficient training data, yet they often neglect physical constraints, resulting in physically invalid solutions. To address this, we introduce a PICNN framework for sound field estimation where the loss function penalizes deviations from the Helmholtz equation. Because standard CNN outputs represent spatially discretized pressure distributions, directly computing the Helmholtz-equation loss is challenging; thus, bicubic spline interpolation is integrated into the PICNN architecture. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that the proposed method successfully achieves both accurate and physically feasible sound field estimations even from sparse measurements.

Creating images from semantic visual knowledge is a difficult but valuable endeavor, offering a means to guide synthesis more precisely than class labels or text descriptions by employing complex, subtle, and unambiguous conditions. While existing generative methods utilize semantic representations, they lack mechanisms to control the generation process beyond defining constraints between objects. For instance, the ability to iteratively generate or modify images by manually inserting specific items is a desirable feature that, to our knowledge, has not been thoroughly explored. This work introduces a transformer-based approach conditioned on scene graphs; unlike recent transformer methods, it incorporates a decoder to autoregressively compose images, thereby enhancing both effectiveness and controllability. The proposed architecture consists of three components: 1) a graph convolutional network to encode input graph relationships; 2) an encoder-decoder transformer responsible for the autoregressive composition of the output image; and 3) an auto-encoder that produces representations serving as inputs and outputs for each generation step within the transformer. Experiments on CIFAR10 and MNIST demonstrate that the model can adhere to semantic constraints defined by scene graphs and model relationships between visual objects by incorporating a user-provided partial rendering of the desired target.

This paper reports on the performance of a prototype Time Projection Chamber (TPC) designed for the International Large Detector concept at the planned International Linear Collider, which utilizes micro-pattern gas detector readout. The prototype, equipped with three independent GEM-based readout modules, operated within a 1 T solenoidal magnetic field and was exposed to a 6 GeV electron beam at the DESY II synchrotron. The study presents findings on hit reconstruction efficiency, drift velocity measurement, space point resolution, and the management of field inhomogeneities.

Complementarity serves as a fundamental principle of quantum mechanics, where preparing an eigenstate for one observable necessitates total randomness in its complementary counterpart. While this principle enables security analyses in quantum cryptography through phase-error correction, its application becomes significantly more nuanced in the device-independent regime, which guarantees security without characterizing the devices. Consequently, security proofs for device-independent protocols are often intricate and distinct from their standard device-dependent equivalents, presenting substantial experimental hurdles, particularly regarding the massive data volumes required. This work elucidates the complementarity-based security origins of device-independent tasks by connecting complementarity with quantum nonlocality, thereby reformulating these schemes as quantum error correction protocols. Extending beyond the identical-and-independent-distribution assumption, we address the most general attacks and generalize sample entropy from classical Shannon theory to facilitate finite-size analysis. Our approach demonstrates robust finite-size performance, shifting device-independent schemes toward practical feasibility. When applied to data from a recent ion-trap-based device-independent quantum key distribution experiment, this method reduces the necessary data size to under one-third of the original requirement. Additionally, the complementarity framework naturally extends to advantage key distillation, thereby simplifying experiments by accommodating higher loss rates and lower transmittance.

6G communication technology represents a revolutionary advancement poised to transform numerous technologies and applications. As a truly AI-driven system operating within an intelligent space, it will facilitate the Internet of Everything (IoE), thereby impacting a wide array of fields. By promising superior Quality of Service (QoS) and Quality of Experience (QoE), the synergy between IoE and 6G will trigger an explosion of applications in the near future, encompassing vehicles, drones, homes, cities, hospitals, and virtually every other sector. Consequently, many existing technologies are expected to become fully dependent on 6G to significantly enhance their performance. As a game-changing force across various domains, 6G will have the capacity to influence countless applications, leading us to envision its extensive potential in the coming years.

This paper reports on both experimental and numerical investigations into the distributions of the reflection coefficient P(R), as well as the imaginary P(v) and real P(u) components of the Wigner reaction K matrix, within irregular, fully connected hexagonal networks under conditions of strong absorption. Experimentally, microwave networks constructed from coaxial cables, joints, and attenuators were employed. Numerically, these physical systems were modeled using quantum fully connected hexagon graphs, where the absorption effects of the attenuators were represented by optical potentials. Both the reflection coefficient and the K matrix distributions were derived from the scattering matrix S, calculated through measurements of the physical networks and computations of the theoretical graphs, respectively. The findings demonstrate a strong concordance between the experimental and numerical results and the exact analytic predictions provided by random matrix theory (RMT).

This study outlines and examines our perspective on advancing and reasoning about innovative and established strategies for curating data-centric geoscience knowledge, encompassing data, experiments, models, methods, conclusions, and interpretations. Such knowledge is generated by applying statistical modeling, machine learning, and contemporary data analytics techniques to geo-data repositories. Furthermore, the work tackles open methodological challenges related to model construction, evaluation, prediction, and forecasting workflows.

Tables are extensively utilized in documents due to their ability to present information in a compact and organized manner. Specifically, within scientific literature, tables consolidate novel findings and experimental outcomes, thereby facilitating research comparison and enhancing comprehensibility for scholars. Given the significant variability in table layouts, it is beneficial to interpret their content and categorize them accordingly. This capability aids in directly extracting information from papers, such as comparing model performances based on their result tables. This study addresses table classification using a Graph Neural Network (GNN), leveraging the table's structural data for the message-passing algorithm. Our model was evaluated on a subset of the Tab2Know dataset; however, due to the limited number of manually annotated examples, we introduced data augmentation techniques applied directly to table graph structures. We obtained promising preliminary results, demonstrating that our proposed data augmentation method is well-suited for graph-based table representations.

Over the last ten years, synthetic biology has advanced significantly in creating modular methods for assembling genetic sequences and engineering diverse biological systems with varied functions across different organisms. Nevertheless, existing approaches in the field tightly couple sequence and function, which hinders abstraction, limits engineering flexibility, and compromises predictability and design reuse. Functional Synthetic Biology seeks to resolve these challenges by prioritizing function over sequence in system design. This shift separates the development of biological devices from their specific applications, necessitating both conceptual and organizational transformations alongside new software tools. Achieving this vision of Functional Synthetic Biology promises greater flexibility in device utilization, enhanced opportunities for reusing devices and data, improved predictability, and reduced technical risks and costs.

Value function approximation is essential for policy evaluation in reinforcement learning, particularly within large or continuous state spaces. This paper introduces a generative approach to policy evaluation using temporal-difference (TD) learning, assuming a Gaussian process (GP) prior for the target value function and modeling instantaneous rewards as probabilistic outputs derived from evaluations at consecutive states. Leveraging a random feature-based approximation of the GP prior, we develop an online scalable method called OS-GPTD to estimate the value function from observed state-reward sequences. To assess OS-GPTD's robustness, including in adversarial scenarios where modeling assumptions fail, we conduct complementary worst-case analyses by upper-bounding the cumulative Bellman error and long-term reward prediction error relative to a fixed-value-function estimator using the full trajectory. Additionally, to overcome the limited expressiveness of a single fixed kernel, we employ a weighted ensemble of GP priors, creating the OS-EGPTD scheme, which jointly infers the value function and interactively selects the optimal GP kernel during execution. Finally, the proposed OS-(E)GPTD methods are evaluated on two benchmark problems.

This 1954 French translation of N. Cuesta's Spanish paper primarily examines partially and totally ordered sets. It focuses on two key topics: constructing new ordered sets from existing families and completing ordered sets using methods similar to Dedekind cuts. Remarkably, the concept of surreal numbers—formally defined by Conway in 1974—appears in this work three decades prior.

This study examines the viability of a high-statistics experiment designed to detect invisible decay modes within nuclear gamma cascades, utilizing 200 kg of Cs(Tl) scintillators currently housed at Texas A&M. The primary objective is to identify missing energy by definitively confirming the absence of a photon in a well-characterized gamma cascade. We present experimental validation of the energy resolution required for such a search. While previous investigations of this detector concept targeted baryonically coupled physics in $E_2$ transitions, we demonstrate that the same methodology can probe particles coupled to photons by observing the conversion of a cascade photon into a hidden particle. Specific processes include photon oscillation into a hidden photon or conversion into an axion-like particle via a magnetic field or the Primakoff effect. This proof-of-concept setup also holds potential for detecting previously unconstrained baryonically coupled scalars and pseudoscalars arising from $E_0$ and $M_0$ transitions. If realized, this experiment would serve as a precursor to a larger, more contained detector capable of rigorously exploring new particles with masses below 4 MeV within the poorly constrained supernova "trapping window" ranging from 100 keV to 30 MeV.

This paper examines the physics case for flavour-violating axions. Specifically, I contend that abandoning the assumption of Peccei-Quinn current universality creates novel avenues, such as weakening the supernova constraint on axion mass, establishing a potential link to the Standard Model flavour problem, and enabling the discovery of axions through dedicated flavoured axion searches.

Over the past ten years, wildfires have grown larger and more destructive, with climate change and urban expansion potentially increasing the likelihood of such large-scale events. While preventive measures can mitigate fire risk, constructing firefighting lines to halt fire spread is expensive to install and maintain, necessitating careful strategic planning. This study approaches wildfire management theoretically by defining a risk function to model fire diffusion. The landscape is represented as a mixed graph where vertices denote areas with a specific probability of ignition, and edges represent the likelihood of fire transmission between them. To minimize risk within budgetary limits, we propose the {\sc Windy Firebreak Location} problem, which determines the optimal placement of these lines. We analyze the computational complexity of this problem, demonstrating its hardness even in planar, bipartite graphs with a maximum degree of four and uniform propagation probabilities. Furthermore, we present an efficient polynomial-time algorithm for solving specific instances involving tree structures.

Overfitting poses a significant challenge for Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) by hindering their ability to generalize to unseen data. To address this, researchers have developed various data augmentation (DA) techniques to enrich or create additional training data, thereby enhancing its quality. This study introduces a novel DA algorithm called VoronoiPatches (VP). Unlike conventional methods, VP employs non-linear recombination by fragmenting and occluding small image patches, utilizing randomly arranged small convex polygons to redistribute information within an image. These transitions between patches and the original image can optionally be smoothed. Experimental results indicate that VP surpasses existing DA methods in reducing model variance and overfitting. The findings demonstrate that augmenting data through non-linear information recombination and the use of non-orthogonal shapes and structures enhances the robustness of CNN models when faced with unseen data.

We introduce GAAF, a Generalised Automatic Anatomy Finder designed to identify generic anatomical locations within 3D CT scans. This end-to-end pipeline consists of specialized modules for data pre-processing, model training, and inference. Central to GAAF is a custom localisation convolutional neural network (CNN) that is compact, lightweight, and adaptable to specific applications. The framework has been evaluated on an open-access dataset, demonstrating accurate and robust performance in localising anatomical features, such as the brainstem's centre-of-mass, particularly in the head and neck region. All source code is freely available at https://github.com/rrr-uom-projects/GAAF.

Network topology significantly influences traffic dynamics, with most real-world systems exhibiting heterogeneous, scale-free characteristics. In such networks, new nodes preferentially attach to hubs, while smaller-degree nodes constrain overall capacity. To enhance transport efficiency, we propose rewiring a portion of the network's links. This paper outlines effective rewiring strategies and validates them through simulations on scale-free networks. Our results demonstrate that these strategies successfully lower the betweenness centrality of high-centrality nodes without altering the network's degree distribution. Ultimately, this approach offers a valuable method for improving overall network performance.

By leveraging gauge/string duality, we investigate specific facets of string breaking within a three-quark system. Our findings indicate that the distance at which strings break is not universal but varies according to the geometric arrangement of the quarks. We estimate that the ratio of this breaking distance in the three-quark system compared to the quark-antiquark system falls roughly between $\frac{2}{3}$ and $1$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that certain geometric configurations permit the existence of multiple distinct breaking distances.

This study investigates the production of heavy Majorana neutrinos via the $B^- \to \pi^+\mu^-\mu^-$ decay channel, utilizing 3 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity gathered by the LHCb detector from proton-proton collisions at the LHC with center-of-mass energies of 7 TeV and 8 TeV. The analysis probes neutrino masses between 250 and 5000 MeV and lifetimes ranging from 0 to 1000 ps. Given the lack of an observed signal, upper bounds are established for the branching fraction ${\cal{B}}(B^- \to \pi^+\mu^-\mu^-$) as a function of both neutrino mass and lifetime; for neutrino lifetimes of 1 ps or less, these limits reach approximately $10^{-9}$. Additionally, constraints are placed on the coupling between the muon and a hypothetical fourth-generation neutrino.

Natural images adhere to statistical patterns derived from the physical structure of our visual environment. A key characteristic of this structure is that images can be characterized by a relatively small number of features. To examine how this sparseness influences the efficiency of neural coding, we developed a new set of random textured stimuli with adjustable sparseness levels, modeled after natural image data. We then assessed the effect of this sparseness parameter on the firing patterns of a population of retinal ganglion cells recorded ex vivo from the rodent *Octodon degus*. Our recordings revealed that the reliability of spike timing fluctuates with sparseness, following a global trend similar to the sparseness distribution found in natural images. These findings suggest that the spike patterns of ganglion cells may adapt to this specific aspect of natural image statistics.

Blazars represent a category of active galactic nuclei characterized by relativistic jets aligned nearly parallel to the observer's line of sight. These objects display highly complex variability, with flares—defined as flux deviations from the mean exhibiting specific shapes and durations—serving as a key diagnostic feature. While blazars are recognized for multi-wavelength flares, they also produce "orphan" flares, which manifest exclusively within a particular energy band. Existing models attempting to explain specific flares, even for individual sources, often conflict with one another and lack a unified framework. This study introduces a cohesive model to account for both orphan and multi-wavelength flares within a single paradigm. The proposed framework posits that blazar emission during a flare comprises two distinct elements: (i) a quasi-stable background component resulting from the superposition of numerous, relatively weak dissipation zones along the jet, and (ii) a transient component driven by a strong energy dissipation event at a random location, responsible for the sudden flux increase. The nature of the emitted flare depends on the dissipation site's distance from the jet base: dissipation close to or far from the supermassive black hole typically favors inverse Compton or synchrotron dominance, respectively, leading to orphan gamma-ray or optical flares. Conversely, dissipation at intermediate distances is expected to produce multi-wavelength flares. The model's efficacy is demonstrated through its successful description of the spectral energy distributions of various flares from the flat spectrum radio quasar 3C 279 and the BL Lac object PKS 2155-304.

This study demonstrates that the traditional image description metric CIDEr-D performs inadequately on datasets featuring significantly longer sentences than those in the MS COCO Captions benchmark. Furthermore, we identify that CIDEr-D suffers from performance degradation due to insufficient multiple reference sentences and high variance in sentence lengths. To address these limitations, we propose CIDEr-R, an enhanced version of CIDEr-D that offers greater flexibility when handling datasets with substantial sentence length variability. Our findings indicate that CIDEr-R yields higher accuracy and aligns more closely with human judgment compared to CIDEr-D, while also demonstrating improved robustness regarding the number of available references. Additionally, our results show that optimizing CIDEr-R via Self-Critical Sequence Training produces descriptive captions; conversely, optimizing CIDEr-D results in generated captions that match the reference length but rely on repetitive word usage to artificially extend sentence length.

We demonstrate that quantum interference influences proximity-induced Rashba spin-orbit coupling in twisted van der Waals stacks of hexagonal layers. Specifically, we compute the quantum phase driving this phenomenon in graphene-transition metal dichalcogenide bilayers as a function of the interlayer twist angle. Our analysis reveals how this phase modulates the spin polarization of graphene bands and explores its implications for spin-to-charge conversion experiments. Furthermore, in twisted trilayers, specific twist angles can either restore or break symmetries, allowing for the deduction of induced spin-orbit coupling effects on spin-lifetime anisotropy and magnetoconductance.

Teleportation of a quantum state has emerged as a focal point within quantum communication, attracting substantial research interest and prompting the development of numerous schemes. This study compares the teleportation of a single qubit across various entangled channels, including the two-qubit Bell state, three-qubit GHZ state, two- and three-qubit cluster states, and the highly entangled five-qubit state proposed by Brown et al., as well as the six-qubit state by Borras et al. We evaluate and contrast the quantum costs associated with each configuration. Additionally, we analyze the impact of six distinct noise models—bit-flip, phase-flip, bit-phase flip, amplitude damping, phase damping, and depolarizing errors—on the communication channels. The investigation examines how the fidelity of the teleported state varies relative to the initial state under these noisy conditions, with results visualized through graphs depicting fidelity changes across different noise parameters ($\eta$). Findings indicate that for $\eta \in [0, 0.5]$, fidelity declines across all channels and noise types. Subsequently, fidelity exhibits an upward trend in the Bell, GHZ, and three-qubit cluster state channels under all noise models. In contrast, the remaining three channels experience significant fidelity drops under amplitude damping, phase damping, and depolarizing noise, reaching zero at $\eta = 1$ specifically for the Brown et al. and Borras et al. channels.

Although numerous methods for anomaly detection in multivariate time series exist, few address federated environments where data is heterogeneously distributed across edge devices and sharing is restricted. This paper explores federated unsupervised anomaly detection and introduces the Federated Exemplar-based Deep Neural Network (Fed-ExDNN). First, we design an Exemplar-based Deep Neural Network (ExDNN) to learn local time series representations by evaluating their compatibility with a local exemplar module containing hidden parameters that capture diverse normal patterns specific to each device. Next, a constrained clustering mechanism (FedCC) operates on a centralized server to align and aggregate parameters from local exemplar modules, creating a unified global exemplar module. Finally, this global module is deployed alongside a shared feature encoder on each edge device, where anomaly detection is performed by assessing the compatibility of test data against the exemplar module. By capturing local normal patterns via ExDNN and aggregating them through FedCC, Fed-ExDNN effectively handles heterogeneous data across multiple edge devices. Extensive experiments on six public datasets demonstrate that both ExDNN and Fed-ExDNN surpass existing state-of-the-art anomaly detection algorithms and federated learning techniques.

Current reading comprehension models rely on recurrent neural networks to process document tokens sequentially. However, as the demand grows for answering complex questions over lengthy documents, this sequential approach becomes a significant bottleneck. Drawing inspiration from how humans utilize document structure, we introduce a new reading comprehension framework. In this approach, documents are represented as trees, and an agent is trained to alternate between rapid navigation of the tree and costly answer extraction. To promote thorough exploration of the document tree, we developed a novel algorithm based on Deep Q-Networks (DQN) that strategically samples tree nodes during training. Our empirical results demonstrate that this algorithm outperforms both standard DQN and a robust information-retrieval (IR) baseline in question answering tasks. Furthermore, combining our model with the IR baseline through ensembling yields additional performance improvements.

Autonomous mapping and exploration of unknown environments using single or multiple robots is a critical area of mobile robotics that has seen extensive research. However, the absence of standardized platforms, metrics, and datasets for evaluating these approaches led to the creation of Explore-Bench, an autonomous robot exploration benchmark. This benchmark features diverse exploration scenarios and introduces two quantitative metrics to assess exploration efficiency and multi-robot collaboration. Explore-Bench is particularly valuable given the recent surge in using deep reinforcement learning (DRL) for exploration tasks, which have yielded promising results. Yet, training DRL models demands large datasets, and existing benchmarks often rely on realistic simulators with slow speeds, making them unsuitable for efficient strategy training. To address this and support both efficient DRL training and comprehensive evaluation, Explore-Bench introduces a three-level platform with a unified data flow and a $12 \times$ speed-up. This platform comprises a grid-based simulator for rapid evaluation and training, a realistic Gazebo simulator, and a remotely accessible robot testbed for high-accuracy physical testing. The benchmark's practicality is demonstrated through the application of one DRL-based and three frontier-based exploration methods, alongside an analysis of performance differences to offer insights into method selection and design. The benchmark is accessible at https://github.com/efc-robot/Explore-Bench.

This study examines how neutrino cooling mechanisms within the core of neutron stars (NSs) influence the light curves of type-I X-ray bursts and X-ray superbursts. Observations of NS thermal evolution suggest the presence of rapid cooling processes, such as the direct Urca (DU) mechanism, which notably lower surface temperatures, although this effect may be mitigated by nucleon superfluidity.
