Through a microscopic analysis of the exotic superconductor UTe$_2$, along with an examination of temperature dependencies and renormalization effects, we demonstrate that the nonreciprocal Meissner effect serves as a valuable tool for investigating parity-mixing characteristics and gap structures in superconductors.

Let $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathbb{N}$ denote the sets of all prime numbers and natural numbers, respectively. This article establishes that there exists a subset of natural numbers with a positive lower density, where each element can be expressed in the form $p+2^{m_1^2}+2^{m_2^2}$ for some $p \in \mathcal{P}$ and $m_1, m_2 \in \mathbb{N}$. This result resolves a problem posed by Chen and Yang in 2014.

Although pretrained language models have achieved notable success, there remains a scarcity of freely accessible, high-quality, general-purpose question-answering (QA) systems. To address this gap, we introduce Macaw, a flexible generative QA system released for community use. Built upon UnifiedQA and T5, Macaw demonstrates robust zero-shot performance across diverse topics, surpassing GPT-3 by more than 10% (absolute) on the Challenge300 benchmark of 300 difficult questions, despite having approximately 11 billion parameters compared to GPT-3's 175 billion. Furthermore, Macaw supports various input-output configurations, such as generating answers from questions, formulating questions from answers, or creating multiple-choice options from both. We detail the system and showcase its ability to deliver surprisingly effective responses on question types outside its training distribution, while also highlighting specific question categories where it struggles to provide insights into the current limitations of pretrained models. Macaw is freely available at https://github.com/allenai/macaw, with hopes that it will be valuable to the community.

Certain one-dimensional quasiperiodic lattices are known to support waves that undergo a sharp localization transition. We theoretically predict and experimentally confirm that, in one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, an initial localization of light can be followed by a second delocalization transition for specific states as the quasiperiodic modulation strength increases, illustrating a reentrant transition. Additionally, we propose that this phenomenon can be qualitatively described by a dimerized tight-binding model incorporating long-range couplings.

A recent study on Unidentified Aerial Phenomena (UAP) in Ukraine (arXiv:2208.11215) describes dark, phantom objects ranging from 3 to 12 meters in size, traveling at speeds up to 15 km/s within a distance of 10-12 km without producing optical emissions. However, I demonstrate that the air friction acting on such objects would have created a luminous fireball. Instead, reducing the inferred distance by a factor of ten aligns perfectly with the characteristics of artillery shells regarding their size and velocity.

Tumor volume and evolving characteristics serve as critical biomarkers for cancer treatment. Consequently, FDG-PET/CT scans are standardly employed for cancer staging and re-staging, leveraging the uptake of radiolabeled fluorodeoxyglucose in high-metabolism areas. However, these metabolically active regions lack specificity, as they may also indicate physiological activity in healthy organs, or inflammation and infection, rendering precise and reliable tumor segmentation a challenging endeavor. The AutoPET challenge addresses this research gap by offering a public dataset of FDG-PET/CT scans from 900 patients to foster advancements in the field. Our contribution to this challenge involves an ensemble of two leading segmentation architectures, nn-Unet and Swin UNETR, enhanced by a maximum intensity projection classifier that functions as a gating mechanism. When this classifier identifies lesions, the resulting segmentations are merged using a late fusion strategy. In our cross-validation involving patients with lung cancer, melanoma, and lymphoma, our solution achieved a Dice score of 72.12%. Code: https://github.com/heiligerl/autopet_submission

The enduring resolution to the Abraham–Minkowski debate regarding electromagnetic momentum relies on decomposing the total momentum of a closed continuum electrodynamic system into distinct matter and field components. By employing a microscopic model of a basic linear dielectric, we derive Lagrangian equations of motion for electric dipoles, demonstrating that the dielectric behaves as an ensemble of stationary simple harmonic oscillators driven by the electric field to generate a polarization response. Macroscopic energy and momentum are defined via the electric, magnetic, and polarization fields propagating through the dielectric as a unified pulse of electromagnetic radiation. We conclude that, for a simple linear dielectric without significant reflections, both macroscopic energy and momentum are entirely of electromagnetic origin.

We present geometric algorithms that extend the classical continued fraction method for the torus to all translation surfaces within hyperelliptic components. These algorithms generate every saddle connection that represents a best approximation in a geometric context, thereby generalizing the standard concept of best approximation found in classical continued fractions. Furthermore, they enable the enumeration of all systoles along a Teichmüller geodesic and all bispecial words occurring in the symbolic coding of linear flows. The elementary steps of these algorithms constitute a geometric, invertible extension of the renormalization moves previously introduced by S. Ferenczi and L. Zamboni for the associated interval exchange transformations.

Although oxygen vacancies are recognized as pivotal to the performance of HfO2-based devices, the atomic mechanisms driving exotic phenomena like wake-up and fluid imprint remain unclear. Guided by a lattice-mode-matching criterion, this study systematically investigates phase transitions among various hafnia polymorphs under the influence of neutral and positively charged oxygen vacancies. By mapping minimum energy pathways using a first-principles-based variable-cell nudged elastic band method, we demonstrate that positively charged oxygen vacancies significantly accelerate the kinetic transition of nonpolar phases to the polar phase. This process is facilitated by a transient high-energy tetragonal phase and the extreme charge-carrier-inert ferroelectricity of the polar $Pca2_1$ phase. The complex interplay between the kinetics of structural polymorphism and the charge state of oxygen vacancies offers crucial insights into the origins of ferroelectricity in HfO2-based thin films, as well as the mechanisms behind wake-up, fluid imprint, and inertial switching.

This study presents a method that breaks down the dynamics of a nonlinear system around an equilibrium point into low-order components, enabling the reconstruction of the complete system behavior. Serving as a nonlinear counterpart to linear modal analysis, the approach utilizes Invariant Spectral Foliations (ISF)—defined as the smoothest invariant foliation near an equilibrium, which is unique under general conditions. The conjugate dynamics derived from an ISF function as a reduced-order model. Notably, an ISF can be fitted directly to vibration data without the need for prior model identification. The theoretical framework is demonstrated through an analytic example and applied to free-vibration data from a clamped-clamped beam.

We present an analytical framework that examines the validity limits of Fermi liquid theory in two-dimensional Fermi systems interacting through long-range Coulomb forces, alongside a comparison with three-dimensional counterparts. Our findings indicate that 2D Fermi liquid theory and quasiparticles remain robust at high energies and temperatures near the Fermi energy, mirroring the behavior observed in 3D systems. Additionally, we derive the phase diagram within the frequency-temperature plane that distinguishes between the collisionless ballistic and collision-dominated hydrodynamic regimes for both 2D and 3D interacting electron systems. Finally, we compute temperature corrections to the renormalized effective mass up to the third order and discuss the applicability of the 2D Wiedemann-Franz law and the 2D Kadowaki-Woods relation.

This study outlines the creation of a collaborative instrument for music and dance, specifically investigating the distinctions between motion and stillness, as well as sound and silence. Inspired by the concept of fostering a genuine partnership between a musician and a dancer, the project developed an instrument designed for active co-performance. Employing a participatory design methodology, we utilized sonification to systematically analyze the dancer's physical movements through a "spatiotemporal matrix," with an emphasis on sonic microinteractions. For the final performance, the system captured muscle activity in the dancer's arm and leg using two Myo armbands, alongside a wireless headset microphone that recorded breathing sounds. The paper reflects on multi-user instrument paradigms, examines our approach to designing a shared instrument via sonification, and considers the performers' subjective assessments of the technology.

We introduced a data-driven method designed to decompose multivariate time series, aiming to uncover multiple phases within the dynamics of complex systems. This methodology extends the Hierarchical Factor Segmentation (HFS) technique into a multi-dimensional framework, establishing a systematic protocol for selecting extreme events across multi-dimensional spaces. For each selected event, we fit an empirical distribution of recurrence times (the intervals between excursions) using a geometric distribution with time-varying parameters, performing these fittings iteratively across all chosen events. Subsequently, we aggregate local recurrent patterns to derive a global dynamic mechanism. To partition the entire time series into segments where variables follow identical distributions, we apply clustering, supplemented by feature weighting techniques to address specific clustering limitations. Simulation results indicate that this expanded approach can identify systematic variations even when joint distributions shift. In real-world applications, we examined the interrelationships among returns, trading volume, and transaction counts for both individual and multiple stocks within the S&P 500. Our analysis successfully identified volatile periods and revealed potential associative links between the stocks.

Quantum state discrimination involves determining unknown states from a specific ensemble through measurements, utilizing various strategies like minimum-error discrimination or unambiguous state identification to achieve optimal results. Maximum-confidence measurements (MCMs) distinguish themselves by maximizing the certainty of identifying inputs based on measurement outcomes, effectively unifying other strategies as specific limiting cases. This study explores MCMs applied to general ensembles of qubit states. We introduce a technique to determine these measurements by leveraging the geometric properties of qubit ensembles, applying it to scenarios involving two and four mixed states, as well as arbitrary numbers of pure states. Furthermore, we compare MCMs against minimum-error and unambiguous discrimination methods for qubits. Our findings offer new interpretations of qubit measurements through the lens of MCM and assist in designing relevant qubit protocols.

Transmission system operators (TSOs) are tasked with ensuring secure and efficient access to the transmission network for all stakeholders. However, this responsibility is becoming increasingly difficult due to rising and unpredictable demand, rapid shifts in the generation mix, and evolving market policies. While TSOs have traditionally sought to enhance technical performance by constructing new overhead lines or physically hardening infrastructure, securing public approval for such projects is often a significant hurdle. Consequently, TSOs are increasingly focused on leveraging the capabilities of existing assets. This study examines the application of modular Flexible AC Transmission Systems (FACTS) devices to modify line characteristics, thereby improving the network's ability to handle uncertain demand without the necessity of building new overhead lines. The proposed approach accounts for demand uncertainty and manages the utilization of current transmission infrastructure. Furthermore, the mathematical findings are verified using a comprehensive non-linear simulation model of three distinct transmission networks.

The ESCULAP project focuses on investigating the external injection of low-energy (10 MeV) electrons into a plasma within the quasilinear regime. This setup will utilize the PHIL photo injector and the LASERIX high-power laser. We will provide an update on the preliminary work regarding the facility and the current status of both machines, alongside presenting simulation results that demonstrate the expected performance capabilities.

Polyphone disambiguation seeks to extract precise pronunciation insights from natural text to ensure reliable Text-to-speech (TTS) performance. However, existing methods depend heavily on extensive annotated datasets and the involvement of language experts, hindering the expansion of high-quality neural TTS to out-of-domain daily dialogues and the world's vast array of languages. This study addresses the polyphone disambiguation challenge through a concise and innovative lens by introducing Dict-TTS, a semantic-aware generative TTS model that leverages an online website dictionary as prior natural language information. We developed a Semantics-to-Pronunciation Attention (S2PA) module that aligns semantic patterns between input text and dictionary entries to derive accurate pronunciations. Notably, this module can be trained end-to-end with the TTS model without requiring any annotated phoneme labels. Experiments across three languages demonstrate that our approach surpasses several robust baseline models in pronunciation accuracy and enhances prosody modeling. Comprehensive analyses further validate the effectiveness of each design component in Dict-TTS. The implementation is accessible at \url{https://github.com/Zain-Jiang/Dict-TTS}.

The kinetic term within the $N$-body Hamiltonian system on a spherical surface is non-separable, rendering standard explicit symplectic integrators unsuitable. By leveraging a hierarchical structure inherent to this kinetic term, we develop an explicit, time-reversible symplectic scheme of second order. Furthermore, we employ iterative applications of this method to derive a fourth-order scheme and validate its computational efficiency.

Ultracold Fermi gases subjected to synthetic gauge fields offer a superior environment for investigating the interplay between lattice frustration and an effective magnetic flux approaching one quantum per particle. The simplest theoretical framework for this scenario involves spinless, noninteracting fermions situated on a triangular two-chain flux ladder. This study examines the model near half-filling, characterized by small, alternating interchain hopping amplitudes along the zigzag bonds. Under these conditions, significant alterations in the ground state properties occur, particularly where flux-induced topological Lifshitz transitions shift toward flux values per diatomic plaquette ($f$) near the flux quantum ($f\sim 1/2$). Lattice geometrical frustration disrupts the $k \to \pi - k$ particle-hole spectral symmetry found in non-frustrated ladders, resulting in the splitting of degeneracies at metal-insulator transitions. A distinctive characteristic of the translationally invariant triangular ladder is the emergence of isolated Dirac nodes at the Brillouin zone boundary, which renders the ground state semi-metallic at $f=1/2$. We compute the orbital current's dependence on flux and identify Lifshitz critical points through singularities in this relationship at fixed chemical potential ($\mu$) and particle density ($\rho$). The lack of particle-hole symmetry in the triangular ladder creates an asymmetry between hole ($\rho<1$) and particle ($\rho>1$) doping, yielding qualitatively distinct outcomes for the phase diagram, Lifshitz points, and the flux dependence of the orbital current under constant $\rho$ versus constant $\mu$ conditions.

Dense particulate suspensions often undergo a stress-induced shift from a liquid-like to a solid-like shear jammed (SJ) state, yet the particle-level mechanisms driving this reversible bulk transition remain unclear. This study investigates the transient stress relaxation of SJ states in a well-defined dense suspension subjected to step strain perturbations. We identify a highly non-exponential relaxation characterized by a sharp, discontinuous stress drop at short times when peak stress values are sufficiently high. High-resolution boundary imaging and normal stress measurements reveal that this stress discontinuity stems from localized plastic events, while system-spanning dilation governs the slower relaxation phase. Furthermore, we discover a compelling correlation between the characteristics of this transient relaxation and the steady-state shear jamming phase diagram derived from the Wyart-Cates Model.

The equivariant coarse Baum-Connes conjecture, initially proposed by Roe [29], serves as a unified framework for addressing both the Baum-Connes conjecture and its coarse variant. In this paper, we establish that if an a-T-menable group $\Gamma$ acts properly and isometrically on a metric space $X$ with bounded geometry and controlled distortion, such that the quotient $X/\Gamma$ admits a coarse embedding, then the equivariant coarse Baum-Connes conjecture is satisfied for this action. This result provides an affirmative answer to the question raised in [8].

We establish upper bounds for the one-arm exponent $\eta_1$ across a range of dependent percolation models that extend beyond standard Bernoulli percolation. Although our primary focus lies on the level set percolation of Gaussian fields, the methodology is applicable to other models within the Bernoulli percolation universality class, such as Poisson-Voronoi and Poisson-Boolean percolation. Specifically, in two dimensions ($d=2$), we demonstrate that $\eta_1 \le 1/3$ for continuous Gaussian fields exhibiting rapid correlation decay, exemplified by the Bargmann-Fock field. In dimensions $d \ge 3$, we prove $\eta_1 \le d/3$ for both discrete and continuous finite-range fields, as well as $\eta_1 \le d-2$ for fields with rapid correlation decay. While these results are well-established for Bernoulli percolation and represent the best-known bounds in general, prior proofs fail to apply to dependent percolation models; consequently, we introduce a novel approach utilizing exploration and relative entropy techniques. Furthermore, the proof incorporates a new Russo-type inequality tailored for Gaussian fields, which we employ to demonstrate the sharpness of the phase transition and the mean-field bound applicable to finite-range fields.

The potential energy surfaces for the hydrogen molecular ion (H$_2^+$) within the Born-Oppenheimer approximation are calculated using the Riccati-Padé method (RPM). The convergence behavior of this approach is examined across various states. For multiple bound states, the equilibrium internuclear distance, the combined electronic and nuclear energy, and the separation constants are determined with 40 digits of precision. In the case of the ground state, these parameters are computed with an accuracy exceeding 100 digits. Furthermore, benchmark electronic energy values at diverse internuclear distances are provided for several other states. The RPM software implementation is released under a free license. These findings represent the most precise results available to date, and the accompanying software offers additional benchmark data.

Recent studies have demonstrated that quantum non-Markovianity can emerge from the mixing of Markovian channels. We address a parallel inquiry: can singularities arise when mixing non-singular channels (those devoid of such features)? Our analysis, focused on qubit Pauli channels, yields a negative answer. Conversely, combining channels that possess singularities can result in a mixed channel where these singularities are eliminated. We categorize singular channels into two distinct types, noting that their mixing produces markedly different singularity characteristics in the outcome. We also highlight the relationship between these phenomena and non-Markovianity, defined via completely positive indivisibility. Ultimately, these findings establish significant constraints on realizing non-invertible quantum channels through the process of channel mixing.

This study introduces a robotic framework for grasping and placing objects without relying on prior knowledge of their geometric shapes. Unlike recent approaches that treat every object as entirely novel, the proposed system identifies previously handled items, enabling online model reconstruction and reuse. Throughout a lifelong manipulation process, the system continuously learns object features and refines their reconstructed models. When a familiar object reappears, the system first recognizes it and then aligns its stored model with the current visual data. This capability significantly lowers shape uncertainty, allowing the robot to reason about unobservable parts of the object and improving manipulation efficiency by reducing the need for active perception during the task. To achieve reusable models, the pipeline utilizes Truncated Signed Distance Functions (TSDF) for representation and a modified particle filter algorithm for pose estimation and tracking of partial models. Additionally, the work presents a method for building and maintaining a dataset of manipulated objects. Real-world experiments demonstrate that reusing models generated during prior interactions makes future manipulation tasks more effective and efficient compared to treating each object as new.

Terahertz (THz) wireless communications are essential for enabling ultra-high-speed applications and services in sixth-generation (6G) networks. Nevertheless, THz systems face significant coverage limitations due to inherent characteristics like high penetration losses, severe path attenuation, and substantial molecular absorption. To overcome these obstacles and maximize the potential of the THz spectrum, this study investigates a hybrid indoor network architecture where RF macrocells ensure coverage and THz small cells deliver high data rates. Leveraging stochastic geometry, we evaluate the performance of this coexisting network regarding coverage probability and average achievable throughput, with analytical findings validated through Monte-Carlo simulations. The research offers key insights for optimizing THz system parameters, such as the deployment density of THz access points (APs) and the bias factor. Results highlight a distinct trade-off between coverage and rate: increasing the fraction of THz APs significantly boosts data rates but can compromise coverage. Additionally, the optimal fraction of THz APs is found to be highly dependent on the user's location within the finite network area.

This paper investigates transmission design for multiuser communication networks assisted by reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS). Unlike most existing works, we focus on long-term channel state information (CSI)-based design, where both base station beamforming vectors and RIS phase shifts are optimized using long-term CSI, thereby substantially lowering channel estimation overhead. Addressing the absence of an explicit ergodic data rate formula, we introduce a novel deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG) algorithm to resolve the optimization problem, utilizing channel vectors generated offline for training. Simulation results indicate that the achievable net throughput exceeds that of conventional instantaneous-CSI-based schemes when channel estimation overhead is accounted for.

Using the non-parametric, Bayesian algorithm CHASSIS and radial velocity data from 174 globular clusters, we have mapped the dark matter density structure in the outer regions (extending to roughly 7 effective radii) of the elliptical galaxy NGC 4636. Our findings indicate a significant dark matter presence, with $R$-band mass-to-light ($M/L$) ratios increasing to approximately 30 near $4R_e$, while the $K$-band $M/L$ ratio at about $3R_e$ reaches nearly 10. These results remain consistent whether the analysis is performed on red and blue globular clusters individually or together. This $M/L$ estimate exceeds values from prior studies utilizing the same kinematic data, and we further observe that the dark matter distribution is strongly concentrated within the inner halo.

Stylometric methods have proven highly effective for real-world authorship attribution. To counter the privacy risks associated with this capability, researchers have developed automated obfuscation techniques designed to hide the stylistic markers that reveal an anonymous author's identity. Recent advancements focus on black-box obfuscation methods that evade attribution classifiers while maintaining the original document's semantics. However, for practical utility under realistic threat models, these techniques must remain effective even when the adversary's classifier differs from the one used during obfuscation. Regrettably, current approaches often fail to generalize to unseen classifiers. This paper introduces an ensemble-based strategy for achieving transferable authorship obfuscation. Experimental results indicate that if an obfuscator can successfully evade an ensemble classifier—comprising multiple base classifiers—it is more likely to succeed against other, different classifiers. Our analysis reveals that this improved transferability stems from the ensemble's ability to synthesize knowledge from individual base classifiers by effectively averaging their decision boundaries.

SMT solvers and equality saturation engines rely on proof certificates derived from e-graph-based congruence closure procedures to facilitate verification and conflict clause generation; reducing the size of these certificates accelerates these processes. Although finding proofs of minimal size is NP-complete, current minimization algorithms for congruence closure produce excessively large proofs and impose asymptotic overhead on the core procedure. This paper presents an O(n^5) algorithm that generates optimal proofs under a novel "proof tree size" metric that directly constrains proof magnitude. We further relax this method into a practical O(n log n) greedy algorithm that produces compact proofs without introducing asymptotic overhead. By integrating these techniques into the egg equality saturation toolkit, we created the first certifying equality saturation engine. Our results demonstrate that the greedy approach within egg generates significantly smaller proofs than the state-of-the-art Z3 SMT solver across a dataset of 3,760 benchmarks.

In late 2019, ASHRAE organized the Great Energy Predictor III (GEPIII) machine learning contest on Kaggle, marking the third such event they hosted and the first since the mid-1990s. Participants were given access to more than 20 million training data points sourced from 2,380 energy meters across 1,448 buildings and 16 different providers. The primary goal was to develop the most precise models for forecasting over 41 million private and public test data points. A total of 4,370 individuals, organized into 3,614 teams from 94 nations, competed by submitting 39,403 predictions. Beyond the top five winning workflows, competitors publicly released 415 reproducible online machine learning notebooks, which included over 40 complete solutions. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the competition's preparation, dataset, participant interactions, generated workflows and models, the winners and their submissions, key lessons learned, and the resulting outputs and future directions. The most successful and accurate approaches relied heavily on large ensembles of gradient boosting tree models, particularly LightGBM. As was the case with the inaugural predictor competition, data preprocessing proved to be a critical differentiating factor.

We present and investigate a novel concept of scattered subspaces relative to a set of subspaces of equal dimension, particularly focusing on partial spreads. Our findings demonstrate that this definition extends existing ideas of subspace scatteredness. We derive multiple upper limits for the dimension of scattered subspaces concerning arbitrary partial spreads, thereby refining results for Desarguesian cases. Additionally, we prove the existence of scattered spaces through a non-constructive method utilizing graph theory. The derived upper and lower bounds offer a precise interpretation as limits for the critical exponent of specific combinatorial geometries. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between our introduced notion of scattered space and rank-metric code theory, yielding new insights into covering radius and the existence of minimal vector rank-metric codes.

The study investigates how spin polarization evolves under an external electric field at collision energies of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=27\,{\rm GeV}$ and $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=200\,{\rm GeV}$. Conducted within a perfect-fluid Bjorken-expanding resistive magnetohydrodynamic framework, the numerical analysis yields new findings. Specifically, the results demonstrate that the electric field exerts a substantial influence on the balance between expansion and dissipation.

Developing scoring functions to effectively analyze and learn the properties of high-dimensional hidden representations in large-scale transformer models like BERT presents significant challenges. This work introduces a novel approach by investigating the topological features of BERT's hidden layers through persistent homology (PH). We present a new metric called the "persistence scoring function (PSF)," which: (i) precisely captures the homology of these high-dimensional representations, demonstrates strong correlation with test set accuracy across diverse datasets, and surpasses existing scoring methods; (ii) reveals insightful "per-class" characteristics after fine-tuning from both qualitative and quantitative perspectives; (iii) exhibits greater stability against perturbations compared to baseline functions, establishing it as a highly robust proxy; and (iv) effectively predicts attack success rates for a broad spectrum of black-box and white-box adversarial attacks. Comprehensive correlation experiments confirm the practical applicability of PSF across various NLP tasks associated with BERT.

We explore the phase diagram of high-pressure molecular hydrogen using path integral molecular dynamics, guided by a machine-learned interatomic potential trained on Quantum Monte Carlo forces and energies. Beyond the known HCP and C2/c-24 phases, we identify two additional stable phases featuring molecular centers within the Fmmm-4 structure; these are distinguished by a temperature-dependent transition in molecular orientation. The high-temperature isotropic Fmmm-4 phase exhibits a reentrant melting line peaking at a higher temperature (1450 K at 150 GPa) than previously thought and intersects the liquid-liquid transition line near 1200 K and 200 GPa.

Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) are standard in robotics for enabling balance and navigation through posture data. However, unlike robots that rely on precise orientation and position metrics, humans and animals intuitively sense their movement within the environment via a rapid perception-action feedback loop. This study introduces an end-to-end framework that trains a visual self-model for legged locomotion by utilizing high-dimensional visual observations and action commands. This model learns the spatial correlation between the robot's body dynamics and corresponding ground texture variations from image sequences. We show that the robot can effectively employ this visual self-model to perform diverse locomotion tasks in real-world settings it has not encountered during training. Consequently, this method enables robots to navigate without IMUs or in environments lacking GPS and with weak geomagnetic fields, such as indoor spaces and urban canyons.

We propose a model-free reinforcement learning (RL) framework for addressing time-consistent risk-sensitive stochastic optimization problems. In this approach, agents evaluate the risk of random variable sequences through dynamic convex risk measures. Utilizing a time-consistent dynamic programming principle to compute policy values, we derive policy gradient update rules to facilitate the discovery of optimal strategies. Furthermore, we introduce an actor-critic algorithm leveraging neural networks for policy optimization. The efficacy and adaptability of this method are validated through its application to three distinct scenarios: statistical arbitrage trading, obstacle avoidance in robotics, and financial hedging.

Inspired by experimental investigations of graphene within the quantum Hall regime, we re-examine the phase diagram of a single graphene sheet at charge neutrality. Due to spin and valley degeneracies, interactions are pivotal in defining the ground state's characteristics. We demonstrate that, generally, within the relevant regime, the phase diagram features a region where magnetic and bond orders coexist. This finding is established using both continuum and lattice models, and we propose that this coexistence phase offers a natural resolution to previously unexplained experimental observations regarding the quantum Hall effect in graphene.

Liger is a second-generation near-infrared imager and integral field spectrograph (IFS) for the W. M. Keck Observatory, designed to leverage the Keck All-sky Precision Adaptive-optics (KAPA) system. Operating across a wavelength range of 0.81 to 2.45 micrometers, Liger employs a slicer and lenslet array IFS configuration with adjustable spatial plate scales and fields of view, offering hundreds of operational modes. Due to the inherent complexity of the raw data formats generated by these modes, the instrument requires a Data Reduction System (DRS) capable of performing real-time data reduction and delivering science-ready products to observers. The DRS processes raw imager and IFS frames from the readout system, generating 2D and 3D data products through specialized quick-look visualization tools tailored for IFS presentation. Additionally, the system will upload reduced data to the Keck Observatory Archive (KOA) for astronomers to access for offline post-processing. This document outlines an initial design for the DRS and specifies the interfaces between the observatory and instrument software systems.

Although super-resolution microscopy in the visible spectrum is a well-established and potent instrument across various fields, comparable techniques have not yet been realized in the infrared (IR) range. This study presents an experimental demonstration of IR super-resolution microscopy ($\lambda_{IR}\approx 10-12\,\mu$m) utilizing IR-visible sum-frequency generation. Employing a wide-field configuration, we imaged localized surface phonon polaritons within 4H-SiC nanostructures to validate the method. Our approach achieves an enhanced spatial resolution of approximately $\lambda_{IR}/9$, allowing for the resolution of polariton resonances in individual sub-diffractional nanostructures separated by sub-wavelength distances. Additionally, we demonstrate that this level of resolution enables the differentiation of spatial patterns corresponding to distinct polariton modes inside single nanostructures.

The first identified interstellar object, 1I/'Oumuamua, displayed several anomalous characteristics during its 2017/2018 transit through the inner solar system, making an in-situ intercept mission highly valuable for scientific discovery. Extending prior Project Lyra research, this study proposes an alternative trajectory utilizing a Jupiter Oberth Manoeuvre (JOM), distinguished by a Mars flyby prior to the Jupiter encounter. Although this path demands a higher total $\Delta V$ (15.6 $kms^{-1}$), entails a longer 29-year flight, and necessitates a 2026 launch with reduced preparation time compared to earlier options, it offers a unique advantage: negligible $\Delta V$ required to reach Jupiter. This "free ride" eliminates the need for an onboard liquid propellant stage, a benefit partially counterbalanced by the necessity of using two or three staged solid rocket motors at Jupiter. For instance, a Falcon Heavy configuration augmented with a CASTOR 30B and a STAR 48B booster could deliver 102kg to 1I/'Oumuamua by 2059, with other scenarios potentially achieving shorter durations or greater payload capacities.

The COVID-19 pandemic has profoundly transformed our daily lives, work environments, and social interactions. As online activities increase, individuals face growing exposure to privacy risks. This paper examines user self-disclosure on social media and the privacy concerns stemming from these behaviors. Drawing on recent news, techniques, and research, we identify three escalating privacy threats associated with the pandemic. Following this, we offer a systematic analysis of potential privacy issues related to the COVID-19 crisis. Finally, we propose a set of research directions concerning online self-disclosure and privacy challenges for future studies, along with possible solutions.

Algorithms are increasingly employed to make high-stakes decisions impacting human lives, such as in college admissions, healthcare, and law enforcement. Although these tools allow us to extract insights from massive datasets, they risk inadvertently reinforcing biases present in that data. This issue has driven growing interest in fair machine learning, a field dedicated to measuring and reducing algorithmic discrimination. Consequently, machine learning models must undergo rigorous testing for bias prior to large-scale deployment. This paper introduces a statistical hypothesis test for identifying unfair classifiers by applying concepts from optimal transport theory. By utilizing the geometry of the feature space, the proposed test statistic measures the distance between the empirical distribution of test samples and the manifold of distributions that ensure fairness for a pre-trained classifier. We establish a rigorous hypothesis testing framework to evaluate the probabilistic fairness of any pre-trained logistic classifier, demonstrating both theoretically and empirically that the method is asymptotically valid. Furthermore, the framework provides interpretability by pinpointing the optimal data perturbation required to render a specific classifier fair.

The potential existence of black hole remnants offers viable candidates for dark matter. This paper examines the feasibility of such remnants by incorporating quantum gravitational corrections to black hole entropy and temperature. Furthermore, the study outlines observational methods for detecting these relics and discusses the associated cosmological constraints.

This study examines free-space optical (FSO) communication links designed for the backhaul connectivity of small cells (SCs), utilizing an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) equipped with FSO hardware as a relay node. We illustrate the deployment of these drone relay stations (DRSs) within high-rise urban environments to establish unobstructed FSO line-of-sight (LOS) connections that avoid building interference. Furthermore, our approach incorporates solar panels on the DRSs, prioritizing sunny locations, and demonstrates the resulting reduction in the number of recharging trips required for the UAV.

We introduce a method beneficial for analyzing network or system performance when the underlying model lacks the Markov property. While performance models frequently rely on Markov chains or processes, the Markov assumption is not always valid, particularly in scenarios involving long-range dependencies. Our approach offers valuable assistance in these non-Markovian situations and similar cases where the property does not hold.

Compact protoplanetary disks with radii smaller than approximately 50 au are frequently observed around young, low-mass stars. This study presents high-resolution ALMA dust continuum observations of a compact disk surrounding CW Tau, conducted at Bands 4 (2.2 mm), 6 (1.3 mm), 7 (0.89 mm), and 8 (0.75 mm). The spectral energy distribution (SED) reveals a spectral slope of $2.0\pm0.24$ from 0.75 to 1.3 mm, whereas the slope between 2.17 and 3.56 mm is significantly steeper at $3.7\pm0.29$. This steep rise aligns with optically thin emission from small grains ($\lesssim$ 350 ${\rm \mu m}$). We applied parametric fitting to the ALMA data to characterize the dust properties of the disk. Notably, assuming a dust-to-gas mass ratio of 0.01, the Toomre Q parameter falls in the range of $\sim$ 1-3, implying that the CW Tau disk could be marginally gravitationally unstable. The total dust mass is estimated at roughly $250M_{\oplus}$ for a maximum grain size of 140 ${\rm \mu m}$ (inferred from prior Band 7 polarimetry), and remains at least $80M_{\oplus}$ even if grains are larger. These findings indicate that the CW Tau disk is surprisingly massive despite its compact nature. Additionally, we clearly detect a gap structure near $\sim$ 20 au, potentially carved by a giant planet. Despite these intriguing features, the CW Tau disk exhibits typical luminosity, size, and spectral index at ALMA Band 6, which may offer insights into the mass budget challenges associated with Class II disks.

The Internet of Things (IoT) represents an evolving paradigm connecting billions of physical objects to the Internet, enabling them to collect and exchange data across various devices and systems. However, these devices were not originally designed with security in mind, creating potential vulnerabilities within multi-device environments. Traditionally, researchers have addressed IoT challenges by surveying developers and experts; yet, this approach lacks scalability due to the impracticality of reaching every developer. An alternative method involves analyzing discussions on prominent online development platforms like Stack Overflow. Nevertheless, identifying IoT-specific issues in these forums is difficult because such conversations often lack relevant categorization tags. To address this, this paper introduces the "IoT Security Dataset," a specialized collection of 7,147 samples dedicated exclusively to IoT security discourse. Since no automated labeling tools exist, these samples were manually annotated. Additionally, multiple transformer models were utilized to automatically identify security-related discussions. Rigorous analysis reveals that IoT security conversations differ significantly in complexity from traditional security topics. We demonstrated a substantial performance decline (up to 44%) for transformer models when applied to cross-domain datasets using the general-purpose "Opiner" dataset, thereby validating our assertion. Consequently, we developed a domain-specific IoT security detector achieving an F1-Score of 0.69. The dataset has been made publicly available to assist developers in understanding security discussions and to encourage vendors to prioritize product security.

User intent classification plays a pivotal role in information retrieval. This study presents a refined taxonomy of user intent, expanding upon the standard distinction between navigational, transactional, and informational queries by subdividing informational queries into three specific categories: instrumental, factual, and abstain. This enhanced classification offers greater granularity, ensures high consistency among annotators, and establishes a robust foundation for automated classification. The new categories enable retrieval systems to differentiate query types and tailor ranking strategies accordingly, such as prioritizing specific results. To annotate the ORCAS dataset using this new taxonomy, we employed a weak supervision framework based on Snorkel, leveraging established heuristics and keywords to generate predictive rules. Subsequent experiments compared various machine learning models trained on Snorkel-generated labels against other methods; the results demonstrated that Snorkel's performance remains competitive and achieves state-of-the-art accuracy. A primary benefit of this rule-based approach is its efficiency for real-world deployment, where intent classification must process every incoming query. The paper also releases the ORCAS-I dataset, a labeled version of the ORCAS click-based Web query dataset containing 18 million connections across 10 million distinct queries.

The second-grade fluid equations serve as a model for viscoelastic fluids, characterized by two parameters: $\alpha > 0$, representing elasticity, and $
u > 0$, representing viscosity. Formally setting both parameters to zero reduces the system to the incompressible Euler equations for ideal fluid flow. This article investigates the limits $\alpha, 
u 	o 0$ of solutions within a smooth, bounded, two-dimensional domain subject to no-slip boundary conditions. The problem bridges the gap between the Euler-$\alpha$ model ($
u = 0$), where recent work by the authors demonstrated convergence to the Euler solution, and the Navier-Stokes case ($\alpha = 0$), where the vanishing viscosity limit remains a significant open question. Three primary results are established. First, we demonstrate that solutions of the second-grade model converge to those of the Euler equations when $
u = \mathcal{O}(\alpha^2)$ as $\alpha 	o 0$, thereby extending the main finding in [19]. Second, we show that convergence of the second-grade fluid to the Euler equations is equivalent to the vanishing of energy dissipation in a suitably thin boundary layer, under the asymptotic regime where $
u = \mathcal{O}(\alpha^{6/5})$ and $
u/\alpha^2 	o \infty$ as $\alpha 	o 0$. This yields a convergence criterion analogous to the well-known Kato criterion for the Navier-Stokes to Euler transition. Finally, we extend Kato's classical criterion to the second-grade fluid model, which holds if $\alpha = \mathcal{O}(
u^{3/2})$ as $
u 	o 0$. The proofs for all these results rely on energy estimates and boundary correctors, adhering to the original methodology proposed by Kato.

Emerging intelligence applications are fueling greater demand for deploying deep neural networks (DNN) across distributed systems. Configuring such distributed deep learning environments requires adjusting numerous parameters for both network/edge devices and DNN models to ensure optimal performance. Simulations are essential in the early stages to assess the scalability of these applications and evaluate the impact of various configurations; however, research into simulating distributed intelligence environments remains nascent. Current frameworks, including NS-3, cannot be easily extended to support distributed learning simulations. To address this, we introduce sim4DistrDL, a novel discrete event simulator comprising both a deep learning module and a network simulation module designed to facilitate the simulation of DNN-based distributed applications. This paper details the design and implementation of this learning simulator and presents a representative use case.

A recently identified family of iron-based superconductors shares the same crystal structure as the well-known 122 iron pnictide group but exhibits a fundamentally different doping condition. Initial findings suggest that superconductivity in these materials is nodeless, even though the typical prerequisites for the $s_\pm$ nodeless state—usually associated with iron superconductors—are absent. While it might initially seem plausible to attribute $d$-wave symmetry to these new compounds, which could theoretically allow for a nodeless state, a rigorous analysis proves this impossible due to the specific 122 crystallographic constraints. Consequently, the range of viable symmetry options is highly restricted, leaving only two possibilities: a standard single-sign $s_{+}$ state or an alternative $s_\pm$ state distinct from the one found in other iron-based superconductors.

Low-light image enhancement is a widespread yet difficult challenge that is crucial for improving the visibility of images taken in dimly lit conditions. Since the Bayer filter on color camera sensors prevents all photons from reaching the sensor, this work first introduces a deep neural network-based simulator to generate monochrome raw images from colored raw data. Subsequently, a fully convolutional network is proposed to enhance low-light images by fusing colored raw data with the synthesized monochrome data. Additionally, channel-wise attention mechanisms are incorporated into the fusion process to facilitate complementary interactions between features from both the colored and monochrome raw images. For training these networks, we developed a dataset of paired monochrome and color raw images called the Mono-Colored Raw paired dataset (MCR), collected using a monochrome camera without a Bayer filter alongside a color camera with one. The proposed pipeline leverages the fusion of virtual monochrome and color raw images, and extensive experiments demonstrate that significant improvements can be achieved by utilizing raw sensor data combined with data-driven learning.

Within gravitational effective theories that incorporate higher curvature terms, cosmological models can exhibit nontrivial de Sitter fixed points. This study investigates the phenomenological consequences of such points, specifically examining a model where a massive scalar field is nonminimally coupled to the Euler density. By analyzing the phase portrait of the resulting dynamical system, we demonstrate that the nature of the fixed point—whether it acts as a sink or a saddle—depends on the magnitude of the coupling. Subsequently, we calculate the perturbation spectra arising near this fixed point to assess its viability as a mechanism for cosmic inflation. Our results identify parameter ranges compatible with cosmological observations, provided that cosmic microwave background anisotropies originate from fluctuations generated in the vicinity of the fixed point. Future observations could further restrict the coupling function within this framework, and we also offer brief remarks on the swampland conjecture.

Overcoming sparse rewards has long been a persistent hurdle in reinforcement learning. Although recent hindsight-based approaches have succeeded across various sparse-reward scenarios, they struggle with complex objectives, such as stacking multiple blocks using a robotic arm in a simulated environment. Meanwhile, curiosity-driven exploration, which leverages the prediction error of a learned dynamics model as an intrinsic reward, has proven effective for navigating numerous sparse-reward settings. This paper introduces a novel approach that integrates hindsight techniques with curiosity-driven exploration and curriculum learning to successfully tackle the difficult sparse-reward block stacking problem. To our knowledge, we are the first to achieve stacking of more than two blocks using solely sparse rewards, without relying on human demonstrations.

This paper addresses the challenge of identifying features linked to extreme values within high-dimensional linear regression. Typically, linear modeling treats abnormal extreme values or outliers as anomalies to be eliminated or handled via robust regression techniques. However, in numerous contexts, these extreme values represent signals of interest rather than errors; examples include spiking neuron traces, financial volatility, and extreme climate events. Consequently, we introduce a novel approach for sparse high-dimensional linear regression tailored to extreme values, grounded in the Subbotin, or generalized normal distribution, which we designate as the extreme value linear regression model. Our methodology employs an $\ell_p$ norm loss function where $p$ is an even integer exceeding two, demonstrating that this loss function amplifies the weight assigned to extreme observations. We establish consistency and variable selection consistency for this framework when paired with a Lasso penalty, naming the resulting procedure the Extreme Lasso. Additionally, we investigate the theoretical influence of extreme value observations on parameter estimates using influence functions. Finally, simulation studies and an application to real-world data confirm that the Extreme Lasso surpasses existing literature methods in selecting features associated with extreme values in high-dimensional regression.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) struggle to learn effectively in environments characterized by uncertainty, noise, or adversarial conditions. To address this, we introduce a novel, efficient, and theoretically sound method for robust learning that integrates Bayesian estimation with Variational Inference. By modeling the propagation of density through DNN layers and resolving it via an Ensemble Density Propagation (EnDP) framework, our approach transmits the moments of the variational probability distribution across the network. This enables the calculation of the mean and covariance for the predictive distribution at the model's output. Empirical evaluations on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate that models trained with this method exhibit significantly enhanced robustness against both random noise and adversarial attacks.

Spoken term discovery from untranscribed audio can be accomplished through a two-stage pipeline. Initially, unlabeled speech is decoded into a sequence of subword units learned and modeled unsupervised. Subsequently, partial sequence matching and clustering are applied to these decoded sequences to identify words or phrases. A key drawback of this method is that errors in subword decoding can negatively affect downstream stages. Although Siamese/Triplet networks offer a way to learn segment representations that enhance discovery, their application in fully unsupervised scenarios is hindered by the lack of training data. To address this, we propose generating training examples from initial hypothesized sequence clusters. These synthesized examples are used to train Siamese/Triplet networks to assess the similarity between speech segments, enabling the re-clustering of all hypothesized subword sequences for spoken term discovery. Experimental results indicate that our approach effectively generates training data for these networks, thereby improving discovery efficacy compared to the original two-stage method.

Berkovich, Chillag, and Herzog previously identified all finite groups $G$ where every nonlinear irreducible character possesses a unique degree. This paper generalizes that finding by demonstrating an analogous characterization for finite solvable groups $G$ containing a normal subgroup $N$, provided that all irreducible characters of $G$ whose kernels do not contain $N$ have distinct degrees.

Neuromorphic image sensors mimic the biological retina to execute visual tasks within electronic hardware. While first-generation devices utilized gain modulation during phototransduction and temporal differentiation at the initial retinal synapse, they failed to incorporate processing from downstream retinal circuits, a field that has seen significant discovery over the last decade. This paper introduces a technology-circuit co-design approach that realizes two motion computations occurring at the retina's output, offering broad utility for vision-driven decision-making in dynamic settings. Simulations conducted on the GlobalFoundries 22nm node demonstrate that leveraging recent breakthroughs in semiconductor chip stacking enables the fabrication of these retina-inspired circuits on existing image sensing platforms. Consequently, Integrated Retinal Functionality in Image Sensors (IRIS) technology has the potential to propel advancements in machine vision, specifically for applications requiring robust, high-speed, energy-efficient, and low-bandwidth real-time decision-making.

Jellyfish galaxies serve as fascinating examples of galaxies experiencing ram-pressure stripping (RPS) within dense environments, characterized by striking star-forming knots within their disks and trailing tails. Using Gemini GMOS/IFU data, we examined the ionized gas properties of five jellyfish galaxies located in massive clusters: MACSJ0916-JFG1 ($z=0.330$), MACSJ1752-JFG2 ($z=0.353$), A2744-F0083 ($z=0.303$), MACSJ1258-JFG1 ($z=0.342$), and MACSJ1720-JFG1 ($z=0.383$). BPT diagrams reveal that the gas ionization in these systems results from diverse mechanisms, including star formation, active galactic nuclei (AGN), or a combination of both. The radial velocity distributions of the ionized gas largely align with the galaxies' disk rotation, although a few high-velocity components in the tails indicate RPS activity. In most star-forming regions, the mean gas velocity dispersion remains below 50 \kms, except near AGNs or shock-heated areas, suggesting that the ionized gas in these regions is dynamically cold. The integrated star formation rates (SFRs) for these galaxies span from $7~{\rm M_{\odot}~{\rm yr^{-1}}}$ to $35~{\rm M_{\odot}~{\rm yr^{-1}}}$, with tail SFRs ranging from $0.6~{\rm M_{\odot}~{\rm yr^{-1}}}$ to $16~{\rm M_{\odot}~{\rm yr^{-1}}}$; these values are significantly higher than those observed in local universe jellyfish galaxies. These elevated SFRs suggest that RPS drives intense star formation in these extreme systems. Furthermore, phase-space diagrams indicate that jellyfish galaxies with greater stellar masses and residing in clusters with higher velocity dispersions tend to exhibit more enhanced star formation. While the gas kinematics and dynamical states of these galaxies resemble those found in the local universe, their star formation rates are markedly higher.

Scintillation in compact radio sources arises from the interference of images produced by multipath propagation, offering insights into the intervening scattering plasma as well as the velocities of both the emitting source and the scattering screen. In the case of FRB20201124A, a repeating fast radio burst that experienced a phase of extreme activity, we detected numerous bursts using observations from the upgraded Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (uGMRT) and the Effelsberg 100\,m Radio Telescope. Bursts occurring close together in time exhibit similar scintillation patterns. By correlating the spectra of burst pairs, we determined scintillation timescales of $14.3\pm1.2$\,min at Effelsberg (1370\,MHz) and $7\pm2$\,min at uGMRT (650\,MHz). The scintillation bandwidth, normalized to 1\,GHz, is $0.5\pm0.1$\,MHz. The inferred interstellar scintillation velocity at Effelsberg is $V_{\mathrm{ISS}}\approx (59\pm7) \sqrt{d_{l}/2\,\rm{kpc}}~{\rm km~s}^{-1}$, which exceeds Earth's orbital velocity for any screen located beyond a lens distance of $d_{l} \gtrsim 400\,$pc. Based on the measured bandwidth, FRB20201124A exhibits comparatively lower scattering than nearby pulsars, being underscattered by a factor of approximately 30 or 1200 relative to the NE2001 and YMW16 model predictions, respectively. This underscattering, combined with the observed scintillation velocity, supports the existence of a scattering screen located closer to Earth at $d_{l} \sim 400\,$pc, rather than at the 2\,kpc spiral arm, which NE2001 identifies as the primary scattering source. Future measurements could determine the screen's distance, geometry, and velocity by modeling annual variations in $V_{\rm ISS}$, utilizing inter-station time delays, or conducting interferometric observations. Measurements of scintillation and scattering in FRBs may aid in refining Galactic electron density models, especially within the Galactic halo or at high Galactic latitudes.

We establish three distinct "codes" for trees through bijections that arise naturally from Tutte's Matrix Tree Theorem, offering significant advantages over Prufer's 1918 construction. The first algorithm provides an explicit bijection inherent in Orlin's constructive proof of Cayley's formula (originally discovered by Borchardt). The second relies on Knuth's proof, while the third implements Joyal's pseudo-bijective approach, which aligns with a prior method by Egecioglu and Remmel. For each code, we present at least two algorithms: one utilizing direct, hands-on manipulation of the tree structure, and the other employing combinatorial and linear algebraic operations on a matrix.

This note investigates whether quantum computational models featuring adaptive measurements can be emulated by those utilizing postselected measurements. We support an affirmative answer to this inquiry and demonstrate that adaptive measurements can indeed be simulated through postselection. Furthermore, we explore significant implications of this finding, including the capacity to resolve #P problems.

Phase retrieval is typically a non-linear, non-convex problem where algorithms often encounter local minima. This study addresses scenarios where measurement samples, usually found in small and disjoint subsets, are coherently linked—a condition well-suited for antenna measurement objectives. We examine two measurement configurations capable of providing this additional coherence: multi-probe systems and holographic setups utilizing multiple reference signals. Several mathematical formulations for this phase retrieval problem are proposed. The most straightforward approach models the issue as a linear system resembling an eigenvalue problem, requiring the identification of a unique non-trivial null-space vector. Consequently, accurate phase reconstruction from partially coherent data becomes feasible through robust solution methods and careful quality assessment. Under ideal, noise-free conditions, the necessary sampling density remains below twice the number of unknowns, though noise and other errors slightly elevate this requirement. Simulations involving Gaussian random matrices and practical antenna measurement cases confirm that the proposed method enables reliable phase reconstruction.

On-the-job learning involves acquiring knowledge continuously within a production setting and an open environment, requiring the system to autonomously handle previously unseen situations and elements. Dialogue systems appear particularly well-suited for this approach, as they can leverage user interactions to gather feedback and iteratively refine their components. Although several dialogue systems implementing on-the-job learning have been constructed and assessed, no comprehensive evaluation methodology currently exists. Consequently, this paper introduces the first general framework for evaluating such systems. Furthermore, we present a task-oriented dialogue system that enhances its natural language capabilities through ongoing user engagement, and we subsequently assess this system using the proposed methodology.

This study presents a measurement of observables sensitive to spin correlations in $t\bar{t}$ production, utilizing 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of $pp$ collision data at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV collected by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. Differential cross-sections are determined for events containing exactly one electron and one oppositely charged muon, as functions of the azimuthal opening angle and the absolute pseudorapidity difference between the lepton candidates in the laboratory frame. Additionally, the azimuthal opening angle is analyzed as a function of the $t\bar{t}$ system's invariant mass. These measured cross-sections are compared against predictions from various NLO Monte Carlo generators and fixed-order calculations. The observed spin correlation level is slightly higher than what the employed generators predict. While the data align well with one specific NLO fixed-order calculation, they show poorer agreement with higher-order predictions. Furthermore, a search for the pair production of supersymmetric top squarks decaying into Standard Model top quarks and light neutralinos is conducted using these leptonic observables. At the 95% confidence level, top squark masses ranging from 170 to 230 GeV are largely excluded for kinematically allowed neutralino masses.

Imaging systems that measure far-field intensity are constrained by Rayleigh's curse, a resolution limit imposed by the finite aperture of the optical setup. Previous proof-of-concept studies and certain two-dimensional experiments have demonstrated that spatial mode demultiplexing (SPADE) maximizes collected field information, thereby achieving resolution that surpasses the Rayleigh criterion. To date, SPADE methods have relied on resolving the lateral splitting of a Gaussian wavefunction. In this work, we examine a scenario involving a bi-photon source generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion, where a horizontal separation is applied to one of the photons. We demonstrate that a separation introduced in the signal photon arm can be super-resolved through coincidence measurements following the projection of both photons onto Hermite-Gauss modes. Notably, the Fisher information linked to this measurement is enhanced by a factor of $\sqrt{K}$ compared to standard SPADE techniques, where $K$ represents the Schmidt number of the two-photon state, a metric quantifying the spatial entanglement between the photons.

This paper demonstrates the existence of a broad class of novel, nontrivial, and smooth traveling waves for the 2D Euler equation located at an arbitrarily small distance from the Couette flow within $H^s$ (where $s<3/2$) regarding vorticity. The velocity of these waves scales as order 1 relative to this distance. These findings stand in sharp contrast to the high-regularity setting in Gevrey spaces (referenced in arXiv:1306.5028), which features an inviscid damping mechanism causing perturbations to relax back toward nearby shear flows. Additionally, this work complements the established result that no nontrivial traveling waves exist in $H^{\frac{3}{2}+}$ neighborhoods of the Couette flow (referenced in arXiv:1004.5149).

This study extends a maximum theorem by Morgan and Scalzo and presents minimax inequality results equivalent to the renowned Ky Fan inequality. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the existence of Nash equilibria established by Morgan and Scalzo corresponds to a classical result found in the literature.

Let $W_{t}$ denote planar Brownian motion initiated at the origin, and let $\theta$ represent the first exit time from the unit disk $D_{1}$. Define
\[
\mu_{ \theta } ( x,\epsilon) =\frac{1}{\pi\epsilon^{ 2} }\int_{0}^{ \theta
}1_{\{ B( x,\epsilon)\}}( W_{t})\,dt,
\]
and let $\mu^{ \ast}_{ \theta }(\epsilon)=\sup_{x\in D_{1}}\mu_{ \theta } ( x,\epsilon)$. We demonstrate that the quantity
\[
\sqrt{\mu^{\ast}_{\theta} (\epsilon)}-\sqrt{2/\pi} \left(\log \epsilon^{-1}-
\frac{1}{2}\log\log \epsilon^{-1}\right)
\]
is tight.

A *proper $t$-edge-coloring* of a graph $G$ refers to a mapping $\alpha: E(G) \rightarrow \{1,\ldots,t\}$ that utilizes every color in the set and assigns distinct colors to any pair of adjacent edges $e, e^{\prime} \in E(G)$. Given a proper edge-coloring $\alpha$ of $G$ and a vertex $v \in V(G)$, the *spectrum of vertex $v$*, denoted $S(v, \alpha)$, comprises the collection of all colors assigned to edges incident to $v$. The *deficiency of $\alpha$ at vertex $v$*, written as $def(v, \alpha)$, represents the minimum count of integers required to be added to $S(v, \alpha)$ to create an interval. Consequently, the *deficiency $def(G, \alpha)$ of a proper edge-coloring $\alpha$ of $G$* is defined as the sum $\sum_{v \in V(G)} def(v, \alpha)$. The *deficiency of a graph $G$*, symbolized by $def(G)$, is determined by $def(G) = \min_{\alpha} def(G, \alpha)$, where the minimum is calculated across all feasible proper edge-colorings of $G$. For a graph $G$, $w_{def}(G)$ and $W_{def}(G)$ denote the smallest and largest values of $t$, respectively, for which a proper $t$-edge-coloring $\alpha$ exists such that $def(G, \alpha) = def(G)$. This study establishes bounds for $w_{def}(G)$ and $W_{def}(G)$. Specifically, it demonstrates that for any natural number $l$, there exists a graph $G$ where $def(G) > 0$ and $W_{def}(G) - w_{def}(G) \geq l$. It is established that for the complete graph $K_{2n+1}$, $def(K_{2n+1}) = n$ (where $n \in \mathbb{N}$). Recently, Borowiecka-Olszewska, Drgas-Burchardt, and Ha{\l}uszczak proposed a conjecture regarding the deficiency of near-complete graphs: if $n \in \mathbb{N}$, then $def(K_{2n+1} - e) = n - 1$. This paper validates that conjecture.

MimbleWimble (MW) represents a privacy-focused cryptocurrency technology distinguished by its unique security and scalability attributes compared to similar protocols. This work examines these properties and introduces a model-driven verification framework designed to certify the correctness of MW implementations. Specifically, we propose an idealized model central to this verification process and define precise sufficient conditions that ensure the model validates relevant security characteristics of MW. Given that MW relies on a consensus protocol, we develop a Z specification for one such protocol and provide an excerpt of the generated $\{log\}$ prototype. This executable model facilitates simulations, enabling the analysis of protocol behavior without the need for low-level programming implementation. Finally, we evaluate the current state of development for the Grin and Beam implementations of MW.

This work examines the capacity of a discrete-time optical fiber model based on the split-step Fourier method (SSFM), focusing on its dependence on the signal-to-noise ratio ($\text{SNR}$) and the number of distance segments, $K$. Analysis reveals that when $K \geq \text{SNR}^{2/3}$ and $\text{SNR} \to \infty$, the capacity of the resulting continuous-space lossless model is lower-bounded by $\frac{1}{2}\log_2(1+\text{SNR}) - \frac{1}{2} + o(1)$, where $o(1)$ vanishes as $\text{SNR}$ increases. As $K$ approaches infinity, the inter-symbol interference (ISI) diminishes to zero via the law of large numbers, causing the SSFM model to converge toward a diagonal phase noise model. Consequently, unlike the discrete-space model which offers only a single signal degree-of-freedom (DoF) at high powers, the continuous-space model supports at least half of the input dimension $n$ in terms of DoFs. This rate is achievable through intensity-modulation and direct detection. Additionally, the pre-log factor of the lower bound for $K = \sqrt[\delta]{\text{SNR}}$ is generally expressed as a function of $\delta$.

Further analysis shows that as the nonlinearity parameter $\gamma \to \infty$, the capacity of the continuous-space model approaches $\frac{1}{2}\log_2(1+\text{SNR}) + o(1)$. The study also considers the SSFM model where the dispersion matrix remains independent of $K$. Under these conditions, with $K = \sqrt[\delta]{\text{SNR}}$ for $\delta > 3$ and $\text{SNR} \to \infty$, the capacity is found to be $\frac{1}{2n}\log_2(1+\text{SNR}) + O(1)$, indicating that this model possesses only one DoF. Finally, numerical simulations of the SSFM model employing back-propagation equalization demonstrate that the maximum achievable information rates (AIRs) follow a double-ascent curve.

This study tackles two critical estimation challenges in linear systems: system identification and model-free state estimation. Specifically, it focuses on ARMAX models with unknown parameters. First, we present a reinforcement learning algorithm for system identification that ensures guaranteed consistency. This algorithm is subsequently leveraged to offer a new approach to model-free state estimation. Finally, these findings are utilized to address the model-free Linear Quadratic Gaussian (LQG) control problem within the reinforcement learning framework.

This study focuses on human activity classification within an indoor radar framework. Human movements produce nonstationary radar returns that manifest as Doppler and micro-Doppler signals. By applying time-frequency (TF) analysis to micro-Doppler signals, it is possible to identify subtle motion variations by accurately exposing the velocity components of distinct body parts. This paper investigates radar-based activity monitoring using a TF-driven machine learning strategy that leverages both temporal and spatial dimensions. The proposed method more effectively captures diverse human motion representations within joint-variable data domains, facilitated by receiver-side beamforming. Data acquisition was conducted via real-time measurements at 77 GHz utilizing four receive antennas, followed by the analysis of micro-Doppler signatures through a machine learning algorithm to classify walking patterns. The results demonstrate the efficacy of this multi-antenna approach in distinguishing and categorizing two individuals walking in opposite directions.

We introduce a supervised method for detecting style shifts in documents, designed to identify the presence of such changes and pinpoint their exact locations. This approach integrates TF-IDF document representations with task-specific engineered features, utilizing an ensemble of diverse classifiers—SVM, Random Forest, AdaBoost, MLP, and LightGBM—to generate predictions. Upon detecting a style change, the model applies a recursive process to determine the precise positions of the shifts. This methodology secured the winning position for the PAN@CLEF 2018 Style Change Detection task.

The emergence of multiple SARS-CoV-2 variants has driven successive waves of COVID-19, each exhibiting distinct effects on patients' respiratory health. This study investigates whether acoustic signals captured from infected individuals contain computable patterns capable of identifying the specific virus variant. We examined the Coswara dataset, which comprises recordings from three groups: healthy individuals, COVID-19 patients during the Delta variant's dominance, and patients during the Omicron surge. Our results indicate that various sound types—including speech, breathing, and coughs—display significant acoustic feature variations when comparing Omicron and Delta infections. Statistical analysis reveals that the area under the curve (AUC) for distinguishing between these two variants significantly exceeds random chance. By fusing scores across multiple sound categories, we achieved an AUC of 89%, with 52.4% sensitivity at 95% specificity. Furthermore, a hierarchical three-class model successfully categorized data as either healthy or COVID-19 positive, and subsequently distinguished between Delta and Omicron variants among positive cases, yielding high accuracy. These findings propose novel methodologies for developing sound-based diagnostic tools for COVID-19.

This study details the synthesis and characterization of superconducting Bi$_2$PdPt, a novel compound within the Bi-Pd family renowned for hosting both topological surface states and superconductivity. The material adopts a hexagonal crystal structure belonging to the $P6_3/mmc$ space group. Comprehensive analyses utilizing transport, magnetization, and specific heat techniques establish bulk superconductivity with a transition temperature of \textit{T}$_{C}$ = 4.0(1) K, indicative of a moderate coupling regime.

Aspect-based sentiment classification (ABSC) represents a difficult subfield of sentiment analysis that is severely hindered by class imbalance. Current approaches typically analyze sentences in isolation, neglecting domain-level inter-sentence relationships, which limits their ability to address imbalance effectively. Intuitively, sentences within the same domain often share high-level semantic connections; leveraging the interaction of these features can enhance semantic representations and better capture similarities and nuances. Motivated by this, we introduce a plug-and-play Pairwise Semantic Interaction (PSI) module. This module accepts pairs of sentences as input, deriving interactive information by learning their semantic vectors. It then employs distinct gating mechanisms to emphasize critical semantic features for each sentence. Furthermore, adversarial interactions between the vectors are utilized to ensure that the semantic representations of the two sentences become more distinguishable. Experiments across four ABSC datasets demonstrate that PSI outperforms many competitive state-of-the-art baselines in most scenarios and significantly mitigates the issue of class imbalance.

This paper introduces ExplainDR, a neural-symbolic learning-based classification model for diabetic retinopathy designed to be both explainable and interpretable. To ensure explainability, we incorporate a high-level symbolic representation into the decision-making process. Specifically, we develop a human-readable symbolic format that adheres to a taxonomy of diabetic retinopathy features related to eye health. These interpretable features are then integrated into the disease prediction process. Experiments on a diabetic retinopathy classification dataset demonstrate that the proposed ExplainDR method achieves promising performance compared to state-of-the-art techniques applied to the IDRiD dataset, while simultaneously delivering interpretability and explainability.

This article reviews knowledge distillation techniques, specifically examining their suitability for retail banking. Predictive machine learning models within banking, particularly in risk and control, often face regulatory and technical constraints that limit their complexity. Knowledge distillation offers a solution by enhancing the performance of simple models without increasing their computational burden, leveraging outputs from more complex, high-performing teacher models. By analyzing recent advancements, we identify three primary approaches: Soft Targets, Sample Selection, and Data Augmentation. We evaluate a subset of these techniques on open-source datasets before testing them on real-world use cases at BPCE, a leading French retail bank. Ultimately, we demonstrate that knowledge distillation can boost model performance while maintaining their original simplicity and structure.

Selecting an appropriate decision threshold is a critical yet difficult challenge in classification tasks. If the decision boundary is not carefully selected, even a highly accurate model will fail to perform effectively. In imbalanced classification scenarios, where one class significantly dominates the other, traditional threshold selection methods often yield poor results. Furthermore, even when thresholds are determined using standard machine learning strategies like SVMs or decision trees, they may eventually fail due to dynamically changing databases or the presence of highly similar identity features, as seen in face recognition and person re-identification systems.
