To address the need for adaptive threshold selection in imbalanced classification and growing database sizes, an online optimization-based statistical feature learning technique has been developed and evaluated on the LFW and self-prepared athletes datasets. This adaptive approach achieved a 12–45% improvement in model accuracy compared to fixed thresholds (0.3, 0.5, 0.7) typically selected through trial and error in classification and identification tasks. The complete algorithm source code is available at: https://github.com/Varat7v2/adaptive-threshold.

This expository piece provides the mathematical foundation for the braid representation calculator presented in arXiv:2212.00831, where such representations define the logic gates accessible to a topological quantum computer for handling encoded qubits. Assuming minimal prior knowledge of category theory, we begin by revisiting the concept of a ribbon fusion category (RFC) and gathering the essential definitions. We then examine how specific RFCs emerge from the representation theory of quantum groups. Finally, we investigate braiding within these categories in depth, given its critical role in the associated quantum computing applications.

Federated Learning (FL) is an emerging distributed machine learning paradigm that enables thousands of edge devices to train models locally without centrally uploading data. However, in real-world resource-constrained environments, system heterogeneity frequently leads to stragglers, which in turn cause significant accuracy drops. To address these challenges, we introduce FedSAE, a novel self-adaptive federated framework that automatically adjusts training tasks and actively selects participants to mitigate performance degradation. First, FedSAE utilizes complete historical training data to predict the affordable workload for each device, thereby estimating reliability and self-adaptively tuning the training load per client in every round. Second, the framework integrates Active Learning to dynamically select participants; by evaluating devices based on their training loss, the server chooses clients with higher value for the global model, thus reducing communication overhead and accelerating convergence. Experimental results demonstrate that in highly heterogeneous systems, FedSAE converges faster than the standard FedAvg approach. Furthermore, across several federated datasets, FedSAE outperforms FedAvg by improving test accuracy by 26.7% and reducing stragglers by an average of 90.3%.

Existing natural language interfaces for self-tracking applications typically rely on custom implementations tailored to specific tracking themes and data formats, limiting their generalizability and scalability across the vast landscape of self-tracking possibilities. Training machine learning models for this domain is difficult given the extensive diversity of topics and data structures involved. This paper introduces a new NLP task designed for self-tracking that retrieves both closed and open-ended information from retrospective activity logs formatted as plain text, alongside a domain-agnostic NLU framework powered by GPT-3. To overcome the cold-start challenge when initiating a new tracking topic, the framework enhances prompts with synthetic data to convert the task into a 10-shot learning scenario. Preliminary results indicate that our method significantly surpasses baseline question-answering models. Furthermore, we explore potential future application areas where NLP and HCI researchers could collaborate.

A variety of object-oriented programming languages now incorporate pattern matching, ranging from historical implementations like Scala and Ceylon to recent integrations in Java, Kotlin, TypeScript, and Flow. However, applying pattern matching to generic class hierarchies frequently triggers confusing type errors across these systems, despite such scenarios occurring naturally in tasks like manipulating typed abstract syntax trees. To address this, compilers must implement subtyping reconstruction, a capability that recovers subtyping information revealed at runtime during the matching process. This paper introduces cDOT, a novel calculus within the Dependent Object Types (DOT) family designed as a formal basis for subtyping reconstruction. Building upon pDOT, which underpins Scala, cDOT can represent sophisticated object-oriented constructs including generic inheritance, type constructor variance, F-bounded polymorphism, and first-class recursive modules. Furthermore, we show that subtyping reconstruction encompasses GADTs by successfully encoding $\lambda_{2,G\mu}$, a standard constraint-based GADT calculus, into cDOT.

Parallel-in-time resolution of evolutionary equations has become a compelling research area, with numerous algorithms developed over the last twenty years. Among these, methods utilizing block $\alpha$-circulant preconditioning have demonstrated significant potential, particularly for wave propagation scenarios. By applying the fast Fourier transform to decompose the circulant matrices, these preconditioned iterations can be executed efficiently using a diagonalization approach, enabling direct parallelization across all temporal levels. While recent years have seen extensive efforts to analyze the convergence of such iterations by examining the spectral radius of the iteration matrix—often resulting in specific studies for each time-integrator—this paper introduces a unified convergence analysis for the algorithm applied to the equation $u'+Au=f$, where the spectrum $\sigma(A)$ lies in the complex upper half-plane. We demonstrate that for any one-step method, including Runge-Kutta schemes with stability function $\mathcal{R}(z)$, the global error decay rate is bounded by $\alpha/(1-\alpha)$, assuming the method is stable (i.e., $\max_{\lambda\in\sigma(A)}|\mathcal{R}(\Delta t\lambda)|\leq1$). For linear multistep methods, this bound adjusts to $c\alpha/(1-c\alpha)$, where $c\geq1$ is a constant inherent to the specific multistep method. Crucially, our proof depends solely on the stability of the time-integrator, and the resulting estimate remains independent of both the step size $\Delta t$ and the spectrum $\sigma(A)$.

Modified gravitational wave propagation serves as a definitive signature of gravitational modifications at cosmological scales and represents the most promising observable for validating such theories. Recent gravitational wave observations have enabled initial investigations into this phenomenon, prompting a brief review of two promising testing methods. We demonstrate that the current detector network can already achieve meaningful precision in estimating the $\Xi_0$ parameter—which characterizes modified wave propagation, where $\Xi_{0, {\rm GR}} = 1$—and that next-generation facilities like the Einstein Telescope will enable sub-percent level measurements.

The interaction line where a fluid, liquid, and solid meet is a widespread phenomenon, making the determination of the maximum velocity for liquid wetting or dewetting on a solid a practically significant challenge. Previous continuum modeling studies indicate that this maximum speed corresponds to a critical capillary number ($Ca_{\mathrm{crit}}$) derived from steady-state solutions of the governing equations; beyond this threshold, no steady state exists. Below $Ca_{\mathrm{crit}}$, both stable and unstable steady solutions are present, forming a fold bifurcation where their branches intersect when plotted against $Ca$. However, the role of this bifurcation structure in transient dynamics remains largely unexplored. This article introduces a computational model and applies dynamical systems theory to demonstrate the critical influence of unstable solutions on transient behavior. By perturbing the stable state using eigenmodes from a linear stability analysis, the study reveals that the unstable branch dictates the eventual dynamical outcomes and that the system can become unstable even when $Ca < Ca_{\mathrm{crit}}$ due to finite amplitude perturbations. Additionally, it is shown that for $Ca > Ca_{\mathrm{crit}}$, trajectories in phase space closely track the unstable branch.

Presently, quantum hardware faces constraints due to noise and limited qubit counts. Consequently, a quantum virtual machine that emulates quantum operations on classical systems serves as a crucial instrument for developing and validating quantum algorithms prior to their deployment on actual quantum devices. Various variational quantum algorithms have already been proposed and evaluated on such virtual machines to overcome these hardware limitations. Our objective is to advance these variational approaches toward practical quantum machine learning applications using cutting-edge quantum computers. This paper introduces our quantum virtual machine, Qsun, which operates based on quantum state wave-functions and offers native tools supporting variational quantum algorithms. Specifically, we implement quantum differentiable programming, essential for gradient-based optimization, utilizing the parameter-shift rule. We further present two representative tests in the domain of quantum machine learning: quantum linear regression and quantum neural networks.

Although transformer-based architectures have recently excelled in semantic segmentation, CNN-based methods remain dominant for real-time applications due to the computational overhead of standard transformers. We introduce RTFormer, an efficient dual-resolution transformer designed for real-time segmentation that offers a superior balance between performance and efficiency compared to CNNs. To maximize inference speed on GPU-like hardware, RTFormer employs GPU-Friendly Attention with linear complexity and eliminates the multi-head mechanism. Furthermore, we discovered that cross-resolution attention efficiently captures global context for high-resolution branches by propagating high-level knowledge from low-resolution branches. Extensive experiments on major benchmarks validate RTFormer's effectiveness, achieving state-of-the-art results on Cityscapes, CamVid, and COCOStuff, along with promising performance on ADE20K. The code is available at PaddleSeg: https://github.com/PaddlePaddle/PaddleSeg.

The differential invariant yield of electrons, originating from the semileptonic decays of heavy-flavor hadrons, was measured at midrapidity across central (0–10%), semi-central (30–50%), and peripheral (60–80%) lead-lead (Pb-Pb) collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}=5.02$ TeV. The transverse momentum ($p_\mathrm{T}$) coverage spanned 0.5–26 GeV/$c$ for the 0–10% and 30–50% centrality classes, and 0.5–10 GeV/$c$ for the 60–80% class. Additionally, the production cross section in proton-proton (pp) collisions at $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV was determined within the $0.5<p_\mathrm{T}<10$ GeV/$c$ range. This cross section aligns closely with the upper edge of perturbative QCD uncertainty bands up to $p_\mathrm{T}=5$ GeV/$c$ and approaches the mean value at higher momenta. The nuclear modification factor ($R_{\mathrm{AA}}$) was calculated to assess the deviation of the electron yield from the incoherent superposition of nucleon-nucleon collisions. By analyzing $R_{\mathrm{AA}}$ across various centrality classes, researchers investigated in-medium energy loss for charm and beauty quarks. The results indicate a suppression of $R_{\mathrm{AA}}$ below unity at intermediate $p_\mathrm{T}$, an effect that intensifies in more central collisions. Furthermore, the measured $R_{\mathrm{AA}}$ reflects modifications to nuclear parton distribution functions (PDFs), such as nuclear shadowing, which leads to a reduction in heavy-quark production at low $p_\mathrm{T}$ during heavy-ion collisions at the LHC.

Numerous machine learning tasks can be formulated as minimization problems and addressed effectively through gradient-based methods. However, the emergence of generative models, especially GANs, has sparked interest in solving min-max games, where conventional optimization strategies often fail. Practitioners frequently encounter issues such as a lack of convergence guarantees or the system settling into a non-optimal cycle. These challenges stem from the min-max architecture of the GAN objective, which introduces complex interdependencies between the competing agents. To resolve this, we propose optimizing an alternative objective that bypasses the min-max structure by leveraging the concept of the duality gap from game theory. We establish new convergence guarantees for this approach and demonstrate that the resulting limit point yields superior solutions compared to existing techniques.

We report the outcomes and discoveries of the inaugural First Nuanced Arabic Dialect Identification Shared Task (NADI), which comprises two subtasks: country-level dialect classification (Subtask 1) and province-level sub-dialect categorization (Subtask 2). The dataset encompasses 100 provinces across 21 Arab nations, sourced from Twitter. Consequently, NADI represents the first shared task focused on naturally occurring, fine-grained dialectal text at a sub-national level. A total of 61 teams from 25 countries registered to compete, highlighting significant community interest. The task received 47 submissions for Subtask 1 from 18 teams and 9 submissions for Subtask 2 from 9 teams.

In this study, we compute the topological entanglement entropy for the BTZ black hole and observe that it matches the value found in fractional quantum Hall states. This equivalence implies that BTZ black holes possess the same topological order as fractional quantum Hall systems, thereby demonstrating the presence of long-range entanglement in these black holes.

This paper aims to generate robust parameters for distinguishing point distributions and dynamical systems by employing diverse metrics, including those in Euclidean and Sobolev-type function spaces. Our primary approach involves analyzing the geometric evolution of hypergraphs formed as radial parameters expand, using a suitable metric within the data point space. Subsequently, we apply Lebesgue and Sobolev norms to compare the fundamental geometric signals derived from this dynamics.

We have developed a computationally efficient frequency-domain waveform tailored for generic circular compact object binaries, specifically those containing neutron stars. Orbital precession is resolved on the radiation reaction timescale and subsequently transformed into the frequency domain to map the non-precessional waveform from the source frame to the laboratory frame. This approach to orbital precession differs from that used for precessional binary black holes because the effective spin parameter ($\chi_{\rm eff}$) is not conserved due to the spin-induced quadrupole moments inherent to neutron stars. Our results demonstrate that the new waveform achieves a mismatch of $\le 10^{-4}$ relative to numerically evolved precessional waveforms for neutron star-black hole systems in at least 90% of configurations, assuming the component masses and spin magnitudes are fixed while initial spin directions are randomized. We anticipate this waveform will be valuable for probing the nature of mass-gap objects, such as the one identified in GW 190814, by measuring their spin-induced quadrupole moments, particularly if these objects possess rapid spins. Furthermore, it is applicable for testing black hole mimickers in precessional binary black hole events, provided these candidates exhibit nontrivial spin-induced quadrupole moments.

Upcoming time-domain initiatives, including the Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time, will significantly expand the number of observed supernovae and other optical transients, necessitating novel data-driven approaches for analyzing their photometric light curves. In response, we introduce PISCOLA ("Python for Intelligent Supernova-COsmology Light-curve Analysis"), an open-source tool that employs Gaussian Processes to fit light curves without relying on pre-existing templates. Validated through extensive simulations of Type Ia supernovae, PISCOLA demonstrates the ability to accurately recover rest-frame peak magnitudes even with survey cadences as sparse as 7 days. When compared against the established SALT2 fitter using real observational data, PISCOLA yields only minor yet statistically significant discrepancies in various light-curve parameters. As a practical demonstration, we applied Non-Negative Matrix Factorization to PISCOLA-derived rest-frame light curves of Type Ia supernovae from the Pantheon sample, achieving performance comparable to standard fitters. Additionally, we derived a Type Ia supernova colour law spanning approximately 3500 to 7000 Å using PISCOLA fits, finding consistent results with both the SALT2 colour law and reddening laws characterized by a total-to-selective extinction ratio $R_V \lesssim 3.1$.

Discourse that is coherent differs from a simple assemblage of sentences because it adheres to various constraints, such as word selection, the logical connection between events, and alignment with general world knowledge. This study investigates whether neural language models internalize these constraints. We develop a flexible suite of tests that examine different dimensions of discourse and dialogue coherence. Contrary to most prior evaluations that focus primarily on sentence reordering, our approach targets specific linguistic features to enable a more granular analysis of coherence and determine what a language modeling objective captures. By extending the evaluation framework introduced by Marvin and Linzen (2018) from syntax to broader linguistic phenomena, we demonstrate that this paradigm is equally effective for assessing the linguistic qualities that define coherence.

Despite over ten years of effort, directly observing the odd-frequency triplet pairing state in superconducting hybrid structures has remained elusive. We propose a feasible experimental setup capable of unambiguously detecting the zero-energy peak arising from proximity-induced equal-spin superconducting triplet correlations. Our theoretical study focuses on a two-dimensional Josephson junction operating in the diffusive regime, where a normal metal layer is sandwiched between two ferromagnetic layers featuring spiral magnetization. By applying an external magnetic field perpendicular to the junction, vortices form within the normal metal. Calculations of the energy and spatially resolved density of states, alongside the pair potential, demonstrate that remarkably, only triplet Cooper pairs persist within the vortex cores. These isolated odd-frequency triplet correlations generate distinct zero-energy peaks in the local density of states, which can be identified via tunneling spectroscopy. Furthermore, the diffusive regime considered here excludes the possibility that Andreev bound states in the vortex core contribute to these zero-energy peaks.

This work investigates low-rank tensor approximations, specifically addressing tensor train (TT) and Tucker decompositions, alongside tree tensor networks and broader tensor network structures. For the TT decomposition, we present a bicriteria $(1 + \eps)$-approximation algorithm featuring a small bicriteria rank and a running time of $O(q \cdot \nnz(A))$ (excluding lower-order terms), which surpasses the additive error method described in \cite{huber2017randomized}. We further demonstrate how to adapt the algorithm from \cite{huber2017randomized} into a relative error framework; however, converting it to a $(1 + \eps)$-approximation with bicriteria rank $r$ inevitably results in a runtime of $O(qr^2 \cdot \nnz(A)) + n \cdot \poly(qk/\eps)$. To our knowledge, this study represents the first polynomial-time approach to relative error approximation for tensor train decomposition. Our primary innovation involves a technique for deriving subspace embeddings with row counts polynomial in $q$ for matrices formed by flattening a tensor train of $q$ tensors. We generalize this algorithm to tree tensor networks and further extend it to general tensor networks defined by arbitrary graphs. This extension leverages the result in \cite{ms08_simulating_quantum_tensor_contraction}, establishing that a general tensor network of rank $k$ can be contracted into a binary tree network of rank $k^{O(\deg(G)\tw(G))}$, thereby reducing the problem to the tree tensor network case. Additionally, we introduce new fixed-parameter tractable algorithms for TT, Tucker, and CP decompositions that are more streamlined than those in \cite{swz19_tensor_low_rank} because they avoid polynomial system solvers. Our method employing Gaussian subspace embeddings with precisely $k$ rows (resulting in an exponentially small success probability) may also hold independent interest.

Consider a Calabi-Yau threefold $X$. A conifold transition involves first contracting $X$ along disjoint rational curves possessing normal bundles of type $(-1,-1)$, followed by smoothing the resulting singular complex space $\bar{X}$ into a new compact complex manifold $Y$. This manifold $Y$ is known as a Clemens manifold and may fail to be Kähler. We demonstrate that any small smoothing $Y$ of $\bar{X}$ satisfies the $\partial\bar{\partial}$-lemma. Furthermore, we establish that the pure Hodge structure of weight three on $H^3(Y)$ is polarized via the cup product. These findings address several inquiries posed by R. Friedman.

This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework of pyramid Markov processes to address fundamental and open issues regarding blockchain selfish mining within a rigorous mathematical context. We begin by outlining a generalized model of selfish mining that incorporates both a two-block leading competitive criterion and a novel economic incentive mechanism. Subsequently, we construct a pyramid Markov process, demonstrating that it is irreducible and positive recurrent, with a stationary probability vector that is matrix-geometric and possesses an explicitly representable rate matrix. Furthermore, we utilize this stationary vector to analyze how numerous orphan blocks contribute to the waste of computational resources. Additionally, we establish a pyramid Markov reward process to examine the long-term average profits of both honest and dishonest mining pools. As a secondary outcome, we develop three approximate Markov processes and offer new insights into the Markov chain and revenue analysis presented in the seminal work by Eyal and Sirer (2014). It is worth noting that pyramid Markov (reward) processes may开辟 a new pathway for researching blockchain selfish mining. Consequently, we hope that the methodologies and findings presented here will illuminate the field of blockchain selfish mining, potentially fostering a series of promising future research endeavors.

Electromyogram (EMG) pattern recognition is valuable for classifying hand gestures and movements in human-machine interfaces and prosthetics, yet it often suffers from reliability issues due to changes in limb position. A common solution is dual-stage classification, which uses additional sensors to identify limb position and then selects from multiple position-specific gesture classifiers. Although this improves performance, it increases model complexity and memory usage, making it challenging to deploy in resource-constrained wearable devices. This paper introduces a memory-efficient approach that fuses accelerometer and EMG signals using a hyperdimensional computing model to emulate dual-stage classification. We present two methods for encoding accelerometer features as keys to retrieve position-specific parameters from multiple superimposed models. Validation on a dataset comprising 13 gestures across 8 limb positions yielded a classification accuracy of up to 93.34%, representing a 17.79% improvement over a model trained on EMG alone. This performance is achieved with only a marginal increase in memory footprint compared to a single-position model, while utilizing 8 times less memory than a traditional dual-stage architecture.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have significantly advanced single image super-resolution; however, substantial information loss during image downscaling makes further improvements, particularly for large upscaling factors, extremely difficult. This paper investigates a novel approach known as reference-conditioned super-resolution, which supplies a reference image with desirable high-resolution textures alongside the low-resolution input. Our primary focus is on transferring these high-resolution textures to the super-resolution output without requiring content similarity between the reference and target images, distinguishing our method from prior example-based techniques. Drawing inspiration from image stylization, we tackle this challenge through neural texture transfer. We have developed an end-to-end trainable deep model that adaptively merges content from the low-resolution image with texture patterns from the reference image to produce detail-rich results. Additionally, we introduce a benchmark dataset for general reference-based super-resolution research, featuring paired reference and low-resolution inputs with varying levels of similarity. Both objective and subjective evaluations confirm the significant potential of utilizing reference images and demonstrate the superiority of our results compared to other state-of-the-art methods.

The evolution of language-centric Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers significant social-good potential, particularly when applied to educational tools. Improving mathematics education across various fields is essential for fostering critical thinking and problem-solving abilities in young learners. As conversational AI systems mature, they are increasingly capable of assisting students in mastering fundamental mathematical concepts. This study introduces a task-oriented Spoken Dialogue System (SDS) designed to facilitate play-based learning of basic math for early childhood education. The system was assessed through real-world school deployments where students engaged with early math concepts via multimodal interactions. We examine efforts to enhance the SDS pipeline for math instruction by investigating the use of MathBERT representations to improve the Natural Language Understanding (NLU) module. Furthermore, we conduct an end-to-end evaluation using real-world deployment data from the Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Intent Recognition, and Dialogue Manager (DM) components to analyze how error propagation impacts overall performance in practical scenarios.

The $s$-Club problem determines if an undirected graph $G$ includes a vertex set $S$ with cardinality at least $k$ such that the induced subgraph $G[S]$ has a diameter no greater than $s$. This study examines variations of the $s$-Club problem that impose extra conditions: every vertex in $G[S]$ must belong to at least $\ell$ triangles within $G[S]$, every edge in $G[S]$ must be part of at least $\ell$ triangles within $G[S]$, or the set $S$ must include a specified collection $W$ of seed vertices. We demonstrate that, in general, these variants are W[1]-hard when parameterized by the solution size $k$, rendering them substantially more difficult than the standard unconstrained $s$-Club problem. Conversely, we present fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithms for scenarios where $\ell=1$ and for instances where the subgraph induced by the seed vertices $G[W]$ forms a clique.

This paper reviews the relationships between classical Markov Decision Process (MDP) algorithms and traditional gradient-based convex optimization techniques. Although some of these connections were established as early as the 1980s, they have recently gained significant traction, resulting in more efficient MDP solvers. Specifically, two prominent MDP methods—Value Iteration and Policy Iteration—correspond to first-order and second-order convex optimization approaches, respectively. Furthermore, recent advancements in quasi-Newton methods have inspired new MDP algorithms, including Anderson acceleration. By categorizing MDP algorithms into first-order, second-order, and quasi-Newton frameworks, we aim to deepen our understanding of these methods and leverage recent progress in convex optimization to design novel MDP algorithms.

Although gravity lacks a fully renormalizable quantum field theory, it still permits predictions that extend beyond classical general relativity. With the advent of gravitational wave astronomy, a critical inquiry arises: can we detect measurable quantum deviations from classical gravity, similar to how quantum optics reveals phenomena unexplainable by classical electrodynamics? This study explores quantum signatures within gravitational waves by applying quantum optical techniques. Specifically, squeezed-coherent gravitational waves capable of displaying sub-Poissonian graviton statistics can amplify or diminish interferometer signals, mirroring the effects of quantum squeezing. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Gaussian quantum states of gravitational waves can be reconstructed through measurements on an ensemble of optical fields interacting with a single gravitational wave instance, thereby creating a viable pathway to observe quantum characteristics of gravity that transcend classical general relativity.

This study examines, within a continuous-time framework, how corporate management navigates a dynamic selection between two voluntary disclosure strategies: "candid" (full transparency) and "sparing" (disclosing only items exceeding a dynamic threshold). We demonstrate that candid behavior yields a reputational premium, though it incurs costs because sparing allows managers to shield low values from downgrades. The optimal choice between these strategies, as well as the timing for switching, is influenced by model parameters such as news intensity, pay-for-performance structures, and the timeline to mandatory disclosure. Management receives private news updates via a Poisson process between fixed mandatory reporting dates (e.g., fiscal quarters or years), where the underlying news generation follows a partially observed Black-Scholes model of economic activity. Derived from this background model, a simple ordinary differential equation (ODE) characterizes equilibrium in the resulting piecewise-deterministic system. Under the assumption of an at-most-single switching policy, we find that firms either maintain a candid strategy indefinitely or alternate between candid and sparing approaches in the sequence that maximizes value, a pattern supported by empirical evidence.

Collaborative Metric Learning (CML) has recently become a potent approach for recommendation systems utilizing implicit feedback collaborative filtering. Nevertheless, conventional CML techniques rely on static user and item embeddings, which are insufficient for modeling the intricate and evolving interests of users. Furthermore, current CML extensions either overlook the heterogeneity in user-item interactions—where a single user may favor vastly different items—or neglect latent item-item dependencies, where an item's attractiveness is influenced not just by its inherent traits but also by a user's prior interactions. This paper introduces a hierarchical CML framework that simultaneously models these latent user-item and item-item relationships using implicit data. Drawing inspiration from knowledge graph embedding translation mechanisms and incorporating memory-based attention networks, our method empirically demonstrates the superiority of this joint relational modeling across multiple real-world datasets, outperforming existing CML architectures. Additionally, our experimental results highlight the limitations of current CML relational models when dealing with highly sparse data.

Spontaneous audio captured in real-world, child-centered environments represents one of the most difficult challenges in speech processing. Despite this difficulty, developing models capable of handling such diverse conditions is highly valuable for language acquisition research, which examines both the quantity and quality of speech heard and produced by children, as well as for early diagnosis and assessing remediation outcomes. This paper introduces our approach to creating an open-source neural network designed to classify audio segments into four categories: vocalizations from the child wearing the recorder, vocalizations from other children, adult male speech, and adult female speech. To achieve this, we assembled a diverse collection of child-centered corpora totaling 260 hours of recordings across 10 languages. Our model serves as a foundation for downstream tasks, such as estimating the number of words spoken by adults or the number of linguistic units produced by children. By integrating SincNet filters with a stack of recurrent layers, our architecture significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art Language ENvironment Analysis (LENA) system, which has been widely used in child language studies.

For natural numbers $h$ and $g$, a subset $X$ of the integers $\mathbb{Z}$ is classified as a $B_{h}^{+}[g]$ set if every real number $n$ can be expressed as a sum of $h$ elements from $X$ in at most $g$ ways, where solutions are considered identical if they differ only by the order of the summands. A multiplicative $B_{h}^{\times}[g]$ set is defined similarly using multiplication. This paper establishes that there exists an absolute constant $g \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for any $h \in \mathbb{N}$ and any finite set $A$ of integers, $A$ must contain either a $B_{h}^{+}[g]$ set $B$ or a multiplicative $B_{h}^{\times}[g]$ set $C$ with the property that $\max \{ |B| , |C| \} \gg_{h} |A|^{(1+ \delta_h)/h }$, where $\delta_h > 0$. Furthermore, when $h$ is sufficiently large, we can choose $g = 1$ and ensure $\delta_h \gg (\log \log h)^{1/2 - o(1)}$.

At the LHC, single top quarks are primarily generated via $t$-channel $W$ boson exchange in the process $q + b \rightarrow q' + t$. This mechanism offers a direct probe of the $Wtb$ vertex, enabling the measurement of the CKM matrix element $V_{tb}$ and the constraint of the bottom quark parton distribution function (PDF). Non-factorisable contributions represent the final missing component of next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) corrections. This presentation is divided into two parts: the first examines the significance of these corrections and details the derivation of the necessary amplitudes, while the second compares recent LHC findings with new calculations for proton-proton collisions at $100 \: {\rm TeV}$, the anticipated energy scale of the Future Circular Collider (FCC).

This work introduces receding horizon control strategies for stochastic discrete-time linear systems subject to additive, potentially unbounded disturbances, while strictly adhering to hard constraints on control inputs. The study formulates the selection of an optimal controller within vector spaces of functions, demonstrating that the resulting optimization yields a tractable convex solution. Assuming the system is asymptotically stable in the absence of inputs and noise, we prove that the state variance remains bounded under hard input constraints for any receding horizon implementation. The article includes multiple examples illustrating how necessary quantities for the optimization formulation can be computed off-line, alongside comparative studies that highlight the efficacy of the proposed control strategies.

This study extends the maximal volume estimation techniques originally formulated by Christodoulou and Rovelli for Schwarzschild black holes and by Zhang et al. for non-rotating BTZ black holes to the context of rotating black holes in 2+1 dimensions. Utilizing the Lagrangian approach established by Christodoulou and Rovelli, we derive the equation governing the maximal hypersurface for the rotating BTZ black hole, corroborating these findings with the maximization method previously applied by Bengtsson et al. to Kerr black holes. We contend that the primary contribution to the hypersurface volume originates from a "steady state radius," which is determined by the mass $M$ and the AdS length scale. This radius is also shown to be derivable through independent considerations of vanishing extrinsic curvature. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the volume of this specific segment of the maximal hypersurface, known as the CR volume, is a function of mass, the AdS length scale, and angular momentum $J$. Finally, we calculate the entropy of a scalar field residing on the maximal hypersurface for a near-extremal black hole, proving that it scales proportionally with the black hole's horizon entropy.

This updated version of ZMCintegral introduces multi-function integration capabilities, enabling the GPU-based evaluation of over $10^{3}$ distinct functions. The Python API retains its design from earlier versions. For integrands with fewer than five dimensions, assessing $10^{3}$ integrations on a single Tesla v100 typically requires under 10 minutes. Additionally, performance demonstrates linear scalability as the number of GPUs increases.

In July 2012, the ATLAS and CMS collaborations at CERN's Large Hadron Collider announced the discovery of a Higgs boson with a mass near 125 GeV. A decade later, with datasets representing a thirty-fold increase in Higgs production, researchers have significantly advanced their understanding of the particle's properties. The CMS experiment has since observed the Higgs across various fermionic and bosonic decay modes, confirmed its spin-parity quantum numbers, precisely measured its mass, and quantified its production cross-sections in different channels. This report presents the most current combined analysis of the Higgs boson's properties, featuring the tightest constraints to date on the cross-section for Higgs pair production, derived from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. All findings remain consistent with Standard Model predictions within their uncertainties. However, substantial evidence suggests the Standard Model serves as a low-energy approximation of a more complete theory, with several unresolved issues rooted in Higgs physics. Examining an order of magnitude more Higgs bosons over the next fifteen years is expected to greatly enhance our comprehension of this critical area.

We examine a holographic thermal state perturbed by a scalar operator whose real-time Green's function features exclusively gapped poles. These poles represent the non-hydrodynamic quasinormal modes of a massive scalar fluctuation within a Schwarzschild black brane background. By varying the scalar mass and consequently the dual operator's dimension, general connections emerge among pole-skipping points, critical points, and quasinormal modes. First, this analysis uncovers a link between the position of a specific mode in the infinite quasinormal tower and the count of pole-skipping points that constrain its dispersion relation at imaginary momenta. Second, we analyze, for the first time, the radii of convergence for derivative expansions centered on these gapped quasinormal modes, finding that these radii are upper-bounded by the collection of all pole-skipping points. Additionally, a transition between two distinct classes of critical points occurs at a specific conformal dimension, suggesting a tight relationship between critical points and pole-skipping points within one of these classes. Numerical evidence confirms that these findings also hold for gapped modes associated with vector and tensor operators.

This study validates and compares COLA (COmoving Lagrangian Acceleration) simulations against two established emulators: Bacco and Euclid Emulator 2. The analysis centers on the non-linear response function, defined as the ratio of the non-linear dark matter power spectrum in a specific cosmology to a reference cosmology (Euclid Emulator 2). We examine variations in three parameters: total matter density, the amplitude of primordial scalar perturbations, and the spectral index. Comparing the COLA non-linear response function with results from the emulators across the redshift range $0 \leq z \leq 3$, we observe excellent agreement for scales up to $k \sim 1 \ h$/Mpc, provided deviations from the reference cosmology remain moderate. Additionally, we verify the implementation of massive neutrinos by testing three mass sums ($0.0$, $0.058$, and $0.15$ eV), demonstrating that the three non-linear prescriptions employed in this work align at the $1\%$ level for $k \leq 1 \ h$/Mpc. Furthermore, we incorporate the Effective Field Theory of Dark Energy into our COLA simulations using the $N$-body gauge method. We evaluate two modified gravity models that either enhance or suppress structure growth at small scales, finding that the response function to changes in modified gravity parameters exhibits only weak dependence on cosmological parameters within these models.

Driven by pressing environmental concerns, power systems must integrate substantial levels of renewable energy, necessitating intelligent grid control strategies. This creates large-scale nonlinear optimization challenges for optimal control, often involving hundreds of millions of variables and constraints. Consequently, traditional interior point methods often become computationally unfeasible, primarily because solving the resulting large linear systems is too demanding.

This document tackles the computational limitations of interior point methods when solving security-constrained optimal power flow problems by implementing a reduced-space quasi-Newton interior point method. This approach leverages high-performance computing through the inherent parallelism of the adjoint method. Combining reduced-space IPM with the adjoint method represents a novel strategy for optimal power flow, previously applied only to PDE-constrained optimization. The methodology is well-suited for high-performance architectures because the adjoint method allows for parallel gradient evaluation, as individual contingency scenarios are modeled by independent constraint sets. Preliminary assessments of performance and convergence were conducted to evaluate this reduced-space approach.

The Snowmass 2021 Implementation Task Force was created to assess proposed future accelerator projects across key dimensions including performance, technological readiness, schedule, cost, and environmental impact. To enable uniform comparisons of proposals ranging from Higgs/EW factories to multi-TeV lepton, hadron, and ep collider facilities—whether utilizing traditional or advanced acceleration technologies—corresponding metrics have been established. This report outlines these metrics and the associated processes, alongside the evaluations of future colliders conducted by the Implementation Task Force.

Random noise serves a constructive function in cognitive processing, yielding quantifiable performance gains in both biological agents and simulations. The phenomenon of stochastic facilitation, where additive noise enhances signal transmission within complex systems, has been observed across various neural settings. Nevertheless, current neuroscience research has not sufficiently examined the specific "colours" of neural noise. While extensive literature documents a 1/f pink noise power spectrum across multiple levels, numerous less rigorous studies incorrectly assume white noise without adequate justification. This work provides a brief overview of noise colours and their beneficial applications in other domains. By recognizing that noise is not merely binary, we can more effectively regularize artificial neural networks and re-examine intriguing findings regarding the brain's utilization of noise.

Consider a simple abelian surface $A$ defined over an algebraically closed field $k$. Let $S$ denote the subset of torsion points $x \in A(k)$ for which there exists a genus 2 curve $C$ and a morphism $f: C \to A$ such that $x$ lies in the image of $f$, and a Weierstrass point of $C$ maps to the origin of $A$. This note establishes that when $k$ has characteristic zero, the set $S$ is finite. This result contrasts with the case where $k$ is the algebraic closure of a finite field, in which $S$ coincides with the entire group $A(k)$, as demonstrated by Bogomolov and Tschinkel. Consequently, for $k = \bar{\mathbb{Q}}$, we deduce that the Kummer surface associated with $A$ possesses infinitely many $k$-rational points that do not lie on any rational curve derived from a genus 2 curve in $A$, differing from the scenario over the algebraic closure of a finite field.

Magnetars, a class of isolated neutron stars characterized by ultra-intense magnetic fields ranging from $10^{14}$ to $10^{15}$ G, are now widely recognized as the drivers behind various astrophysical transients. These nascent, millisecond-period magnetars can convert their spin-down energy into luminous events such as Gamma-ray Bursts (GRBs) with X-ray plateaus, Super Luminous Supernovae (SLSNe), and rapid X-ray transients like CDF-S XT-2. Observations within the Milky Way have identified magnetars aged $10^3$ to $10^4$ years powering diverse phenomena through the dissipation of their magnetic energy, manifesting as giant flares, recurring soft-$\gamma$-ray or hard X-ray bursts, and occasionally fast radio bursts (FRBs). Additionally, magnetar giant flares have been identified as disguised short GRBs originating from nearby galaxies. In this report, we identify a GRB as a hyper flare from a magnetar in a neighboring galaxy. This hyper flare is approximately one thousand times more luminous than a standard magnetar giant flare. A prominent period of roughly 80 milliseconds is detected in the decaying light curve; interpreting this as the rotation period and assuming a magnetic field strength typical for a young magnetar constrains the object's age to just a few weeks. The absence of a preceding superluminous supernova or GRB further suggests the magnetar originated from an off-axis merger of two neutron stars. This discovery bridges the theoretical gap between hypothetical millisecond magnetars and observed Galactic magnetars, indicating a broader pathway for magnetar-powered gamma-ray transients.

This paper introduces a technique for the procedural generation of 3D maps by assembling pre-existing meshes that snap together according to visual constraints defined by the designer. This method overcomes traditional size and layout restrictions, granting designers control over the aesthetic qualities of the maps while providing instant feedback regarding navigability. A prototype built within the Unity game engine is presented, accompanied by case studies such as a multiplayer game application and various illustrative examples demonstrating different parameterization and piece-selection strategies. Serving as both a designer-centric composition tool and a prototyping system for 3D level design, this technique enables the rapid creation of high-quality maps and levels, significantly reducing the time required compared to fully manual approaches.

This paper investigates a Lie conformal algebra of Block type, specifically examining its conformal derivations, rank 1 conformal modules, and low-dimensional cohomology. Additionally, it constructs the vertex Poisson algebra structure linked to this algebra.

The electronic properties of ScS, a transition-metal monochalcogenide featuring a rocksalt crystal structure, have been investigated through magnetization, specific heat, transport, and muon spin rotation/relaxation ($\mu$SR) experiments. These findings collectively confirm bulk superconductivity in ScS with a critical temperature ($T_{C}$) of 5.1(5) K. While specific heat and transverse-field $\mu$SR data suggest a full superconducting gap, zero-field $\mu$SR measurements indicate the emergence of spontaneous static or quasi-static magnetic fields upon entering the superconducting state. We explore potential microscopic causes for this observed time-reversal-symmetry breaking. Since no existing explanation aligns with a conventional pairing mechanism, ScS emerges as a promising new candidate for unconventional superconductivity.

This article examines flagged extensions of convex combinations of quantum channels and establishes general sufficient conditions for the degradability of these extensions. A direct application of these findings provides a bound on the quantum $Q$ and private $P$ capacities for any channel formed as a mixture of a unitary map and another channel, provided the unitary component's probability exceeds $1/2$. We further refine these sufficient conditions specifically for flagged Pauli channels, deriving a set of upper bounds on their quantum and private capacities. Notably, we present new state-of-the-art upper bounds for the quantum and private capacities of the depolarizing channel, BB84 channel, and generalized amplitude damping channel. Additionally, the flagged construction can be readily extended to tensor powers of channels under less stringent degradability requirements, indicating that superior upper bounds may be achievable by analyzing a greater number of channel uses.

This study seeks to enhance the performance of hand keypoint regression and pixel-level hand mask segmentation under novel imaging environments, such as outdoors, despite training only on labeled data from distinct conditions like indoors. Since existing labeled datasets offer limited coverage of real-world variations, it is essential to adapt models trained on source images to unlabeled target images featuring unseen conditions. Although self-training domain adaptation techniques have been developed for both tasks, their efficacy can diminish when target predictions are noisy. Consequently, assigning low confidence weights to these noisy predictions during self-training is critical. To address this, we propose estimating prediction confidence by measuring the divergence between outputs from two separate networks, thereby identifying unreliable predictions. We integrate this confidence estimation into a self-training process via a teacher-student framework: two teacher networks provide supervision to a student network, while the teachers are refined through knowledge distillation from the student. Experimental results demonstrate our method's superiority over state-of-the-art approaches across diverse lighting, grasping objects, backgrounds, and camera viewpoints. Specifically, we achieve a 4% improvement in multi-task scores on the HO3D dataset compared to the latest adversarial adaptation method. Additionally, we validate our approach on the Ego4D dataset, which features egocentric videos with rapid shifts in outdoor imaging conditions.

This study investigates the nature of the first excited 1/2^{+} state in ^9Be, which manifests as a distinct low-lying peak in the cross section of the ^9Be(γ,n)^2α reaction immediately above the ^8Be+n threshold. Employing an α+α+n three-body model, we characterize both the ground and excited unbound states of ^9Be situated above the α+α+n threshold. By applying the complex scaling method to this model, we determine that no 1/2^{+} resonant solutions exist; however, the calculation successfully reproduces the observed low-lying peak in the photodisintegration cross section. Our findings indicate that this peak is primarily attributed to the ^8Be+n component. Additionally, through the analytical continuation of the coupling constant for the three-body interaction within the α+α+n system, we explore the virtual-state character of the 1/2^{+} state.

This book introduces a novel field called Intercenter Geometry, which diverges from both traditional Euclidean and analytic (coordinate) geometry. Its core concept involves representing planar geometric quantities through the lengths of a triangle's three sides and spatial quantities through the lengths of a tetrahedron's six edges. By employing a unified methodology, this approach facilitates the calculation of geometric properties for both triangles and tetrahedrons. This framework has yielded numerous new theorems, formulas, and geometric inequalities, resolving longstanding unsolved problems in classical geometry, such as determining the distance between the centroid and incenter of a tetrahedron. Beyond its theoretical value in expanding mathematical research and fostering innovative methodologies, Intercenter Geometry holds practical application potential, thereby significantly enriching the discipline.

We construct the limiting mixed Hodge structure for a degeneration of compact Kähler manifolds over the unit disk, featuring a central fiber with potentially non-reduced normal crossing singularities, utilizing holonomic D-modules to extend certain findings by Steenbrink. Unlike Steenbrink's results, our limiting mixed Hodge structure lacks a $\mathbb{Q}$-structure; instead, we employ sesquilinear pairings on D-modules as an alternative. The graded quotient of the weight filtration within this limiting mixed Hodge structure can be determined through the cohomology of cyclic coverings of specific intersections among the components of the central fiber.

Person re-identification represents a significant privacy risk within publicly accessible healthcare records. This study examines a novel privacy threat targeting large-scale, publicly shared wearable sensing data that is ostensibly privacy-insensitive. Specifically, we analyze user-specific biometric markers across two contextual dimensions: physiological signals (photoplethysmography and electrodermal activity) and physical movements (accelerometer data). To address this, we introduce PhysioGait, a context-aware model utilizing a Multi-Modal Siamese Convolutional Neural Network (mmSNN). This architecture independently extracts spatial and temporal features before performing sensor fusion via a Siamese loss function to infer individual identity. We validated the PhysioGait attack model using four real-time datasets (three collected under IRB #HP-00064387 and one publicly available) along with two combined datasets, achieving re-identification accuracy rates between 89% and 93%.

We present a method for achieving linear polarization control of exciton-polariton condensates using anisotropic elliptical optical traps. The cavity-induced TE-TM splitting removes the ground state spin degeneracy, resulting in fine structure modes polarized linearly parallel and perpendicular to the trap's major axis, with the condensate occupying the perpendicular mode. These results introduce a novel approach to polarization control, offering promising avenues for spintronics and research into extended systems of interacting nonlinear optical elements featuring anisotropic coupling and tunable fine structure.

This study investigates two co-dimensional thick brane-worlds in a general framework, focusing on extra-dimensional defects generated by two intersecting scalar fields. Typically, such co-dimensional configurations yield a warp factor resembling a string-like defect; however, this work examines an alternative bulk setup using a composite warp factor formed by two intersecting components. With brane localization driven by these crossing scalar fields, the analysis systematically explores solvable models arising from this two co-dimensional arrangement. The resulting solutions are categorized into five distinct models, divided into two subsets, with specific physical properties evaluated for each. In the first subset (Models I and II), Einstein equation solutions are strictly determined up to an arbitrary constant. Conversely, the second subset (Models III, IV, and V) permits an additional degree of freedom not restricted by the Einstein equations. All solutions derive from the assumption of a conformally flat internal metric, consistent with appropriate coordinate choices. While curvature singularities are identified, they do not undermine the physical validity of the solutions, particularly regarding the stress-energy tensor patterns. Notably, Model IV exhibits singularity-free stress-energy tensors and allows for straightforward reductions to $(4+1)$ dimensions. Furthermore, within the frameworks of Models III and IV, brane-world solutions are achieved across two distinct geometries of $\mathbb{S}^{2}$, which can be reduced to both trivial and non-trivial extensions of established $(4+1)$-dimensional brane-worlds.

Addressing and reducing harmful biases in contemporary language models is a critical, unresolved challenge. This study shifts focus to examine the origins of such bias. We utilize a relatively compact language model based on the LSTM architecture, trained on English Wikipedia data. By maintaining complete access to both the dataset and the evolving model parameters throughout every training step, we trace the detailed development of gender representations, identify the dataset patterns driving them, and analyze the relationship between the model's internal states and bias in downstream tasks like semantic textual similarity. Our results reveal that gender representation is dynamic, evolving through distinct phases during training. Additionally, we demonstrate that gender information becomes increasingly localized within input embeddings; consequently, debiasing these embeddings can effectively reduce bias in downstream applications. Monitoring training dynamics also exposes an asymmetry in how male and female genders are encoded in input embeddings, a factor that could cause naive mitigation strategies to inadvertently create new biases. We discuss the broader implications of these findings for mitigation approaches and the potential for extending our methods to larger models, such as Transformers, other languages, and various types of undesirable biases.

Electrons traveling at non-relativistic speeds are described by a wave function that solves the Pauli equation, which represents the low-velocity limit of the relativistic Dirac equation. This work compares two methodologies: the conservative Copenhagen interpretation, which rejects individual electron trajectories but allows for the trajectory of the expectation value via the Ehrenfest theorem (calculated using Pauli's solutions), and the less conventional Bohmian approach, which assigns a velocity field to the electron derived from the same Pauli wave function. The study examines and contrasts the specific trajectories predicted by Bohm against those of the Ehrenfest expectation value, analyzing both their similarities and differences.

Flexible colonoscopes are constrained by their mechanical complexity, leading to patient discomfort and challenging ergonomics for clinicians. Integrating robotics with autonomous control offers a promising approach to alleviate endoscopist workload, shorten training periods, and enhance procedural outcomes. However, previous autonomous control methods relying on heuristic policies struggle to generalize within the unstructured, highly deformable colon environment and often necessitate frequent human intervention. This study introduces Deep Visuomotor Control (DVC), an image-based control framework utilizing Deep Reinforcement Learning, designed to demonstrate adaptive behavior in the colon's convoluted sections. DVC establishes a direct mapping between endoscopic imagery and endoscope control signals. To evaluate this approach, a preliminary study involving 20 expert gastroenterologists used a realistic virtual simulator to compare navigation performance against DVC policies. Results indicated that DVC achieved performance equivalent to human experts on multiple metrics while offering greater safety. Furthermore, a second study with 20 novice participants demonstrated that DVC facilitates easier human supervision compared to current state-of-the-art heuristic controls. Achieving seamless supervision in colonoscopy would allow physicians to concentrate on medical decision-making rather than managing the endoscope's control mechanisms.

We demonstrate that the Wilsonian renormalization group (RG) framework defines a quantum channel operating on the momentum-space density matrices of a quantum field theory. This information-theoretic characteristic of the RG yields a significant implication for the vacuum of theories at a fixed point: there exists no entanglement between different momentum scales. This finding stems from the scale symmetry inherent in such theories and imposes constraints on the structure of the ground state as well as on the expectation values of operators in momentum space.

This work focuses on Markov's extremal problems defined as $M_{n,k}=\sup_{p\in\PP_n\setminus\{0\}}{{\|p^{(k)}\|}_X}/{{\|p\|}_X}$ for $1\le k\le n$, where $\PP_n$ denotes the set of algebraic polynomials of degree at most $n$ and $X$ is a normed space. The study builds upon Markov's original findings regarding the uniform norm on $X=C[-1,1]$ from the late 19th century. The core of the paper addresses extremal problems within the space $X=L^2[(a,b);w]$ for classical weights $w$ on the intervals $(-1,1)$, $(0,+\infty)$, and $(-\infty,+\infty)$. In addition to a concise overview of the fundamental properties of classical orthogonal polynomials on the real line, the paper provides explicit formulas for the $k$-th derivative of these orthonormal polynomials expressed in terms of the polynomials themselves. These formulas are essential for investigating such extremal problems using linear algebra methods. Furthermore, the study presents various results for all classical weight cases, including algorithms for numerically calculating the best constants $M_{n,k}$, along with their lower and upper bounds, asymptotic behavior, and other relevant findings. Finally, the paper also touches upon results concerning Markov's extremal problems applied to specific restricted classes of polynomials.

This study calculates and contrasts the surface energy of gallium liquid droplets wetting cylindrical cavities in multiple configurations; while explicit formulas apply to certain setups, numerical methods are required for others. Driven by these findings, we investigate the more practical scenario of conical cavities. Our findings establish a relationship between conical cavity geometry and the equilibrium wetting angles at the cavity's base and sidewall, conditions that ensure the lateral surface remains dewetted. This offers a significant advancement toward controlling verticality during nanowire growth via the vapor-liquid-solid method.

Although astronomy frequently captivates audiences through compelling narratives, striking visuals, and profound inquiries, leading many to assume it is a natural fit for media coverage, a closer examination reveals a more modest reality. Despite its presence, astronomical reporting remains minimal, often confined to niche sections or specialized publications rather than receiving the widespread attention it might seem to deserve.

Transmon-type superconducting qubits feature non-zero ZZ-interaction terms arising from their finite, albeit small, anharmonicities. These interactions can cause the accumulation of unwanted spurious phases during two-qubit gate operations. While exact ZZ-interaction rates require the full diagonalization of circuit Hamiltonians—a task that becomes computationally prohibitive as the number of modes in the coupler circuit grows—this paper proposes a direct analytical approach for accurately estimating these rates between low-anharmonicity qubits within the dispersive limit of multi-mode circuit-QED. Our method demonstrates excellent agreement with experimental data from multi-qubit devices. As an extension of our prior work in [1], this technique offers a valuable tool for quantum microwave engineers by directly linking ZZ-interaction rates to the impedance matrix entries defined between qubit ports.

We establish general findings that demonstrate the nonfinite axiomatisability of numerous additively idempotent semirings possessing finitely based semigroup reducts. The minimal instance is a commutative $3$-element structure, which we prove also features \texttt{NP}-hard membership within its variety. This specific semiring is unique as the sole nonfinite axiomatisable ai-semiring on $3$-elements, and we show that its nonfinite basis property propagates to many associated semirings, including the natural ai-semiring on $B_2^1$. Furthermore, we substantially expand upon prior group-theory based examples by proving that any finite additively idempotent semiring containing a nonabelian nilpotent subgroup fails to be finitely axiomatisable for its identities.

We provide an explicit description of the Floer cohomology for a family of Dehn twists around disjoint Lagrangian spheres within a $\omega^+$-monotone rational symplectic manifold. Additionally, our framework allows us to define a class in the fixed point Floer cohomology of a Dehn twist in a monotone symplectic manifold by counting half-strips attached to the specified Lagrangian sphere, proving that this class must vanish. Future work intends to leverage this vanishing result to establish a novel geometric proof of Seidel's long exact sequence.

The increasing availability of high-resolution Earth imagery from satellites, drones, and mobile devices at minimal cost presents unprecedented opportunities. This thesis leverages these open-access, high-quality data streams by introducing novel machine learning and big data methodologies designed to support sustainable and resilient agricultural applications. The research focuses on three key themes: monitoring the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), tracking food security, and developing smart agriculture solutions. To address specific challenges within these areas, the thesis develops innovations in processing large-scale Earth Observation (EO) data, overcoming the scarcity of annotated datasets for model training, and bridging the gap between algorithmic outputs and actionable real-world advice. The work demonstrates how big data technologies—including data cubes, distributed learning, linked open data, and semantic enrichment—can transform data deluges into actionable knowledge for users. Furthermore, it advocates for semi-supervised and unsupervised learning approaches to mitigate annotation shortages, enabling robust spatial and temporal model generalization; specifically, it shows that minimal ground truth data can yield high-quality crop type maps and phenology estimates. Finally, the thesis highlights the significant value gap between model predictions and actual decision-making, illustrating how causal and interpretable machine learning can effectively close this divide.

Comparing computer-generated protein structural models is a critical component of protein structure prediction. Its applications include assessing model quality, selecting the best models from numerous candidates, and optimizing energy function parameters for template-free modeling and refinement. While numerous online web servers offer protein comparison methods, they are ill-suited for large-scale model comparisons because: (1) they employ algorithms designed for comparing actual proteins rather than multiple models of the same protein, and (2) most provide only single pairwise comparisons, failing to scale to the thousands of comparisons often required. To address this gap between protein and model structure comparison, we developed the Protein Models Comparator (pm-cmp). To ensure on-demand scalability and handle extensive comparison experiments, pm-cmp was implemented on the cloud. The Protein Models Comparator is a scalable web application that performs fast, distributed comparisons of protein models using RMSD, GDT TS, TM-score, and Q-score metrics. Running on the Google App Engine (GAE) platform, it demonstrates how emerging Platform as a Service (PaaS) technology can simplify the creation of scalable bioinformatics services. pm-cmp's functionality is accessible via an API, enabling full automation of experiment submission and result retrieval. Released as free software under the Affero GNU Public License, the source code is available at: http://www.infobiotics.org/pm-cmp. This article introduces a new web application for large-scale, model-specific protein structure comparison and offers insights into the utility of the GAE platform in scientific computing.

Exciton-polaritons represent hybrid light-matter states formed through strong coupling between active excitonic materials and photonic resonances. Leveraging these hybrid quasiparticles offers a versatile platform for investigating fundamental phenomena, including out-of-equilibrium Bose-Einstein condensation and quantum fluids of light, alongside new mechanisms for optoelectronic applications. In this study, we experimentally examine the generation of exciton-polaritons created by the interaction between hybrid inorganic-organic perovskite excitons and an optical Bound state in a Continuum (BIC) within a subwavelength metasurface, all at room temperature. These resulting eigenmodes, termed polariton BICs (pol-BICs), are detected via reflectivity, resonant scattering, and photoluminescence. Despite having a finite quality factor limited by non-radiative excitonic losses, pol-BICs retain the distinctive traits of BICs: complete decoupling from the radiative continuum in the vertical direction, corresponding to a locally suppressed far-field radiation in momentum space. Crucially, our findings demonstrate that the topological character of the photonic BIC is fully transferred to the pol-BIC, evidenced by the emergence of a polarization vortex in the far-field polaritonic emission. These results establish a foundation for engineering BIC physics in interacting bosonic systems and developing novel room-temperature polaritonic devices.

Multimedia streaming, encompassing both live and on-demand content, forms the backbone of the modern Internet, accounting for over 60% of global traffic. Given this substantial demand, ensuring a superior user experience is both critical and difficult. To assess user Quality of Experience (QoE), numerous researchers employ subjective evaluations where participants rate videos artificially degraded with various temporal and spatial impairments. To assist current initiatives in bridging the divide between objective video QoE metrics and actual user perception, we created DashReStreamer, an open-source framework designed to reconstruct adaptively streamed video within real-world networks. DashReStreamer leverages logs generated by a HTTP Adaptive Streaming (HAS) algorithm operating in uncontrolled environments (such as wired or wireless networks) to encode visual alterations and stall events into a single video file, making these clips suitable for subjective QoE testing under realistic network conditions.

Complementing DashReStreamer, we have reconstructed 234 realistic video clips derived from logs collected from actual mobile and wireless networks. Furthermore, our dataset includes comprehensive video logs containing all decisions made by the HAS algorithm, alongside network bandwidth profiles that depict throughput distribution. We believe this dataset and framework will empower other researchers in their quest to fully understand the dynamics of video QoE.

This review paper aims to offer a comprehensive perspective on recent advancements in understanding the influence of magnetic fields during the embedded stages of star formation. Driven by improved observational tools and parallel developments in numerical models that capture the essential physics of star formation, it has recently become feasible to compare detailed predictions from magnetized models with the observed properties of the youngest protostars. We present an overview of the critical implications of incorporating magnetic fields into state-of-the-art protostellar formation models, highlighting their function in shaping resulting stars and their disks. We examine the significance of magnetic field coupling in determining the efficiency of magnetic processes and review observational studies that constrain the two primary agents responsible for this coupling within star-forming cores: dust grains and ionized gas. We also recall the physical mechanisms and observational techniques used to trace magnetic field topology and intensity in embedded protostars, while reviewing the key steps, successes, and limitations involved in comparing real observations with synthetic data from non-ideal MHD models. Finally, we discuss the principal lines of observational evidence indicating a pivotal role for magnetic fields in star and disk formation, propose a scenario addressing the angular momentum problem in star formation, and highlight the remaining discrepancies between models and observations.

The music sector is a primary field for implementing recommender systems. Unlike most other domains that mostly depend on collaborative filtering (CF), music recommendation systems have historically favored content-based (CB) methods. Recently, hybrid models utilizing both collaborative and content data—termed "content-driven models"—have begun to supersede pure CF or CB approaches. This survey examines 47 papers on content-driven music recommendation. Through comprehensive literature analysis, we introduce an "onion model" with five layers representing distinct content categories: signal, embedded metadata, expert-generated content, user-generated content, and derivative content. We characterize each category across multiple dimensions. Next, we outline six key challenges that structure our discussion: enhancing diversity and novelty, ensuring transparency and explainability, achieving context-awareness, recommending music sequences, improving scalability and efficiency, and mitigating the cold-start problem. We categorize each relevant article based on its content layer, objectives, and methodological choices, while also presenting them chronologically to illustrate the evolution of these strategies. Finally, we highlight the persistent grand challenges that remain unsolved for future research.

Sign Language Translation (SLT) typically begins with a Sign Language Recognition (SLR) system to extract glosses from video, followed by a translation module that converts these glosses into spoken language. This study concentrates on the translation component, presenting the STMC-Transformer, which surpasses current state-of-the-art methods by more than 5 and 7 BLEU points on gloss-to-text and video-to-text translation tasks respectively using the PHOENIX-Weather 2014T dataset, and achieves an improvement of over 16 BLEU on the ASLG-PC12 corpus. Additionally, we highlight a limitation in existing methods that depend on gloss supervision: our STMC-Transformer's video-to-text translation outperforms the translation of ground-truth glosses. This finding challenges previous assertions that translating ground-truth glosses serves as an upper bound for SLT performance, indicating that glosses are an inefficient representation of sign language. Consequently, we recommend future SLT research pursue end-to-end training of recognition and translation models or adopt alternative sign language annotation schemes.

We present the initial findings from a search for leptophobic dark matter (DM) using the Coherent CAPTAIN-Mills (CCM) liquid argon (LAr) detector. In Fall 2019, an engineering run was conducted utilizing 120 photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) and $17.9 \times 10^{20}$ protons-on-target (POT) to characterize the CCM system. This 10-ton detector operated on a strictly light-based principle with a 50 keV threshold, employing coherent elastic scattering off argon nuclei for DM detection. Despite challenges including only 1.5 months of accumulated luminosity, contaminated liquid argon, and suboptimal shielding, the first engineering run achieved sensitivity to unexplored regions of parameter space for light dark matter (LDM) models featuring a baryonic vector portal. With an anticipated background of 115,005 events, we observed $115,005^{+16.5}$ events, consistent with background predictions. For a benchmark mediator-to-dark matter mass ratio of $m_{_{V_B}}/m_{\chi}=2.1$, DM masses in the range $9\,\text{MeV} \lesssim m_\chi \lesssim 50\,\text{MeV}$ have been ruled out at 90% confidence level within the leptophobic model, utilizing the Feldman-Cousins test statistic. An upgraded run involving 200 PMTs, filtered LAr, enhanced shielding, and tenfold increased POT is expected to exclude the remaining thermal relic density parameter space for this model and investigate new parameter spaces for other leptophobic DM scenarios.

It is well established that both the volume and caliber of training data are pivotal for developing effective machine learning models. This paper advances that understanding by highlighting the critical impact of how training examples are sequenced. Curriculum Learning leverages the principle that structured knowledge acquisition accelerates training and enhances comprehension, mirroring human language development where individuals progress from simple sounds to complex sentences. Applying this methodology to Automatic Speech Recognition, we hypothesize that end-to-end models perform superiorly when trained on datasets organized by increasing difficulty. To structure the training set and identify "easy" examples, we investigated various scoring functions utilizing feedback from either external networks or the model itself. Empirical findings indicate that employing different curricula allows for a balanced optimization of both training duration and network performance.

While diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) offers greater sensitivity to microstructural alterations than standard anatomical imaging, it suffers from limited specificity. The DIAMOND model addresses this by partitioning voxel content into diffusion compartments, utilizing diffusion-weighted data to estimate a compartmental non-central matrix-variate Gamma distribution of diffusion tensors. This approach resolves crossing fiber bundles while accommodating their heterogeneity. Alternatively, tensor-valued diffusion encoding employs novel acquisition schemes to directly tag specific features of the intra-voxel diffusion tensor distribution. However, the influence of these schemes on brain microstructural estimation has primarily been examined using only a few parametric models designed for single-fascicle scenarios. In this study, we derive a general Laplace transform for the non-central matrix-variate Gamma distribution, allowing the DIAMOND framework to be extended to handle tensor-valued encoded data. We subsequently evaluate the resulting "Magic DIAMOND" model through both *in silico* simulations and *in vivo* experiments across various combinations of tensor-valued data. By assessing parameter estimation uncertainty via stratified bootstrap, we investigate both voxel-based and fixel-based metrics using multi-peak tractography. Our results demonstrate that the estimated metrics can be robustly mapped along fiber tracks even through regions of fiber crossing, thereby opening new avenues for tractometry and microstructural mapping along specific white-matter tracts.

Our recent study examines the radio-frequency attenuation length of cold polar ice at Summit Station, Greenland, utilizing bistatic radar data collected in summer 2021. This dataset captures echoes from bedrock as well as those originating from stratified impurities or dielectric discontinuities (layers) within the ice.
