Results indicate that incorporating CUT-GAN generated training data yields superior plant detection performance compared to models trained exclusively on real data.

Defects and microstructural characteristics ranging from the atomic scale to the microscale deterministically influence material properties. However, research on material evolution under environmental stimuli typically correlates performance with a single dominant microstructural feature. This study observes the dynamic swelling behavior of Ni-based concentrated solid solution alloys during high-temperature irradiation using continuous, in situ measurements of thermoelastic properties in bulk specimens. Contrary to conventional techniques that rely solely on electron microscopy to identify volumetric porosity, this direct property evaluation captures an integrated response across all defect length scales. Specifically, the evolution of elastic properties during swelling is significantly governed by the entire spectrum of defect sizes, spanning nano- to meso-scales, including some too small to be resolved by imaging. Furthermore, observed changes in thermal transport properties are highly sensitive to the partitioning between electronic and lattice thermal conductivity. This emerging class of in situ experiments, which directly measures integrated performance under relevant conditions, offers unique insights into material dynamics that traditional methods cannot provide.

This paper introduces a learning-based method for multi-view stereo (MVS), which estimates depth maps for a reference frame using posed multi-view images. Our primary approach utilizes a "learning-to-optimize" framework to iteratively index a plane-sweeping cost volume and regress the depth map through a convolutional Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU). Given the critical importance of the cost volume in encoding multi-view geometry, we enhance its construction at both the pixel and frame levels. At the pixel level, we propose disrupting the symmetry of the Siamese network—commonly used for feature extraction in MVS—by inserting a transformer block into the reference image stream while excluding the source images. This asymmetric architecture enables the network to derive global features from the reference image for depth prediction. Addressing inaccuracies in poses between reference and source images, we introduce a residual pose network to correct relative poses, thereby refining the cost volume at the frame level. Extensive experiments on real-world MVS datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art results in both within-dataset evaluation and cross-dataset generalization.

DFT+U offers a practical and economical remedy for the self-interaction error (SIE) inherent in standard approximate density functional theory (DFT) when modeling correlated electronic states. The reliability of DFT+U(+J) simulations depends critically on precise values for Hubbard U and Hund's J parameters, which the linear response (LR) approach determines with both high accuracy and computational efficiency. This research presents a high-throughput computational investigation of U and J values for transition metal d-electron states across a representative collection of more than 2,000 magnetic transition metal oxides (TMOs), establishing a benchmark for researchers utilizing DFT+U in this field. To facilitate this large-scale analysis, an automated atomate workflow was created capable of calculating U and J values on massively parallel supercomputing systems. As a demonstration of this workflow's utility, the study computes the spin-canting magnetic structure and unit cell parameters of the multiferroic olivine LiNiPO4 using derived U and J values for Ni-d and O-p states, subsequently comparing results with experimental data. The findings reveal that both Ni-d U and J corrections significantly influence the Ni-moment canting angle, while the inclusion of an O-p U value yields substantially better agreement between calculated and experimental lattice parameters.

High-intensity, ultrashort pulses from X-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs) are transforming research into fundamental nonlinear x-ray matter interactions and the coupled dynamics of electronic and nuclear systems. To maximize the utility of this advanced tool for sophisticated x-ray spectroscopies, a critical need exists for a high-resolution, noninvasive method capable of characterizing the stochastic nature of incident XFEL pulses. This study introduces a methodology that integrates high-acceptance angle-resolved photoelectron time-of-flight spectroscopy with ghost imaging to significantly improve the quality of x-ray pulse spectral characterization. Deploying this noninvasive, high-resolution diagnostic will greatly benefit the ultrafast x-ray spectroscopy community by acting as a transparent beamsplitter. This enables applications ranging from transient absorption spectroscopy in averaging mode to covariance-based x-ray nonlinear spectroscopies in single-shot mode, where the inherent shot-to-shot fluctuations of self-amplified spontaneous emission (SASE) XFEL pulses serve as a valuable asset.

With restricted vaccine availability and scarce medical resources, devising a pandemic vaccination strategy constitutes an economic challenge. By employing time-series and panel analyses on real-world country-level data, we evaluated the impact of two critical mass vaccination components—dosing intervals and vaccine types—on COVID-19 cases and fatalities. Our findings indicate that both new infections and deaths are significantly reduced as the proportion of the population receiving at least one dose increases. However, given a fixed level of first-dose coverage, expanding the fraction of individuals receiving a second dose yields no additional reductions in cases or deaths. An exception exists for vaccines from China, where significant improvements in both health outcomes are observed only after the completion of two doses. These results endorse a policy of lengthening the gap between the first and second doses for vaccines developed in Europe and the US. Furthermore, as vaccination campaigns advance, rising population mobility partially counteracts the direct benefits of vaccination, indicating that non-pharmaceutical interventions remain essential for controlling transmission during rollout.

An isogeny connecting elliptic curves is defined as an algebraic morphism that also functions as a group homomorphism. Numerous cryptographic applications necessitate the efficient computation of isogenies with large degrees between such curves. For ordinary curves sharing the same endomorphism ring, the most efficient algorithm available previously had a worst-case time complexity that was exponential relative to the input size. This paper demonstrates that, under reasonable heuristics, this problem can be addressed in subexponential time. Our method involves factoring the ideal associated with the isogeny's kernel (modulo principal ideals) into a product of smaller prime ideals, allowing for the direct computation of the corresponding isogenies. When integrated with prior research by Bostan et al., our algorithm generates equations for large-degree isogenies in quasi-optimal time, requiring only the initial curve and the kernel as inputs.

The ATLAS detector analyzed the full LHC Run 2 dataset from 2015 to 2018, comprising an integrated luminosity of $139\,\text{fb}^{-1}$, to measure both inclusive and differential cross sections for the associated production of top-antitop quark pairs and a $Z$ boson ($t\bar{t}Z$) in events featuring exactly three or four isolated electrons or muons. The resulting inclusive cross section was determined to be $\sigma_{t\bar{t}Z}=1.05\pm0.05\,(\text{stat.})\,\pm0.09\,(\text{syst.})\,\text{pb}$, which aligns with the most precise Standard Model theoretical prediction. Furthermore, absolute and normalized differential cross sections were evaluated across various kinematic variables at both parton and particle levels to investigate the kinematics of the $t\bar{t}Z$ system.

The discontinuous precipitation observed in the U-Nb system, described by the transformation $\gamma^{bcc}_{matrix} \rightarrow \alpha^{orth}_{cellular} + \gamma'^{bcc}_{cellular}$, is notable for enabling the formation and growth of the metastable $\gamma'$ phase during the process. Previous hypotheses attempting to explain the thermodynamic driving force suggested that the energy of the $\alpha$ phase creates an intermediate common tangent with the initial potential of the $\gamma$ phase's double-well energy at the $\gamma'$ composition. Although this theory is consistent with experimental data showing a gradual rise in $\gamma'$ composition as temperature increases, it contradicts recent findings indicating a distribution of $\gamma'$ compositions near 50 at\%Nb. To address this discrepancy, the present study examines the origins of U-Nb discontinuous precipitation through fundamental thermodynamics and kinetics using phase-field theory. Results demonstrate that local misfit strain plays a pivotal role in the formation and growth of discontinuous precipitation. Consequently, depending on the magnitude of strain generated at grain boundaries, one can expect either an increasing $\gamma'$ composition or a random distribution of $\gamma'$ compositions around the equiatomic value as temperature rises.

Legal Judgment Prediction stands as a highly regarded domain at the intersection of Law, Artificial Intelligence, and Natural Language Processing. This field involves developing intelligent systems designed to forecast specific judicial attributes, including case outcomes and legal classifications. In this study, we employed AI classifiers to determine judicial results within the Brazilian legal framework. To achieve this, we created a text crawler to retrieve data from official Brazilian electronic legal databases, constructing a dataset focused on second-degree murder and active corruption cases. We utilized various classifiers, such as Support Vector Machines and Neural Networks, to analyze textual features and predict outcomes. Our findings indicate that Regression Trees, Gated Recurring Units, and Hierarchical Attention Networks achieved superior performance metrics across different subsets. Finally, we investigated the internal weights of the Hierarchical Attention Network algorithm to identify key words associated with either the conviction or acquittal of defendants.

This study introduces methodologies for Bayesian inference within time-varying parameter (TVP) quantile regression (QR) models that incorporate conditional heteroskedasticity. By employing data augmentation techniques to ensure conditional Gaussianity, I construct an efficient Gibbs sampling algorithm. High-dimensional parameter spaces are regularized using flexible dynamic shrinkage priors. The approach is applied through a simplified TVP-QR framework based on an unobserved component model to dynamically track inflation distribution quantiles across the United States, the United Kingdom, and the euro area. Out-of-sample forecasting results indicate that the proposed model is competitive, with particular strength in higher-order and tail forecasts. Furthermore, a thorough examination of the resulting predictive distributions shows that they occasionally exhibit skewness and heavy tails.

By applying Morse theory, we establish a canonical representation for a specific class of surfaces, encompassing all properly embedded incompressible surfaces within 3-dimensional handlebodies. Furthermore, we provide a necessary and sufficient criterion to verify the incompressibility of surfaces situated in this standard form. The proposed algorithm is practical, and several examples are presented to demonstrate its functionality.

The analysis of small oscillations in a heavy symmetric top, where the magnitudes of the conserved angular momenta are identical, indicates that the small oscillation approximation remains applicable under these conditions.

Determining the impact of climate change on heavy precipitation remains a central challenge in climate risk analysis. Segmenting the globe into homogeneous sub-regions can enhance precipitation modeling by estimating shared regional distributional parameters. Furthermore, within the detection and attribution (D&A) framework, it is essential to address biases stemming from errors in global climate models (GCMs) to accurately attribute anthropogenic influences. To this end, we introduce an efficient clustering algorithm that, unlike traditional regional frequency analysis (RFA) methods, operates without covariates and explicitly accounts for dependence. This approach relies on a novel non-parametric dissimilarity measure that integrates RFA constraints with pairwise dependence. We establish the asymptotic properties of this dissimilarity estimator and interpret it in the context of generalised extreme value distributed pairs. As a practical D&A application, we cluster annual daily precipitation maxima from 16 GCMs participating in the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project. By merging climatologically consistent subregions across all GCMs, we achieve greater spatial cluster coherence and superior performance compared to methods relying solely on marginal distributions or dependence. Finally, by contrasting precipitation extreme patterns under natural versus total forcing scenarios, we evaluate the specific impact of anthropogenic forcing.

This paper presents a shoebox room simulator capable of systematically creating synthetic datasets of binaural room impulse responses (BRIRs) based on any arbitrary set of head-related transfer functions (HRTFs). Evaluating machine hearing algorithms often necessitates BRIR datasets to emulate the acoustics of diverse environments; however, existing solutions usually rely solely on HRTFs measured from dummy heads, which inadequately capture the high variability in spatial sound perception. Our approach enables the integration of a room impulse response (RIR) simulator with various HRTF sets formatted in the Spatially Oriented Format for Acoustics (SOFA). To make this toolbox accessible to both experts and non-experts, we provide source code and compiled binaries for multiple operating systems, available at https://github.com/spatialaudiotools/sofamyroom/.

Research in Computing Education (CER) is vital for addressing the growing demand for computing skills among students. To ensure the systematic advancement of knowledge, scholarly publications must be sufficiently clear to facilitate replications, meta-analyses, and the development of theory. This study aims to assess the reporting of empirical work in CER literature by determining whether publications provide the necessary information for these three purposes. The investigation addresses three research questions: (RQ1) What proportion of papers in CER venues include empirical evaluations? (RQ2) What are the defining characteristics of these evaluations? (RQ3) Do papers featuring empirical evaluations adhere to reporting standards regarding both the inclusion and labeling of essential details? We conducted a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) of 427 papers published between 2014 and 2015 across five CER venues: SIGCSE TS, ICER, ITiCSE, TOCE, and CSE. Using the CER Empiricism Assessment Rubric, we found that over 80% of the papers contained some form of empirical evaluation, with quantitative methods being the most prevalent. The studies most frequently reported results concerning pedagogical interventions, curriculum, community engagement, or tools. However, there was significant inconsistency regarding whether papers included comparisons between interventions and other datasets or baselines. Furthermore, many papers failed to adequately report research objectives, goals, questions, or hypotheses, as well as details on participants, study design, data collection, and threats to validity. While CER authors are successfully contributing empirical findings, they do not consistently meet all reporting norms. We urge authors to provide clearly labeled details to enable future replications and meta-analyses. As the community expands, reporting practices must mature to foster the establishment of computing education theory that supports future learners.

Stochastic processes characterized by time delays are crucial in science and engineering, particularly when signal transmission and processing involve finite speeds. Yet, rigorous mathematical analyses of their dynamical and thermodynamic behaviors have traditionally been limited to linear models. This work introduces a specific class of stochastic delay processes driven by nonlinear time-local forces and linear time-delayed forces that satisfy fluctuation theorems and approach Boltzmann equilibrium over extended periods. From a control theory perspective, these "equilibrium stochastic delay processes" are inherently stable and energetically passive. Computationally, they offer precise constraints for general nonlinear stochastic delay problems and can serve as foundational models for perturbative analyses in various scenarios. Physically, these processes can be interpreted as an underdamped Brownian particle experiencing either a time-local force within a non-Markovian thermal bath or a delayed feedback force in a Markovian thermal bath. We demonstrate these characteristics numerically using a configuration common to feedback cooling, highlighting potential experimental applications.

This article demonstrates how to address various problems and puzzles using the built-in SAT solver within the computer algebra system Maple. After encoding these challenges into Boolean logic, solutions can be automatically identified—or proven nonexistent—without requiring the implementation of any search algorithms. Specifically, we outline methods for solving the $n$-queens problem, generating and solving Sudoku puzzles, resolving logic puzzles such as the Einstein riddle, tackling the 15-puzzle, addressing the maximum clique problem, and locating Graeco-Latin squares.

Although modern Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) excel at solving diverse problems, their substantial size often prevents deployment on resource-limited edge devices. This paper addresses this issue by minimizing the memory consumption and floating-point operations associated with CNN convolutional layers. We achieve this compression by extending the Kronecker Product Decomposition to handle multidimensional tensors, creating the Generalized Kronecker Product Decomposition (GKPD). Our method produces a plug-and-play module designed as a direct replacement for any standard convolutional layer. Empirical evaluations on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets using ResNet, MobileNetv2, and SeNet architectures confirm the efficacy of our approach. Furthermore, GKPD demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art decomposition techniques like Tensor-Train and Tensor-Ring, as well as other compression strategies such as pruning and knowledge distillation.

This study investigates the Hyers-Ulam stability of perturbations within a homogeneous linear differential system characterized by a $2\times 2$ constant coefficient matrix. We establish new necessary and sufficient conditions for such systems to exhibit Hyers-Ulam stability and, for the first time, determine the optimal (minimal) Hyers-Ulam constant in specific instances. Several examples are presented to demonstrate these findings, and deriving the best Hyers-Ulam constant for second-order constant coefficient differential equations highlights the practical significance of these robust results.

Deep learning has become a prevalent tool for speech enhancement. Beyond evaluating different network architectures, researchers are increasingly focused on refining the loss functions employed during training. Although current approaches incorporate auditory characteristics or signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) formulations, they often lack sufficient correlation with human auditory evaluation scores and may not be optimal for gradient-based optimization. This paper introduces a novel SNR loss function grounded in auditory power compression. Experimental findings indicate that this proposed function exhibits a stronger overall correlation with objective speech intelligibility metrics compared to alternative loss functions. Furthermore, when applied to the same speech enhancement model, this method yields superior training performance relative to other comparative approaches.

Machine teaching represents an inverse learning problem designed to guide a student learner toward a specific target hypothesis, assuming the teacher possesses prior knowledge of the student's learning parameters. While earlier research concentrated on optimizing teaching examples by balancing teaching risk and cost, these methods often fail when the student's learning parameters remain undisclosed. To address this scenario, this paper introduces a distribution matching-based machine teaching strategy. This approach iteratively and backwardly halves the teaching cost to identify an optimal teaching set. Technically, the strategy functions as a cost-controlled optimization process that determines the best teaching examples without needing to explore the student's parameter distribution. Consequently, for any given limited teaching budget, the resulting training examples can be derived in closed form. Both theoretical analysis and experimental results validate this strategy.

Isolated Horizons have been pivotal in gravitational physics, aiding in the analysis of black hole merger endpoints and (quantum) entropy. Specifically, the geometric definition of weakly isolated horizons (WIHs) as quasilocal extensions of event horizons relies solely on geometry and remains independent of the specific variables used to describe the gravitational field. This study examines a canonical decomposition of general relativity utilizing connection and vierbein variables derived from a first-order action. Within this framework, the presence of a (weakly) isolated horizon is identified through specific boundary conditions applied to an internal boundary of the spacetime region. Using the self-dual action, we apply a generalized version of the Dirac algorithm for bounded regions. Although the formalism for gauge theories with boundaries is clear, the selection of dynamical variables on the boundary remains flexible; we investigate this freedom by analyzing various canonical formulations for non-rotating black holes defined by WIHs. Our findings demonstrate that both the degrees of freedom and the energy associated with the horizon are not unique, even when the descriptions are internally consistent. This work extends previous research on isolated horizons by exploring this variable freedom and considering a broader class of horizons, while also addressing earlier results found in the literature.

This review examines searches for axion-like particles (ALPs), offering content that complements other recent surveys. The first section addresses ALPs in extreme environments, specifically within neutron star cores, the magnetospheres of highly magnetized neutron stars (magnetars), and during neutron star mergers. It concentrates on potential ALP signatures in neutron star photon spectra and on gravitational wave and electromagnetic signals arising from mergers. The second section covers recent progress in laboratory-based ALP searches, with a primary emphasis on accelerator facilities, including beam-dump experiments and collider studies. We present a comprehensive, step-by-step discussion of the ALP search pipeline—from production to detection—that is readily applicable to most beam-dump and reactor experiments. Finally, we provide a selective overview of the rapidly evolving field of ultralight dark matter, particularly the formation of Bose-Einstein Condensates (BECs). This concludes with a review of BEC properties, linking them to advancements in numerical simulations and their subsequent implications for experimental searches.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) utilize graph structures by transmitting messages across edges to learn structural features. However, specific topologies can cause inefficient information flow and a phenomenon called oversquashing, which has recently been associated with the graph's spectral gap and curvature. Conversely, augmenting the message-passing graph with additional edges may cause node representations to converge, resulting in oversmoothing. We introduce a computationally efficient algorithm that mitigates oversquashing by systematically adding edges based on spectral expansion. By integrating this with a relational architecture that maintains the original graph structure, we provably prevent oversmoothing. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses existing graph rewiring techniques across various graph classification tasks.

M-dwarf stars are ideal candidates for exoplanet research due to their proximity and advantageous traits for detection and characterization. However, the habitability and atmospheric properties of these systems hinge critically on the history of high-energy radiation—from X-rays to the near-ultraviolet (NUV)—which drives atmospheric escape and photochemistry. Using the Far Ultraviolet M-dwarf Evolution Survey (FUMES), we evaluated the evolution of far-ultraviolet (FUV) radiation, focusing on eight prominent emission lines including Ly$\alpha$, across M-dwarfs with varying rotation periods and ages. We identified tight power-law correlations among spectroscopic FUV features and quantified the intrinsic scatter in quiescent emissions. The luminosity evolution of these features with respect to rotation follows a broken power-law: it remains saturated for rapidly rotating stars and decays as the Rossby number increases, typically with a slope of $-2$, though this may be shallower for Ly$\alpha$. Our regression models allow for FUV emission line luminosity estimates relative to bolometric values, based on known rotation periods, with an accuracy of approximately 0.3 dex across eight distinct UV lines; fit parameters may also vary depending on the atmospheric layer. Furthermore, our detailed analysis of UV luminosity evolution with age reveals that habitable zone planets around lower-mass stars receive significantly higher high-energy radiation exposure than identical planets orbiting more massive hosts. Specifically, exoplanets around early-to-mid M-dwarfs at field ages accumulate 10 to 20 times more EUV energy than modern Earth. Additionally, the majority of this UV exposure occurs within the first billion years of the star's life.

Event representations are crucial for numerous tasks. This paper introduces SWCC, a framework that combines simultaneous weakly supervised contrastive learning with clustering to enhance event representation learning. SWCC leverages event co-occurrence information more effectively by employing a weakly supervised contrastive learning approach capable of handling multiple positive and negative samples, alongside a prototype-based clustering technique that prevents the separation of semantically related events. During training, the model concurrently executes both contrastive learning and clustering. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that SWCC surpasses existing baselines on Hard Similarity and Transitive Sentence Similarity tasks. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of the prototype-based clustering reveals that the resulting prototype vectors implicitly encode diverse relationships between events.

Inspired by recent experimental findings regarding DNA loop extrusion driven by protein motors, this study examines the statistical characteristics of expanding polymer loops using the ideal chain model. These loop conformations are defined statistically through the mean gyration radius and pairwise contact probabilities. We find that the transition between near-equilibrium and highly non-equilibrium statistical regimes is governed by a single dimensionless parameter, representing the ratio of the loop relaxation time to the duration since extrusion began. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that both one-sided and two-sided loop extruding motors generate loops with nearly identical properties. These predictions rely on two rigorous semi-analytical approaches supported by asymptotic analysis of both slow and fast extrusion limits.

The proliferation of Online Social Networks and the commercial potential of popular profiles have drawn many automated programs, referred to as artificial accounts. This study concentrates on distinguishing between human and fake accounts on social networks by utilizing various graph neural networks to effectively encode both account attributes and network graph features. Our approach leverages both network structure and attributes to differentiate humans from artificial accounts, comparing attributed embeddings against traditional graph embeddings. Isolating complex, human-like artificial accounts as a distinct task reveals significant weaknesses in profile-based detection algorithms while highlighting the effectiveness of network-structure-based methods for identifying sophisticated bots. Experimental results indicate that our method achieves competitive performance relative to existing state-of-the-art bot detection systems using only network-driven features. The source code for this research is accessible at: http://github.com/karpovilia/botdetection.

The recent end-to-end object detection pipeline, Detection TRansformer (DETR), has shown promising results; however, it relies heavily on large-scale labeled data and struggles with domain shifts, particularly when labeled data is absent in the target domain. To address these challenges, we introduce MTTrans, an end-to-end cross-domain detection Transformer built upon the mean teacher framework. This approach fully leverages unlabeled target domain data for training and facilitates knowledge transfer between domains using pseudo labels. Additionally, we propose a comprehensive multi-level feature alignment strategy to enhance the quality of pseudo labels generated by the mean teacher framework, utilizing the cross-scale self-attention mechanism from Deformable DETR. This alignment synchronizes image and object features across local, global, and instance levels through domain query-based feature alignment (DQFA), bi-level graph-based prototype alignment (BGPA), and token-wise image feature alignment (TIFA). Furthermore, the pseudo-labeled unlabeled target domain data available for detection training improves feature extraction and alignment, allowing the mean teacher framework and the multi-level feature alignment to be iteratively and mutually optimized within the Transformer architecture. Extensive experiments confirm that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance across three domain adaptation scenarios, notably improving the Sim10k to Cityscapes scenario from 52.6 mAP to 57.9 mAP. The code will be made public.

Large Bayesian VARs have become a standard tool in empirical macroeconomics, where the natural conjugate prior is frequently employed for its ability to streamline posterior simulation and yield valuable analytical outcomes. However, this approach sacrifices modeling flexibility by prohibiting cross-variable shrinkage, which prevents the aggressive penalization of coefficients on other variables' lags compared to own lags. We introduce a new prior that combines the advantages of both approaches: it supports cross-variable shrinkage while retaining key analytical properties, including a closed-form marginal likelihood. Furthermore, this prior enables rapid posterior simulation; for instance, generating 10,000 draws from a BVAR with 100 variables and 4 lags requires less than 30 seconds on a standard desktop. We illustrate the prior's effectiveness through a structural analysis of a 15-variable VAR utilizing sign restrictions to identify five structural shocks.

This study presents findings from a 2018–2019 NICER soft X-ray monitoring campaign of the ultraluminous X-ray pulsar NGC 300 ULX-1. To isolate the source signal, we incorporated data from Swift/XRT and XMM-Newton to model and subtract contamination from the nearby eclipsing binary NGC 300 X-1. By constructing and analyzing 5-day averaged NICER spectra within the 0.4–4.0 keV band, we assessed the source's long-term spectral evolution, determining that an absorbed power-law model offered the best overall fit. During the observation period, the absorbed flux (0.4–4.0 keV) decreased from $2\times10^{-12}$ to below $10^{-13}{\rm\,erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}}$, accompanied by spectral softening where the photon index shifted from $\Gamma\approx1.6$ to $\Gamma\approx2.6$. We attribute this softening to reprocessed emission from the accretion disk edge becoming visible as the pulsar was obscured, potentially by a precessing disk. While some fits were notably enhanced by adding a disk blackbody component, suggesting the pulsar intermittently emerges between partial covering absorber episodes, we propose that the system was observed in a low-flux state caused by line-of-sight absorption. This state was punctuated by occasional pulsar appearances, indicating short-term variability nested within longer-term accretion disk precession timescales.

This paper presents several characterizations of Hom-Leibniz superalgebras and identifies their fundamental properties, which serve as generalizations of known characteristics of Hom-Leibniz algebras. By examining the Hom-Akivis superalgebra linked to a specific Hom-Leibniz superalgebra, we observe that the Hom-super Akivis identity yields an extra property, providing a necessary and sufficient condition for the Hom-super Lie admissibility of these structures. Furthermore, we demonstrate that every (left) Hom-Leibniz superalgebra naturally possesses a Hom-Lie-Yamaguti superalgebra structure.

We posit that topology represents a branch of mathematics focused on properties invariant under equivalence relations, specifically concerning the representation, classification, and comparison of the resulting equivalence classes. Adopting this perspective allows us to extend topological concepts to non-geometric entities. This paper illustrates such an extension by defining sequence topology as the equivalence class of finite integer sequences of identical length subject to relabeling or permutation. The discrepancy between a set of finite integer sequences sharing the same length is quantified by the count of mismatches, whereas the difference between a set of sequence topologies is defined as the minimum discrepancy across all possible combinations of sequences selected, one from each topology. We calculate the total number of distinct sequence topologies for a specific length and label set, establish the minimum upper bound for the difference among sequence topologies, and finally determine the precise difference for a given set of sequence topologies with equal length.

Accurately forecasting network traffic behavior is vital for the efficient administration of contemporary telecommunication systems. However, relying solely on intuitive methods like administrative expertise and market analysis data proves insufficient for building a robust forecasting framework. Consequently, researchers have explored various mathematical models to capture general traffic trends and generate predictions. Despite this, no prior study has comprehensively evaluated different regression models and their ensembles specifically for analyzing real-world anomalous traffic. This paper investigates several regression algorithms—including Extra Gradient Boost (XGBoost), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), Gradient Boosting Regressor (GBR), and CatBoost Regressor—to predict actual traffic with and without outliers, thereby highlighting the importance of outlier detection. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ensemble regression models outperform individual prediction models. We assessed these models using five distinct feature sets with lengths of 6, 9, 12, 15, and 18. Our ensemble approach achieved the lowest average gap of 5.04% between actual and predicted traffic when utilizing nine outlier-adjusted inputs. Overall, our experimental findings suggest that data outliers can substantially degrade prediction quality. Therefore, detecting and mitigating outliers enables regression models to better learn general traffic trends and produce more accurate forecasts.

This paper initially investigates the existence and uniqueness, along with large deviation estimates, for solutions to stochastic Volterra integral equations featuring singular kernels within 2-smooth Banach spaces. Subsequently, these results are applied to a broad range of semilinear stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs) driven by both Brownian and fractional Brownian motions, establishing the existence of unique maximal strong solutions under local Lipschitz conditions. Finally, the study examines high-order SPDEs in bounded Euclidean domains, second-order SPDEs on complete Riemannian manifolds, and stochastic Navier-Stokes equations.

This paper tackles multi-modal pretraining for e-commerce product data. Existing methods for image and text modalities often fail to handle modality-missing and modality-noise, two prevalent challenges in real-world e-commerce environments. To address this, we introduce K3M, a novel approach that incorporates a knowledge modality to mitigate noise and fill gaps in image and text data. The architecture consists of a modal-encoding layer for feature extraction and a modal-interaction layer that models multi-modal relationships. This layer includes an initial-interactive feature fusion model to preserve the independence of image and text modalities, alongside a structure aggregation module that integrates information from image, text, and knowledge modalities. K3M is pretrained using three tasks: masked object modeling (MOM), masked language modeling (MLM), and link prediction modeling (LPM). Experiments on a real-world e-commerce dataset and various product-based downstream tasks show that K3M significantly outperforms baseline and state-of-the-art methods, particularly in scenarios involving modality noise or missing data.

We analyze flux-integrated semi-exclusive differential and integral cross sections for quasi-elastic neutrino charged-current interactions with argon. Using the relativistic distorted-wave impulse approximation, we compute these cross sections and compare our results to recent MicroBooNE data. Our findings indicate that the measured cross sections align well with experimental uncertainties when the nucleon axial mass is set between 1 and 1.2 GeV. Furthermore, the exclusive channel $(\nu_{\mu}, \mu p)$ accounts for approximately 50% of the flux-integrated inclusive cross sections.

Forecasting future observations presents a significant challenge. The two primary methods for measuring prediction uncertainty are prediction regions and predictive distributions; the latter is generally considered more informative due to its utility in various prediction-related tasks. While standard validity, or Type-1 validity, concerns the coverage probability of prediction regions, a corresponding concept for the additional tasks enabled by predictive distributions has been missing. This paper introduces Type-2 validity, which addresses these other tasks. We demonstrate the relationship between Type-2 validity and coherence, showing that imprecise probability frameworks are necessary to attain it. Furthermore, we illustrate that both Type-1 and Type-2 validity can be realized by viewing conformal prediction outputs as the contour functions of consonant plausibility measures. Additionally, we provide an alternative characterization of conformal prediction through a novel nonparametric inferential model construction, where consonance arises naturally, and we prove its validity.

Self-supervised learning focuses on deriving effective representations from unlabeled data. Recent studies indicate that larger models gain more from this approach than smaller ones, significantly narrowing the performance gap between supervised and self-supervised learning for large-scale architectures. Rather than creating a new pseudo-task, this work introduces a model compression technique to distill a pre-trained, deep self-supervised teacher model into a smaller student model. The student is trained to replicate the relative similarity structure found within the teacher's embedding space. On the ImageNet dataset, this method surpasses all prior techniques, including fully supervised models, achieving 59.0% accuracy in linear evaluation (versus 56.5%) and 50.7% in nearest neighbor evaluation (versus 41.4%) when applied to AlexNet. To our knowledge, this marks the first instance where a self-supervised AlexNet exceeds a supervised counterpart in ImageNet classification. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/UMBCvision/CompRess

Matrix-variate structural observations frequently appear in various domains, including multi-layer network analysis and brain image clustering. Although such data have been extensively studied with positive results, critical questions regarding their statistical optimality and computational boundaries remain largely unexplored. This paper introduces a low-rank Gaussian mixture model (LrMM), positing that each matrix-valued observation contains a planted low-rank structure. We derive minimax lower bounds for estimating the underlying low-rank matrix across a broad spectrum of sample sizes and signal strengths. Under a minimal signal strength condition, termed the information-theoretic or statistical limit, we prove the minimax optimality of a maximum likelihood estimator, despite its general computational infeasibility. When the signal exceeds a specific threshold known as the computational limit, we develop a fast spectral aggregation-based estimator and demonstrate its minimax optimality. Furthermore, when signal strength falls below this computational limit, we use the low-degree likelihood ratio framework to argue that no polynomial-time algorithm can consistently recover the underlying low-rank matrix. Our findings uncover multiple phase transitions in minimax error rates and the statistical-to-computational gap, with numerical experiments validating our theoretical results. Finally, we illustrate the effectiveness of our spectral aggregation method using a global food trading dataset.

An isometric path cover, or geodesic cover, refers to a collection of geodesics that collectively include all vertices of a graph, whereas an edge geodesic cover consists of geodesics covering the entire edge set. The geodesic (or edge) cover number is defined as the size of the smallest such cover, and the associated problem involves determining this minimum cardinality. Unfortunately, complete solutions for these problems remain elusive in most cases. This paper establishes that for the $r$-dimensional butterfly graph, the geodesic cover number equals $\lceil (2/3)2^r\rceil$ and the edge geodesic cover number is exactly $2^r$.

We introduce the near-Maximal Algorithm for Poisson-disk Sampling (nMAPS), a method designed to create point distributions for variable-resolution Delaunay triangular and tetrahedral meshes in both 2D and 3D. The algorithm operates in two primary phases: first, an initial point set is generated via a cell-based rejection technique, and second, an efficient background grid identifies and fills gaps to achieve a near-maximal covering. Extensive evaluations indicate that nMAPS produces variable-resolution meshes in linear time relative to the number of accepted points. We illustrate nMAPS's effectiveness by meshing three-dimensional discrete fracture networks (DFN) along with their surrounding volume. Specifically, the planar polygonal boundaries of the fractures serve as the seed for 2D-nMAPS to create a conforming Delaunay triangulation, which then acts as the seed for 3D-nMAPS to generate conforming Delaunay tetrahedra around the network. Under conditions naturally inherent to maximal Poisson-disk samples and met by nMAPS, the resulting 2D Delaunay triangulations are guaranteed to consist solely of well-behaved triangles. Although nMAPS does not offer strict quality bounds for dimensions greater than two, our findings show that low-quality tetrahedra in 3D are rare, easily detectable and removable, ultimately yielding a high-quality balanced mesh.

This paper aims to establish existence and non-existence theorems for deterministic Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equations featuring non-local "gradient terms." Specifically, given a bounded domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ with $N \geq 2$ and a $C^2$ boundary $\partial \Omega$, we examine problems of the form:
\[ \tag{KPZ} \left\{ \begin{aligned} (-\Delta)^s u & = \mu(x) |\mathbb{D}(u)|^q + \lambda f(x), \quad && \mbox{ in } \Omega,\\ u & = 0, && \mbox{ in } \mathbb{R}^N \setminus \Omega, \end{aligned} \right. \]
where $q > 1$ and $\lambda > 0$ are real parameters, $f$ lies in an appropriate Lebesgue space, $\mu$ is in $L^{\infty}(\Omega)$, and $\mathbb{D}$ denotes a nonlocal "gradient term." Based on the magnitude of $\lambda$, we obtain corresponding existence and non-existence outcomes. Notably, our work resolves several open questions raised in [4, Section 6] and [2, Section 7].

The drive for explainability stems from the opacity of black-box machine learning (ML) methods, which hinders trust and adoption of these algorithms. This challenge is equally relevant in Predictive Process Monitoring, where ML-generated predictions require clear explanations to secure user confidence. This study presents a user evaluation of explanation techniques within Predictive Process Monitoring, assessing whether and how provided explanations (i) achieve understandability, (ii) support decision-making, and (iii) can be enhanced for process analysts across varying levels of ML expertise. The evaluation results indicate that while explanation plots are generally comprehensible and beneficial for decision-making among business process management users—regardless of their ML background—significant variations exist in how different plots are understood and utilized, particularly among users with differing degrees of ML knowledge.

It remains uncertain if bulge expansion causes the flattening of the star-forming main sequence (MS) at high masses. To examine how bulges influence the MS, we analyzed the NUV$-r$ color—a reliable tracer of specific star formation rate—in the central ($r<R_{50}$) versus outer regions of 6,401 local star-forming galaxies. Our results show that for galaxies with $M_{\ast}<10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, the central NUV$-r$ is only about 0.25 magnitudes redder than the outer regions. However, above $M_{\ast}=10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, the central NUV$-r$ becomes significantly redder than the outer regions, indicating that bulges in massive galaxies are more evolved. When sorting galaxies by S\'ersic index $n$, those with $n$>2.0 exhibit redder central NUV$-r$ colors than those with $n$<2.0, even when controlling for B/T ratio and $M_{\ast}$. This implies that bulge star formation depends more strongly on $n$ (or central mass density) than on the B/T ratio. Furthermore, the fraction of galaxies with $n$>2.0 rises sharply with mass for $M_{\ast}>10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, aligning with the turnover in the MS at this transition mass. We conclude that the growing proportion of low specific star formation rate, dense bulges in galaxies with $M_{\ast}>10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, rather than an increase in B/T, drives the flattening of the $M_{\ast}$$-$SFR relation at high masses.

It is well-established that irreducible projective representations (Reps) of anti-unitary groups fall into three categories—real, complex, and quaternion—associated with torsion numbers of 1, 2, and 4, respectively. This distinction complicates the derivation of such irreducible projective Reps. This study introduces a physical framework to establish the irreducibility conditions for projective Reps of anti-unitary groups and outlines a practical method to decompose any arbitrary projective Rep into a direct sum of irreducible components. The core strategy involves constructing a Hermitian Hamiltonian matrix that commutes with the representation of every group element $g \in G$, ensuring that each resulting eigenspace constitutes an irreducible representation space of $G$, thereby fully reducing the Rep. This methodology is applied within the $k \cdot p$ effective theory at high symmetry points (HSPs) of the Brillouin zone to analyze quasi-particle excitations in magnetic materials. Following the presentation of criteria to evaluate the strength of single-particle dispersion near an HSP, a systematic procedure for building the corresponding $k \cdot p$ effective model is provided.

The chapter begins by introducing core concepts of quantitative linguistics, such as rank-frequency dependence, Zipf's law, and frequency spectra. The observation that word distributions in texts resemble level occupation in quantum ensembles suggests a superficial analogy with statistical physics. This parallel allows for the definition of physical parameters for texts, including "temperature," "chemical potential," and entropy, creating a set of variables useful for classifying texts as examples of complex systems. Notably, texts may represent the most accessible complex systems for collection and analysis.

Similar methodologies can be applied to study genomes, leveraging established linguistic analogies. We examine specific approaches for defining nucleotide sequences in mitochondrial DNA and viral RNA, illustrating their potential utility as supplementary tools for comparative genomic analysis.

Finally, we address entropy as a parameter readily derived from rank-frequency dependences. While entropy serves as a discriminating factor in certain classification problems for complex systems, its meaningful interpretation is restricted to a specific subset of cases. Consequently, its comprehensive role and significance remain unresolved issues.

We introduce QADI, an automatically gathered dataset comprising tweets from diverse country-level Arabic dialects across 18 nations in the Middle East and North Africa. Our construction methodology involves applying multiple filters to identify users based on their account descriptions, while excluding tweets written in Modern Standard Arabic or containing inappropriate language. The final dataset includes 540,000 tweets from 2,525 users, evenly distributed across 18 Arab countries. Intrinsic evaluation demonstrates that the labels of randomly selected tweets are 91.5% accurate. For extrinsic evaluation, we developed an effective country-level dialect identification system achieving a macro-averaged F1-score of 60.6% across 18 classes.

The interfacial interaction between two materials exhibiting distinct ordered phases, specifically a superconductor (S) and a ferromagnet (F), is fostering novel fundamental physics and cutting-edge applications. Instances such as the development of spin-filter Josephson junctions and the realization of triplet supercurrents indicate the viability of a dissipationless spintronics paradigm grounded in unconventional superconductivity. In this study, we provide evidence for the active quantum utility of S-F-S junctions by detecting macroscopic quantum tunneling within Josephson junctions featuring GdN ferromagnetic insulator barriers. We establish a distinct transition from a thermal to a quantum regime occurring at a crossover temperature of approximately 100 mK under zero magnetic field in junctions that exhibit clear signatures of unconventional superconductivity. Building upon prior demonstrations of passive S-F-S phase shifters in phase qubits, our findings open the path toward the active integration of spin filter Josephson systems into quantum hybrid circuits.

This research conducts a cross-lingual sentiment analysis of news articles by applying zero-shot and few-shot learning techniques. The objective is to categorize Croatian news into positive, negative, and neutral sentiments using a Slovene dataset. The proposed system utilizes a trilingual BERT-based model trained on English, Slovene, and Croatian. The study evaluates various configurations using two-language datasets and introduces a straightforward multi-task model for sentiment classification. Assessments are carried out across single-task and multi-task experiments within both few-shot and zero-shot scenarios for Croatian and Slovene.

Building on a previously proposed formulation of quantum gravity based on world histories, it is suggested that the universe possesses its own intrinsic mass, analogous to particle mass in relativistic mechanics. This mass arises as a distribution of non-zero gravitational constraints that evolve over time due to initial conditions of fundamental dynamic variables. A Euclidean quantum gravity formulation is introduced to determine the initial state serving as the source of this universal mass. Distinct from ordinary matter, this self-mass influences spacetime geometry and establishes a specific reference frame. The existence of such selected reference systems is incorporated through corresponding modifications to the system of quantum gravitational links. A variant of this modification involves an operator representation of gravitational constraints within the Wheeler-De Witt equation; this representation, alongside the universe's state, defines the reference system parameters as a spinor field distribution on a spatial section.

Homomorphic encryption (HE) allows for secure cloud computation by enabling operations directly on encrypted data. However, because HE relies on noisy encryption schemes where errors accumulate with each operation, practical applications are limited by the number of allowable computations. Bootstrapping overcomes this barrier by refreshing ciphertexts, thereby enabling Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) with an unlimited number of operations; yet, this process demands substantial additional computational resources and memory bandwidth. While previous research has introduced hardware accelerators for specific FHE primitives, this work is the first to propose an accelerator that treats bootstrapping as a core capability. We introduce BTS, a Bootstrappable, Technology-driven, Secure architecture for FHE. Our analysis of the challenges inherent in hardware bootstrapping, specifically regarding off-chip memory bandwidth and computation, led us to identify HE parameter sets optimized for modern memory constraints. Leveraging these insights, BTS utilizes a grid of numerous processing elements to maximize the inherent parallelism of HE operations. The architecture includes a specialized network-on-chip designed for deterministic communication patterns. Experimental results demonstrate that BTS achieves execution time improvements of 5,556x on ResNet-20 and 1,306x on logistic regression compared to a CPU, occupying a chip area of 373.6mm² and consuming up to 163.2W of power.

This study introduces an unsupervised learning framework for precoding that trains deep neural networks (DNNs) without target labels by unfolding a proximal "log" barrier function based on an interior point method (IPM). This barrier function originates from a strict power minimization formulation constrained by the signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR). Leveraging known interference through symbol-level precoding (SLP) to reduce transmit power, the proposed method is termed strict Symbol-Level-Precoding deep network (SLP-SDNet). Results indicate that SLP-SDNet surpasses the conventional block-level-precoding (Conventional BLP) scheme and achieves near-optimal performance more rapidly than traditional SLP optimization approaches.

Wegner introduced the collapsibility number of simplicial complexes to analyze the intersection patterns of convex sets, a concept that is also fundamental to various Helly-type theorems. However, literature offers only a limited number of upper bounds for this metric, as deriving non-trivial ones is generally challenging. In this article, we develop a sequence of upper bounds, denoted as $\theta_k(X)$, for the collapsibility number of a simplicial complex $X$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the $\theta_k$ bound is tight when the underlying complex is $k$-vertex decomposable. Finally, we establish an upper bound for $\theta_k$—and consequently for the collapsibility number of a hypergraph's non-cover complex—based on its covering number.

Unsupervised learning is considered vital for most algorithms used in brain image analysis. Deep InfoMax (DIM), a recently developed unsupervised method, offers a flexible, non-linear means of investigating brain structure. This study evaluates various DIM configurations against supervised convolutional neural networks based on AlexNet and ResNet architectures, specifically within the context of Alzheimer's disease progression. The research benchmarks these models using a four-class classification task distinguishing between healthy controls, patients with stable and progressive mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and those with Alzheimer's disease. The analysis utilizes a dataset of 828 participants from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). Experimental results suggest that DIM holds significant promise for future neuroimaging research.

Real-time media monitoring requires organizing and clustering multilingual news articles. While most existing methods prioritize high-resource languages like English, often neglecting low-resource ones, we propose a streamlined online system capable of clustering document streams without relying on language-specific features. Our empirical findings show that utilizing multilingual contextual embeddings for document representation markedly enhances clustering performance. We challenge prior cross-lingual methods by eliminating the prerequisite of constructing monolingual clusters first. By modeling the process as a collection of linear classifiers to group similar documents, our system dynamically merges closely related multilingual clusters in an online manner. This approach achieves state-of-the-art results on a multilingual news stream clustering dataset and introduces a novel evaluation metric for zero-shot news clustering across multiple languages. Additionally, we have released our code as open-source.

Placeholder translation systems allow users to define how specific phrases appear in the final translated sentence. These systems are trained to generate special placeholder tokens, which are later replaced with user-provided terms via context-free substitution. However, this method often yields ungrammatical sentences because the inserted term may require inflection based on the output context, which remains unknown prior to translation. To solve this, we introduce a new placeholder translation approach capable of inflecting specified terms to match the grammatical structure of the resulting sentence. Our method extends the standard sequence-to-sequence architecture by adding a character-level decoder; this component receives the lemma of a user-specified term along with words generated by a word-level decoder to produce the correctly inflected form. We evaluated this approach on a Japanese-to-English translation task within the scientific writing domain, demonstrating that our model successfully incorporates specified terms in their correct forms more effectively than comparable models.

This study examines the source of fountain pressure generated by minor temperature variations in superfluid helium. While Tisza's (1938) osmotic pressure model, which relies on differing fractions of ground-state bosons, is recast as an ideal solution, it is demonstrated to overestimate the fountain pressure by an order of magnitude or more. Conversely, the experimentally validated thermodynamic formulation by H. London (1939)—where the temperature derivative of pressure corresponds to entropy per unit volume—is shown to equate to the equality of chemical potential rather than chemical potential divided by temperature. Specifically, the former arises from minimizing energy at constant entropy, whereas the latter stems from maximizing entropy. Consequently, it is concluded that the fountain effect in superfluids is driven by mechanical, not statistical, forces. This newly identified principle appears to serve as a universal law governing flow in both superfluids and superconductors.

This study investigates the potential for socioeconomic collapse triggered by epidemic spread. We utilize a simplified SIS (susceptible-infected-susceptible) model featuring negative feedback between the number of infected individuals and a collective economic resource, representing the average income or wealth per agent. The system's coupling operates via an activation mechanism, where the recovery rate follows an Arrhenius-like law. In this framework, the economic resource functions as an effective market temperature, while the minimum resource consumption threshold corresponds to activation energy. This interaction can induce a collapsing effect contrary to thermal explosion, potentially driving the system to collapse at non-zero activation energy due to resource scarcity. Consequently, the system may fail to stabilize, preventing a return to either a pre-epidemic stable state or a degraded post-epidemic equilibrium. We demonstrate that such collapse can be partially alleviated through external subsidies, defined as constant resource inflows, or through debt, interpreted as a negative resource. Furthermore, we analyze a basic quarantine scenario, illustrating that its socioeconomic outcomes vary based on initial resource levels (market temperature) and the minimum resource consumption required (activation energy).

Text classification stands as a core task in Natural Language Processing. Although various sequential models can achieve strong predictive performance, they often fail to establish a meaningful link between language semantics and their output predictions. To address this, the paper introduces a new influence score (I-score), a greedy search method named the Backward Dropping Algorithm (BDA), and an innovative feature engineering approach known as the "dagger technique." First, the I-score is developed to identify and select critical linguistic semantics within documents that enhance prediction accuracy in classification tasks. Second, the Backward Dropping Algorithm is proposed to effectively manage long-term dependencies in the data. Additionally, the "dagger technique" is introduced to completely maintain the relationship between explanatory and response variables. These methods are designed to be adaptable across various feed-forward Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), and neural networks in general. The study validates these approaches using a real-world application on the Internet Movie Database (IMDB), demonstrating that implementing the proposed methods reduces error rates by 81% compared to popular baseline models when the I-score and "dagger technique" are not utilized.

This work examines theoretical frameworks for form factors in heavy-meson decays, which represent hadronic manifestations of non-perturbative QCD. Following an introduction to their derivation from QCD factorisation, we trace their development from quark-model approaches to advanced non-perturbative QCD methods, specifically highlighting truncated heavy-light amplitude formulations grounded in Dyson-Schwinger equations. We further evaluate model predictions for the B\to\pi transition form factor and present new findings regarding the g_{D*D\pi} coupling within hadronic D* decays.

We provide an optimal upper bound for the degree of quasi-smooth hypersurfaces that remain invariant under a one-dimensional holomorphic foliation on a compact toric orbifold, specifically a complete simplicial toric variety. This bound relies solely on the degree of the foliation and the degrees of the toric homogeneous coordinates.

A primary objective in genetic research involves pinpointing genes associated with human diseases and traits to elucidate the functional impacts of genetic mutations and improve diagnostic capabilities. While examining individual genes in isolation offers some insights, analyzing gene pathways—collections of interacting genes that jointly execute specific biological functions—yields more biologically relevant outcomes. This gene pathway analysis can be framed as a high-dimensional two-sample testing problem. However, given the typically small sample sizes in gene expression datasets, many current two-sample tests suffer from reduced statistical power because they neglect or inadequately utilize auxiliary information regarding gene interactions within pathways. We introduce T2-DAG, a Hotelling's $T^2$-type test designed to detect differentially expressed gene pathways, which effectively integrates pathway interaction data via a linear structural equation model. Under specific assumptions, we derive the asymptotic distribution of the test statistic. Simulation studies across diverse scenarios demonstrate that T2-DAG surpasses several established methods, maintaining well-controlled type-I error rates while achieving significantly enhanced power, even when faced with incomplete or inaccurate pathway data or unadjusted confounding factors. Furthermore, we apply T2-DAG to identify differentially expressed KEGG pathways across various stages of lung cancer, illustrating its practical utility.

Previous statistical research on earthquake occurrences, utilizing point process methodologies, has primarily relied on earthquake catalogs while neglecting environmental variables. This study introduces inhomogeneous Cox process models designed to quantify the influence of geological factors—including subduction zones, faults, and volcanoes—on the distribution of major earthquakes in Sulawesi and Maluku, Indonesia. Specifically, we evaluate Thomas, Cauchy, variance-Gamma, and log-Gaussian Cox models by examining parametric intensity and pair correlation functions to improve interpretability. Model selection is conducted using the Akaike information criterion (AIC) and envelope tests. Our findings indicate that proximity to subduction zones and volcanoes significantly impacts earthquake risk in the region. Additionally, both the Cauchy and variance-Gamma cluster models provide a strong fit for the major earthquake distribution in Sulawesi and Maluku.

Recently, cache coherence protocols utilizing self-invalidation and self-downgrade have gained traction owing to their simplicity, performance potential, and low energy usage. Nevertheless, these mechanisms induce memory instruction reordering, leading to unintended program behaviors. We introduce a new formal model that encapsulates the semantics of programs executing under such protocols, incorporating a set of fences that interface with the coherence layer. Leveraging this model, we developed an algorithm to analyze reachability and verify if a program adheres to a specified safety property given the current fences. Furthermore, we present a technique for inserting optimal fence sets to guarantee program correctness. This approach employs a counter-example guided insertion strategy and supports diverse fence types with varying costs, requiring the optimization of total cost rather than merely the count of fences. To validate our methodology, we implemented a prototype and tested it across numerous examples and benchmarks, subsequently evaluating the performance of the resulting fenced programs via simulation.

In February 2020, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared the coronavirus disease (COVID-19), caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, a global pandemic. As of now, no treatments or vaccines have received approval following clinical trials. To curb transmission and alleviate pressure on healthcare systems, nations and regions have implemented social distancing protocols, including travel restrictions, school closures, and quarantines. However, these isolation measures have restricted public access to reliable information. Consequently, the South African Minister of Health provides daily updates to the public, detailing confirmed cases along with patient demographics such as age, gender, and travel history. Complementing these announcements, the South African National Institute for Communicable Diseases publishes daily infographics summarizing test volumes, confirmed cases, mortality rates, and affected regions; yet, specific details like patient age and nuanced transmission data remain exclusive to the minister's verbal or written reports. To address this information gap, the Data Science for Social Impact research group at the University of Pretoria has curated publicly available data into computer-readable formats, distributing it via a data repository and an interactive dashboard. This initiative highlighted several challenges regarding public data in South Africa, particularly concerning accessibility, integrity, and data management practices across government departments and the general public. This paper presents potential solutions to these issues, utilizing the aforementioned repository and dashboard as a case study.

Stochastic Programming offers a robust framework for decision-making in uncertain environments, with two-stage stochastic programs (2SPs) representing the most prevalent model class. Exact solutions for 2SPs demand the optimization of an expected value function, a task that is computationally prohibitive; this difficulty is exacerbated when the second stage involves mixed-integer linear (MIP) or nonlinear (NLP) programs, even with specialized algorithms. In such contexts, identifying high-quality first-stage solutions without relying on specific problem structures is vital. We introduce Neur2SP, a novel approach that utilizes a neural network to approximate the expected value function, creating a surrogate model that solves more efficiently than traditional extensive formulations. Crucially, Neur2SP imposes no assumptions regarding problem structure or the second-stage formulation and is compatible with standard MIP solvers. Extensive computational tests across four benchmark 2SP classes—including those with MIP and NLP second stages—highlight the method's efficiency and solution quality. Neur2SP consistently delivers high-quality solutions in under 1.66 seconds, regardless of the number of scenarios, a performance metric that is challenging for conventional 2SP techniques to match. In contrast, the most generic baseline methods typically require minutes to hours to achieve comparable solution quality.

This research investigates prime tensor ideals within tensor abelian categories associated with quiver representations. Specifically, we categorize these ideals in the context of zigzag quivers (restricted to bounded path lengths) where the vertices correspond to the set of integers. Our findings establish a canonical bijection between prime tensor ideals in these categories and prime ideals of a Boolean algebra, namely the power set of integers.

This study identifies and characterizes the potential for green jobs in Argentina—positions poised to benefit from a shift toward a green economy—by applying occupational green potential scores derived from US O*NET data to Argentine household survey records. Our analysis estimates that 25% of the workforce occupies green jobs, defined as those with high green potential. However, when factoring in labor informality, we determine that only 15% of workers and 12% of wage earners hold formal green jobs. Furthermore, we examine the link between greenness scores, with a focus on their connection to decent work, and various individual-level labor and demographic factors. Results indicate that within the full workforce, green potential is relatively higher among men, older individuals, those with very high qualifications, formal employees, and workers in specific sectors including construction, transportation, mining, and industry; these are the groups most likely to benefit from Argentina's economic greening. Conversely, when restricting the sample to wage earners, the green potential score shows a positive association with informality.

In practical applications, the in-control mean and standard deviation of a quality characteristic may fluctuate, making the coefficient of variation (CV) a more suitable metric for evaluating process stability. This study focuses on the statistical design of Run Rules-based control charts for monitoring the CV of multivariate data. The performance of these proposed charts is assessed using a Markov chain approach. Computational results indicate that Run Rules-based charts significantly outperform standard Shewhart control charts. Furthermore, with an appropriately selected scheme, these charts also surpass the Rum Sum control chart in monitoring multivariate CV. An illustrative example from a spring manufacturing process is provided to demonstrate the application of the proposed charts.

Feynman integrals can be expressed using the Mathematica packages AMBRE and MB as multiple Mellin-Barnes integrals, which are subsequently converted into multiple sums via the Mathematica package MBsums.

Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) systems currently face limitations regarding slow processing speeds, poor signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and costly, complex hardware. This study demonstrates the application of a denoising convolutional network to enhance FLIM SNR. This network is integrated into an instant FLIM system characterized by rapid data acquisition through analog signal processing, high SNR achieved via high-efficiency pulse modulation, and a cost-effective design using standard off-the-shelf radio-frequency components. The proposed instant FLIM system simultaneously generates intensity maps, lifetime data, and phasor plots for both *in vivo* and *ex vivo* samples. By applying the trained deep learning denoising model to FLIM data, accurate phasor measurements are achieved. These enhanced phasors are subsequently processed using K-means clustering, an unbiased and unsupervised machine learning technique, to precisely segment different fluorophores. Experimental results on *in vivo* mouse kidneys show that applying deep learning-based image denoising prior to segmentation effectively eliminates noise in the phasor space compared to current methods, resulting in clearer segmentation. Consequently, this deep learning-driven workflow enables fast and accurate automatic segmentation of fluorescence images using instant FLIM. The denoising step proves particularly effective for segmentation when FLIM measurements are noisy, while the clustering process significantly improves the detection of biologically relevant structures in biomedical imaging.

Recent decades have marked a period of extraordinary progress in our understanding of the large-scale universe. Specifically, increasingly precise cosmological observations have revealed the existence of "dark energy," which currently drives the universe's expansion. Conversely, unresolved issues within the standard cosmological model suggest the likelihood of a primordial inflationary epoch. Both of these expansion phases share a common characteristic: they are likely governed by energy forms with properties closely resembling the vacuum energy of classical or quantum fields. Concurrently, quantum field theory in curved spacetime (QFTCS) has emerged as a robust framework for analyzing quantum phenomena in regimes where spacetime curvature is significant but not extreme, offering fresh insights into the structure and dynamics of the quantum vacuum. This dissertation provides a comprehensive overview of QFTCS fundamentals and explores its applications within cosmological spacetimes. Special focus is placed on establishing an empirical definition of particles using an idealized detector model and examining particle creation in expanding FLRW spacetimes. Furthermore, we develop the method of adiabatic renormalization to calculate the renormalized stress tensor in these environments. For a noninteracting scalar field in de Sitter space, we determine that the result manifests as a cosmological constant, though a quantitatively self-consistent value aligning with the background expansion is only achievable at Planckian densities. Additionally, we construct a straightforward inflationary model driven by a self-interacting classical scalar field and demonstrate how the quantized fluctuations of this field could generate a nearly scale-invariant power spectrum, consistent with current CMB observations.

Achieving interactive global illumination in scenes with complex radiometric and geometric properties remains a significant challenge. While specialized sampling techniques work well for specular and near-specular transport due to low directional variance per bounce, resolving high-variance paths involving multiple rough glossy or diffuse events is notoriously difficult with limited samples. We address this by extending unidirectional path tracing through the integration of screen-space reservoir resampling and sparse world-space probes, which markedly enhances sample efficiency for transport terminating at diffuse bounces. Experimental results show clear superiority over both pure path tracing and pure probe-based baselines in terms of equal time and quality. Furthermore, when paired with standard denoisers, this approach enables interactive rendering of global illumination in complex environments.

This paper examines corrections to the mean field theory potential within a nucleon system. We argue that these corrections arise from deforming the Schrödinger equation for nucleons by incorporating a minimal length within the space-time background geometry. This minimal length results from quantum gravitational effects, which influence low-energy quantum mechanical systems. Specifically, since the nucleon mean field potential is modeled by the Woods-Saxon potential, we explicitly analyze the resulting corrections to it. Furthermore, we derive the energy eigenvalue corrections for the deformed Schrödinger equation applied to the Woods-Saxon potential and construct the corresponding wave function.

We report the first successful magneto-optical trap of an atom from Group III of the Periodic Table. Our selected atom, indium, lacks a ground-state transition suitable for standard laser cooling; consequently, we cool atoms on the $\lvert 5P_{3/2},F=6 \rangle \rightarrow \lvert 5D_{5/2},F=7 \rangle$ transition, where the initial state is a long-lived metastable level. By optimizing trap parameters, we achieved atom numbers up to $5\times10^8$ at temperatures around 1 mK. Trap decay measurements yield a one-body lifetime of 12.3 s, consistent with background gas collisions and indicating that our repumpers have successfully eliminated all leakage pathways. Furthermore, we determine a two-body loss rate of $1.6\times 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{cm^3/s}$, a value comparable to those observed in alkali atoms. The techniques presented here can be easily extended to other Group III atoms, and our findings lay the groundwork for creating quantum degenerate gases of these species.
