We establish that the fiber ring of invariant jet differentials for a projective manifold is finitely generated on the regular locus. While Berczi and Kirwan have partially addressed this issue in \cite{BK}, our approach is distinct and complementary. The analytic automorphism group acting on regular $k$-jets of holomorphic curves within a projective variety $X$ constitutes a non-reductive subgroup of $GL_k \mathbb{C}$. Consequently, Chevalley's theorem regarding invariant polynomials in fiber rings does not generally hold. This necessitates alternative techniques for analyzing Cartan subalgebras of the Lie algebra and its associated Weyl group. By combining methods from algebraic Lie groups (which need not be reductive) with foundational results from \cite{BK}, we demonstrate the finite generation of the stalk ring at a regular point.

Humans possess a robust mental representation of environmental entities, which are defined by their attributes; entities sharing these attributes are frequently semantically connected. For instance, if two books share the title "Natural Language Processing," it is reasonable to infer that their topic is also "NLP." Humans generalize such patterns to deduce the conditions under which an entity possesses a specific attribute. To interact effectively with humans, robots must adopt a similar approach to representing entities, attributes, and generalizations. This leads to the development of a contextualized cognitive agent capable of adaptive understanding, where context serves as the basis for accurate interpretation. This research addresses the challenge of acquiring these representations via human-robot interaction. By combining visual perception with natural language input, we incrementally construct a semantic model of the world and employ inductive reasoning to derive logical rules that encapsulate general semantic relations within this model. These relations can enhance human-robot interaction, populate a knowledge base with inferred facts, or reduce uncertainty in the robot's sensory data.

Advances in science and technology have increasingly revealed humanity's capacity to comprehend and control the physical realm, while simultaneously exposing inherent constraints on our ability to predict physical occurrences. This insight has prompted numerous thinkers to question why the universe exhibits the specific degree of regularity we observe. Most explanations frame our cosmos as a probable outcome within a spectrum of potential realities. This study evaluates the likelihood criteria used in these justifications and identifies four alternative universes that, under various definitions of probability, appear more likely than our own.

Predicting molecular conformations (or 3D structures) from molecular graphs is a fundamental problem in many applications. Most existing approaches are usually divided into two steps by first predicting the distances between atoms and then generating a 3D structure through optimizing a distance geometry problem. However, the distances predicted with such two-stage approaches may not be able to consistently preserve the geometry of local atomic neighborhoods, making the generated structures unsatisfying. In this paper, we propose an end-to-end solution for molecular conformation prediction called ConfVAE based on the conditional variational autoencoder framework. Specifically, the molecular graph is first encoded in a latent space, and then the 3D structures are generated by solving a principled bilevel optimization program. Extensive experiments on several benchmark data sets prove the effectiveness of our proposed approach over existing state-of-the-art approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/MinkaiXu/ConfVAE-ICML21.

Mixup functions as a data-dependent regularization method that linearly interpolates input samples and their corresponding labels, a technique proven to enhance accuracy on standard machine learning datasets. Nevertheless, researchers have noted that Mixup can generate out-of-distribution virtual samples and internal contradictions within the augmented training set, which may lead to adversarial outcomes. This paper presents Local Mixup, an approach that reduces the weight of distant input samples during loss computation. We demonstrate that in constrained environments, Local Mixup establishes a trade-off between bias and variance, where the extremes correspond to vanilla training and traditional Mixup. Furthermore, evaluations on standardized computer vision benchmarks indicate that Local Mixup can improve test accuracy.

Massive earth observation satellite data offer significant potential for land use and land cover mapping. However, these mapping tasks remain difficult due to the diversity of land cover classes, data noise, and insufficient labeling. Furthermore, each land cover type exhibits distinct temporal patterns that are only identifiable during specific periods. This article presents a new architecture that integrates UNet with Bidirectional LSTM and Attention mechanisms to simultaneously leverage the spatial and temporal characteristics of satellite imagery, thereby enhancing the identification of unique temporal signatures for each land cover class. We apply this method to map crops across various global regions. Our approach is evaluated both quantitatively and qualitatively against other state-of-the-art techniques using two real-world datasets containing multiple land cover classes. Additionally, we visualize attention weights to demonstrate their effectiveness in reducing noise and pinpointing discriminative time periods.

This paper examines how different particlization scenarios within the hybrid ultrarelativistic quantum molecular dynamics (UrQMD) event generator influence various observables in non-central ($b$ = 5--9 fm) Au + Au collisions across a beam energy range of 1A--158A GeV. These particlization models transition from fluid dynamics to transport descriptions based on diverse hypersurface criteria. Beyond the particlization schemes, we also utilized multiple equations-of-state (EoS) offered by the UrQMD hybrid framework. The study analyzes several observables, including the excitation functions of anisotropic flow coefficients ($v_{1}$ and $v_{2}$), particle species ratios, and the net-proton rapidity distribution shape at mid-rapidity. Our findings aim to aid in predicting and comparing future measurements from the Facility for Antiproton and Ion Research (FAIR) and the Nuclotron-based Ion Collider fAcility (NICA) once data is released. Furthermore, we investigate the optimal pairing of a particlization model and an EoS that most accurately reproduces experimental results.

Large Fabry-Perot Interferometers are integral to various astronomical instruments, notably spectro-polarimeters for 4-meter class solar telescopes. This study presents a comprehensive characterization of a prototype 150 mm Fabry-Perot interferometer featuring a new, fully symmetric architecture. A key contribution is the definition of a novel method to evaluate gravity's impact on the cavity when the system operates in either vertical or horizontal orientations, both common in solar observations. Results demonstrate that the symmetric design effectively constrains the combined influence of pre-load and gravity forces to merely a few nanometers across a 120 mm illuminated area; specifically, gravity contributes approximately 2 nm peak-to-valley (0.3 nm rms) regardless of orientation. We also verify a variation in plate tilt during spectral scans, which can be corrected through adjustments to spacing commands. Furthermore, the dynamical response of this new system meets standard operational requirements. In conclusion, large, fully symmetric Fabry-Perot interferometers are suitable for solar instrumentation in both horizontal and vertical positions, with the vertical configuration offering superior advantages in minimizing the instrument's overall footprint.

This work investigates finite element approaches for symmetric linear hyperbolic systems employing unstructured advancing fronts that adhere to a causality constraint. It establishes convergence theorems and error estimates for mapped tent pitching strategies utilizing standard discontinuous Galerkin discretizations for spatial approximation on these mapped tents. Furthermore, the study develops methodologies to analyze semidiscretization on mapped tents, construct fully discrete schemes, demonstrate local error bounds, verify stability across spacetime fronts, and constrain error propagation through unstructured layers.

This study proposes utilizing configurational temperature ($\Tc$) to quantify the deviation of an active-matter system from thermal equilibrium. This "distance" is assessed via the ratio of the systemic temperature ($\Ts$) to $\Tc$, where $\Tc$ reflects local variations in the potential-energy function, and $\Ts$ represents the canonical-ensemble temperature that yields an identical average potential energy. Since $\Tc$ is local and $\Ts$ is global, the ratio $\Ts/\Tc$ is straightforward to compute in simulations, requiring only equilibrium data alongside a single steady-state active configuration. Validation using radial distribution functions from 3d Kob-Andersen and 2d Yukawa models (with both active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck and active Brownian dynamics) supports the claim that $\Ts/\Tc$ effectively measures equilibrium deviation. Furthermore, in the 2d Yukawa model, the $\Ts/\Tc$ ratio, along with structural and dynamic properties of the homogeneous phase, remains approximately constant along the motility-induced phase separation (MIPS) boundary, confirming that this metric captures the expected constant deviation from thermal equilibrium at that phase boundary. Finally, this measure extends beyond active matter, offering a method to quantify the distance from thermal equilibrium for any system defined by a potential-energy function, such as driven Hamiltonian systems.

We present a thermodynamic analysis of the interaction between new agegraphic dark energy and dark matter within a non-flat cosmological model. In the absence of interaction, each component maintains individual thermodynamic equilibrium; however, introducing an interaction between them induces a stable thermal fluctuation, altering their thermodynamic behavior. We derive a relationship linking the interaction term of the dark sector to this resulting thermal fluctuation.

The Internet of Things (IoT) and sophisticated communication technologies hold significant promise for managing residential energy through demand-side management (DSM). Home Energy Management Systems (HEMS) utilize DSM to automatically regulate electricity consumption and generation within households. By wirelessly gathering data from hardware in homes and the power grid, these systems aim to optimize energy use intelligently while reducing costs. However, HEMS are susceptible to cyberattacks targeting electricity pricing models. Attackers can manipulate price data received by a customer's HEMS, steering optimization algorithms toward suboptimal outcomes. This results in higher electricity bills and undetected demand peaks for the system operator. This paper explores demand-response (DR)-based DSM within HEMS and examines DR optimization via heuristic algorithms. Furthermore, it analyzes the potential and impact of cyberattacks, evaluating the effectiveness of such attacks and the resilience of heuristic algorithms against them. Finally, the article identifies open research questions and outlines future research directions.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are extensively utilized across diverse domains to learn from graph-structured data, often outperforming traditional heuristic methods in tasks like node and graph classification. However, their heavy reliance on smoothed node features rather than graph topology frequently results in subpar performance compared to simple heuristics in link prediction, where structural cues such as overlapping neighborhoods, node degrees, and shortest paths are essential. To overcome this drawback, we introduce Neighborhood Overlap-aware Graph Neural Networks (Neo-GNNs), which extract meaningful structural features directly from adjacency matrices and model overlapping neighborhoods for link prediction. Neo-GNNs extend existing neighborhood overlap-based heuristics and effectively manage overlapping multi-hop neighborhoods. Comprehensive experiments on Open Graph Benchmark (OGB) datasets confirm that Neo-GNNs consistently achieve state-of-the-art results in link prediction. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/seongjunyun/Neo_GNNs.

Active learning seeks to optimize data annotation under resource constraints, yet most current approaches are tailored for balanced datasets, limiting their utility since real-world data is often imbalanced. This paper presents a novel active learning strategy specifically designed for imbalanced scenarios, prioritizing samples from minority classes to balance the labeled subset and enhance their representation. We further compare two training paradigms: the standard deep active learning approach using model fine-tuning per iteration, and a transfer learning-inspired scheme that leverages generic pre-trained models while training shallow classifiers for each iteration. Experiments on three imbalanced datasets demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses competitive baselines. Notably, results reveal that the transfer learning approach outperforms fine-tuning when features are transferable from the generic source to the target unlabeled data—a surprising finding that should motivate further exploration in deep active learning methodologies.

We construct an approximate framework to describe the direct (nonsequential) two-photon double ionization of atoms. Utilizing this model, we compute both generalized total and energy-resolved differential cross sections for helium across photon energies from 39 to 54 eV. When compared with \textit{ab initio} results, the agreement is found to be quantitative. This demonstrates that the intricate ionization process is entirely captured by the simple model, offering valuable insight into the underlying physical mechanisms. Furthermore, we apply the model to determine generalized cross sections for the nonsequential two-photon double ionization of neon.

We have investigated the structural and electronic characteristics of the metallic hexagonal close-packed (hcp) phase of zinc across bulk, monolayer, bilayer, and quantum dot configurations using total energy calculations. Consistent with prior research, our calculated density of states and electronic band structures reveal hybridization of Zn $4s$, $3p$, and $3d$ orbitals in the bulk. Importantly, this orbital hybridization persists in the monolayer, bilayer, and quantum dot systems as well. Additionally, while the monolayer and bilayer configurations exhibit electronic traits typical of lamellar systems, the quantum dot system demonstrates behavior consistent with that of a zero-dimensional (0D) system.

Deep learning has become the prevailing methodology for solving diverse problems, particularly in biometrics like speech and face recognition. These biometric tasks frequently rely on deep learning models to derive image features, referred to as embeddings, where the training loss function plays a critical role in determining embedding quality. This study introduces the D-loss, a loss function grounded in the decidability index, designed to enhance embedding quality for verification processes. Unlike Triplet-based losses, which often suffer from slow convergence due to reliance on hard samples and complex parameter tuning, the D-loss circumvents these drawbacks. The proposed method was evaluated against Softmax (cross-entropy), Triplets Soft-Hard, and Multi Similarity losses across four benchmarks: MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR10, and CASIA-IrisV4. The results demonstrate the D-loss's superiority over other established metrics. Furthermore, the D-loss is characterized by its simplicity, non-parametric nature, and ease of implementation, effectively optimizing both inter-class and intra-class scenarios.

We establish upper limits on the generalization error of learning algorithms by utilizing their \emph{algorithmic transport cost}, defined as the expected Wasserstein distance between an output hypothesis and one conditioned on a specific input. This framework offers a fresh perspective on studying algorithmic generalization through optimal transport, relaxing requirements on the loss function, such as the need for it to be sub-Gaussian or bounded. Additionally, we derive several upper bounds for the algorithmic transport cost expressed via total variation distance, relative entropy (KL-divergence), and VC dimension, thereby connecting optimal transport theory, information theory, and statistical learning theory. Furthermore, we investigate various loss function conditions that allow the generalization error to be bounded by different probability metrics involving the output hypothesis and/or input data distributions. Finally, within our proposed framework, we examine generalization in deep learning, demonstrating that the generalization error in deep neural networks (DNNs) decays exponentially toward zero as the number of layers grows. Our analysis of deep learning generalization primarily leverages the hierarchical architecture of DNNs and the contraction properties of $f$-divergence, findings that may hold independent value for analyzing other hierarchical learning models.

We provide a comprehensive survey of rigorous, formal, and numerical findings regarding the formation of point-like singularities (blow-up) across various evolution equations. By applying a similarity transformation relative to the blow-up point, we map self-similar behavior to the fixed points of a dynamical system. We highlight that examining dynamics near these fixed points offers a powerful method for characterizing singularities, as the resulting dynamics often reduce to very low dimensions. To our knowledge, existing literature examples fall into categories such as stable fixed points, low-dimensional center-manifold dynamics, limit cycles, or traveling waves. For each identified class of singularity, we present detailed illustrative examples.

We introduce and experimentally assess a new secure aggregation algorithm designed for cross-organizational federated learning with a static group of participants. This approach arranges learners in a chain and encrypts all traffic, reducing the aggregator's role to that of a simple message broker. Our method demonstrates superior scalability and lower resource requirements compared to existing solutions, while remaining easy to deploy on constrained platforms. With 36 nodes, our technique outperforms current state-of-the-art secure aggregation by 70x, achieving a 56x improvement with and without failover capabilities, respectively.

Neural networks have demonstrated remarkable success in learning from intricate data distributions by functioning as universal function approximators. Nevertheless, they frequently exhibit excessive confidence in their outputs, resulting in inaccurate and poorly calibrated probabilistic estimates. This issue of overconfidence is particularly pronounced when the data encountered during testing diverges from the training distribution. To address this, we propose a method that identifies regions within the feature space where the model displays unjustified confidence and conditionally increases the entropy of these predictions to align with the label distribution's prior. Our approach yields a better-calibrated network that is independent of the specific model architecture, making it applicable to any neural network that outputs a probability density. We validate the efficacy of our technique on both classification and regression tasks by applying it to recent probabilistic neural network models.

Mean-field variational inference (MFVI) is a widely used estimation technique for Bayesian neural networks (BNNs). This study demonstrates that BNNs utilizing ReLU activation functions generate posteriors that are difficult for MFVI to approximate effectively. We offer theoretical reasoning for this challenge, examine it through empirical analysis, and present experimental results exploring how activation functions influence BNN calibration. Our findings indicate that substituting ReLU with Leaky ReLU produces weight posteriors that are more Gaussian-like and results in a lower expected calibration error (ECE) compared to models using standard ReLU activations.

For over fifty years, exercise testing has served as a highly adaptable instrument for diagnosing and prognosing various conditions, particularly those affecting the cardiovascular and pulmonary systems. Over the past decade, rapid technological progress in wearables and learning algorithms has expanded its application. Among these, Cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPX) stands out as a premier laboratory method for objectively assessing exercise capacity and performance. This non-invasive approach offers an integrative evaluation of the pulmonary, cardiovascular, and skeletal muscle systems by measuring gas exchange. However, interpreting CPX data is complex due to the volume of time-series information required, often leading to a reductionist analysis focused solely on peak values and slopes. This simplification risks discarding valuable trend data embedded within the time series. To address this, our study encodes these time series into images using Gramian Angular Field and Markov Transition Field techniques, then applies a convolutional neural network with attention pooling to classify patients with heart failure and metabolic syndrome. Furthermore, we utilize GradCAMs to visualize the discriminative features identified by the model.

Laparoscopic surgery offers the benefit of eliminating large incisions, which reduces patient pain, discomfort, and blood loss. However, it faces challenges such as limited workspace, unclear communication, and surgeon fatigue resulting from non-ergonomic head positions. This study aimed to pinpoint these critical issues and propose corresponding design requirements and solutions. By employing user and task analysis, we observed surgeons within the operating room to understand their workflows and how they achieve their objectives. Drawing insights from recorded laparoscopic procedures, we identified specific constraints and design necessities to formulate potential remedies. Surgeons typically work in low-light conditions, surrounded by monitors, and rely on verbal cues and gestures for communication. Consequently, conducting user and task analysis enabled us to clarify existing challenges in laparoscopy, specifically highlighting communication limitations and essential design criteria that any solution must meet. Our primary contribution involves establishing design requirements for laparoscopic surgery through this analytical approach; these requirements suggest design solutions aimed at enhancing surgeon comfort and reducing the labor intensity of surgical procedures.

Systematic derivation of embedded-atom method parameters for Co, Nb, and Zr metals has been accomplished. This analytical potential framework accurately reproduces the cohesive energies and structural characteristics of both pure elements and specific alloys using a minimal parameter set. By employing a pair potential that transitions smoothly to zero within an adequate cutoff radius, molecular dynamics simulations calculated radial partial and bond angular distribution functions for these metals and their alloys, yielding strong quantitative alignment with experimental data up to the melting point. Furthermore, atomic short-range order was examined through consecutive Gaussian function decomposition and Honeycutt-Andersen indices.

We introduce the Paired Few-shot GAN (PFS-GAN), a framework designed to train generators using abundant source data alongside limited target data. Although generative modeling usually requires extensive datasets, our approach leverages few-shot learning and domain shift to transfer knowledge between domains, thereby mitigating the problem of producing low-quality generators when trained solely on target data. This method operates under the assumption that cross-domain datasets possess two key characteristics: (1) every target-domain sample has a corresponding source-domain counterpart, and (2) while the two domains share similar semantic content, they differ in visual appearance. The PFS-GAN aims to extract disentangled representations from images, separating them into domain-invariant content features and domain-specific appearance features. Additionally, we incorporate a relation loss applied to content features while shifting appearance features to enhance structural diversity. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms several baselines, yielding superior quantitative and qualitative results for generated target-domain data with increased diversity.

This study aims to examine how large-scale coherent structures form in the flow around a wall-mounted square cylinder, focusing on their influence on urban pollutant dispersion. To achieve this, we evaluate causal connections between modes derived from a reduced-order model, which was constructed using proper-orthogonal decomposition applied to high-fidelity simulation data of the specific flow scenario. We employ conditional transfer entropy, an information-theoretic metric that quantifies the information in one variable's past regarding another, to identify these causal links. This approach elucidates the origins and development of various flow phenomena, specifically to pinpoint the modes driving the formation of primary vortical structures. Our findings reveal that vortex-breaker modes exhibit the strongest causal influence, surpassing higher-order modes, while vortex-generator modes show no significant causal relationships. Furthermore, we validate this methodology by analyzing causal relations in the nine-equation near-wall turbulence model proposed by Moehlis et al. (New J. Phys, vol. 6, 2004, p. 56), obtaining results that align well with established literature on turbulent channel flows.

Cubic Ti$_{1-x-y}$Al$_{x}$Zr$_{y}$N alloys containing 25–70% Al exhibit strong age-hardening properties driven by metastable phase transitions at elevated temperatures, making them promising candidates for ultra-hard nano-coatings. Emerging evidence links this phenomenon to elasto-chemical field-induced phase separation, resulting in compositionally segregated nanocrystalline nitride phases. This study investigates microstructural evolution within the spinodal region of this pseudo-ternary system at 1200 $^\circ$C using an elasto-chemical phase field model. Simulation results demonstrate that elastic interactions between nitride nano-domains significantly influence both microstructural morphology and local chemical phase equilibria. Furthermore, in Al-rich compositional regions, the transformation of AlN-rich phases into their equilibrium wurtzite crystal structure initiates. These findings suggest a broad range of accessible microstructures for these nitride systems, implying that tailored designs could substantially enhance the performance of transition metal nitride-based coatings.

The anisotropic characteristics of SrPt$_{3}$P single crystals were investigated through electrical resistivity and London penetration depth analyses. The upper critical field, $H_{c2}(T)$, was derived from four-probe resistivity data collected with magnetic fields applied along three orthogonal crystal axes. Concurrently, the temperature-dependent London penetration depth, $\lambda(T)$, was extracted from magnetic susceptibility measurements in the Meissner-London state using a tunnel-diode resonator. While $H_{c2}(T)$ and the normal-state resistivity $\rho(T)$ exhibited negligible variation across the three field orientations, the London penetration depth displayed marked unidirectional anisotropy. Specifically, applying a small radiofrequency magnetic field ($H_{rf}$) along the $c"$-axis resulted in an exponential attenuation of low-temperature $\lambda(T)$, as screening currents flowed within the $a"b"$-plane. In contrast, orientations where $H_{rf}$ was parallel to $a"$ or $b"$ yielded a much weaker $\lambda(T)$ dependence, scaling approximately as $T^{2}$. This distinct discrepancy between the anisotropies of the upper critical field, $\gamma_{H}\left(T\right)=H_{c2,ab}/H_{c2,c}=\xi_{ab}/\xi_{c}$, and the penetration depth, $\gamma_{\lambda}\left(T\right)=\lambda_{c}/\lambda_{ab}$, places stringent constraints on the viable order parameter. Although the data do not definitively determine the superconducting gap anisotropy, the results are qualitatively consistent with an order parameter featuring two point nodes and a modulation perpendicular to the nodal plane.

This study presents a solvable, rotationally invariant random matrix ensemble defined by a logarithmic confining potential. Interpretable as a transformed Jacobi ensemble, it features a Lorentzian eigenvalue density in the thermodynamic limit. The analysis demonstrates that spectral correlation functions are described by Gegenbauer polynomials $C_n^{(\lambda)}(x)$ where $\lambda = -1/2$ and $n \ge 2$. A sampling procedure for matrices within this ensemble is outlined and employed to numerically validate several analytical findings. This newly introduced ensemble is highlighted as a potentially valuable component for physical applications.

Adachi, Iyama, and Reiten introduced the theory of $\tau$-tilting, establishing a fundamental bijection between support $\tau$-tilting modules and torsion classes. We extend this result within the framework of Iyama's higher Auslander--Reiten theory. Specifically, for a finite-dimensional algebra $A$ possessing a 2-cluster-tilting subcategory $\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathrm{mod}A$, we establish a correspondence between support $\tau_2$-tilting $A$-modules and torsion pairs in $\mathcal{C}$ that satisfy a specific functorial finiteness condition.

This work investigates Lam\'e operators defined by $L = -\frac{d^2}{dx^2} + m(m+1)\omega^2\wp(\omega x+z_0)$, where $m$ is a natural number and $\omega$ represents a half-period of the Weierstrass function $\wp(z)$. For rectangular period lattices, we select $\omega$ and $z_0$ to ensure the potential is real, periodic, and regular. Building on Ince's established result that the spectrum of such operators exhibits a band structure containing at most $m$ gaps, the first section demonstrates that the open gaps correspond exactly to the initial $m$ gaps. The second section examines the Lam\'e spectrum for a general period lattice under the condition that the potential is complex-valued. We focus specifically on the $m=1$ scenario, where the spectrum comprises two regular analytic arcs, with one extending to infinity, and provide a brief analysis of the $m=2$ case, with special emphasis on rhombic lattices.

Recent studies have highlighted how inaccurate cardinality estimates, specifically underestimations, can severely degrade query performance by generating overly optimistic execution plans that run significantly slower than those based on accurate cardinalities. To mitigate this, cardinality bounding methods compute a strict upper limit on output size by leveraging database statistics like table dimensions and value frequencies. This paper advances that research by introducing the Degree Sequence Bound, a new theoretical limit that incorporates complete degree sequences and maximum tuple multiplicity. Unlike prior approaches that relied solely on maximum degree constraints, this bound offers superior accuracy. Additionally, we outline a practical method for calculating this bound through a learned approximation of the true degree sequences.

We acquired multi-colour light curves for HH Boo and examined the variations in its orbital period. Our analysis suggests a potential mass transfer from the secondary component to the primary, or alternatively, a mass loss rate of -5.04×10⁻⁷ M☉ per year. Upon re-analyzing the available radial velocity data alongside the light curves, we determined the system's inclination to be 69.71(0.16) degrees and calculated the semi-major axis as 2.246(0.064) R☉. The primary component was found to have a mass of 0.92(0.08) M☉ and a radius of 0.98(0.03) R☉, while the secondary component was derived to have a mass of 0.58(0.06) M☉ and a radius of 0.80(0.02) R☉. Based on these findings, we conclude that HH Boo belongs to the A-type subclass of W UMa binaries.

The scarcity of training data in low-resource languages creates significant hurdles for sequence labeling applications like named entity recognition (NER) and machine reading comprehension (MRC), particularly due to inaccuracies in predicted answer boundaries. To address this, we introduce CalibreNet, a two-stage framework: first, any existing sequence labeling method serves as a base model to produce an initial answer; second, CalibreNet refines the boundaries of that answer. To overcome the data scarcity challenge in low-resource settings, we specifically design a novel unsupervised pre-training task for phrase boundary recovery, which strengthens CalibreNet's multilingual boundary detection capabilities. Experimental results on two cross-lingual benchmark datasets demonstrate that this approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on zero-shot cross-lingual NER and MRC tasks.

Quantum technology is reaching a stage of maturity, evidenced by recent space-based experiments and field measurements, enabling its use by non-experts. By integrating advances in microprocessor electronics and database software, robust, modular, and versatile experimental monitoring systems can be developed. This article details a monitoring network deployed across multiple cold atom laboratories sharing a laser system. Diagnosing malfunctions, identifying unexpected behaviors, and passively gathering data on critical parameters—such as vacuum pressure, laser power, and conductor resistance—substantially cuts debugging time. Consequently, this facilitates efficient management of numerous experiments and enables remote operation when physical access is restricted.

This work introduces reductions among optimization problems defined on undirected conservative graphs—edge-weighted graphs lacking negative cycles. We resolve the complexity status of several of these problems and highlight areas that remain challenging. Our primary contribution demonstrates that the shortest odd path problem between two specified vertices, along with related variants such as the shortest odd cycle problem through a specific vertex, is NP-hard. This result provides a negative answer to a long-standing question posed by Lovász (Open Problem 27 in Schrijver's 2003 book). However, the complexity of determining a shortest odd cycle for conservative weights or finding an odd $T$-join of minimum cardinality remains unresolved. Finally, we connect these problems to relevant variants that have either been solved or hold promise.

Software development involves numerous modules, prompting the need to prioritize them so that critical components are tested first. This strategy is essential because regressive testing of every module is often infeasible due to limitations in time and budget. The paper examines key parameters for prioritizing software modules and proposes a measure for determining the optimal time and cost for testing based on a non-homogeneous Poisson process.

While complete phase synchronization is unattainable in standard Kuramoto models with nonidentical oscillators, this study demonstrates that such synchronization is feasible for a broad range of high-dimensional Kuramoto models under these conditions. Specifically, assuming a strongly connected digraph topology, the paper derives a necessary and sufficient condition for achieving complete phase synchronization. The theoretical findings are subsequently corroborated through simulation results.

Lie symmetry analysis is applied to investigate a $1+n$ fourth-order Schrödinger equation, which arises from modifying the deformation algebra under conditions of a minimum length. The study specifically conducts a thorough classification of the scalar field potential function to identify cases where non-trivial Lie symmetries exist and facilitate the simplification of the Schrödinger equation. Subsequently, a qualitative analysis is performed on the resulting reduced ordinary differential equation to elucidate its asymptotic dynamics.

We introduce a forward sufficient dimension reduction technique designed for categorical and ordinal responses by adapting the outer product of gradients and the minimum average variance estimator to multinomial generalized linear models. While prior research has extended forward regression to binary outcomes or applied it pairwise to multinomial data—resulting in lower efficiency—our method offers a more streamlined approach. Similar to other forward regression-based strategies, this technique circumvents the strict distributional assumptions required by inverse regression alternatives. We establish the consistency of the proposed estimator and determine its convergence rate. Furthermore, we outline an algorithm that utilizes repeated applications of existing forward regression procedures and introduce a clustering-based method for estimating tuning parameters. Finally, the efficacy of our estimator and associated algorithms is validated through simulations and real-world applications.

This study replicates a Bayesian educational research initiative examining the link between broadband access and online course enrollment in the United States. We summarize the primary outcomes of our replication and contrast them with the original findings. Drawing from this experience, we illustrate the difficulties inherent in research reproduction, even when code and data are openly accessible and hosted with high quality on GitHub. Furthermore, we examine the implicit assumptions regarding researchers' expertise and analyze how such presumptions can complicate the reproduction of scientific work. Finally, we hope this paper informs the development of reproducibility standards and stimulates discussion on the appropriate content for undergraduate statistics curricula.

Continual Reinforcement Learning (CRL) presents a difficult scenario where an agent must learn to engage with an environment that evolves continuously over time. This paper introduces Avalanche RL, a library designed to facilitate the training of agents on an unending stream of tasks within this setting. Built on PyTorch and compatible with any OpenAI Gym environment, Avalanche RL leverages the architecture of the popular Avalanche library. This foundation enables the reuse of numerous continual learning strategies and strengthens collaboration between researchers in both reinforcement and continual learning. Furthermore, we introduce Continual Habitat-Lab, a new benchmark and high-level library that adapts the photorealistic Habitat-Sim simulator for CRL research. Ultimately, Avalanche RL aims to consolidate various continual reinforcement learning applications into a unified framework, fostering the expansion of the field.

We enhance the class probability outputs of audio event classification models by applying post-processing and utilizing reinforcement learning to simultaneously identify optimal parameters for different stages of this pipeline, including classification thresholds and the kernel sizes of median filters used to smooth predictions. To accomplish this, we establish a reinforcement learning environment where: 1) the state represents the model's class probability distribution for a specific audio sample, 2) the action involves selecting a candidate optimal value for each parameter in the post-processing stack, and 3) the reward is determined by the classification accuracy metric we seek to maximize, specifically the audio event-based macro F1-score. We tested this approach on the class probability outputs from two models submitted to the DCASE Task 4 2020 challenge. Our results demonstrate that using reinforcement learning to determine per-class optimal parameters for the post-processing stack improves the audio event-based macro F1-score by 4-5% compared to using the same stack with manually tuned parameters.

Case Management has progressively evolved to support Knowledge-intensive business process management, leading to the creation of various modeling languages such as Declare, Dynamic Condition Response (DCR), and Case Management Model and Notation (CMMN). Much like extinct human tongues, a language fails if it lacks practical adoption; consequently, assessing user perception is vital to identify areas for improvement. While existing research has examined process designers' views on Declare and DCR, CMMN remains under-studied in this context. This study therefore investigates designers' perceptions of CMMN and DCR regarding usefulness and ease of use, utilizing the Technology Acceptance Model. DCR is incorporated to facilitate comparison with prior findings. The research involved educating master's students over an eight-week period, providing feedback on assignments to mitigate response biases. Perceptions were measured via questionnaires administered before and after feedback on their final exam projects, revealing how feedback influences participant views even among well-trained individuals. Response reliability was validated using Cronbach's alpha, indicating acceptable levels for both perceived usefulness and ease of use for the two languages.

We derive continuity properties for pseudo-differential operators with symbols belonging to quasi-Banach Orlicz modulation spaces when these operators act on other quasi-Banach Orlicz modulation spaces. Specifically, our work extends several findings presented in \cite{GH1,GH2,Toft2,Toft10,Toft16}.

This study introduces a Proper Plasma Analysis Practice (PPAP), an advanced diagnostic protocol for the age of spatially-resolved spectroscopy. We highlight the necessity of executing extinction correction and the direct diagnostic method as a unified, simultaneous process. This strategy is driven by the interdependent nature of critical parameters within these analyses, which can be solved by iteratively converging on a consistent result. By adopting PPAP, we remove superfluous assumptions that hinder the attainment of precise solutions across every pixel of spectral imaging data. Validating PPAP with HST/WFC3 narrowband images of the planetary nebula NGC 6720, we successfully (1) derived self-consistent maps for extinction $c(H\beta)$, electron density/temperature $(n_e, T_e)$, and (2) generated identical metal abundance maps, specifically for nitrogen and sulfur relative to hydrogen, using emission lines from various wavelengths and transition energies. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the derived $c(H\beta)$ comprises both interstellar medium (ISM) and circumsource components, with the ionized gas-to-dust mass ratio in the primary ring ranging from a minimum of 437 to approximately 1600. We conclude that without a deliberate pursuit of self-consistency, uncertainties reaching tens of percent can easily emerge, obscuring real spatial variations at similar magnitudes and thereby negating the value of spatially resolved spectroscopic observations.

Currently, WASP-12b remains the sole confirmed hot Jupiter exhibiting orbital decay, whereas the situation regarding WASP-43b remains contentious. While recent investigations have either supported or excluded the orbital decay hypothesis for WASP-43b, definitive confirmation of its period change requires more precise transit timing data, a capability provided by the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS). This study leverages available TESS data, along with multi-color photometry from the Multicolor Simultaneous Camera for studying Atmospheres of Transiting exoplanets 2 (MuSCAT2) and existing literature, to determine the period change rate of WASP-43b, enhance its precision, and refine the system's parameters. Utilizing a dataset of 129 observed-minus-calculated mid-transit times spanning approximately 10 years, we derived an improved period change rate of $\dot{P} = -0.6 \pm 1.2$ ms yr$^{-1}$, which is statistically consistent with a constant period within $1\sigma$. Consequently, the combined new TESS and MuSCAT2 observations confirm that there is no detected orbital decay for WASP-43b.

Discrete stochastic processes are ubiquitous in natural systems, finding applications in fields ranging from physics and biochemistry to epidemiology, sociology, and finance. Although analytic solutions are often unattainable, current simulation frameworks can produce stochastic trajectories consistent with the governing dynamical laws. However, most simulation algorithms rely on the Markovian assumption, positing that system dynamics are memoryless; under this constraint, future events depend solely on the current state. Mathematically, this assumption models inter-event times as exponentially distributed variables, facilitating exact trajectory simulation via the seminal Gillespie algorithm. Unfortunately, the majority of stochastic systems exhibit memory, an inherently non-Markovian characteristic. Analyzing non-Markovian systems is notoriously difficult, and existing numerical methods are either computationally expensive or limited by strong simplifying assumptions that often conflict with empirical data. To overcome these obstacles, we developed REGIR (Rejection-based Gillespie algorithm for non-Markovian Reactions), a general and scalable framework for simulating non-Markovian stochastic systems with arbitrary inter-event time distributions. REGIR achieves user-defined accuracy while retaining the same asymptotic computational complexity as the Gillespie algorithm. We demonstrate REGIR's modeling power across three key biochemical systems: microbial growth dynamics, stem cell differentiation, and RNA transcription. In each case, REGIR efficiently captures the underlying stochastic processes, proving its utility for accurately investigating complex non-Markovian systems. The algorithm is available as a Python library named REGIR.

This study reports measurements of the $B^0_\mathrm{S}$ $\to$ $\mu^+\mu^-$ branching fraction and effective lifetime, alongside a search for the $B^0$ $\to$ $\mu^+\mu^-$ decay in proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV using the CMS detector at the LHC. The analysis utilizes data from 2016–2018, amounting to an integrated luminosity of 140 fb$^{-1}$. These findings represent the most precise single measurements to date for the $B^0_\mathrm{S}$ $\to$ $\mu^+\mu^-$ branching fraction and the $B^0_\mathrm{S}$ effective lifetime. No significant evidence for the $B^0$ $\to$ $\mu^+\mu^-$ decay was observed. All outcomes align with both standard model predictions and earlier experimental results.

Utilizing engineered coatings to generate robust repulsive Casimir forces offers a solution to the reliability problems caused by adhesive forces in micro- and nano-electromechanical systems. This study employs Lifshitz theory to determine the conditions necessary for repulsive Casimir forces within gyrotropic media, examining two extreme scenarios: ultra-strong gyroelectric and non-gyroelectric states. We demonstrate that in highly gyrotropic materials like Weyl semi-metals, the mechanism driving repulsion stems from the massive interconversion of vacuum fluctuation polarization.

We present an entanglement entropy framework to quantitatively distinguish between the confined and deconfined states of spinons within the spin excitations of quantum magnets. This approach is applied to a parton construction of a honeycomb-lattice antiferromagnet characterized by high-energy anomalous spectra. To facilitate entanglement entropy calculations, we derive an effective Hamiltonian employing the random phase approximation to define the quasiparticles of these spin excitations. We provide a quantitative analysis of the transition from deconfinement to confinement of spinons as the Hubbard interaction increases, demonstrating that magnon fractionalization is avoided in the strong-coupling regime. Furthermore, while the Higgs mode at the $\Gamma_0$ point manifests as a sharp, well-defined peak in the spectra, it is fundamentally decomposed into four degenerate spinon pairs. This study broadens our comprehension of spinon deconfinement and its coexistence with magnons in quantum magnetic systems.

A fundamental component of photonic neural networks is the perceptron. This work presents and validates a complex-valued photonic perceptron implemented on a fully passive silicon photonics integrated circuit, utilizing both time and space multiplexing. A time-dependent bit sequence input is distributed across multiple delay lines, where relative phases are optimized via particle swarm algorithms to achieve specific tasks. By training solely on the phases of propagating optical modes, the design circumvents signal attenuation typically caused by amplitude modulation. Consequently, the perceptron successfully executes binary pattern recognition and multi-bit delayed XOR operations at speeds up to 16 Gbps (constrained by electronic components), achieving bit error rates as low as $10^{-6}$. This fully integrated, scalable, silicon-based architecture serves as an ideal building block for large-scale neural networks.

In [JHEP 09 (2021) 053], Wang et al. examined the polynomial ring of flavor invariants within the leptonic sector involving massive Majorana neutrinos, explicitly constructing finite generating sets for both two- and three-generation models. However, their assertion that these generating sets are finite, derived via Hilbert series using the generalized Molien-Weyl formula, relies on the erroneous claim that the unitary group ${\rm U}(n,\mathbb{C})$ is reductive. This property applies only to linear algebraic groups, and ${\rm U}(n,\mathbb{C})$ is, in fact, not a linear algebraic group. This paper addresses this flaw and resolves the resulting logical gaps in [JHEP 09 (2021) 053], drawing on concepts from linear algebraic group theory, the invariant theory of square matrices, and group theory. Additionally, we clarify certain ambiguous or misleading statements regarding the scope of flavor invariants in the cited work. Notably, despite the incorrect foundational assumption, the calculation results presented by Wang et al. remain valid, as the ring of invariants for ${\rm U}(n,\mathbb{C})$ is isomorphic to that of the reductive group ${\rm GL}(n,\mathbb{C})$.

The standard version of Freiman's 3k-4 theorem asserts that subsets of the integers with cardinality k and a sumset of size approximately 2k are nearly arithmetic progressions. This paper aims to extend that result by restricting the number of permissible summands from one set. Specifically, we demonstrate that if A and B are integer subsets of size k such that the sumset A+X, where X is any four-element subset of B, has a size only slightly exceeding 2k, then A and B must be very close to arithmetic progressions.

The Lagrangian model featuring a distinct extra U(1) symmetry is explicitly detailed. The specific gauge charges assigned to this extra U(1) impose stringent constraints on Lagrangian construction. We estimate and forecast the discovery limits for the Z' boson at both the Tevatron and the LHC. Furthermore, we examine the new contributions to the muon's anomalous magnetic moment at one- and two-loop levels, predicting that the model could account for observed deviations from the Standard Model. Additionally, an electron electric dipole moment may arise due to explicit CP violation within the Higgs sector, with a significant contribution anticipated for a moderately large CP phase associated with the CP-odd Higgs.

Weyl semimetals represent the quintessential example of a gapless topological phase. Although the stability of Weyl nodes, measured by their topological charge, has been thoroughly studied, current research focuses on manipulating their positions to achieve non-Abelian braiding. This requires inducing substantial motion of the nodes through feasible experimental adjustments. We demonstrate that specific symmetry-constrained phase transitions necessitate a significant reorganization of Weyl nodes, causing them to shift between different high-symmetry planes. Furthermore, for certain node pairs possessing nontrivial Euler class topology, this reorganization can only proceed via a braiding mechanism with neighboring nodes. Consequently, small temperature variations compel these nodes to traverse large distances across the Brillouin zone and undergo braiding, a phenomenon illustrated using Cd$_2$Re$_2$O$_7$. This study establishes pathways for easily manipulating Weyl nodes through minor external parameter shifts, facilitating the practical implementation of reciprocal space braiding.

Replicated tree structures are fundamental to distributed file systems and collaborative applications, particularly when clients execute move operations. While local moves across replicas can be secure, remote moves often introduce risks. Concurrent, arbitrary moves on different replicas can trigger bugs, making implementation difficult; prior research has identified issues like data duplication and cycles. This paper introduces an efficient algorithm for handling move operations in distributed replicated trees while guaranteeing eventual consistency. The method focuses on efficient conflict resolution, operates without replica interaction, and performs robustly during network partitions. It employs last-write-wins semantics using globally unique timestamps for conflict management. To prevent cycle formation during move operations, the solution necessitates only a single compensation step. In geo-replicated environments on Microsoft Azure standard instances across three continents, this approach achieves a performance speedup of 68.19× compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

This research examines how large-scale environments influence the proportion of spiral galaxies at redshifts $z=$ 0.3–0.6, analyzed across three bins with $\Delta z=0.1$. The study samples 276,220 massive galaxies within a stellar mass range of $5\times10^{10}$ solar masses (approximately $M^\ast$) spanning 360 deg$^2$, utilizing data from the Second Public Data Release of the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program (HSC-SSP). By integrating projected two-dimensional density maps (Shimakawa et al. 2021) with the CAMIRA cluster catalog (Oguri et al. 2018), we assess the spiral fraction within large-scale overdensities and near red sequence clusters. To minimize labeling expenses, we apply transfer learning, followed by stacking analysis across the full field to address sample size constraints. A morphological classification catalog from Galaxy Zoo Hubble (Willet et al. 2017) was used to train our deep learning model. Leveraging 74,103 sources identified as spirals, we detect moderate morphology-density relations on a ten comoving Mpc scale, attributed to HSC-SSP's extensive field coverage. Additionally, clear deficits of spiral galaxies are confirmed both inside and surrounding 1,136 red sequence clusters. Finally, we test for environmental dependencies on the rest-frame $u-r$ colors of spirals; however, no such trend was found in our dataset.

A primary objective of general intelligence is to acquire new information without erasing previously learned knowledge. The value of learning without forgetting (CF) is twofold: it enables systems to revisit past tasks after mastering new ones, and it facilitates faster acquisition of novel tasks by leveraging existing knowledge. Earlier approaches to CF and bootstrapping have mainly focused on adjusting model weights to adapt to current tasks, often overwriting parameters tuned for previous tasks. However, a critical yet overlooked factor is the initial network topology or architecture. We argue that the structure of biological brains likely evolved specific features to ensure such informational conservation. Specifically, we propose that the highly conserved property of modularity offers a solution to weight-update methods that satisfies both the constraints of preventing catastrophic forgetting and enabling bootstrapping. Finally, we discuss strategies for integrating these two learning objectives into a dynamic, general learning system.

We introduce MeetDot, a videoconferencing platform featuring live translation captions displayed directly on the screen. Designed to bridge language gaps, the system aims to eliminate communication barriers among multilingual users. At present, it supports four languages by combining automatic speech recognition (ASR) and machine translation (MT) in a cascaded pipeline. Although we employ a re-translation strategy for streaming speech, this approach currently causes caption flicker. Given the system's strict latency constraints required for acceptable call quality, we have implemented several features to improve user experience and minimize cognitive load, including smooth scrolling and flicker reduction. Our modular backend architecture enables the integration of various ASR and MT services. Furthermore, we offer an integrated evaluation suite to optimize intrinsic metrics such as accuracy, latency, and erasure. To assess end-to-end performance, we also propose an innovative cross-lingual word-guessing game as an extrinsic metric. We intend to release the system as open-source to support research.

Creating ergodic, stationary visual patterns is essential for applications like texturing, shape modeling, and digital content generation. To ensure these techniques remain widely useful, the synthesis methods must be scalable, diverse, and authentic. This paper introduces an exemplar-based framework designed to capture the underlying statistics of visual patterns, thereby generating new, versatile outputs that satisfy these criteria. Central to this approach is the Implicit Periodic Field Network (IPFN), an implicit architecture built upon generative adversarial networks (GANs) and periodic encoding. IPFN's implicit formulation guarantees scalability by directly mapping input coordinates to features, allowing for efficient computation and the synthesis of patterns at any size, particularly beneficial for 3D shapes. The use of periodic encoding during learning fosters diversity by constraining the network to model exemplar statistics within a spatial latent code periodic field. Furthermore, continuous GAN training procedures enable IPFN to produce tileable patterns featuring smooth transitions and local variations. Finally, the combination of adversarial training and encoded Fourier features allows IPFN to learn high-frequency functions, resulting in authentic, high-quality outputs. We validate this methodology through novel experiments across diverse 2D texture and 3D shape synthesis tasks.

This paper introduces a new approach called "Bridge to Answer," designed to infer accurate responses to video-related questions by utilizing graph interactions across heterogeneous crossmodal graphs. To achieve this, we develop visual graphs conditioned on questions, leveraging the relationship between video content and queries to allow each visual node to integrate both visual and linguistic information through question-to-visual interactions. Furthermore, we introduce bridged visual-to-visual interactions that combine complementary appearance and motion data by using the question graph as an intermediate bridge. This architectural design facilitates reliable message passing through the compositional semantics of the question, enabling the generation of suitable answers. Consequently, our method learns question-conditioned visual representations for both appearance and motion, demonstrating significant efficacy in video question answering tasks. Extensive experiments confirm that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods with superior results across multiple benchmarks.

The ALICE collaboration at the LHC has recently published high-statistics transverse momentum ($p_t$) spectra from proton-proton collisions at center-of-mass energies of 5 TeV and 13 TeV. Data at each energy level were categorized into event classes based on total yields within two distinct, non-overlapping pseudorapidity ($\eta$) regions, referred to as V0M and SPD. For both energies, the spectra derived from these selection criteria were compared against a minimum-bias average (INEL > 0) calculated across the entire event sample. The primary objective was to elucidate the role of jets in high-multiplicity $p$-$p$ collisions, with a specific focus on their contribution to the low-$p_t$ regions of the spectra. Additionally, this work addresses recent assertions regarding "collective" behavior and other potential signatures of quark-gluon plasma (QGP) formation in small collision systems. This study applies a two-component (soft + hard) model (TCM) to analyze the ALICE spectrum data. Consistent with prior TCM investigations of various A-B collision systems, the model successfully separates jet and non-jet contributions to $p$-$p$ spectra across the full $p_t$ acceptance. The analysis distinguishes between spectrum normalizations, jet contributions, and systematic biases arising from V0M and SPD event selections. Statistical significance of deviations between the data and the model is determined. Furthermore, the impact of {\em spherocity} (an azimuthal asymmetry metric generally sensitive to jet production) on the ensemble-mean $p_t$ versus charged particle multiplicity ($n_{ch}$) is examined and found to show little correlation with jet production. Overall, the TCM analysis results align with expectations from a conventional QCD framework describing jet production in $p$-$p$ collisions.

Employing a three-dimensional general circulation model configured with the orbital and planetary parameters of Proxima Centauri b, we demonstrate that atmospheric dynamics on a tidally locked Earth-like exoplanet can sustain a longitudinally asymmetric stratospheric wind oscillation (LASO), which mirrors Earth's quasi-biennial oscillation (QBO). Our simulations indicate that the LASO spans 35–55 km in altitude, repeats every 5–6.5 months, and exhibits wind speed amplitudes ranging from -70 to +130 m/s, peaking at 41 km. Distinct from the QBO, the LASO features longitudinal asymmetries driven by the planet's uneven thermal forcing and its interaction with stationary Rossby waves. While QBO drivers are distributed uniformly, the gravity wave sources fueling the LASO are confined to deep convection at the substellar point and a jet exit zone near the western terminator. Consequently, the western terminator records the strongest winds and earliest reversals, whereas the antistellar point shows only a weak, brief low-speed westward phase. Similar to how Earth's QBO influences water vapor and trace gases like ozone, such atmospheric species on exoplanets would likely undergo comparable fluctuations. Therefore, interpreting observations of tidally locked exoplanets must account for the significant variations in temperature and atmospheric composition expected at the terminators.

This study investigates almost Kenmotsu manifolds (AKMs) equipped with almost Ricci-Yamabe solitons (ARYSs) and their gradient counterparts. We derive the necessary conditions for an AKM supporting an ARYS to be $\eta$-Einstein. Furthermore, we demonstrate that under specific constraints, an ARYS defined on a Kenmotsu manifold reduces to a Ricci-Yamabe soliton. Within this series, it is established that a $(2n+1)$-dimensional $(\kappa, \mu)'$-AKM with a gradient ARYS is either locally isometric to $\mathbb{H}^{n+1}(-4)\times\mathbb{R}^n$ or possesses a soliton vector field that is codirectional with the Reeb vector field. Finally, the characteristics of $3$-dimensional non-Kenmotsu AKMs carrying a gradient ARYS are analyzed.

This work constructs bivariate orthogonal polynomials on algebraic curves defined by $y^m = \phi(x)$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, where $m$ equals 1 or 2 and $\phi$ is a polynomial of any degree $d$, by utilizing univariate semiclassical orthogonal polynomials. We calculate connection coefficients that link these bivariate polynomials to a separate, orthogonal polynomial basis containing them as a subspace. It is demonstrated that the resulting connection matrix is banded, and the connection coefficients along with Jacobi matrices for polynomials of degrees $0$ through $N$ are computed using the Lanczos algorithm within $O(Nd^4)$ operations.

We propose a population-averaged additive subdistribution hazard model designed to evaluate the marginal impact of covariates on the cumulative incidence function when analyzing correlated failure time data under competing risks. This method generalizes the population-averaged additive hazard model by handling potentially dependent censoring caused by competing events other than the primary outcome. Under an assumption of independent working correlations, we employ an estimating equations framework to derive regression coefficients and introduce a sandwich variance estimator. This estimator addresses correlations among both failure times and censoring times, offering robustness against misspecification of the intra-cluster dependency structure. Additionally, we develop goodness-of-fit tests to verify the appropriateness of the additive subdistribution hazard structure for individual covariates and the model as a whole. Simulation studies were conducted to evaluate the proposed methods' performance in finite samples, and the approach is demonstrated through an analysis of the STrategies to Reduce Injuries and Develop confidence in Elders (STRIDE) study.

Let $d$ be an integer exceeding $1$, and fix $t$ such that $\frac{1}{d} < t < \frac{1}{d-1}$. We demonstrate that for any sufficiently large $n_0$ determined by $t$, the $d$-dimensional cubes with side length $n^{-t}$ (where $n \geq n_0$) can exactly pack a cube of volume $\sum_{n=n_0}^\infty \frac{1}{n^{dt}}$. This result advances a prior finding in the three-dimensional setting for the range $1/3 < t \leq 4/11$ with $n_0 = 1$ and extends recent research by Terence Tao regarding the two-dimensional case.

This work establishes criteria determining when affine varieties contain uniruled subvarieties of specific dimensions. These criteria are derived from long exact sequences involving various forms of symplectic cohomology—a Hamiltonian Floer theory applicable to certain open symplectic manifolds, including affine varieties. Although computing symplectic cohomology is generally difficult, we leverage its vanishing and invariance properties to validate these criteria in particular scenarios. Furthermore, we demonstrate applications of these criteria within the birational geometry of log pairs, specifically advancing the Minimal Model Program.

This report presents the initial model-independent determination of charm mixing parameters derived from the $D^0 \to K_S \pi^+ \pi^-$ decay. The analysis utilizes a dataset of proton-proton collisions collected by the LHCb experiment, featuring an integrated luminosity of 1.0 fb$^{-1}$ at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV. The resulting measurements are:
\begin{eqnarray*} x &=& (-0.86 \pm 0.53 \pm 0.17) \times 10^{-2}, \\ y &=&
(+0.03 \pm 0.46 \pm 0.13) \times 10^{-2}, \end{eqnarray*}
where the first uncertainties represent statistical errors (incorporating minor contributions from the strong phase external input provided by the CLEO collaboration), and the second uncertainties correspond to systematic effects.

This work derives the general solution for the Kac--Bernstein functional equation, $f(x+y)g(x-y)=f(x)f(y)g(x)g(-y)$ defined on an arbitrary Abelian group $X$, specifically within the class of positive functions. Furthermore, it investigates solutions in the realm of non-vanishing complex-valued functions that adhere to the Hermitian condition.

Although microcavities hold the promise of revolutionizing chemical processes, the degree to which photonic devices alter molecular material properties remains uncertain, largely due to difficulties in modeling hybrid light-matter excitations that span multiple length scales. We address these challenges by analyzing a photonic wire under strong coupling with a molecular ensemble. Our simulations offer a comprehensive view of how photonic wires influence the spectral and transport characteristics of disordered molecular materials. We observe that molecular observables undergo more significant changes when the cavity resonance is redshifted relative to the molecules and energetic disorder is minimal. These trends are anticipated to apply to higher-dimensional cavities as well; however, they are missed by theories that consider only a single cavity mode. Consequently, our findings highlight critical considerations for future experimental and modeling efforts aimed at discovering new methods to manipulate chemistry using optical cavities.

In the age of big data, massive datasets must be partitioned across multiple computing nodes to build estimators from distributed data. When creating these distributed estimators, minimizing network communication is crucial because data transmission is significantly slower than local computation. This work establishes a general framework for analyzing distributed estimation behavior under communication constraints in nonparametric settings. We extend existing literature by addressing a broad class of models rather than focusing solely on the dominant Gaussian framework. Specifically, we derive minimax lower bounds and matching upper bounds for distributed regression, density estimation, classification, Poisson regression, and volatility estimation under communication limits. To support these findings, we also provide easily verifiable sufficient conditions applicable to all the examples presented.

We re-examine the interpretation of the static, cylindrically symmetric vacuum Levi-Civita metric, utilizing Weyl, Einstein-Rosen, or Kasner-like coordinate systems. Although the axis source is infinite, we derive its Komar mass density by compactifying the space and subsequently expanding the compactification radius. Our analysis demonstrates that employing the Komar mass density ($\mu_K$), calculated within the Einstein-Rosen frame as a metric parameter, offers several benefits: it removes double coverages of the parameter space, vanishes in flat spacetime, and approximates the mass density of an infinite string for small values. Following a thorough examination of both local and global geometry, we address the physical implications of Levi-Civita spacetime. First, we establish that the Newtonian gravitational force is attractive and grows monotonically with any positive $\mu_K$, approaching the inverse of the proper distance in the radial direction. Second, we find that tidal forces between nearby geodesics—representing gravity in the Einsteinian sense—peak at $\mu_K = 1/2$ before asymptotically declining to zero. Physically, the Komar mass density comprises two components: Newtonian gravity and acceleration effects. Increasing $\mu_K$ intensifies Newtonian gravity while simultaneously aligning field lines more parallel; through the equivalence principle, this eventually converts Newtonian gravity into a pure acceleration field, transforming the Levi-Civita spacetime into a flat, Rindler-like geometry. Geometrically, as $\mu_K$ increases from zero to infinity, planar spacetime sections deform into progressively deeper funnels, ultimately degenerating into a cylindrical topology.

This work examines "instantaneous time mirrors" within the framework of surface plasmons, which involve high-frequency waves traveling along a conducting sheet. Originally proposed by M. Fink et al., instantaneous time mirrors rely on singular temporal perturbations in wave equations to generate time-reversed, focused waves. We analyze the time-dependent three-dimensional Maxwell equations coupled with Drude's model for surface currents, modeling the time mirror as an abrupt, significant alteration in the electron Drude weight on the sheet. Our objective is to characterize the resulting time-reversed wave, specifically quantifying the refocusing quality. We demonstrate that this quality is influenced by the source-to-sheet distance and physical parameters such as electron relaxation time. Furthermore, we show that while the time mirror produces a plasmonic wave, it also generates a free-propagating wave that provides resolution in the direction orthogonal to the sheet, unlike the surface wave. Finally, we investigate blurring effects arising from non-instantaneous mirrors.

We uncover universal links connecting three pivotal aspects of classical wave physics: (i) the ponderomotive force exerted on medium particles within an oscillatory wavefield, (ii) the Stokes drift of free particles in a wave field, and (iii) the canonical wave momentum inherent to the medium. This analysis covers both (a) longitudinal sound waves propagating through gases or fluids and (b) transverse electromagnetic waves interacting with electrons in plasmas or metals. Under the assumption of quasi-monochromatic yet arbitrarily inhomogeneous wavefields, we demonstrate that the relationships between the ponderomotive force, Stokes drift velocity, kinetic energy, and canonical wave momentum carried by medium particles are governed by identical, simple expressions in both scenarios. These findings illuminate the fundamental nature of these phenomena, their intricate interplay, and offer utility for applications concerning dynamical transport across diverse wave types.

This research investigates techniques and strategies for efficiently designing algorithms to solve problems involving massive datasets, a domain referred to as Big Data Algorithms. Specifically, the study focuses on Streaming Algorithms, which form the foundation of space-efficient data structures known as Sketches, utilizing sublinear order $o(n)$ memory. Furthermore, the work explores graph problems within the Semi-Streaming model and analyzes the PageRank algorithm as a specific case study. Finally, the development of a library for resolving graph problems, built upon the intensive mathematical computation platform TensorFlow, has been initiated.

This study presents an experimental examination of quantum correlations within a two-qutrit spin system located in a single nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond, operating at room temperature. We observed quantum entanglement between the two qutrits under these conditions and identified non-classical correlations that extend beyond standard entanglement in this high-dimensional context. Our findings highlight the potential of NV centers as multi-qutrit platforms for performing quantum information tasks and establish a robust experimental foundation for investigating the fundamental physics of high-dimensional quantum systems in the future.

Recently introduced, the Multi-coupled Dark Energy (McDE) scenario represents a cosmological model featuring non-standard dark sector physics that nonetheless yields an expansion history nearly identical to the standard $\Lambda$CDM model. This study establishes the first constraints on the McDE framework by contrasting predicted linear density perturbation evolution with a comprehensive suite of recent $f\sigma_{8}$ growth rate datasets, including 6dFGS, LRG, BOSS, WiggleZ, and VIPERS. As anticipated, incorporating growth rate data significantly tightens the limits on model parameters compared to the very loose bounds derived solely from background expansion history. Specifically, the 95% confidence interval for the coupling strength $|\beta|$ shrinks from $|\beta| \leq 83$ (background-only constraints) to $|\beta| \leq 0.88$ (when combining background and linear perturbation constraints). Furthermore, we examine how projections from future wide-field surveys, such as LSST supernova data and Euclid-type growth rate measurements, could further refine these limits, potentially reducing the 95% confidence bound on $|\beta|$ to $\leq 0.85$. Despite these improvements, the constraints remain consistent with a scalar fifth force of gravitational magnitude, and we anticipate that even tighter bounds may emerge from future investigations into nonlinear structure formation within McDE cosmologies. [Abridged]

We present a novel optical diagnostic for gas composition analysis that measures the motion of atoms and molecules confined in deep optical lattices. This non-resonant approach mirrors conventional Raman scattering; however, the resulting spectral features correspond to the oscillatory center-of-mass motion of each species, which is uniquely defined by their polarizability-to-mass ratio. Detection mechanisms vary based on sample density, occurring through optical scattering at higher densities or non-resonant ionization at lower densities. We demonstrate that this technique complements traditional mass spectrometry and propose its integration into current instrumentation.

This study investigates density-based multi-sensor cooperative fusion utilizing random finite set (RFS) multi-object densities (MODs). Current fusion techniques rely on scalar weights to quantify the relative confidence of local MODs, allowing the contribution of each to the global fused result to be adjusted through these weights. However, our analysis indicates that this scalar-based approach is overly simplistic for real-world applications, as the confidence of an MOD is intricate and often spatially varying due to sensor limitations and diverse environmental factors. Consequently, when scalar weights fail to accurately represent these conditions, significant degradation in fusion performance occurs. To address this, we introduce two key contributions. First, we develop a novel heterogeneous fusion method for averaging information among local RFS MODs; by decomposing each local MOD into smaller sub-MODs, we convert the complex fusion task into a more manageable, parallelizable multi-cluster problem. Second, since this strategy is a general procedure requiring no specific model assumptions, we derive detailed heterogeneous fusion equations with a centralized architecture for both the Probability Hypothesis Density (PHD) filter and the Multi-Bernoulli (MB) filter, including their Gaussian mixture implementations. Finally, extensive numerical experiments are conducted to validate the effectiveness of the proposed fusion approaches.

Current consensus emphasizes the necessity of enhancing agricultural monitoring systems to address global changes, a goal supported by timely and precise land use/cover mapping at fine scales. This study proposes a deep learning framework for object-level multi-source land cover mapping. The method extends Recurrent Neural Networks with an attention mechanism tailored for multi-temporal data contexts and introduces a novel hierarchical pretraining strategy that leverages domain-specific knowledge inherent in hierarchical land cover relationships. Experimental results from Reunion Island, a French overseas department, demonstrate the proposed approach's superiority over standard remote sensing techniques for land cover mapping.
