Multi-objective optimization involves identifying multiple competing goals within a specific operation, with solution methods emphasizing the marginal trade-offs involved in prioritizing one objective over another. This paper addresses time-varying multi-objective optimization, where objectives are defined by a continuously changing parameter and a fixed computational budget is available at each moment to adjust decision variables accordingly. We establish regret bounds that provide relative performance guarantees for these competing objectives.
We provide a concise proof of Gao's Quantum Union Bound and Gentle Sequential Measurement theorems.

Historically, astronomy and religion were merged within a single cosmic framework. As science evolved into a separate cultural discipline, astronomy began engaging in diverse and meaningful collaborations with other domains. In the 19th century, astronomical challenges drove the development of mathematical statistics, leading to the modern, expanding field of astrostatistics, which refines methods for analyzing astronomical data. Throughout the 20th century, astronomy forged a deep partnership with physics, making astronomy and astrophysics profoundly interconnected. Similarly, physical chemistry was instrumental in identifying molecules within our galaxy, establishing astrochemistry as a vibrant subfield that illuminates molecular processes in the cosmos. Furthermore, interdisciplinary ties with engineering (for instrument design), Earth sciences (for planetary research), computer science (for astroinformatics), and life sciences (for astrobiology) are increasingly vital. Such cross-disciplinary research has been fundamental to major astronomical breakthroughs and to enhancing the overall quality of the field. To support this progress, it is essential to promote greater flexibility in training young astronomers and to provide adequate funding to cultivate these emerging areas.

Over the past few years, high-performance computing (HPC) systems have increasingly adopted heterogeneous architectures, most notably through the integration of GPU accelerators. These GPUs are sometimes segregated into dedicated partitions, but more often they are embedded directly within compute nodes—frequently with multiple units per node—and serve as the primary source of computational power. Consequently, it is now crucial to update applications running on HPC systems to leverage accelerator hardware. This paper presents a CUDA C++ implementation of the 3D blood flow simulation code, HemeLB, for GPU execution. We demonstrate that utilizing NVIDIA GPU hardware yields substantial performance gains over the original CPU-only version while maintaining the robust strong scaling properties consistently shown by the CPU variant. As HPC approaches the exascale era, we use HemeLB as a case study to discuss the challenges developers will likely encounter when deploying their own applications on future exascale machines.

For the groups $Sp(2n, \mathbb{R})$ and $SO^*(2n)$, we calculate the Dirac index for a broad category of unitary representations identified by Vogan in Section 8 of [Vog84]. This category encompasses all weakly fair $A_{\mathfrak{q}}(\lambda)$ modules, along with (weakly) unipotent representations of $G$, as its two boundary cases. We propose that this set of representations accounts for every unitary representation of $G$ possessing nonzero Dirac cohomology. More generally, for specific irreducible unitary modules within equal rank groups, we elucidate the relationship between potential cancellations in the Dirac index and the parities of their spin-lowest $K$-types.

We present our advancements in simulating Neuberger valence fermions alongside $N_f=2$ Wilson $O(a)$-improved sea quarks. Our analysis involves computing correlators for valence quark masses within both the $\epsilon$- and $p$-regimes, subsequently matching these findings against Chiral Effective Theory predictions in the mixed regime. This procedure enables the extraction of the Low Energy Couplings (LECs) for the $N_f=2$ theory and serves to validate the methodology.

This paper introduces a semantic clustering-based deduction learning method that emulates the human brain's learning and reasoning processes. Drawing on the observation that humans distinguish between fundamentally different categories based on experience—such as not misidentifying an unknown animal as a vehicle—we propose training deep learning models with a clustering prior. This prior guides models to acquire the capacity for semantic deduction and summarization from classification attributes, ensuring that entities like cats are correctly associated with the animal domain and cars with the vehicle domain. Specifically, if an image is labeled as a cat, the model learns to recognize it as definitively distinct from outlier classes unrelated to animals. By achieving high-level clustering within the semantic space, the approach enables models to infer relationships among various classes during training. Furthermore, the study incorporates a semantic prior-based random search for opposing labels to guarantee a smooth cluster distribution and enhance classifier robustness. The method is substantiated both theoretically and empirically through extensive experiments, including comparisons against state-of-the-art classifiers on standard benchmarks and validation of generalization capabilities by introducing noisy labels to datasets. The results confirm the superior performance of the proposed approach.

Hyperuniform many-body systems in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space exhibit completely suppressed normalized density fluctuations at infinite wavelengths and possess unique physical characteristics. This study investigates how localized defects influence density fluctuations across various length scales and impact the hyperuniformity of experimental 2D transition metal dichalcogenide samples. Specifically, we derive atomic coordinates from time-series annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy images of 2D tungsten chalcogenides with a 2H structure, tracking the continuous formation and evolution of electron-beam-induced defects, and build corresponding coordination networks informed by chemical bonding. We calculate diverse pair and bond-orientational statistics to characterize these samples. At low defect levels, the materials remain nearly hyperuniform; however, as defects increase, the approximate hyperuniformity is gradually lost, rendering the system non-hyperuniform even while substantial crystalline regions persist. At high defect concentrations, the structures transition to antihyperuniformity, featuring diverging normalized large-scale density fluctuations. Overall, defected materials display varying degrees of orientational order, with no apparent intermediate hexatic phase. Additionally, we developed a minimalist structural model demonstrating that these experimental samples can be effectively modeled as perturbed honeycomb crystals characterized by small correlated displacements and double chalcogen vacancies.

This paper tackles the collective management of environmental commons with multiple uses using mathematical viability theory. We assume stakeholders can identify variables describing their distinct uses of the commons, their evolution, and the desirable states through analyzing their socioeconomic issues. Subsequently, we examine the guaranteed viability kernel—a subset of desirable states where the commons can be maintained despite conflicting models of its evolution. This method is demonstrated using a lake eutrophication problem.

We demonstrate that a metastable dark matter candidate emerges naturally from the conformal transformation linking the Einstein metric, in which gravitons are normalized, and the Jordan metric, which governs gravity-matter interactions. Although the dark matter sector is largely decoupled from the Standard Model by a high energy scale where the Jordan metric deviates from the Einstein frame, it primarily couples to the Higgs field's energy-momentum tensor within the primordial plasma. This interaction facilitates the production of sufficient dark matter to align with observational data. The effective seclusion of this dark matter ensures a long lifetime for masses below approximately 1 MeV, exceeding both the age of the Universe and current experimental constraints. Consequently, this scenario predicts distinct monochromatic signatures resulting from the decay of the dark matter candidate into neutrinos and/or gamma rays.

For any regularity exponent $\beta<\frac 12$, we construct non-conservative weak solutions to the 3D incompressible Euler equations within the class $C^0_t
(H^{\beta} \cap L^{\frac{1}{(1-2\beta)}})$. Through interpolation, these solutions reside in $C^0_tB^{s}_{3,\infty}$ for $s$ nearing $\frac 13$ as $\beta$ approaches $\frac 12$. Consequently, this finding offers a novel demonstration of the flexible aspect of the Onsager conjecture, one that stands independently of Isett's proof [A proof of Onsager's conjecture, Annals of Mathematics, 188(3):871, 2018]. Equally significant is that the intermittent characteristics of our solutions align with turbulent flows, which exhibit an $L^2$-based regularity index surpassing $\frac 13$. Our methodology extends the authors' prior collaborative work with Buckmaster and Masmoudi [Nonconservative $H^{\frac 12-}$ weak solutions of the incompressible 3D Euler equations, arXiv 2101.09278, 2021], where an intermittent convex integration scheme for the 3D incompressible Euler equations was established. We utilize a scheme featuring higher-order Reynolds stresses, adjusted through a combinatorial arrangement of intermittent pipe flows exhibiting optimal relative intermittency.

Integrating supervised Machine Learning (ML) into Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) presents significant challenges. Effective ML-NIDS development requires training and evaluation on datasets with clearly distinguished benign and malicious labels, a process that depends heavily on expensive expert knowledge. This reliance has historically hindered real-world deployments and led to research papers repeatedly using the same outdated data. Although recent initiatives have begun releasing labeled datasets, most previous studies have merely treated them as standard testbeds, failing to exploit their full potential.

In contrast, this work advocates for leveraging existing labeled data to perform cross-evaluations of ML-NIDS, an approach that has received limited attention and requires specialized handling due to its complexity. We introduce the first cross-evaluation model, which reveals a wider array of realistic use cases, enabling the discovery of previously unknown attributes in state-of-the-art ML-NIDS, such as extending their detection surface without incurring additional labeling costs. However, executing these cross-evaluations is difficult; therefore, we present XeNIDS, the first framework designed for reliable cross-evaluations based on Network Flows. By applying XeNIDS to six prominent datasets, we demonstrate both the hidden potential and the inherent risks associated with cross-evaluating ML-NIDS.

Minkowski's First Theorem and Dirichlet's Approximation Theorem establish upper limits for specific minima associated with lattice points within Euclidean space domains. This study investigates the distribution of these minima, demonstrating that, subject to certain technical constraints, they follow Weibull asymptotics across various natural measures defined on the space of unimodular lattices in $\mathbb{R}^d$. This conclusion stems from broad Poisson approximation principles applicable to shrinking targets, which hold independent significance. Additionally, the appendix reveals that the logarithm laws formulated by Kleinbock-Margulis, Khinchin, and Gallagher can be derived from these distributional findings.

This study introduces a data-driven approach for efficiently addressing parabolic inverse source problems through model reduction. The methodology operates in two phases: an offline stage and an online stage. During the offline phase, we investigate the low-dimensional structures within the solution space of forward parabolic partial differential equations (PDEs) for a specific set of source functions, generating a limited set of Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) basis functions to achieve substantial dimensionality reduction. Utilizing these POD bases, the forward problem is solved with exceptional speed in the online phase. Consequently, we formulate a rapid algorithm for optimizing the parabolic inverse source problem, designated here as the POD algorithm. We establish the convergence of this algorithm for solving forward parabolic PDEs under a weak regularity assumption. Furthermore, we derive error estimates for the POD algorithm applied to parabolic inverse source problems. Numerical experiments are provided to validate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed method. The results indicate that the POD algorithm yields significant computational advantages compared to the finite element method.

Dynamic analysis offers a scalable and efficient approach to examining concurrent programs by targeting specific executions rather than exploring all possible behaviors. A fundamental component of this analysis involves establishing a causal ordering of events, traditionally achieved through vector clocks. These clocks track the logical time of threads but suffer from a performance bottleneck: their core operations, join and copy, incur a time complexity of $\Theta(k)$, where $k$ represents the thread count, making them inefficient for large-scale systems.

This paper introduces "tree clocks," a novel data structure designed to replace vector clocks for determining causal orderings. Unlike vector clocks, joining and copying tree clocks requires time proportional only to the number of modified entries, eliminating the inherent $\Theta(k)$ cost per operation. We demonstrate that tree clocks are optimal for computing the classic happens-before (HB) partial order, as no other structure can achieve a better asymptotic runtime. Furthermore, they prove versatile by supporting the calculation of other partial orders, including schedulable-happens-before (SHB) and Mazurkiewicz (MAZ). Experimental results indicate that substituting vector clocks with tree clocks yields significant speedups: approximately 2.02× faster for MAZ, 2.66× for SHB, and 2.97× for HB on average. These findings suggest that tree clocks have the potential to become a standard tool in concurrent program analysis.

Inelastic neutron scattering data indicates that magnetic interactions in the antiferromagnetic LaFeAsO are two-dimensional. The spin wave velocities within the iron layer and the spin gap magnitude resemble those observed in \textit{A}Fe$_2$As$_2$ based materials. However, the ratio of interlayer to intralayer exchange in LaFeAsO is less than approximately $10^{-4}$, which is comparable to cuprates and roughly 100 times smaller than in \textit{A}Fe$_2$As$_2$ compounds. These findings imply that the effective dimensionality of the magnetic system varies significantly among the parent iron arsenide compounds, and weak three-dimensional interactions may constrain the maximum achievable superconducting $T_{c}$.

Building on our earlier research concerning spherical representations within operator algebras, this paper first proposes analogs of dimension groups by employing operator systems and related structures. Subsequently, we apply these findings to inductive limits of compact quantum groups, deriving a quantum counterpart to Olshanski's concept of spherical unitary representations for infinite-dimensional Gelfand pairs of the form $G < G \times G$ (under diagonal embedding). Notably, this work provides validation for Ryosuke Sato's methodology regarding asymptotic representation theory in the context of quantum groups.

We introduce an enhanced quantum algorithm for determining the Green's function via real-time evolution, applying it to calculate the retarded Green's function for 2-, 3-, and 4-site Hubbard models. This new protocol markedly decreases the count of controlled operations relative to prior methods. This reduction is particularly significant for the 2-site Hubbard model, where we demonstrate that exact time propagation of $|N\pm 1\rangle$ states can be achieved by exponentiating a single Pauli component of the Hamiltonian, enabling execution on a real superconducting quantum processor.

Recently, deep learning approaches for automated personality trait detection have garnered significant interest, particularly given the vast digital footprints individuals leave behind. Furthermore, numerous studies have established a robust connection between personality traits and emotions. Building upon this established correlation, this paper introduces SoGMTL, a novel multitask learning framework designed to predict both personality traits and emotional behaviors concurrently. We also empirically assess and analyze various information-sharing mechanisms between these two tasks. To guarantee high-quality learning, we employ a Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML)-inspired approach for model optimization. Our computationally efficient CNN-based multitask model achieves state-of-the-art results across several prominent personality and emotion datasets, even surpassing performance by Language Model-based methods.

In 2005, Goddard, Hedetniemi, Hedetniemi, and Laskar [Generalized subgraph-restricted matchings in graphs, Discrete Mathematics, 293 (2005) 129-138] posed the question of the computational complexity for identifying the maximum cardinality of a matching that induces a disconnected graph. This paper provides an answer to that inquiry by addressing the generalized task of locating $c$-disconnected matchings, defined as matchings where the induced vertex sets contain at least $c$ connected components. We demonstrate that for any fixed $c \geq 2$, determining such matchings is NP-complete, even when restricted to bounded diameter bipartite graphs; however, the problem is solvable in polynomial time when $c = 1$. When $c$ is part of the input, the problem remains NP-complete for chordal graphs but admits a polynomial-time solution for interval graphs. Additionally, we investigate the parameterized complexity of this issue. We introduce an FPT algorithm parameterized by treewidth and an XP algorithm for graphs with a polynomial number of minimal separators, parameterized by $c$. Complementing these findings, we show that, unless NP $\subseteq$ coNP/poly, the related Induced Matching problem lacks a polynomial kernel when parameterized by either vertex cover or vertex deletion distance to a clique, combined with the size of the matching. Regarding Connected Matching, we outline a method to derive a maximum connected matching in linear time given an arbitrary maximum matching as input.

Kruskal's theorem asserts that a sum of product tensors admits a unique tensor rank decomposition provided the k-ranks of those tensors are sufficiently large. We establish a "splitting theorem" for collections of product tensors, which relaxes Kruskal's k-rank requirement to the conventional notion of rank and modifies the uniqueness conclusion to indicate that the set of tensors splits (meaning the associated matroid becomes disconnected). This splitting theorem yields a broader generalization of Kruskal's theorem. Although various extensions of Kruskal's theorem exist in the literature, they all rely on his original permutation lemma and thus fail to guarantee uniqueness when k-ranks fall below a specific threshold. In contrast, our generalization employs an entirely novel proof technique, encompasses many existing extensions, and is capable of certifying uniqueness even below that threshold. Furthermore, we derive several additional valuable findings regarding tensor decompositions stemming from our splitting theorem. Specifically, we demonstrate sharp lower bounds for tensor rank and Waring rank, thereby extending Sylvester's matrix rank inequality to the realm of tensors. We also establish new uniqueness results for non-rank tensor decompositions.

The CBM experiment at the Facility for Antiproton and Ion Research (FAIR) seeks to investigate the QCD phase diagram under conditions of high net-baryon density through nucleus-nucleus collisions with a center-of-mass energy per nucleon pair ($\sqrt{s_{NN}}$) ranging from 2.9 to 4.9 GeV. To achieve its physics objectives, CBM will employ peak interaction rates reaching up to 10 MHz alongside a sophisticated triggerless data acquisition system, granting unique access to rare physics probes. This presentation will outline CBM's advancements regarding physics performance simulations and the current status of its detector subsystems, highlighting their participation in FAIR Phase-0 initiatives.

This paper examines the phenomenology of a two-dimensional dilute suspension containing active amphiphilic Janus particles. We investigate how the morphology of aggregates formed through self-assembly varies with the magnitude and orientation of active forces. Furthermore, we systematically compare the resulting behaviors across particles with diverse attractive patch coverages. Finally, we demonstrate how colloid geometry and interaction directionality can regulate the physical characteristics of active aggregates, proposing strategies to harness self-propulsion as a tunable driver for self-assembly.

We demonstrate that a hemisphere in Euclidean space $R^{n+1}$, interpreted as a graph, does not admit any smooth perturbations as graphs with mean curvature $H\ge 1$ if the boundary equator remains fixed up to $C^2$. This result extends the \emph{Mean Curvature Rigidity} phenomenon identified by Gromov and Souam regarding non-compact totally umbilic hypersurfaces in space forms, utilizing a Tangency Principle in the proof. Conversely, we establish that nontrivial smooth perturbations with $H\ge 1$ do exist on a great spherical cap when the boundary is fixed up to $C^2$. Comparable findings apply to perturbations that decrease $H$ as well as those involving the $r$ mean curvature function $H_r$. This dichotomy between rigidity and non-rigidity persists even in the 1-dimensional context, encompassing circles and discrete structures such as polygons inscribed in a circle.

This study investigates the screech closure mechanisms across various axisymmetric modes within shock-containing jets. Although shifts in azimuthal mode can account for many discontinuities in the tonal frequencies of screeching jets, no prior explanation existed for the coexistence of multiple axisymmetric modes at distinct frequencies; this paper offers that explanation. Building on previous findings that specific wavenumbers result from wave-shock interactions, the authors identify new pathways for driving upstream-travelling waves capable of completing the resonance loop. Predictions derived from locally parallel and spatially periodic linear stability analyses, alongside the shock-cell wavenumber spectrum, indicate that the A1 mode resonance is closed by a wave produced when the Kelvin-Helmholtz mode interacts with the leading wavenumber of the shock-cell structure. Similarly, the A2 mode closure is attributed to a wave generated by the interaction between the Kelvin-Helmholtz wave and a secondary wavenumber peak, which stems from spatial variations in the shock-cell wavelength. These predictions align closely with experimental data, and the study provides potential justifications for the dominance of each mode based on absolute instability growth rates.

This study introduces an automated approach for segmenting infected and healthy lung regions within CT scans of COVID-19 patients. Since December 2019, the global spread of the novel coronavirus (COVID-19) has profoundly disrupted economic activities and daily life, creating a critical need for computer-aided diagnosis to manage the high volume of infections. Chest CT imaging is highly effective for identifying viral pneumonia, including that caused by COVID-19, making automated quantitative analysis of lung conditions from these volumes essential for diagnostic support. To address this, the paper proposes an automated segmentation technique utilizing a fully convolutional network (FCN) specifically designed for COVID-19. Accurate analysis of both normal and infected lung areas is vital for diagnosing respiratory diseases like COVID-19. The proposed method identifies and segments these regions within CT volumes; to handle the diverse shapes and sizes of infection areas, the FCN incorporates dense pooling connections and dilated convolutions. Applied to CT scans from various COVID-19 cases, the method successfully segmented normal and infected regions across a spectrum from mild to severe disease. Evaluation yielded Dice scores of 0.911 for normal regions and 0.753 for infected regions.

A multitransition database now incorporates new observations of 46 normal galaxies for HCN, HNC, and HCO+ transitions up to J=4-3, expanding the existing coverage to 130 galaxies for HCN/HCO+ and 94 for HNC. The observed near-linear luminosity relations are primarily driven by distance variations rather than intrinsic galaxy physical properties. Significant dispersion exists among individual galaxies regarding both luminosity and line ratios, with these ratios showing poor correlation to luminosities or other lines. Positive correlations with CO and far-infrared (FIR) luminosity are found only in normalized J-transition ladders for HCN and HCO+, as well as in the J=1-0 12CO/13CO isotopologue ratio. HCN and HCO+ exhibit similar intensities, indicating they trace the same gas reservoir; however, in galaxies with active nuclei, HCO+ intensities are suppressed relative to HCN. Although only a small portion of CO emission is directly linked to gas emitting in HCN and HCO+, a substantial fraction of this specific gas appears to be translucent. Consequently, the HCN/CO intensity ratio in galaxy centers does not serve as a proxy for the dense gas fraction, nor do FIR/HCN and FIR/CO ratios indicate star formation efficiency. The observed molecular line emission aligns fully with a model of UV-photon heating enhanced by significant mechanical heating. The gas probed by HCN and HCO+ is characterized by low kinetic temperatures (10–50 K), densities of 10^4–10^5 cm^(-3), and low optical depths in ground-state lines, whereas most CO-sampled gas has densities one to two orders of magnitude lower. Achieving a mechanical heating fraction of 0.5 requires only a modest energy input of approximately 300 Go. Ultimately, accurately understanding star formation necessitates a more robust determination of gas mass than can be derived from the intensities of single HCN or CO transitions.

Future Earth-based gravitational-wave detector searches for a stochastic background may be compromised by correlated noise, such as the well-studied Schumann resonances. Previous research established that "gravitational-wave geodesy" can distinguish genuine background signals from terrestrial artifacts by verifying that observations align with the known geometry of the detector network, yielding a Bayes factor to compare astrophysical versus terrestrial origins. This study further formalizes the geodesy test by mapping distributions of false-alarm and false-acceptance probabilities to quantify how a specific Bayes factor influences confidence in a detection. To establish the false-alarm probability for a given Bayes factor, one requires knowledge of the null hypothesis representing all possible correlated terrestrial signals. Lacking this complete knowledge, we instead construct a conservative, generic space of smooth frequency-domain functions using tailored Gaussian processes, utilizing draws from these processes as proxies for non-astrophysical signals. As a practical demonstration, we apply this framework to the SNR = 1.25 excess observed in a 2/3-power law signal by the LIGO and Virgo collaborations during their second observing run.

By utilizing Rossi's half-plane adaptation of Borel's Theorem, we investigate the zero distribution of linear combinations of $\mathcal{A}$-entire functions (Theorem 1.2). This approach offers a unified framework for analyzing linear $q$-difference, difference, and differential operators featuring entire coefficients that preserve specific subsets of $\mathcal{A}$-entire functions, thereby yielding multiple results analogous to the Hermite-Poulain Theorem for linear finite ($q$-)difference operators with polynomial coefficients. Furthermore, this methodology establishes the existence of infinitely many non-real zeros within certain differential polynomials constructed from functions belonging to specific sub-classes of $\mathcal{A}$-entire functions.

Ensuring software quality relies heavily on unit testing, where developers confirm that production code functions as intended. However, unit test code itself can suffer from defects or poor design, often referred to as "test smells." This study investigates the frequency of "simple stupid bugs" (SStuBs)—a specific category of single-statement bug fixes—comparing their occurrence in test versus production files within popular open-source Java Maven projects. The findings indicate that SStuBs are more prevalent in non-test files, while the majority of fixes in test files involve assertion statements. Additionally, test files containing SStuBs frequently exhibit test smells. We anticipate that these insights will assist tool vendors in enhancing their support for test suite maintenance.

This study examines the control of dynamical systems using competitive analysis. While previous research in this field primarily aims to minimize regret—the performance gap relative to an ideal clairvoyant policy with full knowledge of past, present, and future disturbances—we argue that optimal cost alone offers only a coarse view of ideal closed-loop behavior. Consequently, we propose directly minimizing tracking error against optimal trajectories in hindsight, effectively imitating the clairvoyant policy. Adopting a system-level perspective, we introduce an efficient optimization-based method for designing safe controllers that follow the clairvoyant (FTC). We demonstrate that these controllers achieve minimal regret when no constraints are placed on the noncausal benchmark. Furthermore, numerical experiments illustrate that our policy maintains the characteristic of competitive algorithms by interpolating between classical $\mathcal{H}_2$ and $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ control laws, while consistently outperforming regret minimization approaches in constrained settings due to its enhanced ability to track the clairvoyant trajectory.

Primordial black holes possessing asteroid-like masses represent a promising candidate for dark matter, alongside other potential forms that could create compact dark objects (CDOs). We investigated minute tidal accelerations caused by low-mass black holes or CDOs orbiting close to Earth but detected none. Leveraging approximately a decade of data from superconducting gravimeters located at the Black Forest Observatory in South-Western Germany and at Djougou in Northern Benin, West Africa, we established an upper mass limit for any dark object orbiting Earth as a function of its orbital distance. Specifically, for semi-major axes under two Earth radii, we rule out the existence of black holes or CDOs exceeding a mass of 6.7x10^{13} kg. While lower-mass primordial black holes might face significant constraints due to Hawking radiation, our findings indicate that black holes in Earth's immediate vicinity are highly improbable.

The Brouwer fixed point theorem asserts that every continuous function mapping a disk into itself possesses a fixed point. Employing straightforward geometric methods, we have extended this result to manifolds, demonstrating that any continuous function defined on the boundary of a bounded convex domain within a 2-dimensional Riemannian manifold with a pole—and having at least one fixed point—can be extended to the entire convex domain without introducing any interior fixed points.

This paper introduces a novel method to achieve stable in-phase locking of lasers within an array, irrespective of the array's geometry, orientation, size, period, or specific positioning. The technique involves placing a Gaussian aperture inside the cavity at the array's far-field plane. This approach successfully locked $90$ lasers, each emitting sharp far-field spots with very high power density, across diverse geometric configurations. Stability was maintained even when facing near-degenerate solutions, geometric frustration, or overlapping independent longitudinal modes. Furthermore, the method can suppress internal phase structures to produce pure Gaussian mode outputs characterized by uniform phase and superior overall beam quality. This strategy holds the potential to enhance the performance of recently developed laser simulators utilized for solving various computational challenges.

We present a new method for analyzing animal behavior and its surrounding context by equipping individual free-flying birds with microphone backpacks. While these sensors are increasingly employed by researchers to capture vocalizations from freely moving animals in the field, they can also record specific activities and background contexts. To support this, we explore the automatic annotation of such recordings using two sound scene analysis approaches: a feature-learning-based scene classification method and an event-detection method utilizing probabilistic latent component analysis (PLCA). Our study analyzes recordings from Eurasian jackdaws (*Corvus monedula*) collected in both captive and natural environments. The results align with current state-of-the-art sound scene analysis techniques; we demonstrate that existing recognition quality supports scalable automatic annotation of audio logger data when partial annotations are available. However, we also identify that variations between individual animals and/or their backpacks restrict the ability to generalize findings across subjects. Finally, we examine the relationship between 'scenes' and 'events' in this context, alongside considerations of temporal resolution.

A significant limitation of many current Deep Learning applications is the reliance on extensive datasets. Kolmogorov Complexity suggests an improvement by employing the minimum description length (MDL) principle with computationally universal models. This study investigates the theoretical sample efficiency benefits of this method. We model computationally universal systems using polynomial-time Turing machines and represent Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) operating on finite-precision digits as Boolean circuits. Our analysis reveals direct connections to results in Computational Complexity, establishing both lower and upper bounds on the potential sample efficiency improvements when applying MDL with Turing machines rather than ANNs. These bounds are contingent upon the bit-size of the input Boolean function. Additionally, we demonstrate strong correlations between these bounds and the tightness of longstanding open problems in Circuit Complexity.

We investigate the interaction between chiral and center sector phase transitions in QCD at an imaginary quark chemical potential $\mu=i(2n+1) \pi T/3$. Utilizing a finite size scaling analysis within (2+1)-flavor QCD based on HISQ fermions—featuring a physical strange quark mass and various light quark masses—we demonstrate that the endpoint of the first-order Roberge-Weiss (RW) transition line between center sectors exhibits second-order behavior for light quark masses $m_l\ge m_s/320$, falling into the $3$-d, $Z(2)$ universality class. In an effective spin model describing the RW phase transition, the chiral condensate operator acts similarly to an energy operator. Consequently, for any non-zero quark mass, the chiral condensate displays an infinite slope at the RW transition temperature, $T_{RW}$. Its fluctuation, represented by the disconnected chiral susceptibility, mirrors the specific heat in $Z(2)$ symmetric models and diverges in the infinite volume limit at $T_{RW}$ for all non-zero light quark masses. Our findings suggest that the critical temperatures for the RW and chiral phase transitions coincide in the RW plane; specifically, on lattices with temporal extent $N_\tau=4$, we determine in the chiral limit that $T_{\chi}=T_{RW}=195(1)~$MeV.

Describing the relationship between predictors and responses relies fundamentally on the conditional distribution. We introduce a Wasserstein generative framework designed to learn this distribution. This method employs a conditional generator that maps a known distribution to the desired conditional distribution. The generator is trained by aligning a joint distribution formed with the generator against the target joint distribution, utilizing Wasserstein distance as the metric for this discrepancy. We derive a non-asymptotic error bound for the sampling distribution produced by our approach, demonstrating its ability to alleviate the curse of dimensionality when the data resides on a lower-dimensional manifold. Numerical experiments confirm the method's efficacy, showcasing its utility in conditional sample generation, nonparametric density estimation, prediction uncertainty quantification, handling bivariate responses, as well as image reconstruction and generation.

This paper examines convolution integrals of the form $\int_0^t(t-s)^{\lambda -1}b(s)ds$ featuring hyper-singular kernels, where $\lambda\le 0$ and $b$ is either smooth or belongs to $L^1(\mathbb{R}_+)$. For these values of $\lambda$, the integrals diverge under classical definitions even when $b$ is smooth; however, this paper defines them for $\lambda\le 0$ excluding non-positive integers. The study also addresses integral equations and inequalities utilizing hyper-singular kernels $(t-s)^{\lambda -1}_+$ for $\lambda\le 0$, where $t^\lambda_+=0$ if $t<0$. A primary focus is placed on $\lambda=-\frac 14$ due to its significance for the Navier-Stokes problem (NSP). The research investigates equations of the type $b(t)=b_0(t)+ \int_0^t(t-s)^{\lambda-1}b(s)ds$ with $\lambda\le 0$, proving the existence and uniqueness of solutions specifically for $\lambda=-\frac 1 4$. This particular value is crucial for analyzing the NSP in the boundaryless space $\mathbb{R}^3$. The application of these results leads to the conclusion that the NSP is contradictory: assuming non-trivial initial data $v_0(x)$ with zero divergence ($\nabla \cdot v_0(x)=0$), the derived solution implies $v(x,0)=0$. This paradox suggests that the NSP fails to accurately describe fluid mechanics and consequently lacks a solution.

Although robotics is rapidly becoming ubiquitous, the rush to launch systems often leads to the neglect of security mechanisms during development, deployment, and production. Consequently, modern robotic systems face diverse vulnerabilities, making post-deployment hardening difficult or impossible. This book advocates integrating security from the earliest design stages, specifically addressing the cost-benefit tradeoffs that can hinder the rapid creation of affordable systems. We promote quantitative methods for security management and design, including vulnerability scoring systems adapted for robotics that account for the highly distributed nature of these systems as an interplay of numerous components. Furthermore, we offer game theory as a robust quantitative approach for model-based security, providing a wide range of techniques to optimize defenses against various attacks. Such a multi-perspective approach is essential to tackle the heterogeneity and complexity inherent in robotic systems. Ultimately, this book serves as an accessible entry point for both theorists and practitioners in the field.

Weather's impact on agriculture has emerged as a pressing global issue, creating a demand for effective risk management tools like weather derivatives to protect crop yields from climatic uncertainties. However, widespread adoption among smallholder farmers and agricultural stakeholders is hindered by their reluctance to pay the high premiums associated with basis risks inherent in current product and geographical designs. To address product-design basis risks, this study employed a machine learning ensemble approach to analyze the relationship between maize yields and weather factors, identifying average temperature as the most influential variable. Consequently, a mean-reverting model featuring a time-varying speed of reversion, seasonal means, and local volatility tied to local average temperatures was developed. This framework was further expanded into a multi-dimensional model to account for correlations across different locations. Using these temperature-based models, pricing structures for futures, futures options, and basket futures covering cumulative average temperature and growing degree-days were established. Specifically, futures on baskets mitigate geographical basis risk by allowing buyers to choose optimal weather stations with customized weightings. Ultimately, these pricing models enable farmers and agricultural stakeholders to effectively hedge against the dangers of extreme weather events.

This paper introduces a system that leverages various pre-trained Language Models to assign domain labels to WordNet synsets in a fully unsupervised manner. Unlike previous approaches, the system is not limited to a specific set of domain labels. By utilizing knowledge embedded within different off-the-shelf pre-trained Language Models and specific task formulations, the system infers the domain label for a given WordNet definition. This proposed zero-shot method establishes a new state-of-the-art performance on the English dataset used for evaluation.

This research examines bipartite distance-regular Cayley graphs with diameters of three or four. We establish sufficient criteria for constructing a bipartite Cayley graph on the semidirect product of a group (specifically the component containing the identity) and $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$. These criteria are applied to graphs with diameter three, including scenarios where the conditions fail for particular groups like the dihedral group. Furthermore, we generalize a theorem by Miklavi\v{c} and Poto\v{c}nik, which connects difference sets to bipartite distance-regular Cayley graphs of diameter three, to extend it to diameter four. This extension involves specific partial geometric difference sets and, in antipodal instances, relative difference sets.

Multimodal data is often accessible in medical contexts, and integrating insights from various sources enables clinicians to reach more precise conclusions. Recently, several imaging modalities have been adopted for retinal analysis, including 2D fundus photography, 3D optical coherence tomography (OCT), and 3D OCT angiography. This study examines three deep learning-based strategies for fusing multimodal information to address retinal analysis challenges: early fusion, intermediate fusion, and hierarchical fusion. While the widely used early and intermediate methods are straightforward, they fail to fully leverage the complementary nature of different modalities. We propose a hierarchical fusion technique designed to integrate features across multiple network dimensions and investigate inter-modal correlations. These methods were evaluated for glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy classification using the public GAMMA dataset (containing fundus photos and OCT scans) and a private dataset of OCT angiography images from the PlexElite 9000 system by Carl Zeiss Meditec Inc. In both scenarios, our hierarchical fusion approach yielded superior performance, offering a promising avenue for enhanced clinical diagnosis.

Video deblurring presents a significantly under-constrained challenge because blur varies both spatially and temporally. An intuitive solution involves two stages: first, identifying blurry areas within the current frame, and second, leveraging information from sharp regions in neighboring frames to restore the current frame. To implement this, our approach detects the pixel-wise blur intensity for every frame and integrates this detection with the deblurring process. Consequently, we introduce a novel framework that employs motion magnitude prior (MMP) as a guide for efficient deep video deblurring. Since the distance a pixel travels along its trajectory during exposure correlates positively with motion blur levels, we initially generate synthetic blurry frames and their corresponding pixel-wise motion magnitude maps by calculating the average magnitude of optical flow from high-frequency sharp frames. We subsequently construct a dataset pairing these blurry frames with MMPs, which are then learned via regression using a compact CNN. The resulting MMP encapsulates both spatial and temporal blur information, enabling its integration into an efficient recurrent neural network (RNN) for video deblurring. Finally, we perform extensive experiments on public datasets to demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed methods.

Recent years have seen the development of numerous privacy-preserving frameworks designed to safeguard individual privacy during data analysis. Nevertheless, existing model classes, including simple statistics and generalized linear models, often lack the flexibility needed to accurately approximate real-world data-generating processes. This paper introduces an algorithm for the distributed, privacy-preserving, and lossless estimation of generalized additive mixed models (GAMM) via component-wise gradient boosting (CWB). By leveraging CWB, we recast GAMM estimation as the distributed fitting of base learners using $L_2$-loss. To address the heterogeneity across different data locations, we propose a distributed row-wise tensor product approach that enables the computation of site-specific smooth effects. Our adaptation of CWB retains the key attributes of the original method, such as unbiased feature selection and the capacity to handle high-dimensional feature spaces, while producing model estimates equivalent to those obtained from CWB on pooled data. In addition to deriving the equivalence between the two algorithms, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on a distributed heart disease dataset and compare its performance against state-of-the-art methods.

This note establishes that intrinsic characteristic classes of Lie algebroids, which correspond to the modular class in degree one, exhibit functorial behavior under arbitrary transverse maps and consequently serve as weak Morita invariants. Regarding the modular case, this finding was previously demonstrated by Kosmann-Schwarzbach, Laurent-Gengoux, and Weinstein in Transform. Groups 13 (2008), 727-755. Additionally, Crainic in Comment. Math. Helv. 78 (2003), 681-721 and Ginzburg in J. Symplectic Geom. 1 (2001), 121-169 addressed the result under a connectivity assumption, which we now demonstrate to be superfluous.

Rotating axisymmetric bodies amplify incoming waves through superradiant scattering, and when confined within a cavity, repeated field interactions can induce superradiant instabilities. Although rotating binaries are common in physics and essential to both astrophysics and daily instruments, their inherent complexity has made it difficult to determine exactly how such instabilities arise. This study examines a binary system of two absorbing objects—modeling scenarios like black hole pairs or helicopter blades—revolving around a shared center. We demonstrate that superradiant instabilities indeed occur within the expected timeframes and frequency ranges. These findings offer the first proof that superradiance manifests in highly asymmetric systems, suggesting broad applications in fluid dynamics and astrophysics. Extrapolating to astrophysical black holes, our results suggest that compact binaries could serve as effective particle detectors by transferring a portion of their energy to hypothetical new ultralight fundamental degrees of freedom.

This paper introduces a deep learning approach for designing speckle patterns. After passing through convolutions in our custom framework, Speckle-Net, these patterns exhibit distinctive characteristics. We subsequently apply this method to computational ghost imaging systems. Unlike standard deep learning-assisted ghost imaging techniques, which typically employ networks for object recognition or as imaging algorithms, our innovative approach optimizes the illuminating speckle patterns themselves using Speckle-Net with specific sampling ratios. Consequently, our method surpasses existing ghost imaging techniques, especially in retrieving high-quality images under extremely low sampling ratios. It establishes a new pathway for nontrivial speckle generation by utilizing a standard loss function tailored to specific objectives within a modified deep neural network. Furthermore, this method holds significant potential for applications in dynamic speckle illumination microscopy, structured illumination microscopy, x-ray imaging, photo-acoustic imaging, and optical lattices.

Monitoring numerical simulation traces using Signal Temporal Logic (STL) has become a powerful method for approximating the verification of continuous and hybrid systems. This report investigates an exact verification procedure for STL properties that utilizes monitoring on verified traces represented as Taylor model flowpipes, generated by the Flow* verified integrator. We examine how closely integrating with Flow*'s symbolic flowpipe representation enhances both the precision and efficiency of monitoring. Furthermore, we demonstrate that monitoring performance can be significantly improved by introducing masks, a property-directed refinement that limits flowpipe monitoring to time intervals critical for determining the truth of complex propositions. Finally, we apply these methods to verify properties of a challenging continuous system, assessing the impact of each component of our procedure on overall monitoring performance.

Planetesimal formation remains a critical but elusive stage in the creation of planets, with the streaming instability (SI) generally considered the primary mechanism for dust clumping. Yet, recent analyses indicate that SI can be inhibited by external turbulence, particularly in the weakly turbulent outer regions of protoplanetary disks driven by magneto-rotational instability (MRI). This study employs high-resolution local shearing-box simulations using hybrid particle-gas magnetohydrodynamics (MHD), focusing on ambipolar diffusion as the key non-ideal MHD effect in these outer zones. Our findings reveal that dust backreaction accelerates settling toward the midplane by shortening turbulence correlation times. Even under moderate MRI turbulence, dust clumping proves more favorable than in standard SI scenarios, as the required solid abundance threshold is lower. This enhanced clumping results from the interplay of dust backreaction and local pressure maxima, the latter generated when MRI zonal flows counteract background pressure gradients. Consequently, our results suggest that planetesimal formation is viable within the MRI-turbulent outer protoplanetary disks, particularly within ring-like substructures.

The paper proposes an argumentation tableau, a semantic tableau method designed to derive arguments. It first addresses argument derivation within standard propositional and predicate logic, then presents an extension supporting reasoning with defeasible rules, and finally discusses reasoning by cases using the argumentation tableau.
This paper primarily focuses on examining the quadratic partial sums associated with two-dimensional Walsh-Fourier series.

A straightforward semiclassical H\'enon-Heiles model is developed utilizing Dirac's time-dependent variational principle. By employing a Jackiw-Kerman style Hartree-type two-body trial wavefunction, we derive an effective semiclassical Hamiltonian. Numerical findings demonstrate that quantum effects can indeed generate chaos within the non-chaotic regions of the classical H\'enon-Heiles system.

Building on a concept originally proposed by Pizzetti for the classical Laplacian, we define {\it asymptotic average solutions} that enable pointwise solvability for every Poisson equation $\mathcal{L} u(x)=-f(x)$ with continuous data $f$, where $\mathcal{L}$ represents a hypoelliptic linear partial differential operator possessing a positive semidefinite characteristic form.

The numerical resolution of an ordinary differential equation can be viewed as the precise solution to a slightly altered, nearby equation. This approach, termed backward error analysis, involves studying numerical behavior by examining this modified equation. When the original and modified equations maintain structural consistency, their corresponding exact and approximate solutions retain geometric characteristics, including conserved quantities. Specifically, conjugate symplectic methods applied to Hamiltonian systems preserve a modified symplectic form and a modified Hamiltonian. This work demonstrates how a hybrid of variational and symplectic techniques can determine these modified structures. Unlike other methods, this backward error analysis approach avoids relying on an assumed ansatz; instead, it systematically computes the structures whenever a variational formulation of the method is available. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated using symmetric linear multistep methods featuring matrix coefficients.

With the growing deployment of robots in real-world settings, a primary challenge arises: how to effectively transfer knowledge across environments where shifting constraints and human preferences make adaptation difficult. A core issue is that the full complexity of the deployment environment and its associated tasks often cannot be captured during training. As a result, the abstract representation of tasks humans desire in one setting may not align with the representations the robot has learned in another. We propose that since humans will ultimately judge system success, they are best positioned to communicate which task aspects are critical for the robot. Our key insight is that effective learning from human input depends on first explicitly acquiring high-quality intermediate representations, which can then be leveraged to solve downstream tasks. We identify three domains where this approach can enable interactive systems and outline future research directions to advance collaborative robotics.

The compiler's optimization stage converts a program's intermediate representation (IR) into a more efficient version. Contemporary optimizers, including those in GraalVM, utilize a sophisticated graph-based IR that integrates both data and control flow. This paper defines a semantics for GraalVM's IR within Isabelle/HOL as part of a broader effort to verify its optimization passes. The proposed semantics includes a big-step operational model for data nodes—structured in a graph-based static single assignment (SSA) format—and a small-step operational model for managing control flow, heap operations, exceptions, and method invocations. Furthermore, the authors have formally verified a collection of canonicalization and conditional elimination optimizations against this semantics.

This manuscript addresses the continuous adjoint complement for two-dimensional, incompressible, first-order boundary-layer equations applied to a flat plate. The work is organized into three sections. The first section demonstrates that the adjoint complement can be derived via two distinct approaches: either simplifying the equations before derivation or deriving them first and then simplifying. This simplification involves the classical boundary-layer approximation, while the derivation transforms the primal flow equation into its corresponding adjoint equation. The second section analyzes the coupled primal/adjoint boundary-layer framework, yielding similarity parameters that reduce the Partial-Differential-Equation (PDE) system to a boundary value problem defined by a set of Ordinary-Differential-Equations (ODEs). This reduction supports the formulation of an adjoint complement to the classical Blasius equation. Unlike the primal Blasius equation, this adjoint complement consists of two ODEs that can be simplified based on advection treatment; it is shown that advective fluxes, often debated in literature, vanish in the investigated self-similar boundary-layer flows. Differences between the primal and adjoint Blasius frameworks are examined against numerical solutions, and analytical expressions are derived for the adjoint boundary-layer thickness, wall shear stress, and associated skin friction and drag coefficients. Additionally, an analytical expression for shape sensitivity regarding shear-driven drag objectives is provided. The third section evaluates the predictive accuracy of various Blasius solutions by comparing them with numerical results from Navier-Stokes simulations of a flat plate boundary-layer at Reynolds numbers ranging from 1,000 to 100,000.

We present a boundary state representing a D$p$-brane exhibiting tangential dynamics under the influence of a Kalb-Ramond field, a tachyonic field, and a $U(1)$ gauge potential within a specific gauge choice. Using this framework, we compute the radiation amplitude of a general massless closed string resulting from interactions with these branes. Furthermore, we examine how large separations between the branes affect this radiation, specifically investigating the potential for axion emission in such limits. All calculations are conducted within the context of bosonic string theory.

X-ray imaging may contain complex, predictive features indicating which COVID-19 patients will progress to severe symptoms. If valid, this hypothesis offers practical utility for resource allocation using a cost-effective imaging modality. However, validating this claim requires extensive, well-annotated datasets that include post-imaging severity outcomes. This paper introduces an original methodology to extract semantic features correlated with severity from patient data labeled with ICU admissions, utilizing interpretable models. The approach employs a neural network trained to identify lung pathologies to derive these features, which are subsequently analyzed using low-complexity models to mitigate overfitting and enhance interpretability. The analysis reveals that a limited number of features account for the majority of variance between patients who develop severe symptoms. When applied to a larger, unrelated dataset containing pathology-related clinical notes, the method demonstrated the ability to select images representing learned features, potentially mapping common anatomical locations within the lung. Beyond confirming separability among patients destined for severe outcomes, the proposed statistical approach underscores the significance of features associated with ICU admission that were previously only qualitatively described. Despite handling limited data, the methodology incorporates state-of-the-art lung segmentation and low-complexity modeling to prevent overfitting. The code for the methodology and experiments is publicly available.

Accurately forecasting the performance of AI-driven medical software when facing distribution shifts is vital for assessing safety, efficiency, and usability before clinical implementation. Given the regulatory constraints of medical device software and the scarcity of large, labeled medical datasets, this study addresses the challenge of predicting a black-box model's test accuracy on an unlabeled target domain without altering the original training process or relying on distributional assumptions about the source data. We introduce a black-box test estimation method grounded in conformal prediction and benchmark it against existing approaches using three medical imaging datasets (mammography, dermatology, and histopathology) across various clinically relevant distribution shifts, including institutional, hardware scanner, atlas, and hospital variations. By advancing practical and effective estimation techniques for black-box models, we aim to encourage medical device manufacturers to adopt more standardized and realistic evaluation protocols, thereby enhancing the robustness and reliability of clinical AI tools.

For impartial games $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma'$, the Sprague-Grundy function of their disjunctive sum $\Gamma + \Gamma'$ corresponds to the Nim-sum of their individual Sprague-Grundy functions. This paper introduces $p$-calm subtraction games and demonstrates that for such games $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma'$, the Sprague-Grundy function of the $p$-saturation of $\Gamma + \Gamma'$ equals the $p$-Nim-sum of the Sprague-Grundy functions of their respective $p$-saturations. A $p$-Nim-sum is defined as addition without carry operations in base $p$, while a $p$-saturation of $\Gamma$ refers to an impartial game derived from $\Gamma$ by incorporating additional moves. We establish that both Nim and Welter's game are $p$-calm. Furthermore, leveraging the $p$-calmness of Welter's game, we extend a known relationship between Welter's game and symmetric group representations to the disjunctive sums of Welter's games and representations of generalized symmetric groups, expressing this result combinatorially via Young diagrams.

Efficiently leveraging modern hardware for complex algorithms requires extensive automation, making task-based programming via OpenMP 5.0 a leading solution. This study examines OpenMP 5.0 tasking within a wave equation solver (ExaHyPE) across three distinct architectures and runtime environments. We identify specific task-scheduling deficiencies in existing runtimes, illustrate their detrimental effects on performance, and present strategies to mitigate them. Furthermore, we suggest enhancements to the OpenMP standard.

Effective automatic segmentation of COVID-19 related lung lesions in CT scans demands extensive annotated datasets. Acquiring these annotations via fully manual segmentation is both labor-intensive and relies heavily on expert expertise. Furthermore, significant inter-patient variability in lung lesions, alongside pathologies that visually resemble healthy tissue, complicates the use of current semi-automatic interactive segmentation tools. To overcome these hurdles, we introduce an efficient Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) capable of online learning as annotators provide scribble-based input. A patch-based training strategy accelerates learning from user-labeled samples, while weighted cross-entropy loss mitigates class imbalance arising from such interactions. During inference, the network processes the entire input volume using a fully convolutional approach. Comparative analysis using synthetic scribbles demonstrates that our method surpasses state-of-the-art techniques for annotating COVID-19 lung lesions, delivering a 16% higher Dice score, a threefold reduction in execution time, and a requirement for 9,000 fewer labeled voxels. The online learning capability ensures rapid adaptation to user input, yielding high-quality segmentation results. The source code for ECONet can be accessed at: https://github.com/masadcv/ECONet-MONAILabel.

This study reports findings from a search for events featuring excited leptons (electrons or muons) produced alongside an ordinary lepton of the same flavor, where the excited lepton decays into a lepton and two hadronic jets. The analysis assumes that both the production and decay of these excited leptons proceed through contact interactions characterized by an energy scale $\Lambda$. The branching fraction for this specific decay mode rises with the excited lepton's mass, making it the most sensitive channel for detecting very heavy excited leptons. The investigation utilizes a dataset of proton-proton collisions recorded by the CMS experiment at the LHC with a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} =$ 13 TeV and an integrated luminosity of 77.4 fb$^{-1}$. The primary variable used to distinguish signal from background is the four-body invariant mass of the system comprising two leptons and two jets. No significant excess of events beyond Standard Model predictions was observed. Under the assumption that $\Lambda$ equals the mass of the excited leptons, the study excludes excited electrons and muons with masses below 5.6 and 5.7 TeV, respectively, at a 95% confidence level, establishing the current best limits.

Statistical fault localization (SFL) methods leverage execution profiles and success/failure data from software runs, combined with statistical inference, to automatically rank program elements by their probability of containing faults. These techniques typically rely on a single type of profile data, such as coverage metrics, predicate outcomes, or variable values. However, most SFL approaches measure correlation rather than causation between profile values and execution results, making them vulnerable to confounding bias that skews their scoring. This paper introduces \emph{UniVal}, a novel SFL technique that utilizes causal inference and machine learning to synthesize information from both predicate outcomes and variable values, thereby providing a more precise estimation of the actual failure-inducing impact of program statements. \emph{UniVal} was empirically evaluated against various coverage-based, predicate-based, and value-based SFL methods using 800 program versions containing real faults.

We present a stochastic generalization of the Baez-Fritz-Leinster framework for characterizing Shannon information loss under measure-preserving functions. This approach yields conditional entropy and a related metric termed conditional information loss. While these measures lack full functoriality, they exhibit semi-functoriality—a newly defined concept applicable within any Markov category. Furthermore, we propose an entropic version of Bayes' rule for information measures and offer a characterization of conditional entropy based on this rule.

Painting serves as an artistic method for visual expression, allowing artists to dynamically shift their high-level communication objectives throughout creation. This paper introduces the Framework and Robotics Initiative for Developing Arts (FRIDA), a system that facilitates human-robot collaboration, enabling individuals to create paintings on canvases using simple inputs like text descriptions or images. FRIDA presents key technical advancements in computationally modeling creative painting. First, we constructed a fully differentiable simulation environment based on a "real-to-simulation-to-real" paradigm, demonstrating that our simulated environment offers greater fidelity to reality than current robot painting simulations. Second, to capture the evolving dynamics of creativity, we developed a planning method that continuously optimizes painting strategies in response to the changing canvas relative to high-level goals. Unlike existing methods that handle content generation and action planning separately and sequentially, FRIDA accommodates the stochastic nature of applying paint and brushwork by constantly re-evaluating semantic goals and re-planning based on visual feedback of the painting's progress. We provide detailed accounts of both the technical methodology and system integration.

This research investigates distributed state estimation for both continuous- and discrete-time linear systems. Initially, a straightforward distributed estimator is developed for continuous-time, jointly observable, input-free, multi-channel linear systems where sensed outputs are distributed across a fixed multi-agent network. This framework is subsequently extended to non-stationary networks featuring graphs that switch based on a signal with fixed or variable average dwell times, or switch arbitrarily under specific conditions. Success in solving the problem is guaranteed if a network-wide shared gain is sufficiently large. Alternatively, a fully distributed estimator is examined where each agent adaptively tunes a local gain, though this method faces robustness challenges typical of adaptive control. The study also addresses the discrete-time variant, proposing a corresponding estimator for time-varying networks. For each case, the construction of the estimator is detailed to ensure state estimation errors converge to zero exponentially fast at a user-defined rate, assuming the network graph remains strongly connected at all times. This is achieved using the "split-spectrum" approach and leveraging known properties of invariant subspaces. Furthermore, the proposed estimators are inherently robust against sudden changes in the number of agents or communication links, provided the network maintains redundant strong connectivity and redundant joint observability.

Pairwise learning involves tasks where the loss function is determined by a pair of instances, covering critical areas like metric learning and bipartite ranking. A common strategy for processing streaming data in this context is Online Gradient Descent (OGD), which requires pairing the current instance with a large buffer of prior instances, leading to scalability challenges. This paper introduces straightforward stochastic and online gradient descent methods for pairwise learning. Unlike previous research, our approach pairs the current instance only with the immediately preceding one to determine the gradient direction, thereby enhancing both storage and computational efficiency. We establish new theoretical bounds regarding stability, optimization, and generalization errors applicable to convex and nonconvex, as well as smooth and nonsmooth problems. Additionally, we present innovative techniques to separate the model's dependency on prior instances during both optimization and generalization analyses. Our work addresses an open problem concerning the development of meaningful generalization bounds for OGD utilizing a very small, fixed-size buffering set. Furthermore, we extend our algorithms and stability analysis to create differentially private SGD methods for pairwise learning, yielding significant improvements over current results.

This paper examines the crowdsourced PAC learning of threshold functions using pairwise comparisons. While query-efficient algorithms for scenarios where most crowd workers are accurate have only recently emerged, this work addresses the far more difficult scenario where the majority of workers are incorrect, a condition that typically makes learning infeasible. We demonstrate that under Charikar et al.'s (2017) semi-verified model—where limited access to a trusted oracle providing correct labels is available—it is possible to PAC learn the underlying hypothesis class while significantly reducing labeling costs by leveraging the more accessible comparison queries. Unlike recent advances in semi-verified or list-decodable learning that depend heavily on data distributional assumptions, our PAC guarantee is achieved by harnessing the collective wisdom of the crowd.

A contraction $T$ on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ is defined as pure if the sequence $\lbrace T^{*n} \rbrace_{n}$ converges strongly to $0$. This article establishes that for contractions $T$ commuting with specific, manageable tuples of commuting operators $X = (X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ on $\mathcal{H}$, the following conditions are equivalent: (i) $T$ is a pure contraction, and (ii) the compression $P_{\mathcal{W}(X)}T|_{\mathcal{W}(X)}$ is a pure contraction, where $\mathcal{W}(X)$ denotes the wandering subspace associated with $X$. An operator-valued multiplier $\Phi$ of a vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert space (rkHs) is termed pure contractive when its corresponding multiplication operator $M_{\Phi}$ is a pure contraction. Leveraging the aforementioned result, we demonstrate that operator-valued multipliers $\Phi(\textbf{z})$ for several vector-valued rkHs's over the polydisc $\mathbb{D}^n$ and the unit ball $\mathbb{B}_n$ in $\mathbb{C}^n$ are pure contractive if and only if $\Phi(0)$ constitutes a pure contraction on the underlying Hilbert space; this characterization encompasses Hardy, Bergman, and Drury-Arveson spaces. Finally, we outline applications of this characterization regarding pure contractive multipliers linked to the polydisc.

This paper investigates a ranking challenge within the contextual multi-armed bandit framework. At every time step, a learning agent chooses an ordered sequence of items and receives stochastic feedback for each position. In online recommendation systems, simply displaying the most attractive items in order is suboptimal because rewards depend on both item attributes and their positions, creating a complex reward function; for instance, presenting only high-attractiveness items from a single category fails to provide diversity. We explicitly model these position and item dependencies and develop UCB and Thompson Sampling-based algorithms to address this. We establish that the regret bound over $T$ rounds and $L$ positions is $\Tilde{O}(L\sqrt{d T})$, matching the scaling of prior work with respect to $T$ while growing linearly with $L$. Furthermore, our approach extends existing research by covering broader position dependency scenarios (where position discount is a specific instance) and introducing a more comprehensive contextual bandit model.

We examine recent, high-fidelity ALMA molecular line mapping data of the northeast jet from the young stellar object (YSO) OMC 2/FIR6b (HOPS-60) and conclude that the evidence strongly supports a twin-jet configuration rather than jet rotation, as previously suggested. Interpreting the line-of-sight velocity gradient across the Fir6b jet as rotational implies a launch radius of approximately 2–3 AU; however, the observed jet velocities (100–400 km/s) vastly exceed the escape velocity from such a distance. Consequently, we argue that the northeast jet of FIR6b is better explained by a twin-jet structure, similar to those seen in certain planetary nebulae. Our analysis reveals that the primary, redshifted jet originating from the central YSO actually consists of two narrowly aligned, smaller jets ejected simultaneously but at different angles relative to the sky plane. This dual-jet model eliminates the need to assume jets with such high velocities were launched from extremely large radii to overcome escape velocity. Furthermore, both FIR6b and specific planetary nebulae exhibit asymmetric bipolar jets with unequal intensities and structures. We propose that this oppositional lobe asymmetry arises from a sub-stellar binary companion on an eccentric orbit that is inclined relative to the accretion disk.

Beyond enhancing weather forecast accuracy, uncovering patterns in atmospheric data offers crucial insights for addressing climate change. The Weather4cast competition challenges participants to assess how well machine learning algorithms can forecast future atmospheric conditions. This paper details our third-place submission for Weather4cast, introducing a new Variational U-Net. This architecture merges the probabilistic modeling strengths of Variational Autoencoders with the fine-grained detail recovery capabilities of U-Nets. Building on our fourth-place solution for Traffic4cast 2020, this approach shares significant commonalities, demonstrating its versatility across diverse fields like meteorology and traffic management.

All-atom simulations are gaining traction for investigating the conformational and dynamical characteristics of nucleic acids due to their accuracy and superior spatial and temporal resolution. However, this high fidelity entails significant computational expenses, and the accessible time scales typically confine nucleic acids to weak fluctuations around their ideal structures, limiting the range of explored conformations. We present the RBB-NA algorithm, designed to regulate rigid base parameters during all-atom nucleic acid simulations. By applying appropriate biasing potentials, this method can compel DNA or RNA molecules to adopt specific values for six rotational degrees of freedom (tilt, roll, twist, buckle, propeller, and opening) and/or six translational degrees of freedom (shift, slide, rise, shear, stretch, and stagger). Consequently, the algorithm facilitates the application of sophisticated sampling techniques to examine the structure and dynamics of locally highly deformed nucleic acids. We demonstrate its efficacy through examples involving DNA that is severely twisted, bent, or locally buckled. In these cases, RBB-NA accurately replicates data from unconstrained simulations and other established features of DNA mechanics, while also enabling the exploration of anharmonic behaviors inherent to nucleic acid mechanics under high-deformation conditions.

Function as a Service (FaaS) represents a novel cloud technology featuring automated resource management. Unlike traditional cloud computing, FaaS functions operate for a fixed duration before termination. Additionally, FaaS providers frequently update their platforms, such as modifying idle timeout settings; however, these changes and their effects often remain opaque and can adversely affect function execution. Consequently, this paper presents a methodology to characterize FaaS idle timeout—the duration a provider maintains a function instance alive in the absence of active traffic. The study evaluates three prominent FaaS platforms: AWS Lambda, IBM Cloud Functions, and Azure Cloud Functions. Furthermore, the research investigates how long an instance remains active when a user performs regular polling. Experimental findings indicate that the idle timeout period has undergone evolution between January 2020 and January 2022.

The paper introduces a modified version of the \ssstar Newton method designed to numerically solve generalized equations where the multi-valued component is an SCD (subspace containing derivative) mapping. Assuming a relatively mild regularity condition, this approach demonstrates (local) superlinear convergence. Two practical implementations are derived from the core algorithm, and their performance is evaluated using a generalized equation that models a discretized static contact problem involving Coulomb friction.

Self-supervised contrastive representation learning has achieved remarkable success in vision and natural language tasks, delivering state-of-the-art results with significantly fewer labeled examples. Despite this, applying these methods to real-world tabular data remains largely unexplored due to their domain-specific nature. We introduce SCARF, a simple and broadly applicable contrastive learning approach that generates views by randomly corrupting subsets of features. Evaluated on 69 tabular classification datasets from the OpenML-CC18 benchmark, SCARF enhances deep neural network performance in fully-supervised scenarios, as well as under conditions of label noise and in semi-supervised settings with limited labeled data. Our results demonstrate that SCARF complements current strategies and surpasses alternatives such as autoencoders, supported by comprehensive ablation studies that highlight the significance of various design factors.
