To achieve this, we examine the Iterative Hard Thresholding (IHT) algorithm, widely recognized in literature for its scalability, speed, and ease of implementation. Despite extensive prior research on IHT, we introduce several novel techniques that recover established results while deriving new ones. First, we establish a critical gradient descent property of the hard thresholding (HT) operator, which relates to the distance between sparse points. This property enables the analysis of IHT with a stepsize less than or equal to 1/L (where L is the Lipschitz constant of the objective's gradient), whereas existing literature typically restricts the stepsize to be strictly less than 1/L. Leveraging this advancement, we define and investigate HT-stable and HT-unstable stationary points, demonstrating that regardless of how close an initialization is to an HT-unstable stationary point (a saddle point in the sparse context), the IHT sequence will escape it. Finally, we prove that for any sparse initial point, the IHT sequence converges provided the function values at HT-stable stationary points are distinct.

This study investigates the complexity of the supergranular network by calculating its fractal dimension using digitized Ca II K data from the Kodaikanal Solar Observatory. The dataset comprises 326 visually identified supergranular cells spanning the 23rd solar cycle, with the analysis restricted to well-defined cells. We address the potential selection bias introduced by this criterion, noting that it preferentially selects smaller cells (less than 20 Mm). Within this filtered sample, our analysis of fractal dimensions across the solar cycle reveals an anticorrelation between the fractal dimension and the level of solar activity.

We determine the Ginzburg-Landau (GL) parameters for a three-dimensional attractive Fermi gas near the superfluid critical temperature, comparing various approximations across the BCS to Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC) regimes. Our analysis reveals that incorporating Gaussian fluctuations significantly alters the GL parameters as the system approaches the BEC side of the crossover. By examining the coherence length and critical rotational frequencies, we assess the reliability of fluctuation-inclusive GL theory throughout the BCS-BEC crossover. While Gaussian fluctuations yield qualitatively correct trends for physical quantities from the BCS regime up to the unitary limit, the GL equation with these fluctuations becomes unreliable near the BEC regime.

Over the last thirty years, numerous theoretical metrics have been developed to analyze complex systems. This study uniquely aligns these diverse measures to examine their qualitative similarities, distinctions, and limitations. By employing a Boltzmann machine—a fully connected recurrent neural network with uniform weights—as our primary model, we numerically investigate how complexity evolves in response to network dynamics and parameter variations. Furthermore, we extend an information-theoretic complexity metric to analyze incremental Hebbian learning within Hopfield networks, a fully recurrent architecture designed for autoassociative memory. Our findings indicate that during the Hebbian learning process, the total information flow demonstrates a natural increase in complexity as the network progressively learns additional patterns.

The degree of edge concurrency, defined as the count of edges sharing a node at specific moments, could significantly influence epidemic dynamics within temporal networks. We introduce theoretically manageable Markovian temporal network models where edges continuously switch between active and inactive states. These models exhibit varying levels of concurrency; however, they can be calibrated to maintain identical statistics regarding edge activation and deactivation (and thus the active duration per edge) as well as the topology of the underlying static network. We analytically derive the concurrency metrics for edges incident to a single node across each model. Subsequently, we numerically examine how concurrency affects epidemic propagation using stochastic Susceptible-Infectious-Recovered (SIR) dynamics on these frameworks. Our findings reveal that concurrency amplifies epidemic spreading near the epidemic threshold, though this effect varies in magnitude. Conversely, when the infection rate greatly exceeds the threshold, concurrency tends to suppress spreading. Overall, our simulations suggest that the influence of concurrency on epidemic propagation is relatively limited. We anticipate that these proposed models will prove valuable for exploring the effects of concurrency on diverse collective dynamics, encompassing both infectious diseases and other network processes.

Does the Heisenberg uncertainty principle (HUP) operate along the time dimension identically to how it functions across the three spatial dimensions? While relativity suggests it should, current experimental practices indicate otherwise. Recent breakthroughs in attosecond-scale measurements now make it feasible to resolve this question experimentally.

The most straightforward approach involves measuring the time-of-arrival of a quantum particle; if the HUP applies temporally, the resulting dispersion in arrival times would be measurably greater. We have formulated a standard metric for time-of-arrival and extended it to account for temporal uncertainty, allowing for a direct comparison. As anticipated, the time-of-arrival exhibits increased uncertainty when the HUP holds true along the time axis. These findings are strictly bound by Lorentz covariance, ensuring they are uniquely defined and falsifiable.

Consequently, we face a concrete experimental inquiry. A definitive answer would carry profound implications for understanding the role of time within quantum mechanics and relativity. Furthermore, a positive confirmation would yield significant practical benefits in quantum communication, attosecond physics (such as protein folding studies), and quantum computing.

Density estimation serves as a cornerstone in statistics and machine learning. While Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) is an effective non-parametric approach for low-dimensional data, it struggles in high-dimensional spaces and suffers from linearly increasing computational complexity as the dataset grows. This paper introduces a neural density estimation technique that functions similarly to KDE but eliminates the high prediction overhead. Built upon density matrices—a concept from quantum mechanics—and adaptive Fourier features, this method can be trained without optimization or integrated into deep learning frameworks via gradient descent. Evaluations across various synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that its performance is competitive with state-of-the-art neural density estimation methods.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is a broad scientific field that allows computer systems to tackle problems by mimicking intricate biological functions like learning, reasoning, and self-correction. This paper offers an in-depth review of how AI techniques enhance the performance of optical communication systems and networks. It begins by examining AI applications in optical transmission, covering the characterization and operation of network components, performance monitoring, nonlinear mitigation, and transmission quality estimation. The review then shifts to optical network control and management, addressing topics such as planning and operation within both transport and access networks. Finally, the paper concludes by summarizing the opportunities and challenges in optical networking, highlighting the pivotal role AI is poised to play in the near future.

The Softmax bottleneck, initially recognized in language modeling as a theoretical ceiling on the expressivity of Softmax-based architectures, has also proven relevant in session-based recommender systems (SBRSs), where such models are ubiquitous. These models typically apply a Softmax function atop a final linear layer; however, this layer suffers from rank deficiency linked to matrix factorization, creating the bottleneck. This paper extends the understanding of the Softmax bottleneck within SBRSs by challenging prevailing assumptions. Contrary to the belief that overfitting is exclusive to complex networks, we demonstrate that it occurs in the final linear layer. Additionally, we found that sharing item embeddings between session sequences and the candidate pool induces a tight coupling that exacerbates the bottleneck. To address these issues, we propose a straightforward and effective approach called Dropout and Decoupling (D&D). Experimental results indicate that D&D significantly enhances the accuracy of various Softmax-based SBRS algorithms. Notably, our method achieves performance comparable to, and occasionally superior to, computationally intensive alternatives like MLP and Mixture of Softmaxes (MoS), all while maintaining the same time complexity as standard Softmax-based models.

Downscaling and upscaling are fundamental rescaling operations; however, once an image is downscaled, reconstructing it via upscaling is challenging due to information loss. To enhance compatibility between these processes and improve reconstruction quality, several approaches frame them as a joint encoding-decoding task, ensuring that the downscaled (encoded) low-resolution (LR) image retains the original visual characteristics. Typically, this is achieved by supervising the downscaling module with a bicubically downscaled version of the high-resolution (HR) image. Yet, this bicubic LR guidance can be suboptimal for the subsequent upscaling stage, limiting final reconstruction performance. Instead of direct LR guidance, this paper introduces an additional invertible flow guidance module (FGM). This module transforms the downscaled representation into a visually plausible image during downscaling and reverses the process during upscaling. Leveraging the invertibility of the FGM, the downscaled representation can bypass the need for direct LR guidance, thereby avoiding interference with the downscaling-upscaling workflow. This approach removes constraints on the downscaling module, allowing both the downscaling and upscaling components to be optimized in an end-to-end manner to maximize HR reconstruction. Extensive experiments confirm that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance on both downsampled and reconstructed images.

This study introduces the Quantum Correlation Cost (QCC), which quantifies the quantum correlation consumed during a weak measurement process using the trace norm. It is demonstrated that QCC relates to the trace-norm-based quantum discord (TQD) through a factor dependent solely on the weak measurement's strength, meaning QCC captures only a portion of a system's quantumness compared to TQD. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that this residual quantumness can be extracted not only via subsequent von Neumann measurements but also through a series of infinitesimal weak measurements. These findings are illustrated using a Bell-diagonal state as a specific example.

This paper derives a functional central limit theorem for a specific class of degenerate diffusion processes featuring periodic coefficients, thereby extending classical findings related to uniformly elliptic diffusions. Furthermore, as a practical application, we explore the periodic homogenization of various linear degenerate elliptic and parabolic partial differential equations.

A generalized quasilinear (GQL) approach, introduced by Marston et al. (Phys. Rev. Lett., vol. 116, 104502, 2016), is utilized to analyze turbulent channel flow at a friction Reynolds number of approximately 1700 ($Re_\tau$), focusing specifically on energy transfer within the streamwise wavenumber spectrum. In this framework, the flow is partitioned into low- and high-wavenumber components; the low-wavenumber group is resolved using full nonlinear equations, while the high-wavenumber group is derived from linearized equations based on the former. The GQL method's efficacy is then benchmarked against a standard quasilinear (QL) model (Thomas et al., Phys. Fluids, vol. 26, no. 10, 105112, 2014), which restricts the low-wavenumber group to solely zero streamwise wavenumber. Results indicate that the QL model displays a significantly diminished multi-scale behavior at this moderately high Reynolds number. Conversely, the GQL approximation markedly enhances this behavior by including only a few additional streamwise Fourier modes in the low-wavenumber set, successfully recovering distance-from-wall scaling in both turbulence statistics and spectra. Furthermore, it is suggested that the energy transfer from low to high wavenumbers in the GQL scheme, termed the `scattering' mechanism, relies on the neutrally stable leading Lyapunov spectrum of the linearized high-wavenumber equations. Specifically, if the threshold wavenumber separating the two groups is sufficiently large, the scattering mechanism vanishes entirely due to the linear characteristics governing the high-wavenumber dynamics.

This study presents the application of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) defined on hypercomplex algebras for classifying lymphocytes in digital microscopic blood smear images, a process vital for diagnosing acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), a form of blood cancer. The research utilizes eight hypercomplex-valued CNNs (HvCNNs) in conjunction with real-valued CNNs to perform this classification. Results indicate that HvCNNs outperform real-valued models by achieving higher accuracy with significantly fewer parameters. Specifically, HvCNNs leveraging Clifford algebras to process HSV-encoded images achieved the highest accuracy. On the ALL-IDB2 dataset with a 50% train-test split, our HvCNN reached an average accuracy of 96.6%, nearly matching state-of-the-art models while employing a much simpler architecture and reduced parameter count.

This study introduces a novel method for flow field tomography that leverages the Navier-Stokes and advection-diffusion equations to regularize reconstruction processes. Tomography is increasingly utilized to deduce two- or three-dimensional fluid flow and combustion structures from line-of-sight (LoS) integrated measurements across various imaging techniques. These high-dimensional flow fields are reconstructed from low-dimensional data by inverting a projection model consisting of path integrals along each LoS through the region of interest. While regularization is essential for obtaining realistic estimates, existing methods often employ penalty terms that are only partially compatible with flow physics. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) offer a new framework for inverse analysis, allowing flow field estimates to be regularized using governing physical laws. We demonstrate that PINNs can reconstruct a 2D flow field from sparse LoS-integrated measurements without prior knowledge of boundary conditions by integrating the measurement model into the network's training loss function. The resulting reconstructions significantly outperform those generated by state-of-the-art algorithms, even when PINNs are applied as a post-processing step. However, similar to conventional iterative methods, our approach is prone to semi-convergence under high noise levels. We mitigated this issue by implementing a Bayesian PINN, which provided comprehensive uncertainty quantification, allowed for a more intuitive loss function, and identified the root causes of semi-convergence.

This study investigates the dynamics of an axisymmetric gravity current flowing through an anisotropic porous medium characterized by higher horizontal than vertical permeability. We recognize that the standard model for such currents, driven by a constant point source, exhibits a non-physical singularity at the origin. To resolve this, we introduce a pressure-dominated zone near the source that permits vertical fluid entry, ensuring the current maintains a finite depth; outside this zone, the flow becomes gravity-dominated. While the pressure-driven inner region initially governs the current's expansion, its relative influence diminishes over time. Consequently, at late stages, the current's radius grows proportionally to $t^{3/7}$, and the depth near the origin increases roughly as $t^{1/7}$. The anisotropy of the medium is significant because the vertical permeability continues to impact the late-time flow via the pressure-driven mechanism near the origin. These findings offer quantitative insights into the primary dynamics governing CO$_2$ migration in permeable aquifers, a critical factor in carbon capture and storage applications.

We demonstrate that the gapless boundary signatures—specifically chiral/helical hinge modes or localized zero modes—found in three-dimensional higher-order topological insulators and superconductors with inversion symmetry can be gapped without breaking symmetry by introducing non-Abelian surface topological order. In every scenario, the resulting fractionalization pattern on the surface is `anomalous,' meaning it aligns with symmetry only when situated on the surface of a three-dimensional higher-order insulator or superconductor. Our findings indicate that the interacting expression of higher-order topology manifests as `anomalous gapped boundaries' separating distinct topological orders, where quasiparticles are linked by inversion, potentially alongside other protecting symmetries like time-reversal symmetry and charge conservation.

Proof of work (PoW) serves as a crucial cryptographic mechanism that allows an entity to demonstrate to others that computational effort has been expended to solve a specific task. Its most significant influence has been within the realm of cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and its blockchain infrastructure, which have garnered considerable interest recently due to their diverse application potential and their ability to address fundamental distributed computing challenges under new threat models. PoWs facilitate the linkage of blocks within the blockchain structure, making the feasibility of constructing a sequence of these proofs the central problem of interest. This work investigates the difficulty of generating such a chain of PoWs when facing quantum strategies. We demonstrate that the chain-of-PoW problem can be reduced to a specific challenge termed "multi-solution Bernoulli search," for which we determine the quantum query complexity. This effectively extends a threshold direct product theorem to an average-case unstructured search scenario. Our proof, contributing to current active research, streamlines and broadens the recording technique introduced by Zhandry at Crypto 2019. Furthermore, we re-examine the formal security analysis of the Bitcoin backbone—the core of the Bitcoin consensus protocol—against quantum adversaries, establishing that its security remains valid under a quantum version of the "honest majority" assumption that we define. Our analysis reveals that the Bitcoin backbone protocol remains secure as long as the number of adversarial quantum queries is limited such that each quantum query corresponds to no more than $O(p^{-1/2})$ classical queries, where $p$ represents the success probability of a single classical query to the protocol's underlying hash function. Surprisingly, the wait time required for safe settlement in the presence of quantum adversaries aligns with the safe settlement time observed in classical scenarios.

Since weak values represent average quantities, examining their associated variance is essential for comprehending their role within quantum mechanics. We coherently develop the notion of position-postselected weak variance of momentum, drawing primarily on the works of Moyal (1949) and Sonego (1991). This variance is defined via the Wigner function using standard probability theory constructs. We demonstrate that this quantity is measurable and distinct from a weak value itself, while also establishing a natural link between the imaginary component of the momentum weak value and the quantum potential. Furthermore, we explore how the negativity of the Wigner function results in negative weak variances and the consequences for certain `subquantum' theories. Finally, we discuss the utility of weak variances in investigating determinism and deriving the classical limit through a variational principle.

Certain classes of cubic fourfolds are birational to fibrations over $\mathbb{P}^2$ with rational surface fibers. This relationship tightly links the rationality of the cubic fourfold to the rationality of these surfaces over the function field of $\mathbb{P}^2$ and to the presence of rational sections within the fibration. A key question is whether the existence of a rational section is a necessary condition for the rationality of the cubic. Let $C_{18}$ represent the divisor in the moduli space of smooth cubic hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{P}^5$ consisting of those whose general member contains an elliptic ruled surface linked to a sextic del Pezzo fibration. Cubics within $C_{18}$ are rational if the fibration possesses rational sections. By intersecting $C_{18}$ with the known-rational divisors $C_{14}$, $C_{26}$, and $C_{38}$, we explicitly describe these intersections and present new examples of rational cubic fourfolds whose associated good sextic del Pezzo fibration lacks rational sections. We also examine the divisor $C_{8}$, whose general element is a cubic containing a plane; these cubics are birational to quadric fibrations over $\mathbb{P}^2$. Furthermore, intersections between $C_8$ and the divisors $C_{26}$ and $C_{38}$ yield additional classes of smooth rational cubic fourfolds whose associated quadric surface bundles do not admit rational sections.

Nonnegative matrix factorization enables the automatic, unsupervised discovery of topics within a corpus by approximating a nonnegative matrix as the product of two lower-rank nonnegative matrices. This paper demonstrates that combining this factorization with regression on a continuous response variable yields superior performance compared to conducting regression after topic identification, while simultaneously enhancing model interpretability.

Substituting the standard position-momentum pair (q, p) of the harmonic oscillator with the locally and symplectically equivalent angle-action pair (phi, I) fundamentally alters the global topological structure of the associated phase spaces. While (q, p) resides in a topologically trivial plane (R²), the pair (phi, I>0) exists in a topologically non-trivial, infinitely connected, punctured plane (R²-{0}), characterized by the group SO(1,1,2). Consequently, the resulting symplectic spectrum of the quantum Hamiltonian, influenced by the system's infinitely many covering groups, is expressed as {ħω(n+b), n=0,1,...; b∈(0,1]}, contrasting with the conventional spectrum {ħω(n+1/2)}. The most significant implications likely pertain to infrared vibrations in diatomic molecules, such as molecular hydrogen (H₂). These symplectic spectra could simultaneously resolve two major astrophysical mysteries: the nature of dark (vacuum) energy and dark matter. Regarding dark energy, the zero-point energy (bħω) of free electromagnetic wave modes can be exceedingly small (b ≈ exp(-35) for observed dark energy density). For dark matter, the quantum zero-point energies within the Born-Oppenheimer potentials governing the vibrations of H₂ or other primordial diatomic molecules can be even lower, potentially creating spectrally detuned "dark" H₂ molecules during the universe's "Dark Ages" that form Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs). These findings align surprisingly well with the LambdaCDM cosmological model. Beyond laboratory experiments, investigating 21-cm radio signals from the Dark Ages and other astrophysical observations may further elucidate these theoretical implications.

View a random matrix of size $N$ as an additive perturbation of the complex Ginibre ensemble by a deterministic, finite-rank matrix $X_0$ that remains independent of $N$. If certain eigenvalues of $X_0$ detach from the unit disk, outlier eigenvalues emerge asymptotically at corresponding positions, displaying fluctuations that are notably contingent upon the Jordan canonical form of $X_0$. These observations largely build on the work of Benaych-Georges and Rochet \cite{BR}, Bordenave and Capitaine \cite{BC16}, and Tao \cite{Ta13}. In the scenario where all eigenvalues of $X_0$ reside within the unit disk, we establish that the local eigenvalue statistics at the spectral edge constitute a novel class of determinantal point processes, with correlation kernels defined via repeated erfc integrals. This result finalizes the non-Hermitian counterpart to the BBP phase transition in Random Matrix Theory. Comparable outcomes are observed for the deformed real quaternion Ginibre ensemble.

We introduce a model featuring $D_4$ flavor symmetry within the supersymmetric $SU(5)$ grand unified theory framework to address leptogenesis. In this scenario, neutrino masses are generated via the type I seesaw mechanism, where the spontaneous breaking of the flavor symmetry yields the established trimaximal mixing ($TM_2$). Our analysis indicates that the model predicts a normal hierarchy (NH) for neutrino masses. Furthermore, the predicted interval for the effective neutrino mass $m_{\beta\beta}$ falls within the reach of upcoming neutrinoless double beta decay experiments. Regarding the baryon asymmetry of the Universe (BAU), we examine the unflavored leptogenesis regime by considering the decays of the three right-handed neutrinos $N_i$. We conclude that the observed BAU results from a correction to the Dirac operator, which introduces a novel coupling and a $CP$ phase; both elements are crucial for generating the baryon asymmetry.

The Photon Detectors Topical Group has pinpointed two critical domains where targeted research and development over the coming decade could significantly advance High Energy Physics (HEP) experiments. These areas are defined by the intersection of urgent scientific requirements and recent technological breakthroughs. Key points include:

*   **IF02-1:** While developing detectors capable of counting individual photons across the IR to UV spectrum has been highly active recently, the next step is to adapt these technologies for HEP experiments. This involves scaling up arrays, enhancing energy resolution and timing precision, reducing dark count rates, and broadening wavelength coverage.
*   **IF02-2:** Novel photon detector technologies are being evaluated for upcoming neutrino experiments that surpass current capabilities. Although concept demonstrations are complete, the focus must now shift from theoretical concepts to the construction of functional detectors.
*   **General Context:** The fields governing light generation, detection, and manipulation are advancing rapidly, largely driven by external disciplines. To fully leverage these innovations, the HEP community requires dedicated resources to integrate advanced photonic technologies into particle physics experiments.

This study introduces a novel approach to simultaneously minimize energy usage, transmission latency, and bit error rates within Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) networks. By equipping a UAV with a wireless Bidirectional Relay (BR), the network achieves extended coverage and higher throughput; however, the BR's benefits are offset by transmission delays resulting from UAV motion. These delays increase total energy consumption, which further degrades bit error rate performance, particularly at high signal-to-noise ratios (SNR). Fortunately, wireless communication allows for a trade-off between delay and energy that can enhance overall performance. Consequently, this research seeks to improve UAV network performance by optimizing energy consumption, data transmission delay, and bit error rates. A multi-objective algorithm is utilized to develop an adaptive optimal energy allocation strategy that balances energy usage against transmission delays. Theoretical analysis results are validated through several examples. As demonstrated, the proposed solution effectively harmonizes delay and energy efficiency within a customized system design, thereby improving bit error rates in UAV networks.

A prevalent issue with most zero and few-shot learning methods is their tendency to favor seen classes, leading to sub-optimal outcomes. Current strategies attempt to mitigate this by incorporating unlabeled images from unseen classes (transductive zero-shot) during training to enhance generalization. However, this restricts their application in practical contexts where acquiring data from target unseen classes is impossible or impractical. This work introduces an inductive zero and few-shot learning framework that leverages unlabeled images from auxiliary classes—distinct from both seen and unseen categories—to boost generalization across any-shot scenarios. By employing a product-of-experts formulation and a novel AUD module, we enable the use of these readily available out-of-data samples without incurring annotation costs. Furthermore, we demonstrate the model's efficacy in addressing the more demanding and practical challenge of Generalized Zero-shot learning under limited supervision, where even base seen classes lack sufficient annotated examples.

This paper investigates the thermodynamic properties of Reissner-Nordstr\"om-de Sitter (RN-dS) black holes by examining the relationship between the black hole horizon and the cosmological horizon. The study reveals that the RN-dS black hole undergoes a phase transition when its state parameters meet specific criteria. Through an analysis of the interaction between these two horizons within RN-dS spacetime, numerical solutions for their mutual interaction are derived. This analysis elucidates the force acting between the black hole and the cosmological horizon, which may serve as a candidate to explain the universe's accelerating expansion, thereby offering a novel perspective on exploring the physical mechanisms behind cosmic acceleration.

Binary neutron star mergers occur roughly every ten seconds throughout the cosmos, generating explosive events detectable via both gravitational waves and electromagnetic signals. The binary neutron star merger GW170817 provided transformative, simultaneous observations that yielded critical insights into these cataclysmic collisions, allowing scientists to probe nuclear matter at supranuclear densities, analyze gamma-ray burst jet structures, measure the speed of gravity, and study the local Universe's cosmological evolution, among other discoveries. Despite this abundance of data, the exact timing of the GW170817 remnant's collapse into a black hole remains uncertain. Evidence from other short gamma-ray bursts suggests that a significant proportion of mergers result in long-lived neutron stars. This review examines both observational and theoretical knowledge regarding post-merger remnants of binary neutron stars. Theoretically, we explore the evolution of short- and long-lived remnants, covering fluid dynamics, magnetic fields, and thermal changes. These factors influence the prospects for detecting gravitational waves from such remnants, offering potential new avenues to investigate the hot nuclear equation of state under conditions unattainable in terrestrial labs. Furthermore, we assess the potential for elucidating post-merger physics through current and future electromagnetic observations, including kilonovae and late-stage x-ray and radio afterglows.

This study examines how broadening the options for choosing game and learning partners influences the evolution of cooperation within public goods games on scale-free networks. Our findings reveal three key outcomes: (i) widening the pool of potential game partners hinders cooperation; (ii) expanding the selection range for learning partners fosters cooperation in scenarios where it is otherwise difficult to emerge; and (iii) when cooperation is already likely to develop, a slight increase in learning partner diversity significantly reduces the cooperation rate, whereas further expansion allows the rate to recover. While result (i) aligns with the established hub-centered mechanism that typically supports cooperation on scale-free networks, results (ii) and (iii) stem from a distinct mechanism that has previously been seldom discussed.

Socially-intelligent agents are increasingly significant in the field of artificial intelligence, necessitating systems capable of comprehending social relationships across varied contexts. Inferring the social backdrop of a visual scene requires more than just object recognition; it demands a deeper grasp of the people involved, their attributes, and their interconnections. To address this, an effective computational strategy involves employing an explicit knowledge graph to model human relationships and traits, thereby enabling high-level reasoning. We present a novel, end-to-end trainable neural network designed to generate a Social Relationship Graph—a structured, unified depiction of social ties and characteristics—from a single input image. Our proposed Social Relationship Graph Generation Network (SRG-GN) pioneers the use of memory cells, such as Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), to iteratively refine social relationship states within a graph by leveraging scene and attribute context. By utilizing recurrent connections among these GRUs to facilitate message passing between graph nodes and edges, our network achieves substantial performance gains over prior methods in recognizing social relationships.

The necessity of exotic matter to sustain wormhole geometries has long been a persistent challenge within General Relativity. Recent investigations have attempted to resolve this by employing modified gravity theories, which attribute the wormhole structure to additional curvature terms, thereby satisfying the Null Energy Condition (NEC) and allowing for standard matter. This article explores traversable wormhole solutions supported by normal matter at the throat using the framework of symmetric teleparallel gravity, specifically $f(Q)$ gravity, where $Q$ represents the non-metricity scalar governing gravitational interactions. We analyze three distinct forms of the function $f(Q)$: a linear form $f(Q)=\alpha Q$, a non-linear form $f(Q)=\alpha Q^2 + \beta$, and a more comprehensive quadratic form $f(Q)=\alpha Q^2 + \beta Q + \gamma$, with $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$ serving as constants. For each scenario, the shape function is defined as $b(r) = {\frac{r_{0}\ln(r+1)}{\ln({r_0}+1)}}$, where $r_0$ denotes the throat radius, alongside a specific redshift function. Finally, we evaluate all relevant energy conditions to determine the existence and stability of these wormhole configurations.

To gauge software and hardware adoption within the solar physics community, the SunPy Project distributed a 13-item survey. It received 364 responses from members across 35 nations. The results indicate that 99±0.5% of participants employ software in their research, with 66% utilizing the Python scientific stack. Students are twice as likely as faculty, staff scientists, and researchers to prefer Python over Interactive Data Language (IDL). This trend highlights a significant divergence from the broader astrophysics community; while 44% of astrophysics faculty and scientists sampled by Momcheva and Tollerud (2015) use IDL, 78% of solar physics faculty and staff in our sample do. Furthermore, 63±4% of respondents reported never having taken undergraduate or graduate computer science courses. Most participants rely on consumer-grade hardware for their work. Although 82% process data from space or ground-based missions—including high-volume sources like the Solar Dynamics Observatory and the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope that generate terabytes daily—usage of advanced infrastructure remains limited: only 14% access regional or national clusters, 5% use commercial cloud providers, and 29% depend solely on laptops or desktops. Finally, while 73±4% of respondents incorporate scientific software into their research, only 42±3% do so routinely.

This paper presents a solution for the next destination city recommendation task within a travel reservation system. We introduce a two-stage framework that combines a heuristic method for candidate selection with an attention-based neural network for re-ranking. Drawing inspiration from listwise learning-to-rank techniques and recent advancements in natural language processing, particularly transformer architectures, we applied this approach to the Booking.com recommendations challenge. Our team secured 5th place in the competition, achieving an accuracy@4 score of 0.555 on the held-out dataset.

This paper introduces a quantum Bernoulli noises framework for analyzing quantum walks on hypercubes. We begin by deriving an alternative characterization of a general hypercube, which reveals that the operators $\partial_k^* + \partial_k$ function effectively as shift operators, where $\partial_k$ and $\partial_k^*$ represent the annihilation and creation operators acting on Bernoulli functionals, respectively. Utilizing these operators as shift mechanisms on the position space, we construct a discrete-time quantum walk model on a general hypercube and derive an explicit formula for its probability distribution at any given time. Furthermore, we establish two limit theorems demonstrating that the averaged probability distribution of the walk converges to the uniform probability distribution. Finally, we prove that the walk yields the uniform measure as its stationary distribution on the hypercube, provided the initial state meets certain mild conditions, along with several additional results.

Given the intimate connection between charge and spin order and superconductivity in copper oxide superconductors, understanding competing orders in nickel oxide compounds is vital, especially following the discovery of superconductivity in Nd$_{0.8}$Sr$_{0.2}$NiO$_2$ films. This study presents structural, electronic transport, magnetic, and thermodynamic analyses of single crystals of La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ and La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_6$. La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ exhibits metallic behavior with mixed Ni$^{2+}$ and Ni$^{3+}$ valence states. Resistivity data reveal two transition-like kinks at approximately 110 K and 153 K; the 153 K kink is corroborated by magnetization and specific heat measurements, signaling the emergence of charge and spin order. La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_6$ crystals, derived from the topochemical reduction of La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$, are insulating and display a magnetic susceptibility anomaly near 176 K. The transition-like behaviors observed in La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ and La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_6$ mirror those seen in La$_4$Ni$_3$O$_{10}$ and La$_4$Ni$_3$O$_8$, indicating that charge and spin order are a common characteristic within the ternary La-Ni-O system featuring mixed-valent nickel states.

This study examines the luminous, host-less type Ia supernova 2022ilv, identifying it as a member of the 2003fg-like family, commonly known as super-Chandrasekhar (Ia-SC) events. The ATLAS light curve reveals a brief, pulse-like early excess akin to that observed in SN 2020hvf. Characterized by a broad light curve and early spectra strikingly similar to SN 2009dc, the analysis adopts a redshift of $z=0.026 \pm 0.005$ derived from spectral matching. Modeling indicates a substantial $^{56}$Ni mass between $0.7-1.5$ M$_{\odot}$ and an ejecta mass ranging from $1.6-2.3$ M$_{\odot}$. The early excess is attributed to the interaction of rapidly expanding ejecta with a thin, dense circumstellar shell located approximately $10^{13}$ cm from the progenitor, a few hours post-explosion. This scenario aligns with a double-degenerate model where a white dwarf merger is preceded by the ejection of $\sim 10^{-3}-10^{-2}$ M$_{\odot}$ of hydrogen- and helium-poor, tidally stripped material. Furthermore, a deep pre-explosion Pan-STARRS1 stack finds no host galaxy down to a limiting magnitude of $r \sim 24.5$, suggesting an unexpectedly faint limit for any host with $M_r \gtrsim -11$. This supports the conclusion that such explosions predominantly occur in low-metallicity environments.

This study examines a class of non-smooth, non-convex optimization problems involving penalty constraints connected to variational inequalities (VI), focusing on their shape differentiability. Specifically, it addresses the quasi-brittle fracture problem, which models an elastic body containing a Barenblatt cohesive crack subject to a non-penetration inequality at the crack surfaces. By applying the Lagrange multiplier method and employing smooth penalization via Lavrentiev regularization, a formula for the shape derivative is derived. This explicit formula incorporates both primal and adjoint states, facilitating the identification of descent directions for gradient algorithms aimed at determining an optimal crack shape from boundary data. Additionally, numerical examples illustrating destructive testing in two dimensions are provided.

In dense Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite constellations, centralized minimum-delay routing imposes substantial signaling and computational burdens. This study leverages the deterministic topology of such networks to compute minimum-delay paths between any two nodes. We introduce a distributed probabilistic congestion control mechanism designed to reduce end-to-end latency, which operates atop the existing Datagram Routing Algorithm (DRA). Routing decisions are made using the most recent traffic data from neighboring nodes. Additionally, we analyze congestion patterns generated by a simplified DRA on a uniform infinite mesh. Simulation results comparing our proposed congestion control strategy against the DRA's native mechanism demonstrate significant performance improvements.

Over the past ten years, SLAM systems have seen notable gains in accuracy and speed, expanding their mapping potential. However, sustained long-term operation remains a critical hurdle, largely caused by the diverse range of perturbations robots face. While efforts to enhance SLAM robustness continue, they typically target specific disturbances; generalizing this resilience across a broad spectrum of difficult scenarios remains poorly understood and researched. This paper offers a systematic assessment of the robustness of leading open-source SLAM algorithms under challenging conditions, including rapid motion, uneven lighting, and dynamic environments. These experiments evaluate both isolated and combined perturbations within long-term deployments in unconstrained settings, simulating lifelong operation.

We demonstrate that the conditional gradient method applied to the convex composite optimization problem \(\min_x\{f(x) + \Psi(x)\}\) produces primal and dual iterates where the duality gap converges to zero, assuming a specific {\em growth property} is satisfied and stepsizes are selected appropriately. The convergence rate of this duality gap varies from sublinear to linear based on the strength of the growth property. Furthermore, both the growth property and the resulting convergence guarantees are determined by the pair \((f,\Psi)\) in a manner that is affine invariant and independent of the norm.

We establish that for any subset of the 2-dimensional vector space over a finite field with $q$ elements, if its cardinality is at least $\rho q^2$ where $\frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \ll \rho \leq 1$, then the subset necessarily contains at least $c\rho q^3$ isometric copies of triangles.

The EASIROC chip, an Extended Analogue Silicon Photo-multiplier Integrated Read Out Chip, was designed as the front-end for the camera located at the focal plane of the ASTRI SST-2M telescope prototype. This study details measurement results characterizing EASIROC to assess its adherence to the telescope's focal plane specifications. Specifically, the investigation focused on trigger time walk and jitter variations relative to pulse amplitude. Findings indicate that the EASIROC output signal changes linearly with input pulse amplitude, exhibiting minimal electronic noise and cross-talk (under 1%). Consequently, the results confirm the chip's suitability as a front-end component for the camera prototype, though specific adjustments are required for its implementation in the telescope's final version.

We report detailed near-infrared and sub-millimeter observations of three massive ($>10^{11}\,\rm M_{\odot}$), highly star-forming galaxies located in the core of the RO-1001 group at redshift $z=2.91$. Each galaxy features compact, kiloparsec-scale starburst cores with characteristics indicative of forming bulges, situated within extended, massive stellar disks. Notably, these disks are both distinctly quiescent and severely asymmetric. This configuration suggests that "outside-in" quenching is actively occurring in these group members. We propose a scenario where the significant mass asymmetry in the disks (varying by factors of 1.6 to over 3), likely induced by accreted gas and clumps, suppresses star formation in the outer regions while channeling gas toward the nuclei to fuel central starbursts. The asymmetric side of the disks indicates the impact site of accretion streams, with nearby dust and stellar components directly tracing the inflow direction. Interactions with these accreted clumps, viewed as minor mergers, align the major axes of the three galaxies with external Lyman-$\alpha$-emitting feeding filaments. These findings offer the first observational proof of how cold accretion streams influence galaxy formation and evolution. Currently, this process manifests as the rapid assembly of bulges driven by accretion, while maintaining massive, quiescent, and lopsided stellar disks until a violent major merger occurs.

We establish a sufficient condition for the parameter rigidity of actions by solvable Lie groups, specifically when the first cohomologies of the orbit foliations vanish (an uncountable set of conditions). In certain instances, we demonstrate that the vanishing of only finitely many cohomologies suffices, utilizing the rigidity inherent in quasiisometries. As an application, we prove that specific actions of 2-step solvable Lie groups on mapping tori exhibit parameter rigidity; related cases were previously examined by Matsumoto and Mitsumatsu. Furthermore, we discuss the connection between transitive locally free actions of solvable Lie groups and lattices within such groups, and we leverage rigidity theory concerning lattices in solvable Lie groups to construct transitive locally free actions possessing particular properties.

Integrated photonics holds significant promise for quantum communication devices, offering advantages in scalability, robustness, and complexity. Silicon photonics stands out as a premier platform for quantum photonic technologies, further enhanced by miniaturization, cost-effective manufacturing, and compatibility with CMOS microelectronics. Nevertheless, achieving high-speed modulation of quantum states within standard silicon photonic platforms has been a persistent challenge. This study addresses that limitation by demonstrating high-speed, low-error quantum key distribution using silicon photonic devices that integrate slow thermo-optic DC biases with fast carrier-depletion modulation (10 GHz bandwidth). The potential to scale these integrated circuits and incorporate microelectronics paves the way for advanced integrated quantum communication technologies and broader adoption of quantum-secured communications.

Using the QCD sum rule method, we investigate the mass spectra of $N\Omega$ dibaryons in the $^{3}S_1$ and $^{5}S_2$ channels, corresponding to $J^{P}=1^{+}$ and $2^{+}$, respectively. By constructing two molecular interpolating currents, we compute their correlation functions and spectral densities, extending calculations up to dimension-16 condensates. Our findings suggest the possible existence of an $N\Omega$ bound state in the $^{5}S_2$ channel with a binding energy of approximately $21\ \mathrm{MeV}$. In contrast, the $^{3}S_1$ ($J^{P}=1^{+}$) $N\Omega$ dibaryons are predicted to have masses exceeding the $N\Omega$ and $\Lambda\Xi$ thresholds, allowing them to decay directly into these final states via S-wave transitions. Furthermore, the $^{5}S_2$ $N\Omega$ bound state is expected to decay into octet-octet final states ($\Lambda\Xi$ and $\Sigma\Xi$) through the quark rearrangement mechanism in D-wave. Future relativistic heavy-ion collision experiments may provide evidence for these $N\Omega$ dibaryons.

Recent advancements in artificial intelligence over the past decade have significantly propelled the development of autonomous driving, yet safety concerns persist regarding their deployment in high-risk settings. This thesis aims to create methodological tools capable of generating reliable uncertainty estimates for deep neural networks. Initially, we propose a novel criterion, the true class probability (TCP), which demonstrates superior performance in predicting model failures compared to existing uncertainty metrics. Addressing the fact that the true class is inherently unknown during testing, we develop a specialized learning scheme that utilizes an auxiliary model to learn the TCP criterion from data. The effectiveness of this approach is confirmed through evaluations on image classification and semantic segmentation datasets. Subsequently, we extend this learned confidence framework to domain adaptation tasks, where it enhances the selection of pseudo-labels within self-training methodologies. Finally, we address the challenge of simultaneously identifying misclassifications and out-of-distribution samples by introducing a new uncertainty measure grounded in evidential models and defined on the simplex.

Midlife cognitive function serves as a key indicator for age-related mental deterioration, and statistical models capable of forecasting cognitive performance are valuable for anticipating such decline. Nevertheless, current models often fail to account for the intricate interplay among physical, sociodemographic, psychological, and mental health determinants influencing cognition. Leveraging data from the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) observational cohort study, we modeled numerous variables to forecast executive function and episodic memory. Our analysis incorporated both cross-sectional and longitudinal outcomes characterized by varying degrees of data sparsity. Deep neural network (DNN) models consistently achieved the highest rankings across all cognitive performance prediction tasks, as measured by root mean squared error (RMSE) on out-of-sample data. The differences in RMSE between DNNs and other model types were statistically significant (T(8) = -3.70; p < 0.05). Furthermore, a significant interaction effect between model type and sparsity was observed (F(9)=59.20; p < 0.01), suggesting that the efficacy of DNNs is partly due to their robustness and capacity to model hierarchical relationships among health-related factors. These results highlight the promise of neural networks for analyzing clinical datasets and enhancing our understanding of the drivers behind cognitive decline.

We introduce a space-efficient implementation of the quantum verification of matrix products (QVMP) algorithm, validating its performance through execution on the Aer simulator using both statevector and matrix product state (MPS) simulation techniques. This report details circuit metrics—including gate count, qubit count, and circuit depth—alongside transpilation and simulation times, and provides verification of the Grover oracle's correctness. Our findings indicate that although QVMP is feasible for moderately sized inputs, it fails to scale sufficiently to demonstrate quantum advantage on existing hardware, primarily due to limitations in circuit depth and qubit count. Additionally, the selection of the simulation method significantly influences the size of the transpiled circuit, thereby hindering the development process.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in computer vision over recent decades, largely due to the image convolution operation which enables strong performance on visual tasks. However, this operation is computationally intensive and difficult to implement. To address these challenges, this paper introduces CEMNet, a network designed for training in the frequency domain. The core motivation behind this research is leveraging the Cross-Correlation Theorem to substitute traditional image convolution with straightforward element-wise multiplication in the frequency domain, thereby significantly lowering computational complexity. Furthermore, a Weight Fixation mechanism is introduced to mitigate over-fitting, and the authors analyze the behaviors of Batch Normalization, Leaky ReLU, and Dropout within the frequency domain to develop their CEMNet-specific counterparts. Additionally, to manage the complexities introduced by the Discrete Fourier Transform, a dual-branch network architecture is designed for CEMNet. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that CEMNet achieves competitive performance on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets.

Capturing long-range dependencies is essential for scene understanding in computer vision. While Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved great success, their reliance on local kernels restricts their ability to model long-range structured relationships. Although fully-connected graphs, exemplified by the self-attention mechanism in Transformers, are effective for this purpose, their computational cost is often prohibitive. To address this, we introduce a dynamic graph message passing network that drastically lowers computational complexity compared to existing fully-connected graph approaches. This efficiency is gained by adaptively sampling graph nodes based on the input to facilitate message passing. Leveraging these sampled nodes, our method dynamically predicts node-specific filter weights and an affinity matrix for information propagation. This framework enables the design of a self-attention module and a novel Transformer-based backbone, which we apply to image classification pretraining and various downstream tasks including object detection, instance segmentation, and semantic segmentation. Experimental results demonstrate significant performance gains over strong state-of-the-art baselines across four distinct tasks. Furthermore, our approach surpasses fully-connected graphs while utilizing far fewer floating-point operations and parameters. The code and models will be released publicly at https://github.com/fudan-zvg/DGMN2.

We investigate photo-induced loss in chemically stable bosonic $^{23}$Na$^{87}$Rb and $^{23}$Na$^{39}$K molecules trapped in chopped optical dipole traps, where the molecules experience extended periods in the dark. Given the anticipated short complex lifetimes of approximately $13\mu$s for $^{23}$Na$^{87}$Rb and $6\mu$s for $^{23}$Na$^{39}$K, we expected effective two-body decay to be significantly suppressed within these chopped traps. Contrary to this expectation, we observe near-universal loss even at the minimum chopping frequencies accessible to our measurements. Consequently, our findings either indicate a previously unknown loss mechanism or imply that the complex lifetimes are underestimated by at least one to two orders of magnitude.

Quantum ergotropy measures the maximum work extractable from a quantum state while maintaining constant entropy. Since ergotropy can be formulated as the difference between quantum and classical relative entropies relative to a thermal state, we introduce "classical ergotropy" to quantify work extraction from distributions that vary across energy surfaces. Geometric quantum mechanics offers a unified framework for addressing both quantum and classical contexts, leading to the definition of geometric relative entropy. The discussion concludes by applying these conceptual insights to conditional thermal states, resulting in a refined maximum work theorem.

This study introduces a new zero-shot learning method for personalized speech enhancement utilizing a sparsely active ensemble model. While optimizing denoising systems for specific speakers at test time can enhance performance and lower computational costs, adapting the model during testing is difficult when data from the target speaker is unavailable. To address this, we propose an ensemble architecture where each specialist module handles noisy speech from a unique partition of the training speakers. A gating module then efficiently estimates the characteristics of the test-time speaker via an embedding vector to select the most suitable specialist for denoising. Segmenting the training speakers into non-overlapping, semantically similar groups is a complex and ill-defined task. To resolve this, we first train a Siamese network on noisy speech pairs to maximize or minimize output vector similarity based on whether the utterances originate from the same speaker. Subsequently, we apply k-means clustering to the latent space created by averaged embedding vectors for each training speaker, thereby defining speaker groups and training specialized modules optimized for these partitions. Experimental results demonstrate that ensemble models composed of low-capacity specialists can surpass high-capacity generalist models, offering greater efficiency and better adaptation to unseen test-time speakers.

We experimentally validate a design strategy based on the Purcell effect to achieve superior impedance matching, thereby boosting the radiation efficiency of a compact microwave emitter. By iteratively comparing the phase of the radiated field from the emitter in air versus within a dielectric medium, we optimized a dielectric hemisphere situated above a ground plane around a small monopolar emitter to maximize its efficiency. The resulting system exhibits robust coupling between the emitter and two omnidirectional radiation modes at 2.00 GHz and 2.84 GHz, producing Purcell enhancement factors of 8,360 and 430, respectively, alongside near-perfect radiation efficiency.

This study demonstrates that attaining the capacity region of a 2-user weak Gaussian Interference Channel (GIC) involves iteratively expanding the core of a nested set of Polymatroids—where each set corresponds to a multiple-access channel capacity region—by maximizing the minimum rate, projecting along the orthogonal span, and repeating the process. This approach depends on introducing dummy private messages to account for interference effects within the GIC. Consequently, it is established that utilizing independent Gaussian random codebooks is optimal, with the resulting solution satisfying the boundary conditions defined by HK constraints.

Analyzing the spatial relationship between molecular gas and star formation in galaxies reveals key insights into the physical mechanisms and timelines governing the transition from gas to stars. This study examines the high-resolution relative positioning of CO and H$\alpha$ emission across various galaxy targets to quantify the prevalence of regions at different star formation stages: molecular gas lacking H$\alpha$ signatures, active star-forming gas, and HII regions. Utilizing a large dataset from the PHANGS-ALMA and PHANGS-H$\alpha$ surveys, which covers a broad spectrum of stellar masses and morphological types, we explore how global galaxy properties influence the gas-star formation cycle. At a resolution of 150 pc, the frequency of these distinct stages varies with stellar mass and Hubble type across the observed radial range. Specifically, massive and early-type galaxies contain a significant reservoir of unstar-forming molecular gas, whereas lower-mass galaxies host numerous HII regions, suggesting their birth clouds have dispersed or that they formed from isolated, low-mass clouds. Additionally, galactic structures introduce further complexity to the distribution of CO and H$\alpha$ emission. Observable trends linking galaxy properties to these gas distributions emerge only at spatial scales significantly smaller than 500 pc, underscoring the necessity of high resolution to differentiate the stages of the star formation process.

Graph analytics for large-scale networks has attracted significant attention recently. Numerous algorithms have been developed for vertex-centric distributed frameworks to handle graphs containing hundreds of millions of vertices and edges on commodity clusters and cloud infrastructures. While subgraph-centric programming models offer superior performance compared to vertex-centric ones, directly adapting vertex-centric or shared-memory algorithms to subgraph-centric frameworks is often impossible or results in inefficiency. This paper introduces three subgraph-centric distributed algorithms for triangle counting, clustering, and minimum spanning forest, incorporating variations of both shared and vertex-centric models. These contributions extend existing subgraph-centric algorithms found in literature and enable a more comprehensive evaluation of these graph processing classes and platforms.

This research introduces a generalized multiscale multimesh finite element method ($\text{M}^2$-FEM) designed to overcome persistent obstacles in numerically simulating integral structural theories, which are frequently employed to capture multiscale and nonlocal phenomena. The primary hurdles in solving integral boundary value problems stem from the coupling between the spatial discretization of the global (parent) and integral (child) domains; this coupling limits the efficiency of current algorithms by forcing a compromise between the accuracy of the child domain and the computational resources allocated to the parent domain. A key contribution of this work is the development of a mesh-decoupling strategy that creates independent mesh sets, allowing the parent and child domains to be discretized and approximated separately. This decoupling significantly enhances simulations of integral theories compared to existing state-of-the-art methods by simultaneously improving numerical accuracy and efficiency. Consequently, the proposed algorithm offers greater flexibility in balancing mesh size and computational costs, supports generalized integral kernel functions, and accommodates non-regular (non-rectangular) domains through unstructured meshing. The study validates the approach using a benchmark problem based on an extended version of Eringen's nonlocal elasticity theory—a multiscale framework—that utilizes generalized attenuation kernels and variable nonlocality horizons. Despite this specific application, the $\text{M}^2$-FEM algorithm is highly versatile and applicable to a wide range of integral theories, extending beyond structural elasticity.

A prominent explanation for the recent EDGES-LOW band detection of a strong 21-cm absorption signal near 80 MHz is an excess radio background relative to the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB). This surplus can arise from the decay of unstable particles into low-mass dark photons that possess a non-zero mixing angle with electromagnetism. By applying EDGES-LOW band data, we establish joint constraints on early galaxy characteristics and the parameters of this particle physics framework. Bayesian analysis indicates that a high star formation efficiency is necessary, alongside X-ray emissions of $4-7 \times 10^{48} ~\rm erg$ per solar mass of stars, coupled with suppressed star formation in halos having virial temperatures below $\approx 2\times 10^4$ K. Furthermore, the analysis yields 68 percent credible intervals for the mass of decaying dark matter particles, their lifetime, dark photon mass, and the dark-ordinary photon mixing angle as $[10^{-3.5}, 10^{-2.4}]$ eV, $[10^{1.1}, 10^{2.7}]\times 13.8 ~\rm Gyr$, $[10^{-12.2}, 10^{-10}]$ eV, and $[10^{-7}, 10^{-5.6}]$ respectively. These findings imply an excess radio background approximately 5.7 times stronger than the CMB at 80 MHz, a value roughly three times greater than prior predictions based on simplified 21-cm signal models.

While many cite the growing volume and complexity of evaluations for visualization systems as proof of the field's maturation, I remain skeptical. Specifically, I believe that standard evaluations conducted within the discipline or requested by reviewers provide little useful or transferable insight into visualization systems, irrespective of their statistical rigor or ecological validity. Through a series of thought experiments, I demonstrate that our current understanding of visualization evaluations can be incomplete, arbitrary, or ultimately unhelpful for advancing the field, resembling the "heroic age" of medicine more than the rigorous, evidence-based discipline we should strive to become. In conclusion, I propose that we reconsider our models for designing evaluations and reassess our priorities as a community.

This paper introduces preliminary research on a new Human-Swarm Interaction (HSI) method designed to alter the macroscopic behavior of decentralized robot swarms. By combining a compact but effective hand gesture recognition convolutional neural network (CNN) with the next-generation Robot Operating System (ROS 2)—which facilitates decentralized software implementation for multi-robot systems—we demonstrate that swarms can be programmed to recognize and react to gesture sequences corresponding to various behaviors. Our approach was tested using a set of gestures that adjust the target inter-robot distance among three Turtlebot3 Burger robots to avoid obstacle collisions. Validation was conducted across three distinct Gazebo simulation environments and a physical testbed replicating one of these simulated scenarios.

Abstractive dialogue summarization has recently garnered significant interest. Although existing systems, which are trained to maximize the likelihood of human-written summaries and have achieved notable results, still fall short of producing high-quality outputs regarding coherence and faithfulness as judged by humans, this gap is largely attributed to the misalignment of optimizing for a single reference summary. To address this, we propose integrating multi-level human feedback into the training pipeline to guide models toward capturing human priorities in summaries. Specifically, we solicit human input in two forms: local feedback, where humans highlight essential information to include, and global feedback, where humans evaluate summaries based on coherence, accuracy, coverage, conciseness, and overall quality. By combining these local and global signals, we fine-tune the dialogue summarization policy using Reinforcement Learning. Experiments across multiple datasets confirm that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art supervised baselines in both effectiveness and generalization, particularly according to human evaluations.

We reveal a core property of the QED vacuum within an external electromagnetic (EM) field, demonstrating that the quantized electron vacuum becomes spin-polarized by this field, resulting in a vacuum spin current. We propose an experiment to detect the spin torque generated by this current by observing the rotation of the director axis in a nematic liquid crystal.

Inverse problems involving the reconstruction of piecewise constant fields via multiple level sets present several challenges. From a Bayesian perspective, we assign prior distributions to both the level set functions defining the regions and the parameters governing their magnitudes. To solve the inverse problem and obtain the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate efficiently, we implement a Gauss-Newton method with backtracking line search. Furthermore, we employ the Gauss-Newton Laplace approximation to create a Gaussian representation of the posterior distribution, utilizing preconditioned Krylov subspace methods for sampling. This paper introduces a matrix-free Monte Carlo diagonal estimator to calculate the approximate posterior variance, thereby visualizing uncertainty in parameter reconstructions. Finally, we validate our methodology and solvers on synthetic datasets for photoacoustic and hydraulic tomography (addressing linear and nonlinear problems, respectively) and apply them to real-world X-ray imaging data.

ERC-20 stands as the leading Ethereum standard for fungible tokens, enabling seamless interaction with numerous existing web services and smart contracts. Given its extensive adoption and rising value, security flaws within ERC-20 have become a focal point of recent research. This study systematically categorizes these vulnerabilities and their applicability to ERC-20 tokens, a task not previously undertaken. Leveraging specialized domain knowledge, we introduce a new, open-source implementation of the ERC-20 interface available in both Vyper and Solidity. This version offers superior security characteristics and stricter adherence to best practices compared to the only remaining reference implementation by OpenZeppelin. Furthermore, we evaluate the efficacy of seven general-purpose static analysis tools in detecting ERC-20-specific vulnerabilities using our implementation. Our findings reveal significant inconsistencies among the tools and a prevalence of false positives, indicating substantial potential for their further refinement.

We introduce a measurement operator formalism designed to manage entanglement generation between two atomic gases via quantum nondemolition (QND) measurements. Initially, we demonstrate how the QND entangling protocol simplifies into a positive operator-valued measure and examine its limit as a projection operator that collapses the system into a total spin projection state. Subsequently, we investigate the evolution of the initial wave function under a stroboscopic series of such projections performed in both the x and z bases. This sequence of QND projections amplifies entanglement between the atomic ensembles and drives the state toward a highly entangled configuration. Furthermore, we present several mathematical identities that significantly streamline the state evolution within the projection sequence, enabling the derivation of the exact state with high efficiency. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on the Holstein-Primakoff approximation, our formalism treats the spins of the atomic gases exactly.

Proposed nearly fifty years ago by Thorne, the hoop conjecture posits that black holes satisfy the mass-to-circumference inequality $4\pi {\cal M}/{\cal C}\geq1$, while horizonless compact objects adhere to the reverse condition $4\pi {\cal M}/{\cal C}<1$, where ${\cal C}$ represents the minimum circumference capable of enclosing the object in every azimuthal direction. Recent proofs have established that for this conjecture to hold in horizonless spacetimes featuring spatially regular charged objects, the mass ${\cal M}$ must be defined as the quantity contained within the engulfing sphere rather than the total asymptotic ADM mass. This paper investigates the possibility of formulating a unified version of the hoop conjecture applicable to both black holes and horizonless compact objects. To address this, we examine the mass-to-circumference ratio in Kerr-Newman black holes. We demonstrate that if ${\cal M}$ in the hoop relation refers to the quasilocal Einstein-Landau-Lifshitz-Papapetrou and Weinberg mass enclosed by the horizon, then these charged, spinning black holes exhibit a sub-critical ratio, $4\pi {\cal M}/{\cal C}<1$. Consequently, our findings support the conclusion that no unified version of the hoop conjecture exists that is valid for both black-hole spacetimes and spatially regular horizonless compact objects.
We will characterize robust monetary utility functions defined on the space of real-valued bounded continuous functions over a Polish space.

In Compressive Snapshot Spectral Imaging (CASSI), hyperspectral images (HSI) are reconstructed from single-shot compressive measurements. While model-based approaches utilizing hand-crafted priors attempt to address this, they often yield suboptimal results due to the limited representational power of these manually designed priors. Conversely, deep learning methods that directly learn mappings from compressive inputs to HSIs have achieved superior performance, yet designing effective deep networks remains a non-trivial challenge. This paper introduces a novel HSI reconstruction technique grounded in the Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) estimation framework, employing a learned Gaussian Scale Mixture (GSM) prior. Unlike traditional GSM models that rely on hand-crafted scale priors (such as Jeffrey's prior), our approach utilizes a deep convolutional neural network (DCNN) to learn the scale prior. Additionally, the DCNN estimates the local means within the GSM models. Through end-to-end training, all parameters of both the MAP algorithm and the DCNN are jointly optimized. Comprehensive experiments on synthetic and real datasets confirm that the proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques. The implementation code is accessible at https://see.xidian.edu.cn/faculty/wsdong/Projects/DGSM-SCI.htm.

We present an explicit construction facilitating the decomposition of graph braid groups into graphs of groups, which enables the computation of braid groups for various graphs and establishes two general criteria for non-trivial free product splittings, thereby addressing two questions posed by Genevois. Furthermore, this approach distinguishes specific right-angled Artin groups from graph braid groups. Finally, we offer a concrete example of a graph braid group that is relatively hyperbolic yet not hyperbolic relative to the braid groups of its proper subgraphs, providing a negative answer to another of Genevois's questions.

Although every Finsler metric generates a spray, the reverse is not true. The concepts of scalar and isotropic curvature for sprays serve as generalizations of the corresponding flag curvature notions for Finsler metrics. This paper introduces a new concept, sprays of constant curvature, and demonstrates that in dimensions $n\ge3$, a spray with isotropic curvature does not necessarily possess constant curvature. Furthermore, complete conditions are established for sprays of isotropic and constant curvature to be Finsler-metrizable. Applications of these findings include determining the local structure of locally projectively flat Berwald sprays of isotropic or constant curvature that are Finsler-metrizable, as well as discussing additional metrizability aspects for sprays of isotropic curvature. Additionally, the metrizability problem for sprays of scalar curvature is examined under specific curvature constraints.

This paper establishes various findings concerning chordal and weighted chordal graphs by centering on the concept of exposed edges, defined as edges strictly contained within a single maximal clique. This perspective yields a characterization of chordal graphs through the sequential removal of exposed edges from a complete graph. Notably, in this framework, the connected components formed by the subgraph of exposed edges are 2-edge connected. Leveraging this property, we present an adaptation of Kruskal's second algorithm for computing a minimum spanning tree in weighted chordal graphs. This revised algorithm offers a significant advantage by being local in a crucial manner.

Existing activity tracking systems predominantly rely on data from younger individuals, often resulting in tools that fail to adequately serve older adults. Consequently, gathering training data specifically from this demographic is essential for developing effective trackers for them. To address this, we investigated the viability and obstacles of having older adults provide activity labels using speech. We developed MyMove, a speech-enabled smartwatch application designed to streamline in-situ labeling with minimal user burden. Through a seven-day deployment involving 13 older adults—wearing both a smartwatch and a thigh-mounted monitor—we successfully gathered 1,224 verbal reports and extracted 1,885 activities annotated with effort levels and durations. We then evaluated the utility of these reports as labels and discussed how our methodology and dataset can support personalized activity tracking technologies for older populations.

This study investigates a bouncing scenario for a flat, homogeneous, and isotropic universe by applying the reconstruction technique to a power-law parametrization of the Hubble parameter within a modified gravity framework that incorporates higher-order curvature and the trace of the energy-momentum tensor. The analysis confirms that the conditions for a bounce are met, thereby avoiding the cosmological initial singularity. Furthermore, the model demonstrates that the equation of state parameter crosses the phantom divide. Unlike conventional phantom models, the proposed theory exhibits phantom-condensate behavior near the unstable bouncing point at $ t \simeq 3.08 $, which is designed to facilitate a big bounce. Additionally, the model displays deceleration in the vicinity of this bouncing point, a fundamental characteristic of any bouncing universe.

A binary state on a graph refers to assigning binary values to its vertices. For instance, encoding a network of spiking neurons as a directed graph means that the spikes generated by neurons at a specific moment constitute a binary state on that graph. By varying time and recording the resulting spiking patterns, one generates binary dynamics on the graph, which manifests as a one-parameter family of binary states. This article focuses on the closed neighborhood of a vertex $v$ within a graph $\mathcal{G}$, defined as the subgraph induced by $v$ and all its neighbors. We introduce a topological and graph-theoretic approach to extracting information from binary dynamics on graphs by selecting a small subset of vertices and their corresponding neighborhoods. As a practical demonstration, we apply this method to binary dynamics derived from sample activity on the Blue Brain Project's reconstruction of rat cortical tissue.

Self-organized aggregation is a fundamental behavior in swarm robotics, serving as a prerequisite for more sophisticated collective actions. This paper explores decentralized algorithms enabling heterogeneous robot swarms to self-aggregate at specific target locations. Building on prior research demonstrating that informed robots can guide swarm distribution across sites, we replicated those findings using a streamlined methodology. By eliminating communication protocol constraints and simplifying the state-transition logic of the probabilistic controller, we achieved comparable performance to the original complex system. This simplified approach offers significant benefits regarding portability to physical robots and flexibility; notably, it successfully generates self-organized aggregation responses under a broader range of operating conditions than the more intricate controller.

The AI community has recently achieved significant success in applying language models to "soft theorem proving" over natural language. We introduce a new generative adversarial framework designed to evaluate and enhance the reasoning abilities of these models.
