Upon receiving an input, AppealNet dynamically predicts whether the resource-limited edge device can successfully process the task using its deployed DL model; if not, it requests assistance from a more capable model in the cloud. This functionality is realized through a two-head neural network architecture that explicitly accounts for inference difficulty, thereby optimizing the balance between accuracy and the computational/communication costs of the collaborative system. Experiments across multiple image classification datasets demonstrate that AppealNet achieves energy savings of over 40% compared to existing techniques while maintaining equivalent accuracy.

The task of detecting emerging patterns, defined by a query graph representing a specific interest, can be framed as a continuous query problem on dynamic graphs. We introduce an incremental algorithm designed for processing such continuous queries. This approach relies on query decomposition, breaking the query graph into smaller subgraphs and combining the results of these sub-queries to identify complete matches. The key innovation of our work is utilizing subgraph distributional statistics gathered from the dynamic graph to drive this decomposition. Additionally, we propose a "Lazy Search" algorithm, which determines the search strategy on a per-vertex basis based on the probability of finding a match within that vertex's neighborhood. We also define a metric called "Relative Selectivity" to choose among various query decomposition strategies. Experimental results on real-world datasets, including online news and network traffic streams, as well as a synthetic social network benchmark, show speedups of 10 to 100 times compared to competing methods.

S. Morier-Genoud and V. Ovsienko introduced the concepts of q-rational and q-irrational numbers. This paper examines q-real quadratic irrationals, with a specific focus on q-metallic numbers and the q-rational sequences that converge toward them, analyzing their radii of convergence under the assumption that q is a complex number. We define two sequences based on recurrence relations, extending the q-deformations of Fibonacci and Pell numbers originally proposed by Morier-Genoud and Ovsienko. We provide estimates for the radii of convergence of these sequences and address a conjecture regarding the lower bound for metallic numbers and their convergent rational sequences, as formulated by L. Leclere, S. Morier-Genoud, V. Ovsienko, and A. Veselov. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the radii of convergence for the sequences [n,n,...,n,...]_q and [n,n,...,n]_q specifically when n equals 3 and 4.

This work finalizes the proof of the Trace Theorem within the quantized calculus framework for quasi-Fuchsian groups. The theorem was previously introduced and outlined on pages 322-325 of the book "Noncommutative Geometry" by the first author, but it lacked a complete proof at that time.

The growing volume of smartphone-generated videos necessitates smart editing and enhancement methods capable of running on devices with limited power. While top-performing algorithms for video understanding tasks, such as action recognition and localization, depend heavily on robust spatio-temporal representations for accuracy, effectively learning these representations requires a deep understanding of the object motion patterns within the video. This paper introduces a novel method for analyzing object motion through motion type classification. Our proposed classifier determines a video's motion type by analyzing object trajectories, categorizing them into five primitive classes: linear, projectile, oscillatory, local, and random. We show that representations derived from this motion classification generalize effectively to the challenging downstream task of video retrieval. Additionally, we developed a recommendation system for video playback styles that leverages the predictions made by our motion type classifier.

The Local Unitarity formalism reformulates physical cross-sections so that infrared singularity cancellations between real and virtual contributions occur locally. As a result, phase-space and loop integrals are regulated locally, eliminating the need for counter-terms or dimensional regularisation beyond what is required for ultraviolet stability. This representation is particularly well-suited for direct Monte Carlo integration, providing a straightforward route to automate the calculation of fixed-order differential observables in Quantum Field Theories.

We calculate the large N limit of the partition function for the Euclidean Yang--Mills measure, utilizing either SU(N) or U(N) as the structure group, across all closed compact surfaces—whether orientable or not—with the sole exception of the sphere and the projective plane. Unlike the sphere and likely the projective plane, this limit remains finite. We anticipate that our findings will offer valuable insights into the master field defined on these surfaces.

The proposed Large Hadron electron Collider (LHeC) is designed to collide intense electron beams with protons or heavy ions at the High Luminosity-Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC). Benefiting from a center-of-mass energy exceeding 1 TeV and extremely high luminosity (approximately 1 ab⁻¹), the LHeC will serve as a next-generation facility for deep-inelastic scattering (DIS) and a critical tool for precision Higgs physics, complementing both pp and e⁺e⁻ colliders. Earlier studies utilizing fast simulation frameworks for the LHeC detector demonstrated the potential to achieve uncertainties of 0.8% and 7.4% for the Higgs boson's coupling strengths to b- and c-quarks, respectively. This current study focuses on the primary Higgs decay channel, H → bb, to compare those earlier findings against a fully simulated detector environment. Utilizing the publicly available ATLAS software infrastructure and advanced reconstruction algorithms, we present a novel analysis of the bb decay mode. This approach provides an independent verification of previous results with exceptional precision.

Intelligent systems are revolutionizing both the world and healthcare. We introduce a deep learning model designed to classify cough sounds, distinguishing between healthy children and those with pathological conditions such as asthma, upper respiratory tract infections (URTI), and lower respiratory tract infections (LRTI). To train this deep neural network, we assembled a novel dataset of cough recordings labeled with clinician diagnoses. The selected architecture is a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network utilizing Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs) as features. When trained to differentiate between healthy and pathological coughs in general (or specific respiratory conditions), the model achieved an accuracy exceeding 84% against physician-provided labels. To assess a subject's specific respiratory condition, we aggregated results from multiple cough epochs per individual, yielding a prediction accuracy surpassing 91% for all three respiratory pathologies. However, accuracy decreased when the model was tasked with discriminating among four distinct classes, as certain pathological coughs were frequently misclassified. Nevertheless, if the evaluation considers a healthy cough as correctly identified as healthy and any pathological cough as correctly identified as having a condition, the overall accuracy of the four-class model remains above 84%. Furthermore, a longitudinal analysis of the MFCC feature space, comparing coughs from the same subjects before and after recovery, revealed that pathological coughs, regardless of their underlying cause, occupy the same feature space, making differentiation based solely on MFCCs challenging.

This study presents experimental investigations of spin-wave excitations in individual Ni80Fe20 nanotubes, which are 22 nm thick and approximately 150 nm in diameter, utilizing Brillouin light-scattering (BLS) spectroscopy. By applying microwave irradiation, we observed discrete resonance sets within the nanotube centers spanning frequencies from 2.5 to 12.5 GHz. Through comparison with recent theoretical models and micromagnetic simulations, we distinguished various characteristic eigenmodes associated with axial, mixed, or vortex configurations. Specifically, the mixed and vortex states produce modes exhibiting helical phase profiles, which confirm the unique nature of these modes as non-reciprocal spin waves. These results offer microscopic insights into tubular spin-wave nanocavities and magnetochiral effects, advancing the field of 3D nanomagnonics.

We introduce a laser-plasma facility designed for photon-photon collision experiments aimed at measuring fundamental quantum electrodynamic phenomena, including the linear Breit-Wheeler process with real photons. Developed at the Rutherford Appleton Laboratory using the Gemini laser, this platform employs a laser wakefield accelerator and a bremsstrahlung converter to produce a collimated beam of hundreds of MeV photons. These collide with keV x-ray photons generated by a laser-heated plasma target. To detect the resulting electron-positron pairs, a specialized magnetic transport system directs them toward scintillation-based and hybrid silicon pixel single-particle detectors. We report commissioning results from an experimental campaign utilizing this setup, which successfully demonstrated the generation of both photon sources, the characterization of the magnetic transport, and the calibration of the detectors. Furthermore, we discuss the platform's potential for observing the Breit-Wheeler process and note that its design will facilitate future investigations into strong-field quantum electrodynamic effects, such as the nonlinear Breit-Wheeler and Trident processes, or photon-photon scattering.

Typically, word-alignment tools depend on extensive parallel corpora and utilize IBM model algorithms for processing. However, since the training data for these tools mirrors that of machine translation (MT) systems—particularly neural MT (NMT)—alignments can also be derived directly from the attention heads within trained NMT models. This is advantageous because attention-based NMT can theoretically generate word-alignments as a natural byproduct while simultaneously providing decoder scores for sentence pairs. This study reviews various methods for extracting alignments from alignment scores and investigates how to retrieve such scores from NMT, specifically by inferring alignment probabilities from output sentence and token distributions. We further compare this approach to extracting scores directly from attention mechanisms. Finally, we present a simple feed-forward network that aggregates multiple sources of alignment scores, demonstrating superior performance when these combined extractors are employed.

This paper investigates the task of learning generalized linear models in the presence of adversarial corruptions. We examine the iterative trimmed maximum likelihood estimator, a classical heuristic recognized for its practical efficacy against label noise. For scenarios involving label corruptions, we establish that this straightforward estimator attains minimax near-optimal risk across a broad spectrum of generalized linear models, such as Gaussian, Poisson, and Binomial regression. Furthermore, we adapt the estimator to address the more difficult context of simultaneous label and covariate corruptions, proving its robustness and optimality in this extended setting.

Recommender systems have effectively demonstrated how accessible data can simplify daily digital interactions; however, data privacy remains a paramount concern in the modern era. Following numerous breaches and scandals, users have grown increasingly apprehensive about data sharing. Over the past decade, Federated Learning has risen as a novel, privacy-preserving approach to distributed machine learning, characterized by processing information locally on user devices rather than aggregating it in a central server. We introduce FedeRank (https://split.to/federank), a federated recommendation algorithm that constructs a personalized factorization model on each individual device. This model undergoes synchronous training involving both the central server and federated clients. FedeRank facilitates distributed recommendation computation while granting users control over the extent of their data sharing. Extensive experiments comparing FedeRank against state-of-the-art methods demonstrate its high recommendation accuracy, even when only a minimal fraction of user data is shared. Furthermore, analyses of the diversity and novelty of generated recommendation lists confirm the algorithm's suitability for real-world production deployment.

Pure Transformer architectures have recently achieved competitive accuracy on point cloud learning benchmarks compared to convolutional neural networks. However, current point cloud Transformers are computationally inefficient due to the time wasted structuring irregular data. To address this limitation, we introduce the Sparse Window Attention (SWA) module, which extracts coarse-grained local features from non-empty voxels. This approach eliminates the overhead of structuring irregular data and processing empty voxels while achieving linear computational complexity relative to voxel resolution. Additionally, to capture fine-grained global shape features, we propose a Relative Attention (RA) module, a robust variant of self-attention designed for handling rigid object transformations. By integrating both SWA and RA, we develop PVT, a unified neural architecture for point cloud learning. Compared to prior Transformer- and attention-based models, our method achieves a top classification accuracy of 94.0% and delivers an average 10x inference speedup. Furthermore, extensive experiments confirm PVT's effectiveness on part and semantic segmentation tasks, achieving mIoU scores of 86.6% and 69.2%, respectively.

Fluctuation theorems constitute core principles within non-equilibrium thermodynamics. By examining the fluctuation theorem concerning entropy production alongside an observable, we establish a novel thermodynamic uncertainty relation that remains valid for non-cyclic and time-reversal asymmetric protocols. Additionally, we explore the connection between this uncertainty relation and the correlation existing between entropy and the observable.

This study examines a simple $Z_2$ symmetric extension of the Standard Model (SM) to investigate the characteristics of the electroweak phase transition (EWPT) in the early universe. We demonstrate that introducing a real scalar field alters the phase transition from a smooth crossover observed in the SM to a robust first-order transition. Additionally, we find that the entropy production in this scenario exceeds that of the SM. This enhanced entropy release could result in significant dilution of any pre-existing dark matter particles and baryon asymmetry that were frozen out prior to the onset of the phase transition.

Infinite-layer (IL) nickelates represent a burgeoning class of superconductors, where achieving the Ni$^{1+}$ valence state within a square planar NiO$_2$ framework requires the topotactic reduction of the perovskite phase. Yet, this soft chemistry utilizing hydrogen-based reagents remains in a rapidly evolving stage, accompanied by several unresolved challenges, particularly regarding potential hydrogen uptake. This study investigates the temporal evolution of the topotactic conversion from LaNiO$_3$ to LaNiO$_2$ in powder form using x-ray diffraction and gas extraction methods. Although the powder's hydrogen content rises over time, neutron diffraction reveals no evidence of hydrogen scattering within the LaNiO$_2$ crystal lattice. Instead, the excess hydrogen seems sequestered in grain boundaries or secondary-phase precipitates. Consequently, the average crystal structure and likely the physical properties of the primary LaNiO$_2$ phase remain largely unaffected by hydrogen residues generated during the transformation.

This research offers an automated bibliometric examination of 6,569 papers published across thirteen Brazilian Computer Science Society (SBC) conferences between 1999 and 2021. The main objective was to collect data to assess gender representation in computer science publications. By systematically assigning gender to 23,573 listed authorships, we determined that the gender gap is substantial, with female authors significantly under-represented throughout every year covered by the study.

This study examines gravitational instability within a filamentary molecular cloud under non-ideal magnetohydrodynamic conditions, assuming the filament maintains hydrostatic equilibrium. We incorporate ambipolar diffusion into the model for a filament permeated by a uniform axial magnetic field, formulate the fluid equations in cylindrical coordinates, and apply linear perturbation analysis. By integrating the resulting differential equations, we derive a numerical dispersion relation. Our findings indicate that enhanced ambipolar diffusion accelerates the growth of the most unstable mode and increases the filament's fragmentation scale.

This study examines $5d$ KK dualities, defined as multiple $5d$ gauge theories sharing a common $6d$ infinite coupling limit. We introduce a method to map $4d$ $\mathcal{N}=1$ quivers to their $5d$ dual counterparts, ensuring that the resulting $4d$ quivers remain dual to one another. These $4d$ dualities manifest as infrared equivalences, which can be verified by matching global symmetry anomalies and, in specific instances, proven through sequential application of fundamental Seiberg dualities. Furthermore, we explore dualities arising from Higgsing the same $5d$ theory via two distinct approaches, illustrated with several simple examples.

This study examines collective spin excitations in graphene exhibiting Rashba and valley-Zeeman spin-orbit coupling (SOC), a scenario realized, for instance, when graphene is placed on transition-metal-dichalcogenide substrates. We demonstrate that even without an external magnetic field, the system sustains collective modes representing coupled oscillations between uniform and valley-staggered magnetizations. These modes are observable through both zero-field electron spin resonance (ESR) and zero-field electric-dipole spin resonance (EDSR), where the EDSR signal originates exclusively from Rashba SOC. Furthermore, by analyzing electron-electron interactions using the Fermi-liquid kinetic equation, we reveal that these interactions split both ESR and EDSR peaks into two components. The resulting peak splitting magnitudes and relative resonance weights provide a means to determine spin-orbit coupling constants and many-body interaction parameters that might otherwise remain inaccessible.

The recently noted excess in diphoton events near 750\,GeV can be effectively explained by a new real spin-0 singlet with effective couplings to gauge bosons. In this letter, we first summarize existing constraints on this framework and then investigate its production in association with a gauge boson. We demonstrate the channel's capacity to probe flat directions within the permissible parameter space. Furthermore, we examine two distinct asymmetries to differentiate the CP properties of this singlet in both gluon fusion and vector-boson fusion processes. To this end, we estimate the selection efficiency for signal and background events across eight decay modes: $4\ell, 2j\, 2\ell, 2j\ell\,E_T^\text{miss}, 2\gamma\,2j, 4\ell\,2j, 2\ell\,\gamma\,2j, 4j\,2\ell$, and $4j\,\ell\,E_T^\text{miss}$. We highlight that the unique couplings of this new singlet to Standard Model particles, combined with its higher mass, yield a phenomenology distinct from Higgs searches. Finally, we show that a significant portion of the parameter space can be tested during the current LHC run, with the $2\gamma\, 2j$ channel serving as the dominant mode.

This study reports our initial measurements of identified particle production ($\pi$, $K$, $p$, $K_{s}^{0}$, $\Lambda$, $\phi$, $\Xi^{-}$) and anisotropic flow coefficients ($v_{1}$, $v_{2}$) from Au+Au collisions at a center-of-mass energy per nucleon pair of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 3$ GeV. By comparing experimental data with various theoretical frameworks, including thermal and transport models, we conclude that the matter generated in these 3 GeV collisions exhibits significant differences compared to matter produced at higher energies.

Most active learning acquisition functions rely on either uncertainty or diversity sampling to choose challenging and varied data points from an unlabeled pool. This study introduces a new acquisition function that combines these strengths by selecting *contrastive examples*: data points that are similar in the model's feature space but yield maximally different predictive likelihoods. We evaluate our proposed method, CAL (Contrastive Active Learning), against various acquisition functions across four natural language understanding tasks and seven datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that CAL consistently matches or outperforms the best baseline across all tasks, on both in-domain and out-of-domain data. Additionally, an extensive ablation study and an analysis of the acquired datasets reveal that CAL achieves a superior balance between uncertainty and diversity compared to other strategies.

It is established that repeated projective measurements can either accelerate (the Zeno effect) or decelerate (the anti-Zeno effect) quantum evolution. However, prior investigations into these phenomena for a two-level system strongly coupled to its environment have exclusively focused on repeatedly preparing the system's excited state. This study examines the repeated preparation of an arbitrary state within a two-level system strongly interacting with an environment of harmonic oscillators. To address the strong coupling, we apply a polaron transformation followed by a perturbative method to determine the system's decay rates. Our findings reveal a qualitative shift in these decay rates as the repeatedly prepared state transitions from the excited state toward a superposition of ground and excited states. These results hold significant promise for advancing the quantum control of two-level systems interacting with their environments.

One-dimensional subwavelength atom arrays exhibit multiply excited subradiant eigenstates that resemble free fermions. Previously, these states were linked to subradiant modes with decay rates scaling as $N^{-3}$ (where N is the atom count), a limitation that fundamentally obstructed the optical observation of their fermionic characteristics. This Letter demonstrates that free-fermion states generally emerge whenever the band of singly excited states exhibits a quadratic dispersion relation at the band edge, implying they can also manifest in radiant or even superradiant states. We find that 1D arrays possess free-fermion multiply excited eigenstates that are typically either subradiant or (super)radiant, and we reveal a simple transformation connecting these two families. Leveraging this correspondence, we propose various methods for preparing these states and analyze their signatures for detection via optical means.

Finite groups are termed isospectral when they share identical sets of element orders. It is established that any nonsolvable finite group $G$ isospectral to a finite simple group possesses a unique nonabelian composition factor; specifically, the quotient of $G$ by its solvable radical forms an almost simple group. This paper aims to demonstrate that such an almost simple group constitutes a cyclic extension of its socle. To achieve this, we examine a broader context where $G$ is an arbitrary group featuring a unique nonabelian composition factor, regardless of whether it is isospectral to a simple group. We investigate the prime graph of $G$, defined as a graph with vertices representing prime divisors of $|G|$, where distinct primes $r$ and $s$ are connected if $G$ contains an element of order $rs$. Specifically, we derive sufficient conditions under which a vertex in this graph is adjacent to all other vertices. In addition to proving the primary result, these findings refine a recent theorem by P. Cameron and N. Maslova regarding finite groups almost recognizable by their prime graphs.

We have recently formulated an Effective Field Theory (EFT) to describe rotational bands in odd-mass nuclei. In this study, we apply EFT-based expressions to conduct a Bayesian analysis of rotational energy level data for $^{99}$Tc, ${}^{155,157}$Gd, ${}^{159}$Dy, ${}^{167, 169}$Er, ${}^{167, 169}$Tm, ${}^{183}$W, ${}^{235}$U, and ${}^{239}$Pu. Our Bayesian error model incorporates both experimental uncertainties and EFT truncation errors, while also recognizing that low-energy constants (LECs) at even and odd orders typically differ in magnitude. By employing Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling to investigate the joint posterior distribution of the EFT and error-model parameters, we demonstrate that both the LECs and the expansion parameter, $Q$, can be robustly determined. We derived LECs up to fourth order in the EFT, showing that when EFT truncation errors are properly included in the likelihood function, lower-order LEC results remain stable as higher orders are added. Furthermore, these LEC values prove stable against the inclusion of higher-energy data. For all listed nuclei, we extracted the expansion parameter and observed a distinct correlation between the determined $Q$ values and the expected $Q$ derived from single-particle and vibrational energy scales. Nevertheless, the $Q$ value that governs the actual convergence of the EFT expansion is significantly smaller than the naive estimates based on those energy scales would suggest.

We calculated the isotropic radiation background resulting from Hawking emission by primordial black holes (PBHs) to determine if it could account for the radio wave background excess detected by ARCADE2 and LWA1 at frequencies below approximately 1 GHz. Our findings indicate that even if all dark matter consisted of PBHs, the radio brightness temperature generated by their Hawking evaporation would be on the order of $10^{-46}$ K, making it negligible compared to the cosmic microwave background. This limitation arises because PBHs in the constrained mass range of $\sim10^{12}$-$10^{14}\,$kg emit spectra peaking between $10^5$ and $10^7\,$eV; since the Hawking spectrum is power-law suppressed at lower energies, the resulting flux of $\mu$eV photons is minimal. Although higher-mass PBHs would shift the spectral peak to lower energies, their low number density results in equally low specific intensity. Consequently, Hawking emission from PBHs cannot explain the observed radio background excess. However, we also investigated radio emission from gas accretion onto supermassive PBHs, which can easily generate the strong radio signals required to explain the ARCADE2/LWA1 observations.

We present a theoretical framework for creating a solid-state thermal rectifier by confining the phonon population on one side of an asymmetrically graded film stack. By adapting the phonon gas model to incorporate phonon filtering and population confinement, we show that ideal materials with low phonon anharmonicity can achieve substantial thermal rectification without requiring ballistic phonon transport. Applying this formalism to a 1–5 nm thick diamond film graded to dimensions exceeding 1 μm, we demonstrate theoretical thermal rectification ratios ranging from 0.75 to 6. Consequently, our theoretical approach is poised to facilitate the design of advanced solid-state devices capable of supporting various critical technologies.

Mid-infrared Quantum Cascade Lasers (QCLs) serve as compact, efficient sources well-suited for molecular spectroscopy, including dual-comb applications. Nevertheless, despite over ten years of active research into QCL frequency comb technology, their bandwidth remains constrained to approximately $100$ cm$^{-1}$, which significantly hinders their utility in sensing multi-gas, liquid, and solid samples. Although broad-gain QCLs have been demonstrated, they have failed to expand the comb bandwidth, primarily due to frequency-dependent variations in gain and dispersion; a perfectly flat gain spectrum would eliminate these issues and the parametric gain required to overcome losses at gain clamping. Conversely, comb formation relies on four-wave mixing (FWM), a robust third-order nonlinear process inherent to QCLs. Given the subband structure of these devices, this nonlinearity can be engineered and enhanced to promote comb generation. This study introduces optimized designs featuring broad, flat-top gain spectra covering up to $220$ cm$^{-1}$ and FWM nonlinearities up to 30 times stronger than those in typical bound-to-continuum QCLs. These optimizations employ a nonequilibrium Green's function model with high predictive accuracy while adhering to constraints on gain and current density to ensure device efficiency. Such elevated nonlinearity, paired with moderate, saturable gain, could enable non-classical light generation within QCLs. Furthermore, doubling the spectral bandwidth of QCL combs represents a significant advancement toward high-speed spectroscopy of intricate gas mixtures and liquids.

Soft prompts have recently emerged as a mechanism for adapting frozen large language models (LLMs) to novel tasks. This study reimagines soft prompts specifically for infusing world knowledge into LLMs. We propose a self-supervised learning approach to train these soft prompts using knowledge base data. The resulting soft knowledge prompts (KPs) serve as task-agnostic external memory for LLMs. Through both qualitative and quantitative evaluations, we demonstrate that: (1) KPs can effectively capture the structural patterns of training data; and (2) KPs enhance LLM performance across various knowledge-intensive tasks.

Wireless capsule endoscopy (WCE) involves a patient swallowing a pill-sized camera that traverses the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, capturing and transmitting images to an external receiver. These devices are viewed as a less painful and distressing alternative to traditional endoscopy. During its journey, a WCE device typically generates over 60,000 images that require review by expert physicians to identify frames containing inflammation or disease. Given the volume of data, manual review is laborious, making computer-aided detection a more efficient solution. While various GI anomalies exist, this survey focuses on the most prevalent and critical conditions: ulcers, polyps, and tumors. We present a review of modern computer-aided detection techniques that classify WCE images as either normal or diseased, specifically targeting the detection of tumors, polyps, and ulcers due to their shared category. Additionally, since internal bleeding can be a symptom of these conditions, we also examine existing research on bleeding detection within WCE. Included studies are analyzed in depth regarding their methodologies, findings, and conclusions, with methods further categorized by their technical characteristics. Finally, the paper proposes a framework for the joint classification of these three diseases.

Relic neutrinos from ancient supernovae represent some of the oldest neutrino fluxes accessible to experiment. Consequently, the Diffuse Supernova Neutrino Background (DSNB) offers a potential means to determine whether neutrino masses differed in the past (at redshifts $z\lesssim 5$). Since oscillations within supernovae are highly sensitive to neutrino mass-squared differences and mixing angles, the DSNB energy spectrum becomes a probe for variations in these parameters. By adopting a purely phenomenological model for neutrino mass evolution with redshift, we calculate the anticipated local DSNB spectrum. Given current constraints on oscillation parameters, particularly the smallness of $|U_{e3}|^2$, our analysis suggests that the $\nu_e$ spectrum could deviate significantly from standard predictions if neutrinos were effectively massless at $z\gtrsim 1$, provided the mass ordering is normal. In contrast, the $\overline{\nu}_e$ flux is unlikely to show such deviations. Therefore, measuring both the neutrino and antineutrino components of the DSNB would enable a test of recent theories regarding neutrino mass generation.

Addressing the need to integrate more Bayesian methods into organizational research (as highlighted by Kruschke, Aguinis, & Joo, 2012; Zyphur & Oswald, 2013), this article proposes a Bayesian meta-analysis approach utilizing power priors. The main objective of this method is to enable researchers to regulate the influence of individual studies on the estimated overall effect size through the use of power priors. This approach is grounded in the premise that studies within a meta-analysis vary in reliability; consequently, by assigning greater weight to more reliable studies via power priors, researchers can derive an overall effect size that more accurately reflects the true population effect. We demonstrate the application of this method to organizational research using the relationship between high-performance work systems and financial performance as a case study. Additionally, we offer free online software to facilitate the conduct of the Bayesian meta-analysis presented here, and we conclude with a discussion of research implications and future directions.

Following the announcement of the Earth-like planet candidate KOI-456.04 for the Kepler-160 system on June 4, 2020 (arXiv:1905.09038v2), we conducted a search for artificial radio signals. Utilizing the turboSETI (arXiv:1709.03491v2) and SPANDAK pipelines across the 1-8 GHz range, we specifically targeted narrowband drifting features (2.97 Hz bandwidth, $\pm 4$ Hz s$^{-1}$ drift rate) and wideband pulsed signatures (5 ms duration at all bandwidths) that exhibit artificial dispersion. This investigation yielded no candidates, establishing upper limits on the Equivalent Isotropic Radiated Power (EIRP) of $5.9 \times 10^{14}$ W for narrowband emissions and $7.3 \times 10^{12}$ W for wideband emissions. This paper provides a brief overview of our observational methods and data reduction processes.

This study utilizes the Kempf-Mangano-Mann (KMM) variant of the Generalized Uncertainty Principle (GUP) to investigate how GUP influences the equation of state (EoS) for nuclear and neutron star matter within the Relativistic Mean Field (RMF) framework. These results are then integrated into Serrano-Liška (SL) gravity theory to analyze Neutron Star (NS) characteristics. We establish that nuclear matter properties constrain the GUP parameter to $\beta \leq 2\times10^{-7}$ MeV$^{-2}$, a limit derived under the condition that anisotropy remains smaller than pressure. Applying this upper bound to NS matter while treating the SL parameter $\tilde{c}$ as independent yields an upper limit of $\tilde{c} \leq 10^7$ m$^2$ for the parameter modifying the Einstein field equations. Using $\beta = 2\times10^{-7}$ MeV$^{-2}$ and $\tilde{c} = 10^7$ m$^2$, the resulting mass-radius relations successfully align with NICER observational data for both PSR J0740+6620 ($\sim 2.1M_\odot$) and PSR J0030+0451 ($\sim 1.4M_\odot$). Notably, this $\beta$ upper bound coincides exactly with constraints from the $^{87}$Rb cold-atom-recoil experiment. Furthermore, assuming a dependency between the logarithmic entropy terms in both the GUP and SL models, the SL parameter must satisfy a lower bound of $\tilde{c} > -16\times 10^{-34}$ m$^2$ for $\beta < 2\times10^{-7}$ MeV$^{-2}$. This lower bound is approximately $10^{-40}$ times smaller in magnitude than the upper bound of $10^7$ m$^2$ derived when $\tilde{c}$ is treated as independent.

Self-supervised learning (SSL) models yield speech representations that enhance various processing tasks; however, their application typically demands fine-tuning pre-trained models or creating task-specific architectures with custom loss functions, which incurs significant memory costs and manual effort. Recently, prompting in Natural Language Processing (NLP) has emerged as an efficient method to harness pre-trained language models (LMs). Specifically, prompt tuning optimizes a constrained set of task-specific parameters while keeping the pre-trained model fixed, thereby requiring minimal storage per task. This approach boosts computational and memory efficiency by capitalizing on the pre-trained LM's inherent prediction capabilities. Despite these benefits, the speech community has largely overlooked this paradigm. This paper presents the inaugural investigation into applying prompt tuning for speech processing tasks using Generative Spoken Language Models (GSLMs). Experimental results indicate that prompt tuning achieves performance comparable to fine-tuning specialized downstream models in speech classification tasks while utilizing fewer trainable parameters. Furthermore, the study explores the technique's application in challenging sequence generation tasks, demonstrating its potential while discussing current limitations and future research directions. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ga642381/SpeechPrompt.

The Internal Language Model Estimation (ILME) method significantly enhances the performance of external language model integration with existing end-to-end (E2E) automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems. This approach works by subtracting the internal LM score from the interpolated score of the E2E and external LM during inference. To further optimize ILME-based inference, we introduce an Internal LM Training (ILMT) method that minimizes an additional internal LM loss by updating only the E2E model components influencing internal LM estimation. ILMT encourages the E2E model to develop a standalone language model within its existing architecture without compromising ASR accuracy. Following ILMT, the resulting modular E2E model, which aligns training and inference criteria, allows for more effective elimination of the source-domain internal LM, thereby facilitating superior integration of the target-domain external LM. Experiments conducted on 30K-hour trained recurrent neural network transducer and attention-based encoder-decoder models demonstrate that ILMT combined with ILME-based inference achieves relative word error rate reductions of up to 31.5% on out-of-domain LibriSpeech and 11.4% on in-domain Microsoft production test sets compared to standard E2E training with Shallow Fusion.

In the online learning framework, an algorithm competes with an environment that may incur losses chosen adversarially in each round. This broad setting encompasses non-adversarial scenarios such as offline optimization and saddle point (min-max) problems. However, standard online algorithms generally fail to exploit the specific structures found in these non-adversarial contexts. Recently, minor adaptations to established methods—specifically optimism and adaptive step sizes—have accelerated online learning across various domains, achieving optimal rates in smooth offline optimization and speeding up convergence for saddle points and social welfare in smooth games. This paper extends these techniques of optimism and adaptive step sizes to Lagrangian hedging, a category of online algorithms that subsumes regret-matching and the multiplicative weights update method (hedge). Our contributions include a general regret bound, a path-length regret bound for fixed smooth losses applicable to optimistic variants of regret-matching and regret-matching+, optimistic regret bounds for $\Phi$-regret (which covers external, internal, and swap regret), and optimistic bounds for a broader family of algorithms that includes regret-matching+ as a specific instance.
We demonstrate that the Relativistic Moduli Space approach, when applied to constrained $CP^1$ instantons, provides an accurate description of kink-antikink collisions within the $\phi^4$ model.

Open relation extraction (OpenRE) seeks to group relation instances that share the same underlying semantic relationship, a fundamental step for generalizing relation extraction. However, current OpenRE models, typically trained on datasets created via distant supervision, often suffer from instability and prone to collapse. This paper re-examines the OpenRE process through a causal lens. By modeling OpenRE using a structural causal framework, we determine that these issues arise from spurious correlations between entities, context, and relation types. To mitigate this, we propose \emph{Element Intervention}, which independently intervenes on context and entities to isolate their true causal effects. We present two specific intervention strategies: one based on entity ranking and another on context contrasting. Experiments on unsupervised relation extraction benchmarks demonstrate that our approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods and exhibits robustness across various datasets.

Data movement remains a primary bottleneck in modern system architectures. Near-Data Processing (NDP) addresses this by shifting computation closer to memory to eliminate redundant data transfer. Our proposed Vector-In-Memory Architecture (VIMA) implements large vector instructions adjacent to 3D-stacked memories using dedicated vector functional units, complemented by a small cache for short-term data reuse. This design offers a straightforward programming interface and ensures precise exception handling. When running stream-oriented workloads on a single core, VIMA achieves up to a 26-fold performance improvement over a standard CPU baseline featuring single-core vector operations, while consuming 93% less energy.

This paper presents the initial efforts of a collaboration between Consob and Sapienza University, concentrating on extracting information from documents related to financial instruments. We examine the automation of this process using both rule-based and machine learning approaches and present our preliminary findings.

This study utilizes deep integral-field spectroscopy from the MUSE instrument to examine three planetary nebulae (NGC 6778, M 1-42, and Hf 2-2) characterized by high abundance discrepancy factors (ADF > 20). By generating flux maps for over 40 emission lines, we created spatial distributions for extinction, electron temperature ($T_e$), electron density ($n_e$), and ionic abundances. We assessed how recombination contributions to the auroral [N II] and [O II] lines influence $T_e$ and low-ionization abundance maps using recombination diagnostics. These analyses reveal low $T_e$ values and an inward decreasing $T_e$ gradient across all three nebulae. Spatially, this trend aligns with the rise in heavy element abundances derived from recombination lines in the inner regions, strongly indicating the existence of two distinct gas phases: a cold, metal-rich phase and a warmer phase with standard metallicity. Furthermore, we present the first simultaneous construction of ADF maps for O$^+$ and O$^{2+}$, which show central peaks for all three objects. We demonstrate that the primary challenge in deriving realistic abundances from either forbidden lines (FOLs) or collisionally excited lines (CELs) lies in estimating the relative contribution of each gas component to the H I emission, and we introduce a method to evaluate this. Finally, our findings indicate that in these high-ADF planetary nebulae, the oxygen content in both cold and warm regions is comparable.

The concluding session of FPCP 2008 featured a round-table discussion involving both panelists and the audience. The panel comprised Jeffrey Appel (moderator), Martin Beneke, George W.S. Hou, David Kirkby, Dmitri Tsybychev, Matt Wingate, and Taku Yamanaka. The following text presents an edited transcript of this session.

This study establishes observational limits on the contribution of acoustic waves (5–50 mHz) to solar chromospheric heating. Data were gathered using the Dunn Solar Telescope in New Mexico alongside Atacama Large Millimeter Array observations from April 23, 2017. Analysis of power spectra for Ca II 854.2 nm, H I 656.3 nm, and millimeter continuum emissions at 1.25 mm and 3 mm reveals a power-law behavior at observed frequencies, where specific characteristics (slope, peak, and white noise floors) correlate with solar features such as internetwork, network, and plage. By comparing fields of view near the disk center and solar limb, we distinguish between vertical and transverse plasma motions. Furthermore, acoustic flux in the middle chromosphere is inferred by comparing observations with synthetic data from the time-dependent radiative hydrodynamic RADYN code. Our results indicate that acoustic waves transport approximately 1 kW m$^{-2}$ in the middle chromosphere, a value insufficient to sustain the quiet chromosphere, contradicting earlier studies.

This letter investigates the sensitivity and constraints on the soft-breaking $Z_2$ parameter $m_{12}$ within the Two Higgs Doublet Model (2HDM). In this framework, $m_{12}$ serves as an input parameter alongside the masses of the Higgs bosons ($m_h$, $m_H$, $m_A$, $m_{H^\pm}$), the vacuum expectation value ratio $\tan \beta$, and $\cos(\beta-\alpha)$, where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ represent the mixing angles for the $\mathcal{CP}$-even and $\mathcal{CP}$-odd sectors, respectively. We specifically examine the sensitivity to $m_{12}$ through the decays of the lightest Higgs boson $h$ into two photons, under two assumptions: 1) $h$ corresponds to the state observed at the LHC with a mass of approximately $125 \ \mathrm{GeV}$, and 2) the $h$ couplings to Standard Model particles resemble those of the SM, achieved by adopting the alignment limit where $\cos(\beta-\alpha) = 0$. The primary objective is to establish potential constraints on $m_{12}$ derived from current measurements of the di-photon signal strength, $\mu_{\gamma\gamma}$. These constraints are pertinent to regions of the 2HDM parameter space that satisfy all other theoretical and experimental limits, including those from Liggs rate measurements, Higgs searches, flavor physics, and precision observables. The analysis covers four distinct Yukawa types of the 2HDM, acknowledging that the allowed parameter space varies by model type. Furthermore, we consider a scenario where the Higgs mass spectrum is consistent with a new world average for $m_W$, incorporating the recent CDF measurement.

Inspired by quark-gluon plasma, we have created a simulation technique to derive the spectral function of (Wilson) fermions non-perturbatively within a non-Abelian gauge theory characterized by high gluon occupation numbers [arXiv:2106.11319]. This method was applied to a non-Abelian plasma situated near its non-thermal fixed point, specifically within a far-from-equilibrium self-similar regime, yielding results that align very closely with perturbative hard loop (HTL) calculations. Notably, we have extracted the complete momentum dependence of the damping rate for fermionic collective excitations for the first time, allowing for a comparison with recent non-perturbative determinations of gluonic spectral functions in both two and three spatial dimensions [arXiv:2101.02715, arXiv:1804.01966].

We introduce the Virtual Secure Platform (VSP), the inaugural comprehensive system designed to execute a multi-opcode, general-purpose sequential processor using Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) for Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC). VSP safeguards both data and the functions applied to that data against adversaries during secure computation offloading scenarios, such as cloud computing. We have developed a complete processor architecture featuring a five-stage pipeline that enhances VSP performance by increasing parallelism in circuit evaluation. Furthermore, we designed a custom Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) to minimize the processor's gate count, accompanied by a full suite of toolchains enabling the compilation of arbitrary C programs into this custom ISA. To accelerate instruction evaluation within VSP, we also proposed CMUX Memory-based ROM and RAM constructions over FHE. Experimental results confirm that both the pipelined architecture and the CMUX Memory technique effectively boost the performance of the proposed processor. We offer an open-source implementation of VSP that achieves a per-instruction latency of under one second. Our demonstrations indicate that compared to the fastest existing FHE-based processor, our implementation operates approximately 1,600 times faster.

This study examines the quasiparticle interference (QPI) patterns generated by two neighboring impurities on the surface of a gapped superconductor. We observe that hyperbolic fringes (HF) can emerge in the QPI signal as a result of the loop contribution from two-impurity scattering, with the impurities acting as the foci of these hyperbolas. In systems with a single Fermi pocket, an HF pattern indicates chiral superconducting order when impurities are non-magnetic, whereas magnetic impurities are necessary to produce an HF pattern for non-chiral superconductivity. Conversely, in multi-pocket scenarios, an HF signature also arises from sign-changing order parameters, such as $s_{\pm}$-wave pairing. Finally, we propose twin impurity QPI as a novel analytical tool to supplement investigations into superconducting order derived from local spectroscopy.

This study surveys prominent applications of machine learning (ML) within geophysics and its specialized subfields. We highlight current advancements alongside critical future research trajectories, supported by essential context in meteorology, wind and wave energy, and oil and gas exploration. Our goal is to evaluate past achievements and offer a thorough examination of the synergy between these disciplines to accelerate the development of novel ML approaches in geophysics. Furthermore, we identify potential enhancements, including the adoption of the DataFlow paradigm for ML algorithm implementation to achieve performance acceleration.

Following the discovery of superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene, which launched the field of twistronics, moiré systems continue to reveal remarkable characteristics. We demonstrate that, for a specific moiré periodicity, boron nitride twisted bilayers possess five distinct stackings that maintain monolayer hexagonal symmetry (invariance under 120° rotations), surpassing the traditionally cited two configurations. We propose new definitions and a nomenclature to unambiguously specify the twist angle and stacking sequence for any hexagonal bilayer exhibiting order-3 rotational symmetry. Furthermore, utilizing density functional theory, we analyze how the band structure evolves with the twist angle across all five stacking sequences of boron nitride bilayers. Our results indicate that the band gap remains indirect at every angle and within every stacking configuration, while also identifying specific features that remain invariant within a given stacking sequence regardless of the twist angle.

Group-based cryptography remains an underexplored domain within post-quantum cryptography, with the Semidirect Discrete Logarithm Problem (SDLP) serving as a cornerstone challenge. Yet, the computational complexity of SDLP and its ties to established hardness assumptions—especially concerning resistance to quantum attacks—have remained obscure, representing a major unresolved issue for the field. This paper presents the inaugural comprehensive security analysis of SDLP. Specifically, we establish a link between SDLP and group actions, a framework where quantum subexponential algorithms are already recognized. Consequently, we develop a subexponential quantum algorithm to solve SDLP, effectively categorizing its complexity and clarifying its relationship to known computational problems.

This study examines the Zakharov system in the energy-critical dimension $d=4$ under the condition of energy lying below the ground state. While it is established that such solutions remain global and scatter when restricted to the radial setting, the scattering behavior in the non-radial case remains an open problem. We demonstrate that if scattering does not occur, a minimal energy non-scattering solution below the ground state must exist, and its orbit is precompact modulo translations. This result is derived through a concentration compactness argument, complemented by an enhanced small data theory applicable to energy-dispersed solutions.

Markov decision processes (MDPs) are extensively employed for planning and verification in environments featuring both probabilistic dynamics and controllable or adversarial decisions. While the conventional value iteration algorithm yields only a lower bound on unbounded rewards or probabilities, two recent "sound" methods have been introduced that also provide upper bounds. This paper introduces optimistic value iteration, a novel sound technique that exploits value iteration's typical capacity to generate tight lower bounds. By deriving a lower bound through standard value iteration and using it to conjecture an upper bound—which is subsequently proven correct—this method offers a robust solution. Optimistic value iteration is straightforward to implement, avoids the need for additional precomputations or state space transformations, and applies to both reachability probabilities and expected rewards. Furthermore, extensive experiments using our publicly available implementation in the Modest Toolset demonstrate its high performance.

We examine the solution of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) in two-dimensional spacetime. Adopting Baluni's analysis, a single-flavor model can be studied via Abelian bosonization. The theory is analyzed in the strong-coupling regime, where quarks are significantly lighter than the gauge coupling; under these conditions, the system behaves as a Luttinger liquid.

We have examined halo formation in neutron-rich calcium isotopes using a recently developed relativistic mean-field plus BCS (RMF+BCS) framework, where the single-particle continuum of the RMF is substituted with discrete positive energy states to compute pairing energy. For calcium isotopes near the neutron drip line, adding more neutrons leads to a sharp rise in the neutron root-mean-square radius alongside a minimal gain in binding energy, signaling the emergence of halos. This behavior stems primarily from the progressive occupation of the weakly bound $3s_{1/2}$ orbital. Furthermore, the ability to host several extra neutrons with virtually no increase in binding energy is attributed to pairing correlations.

This study introduces the CoESCA station, designed for surface electron-electron coincidence spectroscopy through a joint effort between Uppsala University and Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin at the BESSY II synchrotron in Germany. After reviewing prior research in electron-electron coincidences, we detail the CoESCA apparatus and its design specifications. The system records shot-to-shot resolved 6D coincidence datasets, capturing the kinetic energy and two emission angles for both coincident electrons. We outline the mathematical framework for analyzing these multi-dimensional datasets, emphasizing coincidence statistics, which define fundamental limits on signal-to-noise ratios and their impact on acquisition durations and raw data volume. The station's capabilities are demonstrated using Auger photoelectron coincidences from silver surfaces, specifically involving Ag 3d core-level photoelectrons and their corresponding MNN Auger electrons. Furthermore, we successfully separated Auger spectra arising from the 3d$_{3/2}$ and 3d$_{5/2}$ core levels and determined the two-hole state energy distributions for these decay channels.

According to the paper "Fourier formula for quantum partition functions" (arXiv:2106.10032 [math-ph]), we demonstrate that for an infinite system of identical bosons interacting through a positive-type pair potential, off-diagonal long-range order exists if and only if a non-zero fraction of the particles constitute infinite permutation cycles. Specifically, Bose-Einstein condensation occurs if and only if the lengths of these diverging cycles grow at least as rapidly as $N^{2/d}$ with respect to the particle number $N$ in dimensions $d \geq 3$. This finding generalizes a corresponding result previously established for the ideal Bose gas.

This study employs direct simulations to examine the motion of slightly deformable, neutrally buoyant prolate capsules—both straight and curved—within unbounded simple shear flow at zero Reynolds number. The curved capsules simulate the crescent-shaped sickle red blood cells characteristic of sickle cell disease (SCD), allowing for an investigation into how deformability and curvature influence dynamics. Results indicate that low-deformability straight capsules tumble within the shear plane, settling into a unique asymptotically stable orbit, a behavior distinct from the infinitely many neutrally stable Jeffery orbits observed in rigid spheroids. Curved prolate capsules exhibit more complex dynamics arising from the interplay of curvature and deformability. Initially, depending on orientation, these capsules may display Jeffery-like motions (tumbling or kayaking) or non-Jeffery-like behavior where the end-to-end vector repeatedly crosses the shear-gradient plane. Over time, however, they converge to a Jeffery-like quasi-periodic orbit irrespective of initial conditions. Furthermore, the long-term trajectory averages can be accurately approximated by analytical Jeffery orbit solutions using an effective orbit constant ($C_{\textnormal{eff}}$) and aspect ratio ($\ell_{\textnormal{eff}}$). As deformability or curvature increases, $C_{\textnormal{eff}}$ decreases, signaling a shift toward log-rolling, while $\ell_{\textnormal{eff}}$ increases slightly with curvature but remains largely unaffected by deformability. Given that blood disorders like SCD alter cell deformability, shape, and interactions, these findings offer significant insights into understanding the pathophysiology of hematologic diseases.

Driven by the growing significance of neural machine translation, research into reference-free quality estimation (QE) has advanced steadily. Although QE is highly practical, traditional manual data creation faces challenges, including the high costs of requiring translation experts and difficulties in scaling data across languages. To address these issues, we introduce QUAK, a fully automated Korean-English synthetic QE dataset. QUAK comprises three subsets—QUAK-M, QUAK-P, and QUAK-H—generated via three language-agnostic strategies that eliminate the need for human intervention. This approach enables significant scalability, resulting in datasets of 1.58M examples for QUAK-P and QUAK-H, and 6.58M for QUAK-M. Our study quantitatively analyzes word-level QE results through various methods and statistical assessments. Furthermore, we demonstrate that efficient data scaling enhances performance, evidenced by meaningful gains in QUAK-M and QUAK-P as data volume increased to 1.58M.

We introduce a novel empirical framework describing the mass assembly of dark matter halos. This approach models the growth of individual halos as a simple power-law function of time, with an index that smoothly transitions from a higher value during the rapid accretion phase at early times to a lower value during the slow accretion phase at late times. Leveraging extensive halo merger trees from high-resolution cosmological simulations, we demonstrate that our three-parameter model, Diffmah, approximates halo growth with an accuracy of approximately 0.1 dex for $t > 1$ Gyr. This accuracy holds for all present-day halos exceeding $10^{11} M_{\odot}$, covering both subhalos and host halos in gravity-only simulations as well as the TNG hydrodynamical simulation. Furthermore, we propose a new model for population-level assembly, DiffmahPop, which not only reproduces average mass growth over time but also accurately reflects the diversity in how individual halos accumulate mass. Implemented in Python using the autodiff library JAX, our model self-consistently accounts for both the mean and variance of the halo mass accretion rate across cosmic time. We show that Diffmah effectively captures the relationship between halo assembly and the large-scale density field (halo assembly bias), while residual errors in the halo assembly history show negligible correlation with the density field. Our publicly available source code enables the generation of Monte Carlo realizations of cosmologically representative halo histories, and its differentiable nature allows for seamless integration into existing analytical halo model frameworks.

This paper introduces a novel, principled method for learning optimal transport between two distributions using samples. Drawing on optimal transport theory, we aim to learn the optimal Kantorovich potential, which defines the corresponding transport map. This is achieved by learning two convex functions through a new minimax optimization strategy. Leveraging recent progress in input convex neural networks, we propose a framework where the gradient of one convex function directly represents the optimal transport mapping. Numerical experiments validate that our method successfully learns the optimal transport mapping, ensuring optimality regardless of neural network initialization. Additionally, the approach effectively handles target distributions with discontinuous supports, as the gradient of a convex function naturally accommodates discontinuous transport mappings.

The Cactus Framework serves as an open-source, modular, and portable programming environment designed for the collaborative creation and deployment of scientific applications within high-performance computing environments. Originating in 1996 through initiatives at the National Center for Supercomputer Applications and the Albert Einstein Institute in Germany, the framework has since evolved alongside significant shifts in hardware infrastructure and its community. This paper examines the framework's resilience through these historical transformations and, leveraging insights from its past, outlines its future trajectory.

Utilizing caching at wireless edge nodes offers a promising approach to enhance spatial and spectral efficiency, thereby reducing network congestion related to content delivery. The coded caching framework, initially introduced by Maddah-Ali and Niesen, accelerates communication efficiency by transmitting multicast messages that serve multiple users simultaneously. While most existing coded caching research assumes users request any content from the entire library, many practical scenarios involve users interested only in a specific subset of content determined by their location. Driven by this insight, this paper addresses the coded caching problem tailored for location-dependent content at edge cache nodes. The study involves a server storing $N$ location-based files (such as High-Definition maps), $K$ edge cache nodes situated in various regions, and $K$ users (e.g., vehicles), where each user resides in the service area of one cache node and accesses its contents with negligible overhead. Based on their location, each user requests a file from a location-specific subset of the library, with the goal of minimizing the worst-case load. For this novel problem, we derive a significant converse bound under uncoded cache placement, demonstrating that a simple achievable scheme is optimal in this setting. Furthermore, this scheme is proven to be order-optimal within a factor of 3. Finally, we extend the location-based coded caching model to the multiaccess topology proposed by Hachem et al., where each user connects to $L$ nearest cache nodes. When $L \geq 2$, we establish the exact optimality regarding the worst-case load.

This paper introduces a criterion to demonstrate boundedness for various operators mapping from $H^1((0,\infty),\gamma_\alpha)$ to $L^1((0,\infty),\gamma_\alpha)$ and from $L^\infty((0,\infty),\gamma_\alpha)$ to $\BMO((0,\infty),\gamma_\alpha)$ under the probability measure $d\gamma_\alpha(x)=\frac{2}{\Gamma(\alpha+1)} x^{2\alpha+1} e^{-x^2} dx$ on $(0,\infty)$ for $\alpha>-\frac12$. We utilize this criterion to derive endpoint estimates for Riesz transforms, maximal operators, Littlewood-Paley functions, multipliers of Laplace transform type, fractional integrals, and variation operators within the Laguerre framework.

This study offers a comparative examination of neutrino models grounded in a wide spectrum of low-scale seesaw mechanisms, specifically type II, inverse (ISS), and linear (LSS) seesaws, which account for the observed smallness of neutrino masses. We explicitly detail the Lagrangians and associated particle content for each framework. To explore light neutrino masses, mixing angles, and flavor structures, we integrate the $A_4$ flavor symmetry into these models. Additionally, we employ symmetries such as $U(1)_{X}$, $Z_4$, and $Z_5$ to ensure the viability of the models. Utilizing recent global fit results for neutrino oscillation parameters, we determine unknown quantities like the lightest neutrino mass and CP-violating phases (Dirac and Majorana). These parameters are derived by solving a system of simultaneous equations generated through $A_4$ product rules within the Lagrangian, considering various vacuum expectation value (VEV) alignments of the triplet flavon field. Subsequently, these derived parameters are applied to analyze charged lepton flavor violation (cLFV), specifically the $\mu \rightarrow e + \gamma$ decay, and are tested against the latest experimental bounds and sensitivities. Although models for type II, ISS, and LSS were constructed to facilitate comparison, this work concentrates its computational efforts on the LSS scenario, with calculations performed to a precision tolerance of $<10^{-5}$.

Conventional link prediction frameworks typically rely on a balanced test set of node pairs to determine link existence. In real-world scenarios, however, such a test set is absent because the ground truth remains unknown, resulting in a search space that scales quadratically with the number of nodes. Given the sparsity of most graphs, the majority of these potential pairs do not represent actual links. Consequently, methods relying on proximity-preserving embeddings or heuristic similarity metrics face a vast, skewed search space containing many pairs that are close in proximity but should not be connected. To address this, we propose LinkWaldo, a framework designed to select a concise set of candidate pairs from this massive, quadratic space. These candidates must exhibit both high proximity and structural resemblance to observed edges. This approach enables the framework to filter out high-proximity, low-resemblance pairs while identifying high-resemblance pairs even with lower proximity. Built upon a model that theoretically integrates Stochastic Block Models (SBMs) with node proximity models, LinkWaldo uses the SBM's block structure to locate regions where new links are likely to appear. Within these regions, proximity metrics identify the most plausible links, while locality-sensitive hashing prevents costly exhaustive searches. LinkWaldo is compatible with any node representation learning method or heuristic proximity definition, allowing it to generate candidate pairs for any link prediction algorithm and unlocking the potential of current and future representation methods for practical link prediction. Evaluated across 13 networks in various domains, LinkWaldo demonstrates that, on average, its candidate sets contain 7–33% more missing and future links compared to those generated by embedding-based and heuristic baselines.
This paper initiates the investigation of Feigin-Odesskii wheel conditions from a geometric perspective and extends the concept to the K-theory Hall algebra of any surface.

Legal practitioners frequently encounter extensive proceedings across diverse case types, including land disputes and corruption cases, making document summarization essential. However, these summaries must specifically capture intent phrases aligned with the case category. To our knowledge, no existing evaluation metric assesses summaries based on intent. We introduce an automated intent-based summarization metric that demonstrates superior agreement with human evaluations compared to traditional metrics like BLEU and ROUGE-L. Furthermore, we have curated a dataset by annotating intent phrases within legal documents and provided a proof of concept for automating this system. All code and data required to reproduce our results are available on GitHub.

The Laplace transform serves as a potent analytical instrument widely applied across various domains of applied mathematics, such as differential equations and probability theory. Much like the inversion of the Fourier transform, deriving inversion formulas for the Laplace transform is fundamental; established methods include the Fourier-Mellin or Bromwich integral and the Post-Widder inversion. This research is driven by an elementary statistical challenge: achieving unbiased estimation of a parametric function involving the scale parameter within the standard model of a random sample drawn from an exponential distribution. By expressing the uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimator (UMVUE) for a parametric function $h(\lambda)$ and its variance as series expansions of Laguerre polynomials and their corresponding Fourier coefficients, this work derives a new inversion formula for the Laplace transform.

MSC: Primary 44A10, 62F10.
Key words and phrases: Exponential Distribution, Unbiased Estimation; Fourier-Laguerre Series; Inverse Laplace Transform; Laguerre Polynomials.

This paper presents a methodology designed to make microscopic transportation models accessible for the statistical analysis of traffic accidents. Our approach facilitates the understanding of both historical losses and potential incidents in modified future systems. From engineering and insurance standpoints, this allows for the evaluation of changes in vehicle and transport system designs regarding their effects on functionality and road safety. Structurally, we approximate the total loss distribution as a mean-variance mixture, which provides valuation procedures as an alternative to Monte Carlo simulation. Specifically, we develop an implementation using the open-source traffic simulator SUMO and demonstrate the approach's potential through counterfactual case studies.

We develop a one-parameter family of solutions for the positive singular Q-curvature problem on compact, nondegenerate manifolds of dimension greater than four that possess finitely many punctures. For dimensions of eight or higher, we require the Weyl tensor to vanish to a sufficiently high order at these singular points. Methodologically, our approach relies on perturbation and gluing techniques, utilizing the mapping properties of the linearized operator within a small neighborhood of each singularity as well as in the surrounding exterior region. Key challenges in this construction involve regulating the convergence rate of the Paneitz operator toward the flat bi-Laplacian in conformal normal coordinates and aligning the Cauchy data of the interior and exterior solutions; the latter issue stems from the absence of geometric Jacobi fields within the kernel of the linearized operator. We address both obstacles by formulating appropriate auxiliary functions.

A Berge cycle of length $k$ in a hypergraph $\mathcal H$ consists of a sequence of distinct vertices and hyperedges $v_1,h_1,v_2,h_2,\dots,v_{k},h_k$ where $v_{i},v_{i+1}\in h_i$ for all $i\in[k]$, with indices taken modulo $k$. While F\"uredi, Kostochka, and Luo recently established sharp Dirac-type minimum degree conditions ensuring Hamiltonian Berge cycles in non-uniform hypergraphs, we provide a sharp P\'osa-type lower bound for both $r$-uniform and non-uniform hypergraphs that guarantees the existence of Hamiltonian Berge cycles.

Investigating the sharpening of the holographic duality between Jackiw-Teitelboim (JT) gravity and its dual matrix model at a finite radial cutoff $\lambda$ via $T\overline{T}$ deformation is a key objective. To advance this, we streamline the analysis by focusing on the Airy model, applying $T\overline{T}$ deformations to its correlators in a manner consistent with deformed JT gravity. Utilizing these correlators, we calculate annealed and quenched free energies for both $\lambda > 0$ and $\lambda < 0$ through an integral representation of the replica method. At leading order in $\lambda$ and low temperatures, we verify that the genus-zero quenched free energy monotonically declines with increasing temperature within the regime of valid perturbation theory. Furthermore, we examine the all-genus quenched free energy at low temperatures, revealing and discussing complexities arising from non-perturbative effects in the Airy model, as well as contributions from the non-perturbative sector induced by the $T\overline{T}$ deformation.

Fanaroff-Riley (FR) 0 radio galaxies represent a distinct class characterized by lower luminosity but significantly higher abundance compared to the well-known FR 1 and FR 2 types, which are currently hypothesized to be sources of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) capable of reaching energies near ${\sim}10^{20}$ eV. This study investigates the feasibility of UHECR acceleration and survival within FR 0 environments. To do so, an average spectral energy distribution (SED) was constructed using data from the FR0CAT catalog. These derived photon fields were treated as targets for UHECRs, which undergo energy losses via electromagnetic pair production, photo-disintegration, photo-meson production, and synchrotron radiation. The analysis evaluates various acceleration mechanisms, specifically Fermi-I order and gradual shear accelerations, alongside particle escape rates. The findings indicate that under a hybrid model combining Fermi and shear accelerations, FR 0 galaxies can contribute to the observed UHECR flux provided the jet Lorentz factor satisfies $\Gamma_\mathrm{j}\gtrsim 1.6$, a threshold where shear acceleration begins to dominate over escape. Furthermore, even in less favorable scenarios, FR 0s may contribute to the cosmic-ray spectrum between the knee and the ankle. These conclusions remain robust across different magnetic turbulence models and shock velocities.

Extratropical cyclones represent large-scale weather phenomena that frequently trigger extreme conditions across Northern Europe, resulting in significant infrastructure damage and loss of life. These systems generate localized vorticity maxima that traverse the Atlantic Ocean, providing a basis for regional climatology. Although substantial progress has been made in creating algorithms to extract cyclone tracks and evolution from reanalysis data, the available record remains relatively brief. This limitation underscores the necessity for a statistical model capable of capturing the extreme characteristics of these systems, particularly their intensity and the spatial variability of their paths. This study introduces a novel simulation-based methodology for modeling the lifecycle of extratropical cyclones, addressing both their tracks and vorticity while integrating various factors of cyclone evolution and motion. By leveraging techniques from extreme value analysis, the approach enables the simulation of storms more severe than those historically observed, offering a valuable instrument for practitioners engaged in risk assessment related to these weather events.

Learning from continuous, non-stationary data streams without supervision represents one of the most significant and difficult challenges for intelligent agents. This work addresses the convergence of unsupervised, streaming, and non-stationary conditions specifically within clustering, or mixture modeling. We present a new clustering algorithm that enables mixture models to dynamically generate new clusters online based on incoming data, operating through a probabilistic, time-varying, and theoretically grounded framework. To accomplish this, we first introduce a new stochastic process, the Dynamical Chinese Restaurant Process (Dynamical CRP), which defines a non-exchangeable distribution over set partitions. We then demonstrate that the Dynamical CRP serves as a non-stationary prior for cluster assignments, resulting in an efficient variational inference method suitable for streaming data. Finally, experimental results confirm that the Dynamical CRP performs effectively on various synthetic and real-world datasets, accommodating both Gaussian and non-Gaussian likelihoods.

Since the 1970s, Mastermind, a traditional two-player game, has garnered significant interest from both the general public and the academic community as a subject of scientific inquiry. Formally defined with $n$ positions and $k$ colors, the game involves a codemaker selecting a secret string $s \in [k]^n$ while the codebreaker attempts to identify $s$ using the minimum number of queries of the form $f_s(x)$, which reveals the proximity of $x$ to $s$. The efficiency of a strategy is evaluated based on the total number of queries required. This study presents a systematic analysis of quantum strategies for Mastermind, achieving a full characterization of quantum complexity and developing optimal algorithms for both non-adaptive and adaptive scenarios. Methodologically, we establish a framework for designing quantum algorithms for the general string learning problem by identifying a novel structure that maximizes quantum speedup in the non-adaptive setting for Mastermind and is likely applicable to other string learning problems involving various query oracles.

This work examines data exchange from relational sources to RDF targets, where target constraints are defined via Shape Expressions (ShEx). We address two core issues: (1) consistency, which verifies whether a solution always exists for any given source instance, and (2) the construction of a universal solution that encapsulates the entire space of possible solutions. Our approach involves utilizing typed IRI constructors within source-to-target tuple-generating dependencies to derive RDF IRIs from relational values, alongside translating ShEx schemas into a corresponding set of target dependencies. Additionally, we identify "key covered" data exchange settings—a decidable property that ensures consistency. Finally, we demonstrate that this property serves as both a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of universal solutions within a practical subclass of weakly-recursive ShEx.

A significant open challenge involves generalizing existing literature on unit disk graphs to hypergraph frameworks. Driven by recent findings that the worst-case efficiency of distributed maximal scheduling algorithms depends on the hypergraph's interference degree, this study examines both the properties of this degree and the structural characteristics of hypergraphs formed under physical constraints. We demonstrate that calculating the interference degree of a hypergraph is NP-hard and establish several key properties regarding this invariant.
