Furthermore, we analyze the realizability of hypergraphs—specifically, which ones can emerge in practice as interference models for wireless networks subject to physical limitations. Building on insights into the worst-case performance of maximal scheduling, we address the natural question of the maximum value of $r$ for which the hypergraph $K_{1,r}$ is realizable, proving that this limit is $r=4$.

Multi-label text classification (MLTC) stands out as both a compelling and demanding endeavor within natural language processing (NLP), offering broader practical utility than its single-label counterpart. To address MLTC challenges, this study introduces a label-interpretable graph convolutional network that represents tokens and labels as nodes within a heterogeneous graph. This architecture captures various relationships, including token-level interactions, while exposing token-label edges to enhance the interpretability of predicted labels. Evaluated across four real-world datasets, the proposed method demonstrates competitive performance against selected baselines, delivering a 0.14 F1 score improvement for small label sets and a 0.07 gain for large label sets.

Dual-energy (DE) chest radiography offers superior diagnostic capabilities compared to standard radiographs by segregating the image into bone and soft tissue components, thereby uncovering lesions that might otherwise be obscured. However, acquiring DE images necessitates two physical scans, requiring specialized equipment and processing, and is susceptible to motion artifacts. Creating virtual DE images from standard, single-shot chest radiographs could enhance diagnostic utility without altering the acquisition process. This study introduces a Multi-scale Conditional Adversarial Network (MCA-Net) capable of generating high-resolution virtual DE bone images from standard radiographs. Trained via adversarial learning, the MCA-Net captures sharp details to produce high-quality bone imagery. Subsequently, virtual DE soft tissue images are derived by applying a cross-projection transformation to the standard radiograph using the generated virtual bone image. Evaluation on 210 patient DE chest radiographs confirmed the algorithm's ability to produce high-quality virtual DE images that preserve critical structures, such as coronary calcium in bone views and lung lesions in soft tissue views. In testing data, the average structural similarity index and peak signal-to-noise ratio for the generated bone images reached 96.4 and 41.5, respectively, significantly outperforming prior methods. Additionally, clinical assessments on a publicly available dataset validate the algorithm's clinical relevance. Consequently, this method yields high-quality DE images with potential applications for radiologists, computer-aided diagnostics, and other diagnostic procedures.

This study introduces an adaptive primal-dual dynamics framework for distributed optimization within multi-agent systems. By integrating an adaptive synchronization law that enhances the coupling strength between primal variables of interconnected agents, the proposed approach accelerates convergence toward the saddle-point solution. The resulting dynamics are modeled as a passive feedback interconnected networked system. Leveraging the system's passivity properties alongside LaSalle's invariance principle for hybrid systems, the authors establish the asymptotic convergence and stability of the saddle-point solution. Furthermore, the analysis of the primal dynamics reveals improved convergence rates under adaptive synchronization, with stronger convergence bounds derived. Robustness is quantified through L2-gain analysis, highlighting the relationship between convergence speed and system robustness. Finally, the efficacy of this dynamic is validated by solving distributed least squares and distributed support vector machine problems.

This study establishes a $(n/m)^{-1/2}$-rate finite sample Berry-Esseen bound for $m$-dependent high-dimensional random vectors within the class of hyper-rectangles. The approach requires minimal assumptions regarding the random vectors, such as nondegenerate covariances and finite third moments. The proof leverages inductive connections between anti-concentration inequalities and Berry-Esseen bounds, drawing inspiration from the telescoping technique of Chen and Shao (2004) and the recursion method of Kuchibhotla and Rinaldo (2020). By executing a dual induction based on these relationships, we derive tight Berry-Esseen bounds applicable to dependent samples.

The performance sensitivity of optical wireless communication (OWC) systems can be significantly enhanced through the use of highly sensitive single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) arrays. However, the throughput of these SPAD-based OWC systems is severely constrained by nonlinear distortion caused by the device's dead time. To address this, optical orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) is utilized to boost spectral efficiency. This study presents a theoretical performance analysis of an OWC system employing SPAD arrays and asymmetrically-clipped optical OFDM (ACO-OFDM), specifically investigating the effects of SPAD nonlinearity. Furthermore, the work compares the proposed ACO-OFDM scheme with direct-current-biased optical OFDM (DCO-OFDM), highlighting their distinct reliable operating regions. Results indicate that ACO-OFDM outperforms DCO-OFDM in low-power scenarios, whereas DCO-OFDM is more advantageous in high-power regimes.
This article demonstrates that the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function necessarily reside on the critical line, a statement known as the Riemann hypothesis.

Network Traffic Classification (NTC) is a critical component of network management tasks, including security services and Quality of Service (QoS) provisioning. While Machine Learning (ML) offers a promising solution for NTC by delivering reasonable accuracy and handling encrypted traffic, these methods often struggle with the scarcity of labeled data prevalent in real-world scenarios. This study explores the potential of Active Learning (AL), a specific ML approach, to address NTC challenges. AL mitigates the reliance on extensive labeled datasets by strategically selecting which instances require labeling. The research begins with an overview of NTC and its core difficulties, followed by a survey of existing ML-based NTC techniques. It subsequently introduces AL, examines its application within NTC, and reviews relevant literature. Furthermore, the study addresses current challenges and open issues in AL-driven network traffic classification. As a technical survey, experiments were conducted to demonstrate the broad utility of AL in this domain. The simulation results indicate that AL can achieve high accuracy using a minimal amount of data.

We introduce a versatile framework capable of handling both singer identity and vocal technique conversion. Trained on non-parallel datasets, our model supports many-to-many mappings and utilizes recent developments in variational autoencoders. By employing distinct encoders to isolate latent representations for singer identity and vocal technique, alongside a shared decoder for reconstruction, the system achieves attribute separation. Conversion is executed through straightforward vector arithmetic within these learned latent spaces. Quantitative evaluations and visualizations of the resulting spectrograms confirm that the model effectively disentangles these attributes and performs successful conversions. To our knowledge, this represents the first deep learning-based approach to jointly address the conversion of both singer identity and vocal technique.

In traveling wave microresonators, cascaded four-wave mixing among optical modes facilitates the creation of frequency combs, notably the fascinating dissipative Kerr solitons (DKS). This study presents a theoretical examination of comb quantum fluctuations to uncover the quantum characteristics of these solitons. We demonstrate that correlations exist among the fluctuations of Kerr frequency comb lines, resulting in multi-color continuous-variable entanglement. Specifically, within the DKS state, coherent comb lines drive photon-pair generation and enable coherent photon conversion across all optical modes, establishing an all-to-all network of quantum entanglement. This broadband multi-color entanglement is both universal and resilient to practical imperfections, such as additional optical loss or significant frequency shifts in a few modes. Our findings highlight the significant quantum nature of DKSs, offering fundamental insights for quantum optics while presenting promising prospects for quantum networks and distributed quantum sensing.

This paper establishes the largest subspace of positive numbers such that the restricted maximal operator of Fejér means remains bounded from the Hardy space $H_{p}$ to $L_{p}$ for all $0<p\leq 1/2$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this result is sharp in a specific sense.

This paper introduces a numerical approach to generate state-feedback control policies for general infinite-horizon, nonlinear optimal control problems featuring continuous states, constant setpoints, and undiscounted costs. Rooted in approximate dynamic programming and closely aligned with approximate policy iteration, this method diverges from existing techniques by mandating the convergence of both the control policy and the system state as termination criteria. Unlike prior methods that often rely on discounted formulations or restrict cost functions to specific subclasses, our approach accommodates bounded and continuous undiscounted cost functions. The study outlines the numerical method, establishes its foundational mathematical properties, and validates it through representative examples, with a freely available MATLAB implementation provided alongside.

This study examines the Einstein-Hilbert action in the first-order formalism coupled to Dirac spinors. Leveraging little group symmetry, we obtain the associated Bargmann-Wigner current, which is conserved yet lacks gauge invariance. Consequently, we develop a gauge-invariant counterpart that is not conserved but remains potentially observable. Due to its non-conservation, we decompose this current into fermionic and gravitational components, deriving their respective broken continuity equations. These equations form the master equations describing the interaction between spin-currents and gravity. Additionally, we establish the corresponding master equations within the weak field approximation.

This paper utilizes the ultrafilter-convergence axiomatics for topological spaces to provide a detailed, accessible categorical introduction to Barr's Set-based relational T-algebras and Burroni's T-preorders internal to a category C (designated as T-spaces in C), where T is a monad replacing the ultrafilter monad on Set. Within this framework, the concepts of compactness, Hausdorff separation (originally defined by Manes), and complete regularity are explored. Drawing on a previously underappreciated result by Burroni, the study's central theorem offers an external fibrational characterization of the category of completely regular T-spaces and its reflective subcategory of compact Hausdorff T-spaces, subject to mild constraints on both C and T.

The velocity coupling term is crucial for accurate numerical simulation and a posteriori error analysis in flow and transport problems, particularly for adaptive mesh refinement. This paper investigates the Enhanced Velocity Mixed Finite Element Method applied to incompressible Darcy flow, aiming to enhance velocity approximation across subdomain interfaces. We propose reconstructing the interface velocity through post-processed pressure. Numerical results demonstrate that this approach improves the convergence rate at the interface.

This work addresses a distributed optimization framework where the objective function comprises a sum of strongly convex, smooth functions and a potentially nonsmooth convex regularizer. Within a multi-agent network, each agent maintains a private cost function and collaborates with neighbors to determine the global optimum. We introduce a quasi-Newton Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) that solves the primal update inexactly using approximated curvature data. By incorporating an intermediate consensus variable, the method yields a block diagonal Hessian, thereby removing the requirement for inner communication loops during the computation of the update direction. We prove global linear convergence to the optimal primal-dual solution without employing backtracking line search, provided the component cost functions are strongly convex and possess Lipschitz continuous gradients. Numerical experiments on real-world datasets confirm the superiority of the proposed approach compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

This study examines the dynamical characteristics of a quantum extension of classical reversible Boolean networks, where each node's state is represented by a single qubit. Beyond standard Boolean logic, the framework incorporates controlled bit-flip and Hadamard operations. The analysis focuses on synchronous update schemes, in which every qubit evolves at each step based on the values held by qubits in the preceding step. We explore the periodic or quasiperiodic dynamics of these quantum networks and assess how single-site perturbations propagate through systems with an input degree of one. Our findings reveal that a non-classical propagation mechanism results in a significantly altered evolution of the Hamming distance between the original and perturbed states.

We introduce two synthetic datasets, Simulated Flying Shapes and Simulated Planar Manipulator, designed to evaluate the learning capabilities of video processing systems. Specifically, these datasets serve as tools for efficiently verifying the validity of deep neural networks intended to encode, reconstruct, or predict sequences of video frames. Each dataset contains 90,000 videos. The Simulated Flying Shapes dataset features scenes with two objects of identical size and shape (rectangle, triangle, or circle) moving toward one another, while the Simulated Planar Manipulator depicts a 3-degree-of-freedom planar arm performing a pick-and-place operation to position a circle of varying sizes onto a square platform. Unlike commonly used datasets such as moving MNIST [1], [2], our collections focus on goal-oriented tasks—such as a manipulator grasping and placing an object—rather than random motions. This distinction renders the datasets more effective for assessing prediction abilities and the learning of complex movements by machine learning models. This technical document provides an introduction to utilizing both datasets.
This document is a written transcript of the theoretical summary lecture delivered at the Strangeness in Quark Matter 2022 conference.

Inspired by Gamow's liquid drop model for large masses, we investigate an isoperimetric problem where the conventional perimeter $P(E)$ is modified to $P(E)-\gamma P_\varepsilon(E)$, with $0<\gamma<1$ and $P_\varepsilon$ representing a nonlocal energy that converges to $P(E)$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$. We demonstrate that for sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, minimizers with unit area are disks. Specifically, in two dimensions, we first establish that minimizers must be convex when $\varepsilon$ is small enough; this convexity implies their boundaries are nearly circular, constituting a small Lipschitz perturbation of a circle. Subsequently, employing a Fuglede-type argument, we prove that for any dimension $n \geq 2$, the unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the unique unit-volume minimizer among centered, nearly spherical sets. Consequently, up to translation, the unit disk is the unique minimizer. This problem corresponds to a generalized version of Gamow's liquid drop model for atomic nuclei, featuring a nonlocal repulsive potential defined by a radial, sufficiently integrable kernel. In this framework, our primary finding indicates that if the kernel's first moment falls below a specific threshold, there exists a critical mass $m_0$ such that for all $m > m_0$, the disk is the unique area-$m$ minimizer up to translation. This result stands in stark contrast to the standard case involving Riesz kernels, where minimizers fail to exist beyond a certain critical mass.

Three key observables—the energy density fluctuation spectrum, baryon asymmetry, and coherent large-scale magnetic fields—offer vital insights into high-energy physics. While inflation accounts for density perturbations, explaining the origins of primordial magnetic fields and baryon asymmetry necessitates physics extending beyond standard cosmological and particle models. This study demonstrates that the mechanism generating primordial helical fields simultaneously drives baryogenesis at the onset of the radiation-dominated era. The proposed model utilizes mass dimension 6 operators featuring Riemann coupling between gravity and the electromagnetic field, without requiring extensions to the Standard Model of particle physics. We explicitly confirm that the production of these helical magnetic fields results in baryogenesis. Furthermore, the model predicts the observed level of cosmic baryon asymmetry across a range of reheating temperatures that align with observational data.

Quantum compiling involves building a quantum circuit $V$ using native gates that are functionally equivalent to a target unitary $U$, a critical step for executing algorithms on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware. However, the vast search space for circuit structures necessitates human expertise and extensive experimentation or modification of existing designs. To address this, we introduce a variational quantum compiling (VQC) algorithm driven by reinforcement learning (RL), enabling the automatic design of quantum circuit structures without human intervention. An agent is trained to sequentially select gates from the native alphabet and their target qubits using double Q-learning with an $\epsilon$-greedy exploration strategy and experience replay. Initially, the agent randomly explores various circuit configurations before iteratively identifying structures with superior performance on the learning task. Simulation results demonstrate that our method achieves exact compilations with fewer gates than prior VQC approaches. Consequently, it mitigates errors arising from decoherence and gate noise in NISQ devices, allowing complex quantum algorithms to run within the available coherence time.

Shape-constrained nonparametric regression has become an increasingly significant field across economics, statistics, operations research, and machine learning. Specifically within productivity and efficiency analysis, recent advances in multivariate convex regression—along with related approaches like convex quantile and expectile regression—have successfully connected traditional deterministic nonparametric and stochastic parametric methodologies. However, the widespread adoption of these sophisticated estimation techniques in empirical practice has been hindered by substantial computational demands and the absence of robust, accessible, and open-source software tools. To overcome this barrier, the Python package pyStoNED offers a free, user-friendly solution for performing multivariate convex regression, convex quantile and expectile regression, isotonic regression, stochastic nonparametric envelopment of data, and associated methods. This paper serves as a tutorial for pyStoNED, demonstrating its utility through applications focused on estimating frontier cost and production functions.

This study examines the challenges facing superluminal "warp drive" travel, specifically focusing on interactions with interstellar matter and curvature effects. Collisions between interstellar dust, photons, and the spacecraft generate a pressure that scales linearly with the ship's apparent velocity, $v_s$. Meanwhile, the force arising from curvature effects comprises two distinct non-trivial components: the radial component scales with $v_s^2$, while the longitudinal component scales with $v_s^4$. These impediments grow significantly more critical as the spacecraft attains higher superluminal velocities.

This study examines the adaptive sparse grid discontinuous Galerkin (aSG-DG) approach for solving high-dimensional partial differential equations (PDEs) and details its software realization. The C++ library, AdaM-DG, which embodies the aSG-DG methodology, can be accessed on Github at \url{https://github.com/JuntaoHuang/adaptive-multiresolution-DG}. This tool is designed to handle a broad spectrum of high-dimensional linear and nonlinear PDEs. We provide an overview of the algorithm's core components and the software's capabilities, such as the utilization of multiwavelets, the construction of bilinear operators, and efficient matrix-vector products tailored for hierarchical data structures. Additionally, we evaluate the package's performance by presenting numerical error metrics and computational costs across several benchmark problems, including linear transport, wave, and Hamilton-Jacobi equations.
I present several progressively stronger conjectures concerning the superadditivity of Kodaira dimension in the context of morphisms between smooth quasi-projective complex varieties.

By naturally extending the classical definition of a Heffter array $H(n,k)$ to groups with order $2nk+1$, we provide direct constructions for elementary abelian Heffter arrays, which specifically include prime Heffter arrays (whose existence was previously established). When $q=2nk+1$ is a prime power, an elementary abelian $H(n,k)$ is termed "over $\mathbb{F}_q$" because its construction leverages both the additive and multiplicative properties of the field of order $q$. We demonstrate that in numerous instances, a direct construction of an $H(n,k)$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$, denoted as $A$, can be readily achieved by requiring $A$ to have rank 1 and potentially a robust set of {\it multipliers}. These multipliers are elements $m \in \mathbb{F}_q$ such that multiplying $A$ by $m$ results in $A$ itself, modulo permutations of rows and columns. An $H(n,k)$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ is defined as {\it optimal} if the size of its multiplier group equals the least common multiple of the odd components of $n$ and $k$, representing the theoretical maximum order. We present an explicit direct construction for a rank-one $H(n,k)$ that achieves near-optimal results for all admissible pairs $(n,k)$, with the exception of {\it demanding} cases where $n$ or $k$ is a power of 2, or where $nk$ possesses only a single odd prime divisor. Additionally, a less explicit construction suggests that optimal rank-one $H(n,k)$ arrays likely exist for every admissible pair $(n,k)$.

We propose a hybrid two-stage design to estimate the reliability of parallel-series and series-parallel systems (via duality) when component reliabilities are unknown and the total number of testable units per subsystem is not predetermined. When the total sample size is large and fixed, we systematically prove asymptotic optimality and validate this result through Monte Carlo simulations.

Semantic hashing converts documents into compact binary vectors, enabling efficient and effective similarity searches within large-scale information retrieval systems. Current state-of-the-art methods prioritize learning hash codes that enhance search effectiveness but typically rely on brute-force linear scans to traverse all codes, overlooking faster alternatives. One such alternative is multi-index hashing, which builds a reduced candidate set for searching; depending on hash code distribution, this can achieve sub-linear search times. This paper introduces Multi-Index Semantic Hashing (MISH), an unsupervised model that learns hash codes optimized for multi-index hashing to ensure both high efficiency and effectiveness. We develop novel, model-agnostic training objectives that are end-to-end trainable and designed to minimize the candidate sets generated by multi-index hashing. These objectives can be easily integrated into existing and future semantic hashing frameworks without being tied to specific code generation methods. Experimental comparisons against state-of-the-art baselines in document similarity search reveal that while multi-index hashing improves baseline efficiency over linear scans, those baselines remain over 33% slower than MISH, which simultaneously achieves state-of-the-art effectiveness.

In the aftermath of the gravitational wave-detected binary neutron star merger associated with the faint gamma-ray burst GRB 170817A (located at a distance of approximately 40 Mpc), we examine constraints on a local population of faint, short-duration gamma-ray bursts (defined here as having a duration $T_{90}<4$ s). We evaluate proposed low-redshift short GRBs and establish statistical limits for a population within $d\lessapprox200$ Mpc using data from Swift/BAT, Fermi/GBM, and CGRO/BATSE. Swift/BAT short GRBs indicate an upper limit for the all-sky rate of less than 4 per year at distances under 200 Mpc, representing fewer than 5% of short GRBs. Cross-correlating selected CGRO/BATSE and Fermi/GBM GRBs with galaxy positions within 100 Mpc yields a less stringent constraint of approximately 12 per year. A separate investigation into correlations arising from SGR giant flares in nearby galaxies ($d<11$ Mpc) sets an upper limit of less than 3 per year. Our findings suggest that events similar to GRB 170817A are likely rare in current short GRB catalogs. The most probable analogue is GRB 050906, whose Swift/BAT position aligned with the galaxy IC0327 at a distance of roughly 132 Mpc. Should binary neutron star merger rates be at the higher end of current estimates, our results imply that only a few percent of such mergers will produce detectable gamma-ray flashes during upcoming LIGO/Virgo science runs.

We introduce several straightforward mass-action systems featuring limit cycles that satisfy the Deficiency-One Theorem. These constructed examples are mass-conserving with a two-dimensional stoichiometric subspace. Leveraging the continuation software MATCONT, we illustrate the limit cycles across all stoichiometric classes simultaneously. The networks consist of trimolecular and tetramolecular reactions, with some displaying two or even three limit cycles. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a mass-action system derived from a bimolecular reaction network with a two-dimensional stoichiometric subspace cannot support a limit cycle.

A comprehensive rate theory for resonance energy transfer is developed to accommodate various degrees of freedom, including rotation, vibration, excitons, and polaritons, as well as coherently coupled composite states. This streamlined rate formula enables the derivation of key relationships: (i) the detailed balance condition under equal donor and acceptor temperatures; (ii) proportionality to the spectral overlap between donor emission and acceptor absorption; (iii) scaling with the effective coherent size, defined as the count of coherently linked molecules; and (iv) spatial and orientational dependencies arising from the interaction potential. When utilized to analyze cavity-assisted vibrational energy transfer, this formalism offers an intuitive and quantitative account of complex phenomena such as cooperativity, resonance, and nonlinearity within the collective vibrational strong coupling regime, as evidenced by recent simulations.

This study investigates the direct formation of the $J^{PC}=1^{++}$ charmonium state $\chi_{c1}(1P)$ through electron-positron annihilation by performing an energy scan near the resonance mass using the BESIII detector at the BEPCII collider. By integrating all collected data samples, an interference pattern emerges between the signal process ($e^+e^-\to \chi_{c1}(1P) \to \gamma J/\psi\to\gamma\mu^+\mu^-$) and background contributions ($e^+e^-\to \gamma_{\mathrm{ISR}} J/\psi\to\gamma_{\rm{ISR}}\mu^+\mu^-$ and $e^+e^-\to\gamma_{\rm{ISR}}\mu^+\mu^-$). A $\chi_{c1}(1P)$ signal is identified with a statistical significance of $5.1\sigma$, marking the first direct observation of a $C$-even state produced in $e^+e^-$ annihilation. The electronic width of the $\chi_{c1}(1P)$ resonance is measured as $\Gamma_{ee}=(0.12^{+0.13}_{-0.08})~\mathrm{eV}$, aligning with the order of magnitude predicted by theoretical models.

When an isolated positive wedge disclination acts upon an infinite, elastically inextensible flat sheet, it transforms the surface into a perfect cone, a state defined by negligible elastic stretching strains. This paper presents rigorous analytical and numerical findings regarding the deformed shape and stress distribution of a bounded Föppl-von Kármán elastic sheet with finite extensibility, highlighting deviations from the idealized cone model. Specifically, permitting elastic extensibility eliminates the localization of the Gaussian curvature field as a Dirac singularity at the defect; instead, significant negative Gaussian curvature persists in regions distant from the defect. Similarly, the stress field loses its Dirac singularity under these conditions. However, as the sheet's Young's modulus increases while maintaining fixed bending modulus and domain dimensions, both the curvature and stress fields approach a Dirac singularity. Notably, even in this limit, true inextensibility is not achieved by the bounded sheet because non-trivial Gaussian curvature remains away from the defect. Additional analyses in the study examine how various boundary conditions (free, simply supported, or partially clamped) influence the Gaussian curvature field outside the defect and affect the buckling transition from a flat to a conical configuration.

We demonstrate that the Euclidean and Lorentzian EPRL vertex amplitudes within covariant Loop Quantum Gravity are connected via a "Wick rotation," which transforms the real Immirzi parameter into purely imaginary values. This finding arises from the concurrent analytic continuation of the gauge groups' $Spin(4)$ and $SL(2,\mathbb{C})$ algebras, group elements, and unitary irreducible representations, specifically applied to the decomposition of both models using $SU(2)$ invariants and booster functions.

The $w_{1+\infty}$ symmetry algebra is present in the Einstein–Yang–Mills theory recently suggested by Strominger. In this work, we establish the supersymmetric $w_{1+\infty}$ symmetry by applying established results regarding the operator product expansions (OPEs) among the graviton, gravitino, gluon, and gluino within the supersymmetric variant of this theory. We explicitly compute four additional commutator relations involving soft currents. Furthermore, we examine the research of Odake et al. and Pope et al., proposing an additional symmetry current linked to the celestial gluino operator. Through this approach, all seven commutator relations are linked to those of the supersymmetric $w_{1+\infty}$ algebra with $SU(N)$ symmetry, subject to the constraints of wedge modes.

This study provides the inaugural comprehensive one-loop calculation of vector boson scattering (VBS) within the non-linear effective field theory defined by the bosonic sector of the electroweak chiral Lagrangian (EChL). Executed under the most general covariant $R_\xi$ gauges, the work simultaneously presents a novel computation for the Standard Model (SM) case for direct comparison. The one-loop VBS amplitude is derived using the diagrammatic method, specifically through the one-particle-irreducible (1PI) Green functions pertinent to these scattering processes. A primary focus of the research is the renormalization of all n-leg one-loop 1PI Green functions, carried out in the most general off-shell scenario with arbitrary external momenta. The paper details the complete renormalization program required for the EChL, which involves deriving counterterms for both electroweak parameters—such as boson masses and gauge couplings—and the EChL coefficients themselves. These latter coefficients are essential for handling the new divergences that arise when computing loops with the lowest chiral dimension Lagrangian. We explicitly list all relevant divergences and counterterms in the $R_\xi$ gauges and establish the full set of renormalization group equations for the EChL coefficients. Finally, we present numerical results for the one-loop cross section in the WZ channel within the EChL framework, comparing them against SM predictions.

Classical molecular dynamics simulations frequently serve as a key element in multi-modal analyses of scattering data, including diffraction and small-angle scattering. However, users of these experimental methods often lack formal training in molecular dynamics theory and practice, which can result in the simulations being treated as a "black box." This article presents an open educational resource (OER) aimed at introducing classical molecular dynamics to practitioners of scattering techniques. The resource is accessible as a series of interactive web pages for students and as an open-source software repository that educators can freely copy, modify, and redistribute. The OER covers topics such as classical atomistic modeling, the parameterization of interatomic potentials, molecular dynamics simulations, common sources of error, and strategies for applying simulations to analyze scattering data.

The nearby, relatively cool neutron star PSR J1957+5033, aged 840,000 years and previously observed only in X-ray and gamma-ray bands, exhibits a temperature of 0.2–0.3 MK, a distance of less than 1 kpc, and a low color excess of $E(B-V) \approx 0.03$. These characteristics render it an optimal target for optical detection to further refine its physical parameters. Consequently, we conducted the inaugural deep optical survey of this pulsar using the 10.4-meter Gran Telescopio Canarias in the $g'$ band, identifying a potential counterpart at $g'=27.63\pm 0.26$. The position of this candidate aligns with the pulsar's X-ray coordinates within 0.5 arcseconds. Under the assumption that this source is the genuine counterpart, we integrated the derived optical flux density with the pulsar's X-ray spectrum. Our analysis indicates that thermal emission from the neutron star's bulk surface can substantially contribute to the observed optical flux. Furthermore, our multi-wavelength spectral study supports the pulsar nature of the detected optical source by yielding physically plausible emission parameters. We demonstrate that incorporating optical data offers new constraints on both the pulsar's temperature and distance.

We reformulate the Foelner condition within an operator algebraic framework and demonstrate that it entails a specific dimension flatness property. Additionally, we establish that the Foelner condition extends current definitions of amenability and that the enveloping von Neumann algebra derived from a Foelner algebra is inherently injective. Leveraging these techniques, we unify existing findings regarding the vanishing of $L^2$-Betti numbers for amenable groups, groupoids, and quantum groups, while also generating a broad new class of algebras exhibiting this vanishing property.

Although non-equilibrium physics, particularly many-body localization (MBL), has garnered growing interest, reliable theoretical methods for investigating these non-equilibrium properties remain scarce. This Letter introduces a systematic methodology to detect MBL phases on a digital quantum computer using the excited-state variational quantum eigensolver (VQE). We present compelling evidence of MBL on actual quantum hardware, suggesting a viable path forward for simulating non-equilibrium systems that exceed classical computational limits during the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era. Furthermore, the proposed MBL probing protocol utilizing excited-state VQE is well-suited for NISQ devices; it can effectively distinguish between MBL and thermal phases using relatively shallow quantum circuits while maintaining robustness against quantum noise.

Topological Data Analysis (TDA), a method emerging from mathematics and data science, is increasingly gaining traction in environmental research. This paper offers an accessible introduction to persistent homology, a specific TDA technique highly effective for image analysis. While briefly covering theoretical foundations, our primary focus is on interpreting the tool's output and the insights it yields. We illustrate these concepts using the Sugar, Fish, Flower, and Gravel Dataset, originally created by Rasp et al. (2020) to study mesoscale cloud organization. We demonstrate how persistent homology and its vectorized form, persistence landscapes, can be integrated with basic machine learning algorithms to achieve strong performance, while also detailing how to explain these outcomes through image-level features. A key advantage of persistent homology is its interpretability; therefore, we examine not only the identified patterns but also the theoretical reasons behind them. Our objective is for readers to gain a deeper comprehension of TDA and persistent homology, learn to identify suitable applications for their own datasets, and understand the results generated by the provided GitHub code examples.

Streaming anomaly detection involves identifying irregular data points within continuous data streams, a task that challenges traditional and deep learning methods due to issues like concept drift and the need for continuous learning. Current state-of-the-art flow anomaly detection techniques often depend on fixed memory structures—such as hash functions or nearest neighbors—which struggle to effectively constrain high-frequency values akin to moving averages, eliminate seamless outliers, or operate within an end-to-end deep learning framework. This paper introduces a novel incremental anomaly detection approach that utilizes random Fourier features combined with quantum measurement mechanisms and density matrices, effectively functioning as an exponential moving average density estimator. Capable of handling potentially infinite data streams with a constant $O(1)$ update complexity, the method is evaluated systematically against 12 leading streaming anomaly detection algorithms across 12 datasets.

This study examines a nonlinear extension of the Caginalp phase field system that incorporates thermal memory. The proposed model serves as a first-order approximation of a thermodynamically consistent framework, drawing inspiration from theories by Green and Naghdi. It consists of two equations derived from phase dynamics and the universal balance law for internal energy, formulated using the phase variable (a non-conserved order parameter) and thermal displacement (the time integral of temperature). The paper establishes existence and continuous dependence results for both weak and strong solutions to the associated initial-boundary value problem. Subsequently, an optimal control problem is analyzed using a specific cost functional, where the distributed heat source and initial temperature function as control variables. The Fréchet differentiability of the control-to-state operator across appropriate Banach spaces is demonstrated, leading to the derivation of meaningful first-order necessary optimality conditions expressed as variational inequalities with adjoint variables. Finally, characterizations of the optimal controls are provided.

Deep learning approaches have shown great promise in the early detection and classification of lung nodules, though most traditional methods ignore uncertain cases by treating the task as a simple binary choice between malignant and benign. Recently, the unsure data model (UDM) addressed this limitation by framing the problem as ordinal regression to include uncertain nodules, outperforming standard binary classification. Building on this, this paper introduces the meta ordinal regression forest (MORF), an advancement over the state-of-the-art deep ordinal regression forest (DORF) in three key areas. First, MORF reduces prediction biases by fully leveraging deep features, whereas DORF requires fixing decision tree compositions prior to training. Second, MORF incorporates a novel grouped feature selection (GFS) module to re-sample decision tree split nodes. Finally, by integrating GFS, MORF utilizes a meta-learning-based weighting scheme to assign tree-specific weights to the selected features, contrasting with DORF's uniform weighting across all trees. Experiments on the LIDC-IDRI dataset confirm that MORF achieves superior results compared to existing methods, including DORF.

Deep algorithm unrolling has become a potent model-based strategy for constructing deep architectures that merge the interpretability of iterative algorithms with the performance benefits of supervised learning, particularly within sparse optimization contexts. This framework is ideal for biological imaging applications, where physics-driven models characterize the measurement process and the target information typically exhibits high structure. In this review, we examine the deep unrolling methodology and demonstrate its enhancements to source localization across various biological imaging scenarios.

We investigate topological physics within a one-dimensional nonlinear system by utilizing a mechanical rotator model featuring alternating spring constants. This nonlinear framework is smoothly linked to an acoustic model, specifically the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, when considering the linear limit. Our numerical analysis demonstrates that the quench dynamics of kinetic and potential energies in the nonlinear model can be effectively explained using the topological and trivial phases established in the corresponding linearized model. This suggests that edge states emerge in the topological phase even within the nonlinear system, potentially representing a form of bulk-edge correspondence for nonlinear dynamics.

Contemporary researchers increasingly leverage platforms like Twitter to disseminate their ideas and empirical findings. Recent research indicates that social media influences a paper's scientific impact; however, existing studies rely solely on tweet counts to measure this activity. To address this limitation, we introduce TweetPap, a large-scale dataset that incorporates temporal data regarding citations and tweets, along with tweet metadata, to quantify and analyze the discourse surrounding scientific papers on social media. This dataset is publicly accessible at https://github.com/lingo-iitgn/TweetPap.

Integrating deep learning with statistical learning offers new perspectives on structured, high-dimensional data. While traditional statistical modeling remains the primary approach for structured tabular data, deep learning can be understood as a form of generalized linear model (GLM) utilizing composite link functions. Through sufficient dimensionality reduction (SDR) and sparsity, nonlinear feature engineering is accomplished. This framework demonstrates that probabilistic methods at the model's output layer enable prediction, interpolation, and uncertainty quantification. Specifically, the approach first generates nonlinear features (factors) using sparse regularization and stochastic gradient optimization, then employs a stochastic output layer to estimate predictive uncertainty. Unlike many statistical models that rely on shallow additive architectures, deep learning utilizes layers of semi-affine input transformations to establish predictive rules. These transformations produce a set of attributes to which standard predictive statistical techniques can be applied, effectively combining scalability, rapid rule construction, and uncertainty quantification. Features are identified via sparse regularization within both supervised and unsupervised learning contexts. The text also clarifies the duality between shallow, wide models (e.g., PCA, PPR, RRR) and deep, skinny architectures (e.g., autoencoders, MLPs, CNNs, LSTMs), highlighting the practical significance of data transformations for designing effective networks. By incorporating probabilistic elements at the output, the model supports predictive uncertainty, while deep Gaussian processes and ReLU trees facilitate interpolation for classification tasks. Applications covering regression, classification, and interpolation are presented, concluding with suggestions for future research directions.

Gaia DR3 offers radial velocities for 33 million stars and spectroscopically determined atmospheric parameters for over five million targets. By integrating these with astrometric data, we can determine orbital and stellar parameters essential for understanding Milky Way populations and conducting galactic archaeology. Utilizing calibrated atmospheric parameters, 2MASS and Gaia-EDR3 photometry, and parallax-derived distances, we apply isochrone fitting to calculate stellar ages, initial masses, and reddenings for targets with spectroscopic data. Additionally, we compute orbital elements (actions, eccentricities, apocentre, pericentre, and Zmax) for all stars with radial velocities and astrometry, employing two literature-based line-of-sight distance sets and an axisymmetric Galactic potential. Comparisons with reference catalogs indicate that reliable ages (with relative uncertainties <50%) are achieved for stars younger than 9–10 Gyr, while older stars often exhibit underestimated ages. Turn-off stars provide the most robust age determinations, even with significant atmospheric parameter uncertainties. For giants and main-sequence stars, age uncertainties remain around 2 Gyr when extinction is below A_V < 2.5 mag. The complete catalogue is publicly downloadable, enabling a comprehensive analysis of the chemo-dynamical properties of the extended Solar neighbourhood, facilitating the characterization of spiral arms, the parameterization of disc dynamical heating, and an in-depth study of the Milky Way's chemical enrichment.

Contemporary natural language understanding models rely heavily on pretrained subword embeddings, yet practical applications often require reasoning about words that were absent or infrequent during the pretraining phase. We demonstrate that natural language inference tasks become significantly more difficult when they hinge on rarer vocabulary. Furthermore, we investigate how models can leverage definitions found in natural text to mitigate this limitation. Although a model's grasp of a definition is typically inferior to a robustly modeled word embedding, this approach recovers the majority of the performance deficit caused by encountering a completely untrained word.

We highlight that the production of new bosons through charged meson decays can significantly boost the sensitivity of beam-focused accelerator experiments to new physics. This improvement occurs because the focused charged mesons undergo three-body decays that avoid the helicity suppression typically affecting their standard two-body decays. Applying this mechanism realistically, we propose it as a way to explain the MiniBooNE low-energy excess, offering plausible dark-sector interpretations. As a proof of concept, we examine two well-motivated dark-sector frameworks: vector-portal dark matter models and models involving long-lived (pseudo)scalars. We argue that the parameter values required to account for the excess remain consistent with current constraints and can be probed by existing and upcoming accelerator-based neutrino experiments.

Machine Learning (ML) offers significant promise for expediting the discovery of novel materials and revealing the characteristics of established ones. However, a primary obstacle in applying ML to Materials Science is the scarcity of experimental data regarding material properties. This study demonstrates a method for deriving material descriptors from atomistic structures found in extensive simulation datasets, which are then utilized to enhance the prediction of experimental properties, specifically the formation energy of solids. By training a Graph Neural Network to regress simulated formation energies based on atomic structures, these learned descriptors are generated. When applied to predict experimental properties, this approach surpasses current methods relying exclusively on chemical composition. Furthermore, the efficacy of this strategy improves under more rigorous generalization constraints, such as when training data is limited or when extrapolating to unseen chemical environments.

We introduce a comprehensive theory describing the coherence of Fano lasers, which rely on a bound state within the continuum. Our findings indicate that these lasers can achieve a reduction in quantum-limited linewidth by several orders of magnitude, a capability that is further enhanced through the introduction of mirror symmetry breaking. However, unlike conventional macroscopic lasers, the linewidth in these systems may broaden again due to optical nonlinearities amplified by intense light localization, a phenomenon that helps identify ideal material platforms. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the coherence of this novel microscopic laser type can be intuitively grasped via a simple, effective potential model. Utilizing this framework, we analyze laser stability and derive how the linewidth depends on the general Fano lineshape. Ultimately, our model supports the integration of additional design parameters and is applicable to a broad range of lasers featuring strongly dispersive mirrors.

We investigate the spin n-point functions of the planar Ising model on a simply connected domain $\Omega$, discretized by the square lattice $\delta\mathbb{Z}^{2}$, under a near-critical scaling limit. Although the scaling limit over the full plane $\mathbb{C}$ has been characterized using fermionic field theory, the limit for a general $\Omega$ remains unexplored. We demonstrate that within a massive scaling regime where the inverse temperature scales as $\beta\sim\beta_{c}-m_{0}\delta$ with a constant $m_{0}<0$, renormalized spin correlations converge to a continuous quantity governed by a boundary value problem defined on $\Omega$. Specifically, when $\Omega=\mathbb{C}$ and $n=2$, our findings recover the renowned formula from [WMTB76] involving the Painlevé III transcendent. To achieve this, we extend the extensive discrete complex analytic framework established in the critical context to the massive setting, thereby inducing a perturbation of standard concepts regarding analyticity and harmonicity.

Self-supervised models for speech processing create representational spaces without relying on external labels, offering a promising approach to reduce the need for expensive manual annotations, an issue especially critical for low-resource languages. However, the nature of these constructed spaces remains unclear: since human perception adapts to the sounds of a listener's native language, do self-supervised models exhibit similar behavior? This study investigates the representational spaces of three state-of-the-art self-supervised models—wav2vec 2.0, HuBERT, and contrastive predictive coding (CPC)—by comparing them with the perceptual spaces of French and English speakers, considering both global trends and behavioral differences between the groups. The findings indicate that while the CPC model displays a minor native language effect, wav2vec 2.0 and HuBERT appear to develop a universal speech perception space that is not specific to any language. Furthermore, when compared to supervised phone recognizers, the self-supervised models capture relatively fine-grained perceptual phenomena, whereas supervised models are more effective at reflecting the coarser, native-language-specific effects observed in human perception.

Perpendicular magnetization is crucial for achieving high-density memory using magnetic materials, a requirement that also demands high-spin polarization of conduction electrons to generate large electric signals via spin-dependent transport. While Heusler alloys are renowned for their half-metallic electronic structures, their typical cubic lattice structure tends to favor in-plane magnetization, thereby suppressing perpendicular magnetic anisotropy (PMA). This research investigates an inverse-type Heusler alloy, Mn$_{2-\delta}$CoGa$_{1+\delta}$ (MCG), featuring slight off-stoichiometry ($\delta$) and anticipated half-metallic properties. In MCG films exhibiting a minor tetragonal distortion of a few percent, we measured a relatively large uniaxial magnetocrystalline anisotropy constant ($K_\mathrm{u}$) of approximately 10$^5$ J/m$^3$ at room temperature. A direct positive correlation was established between the lattice constant $c/a$ ratio and $K_\mathrm{u}$. Kerr microscopy imaging of magnetic domains visually confirmed corresponding changes in domain patterns alongside variations in $K_\mathrm{u}$. Utilizing synchrotron soft x-ray beams for X-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD), we probed the origins of PMA. The XMCD spectra revealed negligible angular variation in the orbital magnetic moment ($\Delta m_\mathrm{orb}$), indicating that the Bruno term plays a minimal role in determining $K_\mathrm{u}$. First-principles calculations successfully accounted for the small $\Delta m_\mathrm{orb}$ and the observed correlation between the $c/a$ ratio and $K_\mathrm{u}$. Based on second-order perturbation theory regarding spin–orbit coupling, the study attributes the magnetocrystalline anisotropy to the mixing of occupied $\uparrow$-spin and unoccupied $\downarrow$-spin states, which is responsible for the PMA in MCG films.

Text embeddings serve as powerful features for applications like semantic search and text similarity computation. While prior research typically trains specialized models tailored to specific use cases with varying datasets, objectives, and architectures, this work demonstrates that large-scale contrastive pre-training on unsupervised data yields high-quality vector representations for both text and code. These same unsupervised text embeddings, which set new state-of-the-art benchmarks in linear-probe classification, also exhibit strong semantic search capabilities, occasionally rivaling fine-tuned models. Our best unsupervised model improves average linear-probe classification accuracy by 4% over the previous best unsupervised model and by 1.8% over the best supervised model across seven tasks. Furthermore, when evaluated on large-scale semantic search, these embeddings achieve relative improvements of 23.4%, 14.7%, and 10.6% over prior unsupervised methods on the MSMARCO, Natural Questions, and TriviaQA benchmarks, respectively. Similarly, by training code embedding models on (text, code) pairs, we achieve a 20.8% relative improvement over the best previous work in code search.

A directed graph has a dichromatic number of at most 2 if its vertices can be 2-colored such that each color class induces an acyclic subgraph. While an oriented graph results from assigning one of two directions to every edge of a graph, this study focuses on oriented graphs with a dichromatic number exceeding 2. Specifically, we examine $3$-dicritical oriented graphs, defined as those where deleting any single arc lowers the dichromatic number to 2. We demonstrate the existence of infinitely many such graphs. Building on Neumann-Lara's identification of the four $7$-vertex $3$-dichromatic tournaments, we identify the $64$ $8$-vertex $3$-dichromatic tournaments that do not contain any of these four. Additionally, we enumerate all $159$ $3$-dicritical oriented graphs on $8$ vertices and establish the minimum number of arcs required for a $3$-dicritical oriented graph, noting that exactly one such graph exists with $7$ vertices and $20$ arcs.

This paper presents an enhanced mixture of probabilistic principal component analysis (PPCA) designed for nonlinear, data-driven process monitoring. To achieve this, the study employs a mixture of probabilistic principal component analysers to construct a model of the underlying nonlinear process using local PPCA models. Additionally, a new composite monitoring statistic is developed by integrating two monitoring statistics from a modified PPCA-based fault detection method, with the weighted mean of these statistics serving as the metric for identifying potential anomalies. The advantages of this proposed algorithm are evaluated against several unsupervised algorithms. Finally, the effectiveness of the scheme is further validated through applications to the Tennessee Eastman process and an autosuspension model.

This article seeks to evaluate the capabilities and practical applicability of Light Fidelity (Li-Fi) as a communication technology by directly comparing it with subdomains of Wireless Fidelity (Wi-Fi), the dominant wireless system. It explores the global potential of Li-Fi through specific use cases and its relationship with Fifth Generation (5G) technology. Finally, the paper outlines the current challenges and future pathways required for this system's development.

In Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), suboptimal or erroneous encoding of information can degrade the quality of representations derived from subsequent sequence elements, ultimately resulting in incorrect predictions and diminished model performance. Similarly, humans can be misled by complex linguistic structures, such as garden path sentences (e.g., "The horse raced past the barn fell"), though they possess the capacity to adjust their understanding and recover once new context becomes available. Drawing inspiration from this human ability, I propose augmenting standard RNNs with a gradient-based correction mechanism. This approach aims to allow models to dynamically refine their internal sentence representations, correcting deviations as they arise. Consequently, this could yield more robust models with flexible representations, even during inference.

I conducted various experiments within the domain of language modeling to evaluate the impact of this mechanism in detail. Specifically, I investigated modifications based on different types of time-dependent error signals and their influence on performance. Additionally, this work includes an analysis of the model's confidence in its predictions during training and on difficult test cases, examining how manipulating this confidence affects outcomes. Finally, I compared the behavior of these novel models against a standard LSTM baseline, conducting a detailed study of error cases to identify areas for future research. My findings indicate that while the proposed method offers promising theoretical guarantees and intuitive appeal, it achieves only minor improvements over the baseline due to practical implementation challenges and the limited efficacy of the tested model variants.

The DARTWARS initiative aims to create advanced traveling wave parametric amplifiers characterized by high gain, extensive bandwidth, significant saturation power, and noise performance approaching the quantum limit. These devices are designed for the 5–10 GHz frequency range, with a target noise temperature of approximately 600 mK. Development proceeds via two distinct methodologies: one utilizing Josephson junctions and the other leveraging the kinetic inductance of superconductors. This specific contribution centers on the Josephson-based traveling wave parametric amplifier, detailing its design, initial measurement results, and an evaluation of the homogeneity within arrays of Josephson junctions.

We demonstrate the existence of a red-blue coloring of $[N]$ that contains no blue 3-term arithmetic progression and no red arithmetic progression of length $e^{C(\log N)^{3/4}(\log \log N)^{1/4}}$. This result implies that the two-colour van der Waerden number $w(3,k)$ is bounded below by $k^{b(k)}$, where $b(k) = c \big( \frac{\log k}{\log\log k} \big)^{1/3}$. Previously, based on empirical data, it was conjectured that $w(3,k) = O(k^2)$.

In the era of surveillance capitalism, it is critical to prioritize trustworthiness when designing new smart services. Edge Intelligence, which integrates AI and edge computing, serves as a pivotal technology for these services, making trustworthy Edge Intelligence a top research priority. However, defining the criteria for trustworthy Edge Intelligence is complex. This paper investigates the requirements for trustworthy Edge Intelligence within the specific context of voice-activated services. We advance the understanding of trustworthiness in this emerging domain through three contributions: first, we introduce a unified framework that jointly evaluates trustworthiness attributes from both AI and IoT perspectives. Second, we present findings from a concrete case study on voice-activated services that illustrates the interconnections among three key attributes: privacy, security, and fairness. Third, drawing on our empirical and analytical results, we identify significant challenges and open questions that outline essential future research directions for trustworthy Edge Intelligence.

Flaky tests pose significant challenges by disrupting automated build pipelines that require all tests to pass and eroding confidence in testing reliability. Although numerous causes of flakiness are known and analysis tools exist to identify them, these methods typically only offer developers advice on refactoring to ensure deterministic outcomes. We contend that a primary source of flakiness is the absence of precise assumptions defining the conditions under which a test is valid. To address this, we propose a sanitization technique that rapidly isolates flaky tests by inferring these assumptions dynamically, enabling automated builds to continue by ignoring problematic tests. We validated this approach on Java and Groovy programs by creating extensions for three major testing frameworks (JUnit4, JUnit5, and Spock) that transparently inject inferred assumptions. Notably, when using JUnit5, these extensions can be deployed without modifying the project's source code. We evaluated the utility of our method using six real-world applications, targeting known flakiness issues stemming from test dependencies on network availability. Our results demonstrate that the approach effectively mitigates failures caused by connectivity problems with high precision and recall.

We consider a generic real singlet scalar extension of the Standard Model, situated in a vacuum defined by $(v,w)$ at the electroweak scale, where $v=246$ GeV represents the Higgs vacuum expectation value and $w$ denotes that of the singlet scalar. By imposing conditions for {\it absolute} vacuum stability, positivity, and perturbativity up to the Planck scale, we demonstrate that the viable parameter space for the model is heavily restricted across various singlet vacuum expectation values ($w = 0.1, 1, 10, 100$ TeV). Furthermore, our results indicate that the singlet scalar mass can range from a few GeV to just below the TeV scale.

The field of exoplanets is currently witnessing a surge in the discovery of new planets and systems. Scientists are keen on deciphering the compositions and internal structures of these extraterrestrial worlds to deduce their formation histories. Crucially, accurately applying the equations of state (EOS) for various materials to internal structure models is essential. Consequently, this guide outlines the precise steps required to convert an EOS into a mass-radius relation for exoplanets, emphasizing the underlying physics and chemistry, and underscores the necessity of visualizing these results.

Menon's identity is a well-known result concerning sums of greatest common divisors and the Euler totient function $\phi$. In a recent publication, Zhao and Cao established a Menon-type identity given by $\sum\limits_{\substack{k=1}}^{n}(k-1,n)\chi(k) = \phi(n)\tau(\frac{n}{d})$, where $\chi$ denotes a Dirichlet character modulo $n$ with conductor $d$. We present an analogous identity in which the greatest common divisor is replaced by a generalized version. Furthermore, we demonstrate that certain arguments utilized in deriving the Zhao-Cao identity can be refined when employing the method we introduce.

Advancing object detection toward open-vocabulary and few-shot transfer has long posed a significant challenge in computer vision. This study investigates a continual learning strategy that enhances a detector's zero/few-shot capabilities through multi-dataset vision-language pre-training. By utilizing natural language as a knowledge representation, we develop methods to aggregate a "visual vocabulary" across diverse datasets and unify the task within a language-conditioned detection framework. Specifically, we introduce OmDet, a novel language-aware detector, along with a new training mechanism. This multimodal detection network overcomes technical hurdles associated with joint training across multiple datasets, enabling generalization to an arbitrary number of datasets without the need for manual label taxonomy merging. Experimental results on COCO, Pascal VOC, and Wider Face/Pedestrian datasets confirm the method's effectiveness, achieving performance equal to or superior to separate training in joint settings. Furthermore, pre-training on over 20 million images featuring 4 million unique object concepts allows the model to be evaluated on 35 ODinW downstream tasks. These results demonstrate that OmDet attains state-of-the-art fine-tuned performance on ODinW. Additionally, analysis indicates that scaling the proposed pre-training approach further improves zero/few-shot tuning capabilities, highlighting a promising direction for future expansion.

The dressing method, utilizing a regularization technique, is employed to derive both higher-order and simple $N$-soliton solutions for the Gerdjikov-Ivanov equation. Through a dressing transformation applied to the eigenfunction of a seed solution, the regularity conditions for the resulting dressed eigenfunctions are determined, thereby defining the connection between the potential and the scattering data.

Decades-old biases rooted in culture, gender, and ethnicity have long shaped human social interactions, influencing machine learning (ML) models and causing significant downstream issues in natural language processing (NLP). Mitigating gender bias in information retrieval (IR) is crucial to prevent the spread of stereotypes. This study utilizes a dataset comprising two elements: (1) a document's relevance to a query and (2) its "gender," determined by substituting pronouns with male, female, or neutral forms. We demonstrate that pre-trained IR models struggle in zero-shot retrieval tasks when subjected to full fine-tuning of a large BERT encoder, whereas lightweight fine-tuning using adapter networks boosts zero-shot performance by nearly 20% compared to baselines. Furthermore, we reveal that these models harbor gender biases, leading to retrieved articles that disproportionately favor males. To address this, we introduce a debiasing method that penalizes the model for preferring males over females, yielding a system that retrieves articles with gender balance.

Numerous online platforms continuously gather real-time data, such as traffic updates, from various Points of Interest (PoIs). A significant challenge in this status acquisition process is determining the optimal upload frequency for each PoI, given their self-interested nature and private, time-varying preferences. This paper addresses a general multi-period status acquisition system designed to maximize aggregate social welfare while maintaining platform freshness, quantified by the age of information metric. To tackle the resulting time-varying information asymmetry, we propose a Long-Term Decomposition (LtD) mechanism. This approach constructs a virtual social welfare function relying solely on current private information, thereby breaking down per-period operations into multiple distributed bidding scenarios for both PoIs and platforms. The LtD mechanism allows platforms to balance payoff maximization against freshness requirements with tunable precision. Furthermore, it achieves social performance comparable to a benchmark with symmetric information and asymptotically satisfies platform freshness constraints. Numerical experiments using real-world data demonstrate that even when platforms prioritize payoff maximization, each PoI secures a non-negative long-term payoff.

Epistemic specifications and logic programs build upon disjunctive logic programs under the stable model semantics by incorporating modal constructs known as subjective literals. These literals enable the verification of whether a standard literal holds true across all or some stable models of a program; these models, referred to as \emph{belief sets}, are aggregated into a \emph{world view}. This framework facilitates the representation of propositions under either open or closed world assumptions. Although multiple formal semantics have been proposed to capture the language's underlying intuitions—creating a fragmented landscape of current research—this paper offers a comprehensive overview of the field's origins and its applicability to knowledge representation and reasoning tasks. Furthermore, it presents a detailed examination of the properties of existing semantics and outlines future research challenges. The work is currently under consideration for publication in the *Theory and Practice of Logic Programming* (TPLP).

This study examines global frequency selection in two-dimensional vortex shedding within the wake of a flat plate. The analysis utilizes mean flow velocity profiles derived from experiments conducted at Reynolds numbers of 1850 and 3350 (defined relative to plate thickness and free-stream velocity), focusing on two trailing edge configurations: blunt and circular. Through local spatio-temporal analysis of these measured profiles, we determine the global shedding frequency, which aligns exceptionally well with experimental data. Complementing these findings, we introduce a novel low-dimensional modeling approach using proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) of the flow fields for flat plate wakes. We find that a model utilizing only two POD modes accurately predicts the global shedding frequency. Furthermore, our results underscore the significance of nonlinear interactions between the mean flow and higher harmonics, providing experimental validation for the theoretical criterion proposed by Sipp & Lebedev (JFM 2007).

Algorithmic approaches for simulating the spatio-temporal dynamics of multi-cellular systems are essential for creating synthetic datasets to benchmark bioinformatics tools and for testing experimental hypotheses across various in-silico environments. Specifically, efficient algorithms are required to resolve the difficult balance between scalability and expressivity, a constraint that often hinders the production of realistic simulations, particularly regarding cancer evolution. We present OG-SPACE, the Optimized Gillespie algorithm for Stochastic sPAtial models of Cancer Evolution, a computational framework designed to simulate the spatio-temporal progression of cancer subpopulations alongside bulk and single-cell sequencing procedures. OG-SPACE adapts the Gillespie algorithm to efficiently manage large cell populations, supporting diverse birth-death processes and interaction rules on arbitrary lattices. The framework outputs visual snapshots of spatial system configurations over time, cell phylogenies, mutational trees, variant allele frequency spectra (for bulk data), and cell genotypes (for single-cell data). OG-SPACE is freely accessible at: https://github.com/BIMIB-DISCo/OG-SPACE

Even without spontaneous emission or laser field modulation, atoms moving through a detuned standing wave can undergo chaotic scattering. Although spontaneous emission partially obscures this phenomenon, Monte Carlo simulations indicate it remains detectable in actual experiments via absorption imaging or atom deposition on a substrate. This chaotic behavior arises from the specific dynamics of atomic dipole moments as they traverse field nodes and exhibits a strong dependence on the atom-laser detuning value.

Fairness assumptions commonly employed to verify liveness properties are often criticized for being overly restrictive or unrealistic. Conversely, justness, which is considered the minimal fairness requirement for such verification, fails to be maintained under classical semantic equivalences like strong bisimilarity. To address this limitation, we propose a more refined alternative to strong bisimilarity known as enabling preserving bisimilarity. We demonstrate that this equivalence preserves justness and functions as a congruence for all standard operators, including parallel composition.

Renal arteries from intact rat kidneys, whose vasculature was infused with the contrast agent Microfil, were analyzed using Micro-CT imaging. An automated algorithm calculated the hierarchical organization of the vessel trees and measured properties of inter-branch segments. These segmented vascular structures, including local diameters and perfusion territories, were mapped onto representative models for visual inspection. By comparing various parameters, key geometrical properties were identified as exhibiting minimal variation across different specimens. The study demonstrates that fractal scaling in non-symmetric branching differs from that in symmetric branching (such as the consistent mean bronchial diameters at each generation observed in lungs). Furthermore, perfused tissue displays negligible inter-specimen variability, suggesting its potential utility in future research aimed at characterizing vascular branching geometry in diseased tissues and organs.

This study examines the configuration space of planar kinematic chains, defined by $n$ links and joints, specifically focusing on conditions that ensure the chain remains closed. We derive explicit formulas for the joint angles required to maintain closure, expressed through a novel set of parameters known as diagonal lengths—the distances from the joints to the origin of the closed chain. Furthermore, we observe that these diagonals reside within a domain characterized by a straightforward structure. We anticipate that this fresh perspective will prove useful for various challenges, including motion planning and singularity analysis for closed kinematic chains. To illustrate the method's practicality, we provide numerical examples.

When a court is aware that a respondent possesses a device password, can it legally compel them to input it? This work proposes a novel perspective on the *foregone conclusion* doctrine established in *Fisher v. US*, which addresses this issue. The ultimate goal of this research area is to develop a framework for determining when testimony implicitly contained within an action is already known to the government. While this paper adopts a narrower scope, it introduces a framework for defining actions where all implicit testimony is, by construction, a foregone conclusion. Our methodology places the burden of proof on the government to show that it is not relying on the respondent's "truthtelling."

Leveraging original legal analysis alongside precise computer science formalisms, we introduce "demonstrability" as a core concept for characterizing compelled acts. Furthermore, we provide a language to assess whether a compelled action meaningfully achieves the government's objectives as effectively as desired. We then apply these definitions to evaluate the compellability of various cryptographic primitives, including decryption, multifactor authentication, commitment schemes, and hash functions. Notably, our framework yields a new conclusion regarding compelled decryption in scenarios involving deniable encryption: while the government may compel the act, the respondent remains free to choose any password.

We introduce a general framework for simulating measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD). This model enables the prediction of experimental results for systems featuring linear channel loss by accurately reproducing gain values, error rates across various bases, and final key rates. It remains applicable to MDI-QKD implementations utilizing any convex source states or coding schemes. Consequently, this tool is essential for characterizing and assessing the performance of diverse MDI-QKD protocols, serving as a valuable resource for research into quantum key distribution.

This paper introduces a novel reconstruction technique designed to investigate the low-mass sector of top-quark pair ($t\bar{t}$) associated production with a generic scalar boson ($\phi$) at the LHC. Compared to existing methods, our approach achieves at least a two-fold improvement in mass resolution within the low-mass region without compromising analytical sensitivity; furthermore, it enhances the mass reconstruction of the 125 GeV Higgs boson for this specific production channel. The study employs an effective Lagrangian to model a scalar with generic Yukawa couplings to top quarks. A comprehensive phenomenological analysis was conducted using Standard Model background and signal events generated via MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO and reconstructed through a kinematic fit. By utilizing CP-sensitive variables, we maximize the discrimination between CP-even and CP-odd components of the Yukawa couplings. Confidence Levels (CLs) for excluding $\phi$ bosons with mixed CP properties were calculated as a function of the top Yukawa couplings. The analyzed mass range extends from slightly above the $\Upsilon$ mass up to 40 GeV, though the methodology remains applicable to arbitrary masses. In the absence of a discovered light scalar, we derive 95% CL exclusion limits for the absolute values of the CP-even and CP-odd Yukawa couplings, which are projected to reach approximately 0.10 and 0.50, respectively, by the end of the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) phase. Finally, we examine how these constraints restrict the parameter space of the complex two-Higgs doublet model (C2HDM).

In V2V Mode-3, eNodeBs allocate subchannels to vehicles to enable their periodic broadcasting of CAM messages \cite{b2}. A critical requirement is ensuring that vehicles within the same cluster transmit on orthogonal time subchannels\footnote{A subchannel is a time-frequency resource unit capable of effectively carrying a CAM message.} to prevent collisions. While resource or subchannel allocation issues are typically modeled as weighted bipartite graphs, this specific scenario introduces an additional time orthogonality constraint that standard graph matching techniques \cite{b3} cannot easily address; consequently, our method explicitly incorporates this constraint. Furthermore, we execute the allocation process sequentially, prioritizing clusters based on their level of constraint. To clarify the nature of the problem, Fig. 1 depicts two partially overlapping clusters where a conflict arises between vehicles $V_8$ and $V_{10}$ because their assigned subchannels fall within the same subframe.

We introduce a spin current diode capable of operating under small applied bias conditions, specifically within the linear-response regime.
