Between these events, the input is maintained using a Zero-Order-Hold mechanism. The analysis demonstrates that the time interval between consecutive triggers is uniformly bounded from below. Consequently, the presence of this minimal dwell-time ensures the closed-loop system avoids Zeno behavior. The well-posedness of the closed-loop system, contingent upon specific model validity conditions, is established. Furthermore, via a Lyapunov-based approach, global exponential convergence of the system to the target setpoint is proven. A simulation case is presented to validate these theoretical findings.

As established in \cite{arkani2018unwinding} by Arkani-Hamed, Thomas, and Trnka, two conjectural characterizations of the tree amplituhedron $\ampli$ were proposed, contingent upon whether $m$ is even or odd: the winding number applies when $m$ is even, whereas the crossing number applies when $m$ is odd. This paper demonstrates that any point residing within the open tree amplituhedron adheres to either the winding or crossing description.

New physics models, whether elementary or composite, frequently produce similar signatures in direct collider searches. A prime example is the production of a light pseudoscalar alongside a monochromatic photon from a Z boson decay at future $e^+e^-$ colliders. We leverage the connection between observing such signals in Z decays and electroweak precision data to differentiate between composite and elementary scalar models. Our findings present a compelling and diverse physics scenario for upcoming colliders, illustrating how a lepton collider operating at the Z mass can serve as a discovery engine for new physics within the Higgs sector.

We present an explicit minimal graded free resolution, expressed through representations of the symmetric group $S_d$, for a Galois-theoretic configuration of $d$ points in $\mathbb{P}^{d-2}$ previously examined by Bhargava regarding ring parametrizations. When applied to the generic fiber of a simply branched degree $d$ cover of $\mathbb{P}^1$ by a relatively canonically embedded curve $C$, this construction yields a novel interpretation of the splitting types of syzygy bundles found in its relative minimal resolution. Specifically, our results demonstrate that these splitting types correspond to scrollar invariants of resolvent covers, subject to a minor shift. This significantly extends an earlier finding by Casnati, who noted that the first syzygy bundle of a degree $4$ cover decomposes according to the scrollar invariants of its cubic resolvent. Furthermore, our work reveals that the splitting types of syzygy bundles, alongside the multi-set of scrollar invariants, fall within a broader class of invariant multi-sets associated with $C \to \mathbb{P}^1$: there exists one such multi-set for every irreducible representation of $S_d$, corresponding to each partition of $d$.

This whitepaper addresses the astrophysical systematics encountered in dark matter research. In both direct and indirect detection efforts, these systematics often represent the primary constraints on sensitivity. Given the diversity of dark matter search methods, there is a corresponding variety of background sources. We examine major systematics across searches utilizing photons (radio and gamma rays), cosmic rays, neutrinos, and gravitational waves. Key topics include astrophysical sources and their interactions that can mimic dark matter signals, which rely on a thorough understanding of the cosmic environment—including gas distributions and magnetic field structures—as well as relevant nuclear astrophysics. Additionally, we discuss the astrophysics of celestial bodies and galaxies used as probes, ranging from black holes to dwarf galaxies. We also cover astrophysical backgrounds associated with probing dark matter distribution and kinematics, which affect a broad spectrum of dark matter studies. Looking ahead, the emergence of multi-messenger astronomy and new analytical techniques to leverage it will provide strategic avenues to better characterize astrophysical backgrounds, thereby enhancing dark matter sensitivity.

Numerous high-dimensional prediction or classification tasks benefit from complementary feature data, such as prior biological insights into (epi)genetic markers. This work addresses scenarios where numerical prior information offers guidance on both the magnitude and direction of feature effects, such as regression coefficients derived from earlier research. We introduce a method for incorporating multiple sources of such prior knowledge into penalized regression models. When appropriate co-data is available, this integration enhances predictive performance, as demonstrated through simulations and practical applications. The proposed method is available in the R package `transreg` (https://github.com/lcsb-bds/transreg).

With deep learning establishing itself as the dominant paradigm in natural language processing, the demand for appropriate active learning strategies has reached a critical level. Although active learning methods leveraging nearest neighbor classifiers have been introduced and shown promising outcomes, current implementations struggle with mutually exclusive classes due to an inability to guarantee inter-class separation. Consequently, informative samples located in margin regions remain undetected, hindering overall active learning performance. To address this, we introduce NCMAL, a novel Nearest Neighbor Classifier with Margin penalty for Active Learning. Our approach first incorporates mandatory margin penalties between classes to ensure both inter-class discrepancy and intra-class compactness. Second, we propose a new sample selection strategy designed to identify informative instances within margin areas. Extensive experiments on various datasets against state-of-the-art methods demonstrate that our approach yields superior results with fewer annotated samples compared to all baselines.

Over recent decades, US wind power generation has expanded substantially, marked by an increase in both the quantity and average size of operational turbines. Utilizing lower specific power—characterized by larger rotor blades relative to turbine capacity—enhances capacity factors and lowers costs; however, this trend simultaneously diminishes system efficiency, defined as the proportion of wind energy passing through the rotor sweep that is converted into electricity. Concurrently, it may reduce output power density, representing the electric power generated per unit of rotor swept area. This study decomposes historical US wind power generation data from 2001 to 2021 to assess the impact of declining specific power on system efficiency and output power density. Additionally, we break down the wind power available to turbines into components driven by shifts in installation locations and variations in average hub heights.

Prostate cancer ranks as the second leading cause of cancer-related mortality for men in the United States. Accurate prostate zonal segmentation is crucial for effective MRI diagnosis; however, current state-of-the-art automated methods often struggle to generate well-contained volumetric segmentations. This challenge arises because specific MRI slices, particularly the base and apex, are significantly more difficult to segment than others. While incorporating cross-slice relationships between adjacent images could address this issue, existing approaches fail to fully learn or utilize these connections. To resolve this, we introduce a novel cross-slice attention mechanism integrated into a Transformer module, designed to systematically capture cross-slice relationships across various scales. This module is compatible with any existing learning-based segmentation framework that includes skip connections. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach effectively captures cross-slice information, enhancing the performance of current state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, our method improves segmentation accuracy in the peripheral zone, ensuring consistent results across all prostate slices, including the apex, mid-gland, and base.

This study develops an effective mathematical model for the well-known slayer exciter transformer circuit. By employing both physical and computational approaches, we analyze various facets of the circuit. Computer simulations are utilized to gather data on diverse circuit parameters, which are then used to generate plots illustrating the behavior of different components. Additionally, we derive an approximate equation designed to maximize the secondary output voltage and discuss a feasible method for constructing the circuit using low-cost materials.

Nonlocal Quantum Electrodynamics (QED), a straightforward extension of the Standard Model, offers an explanation for the lepton $g-2$ anomalies. This approach adheres to the same gauge symmetry as standard QED, requiring no new particles or interactions. By utilizing correlation functions involving nonlocal strength tension and lepton-photon interactions, the theory successfully accounts for the discrepancies observed in both $\Delta a_\mu$ and $\Delta a_e$. Furthermore, applying this same methodology estimates the deviation of the $\tau$ lepton's anomalous magnetic moment from the Standard Model prediction to fall between $1.19\times10^{-5}$ and $3.21\times10^{-3}$, a range encompassed by current experimental uncertainties.
We classify Legendrian torus knots within the standard tight contact structure on S^1 \times S^2 up to Legendrian isotopy.

This paper introduces a block cipher design grounded in quasigroups. The encryption and decryption processes employ quasigroup-based string transformations within their respective round functions. We demonstrate the design's resilience against standard differential, linear, and algebraic cryptanalytic attacks. Furthermore, we conduct a detailed statistical evaluation using the NIST test suite across CBC, CFB, OFB, and CTR modes. By comparing these experimental results with AES-128 under identical conditions, we conclude that our algorithm possesses randomizing capabilities equivalent to those of AES-128.

This study presents an electronic and local structural analysis of double perovskites Sr$_{2-x}$La$_x$CoNbO$_6$ ($x=$ 0--1) via x-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) and extended x-ray absorption fine structures (EXAFS) at the Nb, Co, and Sr $K$-edges. Through $ab$ $initio$ simulations and a thorough examination of the Nb and Co $K$-edge XANES spectra, we confirm that pre-edge features originate from 1$s$ electron transitions to mixed $p-d$ hybridized states. We identify a $z$-out Jahn-Teller (JT) distortion in CoO$_6$ octahedra that diminishes monotonically as the concentration of JT-inactive Co$^{2+}$ ions increases with $x$. Conversely, the $z$-in distortion in NbO$_6$ octahedra stays constant until $x=$ 0.4 before declining with further doping; this abrupt shift in Nb's local coordination drives the evolution of antiferromagnetic interactions in samples where $x \geqslant$ 0.6. Additionally, we correlate the extent of octahedral distortion with the white line intensity in XANES spectra and discuss potential causes. Notably, signatures of KN$_1$ double electron excitation appear in the Sr $K$-edge EXAFS spectra for all compositions, aligning well with the $Z$+1 approximation. Finally, the Co L$_{2,3}$ edge indicates a reduction in crystal field strength and a corresponding increase in charge transfer energy ($\Delta_{ct}$) upon La substitution.
Drawing inspiration from P. Frankl's inductive proof of the LYM-inequality, we present an inductive proof of the Bollob\'{a}s two family theorem.

This work investigates a dependently typed extension of a multi-stage programming language similar to MetaOCaml, incorporating quasi-quotation and cross-stage persistence to treat code fragments as first-class values, alongside an evaluation mechanism for dynamically generated programs. We posit that dependent types can enforce robust invariants on the behavior of such generated code, surpassing basic type safety. However, integrating these features is non-trivial, as the resulting type system must account for type stages, which roughly correspond to the depth of surrounding quotations. To rigorously analyze these properties, we introduce $\lambda^{MD}$, an extension of Hanada and Igarashi's $\lambda^{\triangleright\%}$ calculus that includes dependent types. We demonstrate its key properties: preservation, confluence, strong normalization under full reduction, and progress under staged reduction. Furthermore, inspired by code generators that produce types dependent on external values, we highlight the importance of cross-stage persistence in dependently typed multi-stage programming and identify specific type equivalences that do not stem directly from reduction rules.

We demonstrate that for a reduced algebra $A$ over a characteristic zero field $k$ with a vanishing module of Kähler differentials ($\Omega_{A/k}=0$), $A$ is ind-étale, thereby partially addressing a question posed by Bhatt. Additionally, we apply this finding to establish a rigidity property of Hochschild homology and derive specific cases of Weibel's and Vorst's conjectures, all without requiring noetherian assumptions.

For an odd prime $p$ with $n=2m$, this work introduces a novel Niho-type decimation $d=\frac{(p^{m}-1)^{2}}{2}+1$ applied to $m$-sequences. Leveraging the generalized Niho's Theorem, we demonstrate that the cross-correlation function between a $p$-ary $m$-sequence of period $p^{n}-1$ and its decimated counterpart by $d$ takes on at most six distinct values, with the magnitude of the cross-correlation strictly upper bounded by $4\sqrt{p^{n}}-1$.

This study computes ionization cross-sections for atoms via the absorption of scalar particles across an energy spectrum ranging from a few eV to 100 keV. The analysis encompasses both nonrelativistic particles, such as dark matter candidates, and relativistic particles potentially generated within the Sun. We present numerical results for elements pertinent to direct dark matter detection, including oxygen, sodium, argon, calcium, germanium, iodine, xenon, tungsten, and thallium. We uncover a critical error in prior calculations, demonstrating that they inflated ionization cross-sections by several orders of magnitude because of a violation regarding the orthogonality between bound and continuum electron wave functions. Leveraging our recalculated cross-sections, we interpret recent findings from the Xenon1T experiment to derive the first direct constraints on scalar-electron couplings. We propose that the observed Xenon1T excess may be attributed to scalar emission from the Sun. Although our results face a tension with astrophysical limits comparable to that of the solar axion hypothesis, we establish direct exclusion limits for scalar dark matter in the $\sim 1-10\,\mathrm{keV}$ mass range. Additionally, we update axio-ionization cross-sections and provide accompanying numerical data files.

The iterative weight updates in the AdaBoost machine learning algorithm can be modeled as a dynamical system on a probability simplex. When applied to low-dimensional datasets, AdaBoost often exhibits cycling behavior, which serves as the primary focus of this study. This cyclic nature enables the use of specific computational techniques that are otherwise ineffective for the algorithm's general, non-cycling operation. Leveraging these computational characteristics, we establish a precise link between AdaBoost's cycling and continued fractions dynamics. We then analyze this correspondence to elucidate the mechanisms driving the algorithm into periodic states. Ultimately, this work aims to provide a new, self-contained explanation for the cycling dynamics inherent in AdaBoost.

CNN-based surrogates are increasingly adopted in scientific domains to substitute for traditional, computationally intensive physical methods. While these models deliver satisfactory outcomes with reduced costs on small training sets, our benchmarks reveal that data-loading latency becomes the primary performance bottleneck when scaling to large datasets. Scientific surrogates typically require high-resolution data, often reaching terabyte magnitudes. Although various state-of-the-art data loaders exist to enhance throughput for general CNN training, they perform sub-optimally in surrogate training contexts. To address this, we introduce SOLAR, a specialized surrogate data loader designed to maximize loading throughput. Built upon three key observations from our benchmarking, SOLAR incorporates three novel designs: first, it generates a pre-determined shuffled index list to optimize global access order and buffer eviction, thereby maximizing data reuse and buffer hit rates; second, it balances lightweight computational imbalance against heavyweight loading workload imbalance to accelerate overall training; and third, it refines its data access pattern using HDF5 to improve parallel I/O throughput. Evaluations across three scientific surrogates on 32 GPUs demonstrate that SOLAR achieves up to 24.4X speedup over PyTorch's Data Loader and 3.52X speedup compared to existing state-of-the-art loaders.

Reinforcement learning for recommendation (RL4Rec) is gaining traction due to its ability to rapidly adapt to user feedback. A standard RL4Rec framework typically employs a state encoder to process users' historical interactions and an RL algorithm to execute actions and collect rewards. Previous research compared four state encoders within an environment simulating user feedback from real-world logs, identifying an attention-based encoder as the superior option for achieving peak performance. However, these conclusions are constrained to the actor-critic method, a specific set of four encoders, and evaluation simulators that fail to correct biases in logged data. To address these limitations, we replicate and extend the comparison of attention-based encoders by utilizing the publicly available, debiased SOFA simulator, testing a different RL approach (Deep Q-Networks), incorporating additional state encoders, and applying a distinct dataset. Crucially, our results demonstrate that prior findings do not generalize to the debiased SOFA environment derived from a different dataset or to DQN-based methods when evaluated against a broader range of state encoders.

A defining characteristic of the human moral mind is its adaptability, enabling us to evaluate unfamiliar situations, override established rules, and create new ones spontaneously. Replicating this flexibility remains a primary hurdle in building AI capable of generating human-like moral judgments. This paper presents findings from a study of real-world decision-makers assessing the permissibility of violating the "no cutting in line" norm. By collecting data on how humans judge line-cutting across various scenarios, we propose a modeling approach using a preference-based structure to integrate these reasoning abilities into machines. This method introduces a novel adaptation to standard dual-process theories of moral judgment.

A signed graph $\Sigma$ consists of an underlying graph $G=(V,E)$ paired with a signature function $\sigma:E\rightarrow\{-1,+1\}$ that assigns a sign to each edge. This paper generalizes the concepts of resolving sets and metric dimension, which are commonly used for unsigned graphs, to the domain of signed graphs. We examine the metric dimension across several well-known classes of signed graphs, including a specific subset of signed trees. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the metric dimension of a signed graph remains unchanged when all edge signs are negated.

To explain the radius distribution gap among Kepler exoplanets as an alternative to photo-evaporation, we investigate water worlds using a joint mass-radius-period distribution fitted to transiting Kepler data, including a subset with radial velocity masses. By applying hierarchical Bayesian modeling, we constructed ten mixture models featuring various combinations of compositional subpopulations: planets with gaseous envelopes, evaporated rocky and icy cores, and intrinsically rocky or icy planets. We assessed which combinations were best supported by the data through cross-validation, finding broad support for models containing icy compositions versus those that exclude them. However, significant population-level degeneracies exist between water worlds and planets retaining primordial envelopes. Within models including one or more icy-core subpopulations, the fraction of icy planets varies widely, with a rough upper limit of 50%. Enhanced datasets or alternative modeling techniques may be necessary to better distinguish between these planetary subpopulations.

Characterizing the emission behavior of heavy quarks requires a clear understanding of parton mass and Casimir color factors within quantum chromodynamics parton showers. Recent improvements in jet substructure methods now allow for the isolation and analysis of gluon emissions originating from heavy quarks. This study presents the first direct experimental constraints on the charm-quark splitting function, derived from measuring the groomed shared momentum fraction of the initial splitting in charm jets identified via reconstructed ${\rm D}^0$ mesons. The analysis utilizes proton–proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV, focusing on the low jet transverse-momentum range of $15 \leq p_{\rm T}^{\rm jet~ch} < 30$ GeV/$c$, a regime where mass effects significantly influence emission properties. Additionally, the report details the opening angle of the first perturbative emission from the charm quark and the total count of such emissions. When compared to inclusive-jet measurements, the data indicate that charm quarks exhibit a steeper splitting function relative to gluons and light quarks. Furthermore, charm quarks experience fewer perturbative emissions within the parton shower and demonstrate a lower likelihood of large-angle emissions.

This study extends our previous analysis on fixed cosmology to examine how various assumptions regarding one-loop galaxy bias affect the recovery of cosmological parameters. We analyzed three synthetic galaxy samples designed to replicate the clustering characteristics of the BOSS CMASS and LOWZ catalogues, as well as the SDSS Main Galaxy Sample. By fitting either the real-space galaxy auto power spectrum or the combined galaxy-galaxy and galaxy-matter power spectrum, we assessed the importance of incorporating short-range non-locality versus scale-dependent stochasticity. Evaluations based on goodness-of-fit ($\chi^2$), the unbiasedness of cosmological parameters (FoB), and the figure-of-merit (FoM) indicate that a four-parameter model—comprising linear, quadratic, and cubic non-local bias alongside constant shot-noise, with fixed quadratic tidal bias—offers a robust description for the auto power spectrum of all three samples up to $k_{\rm max}=0.3\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ within an effective volume of $6\,h^{-3}\,\mathrm{Gpc}^3$. Conversely, joint analyses of the two observables struggle at larger scales; achieving comparable $k_{\rm max}$ requires extending the model with either higher derivatives or scale-dependent shot-noise, the latter yielding the most stable outcomes. These results were derived using three distinct, either hybrid or perturbative, prescriptions for the matter power spectrum: \texttt{RESPRESSO}, gRPT, and EFT. Across all scenarios, introducing scale-dependent shot-noise broadens the model's validity range regarding FoB and $\chi^2$. Notably, despite adding extra free parameters, these model extensions do not necessarily enhance the maximum achievable FoM for cosmological parameters $\left(h,\,\Omega_ch^2,\,A_s\right)$, which remain generally consistent with those from the simpler model at smaller $k_{\rm max}$.

Few-shot learning addresses data scarcity issues, but its effectiveness drops significantly when a domain shift occurs between training and test sets, a scenario known as cross-domain few-shot learning. This task is particularly difficult because the target domain remains unseen during training. To mitigate this, we introduce a novel setting that provides some unlabelled data from the target domain, effectively bridging the gap between source and target domains. We constructed a benchmark for this approach using DomainNet \cite{peng2018oment}. Our proposed self-supervised learning method leverages both the labeled training data and the unlabelled target data to maximize knowledge utilization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms various baselines. Additionally, we designed a specialized episodic training pipeline that delivers substantial performance improvements.

We provide a detailed investigation into the morphology of dark matter (DM) halos within a sample of 25 Milky Way-analogous galaxies from the TNG50 simulation. Applying the Enclosed Volume Iterative Method (EVIM), we determine that the DM halos exhibit an oblate-to-triaxial configuration, with a median triaxiality parameter of $T \simeq 0.24$. The halos are classified into three distinct groups: Simple halos, comprising 32% of the sample, maintain consistent principal axis ordering and nearly fixed orientations across all radii. Twisted halos, also representing 32%, undergo gradual rotational shifts along their radial profiles. Stretched halos, making up the remaining 36%, display varying principal axis lengths where eigenvalue ordering changes with radius, accompanied by a $\sim$90-degree re-orientation of the stretching direction. By visualizing the 3D ellipsoids of these halos, we identify, for the first time, evidence of re-orienting ellipsoids in both twisted and stretched categories. Comparing these results with dark matter-only (DMO) simulations reveals that baryonic physics favors a triaxial (prolate) shape. Furthermore, our analysis of substructure in both hydrodynamic and DMO simulations indicates that its influence on halo shape is negligible. We also examine satellite distributions, finding that in simple and twisted halos, the angle between satellite and galaxy angular momentum increases with radius, whereas stretched halos exhibit a uniform angular distribution. Finally, aligning our theoretical findings with existing observational data demonstrates reasonable consistency.

Significant advancements have been achieved in automated reasoning using unstructured natural language by leveraging large language models (LMs) alongside techniques like Chain-of-Thought and Selection-Inference. However, these forward-direction methods, which derive conclusions from axioms, face combinatorial search space explosions and high failure rates on complex, multi-step problems. Classical literature indicates that backward reasoning—from the target conclusion to supporting axioms—is far more efficient for proof discovery. Adapting this insight, we developed LAMBADA, a backward chaining algorithm for LMs that breaks reasoning into four sub-modules executable via few-shot prompting. Our results demonstrate that LAMBADA substantially outperforms state-of-the-art forward reasoning approaches on two difficult logical reasoning datasets, especially when deep and precise proof chains are necessary.

This article introduces a stack-theoretic framework for investigating the universal tropical Jacobian across the moduli space of tropical curves. We present two methodologies for tropicalizing the universal compactified Jacobian over the moduli space of curves: one based on logarithmic geometry and the other on non-Archimedean analytic geometry. The primary outcome from both perspectives is that the tropicalization of the universal compactified Jacobian yields the universal tropical Jacobian, and the tropicalization maps in both contexts align with the tautological morphisms. In a forthcoming sequel, we will apply these techniques to construct explicit polyhedral models for the logarithmic Picard variety.

We examine the trajectory of a point particle moving through a stationary spacetime while subjected to a scalar, electromagnetic, or gravitational self-force. We demonstrate that the conservative component of the first-order self-force induces Hamiltonian dynamics and provide a derived explicit formula for the Hamiltonian within phase space. When applied to Kerr spacetime, our findings extend the Hamiltonian function established by Fujita et al., which was previously restricted to non-resonant orbits. Furthermore, we explore the implications of these results for the first law governing binary black hole mechanics.

In recent years, online reviews have gained significant importance due to their impact on consumer purchasing decisions and business reputations, making the practice of fabricating reviews potentially damaging to both customers and service providers. Although various methods, particularly those utilizing supervised classifiers, have been suggested for detecting opinion spam, this study enhances existing effective features by incorporating the Cumulative Relative Frequency Distribution of each. Through experimental evaluation using real data from Yelp.com, we demonstrate that integrating these distributional features significantly improves classifier performance.

Consider a polynomial $f_0$ of degree $d_1+d_2$ featuring a periodic critical point at $0$ with multiplicity $d_1-1$ and a Julia critical point of multiplicity $d_2$. We demonstrate that if $f_0$ is primitive, lacks neutral periodic points, and is non-renormalizable at its Julia critical point, then the straightening map $\chi_{f_0}:\mathcal C(\lambda_{f_0}) \to \mathcal C_{d_1}$ constitutes a bijection. Specifically, for every $f \in \mathcal C(\lambda_{f_0})$, the iterate $f^{m_0}$ admits a polynomial-like restriction that is hybrid equivalent to a polynomial within $\mathcal C_{d_1}$, where $m_0$ denotes the period of $0$ under $f_0$. Conversely, $f_0$ can be tuned to match any polynomial $g \in \mathcal C_{d_1}$. Consequently, when $d_1=2$, the straightening map $\chi_{f_0}$ is established as a homeomorphism from $\mathcal C(\lambda_{f_0})$ onto the Mandelbrot set. Combined with the primary findings in [SW], this result comprehensively resolves the problem regarding primitive tuning for cubic polynomials possessing connected Julia sets.

This research investigates the finite element discretization of nanofluid convective transport within an enclosure featuring variable properties. The study utilizes the Buongiorno model, which integrates the Navier-Stokes equations for the base fluid, an advective-diffusion equation for heat transfer, and an advection-dominated nanoparticle concentration equation influenced by thermophoresis and Brownian motion. An iterative numerical scheme is developed, merging Newton's method for solving momentum and energy equations with the transport equation for nanoparticle concentration. It is demonstrated that the Stream Upwind Petrov-Galerkin regularization approach is essential for correctly solving the ill-posed Buongiorno transport model when formulated as a variational problem with a mean value constraint. Numerical computations confirm the effectiveness of this proposed approach, showing reasonable alignment with existing experimental data. Furthermore, the experiments indicate that neglecting thermophoresis and Brownian motion in the concentration transport equation prevents the model from capturing the heat transfer degradation caused by suspended nanoparticles, although these terms are shown to be significant near hot and cold walls.

This study analyzes and categorizes sentiments within text data derived from movie reviews by employing a kernel-based method from quantum machine learning. To construct the quantum kernel, we utilize a circuit built from various Pauli rotational gates, where the rotational parameters are classical non-linear functions of the input text data. To evaluate the proposed model's performance, we compared it against decision trees, gradient boosting classifiers, and both classical and quantum support vector machines. The findings indicate that the quantum kernel model, particularly the quantum support vector machine, outperforms all other algorithms across every evaluation metric. Specifically, when compared to a classical support vector machine, the quantum version yields significantly superior results, even with an increased number of features or dimensions. Notably, using a quantum support vector machine with 15 features resulted in a clear 9.4% increase in precision score compared to its classical counterpart.

We address a model governing the stimulated conversion between ultracold bosonic atoms and molecules, initiated by a linearly time-dependent shift across a Feshbach resonance. Our solution indicates that reaction efficiency depends nonexponentially on the transition rate, exhibiting a dynamic phase transition. We discover that the resulting phase features a thermalized energy distribution, where temperature is determined by the transition rate; however, this phase is characterized by significant purely quantum correlations.

We have recently provided an asymptotic resolution to the longstanding Szemerédi and Petruska conjecture. Decades ago, Gyárfás and colleagues noted through a direct yet unpublished argument that this conjecture is equivalent to identifying the maximum order of a 3-uniform $\tau$-critical hypergraph. As a result, our recent findings yield an asymptotically tight upper bound for this maximum order, reigniting interest in this equivalence. In this companion paper, we offer a straightforward proof of said equivalence. Additionally, we provide relevant background information and open problems, while also highlighting applications of the Szemerédi and Petruska conjecture within combinatorial geometry.

Using the bond fluctuation model, we investigate how crosslinking alters brush conformations. While the Flory-Rehner model predicts a $q^{-1/3}$ collapse for highly crosslinked ($q$) uni-axially swollen networks—a trend inconsistent with our simulation results—we demonstrate that brush height reduction is driven by monomer fluctuations perpendicular to the grafting plane rather than network elasticity. Furthermore, we find that crosslinking impacts vary depending on whether reactions occur between monomers on the same chain or different chains. By incorporating the reduction in effective chain length from both reaction types into a function $\beta(q)$, we derive the equilibrium brush height using a Flory approach, yielding $H(q)\approx H_{b}\beta(q)^{1/3}$, where $H_{b}$ represents the height of the non-crosslinked brush.

We performed an extensive theoretical and numerical study of electronic susceptibility, polarizability, plasmons, their damping rates, and static screening within pseudospin-1 Dirac cone materials featuring flat bands, as well as in the general $\alpha - \mathcal{T}_3$ model, at finite temperatures. This work involved computing the polarization function, plasmon dispersions, and associated damping rates across arbitrary temperatures, alongside deriving analytical approximations for the long-wavelength limit at both low and high temperatures. We show that directly applying the integral transformation of the polarization function to dice lattices is invalid, thereby uncovering fundamental properties and defining the applicability boundaries of the flat band dispersion model. At temperatures where $k_B T \ll E_F$, the most significant temperature-induced variations in the polarization function and plasmons arise from the discrepancy between the chemical potential and the Fermi energy. Furthermore, we derived a set of closed-form semi-analytical expressions for the static limit of the polarization function in arbitrary $\alpha - \mathcal{T}_3$ materials at any temperature, providing exact analytical formulas for the high, low, and zero-temperature limits. These results are of immense value for transport and screening calculations in flat band Dirac materials.

Monolayer C$_3$N represents a promising two-dimensional semiconductor characterized by an indirect band gap and notable mechanical, thermal, and electronic attributes. This study details its electronic and dielectric characteristics, with a specific emphasis on the momentum-resolved exciton band structure. We calculate excitation energies and oscillator strengths to distinguish between bright and dark states, contextualizing these findings within the material's crystal symmetry. Our analysis reveals that excitonic states become active at finite transferred momenta: specifically, we identify an indirect exciton at approximately 0.9 eV, which is substantially lower than the direct optical gap of 1.96 eV, alongside excitonic binding energies ranging from 0.6 to 0.9 eV for the lowest energy states. Consistent with trends observed in other 2D materials, we detect a quasi-linear excitonic dispersion near the $\Gamma$ point; however, this dispersion exhibits downward convexity, a feature linked to both C$_3$N's indirect band gap and the dark character of the relevant excitons.
This study focuses on analyzing the structure and characteristics of binary LCD codes that possess automorphisms of odd prime order, while also proposing a method for their construction.

We introduce a 3D immersive visualization system designed to analyze the right-hand techniques of a cello player. By tracking the bow's position and orientation alongside audio recording, we capture the performance data. Given that movements primarily occur within a shallow volume and are largely two-dimensional, we utilize the third dimension to represent time. Our approach investigates diverse mappings of motion and audio data into spatial and other visual attributes. In close collaboration with a cellist, we intend to assess our prototype through a user study involving a group of cellists in the near future.

This position paper investigates language formation and examines the connection between English words' structural properties and their polysemy. By applying Ollivier-Ricci curvature to a large synonym graph to estimate polysemy, it empirically demonstrates that words which are generally easier to pronounce also tend to possess multiple meanings.

The bipartite Turán number $ex(m,n; H)$ represents the maximum edge count in a bipartite graph $G=(X,Y; E)$ with partition sizes $|X|=m$ and $|Y|=n$ that excludes $H$ as a subgraph. This paper establishes $ex(m,n; F_{\ell})$ for any $\ell$ and sufficiently large $n$ relative to $m$ and $\ell$, where $F_{\ell}$ denotes a linear forest composed of $\ell$ vertex-disjoint paths. Additionally, we characterize the extremal graphs achieving this bound. Finally, leveraging these findings, we determine the maximum spectral radius of bipartite graphs free of $F_{\ell}$ and identify all graphs that attain this spectral maximum.

In multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) communications, accurate channel estimation is critical for maintaining synchronization between base stations and users. This study introduces a novel channel estimation technique for MIMO orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) systems that leverages principal component analysis (PCA). The process begins by estimating the channel frequency response using the least squares method, followed by applying PCA to isolate and retain only the dominant singular components of the channel impulse response before converting the result back into the frequency domain. The performance of this proposed method is evaluated against minimum mean square error (MMSE) estimation by analyzing bit error rate as a function of Eb/N0.

This paper introduces Amnestic Forgery, an ontology for metaphor semantics built upon MetaNet and inspired by Conceptual Metaphor theory. By reusing and extending the Framester schema, Amnestic Forgery serves as an optimal design framework for addressing the semiotic and referential dimensions of frames, roles, mappings, and blending. The resource is detailed through its applications, illustrated with examples from metaphor generation and the referential challenges inherent in metaphoric mappings. Both the schema and data are accessible via the Framester SPARQL endpoint.

Dimensionality reduction techniques are vital for analyzing multidimensional data, particularly for time-dependent multivariate datasets where numerous dynamic processes occur. However, there is a scarcity of research utilizing the expressive power of projections within dynamic contexts. This paper introduces a method to evaluate projection techniques for dynamic data and to investigate the link between visual quality and stability. Our approach employs an experimental framework comprising established methods for time-dependent data alongside novel adaptations of static techniques. To facilitate this evaluation, we offer a diverse collection of datasets encoding various dynamic patterns, along with a suite of spatial and temporal stability metrics to assess layout quality. We report on the assessment of 11 methods across 10 datasets using 12 quality metrics, identifying the most suitable approaches for projecting time-dependent multivariate data while examining their design choices and characteristics. All findings are documented and hosted in a public repository to ensure result reproducibility.

We define a $P$-compelling coloring as a proper vertex coloring of a graph where every set containing exactly one vertex of each color satisfies property $P$. The $P$-compelling chromatic number represents the minimum number of colors required for such a coloring. This concept extends the dominator and total dominator chromatic numbers, and we establish general bounds alongside algorithmic findings. Furthermore, we examine specific instances where property $P$ requires the subset to include at least one edge or to be connected.

In the majority of model-based Markov decision process applications, parameters for the unknown underlying model are typically inferred from empirical data. Because of inherent noise, policies derived from these estimated models frequently deviate significantly from the optimal policy of the true model, leading to suboptimal outcomes when deployed in the actual environment and necessitating solutions with enhanced generalization. This study adopts a Bayesian framework, incorporating prior information to regularize the MDP objective function, thereby yielding more robust policies. We introduce two specific methods: one utilizing $L^1$ regularization and another employing relative entropic regularization. Our proposed algorithms are assessed using both synthetic simulations and real-world search logs from a large-scale online retail platform. The findings confirm that regularized MDP policies effectively maintain robustness against noise present in the models.

To proactively ensure a secure online environment for social media users, systems are required to identify harmful content and immediately notify platform moderators. To maintain consistent policy enforcement, moderators rely on comprehensive guidelines. Conversely, most current state-of-the-art models infer abuse from labeled examples, often relying on unreliable spurious cues like group identifiers. This work introduces "policy-aware abuse detection," rejecting the unrealistic assumption that systems can accurately identify abusive phenomena solely by analyzing data. Instead, we propose a machine-readable representation of moderator policies, decomposing them into specific intents and slots. We present a dataset of 3,535 annotated English posts featuring these slots and demonstrate how intent classification and slot-filling architectures can facilitate abuse detection while offering clear rationales for model decisions.

High-resolution hyperspectral images (HSIs) capture spectral responses for every pixel across multiple bands, enabling effective object discrimination in complex environments. Although HSI cameras have become affordable, their algorithmic applications remain underutilized. This paper addresses the novel challenge of weakly-supervised semantic segmentation in cityscapes using HSIs. We leverage the premise that high-resolution HSIs in urban settings offer abundant spectral data that can be readily mapped to semantic categories without manual annotation, thereby facilitating low-cost, highly reliable segmentation. Specifically, we provide a theoretical analysis of HSIs and propose a weakly-supervised framework that enhances coarse labels to a finer granularity by exploiting spectral information. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our approach yields highly competitive labels, surpassing the edge precision of artificial fine labels in certain classes. Furthermore, the refined labels significantly boost overall segmentation performance. These findings underscore the substantial potential of combining HSIs with semantic segmentation for advanced visual tasks.

Emotional expressions are actions that convey an individual's internal feelings or attitudes to others, utilizing both verbal and non-verbal channels. Analyzing complex human behavior involves examining physical cues across multiple modalities, primarily facial expressions, vocal tones, and body gestures. Recently, the study of spontaneous multi-modal emotion recognition has gained significant traction for analyzing human behavior. This paper introduces a novel deep learning framework for audio-visual emotion recognition that capitalizes on recent advancements such as high-performance architectures and knowledge distillation. The system fuses deep feature representations from audio and visual streams using a model-level fusion strategy, followed by a recurrent neural network to model temporal dynamics. The proposed method significantly surpasses state-of-the-art techniques in predicting valence on the RECOLA dataset. Additionally, the custom visual network for facial expression feature extraction achieves superior results compared to existing methods on the AffectNet and Google Facial Expression Comparison datasets.

Neutron stars gradually lose rotational energy through various mechanisms. We present compelling population-level evidence indicating that millisecond pulsars (MSPs) possess a minimum ellipticity of approximately $10^{-9}$ along their spin axis, implying that a subset of these stars primarily decelerates via gravitational-wave emission. Furthermore, we explore the consequences of this lower bound on internal magnetic field intensities and the composition of nuclear matter within neutron stars, demonstrating that upcoming or upgraded Advanced LIGO and Virgo detectors are poised to detect gravitational waves from certain known MSPs in the near term.

We investigated whether the field self-interaction inherent in General Relativity can eliminate the necessity for dark matter to account for the large-scale formation of cosmic structures. Our findings indicate that this self-interaction accelerates structure growth rapidly enough to achieve the densities currently observed, without requiring any free parameters, dark components, or alterations to established physical laws. This outcome contributes to a suite of natural explanations offered by this framework, which also addresses phenomena such as galactic flat rotation curves, supernovae data hinting at dark energy, and galaxy cluster dynamics, thereby strengthening its viability as an alternative to the standard dark universe paradigm.

This research investigates kinetic magnetism within the Fermi-Hubbard model across triangular lattices, ranging from zigzag ladders and multi-legged cylinders to complete two-dimensional structures. The study concentrates on the strong interaction regime ($U\gg t$) with an electron filling factor near unity. At temperatures significantly higher than the hopping energy, the Curie-Weiss behavior of magnetic susceptibility indicates effective antiferromagnetic correlations in hole-doped systems and ferromagnetic correlations in electron-doped ones. We demonstrate that these phenomena stem from magnetic polarons dressing charge carriers moving through a spin-incoherent Mott insulator, where the resulting effective interactions can far surpass standard magnetic super-exchange energies. Specifically, antiferromagnetic polarons in hole-doped triangular lattices arise from kinetic frustration, while Nagaoka-type ferromagnetic correlations in electron-doped systems are driven by propagating doublons. These findings offer a theoretical framework for recent experimental observations in moiré TMDC materials. Furthermore, we examine hole-doped systems in finite magnetic fields to understand many-body states at low temperatures. At low doping levels and intermediate magnetic fields, a magnetic polaron phase emerges, distinct from the fully polarized state by a metamagnetic transition. As the magnetic field decreases, the system exhibits a propensity for phase separation, forming hole-rich regions known as antiferromagnetic spinbags. Finally, we show that ultracold atom experiments, capable of measuring three-point hole-spin-spin correlations, can directly observe these magnetic polarons in triangular lattices.

This study introduces a matrix-scaled consensus algorithm that extends the scaled consensus framework presented in \cite{Roy2015scaled}. While traditional scalar scaled consensus drives agent states toward distinct points along a straight line within the state space—determined by scaling factors and initial conditions—the proposed matrix-scaled approach assigns a positive or negative definite matrix weight to each agent. State updates are calculated as the product of the sum of relative matrix-scaled states and the sign of the agent's matrix weight. Consequently, agents asymptotically converge to final positions that differ from a shared consensus point by the inverse of their individual scaling matrices. This mechanism expands the convergence locus from a one-dimensional line to an open subspace within the state space. The paper provides a detailed convergence analysis for both single and double-integrator agents, supported by simulation results.

We demonstrate that a Weyl law applies to the variational spectrum of the $p$-Laplacian. Specifically, considering the variational spectrum $(\lambda_i)_{i=1}^\infty$ of $\Delta_p$ on a closed Riemannian manifold $(X,g)$, and defining the counting function as $N(\lambda) = \#\{i:\, \lambda_i < \lambda\}$, we establish the asymptotic relation $N(\lambda) \sim c \operatorname{vol}(X) \lambda^{n/p}$. This result validates a conjecture by Friedlander. The proof relies on concepts developed by Gromov and Liokumovich, as well as Marques and Neves.

This paper investigates several multilingual and Russian pre-trained transformer models for the Dialogue Evaluation 2021 shared task on headline selection. Our experiments demonstrate that a combined approach outperforms individual multilingual and monolingual models. We analyze various methods for generating sentence embeddings and developing a ranking model based on them, achieving accuracies of 87.28% and 86.60% on the public and private test sets, respectively.

In thermal Conformal Field Theory (CFT), we employ mixed correlators as precise tools to investigate strong gravity phenomena within their holographic duals. The holographic counterpart of this mixing represents an inelastic transformation between fields driven by gravitational tidal excitation. Our analysis reveals that mixing intensifies at high temperatures, which correspond to large AdS black holes, and is concentrated at small boundary momenta—the dual of the deep bulk where intense gravitational fields reside. Furthermore, we observe substantial $\mathcal{O}(1/G_{N})$ tidal conversion in the low-temperature phase of the $U(N)$ vector model, reinforcing the hypothesis that the bulk dual of this phase contains highly compact objects.

Graphene chemical vapor deposition was investigated using (111)-textured films of Cu, Ni, and Cu$_x$Ni$_y$ as substrates. These metal layers, ranging from 400 to 700 nm in thickness, were sputtered onto $\alpha$-Al$_2$O$_3$(0001) substrates at temperatures between 250°C and 650°C, followed by annealing at 1000°C in a tube furnace. Diffraction analyses revealed that while all films exhibited (111) texture, their grains possessed in-plane orientations separated by $60^{\circ}$. The observed epitaxial relationship for all samples was $[110]_{metal}$||$[10\bar{1}0]_{{Al}_{2}{O}_{3}}$. Pre-deposition reactive sputtering of Al in O$_2$ achieved a single in-plane orientation covering 97% of the Ni film but did not significantly alter the Cu grain structure. Transmission electron microscopy verified the epitaxial alignment and a clean Ni/Al$_2$O$_3$ interface, linking the formation of $60^{\circ}$ twin grains to surface features on the Al$_2$O$_3$. Furthermore, increasing total pressure and Cu vapor pressure during annealing reduced the roughness of both Cu and Cu$_x$Ni$_y$ films. Graphene grown on Ni(111) substrates demonstrated greater uniformity compared to polycrystalline Ni/SiO$_2$, although thickness variations persisted on a scale much smaller than the distance between grains.

We investigate the supersymmetric index of four-dimensional theories resulting from the compactification of the six-dimensional E string theory on a Riemann surface. Specifically, we derive the difference operator that incorporates a specific class of surface defects into the index calculation. This operator is found to be, aside from a constant shift, an analytic difference operator previously analyzed by van Diejen.

The dynamical Casimir effect, which converts virtual photons into real ones, arises from the rapid motion of neutral bodies or swift alterations in their optical characteristics. Enhancing these modulation protocols with spatial precision allows for the tailored manipulation of the spectral, spatial, spin, and entanglement attributes of generated photon pairs. While space-time quantum metasurfaces have previously been suggested as a means to achieve this through optical property modulation, this study presents a mechanical counterpart by examining systems where the lattice structure varies both spatially and temporally. We establish a microscopic framework applicable to both moving mirrors with modulated surface profiles and atomic array meta-mirrors featuring perturbed lattice configurations. This spatio-temporal modulation facilitates the creation of steered, frequency-path entangled photon pairs in both co- and cross-polarized states, as well as vortex photon pairs exhibiting frequency-angular momentum entanglement. Ultimately, the proposed space-time dynamical Casimir effect can be understood as an induced dynamical asymmetry within the quantum vacuum.

Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) is the preferred method for characterizing molecular dynamics. Specifically, in biological macromolecules, pico- to nano-second motions are investigated through nuclear spin relaxation rates, which rely on the temporal fluctuations of spin interaction frame orientations. Over the last four decades, the Model-Free (MF) approach has effectively analyzed these rates without assuming a specific motion type, reporting only the effective amplitude and time-scale. However, deriving a detailed mechanistic understanding from MF analysis alone is challenging, often requiring supplementation with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Despite their inherent limitations in accuracy, these simulations can provide the necessary data to construct explicit motion models tailored for analyzing NMR relaxation data. This work details the construction of such models, with a specific focus on methyl-bearing protein side-chains, and compares them against the MF method. Using synthetic data, we demonstrate that explicit motion models are more robust when rotamer jumps—common in methyl group relaxation—are present. We anticipate that this research will encourage the adoption of explicit motion models for the joint analysis of MD and NMR data.

Let $G$ be a locally compact Lie group with Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$. We introduce a fuzzy counterpart to $G$, termed a fuzzy Lie group $\mathfrak{G_f}$, and construct spherical functions upon it. Furthermore, an analogue of the Helgason existence theorem for spherical functions on $G$ is proven within the context of $\mathfrak{G_f}$.

For every $\lambda > 2$, we define a substitution over an infinite alphabet that generates a substitution tiling with an inflation factor of $\lambda$. Notably, this yields the initial class of substitutive systems featuring transcendental inflation factors that retain the standard dynamical characteristics typically found in primitive substitutions on finite alphabets. We demonstrate that both the corresponding tiling and subshift dynamical systems are strictly ergodic, a property linked to the quasicompactness of the associated substitution operator. Furthermore, we present a specific substitution example with a transcendental inflation factor $\lambda$.

Deep learning approaches for object reconstruction have significantly outperformed traditional methods; however, supervised learning techniques struggle when training and test data exhibit different distributions. While current models often succeed on the synthetic ShapeNet dataset, they frequently fail when applied to real-world images. To mitigate this, unsupervised domain adaptation can transfer knowledge from a labeled synthetic source to an unlabeled real target domain. Addressing the challenge of single-view 3D reconstruction in the real world, we evaluate various domain adaptation strategies inspired by Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), Deep CORAL, and Domain Adversarial Neural Networks (DANN). Based on these findings, we propose a novel architecture that leverages the specific condition where target domain data is unsupervised regarding 3D geometry but supervised for class labels, utilizing a framework built upon the pix2vox network. Experiments were conducted using ShapeNet as the source and the Object Dataset Domain Suite (ODDS) as the target; ODDS comprises real-world, multiview, multidomain images with varying difficulty levels to assess domain gap magnitude. To our knowledge, these results represent the first application of multiview reconstruction literature to the ODDS dataset.

The OPERA experiment, situated within the underground Gran Sasso Laboratory (LNGS), was engineered to achieve the initial detection of neutrino oscillations via direct appearance in the transition from muon neutrinos to tau neutrinos. Its hybrid architecture combines an emulsion/lead target with electronic detectors and is positioned 730 km down the CNGS neutrino beamline from the source. Successful operations using CNGS neutrinos occurred during 2008, 2009, and 2010. Following a concise overview of the beam and setup, this work presents an analysis of events from a sample of $1.89 \times 10^{19}$ protons on target in the CERN CNGS $\nu_{\mu}$ beam, which resulted in the identification of the first candidate $\nu_{\tau}$ charged-current interaction. The event's topology and kinematics are examined in detail, alongside an explanation of background sources and an evaluation of the candidate's statistical significance.

This study presents a search for new heavy resonances decaying into pairs of WW, WZ, ZZ, WH, or ZH bosons within the all-jets final state. Utilizing proton-proton collision data from the CMS detector collected between 2016 and 2018 at the CERN LHC (13 TeV center-of-mass energy, 138 fb$^{-1}$ integrated luminosity), the analysis targets resonances with masses exceeding 1.3 TeV. These resonances decay into highly Lorentz-boosted bosons that manifest as single large-radius jets, which are identified using machine learning methods. No significant deviation from the predicted Standard Model background was found. The analysis observed a maximum local significance of 3.6 sigma (2.3 sigma global) at masses of 2.1 and 2.9 TeV. In the context of a heavy vector triplet model, spin-1 Z' and W' resonances with masses under 4.8 TeV are excluded at the 95% confidence level, establishing the most stringent limits to date. Similarly, in a bulk graviton model, spin-2 gravitons and spin-0 radions with masses below 1.4 and 2.7 TeV, respectively, are ruled out at 95% CL. Additionally, constraints on the production of heavy resonances via vector boson fusion are provided, with 95% CL upper cross-section limits reaching as low as 0.1 fb.

The universal relaxation bound posits that the relaxation times of perturbed thermodynamic systems are lower-bounded by the time-times-temperature (TTT) quantum relation $\tau\times T\geq {{\hbar}\over{\pi}}$. While it is established that certain perturbation modes of near-extremal Kerr black holes, within the regime $MT_{\text{BH}}/\hbar\ll m^{-2}$, exhibit normalized relaxation times $\pi\tau\times T_{\text{BH}}/\hbar$ that oscillate infinitely with negligible constant amplitude around $1$ as $MT_{\text{BH}}/\hbar\to0$, these modes are unsuitable for directly validating the TTT bound across the full parameter space of black-hole spacetime (where $\{T_{\text{BH}},M\}$ denote the Bekenstein-Hawking temperature and mass, and $m$ represents the azimuthal harmonic index of the linearized perturbation mode). This concise paper explicitly demonstrates that all rapidly-spinning Kerr black holes adhere to the TTT relaxation bound. Specifically, through analytical methods, it is proven that all black-hole perturbation modes in the complementary regime $m^{-1}\ll MT_{\text{BH}}/\hbar\ll1$ possess relaxation times satisfying the dimensionless inequality $\pi\tau\times T_{\text{BH}}/\hbar\geq1$.

Recent breakthroughs in machine learning and signal processing have sparked significant interest in Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) owing to their exceptional accuracy and performance in solving complex, engineering-critical challenges. Nevertheless, when these deep learning architectures are employed for high-stakes decisions involving human safety, such as in medical diagnostics or control systems, it is essential to understand, trust, and, most importantly, explain the rationale behind their outputs. In numerous scenarios, artificial neural networks, including DNNs, function as opaque "black boxes" that fail to reveal sufficient insight into their internal mechanisms. While recent initiatives have sought to elucidate the behavior of deep networks, the field of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), dedicated to reasoning about DNN decisions, remains in its early stages. This paper aims to offer a comprehensive review of methods for understanding, visualizing, and explaining both the internal workings and overall behavior of DNNs.

Initially, we review the history of attempts using natural self-adjoint operators to establish the Riemann Hypothesis, noting their previous failures. Section 2 establishes the analytical framework required for rigorous proofs in subsequent sections, distinguishing them from mere heuristics. Section 3 demonstrates the value of constructed pseudo-Laplacians by re-establishing the meromorphic continuation of specific Eisenstein series and deriving a spacing theorem for the zeros of $\zeta_k(s)$ where $k$ is a complex quadratic field with a negative determinant. Finally, Section 4 constructs an automorphic Hamiltonian with a purely discrete spectrum on $L^2(SL_r(\mathbb{Z})\backslash SL_r (\mathbb{R})/SO(r, \mathbb{R}))$, identifies its ground state, and illustrates how it can define a nuclear Fréchet automorphic Schwartz space.

Transferring knowledge across domains holds significant practical value for numerous natural language processing tasks, particularly when target domain data is scarce. This study introduces a novel few-shot method for domain adaptation in Named Entity Recognition (NER). Our proposed two-step framework combines a variable base module with a template module, utilizing simple descriptive patterns to harness insights from pre-trained language models. Despite its simplicity, this versatile approach functions effectively in both few-shot and zero-shot scenarios. Experimental results across various datasets demonstrate that our lightweight method improves upon state-of-the-art baselines by increasing the F1-score by 2-5%.

Unsupervised domain adaptive (UDA) person re-identification (ReID) focuses on transferring knowledge from labeled source domains to unlabeled target domains to facilitate person matching. A primary challenge in this area is generating target domain samples equipped with trustworthy labels for training. To tackle this, we introduce a Disentanglement-based Cross-Domain Feature Augmentation (DCDFA) strategy. This approach ensures that augmented features accurately represent both source and target domain distributions while retaining reliable identity labels. Specifically, we decompose each sample feature into a robust, domain-invariant shared component and a domain-specific component. We then perform cross-domain feature recomposition to increase the diversity of training samples, guided by constraints from cross-domain ReID loss and domain classification loss. Each resulting recomposed feature combines a domain-invariant basis—ensuring dependable identity inheritance—with an enhancement derived from domain-specific features that approximate real-world distributions, creating an "ideal" augmentation. Comprehensive experiments confirm the efficacy of our method, which attains state-of-the-art performance.

When evaluating multi-armed bandit algorithms, the consequences of missing data are frequently neglected. In real-world applications, this issue affects implementation, with the most basic mitigation strategy being to persist with the original sampling protocol while disregarding missing outcomes. This study examines the performance implications of ignoring missing data across various bandit algorithms using an extensive simulation under the assumption that rewards are missing at random. The research specifically targets two-armed bandit algorithms with binary outcomes within the context of small-sample clinical trials for patient allocation, though the findings remain relevant to other domains where missing data is anticipated. We evaluate key operating characteristics, such as expected reward, considering varying probabilities of missingness across both arms. Our primary finding indicates that the effect of ignoring missing data on the expected performance of multi-armed bandit strategies depends on how each algorithm balances the exploration-exploitation trade-off. Specifically, exploration-focused algorithms tend to allocate more samples to arms with higher missing rates, interpreting them as having less observed information and thus appearing more attractive. Conversely, exploitation-oriented algorithms quickly assign high value to arms with current high means, regardless of the number of observations per arm. Additionally, for algorithms prioritizing exploration, we demonstrate that the issue of missing responses can be mitigated through a straightforward mean imputation method.

This paper establishes the persistence property for solutions to the quartic generalized Korteweg-de Vries equation, given initial data in the weighted Sobolev spaces $H^{1/3}(\mathbb{R})\cap L^2(|x|^{2r}dx)$ where $r\in [0,1/6]$.

This paper investigates bubbling solutions for regular $SU(3)$ Toda systems on Riemann surfaces, focusing on two primary challenges: partial blowup and bubble accumulation. We demonstrate that as both parameters approach their critical values, the existence of a single fully bubbling point, combined with a specific curvature condition, ensures that all blowup solutions near that point obey a spherical Harnack inequality. This result effectively eliminates the possibility of bubble accumulation, a finding essential for numerous applications.

It has been demonstrated that for any n greater than 1, the group of holomorphic isometries acting on n-dimensional complex hyperbolic space does not allow non-elementary representations into the isometry group of infinite-dimensional real hyperbolic space.

This study reports the potential detection of a nonmonotonic radial rotation profile in a low-mass, low-luminosity giant star. While low- and intermediate-mass stars typically exhibit rigid rotation on the main sequence, stellar evolution into the giant phase—characterized by core contraction and envelope expansion—generally predicts a profile with a rapidly rotating core and a slower envelope and surface. KIC 9267654, however, displays a surface rotation rate exceeding that of its bulk envelope, contradicting standard angular momentum conservation expectations. We enhance the spectroscopic constraints on the surface rotation, confirm that pulsation frequencies align with previously determined core and envelope rotation rates, and establish that the star lacks significant chemical peculiarities. Furthermore, we evaluate evidence against the presence of a tidally interacting companion. Finally, we explore possible origins for this anomalous rotation profile, such as the accretion of a giant planet or anomalous angular momentum transport via tidal inertial waves driven by a close substellar companion, and advocate for additional observational and theoretical investigations.

This research examines mathematical programs with switching constraints (MPSC) through a topological lens, establishing two fundamental theorems derived from Morse theory. Continuous deformation of lower level sets is feasible away from the W-stationary point set; however, crossing a W-stationary level induces a topological shift in the lower level set through the attachment of a w-dimensional cell, where w corresponds to the W-index of the nondegenerate W-stationary point. This W-index is determined by the count of negative eigenvalues in the restricted Lagrangian's Hessian and the number of bi-active switching constraints. Consequently, the mountain pass theorem for MPSC is demonstrated. Furthermore, the study investigates whether the nondegeneracy assumption for W-stationary points is overly restrictive within the MPSC framework, concluding that all such points are generically nondegenerate. Additionally, the distinction between nondegeneracy and strong stability for W-stationary points is analyzed. A comprehensive characterization of strong stability is provided using first and second-order information of the MPSC defining functions under the linear independence constraint qualification. Notably, for any strongly stable W-stationary point, all bi-active Lagrange multipliers are non-zero.

Rips and Sela defined globally stable cylinders and questioned whether every Gromov hyperbolic group possesses them. We demonstrate that hyperbolic groups admitting a cubulation do indeed contain globally stable cylinders.

This work examines the challenge of scheduling jobs and selecting their speeds across multiple servers subject to a total power limit, with the objective of minimizing the sum of flow time and energy consumption. This scenario extends the classic flow time minimization problem for multiple unit-speed servers by allowing job parallelization, governed by a sub-linear, concave speedup function of $k^{1/\alpha}$ (where $\alpha > 1$) when $k$ servers are assigned, indicating diminishing returns as more servers are added. We demonstrate that when all jobs are present at time $0$, the straightforward EQUI algorithm, which runs all available jobs at an identical speed, achieves a competitive ratio of $\left(2-\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)\frac{2}{\left(1-\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)\right)}$. Furthermore, for the general case where jobs arrive dynamically, we prove that a Last-Come-First-Served (LCFS) based algorithm attains a constant competitive ratio dependent solely on $\alpha$.

Frictional instability, which drives earthquake initiation and dynamics, is primarily governed by the behavior of fragmented rocks within the fault gauge. Simple experimental setups, such as a slowly driven slider atop granular material, have successfully replicated key seismic characteristics, including intermittent dynamics and broad temporal or energetic scales. However, these physical setups often face limitations that hinder the identification of underlying mechanisms, thereby questioning the universality and generality of the observed results. To overcome this, we present a numerical study using two-dimensional discrete element method simulations of a spring-slider experiment. This approach allows for precise control over granular properties and slider surface conditions. Under quasi-static loading, the system exhibits stick-slip behavior, contrasting with stable sliding at finite driving rates, a finding consistent with experimental data. Across extensive parameter ranges involving damping, inter-particle friction, and particle size distribution, the earthquake-like dynamics of the stick-slip regime produce robust, scale-free statistical features also seen in experiments. While these features superficially mirror the primary empirical relations of tectonic seismicity at geological scales, we demonstrate that correlations typical of tectonic aftershocks are missing. Consequently, the origins of the Omori-Utsu relation, aftershock productivity, and Båth's relation in our simulations differ fundamentally from those in natural tectonic events. We contend that this discrepancy likely extends to previous laboratory experiments as well.

This study introduces a new sinogram denoising approach utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) specifically for SPECT imaging. The model was trained using projection data derived from software phantoms. To assess the method's effectiveness, a Shepp Logan phantom with varying noise levels was employed. The denoised sinograms were reconstructed via Ordered Subset Expectation Maximization (OSEM) and contrasted against reconstructions of the original noisy data. Results indicate that the proposed technique substantially reduces noise and markedly enhances image reconstruction quality. Furthermore, real-world DAT-SPECT sinograms are included to validate the method's efficacy and practical capabilities.

Unlike conventional artificial neurons that generate dense, real-valued outputs, biologically-inspired spiking neurons convey sparse, binary data, enabling more energy-efficient implementations. Recent studies demonstrate that spiking neural networks (SNNs) can be trained using the surrogate gradient method, similar to standard recurrent neural networks (RNNs), achieving promising results in speech command recognition. Applying this same approach, we show that SNNs scale effectively to large-vocabulary continuous speech recognition, successfully replacing Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) units in the encoder with negligible performance degradation. This indicates their potential applicability to complex sequence-to-sequence tasks. Furthermore, unlike their non-spiking recurrent counterparts, SNNs exhibit robustness against exploding gradients without requiring gating mechanisms.

Medical tasks often suffer from inter-rater variability stemming from factors like image quality, professional background, training, or ambiguous guidelines. A common strategy to prevent models from favoring a single expert is training deep learning networks with annotations from multiple raters. For artificial intelligence to be successfully integrated into clinical settings, models must generate calibrated outputs that accurately reflect this disagreement among experts. This study compares three label fusion approaches: STAPLE, averaging raters' segmentations, and randomly sampling individual rater segmentations during training. These methods were evaluated using both standard training frameworks and the recently introduced SoftSeg framework, which treats segmentation as a regression task to minimize information loss. Across ten data splits on two public datasets, the results demonstrate that SoftSeg models consistently outperformed conventional counterparts in terms of calibration and the preservation of inter-rater variability, without compromising segmentation accuracy. Specifically, conventional models trained with Dice loss, binary inputs, and sigmoid/softmax activations tended to be overconfident, underestimating uncertainty regarding rater disagreement. In contrast, fusing labels via averaging within the SoftSeg framework resulted in underconfident outputs that overestimated rater disagreement. While the optimal label fusion method varied between the two datasets—suggesting a task-dependent nature—SoftSeg systematically achieved segmentation performance equal to or better than conventional models, while also providing superior calibration and a more faithful representation of inter-rater variability.

Detecting and pinpointing fires within visual data is crucial for managing fire emergencies. While semantic segmentation techniques can identify specific fire pixels, their localized nature often overlooks global contextual cues regarding fire presence that are inherent in image labels. To address this, we introduce a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) designed for simultaneous fire classification and segmentation, thereby enhancing segmentation accuracy. Our approach integrates a spatial self-attention mechanism to model long-range pixel dependencies and a novel channel attention module that leverages classification probabilities as attention weights. By jointly training the network for both tasks, we achieve superior performance compared to single-task segmentation methods and prior fire segmentation approaches.

Predicting overall survival (OS) is a critical metric for assessing glioma prognosis and guiding treatment strategies. Current state-of-the-art approaches rely on a pre-hoc framework that necessitates segmentation maps of tumor sub-regions (necrotic, edema, and enhancing areas) to estimate OS. However, generating these segmentation labels is labor-intensive and costly, as it requires ground truth annotations that are often unavailable in large-scale hospital datasets, thereby limiting the practicality of existing methods. This paper presents a novel post-hoc method for OS prediction that eliminates the need for segmentation map annotations during training. The proposed model takes medical images and patient demographics (specifically age) as inputs to predict OS time and generate a saliency map that localizes the tumor to provide post-hoc interpretability. Crucially, while the model can identify tumor locations, it is trained solely using ground truth OS time labels, requiring no segmentation data. Evaluated on the BraTS 2019 dataset, our approach demonstrates performance comparable to pre-hoc methods while offering the distinct advantage of not depending on segmentation labels for training.

This paper establishes various convergence properties for fine $p$-(super)minimizers defined on quasiopen sets within metric spaces. To achieve this, we derive a Caccioppoli-type inequality and local-to-global principles applicable to these minimizers on such sets. A significant component of this work involves demonstrating that the functions reside in an appropriate local fine Sobolev space. Our findings are proven for complete metric spaces endowed with a doubling measure that supports a $p$-Poincaré inequality, where $1 < p < \infty$. Nevertheless, the majority of these results represent new contributions even for unweighted $\mathbb{R}^n$.
