The \emph{budgeted rooted node-weighted Steiner tree} problem involves a graph $G$ with $n$ nodes, a designated root $r$, and node-specific weights representing costs and prizes. The objective is to identify a tree rooted at $r$ where the cumulative node cost does not exceed a budget $B$, while maximizing the total prize. Conversely, the \emph{quota rooted node-weighted Steiner tree} problem replaces the budget with a real-valued quota $Q$, aiming to minimize the tree's cost subject to achieving a prize of at least $Q$.

For directed graphs featuring an additive prize function, we introduce a method utilizing a standard flow-based linear programming relaxation to construct trees with a favorable balance between prize and cost. This approach yields simple polynomial-time approximation algorithms for both problem variants. Specifically, the algorithm for the \emph{budgeted} problem achieves a bicriteria approximation of $(1+\epsilon, O(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2}n^{2/3}\ln{n}))$ for any $\epsilon \in (0, 1]$. For the \emph{quota} problem, it guarantees a bicriteria factor of $(2, O(n^{2/3}\ln{n}))$. Furthermore, leveraging the same flow-based LP, we present a surprisingly straightforward polynomial-time $O((1+\epsilon)\sqrt{n} \ln {n})$-approximation algorithm for the node-weighted directed Steiner tree problem, valid for any $\epsilon>0$.

In the context of undirected graphs with monotone submodular prize functions over node subsets, we offer a polynomial-time $O(\frac{1}{\epsilon^3}\sqrt{n}\log{n})$-approximation algorithm for the \emph{budgeted} problem that relaxes the budget constraint by at most a factor of $1+\epsilon$, for any $\epsilon \in (0, 1]$. Our methodology also extends to delivering strong approximation results for the \emph{quota} problem.

Identifying object keypoints is a fundamental visual task, yet supervised learning for this purpose typically demands vast amounts of data, which is costly and time-intensive to acquire. To address this limitation, there is increasing focus on semi-supervised learning (SSL), which utilizes a small collection of labeled instances alongside a large pool of unlabeled ones. Within SSL methods, pseudo-labeling (PL) is particularly prominent; it involves assigning pseudo-labels to unlabeled data and iteratively training the model on a mix of labeled and pseudo-labeled samples. The efficacy of PL hinges on selecting high-quality pseudo-labeled instances. While prior research primarily relies on manually defined single confidence thresholds for sample selection, we introduce an automated method using a sequence of dynamic thresholds to curate reliable pseudo-labeled samples, effectively forming a learning curriculum. Comprehensive evaluations across six keypoint localization benchmark datasets show that our approach substantially surpasses existing state-of-the-art SSL techniques.

Glioblastoma Multiforme (GBM) represents a malignant brain tumor, accounting for approximately 48% of all Central Nervous System (CNS) and brain cancers. In the United States alone, over 13,000 individuals die annually from GBM, underscoring the critical need for early diagnostic systems capable of enabling predictable and effective therapies. While chemotherapy is the standard post-diagnosis treatment—functioning by inducing apoptosis in rapidly dividing cells—it proves ineffective when the MGMT promoter sequence is methylated, often resulting in severe adverse effects that reduce patient survival rates. Consequently, identifying the methylation status of the MGMT promoter via non-invasive machine learning (ML) models based on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is essential. Leveraging the Brain Tumor Segmentation (BraTS) 2021 dataset, previously utilized in an international Kaggle competition, we developed four primary models: two radiomic and two convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures, each addressing the binary classification task with iterative enhancements. A key innovation was the creation of a novel ML model called the Intermediate State Generator, designed to standardize the slice thickness across all MRI scans. Through continued refinement, our top-performing model achieved statistically significant ($p < 0.05$) results superior to the best Kaggle submission, boasting a 6% increase in average cross-validation accuracy. This advancement holds the potential to guide more informed chemotherapy decisions, thereby extending the lives of thousands of GBM patients yearly.

Inverse text normalization (ITN) transforms automatic speech recognition (ASR) outputs from spoken to written format. Traditional handcrafted ITN rules are difficult to maintain, while neural modeling approaches depend on large-scale, high-quality spoken-written pairs that are in-domain or from similar domains, both of which demand expensive and intricate annotations. This paper introduces a data augmentation method that effectively creates rich spoken-written numeric pairs from out-of-domain text with minimal human annotation. We empirically show that an ITN model trained with this augmentation technique consistently outperforms models trained solely on in-domain data across all numeric surfaces—such as cardinals, currency, and fractions—achieving an overall accuracy improvement of 14.44%.

This Snowmass whitepaper focuses on physical mathematics, offering a concise overview and emphasizing the primary inquiries derived from a more comprehensive work by the same authors titled "A Panorama Of Physical Mathematics 2021."

We analyzed the thermal conditions of the intergalactic medium (IGM) across ten redshift bins between $z = 2$ and $z = 4$, utilizing 103 high-resolution, high signal-to-noise Ly$\alpha$ forest spectra and four distinct flux distribution statistics. These observations were calibrated against mock spectra generated from extensive hydrodynamical simulations processed with our CITE code, which finely samples the amplitude and slope of the anticipated temperature-density relationship. Inferred thermal parameters derived from the flux power spectrum, Doppler parameter distribution, and wavelet and curvature statistics are consistent within their error margins and collectively reveal the expected peak in temperature and minimum in the slope of the temperature-density relation resulting from HeII reionization. By synthesizing results from these various flux statistics, we determined a peak temperature at mean density of $T_0 = (14750 \pm 1322)$ K and a corresponding minimum slope of $\gamma = 1.225 \pm 0.120$. The peak in thermal evolution is located at $z \approx 3$, aligning with prior studies that indicated such a peak, though those earlier results exhibited significant scatter. Additionally, we employed CITE to compute the IGM's thermal state as predicted by five prominent spatially homogeneous UV-background models. The rapid thermal evolution observed in our data is well replicated by two of these models, provided we assume physically motivated non-equilibrium evolution with photo-heating rates reduced by a factor of approximately 0.7 to 0.8. Conversely, the remaining three models predict a more extended HeII reionization period, featuring a temperature peak that is both earlier and higher than what our measurements indicate.

This work revisits the definition and key features of quadratic gravity theories incorporating torsion. Beginning with the most general Lagrangian density quadratic in both curvature and torsion tensors, we derive necessary conditions for the stability of these theories. This analysis relies on the requirement that General Relativity emerges when torsion vanishes and examines the dynamics of vector and pseudovector torsion fields within the weak-gravity limit. Furthermore, we explicitly derive the gravitational field equations by applying the Palatini variational principle, with the metricity condition enforced through a Lagrange multiplier.

Typical blockchain protocols rely on consensus mechanisms to ensure that mutually distrusting users agree on the execution order of operations on shared data. However, asset transfer systems—the most prevalent blockchain application—can be implemented without consensus. Under the assumption that no account is accessed concurrently (i.e., each account has a single owner), an asset transfer system can be efficiently executed in a purely asynchronous, consensus-free environment. Conversely, implementing asset transfers with shared accounts requires consensus and is impossible otherwise.

This paper introduces CryptoConcurrency, an asset transfer protocol designed to process concurrent accesses in parallel without consensus whenever feasible. Specifically, if simultaneous transfer operations on a specific account do not result in overspending—meaning all transactions can be applied while keeping the balance non-negative—they execute in parallel. If overspending is detected, the account owners may need to interact with an external consensus object. Furthermore, the system allows each account to utilize its own consensus implementation, trusted solely by that account's owners.

This study proposes an agent-centric framework to address novelty within the visual recognition aspect of handwriting recognition (HWR). The goal is to develop an ideal transcription agent capable of matching or exceeding human perception by identifying both familiar and new characters in images, as well as detecting stylistic variations within or between documents. A significant challenge remains the presence of novelty, which has hindered even advanced machine learning algorithms. In handwritten text, novelty may manifest as changes in the writer, character or writing attributes, or the document's overall appearance. Rather than addressing these factors in isolation, we advocate for an integrated agent that can process known characters and novelties concurrently. This work formalizes the domain of HWR with novelty, outlines a baseline agent, establishes an evaluation protocol using benchmark data, and presents experiments that set a new state-of-the-art. The results demonstrate the feasibility of the agent-centric approach, though further research is required to reach human-level reading proficiency. Ultimately, this provides the HWR community with a formal foundation to advance solutions for this complex challenge.

Semileptonic $D \to K \ell \nu$ decays offer a complementary approach to determining the CKM matrix element $V_{cs}$, distinct from studies of leptonic $D_s$ decays. HPQCD presents results from a recently published, refined determination of $V_{cs}$. This work features a new, high-precision calculation of the scalar and vector form factors for $D \to K$ transitions, derived from lattice simulations across eight different $N_f=2+1+1$ MILC gluon field configurations using the HISQ action, three of which utilize physical light quark masses. By combining these theoretical inputs with experimental data, we extract $|V_{cs}| = 0.9663(80)$ for the first time with sub-percent precision. This result is robust, as three distinct methods—each merging our form factors with varying experimental datasets in unique ways—yield results in strong agreement. Our primary approach utilizes $q^2$-binned differential decay rate data, while alternative calculations determine $V_{cs}$ from the total branching fraction and from the experimentally quoted quantity $|V_{cs}|f_+(0)$.

In our prior work, we introduced a covariant BRST quantization of unimodular gravity capable of explaining the small cosmological constant, demonstrating that the theory's physical degrees of freedom match those of general relativity; this was achieved using rank-2 antisymmetric tensor fields for both ghosts and antighosts. In this paper, we present an alternative formulation that employs a vector field for the antighost while maintaining the original ghost structure. This approach yields a considerably simpler covariant quantization with fewer ghosts and eliminates tripole modes within the ghost sector. Furthermore, we confirm that this method also results in only two physical transverse modes, consistent with general relativity.

Cut problems constitute a foundational category within algorithmic graph theory, encompassing well-known instances such as the minimum cut, minimum $s$-$t$ cut, minimum multiway cut, and minimum $k$-way cut. These issues have been the subject of extensive research over many decades. This paper launches the algorithmic investigation of specific cut problems within high-dimensional contexts.

The initial problem addressed is the Topological Hitting Set (THS). It is defined as follows: provided a nontrivial $r$-cycle $\zeta$ within a simplicial complex $\mathsf{K}$, the objective is to identify a set $\mathcal{S}$ of $r$-dimensional simplices with the smallest possible cardinality that intersects every cycle homologous to $\zeta$. Our primary finding demonstrates that THS can be solved in polynomial time for triangulations of closed surfaces. Notably, the optimal solution is characterized by the surface's cocycles. For general complexes, we establish that THS is W[1]-hard relative to the solution size $k$. Conversely, we prove that THS admits a Fixed-Parameter Tractable (FPT) algorithm parameterized by $k+d$, where $d$ represents the maximum degree of the Hasse graph of $\mathsf{K}$.

We further introduce the Boundary Nontrivialization (BNT) problem. Given a bounding $r$-cycle $\zeta$ in a simplicial complex $\mathsf{K}$, BNT requires finding a set $\mathcal{S}$ of $(r+1)$-dimensional simplices with minimum cardinality such that removing $\mathcal{S}$ renders $\zeta$ non-bounding. We show that BNT is W[1]-hard with respect to the solution size parameter. However, for $(r+1)$-dimensional complexes where the $(r+1)$-th Betti number $\beta_{r+1}$ serves as the parameter, we present an FPT algorithm with an $O(\log n)$-approximation. Finally, we offer randomized (approximation) FPT algorithms for the global versions of both THS and BNT.

We introduce a numerical accountant designed to assess the tight $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-privacy loss for algorithms producing discrete one-dimensional outputs. Grounded in the privacy loss distribution formalism, our method leverages recently developed fast Fourier transform-based accounting techniques. Through an error analysis centered on the moment bounds of the privacy loss distribution, we derive rigorous lower and upper bounds for the actual $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-values. As a practical application, we offer a new strategy for accurately accounting privacy in the subsampled Gaussian mechanism, thereby completing prior analyses by establishing strict bounds for the privacy parameters. We validate the accountant's performance using the binomial mechanism, demonstrating that our approach reduces required noise variance by up to 75 percent at equivalent privacy levels compared to existing literature. Additionally, we illustrate the computation of tight bounds for the exponential mechanism when applied to counting queries.

Current data suggests the presence of new physics (NP) in various observables related to $b 	o c \ell^- { ar
u}_\ell$ transitions. In this presentation, I outline measurable angular distributions for ${ ar B} 	o D^* \mu^- { ar
u}_\mu$ and ${ ar B} 	o D^* 	au^- (	o \pi^- 
u_	au) { ar
u}_	au$ decays, incorporating the most comprehensive NP contributions. These angular distributions provide sufficient detail to determine the Lorentz structure of the NP, aiding its identification, and are also capable of detecting non-SMEFT (non-decoupling) NP effects.

This paper addresses the challenge of covering a planar area using unit discs. We establish an enhanced upper bound and the initial nontrivial lower bound on the required number of discs, which vary based on the region's area and perimeter. Additionally, we develop algorithms for efficiently covering convex polygonal regions with unit discs, demonstrating that their computational complexity is pseudo-polynomial relative to the input and output sizes. Furthermore, we prove that these algorithms achieve a constant factor approximation of the optimal covering solution.

A fundamental premise of online advertising is linking a specific ad impression to its corresponding webpage. However, in reality, attributing ads is difficult because of the vast scale, intricate complexity, and varied nature of ad delivery systems. This paper introduces a novel fraud technique termed "placement laundering," which takes advantage of flaws in attribution mechanisms to enable malicious actors to boost revenue by fabricating ad requests that seem to come from reputable publishers. We outline the core characteristics of placement laundering and present details of two real-world instances, one of which exploits the functionality of the widely used SafeFrame environment. Furthermore, we propose a detection method capable of identifying a broad category of laundering schemes and share the results of our testing.

This study investigates how entropic corrections to the Friedmann equations influence the evolution of perturbations during the early universe. We examine two specific modifications to the area law of entropy: Tsallis and Barrow entropies. By applying these corrections, we derive altered Friedmann equations and analyze the development of perturbations in a flat universe containing dark matter and a cosmological constant. Utilizing the spherically symmetric collapse formalism within the linear regime, we discover that the density contrast profile in Tsallis and Barrow cosmologies diverges significantly from standard cosmological models. Our results indicate that the growth rate of matter perturbations is highly sensitive to the values of the Tsallis and Barrow parameters. Specifically, as these correction parameters increase, the total density contrast also rises, suggesting that perturbations evolve more rapidly in a universe governed by Friedmann equations modified by entropic corrections.

This study calculates the up/down-quark mass ($m_{q=u/d}$) within the isoscalar scalar channel using both the Shifman-Vainshtein-Zakharov (SVZ) and Monte-Carlo-based QCD sum rules. The associated spectral function, which accounts for contributions from the $f_0(500)$, $f_0(980)$, and $f_0(1370)$ resonances, was derived from an advanced $U(3)$ chiral analysis. Applying the conventional SVZ QCD sum rules yields a prediction for the average light-quark mass of $m_q(2 \, \text{GeV}) = \frac{1}{2}(m_u(2 \, \text{GeV}) + m_d(2 \, \text{GeV})) = (3.46^{+0.16}_{-0.22} \pm 0.33) \, \text{MeV}$. Conversely, by incorporating uncertainties in input QCD parameters and the spectral functions of the isoscalar scalar channel, the Monte-Carlo-based approach produces $m_q(2 \, \text{GeV}) = (3.44 \pm 0.14 \pm 0.32) \, \text{MeV}$. Both findings are mutually consistent and align well with the Particle Data Group value when uncertainties are considered.

By utilizing copositivity concepts and gauge orbit spaces within the scalar potential of the compact 341 model, we establish analytic necessary and sufficient conditions that ensure the scalar potential remains bounded in every field space direction at the tree level.

This paper presents findings from Edge-TCT and I-V measurements on passive test structures fabricated in the LFoundry 150 nm HV-CMOS process on p-type substrates with initial resistivities between 0.5 and 3 k$\Omega$cm. The samples underwent reactor neutron irradiation up to a fluence of 2$\cdot$10$^{15}$ n$_{\mathrm{eq}}$/cm$^2$. Depletion depth was quantified using Edge-TCT, and the effective space charge concentration, $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$, was derived from the relationship between depletion depth and bias voltage to analyze its variation with neutron fluence. The observed dependence of $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ on fluence varies according to the initial acceptor concentration, consistent with other measurements on p-type silicon. Additionally, a long-term accelerated annealing study of $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and detector current was conducted over 1280 minutes at 60$^\circ$C, revealing that both $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and the reverse-biased detector current behave as anticipated for irradiated silicon.

Exceptional points (EPs) represent unique band singularities that are central to various exotic optical effects and non-Hermitian band theory. This study establishes a topological classification of isolated EPs utilizing homotopy theory. Specifically, the analysis reveals that an $n$-th order EP in two dimensions is entirely defined by the braid group $B_n$, where its eigenenergies form a geometric knot along a closed loop surrounding the EP. The quantized discriminant invariant corresponds to the knot's writhe, while the crossing number of the knot determines the count of bulk Fermi arcs originating from each EP. Additionally, we introduce a non-Hermitian no-go theorem that regulates EP configurations and splitting rules on 2D lattices, extending beyond the traditional fermion doubling theorem. We also offer a straightforward algorithm to construct non-Hermitian Hamiltonians featuring a specified knot. Overall, this framework provides a systematic topological classification of EPs and opens avenues for investigating the fascinating phenomena associated with non-Hermitian band degeneracy.

Utilizing graphene on metallic films for surface plasmon resonance (SPR) sensors offers proven benefits, including corrosion protection and the ease of attaching functional groups for selective detection. Recent studies suggest that few-layer graphene can further boost sensor sensitivity. However, these works often treat graphene as an isotropic thin film, assuming its out-of-plane refractive index matches its in-plane index. This paper critically evaluates the impact of single and few-layer graphene on SPR sensitivity enhancement by modeling the material in three ways: as an atomic-scale 2D sheet, as a thin effective isotropic medium with uniform conductivity across all axes, and as a non-isotropic layer with distinct conductivity perpendicular to the 2D plane. Our findings indicate that only the isotropic layer model—which is recognized as inaccurate for optical graphene modeling—yields significant sensitivity improvements, whereas the more physically accurate models result in negligible contributions.

The recently introduced Detection Transformer (DETR) effectively leverages Transformer architectures for object detection, reaching performance levels comparable to two-stage frameworks like Faster-RCNN. However, DETR is hindered by slow convergence, requiring 500 training epochs to reach high accuracy when trained from scratch. To address this, we introduce a straightforward yet powerful method to enhance the DETR framework: the Spatially Modulated Co-Attention (SMCA) mechanism. SMCA's fundamental concept involves implementing regression-aware co-attention by restricting co-attention responses to peak near initially predicted bounding box locations. By substituting the original decoder co-attention module with our proposed SMCA while leaving the rest of the DETR architecture intact, we significantly accelerate convergence. Moreover, incorporating multi-head and scale-selection attention designs into the comprehensive SMCA allows it to outperform DETR equipped with a dilated convolution backbone, achieving 45.6 mAP at 108 epochs compared to 43.3 mAP at 500 epochs. We conducted extensive ablation studies on the COCO dataset to confirm the efficacy of the proposed SMCA.

This study introduces Hindsight Goal Ranking (HGR), a technique designed to enhance Hindsight Experience Replay (HER) by addressing its reliance on uniform sampling for hindsight goals. Unlike the standard approach, HGR increases the probability of sampling states visited during episodes exhibiting higher temporal difference (TD) errors, treating these errors as an indicator of the learning potential within an experience. The implementation involves a two-step process: first, an episode is selected from the replay buffer based on the average TD error of its constituent experiences, and second, a hindsight goal that results in a larger TD error is prioritized when sampled from the episode's future states. When integrated with the Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) algorithm, an off-policy, model-free actor-critic method, HGR significantly accelerates learning across four complex simulated robotic manipulation tasks compared to non-prioritized versions. Empirical findings indicate that HGR utilizes samples more efficiently than prior methods across all tested scenarios.

Pulsed Doppler radars frequently employ the classic Chinese remainder theorem (CCRT) to address Doppler ambiguities arising from high-speed targets. Additionally, fast-moving objects often suffer from a degradation in signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) following range compression, an issue that subpulse processing (SP) can partially alleviate. Contemporary radar systems integrate these approaches to accurately determine target velocity; however, background noise can degrade Doppler estimation accuracy, necessitating a rigorous statistical evaluation. This study presents a thorough analysis of Doppler estimation, deriving new closed-form equations for the probability of detection (PD) and probability of false alarm (PFA). By incorporating the recently introduced SP method alongside CCRT, we also compare SP performance against traditional pulse processing (PP). Numerical results and Monte-Carlo simulations validate our derived expressions and demonstrate that the SP-plus-CCRT approach significantly lowers the PFA compared to prior research, thereby enhancing radar detection capabilities.

Machine translation is typically defined as producing a single target text from a given source document. In this paper, we explore a more rigorous constraint: jointly generating two texts where each output is effectively dependent on the other. As discussed, this approach serves various practical functions, ranging from multi-target machine translation to creating controlled variations of the target text. We provide an analysis of potential implementations for dual decoding and test it across four applications. By examining the problem from multiple perspectives, we can better underscore the challenges of dual decoding and comprehensively evaluate the advantages of generating coordinated translations over independent ones.

The study investigates double-lepton polarization asymmetries in the exclusive decay B->K_1 l^+ l^- within the Universal Extra Dimension (UED) Model, revealing that these asymmetries exhibit high sensitivity to UED parameters. Consequently, experimental measurements of double lepton polarizations could provide significant insights into physics extending beyond the Standard Model (SM).

We define $D_N$ as the collection of points where a planar Brownian motion completes at least $N$ windings. It is established that the random measure on the plane, defined by the density $2 \pi N 1_{D_N}$ relative to the Lebesgue measure, converges almost surely in the weak sense as $N \to \infty$ to the occupation measure of the Brownian motion.

Understanding cell migration requires insight into how cells apply and respond to forces within their surroundings. For biophysicists modeling cell movement, intracellular stress is a primary focus. Currently, three methods exist to quantify this stress, all operating under the thin plate approximation: two solve the mechanical equilibrium equation within the cell material (Monolayer Stress Microscopy and Bayesian Inference Stress Microscopy), while the third relies on displacement continuity at the cell/substrate interface (Intracellular Stress Microscopy). This study demonstrates via 3D FEM modeling that these approaches do not measure identical quantities, as previously thought; the first two methods compute the sum of active and resistive stresses, whereas the third calculates only the resistive component. Consequently, integrating these techniques could theoretically allow for the isolation of active stress alone.

Deformable registration models frequently employ unsupervised learning strategies to address the scarcity of ground truth deformation fields, typically relying on intensity-based similarity losses to achieve convergence. While effective, this reliance alone is inadequate. In mono-modality deformable registration, perfectly aligned images must not only exhibit negligible intensity differences but also align closely in statistical distribution and boundary regions. Recognizing that well-crafted loss functions can guide models toward optimal convergence, we developed a deformable registration model for T1-weighted MR images by incorporating various image features through a hybrid loss approach. This method successfully registers the OASIS dataset with high precision while maintaining deformation smoothness.

The study of polytopes represented a significant milestone in elementary integral group theory. This paper extends the notion of contra-linearly stochastic lines to H-Positive Definite Monoids. We demonstrate that incorporating the Non-Gaussian assumption grants Sub-Canonical properties to the problem of ordinary Elementary Numerical Operators. Furthermore, we explore the potential for classifying associative, bijective, and conditionally covariant subalgebras, with proofs provided in every section.

Predicting financial time series is notoriously challenging because of their chaotic nature. While statistical methods have delivered reliable outcomes for specific tasks like forecasting market trends or individual stock prices, recent breakthroughs in deep learning and big data analytics have introduced new, promising strategies for this domain. Furthermore, emerging research indicates that hybridizing statistical techniques with machine learning often yields higher forecast accuracy than relying on either approach alone. Building on these insights, this study introduces MegazordNet, a framework that integrates statistical features with a structured deep learning model to enhance time series forecasting. When evaluated on predicting S&P 500 closing prices using various metrics, our approach outperformed standalone statistical and machine learning methods.

Assuming gravitational redshift caused by a central supermassive black hole, we analyzed the redward shifts and widths of H$\beta$ and Fe ii broad emission lines across 1973 SDSS DR5 quasars ($z<0.8$) to determine the virial factor used in estimating black hole masses via reverberation mapping or related methods. While the virial factor was traditionally attributed to the geometric structure of the broad-line region, our results show that for 98% of these quasars, the Fe ii factor exceeds that of H$\beta$. The factor varies significantly between objects and across different emission lines. For most quasars, the H$\beta$ virial factor is higher than the standard averages typically employed in mass calculations. We identified three positive correlations: between the H$\beta$ virial factor and the dimensionless accretion rate, between the H$\beta$ virial factor and the Fe ii/H$\beta$ line ratio, and a three-dimensional correlation linking all three quantities. This suggests the virial factor is primarily governed by the dimensionless accretion rate and metallicity. Additionally, a negative correlation exists between the H$\beta$ redward shift and the scaled broad-line region radius (relative to the black hole's gravitational radius); this relationship is naturally expected if the redshift is predominantly due to black hole gravity. Finally, radiation pressure from the accretion disk may contribute significantly to the virial factor.

The Semi-grant-free (SGF) transmission scheme allows grant-free (GF) users to access resource blocks reserved for grant-based (GB) users without compromising the quality of service for GB users. This study examines the secrecy performance of NOMA-aided SGF systems. Initially, exact and asymptotic analytical expressions for the secrecy outage probability (SOP) are derived for systems with a single GF user. Subsequently, the analysis extends to SGF systems with multiple GF users employing a best-user scheduling scheme, where closed-form expressions for both exact and asymptotic SOP are obtained using order statistics theory. Monte Carlo simulations validate the accuracy of these analytical findings and illustrate how system parameters influence the SOP. The findings reveal that the secrecy performance of SGF systems is primarily determined by the outage target rate for GB users and the secure target rate for GF users.

Using first-principles calculations, we examine the electronic band structure of graphene placed atop various two-dimensional magnetic transition-metal phosphorus trichalcogenide monolayers, MPX$_3$ (where M={Mn,Fe,Ni,Co} and X={S,Se}). A symmetry-based model Hamiltonian is utilized to derive orbital parameters and sublattice-resolved proximity-induced exchange couplings ($\lambda_{\textrm{ex}}^\textrm{A}$ and $\lambda_{\textrm{ex}}^\textrm{B}$) from the low-energy Dirac bands of the induced graphene. The magnetic phase of the MPX$_3$ layer—ranging from ferromagnetic to three distinct antiferromagnetic configurations—dictates entirely different Dirac dispersions, with exchange splittings varying between 0 and 10~meV. Notably, the exchange couplings not only vary in magnitude based on the magnetic phase but also differ in their global sign and type. Crucially, both uniform ($\lambda_{\textrm{ex}}^\textrm{A} \approx \lambda_{\textrm{ex}}^\textrm{B}$) and staggered ($\lambda_{\textrm{ex}}^\textrm{A} \approx -\lambda_{\textrm{ex}}^\textrm{B}$) exchange couplings can be achieved in graphene. Analysis of specific cases reveals that interlayer distance and transverse electric fields serve as effective tuning mechanisms for these exchange splittings. Specifically, reducing the interlayer distance by merely 10% yields a five-fold increase in proximity exchange, whereas applying an electric field of a few V/nm enables tunability of the exchange by tens of percent. Additionally, the dependence on the Hubbard $U$ parameter is found to be minimal, and the influence of spin-orbit coupling on the proximitized Dirac dispersion is negligible compared to the exchange coupling effects.

Hyper-parameter tuning (HPT) is essential for numerous machine learning (ML) algorithms, yet its expansive search space often makes the process time-consuming and resource-heavy. Although leveraging public cloud resources offers convenience for training ML models, it comes at a high expense. Consequently, accelerating HPT while simultaneously lowering costs is a critical challenge for cloud-based ML users. This paper introduces SpotTune, a method designed to utilize transient, revocable cloud resources through specialized strategies to execute HPT in a parallel and cost-effective manner. By orchestrating HPT on transient servers, SpotTune employs two primary techniques: fine-grained cost-aware resource provisioning and ML training trend prediction, aiming to minimize both monetary expenditure and runtime. Evaluation results demonstrate that SpotTune can cut costs by as much as 90% while achieving a 16.61-fold improvement in performance-cost efficiency.

High-performing deep learning models typically incur significant computational expenses. This paper integrates two strategies designed to lower these costs while maintaining model efficacy: pruning and early exit networks. We assess two pruning methodologies for early exit networks: (1) simultaneous pruning of the entire network and (2) sequential pruning of the base network followed by additional linear classifiers. Experimental findings indicate that simultaneous pruning is generally the superior approach. However, at high accuracy levels, both methods yield comparable results, suggesting that the pruning and early exit processes can be decoupled without compromising optimality.

Extending beyond space-coding metasurfaces, space-time digital metasurfaces significantly broaden the utility of digital metamaterials by enabling the concurrent control of electromagnetic waves across both spatial and frequency domains. This study introduces a set of practical closed-form equations for large digital metasurfaces to predict the absolute directivity of scattered beams. These formulas are derived using a superposition of terms with unequal coefficients, Huygens' principle, and an appropriate time-varying biasing mechanism. Furthermore, within a harmonic beam steering framework, two distinct analytical expressions were derived to calculate the exact total radiated power at harmonic frequencies and for end-fire scattered beams, based on several suitable assumptions. Despite these simplifications, the formulas provide a rapid and accurate estimation tool for designing large digital metasurfaces with specific power intensity patterns. The analysis addresses the impact of quantization levels and metasurface dimensions on power manipulation performance, as well as the constraints on maximum scan angles in harmonic beam steering. Numerical simulations conducted in MATLAB confirm the theoretical predictions with strong agreement. Given the constraints outlined, this phase-only meta-particle approach can be applied to any desired frequency. The author concludes that this straightforward method opens new avenues for applications including multi-target radar and THz communication systems.

Two distinct methodologies are employed to derive viscoelasticity, expressed through a fluctuating conformation tensor, based on the dynamics of a finite number of dumbbells. The initial method utilizes stochastic calculus exclusively, serving as a reference standard for the second approach, which is grounded in thermodynamic principles and relies on the Helmholtz free energy and a generalized relaxation tensor. The study demonstrates that the outcomes of these two approaches coincide only when a finite-size contribution to the conformation tensor's Helmholtz free energy is incorporated. Using statistical mechanics, this paper explicitly derives this non-zero finite-size contribution for a broad range of models whenever the observed volume contains a finite number of dumbbells. It is further observed that the generalized relaxation tensor for the conformation tensor requires no such finite-size correction.

Within the decentralized finance (DeFi) landscape, lenders provide flash loans to borrowers—transactions that must be repaid with fees before concluding, allowing asset borrowing without upfront collateral. While powerful, these loans enable malicious actors to accumulate significant assets and launch costly exploits against DeFi protocols. This paper presents a novel framework for the automated synthesis of adversarial contracts designed to exploit such protocols via flash loans. To circumvent the inherent complexity of DeFi systems, we introduce a method that approximates protocol behaviors using numerical techniques, specifically polynomial linear regression and nearest-neighbor interpolation. We subsequently formulate an optimization query based on these approximations to identify an adversarial attack sequence of function invocations with optimal parameters that maximizes profit. Furthermore, we propose a counterexample-driven refinement technique to enhance approximation accuracy. Our framework is implemented in a tool named FlashSyn, which we evaluated against 12 DeFi protocols known to have suffered flash loan attacks, as well as protocols from the Damn Vulnerable DeFi challenges. The results demonstrate that FlashSyn successfully automatically synthesizes adversarial attacks for every tested protocol.

Financial advisors utilize client questionnaires and discussions to construct investment portfolios aligned with individual objectives. Financial institutions assign risk ratings to their securities, which guide both clients and advisors in selecting portfolios that match stated risk tolerances. This study compares clients' Know Your Client (KYC) risk profiles with their actual portfolio risk selections using a value-at-risk (VaR) discrepancy methodology. By applying VaR to measure both elicited and revealed risk, the research assesses whether clients are over- or under-risked, evaluates how shifts in KYC risk influence portfolio configuration, and examines the impact of cash flows on portfolio risk. The paper demonstrates VaR's effectiveness using a dataset from a private Canadian financial dealership comprising over 50,000 accounts, 27,000 clients, and 300 advisors. Employing a unified measure for both elicited and revealed risk allows for an assessment of how closely a client's portfolio aligns with their stated goals. The authors argue that utilizing VaR to quantify client risk offers advisors critical insights to ensure KYC compliance, tailor portfolios to client goals, communicate strategies for aligning portfolios or updating goals, and monitor risk position changes across their practice.

This paper introduces a novel online multi-agent trajectory planning algorithm designed to ensure safe and dynamically feasible paths within cluttered settings. By employing a linear safe corridor (LSC) to define a distributed trajectory optimization problem using solely feasible constraints, the method avoids reliance on slack variables or soft constraints to prevent optimization failures. Additionally, a priority-based goal planning approach is implemented to avert deadlocks without requiring a separate mechanism to determine which robot should yield. On an Intel i7 laptop, the algorithm successfully computes trajectories for 60 agents at an average rate of 15.5 ms per agent, achieving flight distances comparable to baseline methods that utilize soft constraints. The approach was confirmed to reach goals without deadlock in both random forest and indoor scenarios, with its safety and operability further validated through a real-world flight test involving ten quadrotors navigating a maze-like environment.

This paper investigates the aggregation of fuzzy preferences within societies that are not necessarily finite. We define a class of complete preference models, characterized by possibility and impossibility results, where transitivity holds for any t-norm. To achieve this, we represent each model using specific crisp binary relations and utilize the findings established by Kirman and Sondermann.

This study presents findings from a search for a standard model-like Higgs boson with a mass between 70 and 110 GeV that decays into two photons. The analysis utilizes data from the CMS experiment, gathered during proton-proton collisions in the 2012 and 2016 LHC runs, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 19.7 and 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ at center-of-mass energies of 8 and 13 TeV, respectively. The paper details the observed and expected 95% confidence level upper limits on the product of the cross section and branching fraction for the diphoton decay channel. For the 2012 and 2016 datasets individually, the observed limits span from 129 to 31 fb and 161 to 26 fb, respectively. A statistical combination of these results within the shared mass range of 80 to 110 GeV establishes an upper limit on the cross-section times branching fraction, normalized to standard model predictions, varying from 0.7 down to 0.2. Two significant exceptions are noted: a rise to 1.1 near the Z boson peak, potentially caused by Drell-Yan dielectron events misidentified as isolated photons, and a local excess relative to standard model expectations peaking at a mass hypothesis of 95.3 GeV, with local and global significances of 2.8 and 1.3 standard deviations, respectively.

This research investigates the factors influencing organizational employees' motivation to defend against cyber threats. The study examines the relationships between protection motivation and variables including fear of cyberattacks, perceived severity, vulnerability, and threats, as well as perceived efficacy, self-efficacy, costs, mandatoriness, and psychological reactance. Utilizing a cross-sectional design, the researchers administered a survey to academics across six Slovenian universities from June to September 2017. While 324 individuals completed the English-language questionnaire (yielding a 7.6% response rate), data from 255 respondents remained after excluding incomplete entries. A Slovenian translation of the survey instrument is also accessible.

The convergence status of the Flint-Hills series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^3\sin^2(n)}$ remains unresolved. Alekseyev (2011) linked this problem to the irrationality measure of $\pi$, showing that $\mu(\pi) > \frac{5}{2}$ leads to divergence. In this work, we demonstrate a nearly reciprocal result: $\mu(\pi) < \frac{5}{2}$ implies convergence. Our findings regarding the density of close rational approximations may also hold independent significance. We briefly examine the unresolved boundary case where $\mu(\pi) = \frac{5}{2}$, suggesting that resolving it would be challenging.

Orthogonal polynomials $P_{n}(\lambda)$ exhibit oscillatory behavior with respect to $n$ as $n\to\infty$ when $\lambda$ lies within the absolutely continuous spectrum of the associated Jacobi operator $J$. We demonstrate that, regardless of specific constraints on the operator $J$'s coefficients, the amplitude and phase components in the asymptotic expressions for $P_{n}(\lambda)$ satisfy particular universal relationships detailed in this work. Our methodology centers on analyzing operators that diagonalize Jacobi operators, which are defined using the orthogonal polynomials $P_{n}(\lambda)$ and map from the function space $L^2 (\Bbb R)$ to the sequence space $\ell^2 ({\Bbb Z}_{+})$. By examining these operators in a broad context, we establish the necessary and sufficient conditions required for their boundedness.

Shape space learning aims to map a training set of shapes to and from a latent representation space while ensuring strong generalization. Since real-world shape collections often exhibit symmetries—defined as transformations that preserve the shape's essential nature—a natural approach is to design encoders and decoders that are equivariant to these symmetries. This paper introduces a framework for integrating equivariance into both encoders and decoders through two main contributions: first, adapting the recent Frame Averaging (FA) framework to create generic, efficient, and highly expressive equivariant autoencoders; and second, developing autoencoders that are equivariant to piecewise Euclidean motions applied to distinct parts of a shape. To our knowledge, this represents the first fully piecewise Euclidean equivariant autoencoder construction. The training process is straightforward, relying on standard reconstruction losses without the need for novel loss functions. Our architectures combine standard backbone networks with appropriate frame averaging to achieve equivariance. Evaluations on rigid shape datasets using implicit neural representations and articulated shape datasets using mesh-based neural networks demonstrate state-of-the-art generalization to unseen shapes, significantly outperforming relevant baselines. Notably, the method shows marked improvements in generalizing to previously unseen articulated poses.

Separative von Neumann regular rings are plentiful. For instance, all regular self-injective rings, unit regular rings, and regular rings with a polynomial identity are separative. It is still an open question whether any non-separative regular rings exist. This note investigates various conditions that ensure a von Neumann regular ring is separative. We demonstrate that such a ring $R$ is separative if it satisfies any of the following criteria: (1) $R$ is a CS ring; (2) $R$ is pseudo injective (or auto-injective); (3) $R$ possesses the closure extension property, meaning the essential closures in $R$ of two isomorphic right ideals are also isomorphic. Additionally, we provide an alternative characterization of regular perspective rings (Proposition 3.3).

This study reports a measurement of the $W$ boson mass utilizing proton-proton collision data from 2011 collected at the LHC with the ATLAS detector. The dataset corresponds to a centre-of-mass energy of 7 TeV and an integrated luminosity of 4.6 fb$^{-1}$. The analysis includes $7.8 \times 10^6$ events in the $W\rightarrow \mu \nu$ channel and $5.9 \times 10^6$ events in the $W\rightarrow e \nu$ channel. The mass value is derived by fitting templates to the reconstructed distributions of the charged lepton transverse momentum and the $W$ boson transverse mass for both decay modes. The results are:
\begin{eqnarray} m_W &=& 80370 \pm 7 \, (\textrm{stat.}) \pm 11 \, (\textrm{exp. syst.}) \pm 14 \, (\textrm{mod.
syst.}) \, \textrm{MeV} &=& 80370 \pm 19 \, \textrm{MeV}, \end{eqnarray}
where the uncertainties represent statistical, experimental systematic, and physics-modelling systematic contributions, respectively. Additionally, the mass difference between the $W^+$ and $W^-$ bosons is determined to be $m_{W^+}-m_{W^-} = -29 \pm 28$ MeV.

Federated Learning (FL) enables edge devices to jointly train a shared predictive model without transferring their local data to the cloud, effectively separating machine learning capabilities from centralized data storage. Although algorithmic progress in FL has been significant, practical support for executing these algorithms on edge devices remains limited. This paper investigates on-device FL implementation across a range of smartphones and embedded systems using the Flower framework. Furthermore, we assess the system-level costs associated with on-device FL and propose how quantifying these costs can guide the development of more efficient FL algorithms.

This study focuses on the numerical approximation of backward stochastic differential equations (BSDEs). We introduce a novel algorithm grounded in the regression-later approach and the least squares Monte Carlo method. We establish conditions ensuring the convergence of our numerical scheme and present two practical experiments to demonstrate its efficacy.

Sheared multi-component bulk metallic glasses exhibit properties defined by their inherent chemical and structural disorder. This study examines the evolution of local microstructural elastic modulus during the plastic yielding transition in six Ni-based multi-component glasses, which possess compositional traits typically linked to solid solution formability. Our findings reveal that elastic modulus fluctuations exhibit consistent percolation characteristics, indicating universal behavior regardless of chemical composition and yielding sharpness. Specifically, elastic heterogeneity increases upon shearing as elastically soft clusters percolate through a generally rigid amorphous matrix, a phenomenon consistent with previous studies on granular media and colloidal glasses. We identify distinct signatures of a percolation transition marked by spanning clusters that display universal scale-free characteristics and critical scaling exponents. Prior to yielding, both the spatial correlation length and mean cluster size diverge, with associated critical exponents showing only a weak dependence on compositional variations and macroscopic stress-strain curve specifics.

This paper addresses a graph search problem where a team of searchers aims to locate a mobile target within a graph. Under the assumptions that (a) searchers have restricted visibility, (b) they move at unit speed, and (c) the target possesses infinite speed, we define the Limited Visibility Graph Search (LVGS) problem. We introduce the LVGS algorithm, which generates a search schedule guaranteed to capture the target in the minimum number of steps. This algorithm is derived by adapting Guibas and Lavalle's method for searching polygonal regions.

Chemotaxis refers to the directed motion of organisms, ranging from bacteria to multicellular entities, driven by chemical cues. Two prominent mathematical frameworks for this phenomenon are the Keller-Segel equation, which operates at the macroscopic scale, and the chemotaxis kinetic equation, which functions at the mesoscopic level; these models are asymptotically equivalent within the parabolic regime. The organism's reaction to chemical stimuli is encoded in the diffusion and advection coefficients of the Keller-Segel model or within the turning kernel of the kinetic equation. Experimental data tracking the temporal dynamics of population movement under specific stimuli allows researchers to infer the chemotactic response, forming an inverse problem. This paper examines the relationship between the inverse problems associated with both macroscopic and mesoscopic forward models using a Bayesian framework to determine the posterior distribution of the organism population's turning kernel. Furthermore, we demonstrate the asymptotic equivalence between these two posterior distributions.

This theoretical investigation examines the photoexcitation of highly charged ions from their ground states, a process feasible at CERN's Gamma Factory. A primary focus is the influence of mixing between opposite-parity ionic levels—caused by both external electric fields and the weak electron-nucleus interaction—on excitation rates. Utilizing relativistic Dirac theory to revisit the well-established "Stark-plus-weak-interaction" mixing found in neutral atoms, we conduct detailed calculations for ${\rm 1s}_{1/2} \to {\rm 2s}_{1/2}$ and ${\rm 1s}^2 \; {\rm 2s}_{1/2} \to {\rm 1s}^2 \; {\rm 3s}_{1/2}$ (M1 combined with parity-violating-E1) transitions in hydrogen- and lithium-like ions, respectively. Specifically, we analyze the disparity in excitation rates resulting from right- versus left-circularly polarized incident light. This difference, stemming from parity-violating level mixing, is typically quantified via the circular-dichroism parameter. We posit that future circular dichroism measurements using highly charged ions within the SPS or LHC rings could yield significant insights into the strength of the electron-nucleus weak-interaction coupling.

We re-examine traditional string problems within the realm of parameterized complexity, analyzing them via dynamic data structures. Rather than seeking static algorithms for efficient instance resolution, our objective is to create data structures that can efficiently maintain a solution—or determine its absence—following updates to the input. First, we address the Closest String problem by developing randomized dynamic data structures featuring amortized update times of $d^{\mathcal{O}(d)}$ and $|\Sigma|^{\mathcal{O}(d)}$, where $\Sigma$ represents the alphabet and $d$ denotes the maximum distance bound. These results stem from integrating established static Close String methods with color-coding techniques. Subsequently, leveraging a finding by Frandsen et al.~[J. ACM'97], we derive a meta-theorem that yields dynamic data structures for parameterized string problems with worst-case update times of $\mathcal{O}(\log \log n)$, where $k$ is the parameter and $n$ is the string length. We demonstrate the meta-theorem's effectiveness by constructing such structures for Disjoint Factors and Edit Distance. Furthermore, we present explicit data structures for these problems with worst-case update times of $\mathcal{O}(k2^{k}\log \log n)$ and $\mathcal{O}(k^2\log \log n)$, respectively. Finally, we explore how a lower bound framework introduced by Amarilli et al.~[ICALP'21] implies that achieving an update time of $\mathcal{O}(f(k))$ for Disjoint Factors and Edit Distance is improbable, even when the parameter $k$ remains constant.

We present a method for selecting objects within neural volumetric 3D representations, including multi-plane images (MPI) and neural radiance fields (NeRF). By utilizing a collection of foreground and background 2D user scribbles from a single view, our system automatically generates a 3D segmentation of the target object, enabling its rendering in novel perspectives. This capability is achieved through a new voxel feature embedding that integrates the neural volumetric 3D representation with multi-view image features from all input angles. To assess our method, we have created a novel dataset comprising human-annotated segmentation masks for objects in real-world multi-view scene captures. Our results demonstrate that this approach surpasses robust baselines, including both 2D segmentation and 3D segmentation techniques adapted for this specific task.

Reconstructing 3D shapes from a single image remains a significant and enduring challenge in computer vision. Although numerous recent studies have advanced state-of-the-art performance during the deep learning era, a more challenging and less explored problem persists: generalizing learned capabilities to unseen object categories with vastly different geometric distributions. This paper introduces the concept of compositional generalizability and proposes a novel framework designed to improve generalization to such unseen categories. We decompose the 3D shape reconstruction task into specific sub-problems, each addressed by a dedicated neural sub-module optimized for generalizability. Our approach is based on the intuition that while object geometries may vary significantly (e.g., between chairs and cabinets), certain elements are commonly shared across categories, including object parts (such as slates and cylinders), their relationships (like adjacency and translation symmetry), and shape substructures (including T-junctions and symmetric part groups). Experiments conducted on PartNet demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches, validating both our problem factorization strategy and network architecture.

This paper introduces a novel class of DNA codes defined over two noncommutative rings, $E$ and $F$, each of order four and characteristic 2. These codes are constructed using quasi self-dual codes over $E$ and $F$. By leveraging quasi self-duality, we characterize the fixed GC-content constraint weight distributions and the reverse-complement constraint minimum distributions for these codes.

The lottery ticket hypothesis establishes the link between neural network structure, initialization parameters, and learning capacity. However, the original approach, which involves pruning and weight resetting only after training convergence, suffers from the loss of learned knowledge and incurs high training costs. To address these issues, we introduce a strategy integrating neural architecture search with a pruning algorithm. This method recursively searches for and expands network structures within existing winning ticket sub-networks, enabling continuous training and pruning without performance degradation. Through this recursive process, we generate deeper sub-networks that exhibit superior generalization and test results. This approach resolves challenges such as performance drops after pruning, the forgetting of weights inherent in the original hypothesis, and the difficulty of creating winning tickets when the final architecture is undefined. We validate this strategy using the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets. Furthermore, by connecting our findings to related biological phenomena and recent lottery ticket research, we propose a new hypothesis to explore the factors that maintain a network's "juvenile" state—specifically, the elements influencing a neural network's learning potential and generalization performance throughout training.

We present the concept of a submersion connecting two spray structures and introduce a submersion technique within spray geometry. Leveraging this approach alongside global invariant frames on a Lie group, we establish a comprehensive theoretical framework for homogeneous spray geometry. On a homogeneous spray manifold $(G/H,\mathbf{G})$ featuring a linear decomposition $\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{h}+\mathfrak{m}$, we define the spray vector field $\eta$ and the connection operator $N$, thereby extending concepts familiar from homogeneous Finsler geometry. We demonstrate the correspondence between $\mathbf{G}$ and $\eta$ under reductive decompositions, as well as the link between geodesics on $(G/H,\mathbf{G})$ and the integral curves of $-\eta$. Furthermore, we derive the ordinary differential equations on $\mathfrak{m}$ that govern parallel translations on $(G/H,\mathbf{G})$ and compute the S-curvature and Riemann curvature, which generalize L. Huang's curvature formulae for homogeneous Finsler manifolds.

Following an examination of the challenges in extracting $\alpha_s$ from tau decays caused by Duality Violations and the asymptotic character of the OPE, we present a novel determination utilizing an enhanced vector isovector spectral function. This function relies exclusively on experimental data, achieved by (i) merging ALEPH and OPAL findings for $2\pi$ and $4\pi$ channels and (ii) substituting previously Monte Carlo-estimated contributions from $K^-K^0$ and higher-multiplicity exclusive modes with new BaBar experimental results for $K^-K^0$ and values derived from $e^+ e^-$ cross sections and CVC for the remaining modes. Our analysis yields $\alpha_s(m_\tau)=0.3077\pm 0.0075$, corresponding to $\alpha_s(m_Z)=0.1171\pm 0.0010$. We also address certain criticisms of our methodology raised by Pich and Rodriguez-Sanchez.

International Trade (IT) is pivotal to the modern global economy, fundamentally shaping national development paths by linking production and consumption across borders. While the literature extensively covers IT's evolving structure and drivers, its interactions with other complex dynamics remain underexplored. This study aims to investigate the relationships between IT, International Migration (IM), and Foreign Direct Investment (FDI). The methodology involves initially analyzing these issues through a multiple-network lens before applying specialized econometric techniques. Regarding IM, the research identifies a general positive correlation with IT, pinpointing specific product categories where this link is most pronounced and validating them against prior classifications. Furthermore, by utilizing spatial econometrics and redefining country neighbors based on intense migration flows, the study reveals that migrants from third countries exert a stronger competitive effect on certain goods. In the context of FDI, initial analysis shows that correlations between IT and FDI are primarily driven by economic and demographic scale as well as geographic distance. Subsequently, employing a Heckman selection model within a gravity framework, the study examines non-linear influences stemming from distance, Global Supply Chain positioning, and Regional Trade Agreements. Ultimately, the findings demonstrate that the relationship between IT and FDI varies by sector: they act as complements in manufacturing but as substitutes in services.

Let $Y$ be an integral nodal projective curve of arithmetic genus $g \ge 2$ with $m$ nodes, defined over an algebraically closed field $k$, and let $x$ be a nonsingular closed point on $Y$. Given coprime integers $n$ and $d$ with $n \ge 2$, we fix a line bundle $L$ of degree $d$ on $Y$. Denoting the (compactified) "fixed determinant moduli space" by $U_Y(n,d,L)$, we demonstrate that the restriction $\mathcal{U}_{L,x}$ of the Poincaré bundle to $x \times U_Y(n,d,L)$ is stable under the polarization $\theta_L$. Furthermore, its restriction to $x \times U'_Y(n,d,L)$—where $U'_Y(n,d,L)$ represents the moduli space of vector bundles of rank $n$ and determinant $L}$—is stable under any polarization. Finally, we establish that the Poincaré bundle $\mathcal{U}_{L}$ on $Y \times U_Y(n,d,L)$ is stable with respect to the polarization $a \alpha + b \theta_L$, where $\alpha$ is a fixed ample Cartier divisor on $Y$ and $a, b$ are positive integers.

Session-based recommendation focuses on predicting the next item by analyzing user interactions within brief timeframes. Unlike other recommendation approaches, this paradigm is more susceptible to data sparsity because it relies on very limited short-term user activity. Self-supervised learning offers a promising solution by identifying ground-truth samples directly from raw data; however, current self-supervised recommendation models typically depend on item or segment dropout for data augmentation. This approach is ill-suited for session-based recommendation, as dropout further reduces data density, resulting in unusable self-supervision signals. To address this, we integrate self-supervised learning with co-training to create a framework designed to enhance session-based recommendation. Specifically, we utilize the session-based graph to generate two distinct views that capture the internal and external connectivity of sessions. We then construct separate graph encoders for these views, which recursively exploit their unique connectivity information to produce ground-truth samples that mutually supervise each other through contrastive learning. Unlike dropout strategies, our proposed self-supervised graph co-training maintains complete session information and achieves authentic data augmentation. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that self-supervised graph co-training significantly improves session-based recommendation, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

The linear evolution PDE $\partial_t u(x,t) = -\mathcal{L} u$, where $\mathcal{L}$ is a time-independent, strongly elliptic operator, is examined to determine whether arbitrary solutions can be constructed by superposing snapshots from a single or finite set of solutions. Our findings indicate that this capability hinges on the growth rate of the eigenvalues, $\mu_n$, of $\mathcal{L}$ with respect to $n$. When the condition holds, we propose a straightforward data-driven method for model reduction and approximating arbitrary PDE solutions without prior knowledge of the governing equation. Numerical experiments are included to validate our theoretical analysis.

Biclique-colouring assigns colours to graph vertices such that no maximal complete bipartite subgraph containing at least one edge is monochromatic. We demonstrate that verifying whether a specific vertex-colouring function constitutes a valid biclique-colouring is coNP-complete, a finding that supports the pursuit of structured graph classes where this problem admits efficient solutions. Our analysis focuses on powers of paths and powers of cycles, determining their respective biclique-chromatic numbers. Specifically, the biclique-chromatic number of a path power $P_n^k$ is $\max(2k + 2 - n, 2)$ when $n \ge k + 1$, and exactly $n$ otherwise. For cycle powers $C_n^k$, the biclique-chromatic number is at most $3$ if $n \ge 2k + 2$, and exactly $n$ otherwise; we also identify the cycle powers that are 2-biclique-colourable. All proofs are algorithmic, yielding polynomial-time biclique-colouring algorithms for the studied graph classes.

We have investigated the zero-point offset in Gaia EDR3 parallaxes using a sample of 0.3 million giant stars from LAMOST data, which boasts a distance accuracy exceeding 8.5%. Official zero-point corrections significantly mitigate the global parallax offset in Gaia EDR3; prior to correction, the global offsets were $-$27.9 $\mu$as and $-$26.5 $\mu$as for five- and six-parameter solutions, respectively, dropping to $+$2.6 $\mu$as and $+$2.9 $\mu$as after correction. The bias in raw parallax measurements shows strong dependence on $G$ magnitudes, spectral colors, and stellar positions. While official corrections effectively reduce bias patterns related to $G$ magnitudes, they fail to fully address those linked to spectral colors and positions. This study presents, for the first time, a spatially dependent zero-point correction model for the Gaia EDR3 five-parameter solution within the LAMOST footprint, leveraging the substantial size of our stellar sample.

Mapping correspondences between two images is a key focus in computer vision research. However, estimating the relationship between such images is frequently disrupted by outliers, often resulting from noise in prior processing steps. This paper introduces a convolutional neural network capable of filtering outlier noise. The model outputs the probability that a pair of feature points represents an inlier while simultaneously regressing the essential matrix to determine the camera's relative pose. We conceptualize outlier rejection as a noise elimination task, utilizing a soft threshold function which proves highly effective for this purpose. Consequently, we developed an adaptive denoising module based on the soft threshold function to strip noise components from outliers, thereby lowering the likelihood that they are misclassified as inliers. Experiments conducted on the YFCC100M dataset demonstrate that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in relative pose estimation.

This study investigates how information transmission biases emerge from the interaction between network structure and information dynamics within synthetic scale-free networks that exhibit either homophily or heterophily. We introduce straightforward mathematical tools to measure these biases. Results indicate that neither Simple nor Complex Contagion models alone can account for significant biases; however, a Hybrid Contagion model, which incorporates both mechanisms, generates three distinct homophily-dependent biases: emissivity and receptivity biases, as well as echo chambers. Simulations conducted on an empirical network with high homophily validate the presence of these biases. Our findings illuminate the underlying mechanisms driving inequalities in information source visibility, restricted access to information, and communication barriers between distinct groups.

We present the concept of p-adic magic contraction within the framework of p-adic Hilbert space. Furthermore, we establish the p-adic Halmos dilation, p-adic Egervary N-dilation, p-adic von Neumann inequality, and p-adic Sz.-Nagy dilation specifically for this class of p-adic magic contractions.

The scalar one-loop 4-point function featuring a single massless vertex is calculated analytically using the loop regularization technique. This approach introduces a characteristic scale $\mu_{s}$ to manage divergent integrals. As $\mu_{s}\rightarrow 0$, the infrared divergent components, which appear as $\ln^{2}(\lambda^{2}/\mu^{2}_{s})$ and $\ln(\lambda^{2}/\mu^{2}_{s})$ (with $\lambda$ being a constant dependent on masses and Mandelstam variables), are cleanly distinguished from the infrared stable parts. The final result is presented explicitly through $44$ dilogarithms within the kinematic domain where this evaluation holds.

While classical simulations can exactly determine the wave function of quantum circuits (QCs), they are currently restricted to approximately 50 qubits because their memory and computational requirements grow exponentially with the number of qubits. As quantum hardware progresses toward hundreds of interacting qubits, creating robust methods for approximating QC simulations has become essential. In this study, we present an efficient simulation technique for QCs inspired by density functional theory (DFT), a standard method for analyzing many-electron systems. We demonstrate accurate simulations of diverse QCs utilizing universal gate sets, achieving scales of up to one billion qubits with only laptop-based computing. Our approach predicts marginal single-qubit probabilities (SQPs) with greater than 90% accuracy, maintaining memory and computational costs that scale linearly with qubit count, despite the theoretical exponential cost of calculating SQPs. These results are achieved by employing a mean-field description of QCs and developing optimal single- and two-qubit gate functionals—similar to exchange-correlation functionals in DFT—to evolve SQPs without explicitly computing the QC wave function. These findings establish a path for accurately simulating large-scale QCs and offer a framework for adapting electronic structure methods to the field of quantum circuit simulation.

We investigate pairs of subsets $A$ and $B$ within a compact abelian group $G$ characterized by a small sumset $A+B = \{a+b : a\in A, b\in B\}$. Denoting $m$ and $m_{*}$ as the Haar measure and inner Haar measure on $G$, respectively, we classify all Haar measurable pairs $A, B$ with $m(A), m(B) > \varepsilon$ that satisfy $m_{*}(A+B) \leq m(A) + m(B) + \delta$, where $\delta = \delta(\varepsilon) > 0$ is sufficiently small. Additionally, we examine scenarios involving a small $\delta$-popular sumset, defined as $A+_{\delta}B := \{t\in G : m(A\cap (t-B)) > \delta\}$. We demonstrate that for any $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists a $\delta > 0$ such that if $A$ and $B$ are subsets of $G$ with $m(A), m(B) > \varepsilon$ and $m(A+_{\delta}B) \leq m(A) + m(B) + \delta$, then sets $S, T \subseteq G$ exist where $m(A\triangle S) + m(B\triangle T) < \varepsilon$ and $m(S+T) \leq m(S) + m(T)$. Leveraging established results, this final inequality provides significant structural insights into $S$ and $T$, and consequently into $A$ and $B$.

Real-world spatio-temporal datasets frequently suffer from inaccuracies or incompleteness caused by various data loading delays. For instance, a tensor tracking case counts across locations, diseases, and time may experience delayed updates for specific slices. Restoring these missing or noisy (under-reported) entries can be framed as a generalized tensor completion task. However, standard completion methods typically rely on two assumptions that often fail in spatio-temporal contexts: that missing data is randomly distributed and that noise per element is independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) with zero mean. In practice, we often encounter multiple tensor versions with varying degrees of under-reporting noise, where the noise intensity fluctuates based on time or location as updates accumulate. We address this by modeling the data as a multi-version tensor, introducing an additional mode to capture update dynamics. We propose a low-rank tensor model to forecast these temporal updates, demonstrating its ability to accurately predict ground-truth values in real-world scenarios. Our approach achieves up to 27.2% lower root mean-squared error than the leading baseline. Furthermore, we extend the method to track data evolution over time, resulting in substantial computational efficiency gains.

Naturalistic driving data (NDD) serves as a critical resource for analyzing crash causation, human factors, and advancing countermeasures for accident prevention, often incorporating video recordings. Although NDD datasets frequently contain vast amounts of video footage, human annotators can only process a tiny fraction, leading to significant underutilization of available data. This paper investigates a computer vision approach to automatically extract relevant information from these videos. Specifically, we developed a 3D ConvNet algorithm designed to automatically identify cell-phone-related behaviors. Experimental results indicate that our method can segment video clips, approximately 79% of which contain the automatically labeled cell phone behaviors. When combined with human verification of these extracted segments, this approach enables the identification of cell-phone-related driver behaviors far more efficiently than manual video review.

Any permutation of weights and biases within a specific neural network architecture yields the same functional behavior, implying that training algorithms encounter millions of equivalent optimal solutions within the parameter space, even for modest network sizes. To the authors' knowledge, this phenomenon has not been previously documented. To constrain the parameter search space, a novel method is introduced that enforces monotonically increasing configurations for bias vectors across each layer. This is accomplished by integrating inequality constraints on the bias vectors into standard learning problems. A Moreau-Yosida regularization-based algorithm is proposed to manage these constraints, and its theoretical convergence is proven. Applications to standard trigonometric functions and more complex stiff ordinary differential equations in chemically reacting flows demonstrate the significant advantages of this approach.

Small-scale transients in the Solar corona exhibit significantly higher frequencies than flares and are crucial to coronal dynamics. This study examines three distinct transients identified by Hi-C and confirmed via Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) EUV channels on the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO). We employed 0-D enthalpy-based hydrodynamical simulations to generate synthetic light curves for comparison with AIA data. These transients were modeled as loops approximately 1.0 Mm in length, depositing energies around $10^{23}$ ergs within roughly 50 seconds. The resulting synthetic light curves demonstrate reasonable agreement with observations. During the initial phase, conductive flux from the corona exceeds radiative flux, similar to impulsive flaring events. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the time-integrated net enthalpy flux is positive, meaning energy flows into the corona. The ability to model these transients using the same physical mechanisms as nanoflares, microflares, and large flares suggests they may share a common origin.

We analyzed CO absorption lines against the continuum emitted by dust heated in the obscuring tori surrounding active galactic nuclei (AGNs). Utilizing three-dimensional non-LTE line transfer simulations that account for dust thermal emission, we examined the formation of absorption lines from CO rotational transitions. Following the approach in Papers I–III of this series, we employed post-processed radiative transfer calculations based on the "radiation-driven fountain model" (wada2016), which generates a geometrically thick structure around the nucleus consistent with the spectral energy distribution of the Circinus galaxy, a nearby type-2 Seyfert. Our results indicate that continuum-subtracted channel maps for the $J = 4-3$ and higher transitions reveal absorption regions along the disk mid-plane when viewed edge-on. These spectra display a mix of emission and multiple absorption features, mirroring the torus's internal inhomogeneous and turbulent nature. The most profound absorption arises from gas on the near-side of the torus between $r = 10$ and 15 pc, situated in front of AGN-heated dust within $r \simeq 5$ pc. Furthermore, resolving these absorption features requires a spatial resolution of 0.5–1.0 pc, and observation is feasible only at inclinations close to edge-on ($\sim 85^\circ$). These findings suggest that integrating our radiation-hydrodynamic model with high-resolution ALMA observations of CO (7-6) could yield new insights into the internal structure of molecular tori in nearby AGNs.

Although recent deep neural network (DNN)-based single-channel speech enhancement techniques have yielded impressive outcomes, they often struggle with generalization in real-world scenarios. Similar to other data-driven approaches, these DNN models suffer from substantial performance drops when encountering untrained data. To address this, we leverage the benefits of multi-target joint learning to enhance model generalization, proposing a lightweight and computationally efficient dilated convolutional network (DCN) for robust speech denoising.
