By modeling the spectrum of the cold phase of J122809.72+440514.8 ($T_{\text{eff}}=9300\,$K) with the CMFGEN code, we estimated a mass loss rate of $\dot{M} = 5.2\times10^{-3}\,M_{\odot}\,yr^{-1}$. Ultimately, J122809.72+440514.8 and J122817.83+440630.8 were classified as LBVs, while the remaining two stars were identified as LBV or B[e]-supergiant candidates.

This paper demonstrates that introducing appropriate noise resolves the non-uniqueness issue in solutions to the tree dyadic turbulence model. We establish weak probabilistic uniqueness for all $l^2$-initial conditions by employing a method grounded in the characteristics of the $q$-matrix linked to a continuous-time Markov chain.

Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) is a rapidly emerging technique gaining traction among computational scientists in the field of nonintrusive reduced-order modeling. A key advantage of DMD lies in its solid theoretical foundation within Koopman approximation theory, effectively positioning it as a data-driven implementation of the renowned Koopman operator. However, achieving a stable DMD implementation requires computing the singular value decomposition of the input data matrix, a process that becomes computationally prohibitive for high-dimensional systems. To mitigate this challenge, we propose a framework utilizing sketching methods, where a matrix sketch is a significantly smaller matrix that adequately approximates the original system. This compression is achieved by applying specific random transformations to the input matrix. Consequently, costly computations can be performed on this reduced matrix, thereby accelerating the resolution of the original problem. We validate this approach through numerical experiments using the spherical shallow water equations as a representative model for geophysical flows. Various sketching techniques are assessed for their ability to capture the data matrix's range and co-range. Our results demonstrate that the proposed sketching-based framework accelerates multiple stages of the DMD algorithm compared to classical methods operating directly on raw data. This leads to substantial computational efficiency, which is crucial for enabling digital twins of high-dimensional systems.

The AMS-02 experiment has delivered high-precision measurements across multiple cosmic-ray (CR) species. This percent-level accuracy enables the detection of subtle spectral variations among these species, thereby allowing for a rigorous test of CR acceleration universality, a principle central to the standard shock acceleration model. Although pre-AMS-02 data already suggested a breakdown in universality between protons and helium, it remains uncertain whether helium and heavier nuclei can be reconciled under a universal framework. To investigate this, we conducted a joint analysis incorporating AMS-02 data for antiprotons, protons, helium, helium-3, boron, carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen. We examined two competing propagation models: one featuring a diffusion coefficient break at a few GVs without reacceleration, and another involving reacceleration alongside breaks in the primary injection spectra. Additionally, we accounted for uncertainties in nuclear production cross-sections for secondaries by incorporating nuisance parameters into the fit, utilizing Monte Carlo methods to explore the resulting parameter space. Our findings reveal that, contrary to naive expectations, CR universality is violated in standard scenarios not only for helium but also for carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen; explaining the observed spectra necessitates different injection slopes (at a level of $\Delta \sim 0.05$). As an alternative, we investigated further propagation scenarios inspired by non-homogeneous diffusion that might preserve universality. Finally, we assessed the universality of CR propagation itself by comparing properties derived from light nuclei ($\bar{p}$, p, He, $^3$He) against those inferred from heavier nuclei (B, C, N, O).

Document Visual Question Answering (VQA) represents an emerging research area at the intersection of Natural Language Processing and Computer Vision, focusing on interpreting visually complex documents to respond to natural language queries. This study introduces TAT-DQA, a new dataset comprising 3,067 document pages featuring both unstructured text and semi-structured tables, along with 16,558 question-answer pairs derived from the TAT-QA dataset. Sourced from real-world financial reports, these documents are rich in numerical data, necessitating discrete reasoning capabilities to address the questions effectively. Building on TAT-DQA, we propose MHST, a novel model that integrates multi-modal information—specifically text, layout, and visual imagery—to intelligently select strategies such as extraction or reasoning for various question types. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MHST significantly outperforms baseline methods, though its performance still trails that of expert humans. We anticipate that the TAT-DQA dataset will advance research into deep document understanding that combines vision and language, particularly in scenarios demanding discrete reasoning. Additionally, we hope the MHST model will inspire the development of more sophisticated Document VQA architectures in the future. The dataset will be made publicly available for non-commercial use at https://nextplusplus.github.io/TAT-DQA/.

This study establishes error bounds for continuous-time regression on specific subsets of Riemannian manifolds. The regression task, governed by a nonlinear evolution law with values on the manifold, is formulated as an optimal estimation problem within a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). We introduce a novel concept of persistency of excitation (PE) tailored for manifold-based estimation and derive convergence rates for continuous-time estimates based on this condition. The paper further examines and analyzes two methods for approximating the exact regression solution. Finally, numerical simulations are presented to demonstrate the qualitative properties of the estimated functions, including results from function estimates along a Lorenz system trajectory and an analysis of the two approximation methods applied to motion capture data.

Fake news spreads rapidly across social media, reaching global audiences and endangering communities. While deep learning models perform well on labeled data for specific events, their efficacy often drops when encountering new events due to domain shifts. This creates a significant hurdle for existing detection systems when dealing with emergent events where large, labeled datasets are scarce. Furthermore, adapting to new events typically requires training a model from scratch or extensive fine-tuning, which is often costly, impractical, and difficult to sustain in real-world scenarios. To overcome these limitations, we introduce MetaFEND, an end-to-end framework designed to rapidly learn fake news detection for emerging events using only a small number of verified posts. By combining meta-learning with neural process methods, our approach leverages the strengths of both techniques. Specifically, we incorporate a label embedding module and a hard attention mechanism to better manage categorical data and filter out irrelevant content. Extensive experiments on multimedia datasets from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate that MetaFEND effectively detects fake news in previously unseen events, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods.

Interference serves as the fundamental process that organizes waves into remarkable patterns. Currently, structured waves are pivotal for sensing, imaging, trapping, and foundational research, driving a surge of intriguing investigations. By employing a coherent optical field as a probe, we demonstrate how to shape light into distributions featuring collapse and revival patterns within their wavefronts. These configurations arise from the Fourier spectrum of an arrangement of aperiodic diffracting elements. Notably, the resulting interference can exhibit quasiperiodic diffraction peaks across multiple spatial scales, despite the underlying structure lacking periodicity. We draw a parallel between this behavior and revival phenomena observed in the time evolution of quantum mechanical systems, validating our theoretical framework through both numerical simulations and experimental results that show strong agreement.

This research investigates the creation of autonomous agents capable of executing sequences of actions derived from human instructions to fulfill specific tasks. While recent advancements have been substantial for short-horizon tasks, agents often struggle with long-horizon tasks that require extended action sequences, frequently resulting in missed instructions, getting stuck, or task failure. To overcome this, we introduce M-TRACK, a model-agnostic, milestone-based task tracker designed to guide and monitor agent progress. Our approach includes a milestone builder that annotates instructions with necessary navigation and interaction checkpoints for step-by-step completion, and a milestone checker that systematically evaluates progress within the current milestone to decide when to advance. Evaluated on the challenging ALFRED dataset, M-TRACK achieves significant relative improvements of 33% and 52% in unseen success rates compared to two competitive baseline models.

This work introduces a probabilistic perspective on multiple kernel learning that unifies established regularised risk methods with recent developments in approximate Bayesian inference relaxations. The proposed framework offers a versatile objective function applicable to regression, robust regression, and classification tasks; this function serves as a lower bound on the marginal likelihood and encompasses numerous regularised risk approaches as specific instances. Additionally, we develop an optimization algorithm that is both computationally efficient and provably convergent.

This paper derives the precise expression for Klein's fundamental second-kind 2-form specifically for $C_{ab}$ curves. Although Klein originally resolved this issue in the 19th century regarding hyper-elliptic curves, significant advancement on extending it to broader classes remained stagnant for over a century. Recent efforts by multiple authors have addressed this by solving the problem for specific subclasses of $C_{ab}$ curves, utilizing numerical methods to obtain individual solutions. This formula establishes a standard cohomological basis for these curves, offering extensive applications across algebraic geometry, physics, and applied mathematics, extending beyond the general analysis of sigma functions.

This study tackles the challenge of identifying non-persistent changes that begin and end at unknown moments. We re-examine the rationale for several well-known maximum likelihood ratio methods and analyze their operational performance.

Depth completion aims to reconstruct a dense depth map from a sparse input and an RGB image. While recent methods leverage color images to infer depth at missing pixels, relying solely on color fails to capture essential semantic scene understanding, leading to performance degradation under sudden lighting variations like shadows. To address this, we introduce a novel three-branch architecture featuring color-guided, semantic-guided, and depth-guided components. The color-guided branch processes the sparse depth map and RGB image to produce a color depth map containing scene cues such as object boundaries. This output, combined with the semantic image and sparse depth map, feeds into the semantic-guided branch to estimate semantic depth. Subsequently, the depth-guided branch integrates the sparse, color, and semantic depth maps to generate the final dense depth map. These three depth representations are adaptively fused to form the backbone's output. Furthermore, we implement a Semantic-Aware Multi-Modal Attention-Based Fusion Block (SAMMAFB) to merge features across all branches and employ CSPN++ with Atrous convolutions to refine the resulting dense depth map. Extensive experiments on the KITTI benchmark demonstrate that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance at the time of submission.

This study employs low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate the dynamic bonding of gold atoms on surfaces under low coordination conditions. Using an atomically sharp gold tip, researchers deposit a gold adatom with atomic precision either at a first hollow site adjacent to a step edge or at a distant location. To distinguish the bonding behaviors associated with these two distinct placements, the work combines classical molecular dynamics simulations at 4.2 K with density functional theory calculations. Furthermore, these computational methods provide insights into classifying the crystalline structure of STM tips based on their experimental outcomes.

Bayesian optimization (BO) has emerged as a favored approach for globally optimizing costly real-world functions. Contrary to the widespread notion that BO is exclusively designed for black-box functions, its successful deployment actually depends on domain knowledge regarding function characteristics. This expertise is frequently encoded in Gaussian process priors that define initial beliefs about the functions. Nevertheless, even with expert input, selecting an appropriate prior remains challenging, particularly for hyperparameter tuning in complex machine learning models where optimization landscapes are often intricate and hard to interpret. We propose an alternative method for establishing these functional priors, specifically targeting scenarios where data from similar functions enables the pre-training of a more constrained distribution. Theoretically, we demonstrate that BO utilizing pre-trained priors achieves bounded regret. To validate this approach within realistic model training environments, we assembled a substantial multi-task hyperparameter tuning dataset by evaluating tens of thousands of configurations of near-state-of-the-art models across popular image, text, and protein sequence datasets. Our findings indicate that, on average, our method locates optimal hyperparameters at least three times more efficiently than the leading competing techniques.

In the limit where the deformation parameter $\lambda$ vanishes, the complete (anti)commutator relations for the ${\cal N}=4$ supersymmetric linear $W_{\infty}[\lambda=0]$ algebra are established for any weights $h_1$ and $h_2$ of the currents involved. The $w_{1+\infty}$ algebra emerges from this structure by taking the limit where the deformation parameter $q$ approaches zero, accompanied by appropriate current contractions. Conversely, for nonzero $\lambda$, the full structure of the ${\cal N}=4$ supersymmetric linear $W_{\infty}[\lambda]$ algebra is determined for an arbitrary weight $h_1$, provided the second weight $h_2$ satisfies the constraint $h_1-3 \leq h_2 \leq h_1+1$. Additional terms appear on the right-hand sides of the (anti)commutators beyond those found in the $\lambda=0$ case specifically when $h_2$ falls outside this defined region, regardless of the arbitrary weight $h_1$.

Although lubricants are commonly employed in macroscopic mechanical systems to mitigate friction and wear, their efficacy at the microscopic level remains uncertain. To address this, this study employs classical molecular dynamics simulations to examine rotational motion transmission between two nanoscale diamond solid-state gears immersed in various lubricant molecules. Our findings indicate that lubricants facilitate the synchronization of rotational transmission between the gears, irrespective of the specific molecular species or the center-of-mass separation distance. Furthermore, we analyzed the impact of the driving gear's angular velocity, revealing its connection to the bond formation dynamics between the gears.

Establishing whether two knots are equivalent, or more accurately, isotopic, represents a cornerstone issue in topology. In this work, we cast this challenge within the framework of Predicate Calculus by leveraging braid-based knot representations and foundational topological theorems. Specifically, Knot theory is expressed through a language featuring the signature $(\cdot,T,\equiv, 1,\sigma,\bar\sigma)$, where $\cdot$ serves as a binary operation, $T$ as a unary operation, $\equiv$ as a binary relation, and $1$, $\sigma$, and $\bar\sigma$ as constants. We outline a finite collection of axioms that define this language as a first-order theory. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any knot can be encoded as a term $b$ constructed from $1$, $\sigma$, $\bar\sigma$, and $T$, such that two knots represented by terms $b_1$ and $b_2$ are equivalent precisely when $b_1 \equiv b_2$. This approach generates a diverse array of significant mathematical problems situated within First Order Logic.

P-wave superfluids exhibit unique topological properties crucial for robust quantum state control, yet achieving this state experimentally poses significant difficulties. This study investigates s- and p-wave superfluidity within mixtures of fermionic and spinor bosonic gases, establishing a comprehensive set of gap equations for both phases. By numerically solving these equations for the s-wave component, we determine the specific physical requirements necessary to realize a pure p-wave state in a controlled atomic physics setting, free from s-wave contamination.

Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), the established framework for strong interactions, governs the dynamics between quarks and gluons. The observable particles resulting from these interactions are hadrons, composed of quarks and gluons. However, because QCD is strongly coupled at the distance scales relevant to observable hadrons, it lacks rigorous, first-principle methods to derive hadronic spectra and properties directly from the QCD Lagrangian, with the notable exception of Lattice QCD simulations, which currently struggle to address all facets of complex, short-lived states. Consequently, numerous "QCD-inspired" phenomenological models have been developed. A shared characteristic of these models is the prediction of hadrons with substructures more intricate than the standard quark-antiquark mesons and three-quark baryons of the original quark model, which effectively describes most low-mass hadrons. Recently, experimental evidence has emerged for various non-standard candidates, including multi-quark mesons, meson-gluon hybrids, and pentaquark baryons containing heavy charm or bottom quarks. This review examines the experimental data supporting these states and compares their measured properties against standard quark-model expectations and predictions from models of non-standard hadrons. We conclude that the spectroscopy of all hadrons except the simplest ones remains unexplained.

This study addresses the topological equivalence of functions defined on a compact surface $M$ that possess isolated critical points on the boundary, where these points are also isolated when restricted to the boundary. We designate this class of functions as $\Omega(M)$. First, we established a topological classification for these functions within neighborhoods of their critical points. Second, we developed a method to construct a chord diagram based on the neighborhood of a critical level. Additionally, we examined the minimum number of critical points required for such functions. Finally, we formulated a criterion for determining the global topological equivalence of functions within $\Omega(M)$ that feature exactly three critical points.

We introduce a generalized entanglement measure within the framework of AdS/CFT correspondence. Unlike standard entanglement entropy, which corresponds to the area of a Ryu-Takayanagi surface for a spatial subregion, our approach incorporates entanglement among spatial degrees of freedom as well as across different fields in the boundary theory. Additionally, we account for the contributions of strings with varying winding numbers in the bulk geometry. Applying this measure to the D1/D5 system at and near the orbifold point, we calculate it for a thermal state dual to the BTZ black hole. Our results indicate that this generalized entanglement entropy is dual to the length of a geodesic possessing a non-zero winding number. These geodesics traverse the entire bulk geometry, accessing the entanglement shadow up to the horizon in one-sided black holes and probing wormhole growth in two-sided black holes over arbitrarily long durations. Consequently, we suggest that the entanglement structure of the boundary state suffices to reconstruct asymptotically AdS$_3$ geometries, provided one accounts for extremal surface barriers.

This paper investigates a class of Schrödinger-Poisson systems featuring multiple competing potentials and a critical Sobolev exponent. Unlike problems with only positive potentials, this issue requires a distinct approach due to the weight potential set $\{Q_i(x) | 1 \le i \le m\}$, which includes nonpositive, sign-changing, and nonnegative elements. By employing the ground energy function and detailed analysis, we first establish the existence of a ground state solution $v_\varepsilon$ in the semiclassical limit using the Nehari manifold and the concentration-compactness principle. Furthermore, we demonstrate that $v_\varepsilon$ converges to the ground state solution of the associated limiting problem while concentrating at a specific set determined by the potentials. Additionally, we examine various properties of this ground state solution and derive a sufficient condition for its nonexistence.

This study examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation characterized by nonlocal flux and fractional dissipation, defined as $u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0$ for $(t,x)\in R^{+}\times S$, where $S=[-\pi,\pi]$, $\kappa\geq0$, and $0<\alpha\leq1$. We first demonstrate local-in-time well-posedness within the space $H^{3}(S)$. When $\kappa=0$, we show that solutions originating from smooth, odd initial data inevitably develop singularities in finite time. Furthermore, even with the inclusion of a weak dissipation term $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$, we prove that finite-time blowup still occurs.

A subset of young neutron stars, known as magnetars, possesses ultra-intense magnetic fields. Existing models attributing these fields to specific, extreme conditions conflict with the observation that magnetar birth rates match those of core-collapse supernovae. We propose that this apparent contradiction can be resolved if toroidal magnetic fields undergo oscillations after the proto-neutron star (PNS) dynamo phase. The final field strength depends on the oscillation phase at which the process halts, resulting in either very high fields ($\gtrsim 10^{15}\,{\rm G}$) for magnetars or relatively lower ones ($\sim 10^{14}\,{\rm G}$) for ordinary neutron stars. Using a shear-driven dynamo model to generate PNS magnetic fields, we demonstrate that toroidal fields do indeed oscillate post-dynamo. We argue that these Alfv\'enic oscillations determine whether a neutron star becomes a magnetar or a standard one, contingent upon the phase at which the magnetic fields freeze.

Dual-phase liquid xenon time projection chambers (TPCs) have been among the most effective tools for direct dark matter detection, enhancing sensitivity to weakly interacting massive particles by nearly five orders of magnitude over recent decades. Nevertheless, scaling these dual-phase systems to the ~50-tonne sensitive mass required for next-generation experiments remains a significant challenge, primarily due to difficulties in achieving sufficiently high electric field strengths for electron drifting and maintaining low background rates. To address this, we propose a single-phase liquid xenon TPC with a detector geometry resembling a Geiger counter as a viable alternative for future searches. This design prioritizes signal uniformity over isolated charge detection. Preliminary field simulations and signal reconstruction studies indicate that this single-phase approach is technically feasible and capable of delivering the robust signal performance necessary for direct dark matter detection.

Knowledge-dependent tasks generally rely on two knowledge sources: parametric knowledge acquired during training and contextual knowledge provided at inference. To investigate how models integrate these sources, we formalize the concept of knowledge conflicts, defined as instances where contextual information contradicts learned information. By analyzing the behavior of widely used models, we quantify their excessive dependence on memorized data—a primary driver of hallucinations—and identify key factors that intensify this issue. Furthermore, we introduce a straightforward method to reduce reliance on parametric knowledge, which curbs hallucinations and enhances out-of-distribution generalization by 4% to 7%. Our results highlight the necessity for practitioners to assess a model's propensity to hallucinate versus retrieve information, demonstrating that our mitigation strategy fosters better generalization to time-dependent queries. To facilitate these practices, we have made our framework for generating knowledge conflicts publicly available.

Network design challenges focus on determining cost-effective structures like routes, trees, and subgraphs, often with the goal of minimizing hop length or diameter. However, introducing hop constraints makes these optimization problems significantly more difficult and less understood compared to their unconstrained versions, largely because hop-constrained distances in graphs deviate strongly from metric properties. Despite this, we demonstrate that hop-constrained distances can be effectively approximated using distributions of "partial tree metrics." We leverage this insight to create a robust algorithmic framework that, akin to traditional probabilistic tree embeddings, transforms hop-constrained problems in general graphs into hop-unconstrained problems on trees. Applying this approach, we achieve the first poly-logarithmic bicriteria approximations for numerous classic hop-constrained network design issues, including Steiner forest, group Steiner tree, group Steiner forest, buy-at-bulk network design, as well as their online and oblivious counterparts.

We present a method for assigning segments of a document to a group of unknown writers, requiring no prior knowledge of their stylistic traits. By employing several independent clusterings of the input text, we isolate sections that are either alike or distinct from one another. Furthermore, we outline the algorithms needed to synthesize these multiple clusterings into a coherent result. Finally, we demonstrate the technique's effectiveness on texts exhibiting diverse writing styles.

This paper outlines High-Performance computing initiatives utilizing FPGAs to accelerate pulsar and transient searches for the SKA, featuring case studies from SKA and pathfinder telescopes that underscore future prospects. It examines the paradigm shift from offline radio telescope data processing to digitizing hundreds or thousands of antenna outputs across vast bandwidths, generating numerous beams, and integrating this data into SKA real-time pulsar search pipelines. The work provides an overview of various accelerator architectures, with a focus on new generation Field Programmable Gate Array-based systems, highlighting their essential role in delivering high-performance computing and managing SKA's massive data volumes. Additionally, the paper evaluates the power-performance efficiency of this emerging technology and explores potential future scenarios.

We introduce an efficient method for executing a multiplex-controlled phase (MCP) gate, where several photonic qubits jointly control a single target photonic qubit within a circuit quantum electrodynamics (QED) framework. This multiqubit gate is implemented using a two-level superconducting qubit as a coupler to link multiple cavities. The approach is notably simple, requiring only a single operational step, and highly versatile, as the logic states of each photonic qubit can be encoded using a vacuum state paired with any orthogonal or quasi-orthogonal non-vacuum state (such as Fock states, superpositions, cat states, or coherent states). Key advantages include the avoidance of decoherence from higher energy levels by utilizing only two levels of the coupler, an operation time that remains independent of the qubit count, and deterministic execution without the need for measurement. As a demonstration, we numerically evaluate the experimental feasibility of a three-qubit MCP gate where photonic qubits are encoded via vacuum and cat states. Furthermore, this scheme is broadly applicable to various physical systems involving multiple microwave or optical cavities coupled to a two-level coupler, such as natural or artificial atoms.

We identify rational solutions for a KdV-like equation derived from polynomial solutions of the associated generalized bilinear equation. By employing a specific set of polynomials that adhere to a quadratic difference equation, we establish that the bilinear equation admits no solutions with a degree (in the spatial variable) exceeding 5. Consequently, we provide an affirmative resolution to a conjecture proposed by Yi Zhang and Wen-Xiu Ma regarding these solutions.
This study extends a series examining errors in published claims regarding fixed points within digital metric spaces.

In this paper, we provide a negative response to a reverse question posed by Graeme L. Cohen and Herman J. J. te Riele, demonstrating that no fixed integer $m$ satisfies $\sigma^k(m) \equiv 0 \pmod m$ for all iterations $k$ of the sum-of-divisors function. This conclusion relies on H. Lenstra's results regarding aliquot sequences. Furthermore, we establish the existence of integers $m$ for which the sequence $\sigma_k(m) \bmod m$ exhibits periodicity with a small period $L=2$, where this period divides the least common multiple of $1$ and each exponent in the prime factorization of $m$. We also introduce a new equivalence to the Riemann hypothesis based on congruences and divisibility properties of the sum-of-power-divisor function. Additionally, numerical evidence from stochastic and statistical contexts, particularly Random Matrix Theory, is presented to derive a novel fitting distribution model for the behavior of the sequence $\sigma_k(m) \bmod m$.

Control systems that remain invariant under Lie groups of transformations are analyzed through a geometric framework grounded in Lie symmetry. This approach yields a sufficient condition for dynamic feedback linearizability and reveals a systematic method for deriving all smooth, generic system trajectories. The theory requires no assumptions beyond the system's smoothness and the presence of symmetry; consequently, it accommodates fully nonlinear, time-varying control systems and imposes no restrictions on the local form of the dynamic compensator. Significant focus is placed on the intrinsic geometric structures inherent to symmetric control systems, independent of specific coordinates. To demonstrate practical application, the paper details illustrative cases, such as vertical take-off and landing systems, highlighting the critical role of Lie symmetry in dynamic feedback linearization. These are supplemented by simpler pedagogical examples to aid comprehension. Furthermore, the theoretical constructions have been implemented within the Maple package DifferentialGeometry.

Ensembles of independently trained neural networks represent a cutting-edge technique for estimating predictive uncertainty in Deep Learning, effectively approximating the posterior distribution as a mixture of delta functions. However, because their training depends on the non-convexity of the loss landscape and random initialization of individual models, the resulting posterior approximation lacks control. This paper introduces a principled solution to this issue by minimizing an $f$-divergence between the true posterior and a kernel density estimator (KDE) within a function space. We examine this objective combinatorially, demonstrating that it is submodular regarding mixture components for any $f$. Building on this, we address greedy ensemble construction; by analyzing the marginal gain in negative $f$-divergence—which measures the improvement in posterior approximation from adding a new KDE component—we derive a new diversity term for ensemble methods. Our approach's effectiveness is validated on computer vision out-of-distribution detection benchmarks across various architectures and datasets. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Oulu-IMEDS/greedy_ensembles_training.

This paper establishes a Faber-Krahn type inequality concerning the first eigenvalue of the Hermite operator under Robin boundary conditions. We demonstrate that the optimal domain is a half-space and provide a detailed analysis of the equality case within this inequality.

Accurately quantifying uncertainty remains a significant hurdle in deep learning, particularly because neural networks often commit overconfident errors by assigning high certainty to out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs. While the prevailing methods for estimating predictive uncertainty—such as Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) and deep ensembles that aggregate predictions from multiple networks—are popular, their utility in real-time, industrial settings is constrained by substantial memory and computational demands. Moreover, these ensemble or Bayesian approaches do not inherently resolve all deficiencies of the base networks they utilize. This research investigates principled strategies to enhance the uncertainty capabilities of a single deterministic network. By framing uncertainty quantification as a minimax learning problem, we establish that distance awareness—the capacity to measure how far a test instance lies from the training data—is a prerequisite for achieving high-quality, minimax-optimal uncertainty estimation. We introduce Spectral-normalized Neural Gaussian Process (SNGP), a straightforward technique that boosts the distance-awareness of contemporary deep neural networks through two modifications: (1) applying spectral normalization to hidden weights to ensure bi-Lipschitz smoothness in representations, and (2) substituting the final output layer with a Gaussian process layer. Extensive evaluations across various vision and language benchmarks demonstrate that SNGP surpasses other single-model methods in prediction accuracy, calibration, and OOD detection. Additionally, SNGP offers synergistic advantages when combined with established techniques like deep ensembles and data augmentation, positioning it as a simple and scalable component for probabilistic deep learning. The source code is available at https://github.com/google/uncertainty-baselines.

Deep neural networks have become indispensable for various applications, including vision, reinforcement learning, and classification, owing to their robust empirical performance. However, their lack of interpretability restricts their use in safety-critical domains like medical imaging. While neural tangent kernels (NTKs), which resemble kernel machines, offer some interpretability, we propose a novel architecture that combines multiple NTKs to enhance clarity regarding both classification and individual layers. Unlike previous approaches that model an entire network with a single NTK, our method assigns one kernel to each layer. We validate this model's interpretability on two datasets, demonstrating that the multi-kernel framework effectively reveals the interaction between layers and final predictions.

This work generalizes the classical Hilbert property from varieties over fields to arithmetic schemes over integral domains by requiring that the set of near-integral points, as defined by Vojta, forms a non-thin set. Furthermore, we extend the findings of Bary-Soroker-Fehm-Petersen and Corvaja-Zannier by establishing multiple structural theorems concerning products and finite étale covers of arithmetic schemes that possess the Hilbert property.

Eye movements are crucial for non-verbal communication in human-robot interactions, yet replicating the human oculomotor system in robotic eyes remains a significant challenge. This paper investigates the control of a realistic robotic eye model utilizing a cable-driven system that mimics the six degrees of freedom of extra-ocular muscles. The biomimetic approach presents unique difficulties, particularly the requirement to manage pretension in each muscle to avoid cable slack and loss of control during motion. We constructed a robotic prototype, developed a nonlinear simulator, and implemented two control strategies. The first method linearizes the nonlinear model via local derivative techniques to design linear-quadratic optimal controllers that optimize a cost function balancing accuracy, energy usage, and movement speed. The second approach employs a recurrent neural network to learn system dynamics from sample trajectories, paired with a nonlinear trajectory optimization solver to minimize a comparable cost function. Our focus was on generating rapid, fully unconstrained saccadic movements and deriving control signals for six cables that satisfy multiple dynamic optimization criteria. The model accurately replicates the three-dimensional rotational kinematics and dynamics of human saccades. Experimental results show that while both methods achieve similar outcomes, the nonlinear method offers greater flexibility for future model enhancements, as calculating the position-dependent pretensions and local derivatives required for the linearized model becomes increasingly cumbersome.

We hypothesize that a random walk and its associated diffusion within relativistic velocity space provide a suitable framework for modeling the acceleration of relativistic jets. By examining a basic toy model, we illustrate the principal characteristics of velocity space diffusion across both non-relativistic and relativistic domains.

The utility of conversational AI platforms like Siri and Alexa is evident in their daily impact on our lives, largely driven by machine learning models that evolve to enhance user experience. However, advancing these models presents a challenge: they must effectively handle both high-frequency and low-frequency usage scenarios, necessitating fine-grained strategies for specific data subsets. This paper investigates the recent concept of slice-based learning (SBL) to enhance a baseline conversational skill routing system, specifically targeting critical yet low-traffic queries. We begin by establishing labeling functions to create weakly supervised data for these tail intents, then extend the baseline model into a slice-aware architecture capable of monitoring and optimizing performance for selected low-frequency intents. Experiments conducted on de-identified live traffic from a commercial conversational AI system demonstrate that this slice-aware approach improves model performance on tail intents while preserving overall system efficacy.

This paper provides a geometric characterization of the foliation associated with a generic real analytic family unfolding a real analytic vector field possessing a weak focus at the origin. It demonstrates that two such families are orbitally analytically equivalent precisely when the corresponding families of diffeomorphisms unfolding the complexified Poincaré map at the singularities are conjugate. Furthermore, by shifting the leaves of the formal normal form within the blow-up via a fibered transformation along a suitable complex cross-section (quasiconformal surgery), one constructs an abstract manifold of complex dimension 2 endowed with an elliptic holomorphic foliation, where the monodromy map matches a specified family of admissible diffeomorphisms.

The serverless computing paradigm reinforces the cloud trend of abstracting resource management by having serverless platforms handle application deployment and scaling. Coupled with a pay-as-you-go billing structure that charges only for actual processing time, this model incentivizes efficient resource utilization. However, the pursuit of such efficiency often results in the "cold start" problem, characterized by delays in executing serverless applications. While snapshot-based methods have been widely explored as a solution, there is a notable gap in research regarding their trade-offs. This study addresses that gap by comparing two cold start mitigation strategies: Prebaking and SEUSS. We evaluated their performance across functions of varying complexity, including a NoOp function, a Markdown-to-HTML converter, and a function loading 41 MB of dependencies. Preliminary findings indicate that Prebaking outperformed the baseline by 33% for the NoOp function and by 25% for the Markdown function. Additionally, further analysis demonstrated that Prebaking's warmup mechanism reduced the processing time for the first Markdown request by 69%.

We present a minimal hydrodynamic framework for contractile swimmer assemblies within binary-fluid emulsion droplets, omitting an orientational order parameter. This model employs two coupled scalar fields, $\phi$ and $\psi$, representing the droplet interface and the internal activity of the swimmers, respectively, both of which interact with the velocity field $\bm u$. At low activity levels, the model predicts a self-propelling droplet whose center of mass moves rectilinearly; this motion is driven by the spatiotemporal dynamics of $\psi$, generating a time-varying vortex dipole at one droplet end. As activity increases, the center of mass exhibits chaotic super-diffusive behavior, quantified via its mean-square displacement, while the droplet interface displays multifractal fluctuations, for which we compute the spectrum of exponents. Finally, we discuss the experimental relevance of these findings regarding active droplets containing contractile swimmers.

Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) holds significant promise for reducing domain shifts by transferring models from labeled source domains to unlabeled target domains. Although UDA has been extensively applied to various complex vision tasks, research focusing on lane detection for autonomous driving remains limited, primarily due to a scarcity of publicly available datasets. To address this gap and advance research in this area, we introduce CARLANE, a comprehensive three-way sim-to-real domain adaptation benchmark designed for 2D lane detection. CARLANE integrates single-target datasets (MoLane and TuLane) and a multi-target dataset (MuLane), constructed across three distinct domains that feature diverse scenes and comprise a total of 163K unique images, with 118K annotated. Furthermore, we provide and evaluate systematic baselines, including our proposed method based on Prototypical Cross-domain Self-supervised Learning. Our findings reveal that false positive and false negative rates for current domain adaptation approaches remain high relative to fully supervised baselines, underscoring the necessity of benchmarks like CARLANE to bolster UDA research in lane detection. All resources, including the CARLANE benchmark, evaluated models, and their implementations, are publicly accessible at https://carlanebenchmark.github.io.

Achieving hand segmentation and detection in completely unconstrained RGB environments is vital for numerous applications, yet current datasets fall short due to insufficient size and variety caused by the impracticality of manually annotating vast amounts of data. Consequently, existing methods rely heavily on restrictive assumptions, such as specific lighting conditions, consistent skin tones, and controlled settings. This paper introduces Ego2Hands, a large-scale, semi-automatically annotated RGB-based egocentric dataset for hand detection and segmentation. We also present a color-invariant compositing technique that generates training data with significant scale and diversity. For quantitative evaluation, we created a manually annotated benchmark set that surpasses existing standards in quantity, diversity, and accuracy. Furthermore, we conducted cross-dataset evaluations and a comprehensive analysis of state-of-the-art models on Ego2Hands, demonstrating that our dataset and generation method enable models to generalize to unseen environments without requiring domain adaptation.

Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) integrated with communication is an emerging field that promises to deliver insights into propagation environments and transceiver locations, thereby enabling new services for the Internet of Things and environment-aware communication. While leveraging crowdsourced data from multiple agents holds significant potential for enhancing SLAM performance, practical measurement uncertainties and biased estimations from these agents can lead to severe errors. To address these challenges, this study proposes a robust SLAM method incorporating measurement plug-and-play and crowdsourcing mechanisms. Initially, measurements are categorized based on their unknown biases, and a measurement plug-and-play mechanism is realized by extending the classic belief propagation (BP)-based SLAM approach. This mechanism achieves high accuracy and robustness in difficult scenarios without requiring prior information about anchors or agents, effectively estimating time-varying agent locations, radio features, and corresponding measurement biases (including clock, orientation, and received signal strength model parameters). Subsequently, a probabilistic crowdsourcing-based SLAM mechanism is established, allowing multiple agents to cooperatively construct and refine radio maps in a decentralized fashion. This study introduces the first BP-based crowdsourcing approach that resolves "double count" and "data reliability" issues through the flexible application of probabilistic data association methods. Numerical results demonstrate that the crowdsourcing mechanism further enhances mapping accuracy, which in turn guarantees decimeter-level localization precision for each agent even in challenging propagation environments.

This study investigates the extreme ultraviolet (EUV) emission characteristics of tin plasmas generated by irradiating preformed liquid tin targets with nanosecond-duration, 2-$\mu$m-wavelength laser pulses. Utilizing a two-pulse configuration, a pre-pulse reshapes tin microdroplets into thin disks before the primary 2-$\mu$m pulse generates the EUV-emitting plasma. Experiments on targets ranging from 30 to 300 $\mu$m in diameter reveal that EUV efficiency near 13.5 nm scales with the fraction of laser light overlapping the target. Subsequent analysis of varying drive laser intensities (0.6–1.8$\times 10^{11}$ W/cm$^2$) and pulse lengths (3.7–7.4 ns) shows that the angular distribution of emission within a 2% bandwidth around 13.5 nm, specifically in the backward hemisphere, remains largely unaffected by changes in intensity or duration. However, as target diameter increases, emission becomes more anisotropic, directing a larger portion of light forward along the incoming beam. Comparative experiments using a 1-$\mu$m drive laser yield similar setups; however, spectra recorded between 5.5 and 25.5 nm indicate significant self-absorption at 13.5 nm for the 1-$\mu$m case, whereas the 2-$\mu$m case exhibits only opacity-related broadening. These findings highlight the superior performance and capabilities of 2-$\mu$m-driven plasmas from disk targets compared to their 1-$\mu$m counterparts, offering strong justification for employing 2-$\mu$m lasers in future high-power EUV sources.

This study introduces a product quadrature rule utilizing filtered de la Vall\'ee Poussin polynomial approximations to compute the finite Hilbert transform over the interval [-1; 1]. Convergence properties are established within the weighted uniform norm for functions residing in specific Besov type subspaces. The paper further includes multiple numerical experiments that benchmark the proposed rule against other established formulas found in existing literature.

This study examines the Age of Information (AoI) within a discrete-time status updating framework, specifically targeting the derivation of the stationary AoI distribution under a Ber/G/1/1 queue model. Leveraging standard queueing theory, we demonstrate that by employing a two-dimensional state vector to concurrently monitor both AoI and packet age, the stationary AoI distribution can be obtained through the analysis of the resulting two-dimensional stochastic process's steady state. We provide a general formula for the AoI distribution and derive its explicit form when service times follow a geometric distribution. Furthermore, we compare discrete and continuous AoI metrics, illustrating the mean values for both discrete and continuous AoI in a system utilizing an M/M/1/1 queue. While the stationary AoI distribution for certain continuous-time single-server systems has been previously established, this paper proves that standard queueing theory remains applicable for analyzing discrete AoI, offering an even more robust analytical approach than methods currently used for continuous AoI.

This research investigates the thermodynamic equilibrium spectra of the Charney-Hasegawa-Mima (CHM) equation within its weakly nonlinear regime. Unlike the 2D Euler and Gross-Pitaevskii equations, which possess only two adiabatic invariants, the CHM equation features three. We examine how this additional invariant significantly expands the range of accessible equilibrium spectra. Specifically, we analyze the singular limits of these spectra where condensates form, defined as scenarios in which a single Fourier mode or a pair of modes accumulates a macroscopic portion of the total invariants. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these equilibrium condensates offer a straightforward explanation for the distinct structures seen in finite-sized CHM systems, including highly anisotropic zonal flows, large-scale isotropic vortices, and small-scale vortices. Finally, we illustrate the connection between these condensates and combinations of negative thermodynamic potentials, such as temperature.

Self-supervised learning (SSL) techniques, which generate data representations without explicit labels, have become increasingly popular in speech processing, especially for single-talker contexts. Nevertheless, these models frequently exhibit reduced performance in multi-talker settings, likely due to domain mismatches, thereby restricting their practical utility. This paper explores adapting upstream SSL models for multi-talker automatic speech recognition (ASR) under two scenarios. First, for segmented utterances, we demonstrate that incorporating a target speaker extraction (TSE) module utilizing enrollment embeddings complements mixture-aware pre-training. Second, for unsegmented mixtures, we introduce a novel joint speaker modeling (JSM) method that consolidates information from all speakers via their embeddings. Controlled experiments on Libri2Mix reveal that leveraging speaker embeddings yields relative word error rate (WER) reductions of 9.1% and 42.1% over robust baselines for segmented and unsegmented cases, respectively. Furthermore, we validate the efficacy of our models on real conversational mixtures using the AMI dataset.

This study presents the inaugural femtoscopic analysis of baryon pairs—including p-p, p-$\Lambda$, and $\Lambda$-$\Lambda$—conducted by the ALICE experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) during proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}$ = 7 TeV. The results confirm the viability of such measurements at ultrarelativistic energies. By applying the femtoscopy technique, the research aims to place constraints on the hyperon-nucleon and hyperon-hyperon interactions, which remain poorly understood. A novel approach is introduced to assess the impact of residual correlations arising from resonance decays and experimental impurities. The correlation functions for p-p, p-$\Lambda$, and $\Lambda$-$\Lambda$ were fitted concurrently using a newly developed tool for femtoscopy in small systems called 'Correlation Analysis Tool using the Schrödinger Equation' (CATS). Assuming a common source for the three particle pairs in pp collisions, the source radius is determined to be $r_{0} = 1.125\pm0.018$ (stat) $^{+0.058}_{-0.035}$ (syst) fm. The sensitivity of the p-$\Lambda$ correlation to various scattering parameters, which define the interaction between the two particles, was evaluated; however, current statistics are insufficient to distinguish between different models. Furthermore, the $\Lambda$-$\Lambda$ correlation function measurement restricts the phase space of the strong interaction's effective range and scattering length. Finally, discrepancies between the measured scattering parameters and the resulting correlation functions at LHC and RHIC energies are examined within the framework of various theoretical models.

We derive an optimal subset of architectural parameters for the BERT model (Devlin et al., 2018) by utilizing recent advances in neural architecture search algorithms. This streamlined variant, named "Bort," is significantly more compact: excluding the embedding layer, its effective size is merely 5.5% of BERT-large, and its net size is 16%. Bort can be pretrained in just 288 GPU hours, representing only 1.2% of the time needed for the top-performing parametric variant, RoBERTa-large (Liu et al., 2019), and approximately 33% of the GPU hours required to train BERT-large on identical hardware. Furthermore, Bort operates 7.9 times faster on CPUs. Despite its size, it outperforms other compressed architectures and even certain uncompressed variants, achieving absolute performance gains ranging from 0.3% to 31% over BERT-large across various public natural language understanding benchmarks.

The absolute atomic mass of $^{208}$Pb has been measured with a fractional uncertainty of $7\times 10^{-11}$ by utilizing the high-precision Penning-trap spectrometer Pentatrap. This determination involved calculating the cyclotron-frequency ratio $R$ between $^{208}$Pb$^{41+}$ and $^{132}$Xe$^{26+}$, alongside the binding energies ($E_{\text{Pb}}$ and $E_{\text{Xe}}$) for the missing 41 and 26 electrons, derived via the ab initio fully relativistic multi-configuration Dirac-Hartree-Fock (MCDHF) method. The ratio $R$ was obtained with a relative precision of $9\times 10^{-12}$, while the binding energy calculations carried uncertainties of 9.1 eV and 2.1 eV, respectively. These figures yielded a neutral atomic mass of $207.976\,650\,571(14)$ u (where $1\,\text{u}=9.314\,941\,024\,2(28)\times 10^{8}$ eV/c$^2$). This value aligns with the Atomic-Mass Evaluation (AME) 2020 within $1.2\sigma$ but achieves nearly two orders of magnitude better precision. Consequently, this result enhances the mass precision for 14 nuclides in the Z=81–84 range and represents the most precise mass known for any nuclide with $A>200$. Furthermore, this measurement establishes a new reference mass region applicable for the high-precision determination of transuranium nuclides, including superheavy elements.

We demonstrate that an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^d$ admitting a fibration by unit $n$-spheres must satisfy $d \geq 2n+1$; furthermore, when $d = 2n+1$, the spheres are necessarily pairwise linked and $n$ belongs to the set $\left\{ 0, 1, 3, 7 \right\}$. For each of these admissible values of $n$, we provide constructions of unit $n$-sphere fibrations within $\mathbb{R}^{2n+1}$.

This paper extends certain established fixed point theorems for nonexpansive mappings within metric spaces to primitive uniform spaces. The reasoning used in the proofs appears to offer a natural pathway for deriving further general results.

The Moving Discontinuous Galerkin Finite Element Method with Interface Condition Enforcement (MDG-ICE) is utilized for simulating viscous flows. By employing a weak formulation that independently enforces conservation laws, constitutive relations, and interface conditions, the method facilitates the detection of interfaces and under-resolved flow features. To address the resulting overdetermined system, the discrete domain geometry is treated as a variable, allowing the method to implicitly identify unknown interfaces and shift the grid to capture sharp yet smooth gradients; this achieves a form of anisotropic curvilinear $r$-adaptivity. This strategy eliminates low-order errors typically associated with shock capturing, artificial dissipation, or limiting techniques. The method's effectiveness is validated through various test cases, culminating in a two-dimensional compressible Navier-Stokes simulation of a Mach 5 viscous bow shock at a Reynolds number of $10^{5}$. Unsteady problems are solved with time accuracy using a space-time formulation, where the transient issue is cast as a higher-dimensional steady-state problem. Results demonstrate that the approach accurately resolves and transports viscous structures without dependence on numerical dissipation for stabilization.

This letter explores the fabrication of programmable integrated circuits utilizing disordered Chern insulators (CIs). We propose specific schemes for creating low-dissipation logic devices and interconnecting wires. By employing external-gate-induced step voltages, we construct spatially adjustable channels that serve as alternatives to traditional wiring. Numerical simulations demonstrate that these external gates enable the programming of arbitrary wire configurations, facilitating $n$-to-$m$ connections. Our findings indicate that electron transport within these channels is dissipationless and remains robust against fluctuations in gate voltage and disorder strength. Additionally, we introduce seven fundamental logic gates that differ from conventional designs. This proposal holds promise for advancing low-power integrated circuits and offers insights into constructing integrated circuits based on topological materials.

We introduce a high-performance, networked graphics framework that integrates server-side dynamic, high-quality ray-traced global illumination with client-side direct illumination and primary visibility calculations. This architecture delivers the visual fidelity of real-time ray tracing on low-power and legacy devices while ensuring low latency and a mobile form factor. By distributing the rendering pipeline across a network, the system offloads diffuse global illumination computation to a remote server. This process employs a recent irradiance volume representation paired with a novel, perceptually driven update strategy that utilizes lossless, hardware-accelerated HEVC encoding. Our experimental implementation successfully streams thousands of irradiance probes per second with a throughput under 50 Mbps, achieving a 99.4% bandwidth reduction compared to traditional lossless texture compression at 60 Hz. This efficiency enables higher quality and lower latency graphics than current remote rendering solutions based on video streaming. Furthermore, our split-rendering approach decouples remote computation from local display, thereby eliminating constraints on local refresh rates and resolution.

This article offers a proof-of-concept demonstrating the viability of establishing a covert channel between a command-and-control server and malware within an organization by repurposing an organizational scanner as an interaction medium. The study leverages the light sensitivity of flatbed scanners, employing a light source to transmit data into the target facility. The authors detail an implementation of this technique for various objectives, including initiating ransomware attacks, across multiple experimental configurations involving: (1) a stationary laser setup, (2) a drone-mounted laser, and (3) a compromised smart bulb accessed from a passing vehicle. Experimental results show successful data infiltration using diverse light sources, such as infrared, from distances reaching up to 900 meters. Finally, the article examines potential countermeasures to mitigate this threat.

Although the restricted isometry property (RIP) is a crucial condition in compressed sensing, existing optimal matrix constructions rely on randomness. This paper utilizes the pseudorandom characteristics of the Legendre symbol to minimize the number of random bits required for an RIP matrix with Bernoulli entries. While the Legendre symbol is effective, our primary finding extends naturally to any small-bias sample space. Furthermore, we hypothesize that our Legendre symbol-based construction may ultimately require no random bits at all.

We report measurements of elemental abundances and molecular hydrogen (H2) content for a Damped Lyman-{\alpha} (DLA) system characterized by an exceptionally high neutral hydrogen column density, log N(H i) (cm-2) = 22.0 +/- 0.10, located at zabs = 3.287 along the sightline to the QSO SDSS J 081634+144612. Utilizing a high signal-to-noise, high-resolution VLT-UVES spectrum, we determined column densities for H2, C i, C i^*, Zn ii, Fe ii, Cr ii, Ni ii, and Si ii. The system exhibits an overall metallicity of [Zn/H] = -1.10 +/- 0.10 relative to solar values. Two distinct H2 absorption components were identified at redshifts z = 3.28667 and 3.28742, separated by approximately 52 km s-1, with transitions observed in rotational levels up to J = 3. We calculated a total H2 column density of log N(H2) (cm-2) = 18.66 and a mean molecular fraction f = 2N(H2)/[2N(H2) + N(H i)] = 10-3.04+/-0.37, values consistent with other known H2-bearing DLAs. Based on the observed abundance ratios, we infer the presence of dust within the Interstellar Medium (ISM) of this galaxy, particularly enhanced in the H2-rich clouds. Nevertheless, the total dust content along the line of sight is insufficient to cause significant reddening of the background QSO. Physical conditions within the H2-bearing clouds were derived directly from H2 column densities across various rotational levels, along with C i and C i^* measurements, yielding a kinetic temperature of T = 75 K and a particle density range of nH = 50-80 cm-3. The neutral hydrogen column density of this DLA is comparable to the mean H i column density of DLAs associated with {\gamma}-ray bursts (GRBs). Our investigation into the relationship between GRB-DLAs and high-column-density QSO-DLAs reveals no significant differences in properties, such as metallicity and depletion, between the two populations for systems with log N(H i) > 21.5.

Supermassive black holes located at galactic centers can propel relativistic plasma jets along their polar axes. The study of black-hole jets remains a vibrant area of astrophysical research due to numerous unresolved questions regarding jet launching mechanisms, particle acceleration within the jets, and radiative processes. This work specifically addresses the latter, offering a review of our current understanding of radiative emission in supermassive black-hole jets.

Algorithms for grammars and transducers utilizing context-free derivations encompass hypergraph reachability, shortest path calculations, and the pruning of "relatively useless" arcs via inside-outside techniques, specifically those not employed in any near-shortest paths.

This study introduces a generative random network model featuring core-periphery characteristics, where the core nodes function as sublinear dominators—meaning that for a network of $n$ nodes, the core comprises $o(n)$ nodes yet controls the entire system. We demonstrate that networks produced by this model display power law degree distributions and small-world properties, and we validate the model by fitting it to diverse real-world networks.

Current comprehension of the brain's structure and its link to human traits depends heavily on how we model the structural connectome. Typically, the brain is segmented into regions of interest (ROIs), with the connectome depicted as an adjacency matrix quantifying connections between these regions; however, subsequent statistical analyses are often constrained by the arbitrary selection of these ROIs. This article introduces a new tractography-based framework for representing brain connectomes that clusters fiber endpoints to create a data-driven parcellation specifically designed to explain inter-individual variation and forecast human traits. This method yields Principal Parcellation Analysis (PPA), which encodes individual connectomes as compositional vectors derived from a population-level basis of fiber bundles. PPA minimizes subjectivity and streamlines statistical evaluation. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach using Human Connectome Project (HCP) data, revealing that PPA connectomes enhance predictive power for human traits compared to classical connectome methods, while significantly improving parsimony without sacrificing interpretability. The PPA package is publicly accessible on GitHub and can be routinely applied to diffusion imaging data.

This article aims to characterize the left and right invertibility of $T_n^d(A)$, a partial upper triangular operator matrix with specified diagonal entries and unspecified off-diagonal elements, using solely the diagonal entries. Our findings generalize and correct the work of Zhang S. and Wu Z. (2012) by establishing results without requiring the separability condition. Furthermore, we derive appropriate $n$-dimensional analogues under the same relaxed assumptions. In the context of Hilbert spaces, our approach recovers several perturbation results from Djordjević D. S. (2002) and yields results consistent with those of Du H. K. and Pan J. (1994), as well as Han J. K., Lee H. Y., and Lee W. Y. (2000).

Using K-type giants from the LAMOST survey, we investigate the vertical kinematic structure of the Galactic disk within a Galactocentric radius of $R=5-15$ $\rm{kpc}$ and extending up to $3$ $\rm{kpc}$ from the Galactic plane. Analysis of robust three-dimensional velocity moments reveals a phenomenologically wobbly disk. Radial motion is dominated by an outflow in the inner disk, whereas the outer disk exhibits alternating inward and outward flows. Vertically, the bulk motion combines breathing and bending modes; beyond $R_0$, an upward bending mode and a contraction-like breathing mode (with amplitudes growing with height above the plane) prevail, while inside $R_0$, reversed modes occur with significantly smaller amplitudes. The mean azimuthal velocity declines with increasing distance from the plane, showing shallower gradients at larger radii. Additionally, southern disk stars rotate faster than their northern counterparts. The orientation of the velocity ellipsoid varies with radius: between $5<R<9$ $\rm{kpc}$, the gradient of the tilt angle relative to $\arctan(Z/R)$ drops from $\sim0.83$ in the inner disk to $\sim0.52$ in the outer disk, and within $9<R<15$ $\rm{kpc}$, the tilt deviates from vertical antisymmetry. Finally, a distinct flaring signature is identified in both the north and south disks based on the observed vertical structures of the velocity ellipsoid.

This study addresses static parameter estimation for a specific class of continuous-time state-space models. The objective is to derive an unbiased estimate of the log-likelihood gradient (score function) that remains valid even when the model's stochastic processes require temporal discretization. To accomplish this, we employ a doubly randomized approach, featuring a newly developed coupled conditional particle filter (CCPF) at the second randomization stage. This innovative estimator supports gradient-based optimization techniques, including stochastic-gradient Langevin descent. We demonstrate the proposed method through numerical examples involving stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and evaluate its performance against the Rhee & Glynn estimator.

Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) function as nonlinear sieves, offering superior approximation of complex, high-dimensional functions compared to linear sieves. This study evaluates diverse ANN architectures within nonparametric instrumental variables (NPIV) models involving moderately high-dimensional covariates common in empirical economics. We introduce two efficient methods for estimating and inferring a weighted average derivative (WAD): an orthogonalized plug-in approach using optimally-weighted sieve minimum distance (OP-OSMD) and a sieve efficient score (ES) method. Both WAD estimators employ ANN sieves to approximate the unknown NPIV function, achieving root-n asymptotic normality and first-order equivalence. A comprehensive guide is provided for practitioners to implement these procedures. Through simulations featuring smooth NPIV functions with up to 13 continuous covariates, varying nonlinearities, and covariate correlations, we compare their finite-sample performance. Key Monte Carlo results indicate that: 1) tuning and optimization in ANN estimation require greater care; 2) with appropriate tuning, both ANN estimators across different architectures perform robustly; 3) OP-OSMD estimators are generally easier to tune than ES estimators; 4) achieving stable inferences is more challenging with ANNs than with spline estimators; and 5) discrepancies exist between current implementations and theoretical approximations. Finally, we apply ANN-based NPIV to estimate average partial derivatives in two empirical demand contexts involving multivariate covariates.

This study investigates quark and gauge field dynamics within a flux tube model, focusing on low-energy states exhibiting approximate cylindrical symmetry in QCD and QED interactions. By employing the action integral, we decompose the (3+1)D framework into transverse and longitudinal degrees of freedom to solve the resulting equations of motion. Our analysis suggests the existence of localized, stable collective excitations for both QCD and QED, manifesting as particles with masses determined by the respective coupling constants and the flux-tube radius. In addition to established stable QCD modes within the quark-QCD-QED system, we propose that stable QED collective excitations could serve as viable candidates for explaining various anomalous particles recently detected in the tens of MeV energy range.

The increasing integration of IoT devices in healthcare has allowed researchers to harness intelligence from the vast data these devices generate, with health monitoring and diagnosis being the primary beneficial applications. While initial efforts prioritized high prediction accuracy, the focus has gradually shifted toward efficiency and throughput, goals that are effectively met by processing device data in a distributed fashion. Given the extensive landscape of machine learning algorithms, identifying the most effective ones for specific scenarios remains challenging. This literature review examined distributed machine learning algorithms tested in selected studies to pinpoint those yielding the highest prediction accuracy across various healthcare contexts. Although no single algorithm demonstrated consistent superiority, Random Forest emerged as the top performer in several studies, offering a valuable starting point for future research on collaborative machine learning within IoMT environments.

A recent study on a vector formulation of Witsenhausen's counterexample demonstrated that, as the vector length approaches infinity, specific quantization-based control methods are provably within a constant factor of the optimal cost across all problem parameters. This paper extends the analysis to finite vector lengths by treating dimension as an additional parameter. Employing a large-deviation "sphere-packing" approach, a lower bound for the optimal cost in the finite-dimensional setting is established, utilizing projections of the infinite-length bound. Leveraging this new lower bound, the study proves that effective lattice-based control strategies achieve a constant-factor approximation of the optimal cost uniformly for all parameters, including vector length. Furthermore, regarding Witsenhausen's original scalar problem, numerical evidence indicates that the gap between standard lattice-based strategies and the derived lower bound never exceeds a factor of 8.

We introduce a semi-classical approach to derive the effective low-energy quantum Hamiltonian for weakly anharmonic superconducting circuits featuring mesoscopic Josephson junctions connected to electromagnetic environments composed of arbitrary combinations of distributed and lumped components. This framework utilizes a convenient basis representing multi-mode physics, defined by the quantized eigenmodes of the linearized circuit and fully specified by a classical linear response function. The method is applied to numerically compute the low-energy spectrum of a 3D-transmon system, yielding results that quantitatively match experimental measurements.

This study optimizes path planning for a trunk-and-branch topology network situated on an irregular 2D manifold within 3D Euclidean space, specifically addressing submarine cable network design. Expanding upon previous work that focused solely on construction expenses (labor, equipment, and materials) and resilience enhancements, this research integrates the total costs of branching units and the strategic selection of submarine cable landing stations, which can be located anywhere along a connected coastal region. These factors are critical to the economics of cable deployment and substantially alter the modeling and optimization framework. The problem is formulated as a variant of the Steiner tree problem where the number of Steiner nodes is variable but incurs a penalty, termed the "weighted Steiner node problem." Unlike the standard Euclidean Steiner tree problem, which mandates a degree of three for Steiner points, this model accommodates varying node degrees when costs are involved. We demonstrate that our algorithm effectively handles Steiner nodes with degrees exceeding three, facilitating network cost optimization. Furthermore, the optimal solution is derived in polynomial time through dynamic programming.

Anomalies offer a potent method for identifying viable lattice regularizations of quantum field theories. We contend that within a specific spacetime dimension, a manifestly symmetric and local lattice regularization can only match the continuum anomaly of a given symmetry if either the symmetry action is off-site or the anomaly is reproduced precisely on the lattice. Focusing on (1+1)-dimensional asymptotically free Grassmannian nonlinear sigma models (NLSMs) with a $\theta$ term as prototype QCD models, we demonstrate lattice regularizations realizing both scenarios. Regarding the first scenario, we show that Grassmannian NLSMs can emerge from $\mathrm{SU}(N)$ antiferromagnets with a clear continuum limit, successfully capturing both the infrared physics of $\theta$ vacua and the ultraviolet physics of asymptotic freedom. These findings facilitate the use of novel classical algorithms for lattice Monte Carlo simulations of these quantum field theories and offer a practical setup for quantum simulation. Conversely, we reveal that, somewhat unexpectedly, the standard lattice regularization of $\theta$ vacua proposed by Berg and Lüscher reproduces the anomaly exactly on the lattice, thereby exemplifying the second possibility.

Utilizing diverse offline robot datasets necessitates addressing data heterogeneity. This paper specifically examines the challenge of learning from data collected at varying control frequencies. Differences across laboratories in controller discretization, sensor sampling rates, and task requirements often result in aggregated datasets containing mixed frequencies. We investigate the performance of offline reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms when trained on such multi-frequency data. Our observations reveal that $Q$-values propagate at disparate rates depending on the discretization, creating significant learning difficulties for standard offline RL methods. We propose a straightforward yet effective solution that ensures consistency in $Q$-value update rates to stabilize the learning process. By scaling the value of $N$ in $N$-step returns according to the discretization size, we effectively balance $Q$-value propagation, resulting in more stable convergence. Empirical evaluation across three simulated robotic control tasks demonstrates that this simple approach outperforms naive data mixing by an average of 50%.

A swarm robotic system comprises a group of robots executing collaborative tasks without centralized control. While swarms theoretically offer flexible and scalable solutions, creating individual control algorithms that ensure specific global behaviors remains challenging. To enhance confidence in swarm behavior, researchers have proposed formal methods. This work suggests modeling swarms as hybrid systems and employing reachability analysis to verify their properties. Furthermore, we outline associated challenges and share insights from applying hybrid formalisms to verify a specific swarm robotic system.

Multi-photon entangled graph states serve as a cornerstone for quantum sensing, distributed computing, and communication networks. Although these states can theoretically be generated deterministically using quantum emitters like superconducting qubits, atomic systems, or optically active defects, developing efficient production methods has remained a persistent challenge. In this work, we introduce an algorithm that, for any specified multi-photon graph state, calculates the requisite number of quantum emitters and the exact sequence of operations needed to create it. Both the algorithm and the derived operation sequences scale polynomially with the size of the photonic graph state, enabling the efficient generation of graph states comprising hundreds or even thousands of photons.

This study examines the Englert-Brout-Higgs-Guralnik-Hagen-Kibble mechanism within non-Hermitian field theories possessing local non-Abelian gauge symmetry across various parameter space regions. We show that the two core functions of the mechanism—endowing gauge vector bosons with mass and eliminating massless Goldstone bosons—remain synchronized in all regimes defined by modified CPT symmetry. Specifically, in parameter domains where "would-be" Goldstone bosons can be identified, gauge bosons acquire mass and the Goldstone modes disappear. The mechanism holds at standard exceptional points; however, it fails at zero exceptional points, where the eigenvalues of the mass squared matrix vanish regardless of symmetry breaking. At these points, the mechanism collapses because Goldstone bosons cannot be identified, leaving gauge vector bosons massless. This failure aligns with the vanishing of the CPT inner product for symmetry-breaking vacua defined on the eigenvector space of the mass squared matrix. We confirm this behavior in an SU(N) theory featuring complex scalar fields in both fundamental and adjoint representations.

Recent developments have introduced numerous adversarial attacks and defenses for Deep Neural Networks (DNNs).
