Our findings indicate that while newer designs build upon past techniques with enhancements, they do not consistently surpass pre-Optane era solutions. Furthermore, PM indexes often match or exceed the performance of indexes optimized specifically for DRAM, suggesting the viability of a unified architecture for both memory types. In terms of functionality, these indexes currently lack robust support for variable-length keys and effective handling of NUMA effects. Drawing from these insights, we derive new design principles and outline future research directions.

Research on inter-organizational networks faces the significant challenge of accounting for interdependence among ties when analyzing tie formation. This study addresses that issue through an equilibrium framework, modeling firms' decisions to establish connections as a strategic game where links are formed only if the net payoffs are positive. We characterize these equilibrium networks as Exponential Random Graph Models (ERGM) and estimate firm payoffs using Bayesian methods. Applying this framework to a co-investment network of venture capital firms in the medical device sector demonstrates its utility, allowing for economic interpretations of ERGM parameters. Our findings reveal that firms leverage transitivity by relying on joint partners and exhibit homophily by preferring ties with similar firms, even after controlling for tie interdependence. A key advantage of this structural approach is its capacity to simulate economic shocks and policy counterfactuals. Testing scenarios involving new firm entry and regulatory changes, specifically minimum capital requirements, we demonstrate that both factors increase the density and clustering of the co-investment network.

This study investigates how the electronic properties at the surface of a high-temperature superconductor vary under different vacuum conditions using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES). Typically, when vacuum conditions are suboptimal, the carrier concentration in Bi2Sr2CaCu2O{8+x} (Bi2212) rises over time as the material absorbs oxygen from CO2 and CO molecules, which are common contaminants in ultra-high vacuum (UHV) systems. However, we observed that in a high-quality vacuum at low temperatures, the Bi2212 surface remains stable with a constant carrier concentration. Conversely, at elevated temperatures, the carrier concentration drops due to oxygen loss from the Bi-O layer. These opposing effects enable in-situ control of carrier concentration. Our findings suggest the potential to examine the electronic properties of cuprates across the doping phase diagram on a single sample, ensuring consistent impurities and defects. Furthermore, we anticipate this approach could be applied to other surface-sensitive methods, such as scanning tunneling microscopy/spectroscopy.

This study examines the influence of scalar fields on the thermodynamics of charged anti-de Sitter (AdS) black holes, focusing on a specific set of exact (3+1)-dimensional hairy charged AdS black hole solutions within Einstein-Maxwell-scalar gravity. These solutions are particularly notable for possessing a stable ground state and a finite horizon area as the temperature approaches zero. Our findings demonstrate that these black holes satisfy the reverse isoperimetric inequality and exhibit reentrant phase behavior within an intermediate charge range, marking the first instance of such behavior in (3+1) dimensions within a consistent theoretical framework.

Literature has established that a single quantum particle can function as a thermodynamic machine due to energy quantization, a property without a classical counterpart. However, the behavior shifts significantly when examining a collection of non-interacting, massive, indistinguishable quantum particles. This thermodynamic machine relies on particle statistics, chemical potential, and system dimensionality. Our comprehensive analysis reveals the core characteristics of quantum Stirling cycles through the lens of particle statistics and dimensionality, facilitating the design of quantum heat engines and refrigerators by leveraging quantum statistical mechanics. Specifically, we demonstrate that particle statistics exhibit distinct behaviors in one dimension compared to higher dimensions, highlighting the prominent role of quantum thermodynamic signatures in lower-dimensional systems.

Derivative-matching approximations are formulated as power series derived from specific functions. This approach relies on the availability of known special values for Bell polynomials of the second kind, details of which can be found in existing literature. The concepts outlined here hold potential utility within numerical mathematics.

While gauge invariance serves as a foundational postulate in theories like quantum electrodynamics, experimental imperfections in quantum simulations often compromise this symmetry. A recent study [Halimeh and Hauke, Phys. Rev. Lett. 125, 030503 (2020)] demonstrated that in finite-size spin-$1/2$ quantum link lattice gauge theories, applying an energy-penalty term with a sufficiently large strength $V$ suppresses unitary gauge-breaking errors of magnitude $\lambda$ by a factor proportional to $\lambda^2/V^2$, valid across all accessible evolution times. We present numerical evidence that this finding holds for quantum link models in the thermodynamic limit and for systems with higher spin values $S$. Analytically, we show that short-time dynamics correspond to an *adjusted* gauge theory, valid up to a timescale of at least $\tau_\text{adj}\propto\sqrt{V/V_0^3}$, where $V_0$ is an energy factor. Additionally, our analysis predicts that a renormalized gauge theory prevails at intermediate times until a timescale of $\tau_\text{ren}\propto\exp(V/V_0)/V_0$. In these emergent frameworks, $V$ remains independent of the system volume and scales at worst as $\sim S^2$. Finally, numerical results confirm that robust gauge invariance persists even with a single-body gauge-protection term, which is experimentally feasible to implement in ultracold-atom experiments and NISQ devices.

This study addresses two primary inquiries concerning a convex body $C\subset\mathbb{R}^d$, a positive integer $k$, and a finite set $S\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ (or a finite Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$). The first question asks for the number of homothets of $C$ needed to cover $S$, under the constraint that no single homothet covers more than $k$ points (or possesses a measure exceeding $k$). The second question seeks the maximum number of homothets of $C$ that can be packed, provided each covers at least $k$ points (or has a measure of at least $k$). We demonstrate that, assuming $S$ is not excessively degenerate, the solution to both problems is $\Theta_d(\frac{|S|}{k})$, with the implicit constant remaining independent of the dimension $d$. This result is optimal up to a multiplicative factor, and analogous findings apply to measures. Furthermore, we extend the standard notions of covering and packing densities for a convex body $C$ to Borel measure spaces in $\mathbb{R}^d$; utilizing the established bounds, we prove these densities are bounded below and above, respectively, by functions of $d$. As an intermediate outcome, we offer a straightforward proof for the existence of weak $\epsilon$-nets of size $O(\frac{1}{\epsilon})$ within the range space generated by all homothets of $C$. Drawing on recent developments in discrete geometry, we conduct a more thorough analysis of the specific case where $d=k=2$. Additionally, we present polynomial-time algorithms for constructing packings or coverings that achieve the $\Theta_d(\frac{|S|}{k})$ bound when $C$ is an Euclidean ball. Finally, we establish that determining whether $S$ can be covered by $\frac{|S|}{4}$ squares, each containing exactly four points, is NP-hard when $C$ is a square.

We demonstrate that every continuous $\mathbf{C}$-linear Lie algebra splitting of the symbol map, originating from the Atiyah algebra of a vector bundle over a complex manifold, corresponds to a differential operator of order no greater than the bundle's rank plus one. Vector bundles admitting such a splitting may be characterized as \emph{infinitesimally equivariant} bundles; furthermore, our theorem indicates that, in a specific categorical sense, these bundles reside in the formal neighbourhood of vector bundles possessing a flat connection.

Evaluating and enhancing policies constitutes a fundamental challenge in Reinforcement Learning (RL). While conventional RL approaches typically derive a value function for a solitary policy, a growing alternative focuses on learning one value function applicable to numerous policies. This work integrates the actor-critic framework of Parameter-Based Value Functions with the policy embedding strategy of Policy Evaluation Networks to create a unified value function capable of assessing—and thereby aiding the improvement of—any policy encoded by a deep neural network. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the method's competitiveness. Specifically, in continuous control tasks involving infinite state spaces, the value function reduces prediction error by concurrently learning a compact set of "probing states" and a mapping from actions taken within these states to the policy's cumulative return. This approach distills essential abstract environmental knowledge into a minimal set of states sufficient to characterize the behavior of diverse policies. Policy optimization occurs exclusively through adjustments to actions within these probing states, guided by the gradients of the value function's predictions. Notably, the behaviors of near-optimal policies in the Swimmer-v3 and Hopper-v3 environments can be replicated merely by understanding actions for three and five such learned states, respectively. Furthermore, the value function, trained to evaluate neural network policies, exhibits invariance to architectural variations, enabling zero-shot learning of linear policies that match the performance of the best policy observed during training. The associated code is publicly available.

We report a search for seven lepton-flavor-violating neutral charm decays of the form $D^{0}\rightarrow X^{0} e^{\pm} \mu^{\mp}$, where $X^{0}$ denotes a $\pi^{0}$, $K^{0}_{\rm S}$, $\bar{K^{*0}}$, $\rho^{0}$, $\phi$, $\omega$, or $\eta$ meson. This analysis utilizes $468$ fb$^{-1}$ of $e^+e^-$ collision data gathered at or near the $\Upsilon(4S)$ resonance using the BaBar detector at the SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory. No significant signals were detected, leading to 90\% confidence level upper limits on the branching fractions ranging from $(5.0 - 22.5)\times 10^{-7}$. These constraints are one to two orders of magnitude tighter than those from prior measurements.

This study proposes a theoretical framework linking program size theory with psychology by introducing a concrete language of thought, termed LT^2C^2, grounded in Turing-computable Kolmogorov complexity. This language is designed to meet three criteria: 1) simplicity allowing for the computation of complexity for any finite binary sequence, 2) reliance on tangible human reasoning operations (e.g., printing, repeating), and 3) sufficient power to generate all sequences without becoming so potent that it detects human-invisible regularities. We first define LT^2C^2, establishing its syntax, semantics, and a corresponding notion of program size. This approach yields a polynomial-time computable Kolmogorov complexity function and induces a prediction algorithm aligned with Solomonoff's inductive inference theory. Subsequently, we validate the language's efficacy by analyzing regularities in strings generated by participants attempting to create random sequences. Participants demonstrated a deep grasp of randomness, avoiding common errors like overestimating alternation frequency. We hypothesized that residual regularities would reflect the algorithmic nature of human cognition through specific patterns. Relative to LT^2C^2, Kolmogorov complexity satisfied three anticipated tests: 1) human sequences exhibited lower complexity than control pseudo-random number generator sequences, 2) human sequences were non-stationary, displaying declining complexity values due to fatigue, and 3) individual participants showed algorithmic stability, as fitting partial sequences more effectively predicted subsequent ones compared to average fits. This research builds upon prior attempts to merge Kolmogorov complexity and algorithmic information theory with psychology by explicitly...

Our paper [arXiv:2111.13727(2021)] contends that the conventional view of interference as a problematic aspect fails to grasp the fundamental nature of quantum theory, challenging assertions made by Feynman and others. We support this by presenting a "toy field theory," a physical framework that replicates this interference phenomenology without abandoning the classical worldview. In response to a Comment by Hance and Hossenfelder [arXiv:2204.01768(2022)] that disputes our findings, we correct their errors and address their critiques, thereby offering a chance to further elucidate the concepts introduced in our original work.

This study introduces networked dynamics to address resource allocation challenges within time-varying multi-agent systems. In this framework, an agent's state corresponds to its utilized resources or generated utilities, constrained by a fixed total resource pool. The objective is to minimize a global cost function while maintaining this constant resource sum. Each agent operates with limited information, accessing only its own state and cost function along with those of its immediate in-neighbors. This approach is driven by distributed applications including mobile edge computing, economic dispatch in smart grids, and multi-agent coverage control. The proposed method offers rapid convergence compared to linear dynamics and accommodates relaxed network connectivity alongside quantized communication links. It achieves an optimal solution across switching (potentially disconnected) undirected networks, provided that the union of the network over specific bounded, non-overlapping time intervals contains a spanning tree. The analysis establishes the feasibility of the solution, the uniqueness of the optimal state, and convergence to the optimal value under the suggested dynamics. Furthermore, these results apply to similar first-order allocation dynamics featuring strongly sign-preserving nonlinearities, such as actuator saturation.

Training models on extensive datasets like ImageNet is a standard approach in computer vision, particularly beneficial for tasks with limited data where high-capacity models might otherwise overfit. This study examines a self-supervised pre-training framework that relies exclusively on target task data, focusing on smaller datasets such as Stanford Cars, Sketch, and COCO, which are significantly less extensive than ImageNet. Our research demonstrates that denoising autoencoders, including BEiT and a novel variant proposed here, exhibit greater robustness regarding pre-training data size and type compared to popular self-supervised methods based on image embedding comparison. We achieve competitive results against ImageNet pre-training across diverse classification domains. Notably, on the COCO dataset, pre-training solely with COCO images yields detection and instance segmentation performance that exceeds that of supervised ImageNet pre-training in a comparable setting.

Approximately 20% of planetary nebulae result from a common envelope (CE) interaction, wherein a companion star spirals into the envelope of an asymptotic giant branch (AGB) star, ejecting the nebula and forming a compact binary. This study utilizes 3D smoothed particle hydrodynamics simulations to model the CE interaction between a 1.7 $M_{\odot}$ AGB star and a 0.6 $M_{\odot}$ companion. The AGB star's structure is defined by a 1D model at its seventh thermal pulse, with the interaction occurring during the expansion phase when the stellar radius reaches 250 $R_{\odot}$. Post-interaction orbital separations range from 20 to 31 $R_{\odot}$, increasing further when recombination energy is accounted for. Given the observed rapid in-spiral timescales, we propose that thermal pulses can initiate CEs, thereby enhancing the capacity of AGB stars to capture companions and suggesting a larger population of post-AGB, post-CE binaries than previously anticipated. Simulations incorporating a tabulated equation of state indicate that significantly more gas is unbound, likely removing the entire envelope within short timeframes. Additionally, the resulting CE shape is more spherical for AGB stars compared to red giant branch stars, a feature that becomes even more pronounced with recombination energy. Consequently, the planetary nebula generated from this CE is expected to exhibit distinct characteristics from those predicted by Zou et al. (2020).

Identifying low-dimensional structures in real-world networks demands an appropriate null model to characterize the absence of meaningful patterns. This study presents a spectral method for uncovering such structures and the participating nodes, applicable to any null model. By employing generative models to predict the expected eigenvalue distribution under a chosen null model, we identify instances where the data network's eigenspectra surpass these estimated thresholds. Testing on synthetic networks, this spectral estimation technique effectively distinguishes between random and community structures, accurately recovers community counts and memberships, and filters out noise nodes. When applied to real networks, it either identifies a substantial proportion of noise nodes or finds no deviation from the null model, offering a sharp contrast to conventional community detection approaches. Across all evaluations, we observe that the selection of a null model can significantly influence conclusions regarding the existence of network structure. Consequently, this spectral estimation framework serves as a promising foundation for detecting low-dimensional structures in real-world networks—or confirming their absence.

The transition from diffuse to dense clouds alters dust properties due to ice formation and grain coagulation, though many details of this transformation remain uncertain. We analyzed 2-20 micron spectra of 49 background stars located behind the Perseus and Serpens Molecular Clouds to determine correlations between near-infrared continuum extinction ($A_K$) and the depths of the 3.0 micron H$_2$O ice ($\tau_{3.0}$) and 9.7 micron silicate ($\tau_{9.7}$) absorption features. The $\tau_{9.7}/A_K$ ratio shifts significantly, ranging from values near 0.55 typical of the diffuse interstellar medium down to approximately 0.26 in denser regions. This ratio reaches its minimum at extinctions of $A_K \sim 1.2$ (corresponding to $A_V \sim 10$ in Perseus, Lupus, and dense cores) and $A_K \sim 2.0$ ($A_V \sim 17$ in Serpens). The observed decrease in the $\tau_{9.7}/A_K$ ratio from diffuse to dense environments aligns with moderate grain growth up to roughly 0.5 microns; this growth increases the near-infrared color excess (and thus $A_K$) without altering the profiles of the ice or silicate bands. This process appears linked to ice column densities and the thresholds for dense core formation, underscoring the critical role of density. Following corrections for foreground extinction in Serpens, the threshold for H$_2$O ice formation is estimated between $A_K = 0.31$ and $0.40$ ($A_V = 2.6$–$3.4$) across all clouds, indicating that grain growth occurs subsequent to ice formation. Additionally, the target 2MASSJ18285266+0028242 in Serpens exhibits an exceptionally high abundance of CH$_3$OH ice, approximately 21% relative to H$_2$O, which is more than four times greater than in other observed targets.

TeV photons originating from extragalactic sources are absorbed within the intergalactic medium, triggering electromagnetic cascades that serve as a distinctive means to investigate cosmological-scale universe properties. We introduce a novel Monte Carlo code specifically designed for the physics of these cascades. Validated against both established results and analytical approximations, this tool is now publicly accessible. Utilizing this numerical framework, we examine key cascade characteristics—including spectrum, halo extension, and time delays—and analyze their sensitivity to various physical parameters such as the extragalactic magnetic field, extragalactic background light, source redshift, source spectrum, and beaming emission. Furthermore, we highlight the constraints of analytical solutions, noting that such approximations typically consider only the first generation of photons while neglecting higher branches of the cascade tree.

This work examines monotone P1 finite element schemes applied to unstructured meshes for fully non-linear, degenerately parabolic Isaacs equations featuring isotropic diffusions, which originate in stochastic game theory and optimal control. We demonstrate uniform convergence toward the viscosity solution. To address singular behavior at boundaries and to handle consistency condition violations by numerical operators identified in the Barles and Souganidis framework, we employ elliptic projections. Boundary conditions can be enforced either in the viscosity sense, the strong sense, or a hybrid of both. Furthermore, the proposed monotone numerical approach generates well-posed finite-dimensional systems that can be efficiently solved using Howard's method.

We investigate the topological abelian BF theory on a generic 3D manifold with a radial boundary, aiming to determine how and where the boundary retains memory of the background metric's details. Our analysis reveals that certain features are topologically protected and independent of the bulk metric. The holographically induced 2D action relies on two scalar fields and can be decomposed into two Luttinger actions representing chiral bosons propagating along the 3D bulk's edge. Consequently, these edge excitations experience acceleration due to the non-flat geometry of the bulk spacetime, resulting in chiral velocities that vary locally based on the determinant of the induced boundary metric. We identify three potential motion scenarios for edge quasiparticles: unidirectional, bidirectional (opposite), or single-mode propagation. However, imposing the requirement that the 2D Hamiltonian remains bounded from below eliminates the unidirectional case; thus, systems with parallel Hall currents (such as the Fractional Quantum Hall Effect at $\nu=2/5$) cannot be modeled by a BF theory with a boundary, regardless of the bulk geometry, due to positive energy constraints. This leaves two viable physical scenarios: edge modes moving in opposite directions (observed in FQHE with $\nu=1-1/n$ and Helical Luttinger Liquids) or a single moving mode (as in the Quantum Anomalous Hall effect). Imposing Time Reversal symmetry further restricts the system to modes with equal and opposite velocities, characteristic of Topological Insulators. The key novelty compared to a flat bulk background is that these modes possess local velocities, effectively describing Topological Insulators with accelerated edge states.

Although cardiac magnetic resonance parametric T1 maps are conventionally reconstructed via non-linear fitting, this approach is constrained by significant computational expenses and limited robustness. Consequently, this study introduces a recurrent neural network (RNN) designed to enable the rapid and reliable reconstruction of cardiac T1 maps.

We introduce e3nn, a generalized framework for constructing trainable functions that are equivariant under E(3) transformations, commonly referred to as Euclidean neural networks. Designed to inherently handle geometry and geometric tensors representing 3D systems, e3nn ensures predictable behavior when the coordinate system changes. At its core lie equivariant operations, such as the TensorProduct class and spherical harmonics functions, which can be combined to build more sophisticated modules like convolutions and attention mechanisms. These fundamental operations enable the efficient formulation of various E(3) equivariant architectures, including Tensor Field Networks, 3D Steerable CNNs, Clebsch-Gordan Networks, SE(3) Transformers, and others.

Using Johnson's operator formula for the equivariant Gromov-Witten theory of $\mathbb{P}^1$-orbifolds, we present a novel method for the operator formalism developed by Okounkov and Pandharipande, which addresses the $\mathbb{C}^*$-equivariant Gromov-Witten theory of $\mathbb{P}^1$ relative to one or two points. Furthermore, we generalize their non-equivariant operator formalism to accommodate cases involving negative contact orders.

Extensive training with large-scale image-text pairs endows the CLIP model with robust generalization capabilities. However, acquiring similarly vast video datasets is currently impractical, prompting recent research to focus on effectively transferring image-based CLIP to the video domain. Existing methods often introduce complex parametric modules to capture temporal dynamics and inter-frame relationships, requiring intricate design. Moreover, models trained directly on videos frequently suffer from overfitting to specific task distributions and exhibit poor generalization. This raises a critical question: How can image-level CLIP representations be effectively transferred to videos? In this work, we demonstrate that a straightforward Video Fine-tuned CLIP (ViFi-CLIP) baseline is largely sufficient to overcome the domain gap between images and videos. Qualitative analysis reveals that ViFi-CLIP implicitly models temporal cues by applying frame-level processing via the CLIP image encoder, followed by feature pooling and similarity matching with text embeddings. This fine-tuning strategy enables the model to concentrate on scene dynamics, moving objects, and interactions between objects. For low-data scenarios where complete fine-tuning is not feasible, we introduce a "bridge and prompt" approach: first using fine-tuning to bridge the domain gap, then learning prompts for both language and vision to adapt CLIP representations. We comprehensively evaluate this simple yet powerful baseline across zero-shot, base-to-novel generalization, few-shot, and fully supervised settings on five video benchmarks. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/muzairkhattak/ViFi-CLIP.

Detecting binary changes in bi-temporal co-registered hyperspectral images is difficult because of the high volume of spectral bands, prompting researchers to employ dimensionality reduction. This study introduces a new feature extraction framework utilizing a feature fusion deep convolutional autoencoder to identify changes between such image pairs. By integrating features from successive levels and diverse receptive fields, this approach offers a significant advantage over current methods. Furthermore, the proposed technique is entirely unsupervised, providing a more streamlined alternative to supervised or semi-supervised methods that rely on labeled data. Various algorithms were applied to the extracted features to detect differences between the two images, demonstrating that the proposed method consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art unsupervised change detection techniques across all datasets.

The study investigates visco-resistive magnetohydrodynamic turbulence generated by a two-dimensional shear layer stabilized by an external body force, analyzing it through the decomposition of dissipationless linear eigenmodes derived from initial profiles. While the down-gradient momentum flux is attributed to large-scale instability, a continuous up-gradient transport driven by large-scale, linearly stable yet nonlinearly excited eigenmodes is identified; this up-gradient flux nearly offsets the down-gradient transport from unstable modes. This balance occurs because stable modes reduce large-scale turbulent fluctuations by transferring energy to the mean flow. This mechanism explains the well-established observation that coherent vortices, resulting from the nonlinear saturation of the instability, diminish turbulent transport and fluctuations, as these vortices consist of stable and unstable modes with comparable amplitudes. The influence of magnetic fields on these nonlinearly excited stable modes is subsequently quantified. Even under a strong magnetic field that nearly suppresses the instability, the up-gradient transport by stable modes remains at least two-thirds of the down-gradient transport by unstable modes, a ratio that increases to as much as 98% for weaker fields. These findings remain consistent across variations in magnetic Prandtl number and forcing intensity. Furthermore, although continuum modes are energetically minor, they are crucial for accurately representing magnetic fluctuations and Maxwell stress. An analytical scaling law is derived for the saturated amplitudes of these turbulent modes, predicting an inverse Fourier wavenumber fall-off rate, a result confirmed by numerical simulations.

Rising vapor pressure deficit (VPD) heightens the atmosphere's demand for water. Although higher evapotranspiration (ET) due to this increased demand appears logical, plants can counteract it by closing their stomata when VPD rises. This study investigates which factor dominates: the atmospheric drive increasing ET or the plant's stomatal response decreasing it. By integrating the Penman-Monteith equation with semi-empirical models of optimal stomatal regulation and water use efficiency, we established a theoretical framework to evaluate ET responses to VPD. The model indicates that ET reactions to rising VPD can range from strongly positive to negative, depending on environmental conditions and plant traits, thereby illustrating the variety of plant water management strategies.

Variations in ET response are driven by three main factors: (1) climate, where tropical and temperate zones are more prone to positive ET responses than boreal or arctic regions; (2) photosynthetic pathway, with C3 plants more likely to show increased ET compared to C4 plants; and (3) plant type, as crops tend to exhibit positive responses while shrubs and gymnosperm trees are more likely to show negative ones. Derived from existing literature linking plant parameters to climatic and biological characteristics, these findings underscore the value of our simplified framework for analyzing complex land-atmosphere interactions. This approach isolates the specific effect of VPD on ET, a relationship that is difficult to isolate in natural environments where multiple processes evolve simultaneously.

Let $\mathcal{S}=\{1^2,2^2,3^2,...\}$ denote the set of perfect squares, and let $\mathcal{W} \subset \mathbb{N}$ be an additive complement to $\mathcal{S}$ such that $\mathcal{S} + \mathcal{W}$ contains all natural numbers greater than or equal to some $N_0$. Define $\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{W}}(n)$ as the count of pairs $(s,w)$ where $n=s+w$, $s \in \mathcal{S}$, and $w \in \mathcal{W}$. Chen and Fang [5] established that $$ \sum_{n=1}^NR_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{W}}(n)-N\gg N^{1/4}\log N. $$ In this note, we enhance their finding by proving that $$ \sum_{n=1}^NR_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{W}}(n)-N\gg N^{1/3}. $$

This study details the frequency stabilization of a 739 nm Ti:sapphire laser to a hyperfine component of the $^{127}I_{2}$ B(1)-X(11) P(70) transition via acousto-optic modulation transfer spectroscopy (MTS). When stabilized, the system achieves a frequency stability of $3.83\times 10^{-11}$ at an averaging time of 13 seconds. The selected molecular iodine hyperfine transition serves as an optimal frequency reference for locking lasers in experiments involving trapped ytterbium ions, as its second harmonic aligns with the $^{2}S_{\frac{1}{2}}-^{2}P_{\frac{1}{2}}$ transition of the ytterbium ion at 369.5 nm. By examining line broadening caused by iodine vapor pressure and laser power, the locking mechanism was optimized to reach the theoretical signal-to-noise ratio (TSNR) of this specific iodine transition.

The study of thin gaseous disks is frequently linked to galactic phenomena such as starburst rings and dense circumnuclear molecular disks, where the self-gravity of the gas within the two-dimensional disk plays a significant role in matching detailed observations and numerical simulations. To address these applications, a novel technique for computing the gravitational force of a 2D disk is introduced. Rather than solving the full potential function, this method calculates forces in infinite planes using both Cartesian and polar coordinates via a reproducing kernel approach. Specifically, within the constraints of a 2D disk, the force is expressed as a double summation of the convolution between surface density and a fundamental kernel, utilizing a fast Fourier transform. This strategy reduces the total computational complexity from $O(N^2\times N^2)$ to $O((N\times \log_2(N)^2)$, where $N$ represents the number of zones per dimension. Notably, the method does not require softening. While similar to spectral methods, it avoids the need for periodic boundary conditions. Furthermore, the approach demonstrates near second-order accuracy for smooth surface densities in a Cartesian coordinate system.

The Hateful Memes dataset presents a novel multimodal classification challenge dedicated to identifying hate speech within memes. By incorporating challenging examples, the dataset ensures that reliance on unimodal features is insufficient, necessitating multimodal approaches for success. As noted by Kiela, current state-of-the-art methods underperform significantly compared to human accuracy (64.73% versus 84.7%). I introduce a new model that integrates multimodal analysis with rule-based mechanisms, achieving the top ranking with an accuracy of 86.8% and an AUROC of 0.923. These rules, derived from the training data, specifically target the enhancement of classification performance on difficult samples.

This research investigates traversable wormholes devoid of tidal forces within the $f(R)$ gravity metric framework. We analyze three distinct wormhole shape functions to evaluate their structural viability and establish the relationship between these functions and the $f(R)$ gravity model, highlighting the model's dependency on the shape function. Furthermore, we derive a wormhole solution for the Starobinsky model within the $f(R)$ gravity formalism, surrounded by a cloud of strings; in this scenario, the shape function relies on both the Starobinsky parameter and the cloud of strings parameter. The wormhole's structure and height are significantly influenced by the cloud of strings parameter, whereas they exhibit lower sensitivity to the Starobinsky parameter. We examine the energy conditions and determine the ranges of null energy condition violation across all studied wormhole configurations. Additionally, quasinormal modes for scalar and Dirac perturbations are analyzed using higher-order WKB approximation methods. Results indicate that quasinormal modes for toy shape functions are highly sensitive to model parameters. Specifically, for the Starobinsky model, scalar perturbations show increased quasinormal frequencies and damping rates with a higher Starobinsky parameter, while Dirac perturbations display decreased frequencies and increased damping rates under the same condition. The cloud of strings parameter also exerts a notable and distinct influence on the quasinormal modes of the Starobinsky wormhole.

Topological edge solitons, which bifurcate from linear edge states to gain topological protection, are a focal point in the rapidly expanding field of topological photonics due to their immunity to disorder and defects during propagation. Valley Hall systems are particularly promising for realizing these solitons because they generate topological phases without the need for external or artificial magnetic fields or longitudinal potential modulations. This study reports on various types of vector valley Hall edge solitons that emerge at the domain walls of superhoneycomb lattices, specifically bright-dipole, bright-tripole, dark-bright, and dark-dipole configurations. Unlike conventional scalar topological solitons, these vector states function as envelope solitons derived from edge states across different branches and Bloch momenta. These solitons exhibit remarkable robustness, maintaining stable long-distance propagation and successfully navigating sharp bends in the domain wall. Furthermore, the presence of counter-propagating valley Hall edge solitons at the same domain wall enables the investigation of their structural resilience during nearly elastic collisions. These findings highlight the diversity of soliton families within valley Hall systems and suggest new possibilities for manipulating light fields and designing nonlinear topological functional devices.

The exclusive process $\gamma p \to p K^+ K^-$ was investigated within a photon energy spectrum of $3.0 - 3.8 \mbox{ GeV}$ and a momentum transfer interval of $0.6<-t<1.3 \mbox{ GeV}^2$. Data acquisition was performed using the CLAS detector at the Thomas Jefferson National Accelerator Facility, accumulating an integrated luminosity of roughly 20 pb$^{-1}$ in this kinematic region. The reaction was identified by tracking the $K^+$ and proton in CLAS while reconstructing the $K^-$ using the missing-mass method. Moments derived from the di-kaon decay angular distributions were analyzed to extract physical parameters. While the $P$-wave contribution from the dominant $\phi$ meson was observed, evidence for $S-P$ interference was also identified. Differential production cross sections ($d\sigma/dt$) for individual waves within the $\phi$ resonance mass range were calculated and contrasted with a Regge-inspired model prediction. Notably, this study represents the first measurement of the $t$-dependent cross section for the $S$-wave component in elastic $K^+K^-$ photoproduction.

We introduce a bottom-up framework for cumulatively learning numerous concepts representing meaningful character strings, along with their associated part-based and predictive relationships. This self-supervised approach utilizes discovered concepts simultaneously as both predictors and prediction targets. We define an objective function for segmentation based on learned concepts, which is derived by comparing against a baseline system; this objective encourages the formation and application of larger concepts, thereby enabling the prediction of longer text spans. Additionally, we outline a straightforward method to foster exploration by testing newly generated concepts during segmentation. To clarify the conditional distributions learned among concepts, we propose a layered architecture that roughly mirrors a part-whole hierarchy. Despite using basic segmentation and learning algorithms, the system proves promising: small-scale experiments yielded tens of thousands of concepts, and text segmentation improved significantly. When processing spaceless English text starting from characters, the learned concepts largely align with word or phrase boundaries, and the frequency of incorrect splits within words diminishes as larger concepts are identified and integrated. We also present encouraging results where binary input text is used, beginning with just two concepts, "0" and "1." The system remains transparent, allowing clear identification of learned concepts, their activity during segmentation, and how the input is interpreted. We anticipate this framework to be extensible and discuss existing limitations alongside potential avenues for improving learning and inference capabilities.

The decline in network camera costs, combined with increased connectivity, has allowed global entities to implement extensive camera networks. These devices provide real-time visual information valuable for analyzing traffic, managing emergencies, enhancing security, and supporting other applications. Despite the abundance of network camera data, collection remains challenging due to inconsistencies in programming interfaces and website architectures. Existing methods depend on manually parsing target sites, a process that is time-consuming. We have developed a generalized, automated approach to aggregate data from thousands of uniquely structured web pages. By analyzing diverse web page layouts and identifying shared traits across 73 sample network camera websites (each containing multiple pages), we created an automated discovery module that crawls and consolidates camera data. This system successfully extracted 57,364 network cameras from 237,257 unique web pages.

Clustering and community detection within networks are widely studied topics spanning multiple disciplines. Our focus is specifically on identifying communities of scientific publications connected through citations, which can reveal groups of scientists with shared interests. Building upon the established k-core algorithm, we have created a modular pipeline designed to detect these publication communities. We benchmark our method against the widely adopted Leiden algorithm for community detection. Using both quantitative and qualitative metrics, we evaluate the results on a citation network comprising over 14 million publications related to extracellular vesicles.

A Kramers-Kronig receiver that incorporates a continuous wave tone, digitally inserted at the transmitter, is paired with a digital resolution enhancer to constrain the rise in transmitter quantization noise. The study demonstrates improved performance alongside the capability to decrease the bit count required for the digital-to-analog converter.

While a core goal of news reporting is to document events factually by detailing the 5 Ws and capturing public responses through reported statements, current news summarization research largely overlooks these reactions. This study introduces a new task focused on summarizing the statements made by various speakers regarding specific events. To support this, we developed SUMREN, a multi-document benchmark containing 745 summaries of reported remarks from 633 articles covering 132 events involving different public figures. We also devised an automatic method for generating silver training data, enabling smaller models such as BART to reach GPT-3 performance levels on this task. Furthermore, we present a pipeline-based framework for summarizing reported speech, which empirical results show produces summaries that are both more abstractive and factual than traditional query-focused approaches.

Although the BERT model has proven effective for open-domain question answering, prior approaches trained it by treating passages associated with the same query as independent instances, leading to incomparable answer scores across different passages. To resolve this, we introduce a multi-passage BERT architecture that globally normalizes answer scores across all passages for a given question, thereby enabling the model to identify superior answers by leveraging additional context. Furthermore, we observe that partitioning articles into 100-word segments using a sliding window boosts performance by 4%, while integrating a passage ranker to prioritize high-quality texts yields an additional 2% improvement. Experiments across four standard benchmarks demonstrate that our multi-passage BERT surpasses all state-of-the-art models. Specifically, on the OpenSQuAD dataset, our approach achieves a 21.4% increase in Exact Match (EM) and a 21.5% increase in $F_1$ score compared to non-BERT models, and a 5.8% EM and 6.5% $F_1$ gain over existing BERT-based models.

Score-based generative models currently achieve top-tier results in generative modeling and density estimation. While these models usually presuppose flat data geometry, recent advancements have enabled data synthesis on Riemannian manifolds. However, existing acceleration techniques for diffusion sampling do not apply to Riemannian contexts, and Riemannian score-based approaches have yet to address dataset interpolation. To address these gaps, we present \emph{Riemannian Diffusion Schr\"odinger Bridge}. This approach extends the Diffusion Schr\"odinger Bridge framework from \cite{debortoli2021neurips} to non-Euclidean spaces and broadens Riemannian score-based models to operate beyond the first time reversal. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method using both synthetic datasets and real-world Earth and climate data.

Within the HL-LHC upgrade initiative, the CMS collaboration is swapping its current endcap calorimeters for a new high-granularity calorimeter (CE). This innovative sampling calorimeter features exceptional transverse and longitudinal readout capabilities across both its electromagnetic and hadronic sections. Given its compact size, superior intrinsic time resolution, and resistance to radiation, silicon was selected as the active material for areas facing high radiation doses. These silicon sensors are manufactured as 20 cm (8") hexagonal wafers and divided into hundreds of individually readout pads. To validate the sensors, an irradiation test using neutrons was performed on 8" wafers at the Rhode Island Nuclear Science Center (RINSC), followed by electrical characterization during 2020-21. This paper documents this key milestone in the CE's R&D efforts, detailing the supporting infrastructure and protocols, and presents the findings regarding the electrical performance of the irradiated silicon sensors.

For any positive integer $k$, this paper employs a modular approach to demonstrate that, assuming the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH), the Diophantine equation $x^2+(2k-1)^y=k^z$ possesses a unique positive integer solution $(x,y,z)=(k-1,1,2)$ whenever $k\equiv 0 \pmod{4}$, $30< k<724$, and $2k-1$ is an odd prime power. These findings address several challenging instances of Terai's conjecture regarding this equation.

This paper investigates the temperature front problem within the 3D viscous Boussinesq framework. We demonstrate that $C^{k,\gamma}$ (where $k\geq 1$ and $0<\gamma< 1$) and $W^{2,\infty}$ regularity for a temperature front remains locally invariant throughout the evolution and is globally maintained provided a smallness condition holds in a critical space. Notably, beyond offering an alternative proof of the primary result found in \cite{GGJ20}, we broaden its scope to encompass a more extensive class of regular patches.

RDF and property graph models share foundational similarities, such as utilizing basic graph concepts like nodes and edges; however, they diverge in their modeling strategies, expressiveness, serialization methods, and target applications. As the de-facto standard for Semantic Web knowledge graphs, RDF is backed by a robust ecosystem for inference and processing. Conversely, the property graph model excels in scalable analytical tasks, including graph traversal, path analysis, and graph matching. While RDF-star extends RDF to treat metadata as a first-class citizen, existing literature offers various methods for converting between property graphs and RDF, yet most fail to handle RDF-star graphs fully. Consequently, this paper advances the field by addressing the transformation of RDF-star graphs into property graphs. We identify specific scenarios to evaluate these transformation approaches, categorizing them into two distinct classes and analyzing them against test cases. The insights derived from this analysis will serve as a foundation for developing comprehensive transformation solutions in the future.

Very recently, the BESIII collaboration identified a charged hidden-charm state with strangeness, denoted as $Z_{cs}(3985)^{-}$, observed in the recoil mass spectrum of $K^+$ within the processes $e^+e^-\to D_s^{*-}D^0K^+$ or $D_s^{-}D^{*0}K^+$. This newly discovered charged structure serves as a strangeness-containing counterpart to the well-established $Z_{c}(3885)^{-}$, which was detected in $e^+e^-\to D^{*-}D^0\pi^+$. In this study, we introduce a new framework to elucidate the nature of $Z_{cs}(3985)$. Through a combined analysis of the $K^+$ recoil mass line shapes at five center-of-mass energies ($\sqrt{s}=4.628, 4.641, 4.661, 4.681, 4.698$ GeV), we demonstrate that $Z_{cs}(3985)$ can be interpreted as a reflection structure of the charmed-strange meson $D_{s2}^{*}(2573)$. This meson is generated via the open-charm decay of $Y(4660)$ accompanied by a $D_s^*$ meson. Additionally, based on our proposed reaction mechanism, we predict the angular distribution of the final-state $D_s^{*-}$ in the process $e^+e^-\to D_s^{*-}D^0K^+$, which may provide a crucial test for the non-resonant nature of $Z_{cs}(3985)$.

Tunneling is a unique quantum phenomenon lacking a classical counterpart, capable of competing with Coulomb forces to generate intricate behaviors. While phosphorus dopants in silicon can be positioned with atomic precision to explore these competing regimes, they typically rely on crystal band symmetry-based wavefunctions that are intrinsically sensitive to tunneling effects. This study directly visualizes lattice-aperiodic valley interference between coupled silicon atoms using scanning tunneling microscopy. Our atomistic analysis reveals how envelope anisotropy, valley interference, and dopant positioning influence the Heisenberg spin exchange interaction. We demonstrate that the exchange interaction can be made resilient to valley interference by strategically aligning dopants along specific in-plane crystallographic directions. This approach restores a vacuum-like behavior, maximizing exchange based on donor orbital overlap and restricting pair-to-pair variations to under a factor of ten, given the precision of dopant placement. This robustness persists across a broad distance spectrum, spanning the strongly Coulomb-interacting regime essential for high-fidelity quantum computation to the tightly coupled donor arrays valuable for quantum simulation in silicon.

Few-shot learning represents a critical yet difficult challenge in machine learning, focusing on acquiring knowledge from a minimal number of labeled training instances. This field has gained significant research momentum because deep learning models typically demand vast labeled datasets, which are often impractical to obtain in real-world scenarios. Furthermore, mastering tasks with limited examples aligns closely with human learning capabilities. Few-shot learning has demonstrated substantial potential across various machine learning domains, especially in image classification. As a relatively recent technique, much of the current research concentrates on addressing fundamental issues using standard image datasets like Mini-ImageNet and Omniglot. However, this approach also presents a unique opportunity to tackle low-resource languages such as Amharic. This study investigates offline handwritten Amharic character recognition through the application of few-shot learning. Specifically, it implements prototypical networks—a widely used and straightforward few-shot learning method—as a baseline. Leveraging the inherent row-wise and column-wise similarities within the Amharic alphabet, the study proposes a novel method for augmenting training episodes. Experimental results indicate that this proposed approach surpasses the baseline performance. Notably, this research marks the first implementation of few-shot learning for Amharic characters. Beyond this achievement, the findings offer new avenues for exploring the impact of training episodes on few-shot learning, addressing a key area requiring further investigation. The datasets utilized in this study were gathered from native Amharic speakers via a custom Android application developed specifically for this research.

This study tackles joint direction-of-arrival (DoA) and range estimation using a frequency diverse coprime array (FDCA). By integrating coprime array structures with coprime frequency offsets, we establish a two-dimensional space-frequency virtual difference coarray that mimics a uniform array with uniform frequency offsets, thereby expanding the degrees-of-freedom (DoFs). Although this approach increases DoFs, reconstructing the doubly-Toeplitz covariance matrix remains computationally demanding. To address this, we introduce an interpolation algorithm grounded in decoupled atomic norm minimization (DANM), which transforms the coarray signal into a simplified matrix format. Building on this, we formulate a relaxation-based optimization problem to facilitate joint DoA-range estimation with improved DoFs. The resulting coarray signal allows for the use of established subspace-based spectral estimation techniques. Furthermore, the proposed DANM problem is recast as an equivalent rank-minimization problem, solved via cyclic rank minimization. This method circumvents the approximation errors inherent in nuclear norm-based techniques, yielding superior root-mean-square error performance that approaches the Cramer-Rao bound. Both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations validate the efficacy of the proposed method.

We introduce an adaptive sampling technique for estimating the probability of rare events across diverse flight conditions for a collection of three-dimensional aircraft configurations. This study presents a fully automated workflow to generate parameterized airplane geometries and construct volumetric meshes suitable for viscous CFD analysis. Leveraging this automatic geometry and meshing process, we execute the adaptive sampling procedure to determine rare event probabilities. Our results indicate that the computational expense of this adaptive sampling method is hundreds of times less than that of a brute-force Monte Carlo approach.

Deepfakes present a significant risk of visual misinformation to society, with face manipulation—altering attributes like age or hair color in images—serving as a primary example. Current state-of-the-art manipulation methods depend on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). This paper introduces UnGANable, the first defense system targeting GAN-inversion-based face manipulation. Specifically, UnGANable defends against GAN inversion, a critical step in the manipulation process, by searching for alternative "cloaked images" near the original "target images" within the image space. These cloaked images can disrupt the inversion process when posted online. We evaluated five distinct defense strategies across five scenarios, accounting for varying levels of defender background knowledge, against two leading inversion techniques: optimization-based and hybrid inversion. Extensive testing on four popular GAN models using two benchmark face datasets demonstrates that UnGANable delivers remarkable effectiveness and utility, surpassing multiple baseline methods. Additionally, we examined four adaptive adversaries attempting to bypass UnGANable, finding that some were marginally successful.

Resolving specific toroidal orbifolds, such as T6/Z2xZ2, yields non-unique outcomes because the resolution of their local singularities depends on the chosen triangulation. This dependence causes a vast proliferation of topologically distinct smooth geometries for any single orbifold. By introducing a parameterization to track the triangulations at all resolved singularities simultaneously, one can determine (self-)intersection numbers and integrated Chern classes for any specific configuration. Using this approach, consistency conditions for line bundle models and the resulting chiral spectra can be calculated for every possible triangulation. Furthermore, by combining Bianchi identities across all triangulation options, simpler yet more stringent conditions emerge; when these are met, flop transitions between all different triangulations become permissible. Various methods are illustrated through concrete models applied to resolutions of the T6/Z2xZ2 orbifold.

The concept of a "centre" has been established across numerous algebraic structures in mathematics; for instance, the centre of a monoid invariably yields a commutative submonoid. In category theory, monads serve as crucial algebraic structures for modeling computational effects within programming languages. This paper demonstrates how the notion of a centre can be generalized to strong monads defined on symmetric monoidal categories. Specifically, we prove that if the centre of a strong monad $\mathcal T$ exists, it generates a commutative submonad $\mathcal Z$ where the Kleisli category of $\mathcal Z$ is isomorphic to the premonoidal centre (following Power and Robinson) of the Kleisli category of $\mathcal T$. We establish three equivalent criteria characterizing the existence of the centre for $\mathcal T$ and demonstrate that every strong monad on many prominent naturally occurring categories possesses a centre, indicating the ubiquity of this new concept. Furthermore, we offer a computational interpretation by refining Moggi's monadic metalanguage. This refinement enables the immediate identification of a broad class of contextually equivalent programs for computational effects modeled by monads with a non-trivial centre, leveraging the enhanced syntactic structure provided by the refinement.

This research examines an online caching scenario where local storage mitigates retrieval expenses from a remote server. The cache updates its configuration following request batches and can retain a fractional portion of any file. We investigate no-regret algorithms grounded in Online Mirror Descent (OMD) approaches, demonstrating that the optimal OMD strategy varies according to the diversity of requests within a batch. Furthermore, we establish that when the cache is required to store complete files instead of fractions, OMD methods can be integrated with a randomized rounding technique that maintains regret performance guarantees.

The advent of Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) represents a pivotal milestone in the evolution of representation learning models. Beyond their own significant achievements, VAEs have inspired a lineage of innovations, including the Wasserstein Autoencoder (WAE). As a successor in this domain, WAE inherits the strengths of its predecessor while delivering enhanced generative capabilities that rival Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). Although recent years have seen a notable revival in the statistical analysis of GANs, comparable investigations into Autoencoders remain scarce, despite their broad applicability and strong empirical results. To address this gap, this paper examines the statistical properties of WAE. We first establish statistical guarantees that WAE recovers the target distribution within the latent space by leveraging Vapnik-Chervonenkis (VC) theory. Our primary result confirms the model's ability to regenerate the input distribution by exploiting the potential of Optimal Transport under the Wasserstein metric. Ultimately, this study elucidates the range of distributions that WAE can reconstruct following the compression inherent in its latent representation.

Experiments in levitated optomechanics conducted under ultra-high vacuum conditions necessitate the clean loading of silica nanoparticles with radii down to approximately 50 nm. We introduce an affordable and straightforward technique for dry-launching these particles by shaking them off a polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) surface. This method successfully launches individual silica nanoparticles with a minimum radius of 43 nm, a capability attributed to the minimal stiction between the particles and the launch surface. Nanoparticles with radii of 43 nm and 71.5 nm are emitted with high flux and a narrow angular spread of roughly $\pm 10^\circ$, facilitating their capture by a tightly focused optical tweezer within a few minutes. The observed velocities are notably below 1 m/s. This demonstrated approach enables the controlled loading of dry nanoparticles as small as 43 nm into optical traps in (ultra-)high vacuum environments, though we expect that loading even smaller particles remains feasible.

Multifidelity and multioutput optimization algorithms are gaining significant attention across various computational design fields because they enable the intelligent use of cost-effective computational proxies to enhance experimental searches for high-performance species. Evaluating these algorithms typically relies on benchmarks based on either analytic functions or existing multifidelity datasets. However, analytic functions often fail to represent real-world problems accurately, whereas preexisting datasets prevent a systematic analysis of how the characteristics of lower-fidelity proxies influence outcomes. To address this limitation, we introduce a methodology for the systematic generation of synthetic fidelities derived from existing datasets. This approach facilitates the creation of benchmarks that are both representative of practical optimization challenges and capable of systematically investigating the impact of lower-fidelity proxy characteristics.

Detecting collisions between objects is essential for simulating, controlling, and training robotic systems. Yet, standard collision detection algorithms are fundamentally non-differentiable, which restricts their use in gradient-based optimization methods. To address this, we introduce DCOL: a rapid and entirely differentiable collision-detection framework capable of analyzing interactions between a collection of composable, highly expressive convex primitive shapes. By casting the collision detection task as a convex optimization problem that computes the minimum uniform scaling factor required for primitives to intersect, we achieve full differentiability regarding each primitive's configuration. This approach provides a collision metric and contact points for every object, regardless of interpenetration levels. We validate DCOL's effectiveness across various robotics applications, including trajectory optimization and contact physics, and have released an open-source implementation.

The extragalactic radio sky is generally stable at the mJy level, with only about 3% of persistent sources showing variability, primarily driven by AGN. In the fainter regime (<mJy), the source population is thought to shift from AGN dominance to one dominated by star formation, alongside the emergence of radio-quiet AGN; however, the variable component in this sub-mJy range remains poorly understood. This study offers the first insights into the $\mu$Jy variable sky through a detailed analysis of deep VLA observations in the GOODS-N field. By examining approximately 480 radio sources across five epochs spanning 22 years, we identified 10 sources exhibiting variability, which we attribute to AGN activity. Our findings confirm and expand upon prior surveys, indicating that variability in the faint radio sky is relatively low, with no more than 2% of sources showing significant changes between any two epochs. Specifically, 70% of variable sources display fluctuations over timescales of a few days, whereas the fraction drops to less than 1% over decadal periods, suggesting that radio variability peaks at shorter intervals as other studies propose. Furthermore, 80% of these variable sources have VLBI counterparts. Utilizing multi-wavelength data, we infer that these are likely core-dominated FR-I sources, aligning with postulations from wide-field VLBI surveys and semi-empirical simulations.

The LHCb Collaboration recently reported the discovery of a new hidden-charmed strange pentaquark state, $P_{cs}(4459)^0$, but the spin-parity quantum numbers remain undetermined due to limited data. To clarify these properties, we analyze its observed decay channel, $P_{cs}(4459)^0 \rightarrow J/\psi \Lambda$, using the QCD sum rule approach. Assuming a diquark-diquark-antiquark substructure and assigning the quantum numbers $J^P=\frac{1}{2}^-$, we calculate the strong coupling constants governing this decay and subsequently determine the decay width. The resulting width aligns with experimental findings, thereby validating the proposed $J^P=\frac{1}{2}^-$ assignment and supporting the compact pentaquark nature of the $P_{cs}(4459)^0$ state.

The C-metric is utilized to describe accelerating black holes, and this study investigates their causal structure through the analysis of null geodesics. We explicitly construct the corresponding Penrose diagrams. Initially, we verify established results concerning sub-accelerating black holes before expanding the analysis to super-accelerating scenarios, where an additional essential singularity emerges. Furthermore, we examine accelerating black holes with negative masses, demonstrating their equivalence to the geometry of standard black hole metrics beyond conformal infinity. Finally, we compare these findings with Schwarzschild geometry to enhance comprehension and underscore the significance of these novel characteristics.

Laue diffraction microscopy employs polychromatic Laue micro-diffraction to analyze material structures with sub-micron resolution across three dimensions. This technique measures local crystallographic orientations, orientation gradients, and strains, storing the results in HDF5 image format for subsequent analysis using a depth reconstruction algorithm. However, the existing algorithm is computationally intensive, requiring up to two weeks to process data from a single experiment. To address this bottleneck, this paper introduces a scalable GPU-based solution for depth reconstruction. Testing indicates that this approach accelerates processing times by a factor of 10 to 20 compared to previous CPU implementations across various input sizes.

"How many days in the last 30 days did you experience poor mental health?" This question captures self-reported mental well-being and correlates with key covariates from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES). However, the resulting count data pose significant distributional issues, including overdispersion, zero-inflation, a 30-day upper bound, and clustering at five- and seven-day intervals. To address these complexities, we propose a semiparametric estimation and inference framework for count data regression. Our approach defines a data-generating process through the Simultaneous Transformation and Rounding (STAR) of a latent Gaussian regression model. The transformation is estimated nonparametrically, while the rounding operator ensures the discrete and bounded support of the data. Maximum likelihood estimators are derived using an EM algorithm compatible with any continuous model estimable via least squares. STAR regression features asymptotic hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, information-criteria-based variable selection, and tailored diagnostics. Simulation studies confirm the framework's effectiveness. When applied to analyze factors influencing self-reported mental health, STAR demonstrates markedly better goodness-of-fit than existing count data regression models.

This study introduces a visual analytics framework designed to handle intricate user interactions via a command-line interface within distributed data analysis environments. The framework enables users to manage access to distributed servers, ingest source data, execute data-driven analyses, track progress, and investigate results through interactive visualizations. By embedding generalized functionalities and access protocols into a user interface, we integrate it with a distributed analysis system. To validate this proof of concept, we illustrate two use cases drawn from earth science and the Sustainable Human Building Ecosystem research domains.

This paper introduces a novel hybrid mobile robot featuring controllable stiffness and a deformable shape. Unlike traditional mobile agents, our system transitions between rigid and compliant phases by solidifying or melting Field's metal within its structure, allowing it to modify its shape via the movement of its active components. In its soft configuration, the robot's main body can curve into circular arcs, enabling it to adapt to surrounding curved surfaces. This variable geometry generates new motion capabilities that standard fixed-geometry models cannot describe. Consequently, we have developed a unified mathematical framework to capture the differential kinematics of both rigid and soft states. Furthermore, an optimized control strategy is proposed to determine the most suitable phase states and motion modes required to achieve a target pose-shape configuration. The efficacy of this approach is validated through numerical simulations and experiments on a prototype system. The simulation source code is accessible at https://github.com/Louashka/2sr-agent-simulation.git.

In high-stakes scenarios where humans make final decisions, explaining AI predictions has become not only crucial but essential. This study introduces two new architectures for self-interpretable image classifiers that prioritize explanation before prediction by leveraging visual connections between a query image and exemplars, rather than relying on post-hoc methods. While these models achieve marginal performance drops (1 to 2 points) on in-distribution data compared to ResNet-50 and kNN classifiers, they consistently outperform them on out-of-distribution datasets by 1 to 4 points. Large-scale human evaluations on ImageNet and CUB datasets reveal that our correspondence-based explanations are more beneficial to users than those provided by kNN, specifically aiding users in more accurately identifying and rejecting incorrect AI decisions. Notably, this research demonstrates, for the first time, the ability to achieve complementary human-AI team accuracy in image classification tasks, surpassing the performance of either AI or humans working alone.

We introduce a Riemann-Hilbert problem associated with a family of $q$-orthogonal polynomials, $\{ P_n(x) \}_{n=0}^\infty$, to derive their asymptotic behavior as the degree $n$ tends to infinity. Our findings reveal that these polynomials exhibit universal characteristics in the limit $n\to\infty$. Specifically, the asymptotic behavior near the smallest zeros, where $x \sim q^{n/2}$, and the norm $\|P_n\|_2$ are shown to be independent of the weight function as $n$ approaches infinity.

This paper addresses two inquiries concerning the exceptional behavior of preperiodic points for polynomials in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$. We demonstrate that for every integer $d \geq 2$, there exists a polynomial $f_d(x) \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$ with degree between 2 and $d$ inclusive, possessing at least $d + \lfloor \log_2(d)\rfloor$ rational preperiodic points. Additionally, we prove that for infinitely many values of $d$, both $f_d(x)$ and $f_d(x) + 1$ share at least $d^2 + d\lfloor \log_2(d)\rfloor - 2d + 1$ common complex preperiodic points.

Locality serves as a fundamental simplifying characteristic in numerous physical systems, a feature that cluster expansion techniques are designed to leverage. Historically utilized in statistical physics to demonstrate the uniqueness of Gibbs states and correlation decay at elevated temperatures, these methods are now applied to quantum many-body systems governed by local Hamiltonians. This approach examines the dynamics of both local observables and non-local metrics, such as the Loschmidt echo. We demonstrate that when starting from a product state, cluster expansions allow for efficient classical simulation of system dynamics up to a specific time horizon, regardless of system size, with computational costs scaling polynomially with both system size and inverse approximation error. For local observables, analytic continuation extends the valid evolution time to any constant. In multi-dimensional settings, our method exhibits a superior dependence on approximation error compared to algorithms relying on the Lieb-Robinson bound. The efficacy of these algorithms hinges on the convergence of the cluster expansion, yielding significant physical insights, including a new quantum speed limit, constraints on dynamical phase transitions, and concentration bounds for product states evolved over short durations.

Building upon general semiclassical equations of motion for electrons under electric and magnetic fields, we generalize the Chambers formula to incorporate time-dependent electric fields alongside magnetic fields, as well as bands featuring Berry curvature. This framework enables the calculation of the conductivity tensor ${\sigma}_{{\alpha}{\beta}}(B,{\omega})$ for both two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) systems with Berry curvature in the presence of a magnetic field. We subsequently apply these results to magnetotransport phenomena in metals undergoing Fermi surface topological transitions in 2D. Specifically, utilizing a rectangular lattice and a model analogous to overdoped graphene, we examine how various types of Fermi surface topological transitions manifest in the Hall coefficient, Hall conductivity ${\sigma}_{xy}$, and longitudinal conductivity ${\sigma}_{xx}$. Furthermore, we analyze the frequency-dependent behavior of these quantities under time-varying electric fields. As a concrete example of non-zero Berry curvature, we investigate the magnetotransport properties of the Haldane model within this context. Additionally, we derive formulas for linear and nonlinear electric currents up to the second order in the electric field ($E^2$).

Recent research has explored a generalized Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) for multiple integers within residue sets where the mapping between remainders and integers across several moduli is unknown, alongside a robust CRT for recovering a single integer from faulty remainders. This paper addresses the reconstruction of two integers from their respective residue sets, handling scenarios where remainders are both misordered and potentially erroneous. We demonstrate that robust reconstruction is achievable if the remainder errors remain below $M/8$, with $M$ representing the greatest common divisor of all moduli. Furthermore, we introduce an efficient reconstruction algorithm and provide simulations to validate its performance. This work is driven by and applicable to the estimation of multiple frequencies from multiple undersampled waveforms.

Keystroke dynamics have long been utilized in psycholinguistics and writing research to understand cognitive processes. However, the question remains whether these logs contain specific signals capable of enhancing natural language processing models. We hypothesize that keystroke dynamics encode information regarding syntactic structure that can aid in shallow parsing. To validate this, we treated keystroke-derived labels as an auxiliary task within a multi-task bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (bi-LSTM) framework. Our findings demonstrate promising performance on two shallow parsing tasks: chunking and CCG supertagging. The proposed model is straightforward, benefits from the ability to incorporate data from diverse sources, and yields models that significantly outperform those trained solely on text annotations.

We examine short-range Ising spin glasses in equilibrium with infinite system size, demonstrating that for a fixed bond configuration and a specific Gibbs state selected from an appropriate metastate, every translation- and locally-invariant function (such as self-overlaps) associated with a single pure state within the Gibbs state's decomposition yields an identical value across all pure states comprising that Gibbs state. We outline various important applications of this result to spin glasses.

Understanding the ventilation strategy for supercavities is crucial for designing high-speed underwater vehicles that utilize an artificial gas pocket behind a flow separation device to reduce drag. This study examines how flow unsteadiness influences the ventilation requirements needed to form (CQf) and collapse (CQc) a supercavity. Introducing unsteadiness into the incoming flow increases the required CQf at low free stream velocities but decreases it at high velocities. High-speed imaging reveals distinct differences in the recirculation region's behavior between low and high free stream velocities under unsteady conditions. At low velocities, the recirculation zone downstream of the cavitator shifts vertically due to flow unsteadiness, reducing the probability of bubble collision and coalescence, which is vital for supercavity formation. Conversely, at high velocities, the recirculation region remains largely unaffected by flow unsteadiness, requiring less ventilation to form a supercavity than in steady flows. This difference is attributed to increased transverse Reynolds stress that facilitates bubble collisions within the confined recirculation space. The collapse ventilation requirement (CQc) is heavily dependent on the vertical component of flow unsteadiness and free stream velocity. Flow unsteadiness significantly enhances interfacial instability at the upper rear of the supercavity, causing the distorted interface to shed additional bubbles and thereby increasing CQc. Further analysis quantifies this additional bubble leakage rate, indicating that the development and amplitude of interfacial instability account for the variation in CQc across a wide range of flow unsteadiness. Ultimately, this study offers valuable insights for developing practical ventilation strategies for supercavitating vehicles.

In 1992, Godsil and Hensel presented a landmark study on distance-regular antipodal covers of the complete graph, which notably established a significant link to equi-isoclinic subspaces. This relationship appears to have been neglected, as numerous direct implications have not been thoroughly documented in existing literature. To address this gap, we initially explain how Godsil and Hensel's method leverages representation theory to generate equi-isoclinic tight fusion frames. Utilizing this framework on Mathon's construction yields $q+1$ planes within $\mathbb{R}^{q+1}$ for any even prime power $q>2$. Although these results stem from the Godsil-Hensel finding from three decades ago, infinitely many of these parameter sets have never been explicitly stated before. Furthermore, drawing on concepts from Et-Taoui, we explore a productive interaction with complex symmetric conference matrices.

The high-spin level structure of the neutron-rich nucleus 91Y was reexamined using the 82Se(13C, p3n)91Y reaction. A newly constructed level scheme, which incorporates several pivotal levels, resolves ambiguities present in previous investigations. These levels are defined by the disruption of Z=38 and N=56 subshell closures, a phenomenon involving spin-isospin dependent central forces and tensor forces.

Recent breakthroughs in self-supervised learning (SSL) have enabled the acquisition of adaptable visual representations from unlabeled datasets. Models fine-tuned on pretrained SSL features now achieve performance levels comparable to those fine-tuned on state-of-the-art supervised learning (SL) representations. Despite these advances, the generalizability of SSL remains underexplored. This article presents a comprehensive domain-based analysis of the generalizability of both pretrained SSL and SL representations within transfer learning classification tasks.
