This outcome aligns with our simulation study based on the SPM, which shows that while the naive model performs better for existing participants, the SPM is more effective for predicting outcomes among dropouts.

The Locally Competitive Algorithm (LCA) leverages local competition among non-spiking leaky integrator neurons to derive sparse representations, enabling real-time operation on massively parallel neuromorphic systems like Intel's Loihi. This study addresses the challenge of inferring sparse representations from streaming video using unsupervised dictionaries of spatiotemporal features optimized for sparse reconstruction. While non-spiking LCA has previously facilitated the unsupervised learning of convolutional kernels from raw, unlabeled video, we demonstrate that unsupervised dictionary learning can be efficiently executed with spiking LCA (S-LCA) via accumulator neurons. These neurons integrate a standard leaky-integrate-and-fire (LIF) mechanism with an extra state variable designed to minimize the gap between integrated inputs and spiking outputs. We show that dictionary learning remains effective across diverse dynamical regimes, ranging from graded to intermittent spiking, for both static images from the CIFAR dataset and video frames from a DVS camera. In a classification task involving a rapidly flipped deck of cards observed by a DVS camera, performance remained virtually unchanged as the model transitioned from graded to spiking inference. We conclude that accumulator neurons are poised to be a critical component in future neuromorphic hardware, facilitating online unsupervised learning of spatiotemporal dictionaries tailored for the sparse reconstruction of streaming video from event-based DVS cameras.

The Single Source Replacement Paths (SSRP) problem involves calculating the shortest distance $d(s,t,e)$ from a source vertex $s$ to every other vertex $t$ in a graph, excluding a specific edge $e$. A Single-Source Distance Sensitivity Oracle (DSO) is a data structure designed to return this distance for any given pair $(t,e)$. This work presents a deterministic method to compress the results of the SSRP problem for graphs with $n$ vertices, $m$ edges, and integer weights in $[1,M]$, resulting in a DSO with $O(M^{1/2}n^{3/2})$ space and $\widetilde{O}(1)$ query time. This space complexity is optimal relative to the word size, and the approach extends to handling vertex failures as well.

Previous work by Chechik and Cohen (SODA 2019) offered a combinatorial, randomized SSRP algorithm with $\widetilde{O}(m\sqrt{n}+n^2)$ time complexity for undirected, unweighted graphs, while Grandoni and Vassilevska Williams (FOCS 2012, TALG 2020) provided an algebraic, randomized algorithm with $\widetilde{O}(Mn^\omega)$ time for weighted graphs, where $\omega < 2.373$. This study derandomizes both algorithms for undirected graphs, maintaining their asymptotic running times, and applies the proposed compression technique to create deterministic Single-Source DSOs. These preprocessing times represent polynomial improvements over earlier oracles that required $o(n^2)$ space.

Furthermore, for sparse graphs where $m=O(n^{5/4-\varepsilon}/M^{7/4})$, the preprocessing time can be reduced to randomized $\widetilde{O}(M^{7/8}m^{1/2}n^{11/8})$, which simplifies to $O(n^{2-\varepsilon/2})$ for any constant $\varepsilon > 0$. This marks the first truly subquadratic time algorithm for constructing Single-Source DSOs on sparse graphs.

Social network analysis (SNA) has emerged as an increasingly popular method for quantitatively examining student collaboration. This study analyzes collaboration networks derived from student self-reports regarding homework in two courses at the University of Colorado Boulder and one at the Colorado School of Mines. Since all three courses took place during the COVID-19 pandemic, the data enables a comparison between the fully remote format at the Colorado School of Mines and findings from a prior pre-pandemic study of a hybrid format at the same institution. By computing nodal centrality metrics and assessing their correlation with academic performance, the study found significant variation across the courses. The remote course at the Colorado School of Mines exhibited strong correlations between various centrality measures and performance, aligning with patterns observed in the earlier hybrid study. In contrast, the University of Colorado Boulder courses displayed weaker correlations, with one showing virtually no link between student connectivity and performance. Collectively, these results suggest that the specific course context and environment are more critical than the instructional format (remote, hybrid, or in-person) in fostering a relationship between collaboration and performance. Furthermore, a supplementary investigation into the impact of missing nodes on calculated correlations revealed that such omissions tend to shift correlations toward zero. This finding supports the conclusion that the statistically significant correlations identified in this research are not spurious.

This paper investigates a specific class of quantum stochastic differential equations that model system-environment interactions under the quantum noise approximation. The framework utilizes symmetric Fock space over $L^2(\mathbb{R}_+)$ to represent quantum noise. By leveraging an isomorphism between this space and the space of square-integrable functionals of a Poisson process, the equations are recast as classical stochastic differential equations driven by Poisson processes. This approach yields a discontinuous dynamical state reduction, which is contrasted with the Ghirardi-Rimini-Weber model. The study identifies a purely quantum norm process that functions as an observer in the Everettian sense, encoding all events within the system space. Furthermore, an algorithm by Dalibard et al. for numerically solving quantum master equations is reinterpreted within the context of unravellings, enabling the calculation of trajectories for expected values of system observables.

Let $D$ denote a weighted oriented graph with underlying graph $G$, where $I(D)$ and $I(G)$ represent their respective edge ideals. We demonstrate that the regularity of the edge ideal for a specific class of weighted oriented graphs remains unchanged even after incorporating certain types of new edges. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the regularity of the edge ideal of a weighted oriented path or cycle and the regularity of its underlying graph, under the condition that vertices in $V^+$ act as sinks.

We introduce an infinite set of recursive equations designed to enumerate binary integer partitions under natural divisibility constraints, demonstrating that these counts are connected through partial sums. Furthermore, we analyze these partitions within the framework of graded polynomial rings and utilize this perspective to determine the free rank of specific homology modules in stable homotopy theory via the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra.

This study introduces a new closed-loop control framework designed for autonomous obstacle avoidance on curved roads. The framework offers two core capabilities: (i) collision-free trajectory planning via Model Predictive Control (MPC) and (ii) a torque vectoring controller for lateral and yaw stability, developed using optimal control principles. The paper evaluates trajectory planning strategies employing nominal, offset-free, and robust MPC, alongside the independent implementation of torque-vectoring control. Simulation outcomes validate the advantages of this hierarchical approach, including: (i) elimination of non-convex collision avoidance constraints, (ii) assurance of convexity during driving on curves, (iii) guaranteed trajectory feasibility during acceleration or deceleration while executing lateral maneuvers, and (iv) robustness against low-friction surfaces. Furthermore, to assess the control structure's performance in emergency and dynamic conditions, the framework was tested under varying curvature values and low-friction scenarios. Results indicate that the proposed collision avoidance system significantly enhances vehicle safety during emergency driving. To verify the effectiveness of this system, the study utilizes a high-fidelity co-simulation environment combining IPG CarMaker and Simulink.

De Haas-van Alphen (dHvA) oscillations represent fluctuations in magnetization relative to the inverse magnetic field. Traditionally viewed as a signature of the Fermi surface and thus exclusive to metals, these oscillations have recently been demonstrated both theoretically and experimentally to occur in specific insulators characterized by narrow gaps and inverted band structures. This study presents a perturbative theory, accurate to the leading order of interaction strength, to examine how many-body interactions influence these unconventional oscillations. Our findings reveal an anomalous interaction effect in insulators: unlike in metals, where interactions typically suppress the oscillation amplitude, they can enhance it. This enhancement persists at both zero and finite temperatures and becomes particularly significant when the gap parameter is comparable to the Landau level spacing.

We introduce a quantum framework for analyzing Jeans gravitational instability within the Newtonian limit of a gravity model featuring non-minimal matter-curvature coupling. Utilizing Wigner functions to represent quantum states in classical phase space, we develop a quantum kinetic approach that extends the classical method previously outlined by C. Gomes (Eur. Phys. J. C 80, 633 (2020)). This formulation enables an examination of how non-minimal coupling, quantum phenomena, and kinetic effects (specifically those arising from finite temperature) interact to influence the Jeans criterion. Furthermore, we analyze specific instances of the model, including general relativity, $f(R)$ theories, and pure non-minimal coupling, and compare these results against the observed stability of Bok globules.

This research investigates partial derivatives within the product of two metric measure spaces, specifically addressing the calculus via modules framework initiated by the first author. Our primary contributions include: 1) Generalizing Schwarz's theorem regarding the symmetry of mixed second derivatives to this non-smooth setting; and 2) Establishing a comprehensive set of equivalences linking the condition $f\in W^{2,2}(\X\times\Y)$ with the requirements that $f(\cdot,y)\in W^{2,2}(\X)$ and $f(x,\cdot)\in W^{2,2}(\Y)$ for almost every $y$ and $x$, respectively. In this context, $\X$ and $\Y$ are $\RCD$ spaces, ensuring that second-order Sobolev spaces are properly defined. These findings rely on an analysis of Sobolev regularity and the concept of differentials for maps taking values in a Hilbert module; we primarily apply this notion to the map $x\mapsto\d_\sy f(x,\cdot)$ to construct its differential, $\d_\sx\d_\sy f$, subject to suitable regularity conditions.

Data visualizations are now ubiquitous across all fields, serving as the main method for data analysis and insight communication. However, the heavy dependence on visual encoding creates significant accessibility barriers for individuals who are blind or have vision impairments, contributing to their underrepresentation in STEM disciplines. This study investigates the experiences of blind and visually impaired professionals within the geosciences regarding their access to data visualizations. Through in-depth, semi-structured interviews with seven professionals, the research examined accessibility challenges and opportunities for improvement using a socio-technical framework. Reflexive thematic analysis highlighted how visualizations negatively impacted career trajectories, the scarcity of tools for data exploration, difficulties in accessing peer work, and the disconnect between the pace of visualization development and accessibility research. The article also presents recommendations from participants aimed at addressing these specific barriers.

The widespread availability of large-scale annotated image datasets has enabled pre-trained models to achieve exceptional results in medical image classification. Nevertheless, developing robust classifiers for datasets characterized by data irregularity or class imbalance remains a significant challenge, particularly within medical imaging. This paper introduces a novel deep convolutional neural network named Self-Supervised Super Sample Decomposition for Transfer learning (4S-DT). By employing a generic self-supervised sample decomposition strategy, 4S-DT facilitates a coarse-to-fine transfer learning process from general image recognition tasks to specific chest X-ray classification. Our primary contribution lies in a new self-supervised mechanism driven by the super sample decomposition of unlabeled chest X-ray images. Furthermore, 4S-DT enhances the robustness of knowledge transfer through a downstream learning strategy that utilizes a class-decomposition layer to streamline the local data structure. This downstream class-decomposition mechanism allows the model to address various dataset irregularities by analyzing class boundaries. We validated this approach using 50,000 unlabeled chest X-ray images for coarse-to-fine transfer learning, specifically applying it to COVID-19 detection. On a large dataset, 4S-DT achieved a detection accuracy of 99.8% (95% CI: 99.44%, 99.98%), while on an extended test set enriched with augmented images from a small dataset, it reached 97.54% accuracy (95% CI: 96.22%, 98.91%), successfully identifying all real COVID-19 cases. This performance represents the highest accuracy recorded compared to other methods.

Preserving and regulating the quantum characteristics of an open quantum system throughout its evolution is critical for both foundational research and technological applications. This study evaluates the ability of a frequency-modulated qubit situated within a leaky cavity to enhance its dynamical quantum properties. In this setup, the qubit's transition frequency undergoes sinusoidal modulation driven by an external field. We demonstrate that an optimized quantum witness successfully detects the protection of quantum coherence afforded by this frequency modulation, whereas a conventional witness does not. Furthermore, we observe an acceleration in the qubit's evolution when the driving field's modulation parameters are appropriately tuned. Significantly, by proposing a new figure of merit, $R_g$, we reveal that the relationship between the Quantum Speed Limit Time (QSLT) and non-Markovianity varies according to the system's initial state, thereby extending earlier understandings of the link between these two dynamical attributes. Consequently, the frequency-modulated qubit model exhibits profound dynamical behaviors with promising applications in mitigating decoherence.

Chaotic microcavities have served as the fundamental arena for investigating quantum chaos. This study extends wave chaos theory to cavity lattice systems, revealing an intrinsic link between crystal momentum and internal cavity dynamics that replaces the function of deformed boundaries found in traditional microcavity problems. This discovery establishes a novel platform for the in-situ analysis of light dynamics within microcavities. In the perturbative regime, weak momentum coupling induces a dynamical localization transition, causing degenerate scar-mode pairs to hybridize and localize non-trivially around regular phase space islands. Conversely, when momentum coupling reaches its maximum at the Brillouin zone boundary, both inter-cavity chaotic mode coupling and wave confinement undergo significant changes. This work pioneers the exploration of intertwined quantum chaos in periodic systems and offers valuable applications for controlling light dynamics.

**Objective:** We created a domain decomposition-based hybrid volume surface integral equation (VSIE) approach designed to deliver rapid and precise magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) simulations that account for both local and remote conductive components. **Methods:** The conductive surfaces within MRI configurations were partitioned into two distinct domains, each optimized for specific electromagnetic (EM) modeling. Interactions between the human body and EM waves from local radiofrequency (RF) coils were handled using the precorrected fast Fourier transform, while engagements with remote conductive structures (such as the RF shield and scanner bore) were addressed via a new cross tensor train-based algorithm. We evaluated this hybrid-VSIE against other VSIE techniques using realistic MRI simulation environments. **Results:** The hybrid-VSIE emerged as the sole practical solution for simulations requiring 1 mm isotropic voxel resolution (VIR). At 2 mm VIR, our method achieved a speedup of at least 23 times and reduced memory requirements by a factor of 760 compared to conventional VSIE methods. **Conclusion:** Compared to traditional numerical EM simulation approaches, the hybrid-VSIE showed significant enhancements in convergence times across various realistic MRI scenarios. **Significance:** The computational efficiency of this novel hybrid-VSIE method holds the potential to facilitate rapid simulations of intricate and comprehensive MRI setups.

Simultaneous evolution of robotic controllers and morphologies often results in a "brain-body mismatch." To address this, we propose a lifetime learning framework within a modular robot system where offspring inherit parental bodies through recombination and mutation. Offspring brains are generated via two distinct approaches: pure evolution, where the brain is directly inherited, and a hybrid method combining inheritance with the RevDEknn learning algorithm. Experiments conducted in the Revolve simulator compare these methods using metrics for efficiency, efficacy, and morphological intelligence. The results indicate that the evolution-plus-learning approach yields superior fitness and promotes greater morphological evolution. This provides quantitative evidence that brain modifications can drive body changes, supporting the concept of morphological intelligence, which is measured by the learning delta—the capacity of a morphology to enhance learning.

This work explores recent efforts to link twistor theory with higher-spin theories and the IKKT matrix model. After briefly reviewing the higher-spin algebra $hs$ in four-dimensional spacetime, we demonstrate how higher-spin symmetry can be represented by $hs$-valued sections or holomorphic differential forms on (non-commutative) twistor space. This approach offers a streamlined method for deriving local higher-spin theories in spacetime from actions defined on (non-commutative) twistor space. Notably, certain higher-spin theories derived through this twistor framework exhibit non-trivial scattering amplitudes in flat space.

Radar Wind Profilers (RWP) are proven tools for studying the atmospheric boundary layer, offering significant benefits such as all-weather operation and long-range capabilities. However, a primary drawback is their relatively lengthy integration time when compared to instruments like lidars. This study demonstrates that for L-band RWPs, combining Autoregressive (AR) modeling of antenna signals with the Maximum Entropy Method (MEM) enables accurate estimation of radial wind velocity profiles even with very brief time samples. Performance was systematically evaluated using synthetic data, and these numerical findings were corroborated by experimental data collected near the runways of Paris Charles de Gaulle (CDG) Airport, France, and validated against a colocated optical lidar at the Payerne Aerological station in Switzerland. The results indicate that the AR-MEM approach yields reliable wind estimates with integration times as short as 2.5 seconds, a threshold where traditional spectral methods struggle to produce measurements. Furthermore, this technique reduces the impact of uncooperative flyers on atmospheric echo processing, thereby enhancing the overall success of the wind estimation algorithm.

The "old" conformal bootstrap, initially developed by Migdal and Polyakov (MP) as a self-consistent approach to determining conformal dimensions, is revisited in this study. We employ efficient multi-loop Feynman integral techniques to solve the associated equations, deriving solutions at first order in the skeleton expansion for finite coupling and integer spacetime dimensions. Particular attention is given to the $\phi^3$ theory in seven dimensions and the $O(N)$ vector models in three dimensions.
This paper challenges certain conjectures proposed by Marques and Lengyel regarding the $p$-adic valuations within the Tribonacci sequence.

This work investigates superintegrable classical Hamiltonian systems within two-dimensional Euclidean space $E_2$, focusing specifically on Hamiltonians that permit separation of variables in Cartesian coordinates, expressed as $V(x,y)=V_1(x)+V_2(y)$. The analysis is limited to cases where the Hamiltonian $\mathcal H$ possesses a polynomial integral of order $N>2$, considering exclusively doubly exotic potentials—those where neither separated component satisfies any linear ordinary differential equation. An enhanced method for determining these higher-order superintegrable systems is presented, relying on non-linear compatibility conditions and the algebra of integrals of motion as its fundamental components. The approach is fully demonstrated by solving the $N=5$ case, which marks the first appearance of doubly exotic confining potentials. Additionally, the general scenario for $N>2$ and the formulation of the inverse problem in superintegrability are briefly addressed.

The concept of partial PT-symmetry is explored within a standard Fock space framework, interpreted as a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS). This symmetry is also examined in the context of a non-Hermitian Bose-Hubbard Hamiltonian featuring two boson operators, along with its corresponding eigenstates. Additionally, the study addresses the occurrence of symmetry breaking.

Deep Neural Network (DNN) driven video analytics enables numerous computer vision applications to attain high recognition accuracy. To mitigate inference latency and bandwidth expenses, these DNN models are often deployed on edge nodes located near end users. Nevertheless, the constrained processing power of individual edge nodes can lead to significant delays when faced with overloaded inference requests. Although previous efforts have focused on optimizing configurations within a single edge node, we identify that collaborative work among multiple edge nodes can leverage idle resources to enhance total processing capacity and resource efficiency. Consequently, we introduce EdgeVision, a Multiagent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) framework designed for collaborative video analytics across distributed edges. This system allows edge nodes to jointly learn optimal strategies for video preprocessing, model selection, and request routing, aiming to minimize overall costs. We employ an actor-critic based MARL algorithm incorporating an attention mechanism to derive these optimal policies. Furthermore, we constructed a multi-edge-node testbed and utilized real-world datasets to assess the method's performance. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our approach improves overall rewards by 33.6% to 86.4% compared to the most competitive baseline methods.

This study introduces the Adaptive Decision Forest (ADF), an incremental machine learning framework designed to generate decision forests for classifying new records. Leveraging two novel theorems, we propose a new splitting strategy named iSAT, enabling ADF to classify records belonging to previously unseen classes. ADF effectively identifies and manages concept drift without discarding previously acquired knowledge. Additionally, the framework can process big data provided the information is partitioned into batches. We evaluated ADF across six datasets—five natural and one synthetic—and compared its performance against eight state-of-the-art methods. Statistical analyses using the sign test and Nemenyi test confirm that the proposed framework significantly outperforms existing techniques.

Over the past few years, hundreds of new YouTube channels have emerged, producing and distributing animation, superhero, and comic-themed videos aimed at children. Regrettably, a significant portion of this content contains disturbing, violent, or sexual material unsuitable for its intended audience. This study examines YouTube channels identified in prior research as posting either appropriate or disturbing content for kids. We observe a notable gap between YouTube's internal flagging of inappropriate channels and the reality of disturbing content that remains accessible on the platform. Specifically, nearly 60% of videos manually classified as disturbing in a 2019 study—originally bootstrapped using terms like "Elsa" and other child-related keywords—were still available as of mid-2021. Furthermore, 44% of the channels that uploaded such content had not yet been suspended or had their videos removed. For the first time, we also analyze the "madeForKids" feature, introduced by YouTube in late 2019, comparing its application on channels sharing disturbing versus suitable content. Our findings indicate that channels posting disturbing material are less likely to be marked as "madeForKids" than those sharing appropriate content. Additionally, these channels exploit various channel attributes, such as keywords, descriptions, topics, and posts, to attract young viewers, often employing game-related terminology. Finally, we utilize a set of channel and content features to train machine learning classifiers capable of predicting, at the time of channel creation, whether a channel will eventually host disturbing content. These classifiers could assist YouTube moderators in identifying potentially suspicious accounts without the need to review individual videos, thereby helping to mitigate such incidents.

The origin of radiation in Radio-Loud Narrow-Line Seyfert 1 (RL-NLS1) galaxies, spanning from X-ray to $\gamma$-ray energies, remains unresolved. Although the leptonic model is commonly used to fit the spectral energy distribution (SED), hadronic mechanisms might also contribute to the high-energy output of certain $\gamma$-ray loud NLS1s. We investigate the RL-NLS1 PKS 1502+036 by comparing its observed SED with theoretical predictions from both leptonic and lepto-hadronic frameworks. In our lepto-hadronic analysis, we consider proton synchrotron emission and proton-photon interactions (specifically Bethe-Heitler and photopion processes), accounting for pair production within the resulting electromagnetic cascade. Our findings indicate that the leptonic model successfully reproduces the SED, attributing X-ray to $\gamma$-ray emission to inverse Compton scattering. Conversely, while proton synchrotron radiation could theoretically account for the high-energy component, it requires extreme physical parameters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that $p\gamma$ interactions and the associated cascade processes fail to explain the observed SED. Consequently, our results suggest a leptonic origin for the multi-wavelength emission of PKS 1502+036.

We have conducted numerical investigations into the large-scale expansion of heavy ions within a cold background plasma. Our analysis identified two distinct collective behaviors arising from variations in the initial total mass of the traversing heavy ions, demonstrating that this mass difference alone can trigger entirely different plasma collective dynamics. Utilizing a hybrid simulation model—where ions are modeled as classical particles and electrons as a massless fluid—we observed that the imbalance between electric and magnetic forces acting on the heavy ions drives them to form divergent collective patterns over time. These patterns result in markedly different stopping behaviors for the moving ions and opposite drifting directions for the electron fluid at the plasma's expanding rim. Additional numerical and analytical calculations indicate that this force imbalance is influenced not only by the plasma ion number densities but also by spatial variations in the magnetic fields. Ultimately, our study reveals that the collective behavior of heavy ions is highly non-linear, with this non-linearity capable of inducing diverse phenomena during the system's large-scale evolution.

A universal register machine, a formal computational model, can be simulated within the Game of Life, a two-dimensional cellular automaton. This study conducts a spectral analysis on the dynamical evolution of the register machine operating on the Game of Life array. By partitioning the array into smaller sectors, we calculate the power spectrum based on the evolution within each region. These spectra fall into four distinct shape-based categories: null, white noise, sharp peaks, and power law. By encoding the spectral shape as a specific mark, we create a visualization of sector activity throughout the computation. For instance, this approach allows us to trace pulses moving between machine components and identify frequently updated registers. Ultimately, this method reveals the functional distinctions across different regions of the computational system.

We conducted a comprehensive morphological, kinematic, and chemical investigation of the disrupting cluster UBC 274 (age 2.5 Gyr, distance 1778 pc) to characterize its global properties. Utilizing Gaia EDR3 data, HDBSCAN was employed to generate an updated membership list extending up to 50 pc from the center and reaching a magnitude limit of $G=19$. High-resolution, high signal-to-noise spectra were analyzed to determine atmospheric parameters for six giant and subgiant stars, alongside individual abundances for 18 chemical species. The cluster exhibits a highly eccentric (0.93) component tilted approximately 10 degrees relative to the Galactic plane, a morphology consistent with test-particle simulations of a disrupting cluster. Chemical analysis reveals a subsolar metallicity of [Fe/H]$=-0.08\pm0.02$. The abundance pattern aligns with that of Ruprecht 147, which shares a similar age but is located nearer to the Sun, with the notable exception of neutron-capture elements, which show an overabundance of $[n\mathrm{/Fe]}\sim0.1$. The cluster's elongated shape corresponds to the inner section of its tidal tail, reflecting the anticipated dynamical disruption process. We identified significant mass segregation, with the most massive stars being 1.5 times more concentrated than the rest. The observed neutron-capture element overabundance may be attributed to the metallicity dependence of their yields, a phenomenon predicted by certain models due to their secondary nature. Furthermore, UBC 274 demonstrates high chemical homogeneity, with variations of only 0.03 dex within the sampled region of its tidal tails.

This article investigates non-radiative and radiative relaxation mechanisms within a hybrid system comprising Ag nanoparticles and CdTe quantum dots, utilizing transient transmission spectroscopy. Upon 400 nm excitation, the ultrafast transient transmission of the hybrid exhibits a rapid hot electron recovery on a picosecond scale, contrasted with a slower recovery over tens of picoseconds. Additionally, the presence of Ag nanoparticles enhances the contribution of CdTe quantum dots to the transient transmission, yet it simultaneously quenches the radiative relaxation of these dots. These findings offer crucial insights into the relaxation processes governing charge transport and photoluminescence quenching in metal-semiconductor hybrids.

In an era where reliance on Deep Learning (DL) models is growing, ensuring their security has become paramount. This study investigates security vulnerabilities within DL systems and utilizes experimental analysis to determine strategies for constructing more resilient architectures. Through experiments designed to evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of a novel method for enhancing robustness against adversarial attacks, the research demonstrates significant improvements. These findings offer fresh insights and actionable recommendations for both researchers and practitioners aiming to develop superior DL algorithms.

Accurately correcting for dust reddening is essential for determining the true physical properties of celestial objects. While the Schlegel et al. (SFD) and Planck 2D extinction maps are commonly employed for this purpose, this study utilizes precise reddening measurements from approximately two million stars in the Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope (LAMOST) Data Release 5 (DR5) and Gaia DR2 to evaluate and calibrate the SFD and Planck maps across middle and high Galactic latitudes. Our analysis reveals that all four maps achieve comparable precision in reddening correction but exhibit small, yet significant, spatially varying biases. These biases align between the SFD and Planck2014-R maps, as well as between the Planck2014-Tau and Planck2019-Tau maps. Specifically, biases in the SFD and Planck2014-R maps correlate strongly with dust temperature and extinction, whereas those in the Planck2014-Tau and Planck2019-Tau maps show a weak temperature dependence but a strong reliance on the dust spectral index. We provide corrections for the SFD and Planck extinction maps within the LAMOST footprint, alongside empirical relations applicable beyond it. These findings offer critical insights for refining all-sky Galactic extinction maps and establish a robust foundation for achieving high-precision extinction corrections in modern astronomy.

Regular nested word languages, also known as visibly pushdown languages, properly extend regular word languages while maintaining their essential closure and decidability characteristics. Earlier research demonstrated that moving to 2-nested words—words augmented with two matchings, or 2-visibly pushdown languages—yields limited success because the associated automata model fails to be closed under determinization. Drawing inspiration from homomorphic representations of indexed languages, this study defines a specific subset of 2-nested words termed "2-wave words." This new class strictly encompasses the class of nested words and retains its primary properties. Specifically, we establish that the corresponding automaton model is closed under determinization, offer a logical characterization of the recognized languages, and demonstrate that the associated graphs possess bounded treewidth. These findings lead to significant closure and decidability results. Finally, we prove that the word projections of these languages fall within the class of linear indexed languages.

We consider the proton's mass as its total static energy, which is partitioned into distinct contributions from quarks and gluons. By employing the core principles of the hadron bag model, we investigate the proton's structure and determine that the computed values for temperature, radius, and the bag constant align closely with QCD predictions, provided the proton is treated as a thermal equilibrium system of quarks and gluons.

We introduce an unsupervised learning approach designed to separate speech into distinct content and speaker identity representations. To validate the efficacy of this disentanglement, we apply the method to the demanding one-shot cross-lingual voice conversion task. Drawing inspiration from $\beta$-VAE, we develop a learning objective that equilibrates the information retained by the content and speaker encodings. Furthermore, inductive biases inherent in our architectural design and training dataset reinforce this desired separation. Comprehensive evaluations, both objective and subjective, confirm the proposed method's success in achieving speech disentanglement and performing one-shot cross-lingual voice conversion.

This study examines the gravity- and surface-tension-driven one-phase Muskat problem within an unstable regime where fluid overlays a dry area. Employing a new method based on depth-averaged formulations, we establish two asymptotic approximations for this scenario. The lower-order model corresponds to the classical thin film equation, whereas the higher-order model yields a novel, refined thin film equation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that both models achieve the optimal order of convergence with respect to the shallowness parameter when matched against original Muskat solutions, even under low-regular initial data conditions.

Optimization methods are crucial across various scientific and practical domains, generating significant interest within the research community. This demand has led to the emergence of numerous open-source libraries, which in turn accelerate the development of novel techniques and applications. This paper introduces LibOPT, a new library designed for the rapid prototyping and implementation of nature-inspired optimization strategies. Currently, LibOPT incorporates 15 optimization techniques and 112 benchmark functions, while also supporting 11 hypercomplex-based approaches, distinguishing it as one of the first libraries to offer such capabilities. The work demonstrates how users can readily utilize and extend LibOPT within the C programming paradigm, providing examples that include source code utilizing benchmark functions.

Transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) exhibit charge carriers endowed with spin, pseudospin, and valley degrees of freedom linked to magnetic moments. Specifically, monolayer and bilayer configurations of TMDCs, such as MoS$_2$, induce robust couplings between spin and pseudospin phenomena, a characteristic that has heightened interest in their application for advanced technological devices. Concurrently, high-order harmonic generation (HHG) has emerged as a powerful tool for probing the electronic structure of solids, including energy dispersion, Berry curvature, and topological attributes. In this work, we present theoretical findings based on employing HHG to examine how the structural variations of monolayer and bilayer MoS$_2$ influence nonlinear optical emission. Utilizing a simplified model of MoS$_2$ with 3R AB stacking, we demonstrate that the pseudospin and valley indices—manifested through Berry curvature and dipole transition matrix elements—can be encoded within high-energy photon emissions when the material is driven by circularly polarized lasers (CPL). This theoretical study is anticipated to facilitate the ultrafast control of valleytronics and raise new inquiries regarding spin-orbit coupling (SOC) effects in TMDCs, Weyl semimetals, and the topological phases and transitions found in topological insulators.

We investigate the challenge of synchronizing lip movements in video with the accompanying audio stream. Our approach identifies an optimal alignment through a dual-domain recurrent neural network trained on synthetic data created by dropping and duplicating video frames. After determining the alignment, we adjust the video to synchronize the two sources. Our method significantly outperforms existing literature techniques across various established and new benchmarks. As a practical application, we demonstrate the robust alignment of text-to-speech generated audio with pre-existing video streams. Our code and samples are accessible at https://github.com/itsyoavshalev/End-to-End-Lip-Synchronization-with-a-Temporal-AutoEncoder.

Two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides (2D-TMDs), known for their stable and chiral excitons, show significant potential in nanophotonics due to their unique optical characteristics. While chemical vapor deposition (CVD) enables the fabrication of nanostructures with varied geometries, understanding the optical behavior of more complex shapes remains limited. Researchers have successfully synthesized WS2 nanostructures spanning from monolayers to hollow pyramids. Notably, these hollow pyramids display significantly diminished photoluminescence compared to standard layered tungsten disulfide, allowing for a more detailed analysis of their distinct Raman signals. When excited resonantly, they reveal numerous higher-order phononic resonances. Unlike monolayers, the optical response of these pyramids varies based on position; differences in peak intensity, ratios, and spectral positions indicate local variations in atomic arrangement across the crater and sides. This position-dependent optical behavior is linked to the nanogeometry induced during growth, marking initial progress toward developing tunable nanophotonic devices applicable in opto-electronics and non-linear optics.

Using the 13.7 m telescope at the Purple Mountain Observatory, we conducted an unbiased survey of CO (J=1-0) emission across the Galactic plane, spanning longitudes from l=34.75° to 45.25° and latitudes from b=-5.25° to 5.25°. This extensive 100 square degree region was sampled every 30 arcseconds with a velocity resolution of approximately 0.2 km/s, focusing on velocities between -60 km/s and -10 km/s. Analysis of the 12CO data identified over 500 molecular clouds (MCs), with 131 of these also showing 13CO emission. These distant MCs, located beyond the solar circle and primarily within the Galactic plane, reveal the large-scale molecular gas structure across a 10-degree azimuthal range. We propose that this segment corresponds to the Outer Arm. The physical mid-plane of the Outer Arm appears slightly offset from the IAU-defined plane on large scales, likely due to the warping of the disk at Galactocentric distances greater than ~10 kpc and the apparent tilt caused by the Sun's vertical height relative to the disk within the solar circle. Assuming the inner Galaxy is flat, we calculate an upper limit for the Sun's offset from the Milky Way's physical mid-plane of approximately 17.1 pc. Furthermore, we examine correlations among the physical parameters of these distant MCs, finding results consistent with previous studies.

Searching for dark matter axions using haloscopes critically depends on precise tuning, especially given the axion's unknown mass to the scientific community. Currently, most haloscope tuning mechanisms rely on mechanical devices, which are prone to failure due to the harsh operational environments. In contrast, electronic tuning utilizing ferroelectric materials offers a more robust alternative less susceptible to mechanical breakdowns, thereby enhancing and expanding existing systems. This study introduces and designs a novel approach employing Potassium Tantalate ($KTaO_3$ or KTO) as a tuning element within haloscopes based on coupled microwave cavities. Specifically, we adapt the structures from the Relic Axion Detector Exploratory Setup (RADES) group, which utilize metallic irises to couple multiple cavities. We demonstrate how $KTaO_3$ films can replace traditional inductive or capacitive metallic windows to serve as these interresonator couplings. These innovations represent a significant upgrade over current dark matter axion systems, achieving a tuning range of $2.23\%$, a substantial improvement compared to previous achievements of less than $0.1\%$ for similar tuning classes. The theoretical and simulated results presented here highlight the potential of integrating ferroelectric media into multicavity resonant haloscopes for axion detection.

The exceptional characteristics of borophene, such as mechanical flexibility, polymorphism, and opto-electrical anisotropy, have sparked significant research interest. Recently, a new semi-hydrogenated borophene variant, designated $\alpha'$-4H, was synthesized as large-scale, freestanding samples, demonstrating remarkable air stability and semiconducting behavior. In this study, we employ density functional theory (DFT) and many-body perturbation theory (MBPT) to analyze the electronic and excitonic optical properties of $\alpha'$-4H. DFT calculations indicate that hydrogenation disrupts the mirror symmetry and increases the buckling height of pure $\alpha'$-borophene, leading to orbital hybridization and the opening of an indirect band gap of 1.49 eV. When corrected using G0W0, GW0, and GW levels of theory, this band gap value adjusts to 1.98, 2.23, and 2.52 eV, respectively. Solving the Bethe-Salpeter equation yields an optical band gap of 2.40 eV, corresponding to a highly stable, strongly bound bright exciton with a binding energy of 1.18 eV. Notably, these excitonic states remain robust under tension up to 10%, maintaining dynamic stability in the monolayer. Additionally, we investigated bilayer $\alpha'$-4H structures with various stacking configurations; due to weak van der Waals interactions between layers, the bilayer retains most of the monolayer's structural and electronic attributes. This work elucidates the fundamental physics governing the structural, electronic, and optical features of $\alpha'$-4H borophene, positioning it as a highly promising candidate for flexible optoelectronic applications.

This study introduces a mixed-N-spin chain featuring an Ising-XY model, specifically focusing on a (1/2, 1, 1/2) three-spin cell. In this configuration, the (1, 1/2) spin pair interacts via an Ising-type force, while the (1/2, 1/2) pair exhibits combined XY-type and Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interactions. The system, maintained in thermal equilibrium under a uniform external magnetic field $B$, includes single-ion anisotropy (coefficient $\zeta$) for the integer-spin component. We analyze the quantum entanglement between the half-spins using concurrence, alongside classical correlations (CC), examining how temperature, magnetic field, and DM interactions influence these metrics. Furthermore, the impact of single-ion anisotropy on half-spin correlations is confirmed. Drawing on the tripartite spin model framework proposed by Rossini, Giovannetti, and Fazio as an ideal quantum channel, we theoretically calculate the information transmission rate. Our results highlight distinct behavioral differences between this proposed model and earlier simple chains lacking integer spins and DM interactions, specifically regarding information transfer protocols.

Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) stands as a pivotal 3D imaging technology, offering micron-level depth resolution for biological imaging. This precision far exceeds the typical millimeter-scale limits of Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR), which are constrained by the impulse response of detection electronics. However, OCT's reliance on coherence renders it impractical for LiDAR applications, where mechanical motion often disrupts coherence. We introduce a quantum interference-based method for LiDAR that attains OCT-like depth resolution without demanding high stability. Our demonstration achieves an effective impulse response of 70 μm, enabling the discernment of ranging and multiple reflections with significantly higher resolution than conventional LiDAR. This improved resolution facilitates applications such as 3D facial recognition, detection and tracking of small features, and enhances complex time-of-flight techniques, including imaging through obscurants and non-line-of-sight imaging.

Sparse Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) represent a robust approach for structured prediction in computer vision and natural language processing, yet solving them at scale remains difficult. This paper introduces a new safe dynamic screening technique that utilizes precise dual optimum estimation to detect and eliminate irrelevant features throughout training. Consequently, the problem size shrinks continuously, yielding substantial computational savings without compromising the accuracy of the final model. To our knowledge, this is the inaugural screening method to apply dual optimum estimation—leveraging the strong convexity and intricate structure of the dual problem—to dynamic screening, thereby merging the benefits of both static and dynamic approaches while mitigating their respective limitations. Our estimation surpasses those relying on the duality gap in accuracy, resulting in a more potent screening rule. Furthermore, this work marks the first application of screening methods in sparse CRFs and broader structure prediction models. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets confirm that our method achieves significant speedups.

The concept of matching Rota-Baxter algebras was recently proposed by Gao, Guo, and Zhang in their 2020 work in the *Journal of Algebra* (552, 134-170), driven by the investigation into the algebraic renormalization of regularity structures. This framework extends the understanding of multiple integral operators featuring kernels. The same authors previously established matching dendriform algebras as the foundational structure for matching Rota-Baxter algebras. In this paper, we present matching relative Rota-Baxter algebras, which likewise relate to matching dendriform algebras. We formulate a matching associative Yang-Baxter equation, where its solutions generate matching relative Rota-Baxter algebras. Furthermore, we define the cohomology of a matching relative Rota-Baxter algebra, deriving it from classical Hochschild cohomology alongside a novel cohomology arising from matching operators. As an application, we demonstrate that this cohomology controls the formal deformation theory of these algebras. Finally, utilizing multiplicative nonsymmetric operads, we define the cohomology for matching dendriform algebras and establish a morphism from the cohomology of a matching relative Rota-Baxter algebra to that of its induced matching dendriform algebra. The paper concludes with an examination of homotopy matching dendriform algebras.

Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) solvers have proven effective in addressing numerous formal verification challenges, including bounded model checking (BMC) across diverse systems ranging from integrated circuits to cyber-physical systems. Conventionally, BMC involves verifying the satisfiability of a potentially lengthy quantifier-free formula. Alternatively, BMC issues can be naturally formulated as quantified formulas regarding the number of checking steps. This paper explores an approach that leverages decision procedures capable of handling quantifiers to validate these quantified formulas. While this method has previously been utilized for purely discrete systems via Quantified Boolean Formula (QBF) encodings solved by QBF solvers, we introduce a novel quantified encoding of BMC specifically for rectangular hybrid automata (RHA). Due to the modeling of continuous states through real-valued variables and dense time, this encoding necessitates the use of more general logics. We implemented a preliminary prototype using the HyST model transformation tool to generate quantified BMC (QBMC) queries for the Z3 SMT solver. Our experimental results, evaluated on timed and hybrid automata benchmarks such as the Fischer and Lynch-Shavit mutual exclusion algorithms, are presented alongside a comparison with quantifier-free BMC methods like dReach (utilizing dReal) and HyComp (based on nuXmv and MathSAT). Given these encouraging outcomes, QBMC holds potential as a scalable and effective analysis technique for RHAs and other hybrid automata, contingent upon future advancements in quantifier handling within SMT solvers like Z3.

In contrast to standard linear regression, which focuses solely on the relationship between covariates and the expected value of the conditional response, quantile regression models the entire conditional response distribution. Although established methods exist for continuous variables and certain discrete data types, there remains a lack of widely accepted approaches for ordinal variables, which are crucial in many medical applications. This paper reviews two current ordinal quantile regression techniques and highlights their limitations. We then introduce a novel method called Bayesian ordinal quantile regression with a partially collapsed Gibbs sampler (BORPS). Simulation studies demonstrate that BORPS outperforms existing methods. Furthermore, we apply BORPS to data from the Fragile Families and Child Wellbeing Study to disentangle associations with early puberty in both genders. The software is accessible at: GitHub.com/igrabski/borps.

By applying the $H^\infty$-functional calculus to quaternionic operators, this work demonstrates the generation of fractional powers for specific densely defined differential quaternionic operators of order $m\geq 1$, which act on the right linear quaternionic Hilbert space $L^2(\Omega,\mathbb C\otimes\mathbb H)$. The operators under consideration take the form $$ T=i^{m-1}\left(a_1(x) e_1\partial_{x_1}^{m}+a_2(x) e_2\partial_{x_2}^{m}+a_3(x) e_3\partial_{x_3}^{m}\right), \ \ \ x=(x_1,\, x_2,\, x_3)\in \overline{\Omega}, $$ where $\overline{\Omega}$ represents the closure of a bounded domain $\Omega$ with a $C^1$ boundary, or an unbounded domain in $\mathbb R^3$ with a sufficiently regular boundary satisfying property $(R)$. Here, $\{e_1,\, e_2,\, e_3\}$ denotes an orthonormal basis for the imaginary units of $\mathbb H$, and $a_1,\,a_2,\, a_3: \overline{\Omega} \subset\mathbb{R}^3\to \mathbb{R}$ are the real-valued coefficients of $T$. Specifically, sufficient conditions on these coefficients are established to ensure the generation of the fractional powers of $T$, denoted as $P_{\alpha}(T)$ for $\alpha\in(0,1)$, even when the components of $T$, defined as $T_l:=a_l\partial_{x_l}^m$, do not commute.

We investigate a cosmological model where the expansion of the Universe cycles through repeating $\Lambda$CDM phases, interspersed with inflationary and radiation-dominated epochs. This periodic $\Lambda$CDM cosmology arises from the hypothesis that both current accelerated expansion and primordial inflation stem from the same dark energy source. In a phase space plotting the matter density parameter $\Omega_m$ against the radiation density parameter $\Omega_r$, the trajectory $\Omega_m(\Omega_r)$ forms a closed loop, suggesting a perpetual cycle where the cessation of acceleration in one $\Lambda$CDM phase triggers the onset of a new inflationary phase. This scenario necessitates an interaction between matter and/or radiation and dark energy. We analyze the simplest iteration of this model, featuring vacuum energy coupled to radiation. From the matter-dominated era up to the present, the model mimics standard $\Lambda$CDM behavior, followed by an inflationary period. However, a rapid and sudden decay of dark energy into radiation periodically halts accelerated expansion, resulting in a radiation-dominated epoch before a fresh $\Lambda$CDM expansion begins. Constraints derived from Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations utilizing supernova, Hubble, BAO, and CMB data indicate that this model fits observational evidence as effectively as the standard $\Lambda$CDM paradigm.

This work investigates a broad extension of Markov numbers, inspired by a particular generalized cluster algebra derived from a Chekhov-Shapiro orbifold. We provide a clear algorithm for calculating these generalized Markov numbers and highlight multiple patterns that mirror those found in standard Markov numbers. Furthermore, we derive formulas connected to continued fractions and snake graphs.
We investigate a specific class of almost-coupling Poisson and Dirac structures on a foliated manifold under a compact Lie group $G$ action, utilizing deformation theory and averaging techniques.

Stability, safety, and reachability represent fundamental attributes of dynamical systems. Although abstraction-based formal methods can effectively manage reach-avoid-stay objectives through verification and control synthesis, these techniques often incur high computational costs due to state-space discretization. Conversely, Lyapunov methods characterize safety and stability qualitatively without requiring discretization. Recent advancements in converse Lyapunov-barrier theorems have further shown approximate completeness for verifying reach-avoid-stay specifications in systems governed by nonlinear differential equations. This paper extends the Lyapunov-barrier characterization to broader classes of hybrid systems defined by differential and difference inclusions, utilizing the topology of hybrid arcs. We demonstrate that Lyapunov-barrier functions serve as both sufficient conditions for guaranteeing reach-avoid-stay specifications in well-posed hybrid systems and as necessary conditions for systems subjected to arbitrarily small perturbations, provided mild constraints are met. Numerical examples are included to validate these primary findings.

We introduce a unified methodology for estimating the largest and smallest singular values of inhomogeneous random rectangular matrices, utilizing the non-backtracking operator and the Ihara-Bass formula applicable to general Hermitian matrices with a bipartite block structure. Our primary contributions are probabilistic upper and lower bounds for the extreme singular values of large rectangular random matrices $X$, expressed through the maximal and minimal $\ell_2$-norms of the rows and columns of $X$'s variance profile. These proofs rely on establishing probabilistic upper bounds for the spectral radius of an associated non-backtracking matrix $B$. The resulting two-sided bounds are applicable to the centered adjacency matrices of sparse inhomogeneous Erd\H{o}s-R\'{e}nyi bipartite graphs across a broad spectrum of sparsity levels. Specifically, for Erd\H{o}s-R\'{e}nyi bipartite graphs $\mathcal{G}(n,m,p)$ where $p=\omega(\log n)/n$ and $m/n\to y \in (0,1)$, our sharp bounds demonstrate that no outliers exist outside the support of the Mar\v{c}enko-Pastur law almost surely. This finding generalizes the Bai-Yin theorem to the context of sparse rectangular random matrices.

This study presents the first direct search for dark matter utilizing Gaia observations, which may harbor signals from mirror stars—exotic compact objects composed of atomic dark matter with minimal kinetic mixing between the dark and standard model photons. These mirror stars accumulate small quantities of interstellar matter within their cores, producing distinctive optical/IR and X-ray emissions. We establish a comprehensive pipeline for identifying mirror stars using Gaia data alongside other stellar catalogs and apply this methodology to search for toy mirror stars, employing simplified calculations of their optical/IR emissions across a broad spectrum of hidden sector and mirror star parameters. Furthermore, we derive projected exclusion limits on the abundance and characteristics of mirror stars should no candidates be detected, illustrating Gaia's potential as a novel and uniquely potent tool for probing atomic dark matter. Our research offers a foundational framework for future realistic searches that will incorporate a more rigorous treatment of captured interstellar gas.

This study examines the Cauchy problem for the Hunter-Saxton equation on the real line. Initially, we prove local well-posedness for the integral formulation of the equation by developing specialized spaces, $E^s_{p,r}$, that combine Lebesgue and homogeneous Besov spaces. Subsequently, we demonstrate global existence and derive a sufficient condition for the finite-time blow-up of strong solutions. Finally, we address the ill-posedness and unique continuation properties of the Hunter-Saxton equation.

This study reports measurements of exclusive and semi-exclusive charged pion pair ($\pi^+\pi^-$) production in proton-proton collisions, where the central rapidity region is probed and the scattered protons remain intact or diffractively dissociate without detection. Conducted with the CMS detector at the LHC, the analysis utilizes a dataset with an integrated luminosity of 450 inverse microbarns collected at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV. For single-pion transverse momentum $p_t > 0.2$ GeV and absolute rapidity $|y| < 2$, the measured dipion cross section is $26.5 \pm 0.3 \text{ (stat)} \pm 5.0 \text{ (syst)} \pm 1.1 \text{ (lumi)}$ microbarns. Differential cross sections as functions of the pion pair's invariant mass, $p_t$, and rapidity, as well as the single-pion $p_t$, are evaluated against phenomenological models.

We report the first lattice QCD calculation of unpolarized proton isovector transverse-momentum-dependent parton distribution functions (TMDPDFs), which are crucial for predicting multi-scale semi-inclusive observables within the Standard Model. Utilizing an $N_f=2+1+1$ MILC ensemble featuring valence clover fermions on a highly improved staggered quark (HISQ) sea, we computed quark momentum distributions for protons with large momenta. Our approach employs state-of-the-art methods for renormalization and extrapolation regarding correlation distance. We incorporated one-loop contributions from the perturbative matching kernel to light-cone TMDPDFs and investigated dependencies on pion mass and hadron momentum. Our findings show qualitative agreement with phenomenological TMDPDFs, offering a pathway to predict high-energy scattering events from first principles.

This study expands upon our prior discrete-to-continuum methodology to formulate a continuum variational model for a hexagonal twisted bilayer material with a fixed layer. The discrete energy framework incorporates elastic components alongside a weak interaction term, compatible with either Lennard-Jones or Kolmogorov-Crespi potentials. To verify the model, we conducted numerical simulations comparing the proposed continuum approach against the original discrete formulation; these results align well with experimental data, such as that observed in twisted bilayer graphene.

Executing algorithms is a core challenge that has been extensively researched. Previous studies~\cite{veli19neural} demonstrate that achieving systematic generalization in graph algorithms requires access to intermediate program steps. However, in many reasoning tasks involving algorithmic logic, only input-output pairs are available. Drawing inspiration from successful pre-training methods in Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Computer Vision, this work explores transferring algorithmic reasoning capabilities. Specifically, we examine how knowledge from algorithms with known execution traces can be applied to solve similar tasks lacking such traces. Our investigation covers two primary categories of graph algorithms: parallel methods like Breadth-First Search and Bellman-Ford, and sequential greedy approaches like Prim's and Dijkstra's algorithms. Given the fundamental distinctions between algorithmic reasoning and feature extractors used in NLP or Computer Vision, we hypothesize that standard transfer learning techniques are insufficient for systematic generalization. To test this empirically, we constructed a dataset comprising nine algorithms across three graph types. Our experiments confirm that multi-task learning, rather than standard transfer methods, effectively facilitates the transfer of algorithmic reasoning knowledge.

This study examines a class of "box-like" statistically self-affine functions, calculating the almost-sure box-counting dimension of their graphs. Additionally, we investigate the differentiability of these functions, demonstrating that, based on a specific computable functional of the model, they are almost surely either differentiable almost everywhere or non-differentiable almost everywhere.

Using a newly developed high-temperature probe featuring mechanical pin connectors rather than conductive paste, we investigated the resistivity of single-crystalline Nd2Fe14B as a function of temperature. Warming and cooling cycles consistently yielded a Curie temperature near Tc = 580 K. Notably, anomalous discrete jumps appeared exclusively in cooling curves within the 400–500 K range, absent during warming. Interestingly, these jumps coincided with an increase in resistivity. This behavior is attributed to the temperature-dependent striction effect caused by magnetic domain re-orientation occurring well below the Curie temperature.

Rather than employing synthetic translations primarily for data augmentation across various NLP tasks, this study investigates their utility in refining imperfect reference translations within mined bitexts. Our findings indicate that synthetic samples can enhance bitext quality without requiring additional bilingual supervision when they substitute original entries based on a semantic equivalence classifier designed to reduce NMT noise. This improvement in bitext quality is validated both intrinsically through human evaluation and extrinsically via bilingual induction and machine translation tasks.

The muon anomalous magnetic moment remains a focal point of research because of the potential discrepancy between experimental measurements and Standard Model predictions. To decrease uncertainties regarding the hadronic light-by-light contribution, we establish short-distance constraints within the Melnikov-Vainshtein regime, facilitating data-driven analyses. In this kinematic domain, two of the four electromagnetic currents in the four-point function defining the hadronic light-by-light tensor are nearly coincident. We achieve these constraints by constructing a systematic operator product expansion of the relevant tensor up to next-to-leading order in the operator expansion. Furthermore, we calculate the leading $\alpha_s$ contributions and derive constraints for the next-to-leading operators that remain valid nonperturbatively.

We introduce a straightforward framework where dark matter (DM) arises as a stable, neutral hadronic relic from thermal freeze-out, with its stability guaranteed by an exact $\operatorname{U}(1)_D$ symmetry. In this model, neutrinos acquire radiatively induced Majorana masses through the exchange of colored DM particles. Both the dark matter and neutrino mass share a common origin, resulting in a predicted lower bound for neutrinoless double beta decay. Future hadron collider experiments and lepton flavor violation searches may detect additional phenomenological signals, while direct detection experiments utilizing nuclear recoil measurements will provide crucial tests of this proposal.

This study presents a search for narrow resonances decaying into bottom quark-antiquark pairs, utilizing a dataset from proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} =$ 8 TeV with an integrated luminosity of 19.7 fb$^{-1}$. By employing triggers that identify jets from bottom quarks, the search extends to lower masses than typical LHC resonance searches into jet pairs. No significant excess over background predictions was observed. Consequently, constraints were established on the product of cross section and branching fraction for spin 0, 1, and 2 resonances within the 325-1200 GeV mass range. These findings substantially enhance the existing limits for resonances decaying into jet pairs in the 325-500 GeV region.

Machine learning has been extensively utilized to classify topological phases, with various data formats proposed to maximize information extraction from target systems. Given the inherent complexity of quantum physics, sophisticated mathematical frameworks are essential for designing these models. This study integrates quaternion algebras into both supervised and unsupervised learning frameworks to classify two-dimensional Chern insulators. In the unsupervised approach, we apply Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to quaternion-transformed eigenstates to differentiate topological phases. For supervised learning, we enhance a standard convolutional neural network by incorporating a single quaternion convolutional layer. This model accepts quaternion-transformed configurations as input and successfully distinguishes all distinct topological phases, including those not encountered during training. Our findings highlight the efficacy of quaternion algebras in extracting critical features from data and demonstrate the superiority of quaternion-based neural networks over conventional ones for topological phase classification tasks.

This note provides a quantitative analysis of publication length trends in ACM CSCW between 2000 and 2018, specifically highlighting key shifts in editorial and review policies. The central theme is the ascent and subsequent decline of the 4-page note, a distinct submission category introduced in 2004 alongside the standard 10-page double-column full paper. Between 2004 and 2012, these 2,500 to 4,500-word notes consistently accounted for 20% to 35% of all publications. However, in 2013, official page limits were abolished, and no formal distinction remained between full papers and notes. Consequently, the note genre vanished entirely, paralleling a trend toward steadily increasing paper lengths. These findings are examined in relation to local CSCW concerns as well as broader theoretical debates regarding genre theory, and how socio-technical structures and affordances influence participation in distributed, computer-mediated organizations and user-generated content platforms. While numerous potential explanations exist for the note's disappearance and the rise of longer papers, identifying these remains a topic for future research. The discussion concludes by exploring the implications for the CSCW community, particularly regarding how genre norms affect which types of scholarship and scholars flourish, and whether new top-down regulations or bottom-up guidelines should be established concerning paper length and contribution types.

We report the identification of ATLAS18mlw as a tidal disruption event (TDE) located in the galaxy WISEA J073544.83+663717.3, situated 334 Mpc away. First detected by the Asteroid Terrestrial Impact Last Alert System (ATLAS) on March 17.3, 2018, its nature as a TDE was only recently confirmed through the re-analysis of a SuperNova Integral Field Spectrograph (SNIFS) spectrum. Obtained by the Spectral Classification of Astronomical Transients (SCAT) survey, this spectrum reveals a prominent blue continuum alongside a broad H$\alpha$ emission line. In this work, we analyze approximately six years of optical photometry starting prior to the event to limit AGN activity, present optical spectroscopy of the transient, and examine host galaxy properties using archival data and a host spectrum. ATLAS18mlw appeared in ground-based light curves for about two months. By fitting a blackbody model to the transient spectrum and applying a bolometric correction to the optical light curve, we determine that ATLAS18mlw is likely a low-luminosity TDE with a peak luminosity of log(L [erg s$^{-1}$]) = $43.5 \pm 0.2$. The TDE classification is reinforced by the quiescent, Balmer-strong nature of the host galaxy. Additionally, we calculated the decline rate from the bolometric light curve, finding $\Delta L_{40} = -0.7 \pm 0.2$ dex, which places ATLAS18mlw among the increasing group of "faint and fast" TDEs characterized by low peak luminosities and rapid declines.

Ultra-Wideband (UWB) is a pivotal technology enabling the Internet of Things (IoT) to achieve precise, energy-efficient, and dependable monitoring, screening, and localization within indoor spaces. However, the accuracy of UWB-based localization systems often deteriorates due to Non-Line-of-Sight (NLoS) links between mobile users and UWB beacons. To counteract the adverse impacts of NLoS connections, we developed a Reinforcement Learning (RL) anchor selection framework designed to handle the dynamic characteristics of indoor settings. Nevertheless, current RL models in this domain struggle to generalize effectively to new environments and require extensive time to converge on an optimal policy. Addressing these issues, we introduce the Jump-start RL-based UWB NOde selection (JUNO) framework, which enables real-time location estimation without depending on intricate NLoS identification or mitigation techniques. We assessed the JUNO framework's performance based on location error, simulating a mobile user traversing an ultra-dense indoor environment with a high probability of NLoS occurrences. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

Despite the non-detection of genuine metal-free "Population III" stars, their characteristics and those of their supernovae are inferred from the chemical signatures imprinted on subsequent stellar generations. This study presents the identification of AS0039, an ultra-metal-poor star located in the Sculptor dwarf spheroidal galaxy. With an iron abundance of [Fe/H]$_{\rm LTE}=-4.11$, AS0039 holds the record for the most metal-deficient star found in an external galaxy to date. Unlike most Milky Way stars at this metallicity level, AS0039 shows no carbon enhancement; instead, it exhibits [C/Fe]$_{\rm LTE}=-0.75$ and A(C)=+3.60, representing the lowest carbon abundance ever recorded in a star. Furthermore, the star displays a lack of $\alpha$-element uniformity, characterized by exceptionally low values of [Mg/Ca]$_{\rm NLTE}=-0.60$ and [Mg/Ti]$_{\rm NLTE}=-0.86$, which stands in sharp contrast to the near-solar ratios typical of carbon-normal stars in the Milky Way halo. This distinctive abundance pattern suggests that AS0039 originated from material enriched primarily by a $\sim$20 $M_\odot$ progenitor star that underwent an unusually energetic explosion ($E=10\times10^{51}$ erg). Consequently, AS0039 constitutes some of the earliest observational evidence for zero-metallicity hypernovae and offers a rare chance to explore the varied nature of Population III stars.

This research investigates proton-induced knockout reactions using a theoretical approach that integrates {\it ab initio} Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) wave functions with the Faddeev/Alt-Grassberger-Sandhas few-body formalism. Newly developed QMC wave functions for $^{12}$C produce, for the first time, outcomes consistent with experimental rms radii, electron scattering measurements, and (p,2p) total cross-section data. For nuclei with $\mathrm{A}\leq 12$ and $(N-Z) \leq 3$, our findings indicate that the theoretical ratios of (i) {\it ab initio} to Mean Field Approximation cross sections ($\mathcal{R}_\sigma$) and (ii) the corresponding spectroscopic factors ($\mathcal{R}_\Sigma$), summed over states below the particle emission threshold, exhibit only a moderate dependence on the nucleon separation energy ($S_{\rm N}$). These ratios result from a subtle balance between the radii of the parent and residual nuclei and the nucleon separation energy, and are consistently lower for the knockout of the more correlated, neutron-deficient nucleons. Furthermore, in the symmetric $^{12}$C nucleus, theoretical ratios suggest that protons remain more correlated than neutrons.

Active learning has gained traction for screening functional materials from established databases based on specific properties. However, popular repositories like ICSD and the Materials Project contain only a minuscule fraction of the vast chemical design space. To address this, we introduce an active generative inverse design framework that integrates active learning with deep variational autoencoders and generative adversarial networks to identify novel materials with target properties across the entire chemical design space. This approach successfully discovered new thermodynamically stable materials with high band gaps (SrYF$_5$) and semiconductors within specified band gap ranges (SrClF$_3$, CaClF$_5$, YCl$_3$, SrC$_2$F$_3$, AlSCl, As$_2$O$_3$), all confirmed via first-principles DFT calculations. Our experiments demonstrate that while active learning may generate chemically infeasible candidates, these samples are crucial for training effective screening models to filter desired materials from those produced by the generative architecture. Consequently, our active generative inverse design method proves highly effective.

Addressing Gromov's inquiry regarding whether bi-invariant metrics on compact Lie groups are extremal relative to other metrics, this note establishes that for a compact connected semi-simple Lie group $G$, such metrics are indeed extremal—and specifically rigid—when contrasted with left-invariant metrics. Furthermore, this finding extends to compact connected homogeneous manifolds of the form $G/H$, provided $G$ is compact, connected, and semi-simple.

The coherent motion of cold atoms within a standing-wave field is understood as propagation through two optical potentials. It is demonstrated that wave-packet dynamics may exhibit either regular or chaotic behavior, with transitions occurring between these potentials after the atoms pass field nodes. Signatures of de Broglie-wave chaos appear in the evolution of position and momentum probabilities, as well as in the Wigner function. The likelihood of these transitions is governed by the ratio of squared detuning to Doppler shift and is notably high in the parameter regime where classical motion is chaotic.

Particle Filtering (PF) represents a well-established framework for inference within non-linear state-space models. Resampling is a critical component of PF, essential for achieving low-variance likelihood and state estimates. However, conventional resampling techniques render PF-based loss functions non-differentiable regarding model and PF parameters. Furthermore, within a variational inference setting, resampling produces high-variance gradient estimates for the PF-based evidence lower bound. By utilizing optimal transport concepts, we propose a principled differentiable particle filter and establish convergence guarantees. We validate this innovative approach across various applications.

We report measurements of the expansion of Kepler's Supernova Remnant (SNR) across three epochs of Chandra X-ray observations conducted in 2000, 2006, and 2014. As the remnant of a historical supernova observed in 1604 CE, Kepler's SNR offers a unique chance to study the real-time dynamical evolution of such an object. Analyzing the asymmetry in forward shock velocity can also yield insights into the explosion's nature and the density of the surrounding circumstellar material. By integrating 2014 data with observations from 2000 and 2006, we track the proper motion of filaments along the SNR's outer rim. Previous research has identified proper motion differences of up to a factor of three between the northern and southern regions of the remnant. Utilizing this extended time baseline, our results align with prior studies but feature reduced uncertainties. Furthermore, the inclusion of a third observation epoch allows us to investigate potential systemic velocity changes, specifically blast wave deceleration, similar to recent findings in Tycho's SNR. We find little to no conclusive evidence of such deceleration and conclude that Kepler's SNR is interacting with circumstellar material that maintains roughly constant density, although this density varies significantly around the periphery.

This paper introduces an architecture utilizing Symbolic Reinforcement Learning (SRL) to ensure safety in Radio Access Network (RAN) applications. Specifically, we offer a fully automated workflow where users define high-level logical safety constraints for a specific cellular network topology, enabling the network to achieve optimal performance as measured by Key Performance Indicators (KPIs).
