We demonstrate that for any $p \in (0,1)$, the quenched density of the point on a point-to-point polymer of length $t$ located at distance $pt$ from the origin converges in law to a specific random density function as $t \to \infty$, provided the path is centered around its random mode $\mathcal{M}_{p,t}$ and no additional scaling is applied. Similarly, for point-to-line polymers of length $t$, the quenched density of the endpoint, when centered around its random mode $\mathcal{M}_{*,t}$, converges in law to an explicit random density. These limiting random densities are proportional to $e^{-\mathcal{R}_\sigma(x)}$, where $\mathcal{R}_\sigma(x)$ represents a two-sided 3D Bessel process with a suitable diffusion coefficient $\sigma$. Furthermore, the distributions of the random modes $\mathcal{M}_{*,t}$ and $\mathcal{M}_{p,t}$ converge upon $t^{2/3}$ scaling to the maximizer of the $\operatorname{Airy}_2$ process minus a parabola and to points on the geodesics of the directed landscape, respectively. The localization results presented here confirm the folklore "favorite region" conjecture. Additionally, our proof methods enable the derivation of properties for the KPZ equation, including ergodicity and limiting Bessel behaviors near the maximum.

We employ the amplitude soft bootstrap technique to investigate the landscape of effective field theories (EFTs) involving massless vectors and scalars. It is established that imposing vanishing soft limits uniquely identifies a specific subset of EFTs, namely non-linear sigma models, scalar Galileons, and Born-Infeld theories. Leveraging amplitude analysis, we propose no-go theorems for higher-derivative vector theories and those featuring coupled vectors and scalars. Subsequently, we consider more general soft theorems where the non-trivial component of the soft limit for an $(n+1)$-point amplitude is expressed as a linear combination of $n$-point amplitudes. We derive the structure of these soft theorems for arbitrary power-counting and particle spins, then apply them within the soft bootstrap framework for Galileon power-counting and coupled scalar-vector systems. This approach unifies the characterization of known Galileon theories and reveals a novel exceptional model: the Special scalar-vector Galileon.

This study addresses data-driven predictive control for discrete-time linear time-periodic (LTP) systems with a known period but unknown dynamics. The proposed method extends established data-driven techniques for linear time-invariant (LTI) systems, specifically Data-enabled Predictive Control (DeePC) and Subspace Predictive Control (SPC). The approach relies on a comprehensive theoretical framework of behavioral systems theory adapted for LTP systems, including a generalized version of the fundamental lemma. For deterministic LTP systems, the algorithm yields results equivalent to standard Model Predictive Control (MPC). Furthermore, the algorithm's robustness against noisy data is demonstrated through simulations involving a regularized variant applied to a stochastic multi-input multi-output LTP system.

We introduce general one-loop contributions to the decay processes $H\rightarrow f\bar{f}\gamma$, encompassing all potential exchanges of additional heavy vector gauge bosons, heavy fermions, and charged (as well as neutral) scalar particles within loop diagrams. Consequently, the derived analytic results apply to a broad spectrum of Beyond the Standard Model (BSM) theories. The analytic expressions for the form factors are formulated using Passarino-Veltman functions adhering to the standard notation of {\tt LoopTools}, enabling the numerical computation of decay rates via this package. These calculations are subsequently applied to the Standard Model, the $U(1)_{B-L}$ extension, and the Two-Higgs-Doublet Model, with phenomenological outcomes for all these frameworks analyzed. We find that new physics effects yield significant contributions, making them detectable at future colliders.

This paper tackles the challenge of efficient blind deblurring by introducing a collection of lightweight Deep-Wiener-Networks capable of real-time performance. The architecture comprises a deep neural network designed to estimate Wiener network parameters and a subsequent Wiener network dedicated to the deblurring process. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms the State of the Art regarding inference time and parameter count. Specifically, two of our models achieve a processing speed of 100 images per second, meeting the requirements for real-time deblurring. Future work may explore practical real-world applications of these models.

This study identifies a Critical Energy induced Enhancement (CEE) mechanism applicable to general three-body open-charm processes in $e^+e^-$ collisions, leveraging the unique kinematic characteristics of such annihilation events with three-body final states. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the process $e^+e^-\to BC\to B(C\to DE)$. When the center-of-mass (CM) energy reaches a critical condition defined by $\sqrt{s}=m_B+m_C$, a distinct reflection peak emerges for an intermediate $C$ state near the threshold of the invariant mass distribution for $m_{BE}$ or $m_{BD}$, a phenomenon highly sensitive to the CM energy. This reflection enhancement at critical energy suggests that new clusters of charmoniumlike structures can be experimentally identified. Using the example of $e^+e^-\to D_s^{*-}D_{s2}^*(2573)^+ \to D_s^{*-}(D^0K^+)$ at $\sqrt{s}=4.680$ GeV, we demonstrate this novel effect. Crucially, we propose a series of optimal CM energy points for searching new charmoniumlike structures in three-body open-charm processes from $e^+e^-$ annihilation, which are accessible for investigation at BESIII and potentially at BelleII.

This paper examines the geometric superspace framework applied to boundary issues in supergravity, reconstructing the geometric formulation of four-dimensional supergravity Lagrangians when spacetime possesses a non-trivial boundary. Initially, we concentrate on pure $\mathcal{N}=1$ and $\mathcal{N}=2$ theories featuring a negative cosmological constant. In these scenarios, maintaining supersymmetry invariance of the action necessitates adding topological boundary terms that supersymmetrize the Euler-Gauss-Bonnet term. Furthermore, the boundary values of super field-strengths are determined dynamically to be constant, reflecting the vanishing of $\mathrm{OSp}(\mathcal{N}|4)$-covariant supercurvatures at the boundary. Subsequently, we address the case of a vanishing cosmological constant; here, incorporating boundary terms with additional fields—which act as auxiliary fields for the bulk theory—restores supersymmetry. Across all aforementioned cases, the complete supersymmetric Lagrangian can be reformulated in a MacDowell-Mansouri-like structure. Finally, we discuss the application of these findings to specific problems involving asymptotic boundaries, which are pertinent to holographic analysis.

The NA48/2 experiment at CERN presents the initial detection of the $K^\pm \to \pi^\pm \pi^0 e^+ e^-$ decay, based on data from $1.7 \times 10^{11}$ charged kaon decays collected between 2003 and 2004. With a candidate sample of 4919 events containing 4.9% background, the branching ratio across the complete kinematic range was measured as BR($K^\pm \to \pi^\pm \pi^0 e^+ e^-$) = $(4.24 \pm 0.14) \times 10^{-6}$. An analysis of the kinematic distribution reveals evidence for a structure-dependent component consistent with chiral perturbation theory predictions. Additionally, various P- and CP-violating asymmetries were calculated.

Boundary AdS correlators and their duals serve as the primary dynamic observables linking bulk AdS theories with boundary conformal field theories. We demonstrate that tree-level AdS boundary correlators for generic states can be represented as specific nonlocal differential operators acting on contact Witten diagrams. Furthermore, we express these boundary correlators in a format closely resembling flat space amplitudes, where Mandelstam variables are substituted with particular combinations of single-state conformal generators. We establish that all tree-level AdS boundary correlators admit a differential representation and outline the process of converting these expressions into position space. The construction is illustrated by calculating boundary correlators for scalars interacting with gluons and gravitons; upon conversion to position space, these yield established results. Additionally, we define color-kinematics duality and BCJ relations analogously to their flat space versions, showing they are upheld by scalar correlators involving gluon exchange. Finally, we explore potential methods for the double copy, concluding that a direct generalization likely necessitates nontrivial extensions.

Research into the production of light hadrons and nuclei is essential for characterizing the hot, dense fireball generated in ultra-relativistic heavy ion collisions and for exploring hadronization mechanisms at the LHC. Observables analyzed as a function of charged particle multiplicity in proton-proton and proton-lead collisions have revealed unexpected features that are qualitatively similar to those seen in larger colliding systems. The ALICE experiment, utilizing its superior tracking and particle identification capabilities, has conducted a comprehensive and systematic investigation of strange and non-strange hadrons, short-lived hadron resonances, and light (anti-)(hyper-)nuclei. This presentation offers a critical overview of these findings by comparing them with the statistical hadronization model.

This study reports experimental findings on a Bose gas confined in a quasi-2D geometry near the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition temperature. By analyzing the density profiles both \textit{in situ} and following time-of-flight expansion, as well as measuring the coherence length, we distinguish various states of the gas. Notably, we observe the emergence of a bimodal distribution lacking long-range order. In this specific state, the gas exhibits a coherence length exceeding that of a thermal cloud; it is quasi-condensed but does not display superfluidity. The experimental data suggests that we are witnessing the superfluid transition, specifically the BKT transition.

Reconstructing photorealistic objects from limited viewpoints is fundamentally ambiguous and relies on learning appropriate reconstruction priors. While previous studies on sparse rigid object reconstruction effectively utilized large datasets like CO3D to learn these priors, this paper extends that methodology to dynamic objects. Using cats and dogs as a representative case, we present Common Pets in 3D (CoP3D), a crowd-sourced dataset comprising approximately 4,200 distinct pets, marking one of the first large-scale benchmarks for non-rigid 3D reconstruction in uncontrolled environments. We also introduce Tracker-NeRF, a technique for learning 4D reconstruction from this data. During inference, Tracker-NeRF takes a small number of frames from an unseen object to predict the 3D trajectories of its points and synthesize novel views that interpolate across both viewpoint and time. Experiments on CoP3D demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing baselines in non-rigid new-view synthesis.

The hippocampus frequently reveals intriguing and perplexing phenomena, including landmark vector cells, splitter cells, and event-specific representations. In the absence of a unifying framework to account for these diverse findings, individual experiments often appear to uncover new anomalies or distinct coding types. In this work, we propose a unifying principle: the mental representation of space emerges from latent higher-order sequence learning. By conceptualizing space as a sequence, we can explain numerous observed phenomena and suggest that interpreting sequential neuronal responses through spatial and Euclidean frameworks—specifically the place-field mapping methodology—may itself generate apparent anomalies. Our proposed model, the Clone-structured Causal Graph (CSCG), employs a specialized higher-order graph structure to learn latent representations by mapping sensory inputs to unique contexts. By learning to compress sequential and episodic experiences using CSCGs, cognitive maps emerge; these are mental representations of spatial and conceptual relationships within an environment that facilitate planning, introspection, consolidation, and abstraction. We demonstrate that our model succinctly and mechanistically explains over a dozen distinct hippocampal phenomena, spanning from classic experimental reports to the most recent discoveries.

Multi-threaded applications can leverage the full capabilities of many-core systems; however, Network-on-Chip (NoC) inter-core communication accounts for 60–75% of the miss latency these applications encounter. This delay in delivering critical data to requesting cores significantly degrades performance. This brief offers insights into how multi-threaded applications request critical data from memory, analyzes the causes of NoC-induced delays and their impact on performance, and demonstrates how NoC-aware memory access optimizations can substantially enhance efficiency. Experimental evaluation of early restart memory access optimization shows that prioritizing critical data through NoC resource exploitation reduces miss penalties by 10–12% and boosts system performance by 7–11%.

These notes result from courses delivered to undergraduate and graduate students from the University of Western Australia, the Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Rio de Janeiro, the Indian Institute of Technology Gandhinagar, and the Ukrainian Catholic University during 2021 and 2022.

The maximum parsimony distance, $d_{\textrm{MP}}(T_1,T_2)$, and the bounded-state variant, $d_{\textrm{MP}}^t(T_1,T_2)$, quantify the disparity between two phylogenetic trees $T_1$ and $T_2$ by evaluating the maximum difference in their parsimony scores across any character (where $t$ denotes the state limit for the latter). Although computing $d_{\textrm{MP}}(T_1, T_2)$ is known to be fixed-parameter tractable with a linear kernel, this property remained unproven for $d_{\textrm{MP}}^t(T_1, T_2)$. This paper establishes that computing $d_{\textrm{MP}}^t(T_1, T_2)$ is indeed fixed-parameter tractable for every $t$. Specifically, we demonstrate that the problem admits a kernel of size $O(k \lg k)$, with $k$ representing the distance value $d_{\textrm{MP}}^t(T_1, T_2)$. Central to our proof is the introduction of "leg-disjoint incompatible quartets," a concept that may hold independent significance.

This review addresses the "problem of time" in quantum physics, outlining its historical context and the objections against treating time as a quantum observable. It argues that unresolved issues necessitate a treatment of time as an observable, noting that the absence of a consistent temporal theory currently obstructs the development of a complete quantum gravity framework. The paper contends that adopting an intrinsic measurement of quantum time alongside conventional external time is a compelling solution. Recent work has sought to revitalize the Page and Wootters (1983) proposal by clarifying its original ambiguities and expanding its interpretive scope. These new contributions highlight the necessity of transcending the constraints of standard quantum mechanics. Additionally, the review examines the covariant loop quantum gravity perspective, which advocates for disregarding time entirely. Ultimately, this work aims to advance the unification of relativity and quantum physics by establishing the necessary conceptual foundations, intentionally omitting technical details to maintain clarity and simplicity, with readers directed to original references for deeper technical insights.

Recent theoretical work by Chen et al. (2021) established an intermediate-scale gyrokinetic-electron framework for nonuniform tokamak plasmas, revealing that a Navier-Stokes-like nonlinearity couples electron-temperature-gradient (ETG) modes with zonal flows (ZFs). These coupled modes operate at scales shorter than the ion gyroradius but longer than the electron gyroradius. This intermediate-scale ETG-ZF interaction is typically more robust than the Hasegawa-Mima nonlinearity found in fluid models and is expected to drive significant zonal flow generation and regulate ETG modes. This study presents electron-scale, continuum gyrokinetic simulations covering both single-mode ETG scenarios and full-spectrum ETG turbulence. Investigations into zonal flow generation from single ETG modes confirm agreement with theoretical predictions. Furthermore, full-spectrum results are qualitatively interpreted through the lens of single-mode findings, demonstrating that ETG-driven zonal flows effectively regulate intermediate-scale electron heat flux transport within the theoretically predicted range.

We present a universal formula for the gravitational radiation energy spectrum, $dE^{GW}/d\omega$, at sub-leading order arising from generic hard gravitational scattering events involving multiple particles or bodies. This result encompasses all $\mathcal{O}(\omega)$ corrections to the radiation flux for general $2\rightarrow N$ collisions, covering both massive and massless scenarios. Furthermore, we analyze how quantum spin influences the radiation energy flux in particle collisions. Specifically, we examine the case of elastic gravitational scattering between two massive bodies ($m+M\rightarrow m+M$), demonstrating that all $\mathcal{O}(\omega)$ contributions to the energy flux precisely cancel out in this instance. However, for inelastic $2\rightarrow 2$ scattering, the inclusion of sub-leading soft gravitons yields a non-zero radiation flux, which admits a simple expression within certain asymptotic limits. These findings are applicable to black hole collisions and may have testable implications for gravitational wave physics.

We introduce a technique to investigate how parton showers accumulate large logarithms. This approach involves applying a suitable integral transform to the distribution of the relevant observable. Subsequently, the parton shower is restructured to yield the transformed distribution as an exponential, allowing for the calculation of terms within the perturbative expansion of that exponent. We demonstrate this framework by applying it to the thrust distribution in electron-positron annihilation across various shower algorithms. Among the tested methods, the most broadly applicable strategy involves determining specific perturbative coefficients in the exponent via numerical integration and verifying their consistency with the next-to-leading-log summation of thrust logarithms.

The roots of a complex polynomial vary continuously with respect to its coefficients, meaning that an infinitesimal change in the coefficients leads to an infinitesimal change in the roots. This result can be demonstrated concisely and directly using the method of infinitesimals.

The spherical model, a well-known exactly solvable framework, has been utilized to characterize various critical phenomena, including ferromagnetic transitions, Bose-Einstein condensation, spin-glass and glass transitions, as well as jamming. Inspired by recent advances in active matter physics, this study investigates the spherical model subjected to an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck type self-propulsion force characterized by a persistent time $\tau_p$. Our findings indicate that the system displays Ising universality when $\tau_p$ is finite, whereas in the limit as $\tau_p$ approaches infinity, the behavior aligns with the random field Ising universality class.

Current analyses of quantum reservoir computing (QRC) systems driven by classical inputs predominantly rely on the density matrix formalism. However, this paper demonstrates that alternative representations offer superior insights for addressing design and evaluation challenges. Specifically, system isomorphisms have been derived that unify the standard density matrix approach with an observable-space representation utilizing Bloch vectors based on Gell-Mann bases. It is shown that these vector-based formulations correspond to state-affine systems (SAS) previously identified in classical reservoir computing literature, for which extensive theoretical results already exist. Leveraging this connection, the study proves that key properties regarding fading memory (FMP) and the echo state (ESP) are representation-independent, while also clarifying fundamental theoretical questions within finite-dimensional QRC. Notably, the authors formulate a necessary and sufficient condition for the validity of ESP and FMP and characterize contractive quantum channels with exclusively trivial semi-infinite solutions by identifying the existence of input-independent fixed points.

Hybrid photon-atom integrated circuits, featuring photonic microcavities and trapped single neutral atoms within their evanescent fields, hold significant promise for quantum information processing. In this architecture, atoms supply the long-lived memory and single-photon nonlinearity that complement the superior passive photonic components found in traditional quantum circuits. This study proposes a stable realization of such hybrid circuits using an unsuspended photonic chip. By utilizing high-order modes within a microring, we achieve a feasible evanescent-field trap potential of approximately 0.3 mK with only ~10 mW of cavity power, a substantial reduction from the ~100 mW typically needed in schemes relying on fundamental modes. Consequently, our approach enables stable single-atom trapping with relatively low laser power, paving the way for future research into high-fidelity quantum gates, single-photon generation, and controllable atom-array-based many-body quantum physics.

Active Galactic Nuclei (AGNs) have recently been suggested as standardizable candles, utilizing a discovered non-linear correlation between their X-ray and optical-ultraviolet (UV) luminosities to independently determine distances. This study employs these observables for the first time to constrain parameters in f(R) gravity models—specifically the Hu-Sawicki and exponential variants—alongside cosmological parameters. The significance of these modified gravity theories stems from their ability to account for the universe's late-time accelerated expansion without invoking a dark energy component. Our analysis incorporates additional datasets, including Hubble parameter estimates from Cosmic Chronometers, the Pantheon Type Ia supernova sample, and Baryon Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) measurements. Our findings indicate that the allowed parameter space for these models becomes more constrained when AGN and BAO data are combined with Cosmic Chronometer and supernova data, with the BAO dataset providing the tightest constraints. Furthermore, while our results align with the $\Lambda$CDM model, the data also permit small deviations from General Relativity that can be effectively described by the f(R) models examined here.

Cyber-physical systems, which integrate hardware and software, underpin operational workflows in production, logistics, maintenance, and material handling. This integration aligns the digital and physical realms, enabling detailed process tracking via sensors. The vast volume of event data produced by these operations presents both opportunities and challenges for process mining techniques, which facilitate process discovery, performance analysis, and conformance checking. Current tools already allow for the automatic generation of process models and the identification of compliance and performance issues. Within the DFG-funded Cluster of Excellence "Internet of Production" (IoP), process mining is employed to construct "digital shadows" that enhance diverse operational processes. However, given the dynamic, distributed, and complex nature of these operations, research is driven by IoP challenges to develop advanced methods in comparative process mining (analyzing process variants across different products, locations, and times), object-centric process mining (managing interactions among various object types), and forward-looking process mining (addressing "what if" scenarios). By tackling these hurdles, the goal is to create valuable "digital shadows" capable of eliminating operational friction.

This paper outlines the creation of an annotated corpus and the training of models specifically for classical French theatre, with an emphasis on verse comedies. Initially developed as a precursor to the stylometric analysis detailed in Cafiero and Camps [2019], the study leverages a modern neural network-based lemmatiser and a CRF tagger. This approach achieves accuracies surpassing the current state-of-the-art on in-domain tests and demonstrates robustness in out-of-domain scenarios, extending effectively to 20th-century novels.

Off-policy evaluation typically encompasses two interconnected tasks: estimating a policy's expected return and determining its value function (or other relevant metrics like density ratios). Although recent advancements in marginalized importance sampling (MIS) have established provable guarantees for the former task under realizability assumptions, the latter remains feasible only under significantly stricter conditions, such as the use of excessively expressive discriminators. This study establishes guarantees for off-policy function estimation under realizability alone by applying appropriate regularization to MIS objectives. Unlike standard regularization methods in MIS, our approach offers greater flexibility, accommodating any user-defined distribution where the learned function approximates the ground truth. We precisely characterize the optimal dual solution required from the discriminator class, which defines the data-coverage assumption for value-function learning. Furthermore, we observe that the regularizer can be modified to relax data-coverage constraints, effectively eliminating them entirely when strong side information is available.

Although hypothetical axions and axion-like particles (ALPs), which interact weakly with photons, have not yet been experimentally detected, advancements in laser technology offer new prospects. By utilizing laser-plasma interactions, laboratories can now generate quasi-static electric and magnetic fields that are significantly stronger and more compact than those produced by traditional large-scale magnets, thereby enhancing the search for axions. This study examines the viability of exploring ALPs using planar or cylindrically symmetric laser-plasma fields as a background environment, probed by an x-ray free-electron laser. In this setup, both the background and probe fields are polarized; consequently, the presence of ALPs within the relevant parameter space would induce a measurable rotation in the probe's polarization. Furthermore, structured fields within the plasma provide a tunable transverse interaction profile and boost the signal-to-noise ratio through phase-matching. Focusing on ALP masses between $10^{-3}$ eV and 1 keV, the article presents preliminary schemes and estimations regarding ALP production and the resulting polarization rotation of probe photons, highlighting the potential for future laboratory-based laser-plasma ALP sources.

Emergent quantum phenomena in materials, characterized by exotic quasi-particle excitations, stem from electron collective behavior, frustration-induced quantum fluctuations, and entanglement. This study reports on the recently synthesized frustrated antiferromagnet Li4CuTeO6, combining thermodynamic and muon spin relaxation data with ab initio density functional theory and exact diagonalization calculations. In this system, Cu2+ ions (S = 1/2) form disordered spin chains and ladders along the [101] direction, connected by weak random inter-chain couplings. Despite strong antiferromagnetic interactions between Cu2+ moments—evidenced by a large effective Curie-Weiss temperature of -154 K—thermodynamic measurements reveal no long-range magnetic order or spin freezing down to 45 mK. Muon spin relaxation findings align with these thermodynamic observations. Furthermore, the scaling of magnetization and specific heat with temperature and magnetic field demonstrates a data collapse, indicating the existence of random singlets within a disorder-driven, correlated, and dynamic ground state.

This study examines the scalability of leading user profiling technologies across various online environments. Specifically, it seeks to evaluate the reliability and constraints of existing computational stylometry methods when applied to underground forums, which often feature distinct user demographics—predominantly male, younger, and more tech-savvy—and are frequented by cyber offenders attempting to conceal their identities. Due to the absence of ground truth or validated historical criminal data for verification, we gathered new datasets from clearweb forums. These forums include available user demographics and represent user populations more closely aligned with underground spaces (such as tech communities) compared to standard social media benchmark datasets, which typically exhibit a more balanced demographic distribution.

Recent research has investigated the classical simulation of quantum circuits with limited non-Clifford gates using the stabilizer formalism, where the computational expense hinges on the stabilizer rank $\chi$—the minimum number of stabilizer states required to superpose into a given pure state $\psi$. This work establishes a thorough mathematical framework for both exact and approximate stabilizer ranks and introduces a suite of classical simulation algorithms that offer broader applicability and marked performance improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods. A key advancement is the ability to simulate circuits featuring Clifford gates alongside arbitrary diagonal gates, thereby expanding upon prior algorithms restricted to the Clifford+T gate set. By implementing these new techniques, we successfully simulated quantum algorithms comprising 40–50 qubits and more than 60 non-Clifford gates without relying on high-performance computing resources. Specifically, we demonstrated a simulation of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) that processed superpositions of approximately $10^6$ stabilizer states and sampled the complete $n$-bit output distribution, surpassing earlier efforts that utilized only $\sim 10^3$ stabilizer states and sampled single-qubit marginals. Additionally, we simulated instances of the Hidden Shift algorithm with circuits containing up to 64 T gates or 16 CCZ gates, illustrating the efficiency gains achieved by optimizing the decomposition of non-Clifford components.

Vision Transformers (ViT) are increasingly challenging Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) in medical imaging applications like classification and segmentation. Although CNNs are already known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks, recent studies indicate that ViTs face similar risks, experiencing substantial performance drops when subjected to such attacks. This susceptibility to meticulously crafted adversarial examples casts doubt on the safety of deploying ViTs in clinical environments. To address this, we introduce a novel self-ensembling technique designed to bolster ViT robustness against adversarial threats. Our proposed Self-Ensembling Vision Transformer (SEViT) capitalizes on the observation that feature maps extracted from the initial layers of a ViT remain largely stable despite adversarial perturbations. By training multiple classifiers on these intermediate features and aggregating their outputs with the predictions from the final ViT classifier, the model achieves greater resistance to adversarial inputs. Furthermore, assessing the consistency across these diverse predictions aids in identifying adversarial samples. Experiments conducted on chest X-ray and fundoscopy datasets confirm the effectiveness of the SEViT architecture in defending against various adversarial attacks within a gray-box scenario, where the attacker possesses full knowledge of the target model but not the defense mechanism. Code: https://github.com/faresmalik/SEViT

MA2Z4 monolayers represent a novel category of hexagonal, non-centrosymmetric materials that exhibit remarkable spin-valley phenomena. Although only MoSi2N4 and WSi2N4 have been synthesized to date, theoretical models suggest a broader family of two-dimensional materials with intriguing (opto)electronic characteristics. This study investigates, via first-principles methods, the chemical trends in band gaps and spin-orbit splittings for selected MSi2Z4 compounds (where M = Mo, W and Z = N, P, As, Sb). Effective Bethe-Salpeter-equation calculations indicate substantial exciton binding energies. Furthermore, the evolution of excitonic energies under external magnetic fields is modeled by determining effective g-factors and diamagnetic coefficients, enabling direct comparison with experimental data. Notably, large positive g-factors are predicted for excitons associated with higher conduction bands. These findings position MSi2Z4 monolayers as a promising platform for exciton research and optoelectronic applications, including heterostructure designs. Additionally, the heaviest compound examined, WSi2Sb4, displays spin-orbit induced band inversion, a definitive indicator of its topological properties.

The surge in aerial image availability and volume, combined with advancements in computing power and growing application interest, has enabled the transition of object detection and domain adaptation research from theory to production. However, the massive scale of aerial datasets, which contain numerous dense and small objects per frame, presents significant hurdles. Deep learning for aerial imagery has historically struggled due to insufficient training data, prompting researchers to adopt domain adaptation (DA) techniques to leverage labeled source data for unlabeled target domains. This approach addresses two primary challenges: the substantial variability between datasets—encompassing factors like object size, class distribution, feature uniformity, acquisition methods, distance, and weather—and the difficulty of detecting small, densely overlapped objects in satellite imagery, which often causes state-of-the-art models to fail in capturing local features and generating accurate region proposals. To address these issues, we propose a dual solution: a domain discriminator designed to align local feature spaces across domains, and a novel pipeline that enhances the back-end through spatial pyramid pooling, a cross-stage partial network, and heatmap-based region proposal networks. Furthermore, we introduce a new image difficulty score to guide object localization and identification by adaptively adjusting the focal loss measure. Our proposed model surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods by 7.4%.

This study introduces the initial doping of crystalline methylammonium lead bromide (MAPbBr$_3$) perovskite thin films with CdSe/CdZnS core/shell quantum dots (QDs) via a soft-chemistry technique that maintains their high quantum yield and exceptional fluorescence characteristics. The resulting 100 nm thick MAPbBr$_3$ films contain colloidal QDs doped at volume concentrations ranging from 0.025% to 5%; the QDs' organic ligands are replaced with halide ions to facilitate intimate contact with the perovskite matrix. Ensemble photoluminescence (PL) data confirm that QD emission persists within the MAPbBr$_3$ host, while ensemble photoluminescence excitation (PLE) spectra reveal wavelength-dependent coupling between the QDs and the matrix. Spatially resolved PL measurements indicate a strong correlation between QD locations and enhanced matrix PL signals. Furthermore, fluorescence lifetime imaging (FLIM) shows that the MAPbBr$_3$ emission lifetime is prolonged near QDs. Combined with the increased matrix PL intensity, this suggests QDs function as nucleation sites that enhance MAPbBr$_3$ crystallinity and boost its emission quantum yield. Antibunching measurements confirm single-photon emission from individual QDs embedded in the perovskite, and blinking statistics analysis demonstrates improved photostability for these QDs compared to bare CdSe/CdZnS counterparts. High doping levels pave the way for hybrid-based LEDs, whereas low doping concentrations could enable hybrid single-photon sources integrated into field-effect devices, offering a solid-state alternative for high-quantum-yield CdSe-based QDs in nanophotonic applications.

We contend that the concept of identical particles loses its validity within quantum systems influenced by non-commutative deformations of space-time symmetries. These frameworks are defined by a four-momentum space structured as a non-abelian Lie group. Our investigation highlights that for systems comprising multiple particles, the sole well-defined quantum number is the total momentum, derived from the non-abelian combination of individual momenta, which themselves are no longer uniquely determined. Consequently, our findings indicate that all prior efforts to construct Fock spaces for these models were fundamentally flawed and ultimately failed. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the natural braiding of momentum quantum numbers, which governs the exchange of factors in state tensor products, remains covariant under relativistic transformations, thereby resolving a persistent issue in the field.

A set of orthogonal multipartite quantum states is defined as genuinely nonlocal (or distinguishability-based genuinely nonlocal) if it remains locally indistinguishable across every possible bipartition of the subsystems. While this form of multipartite nonlocality arises more naturally than the recently popular concept of "strong nonlocality" within the framework of local distinguishability, it has received comparatively little attention. This study investigates the distinguishability-based genuine nonlocality of a specific class of genuinely multipartite entangled states known as Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ)-like states. We demonstrate that any subset of five states from the three-qubit GHZ basis exhibits genuine nonlocality, whereas any subset of four does not. Furthermore, for general tripartite systems, we establish a universal upper bound on the cardinality required for an arbitrary set of GHZ-like states to be genuinely nonlocal. Although not strictly required, entanglement is widely believed to increase the difficulty of state discrimination in various contexts; literature in bipartite systems has often sought small nonlocal sets composed of maximally entangled states to support this view. Extending this to the tripartite case with GHZ-like states, we identify small genuinely nonlocal sets where the cardinality scales linearly with the local dimension $d$. This finding not only reinforces the perspective that entanglement complicates discrimination in multipartite scenarios but also highlights potential substantial distinctions between strong nonlocality and standard distinguishability-based multipartite nonlocality.

Optical fibers are acknowledged as a leading host material for maintaining high phase coherence during optical frequency transfer across thousands of kilometers. While pioneering efforts relied on active phase noise cancellation (ANC) to suppress environmental perturbations, this method requires an ideal phase detector with high resolution and an unlimited detection range to extract noise, especially in noisy fiber links. We show that passive phase noise cancellation (PNC) is preferable for such links and does not require a phase detector. To mitigate the radio frequency (RF) influence from local time bases found in conventional active or passive techniques, we introduce a fiber-pigtailed acousto-optic modulator (AOM) that utilizes two diffraction orders (0 and +1) with specifically allocated driving frequencies to eliminate the time base effect. Using this approach, we successfully transferred coherent light through a 260 km noisy urban fiber link, effectively removing RF reference effects. After passive compensation, we achieved a fractional frequency instability of $4.9\times10^{-14}$ at 1 second integration time, scaling down to the $10^{-20}$ level at 10,000 seconds in modified Allan deviation over the 260 km link. The frequency uncertainty of the light retrieved after this noise-compensated transfer, relative to the input, was $(0.41\pm4.7)\times10^{-18}$. This proposed technique facilitates the broad distribution of ultrastable frequency references with high coherence, free from RF reference artifacts, and enables diverse applications beyond metrology within fiber networks.
This paper establishes the derivation algebra and automorphism group for twisted deformative Schrödinger-Virasoro Lie algebras.

We establish a dynamical bound governing the spread of correlations in local random quantum circuits, which are lattice spin systems characterized by piecewise quantum operations occurring in space and time with classical probabilities. These correlations are measured using the Frobenius norm of the commutator between two positive operators defined on space-like separated local Hilbert spaces. For times scaling as $t=O(L)$, correlations propagate to distances $\mathcal{D}=t$ at most diffusively, accompanied by extensively suppressed distance-dependent corrections; however, when $t=o(L^2)$, the entire system becomes nearly uniformly correlated, featuring exponentially suppressed distance-dependent corrections and approaching the asymptotic maximum of achievable correlations.

Recent years have witnessed significant progress in symbolic-numerical eigenvalue methods for resolving polynomial systems, and this paper contributes to that evolution. We introduce an algorithm capable of reliably and efficiently solving systems that possess isolated solutions. In cases where the system is overdetermined, the approach reduces the problem to an eigenvalue computation in a manner that is both simpler and substantially faster than prior techniques, potentially surpassing the performance of homotopy continuation methods. To support these claims, we offer numerous examples along with a proof-of-concept implementation in the Julia package EigenvalueSolver.jl.

Image segmentation data often lack a unified grid, a challenge especially prevalent in medical imaging due to variations in resolution, field-of-view, and orientation across different subjects and modalities. Consequently, images and corresponding labels are typically resampled onto a common grid during pre-processing. However, this resampling process induces blurring and partial volume effects, which degrade effective resolution and diminish structural contrast. To address this, we introduce a splat layer designed to automatically manage input resolution discrepancies. This layer maps each image to a mean space for the forward pass; since the splat operator acts as the adjoint of the resampling operator, predictions can be pulled back to the native label space for loss computation. This approach eliminates the necessity for explicit interpolation-based resolution adjustment. Evaluations on two public datasets, featuring both simulated and real multi-modal MRI scans, demonstrate that this model yields superior segmentation performance compared to traditional pre-processing resampling.

Let $(f_{n})_{n}$ be an orthonormal system of continuous functions in $L^{2}(D)$, where $D \subset \mathbb{R}^{d}$ is compact, and let $(\lambda_{n})_{n}$ be a sequence of strictly positive coefficients that form a convergent series. We demonstrate that these functions and coefficients correspond to the eigenfunctions and eigenvalues of a covariance operator linked to a continuous positive-definite kernel if and only if the sequence of partial sums $\sum_{j \leq n} \lambda_{j} f_{j}^{2}$ is equicontinuous on $D$.

Recent discoveries of superconducting diodes have expanded the realm of conventional electrical nonreciprocity into the superconducting domain. Typically, diode performance is regulated by external magnetic fields, a method that risks disrupting the system's superconductivity. This study introduces an all-electrical topological Josephson diode (TJD) situated within a time-reversal symmetry-broken quantum spin Hall insulator characterized by anisotropic helical edge states. Leveraging the anisotropy and helicity of these edge states, the electrostatically induced Doppler energy shift enables a new diode mechanism. This mechanism achieves a topologically protected maximum efficiency of $40\%$ in a single-edge configuration, which can be enhanced to $90\%$ using a double-edge interferometer. Crucially, the device functions entirely through electrical means, allowing both efficiency and polarity to be precisely tuned via electrostatic gate voltage. The proposed gate-controllable TJD falls within current experimental capabilities and promises to provide essential components for *topological superelectronics*, effectively integrating topological materials, superconductivity, and nonreciprocal quantum transport.

The in-situ assessment of tungsten surface enrichment in EUROFER steel, induced by 250 eV deuterium sputtering, was conducted using low energy He$^{+}$ ion scattering spectroscopy. Samples were subjected to irradiation across a temperature range of 300 K to 800 K, utilizing a deuterium atom flux of 2e18 m$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$ and fluences reaching up to 1.1e23 m$^{-2}$. While room temperature measurements revealed a distinct rise in tungsten surface density, the enrichment observed at 520 K was reduced to half its magnitude. At 800 K, no detectable tungsten surface enrichment occurred. Based on these findings, an upper limit of 1.6 eV was established for the diffusion activation energy of tungsten within EUROFER.

This research investigates the near-threshold molecular and collisional dynamics of a strong $^{40}$K p-wave Feshbach resonance using a multifaceted approach combining experimental measurements, numerical simulations, and theoretical modeling. Dimer spectroscopy is performed via radio-frequency spin-flip association in the MHz range and resonant association in the kHz range. A model incorporating both Franck-Condon overlap amplitudes and inhomogeneous broadening significantly reduces systematic uncertainties in the measured binding energy. Coupled-channels calculations utilizing mass-scaled $^{39}$K potentials align well with observed binding energies and uncover a low-energy p-wave shape resonance in the open channel. Contrary to standard expectations, we detect a nonlinear variation of binding energy with the magnetic field, attributing this to the interaction between the closed-channel ramping state and the near-threshold shape resonance in the open channel. We construct an analytic two-channel model that accounts for both resonances and dipole-dipole interactions, demonstrating that the latter become critical at low energies. By parameterizing the energy dependence of the scattering phase with this model, we classify the studied $^{40}$K resonance as broad. Throughout the study, we contrast these findings with the well-understood s-wave case and highlight the significant influence of van der Waals physics. Ultimately, our enhanced understanding of p-wave resonance dimer physics establishes a robust basis for future investigations into few- and many-body orbital phenomena.

Parkinson's disease causes various speech deficits that hinder communication. Automatically analyzing patient speech enables the creation of computer-aided tools to assist in diagnosis and assess disease severity. This paper presents a methodology for classifying Parkinson's disease from speech samples across three languages: Spanish, German, and Czech. The proposed approach utilizes convolutional neural networks trained on time-frequency representations and employs a transfer learning strategy across these languages. This transfer learning scheme is designed to enhance model accuracy by initializing neural network weights with utterances from a language different from the test set. Results indicate that this strategy can improve model accuracy by up to 8% when the base model is sufficiently robust. Furthermore, models utilizing transfer learning generally achieve better balance between specificity and sensitivity compared to those trained without it.

By integrating mapping-mode mid-infrared Spitzer spectra with complementary infrared imaging, we conducted a spatially resolved analysis of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) emission in the central regions of 66 nearby galaxies, split nearly evenly between star-forming systems and low-luminosity active galactic nuclei (AGNs). Combined with existing data on quasars, this study seeks to characterize PAH physical properties across a wide spectrum of black hole accretion power, aiming to identify observational diagnostics that reveal how AGNs influence their host galaxies. While PAH emission in star-forming regions shows a strong correlation with far-ultraviolet luminosity, AGN regions generally exhibit a deficiency in PAHs. Furthermore, AGN areas display, on average, reduced 6.2 μm/7.7 μm and enhanced 11.3 μm/7.7 μm band ratios. Although the current dataset is limited, it indicates that these anomalous ratios cannot be attributed solely to the AGN radiation field. Instead, they suggest that small grains may be destroyed by the combined impact of radiative processes and shocks, phenomena likely linked to jets and outflows associated with highly sub-Eddington, radiatively inefficient AGNs. While quasars also show a PAH deficit and atypical band ratios, their specific characteristics differ from those of less accreting AGNs, potentially signaling fundamental differences in their energy feedback mechanisms.

We establish sectorial extension theorems for Beurling-type ultraholomorphic function classes defined by weight functions exhibiting a regulated loss of regularity. Our proofs rely on a reduction lemma by the second author, which adapts recent results by Jim\'{e}nez-Garrido, Sanz, and the third author on the Roumieu case to the Beurling setting. To manage the opening of the sectors where these extensions hold, we employ the (mixed) growth index and the quasianalyticity order of the weight functions. Consequently, we derive analogous extension results for classes defined by weight sequences and provide insights into the existence of continuous linear extension operators.

This work offers a pedagogical overview of $L_\infty$-algebras and their role in structuring the symmetries and dynamics of both classical field theories and conventional noncommutative gauge theories, which emerge as low-energy effective descriptions in string theory. We examine recent advances that introduce field theories with braided gauge symmetries as a solution to persistent challenges in standard noncommutative frameworks, specifically addressing limitations on gauge algebras and matter fields. These constructions rely on Drinfel'd twist deformation theory, reviewed here in detail, and are governed by a novel homotopy algebraic structure termed the "braided $L_\infty$-algebra." Furthermore, we explore several new theoretical aspects of these models and provide three concrete examples: the standard noncommutative scalar field theory interpreted as a braided field theory, a braided $BF$ theory in arbitrary dimensions viewed as a higher gauge theory, and a newly formulated braided version of noncommutative Yang-Mills theory applicable to arbitrary gauge algebras.

Finding the ideal cloud destination for migrating on-premises SQL environments remains a significant hurdle. Existing tools are often slow, prone to errors, demand extensive manual input, and struggle to offer suitable suggestions. We introduce Doppler, a scalable recommendation engine that delivers appropriately sized Azure SQL Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) targets without needing access to sensitive customer queries or data. Doppler employs a new price-performance approach that enables users to receive a personalized ranking of relevant cloud options based solely on low-level resource metrics like latency and memory consumption. Additionally, Doppler leverages insights into Azure customer behavior to steer new migration clients toward the single best target. Testing over a nine-month span with both prospective and current clients demonstrates that Doppler can pinpoint optimal destinations and adjust to evolving workloads. It has also identified cost-reduction opportunities for over-provisioned users without sacrificing capacity or other necessities. Doppler is now integrated into the Azure Data Migration Assistant v5.5, which processes hundreds of assessment requests every day.

Recent advancements in accessible, high-performance computing have propelled significant strides in Deep Learning and Computer Vision, which have subsequently accelerated progress in Autonomous Driving and Navigation Systems. While existing research predominantly targets driving scenarios in Europe and America, this paper focuses specifically on the Indian driving context. To address this, we introduce a novel architecture called DR-Gaze, designed to map a driver's gaze onto the road surface. We benchmark our results against prior studies and state-of-the-art methods using the DGAZE dataset. Our code will be made publicly available upon the acceptance of this paper.

Code-Switching (CS) is a prevalent linguistic behavior in multilingual groups, defined by the alternation between languages during speech. This study investigates end-to-end speech recognition for Mandarin-English CS, analyzing specific challenges such as property mismatches between languages in a CS pair, the unpredictability of switching points, and data scarcity. We enhance the state-of-the-art end-to-end system through several strategies: merging nonlinguistic symbols, incorporating language identification via hierarchical softmax, modeling sub-word units, artificially reducing speaking rates, and augmenting data using speed perturbation alongside multiple monolingual datasets. These improvements aim to boost performance on both CS and monolingual benchmarks, ensuring applicability in real-world scenarios. Additionally, we examine the impact of various language model integration methods on the proposed model's performance. Experimental results demonstrate that all proposed techniques enhance recognition accuracy. The best combined system achieves up to a 35% relative improvement in mixed error rate over the baseline, delivering acceptable performance on monolingual benchmarks as well.

Decision trees are frequently favored for embedded machine learning due to their simplicity and scalability. Hoeffding Trees, a specific variant, utilize the Hoeffding Bound to identify data patterns without the need for continuous storage of samples, making them ideal for embedded deployment. This study examines the features of a Hardware Logic Synthesis (HLS) implementation of the Hoeffding Tree, with parameters defined by feature dimension (D), output class count (K), and maximum tree depth (Nd). Targeting the Xilinx MPSoC ZCU102, the evaluation assesses resource usage and clock frequency across varying class and feature sizes, execution time on synthetic datasets with different sample counts (N), and performance metrics on two UCI datasets. Specifically, for a configuration of D=3, K=5, and N=40,000, a single tree running at 103 MHz delivers inference 8.3 times faster than a 1.2 GHz ARM Cortex-A53 core. Furthermore, the proposed implementation achieves classification accuracy on UCI datasets comparable to a reference Hoeffding Tree solution.

We construct the full set of modes and the Hadamard function for a scalar field within and outside a sphere embedded in (D+1)-dimensional de Sitter spacetime, which is foliated by spaces of negative constant curvature. The field is subject to Robin boundary conditions on the sphere. We explicitly isolate the contributions to the Hadamard function arising from the sphere and examine the vacuum expectation values (VEVs) of the field squared and the energy-momentum tensor within the hyperbolic vacuum. In the limit of flat spacetime, the resulting state corresponds to the conformal vacuum in the Milne universe, distinct from the maximally symmetric Bunch-Davies vacuum. The vacuum energy-momentum tensor features a nonzero off-diagonal component representing radial energy flux; this is a purely sphere-induced effect absent in boundary-free geometries. Depending on the Robin boundary condition constant and the radial coordinate, this energy flux may be directed either toward or away from the sphere. During early cosmological expansion, curvature effects on sphere-induced VEVs are negligible, with leading expansion terms matching those of a sphere in the Milne universe, whereas gravitational field influence becomes significant at late stages. The decay of these VEVs over time is either monotonic or damped oscillatory, contingent on the field mass and curvature coupling parameter. Furthermore, at large distances from the sphere, the fall-off of sphere-induced VEVs with respect to geodesic distance is exponential for both massless and massive fields.

Fall detection for the elderly is a well-studied challenge with various proposed solutions, ranging from wearable to non-wearable methods. Although current techniques achieve high detection rates, their uptake remains limited due to the requirement of wearing devices and privacy issues. This paper introduces a novel, non-intrusive, and scalable non-wearable solution deployed on an autonomous mobile robot equipped with a microphone. The method utilizes ambient sound captured within homes, specifically focusing on bathrooms—a high-risk area where existing methods often fail due to privacy constraints. Our approach employs a Transformer architecture to classify noisy bathroom audio into fall or no-fall categories, achieving an accuracy of 0.8673. Furthermore, this solution is adaptable to other indoor settings and is well-suited for deployment in elderly care homes, hospitals, and rehabilitation centers, eliminating the need for wearable devices or constant visual surveillance.

This study details the measurement of freeze-out radii for identical-charge pion pairs in Pb--Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=2.76$ TeV, analyzing variations with collision centrality and the pair's average transverse momentum, $k_{\rm T}$. Both three-dimensional femtoscopic radii and direction-averaged one-dimensional radii are determined. The observed radii exhibit a power-law decrease as $k_{\rm T}$ increases, aligning qualitatively with hydrodynamic predictions for a collectively expanding system. Additionally, the radii scale linearly with $\left< \mathrm{d}N_{\rm ch}/\mathrm{d}\eta \right>^{1/3}$. When compared to global femtoscopic data from heavy-ion collisions, the trends resemble those at lower $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$, except for a noted reduction in the $R_{\rm out}/R_{\rm side}$ ratio, which matches specific hydrodynamic model forecasts. These findings further substantiate the creation of a collective, strongly coupled medium in heavy-ion collisions at the LHC.

This paper seeks to prove first and second fundamental theorems concerning $GL(V)$-equivariant polynomial maps that send $k$-tuples of matrix variables from $End(V)^k$ to tensor spaces $End(V)^{\otimes n}$, following the tradition of H. Weyl's *The classical groups* \cite{Weyl} and the principles of symbolic algebra.

Conventional methods for achieving group fairness in algorithmic decision-making strive to balance "total" error rates across various population subgroups. Conversely, we contend that fairness initiatives should prioritize equalizing errors stemming from model uncertainty (epistemic uncertainty)—which arises from insufficient knowledge of the optimal model or limited data—rather than those caused by inherent data uncertainty (aleatoric uncertainty). By linking predictive multiplicity to model uncertainty, we suggest that techniques derived from predictive multiplicity can pinpoint errors attributable to the former. We introduce scalable convex proxies to generate classifiers demonstrating predictive multiplicity and empirically validate that our approach matches the performance of current state-of-the-art methods while being up to four orders of magnitude faster. Furthermore, we develop methods to equalize group error rates driven by model uncertainty in algorithmic decision-making, confirming their efficacy through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

This paper investigates fundamental issues in geometric analysis on Riemannian manifolds. Specifically, it addresses whether $L^p$-Calderón-Zygmund inequalities hold for a broad class of non-compact Riemannian manifolds without requiring a positive injectivity radius. We provide an affirmative answer for the range $1 < p < 2$ assuming a lower bound on the Ricci curvature. For $p > 2$, we extend the work of Güneysu-Pigola (2015) by establishing sufficient geometric conditions for the validity of these inequalities, which include Kato class bounds on the Riemann curvature tensor and the covariant derivative of the Ricci curvature. Throughout the proofs, probabilistic techniques, such as Hessian formulas and Bismut-type representations for heat semigroups, are instrumental.

In 1994, Alcubierre suggested that the special relativistic prohibition against superluminal travel could be circumvented when analyzed globally within certain general relativistic frameworks. While early findings deemed this scenario unphysical due to the apparent requirement of negative mass-energy density, recent theoretical investigations imply that such a condition may not be universally necessary. This paper examines solutions to the Einstein equations derived from the original Alcubierre warp drive metric, incorporating diverse matter-energy sources including dust, perfect fluids, anisotropic fluids, and perfect fluids with a cosmological constant. Additionally, we demonstrate a connection between some of these solutions and shock waves governed by the Burgers equation.

This study presents the initial analysis of the electrical and magnetic characteristics of the triangular-lattice material Zr$_2$NiP$_2$ (space group $P$6$_3$/$mmc$). The temperature-dependent electrical resistivity aligns with the Bloch-Gr\"uneisen-Mott law, indicating standard metallic behavior. Neither electrical nor magnetic measurements reveal any phase transition, and negligible magnetization is observed ($M_0$ $<$ 0.002$\mu_\mathrm{B}$/Ni) across the range from 1.8 K to 7 T. First-principles calculations for Zr$_2$NiP$_2$ successfully explain these metallic and nonmagnetic properties.

We performed three-dimensional hydrodynamical simulations of common envelope jets supernova (CEJSN) events, assuming a neutron star (NS) emits jets while orbiting within the outer layers of a red supergiant (RSG) envelope. Our findings indicate a negative jet feedback coefficient of approximately 0.1 to 0.2, representing the reduction in mass accretion onto the NS as jets strip envelope mass and inflate cocoons. These results suggest that most CEJSN systems undergo grazing envelope evolution (GEE) prior to transitioning into full common envelope evolution (CEE). Additionally, the jets generate upward and downward flows within the RSG envelope; combined with the star's strong convection, this implies that convective energy transport is crucial in CEJSNe. Due to computational constraints, our simulations omitted the NS's gravity, the accretion process, the jet launching mechanism, and the gravity of the deformed envelope. Future simulations of CEE involving NS or black hole companions should incorporate NS accretion (with variable jet power), the full gravitational interaction between the NS and RSG, and the effects of strong convective energy transport.

1ES 1927+654 represents a unique active galactic nucleus and one of the most unusual X-ray nuclear transients. In early 2018, this well-known AGN experienced a "changing-look" event characterized by the emergence of broad optical emission lines and a surge in optical flux. However, by July 2018, the X-ray luminosity had plummeted by more than two orders of magnitude, signaling a drastic transformation in the inner accretion flow. Utilizing three years of data from NICER, XMM-Newton, and NuSTAR, we detail the X-ray evolution of 1ES 1927+654, which unfolds in three distinct stages: (1) an initial super-Eddington phase marked by rapid fluctuations in X-ray luminosity and spectral properties, (2) a stable super-Eddington phase at peak luminosity, and (3) a gradual return to pre-outburst levels and spectral characteristics. For the first time, we observed the emergence of an X-ray corona as the spectrum shifted from thermally dominated to primarily Comptonized. Additionally, we traced the evolution of a prominent broad feature near 1 keV in early spectra, demonstrating that it can be modeled via blueshifted reflection (z = -0.33) from a single-temperature blackbody irradiating spectrum using xillverTDE, a novel variant of xillver models. Consequently, we suggest that this 1 keV feature originates from reflected emission off the base of an optically thick outflow driven by a geometrically thick, super-Eddington inner accretion flow, thereby linking the inner accretion flow with outflows generated during extreme accretion events such as tidal disruption events. Finally, we compare 1ES 1927+654 with other nuclear transients and explore the applications of xillverTDE to super-Eddington accretors.

Let $p$ denote an odd prime and $F_\infty$ represent a $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension of a number field $F$. For an elliptic curve $E$ defined over $F$, this work investigates the structure of the fine Selmer group over $F_\infty$. Under specific conditions, it is demonstrated that the fine Selmer group forms a cofinitely generated module over $\mathbb{Z}_p$, and an upper bound for its corank (also known as the $\lambda$-invariant) is derived using several local and global invariants.

The MediaEval campaign's annual Predicting Media Memorability task, initiated in 2018, has employed various datasets and tasks over the years. This approach has enabled the comparative analysis of numerous memorability prediction methods on identical data in a reproducible manner, facilitating their refinement and enhancement. The resources developed for calculating media memorability are now utilized by researchers far beyond the scope of the evaluation campaign itself. This paper offers a summary of the task, highlighting the collective insights gained for the broader research community.

This paper introduces two finite element formulations for the Laplace problem and establishes their equivalence. We then compare the resulting solutions by varying the ordering of shape functions and the mesh refinement level (specifically using a star pattern with rhomboidal elements). Finally, we provide an overview of the LLNL (Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory) MFEM library, which was utilized to generate these solutions.

Music genre stands as a critical and distinguishing factor for audio and music content. Although visual methods utilizing spectrograms have been investigated for genre classification, the scarcity of high-quality data and augmentation strategies hinders the effective application of deep learning. This study explores the utility of graph neural networks (GNNs) for this task, leveraging their robust inductive biases, and demonstrates that a hybrid CNN-GNN architecture achieves state-of-the-art performance on the GTZAN and AudioSet (Imbalanced Music) datasets. Additionally, we examine Siamese Neural Networks as a functional equivalent to GNNs for learning edge similarity weights. Finally, we conduct visual analysis to interpret the model's field-of-view within the spectrogram in relation to genre labels.

This paper provides explicit evaluations for specific infinite series containing generalized (alternating) harmonic numbers. Furthermore, we derive additional formulas related to these generalized (alternating) harmonic numbers.

This study investigates the Fermi surfaces and superconducting properties of CaSb$_2$ single crystals, which exhibit superconductivity below a critical temperature ($T_{\text{c}}$) of approximately 1.8 K and were synthesized via the self-flux method. Analysis of de-Haas-van-Alphen and Shubnikov-de-Haas oscillation frequencies confirms a quasi-two-dimensional (quasi-2D) Fermi surface, aligning with theoretical predictions of Dirac lines from first-principles calculations. Superconducting state measurements suggest CaSb$_2$ behaves as a type-I superconductor with a Ginzburg-Landau (GL) parameter near unity. The temperature evolution of the upper critical field ($H_{\text{c2}}$) is accurately modeled using a two-band superconducting framework, and the enhancement of the effective mass derived from $H_{\text{c2}}$ at 0 K corresponds to the quasi-2D band identified through quantum oscillations. Consequently, our findings indicate that a quasi-2D band featuring Dirac lines plays a significant role in the superconductivity of CaSb$_2$.

We introduce CatEff, an effect system grounded in category-graded algebraic theories that align with category-graded monads. This system features category-graded operations and handlers, where effects are stratified by morphisms within the grading category; these morphisms capture fine-grained effect structures, such as dependencies or state sorts. Handlers in CatEff serve as implementations for these category-graded effects. To provide semantics for CatEff, we define the concept of a category-graded algebraic theory and establish both soundness and adequacy. Furthermore, we illustrate the utility of category-graded effects by demonstrating a protocol for the transmission and reception of typed data.

Achieving quantum computational advantage requires scaling to many qubits with high-precision control to exponentially surpass classical hardware and algorithmic advances. In this study, we introduce \textit{Zuchongzhi}, a two-dimensional programmable superconducting processor featuring 66 functional qubits arranged in a tunable coupling architecture. To evaluate the system's performance, we executed random quantum circuit sampling as a benchmark on up to 56 qubits across 20 cycles. The classical computational cost for this task is estimated to be 2–3 orders of magnitude greater than that of the previous 53-qubit Sycamore processor [Nature \textbf{574}, 505 (2019)]. We project that the sampling task completed by \textit{Zuchongzhi} in approximately 1.2 hours would require the most powerful supercomputer at least 8 years to finish. This work demonstrates a clear quantum computational advantage that is practically impossible for classical systems to achieve within a reasonable timeframe. Furthermore, this high-precision, programmable platform provides a new avenue for investigating novel many-body phenomena and executing complex quantum algorithms.

We present a specific subclass of weighted automata defined over the rationals, termed image-binary automata. These automata recognize regular languages, achieve exponential succinctness compared to equivalent NFAs, and support polynomial-time operations for complementation, union, and intersection. This performance stands in contrast to unambiguous automata, where complementation incurs a superpolynomial increase in state count. Furthermore, we investigate the infinite-word variant, known as image-binary B\"uchi automata. Similar to unambiguous B\"uchi automata, these structures are suitable for probabilistic model checking. Additionally, we develop translation algorithms that convert $k$-ambiguous B\"uchi automata into image-binary B\"uchi automata, thereby enabling model-checking procedures with optimal computational complexity.

Controlling individual molecules is central to studying chemical reactivity at ultra-low temperatures. This study presents the first investigation into the formation of long-lived intermediates during the time-dependent scattering of cold $^{23}$Na$^{87}$Rb bialkali molecules, both with and without infrared trapping light. Over the approximately 50-nanosecond lifetime of the intermediate complex, we observe an unconventional roaming phenomenon where, for several tens of picoseconds, either NaRb or dissociated Na$_2$ and Rb$_2$ pairs with large separations form before recombining into the four-atom complex. Additionally, we quantify the probability of molecular loss when the trapping laser is active during the collision. Our findings indicate that at a wavelength of 1064 nm, the Na$_2$Rb$_2$ complex is rapidly destroyed, leading to the quick loss of $^{23}$Na$^{87}$Rb molecules.

A set of multipartite orthogonal product states exhibits strong nonlocality when it is locally irreducible across all bipartitions, demonstrating strong quantum nonlocality without entanglement. Since unextendible product bases (UPBs) are known to exhibit quantum nonlocality without entanglement, investigating their strong nonlocality is of significant interest. However, most UPBs with minimal sizes fail to display this strong form of nonlocality. In this work, we construct a series of UPBs with larger sizes in $d_A\otimes d_B\otimes d_C$ and $d_A\otimes d_B\otimes d_C\otimes d_D$ systems where $d_A, d_B, d_C, d_D\geq 3$, proving that these bases possess strong quantum nonlocality. This finding resolves an open question posed by Halder \emph{et al.} [Phys. Rev. Lett. \textbf{122}, 040403 (2019)] and Yuan \emph{et al.} [Phys. Rev. A \textbf{102}, 042228 (2020)] for any three- and four-partite systems. Additionally, we introduce an entanglement-assisted protocol for locally distinguishing the UPB in $3\otimes 3\otimes 4$, which utilizes fewer entanglement resources than the teleportation-based approach. These results establish a clear link between strong quantum nonlocality and UPBs.

Weakly Supervised Semantic Segmentation (WSSS) presents significant difficulties, especially when attempting to predict pixel-level details using only image-level labels. To bridge this gap, Class Activation Maps (CAMs) are typically generated to create pixel-level pseudo-labels; however, CAMs in Convolutional Neural Networks often suffer from partial activation, where only the most discriminative regions are highlighted. Conversely, Transformer-based methods excel at capturing global context through long-range dependency modeling, which may mitigate the "partial activation" problem. This paper introduces the first Transformer-based WSSS approach, featuring the Gradient-weighted Element-wise Transformer Attention Map (GETAM). GETAM provides fine-grained activation across all feature map elements, exposing various object components throughout transformer layers. Additionally, we propose an activation-aware label completion module to produce high-quality pseudo-labels. These techniques are integrated into a comprehensive end-to-end WSSS framework utilizing double backward propagation. Extensive experiments on the PASCAL VOC and COCO datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art end-to-end approaches and surpasses most multi-stage methods.

We investigate an early dark energy (EDE) model formulated as a K-essence scalar field within the FLRW cosmological framework. This approach employs an effective state equation parametrized by redshift $z$, satisfying tracker conditions during radiation domination while ensuring late-time accelerated expansion akin to a cosmological constant. We derive all dynamical variables for the EDE system, utilizing Type Ia supernova luminosity distances to optimize the model's free parameters. Additionally, we constrain the model using Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) predictions for light nuclear abundances, summarizing the requisite conditions to simultaneously achieve BBN consistency and late-time cosmic acceleration.

This paper addresses the challenge of minimizing a large sum of smooth convex functions under numerous constraints imposed by potentially non-smooth convex functions, a problem prevalent in fields like machine learning and signal processing. We introduce a novel Random Projection Method (RPM) designed to solve this problem efficiently. Our approach integrates two key algorithmic innovations. First, rather than projecting onto a subset of the feasible region at each step, we employ a relaxed projection onto a half-space approximation, which yields a closed-form formula and substantially lowers computational costs per iteration. Second, leveraging the structure of the objective as a sum of convex functions, we incorporate variance reduction techniques to enhance empirical convergence. Theoretically, under an error bound condition and other standard assumptions, we demonstrate that the algorithm almost surely converges to an optimal solution, with the optimality gap decreasing at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{K})$ and the feasibility gap at $\mathcal{O}(\log(K)/K)$. Additionally, we establish that the error bound condition holds under mild assumptions, a result of independent interest. Finally, numerical experiments on synthetic instances illustrate the practical efficacy of the variance reduction technique and the superiority of our proposed RPM compared to two existing methods.

While it is established that flat systems can be linearized through quasi-static feedback of generalized states, the possibility of achieving this via quasi-static feedback of classical states remains an open question, despite its significant practical value for controller design. This paper demonstrates that for $(x,u)$-flat systems, such a linearizing feedback always exists and offers a systematic method for its construction. Furthermore, since exact linearization often serves merely as an intermediate stage in flatness-based tracking control, we also illustrate how the tracking error dynamics can be stabilized using feedback of the classical state rather than a generalized one.

Mathematical modeling of a three-tiered food web involved in anaerobic chlorophenol mineralization indicates that specific ecological interactions—namely competition, syntrophy, and product inhibition—give rise to complex dynamical behaviors. Earlier numerical studies suggested that a Hopf bifurcation could occur at an interior equilibrium point, noting that external substrate inputs can both suppress periodic solutions and broaden the stable positive steady state associated with complete mineralization. This study extends those findings to a generalized model, demonstrating that the introduction of multiple substrates increases dynamical complexity and confirms a supercritical Hopf bifurcation driven by changes in operational parameters. Additionally, numerical estimates reveal that fluctuations in the dilution rate can induce Bogdanov-Takens and Bautin bifurcations. Finally, by applying persistence theory across various parameter sets, we establish unique persistence scenarios when chlorophenol and hydrogen are externally added to the system, a finding that aligns with recent applied research emphasizing hydrogen's role in sustaining stable anaerobic microbial communities.
