We provide mathematical justification for this framework and demonstrate that, under this new phase space, the system exhibits critical behavior and mimics a Van der Waals fluid when the cosmological constant (treated as pressure) is held constant while the charge varies. We derive the system's Gibbs free energy, identifying a swallow-tail structure in the Gibbs diagrams that signifies a first-order phase transition. Furthermore, our calculation of critical exponents reveals that although thermodynamic quantities rely on metric parameters such as $z$, $p$, and $n$, the critical exponents themselves remain identical to those of the Van der Waals fluid-gas system. This alternative perspective on the phase space of Lifshitz dilaton black holes is intuitively understandable, as it can be visualized as a single black hole acquiring charge to induce a phase transition. These findings further corroborate the viewpoint proposed in \cite{Dehy}.

The density matrix framework serves as a cornerstone for investigating numerous issues in quantum information processing. Within this framework, the Hilbert-Schmidt and Bures-Hall ensembles stand out as the most prominent and physically significant measures. This study introduces a generalized ensemble of density matrices, called the quantum interpolating ensemble, which bridges the gap between these two distinct ensembles. To elucidate the characteristics of this new ensemble, we derive exact analytical expressions for the mean entanglement entropies, thereby extending several recent findings. Additionally, we examine essential properties of the associated orthogonal polynomials, which are crucial for extracting further statistical data regarding the entropies. Numerical simulations confirm the practical utility of this proposed ensemble in assessing the entanglement levels of quantum states.
We provide a complete classification of codimension one distributions of degree $2$ on $\mathbb{P}^3$ based on the invariants of their associated tangent sheaves.

MAGIC's recent observation of blazar 3C279 has validated earlier hints from H.E.S.S., suggesting that the cosmos is more permeable to very-high-energy gamma rays than previously believed. This finding aligns with data from nearby blazars if photons convert into ultra-light Axion-Like Particles within extragalactic magnetic fields. The resulting "DARMA scenario" is poised for near-future verification through the Fermi LAT satellite and ground-based instruments, including the Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov Telescopes H.E.S.S., MAGIC, CANGAROO III, and VERITAS, as well as the Extensive Air Shower arrays ARGO-YBJ and MILAGRO.

Let $\mathcal{H}_{k,g}$ denote the Hurwitz stack that parametrizes degree $k$, genus $g$ covers of $\mathbb{P}^1$. We introduce the tautological ring for $\mathcal{H}_{k,g}$ and demonstrate that, for $k \leq 5$, every Chow class is tautological up to codimension approximately $g/k$, with the possible exception of classes supported on the locus of "factoring covers." The framework established in this work underpins our subsequent research, where we derive new findings regarding the structure of the Chow ring for $k \leq 5$.

This research employs a deep learning strategy to reconstruct high-resolution turbulent flow fields from sparse data. The proposed model utilizes a multi-scale enhanced super-resolution generative adversarial network (GAN) integrated with a physics-based loss function. Its capability to generate high-resolution laminar flows was first validated using data from flow around a square cylinder, demonstrating accurate reconstruction even with limited spatial inputs. Subsequently, the model's performance in handling wall-bounded turbulent flows was evaluated using turbulent channel flow data. The instantaneous and statistical outcomes aligned closely with ground truth data, confirming the model's ability to effectively map coarse inputs to high-resolution outputs. Additionally, a careful analysis revealed that the computational cost remains low. These findings indicate that physics-guided GAN models trained on high-fidelity data offer a practical and efficient solution for reconstructing detailed turbulent flow fields from extremely coarse datasets.

This paper reviews pseudo-complex General Relativity (pc-GR), focusing primarily on its observational implications. It begins by justifying the choice of an algebraic extension and demonstrating the viability of the pseudo-complex approach, followed by the formulation of pc-GR. Subsequently, various observational consequences are examined, including the perihelion shift of Mercury, Quasi Periodic Objects, accretion disc emission profiles, the pc-Robertson-Walker cosmological model, neutron stars, and the gravitational ring-down modes of black holes.

This study introduces NeuMap, an end-to-end neural approach for camera localization that encodes entire scenes into latent code grids. A Transformer-based auto-decoder then utilizes these codes to regress the 3D coordinates of query pixels. Unlike state-of-the-art methods that rely on storing gigabytes of per-point features for each scene as 3D point clouds—and suffer significant performance degradation under compression—NeuMap achieves extreme compression with minimal accuracy loss. This is accomplished through two key components: learnable latent codes for scene storage and a scene-agnostic Transformer auto-decoder for coordinate inference. The scene-agnostic architecture, trained on large-scale data, learns robust matching priors, allowing the network weights to remain fixed while optimizing codes rapidly for new scenes. Extensive testing across five benchmarks demonstrates that NeuMap significantly outperforms existing coordinate regression methods and matches the performance of feature matching approaches while drastically reducing scene representation size. For instance, on the Aachen Night benchmark, NeuMap attains 39.1% accuracy using only 6MB of data, whereas other methods require 100MB to several gigabytes and often fail under high compression. The project code is accessible at https://github.com/Tangshitao/NeuMap.

Elastic turbulence (ET) is a chaotic flow phenomenon found in dilute polymer solutions without inertia, first identified experimentally in curved settings. It was previously believed that inducing ET in parallel flows necessitated a finite amplitude perturbation to create streamline curvature. This study demonstrates, however, that self-sustaining ET can arise from a linear instability within inertialess planar Couette flow, a configuration formerly thought to be stable against all initial disturbances. This novel linear instability stems from finite polymer diffusivity and persists across a broad spectrum of realistic parameters and various boundary conditions for the polymer conformation tensor. Numerical simulations reveal that this instability produces a three-dimensional, self-sustaining chaotic state, representing what appears to be the first numerical evidence of ET in a parallel flow.

In this study, we synthesized Cs$_2$LiRuCl$_6$ for the first time and determined its crystal structure alongside an investigation of its magnetic properties. The material adopts a hexagonal lattice formed by linear chains of face-sharing RuCl$_6$ and LiCl$_6$ octahedra. Within two-thirds of these chains, Ru$^{3+}$ and Li$^+$ sites exhibit near-perfect order, whereas the remaining chains display site disorder, a configuration analogous to the ground state of an antiferromagnetic Ising model on a triangular lattice. Electron paramagnetic resonance measurements yielded $g$ factors for the effective spin-1/2 Ru$^{3+}$ ions of $g_c\,{=}\,2.72$ and $g_{ab}\,{=}\,1.50$ for magnetic fields aligned parallel and perpendicular to the $c$ axis, respectively. The magnetization curves show strong anisotropy for both $H\,{\parallel}\,c$ and $H\,{\perp}\,c$, yet they align closely when normalized by their respective $g$ factors. Analysis of magnetization and specific heat data indicates that Cs$_2$LiRuCl$_6$ behaves as a coupled one-dimensional $S\,{=}\,1/2$ Heisenberg-like antiferromagnet with an exchange constant of $J/k_{\rm B}\,{\simeq}\,3.7$ K. Long-range three-dimensional magnetic ordering emerges at $T_{\rm N}\,{=}\,0.48$ K, and a magnetic phase diagram corresponding to $H\,{\parallel}\,c$ is provided.

The "Bargmann framework" enables the demonstration of equivalence between the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator and a spin-zero particle subjected to a circularly polarized periodic gravitational wave. By extending the symmetries of this latter system—which encompass Carroll symmetry—we obtain conserved charges for the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator.

We introduce two novel algorithms, FedDR and asyncFedDR, designed to address a fundamental nonconvex composite optimization problem within federated learning. These methods integrate a new approach combining nonconvex Douglas-Rachford splitting, randomized block-coordinate techniques, and asynchronous execution, while remaining capable of handling convex regularizers. In contrast to recent literature methods such as FedSplit and FedPD, our algorithms update only a subset of users per communication round, potentially asynchronously, thereby enhancing practicality. They effectively manage statistical and system heterogeneity—the two primary challenges in federated learning—while attaining the best known communication complexity. Specifically, under standard assumptions, our algorithms achieve a communication complexity that matches the theoretical lower bound up to a constant factor. Furthermore, numerical experiments on both synthetic and real datasets demonstrate the superiority of our methods over existing algorithms.

A previous publication by the author inquired whether a one-dimensional space $X$, which is not almost zero-dimensional, could exist such that its hyperspace of compact subsets also possesses one-dimensional dimension. In this brief note, we present examples of spaces $X$ that are neither almost zero-dimensional nor one-dimensional, yet whose hyperspaces of compact subsets are likewise one-dimensional.

We experimentally investigate the behavior of long waves within a turbulent regime of bending waves in a thin elastic plate, driven by monochromatic forcing at a frequency $f_0$ significantly higher than the characteristic bending wave frequencies. This condition establishes a range of conservative scales for $f<f_0$, where the average energy flux is zero. In this regime, we observe a flat power density spectrum for the orthogonal velocity, indicating energy equipartition across modes. Consequently, the average energy per mode, $\beta^{-1}$—which serves as an analog to temperature—completely characterizes the large-scale turbulent wave field. We provide a formula for $\beta$ dependent on the forcing frequency and amplitude, as well as the properties of the plate.

We introduce nBIIG, a neural system designed to generate Business Intelligence (BI) insights. The system processes a given table by performing diverse analyses to produce corresponding RDF representations, which a neural model then converts into fluent textual insights. These insights assist analysts through a human-in-the-loop approach, enhancing the creation of compelling table reports. The underlying generative neural model is trained on extensive, carefully distilled data curated from multiple BI domains. Consequently, the system can produce faithful and fluent insights for open-domain tables, ensuring its practicality and utility.

Machine learning models have become a cornerstone of modern indoor positioning systems due to their superior ability to extract meaningful environmental data. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are among the most prevalent neural networks because they excel at identifying complex patterns within input data. Another widely utilized approach in indoor positioning is the Extreme Learning Machine (ELM), which offers rapid learning speeds alongside satisfactory generalization performance. This paper introduces a lightweight integration of CNNs and ELMs designed to deliver fast and accurate classification of buildings and floors, specifically optimizing for devices with limited power and resources. Consequently, the proposed model achieves a 58% speed improvement over the benchmark while maintaining classification accuracy with a marginal gain of less than 1%.

This study presents a theoretical investigation into the photovoltaic Hall effect, specifically transverse photoconductivity driven by circularly polarized radiation, as well as linearly polarized radiation inducing intraband optical transitions within a two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG). We establish a microscopic framework for these phenomena by analytically solving the Boltzmann equation for arbitrary electron spectra and scattering mechanisms. Calculations of transverse photoconductivity are performed for 2DEGs exhibiting both parabolic and linear dispersion relations, considering short-range and Coulomb scatterers across various temperatures. Our findings indicate that transverse electric current is markedly amplified at frequencies near the inverse energy relaxation time; however, at higher frequencies, both the excitation spectrum and current direction become dependent on the specific scattering mechanism. Additionally, we examine how thermalization processes arising from electron-electron collisions influence photoconductivity.

Modeling thematic fit, a task involving verb-argument compositional semantics, typically demands extensive labeled datasets. This study substitutes layers in a linguistically annotated large corpus with outputs from superior, modern taggers. Using a high-performing neural method, we evaluate how these updated corpus versions affect verb-argument fit modeling. Our findings indicate that enhanced annotation quality significantly lowers data requirements while improving supervised predicate-argument classification. However, when applying the model to psycholinguistic tasks beyond the training goal, we observe clear improvements at scale in only one of two thematic fit estimation tasks, with no significant gains in the other. Additionally, while quality generally improves with larger training sets, it may plateau or even decline in specific tasks. We also examined the impact of role set size. Collectively, these results suggest that the interplay between data quality and quantity is insufficient on its own. We replicate prior research with modifications to certain role representation details, establishing a new state-of-the-art in event modeling using a fraction of the original data, and we release the updated corpus publicly.

Entity information networks are utilized to depict structural connections between entities, and their adaptability to heterogeneity and extensibility has led to increasing applications in relationship modeling. Although numerous studies on entity information network modeling have emerged recently, few address equipment-standard systems characterized by multi-layer, multi-dimensional, and multi-scale properties. To effectively handle complex challenges within such systems—including standard revision, control, and production design—this paper introduces a heterogeneous information network model specifically for equipment-standard systems. The proposed framework incorporates three entity types and six relationship types, employing various similarity-measuring methods during the modeling process. Experimental results demonstrate that this model accurately captures entity relationships and exhibits efficient time performance.

We have developed a framework for evaluating subscription-based businesses using a unified metric known as SCV (Single Customer Value). A key advancement in this paper is modeling customer churn as an exponential decay variable, a structure derived directly from experimental data within the subscription sector. Utilizing a Bayesian probabilistic model, we calculated the expected revenue contribution of an individual user. Our approach yields an exact closed-form solution for the constant churn model and an approximate closed-form solution for the exponential decay model. Furthermore, we outline a general methodology for decision-making through the sensitivity analysis of the model equations, demonstrated via a real-world case study of a food subscription business.

Self-supervised vision transformers have recently garnered significant attention due to their exceptional representation learning capabilities. However, the prevailing approach, contrastive learning, predominantly depends on instance discrimination to achieve a global understanding of images. This study introduces Reconstructive Pre-training (RePre), which integrates local feature learning into self-supervised vision transformers by augmenting contrastive frameworks with a parallel branch dedicated to reconstructing raw image pixels. RePre utilizes a lightweight convolutional decoder to fuse multi-hierarchy features from the transformer encoder, providing rich supervisory signals ranging from low-level to high-level semantics that are essential for the model's performance. The results demonstrate that RePre yields substantial improvements across various contrastive frameworks and transformer architectures, achieving downstream transfer performance that surpasses both supervised pre-training and current state-of-the-art self-supervised methods.

Accurate and early diagnosis of parkinsonian syndromes is essential for delivering proper patient care and facilitating participation in therapeutic trials. The midbrain's red nucleus plays a pivotal role in these conditions and can be visualized using iron-sensitive MRI sequences. By leveraging various iron-sensitive contrasts, researchers can generate different MRI data types; combining these multimodal datasets holds promise for enhancing the segmentation of the red nucleus. However, existing multimodal segmentation algorithms are often computationally intensive, struggle with missing modalities, and require annotations for every data type. This paper introduces a novel model that incorporates prior knowledge from diverse contrasts to segment the red nucleus. The methodology involves three primary stages: first, the image is decomposed into high-level structural information and low-frequency contrast information; second, a network processes the high-frequency data to extract anatomical features, while a separate module handles the list of multimodal low-frequency inputs; finally, feature fusion is executed to finalize the segmentation. The model was tested using several iron-sensitive contrasts, including iMag, QSM, R2*, and SWI. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method significantly outperforms a baseline UNet model, particularly when the training dataset is very small.

This study introduces a novel Adaptive-Robust Control (ARC) framework designed for a specific category of uncertain Euler-Lagrange (EL) systems, provided the uncertainty upper bound adheres to a linear-in-parameters (LIP) structure. Traditional ARC approaches typically depend on knowing the system's structure or assume that total uncertainties or their time derivatives are bounded by a constant value. However, unmodeled dynamics and modeling inaccuracies often make true structural knowledge unavailable. Furthermore, assuming a constant upper bound for uncertainties (or their derivatives) in this system class imposes premature restrictions on the states. Conventional ARC laws also suffer from the overestimation-underestimation issue regarding switching gains. To address these challenges, an Adaptive Switching-gain based Robust Control (ASRC) method is proposed, which resolves the switching gain overestimation-underestimation problem. Additionally, ASRC eliminates the need for assumptions about constant uncertainty bounds and handles uncertainties whether they are linear or nonlinear in parameters. Experimental validation using a wheeled mobile robot demonstrates that ASRC achieves superior control performance compared to adaptive sliding mode control.

This work investigates the algorithmic characteristics of first-order monomodal logics applied to frames such as $\langle \mathbb{N}, \leq \rangle$, $\langle \mathbb{N}, < \rangle$, $\langle \mathbb{Q}, \leq \rangle$, $\langle \mathbb{Q}, < \rangle$, $\langle \mathbb{R}, \leq \rangle$, and $\langle \mathbb{R}, < \rangle$, alongside related systems. The analysis focuses on languages constrained by the count of individual variables, as well as the quantity and arity of predicate symbols. We demonstrate that logics based on $\mathbb{N}$ are $\Pi^1_1$-hard—implying they are not recursively enumerable—when using two individual variables, one monadic predicate letter, and one propositional letter. Furthermore, we establish that the logics derived from $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}$ are $\Sigma^0_1$-hard under identical linguistic restrictions. Comparable findings are reported for several associated logics.

We enhance the $\ell^p(\mathbb Z^d)$-boundedness range for the integral $k$-spherical maximal functions originally defined by Magyar. Earlier optimal bounds for the complete $k$-spherical maximal function necessitated that the dimension $d$ increase at least cubically relative to the degree $k$. By merging concepts from our earlier research with recent breakthroughs in Weyl sum theory by Bourgain, Demeter, Guth, and Wooley, we lower this requirement to a quadratic relationship. Consequently, we establish improved bounds for the ergodic Waring–Goldbach problem.

Large-scale deep neural networks (DNNs), including convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have demonstrated remarkable success in audio classification due to their robust capacity and generalization capabilities. Nevertheless, training DNNs on low-resource tasks often leads to overfitting on limited data and the acquisition of excessive redundant information. To tackle this challenge, we propose employing the variational information bottleneck (VIB) method to curb overfitting and filter out irrelevant details. Our experiments were conducted on a 4-layer CNN, though the VIB framework is modular and can be readily integrated with various other state-of-the-art architectures. Evaluations across several audio datasets reveal that our approach substantially surpasses baseline methods, achieving over a 5.0% gain in classification accuracy under certain low-resource conditions.

This paper connects the stated skein modules of the Kauffman bracket to two distinct constructions of quantum representation spaces developed by Habiro and Van der Veen (with the second author). Leveraging this relationship, we derive a description of the classical limit for stated skein modules, establish both a quantum Van Kampen theorem and a quantum HNN extension theorem within this framework, and provide a novel characterization of the skein modules associated with mapping tori and link exteriors.

This study examines the existence and regularity of weak solutions to a one-dimensional parabolic differential equation featuring a non-constant Hölder continuous diffusion coefficient and a rough forcing term. These findings are directly applicable to the analysis of the one-dimensional Ericksen-Leslie model for nematic liquid crystals. The approach relies on the Hölder continuity of the diffusion coefficient, a property derived from physical considerations and the specific analysis of the Ericksen-Leslie system. Furthermore, the Hölder exponent of the solution is shown to depend explicitly on the Hölder exponent of the diffusion coefficient.

As the lattice spacing vanishes, we examine the dimer model on isoradial graphs subjected to singular $SL(N,\mathbb{C})$ gauge fields that remain flat except at specific punctures. We analyze the cluster expansion of this twisted dimer partition function and demonstrate its correspondence with the cluster expansion of the 2D Dirac partition function under the same gauge field, a quantity often identified as a tau function. This work reproduces and extends several calculations by Dubédat (J. Eur. Math. Soc. 21 (2019), no. 1, pp. 1-54). Specifically, we match the cluster expansions of both sides term-by-term, showing that each term consists of a specific holomorphic integral plus its conjugate. On the dimer side, we compute the expansion terms by leveraging exact lattice identities involving discrete exponential functions and the inverse Kasteleyn matrix. On the fermion side, the cluster expansion yields two new series representations for tau functions: one based on the Fuchsian representation and the other on the monodromy representation.

Dense active matter, whether in fluid or amorphous-solid states, has become a significant model for understanding dynamics within living cells and multicellular systems. Researchers developed an extension of the random first-order transition (RFOT) theory to incorporate activity by adding individual particle activity to the system's free energy, modeled as the potential energy of an active particle confined by a harmonic potential representing the surrounding medium. This active-RFOT framework successfully explained the variation in structural relaxation times within active glasses, as derived from simulations, in relation to activity parameters such as the active force magnitude ($f_0$) and its persistence time ($\tau_p$). However, notable discrepancies emerged under conditions of high activity (large $f_0$ and/or $\tau_p$). To address this, we extended the active-RFOT model for high-activity regimes by employing an activity-dependent harmonic confining potential, solved self-consistently. This enhanced model forecasts qualitative shifts in the high-activity regime that align with simulation outcomes in both three-dimensional and two-dimensional active glass models.

This work investigates acoustic wave propagation in the time domain when a micro-bubble, characterized by significantly lower mass density and bulk modulus than the surrounding vacuum, is present. The primary objective is to quantify the pressure generated in the immediate vicinity of the bubble (at a distance scaling with its radius). Our findings indicate that at this close range, the dominant field mimics the wave produced by a point-like obstacle, formally represented by a Dirac-like heterogeneity at the bubble's location, where the scattering coefficient reflects the contrast between the bubble and the background. Consequently, by adjusting the bubble's material properties, one can achieve a specific target pressure level. This capability is particularly relevant for acoustic cavitation applications, which require sufficient but controlled pressure to eliminate anomalies. The analysis relies on time-domain integral equations and asymptotic methods. A key aspect of this approach is how the disparate scales between the bubble and the background induce resonances, such as the Minnaert resonance, in the time-harmonic regime. These critical scales and resulting resonances are also evident in the time-domain estimates of the acoustic wave, highlighting that achieving the desired near-field pressure is feasible only through such resonating bubbles.

This study investigates the strong decay characteristics of higher excited heavy-light mesons, ranging from the first radially excited states to the first $F$-wave states, utilizing a constituent quark model. The analysis reveals that numerous missing excitations possess promising prospects for discovery in upcoming experiments due to their narrow widths; notably, several of these decay predominantly into first orbital excitations rather than ground states. Consequently, future observational efforts should prioritize decay channels leading not only to ground states but also to low-lying $P$-wave excitations with $J^P=0^+,1^+$. Additionally, the nature of the recently observed states $D_J(3000)$, $D_J^*(3000)$, and B(5970) is examined. It is predicted that $D_J(3000)$ acts as a partner to $D_{sJ}(3040)$, likely identified as the high-mass mixed state $|2{P_1}>_L$ ($J^P=1^+$) resulting from $2^1P_1$-$2^3P_1$ mixing. While the $D_J^*(3000)$ resonance appears to favor the $1^3F_4$ assignment, quantum numbers of $J^P=0^+$ and $2^+$ cannot be entirely ruled out, necessitating further experimental data to establish its $J^P$ values. Finally, the B(5970) resonance is most likely identified as the $1^3D_3$ state with $J^P=3^-$.

Vision-based formation control systems have recently gained significant interest from both researchers and industry practitioners due to their suitability for GPS-denied environments. However, ensuring safety in such systems remains challenging because of the absence of formal specifications for computer vision and the complex effects of estimation inaccuracies on distributed control. This paper proposes a safety assurance technique that integrates (1) the creation of a piecewise approximation for worst-case perception errors and (2) a classical Lyapunov-based safety analysis of the consensus control algorithm. This analysis establishes an ultimate bound on the relative distance between drones, which serves to guarantee safe separation among all units. We implemented a vision-based control system within the photo-realistic AirSim simulator. By constructing piecewise approximations for varying perception errors across different environments and weather conditions, we successfully validated the safe separation guarantees provided by our analysis under diverse weather scenarios using AirSim simulations.

This preprint, accepted for CICM 2020, introduces a dataset formalized in Isabelle/HOL to express and verify properties of graph trails. We establish reasoning for strictly increasing and decreasing trails within weighted graphs and prove lower bounds regarding trail lengths. This is achieved by extending the Isabelle/HOL graph theory library with an algorithm that calculates the length of the longest strictly decreasing trail from a given vertex for a specific weight distribution, alongside a proof demonstrating that any decreasing trail is inherently an increasing one.

Darkness-captured image frames present unique challenges; simply applying a constant multiplier fails to restore them because shot noise, quantization artifacts, and camera non-linearities result in poor color and luminance estimation. While existing techniques rely on learning mappings from real dark-bright pairs—which are difficult to acquire—recent research demonstrates that simulated data pairs yield tangible restoration improvements, likely due to the ease of generating vast datasets. This paper introduces a method where enforcing equivariance (ensuring a pixel's color remains consistent regardless of cropping) surpasses current state-of-the-art performance. Additionally, we demonstrate that incorporating a scale selection mechanism enhances reconstruction quality, and our approach effectively improves video restoration as well. The proposed methods are assessed through both quantitative and qualitative evaluations.

Functional datasets often rely on parametric templates to represent typical function shapes, yet these templates can introduce substantial bias, compromising their utility and interpretability. To address model misspecification, we enhance the parametric template with an infinite-dimensional nonparametric functional basis. These basis functions are derived from the data and constrained to be orthogonal to the parametric component, ensuring clear separation between the two terms. This orthogonality is crucial to avoid functional confounding, which would otherwise cause severe bias in the parametric estimates. The nonparametric factors are regularized using an ordered spike-and-slab prior, enabling consistent rank selection and satisfying various desirable theoretical properties. The method's flexibility is demonstrated through applications to synthetic data, human motor control data, and dynamic yield curve data. Compared to parametric and semiparametric alternatives, the proposed semiparametric functional factor model eliminates bias, reduces excessive posterior and predictive uncertainty, and offers reliable inference regarding the effective number of nonparametric terms, all with minimal added computational cost.

Recent multi-wavelength ALMA observations of the protoplanetary disk around Elias 2-27 have uncovered a two-armed spiral structure. Given the system's youth, the disk-to-star mass ratio derived from dust continuum data, and its spiral morphology, it serves as an ideal setting to study self-gravity's role in early star formation. This is significant because gravitational instabilities may be the primary mechanism for forming planetesimals and planets. In this Letter, we fit the rotation curve derived from CO data with a theoretical model incorporating both stellar and disk self-gravity contributions, comparing it against purely Keplerian and simple power-law models. Our analysis indicates that the rotation curve, particularly for the $^{13}$CO isotopologue, is best explained by including disk self-gravity alongside the star's influence. Consequently, we provide the first dynamical mass estimates for the system: a disk mass of $0.08\pm0.04\,M_{\odot}$ and a stellar mass of $0.46\pm0.03\,M_{\odot}$ (in the general case), with the latter aligning well with prior estimates. These values imply the disk comprises 17% of the star's mass, suggesting it is susceptible to gravitational instabilities, which strongly supports the hypothesis that the observed spiral arms were generated by such instabilities.

Beyond the Gnevyshev-Ohl rule (GOR), a relationship has been identified between odd and even cycles within the 22-year Hale solar cycle. Specifically, three years prior to the 11-year minimum ($m$), the relative sunspot number (SN) of an odd cycle exhibits a strong correlation with the peak of the following even cycle ($\rho=0.94$), whereas the link to the preceding even cycle is weaker. Similar to the GOR, cycles are paired, but this relationship opposes the traditional rule. Consequently, we propose using SN$_{m-3}$ from the descending phase of the previous odd cycle as a precursor for the subsequent EVEN cycle, designated as MI3E (Figure 3a); however, this method yields less reliable results when predicting odd cycles or ignoring parity, as noted in Braj\v{s}a et al. (2022). For forecasting the amplitude of an ODD cycle, we suggest using the seventh-year precursor to its maximum ($M$), termed MA7O -- SN$_{M-7}$ on the descending phase of the previous even cycle (Figure 3b). This approach also enables the prediction of years near the maximum with high accuracy ($\rho=0.90{-}0.94$). These methods facilitate the prediction of cycles regardless of parity. Based on these forecasts, Solar Cycle 25 is expected to reach a maximum of 154 units in 2023, with prediction errors of $\pm25$ (68% confidence) and $\pm53$ (95% confidence). In 2024, SN values are projected to remain nearly as high at 147 units, suggesting that with finer time averaging, the maximum will occur by the end of 2023.

Among various extended gravity frameworks, $f(R,T)$ gravity has attracted significant attention recently due to its promising cosmological outcomes. While logarithmic modifications in alternative gravity theories have been widely investigated, this study specifically introduces a logarithmic correction to the trace term $T$, defining the functional form as $f(R,T)=R + 16 \pi G \alpha \ln T$, where $\alpha$ represents a free parameter. By utilizing the dark energy density parameter $\Omega_{\Lambda}$ and the Hubble parameter $H_0$ to constrain $\alpha$, we determine a lower bound of $\alpha \ge - 9.93 \times 10^{-29}$. Furthermore, the cosmological implications of this model are analyzed.

Solar eruptive phenomena, including flares and coronal mass ejections, involve the swift release of energy, resulting in radiation across the electromagnetic spectrum and a sudden surge in particle kinetic energy. These events significantly impact space weather, making it essential to comprehend their origins, specifically the eruptive capacity of active regions (ARs). This study compares two distinct approaches previously used to analyze physical parameter variations during the pre-flare phase of flaring ARs: (i) the evolution of magnetic flux and the accumulation of magnetic helicity, and (ii) the fractal and multi-fractal characteristics of flux concentrations within ARs. The analysis utilizes photospheric time-series data from the Solar Dynamics Observatory spanning March 2011 to June 2013. Two separate AR samples were examined: one featuring high-energy M- and X-class flares capable of affecting both near-Earth space and the terrestrial environment, and another comprising regions with no flares or only minor C- and B-class events. The findings indicate that these two methods are complementary in evaluating AR eruptive potential and can be utilized to identify regions prone to flaring. Consequently, this case study suggests that combining multiple methodologies may enhance the reliable detection of AR eruptive potential and improve our understanding of pre-flare conditions.

We introduce a comprehensive framework, termed the "landscape," designed to map the space of Lorentz-invariant effective field theories applicable to any gauge symmetry and field configuration. Leveraging the amplitude-operator correspondence, we systematically develop various operator bases within this landscape to highlight distinct characteristics: operator independence (y-basis), flavor relations (p-basis), and conserved quantum numbers (j-basis). The transformation matrices connecting these bases reveal model-independent operator properties, including insights into their ultraviolet origins. We demonstrate this capability by analyzing dimension-9 operators pertinent to neutron-antineutron oscillation.

This paper outlines our methodologies for identifying hate speech targeting women and immigrants on Twitter within multilingual environments, specifically focusing on English and Spanish. Developed for SemEval-2019 Task 5, the challenge required participants to create algorithms capable of detecting such hate speech in these two languages with specified targets. Our approach integrates two deep neural networks—a Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) and a Character-level Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)—alongside a machine learning model that leverages linguistic features. Our proposed system achieved F1 scores of 57 and 75 for Task A in English and Spanish, respectively. For Task B, the scores were 67 for English and 75.33 for Spanish. Compared to baselines, Task A (Spanish) and Task B (both languages) saw F1 score improvements of 2, 10, and 5 points, respectively. Additionally, we introduce visually interpretable models to mitigate generalizability issues inherent in custom machine learning architectures by analyzing the annotated dataset.

We introduce a Hodge-theoretic invariant designed to quantify the potential violation of an Arakelov-type inequality in higher dimensions, which extends the classical Arakelov inequality applicable to regular quasi-projective curves. Our results demonstrate that for families of manifolds possessing an ample canonical bundle, this invariant remains uniformly bounded. Consequently, we prove that such families, regardless of the base dimension, satisfy the specified Arakelov inequality, thereby resolving a question posed by Viehweg.

We investigate whether a quantum channel can map one pair of quantum states to another. While quantum statistical comparison and relative majorization offer necessary and sufficient criteria for such a transformation, these conditions are often hard to verify practically. Drawing on Matsumoto's work, we relax the strict requirement by permitting small errors in the transformation. This approach yields a straightforward sufficient condition based on the one-shot relative entropies of the state pairs. In the asymptotic limit, where we examine sequences of state pairs under mild convergence assumptions, the quantum relative entropy emerges as the sole determinant for feasibility. Specifically, if the initial pair's relative entropy exceeds that of the target pair, a transformation with exponentially decreasing error is achievable; conversely, if the target's relative entropy is higher, any such transformation will exhibit an error that converges exponentially to one. Consequently, the rate of transforming state pairs is determined by the ratio of their respective relative entropies. We also explore applications within the resource theories of athermality and coherence.

The critical Burgers equation, expressed as $\partial_t u + u \partial_x u + \Lambda u = 0$, serves as a simplified model to examine the interplay between transport and diffusion concerning shock formation in fluids. It is established that smooth initial conditions do not lead to shocks within a finite timeframe. However, the long-term dynamics for "shock-like" initial data, defined by limits $u_0 \to \pm a$ as $x \to \mp \infty$, remain less understood. We characterize this asymptotic behavior within a broader framework of multidimensional critical scalar conservation laws, $\partial_t u + \text{div}f(u) + \Lambda u = 0$, assuming the initial data approaches limits at infinity. These long-time behaviors are described by specific self-similar solutions, the stability of which is proven using optimal diffusive rates.

Non-Hermitian topology has recently become a prominent area of research within condensed matter physics. In this study, we introduce a new interdisciplinary framework based on rock-paper-scissors (RPS) cycles from evolutionary game theory. By examining the topological characteristics of the associated payoff matrix, we demonstrate the appearance of an exceptional point and the skin effect. Additionally, our analysis of an RPS chain reveals remarkable dynamical behaviors, including the directed flow of population density through the bulk and a significant increase in population density specifically at the right boundary. These findings establish new pathways for advancing both non-Hermitian topology and evolutionary game theory.

Although a submarine traveling at relativistic horizontal speed appears to float in its own frame, it sinks within Earth's rest frame as a result of length contraction. By applying spacetime geometry and Lorentz transformations, we demonstrate that the resolution depends on how metric components transform between relatively moving reference frames. This approach eliminates reliance on prior assumptions regarding the transformation of Newtonian gravitational forces. Furthermore, our method of background Lorentz transformations is technically more straightforward than earlier treatments within general relativity. Additionally, we offer a fresh, intuitive explanation of the paradox and correct a previously erroneous expression for gravitational force attributed to Supplee that has been repeatedly cited in the literature.

This study investigates inverse reinforcement learning for autonomous navigation, utilizing distance and semantic category data. The primary goal is to derive a cost function that accounts for expert demonstrations, based solely on the expert's observations and state-control trajectories. We introduce a map encoder to predict semantic category probabilities from observation sequences and a cost encoder, implemented as a deep neural network processing these semantic features. Because the expert's cost function is not directly visible, model parameters are optimized by minimizing the discrepancy between demonstrated controls and a policy generated from the estimated cost. We propose a novel expert behavior model that facilitates error minimization through a closed-form subgradient calculated over a subset of promising states identified by a motion planning algorithm. This method enables the generalization of learned behaviors to novel environments with different spatial arrangements of semantic categories. We evaluate the various components of our model within a Minigrid environment and demonstrate its ability to learn adherence to traffic rules in the CARLA autonomous driving simulator by leveraging semantic observations of buildings, sidewalks, and road lanes.

This study investigates $Sp(4)$ gauge theory featuring two fundamental fermions within the framework of composite Goldstone Dark Matter. We report initial lattice findings regarding the mass of the pseudoscalar iso-singlet meson $\eta'$, utilizing unimproved Wilson fermions alongside the standard plaquette action. Our results indicate that the $\eta'$ mass is marginally higher than that of the non-singlet pseudoscalars $\pi$ yet lower than the vector mesons $\rho$, a trend observed across multiple ensembles where $m_\pi/m_\rho \geq 0.77$. Such a mass hierarchy holds potential significance for constructing models in physics beyond the Standard Model. Additionally, we demonstrate that for $N_f=1+1$ flavours, disconnected contributions to the unflavoured pseudoscalar $\pi^0$ are negligible. Complementing this, we calculate the $\pi\pi$ scattering length $a_0$, suggesting that the examined ensemble could be phenomenologically applicable to Dark Matter scenarios like the Strongly Interacting Massive Particles (SIMPs) paradigm.

We introduce a formulation and implementation of the DFT+$U$ method based on the linear combination of numerical atomic orbitals (NAO). This implementation facilitates not only single-point total energy and electronic structure calculations but also computes atomic forces and stresses, thereby enabling complete structural relaxations for periodic systems. Additionally, it supports non-collinear spin textures with self-consistent treatment of spin-orbit coupling (SOC). The core of our approach lies in defining the correlated subspace appropriately when multiple atomic orbitals share the same angular momentum; this is achieved through a "Mulliken charge projector" built from the most localized orbital within the $d/f$ angular momentum channel. The Hubbard $U$ and Hund $J$ parameters are estimated using a screened Coulomb potential of the Yukawa type, where the screening parameter is either selected semi-empirically or derived from the Thomas-Fermi screening model. Benchmark studies were conducted on four late transition metal monoxide bulk systems (MnO, FeO, CoO, NiO) and the 5$d$ compound IrO$_2$. For the monoxides, we evaluated the performance of our DFT+$U$ method regarding band gaps, magnetic moments, electronic band structures, forces, and stresses. For IrO$_2$, we assessed the efficacy of the DFT+$U$+SOC implementation. Systematic comparisons with experimental data and results from other implementation schemes confirm the validity of our NAO-based DFT+$U$ formalism and its practical application.

Creating robust control strategies to counter stealthy attacks is vital for modern cyber-physical systems. While designing anomaly detectors often relies on Gaussian noise models for simplicity, this assumption can cause the actual false alarm rate to far exceed expectations. We introduce a distributionally robust anomaly detector that operates within moment-based ambiguity sets for noise distributions. By employing generalized Chebyshev inequalities, we establish a detection threshold ensuring the true false alarm rate remains below a specified upper limit. Additionally, we demonstrate a critical trade-off between the worst-case false alarm rate and the vulnerability to stealthy attacks by efficiently calculating an outer ellipsoidal bound for the states reachable by an attacker under our robust threshold. A numerical example illustrates this trade-off, and the proposed method is compared against a conventional chi-squared detector.

Within a social group, members are designated as agents, any two of whom may engage in interaction. These interactions involve information exchange and incur an energy cost. Non-reducible subgroups of interacting agents exist, and the overall configuration of these interactions constitutes a macroscopic structure. Statistical equilibrium, achieved through microreversibility, is defined by the maximization of entropy alongside the minimization of energy costs associated with information transfer. This results in a structure equivalent to random cellular networks, as referenced by N. Rivier in *Physica* 23D (1986), pp. 129-137. We apply Rivier's methods to analyze agent social behavior. Furthermore, three empirically observed dependencies regarding personal radius in relation to various factors allow us to characterize the quantization that verifies information.

Automatically detecting human stress holds significant value for artificial intelligence agents operating within affective computing and human-computer interaction contexts. While stress and emotion are both affective states, stress notably influences how emotions are regulated and expressed. Despite the existence of various multimodal methods for stress detection, research into the underlying interdependence between stress and emotion remains limited. This study examines the potential of emotion recognition as an auxiliary task to enhance stress detection performance. We introduce MUSER, a transformer-based architecture coupled with a novel multi-task learning algorithm that employs a speed-based dynamic sampling strategy. Assessments on the Multimodal Stressed Emotion (MuSE) dataset demonstrate that our model effectively leverages both internal and external auxiliary tasks for stress detection, achieving state-of-the-art results.

PanGEA, the Panoramic Graph Environment Annotation toolkit, is a lightweight solution designed to gather speech and text annotations within photo-realistic 3D settings. By immersing annotators in a web-based simulation, PanGEA enables them to move freely while speaking and listening. The toolkit features integration with databases and cloud storage, along with utilities for automatically aligning recorded audio with manual transcriptions and annotator poses. Out of the box, it supports two primary tasks: collecting navigation instructions and following them. However, it is easily adaptable for other activities such as annotating walking tours, identifying and labeling landmarks or objects, and similar applications. Drawing from a 20,000-hour annotation project that produced the Room-Across-Room dataset, we share best practices gained through using PanGEA. We aim for our open-source toolkit and associated insights to accelerate future data collection and foster innovation in grounded language tasks supported by such environments.

The presence of mutually correlated, thin, rotating planes of satellite galaxies surrounding both the Milky Way (MW) and Andromeda (M31) demands an explanation. Prior research within Milgromian dynamics (MOND) suggested that a historical encounter between the MW and M31 could have generated these structures. This study presents the first hydrodynamical MOND simulation of the Local Group utilizing Phantom of RAMSES. We demonstrate that an MW-M31 collision at $z \approx 1$, featuring a perigalactic distance of roughly 80 kpc, can result in two disc galaxies at $z=0$ that align similarly to observed galactic discs and maintain a separation consistent with the current distance between M31 and the MW. Crucially, the tidal debris is distributed in phase space to resemble the observed satellite planes for both galaxies, exhibiting the correct preferred orbital poles. The resulting MW-M31 orbital geometry aligns with the currently observed proper motion of M31, even though this parameter was not explicitly constrained during the exploration of the parameter space. The mass of the tidal debris around the MW and M31 at $z=0$ closely matches the observed masses in their respective satellite systems. The remnant discs of both galaxies display realistic radial scale lengths and velocity dispersions, with the simulation naturally producing a significantly hotter stellar disc in M31 compared to the MW. However, aligning this scenario with the ages of stellar populations in satellite galaxies would necessitate either a higher fraction of stars originally formed in the outskirts of the progenitors migrating into the tidal debris, or that the MW-M31 interaction took place at $z>1$.

Denoting the 2-primary Steenrod algebra by $\mathbb A$, we define it as the algebra of stable natural endomorphisms of the mod 2 cohomology functor on topological spaces. Within algebraic topology, determining the cohomology of $\mathbb A$ at the prime 2 is a central problem, as this cohomology constitutes the initial page of the Adams spectral sequence that converges to the stable homotopy groups of spheres. A particularly effective method for characterizing this cohomology is the Singer algebraic transfer of rank $n$, detailed in [Math. Z. 202 (1989), 493-523]. This tool maps a specific subquotient of a divided power algebra into the cohomology of $\mathbb A$. Although Singer conjectured that this transfer acts as a monomorphism, the conjecture remains unproven for $n \geq 4$. This brief note confirms the conjecture for ranks 4 and 5, along with certain generic degrees.

This study introduces galactic magnetic dynamo models that are scale-invariant and self-similar, derived from classic equations, and qualitatively compares them with recent observations of magnetic fields in edge-on spiral galaxies. The axially symmetric dynamo magnetic field is categorized by its distinct sources: advected flux and sub-scale turbulence. Under plausible physical conditions, the diffusion term is disregarded. Time evolution is governed by globally conserved quantities. Our findings indicate that magnetic scale heights grow with both radius and wind velocity. We propose that AGN outflows play a crucial role in the large-scale galactic dynamo, driven by the dynamo action of increasing sub-scale vorticity. Consequently, we predict a correlation between the morphology of coherent galactic magnetic fields (specifically extended polarized flux) and the presence of an AGN.

This study presents the inaugural large-scale, data-driven assessment of various attributes' predictive capabilities regarding the risk of cyberattack data breaches. Driven by the swift escalation of third-party facilitated cyberattacks, it offers the first quantitative empirical proof that digital supply-chain characteristics are vital indicators of enterprise cyber risk. By utilizing external-in cyber risk scores intended to reflect the quality of internal cybersecurity management and enhancing them with supply chain features derived from observed third-party attack patterns and network science principles, the research demonstrates that supply chain network attributes significantly boost the detection power for predicting enterprise cyber risk compared to using enterprise-only metrics. Specifically, integrating these supply chain features into a base model relying solely on internal enterprise data increases the out-of-sample AUC by 2.3%. Given that cyber data breaches represent low-probability, high-impact events, these enhancements in predictive accuracy hold substantial value. Moreover, the model identifies several third-party cyberattack and breach mechanisms as key risk drivers, offering crucial insights into effective interventions for risk mitigation.

Feature extraction serves as an effective strategy for mitigating dimensionality challenges inherent in high-dimensional datasets. Given the recent surge in interest toward contrastive learning as a prominent self-supervised technique, this study introduces a unified framework grounded in a novel perspective of contrastive learning (CL), applicable to both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework initially establishes two distinct CL graphs to precisely define positive and negative pairs, followed by the determination of a projection matrix through the minimization of a contrastive loss function. Furthermore, the approach integrates both similar and dissimilar samples to harmonize unsupervised and supervised extraction processes. Specifically, the study proposes three methodologies: an unsupervised contrastive learning approach, along with two distinct supervised contrastive learning methods. Extensive numerical experiments conducted across five real-world datasets confirm that the proposed framework outperforms existing methods.

Intersection cohomology extends classical cohomology, enabling the application of Poincaré duality to a broad category of spaces referred to as stratified pseudomanifolds. A robust theoretical framework for deriving intersection cohomology involves classifying sheaves that adhere to the Deligne axioms. We establish an abstract formulation of these axioms and subsequently apply it within a simplicial complex setting, utilizing a category of simplicial sheaves inspired by the research of D. Chataur, D. Tanr\'e, and M. Saralegi-Araguren. By defining a specific topology on the triangulation of a stratified pseudomanifold, we identify a family of sheaves that satisfy the simplicial Deligne axioms, thereby providing a method to construct intersection cohomology from simplicial sheaves.

Parton distributions can be characterized by the entanglement entropy between the spatial region probed in deep inelastic scattering (DIS) and the remainder of the proton. At very small $x$, the proton approaches a state of maximal entanglement. This framework establishes a direct relationship, $S = \ln N$, linking the entropy of the resulting hadronic state ($S$) to the mean number of color-singlet dipoles ($N$) within the proton's wave function. In the small-$x$ regime, this dipole multiplicity corresponds to the gluon structure function, $N = xG(x,Q^2)$.

The H1 Collaboration recently investigated the entropy of the produced hadronic state in DIS and its connection to the gluon structure function, observing a significant discrepancy with the predicted relation. In this letter, we contend that a more precise description of the number of color-singlet dipoles for the H1 kinematics—specifically where hadrons are detected in the current fragmentation region—is provided by the sea quark structure function, $x\Sigma(x,Q^2)$, rather than $xG(x,Q^2)$. Although sea quarks arise from gluon splitting and thus $x\Sigma(x,Q^2)$ approximates $xG(x,Q^2)$ at small $x$, this proportionality is altered in the current fragmentation region due to the virtual photon's production of quark-antiquark pairs. Furthermore, the dipole multiplicity in this region is relatively low, necessitating $\sim 1/N$ corrections to the asymptotic formula $S = \ln N$. Incorporating both these adjustments demonstrates that the H1 data aligns well with the entanglement-based prediction.

In many practical scenarios, the true background model is inaccessible for foreground estimation, necessitating its derivation from cluttered image sequences. We introduce a sequential approach for static background estimation under these constraints, characterized by minimal computational and memory demands. The analysis proceeds block-by-block, maintaining a representative set of distinct blocks for each location along its temporal trajectory. Background estimation is performed within a Markov Random Field framework, where the optimal labeling is determined via iterated conditional modes. Clique potentials are derived from the combined frequency response of each candidate block and its neighborhood, operating on the assumption that the most suitable block yields the smoothest response, thereby implicitly enforcing spatial continuity of scene structures. Experiments on real-world surveillance footage demonstrate that the proposed method achieves significantly superior background estimates—both qualitatively and quantitatively—compared to median filtering and the recently introduced "intervals of stable intensity" technique. Additionally, tests on the Wallflower dataset indicate that integrating this method with a foreground segmentation algorithm enhances segmentation performance.

Although tidal disruption accretion (TDA) of stars by massive black holes (MBHs) in dense nuclear star clusters (NSCs) could significantly contribute to MBH growth, it has largely been neglected in favor of gas accretion (GA) in most numerical studies. This work incorporates a TDA growth channel into the high-resolution adaptive mesh refinement code Enzo to examine its impact on the early evolution of MBH seeds. Our results indicate that, in certain simulations, an MBH seed can rapidly increase from $10^3\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ to over $10^6\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ within 200 million years. While GA alone yields slower growth, TDA can accelerate this rate by more than an order of magnitude. However, TDA primarily drives early-stage expansion (from $10^{3-4}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ to $\lesssim10^{5}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$), with GA dominating the subsequent evolution. Additionally, we observed that active TDA suppresses nearby star formation, occasionally creating a gas cavity spanning a few parsecs. This occurs because rapid MBH growth via both mechanisms allows the black hole to consume surrounding gas faster than inflows can replenish it. Ultimately, this study highlights the necessity of accounting for diverse accretion channels to better understand the origins of supermassive black holes at high redshifts.

This study demonstrates that large pre-trained language models possess an innate ability to detect label errors in natural language datasets. Specifically, analyzing out-of-sample data points sorted by fine-tuned task loss in descending order significantly surpasses the performance of more intricate error-detection strategies introduced in prior research. To facilitate this, we propose a new approach for injecting realistic, human-generated label noise into established crowdsourced datasets like SNLI and TweetNLP. Our findings indicate that this type of noise mirrors the characteristics of genuine, manually verified errors and is more difficult to identify than current synthetic noise, thereby posing greater challenges for model robustness. Consequently, we contend that human-originated noise serves as a superior benchmark for evaluation compared to synthetic alternatives. Furthermore, by employing crowdsourced verification to assess real error detection on the IMDB, Amazon Reviews, and Recon datasets, we confirm that pre-trained models achieve an absolute Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve that is 9–36% higher than that of existing models.

We present a method capable of efficiently learning distributions over articulation model parameters directly from depth images, eliminating the requirement for prior knowledge of articulation categories. Unlike existing approaches that derive articulation models from raw observations by merely predicting point estimates—which often fail to ensure safe manipulation of articulated objects—our solution offers a more robust framework. Our primary contributions include a new representation for distributions over rigid body transformations and articulation parameters, grounded in screw theory, von Mises-Fisher distributions, and Stiefel manifolds. This combination yields an efficient and mathematically rigorous representation that inherently satisfies the geometric constraints of rigid transformations and articulations. Utilizing this framework, we developed DUST-net, a novel deep learning approach that performs category-independent articulation model estimation while quantifying model uncertainties. We validated our method on multiple benchmark datasets and real-world objects, comparing it against two state-of-the-art techniques. Our results demonstrate that DUST-net successfully learns articulation model distributions for novel objects across various categories, generating point estimates with superior accuracy compared to existing methods and effectively capturing parameter uncertainty arising from noisy inputs. Project webpage: https://pearl-utexas.github.io/DUST-net/

Observing young stellar objects is crucial for validating theories of planet formation. PDS 70 stands out as a rare system with strong evidence for two planetary-mass companions located within the gap of its transition disk. These planets are thought to be in their final accretion phase, drawing material from the protoplanetary disk via a circumplanetary disk (CPD). This study aims to construct a three-dimensional radiative transfer model for the dust component of the PDS 70 system that reproduces global features observed at 855 $\mu\, \mathrm{m}$ using ALMA and 1.25 $\mu\, \mathrm{m}$ using VLT/SPHERE. By iteratively adjusting protoplanetary disk properties until the model matches both datasets, we investigate the physical characteristics of companion PDS 70 c and its potential CPD. The resulting model jointly explains the system's appearance in submillimeter and polarized-scattered light, indicating spatial dust segregation within the protoplanetary disk. Furthermore, submillimeter modeling of PDS 70 c supports the existence of an optically thick CPD with a dust mass upper limit of 0.7 $M_\oplus$. Analysis of the CPD's thermal structure reveals that planet luminosity is the primary heat source for dust within 0.6 au, whereas stellar photons dominate heating at greater distances.

Utilizing the small amplitude expansion, an entropy current was recently developed for the horizons of dynamical black holes within any higher-derivative theory of gravity. This note dualizes that horizon current into a boundary counterpart for asymptotically AdS black holes, where the dual description involves dynamical fluids on the AdS boundary. This boundary current is derived through mapping functions that correspond each horizon point to a specific boundary point. When applied to Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet black holes, we find that up to the first order in the derivative expansion, Gauss-Bonnet terms introduce no additional corrections to fluid entropy, as anticipated. However, at the second order, the boundary current non-trivially depends on the specific choice of the horizon-to-boundary map, which cannot always be fully expressed via fluid variables. Consequently, the boundary entropy current resulting from this dualization generally lacks a fluid dynamical description.

A complex algebraic surface $S$ qualifies as a $\mathbb{Q}$-homology plane if $H_{i}(S,\mathbb{Q})=0$ for all $i>0$. Palka's Negativity Conjecture posits that $\kappa(K_{X}+\tfrac{1}{2}D)=-\infty$, where $(X,D)$ represents a log smooth completion of $S$. This work provides a comprehensive characterization of smooth $\mathbb{Q}$-homology planes that meet the criteria of the Negativity Conjecture, focusing specifically on those of log general type, as the geometry of others is already established. It is demonstrated, aligning with the conjectures of tom Dieck and Petrie, that these surfaces form a finite number of discrete series, each generated uniformly from line and conic arrangements on $\mathbb{P}^{2}$. Consequently, it is deduced that these surfaces satisfy both the Rigidity Conjecture proposed by Flenner and Zaidenberg and a conjecture by Koras stating that the number of automorphisms of $S$ is at most 6.

This paper introduces a Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework based on Risk-Averse Priced Timed Automata (PTA) to enhance the flexibility of cyber-physical systems. To achieve greater flexibility, our risk-averse approach addresses a multi-objective optimization problem that concurrently minimizes both cost and risk. While cost minimization reduces the effort required to complete a task, risk minimization ensures task feasibility even under uncertain conditions. By navigating the trade-off between these two objectives, our framework generates risk-averse control actions. Furthermore, the dynamic decision-making algorithm of the proposed risk-averse PTA MPC demonstrates a more responsive reaction to PTA changes compared to traditional PTA MPC lacking risk-averse capabilities. A manufacturing system case study is provided to illustrate the application of this control strategy.

This study investigates how dissipation-assisted operator evolution (DAOE) influences the scaling of transport in one-dimensional spin chains using non-equilibrium steady states. We analyze three XXZ family models: the chaotic XXZ model with staggered anisotropy; the Bethe ansatz integrable XXZ model (which is free fermion integrable at zero interaction and lacks an external field); and the free-fermion integrable, Anderson localized disordered XY model. Our results indicate that DAOE's impact on transport is governed by its influence on the system's conserved quantities. Specifically, if DAOE maintains these symmetries, the transport scaling remains unchanged; however, when DAOE breaks these conserved quantities, the system transitions toward diffusive transport scaling.

Recent initiatives have effectively leveraged satellite imagery and alternative data sources to map welfare accurately in data-scarce areas. However, existing research has primarily concentrated on forecasting asset indices, a type of welfare measure that is largely unaffected by short-term fluctuations in well-being. We propose that predicting more volatile indicators, such as consumption expenditure, would see substantial improvements by integrating high-frequency data sources. Specifically, incorporating daily weather data into our models significantly enhances the accuracy of consumption predictions compared to approaches relying solely on satellite imagery.

Early lightcurves of Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) offer a means to evaluate predictions regarding their progenitor systems. In the single-degenerate scenario, where a white dwarf accretes from a Roche-lobe-overflowing non-degenerate companion, the resulting ejecta-companion collision should generate shock heating and an early ultraviolet (UV) excess. However, this signature is only visible when the viewing angle is favorable, occurring in roughly 10% of cases. By modeling the 2018 ZTF sample of 127 SNe Ia with companion-shocking simulations, we recovered an early excess rate of $12.0\pm3.6\%$. This finding aligns with rates derived from other literature and supports the hypothesis that SNe Ia primarily arise from single-degenerate systems. Furthermore, we detected early excesses exclusively in spectroscopically normal SNe Ia, contradicting previous claims that they are more common in overluminous events. We also demonstrate that the detection of these excesses depends on methodology. Consequently, we advocate for high-cadence, multiwavelength early observations of large SNe Ia samples to statistically test progenitor model predictions, alongside improvements to current modeling techniques.

We develop a family of embedded pairs designed for optimal strong stability preserving (SSP) explicit Runge-Kutta methods of orders $2 \leq p \leq 4$, intended for solving spatially discretized hyperbolic PDEs. This construction prioritizes non-defective methods, a large region of absolute stability, and optimal error metrics as outlined in [5,19]. The resulting embedded pairs enable SSP methods to dynamically adjust step-sizes based on local error estimates without compromising their intrinsic nonlinear stability. Numerical experiments evaluate the overall efficacy of these methods, balancing precision against computational cost while accounting for both accuracy and stability.

Successful innovations expand geographically by spreading across various settlements and distances. For many decades, spatial diffusion has been theorized to follow an urban hierarchy, moving from major cities to medium-sized ones, and subsequently to smaller towns. However, the influence of geographical distance, a key component of diffusion, remained elusive in hierarchical models due to a lack of data on specific spreading events. This study utilizes spatial patterns of individual invitations on a social media platform, tracking communications from registered to new users throughout the platform's entire lifespan. This approach allows us to separate the effects of urban hierarchy from those of distance by analyzing the origin and destination of these flows across an extensive timescale. We show that hierarchical diffusion largely coincides with diffusion over short distances, and these factors evolve together over time, necessitating a joint analysis. Subsequently, a regression model estimates the number of invitations exchanged between town pairs annually, incorporating population sizes of source and target towns, their combinations, and the distance separating them. Our findings confirm that while hierarchical diffusion initially dominates among large towns, it expands to include all settlement sizes during the middle phase of the life cycle as adoption accelerates. Contrary to previous gravity models, we observe that after distance plays an intensifying role in the middle stage, its effect surprisingly weakens in the final years of diffusion. Ultimately, our results underscore the primacy of urban hierarchy in spatial diffusion and provide insights for forecasting local innovation adoption.

This study examines characteristics of heavy-tailed Sibuya-like distributions concerning thinning, self-decomposability, and branching processes. By extending the thinning operation for non-negative integer-valued random variables to scaling by arbitrary positive numbers, we define a novel class of probability distributions. These distributions feature a generating function $Q(w)$ representable as a Laplace transform $\varphi(1-w)$ and a probability mass function $p_n$ that follows a straightforward one-step recurrence relation between $p_{n+1}$ and $p_n$. We demonstrate that both the compound Poisson-Sibuya and shifted Sibuya distributions fall within this class. Leveraging the shared Markov property in stationary solutions of birth and death equations, we identify the Sibuya distribution and its variants as specific solutions to these equations. Furthermore, we determine the conditions under which a non-negative integer-valued heavy-tailed random variable possesses a finite $r$-th absolute moment for $0 < r < a < 1$.

This study details microscopic simulations of high-energy cosmic-ray air showers penetrating high-altitude ice layers typical of polar regions. By integrating the CORSIKA Monte Carlo code with the Geant4 simulation toolkit, we focus on the particle cascade within the ice to characterize its key features. We analyze how the ice layer affects the total particle count as a function of shower depth and provide a general parameterization of the charge distribution in the cascade front relative to the air shower's Xmax, facilitating analytical and semi-analytical calculations of expected Askaryan radio emission. Our results demonstrate that the shower core dominates propagation through the ice, creating an in-ice cascade that closely resembles a neutrino-induced one. Furthermore, we present findings from microscopic simulations of the Askaryan radio emission, confirming that emission is core-dominated, and we discuss the feasibility of detecting the plasma generated by this cascade in ice using RADAR echo techniques.

Healthcare practitioners utilize treatment search engines to locate suitable clinical trials and early access programs for their patients efficiently. Nevertheless, trust in these systems diminishes when their internal mechanisms remain opaque and unexplained. This paper introduces a model-agnostic explainable framework designed to clarify the rationale behind specific clinical trial retrievals in response to queries. To achieve this, the engine extracts features from clinical trials by integrating knowledge graphs, trial data, and supplementary medical resources, while a crowdsourcing approach is employed to assess feature importance. Based on this methodology, the reasoning for retrieval is articulated in accessible language, enabling healthcare professionals to easily comprehend it. Furthermore, an explainability score is calculated for each retrieved item to facilitate ranking. Validation through experiments with medical professionals indicates that the proposed approach fosters trust among both targeted and non-targeted users, offering them reliable explanations and item rankings.

This study examines self-consistent ambipolar charge kinetics at a negatively biased semiconductor-plasma interface. Focusing on a thin germanium layer featuring nonpolar electron-phonon scattering, situated between an Ohmic contact and a collisionless argon plasma, we computed the current-voltage characteristics. The results demonstrate that these characteristics are influenced by the semiconductor's electron microphysics. Furthermore, we derived spatially and energetically resolved fluxes and charge distributions within the layer to visualize the charge carriers driving transport. Although the findings are not strictly quantitative due to simplified modeling of the germanium band structure and the omission of non-conserving scattering mechanisms—such as impact ionization and electron-hole recombination, which are significant at the relevant energies—the results clearly establish two points: (i) the interface current is transported by relatively hot carriers, and (ii) the perfect absorber model, frequently applied to plasma-solid interfaces, is invalid for semiconducting interfaces.

We introduce Bh\=a$\unicode{x1E63}$\=acitra, a dialect mapping system for South Asia founded on a database of linguistic studies from the region that are annotated with topic and location information. We examine language coverage and explore applications in typology by visualizing sample datasets. Beyond facilitating feature mapping, the tool also functions as an innovative interactive bibliography for scholars of South Asian languages.

We introduce the first comprehensive 3D kinematic study of 3,133 white dwarfs, utilizing Gaia astrometry combined with radial velocities sourced from both Gaia and ground-based spectroscopy. The dataset comprises isolated white dwarfs with direct velocity measurements and members of common proper motion pairs featuring nondegenerate companions with known radial velocities; a subset of these pairs also includes measured metal abundances from large-scale surveys or our follow-up work. Employing white dwarfs as astrophysical clocks, we interpolated dedicated evolutionary models to derive their masses and total ages. Additionally, we leveraged the nondegenerate companions in common proper motion systems to chemically characterize the population. By integrating precise radial velocities with Gaia astrometry and proper motions, we calculated the velocity components of the sample within the Galactic rest frame and their corresponding orbital parameters. Located primarily within approximately 300 pc of the Sun, the sample consists overwhelmingly (90–95%) of thin-disk stars on nearly circular orbits, while the remaining 5–10% exhibit eccentric trajectories indicative of the thick disk. We identified seven isolated white dwarfs and two common proper motion pairs as halo members. Our analysis of the age-velocity dispersion relation for thin-disk stars reveals signatures of dynamical heating and saturation occurring after 4–6 Gyr.
