Furthermore, we detected a mild anti-correlation between [Fe/H] and the radial component of the mean velocity dispersion, indicating that dynamical mixing occurs within the Galactic disk, a phenomenon previously observed in FGK star samples. [Abridged]

Human motion analysis is a fundamental area of interest across various fields, including Human-Computer Interaction, entertainment, Virtual Reality, and healthcare. While deep learning has delivered remarkable success in real-time human pose estimation, these models frequently struggle to generalize to unseen individuals due to high inter-subject variability, a challenge exacerbated by the scarcity of specialized datasets in domains like healthcare. Collecting such data is often prohibitively time-consuming, difficult, and costly; therefore, developing methods for human motion synthesis is a critical problem within deep learning and computer vision. This paper introduces a novel approach to controllable human motion synthesis by employing end-to-end training with attention-based probabilistic deep adversarial models. We demonstrate the ability to generate synthetic human motion across both short and long time horizons using adversarial attention. Additionally, we show that augmenting existing datasets with these synthetic motions can significantly enhance the classification performance of deep learning models when real-world data is insufficient.

To address long-tail scenarios in sequence labeling (SL), this study proposes Graph Neural Network-based Sequence Labeling (GNN-SL). This approach enhances standard SL models by integrating similar tagging examples retrieved from the entire training dataset. Because not every retrieved example aids prediction, we build a heterogeneous graph and utilize Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to facilitate information transfer between the input word sequence and these retrieved examples. The augmented node, which aggregates data from its neighbors, performs the final prediction. This method allows the model to directly access similar tagging instances, thereby improving overall prediction quality. Extensive experiments across three representative SL tasks—Named Entity Recognition (NER), Part of Speech Tagging (POS), and Chinese Word Segmentation (CWS)—demonstrate the model's significant performance. Specifically, GNN-SL achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) results on the CWS task with scores of 96.9 (+0.2) on PKU, 98.3 (+0.4) on CITYU, 98.5 (+0.2) on MSR, and 96.9 (+0.2) on AS, while also matching SOTA performance on NER and POS datasets.

We present the inaugural infinite families of locally arc transitive graphs where the automorphism group acts quasiprimitively on exactly one of its two vertex orbits, specifically within the twisted wreath category. This research advances the classification initiative launched by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by demonstrating that the star normal quotient twisted wreath category encompasses infinitely many such graphs.

An "open" or $(\mu,P,T)$-ensemble characterizes equilibrium systems where the control variables are chemical potential, pressure, and temperature. Because the associated free energy vanishes identically due to the Euler relation, this unconstrained ensemble is rarely applied to standard thermodynamic systems. In contrast, it is highly suitable for black holes, as their entropy behaves as a quasi-homogeneous function of extensive variables, governed by the scaling rules of the Smarr formula. After briefly outlining thermodynamics within this open framework, we derive the general expression for logarithmic corrections to the entropy of a typical system arising from fluctuations in energy, thermodynamic volume, and a generic charge $N$. Finally, we apply this result to determine the exact analytic form of the logarithmically corrected entropy for charged and rotating black holes situated in anti-de Sitter spacetimes.

We examine a Higgs transition occurring between a U(1) Dirac spin liquid and a gapless $\mathbb{Z}_2$ spin liquid. This $\mathbb{Z}_2$ phase is significant for the spin $S=1/2$ square lattice antiferromagnet, where recent numerical evidence suggests its existence in highly frustrated regimes of the $J_1$-$J_2$ model, specifically between the disappearance of N\'eel order and the emergence of valence bond solid (VBS) order. The nearby Dirac spin liquid is unstable to monopole proliferation on the square lattice, eventually resulting in either N\'eel or VBS ordering. Consequently, we propose that this Higgs transition serves as the critical theory distinguishing the gapless $\mathbb{Z}_2$ spin liquid of the $J_1$-$J_2$ model from one of its adjacent ordered phases. The transition to the other ordered phase can be treated uniformly as a transition into an unstable SU(2) spin liquid, which was previously analyzed. By investigating the deconfined critical theory separating the U(1) Dirac spin liquid from the gapless $\mathbb{Z}_2$ spin liquid using a $1/N_f$ expansion (where $N_f$ scales with the fermion count), we identify a stable fixed point characterized by anisotropic spinon dispersion and a dynamical critical exponent $z \neq 1$. We explore the implications of this anisotropy by computing the angular profiles of equal-time N\'eel and VBS correlation functions, finding them to be distinct. Furthermore, we highlight how this anisotropy affects the scaling dimension of monopoles.

This study examines how new physics, motivated by flavor anomalies, influences neutrino oscillations within a dense dark matter halo. Drawing inspiration from a model featuring a Majorana dark matter fermion and two new scalar fields that contribute to the $b \to s \mu^+ \mu^-$ transition at the one-loop level, we analyze how neutrino-dark matter interactions alter the oscillation patterns of ultra-high energy cosmic neutrinos traversing a muonphilic halo near the Milky Way's center. Our findings indicate that these interactions cause the flavor ratios of neutrinos arriving at Earth to deviate from those predicted by vacuum oscillations. Furthermore, we investigate a $Z'$ model based on $L_{\mu}-L_{\tau}$ symmetry with a vector-like fermion as the dark matter candidate; in this scenario, neutrino flavors decouple, resulting in flavor ratios similar to vacuum oscillations. Consequently, interactions with dense dark matter halos offer a valuable method for distinguishing between flavor models that involve dark matter connections.

High-performance quantum memory is critical for both extensive quantum communication networks and intricate large-scale computing systems. This study examines the potential of Er$^{3+}$:Y$_2$SiO$_5$ crystals to function as a quantum memory for propagating microwave photons, utilizing methodologies typically applied to dense optical ensembles. Our research involved conducting high-resolution microwave spectroscopy on the Er$^{3+}$:Y$_2$SiO$_5$ material, which revealed both electronic spin and hyperfine transitions. Additionally, we investigated spectral hole burning and analyzed spin relaxation processes at millikelvin temperatures to identify primary relaxation mechanisms, thereby establishing a foundation for future investigations into this field.

Most existing supervised automatic music transcription (AMT) models suffer from poor generalization, struggling to transcribe real-world recordings from diverse genres absent from their labeled training data. To address this, we introduce ReconVAT, a semi-supervised framework that utilizes vast amounts of unlabeled music data. By incorporating reconstruction loss and virtual adversarial training, ReconVAT, when paired with standard U-net architectures, delivers competitive performance on benchmark datasets like MAPS and MusicNet. Notably, in the few-shot setting for the MusicNet string part dataset, ReconVAT achieves F1-scores of 61.0% (note-wise) and 41.6% (note-with-offset-wise), representing significant gains of 22.2% and 62.5% over supervised baselines. Furthermore, the framework highlights the potential for continual learning with new data, offering practical benefits for scenarios where data streams are continuously generated.

Numerous resource allocation challenges in wireless communications can be modeled as Generalized Assignment Problems (GAP). As a generalized variant of the Linear Sum Assignment Problem (LSAP), GAP presents greater complexity due to the simultaneous presence of equality and inequality constraints. We introduce a novel Deep Unsupervised Learning (DUL) framework designed to resolve GAP efficiently. Specifically, this method trains a Deep Neural Network (DNN) via a tailored loss function that integrates the objective function with penalty terms for both constraint types. Additionally, we utilize a Softmax activation function at the DNN's output combined with tensor splitting; this strategy simplifies the loss function and ensures compliance with equality constraints. In a case study, we apply this DUL approach to a standard user-association problem in wireless networks, formulating it as a GAP. Numerical findings indicate that the proposed DUL method achieves near-optimal solutions with substantially reduced time complexity.

Recent shadow tomography protocols utilize classical shadows of quantum states to forecast numerous target functions of an unknown state. Distinct from full quantum state tomography, this approach does not demand precise recovery of the density matrix for high-rank mixed states; instead, it achieves multiple accurate predictions with high confidence using a moderate number of measurements. While the influential algorithm by Huang, Kueng, and Preskill (arXiv:2002.08953) relies on specific random unitary circuits, this paper demonstrates a method that bypasses those transformations by employing an arbitrary informationally complete POVM. We show that this procedure can reliably compute k-bit correlation functions for quantum states. Furthermore, we establish that the median of means procedure used by Huang et al. is unnecessary for this specific application. Finally, we examine the differences between computing correlation functions and the fidelity required for reconstructing low-rank density matrices.

We have identified a category of browser-based covert channels that evade existing defenses, termed "pool-party" attacks. These attacks enable websites to establish covert communication by manipulating limited, unpartitioned resource pools. While this class of attack has been recognized previously, our research demonstrates that it is more widespread, easier to exploit, and offers a broader range of exploitation vectors than previously understood. These channels possess sufficient bandwidth to transmit cookies and identifiers across site boundaries under realistic, real-world conditions. We detected pool-party attacks in all major browsers and confirmed their viability as cross-site tracking mechanisms (requiring approximately 0.6 seconds in Chrome and Edge, and 7 seconds in Firefox and Tor Browser).

Our paper offers four key contributions: first, we detail pool-party covert channel attacks that leverage constraints in application-layer resource pools within browsers. Second, we prove that these attacks are practical for tracking users across all popular browsers and provide open-source implementations, which we evaluated using a representative web crawl. Third, we demonstrate that in Gecko-based browsers (including Tor Browser), pool-party attacks facilitate cross-profile tracking, such as linking behavior between standard and private browsing sessions. Finally, we propose potential mitigation strategies and defensive measures.

Current state-of-the-art reinforcement learning (RL) methods often rely on random sampling, such as $\epsilon$-greedy, for exploration; however, this approach struggles with difficult exploration environments like Montezuma's Revenge. To overcome this, previous research has introduced intrinsic rewards—also known as curiosity or exploration bonuses—that incentivize agents to visit novel states, yielding strong results on hard exploration tasks. Yet, on simpler tasks, agents become distracted by these intrinsic signals and engage in unnecessary exploration despite having access to sufficient extrinsic rewards. Consequently, overly curious agents often underperform compared to those trained solely on task rewards. This inconsistency in performance across different task difficulties has hindered the broad adoption of intrinsic rewards in RL. We introduce Extrinsic-Intrinsic Policy Optimization (EIPO), a principled constrained optimization framework that automatically adjusts the weight of intrinsic rewards: suppressing them when exploration is superfluous and amplifying them when necessary. Our approach delivers superior exploration capabilities without requiring manual tuning to balance intrinsic and task rewards. Empirical results demonstrating consistent performance improvements across sixty-one ATARI games support our findings. The code is accessible at https://github.com/Improbable-AI/eipo.

While topological band theory has successfully identified and categorized numerous novel phases in insulators and semimetals, it lacks the capability to detect topological effects in metallic or gapless materials. To address this, we propose a framework for topological metals utilizing the spectral localizer and its associated Clifford pseudospectrum. This approach can identify boundary-localized states even when degenerate bulk bands exist and quantify their topological protection without requiring a bulk band gap. We validate the method's broad applicability across symmetry classes in two lattice models—a Chern metal and a higher-order topological metal—and demonstrate that their topology remains robust against significant perturbations. By establishing invariants for metallic and gapless systems, this work opens the door to discovering topological phenomena in diverse natural, photonic, and artificial materials that were previously inaccessible.

Term enrichment analysis enhances biological interpretation by linking experimentally or computationally derived data to annotations from controlled vocabularies. This workflow typically calculates statistical significance for each term and utilizes the most significant terms—often weighted—to characterize specific sets of biological entities. However, many current enrichment methods are limited; they may require arbitrary selection thresholds for top entities, ignore entity weights, rely on extensive simulations for statistics, or assume a normal weight distribution. Furthermore, most existing approaches struggle to assign accurate statistical significance to terms containing few entities. To address these limitations, we developed SaddleSum, a novel method based on the well-known Luganani-Rice formula. Unlike its predecessors, SaddleSum operates without these constraints and has been benchmarked against multiple existing techniques. By properly incorporating entity weights, SaddleSum demonstrates internal consistency and stability regardless of the number of top entities selected. Making minimal assumptions about the input data, this universal method is applicable beyond microarray analysis. Utilizing an asymptotic approximation, SaddleSum generates a term-size-dependent score distribution function that ensures accurate statistical significance even for terms with few entities. Consequently, SaddleSum allows researchers to confidently interpret significance assignments for small terms, which are frequently the most biologically specific.

We contend that STAR's measurements of $J/\psi$ photoproduction in $d+Au$ ultraperipheral collisions (UPCs) at non-zero momentum transfer ($t \neq 0$) mainly investigate elastic and potentially nucleon-dissociative $J/\psi$ photoproduction occurring on quasi-free nucleons, while remaining largely unaffected by anticipated but weak nuclear modifications to the deuteron's gluon distribution. By examining the STAR detector's capacity to select UPC events, we investigate whether the contribution from nucleon-dissociative $J/\psi$ photoproduction is negligible and demonstrate that this assumption yields an excellent fit to the $t$ dependence of the STAR total cross section.

Drawing inspiration from statistical practice, this work employs category theory to define Borel data structures and investigate exchangeability within an abstract setting. It establishes a generalized version of de Finetti's theorem and utilizes natural transformations to formulate functional representation theorems (FRTs). These proofs rely on a classical theorem by D.N. Hoover regarding functional representations for exchangeable arrays indexed by finite integer tuples, combined with an universality result for Borel data structures. A specific subset of Borel data structures, termed "array-type," is introduced via a new concept known as an indexing system. By examining natural transformations that map to arrays, the study derives explicit FRTs that align with established Aldous-Hoover-Kallenberg-type theorems for (jointly) exchangeable arrays in various examples. Furthermore, the proposed abstract "index arithmetic" unifies and extends the technical arguments frequently found in exchangeability literature. Ultimately, the category-theoretic framework is applied to delineate how an abstract concept of separate exchangeability can be derived, once again grounded in statistical applications.

This paper explores the internal relationship between Hamiltonian optics and the scalar wave theory of light rays. It demonstrates that solutions to the reduced wave equation resemble Huygens' wavelets and provide insight into Snell's law of refraction. Furthermore, this model enables the derivation of a reflection coefficient for $s$-polarized light that aligns with Fresnel's equations.

Significant research in Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has focused on algorithmic development to create more efficient and cost-effective methods. However, investigation into the initialization of these techniques remains scarce; consequently, most current NAS approaches rely on stochastic initialization because gathering prior information is expensive. Nevertheless, the recent emergence of NAS benchmarks has facilitated prototyping with limited computational resources. This study proposes accelerating a NAS algorithm through a data-driven initialization technique that leverages these benchmarks. Specifically, we introduce a two-step methodology: first, a calibrated clustering analysis of the search space is conducted, and second, the resulting centroids are extracted to initialize the NAS algorithm. We evaluated this approach using Aging Evolution, an evolutionary algorithm, on the NAS-bench-101 dataset. The results demonstrate that compared to random initialization, this method achieves faster convergence and superior performance in the final solution.

The "TAP and the Data Models" Bird of Feathers session aimed to discuss the importance of allowing TAP services to handle IVOA standardized data models and to refine the necessary functionalities for implementing this capability.

This study presents findings from a search for the lepton flavor violating decay $\tau \to 3\mu$ within proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV. The analysis utilizes a dataset of 33.2 fb$^{-1}$ collected by the CMS experiment at the LHC in 2016, encompassing $\tau$ leptons originating from both W boson decays and heavy-flavor hadrons. No statistically significant excess over the predicted background was detected. Consequently, an upper limit on the branching fraction $\mathcal{B}(\tau \to 3\mu)$ of $8.0 \times 10^{-8}$ is established at the 90% confidence level, which is consistent with the expected limit of $6.9 \times 10^{-8}$.

All-van der Waals heterostructures consist entirely of two-dimensional crystals for their active layers, gate dielectrics, and electrodes. Because these 2D materials lack dangling bonds in their bulk, they support exceptionally clean electron systems. This work outlines techniques for achieving nanoscale electrostatic control while avoiding contamination at critical interfaces. Specifically, we employ a resist-free local anodic oxidation method to pattern sub-100 nm features in graphite gates, which are subsequently integrated into the heterostructure. Utilizing a quantum point contact as a reference device, we demonstrate the selective separation of both integer and fractional quantum Hall edge modes under high magnetic fields. Additionally, we observe signs of delicate interaction-driven edge reconstruction, such as the emergence of a quantum dot at an electrostatic potential saddle point. These findings establish a foundation for high-precision nanoscale investigations of correlated states in these materials, including the potential for single anyon control within the fractional quantum Hall regime.

This study introduces a deep learning framework designed for symbol estimation and detection within signals conveyed via reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS). The architecture employs fully connected layers to derive channel conditions and phase shifts from signals reflected by the RIS. By enabling symbol detection without the need for pilot signaling, this approach minimizes transmission overhead. Furthermore, the method demonstrates superior performance compared to conventional detectors, as evidenced by improved bit-error rates.

Algorithms frequently execute a comparable number of computations for both "easy" and "difficult" problem instances; specifically, nearest neighbor algorithms typically maintain consistent running times regardless of the specific instance. This paper addresses the approximate k-nearest-neighbor problem, which involves identifying a subset of approximately k points from a given set that includes the k nearest neighbors of a query point. We introduce an algorithm utilizing adaptive distance estimation and demonstrate that it is essentially optimal among methods restricted to this approach. Furthermore, we provide both theoretical and experimental evidence showing that this algorithm can achieve substantial speedups compared to the naive method.

This study investigates inertial modes within a spherical Couette flow experiment characterized by a radius ratio of $\eta = 1/3$. Inertial modes are linear wave patterns restored by the Coriolis force, commonly observed in rapidly rotating fluids. While recent experiments confirmed their existence in spherical Couette systems where the inner sphere rotates slower than the outer sphere ($\Omega_{i}<\Omega_{o}$), only a limited set of specific modes had been identified previously. By varying the Rossby number across the range $-2.5 < Ro = (\Omega_{i}-\Omega_{o})/\Omega_{o} < 0$ at two constant values of $\Omega_{o}$, we identify similar inertial modes. However, the flow dynamics observed here differ significantly from prior spherical Couette experiments. We demonstrate that the kinetic energy of the dominant inertial mode rises sharply as the Rossby number decreases, ultimately causing wave breaking and the emergence of small-scale structures at a critical Rossby number. This specific transition in spherical Couette flow has not been documented before. Furthermore, this critical Rossby number scales with the Ekman number as $E^{1/5}$. Beyond this transition, the proliferation of small-scale features transfers energy to create a massively amplified mean flow along the tangent cylinder. In this context, we explore the interaction between the dominant inertial modes and a geostrophic Rossby mode, which excites secondary modes satisfying the triadic resonance condition.

BERT-based contextual ranking models are now widely utilized for various passage and document ranking tasks; however, their resilience against adversarial inputs remains insufficiently investigated. This paper contends that BERT-rankers are vulnerable to attacks targeting retrieved documents relative to a query. To demonstrate this, we introduce algorithms employing gradient-based optimization to perturb both highly relevant and non-relevant documents. Our approach involves adding or substituting a minimal number of tokens to significantly alter a document's rank, either promoting or demoting it. Experimental results indicate that even a few tokens can drastically shift document rankings. Furthermore, our findings reveal that BERT-rankers heavily depend on the beginning of documents for relevance assessment, rendering the initial section more prone to adversarial manipulation. Notably, we identified a limited set of recurring adversarial words that consistently induce successful rank changes for any relevant or non-relevant document. Finally, these adversarial tokens exhibit specific topic preferences across datasets, highlighting potential biases originating from BERT's pre-training or downstream data sources.

This preliminary research details the creation of an artificial intelligence-driven algorithm for segmenting medical images to quantify bone growth adjacent to metallic implants. To address the challenge of estimating new bone tissue formation caused by artifacts—distortions and errors inherent in imaging—two databases of computerized microtomography scans were utilized: 100 images for training and 196 for testing. In the training set, both bone and implant tissues were manually segmented. The study employed a U-Net architecture, a convolutional neural network specifically designed for medical image segmentation. Regarding accuracy, the model achieved approximately 98%. After generating predictions on the test set, the total pixel count representing bone tissue was determined, yielding a volume roughly 15% of that estimated by conventional techniques, which tend to overestimate growth. While the method demonstrates strong performance and promising results, there remains significant room for enhancement by adjusting network parameters or expanding the database to improve training.

Abstractive conversation summarization has gained significant recent interest, yet generated summaries frequently lack precision due to issues like redundancy, incompleteness, or factual errors, largely stemming from the unstructured and complex nature of human dialogue. To address this, we propose explicitly modeling the rich structural elements within conversations to achieve more accurate summarization. Our approach involves encoding dialogues through structured graphs that capture discourse relations between utterances and action triples ("who-doing-what") within them, followed by a multi-granularity decoder that synthesizes summaries by integrating information across all levels. Experimental results demonstrate that our models surpass state-of-the-art techniques and exhibit strong cross-domain generalization, as validated by both automatic metrics and human evaluations. We have made our code publicly available at https://github.com/GT-SALT/Structure-Aware-BART.

This research investigates the non-asymptotic advantages of double $\ell_1$-regularization applied to heterogeneous overdispersed count data modeled through negative binomial regression. Leveraging restricted eigenvalue conditions and concentration inequalities from empirical processes, we establish oracle inequalities for Lasso estimators of two partial regression coefficients for the first time. Additionally, based on these oracle inequalities, we provide theoretical assurances regarding the consistency and convergence rates of the estimators, which support subsequent statistical inference. Ultimately, both simulation studies and an analysis of real-world data confirm the efficacy of the proposed methods.

We present the detection and validation of Kepler-7b, a transiting exoplanet characterized by an exceptionally low density. Its mass is under half that of Jupiter (Mp = 0.43 Mj), yet its radius is 50% larger (Rp = 1.48 Rj), yielding a density of 0.17 g/cc, which ranks as the second-lowest among known extrasolar planets. The planet orbits with a period of 4.886 days around a host star slightly hotter than the Sun (Teff = 6000 K). However, this star is significantly more massive (Mstar = 1.35 Msun) and larger (Rstar = 1.84 Rsun) than our Sun, suggesting it is nearing the end of its Main Sequence lifespan.

The Warm Plasma Dispersion Relation, applicable to waves within the electron cyclotron resonance frequency range, can be expressed as a bi-quadratic equation for $N_\perp$, where the coefficients depend on $N_\perp^2$, necessitating an iterative solution. However, this iterative approach is poorly understood and fails to converge at the second harmonic resonance layer, particularly at higher densities where coupling with electron Bernstein waves occurs. This study addresses the convergence issues of the iterative method to determine the dispersion relation's topology near the second harmonic using a fully relativistic code for oblique waves. A feed-forward controller is introduced, capable of adjusting the rotation of the $N_\perp^2$ step within the complex plane while constraining the step size. The implementation of this controller demonstrates the stabilization of unstable solutions and enhances the overall robustness of the iteration. Consequently, this enables the assessment of coupling between the fast extraordinary mode and electron Bernstein waves at the second harmonic resonance layer for non-perpendicularly propagating waves.

Traditionally, scene text detection and document layout analysis have been handled as distinct tasks within separate image domains. This paper unifies these approaches by introducing the novel task of simultaneous scene text detection and layout analysis. To support this, we present the first hierarchical dataset for scene text, which facilitates this new research direction. Furthermore, we propose a method capable of jointly detecting scene text and clustering text regions in a unified manner. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our unified model outperforms several well-designed baseline methods. Additionally, it achieves state-of-the-art results across multiple scene text detection datasets without requiring complex post-processing. Dataset and code are available at: https://github.com/google-research-datasets/hiertext and https://github.com/tensorflow/models/tree/master/official/projects/unified_detector.

I present experimental findings from heavy ion collisions at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider, tailored for a general audience. Key topics include elliptic flow and nearly ideal hydrodynamics; the suppression of high-energy particles and the R_AA ratio; and electromagnetic signals such as direct photons and dileptons. A particularly intriguing question remains: why do heavy charm quarks behave so similarly to light quarks?

This note examines both real and complex methodologies within harmonic analysis, highlighting a shared foundation in the covariant transform derived from the affine group.
Keywords: wavelet, coherent state, covariant transform, reconstruction formula, the affine group, ax+b-group, square integrable representations, admissible vectors, Hardy space, fiducial operator, approximation of the identity, maximal functions, atom, nucleus, atomic decomposition, Cauchy integral, Poisson integral, Hardy–Littlewood maximal functions, grand maximal function, vertical maximal functions, non-tangential maximal functions, intertwining operator, Cauchy–Riemann operator, Laplace operator, singular integral operator, SIO, boundary behaviour, Carleson measure.

Developing biologically plausible learning algorithms is crucial for elucidating brain function, yet most current approaches fail to scale to real-world applications, thereby limiting their utility as models for actual brain learning. Consequently, there is a pressing need to investigate algorithms that offer robust theoretical guarantees while matching the performance of backpropagation (BP) on complex tasks. Difference Target Propagation (DTP) represents such an algorithm, recently linked to Gauss-Newton (GN) optimization. However, the rigorous conditions required for this connection prevent the layer-wise training of feedback pathway synaptic weights—a method that is more biologically realistic. Furthermore, the alignment between DTP weight updates and loss gradients is only weakly guaranteed and relies on highly specific architectural conditions. This paper introduces a novel feedback weight training scheme that ensures DTP approximates BP while restoring layer-wise feedback weight training without compromising theoretical guarantees. We support our theory with experimental evidence, reporting the highest performance ever achieved by DTP on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet 32×32.

We present the implementation of micro-electro-mechanical-system (MEMS) scanning mirrors as active components for locally optically pumping ultra-cold atoms confined within a magneto-optical trap. A duo of MEMS mirrors directs a focused resonant beam across a cloud of trapped \textsuperscript{87}Rb atoms, which are shelved in the \textit{F}=1 ground state, enabling spatially selective fluorescence of the ensemble. Two-dimensional manipulation is achieved by projecting geometrical patterns along the imaging axis of the cold atom cloud. This method of controlling atomic ensembles using a microfabricated mirror pair holds promise for applications such as single-atom selection, localized optical pumping, and arbitrary shaping of the cloud. Furthermore, this technique offers substantial potential for miniaturization and the development of portable control systems for quantum optical experiments.

This paper outlines the design, assembly, and operational use of a novel intensity interferometer situated at Southern Connecticut State University in New Haven, Connecticut. Although the study primarily analyzes data from an initial two-telescope setup, the full system currently comprises three portable 0.6-meter Dobsonian telescopes equipped with single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) detectors positioned at the Newtonian focus of each unit. Photons recorded at each station are time-stamped and processed by timing correlators capable of achieving cross-correlation precision of 48 picoseconds. We present our results from 16 successful observing nights at the university, noting that the instrument's components were also temporarily deployed at Lowell Observatory to configure the Perkins and Hall telescopes as an intensity interferometer. A detailed performance characterization reveals a 6.76-sigma correlation peak for unresolved stars and results consistent with partial or no detection at baselines sufficient to resolve the stars. Based on these findings, we estimate Arcturus's angular diameter to be greater than 15 mas and Vega's to fall between 0.8 and 17 mas. Despite significant uncertainties, both measurements align with data obtained from amplitude-based long-baseline optical interferometers.

Amidst the surge of fake news and deepfakes, numerous instances have emerged where altered images are disseminated via newspapers, utilized in legal proceedings, and shared on social media for defamation. Detecting such manipulated imagery is a critical challenge we address in this study. We concentrate on techniques that employ both Deep Learning and image transformation strategies to identify tampering, subsequently evaluating and comparing their performance and robustness. Furthermore, we aim to localize the forged regions within an image and generate corresponding masks. Finally, based on our findings, we propose recommendations and methodologies to develop a more resilient framework for detecting and pinpointing forgeries.

This work offers a concise overview of clipping and intersection algorithms in both 2D and 3D environments, accompanied by a comprehensive list of pertinent references. Certain algorithms leverage the projective extension of Euclidean space alongside vector-vector operations, thereby enabling compatibility with GPU and SSE architectures.

Over the past ten years, computational methods have become pivotal in material design, enabling faster development cycles at lower costs, with machine learning gaining significant traction in photonics. However, optimizing the inversion of Maxwell's equations remains a complex challenge that demands advanced software. This paper introduces Neural Inverse Design of Nanostructures (NIDN), an innovative open-source platform that utilizes a physics-based deep learning approach to create complex, stacked nanostructures. Unlike derivative-free or purely data-driven methods, NIDN employs gradient-based neural network training to directly optimize material properties and structural geometry according to target spectral features. The tool integrates two distinct solvers: rigorous coupled-wave analysis and the finite-difference time-domain method. Its effectiveness and accuracy are validated through various synthetic cases, including the design of a 1550 nm filter and anti-reflection coating, with results aligning closely with experimental benchmarks, other simulation tools, and desired spectral targets. Due to its modular architecture for both neural networks and Maxwell solvers, along with its open-source and permissive licensing, NIDN is well-positioned to advance computational material design across diverse applications.

This paper aims to measure BERT's syntactic capabilities within an evaluation framework involving non-context-free patterns, such as those found in Dutch. We created a test suite grounded in a mildly context-sensitive formalism to generate grammars that model specific linguistic phenomena, namely control verb nesting and verb raising. By combining these grammars with a limited lexicon, we produced a substantial corpus of naturalistic sentences, annotated with verb-subject relationships, which function as the test bed for an attention-based span selection probe. Supported by thorough analysis, our findings indicate that the examined models are unable to implicitly acquire the dependencies under study.

This work introduces a novel numerical procedure called Trust-Region Stochastic Tuning for Matrix Incoherence (TRSTMI) designed to construct low coherence matrices, alongside a detailed analysis of experimental outcomes from a CPU/GPU parallelized implementation. These trials indicate that this approach outperforms existing methods when dealing with large matrices. Furthermore, we propose new conjectures regarding optimal complex matrices, driven by and informed by the experimental findings.
We present a q-analogue of Gauss' divisibility theorem.

The connection between passive and positive real systems has been thoroughly examined in existing literature. This paper explores their relationship with the more recently introduced concept of port-Hamiltonian descriptor systems. It is established that port-Hamiltonian systems are passive, and passive systems are positive real; consequently, the conditions under which the converse implications hold are investigated. Additionally, the paper examines the interplay between passivity, KYP inequalities, and finite available storage.

Systems programming frequently involves managing critical resources such as file handles, network connections, and dynamically allocated memory. Adhering to specific protocols for these resources is essential, as deviations can result in a spectrum of bugs—from type mismatches and data races to use-after-free errors and memory leaks—many of which compromise security. Although statically typed languages inherently guarantee type soundness and memory safety, they often fail to address problems stemming from improper resource management. A key approach to solving this is adopting linear and affine types to enforce single-threaded resource usage; however, the limited languages that support these types demand extensive type annotations.

This paper introduces Affe, an extension of ML that enforces linearity and affinity through kinds and constrained types. Drawing inspiration from Rust, Affe also supports both exclusive and shared borrowing of affine resources. Crucially, Affe maintains the core characteristics of the ML family: it is an impure, strict functional expression language featuring complete principal type inference and type abstraction. Unlike other systems requiring explicit linearity annotations, Affe imposes no such requirements on expressions while fully supporting standard functional programming idioms.

Object detection and classification within aerial imagery support various applications, including urban planning, crop monitoring, and traffic surveillance. Nevertheless, the small scale of objects and noise inherent in aerial photographs make feature extraction difficult. This study assesses CenterNet, a leading real-time 2D object detection technique, using the VisDrone2019 dataset. Furthermore, we analyze the model's performance by testing different backbone networks alongside various training and testing resolutions.

This study presents, for the first time, predictions of axion spectra and corresponding luminosities for various low-mass stars, including one- and two-solar-mass stars during both main-sequence and post-main-sequence evolutionary phases. We also calculate the X-ray excess emission generated when axions convert back into photons within the strong magnetic fields present in these stellar envelopes. Consequently, each star possesses a distinct axion spectrum and axion luminosity ($L_a$); if the star's envelope contains a strong magnetic field, it will additionally exhibit a characteristic X-ray spectrum and X-ray luminosity ($L_{a\gamma}$). This axion-derived radiation contributes to the star's total electromagnetic X-ray spectrum and X-ray luminosity ($L_X$). The research examines axion models featuring an axion-photon coupling constant of $5 \times 10^{-11} \text{ GeV}^{-1}$, a value slightly below the current upper limit of $6.6 \times 10^{-11} \text{ GeV}^{-1}$ established by CAST and IAXO helioscopes. The parameter space explored covers multiple axion models, including DFSZ and KSVZ. Our findings indicate that axions with masses between $10^{-7}$ and $10^{-5} \text{ eV}$ and the specified coupling constant yield emission spectra with an average axion energy ranging from 1 to 5 keV and an $L_a$ between $10^{-6}$ and $7 \times 10^{-3} L_\odot$. Furthermore, we predict that $L_{a\gamma}$ will vary from $5 \times 10^{-8}$ to $10^{-5} L_\odot$ for stars possessing an average atmospheric magnetic field of $3 \times 10^4 \text{ G}$. In many cases, these predicted $L_{a\gamma}$ values exceed the observed $L_X$ in certain stars. Thus, these preliminary results highlight the potential for next-generation stellar X-ray missions to constrain various axion model classes.

Advances in fabrication technologies, particularly 3D printers, now enable individuals to freely produce a wide range of products. To establish clear liability for these items, creators must maintain a fabrication record that is both unalterable and permanently accessible. This paper introduces "Fabchain," a proposed solution designed to log fabrication history in this specific manner. Leveraging blockchain as an auditable communication channel, Fabchain oversees print jobs on a fabricator's 3D printer while preserving a complete job history. The system was implemented on Ethereum, and its performance in recording print jobs was assessed. Results indicate that Fabchain can process a print job sequence in under one minute on the Ethereum test network. We conclude that Fabchain effectively manages print jobs within a reasonable timeframe for 3D printing while meeting the essential criteria of immutability and sustainability.

Contemporary neural networks frequently possess a parameter count far exceeding their training dataset size. We demonstrate that this surplus capacity enables the embedding of covert machine learning models within trained networks. Our proposed framework conceals a secret neural network with any desired functionality inside a carrier network. We provide theoretical proof that detecting the secret network is computationally infeasible and show empirically that the carrier network does not reveal the secret network's disguise. This paper introduces a previously unknown steganographic method that could be exploited by adversaries if left unregulated.

This study introduces a hybrid multiscale finite element method (MsFEM) incorporating the Local Orthogonal Decomposition (LOD) technique to address multiscale problems featuring singularities in specific regions of the computational domain. For instance, in modeling steady flow through highly heterogeneous porous media driven by extraction wells, singularities occur near the wells. The core strategy involves applying the traditional finite element method (FEM) directly to a fine mesh within the problematic area while employing LOD-based MsFEM on a coarse mesh for the remainder. A critical challenge lies in defining local correctors for basis functions near the interface between coarse and fine meshes, necessitating careful handling. The proposed approach leverages the strengths of both traditional FEM and LOD-based MsFEM, offering a significant reduction in degrees of freedom compared to standard FEM and potentially higher accuracy for problems involving singularities than LOD-based MsFEM alone. Error analysis is conducted for highly varying coefficients without requiring assumptions regarding scale separation or periodicity. Numerical experiments involving periodic and random highly oscillating coefficients, multiscale problems on an L-shaped domain, and scenarios with high-contrast channels or well-singularities are provided to validate the method's efficiency and accuracy.

We investigate the estimation of the density $f(\boldsymbol x)$ for a random vector ${\boldsymbol X}$ within $\mathbb R^d$. For a spanning tree $T$ over the vertex set $\{1,\dots ,d\}$, the associated tree density $f_{T}$ consists of products of bivariate conditional densities. An optimal spanning tree is defined as the one that minimizes the Kullback-Leibler divergence between $f$ and $f_{T}$. Using independent and identically distributed data, we identify an optimal tree $T^*$ and efficiently construct a tree density estimate $f_n$. This estimator satisfies $\lim_{n\to \infty} \int |f_n(\boldsymbol x)-f_{T^*}(\boldsymbol x)|d\boldsymbol x=0$ almost surely, without requiring any regularity conditions on $f$. Furthermore, if $f$ is Lipschitz continuous with bounded support, the expected $L_1$ error between $f_n$ and $f_{T^*}$ is $O\big(n^{-1/4}\big)$, achieving a dimension-free convergence rate.

This study explores the decay characteristics of axially symmetric solutions to the steady incompressible magnetohydrodynamic equations in $\mathbb{R}^3$ possessing a finite Dirichlet integral. Initially, we establish decay rates for general D-solutions to the axisymmetric MHD system. Furthermore, when the magnetic field comprises solely the swirl component ${\textbf {h}}(r,z)= h_{\theta}(r,z) {\mathbf e_{\theta}}$, we achieve improved decay rates. The final analysis investigates the decay behavior along the $Oz$ axis within this specific class of D-solutions characterized by a purely swirl magnetic field. The primary methodology employed involves integrating scaling arguments, the \textit{Brezis-Gallouet inequality}, and weighted energy estimates.

Major blockchains like Ethereum utilize user-defined smart contracts to process intricate transactions within blocks. However, processing smart contract atomic units (AUs) sequentially underutilizes the parallel processing capabilities of modern multi-core systems; introducing concurrency to AU execution significantly enhances efficiency and throughput. This paper introduces a concurrent miner that constructs blocks by executing AUs in parallel using optimistic Software Transactional Memory (STM). The miner efficiently categorizes independent AUs into a concurrent bin while organizing dependent AUs into a block graph (BG). Furthermore, we propose a concurrent validator that re-executes these AUs deterministically and in parallel—following the miner's sequence of a concurrent bin and BG—to verify the proposed block. We rigorously demonstrate the correctness of this concurrent execution model and achieve substantial performance improvements over current state-of-the-art solutions.

Models featuring scalar doublets alongside charged scalar singlets possess a distinctive characteristic: they allow couplings between a single $Z$ boson and two charged scalars of differing masses. This feature is frequently overlooked in phenomenological studies because it does not appear in models containing only additional scalar doublets. This paper investigates the implications of this property in detail, focusing on processes such as $h \rightarrow Z \gamma$, $B \to X_s \gamma$, and the decay of a heavy charged scalar into a lighter one accompanied by a $Z$ boson. We recommend actively searching for this specific decay mode at the LHC, utilizing the scalar sector of the Zee model as a representative framework. Furthermore, we propose benchmark scenarios that satisfy all existing experimental constraints and may be accessible to current or near-future LHC capabilities.

The dressing technique utilizing the $2\times2$ matrix $\bar\partial$-problem is extended to analyze the canonical form of AB equations, where soliton solutions are derived from the properties of Cauchy matrices. Additionally, the asymptotic behaviors of $N$-soliton solutions are examined.

We introduce a precisely defined and characterized all-sky catalog of classical Cepheids in the Milky Way, created by merging data from two time-domain surveys: Gaia DR2 (Gaia Collaboration et al. 2018) and ASAS-SN (Shappee et al. 2014). Initially, we leverage Gaia's parallax and variability metrics to identify approximately 30,000 bright (G<17) Cepheid candidates with absolute magnitudes M_K < -1. Subsequently, we examine their ASAS-SN V-band light curves to derive periods and classify them based on Fourier parameters. This process yields roughly 1,900 probable Galactic Cepheids, which we estimate are over 90% complete and pure under our chosen selection criteria. This represents the most extensive all-sky sample of Milky Way Cepheids with a well-characterized selection function, essential for population studies and the systematic spectroscopic follow-up planned for SDSS-V. Approximately 130 of these Cepheids remain undocumented in the literature, even as potential candidates.

Establishing robust and unconditionally secure quantum networks fundamentally relies on creating quantum nonlocal correlations across realistic channels. Although loophole-free Bell tests certify entanglement in device-independent settings, they are highly vulnerable to the noise and signal loss inherent in practical communications. Quantum steering offers a solution by redefining nonlocality in an asymmetric framework, thereby relaxing the stringent technological demands of Bell tests and enabling one-sided device-independent networks to function under real-world conditions. This study presents a noise-resilient and loss-tolerant steering test optimized for single-detector measurements that leverages high-dimensional entanglement. We demonstrate the superiority of these systems over qubit-based approaches by experimentally achieving detection-loophole-free steering in 53 dimensions. This feat was accomplished under simultaneous adverse conditions equivalent to 14.2 dB of loss (simulating 79 km of fiber) and 36% white noise. Furthermore, we reveal that utilizing higher dimensions counter-intuitively drastically reduces total measurement time; doubling the Hilbert space dimension accelerated the steering violation by nearly two orders of magnitude. By overcoming the limitations of device-independent entanglement distribution, our resource-efficient, loss-tolerant, and noise-robust demonstration of quantum steering establishes it as a vital component for realizing long-distance, device-independent quantum communication.

The metaverse, envisioned as the next evolution of the Internet, comprises multiple interconnected virtual environments known as "verses." While this concept has garnered significant attention, the security challenges inherent in these digital realms remain underexplored. This study examines the privacy and security risks associated with the metaverse, focusing on virtual reality headsets as the primary access devices. Since user identity verification is essential for logging into these platforms, ensuring the security of this authentication phase is critical. The paper compares the security efficacy of primary authentication methods used in virtual reality settings, specifically analyzing information-based, biometric, and multi-modal approaches. These techniques utilize diverse data types, including 3D patterns, PINs, and biometric information, to verify user identity. The analysis evaluates the advantages and disadvantages of each method and concludes with recommendations for enhancing the safety of these authentication systems, along with suggestions for future research.

The Ultraviolet Transient Astronomical Satellite (ULTRASAT) is a geostationary UV space telescope scheduled for launch in 2024, spearheaded by the Weizmann Institute of Science and the Israel Space Agency. The development of the telescope's core UV-sensitive camera is assigned to DESY in Germany. This camera utilizes four back-side illuminated CMOS sensors to create a total sensitive area of approximately 90mm x 90mm, covering a field of view of roughly 200 deg², with each sensor boasting 22.4 megapixels. The Schmidt optical design places the detector within the optical path to minimize the assembly's footprint, necessitating that readout electronics be housed in a remote unit outside the telescope. Due to the telescope's short focal length, sensor positioning along the optical axis must be accurate within ±50 µm, and the sensor surface must maintain a flatness of ±10 µm. While the telescope operates at approximately 295K, the sensors must be cooled to 200K to reduce dark current, yet also capable of being heated to 343K for decontamination purposes. This paper outlines the preliminary design of the UV-sensitive ULTRASAT camera.

We investigate the feasibility of performing text simplification without depending on a "parallel" corpus, which consists of sentence-level alignments between complex and simple ground-truth texts. To explore this, we propose several concepts, including the novel Conjoined Twin Networks, Flip-Flop Auto-Encoders (FFA), and Adversarial Networks (GAN). We compare Jensen-Shannon (JS-GAN) against Wasserstein GAN to evaluate their performance impact, finding that the former yields superior results. Experiments using a large Wikipedia-derived dataset demonstrate that Twin Networks combined with FFA and JS-GAN significantly outperform existing state-of-the-art systems. Additionally, we contextualize our approach relative to fully supervised methods found in prior literature and illustrate qualitative distinctions among simplified sentences produced by supervision-free models through specific examples.

We perform a comprehensive empirical study to explore the landscape of distributional robustness in question answering. This investigation covers over 350 models across 16 QA datasets, encompassing a wide range of architectures, sizes, and adaptation techniques such as fine-tuning, adapter tuning, and in-context learning. Our results show that model variations often have no impact on robustness, with in-distribution performance being the sole determinant of out-of-distribution performance. Furthermore, we observe that: i) zero-shot and in-context learning approaches demonstrate greater resilience to distribution shifts compared to fully fine-tuned models; ii) few-shot prompt fine-tuned models outperform few-shot fine-tuned span prediction models in terms of robustness; and iii) parameter-efficient and robustness-enhancing training methods yield no significant improvements in robustness. Additionally, we have publicly released all evaluation data to facilitate further analysis of robustness trends in QA models.

"Natural Language," whether it is spoken and perceived by humans or processed and created by machines, relies on interconnected systems that mirror creative processes across semantic, syntactic, phonetic, linguistic, social, emotional, and cultural dimensions. The capacity to generate innovative and practical actions through repeated practice lies at the core of both human language and artificial intelligence. This paper examines the modalities involved in language-like applications utilized by computers and programmers, with the goal of refining our inquiry to more effectively address context, self-awareness, and embodiment.

The surge in volume and prevalence of misinformation on social media necessitates systems capable of assisting fact-checkers by prioritizing high-risk content. While previous research on content prioritization has largely concentrated on English-language news articles, misinformation is increasingly emerging within user-generated content. This paper introduces a novel dataset designed to prioritize check-worthy posts from multi-media content in Hindi. This dataset is distinguished by its focus on user-generated content, its use of the Hindi language, and its accommodation of multi-modality in social media posts. Additionally, we provide metadata for each post, including share and like counts from ShareChat, a prominent Indian social media platform, to facilitate analyses on the correlation between virality and misinformation. The data is available on Zenodo (https://zenodo.org/record/4032629) under a Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY 4.0).

Surface enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) offers high optical sensitivity and chemical specificity for detecting single-molecule spectroscopic signatures, yet enabling this within optically trapped nanoparticles at low laser intensities remains a major hurdle. This letter demonstrates the detection of single-molecule SERS signals from reversible assemblies of trapped plasmonic nanoparticles using a single 633 nm laser excitation. Crucially, the optical trap is generated by the thermoplasmonic field of a single gold nanoparticle deposited on a glass substrate. We utilize a bi-analyte SERS approach to verify single-molecule statistical characteristics and determine the key parameters of the thermoplasmonic tweezer required for such sensitivity. Additionally, we illustrate the platform's capability to trap individual gold nanoparticles and transport nanoparticle assemblies using low power ($\approx$0.1 mW/$\mu$m^2). Given that the setup relies on a dropcasted gold nanoparticle, we anticipate its potential for forming reconfigurable plasmonic metafluids in physiological and catalytic settings, as well as its adaptability for in-vivo plasmonic trapping applications.

In certain neural networks, specific neurons map directly to natural "features" within the input. These \emph{monosemantic} neurons are invaluable for interpretability research because their functions are easily deciphered. This study presents initial efforts to engineer monosemanticity in simplified models. We discovered that models can achieve higher monosemanticity without raising the loss function merely by shifting to different local minima during training. Specifically, loss minima exhibiting greater monosemanticity tend to possess moderate negative biases, a property we leverage to construct highly monosemantic architectures. We successfully interpret these models mechanistically, accounting for residual polysemantic neurons and revealing a straightforward yet unexpected algorithm. Furthermore, increasing the number of neurons per layer enhances monosemanticity, though at a higher computational expense. These results suggest several new research directions for engineering monosemanticity, which we plan to explore in future work.

To mitigate nonlinear interference (NLI) caused by correlated symbols in optical transmission, the energy dispersion index (EDI) was recently introduced as a key metric. This paper presents a novel shaper architecture designed to lower the EDI of transmitted symbols, thereby enhancing the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). We refer to this design as the list-encoding constant-composition distribution matcher (L-CCDM). The L-CCDM incorporates an extra EDI selection module that integrates seamlessly with standard probabilistic amplitude shaping (PAS) frameworks. Numerical simulations of a multi-span, multi-channel system demonstrate that, relative to conventional constant-composition distribution matching (CCDM) using 256-ary quadrature amplitude modulation (256QAM), the proposed architecture achieves an effective SNR improvement of 0.35 dB, an information rate increase of 0.22 bit/4D-symbol, or a transmission reach extension of 8%.

Robust overfitting is a prevalent issue in adversarial training for deep neural networks, yet its precise origins remain unclear. This study investigates the root causes by contrasting the data distributions between non-overfitting scenarios (using weak adversaries) and overfitting scenarios (using strong adversaries). We observe that weak adversaries primarily generate adversarial examples with small losses, whereas strong adversaries produce a more diverse distribution spanning both large-loss and small-loss data. Based on these findings, we developed data ablation experiments to determine that certain small-loss samples, which are insufficiently challenging for strong adversaries, contribute to robust overfitting. To address this, we introduce *Minimum Loss Constrained Adversarial Training* (MLCAT). In each minibatch, MLCAT processes large-loss data conventionally while applying additional mechanisms to increase the loss of small-loss data. Technically, MLCAT prevents the model from overfitting to easily learnable samples; philosophically, it embodies the principle of maximizing the utility of every adversarial example; and algorithmically, we implemented two versions of MLCAT. Extensive experiments confirm that MLCAT successfully eliminates robust overfitting and significantly enhances adversarial robustness.

Musical audio is fundamentally characterized by three physical attributes: frequency, time, and magnitude, which align with the neural coding mechanisms of the human auditory system for music perception. Drawing inspiration from these inherent traits, a frequency-temporal attention network has been developed to emulate human hearing for singing melody extraction. Specifically, this model integrates frequency-temporal attention modules and a selective fusion module that correspond to the aforementioned three properties. The frequency attention module identifies activation frequency bands similar to those in the cochlea, while the temporal attention module analyzes time-based patterns. Furthermore, the selective fusion module recalibrates magnitudes and merges raw data to facilitate prediction. Additionally, a separate branch is introduced to concurrently predict the presence of singing voice melodies. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that the proposed model surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches.

This study combines photometric and spectroscopic data to analyze HD 50526, an ellipsoidal binary classified as a Double Periodic Variable. By mining existing photometric surveys and conducting new spectroscopic observations between 2008 and 2015 using various spectrographs, we derived the system's orbital and stellar parameters. Radial velocities were analyzed using the genetic PIKAIA algorithm, while Doppler tomography maps for the H$\alpha$ and H$\beta$ lines were generated with the Total Variation Minimization code. Furthermore, an optimized simplex algorithm solved the inverse problem to fit the light curve to the optimal stellar parameters. Our results indicate an orbital period of $6.701 \pm 0.001 ~\mathrm{d}$ and a long photometric cycle of $191 \pm 2 ~\mathrm{d}$. Spectral features of the cooler component were identified and modeled as a giant with $\log{g} = 2.79 \pm 0.02 ~\mathrm{dex}$, a mass of $1.13 \pm 0.02 ~\mathrm{M_{\odot}}$, and an effective temperature of $10500 \pm 125 ~\mathrm{K}$. Additionally, we determined a mass ratio of $q= 0.206 \pm 0.033$, characterizing the hotter star as a B-type dwarf with a mass of $5.48 \pm 0.02 ~\mathrm{M_{\odot}}$. The $V$-band orbital light curve is successfully modeled by including an accretion disk around the hotter star, which fills its Roche lobe, has a radius of $14.74 \pm 0.02 ~\mathrm{R_{\odot}}$, and a temperature of $9400 ~\mathrm{K}$ at its outer edge. Two bright spots within the disk explain the global light curve morphology. Finally, the Doppler tomography maps of H$\alpha$ and H$\beta$ reveal complex mass flux structures within the system.

Recently, leveraging modern language models to train learnable metrics has become a promising avenue for automatically evaluating machine translation. However, current human evaluation datasets for text simplification fall short due to insufficient annotations, a narrow range of simplification types, and reliance on outdated models, rendering them inadequate for this purpose. To overcome these limitations, we present the SIMPEVAL corpus, which includes SIMPEVAL_ASSET—featuring 12,000 human ratings across 2,400 simplifications from 24 systems—and SIMPEVAL_2022, a rigorous benchmark with over 1,000 human ratings of 360 simplifications, including outputs from GPT-3.5. By training on SIMPEVAL_ASSET, we developed LENS, a Learnable Evaluation Metric for Text Simplification. Comprehensive empirical findings demonstrate that LENS exhibits superior correlation with human judgment compared to existing metrics, thereby advancing the field of text simplification evaluation. Additionally, we introduced RANK & RATE, an interactive human evaluation framework that enables list-wise rating of simplifications from multiple models, ensuring both consistency and accuracy in the annotation process. Our metric, the dataset, and the annotation toolkit are accessible at https://github.com/Yao-Dou/LENS.

Investigating how multilegged robotic systems can efficiently adapt to changing environments promises significant advancements in robotic control and locomotion. This paper examines the performance limits of enumerative (factorial) encoding for hexapod gaits, specifically focusing on rapid recovery following leg failures. Computational experiments utilizing five nature-inspired, gradient-free optimization heuristics demonstrate that feasible recovery strategies can be generated with minimal computational effort, achieving close alignment with desired locomotion directives. For example, viable gait strategies were produced with an average directional deviation of 2.5 cm (10 cm.) using only 40–60 (20) evaluations. These findings suggest the potential for enabling efficient adaptation to new conditions and further investigating canonical representations for solving adaptation challenges in robotic locomotion.

Optimally designed control of quantum systems is becoming increasingly vital for developing novel and more efficient quantum technologies. In this study, we examine a scenario where an arbitrary quantum system is controlled through its interaction with an auxiliary quantum system that has been optimally initialized. We demonstrate that the quantum channel capacity dictates the scaling behavior of the optimal control error. Specifically, we prove that minimizing the control error requires maximizing the quantum capacity of the channel that maps the initial control state to the target state of the system; essentially, this involves optimizing the flow of quantum information from the controller to the target. We provide analytical results supported by numerical evidence for cases involving qubits or single bosonic modes, and these findings are applicable to a broad range of platforms for controllable quantum devices.

Photo Rater is a computer vision initiative leveraging neural networks to assist photographers in identifying the optimal image from a series captured within the same scene. Known in photography as "culling," this manual process can be laborious and time-intensive. To automate it, Photo Rater employs three distinct neural networks: one evaluates overall image quality, another detects blur caused by camera shake or incorrect focus, and the third assesses general aesthetics, including composition. After processing each image through these networks, the system generates a final score, ranks the photos accordingly, and displays the results to the user.

This study examines the quantum mechanisms governing energy and charge transport within a wheel-shaped artificial photosynthetic complex comprising six light-harvesting chromophores and a fullerene electron acceptor. By deriving exact non-Markovian equations for the Heisenberg operators of this system interacting with a Gaussian heat bath, we model quantum phenomena occurring on femtosecond scales. This approach allows us to explore strong system-bath coupling regimes where reorganization energies match intersite exciton couplings. Our findings demonstrate that energy from initially excited antenna chromophores is efficiently channeled to the porphyrin-fullerene reaction center, establishing a charge-separated state within picoseconds and achieving a quantum yield near 95%. In the single-exciton regime, resonant energy exchange between two antenna chromophores exhibits quantum beatings with a decoherence time of approximately 100 fs. Furthermore, analysis of the double-exciton regime, where two porphyrins in the reaction center are initially excited, reveals significant quantum oscillations in fullerene charge with a decoherence time of roughly 20 fs at liquid nitrogen temperatures. These outcomes provide a method for directly observing quantum effects in artificial photosynthetic architectures.

This paper investigates Ramsey numbers $R(r,s)$ by applying Hilbert's Nullstellensatz and Alon's Combinatorial Nullstellensatz. We develop polynomial encodings where the solutions represent Ramsey graphs of order $n$ that avoid containing copies of $K_r$ or $\bar{K}_s$. When these systems lack solutions for $n \ge R(r,s)$, we construct Nullstellensatz certificates with degrees matching the restricted online Ramsey numbers defined by Conlon, Fox, Grinshpun, and He. Additionally, we demonstrate that these findings extend to other concepts in Ramsey theory, such as Rado, van der Waerden, and Hales-Jewett numbers. Lastly, we define a new family of numbers connected to the coefficients of a specific "Ramsey polynomial," which provides lower bounds for Ramsey numbers.

For decades, the prohibitive computational burden of nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) has hindered its application in robots requiring high sampling rates. This study addresses policy learning for constrained nonlinear MPC, specifically targeting unmanned surface vehicles (USVs), by training the nonlinear MPC policy offline for online deployment to mitigate computational complexity. We introduce a Deep Neural Network (DNN)-based Policy Learning MPC (PL-MPC) approach that eliminates the need for solving nonlinear optimal control problems in real-time. The paper details the development of the policy learning methodology and the design of the PL-MPC algorithm. Furthermore, we propose a strategy to guarantee the practical feasibility of implementation, providing theoretical proof that the closed-loop system achieves asymptotic stability in probability. The proposed PL-MPC algorithm is successfully applied to USV motion control, demonstrating the ability to operate at sampling rates up to $5$ Hz with high-precision control. The experiment video is available at: \url{https://v.youku.com/v_show/id_XNTkwMTM0NzM5Ng==.html}

The Poisson-Exponential distribution describes the maximum of independent and identically distributed exponential random variables, where the count follows a zero-truncated Poisson distribution. This distribution is utilized in reliability studies to model monotone hazard rates. This paper introduces Stein's method specifically for Poisson-Exponential distributions and establishes upper bounds for total variation approximation errors when approximating both standard and Generalized Poisson-Exponential distributions using other Poisson-Exponential distributions. Furthermore, by utilizing standardized Stein equations, the study derives upper bounds for the bounded Wasserstein distance when approximating the maximum of a zero-truncated Poisson number of i.i.d. geometric random variables with a Poisson-Exponential distribution. These findings are applied to evaluate the bounded Wasserstein distance between the maximum waiting time of Bernoulli sequence patterns and a Poisson-Exponential distribution. Finally, the theoretical results are demonstrated numerically by approximating a Generalized Poisson-Exponential distribution with Poisson-Exponential distributions across two real-world datasets.

This paper examines a mathematical model of heat transfer in a semi-infinite material with a variable cross-section, where the radial temperature gradient is negligible compared to the axial component. Specifically, the temperature distribution in both the liquid and solid phases of such a body is represented by a Stefan problem for a generalized heat equation. The solution method relies on the similarity principle, which reduces the generalized heat equation to a nonlinear ordinary differential equation. Furthermore, we derive temperature solutions for both phases and identify the free boundaries that define the locations of melting and boiling interfaces. Finally, the existence and uniqueness of the solution are established using Banach's fixed point theorem.

This study examines how the Basset history force influences the sedimentation of nearly neutrally buoyant particles, such as marine snow, within a three-dimensional turbulent flow. The particles are defined by Stokes numbers significantly below unity and still-water settling velocities, normalized by the Kolmogorov velocity, that are approximately one. Incorporating the history force into the Maxey-Riley equation results in individual particle trajectories that diverge substantially from those of inertial particles lacking this force and from ideal settling tracers. However, when analyzing a large ensemble of particles, the statistical characteristics of these three dynamical systems converge. The primary impact of the history force is a gradual, power-law approach toward an asymptotic settling velocity for the center of mass, which numerical analysis identifies as the settling velocity in quiescent fluid. Following an initial ballistic expansion phase lasting roughly one large eddy turnover time, the spatial spread of the ensemble increases diffusively. We show that the center-of-mass settling of these light aggregates is best modeled by the still-fluid dynamics derived with the history force, overlaid with fluctuations that closely mirror those of the turbulent velocity field.

**Background:** Although approximately 2,500 nuclear masses have been measured experimentally, theoretical calculations predict the existence of over 7,000 isotopes ranging from Hydrogen (Z=1) to Oganesson (Z=118), making the exploration of the remaining masses a prominent topic in nuclear physics. Machine learning has emerged as a potent instrument for extracting complex representations from big data across various disciplines. **Purpose:** This study employs the Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), a highly efficient algorithm, to predict the masses of unknown nuclei and investigate the neutron-rich region of the nuclear landscape by learning from measured nuclear masses. **Results:** Utilizing experimental data from 80% of known nuclei for training, the root mean square deviation (RMSD) between predicted and experimental binding energies for the remaining 20% was approximately 0.234 MeV, 0.213 MeV, 0.170 MeV, and 0.222 MeV for the LightGBM-refined LDM, DZ, WS4, and FRDM models, respectively. These figures represent reductions of roughly 90%, 65%, 40%, and 60% compared to the original mass models. Furthermore, the RMSD for 66 newly measured nuclei included in AME2020 showed significant improvement. The one-neutron and two-neutron separation energies predicted by these refined models align with several theoretical predictions derived from various physical models. **Conclusions:** LightGBM can effectively refine theoretical nuclear mass models to predict the binding energies of unknown nuclei. Additionally, the correlation between input characteristic quantities and output can be interpreted using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), a popular explainable AI tool, which may offer new insights for developing theoretical nuclear mass models.

Model selection or sparse modeling with categorical variables remains difficult even with a moderate number of predictors, as encoding each category typically requires a separate parameter. Although Group Lasso is a recognized efficient method for selecting both continuous and categorical variables, it often yields distinct estimates for each level of a selected factor, resulting in non-sparse fitted models that are hard to interpret. To achieve sparsity with Group Lasso, we propose a two-step approach: first, use Group Lasso to reduce data dimensionality; second, select the final model by applying an information criterion to a restricted set of models generated by clustering the levels of individual factors. We evaluate the algorithm's selection accuracy in sparse, high-dimensional settings and test it on both synthetic and real datasets, demonstrating superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods in terms of prediction accuracy and model dimensionality.

A systematic investigation into the crystal, local, magnetic, and transport properties of quenched and temper-annealed Ni$_{2-x}$Mn$_{1+x}$Sn alloys reveals the formation of Mn$_3$Sn-type structural defects arising from antisite disorder, where Mn and Sn atoms interchange positions between the Y and Z sublattices of the X$_2$YZ Heusler structure. This disorder results from Mn substituting Ni at the X sites. Upon temper annealing, these defects segregate and phase-separate into distinct $L2_1$ Heusler and $D0_{19}$ Mn$_3$Sn phases.

The field of remote sensing encompasses a variety of acquisition modalities, each possessing distinct advantages and limitations. However, existing literature and open datasets predominantly focus on electro-optical (optical) imagery for high-resolution detection and segmentation tasks. Although optical data is favored in geospatial contexts, its utility is restricted by the need for clear skies and minimal cloud cover. In contrast, Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) offers the distinct ability to operate through clouds and in all weather conditions, day or night. This makes SAR data invaluable for disaster response scenarios where optical sensors are often obscured. Despite these benefits, researchers face a scarcity of open SAR data, especially at very-high spatial resolutions (Ground Sample Distance <1m), limiting the exploration of SAR's potential for such applications.

To bridge this gap, we introduce the Multi-Sensor All Weather Mapping (MSAW) dataset and challenge, which integrates both SAR and optical modalities.
