Focused on mapping and building footprint extraction using these combined sources, MSAW covers 120 km² across multiple overlapping acquisitions and includes annotations for over 48,000 unique building footprints. This resource facilitates the development and evaluation of algorithms for multi-modal data. We established a baseline and benchmark for SAR-based building footprint extraction, demonstrating that state-of-the-art segmentation models pre-trained on optical data and subsequently fine-tuned on SAR data achieve an F1 score of 0.21, significantly outperforming models trained exclusively on SAR data, which scored 0.135.

Associative memory algorithms generally depend on networks of numerous interconnected units, with the Hopfield model serving as the standard example; its quantum extensions typically utilize open quantum Ising models. In contrast, we introduce an associative memory implementation using a solitary driven-dissipative quantum oscillator, leveraging its infinite phase-space degrees of freedom. This approach enhances the storage capacity of discrete neuron systems across a broad regime and demonstrates successful discrimination among $n$ coherent states, which encode the stored patterns. These patterns can be adjusted continuously by varying the driving strength, effectively forming a modified learning mechanism. Furthermore, we establish that the associative memory capacity is intrinsically linked to the presence of a spectral gap in the Liouvillian superoperator, a condition that creates a significant timescale separation in the dynamics associated with a metastable phase.

This paper addresses the problem of establishing a lower bound on error covariance in Kalman filtering. A sensor transmits a set of measurements to a fusion center, which possesses perfect knowledge of the dynamic model and uses them to estimate system states, but must be constrained so that these estimates do not exceed a specified level of accuracy. We introduce a measurement noise manipulation strategy to guarantee a lower bound on state estimation accuracy. Our proposed method ensures a lower bound on the steady-state estimation error of the Kalman filter by utilizing mathematical tools from eigenvalue analysis.

By integrating interface-pinning simulations with numerical integration of the Clausius-Clapeyron equation, we precisely calculate the coexistence pressure of the melting line and the fluid/crystal densities for the Weeks-Chandler-Andersen (WCA) system across a temperature range spanning four decades. These results facilitate a comparison of melting-line predictions generated by the Boltzmann, Andersen-Weeks-Chandler, Barker-Henderson, and Stillinger hard-sphere approximations. The Andersen-Weeks-Chandler and Barker-Henderson theories emerge as the most accurate, both performing exceptionally well in the zero-temperature limit, for which analytical expressions are derived in this work.

Mobile app screen recordings are a widely used and accessible method for users to demonstrate app usage, appearing in online tutorials, reviews, and bug reports. However, reproducing touch interactions solely from video pixel data remains challenging for both humans and automated systems. This paper presents a method to extract and replay user interactions from mobile app videos using exclusively pixel information from video frames. To detect these interactions, we combine heuristic-based image processing with convolutional deep learning to segment recordings, classify interaction types, and pinpoint interaction locations. For replaying interactions on different devices, we utilize UI element detection to match screen components. We assessed our pixel-based approach using the Rico mobile app dataset and a newly created dataset comprising 64 apps across both iOS and Android platforms. Our results show that the end-to-end system successfully replays the majority of interactions on different devices (84.1% for iOS and 78.4% for Android). This advancement supports various applications, such as automatically annotating interactions in existing videos, facilitating automated UI testing, and generating interactive app tutorials.

This study introduces a strategy utilizing site-bond percolation to curb the spread of *Phytophthora* zoospores in plantations by installing physical barriers between adjacent plants. The analysis distinguishes two clustering mechanisms: i) the distribution of pathogen presence identified through soil testing, which aligns with standard site-bond percolation; and ii) the pattern of visibly diseased plants detected via inspection, where the percolation threshold follows a Tsallis distribution in the absence of barriers. We derive the equations for the minimum barrier density required to stop the formation of a spanning cluster for both scenarios. Although the research targets a specific pathogen, the proposed model is applicable to other diseases that transmit between neighboring plants. Additionally, the strategy's implementation is demonstrated using three commercially significant varieties of Mexican chili plants.

This study investigates turbulent drag reduction using streamwise-travelling waves of spanwise wall oscillation across a broad spectrum of Reynolds numbers. In Part 1, wall-resolved large-eddy simulations of channel flow analyze the impact of wave frequency and wavenumber on drag reduction at friction Reynolds numbers of $Re_\tau = 951$ and $4000$. The investigation is confined to the inner-scaled actuation (ISA) pathway, which reduces drag by directly damping near-wall turbulent scales. Results indicate that the extent of turbulence attenuation and subsequent drag reduction varies with the near-wall Stokes layer protrusion height, $\ell_{0.01}$. A specific frequency range is identified where the Stokes layer suppresses turbulence, elevating the turbulence generation cycle and thickening the viscous sublayer; within this range, drag reduction rises as $\ell_{0.01}$ increases to 30 viscous units. Conversely, outside this range, intense Stokes shear strain amplifies near-wall turbulence, causing drag reduction to decline with higher $\ell_{0.01}$. Furthermore, within the examined parameter and Reynolds number limits, the power cost of the ISA pathway consistently outweighs any drag reduction benefits. These findings motivate the exploration of the outer-scaled actuation (OSA) pathway in Part 2, where drag reduction is achieved by actuating outer-scaled motions.

Classical novae are driven by thermonuclear explosions on the surfaces of white dwarfs (WDs) that are gaining mass. Observations revealing heavy element enrichments in nova ejecta suggest that material from the accreted layers mixes with the outer layers of the underlying WD before the outburst; however, the exact proportion of this mixing remains unclear. This study aims to identify specific elemental abundance ratios within nova outbursts that can serve as indicators for estimating the WD mixing fraction. Using the stellar evolution code MESA, we simulated nova outbursts across various WD mixing fractions, with initial carbon-oxygen WD masses spanning $0.7-1.0\,M_\odot$. Our findings identify four abundance ratios—$\rm (H+He)/\sum CNO$, $\rm (H+He)/Ne$, $\rm \sum CNO/Mg,$ and $\rm \sum CNO/Si$—that effectively constrain the mixing fraction, with $\rm (H+He)/\sum CNO$ proving to be the most reliable metric. We applied these ratios to estimate mixing fractions in several representative classical novae and discovered a correlation where higher metallicities (indicating greater WD mixing) are associated with longer $t_{\rm 2}$ values (the time required for the luminosity to decline by two magnitudes from its peak). These results provide valuable constraints on the mixing mechanisms operating in classical novae.

For any genus $g \geq 3$, we construct Lefschetz fibrations over the two-sphere with slopes approaching $2$ arbitrarily closely. These fibrations can be selected to have minimal total spaces that are simply connected. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that neither the infimum nor the supremum of the slopes across all such Lefschetz fibrations is actually attained.

In recent years, embedded systems have evolved to demand not only hard real-time performance and reliability but also diverse functional capabilities, including networking. While hypervisor-based virtualization offers a promising solution to meet these needs, most existing hypervisors are tailored for general-purpose computing, relying on extensive system stacks that render them unsuitable for mixed-criticality embedded real-time environments. Furthermore, even hypervisors specifically designed for embedded use often fail to account for the variety of real-time requirements and the rapid advancements in scheduling theory. This paper introduces T-Visor, a hypervisor engineered specifically for mixed-criticality embedded real-time systems. Supporting the ARM architecture, T-Visor achieves full virtualization via ARM Virtualization Extensions. To ensure real-time behavior, it incorporates a flexible scheduling framework that allows developers to choose the most appropriate algorithm for their specific needs. Evaluation results demonstrate that T-Visor outperforms Xen/ARM, leading to the conclusion that our design and implementation are better suited for embedded real-time applications than current hypervisor solutions.

Time serves as a central parameter in our most fundamental descriptions of natural laws. Relativity theory demonstrates that the comparison of times measured by different clocks relies on their relative motion and the strength of the gravitational field in which they exist. In standard cosmology, the time parameter corresponds to that measured by fundamental clocks (i.e., clocks at rest relative to the expanding space). This proper time is traditionally assumed to flow at a constant rate throughout the entire history of the universe. We propose an alternative hypothesis: the rate at which cosmological time flows depends on the dynamical state of the universe. In thermodynamics, the arrow of time is closely linked to the second law, which states that the entropy of an isolated system will always increase over time or, at best, remain constant. Consequently, we assume that the time measured by fundamental clocks is proportional to the entropy of the region of the universe causally connected to them. Under this simple assumption, we demonstrate that it is possible to construct toy cosmological models that exhibit accelerated expansion without requiring dark energy, while maintaining a spatially closed and finite geometry, thereby avoiding the need to handle infinite values.

Effective feature representation is crucial for classifying remote-sensing images. Although deep convolutional neural networks excel at integrating information, their vast parameter counts often render learned features opaque and challenging to transfer to other models. To enhance the representation of statistical texture data for such classification tasks, this study explores a novel histogram neural network that performs joint dimensionality reduction and classification. Inspired by t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE), our method integrates a classification loss function applied directly within a low-dimensional embedding space. We evaluate the resulting sample embeddings against those generated by t-SNE, comparing both quantitative classification accuracy and qualitative visualizations. Additionally, we examine the impact of different divergence measures within the t-SNE objective. The proposed approach offers key benefits, including the ability to easily embed out-of-sample points and reduce feature dimensions while preserving class separability. Experimental results indicate that this method sustains or enhances classification performance while uncovering neural network feature characteristics that could prove valuable for other applications.

Strongly-coupled nanomagnetic arrays are increasingly utilized as model platforms for reconfigurable magnonics. The intense inter-element coupling generates significant spectral variations across a wide range of microstates by altering the dipolar field environment. Although early results have been promising, the challenge of rapidly and scalably accessing diverse, spectrally distinct microstates remains unsolved. This study introduces a method involving a modified square artificial spin ice, where a "staircase" portion of the bars is widened relative to the rest of the array. This modification enables the preparation of any ordered vertex state using straightforward global-field techniques. The accessible microstates span from the system's ground state to high-energy "monopole" configurations, exhibiting rich and unique magnon spectra specific to each state. Both remanent and in-field conditions reveal microstate-dependent mode hybridization and anticrossings, with dynamic coupling strength adjustable through microstate selection. Experimental coupling strengths reach up to g / 2π = 0.15 GHz. Furthermore, controlling the microstate facilitates precise adjustments of mode frequencies, the creation or closure of gaps, and the active selection of mode numbers.

This is a highly subjective survey paper designed for non-specialists, addressing group actions on Gromov hyperbolic spaces. The initial section introduces hyperbolic groups, whereas the remainder of the work examines mapping class groups and $Out(F_n)$, detailing how their large-scale geometry can be understood through actions on various hyperbolic spaces derived from projection complexes. The paper notes that the current comprehension of $Out(F_n)$ lags significantly behind that of mapping class groups and concludes by presenting several open questions.

Acoustic signals generated by nearby fireballs (within 200 km) detected by extensive ground networks can help estimate both the trajectory orientation and fragmentation sites of bolides (Pujol et al., 2005; Kalenda et al., 2014; Edwards and Hildebrand, 2004). While differentiating between ballistic arrivals from the cylindrical shock and signals from quasi-spherical fragmentation sources remains difficult, this distinction is achievable by analyzing acoustic paths and timing data from ground sensors. This paper introduces an integrated computational tool, the Bolide Acoustic Modelling program (BAM), designed to calculate fireball trajectories and energy release. We present a novel method for deriving energy release during fragmentation events exclusively from acoustic data and integrate it into BAM. Additionally, we investigate how uncertainties in atmospheric models affect seismo-acoustic solutions and energy estimates. When applied to the Stubenberg meteorite event, BAM determined that the ballistic energy was approximately $5 \times 10^{10}$J, aligning well with the optical estimate of $4.36 \times 10^{10}$J. The acoustic analysis further revealed a combined fragmentation energy of $1.47^{+0.28}_{-0.12} \times 10^{10}$J, representing roughly one-third of the total ballistic or optical energy. Finally, we demonstrate that deriving fireball velocities from acoustic data alone is highly challenging, though feasible for slow, deeply penetrating fireballs with shallow entry angles observed over dense seismic or infrasound networks.

The LHC lifetime frontier and visible decay searches at fixed-target facilities are poised to investigate the dark sector in the near term. A compelling framework for resolving the coincidence between visible and dark matter involves composite asymmetric dark matter coupled via a dark photon portal. Within this model, dark strong dynamics endows the dark sector with complex structure: the lightest dark nucleon constitutes the dark matter, while symmetric components are depleted through strong annihilation into dark pions. Dark photons help address cosmological issues and simultaneously extend the lifetimes of dark hadrons in terrestrial settings. Since dark hadrons are produced via the same dark photon, this study examines visible decay searches for composite asymmetric dark matter. For dark nucleons in the few-GeV range, the LHC lifetime frontier, along with MATHUSLA and FASER, could detect their decays if the dark photon kinetic mixing angle satisfies $\epsilon \gtrsim 10^{-4}$. Conversely, fixed-target experiments like SeaQuest, complemented by the LHC lifetime frontier, will achieve high sensitivity to dark pions with masses below the GeV scale and kinetic mixing $\epsilon \gtrsim 10^{-4}$. These projected reach limits for dark hadrons in dark photon parameter space are comparable to the anticipated sensitivities of future dark photon searches at Belle-II and LHCb.

Recent advancements in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) now enable the creation of high-resolution, realistic images from natural language inputs like captions. Moreover, conditional GANs permit steering the generation process using labels or text descriptions. Nevertheless, achieving fine-grained control over image composition—specifically the precise placement of objects—remains challenging, particularly for scenes involving multiple distinct items at varying spatial coordinates. We present a novel method that facilitates the positioning of any number of objects within an image by incorporating an object pathway into both the generator and discriminator. This approach requires only bounding boxes and corresponding object labels, eliminating the need for detailed semantic layouts. The object pathway concentrates exclusively on individual items and is applied iteratively at the coordinates defined by the bounding boxes, whereas the global pathway attends to the image background and overall structure. We evaluated our method on the Multi-MNIST, CLEVR, and the more intricate MS-COCO datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that the object pathway successfully governs object placement and enables the modeling of complex scenes with multiple entities at diverse locations. Additionally, we verified that the object pathway learns features specific to individual objects, while the global pathway captures broader image characteristics and background details.

This study introduces three new block-structured multigrid relaxation strategies—grounded in distributive, Braess-Sarazin, and Uzawa methods—for resolving Stokes equations discretized via the mark-and-cell scheme. While our previous research \cite{he2018local} examined these schemes using weighted Jacobi iterations to handle the Laplacian component of the Stokes equations, demonstrating optimal smoothing factors of $\frac{3}{5}$ for distributive and inexact Braess-Sarazin variants and $\sqrt{\frac{3}{5}}$ for $\sigma$-Uzawa relaxation, this work advances the approach by incorporating mass-based approximations. Specifically, we utilize the mass matrix $Q$ derived from bilinear finite elements to directly approximate the inverse of the scalar Laplacian operator, replacing the Jacobi iteration. Through local Fourier analysis, we theoretically determine the optimal smoothing factors for these updated schemes: mass-based distributive and Braess-Sarazin relaxations achieve a factor of $\frac{1}{3}$, while mass-based $\sigma$-Uzawa relaxation reaches $\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}$. Importantly, these mass-based methods incur no additional computational cost compared to the original Jacobi-based versions and eliminate the necessity of computing a matrix inverse, rendering them highly advantageous.

Latent dynamics models have become essential for analyzing and interpreting the activity of neural populations. Recent efforts have sought to integrate concurrently recorded behavioral data into these frameworks to better separate sources of variability within the latent space. However, existing methods struggle to accurately capture underlying neural dynamics, such as linear patterns, and often fail to establish a clear temporal relationship between learned dynamics and observed behavior. To address these limitations, we propose Targeted Neural Dynamical Modeling (TNDM), a nonlinear state-space model that simultaneously accounts for neural activity and external behavioral variables. TNDM separates neural dynamics into behaviorally relevant and irrelevant components; the relevant dynamics drive a flexible linear decoder to reconstruct behavior, while both dynamic sets feed into a linear decoder with no time lag to reconstruct neural activity. We realized TNDM as a sequential variational autoencoder and tested it on both simulated data and recordings from a monkey's premotor and motor cortex during a center-out reaching task. Our results demonstrate that TNDM successfully learns low-dimensional latent dynamics that strongly predict behavior while maintaining a high fidelity fit to the neural data.

Opinion summarization focuses on profiling a target by extracting opinions across numerous documents. Since acquiring high-quality annotations for thousands of documents is challenging, most current methods adopt a semi-supervised approach, often relying on aspect and sentiment analysis as proxies to identify opinions. This paper introduces FineSum, a novel framework that advances the field through three key improvements: (1) minimal supervision, requiring only aspect names and a limited set of aspect/sentiment keywords; (2) fine-grained opinion analysis, which extends sentiment evaluation to the sub-aspect level; and (3) phrase-based summarization, which presents opinions as concise phrases. FineSum automatically extracts opinion phrases from raw data, categorizes them by aspect and sentiment, and builds multiple fine-grained clusters under each category. Each cluster contains semantically consistent phrases reflecting uniform sentiments toward specific sub-aspects or features (e.g., positive reactions to "burgers" within the "food" aspect). The system trains an opinion-oriented spherical word embedding space to offer weak supervision for the phrase classifier and utilizes aspect-aware contextualized embeddings from the classifier to perform phrase clustering. Both automated benchmark evaluations and quantitative human assessments confirm the method's effectiveness.

Precise language alignment is essential for enhancing cross-lingual pre-trained models (XLMs). Inspired by the natural occurrence of code-switching (CS) among multilingual speakers, CS serves as a potent data augmentation technique that provides word- or phrase-level alignment, differing from the sentence-level alignment found in parallel corpora. Current methods typically rely on dictionaries or parallel sentences with word alignments to create CS data by randomly swapping words; however, these approaches often yield suboptimal results because dictionaries ignore semantics and random swapping can break syntactic validity. This paper introduces EntityCS, a method centered on entity-level code-switching to capture fine-grained cross-lingual meanings while maintaining syntactic integrity. By leveraging Wikidata and English Wikipedia, we construct an entity-focused CS corpus by replacing entities with their multilingual counterparts. Additionally, we develop entity-oriented masking strategies for intermediate training on this corpus to bolster entity prediction capabilities. Experiments across four entity-centric downstream tasks demonstrate consistent performance gains over baselines, with a significant 10% improvement in Fact Retrieval. We have made the corpus and models publicly available to support future research on code-switching and to enrich XLMs with external knowledge.

Soft hadronic collisions involving the multi-production of (anti)quarks alongside soft photon emission are modeled using higher Fock states of the colliding hadrons, which incorporate a photon component. The distribution functions for these Fock states are determined using the Quark-Gluon String Model, while photon radiation from quarks is explained through color-dipole phenomenology. The calculated results align well with existing data across a broad spectrum of photon transverse momenta.

We present both analytical and numerical investigations into the magnetotransport properties of strained graphene within a Corbino geometry under an external perpendicular magnetic field. Utilizing the Landauer-Büttiker formalism, we compute the conductance of a Corbino disc subjected to uniaxial and inhomogeneous strain. Our findings indicate that the oscillation period of conductance as a function of magnetic flux is influenced by uniaxial strain, while conductance exhibits a sharp decline along the axis of graphene stretching. Conversely, the conductance amplitude can be controlled through induced pseudomagnetic flux. Furthermore, inhomogeneous strain generates a valley-polarized regime, and we identify a broad energy range where the system remains fully valley polarized.

Gamma-ray Burst (GRB) prompt emission spectra are frequently modeled using the empirical "Band" function, which consists of two smoothly connected power laws, typically with a low-energy (sub-MeV) slope of $\alpha_{B}\simeq -1$. However, in a minority of long GRBs, this power law divides into two components, creating a break ranging from a few keV to hundreds of keV alongside the standard $\sim$ MeV $\nu F_{\nu}$ peak. The spectral slopes below and above this break are generally -0.6 and -1.5, respectively. If such breaks are common, the observed $\alpha_{B}$ value might represent an average of the slopes on either side of the break in Band-function fits.

Our analysis of 27 bright long and short GRBs detected by the Fermi satellite reveals low-energy breaks between 80 keV and 280 keV in 12 long GRBs, but none in short events. Spectral simulations demonstrate that moving the break closer to (or farther from) the peak energy results in a harder (or softer) fitted $\alpha_{B}$. The hard average slope of $\alpha_{B}\simeq-0.38$ observed in short GRBs implies that their breaks lie close to the peak energy. Furthermore, we find that for 15 long GRBs best fitted solely by the Band function, a break likely exists but remains undetectable in Fermi/GBM data due to either low energies near the detector limit (for soft $\alpha_{B}\lesssim-1$) or proximity to the peak energy (for hard $\alpha_{B}\gtrsim-1$). While a spectrum featuring two breaks may be typical of GRB prompt emission, current detectors struggle to identify it. However, the instrumental design planned for the THESEUS space mission, which spans 0.3 keV to several MeV with a larger effective area than Fermi/GBM, could uncover a greater proportion of GRBs exhibiting spectral energy breaks.
Estimates for the Kolmogorov widths of finite-dimensional ball intersections are derived.

Phononic frequency combs have garnered growing interest both as a novel form of nonlinear behavior in vibrational systems and for their practical applications. While it is generally assumed that generating a comb requires at least two modes, this paper demonstrates that a single nanomechanical mode, when driven by a resonant monochromatic force, can produce a comb. This phenomenon occurs under weak driving conditions where the anharmonic component of the mode's potential energy remains minimal. We attribute this effect to negative nonlinear friction induced by the resonant drive, which destabilizes vibrations at the drive frequency. By directly mapping the trajectories of the resulting oscillations in the rotating frame, we illustrate how these oscillations generate the frequency comb observed in the laboratory frame. These findings extend beyond the realm of nanomechanics, proposing a fundamentally new method for creating tunable frequency combs within single-mode vibrational systems.

Distributed access control is essential for massive machine-type communication (mMTC). In this context, centralized resource allocation lacks scalability due to the need for frequent transmission of resource configurations from the base station to a vast number of devices. This study explores distributed reinforcement learning for resource selection that operates independently of centralized control. A defining characteristic of mMTC is the sporadic and dynamic nature of traffic; however, existing research on distributed access control typically assumes static traffic loads or relies on gradual adaptation to dynamic changes. To minimize the adaptation period, we train TinyQMIX—a lightweight multi-agent deep reinforcement learning model—to learn a distributed wireless resource selection policy across various traffic patterns prior to deployment. Consequently, the trained agents can rapidly adapt to dynamic traffic conditions, resulting in low access delays. Numerical results are provided to validate these claims.

Annotating prepositional supersenses is labor-intensive and demands specialized expertise. In this study, we introduce two viable approaches to generate these annotations by soliciting surface-level substitution and similarity assessments. Findings from four pilot studies indicate that both methods hold promise for producing annotations of quality comparable to those created by experts.

Stencil computation represents a critical kernel in numerous scientific and engineering domains. While extensive research has targeted vectorization to leverage in-core data parallelism, existing methods often face challenges, such as data alignment conflicts or degraded locality when combined with tiling. This paper introduces a novel transpose layout that simultaneously maintains data locality for tiling and minimizes reorganization overhead for vectorization. Furthermore, we propose a temporal computation folding technique that exploits register reuse to reduce arithmetic redundancy, mitigate register pressure, and enable generalization through a linear regression model. Experiments conducted on AVX-2 and AVX-512 architectures demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive performance.

Theoretical analysis investigates the generation of traveling sine-Gordon breathers arising from the nonlinear supratransmission effect within a long Josephson junction subjected to appropriate magnetic pulses, while incorporating dissipation, current bias, and thermal noise. Simulation results demonstrate that, contingent upon the pulse morphology and key system parameters, this setup can produce exclusively breather excitations. Additionally, the probability of generating breathers alone exhibits a nonmonotonic dependence on noise intensity. Finally, the dynamics of these supratransmission-induced breathers are analyzed through metrics including their radiative decay lifetime and the medium's energy.

Ground-state moments of inertia (MoI) have been examined for approximately 1700 even-even nuclei spanning from the proton to the neutron drip line, extending up to $Z=120$ and $N=184$, using a cranked Skyrme-Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov equation solved in coordinate space. This model accurately reproduces experimental data for over 300 deformed nuclides. The findings indicate that MoI values rise significantly near the drip lines, although the associated deformation is less pronounced than predicted by empirical relations. Furthermore, systematic measurements of excitation energies and transition probabilities to the first $I^\pi=2^+$ state in neutron-rich nuclei provide insights into deformation evolution and help constrain effective pair interactions.

We investigate the Bethe/gauge correspondence at a specific point in the Coulomb moduli space where the integrable system displays degenerate level splitting. This study focuses on four-dimensional pure $\mathcal{N}=2$ supersymmetric $U(N)$ gauge theory, utilizing a half-BPS surface defect formed via an orbifold or a degenerate gauge vertex. We demonstrate that non-perturbative Dyson-Schwinger equations yield both Schrödinger-type and Baxter-type differential equations for the corresponding surface defect partition functions. At this special locus, the partition function decomposes into distinct components, allowing us to recover the Bethe/gauge dictionary for each individual summand.

Integrable optics represents a novel advancement in particle accelerator engineering, offering robust nonlinear focusing without triggering parametric resonances. A key application of this technology is to surpass conventional intensity constraints in accelerators caused by betatron tune-spread and collective instabilities. Over the coming years, the performance of high-intensity integrable systems will be rigorously evaluated at the Fermilab Integrable Optics Test Accelerator (IOTA) and the University of Maryland Electron Ring (UMER). We propose an integrable Rapid-Cycling Synchrotron (iRCS) to replace the Fermilab Booster, aiming to deliver multi-MW beam power for Fermilab's high-energy neutrino initiatives. This paper outlines the machine parameters and details a strategy for lattice optimization. Fundamentally, integrable optics relies on arcs with integer-pi phase advance succeeded by drifts featuring matched beta functions. We present a sample integrable lattice incorporating characteristics of a modern rapid-cycling synchrotron, including long dispersion-free drifts, minimal momentum compaction, superperiodicity, chromaticity correction, separate-function magnets, and bounded beta functions.

Determining heritability is a core objective in genetics, addressing how much genetic variation drives differences in specific traits. While traditional methods for estimating trait heritability originated in quantitative genetics, the advent of modern sequencing has enabled the analysis of whole-genome sequences alongside extensive phenotypic data across large populations. This surge in data volume has spurred the creation of new machine learning techniques for inferring heritability. This review systematically outlines recent progress in machine learning applications for heritability estimation, with a specific focus on bacterial genomes. In bacteria, heritability is critical for understanding key phenotypes like virulence and drug resistance, issues that have gained urgency due to the escalating global threat of antimicrobial resistance. We highlight applications of these emerging machine learning methods to quantify the heritability of antibiotic resistance in various pathogens, offering valuable insights and lessons for future research utilizing machine learning in heritability inference.

This study demonstrates the application of the two-photon absorption transient current technique to wide bandgap semiconductors, specifically to investigate the charge transport properties of single-crystal Chemical Vapor Deposition (scCVD) diamond. In this setup, femtosecond laser pulses excite charge carriers within the diamond sample via the simultaneous absorption of two photons. Because two-photon absorption inherently restricts carrier generation to the three-dimensional space surrounding the laser's focal point, this localized injection enables the probing of bulk semiconductor properties with high 3-D spatial resolution. By leveraging this spatial confinement, we mapped the internal electric field of the diamond at various depths and compared these results against an X-ray diffraction topograph of the sample. Ultimately, this method offers a unique approach for examining spatial variations in charge transport characteristics within transparent, wide-bandgap semiconductors.

For many decades, astronomers have measured electromagnetic radiation across the entire energy spectrum with remarkable precision. While the low-energy radio portion of this spectrum is relatively well-understood, a persistent gap between theoretical predictions and observational data has led to numerous proposed models for radio sources. This study demonstrates that residual electron-proton interactions in the early universe—known as cosmic free-free emission—resolve this discrepancy. Although the concept of cosmic free-free emission has been hypothesized for some time, this work marks the first calculation of its signal's amplitude and shape, alongside the proof of its existence. Based on current data, we estimate this emission becomes significant at a redshift of approximately $z \simeq 2150$. This signal, arising from fundamental particles and interactions, offers the lowest-energy test from the early universe of Quantum Electrodynamics, a cornerstone of modern physics. Future deep radio surveys will be capable of detecting these primordial signals with higher precision, thereby strengthening our comprehension of the radio sky.

We introduce a rapid asynchronous Byzantine agreement protocol for systems with $n > 3t + 1$ processes, where $t$ denotes the maximum number of tolerated faults, achieving agreement in $O(t)$ expected time. This surpasses the $O(n^2)$ expected time previously established by Abraham, Dolev, and Halpern [PODC 2008]. Additionally, when $n = (3 + \varepsilon)t$ for any $\varepsilon > 0$, our protocol achieves agreement in $O(1 / \varepsilon)$ expected time, an improvement over the results of Feldman and Micali [STOC 1988], which offered constant expected time only when $n > 4t$.

This paper introduces a mixture composite regression model designed for analyzing claim severity, which often presents challenges like multimodality, heavy tails, and systematic data effects. The proposed model simultaneously addresses attritional and large claims by incorporating systematic effects into both the mixture components and the mixing probabilities. To fit the model, we employ a group-fused regularization technique that identifies explanatory variables significantly influencing the mixing probabilities and individual mixture components. Furthermore, we establish an asymptotic theory for this regularized estimation method and implement fitting using a new Generalized Expectation-Maximization algorithm, demonstrating the approach with real motor insurance data.

Self-supervised pretraining has become the preferred approach for natural language processing and is quickly becoming dominant in vision tasks. It has recently surpassed supervised pretraining in numerous downstream vision applications, representing a significant breakthrough. This advantage stems from the limitations of incomplete labeling in supervised training, where images containing multiple concepts are often annotated with only a single dominant class. While Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) theoretically avoids this constraint, the specific pretext tasks used often reinforce the focus on a single concept. This study explores the potential of modeling all concepts within an image without relying on labels. To this end, the proposed MC-SSL0.0 framework advances Multi-Concept Self-Supervised Learning by moving beyond single-label modeling to effectively leverage information from all concepts present. Built on two core principles—group masked model learning and pseudo-concept learning via a momentum encoder within a teacher-student framework—experimental results on multi-label and multi-class classification tasks show that MC-SSL0.0 exceeds the performance of existing SSL methods and even supervised transfer learning. The source code will be released publicly to enable the community to train on larger datasets.

The surging need for highly personalized novel therapeutics, such as gene therapies for tailored cancer treatment and rapidly evolving vaccines, is exerting significant pressure on the traditional timelines of pharmaceutical R&D and manufacturing, forcing a faster transition from design to production. This shift has already catalyzed technological transformations within the industry, driving a move away from the conventional model of large-scale batch production toward flexible, modular continuous biomanufacturing—a trend bolstered by advancements in single-use equipment. Unlike the past era characterized by lengthy design cycles, low product variability, and rigid systems, modern pharmaceutical companies are now addressing the critical challenge of aligning design and process control with the accelerated capabilities of these new technologies to enable rapid, flexible production runs. This tutorial explores key operational research challenges and potential solutions to address this issue. We begin by outlining technical hurdles and innovative methods for designing next-generation drugs, followed by an examination of process modeling and control strategies required to manufacture them efficiently and successfully.

The CogSense system, proposed in this paper, draws inspiration from mammalian brain cognition and perception to detect perception errors and adapt perception parameters using probabilistic signal temporal logic. As a specific application, a contrast-based perception adaptation method is introduced and validated. This approach assesses perception errors by employing heterogeneous probe functions derived from detected objects, followed by solving a contrast optimization problem to rectify these errors. The CogSense probe functions leverage object characteristics—specifically geometry, dynamics, and detected blob image quality—to formulate axioms within a probabilistic signal temporal logic framework. By evaluating these axioms, the system formally verifies the validity of detections. Furthermore, utilizing these CogSense axioms, probabilistic signal temporal logic-based constraints are generated to resolve the contrast-based optimization problem, thereby minimizing both false positives and false negatives.

This paper introduces mmPose-NLP, a new Sequence-to-Sequence (Seq2Seq) skeletal key-point estimator that leverages Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques and millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar data. To our knowledge, this is the inaugural method capable of accurately estimating up to 25 skeletal key-points using solely mmWave radar data. Skeletal pose estimation is vital for various applications, including autonomous driving, traffic surveillance, patient monitoring, gait analysis, and defense security forensics, supporting both preventive and actionable decision-making. Unlike traditional optical sensors, mmWave radars offer superior robustness against adverse weather and varying lighting conditions, where optical performance often degrades. In the proposed approach, mmWave point-cloud (PCL) data is voxelized, analogous to NLP tokenization. A sequence of $N$ voxelized frames, similar to a text paragraph, is processed by the mmPose-NLP architecture to predict voxel indices corresponding to the 25 skeletal key-points, akin to keyword extraction. These indices are then converted into real-world 3-D coordinates using a voxel dictionary from the tokenization stage. Accuracy was evaluated using Mean Absolute Error (MAE) against ground truth, with mmPose-NLP achieving localization errors under 3 cm across depth, horizontal, and vertical axes. Additionally, the study analyzed the impact of varying the number of input frames ($N = 1$ to $10$) on performance. This paper details a comprehensive methodology, results, discussions, and limitations. All source code and results are publicly available on GitHub to support further research and development in this emerging field of mmWave-based skeletal key-point estimation.

We examine a $U(1)_{L_\mu - L_\tau}$ extended left-right symmetric gauge theory in which neutrino masses arise via the inverse seesaw mechanism. Within this framework, the muon $(g-2)$ anomaly is explained by the exchange of $Z_{\mu\tau}$, the gauge boson associated with the $U(1)_{L_\mu - L_\tau}$ symmetry. The model's symmetries impose a specific two-zero texture on the light neutrino mass matrix, resulting in non-trivial constraints on the minimum neutrino mass. Furthermore, the theory predicts observable charged lepton flavor violation within the $\mu-\tau$ sector.

Prior research indicates that the stellar mean metallicity and [Mg/Fe] ratios in massive elliptical (E) galaxies imply an extremely rapid star formation timescale, a finding that conflicts with both stellar population synthesis (SPS) models and hierarchical assembly theories. To address this, the GalIMF chemical evolution code was employed, re-evaluating star formation timescales (SFTs) by incorporating an environment-dependent stellar initial mass function (IMF) within the integrated galaxy initial mass function (IGIMF) framework, rather than relying on a fixed canonical IMF. GalIMF's distinct feature is its capacity for the galaxy-wide IMF and chemical enrichment to evolve alongside changing physical conditions. Consistency between these recalculated SFTs and independent SPS results is achieved if the yield of type Ia supernovae (SNIa) per unit stellar mass rises with increasing E galaxy mass. This occurs naturally because galaxies with higher star-formation rates generate more massive star clusters, thereby producing a greater number of SNIa progenitors per star. Calculations reveal that E galaxies with a stellar mass near $10^{9.5} M_\odot$ possessed the longest mean SFTs of approximately 2 Gyr. In contrast, the majority of more massive E galaxies formed more quickly (SFT $\approx$ 1 Gyr), resulting in the observed dominance of M dwarf stars and elevated dynamical mass-to-light ratios. Meanwhile, lower-mass galaxies tend to deplete their gas reservoirs more readily due to shallower gravitational potentials, leading to similarly short mean SFTs. For the first time, this study reconciles star formation timescales for early-type galaxies across chemical enrichment and SPS modeling, offering a refined understanding of how star formation environments influence the total number of SNIa per unit of stellar mass formed.

There is increasing acknowledgment that introductory labs should move beyond "cookbook" formats toward more meaningful learning experiences. To evaluate the merits and drawbacks of combining cookbook-style and inquiry-based approaches, researchers observed an introductory lab course undergoing reform using a reflexive ethnographic protocol, alongside administering pre- and post-E-CLASS surveys. The resulting data analysis aimed to pinpoint current lab deficiencies and identify opportunities for enhancement.

Color-based re-identification techniques typically utilize distance functions to assess similarity between individuals. This paper investigates the performance of various histogram distance metrics across different color spaces. We examine whether specific distance measures or color spaces offer superior discrimination capabilities. Through experiments conducted on multiple image databases, we evaluate these metrics to determine optimal configurations. A ranking system is established based on the area under the CMC curve, serving as the primary indicator for identifying the most effective distance measure and color space for the tested datasets. Additionally, we analyze other parameters, including horizontal stripe segmentation and the number of histogram bins.

Accurately estimating instruction-level throughput is vital for numerous domains, including multimedia, low-latency networking, medical, automotive, avionics, and industrial control systems, as these rely on precise and calculable timing guarantees for their software. However, determining the exact execution duration or halting behavior of a program is generally undecidable. Consequently, current state-of-the-art tools typically restrict themselves to subsets of operations and rely on simplifying assumptions. Identifying the specific constraints and regions of interest usually demands access to source code, specialized utilities, and expert domain knowledge. Since any modification to a single instruction necessitates re-running this analysis, the iterative development of timing-critical code incurs substantial costs.

This paper introduces MCAD, a novel and lightweight framework designed to detect the impact of code modifications on the microarchitectural level within binary programs. By emulating full program execution using QEMU and passing traces to LLVM for instruction-level analysis, MCAD delivers accurate differential throughput estimates. This approach enables developers to iterate rapidly with minimal overhead using standard tools; pinpointing execution paths that are less sensitive to timing variations compared to critical paths takes only minutes within MCAD. To our knowledge, this marks a completely new capability that accelerates differential throughput estimation turnaround times by several orders of magnitude relative to existing tools. Our comprehensive evaluation demonstrates that MCAD scales effectively to real-world applications such as FFmpeg and Clang, which contain millions of instructions, achieving a geometric mean error of less than 3% against ground truth timings obtained from hardware performance counters on x86 and ARM architectures.

We analyze the rotational dynamics of a thin galactic disc containing both stars and gas, subjected to an external tidal field, and derive the coupled differential equations that describe the evolution of instabilities. By linearizing these governing equations, we obtain a modified dispersion relation and a stability criterion to assess the stability of this two-fluid disc under tidal influence. Finally, we discuss potential applications and methodologies related to this work.

A graph $H$ is defined as ubiquitous if the condition that every natural number $n$ yields $n$ vertex-disjoint $H$-minors in a graph $G$ implies that $G$ actually contains infinitely many vertex-disjoint $H$-minors. Andreae conjectured that all locally finite graphs possess this property. We present a counterexample to this conjecture by utilizing a disconnected graph. The question of whether every connected locally finite graph is ubiquitous remains unresolved.

Bayesian networks serve as a potent instrument for analyzing probabilistic causality across numerous scientific disciplines; however, they are fundamentally rooted in classical mechanics. Specifically, they inherently produce Bell inequalities. Motivated by this link, we have extended the formalism of classical Bayesian networks to explore non-classical correlations within any causal architecture. Our proposed framework of "generalised Bayesian networks" substitutes latent variables with resources from any generalised probabilistic theory, encompassing quantum mechanics as well as alternatives like Popescu-Rohrlich boxes. We derive three primary findings. First, we demonstrate that all observable conditional independences mandated by classical theory remain valid in this generalised context by extending the classical $d$-separation theorem. Second, we identify that theory-independent constraints on probabilities can exceed these conditional independences; for instance, we show that no probabilistic theory allows for perfect correlation among three parties relying solely on bipartite common causes. Finally, we initiate a classification of causal structures, such as the Bell scenario, capable of distinguishing between classical, quantum, and general-probabilistic correlations.

Control variables serve as a crucial method for addressing endogeneity within econometric frameworks characterized by nonseparable or multidimensional heterogeneity. This approach accommodates discrete instruments, establishing identification conditions across various constraints regarding how endogenous variables and controls influence the outcome. The analysis examines numerous structural parameters of interest, including average and quantile treatment effects. These theoretical findings are demonstrated through an empirical application focused on estimating Engel curves.

We define the diameter cover number, $D^t_r(G)$, as the smallest integer $d$ for which, in any $r$-coloring of the edges of graph $G$, one can find $t$ monochromatic subgraphs each with a diameter no greater than $d$ that collectively include every vertex of $G$. This study investigates this parameter specifically for two colors and two subgraphs within complete multipartite graphs containing at least three parts. We establish the precise value of $D_2^2(G)$ for all complete tripartite graphs and for nearly all complete multipartite graphs with more than three parts.

Off-policy Evaluation (OPE), or offline evaluation broadly, assesses the performance of hypothetical policies using solely historical log data. This approach is especially valuable in high-stakes, costly domains like recommender systems and precision medicine. However, as numerous OPE estimators have emerged—many requiring hyperparameter tuning—practitioners face a growing challenge in selecting and configuring the most appropriate estimator for their specific needs. Currently, identifying a reliable estimator from research literature is often problematic because existing experimental protocols typically test only a limited range of hyperparameters and evaluation policies, making it hard to determine which estimator is truly safe. To address this, we introduce Interpretable Evaluation for Offline Evaluation (IEOE), a novel procedure designed to assess the robustness of OPE estimators regarding hyperparameter and policy variations in an interpretable way. Utilizing IEOE, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation of diverse existing estimators on the Open Bandit Dataset, a large-scale public real-world benchmark for OPE. Our results demonstrate that this procedure effectively evaluates estimator robustness against hyperparameter choices, helping users avoid unsafe methods. Furthermore, we applied IEOE to real-world e-commerce data to illustrate its practical implementation.

Voyager probe data have yielded the first measurements of cosmic ray intensities at MeV energies, a previously uncharted range. However, simple extrapolations of GeV-energy models, such as those from AMS-02, fail to match these findings because they predict intensities that are too high. This discrepancy is frequently addressed by arbitrarily introducing breaks in the source spectrum or diffusion coefficient, lacking a robust physical justification. In contrast, we propose that the discrete nature of cosmic ray sources—often overlooked—is the more plausible explanation. By modeling the intensity distribution expected from a statistical ensemble of discrete sources, we demonstrate that the mean value is unrepresentative and exhibits a spectral shape distinct from typical source configurations. Nevertheless, Voyager data for both protons and electrons align well with the median of this intensity distribution. Crucially, this model accounts for the Voyager observations without necessitating any unphysical spectral breaks.

Soft, smooth particles discharged from a silo exhibit unique behaviors, such as intermittent flow and temporary blockages. This study investigates soft, low-friction hydrogel spheres within a quasi-2D silo, enhancing their competitive dynamics during discharge by introducing an obstacle before the outlet. High-speed optical imaging captures the discharge process, while machine learning (specifically MASK R-CNN) identifies and tracks every particle in the field of view. Using particle tracking velocimetry (PTV), the analysis examines velocity fields, egress times, packing fractions, and kinetic stress. Although placing an obstacle before a narrow gate can lower stress and improve efficiency in pedestrian dynamics, the opposite occurs with these soft grains; an obstacle above the orifice consistently reduces flow rates and, in certain instances, increases the likelihood of clogging.

We introduce PyTorch Geometric Temporal, a deep learning framework that unifies state-of-the-art machine learning algorithms for neural spatiotemporal signal processing. The library aims to provide researchers and practitioners with a streamlined, user-friendly environment for temporal geometric deep learning. Built upon the PyTorch ecosystem, the framework features optimized neural network layers, temporal snapshot generators for efficient batching, and built-in benchmark datasets, all demonstrated through a tutorial-style case study. Experimental results highlight the models' predictive capabilities on real-world challenges, including epidemiological forecasting, ride-hail demand prediction, and web traffic management. Furthermore, our runtime sensitivity analysis suggests the framework is capable of handling web-scale datasets characterized by complex temporal features and spatial structures.

Building on recent progress in retrieval-augmented NLP techniques~\citep{khandelwal2019generalization,khandelwal2020nearest,meng2021gnn}, this paper presents a $k$ nearest neighbor NER ($k$NN-NER) framework. This approach enhances the distribution of entity labels by incorporating $k$ nearest neighbors retrieved from the training set, thereby improving the model's ability to address long-tail scenarios and boosting few-shot learning performance. Notably, $k$NN-NER introduces no extra operations during training; by seamlessly integrating nearest neighbor search into standard NER models, it consistently surpasses baseline methods. We achieve a new state-of-the-art F1-score of 72.03 (+1.25) on the Chinese Weibo dataset and observe gains across various widely used NER benchmarks. Furthermore, $k$NN-NER delivers results comparable to vanilla NER models using 40\% less training data. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/ShannonAI/KNN-NER}.

This study outlines a method for extracting plasma parameters from I-V Langmuir curves using the Druyvesteyn equation, introducing two novel parameters, $q$ and $r$, alongside the standard set of plasma potential ($V_p$), floating potential ($V_f$), electron density ($n$), and electron temperature ($T$). These new parameters are especially effective for characterizing non-Maxwellian distributions. The approach relies on fitting the I-V Langmuir curve to a $q$-Weibull distribution function, inspired by recent research utilizing the $q$-exponential distribution derived from Tsallis statistics. We derive the conventional plasma parameters using three distinct methods: numerical differentiation via Savitzky-Golay (SG) filters, the $q$-exponential distribution, and the $q$-Weibull distribution. We identify limitations in the $q$-exponential function, noting that it requires pre-trimming experimental data where $V>V_p$, which reduces accuracy compared to SG-based numerical differentiation. To address this, the $q$-Weibull function is presented as a natural generalization of the $q$-exponential distribution, offering superior flexibility in modeling concavity changes near $V_p$. We apply this procedure to analyze measurements from a nitrogen ($N_2$) cold plasma, acquired using a single Langmuir probe at varying heights from the cathode. Our results indicate that the $q$ parameter maintains a highly stable numerical value across different heights. While this work highlights the advantages and limitations of applying non-extensive statistics to plasma diagnostics, the physical interpretation of these non-extensive parameters within plasma physics remains unclear and warrants further investigation.

Starting from the conservation of momentum, a multiphase mechanical energy balance is formulated to address multiple material phases and interfaces within a moving control volume. This balance is applied to a control volume fixed to a three-phase contact line as it advances across a rough yet chemically uniform solid surface. By employing semi-quantitative models for material behavior within this volume, an order-of-magnitude analysis identifies significant terms, yielding an equation capable of predicting contact angle hysteresis based on interface dynamics near the three-phase line. Beyond this equation, the theory clarifies several points in wetting literature: (1) static contact angle hysteresis depends on conditions at the three-phase contact line rather than the broader flow system; (2) hysteresis arises from energy-dissipating interface "jumps" instead of direct contact line deformation; (3) predicting hysteresis requires interfacial dynamics, which must be interpreted through energy conservation; and (4) dynamic contact angles are influenced by kinetic energy transport around the three-phase line and local energy dissipation. The framework relies on assumptions of incompressible Newtonian fluids, reversible interface formation, and zero-strain solids; future research may relax these assumptions to broaden the theory's applicability.

Models exhibiting real eigenenergies are prized in non-Hermitian physics due to their inherent stability. However, most existing examples rely on specific symmetries like PT-symmetry, which limits the observation of certain exotic non-Hermitian phenomena. This study explores the non-Hermitian skin effect as an alternative mechanism to ensure real spectra and system stability. We present various ansatz models across different energy dispersion classes that feature extensive regions of real spectra without relying on apparent symmetries. These minimal local models are readily implementable in non-reciprocal experimental platforms, such as electrical circuits utilizing operational amplifiers.

Understanding experimental scientific papers relies on the concepts of tasks, datasets, and evaluation metrics. However, prior research on information extraction in scientific literature has primarily focused on abstracts alone, often failing to recognize datasets as distinct entities (Zadeh and Schumann, 2016; Luan et al., 2018). This paper introduces a new corpus featuring domain expert annotations for Task (T), Dataset (D), and Metric (M) entities across 2,000 sentences selected from NLP papers. We present experimental results on TDM extraction utilizing a straightforward data augmentation technique and apply our tagger to approximately 30,000 NLP papers from the ACL Anthology. To support community research in scientific publication summarization (Erera et al., 2019) and knowledge discovery, this corpus is made publicly available.

The composition of the human gut microbiome significantly impacts overall health, prompting widespread adoption of microbiome therapies, such as over-the-counter probiotics designed to modify microbial communities. Despite considerable commercial promise, the specific determinants of whether these targeted treatments succeed or fail remain poorly understood. This study examines the biological interactions facilitating the successful colonization of a novel bacterial strain introduced via probiotic administration. Utilizing pairwise genome-scale metabolic modeling combined with generalized resource allocation constraints, we constructed an interaction network encompassing 818 species with established models in the AGORA database. By generating induced sub-graphs from taxa identified in three experimental engraftment studies, we evaluated the probability of an invader's colonization based on network architecture. To achieve this, we employed a suite of dynamical models linking network topology to growth dynamics. Our findings demonstrate that a generalized Lotka-Volterra model effectively predicts whether a specific probiotic or invasive strain will successfully establish itself within an individual's microbiome. Moreover, the mechanistic framework of this model proves valuable for identifying the specific microbe-microbe interactions that potentially drive engraftment.

CAPTCHAs and HIPs serve as security measures designed to stop the automated abuse of services, yet they remain vulnerable to learning attacks where adversaries utilize them as oracles. Recently, Kwon and Cha introduced a new algorithm aiming to evade these learning attacks and identify all bots by incorporating uncertainty into challenge grading and employing trap images to detect bots. The authors claim that a major IT corporation is evaluating their proposal for widespread adoption. However, we identify two critical design flaws in their approach concerning trap images and uncertainty grading, both of which inadvertently leak information about correct image grading. By exploiting these vulnerabilities, an attacker can leverage an UTS-CAPTCHA as an oracle to execute a learning attack. Our testing demonstrates that these flaws allow an attacker to boost an initial reasonable success rate to 100%.

The Semi-iNat dataset presents a significant challenge for semi-supervised classification due to its long-tailed class distribution, fine-grained categories, and domain discrepancies between labeled and unlabeled data. It serves as the foundation for the second iteration of the semi-supervised recognition challenge at the FGVC8 workshop during CVPR 2021. Unlike its predecessor, Semi-iNat (i) features images from species across various kingdoms within natural taxonomy, (ii) operates on a larger scale comprising 330,000 images with 810 in-class and 1,629 out-of-class species, and (iii) omits specific in/out-of-class labels, instead offering coarse taxonomic annotations (kingdom and phylum) for unlabeled images. This document outlines the dataset details and baseline results, which are accessible at \url{https://github.com/cvl-umass/semi-inat-2021}.

Axions represent a leading candidate for dark matter, with recent attention turning toward detecting photons generated by their resonant conversion within the magnetospheres of neutron stars. Although several groups have started gathering radio data to hunt for this signal, a more robust theoretical prediction for the corresponding radio lines is still required. This study derives detailed characteristics of the signal, determining both its line shape and temporal evolution. The primary physical mechanisms driving these features are refraction within the plasma and gravitational effects, which together induce significant lensing that fluctuates throughout the pulse period. Additionally, the co-rotation of the plasma with the pulsar distorts the frequencies, resulting in a Doppler-broadened signal whose width changes over time. To generate these predictions, we trace curvilinear rays to the observer using the complete equations of Hamiltonian optics for a dispersive medium in curved spacetime. For the first time, we provide a comprehensive description of the signal's detailed shape and its time-dependent variations, which are more prominent than in previous studies. These predicted signal features will be crucial for future dark matter searches of this nature.

This paper examines Augmented Reality (AR) and its diverse real-world applications. The introductory section provides a brief history of both AR and Virtual Reality (VR) before detailing the characteristics and essential services of AR. The study outlines AR technologies and their workflow, encompassing the complete AR process which involves Image Acquisition, Feature Extraction, Feature Matching, Geometric Verification, and Associated Information Retrieval. Since feature extraction is the core component of AR, the paper provides an in-depth analysis of this specific stage.

Active plasma resonance spectroscopy (APRS) serves as a process-compatible diagnostic technique that leverages the inherent capacity of plasmas to resonate at or near their electron plasma frequency. The Multipole Resonance Probe (MRP) represents a specific APRS configuration characterized by significant geometric and electrical symmetry, allowing its operating principles to be modeled using an idealized geometry well-suited for theoretical analysis. In pressure regimes of a few Pascals or less, kinetic effects emerge that the Drude model fails to predict; consequently, this study establishes a dynamic model describing the interaction between an idealized MRP and a plasma. The resulting framework elucidates plasma kinetic behavior and explains how these effects influence resonance structures. Analogous to particle-in-cell methods, the proposed spectral kinetic method iteratively calculates the electric field at individual particle locations without relying on numerical grids. This optimized analytical approach ensures simulation efficiency. Ultimately, this work aims to address the limitations of the Drude model, particularly regarding pure collisionless damping induced by kinetic effects, and introduces a formula for deriving electron temperature from the half-width.

It is widely recognized that glassy materials experience aging, meaning their properties evolve gradually over time. While there is increasing evidence that dense active and living systems display numerous glassy characteristics, the specific manifestations of physical aging in such active glassy materials remain largely unclear. Our objective is to investigate whether active and passive thermal glasses age through fundamentally distinct mechanisms. To achieve this, we conduct numerical simulations of aging dynamics following a high-to-low temperature quench for two-dimensional passive and active Brownian model glass-formers. Our findings indicate that aging in active thermal glasses results from a time-dependent interplay between thermal and active effects, characterized by an effective temperature that explicitly evolves with the material's age. Furthermore, unlike the phenomenology of passive aging, we observe that dynamic heterogeneity in active aging systems remains relatively small and remarkably constant over time. Consequently, we conclude that the common mapping between active systems and passive ones with elevated effective temperatures strictly fails during aging, and that the aging dynamics of thermal active glasses differ significantly from both passive and athermal active scenarios.

Over the past several years, the UK has experienced political instability characterized by Brexit and leadership crises. This study investigates how the global health emergency, COVID-19, impacted the volume, nature, and subjects of abuse directed at UK politicians during their public engagements. Specifically, this research analyzes Twitter abuse in responses to Members of Parliament (MPs) between June and December 2020, serving as a follow-up to an earlier analysis of online abuse during the first four months of the pandemic. The paper assesses overall abuse rates, reactions to various political parties and the government, and the connection between online hostility and specific topics such as Brexit, the government's pandemic response, policies, and social issues. Additionally, the study examines the prevalence of conspiracy theories within abusive replies to MPs during this period. Findings reveal that abuse levels against UK MPs reached an all-time high in December 2020, with 5.4% of all reply tweets to MPs being abusive. This figure was nearly 1% higher than the levels observed in the two months prior to the General Election. Furthermore, marking a shift from the initial four-month trend, MPs from the Conservative party received the highest percentage of abusive replies from July 2020 onwards. This trend remained above 5% starting in September 2020, coinciding with the deepening of the COVID-19 crisis and the nearing completion of Brexit negotiations with the EU.

This study presents a search for electroweak production of charginos and sleptons resulting in final states containing two electrons or muons. The analysis utilizes 139 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data recorded by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider with a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV. Three $R$-parity-conserving scenarios, in which the lightest neutralino serves as the lightest supersymmetric particle, are examined: the production of chargino pairs decaying through either $W$ bosons or sleptons, and the direct production of slepton pairs. Although the analysis is optimized for the first scenario, the findings are also interpreted within the other two frameworks. No significant deviations from Standard Model predictions are found, and 95% confidence level limits are established on the masses of relevant supersymmetric particles for each scenario. Assuming a massless lightest neutralino, masses up to 420 GeV are excluded for chargino pair production via $W$-boson-mediated decays, while up to 1 TeV is excluded for slepton-mediated decays. Furthermore, for slepton-pair production, masses up to 700 GeV are excluded under the assumption of three generations of mass-degenerate sleptons.

This paper introduces Ensemble Feature Importance (EFI), an open-source Python toolkit designed to offer machine learning researchers, domain specialists, and decision-makers robust and accurate quantification of feature importance, along with more reliable mechanistic interpretations for prediction tasks using fuzzy sets. Developed to tackle uncertainties in quantifying feature importance and the lack of trustworthy interpretations arising from the variety of machine learning algorithms, calculation methods, and dataset dependencies, EFI combines results from multiple models and diverse feature importance approaches. It utilizes data bootstrapping and decision fusion techniques—including mean aggregation, majority voting, and fuzzy logic—to merge these results. The primary attributes of the EFI toolbox include: (i) automatic optimization of machine learning algorithms, (ii) automatic calculation of feature importance coefficients from optimized algorithms and various calculation techniques, (iii) automatic aggregation of these coefficients using multiple decision fusion methods, and (iv) fuzzy membership functions that illustrate the importance of each feature regarding the prediction task. The paper details the toolbox's key modules and functions, illustrating their application with a simple example using the widely recognized Iris dataset.

This study introduces novel full-sky temperature and polarization maps across five frequency bands ranging from 23 to 94 GHz, derived from the first five years of the WMAP sky survey. These five-year maps benefit from enhanced data processing, facilitated by the extended observation period and a more rigorous analysis of instrument calibration and in-flight beam response. We have implemented new tests for systematic errors within the polarization data, concluding that Ka band data (33 GHz) is viable for cosmological analysis following foreground removal, thereby substantially lowering overall polarization uncertainty. Utilizing five-year WMAP data, we find no compelling evidence against the minimal six-parameter LCDM model, which describes a flat universe dominated by a cosmological constant with adiabatic, nearly scale-invariant Gaussian fluctuations.

By combining WMAP data with Type Ia supernovae and Baryon Acoustic Oscillation measurements, we determine the following parameters (68% CL uncertainties): Omega_bh^2 = 0.02267 \pm 0.00059, Omega_ch^2 = 0.1131 \pm 0.0034, Omega_Lambda = 0.726 \pm 0.015, n_s = 0.960 \pm 0.013, tau = 0.084 \pm 0.016, and Delta_R^2 = (2.445 \pm 0.096) x 10^-9. Derived values include sigma_8 = 0.812 \pm 0.026, H_0 = 70.5 \pm 1.3 km/s/Mpc, z_{reion} = 10.9 \pm 1.4, and t_0 = 13.72 \pm 0.12 Gyr. We establish a new upper limit on the tensor-to-scalar ratio of r < 0.22 (95% CL). Additionally, we derive stringent simultaneous constraints on the constant dark energy equation of state and spatial curvature: -0.14 < 1+w < 0.12 and -0.0179 < Omega_k < 0.0081 (both 95% CL). The number of relativistic degrees of freedom is measured as N_{eff} = 4.4 \pm 1.5, aligning with the standard value of 3.04, while models proposing N_{eff} = 0 are excluded with greater than 99.5% confidence.

A bounded container holds a set of elements that can be added or removed provided the total count does not surpass a fixed limit. We evaluate concurrent implementations of such containers based on their memory efficiency, specifically regarding the extra memory required beyond storing the actual data. A memory-optimal approach utilizes the smallest possible overhead, keeping both data and metadata as compact as possible to minimize cache misses and reduce unnecessary memory reclamation. This paper demonstrates that non-blocking implementations of a broad category of element-independent bounded containers—including queues, stacks, and pools—must sustain memory overhead that scales linearly with the number of concurrent processes. However, in specific scenarios where the ABA problem is eliminated, such as when hardware supports LL/SC instructions or elements are distinct, this lower bound can be avoided; we present lock-free bounded queues with constant memory overhead for these cases. For the general scenario, we introduce a CAS-based bounded queue implementation that asymptotically aligns with our established lower bound. We believe these findings establish a new research direction focused on the phenomenon of memory optimality.

Broadband and narrowband wavelength-selected XUV pulses were employed in time-resolved XUV-IR photoion mass spectroscopy of naphthalene, revealing a fragmentation probability increase with a lifetime of $92\pm4$~fs. This duration remains constant regardless of the XUV excitation wavelength and applies uniformly to all low appearance energy fragments observed. Integrating experimental results with a statistical multi-state vibronic model indicates that the signals monitor vibrational energy redistribution on the ground state cation's potential energy surface. Specifically, populations of out-of-plane ring twist and out-of-plane wave bending modes may facilitate new IR absorption pathways, thereby promoting enhanced fragmentation.

Current NFTs face limitations regarding single-use incentives and product isolation. Because distinct NFTs lack interconnectivity, creators fail to derive ongoing benefits after an initial sale, leading to contentious issues surrounding profit distribution. This research introduces a referable NFT framework designed to sustain incentives over time. By constructing a referable NFT (rNFT) network, we aim to boost visibility and strengthen the referral links between inclusive items. Furthermore, we employ a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) topology to establish weighted and labeled directed edges between every pair of NFTs, facilitating advanced functionalities. The proposed scheme is implemented in accordance with Ethereum Improvement Proposal (EIP) standards, specifically utilizing the EIP-1155 standard. Additionally, we present a mathematical formulation to evaluate the utility for each rNFT participant, offering broad guidance across multiple parameters. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the inaugural study to construct a referable NFT network that explicitly delineates the virtual interconnections among NFTs.

While host star activity is thought to significantly influence exoplanet habitability, coronal mass ejections (CMEs) in solar-like and late-type stars remain difficult to detect. This study presents observational findings on flares from two M-dwarfs, utilizing high-cadence data from the Ground Wide-angle Camera system. Fast, time-resolved spectroscopy of both events revealed symmetric broad H$\alpha$ emission characterized by near-zero bulk velocities but large projected maximum velocities reaching approximately 700–800 km s$^{-1}$. Such broadening may stem from either Stark (pressure) effects or CMEs originating at the stellar limb. Under the CME hypothesis, the estimated masses range from $\sim4\times10^{18}$ g to $2\times10^{19}$ g. Furthermore, spectral analysis of the narrow H$\alpha$ emission showed temporal shifts in the line center, with amplitude variations of tens of km s$^{-1}$ attributed to chromospheric evaporation in one case and a binary system in the other.
