Regarding the non-negative version, we demonstrate that a widely used heuristic achieves an $O(\log |X|)$ approximation on graphs meeting two specific width-related properties (such as series-parallel graphs) and improves the known worst-case lower bound from $\Omega(\sqrt{m})$ to $\Omega(m / \log m)$ for sparse graphs, where $m$ denotes the edge count. For the negative-weight variant, we present a $(\lceil \log \Vert X \Vert \rceil +1)$-approximation algorithm utilizing a power-of-two strategy, parity correction techniques, and the decomposition of unitary flows ($\Vert X \Vert \leq 1$) into at most $w$ paths, where $w$ is the width and $\Vert X \Vert$ represents the maximum absolute flow on any edge. Furthermore, we refute a conjecture by Kloster et al. [ALENEX 2018] concerning the linear independence of minimum non-negative flow decompositions, yet confirm that the conjecture's practical consequence—assigning polynomial-time weights to a given path set to decompose a flow—remains valid for the negative-weight case.

Epidemic models typically capture the hallmark traits of infectious disease transmission through coupled non-linear differential equations that account for various health statuses, such as Susceptible, Infected, and Recovered. However, this compartmental framework offers an incomplete view of epidemic dynamics because it overlooks stochastic and network influences, as well as the critical role of the measurement process, which underpins the estimation of epidemiological parameters and incidence rates. To address these gaps, we expand upon standard epidemiological models by incorporating a measurement (testing) framework that accounts for false positives, false negatives, and biased sampling. By analyzing a model-generated ground truth alongside simulated observation processes (virtual measurements), we can better understand the constraints of purely data-driven methods used to evaluate epidemic conditions. Our findings indicate that epidemic monitoring, simulation, and forecasting constitute "wicked problems," as relying on conventional data-driven approaches within complex systems characterized by non-linear dynamics, network effects, and uncertainty can lead to misleading conclusions. Nonetheless, certain errors can be mitigated by integrating scientific knowledge of both spreading dynamics and measurement mechanisms. Consequently, we conclude that such corrections should be integral components of future efforts in epidemic monitoring, modeling, and forecasting.

This paper presents our system for SemEval-2018 Task 11, which focuses on Machine Comprehension utilizing Commonsense Knowledge. We employ Three-way Attentive Networks (TriAN) to capture interactions among the passage, question, and answers. To integrate commonsense knowledge, we enhance the input with relation embeddings derived from the general knowledge graph ConceptNet (Speer et al., 2017). Consequently, our system attains state-of-the-art performance, achieving 83.95% accuracy on the official test set. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/intfloat/commonsense-rc.

This document outlines the annotation protocols employed to build the Turku Paraphrase Corpus. Developed in tandem with the actual annotation process, these guidelines were continuously revised and expanded throughout the project. The paraphrase annotation framework utilizes a primary scale of 1–4, where scores 1 and 2 denote negative candidates (non-paraphrases), and scores 3 and 4 indicate paraphrases valid within the specific context, if not universally. Beyond this base labeling, the scheme incorporates additional subcategories (flags) to classify various types of paraphrases under the two positive labels, enabling fine-grained categorization. This methodology was applied to annotate more than 100,000 Finnish paraphrase pairs.

This dissertation offers a semiclassical examination of conical topology change within $1+1$ spacetime dimensions, assuming a classical, fixed background while quantizing the coupled scalar field. The stress-energy tensor's vacuum expectation value is derived using two distinct methods: one based on the explicit construction of the Sorkin-Johnston state on the cone alongside a novel regularization technique, and the other utilizing the conformal vacuum with standard point-splitting renormalization. The results indicate that conical topology change avoids the pathologies typically associated with trousers-type topology change. This finding offers preliminary support for conjectures by Sorkin and Borde, which categorize topology-changing spacetimes based on their Morse critical points, specifically suggesting that cones and yarmulkes in $1+1$ dimensions lack critical points with a unit Morse index.

Vital sign monitoring is essential in various medical and health contexts, yet widely deployed contact and wearable sensors are ineffective for patients with burn injuries or infants lacking sufficient surface area for attachment. While camera-based imaging offers a contactless alternative, it remains vulnerable to ambient light variations and raises privacy issues. This study presents the first demonstration of a photonic radar system designed for non-contact vital signal detection to address these limitations. By utilizing synthesized radar signals with a bandwidth reaching 30 GHz, the system achieves millimeter-level range resolution. This high precision allows for accurate respiratory monitoring using breathing simulators and a cane toad as a human surrogate. Furthermore, the optical signals produced by this setup facilitate vital sign detection through Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR). This demonstration highlights the potential of a sensor-fusion architecture that integrates the complementary strengths of radar and LiDAR to enhance sensing accuracy and system resilience. Ultimately, this work establishes a novel technical foundation for contactless, high-resolution, and privacy-preserving vital sign detection, addressing the growing needs of future medical and healthcare applications.

We computed the total cross sections and transverse momentum spectra for the production of the mysterious $\chi_{c,1}(3872)$ (also known as X(3872)) under various hypotheses, including the $c \bar c$ configuration and the $D^{0*} \bar{D}^0 + D^0 \bar{D}^{0*}$ molecular model. For the $c \bar c$ scenario, we utilized the derivative of the wave function derived from potential model calculations. Unlike previous studies on molecular states, our analysis incorporates both single parton scattering (SPS) and double parton scattering (DPS) contributions, with the DPS component yielding a smaller effect than SPS. Our estimated upper limit for DPS production falls significantly below CMS experimental data. We compared our findings with results from CMS, ATLAS, and LHCb, concluding that reasonable cross sections are achievable in both the $c \bar c$ and molecular $D \bar{D}^*$ frameworks, and a hybrid scenario remains a viable possibility.

The examination of Bell-EPR nonlocal correlations within a microscopic measurement theory framework suggests the presence of new quantum nonlocality effects, specifically manifesting as distant correlations between elementary quantum systems or particles. The study applies the Doebner-Goldin nonlinear quantum formalism to describe these nonlocal correlations and compares the findings with results from various cosmophysical experiments.

We introduce a class of mappings between holomorphically embedded null curves that extend conformal transformations to any complex dimension. In four dimensions, analogous mappings can be defined for self-dual surfaces, which generalize flat $\alpha$-planes; these are termed causal and self-dual morphisms, respectively. It is demonstrated that both types of maps admit an infinite family of non-trivial examples within four dimensions.

Current solutions for tracking mobile entities indoors using visual inertial odometry or fine-grained ranging (RF, ultrasonic, IR, etc.) function well under favorable conditions but fail in dynamic environments lacking such conditions, such as first responder operations or multi-player AR/VR gaming. These scenarios demand infrastructure-free solutions that are robust to node mobility and varying visual conditions. Consequently, a robust RF-based approach is required, specifically addressing a novel, latency-constrained variant of the infrastructure-free (peer-to-peer) localization problem, where accurate tracking imposes strict latency budgets affecting both computation and range collection.

This work introduces DynoLoc, a system designed to solve this latency-bounded, infrastructure-free RF localization challenge. DynoLoc resolves the fundamental tradeoff between latency and accuracy by incorporating design elements that adaptively utilize ranging resources to estimate joint node topology. It employs robust algorithms to maintain high localization accuracy despite practical environmental artifacts like wireless connectivity issues, multipath effects, and node mobility. This enables DynoLoc to track networks of dozens of mobile entities at speeds of 1–2 m/s every second with median accuracies under 1–2 meters (compared to over 5 meters for baselines), all without infrastructure support. The system's efficacy is demonstrated through real-world applications, including a firefighter drill, multi-player AR/VR gaming, and active shooter tracking by first responders.

This study investigates the production of light Higgs bosons ($H_1$) in pairs via supersymmetric cascade decays, focusing on final states characterized by low missing transverse momentum. The analysis utilizes a CMS dataset from LHC proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV, comprising an integrated luminosity of 138 fb$^{-1}$. The search specifically targets events where both $H_1$ bosons decay into $\mathrm{b\bar{b}}$ pairs, which are identified as large-radius jets through substructure methods. No significant excess over standard model background predictions was observed. These results are interpreted within the next-to-minimal supersymmetric extension of the SM, considering a scenario where a light singlino drives squark and gluino cascades that predominantly yield a highly Lorentz-boosted singlet-like $H_1$ and a low-transverse-momentum singlino-like neutralino. Consequently, upper limits were established on the product of the pair-production cross-section for squarks or gluinos and the squared $\mathrm{b\bar{b}}$ branching fraction of the $H_1$, based on a benchmark model with nearly mass-degenerate gluinos and light-flavor squarks. Assuming an $H_1$ branching fraction to $\mathrm{b\bar{b}}$ similar to the standard model, $H_1$ bosons with masses between 40 and 120 GeV, originating from squark or gluino decays with masses ranging from 1200 to 2500 GeV, are excluded at the 95% confidence level.

Significant research has been conducted on detecting road surface damage using image processing, achieving high accuracy; however, most studies merely identify the presence or absence of damage. In practical scenarios, road managers require specific information on damage types to execute effective repairs. Furthermore, the lack of a standardized, openly available dataset due to varying data acquisition methods in previous studies has resulted in the absence of a benchmark. This study addresses these gaps with three main contributions. First, we present, to our knowledge, the first large-scale road damage dataset containing 15,435 instances across 9,053 images captured via a smartphone mounted on a vehicle. Developed in collaboration with seven Japanese municipalities over more than 40 hours, the dataset encompasses diverse weather and lighting conditions, with each image annotated to indicate the location and type of damage. Second, we trained a state-of-the-art convolutional neural network object detection model on this dataset and evaluated its accuracy and runtime performance on both a GPU server and a smartphone. Finally, we demonstrate that the proposed method can classify road damage into eight distinct categories with high accuracy. The dataset, experimental results, and the accompanying smartphone application are publicly accessible at https://github.com/sekilab/RoadDamageDetector/.

We examine classical and quantum computing through the lens of their respective Hamiltonian dynamics. This framework enables the introduction of quantum computations that process both data and program instructions in parallel. By utilizing mixed quantum-classical dynamics, we aim to determine the total computational cost for quantum systems interfaced with classical terminals.

Coverage Path Planning entails visiting every free state within an obstacle-filled environment. This paper investigates that challenge in initially unknown settings to simulate the operation of a vacuuming robot. A review of previous research indicates that applying learning techniques to this problem has seen limited progress. We examine modeling Coverage Path Planning via Deep Reinforcement Learning and evaluate its performance against the proprietary algorithm used in Roomba, a widely used vacuum robot.

The growing integration of algorithms in business has heightened concerns about potential reputational and financial harm. This issue arises partly because the United States currently lacks stringent legislative prohibitions or standardized protocols for quantifying such damages. Consequently, governments are introducing new laws and enforcing bans, regulators are imposing fines, and the judiciary is deliberating on the legal status of artificial intelligence as a decision-maker. Across sectors ranging from autonomous vehicles and banking to healthcare, housing, and legal judgments, algorithms with minimal human oversight are poised to make vast numbers of decisions. To address this, a comprehensive algorithm audit system is needed—one that provides systematic verification of legality, ethics, and security, akin to financial audits. Establishing a modern framework for auditing and assuring these algorithms will help professionalize and industrialize AI, machine learning, and related technologies. Key stakeholders in this emerging domain include policymakers, regulators, industry experts, and entrepreneurs. Furthermore, we anticipate that audit thresholds and frameworks will offer critical insights for those focused on governance and standardization. This paper seeks to examine the essential components required for auditing and assurance while stimulating dialogue within this innovative field of study and practice.

Computer vision algorithms currently match or exceed human performance in visual tasks such as object recognition (particularly fine-grained categories), segmentation, and reconstructing 3D objects from 2D images. However, humans retain an advantage in higher-level image analysis, notably in applying a "theory of mind" to distinguish whether an observed action was intentional. This paper presents an algorithm that determines the intentionality of an agent's behavior by analyzing its 3D kinematics through the lens of self-propelled versus Newtonian motion. By incorporating this fundamental physical knowledge, we developed a simple, unsupervised method. To validate the approach, we created three datasets ranging from abstract geometric animations to realistic video clips depicting both intentional and unintentional actions. Experimental results demonstrate that the algorithm can accurately identify intentionality without training data, achieving quantitative performance comparable to various supervised baselines and producing qualitatively sensible intentionality segmentation.

This study examines the computational complexity and approximation strategies for covering a set of non-crossing straight line segments, which form a planar graph drawing $G=(V,E)$, using the minimum number of disks with a fixed radius $r>0$. Such geometric challenges are relevant to network security. We demonstrate that the problem is strongly NP-hard for edge sets derived from Delaunay triangulations, Gabriel graphs, and other common network design subgraphs, provided the radius $r$ falls within the range $[d_{\min}, \eta d_{\max}]$, where $d_{\min}$ and $d_{\max}$ represent the shortest and longest Euclidean edge lengths, respectively, and $\eta$ is a constant. Furthermore, we introduce a fast $O(|E|\log|E|)$-time algorithm achieving a constant-factor approximation for planar straight line drawings where the edge lengths are uniformly bounded by a linear function of $r$ (specifically, $r \geq \eta d_{\max}$ for some constant $\eta > 0$).

This paper investigates the solvability of a specific category of fractional backward stochastic differential equations (BSDEs) characterized by a delayed generator. Within this framework, the generator incorporates not only the current solution values but also historical ones. By imposing a Lipschitz condition, we establish both the existence and uniqueness of these BSDEs and derive a corresponding comparison theorem for this class.

Exceptional points (EPs) have recently garnered significant interest within non-Hermitian systems, particularly regarding applications in sensing and mode switching. Research has intensely focused on the nontrivial topological structures of EPs, especially those involving encircling trajectories, making the generation of multiple EPs a critical challenge across various disciplines. While previous approaches to creating multiple EPs have relied on multi-level or composite physical systems with Hermitian couplings, this study demonstrates the generation of multiple EPs within a single microcavity using two-level systems. This is achieved through a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian characterized by imaginary (dominant) coupling. Notably, the topological structures of the Riemann surfaces arising from non-Hermitian coupling display distinct features compared to those produced by Hermitian coupling. These characteristics were validated by encircling multiple EPs and employing a Riemann sphere.

We describe recent advancements in transforming differential equations for Feynman master integrals into their canonical form, utilizing a technique introduced by Roman Lee. For the first time, we introduce Fuchsia, an open-source Python implementation of the Lee algorithm that leverages the mathematical capabilities of the free computer algebra system SageMath. We validate Fuchsia by applying it to reduce differential equations for next-to-leading-order (NLO) contributions to QCD splitting functions, which involve both loop and leg integrals.

This paper introduces a dataset designed to capture diverse visual formats across varying luminance conditions. Although RGB cameras offer intuitive data, vision-based robotic systems often fail catastrophically under changing light. While solutions like robust algorithms or alternative sensors (e.g., thermal and event cameras) have been proposed, datasets utilizing these non-standard sensors remain scarce. To address this, we present a dataset recorded using alternative vision sensors, both handheld and vehicle-mounted, repeatedly within the same environment under different conditions. Our goal is to acquire co-aligned visible information from these sensors. Our system independently measures infrared dissipation to capture data less reliant on visible light intensity, utilizes structured reflection for depth, and records instantaneous luminance changes. We provide these measurements alongside inertial sensor data and ground truth to facilitate the development of robust visual SLAM in poor lighting. The complete dataset can be accessed at: https://visibilitydataset.github.io/

In panoramic photography, cameras are typically aligned with the vertical axis, or gravity direction. Modern devices like smartphones and tablets include Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) that accurately measure the gravity vector. Leveraging this prior knowledge allows us to assume the camera y-axes are aligned, reducing their relative orientation to a single degree of freedom (1-DOF). Building on this assumption, we introduce novel minimal solutions for stitching panoramic images captured by cameras sharing the same optical center, meaning they undergo pure rotation. We evaluate four practical camera setups, accounting for unknown fixed or varying focal lengths with or without radial distortion. Our solvers were tested on synthetic data and over 500,000 real image pairs from the Sun360 dataset and our own smartphone captures using IMU-equipped devices. Results demonstrate that our methods surpass state-of-the-art techniques in both accuracy and processing speed.

Accelerating advancements in streaming data technologies are driving greater focus on monitoring human behavior. Wearable sensors, particularly wrist-worn actigraphs that track gross motor activity, have become ubiquitous. These devices continuously log individual activity levels, generating vast quantities of high-resolution data that can be instantly downloaded and analyzed. Although this "big data" encompasses both spatial and temporal dimensions, the variation within it is best modeled by treating stochastic evolution as a temporal process while addressing spatial components separately. We introduce a comprehensive Bayesian hierarchical modeling and inference framework designed to handle the massive scale of actigraphy databases while enabling full inference. Leveraging recent field developments, we develop Nearest Neighbour Gaussian Processes (NNGPs) tailored for actigraphy to facilitate computation at large temporal scales. Specifically, we construct a temporal NNGP and emphasize the optimized implementation of the collapsed algorithm within this context. This strategy allows for enhanced model scalability alongside complete inference capabilities. We evaluate and validate our methods using simulated data before applying and verifying their predictive performance on an original dataset from a health study conducted by the Fielding School of Public Health at the University of California, Los Angeles.

This study examines resonance characteristics in three-body systems, focusing on examples from $^{12}{\rm C}$ and $^{24}{\rm Mg}$. Employing a microscopic cluster model grounded in the hyperspherical formalism for the generator coordinate, we describe the $^{12}{\rm C}$ nucleus as an $\alpha+\alpha+\alpha$ configuration and $^{24}{\rm Mg}$ as an $^{16}{\rm O}+\alpha+\alpha$ system. Our primary focus is on resonances, involving a review of techniques that extend variational methods to this domain. We analyze $0^+$ and $2^+$ states in both nuclei and demonstrate that a resonance's root-mean-square radius is highly sensitive to the choice of variational basis. This sensitivity impacts calculations and measurements of the Hoyle state ($0^+_2$ in $^{12}{\rm C}$). Furthermore, in $^{24}{\rm Mg}$, we identify two $0^+$ resonances located just below the three-body threshold.

Plasma serves as an ideal environment for creating robust microscopic magnetic structures and controllable electromagnetic radiation with defined topologies, owing to its unique capacity to support and steer high currents and intense fields. Through theoretical analysis and simulations, we demonstrate the efficient production of multi-megagauss magnetic fields and adjustable optical vortices when a sharp relativistic ionization front traverses a longer-wavelength Laguerre-Gaussian (LG) laser pulse possessing orbital angular momentum (OAM). The frequency of the optical vortex can be upshifted across a broad spectrum merely by adjusting the plasma density, while its temporal duration is simultaneously compressed. The topological charges of both the magnetic and optical vortices can be tuned by manipulating the OAM mode of the incoming LG laser and/or by regulating the ionization front's density and topology. Furthermore, at relatively high (low) plasma densities, the majority of the incident LG laser pulse's energy is converted into the magnetic (optical) vortex.

We investigate quantum chaos diagnostics applied to variational circuit states generated with random parameters, examining their relationship with circuit expressibility and control parameter optimization. Through measurements of the operator spreading coefficient and the eigenvalue spectrum of the modular Hamiltonian of the reduced density matrix, we reveal the universal structure characteristic of random matrix models in high-depth circuits. Furthermore, we design distinct layer unitaries aligned with GOE and GUE distributions to assess their Variational Quantum Algorithm (VQA) performance. Finally, our research underscores a potential conflict between OTOC-based and BGS-type methods for diagnosing quantum chaos.

The ultra-faint dwarf galaxy Reticulum II appears to have been enriched by a solitary, rare, and highly productive r-process event. Consequently, the galaxy's r-process composition offers a distinct chance to investigate metal mixing within a surviving first-generation galaxy. By employing multi-object high-resolution spectroscopy via VLT/GIRAFFE and Magellan/M2FS, we identified 32 definitive member stars and determined abundances for Mg, Ca, Fe, and Ba where feasible. Our analysis reveals that $72^{+10}_{-12}$% of these stars exhibit r-process enhancement, characterized by a mean $\left\langle\mbox{[Ba/H]}\right\rangle=-1.68~\pm~0.07$ and an unresolved intrinsic dispersion of $\sigma_{\rm [Ba/H]} < 0.20$. These uniform r-process abundances suggest that Ret II's metals were thoroughly mixed before the formation of r-enhanced stars, a process simulations indicate requires at least 100 Myr of mixing between star formation bursts. This finding constitutes the first direct proof of bursty star formation in an ultra-faint dwarf galaxy. Furthermore, the homogeneous dilution pattern favors a rapid, high-yield r-process origin, such as collapsar disk winds or prompt neutron star mergers. Additionally, data from [Ba/H] and [Mg/Ca] indicate that r-enhanced stars in Ret II formed without significant accretion of pristine gas, potentially implying that approximately 70% of the galaxy's stars emerged after reionization.

Spacelike and timelike generalized parton distributions (GPDs) have been explored through charged-lepton scattering and electron-positron collisions, utilizing deeply virtual Compton scattering and two-photon processes, respectively. Future measurements are anticipated at hadron accelerator facilities. These GPDs are essential for elucidating the origins of hadron masses and spins in relation to quarks and gluons, as well as for investigating internal hadronic pressure to understand stability. While gravitational form factors were once deemed purely theoretical due to the weakness of gravitational interactions in microscopic systems, advancements in hadron tomography now allow their extraction from actual GPD data without direct gravitational measurements. Future neutrino reactions, such as those at Fermilab's Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility, offer a complementary approach to study flavor dependence. This overview summarizes GPDs and examines potential neutrino GPD measurements via single-pion production processes: $\nu + N \to \ell^- + N' + \pi$ and $\bar\nu + N \to \ell^+ + N' + \pi$.

A 0-1 matrix $M$ contains a pattern $P$ if $P$ can be derived from $M$ by removing rows and/or columns and converting some 1s to 0s. The saturation function $\mathrm{sat}(P,n)$ represents the minimum number of 1s required in an $n \times n$ 0-1 matrix that avoids $P$, yet becomes an occurrence of $P$ if any single 0 is changed to a 1. Recently, Fulek and Keszegh demonstrated that the saturation function is either bounded or grows linearly as $\Theta(n)$. Extending their findings, we identify a broad class of patterns with a bounded saturation function, which includes infinitely many permutation matrices as well as infinitely many non-permutation matrices.

Nonlinear Thomson scattering involves relativistic electrons reflecting and re-emitting laser photons, thereby transforming optical light into x-rays or higher frequencies. Although this extreme frequency up-conversion holds promise for investigating high-energy-density matter and exploring new frontiers in nonlinear quantum electrodynamics, traditional approaches face inherent limitations regarding how radiated power scales with laser intensity. This study reveals that spatiotemporal pulse shaping, which provides ponderomotive control, unlocks novel regimes of nonlinear Thomson scattering that dramatically improve the scaling of radiated power, emission angles, and frequency relative to laser intensity. By precisely tuning the velocity of the intensity peak, a shaped pulse can amplify radiated power by orders of magnitude. This superior intensity scaling facilitates operation at much lower electron energies and may render high-energy electron accelerators unnecessary.

This paper examines the interaction between scalar (Higgs) particles ($\phi$) and gravitons ($h$), along with their potential consequences. By analyzing the scaling properties of spinor variables under the little group, we derive the general structure of the 3-point interaction $\phi(p) h(1)h(2)$; the resulting vertices are notably simple, suggesting that further simplifications may exist within the extended scalar action. To explore this, we analyze an extended Einstein-Hilbert action that incorporates minimal coupling alongside terms like $\phi R^2$, $\phi R^{\mu
u} R_{\mu
u}$, and $\phi R^{\mu
uho\sigma} R_{\mu
uho\sigma}$, plus an additional term, $\epsilon_{\mu
u \alpha eta} \phi_5 R^{\mu
u}_{ho\sigma} R^{\alpha etaho\sigma}$, specific to pseudo-scalar ($\phi_5$) cases. We observe that the derived vertices obey KLT-type relations, meaning they can be expressed as the square of the Higgs-gluon coupling. Furthermore, we determine that the amplitude for Higgs decay into a pair of on-shell gravitons receives contributions solely from the square of the Riemann tensor. Comparable findings emerge for the 3-body decay $\phi 	o h h^* (	o XX)$, where an off-shell graviton ($h^*$) transitions into a final state $XX$. Although these quadratic terms might be expected to generate novel loop effects, we discover that the new contribution arising from this non-minimal coupling to the graviton self-energy also vanishes for on-shell gravitons.

Patch-based sparse representation modeling has demonstrated significant promise in reconstructing images via compressive sensing (CS). Nevertheless, this approach often faces limitations, including high computational costs associated with dictionary learning and a failure to account for relationships between similar patches. This paper introduces a Group-Based Sparse Representation method with Non-Convex Regularization (GSR-NCR) for image CS reconstruction. GSR-NCR integrates both local sparsity and nonlocal self-similarity within a single framework. Unlike prior methods relying on sparsity-promoting convex regularization, we apply a non-convex weighted Lp penalty (where 0 < p < 1) to the group sparse coefficients of the data matrix, moving beyond traditional L1-based regularization. To mitigate computational complexity, we replace the high-cost dictionary learning from natural images with a Principal Component Analysis (PCA)-based dictionary for each group. Furthermore, to ensure the scheme remains tractable and robust, we devised an efficient iterative shrinkage/thresholding algorithm to address the non-convex optimization challenge. Experimental outcomes indicate that the proposed method surpasses numerous state-of-the-art techniques in image CS reconstruction.

A core strategy in neuroscience involves testing hypotheses using neuropsychological and behavioral data to determine if specific variables, such as life events, correlate with outcomes like depression. Recently, deep learning has emerged as a viable alternative for predicting outcomes from multiple factors and pinpointing the most predictive ones. However, its influence has been constrained because it lacks a connection to the statistical significance of the factors that support established hypotheses. This article introduces a flexible, scalable method grounded in permutation testing, which embeds hypothesis testing directly into data-driven deep learning workflows. We demonstrate this approach by analyzing yearly self-reports from 621 adolescents in the National Consortium of Alcohol and Neurodevelopment in Adolescence (NCANDA) to forecast negative valence, a symptom of major depressive disorder defined by the NIMH Research Domain Criteria (RDoC). Our method effectively isolates categories of risk factors that provide further insight into the symptom.

Recently, there has been significant interest in utilizing general-purpose neural architectures to supplant hand-crafted designs or inductive biases. Nevertheless, current tracking methods depend on tailored sub-modules and require prior knowledge for architectural selection, which impedes the development of more general systems. This paper introduces SimTrack, a Simplified Tracking architecture that employs a transformer backbone to handle both feature extraction and interaction simultaneously. Diverging from traditional Siamese trackers, SimTrack serializes input images and concatenates them directly before processing through a single-branch backbone. This approach allows feature interactions within the backbone to eliminate the need for explicitly designed interaction modules, resulting in a more efficient and effective framework. Additionally, to mitigate information loss caused by down-sampling in vision transformers, we propose a foveal window strategy that offers diverse input patches while maintaining acceptable computational costs. On the LaSOT and TNL2K datasets, SimTrack achieves AUC improvements of 2.5% and 2.6% over the baseline, respectively, delivering performance competitive with specialized tracking algorithms without relying on complex, unnecessary components.

There is growing interest in estimating heterogeneous causal effects within both randomized and observational studies, yet research addressing this heterogeneity in instrumental variables (IV) contexts remains scarce. This study introduces a method for estimating heterogeneous causal effects using an IV approach, which consists of two components. First, it leverages domain expertise and interpretable machine learning techniques, such as classification and regression trees, to identify potential effect modifiers. Second, it employs closed testing to assess the statistical significance of these modifiers while rigorously controlling the familywise error rate. Applying this method to the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment to evaluate the impact of Medicaid on the number of days an individual's health limits their usual activities, we identified heterogeneity among older English-speaking men who do not identify as Asian, as well as younger individuals with at most a high school diploma or GED who prefer English.

Landslide velocity is a critical factor in calculating impact forces and the extent of devastation. Drawing on Pudasaini and Krautblatter (2022), I have formulated a new extended velocity model that incorporates the force generated by the hydraulic pressure gradient, a component previously ignored by all analytical landslide velocity models. Through a rigorous conversion of this force into inertia, I created two equivalent systems designed to yield identical results; however, this outcome contradicts conventional wisdom and prompts the question of whether new balance equations are required. Comparing velocity models that either exclude or include the hydraulic pressure gradient force reveals distinct analytical solutions. The proposed model is comprehensive and elegant, representing a significant advancement by uncovering a serendipitous pressure-inertia paradox where mass initially moves upstream before reversing direction and accelerating downslope. As the force associated with the hydraulic pressure gradient increases, the divergence between the extended and simple solutions becomes pronounced, highlighting its significance. While viscous drag significantly influences landslide dynamics, no explicit mechanical or analytical model previously existed for it. The refined form of the new velocity equation yields a mechanically robust, dynamically evolving analytical model for viscous drag, marking the first of its kind. A dimensionless drag number is established. Contrary to standard practices, it has been demonstrated that drag behaves fundamentally differently during expanding versus contracting motions, offering a novel perspective. Although drag coefficients align closely with common empirical or numerical values, this work provides an innovative, physically grounded analytical framework for simulating drag in mass flow.

This note presents a streamlined, dimension-independent proof of the logarithmic Sobolev inequality on the Heisenberg groups $H_n=\R^{2n+1}$ by leveraging measure-preserving transformations of Brownian motion. We have rectified several significant errors and simplified the associated arguments.

We establish anti-concentration bounds for the inner product of two independent random vectors. Specifically, we demonstrate that for subsets $A$ and $B$ of the cube $\{\pm 1\}^n$ satisfying $|A| \cdot |B| \geq 2^{1.01 n}$, if $X \in A$ and $Y \in B$ are chosen independently and uniformly at random, the probability that their inner product $\langle X, Y \rangle$ equals any specific value is bounded by $O(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}})$. Building upon Halász's results, we derive even stronger bounds in scenarios where the selection of $x$ lacks structure. Furthermore, we outline applications of these findings in communication complexity, randomness extraction, and additive combinatorics.

Angular correlation spectra of $e^+e^-$ pairs generated via the $^{7}$Li($p$,$\gamma$)$^{8}$Be reaction were investigated at the sharp $E_p$= 441 keV resonance and at proton beam energies of 650, 800, and 1100 keV. While the spectra recorded at the resonance align with the M1 internal pair creation mechanism, notable anomalies in the $e^+e^-$ angular correlations were detected in the off-resonance regions (corresponding to direct proton capture). These anomalies provide support for the creation and decay of the hypothetical X17 particle.

We investigate the minimizers of inhomogeneous variational problems that are $L^{2}$-critical, featuring a spatially decaying nonlinear term within an open bounded domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^{N}$ containing the origin. We establish the existence of a threshold $a^{*}>0$ such that minimizers exist for $0<a<a^{*}$ but fail to exist for any $a>a^{*}$. Unlike the homogeneous scenario, we demonstrate that at the threshold $a^{*}$, the presence or absence of minimizers depends on the specific value of the trapping potential $V(0)$. Furthermore, under appropriate conditions on $V(x)$, we utilize a detailed analysis of the concentration behavior of minimizers as $a$ approaches $a^{*}$ from below to prove their local uniqueness in a neighborhood of this threshold.

This work presents an analytical investigation of boundary conditions for lattice-based Dirac fermion models, which characterize first and second-order topological insulators. By solving these conditions, we derive the dispersion relations for edge and hinge states, highlighting how Hamiltonian symmetry can impose constraints on the boundary conditions. Furthermore, we illustrate an edge-hinge counterpart to the bulk-edge correspondence, showing that the nontrivial topology of a gapped edge state necessitates the gaplessness of the corresponding hinge state.

We demonstrate that within a Finsler manifold characterized by vanishing $\chi$-curvature (including cases with constant flag curvature), certain non-Riemannian geometric structures remain invariant along geodesics, thereby generating a collection of non-Riemannian first integrals. These integrals can be expressed in two alternative forms: either utilizing the mean Berwald curvature or as functions dependent on both the mean Cartan torsion and the mean Landsberg curvature.

Ex vivo dynamic optical coherence tomography (OCT) demonstrates label-free metabolic imaging of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) in mouse livers. This study utilizes a methionine choline-deficient (MCD)-diet model, comparing normal-diet controls with mice fed the MCD diet for one and two weeks. The dynamic OCT technique employs repeating raster scans combined with logarithmic intensity variance (LIV) analysis, allowing for volumetric metabolic imaging using a standard-speed system (50,000 A-lines/s). This method clearly visualizes three-dimensional metabolic domains linked to lipid droplet accumulation and inflammation. Specifically, the normal-diet liver displays highly metabolic, vessel-like structures within peri-vascular hepatic zones, whereas the 1-week MCD-diet liver reveals ring-shaped, highly metabolic formations composed of lipid droplets. In contrast, the 2-week MCD-diet liver shows fragmented, vessel-like structures associated with inflammation. These findings suggest that volumetric LIV imaging is an effective tool for visualizing and evaluating NAFLD abnormalities.

The easy availability of vast, multi-dimensional data has prompted machine learning researchers to shift focus from correlation-based approaches to causality-based learning, known as causal machine learning. In recent years, significant efforts have been dedicated to developing causal learning algorithms to help artificial intelligence attain human-level intelligence. However, a primary obstacle in current research is the scarcity of ground-truth data, which severely hampers algorithm evaluation. This limitation stifles the cross-fertilization between AI and causal inference, preventing both fields from leveraging each other's advancements. To bridge the gap between traditional causal inference (relying on statistical methods) and causal learning within the context of big data (the intersection of causal inference and machine learning), this survey reviews standard datasets, evaluation metrics, and methodologies using a pipeline analogous to conventional machine learning. We concentrate on two fundamental tasks: causal inference and causality-aware machine learning, while also addressing the shortcomings of existing evaluation protocols. Furthermore, we explore popular causal inference tools and packages, concluding with the main challenges and opportunities for benchmarking causal learning algorithms in the big data era. Ultimately, this survey aims to highlight the critical need for publicly accessible benchmarks and consensus standards for evaluating causal learning on observational data, thereby fostering broader discussions and collaboration to drive innovation and application in this field.

This study introduces a non-computational technique to mitigate image degradation caused by diffraction in lensless microscopy. Since all optical images, whether lens-based or not, inherently represent diffraction patterns that retain visual information up to a limit defined by point spread functions (such as airy disks), a highly diverging beam can be utilized to proportionally reduce the spatial extent of these functions within the transformed projective space. This reduction facilitates the spatial unmixing of visual data. The proposed principle was experimentally confirmed through the lensless imaging of red blood cells (approximately 6-9 micrometers in diameter) and photolithography masks with micrometer-scale features. Key benefits of this non-computational shadow microscopy approach include an enhanced depth of field and a significant increase in the working distance between the sensor and the sample. Furthermore, this imaging method is applicable as a projection technique in multi-angle optical computed tomography (CT).

Chimeras emerge in networks comprising two coupled oscillator populations when synchronization occurs within one group while the other remains asynchronous. This study examines such chimeras in networks of planar oscillators, where one dynamic parameter is randomly selected from a uniform distribution. Utilizing a generalization of the methodology from [C.R. Laing, Physical Review E, 100, 042211, 2019], which previously addressed identical oscillators, we investigate the existence and stability of chimeras in these heterogeneous networks under the limit of infinite oscillators. Across all scenarios, increased heterogeneity eliminates the stable chimera state via a saddle-node bifurcation. These findings enhance our understanding of how robust chimeras in general oscillator networks are against heterogeneity.

This work investigates the statistical properties of quantum entanglement in bipartite fermionic Gaussian systems, quantified via von Neumann entropy. While recent studies have derived formulas for the average von Neumann entropy with and without particle number constraints, this paper presents exact, explicit formulas for the variances in both scenarios. Specifically, the results for the unconstrained case settle a recent conjecture regarding that variance. Unlike previous approaches to calculating variances across generic state models, our proof hinges on a novel simplification framework. This framework introduces new tools for reducing finite summations involving what we term "dummy summation" and re-summation techniques. Additionally, as a secondary outcome, this proposed framework yields various new transformation formulas for hypergeometric functions.

We experimentally demonstrate the integration of silicon-vacancy centers in nanodiamonds (SiV-NDs) with an optical nanofiber (ONF). Using microwave plasma-assisted chemical vapor deposition, we cultivate SiV-NDs on seed NDs dispersed across a quartz substrate. Initially, we identify and characterize these SiV-NDs on the quartz surface via an inverted confocal microscope and an atomic force microscope (AFM). Following this, we utilize the AFM tip to lift SiV-NDs from the substrate and deposit them onto a free-standing ONF. Finally, we systematically evaluate the fluorescence emission spectrum, photon count rate, and intensity correlations of the SiV-NDs.

Multiparty session types (MSTs) offer a robust framework for specifying and verifying message-passing software. In MST theory, a global type defines interactions across all roles, while local specifications for individual roles are derived by projecting the global type onto specific message exchanges. When a global type successfully projects onto every role, the resulting composition is guaranteed to be deadlock-free and to exhibit precisely the behaviors defined globally. The usability of MSTs hinges on the projection operation: enhancing its expressiveness enables the type-checking of more systems but complicates the associated soundness proofs. This paper generalizes the standard projection mechanism in MSTs, facilitating the modeling and type-checking of numerous distributed system design patterns—such as load balancing—that are rejected by traditional methods. The core of this new projection lies in a causality analysis between messages, with the soundness proof leveraging novel graph-theoretic techniques from message-sequence chart theory. We validate the effectiveness of this enhanced projection by demonstrating numerous global types for common patterns that our method can handle, whereas the standard projection cannot.

This research introduces a new method for successive interference cancellation (SIC) ordering and beamforming within a multi-carrier, multi-user non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) system equipped with multiple antennas. The study develops a joint algorithm optimizing beamforming, subcarrier allocation, user association, and SIC sequence to maximize worst-case energy efficiency (EE). Since this results in a challenging non-convex mixed integer non-linear programming (MINLP) problem, the authors apply linearization and relax integer constraints, followed by the Dinkelbach algorithm to simplify the formulation. The non-convex optimization is further transformed into an equivalent rank-constrained semidefinite programming (SDP) problem, solved via SDP relaxation and sequential fractional programming. Additionally, an alternative optimization-based approach is utilized to balance computational complexity with performance. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed SIC ordering strategy surpasses conventional methods found in existing literature.

Quantum LDPC codes represent a promising avenue for low-overhead quantum computing. This paper introduces a generalized Union-Find decoder tailored for quantum LDPC codes. We demonstrate that this decoder can correct all errors with a weight up to $An^{\alpha}$ (where $A, \alpha > 0$) across various classes of quantum LDPC codes, including toric and hyperbolic codes in dimensions $D \geq 3$, as well as quantum expander codes. To establish this finding, we define a covering radius metric that quantifies the spread of an error based on its syndrome; we anticipate this concept may prove useful in areas beyond decoding. Additionally, numerical simulations indicate that our Union-Find decoder surpasses the belief propagation decoder in the low error rate regime for a quantum LDPC code with a length of 3600.

Traditional toxicity assessments for chemical compounds have depended on animal testing, yet there is a growing global need for non-animal predictive methods. This study aimed to develop a classification system for compounds using *in vitro* gene expression profiles, drawing on data previously analyzed by our team regarding nine substances commonly used in chemical management. Although we initially employed agglomerative hierarchical clustering, we encountered a statistical challenge: selecting representative RNAs for clustering from a pool of over 30,000 transcripts. To address this, we formulated a combinatorial optimization problem that considered both gene expression levels and the correlation between expression profiles, solving it via a simulated annealing algorithm. Consequently, the nine compounds were successfully categorized into two distinct groups using 1,000 extracted RNAs. This proposed methodology facilitates read-across, a key framework for toxicology prediction, based on *in vitro* gene expression data.

Spin chains serve as versatile platforms for quantum computation and information processing, facilitating the modeling, demonstration, and understanding of key phenomena such as high-fidelity quantum state transfer, entanglement generation and distribution, and resource creation for measurement-based quantum computing. This paper investigates a more intricate 2D spin network (SN) constructed by applying appropriate unitary transformations to two initially uncoupled spin chains. By restricting the analysis to the single-excitation subspace of this network, it is shown that the system functions effectively as a router, guiding information flow through the network. Additionally, the study demonstrates the network's capability to generate maximally entangled states between two specific sites. The research further illustrates that this 2D SN can operate as a sensor to detect unknown phases applied to a system spin. Finally, a comprehensive modeling analysis of static disorder reveals that the system maintains robustness against various types of disorder.

We present experimental results on the dynamics of vibrated particles confined within a two-dimensional vertical container, driven by the inquiry: how can we optimize a specific external vibration to maximize internal disorder (for blending) and agitation (for vibration absorption)? Granular media serve as analogs to classical thermodynamic systems, where energy input via shaking induces fluidization by adjusting oscillation amplitude or frequency. Alternatively, we investigate the effects of altering container geometry while maintaining constant energy injection. Our approach involves reshaping the container base into a V-shape to disrupt the symmetry of the internal particle arrangement. The resulting lattice exhibits a coexistence of a compact, hexagonal, solid-like crystalline phase and a loose, amorphous, fluid-like phase under any level of thermal agitation. We demonstrate that both the solid-to-fluid volume fraction and granular temperature are influenced not only by external vibration but also by the number of topological defects induced by the container's asymmetry. The former depends on energy fluctuation statistics, while the latter aligns with a two-dimensional melting transition described by KTHNY theory.

To counter spoofing vulnerabilities in Phasor Measurement Units (PMUs), we introduce the Stochastic Reachability-based Distributed Kalman Filter (SR-DKF), a set-valued state estimation method designed to ensure secure GPS timing across receiver networks. By leveraging stochastic reachability, this approach estimates both GPS time and its stochastic reachable set, represented through probabilistic zonotopes (p-Zonotopes). Although it requires known measurement error bounds only under non-spoofed conditions, our two-tier strategy first mitigates measurement-level spoofing by detecting deviations in measurement innovation from the expected p-Zonotope, and secondly conducts state-level timing risk analysis by calculating the intersection probability between the estimated p-Zonotope and an unsafe set defined by IEEE C37.118.1a-2014 standards. We validated the SR-DKF using a simulated receiver network subjected to coordinated signal-level spoofing, demonstrating enhanced GPS timing accuracy and effective spoofing mitigation. Furthermore, we assessed the robustness of the estimated timing risk across varying numbers of receivers.

This study examines topological defects within the (1+1)-dimensional $\lambda\phi^4$ theory set against a Lorentz-violating background. While M. Barreto et al. (2006) \cite{barreto2006defect} demonstrated that no original effects arise in the leading order of a single scalar field model, we introduce a novel Lorentz-violating term at the next-to-leading order. This term resists absorption through any redefinition of scalar fields or coordinates and represents the lowest-order contribution capable of producing tangible effects on kink properties. We compute the resulting corrections to both the kink's shape and mass, perform kink quantization to derive revised modes, and determine that both bound and continuum states are altered by this violation of Lorentz symmetry.

Characters represent the smallest textual units capable of extracting stylometric signals for author identification. This study examines the efficacy of character-level features in authorship attribution within Bangla literature, yielding promising yet improvable results. The proposed model demonstrates significantly superior time and memory efficiency compared to word-level alternatives, though it achieves accuracy that is 2–5% lower than top-performing word-based models. Comparative analysis of various word-based approaches reveals that the proposed model's performance improves as dataset size increases. Additionally, we evaluated the impact of pre-training character embeddings on a diverse Bangla character set, finding that pre-training enhances performance by up to 10%. The study utilized two datasets ranging from 6 to 14 authors, which were balanced prior to training, to compare outcomes.

Despite the formidable hurdles facing the development of practical quantum computers, rapid advancements in emerging quantum technologies are making this objective increasingly attainable. Central to this progress is quantum entanglement, a resource that enables quantum computations to surpass classical capabilities. However, detecting entanglement is often complex. A primary obstacle is that conventional methods quickly become impractical when applied to systems with more than a few qubits, largely because they require extensive measurements across numerous state copies. Since experimental setups frequently involve a very limited number of copies—especially in large-scale quantum systems—these traditional approaches face significant constraints. This article presents an overview of a probabilistic method capable of identifying genuine multipartite entanglement with high confidence using an exceptionally small number of state copies. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that this protocol maintains efficiency even under noisy conditions, thereby validating its practicality for near-term quantum devices and complex experimental environments.

Training change detectors typically relies on bi-temporal images captured at different times within the same region, yet acquiring labeled pairs is costly and labor-intensive. While various unsupervised methods have been introduced to mitigate this, they still necessitate access to unlabeled bi-temporal data. This paper presents a novel unsupervised change detection approach based on image reconstruction loss, which operates using only unlabeled single-temporal images. The underlying reconstruction model is trained to regenerate the original source image by processing pairs consisting of the source image and a photometrically transformed version of itself. During inference, the model accepts bi-temporal images as input and attempts to reconstruct one of them; areas exhibiting significant discrepancies between the two images result in elevated reconstruction loss, thereby indicating change. Our detector demonstrates substantial performance across multiple benchmark datasets despite relying solely on single-temporal input. The associated code and trained models will be made publicly available to ensure reproducibility.

Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) are planar arrays capable of manipulating reflection to create partially controllable propagation environments. While RIS has garnered significant interest from both academia and industry, most researchers analyzing RIS-assisted systems rely on the simple Rician model. Although this model facilitates theoretical analysis, its stochastic Non-Line-of-Sight (NLoS) component fails to account for deployment geometry, rendering it unsuitable for evaluating 3GPP standardization proposals. This article adapts the widely used Quasi Deterministic Radio channel Generator (QuaDRiGa) for RIS-assisted scenarios and contrasts it with the Rician model. The comparison reveals that geometry-inconsistent NLoS modeling within the Rician framework yields inflated estimates of achievable rates. In contrast, our approach leverages QuaDRiGa's strengths, including spatial consistency in Large Scale Fading, support for User Equipment mobility, and alignment between Large Scale and Small Scale Fading. Additionally, QuaDRiGa provides calibrated scenario parameters that guarantee 3GPP compatibility. Ultimately, this method is versatile enough to be applied to any model or software originally designed for conventional MIMO, enabling researchers to construct simulation platforms for RIS-assisted systems.

We introduce an algorithm designed to determine the $C^\infty$-ring structure of any Weil algebra, enabling both numerical and symbolic analysis involving higher infinitesimals. This approach begins by outlining (Forward-mode) automatic differentiation (AD) through the lens of $C^\infty$-rings. Originally formulated by Lawvere, $C^\infty$-rings serve as the cornerstone of smooth infinitesimal analysis and synthetic differential geometry. We contend that viewing AD within this $C^\infty$-ring framework establishes a cohesive theoretical foundation and provides modular mechanisms for representing multivariate partial derivatives. Specifically, higher-order Forward-mode AD can be encapsulated as a Weil algebra, with tensor products utilized to combine them for achieving multivariate higher-order AD. Furthermore, the algorithms presented herein offer educational value for teaching and exploring smooth infinitesimal analysis.

BlockSystems.jl and NetworkDynamics.jl are two innovative software packages designed to enable highly efficient transient stability simulations for power networks. These tools allow users to define inputs and power system configurations in a modular, equation-based format that maintains both high speed and detailed modeling fidelity. Developed in the high-level, high-performance language Julia, the software benefits from a robust open-source ecosystem featuring advanced solvers and machine learning algorithms. Driven by recent interest in the Nordic inertia challenge, the Nordic5 test case has been implemented and its control parameters optimized by leveraging the machine learning and automatic differentiation features of the software stack.

We elucidate the proximity of a second-order fully nonlinear equation to uniform ellipticity by analyzing the large eigenvalues of its linearized operator. This approach offers a novel and effective framework for comprehending the structure of fully nonlinear equations in both elliptic and parabolic contexts. Applying this method, we resolve a fully nonlinear variant of the Loewner-Nirenberg problem and a noncompact, complete version of the fully nonlinear Yamabe problem. However, the intricacy of our method is underscored by a topological obstruction.

We investigate KIC9773821, a $\delta$ Scuti--red giant binary system and the first double-pulsator of its type, which was monitored by the \textit{Kepler} mission over four years. Our primary objectives are to confirm the system's physical binding rather than a chance alignment and to determine the evolutionary stage of the red giant using asteroseismology. Additionally, we aim to derive a dynamical mass and an age estimate for the $\delta$ Sct component, which would facilitate further mode identification through advanced asteroseismic modeling. Using HERMES@Mercator spectroscopy, we measured spectroscopic parameters and radial velocities (RVs) for the red giant. By combining light-arrival-time delays from the $\delta$ Scuti pulsations with the red giant's RVs, we established that the system is bound and derived its orbital parameters, including the mass ratio. Asteroseismic modeling of the red giant's individual frequencies yielded a mass of $2.10^{+0.20}_{-0.10}$ M$_{\odot}$ and an age of $1.08^{+0.06}_{-0.24}$ Gyr. We identified the red giant as a helium-burning secondary clump star, verified its adherence to the standard $\nu_{\rm max}$ scaling relation, and confirmed that its observed period spacings align with theoretical predictions from the MESA code. These findings also constrain the mass and age of the $\delta$ Sct star. Utilizing these constraints, we constructed $\delta$ Sct models within a reduced parameter space, successfully identifying four out of its five pulsation modes.

We investigate the Josephson effect arising from a domain wall within an electron-hole double layer of two chiral metals, focusing on s-wave pairing. This domain wall, resulting from a discontinuity in the order parameter phase, generates two independent evanescent zero-energy modes at an exceptional point. By applying the continuity equation to couple quasiparticle currents with supercurrents, we derive a unique solution that involves a superposition of these zero-energy modes, where the relative phases of the coefficients correspond to the direction of the macroscopic supercurrents. In a toroidal configuration, the effective Josephson current circulates around the domain walls, a setup that can be physically realized on the surface of a ring-shaped topological insulator.

Interactions between electrons and antiferromagnetic magnons (AFMMs) play a pivotal role in numerous correlated materials, serving as the most likely pairing mechanism in high-temperature superconductors like cuprates and iron pnictides. Yet, unlike well-documented electron-phonon interactions (EPIs), definitive evidence of how electron-AFMM interactions (EAIs) reshape band structures remains absent, leaving critical details such as interaction strength and doping trends unknown. In this study, we directly detect a kink in the band dispersion within Ba$_{1-x}$K$_x$Mn$_2$As$_2$ caused by EAIs, revealing fundamental properties of these interactions. We determined that the EAIs coupling constant can reach values as high as 6, exhibiting profound dependencies on both doping and temperature—behaviors that starkly contrast with EPIs and challenge existing theoretical frameworks. This massive renormalization of electronic bands pushes the system toward the Stoner criterion, resulting in the observed ferromagnetic state in Ba$_{1-x}$K$_x$Mn$_2$As$_2$. These findings broaden our understanding of EAIs and may aid in deciphering the behavior of other correlated materials where such interactions are crucial, including high-temperature superconductors.

Semantic segmentation has emerged as a pivotal area in computer vision, effectively addressing complex challenges in object detection and recognition. We introduce an object-by-object learning framework designed to identify 11 categories of facial skin lesions using semantic segmentation. Identifying individual lesions within dense clusters remains difficult due to visual ambiguities; however, we note that certain object classes exhibit co-occurring visual relationships (such as wrinkles with age spots or papules with whiteheads). Leveraging rich contextual information to resolve these issues, we propose REthinker blocks. These blocks integrate locally constructed convLSTM/Conv3D layers with an SE module acting as a one-shot attention mechanism. This architecture enhances the network's sensitivity to both local and global contexts, facilitating the detection of ambiguously appearing objects and their inter-class co-occurrences. Experimental results on a prepared dataset demonstrate that our model achieves a Mean Intersection over Union (MIoU) of 79.46%, marking a 15.34% improvement over Deeplab v3+ (which achieved an MIoU of 64.12%).

This study examines sequential changepoint detection under the assumption that the duration of a change is finite but unknown, a scenario critical for applications like signal and image processing where events emerge and vanish at uncertain times or locations. Departing from the standard quickest change detection criterion, which seeks to minimize expected detection delay for a fixed average run length to false alarm, we instead employ a reliable maximin approach. This method aims to maximize the minimum probability of detection within a specific time or spatial window, subject to a constraint on the local maximum probability of false alarm in that same window. Our analysis demonstrates that the optimal detection strategy is a modified CUSUM procedure. We subsequently compare the performance of this optimal method against the widely used Finite Moving Average (FMA) and standard CUSUM algorithms via Monte Carlo simulations. The results indicate that the latter two algorithms typically perform nearly as well as the optimal solution. However, the FMA algorithm offers a significant advantage by remaining independent of signal intensity, a parameter often unknown in practice. Finally, we apply the FMA algorithm to the task of detecting faint satellite streaks in optical imagery.

This study generalizes the celebrated concentration-compactness principle established by P.L. Lions to the framework of Orlicz spaces. As a practical application, we demonstrate an existence theorem for certain critical elliptic problems characterized by nonstandard growth conditions.

The surge in decoded protein sequences from genomes is creating new opportunities to utilize transformer neural networks for connecting sequence data with protein function. Recent studies indicate that the vast volume of known protein sequences enables transformers to learn robust, task-agnostic sequence representations. This paper argues that developing joint representations of both sequence and structure produces superior embeddings for function-prediction tasks. We introduce a transformer architecture that incorporates attention mechanisms for both sequence and tertiary structure. Our findings demonstrate that these combined representations outperform sequence-only models, resulting in enhanced performance across multiple metrics for determining superfamily membership.

Many devices and users increasingly demand low latency, a requirement that traditional cloud computing cannot satisfy, thereby validating the shift toward a new paradigm. Edge computing addresses this by relocating computational resources to the network's periphery, positioning them closer to data generation and consumption points. Nevertheless, this approach introduces distinct challenges. Unlike data centers optimized for economies of scale, the edge environment features highly heterogeneous devices; for instance, mobile units like vehicles create dynamic network topologies that complicate system architecture. While Internet of Things (IoT) devices generate vast amounts of data suitable for edge processing, this paper examines the primary obstacles in edge computing and proposes solutions to deliver a seamless cloud experience. Specifically, we suggest leveraging technologies such as containers and WebAssembly to effectively manage application execution across diverse hardware.

The Zernike wavefront sensor (ZWFS) falls within the broader category of Fourier-filtering wavefront sensors (FFWFS). Renowned for its exceptional sensitivity despite a limited dynamic range, it serves as an ideal component for second-stage adaptive optics (AO) systems or for calibrating quasi-static aberrations. Structurally, the ZWFS utilizes a focal plane mask featuring a phase-shifting dot defined by two parameters: its diameter and depth. This study aims to enhance sensor performance by adjusting the dot's diameter. We first establish a general theoretical framework offering an analytical description of FFWFS characteristics, followed by predictions of ZWFS sensitivity across various dot diameter and depth configurations. These analytical results are subsequently validated through end-to-end simulations. Consequently, we propose a modified ZWFS shape with highly advantageous properties. Our findings demonstrate that sensitivity can be optimized by altering the dot diameter, potentially reaching the theoretical limit, though this involves a trade-off regarding sensitivity at low spatial frequencies. For instance, a ZWFS with a dot diameter of $2\lambda/D$ (denoted as Z2WFS) shows double the sensitivity of the conventional $1.06\lambda/D$ ZWFS for all phase spatial components except tip-tilt modes. Notably, this sensitivity improvement does not compromise the dynamic range, which remains comparable to that of the classical design. This research paves the way for the development of diameter-optimized ZWFS units.

Federated learning represents an emerging approach that separates data gathering from model training through multi-party computation and aggregation. As a versatile framework, it holds promise for integration with other learning systems. This survey provides a focused examination of federated learning combined with various algorithms, investigating methods to enhance the standard federated averaging technique. It also reviews model fusion strategies, including adaptive aggregation, regularization, clustering, and Bayesian approaches. Aligning with current trends, the paper further explores "federated x learning," where federated learning intersects with paradigms such as multitask, meta, transfer, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning. Finally, this review outlines the state of the art, identifies key challenges, and suggests future directions.

It is widely recognized that linear codes with few weights find significant utility in secret sharing schemes \cite{JY2006,CC2005}. Specifically, projective two-weight codes are particularly valuable due to their close connections to finite projective spaces, strongly regular graphs, and combinatorial designs \cite{RC1986,CD2018,P1972}. In this work, we introduce two such applications.

For biological organisms facing environmental constraints, minimizing energy usage and optimizing reaction speeds are paramount, a goal mirrored in engineered systems that prioritize rapid and energy-efficient solutions. At the neuronal level, this translates to generating the necessary outcomes using the fewest and earliest possible spikes. Time-to-first-spike coding naturally aligns with these objectives as intrinsic learning features. This work presents a rigorous derivation of a learning rule tailored for first-spike timing in leaky integrate-and-fire networks, depending exclusively on input and output spike events, and demonstrates its ability to execute error backpropagation within hierarchical spiking architectures. Additionally, we validate the framework on the BrainScaleS-2 neuromorphic platform, illustrating its capacity to exploit the system's inherent speed and efficiency. Finally, we assess the approach's adaptability across various neuromorphic technologies by analyzing the impact of characteristic distortions introduced by these substrates on performance.

Neuro-Evolution, which merges deep neural networks with evolutionary algorithms to automate or enhance network construction, has recently become a prominent area of interest within the deep learning community. Recent developments in this field have achieved accuracy levels comparable to manually designed networks. This study introduces a two-stage framework: first, a convolutional autoencoder evolved via an iterative mutation process compresses input data efficiently; second, another evolved convolutional neural network classifies this compressed information. The evolutionary process continuously generates new network architectures by mutating existing ones. Furthermore, the proposed method evaluates the balance between compression rates and information loss across various autoencoders to identify the optimal compressor for the subsequent classification step. The entire framework was implemented and evaluated on the CIFAR-10 dataset, with results analyzed and potential future research directions discussed, including strategies to boost efficiency and explore specific application domains.

Code reviews are essential for ensuring software quality, enabling reviewers to evaluate and critique new patches prior to their integration. However, it remains unclear to what degree coding patterns—specifically repetitive code structures—evolve between a patch's initial submission and the final decision made during the review. This study re-examines coding patterns within code reviews to determine if such changes occur during the review process. By analyzing 27,736 reviewed OpenStack patches, we compare pre-review (initial submission) and post-review (after review) versions to measure differences in coding patterns. The results indicate that patches following a review tend to align more closely with the coding patterns of accepted patches than they did upon first submission. Furthermore, accepted patches exhibit coding patterns similar to those of previously accepted patches. These findings offer insights into the review process, highlighting the potential for automated tools to assist newcomers and establishing a foundation for future research on conformance and its impact on efficient code reviews.

This work investigates the global existence of Einstein-Maxwell equations on $\mathbb{R}^4$. By employing a technique grounded in wave and Lorentzian gauge conditions, we derive refined estimates. Our primary result demonstrates that the Einstein-Maxwell system admits a global-in-time solution provided the initial data is sufficiently small.

UTe2 stands out as a leading candidate for spin-triplet superconductivity, where a paramagnetic normal state transitions into superconductivity driven by spin fluctuations. The discovery of various anomalous superconducting behaviors has established UTe2 as an ideal system for investigating unconventional superconductivity, yet a deeper understanding of how the normal-state fermiology influences these phenomena remains an open question. In this study, we demonstrate theoretically that electron correlations drastically alter the normal-state fermiology, giving rise to a correlated Fermi surface (FS) driven by Kondo resonance at low temperatures. This emergent correlated FS offers a unified explanation for diverse unconventional superconducting properties. Specifically, the geometry of this correlated FS naturally accommodates topological superconductivity when odd-parity pairings become the dominant instability due to strong ferromagnetic spin fluctuations. Furthermore, two degenerate pairs of odd-parity channels appear as accidental solutions, providing a natural explanation for multicomponent superconductivity that breaks time-reversal symmetry. Notably, the resulting time-reversal-breaking state functions as a Weyl superconductor, where Weyl points migrate along the correlated FS as the relative strength of the nearly degenerate pairing solutions changes. We conclude that the correlated normal-state fermiology identified here provides a comprehensive framework for describing unconventional superconductivity in UTe2.

This paper establishes various weighted Poincaré inequalities featuring variable exponents on Carnot groups and Carnot-Carathéodory spaces by employing diverse techniques. Specifically, for vector fields meeting H\"{o}rmander's condition within variable non-isotropic Sobolev spaces, we introduce a weight belonging to the variable Muckenhoupt class $A_{p(\cdot ),p^{\ast }(\cdot )}$, provided the exponent $p(\cdot )$ adheres to suitable hypotheses; this yields first-order weighted Poincaré inequalities with variable exponents. Furthermore, we develop higher-order weighted Poincaré inequalities with variable exponents for Carnot groups. A pivotal element in these findings is demonstrating the boundedness of the fractional integral operator on Lebesgue spaces characterized by weighted and variable exponents over spaces of homogeneous type. Additionally, utilizing alternative methods, we extend certain results to scenarios where the exponent undergoes a jump discontinuity and the weight resides in a restricted Muckenhoupt class. Ultimately, we apply these weighted Poincaré inequalities to prove the existence and uniqueness of a minimizer for the Dirichlet energy integral associated with a degenerate $p(\cdot )$-Laplacian problem subject to zero boundary conditions in Carnot groups.

The normal-state characteristics and superconductivity of NbN films can be adjusted across a broad spectrum, offering an ideal system to systematically examine the progression of superconducting performance. This study reports the upper critical field of NbN films for both parallel ($B\parallel$ film) and perpendicular ($B\perp$ film) magnetic field orientations across a wide temperature range. Eight samples, with critical temperatures ($T_c$) varying from 2.5 K to 9.8 K, were analyzed. By modifying the film growth conditions, the normal-state resistivity was varied by a factor of over six. Results indicate that the upper critical field magnitudes in both orientations ($B_{c2}^{\perp}$ and $B_{c2}^{\parallel}$) surpass the paramagnetic limiting field $B_p$.
