The temperature dependence of $B_{c2}^{\perp}$ aligns with the extended Werthamer--Helfand--Hohenberg (WHH) model that accounts for Pauli spin paramagnetism. Conversely, the $B_{c2}^{\parallel}$ versus temperature data exhibits signatures of two-dimensional superconductivity near $T_c$. Finally, the evolution of the Maki parameter in relation to other factors, including the slope of the upper critical field near $T_c$ and normal-state resistivity, is discussed to elucidate the nature of the Pauli paramagnetic effect within this system.

This report details our advancements in creating a low-frequency magnetic particle imaging (MPI) scanner utilizing an atomic magnetometer (AM), designed to operate without Specific Absorption Rate (SAR) or Peripheral Nerve Stimulation (PNS) limitations. We tackle significant coil and sensor design challenges inherent to specific AM characteristics. Unlike our prior work, we have shifted the AM's operational mode to detect weak magnetic nanoparticle (MNP) response fields amidst nearby strong drive and selection fields. Our findings demonstrate that a pump-probe AM configuration within a buffer gas-filled alkali vapor cell can withstand mT/m gradients while retaining a sensitivity in the low pT/Hz^(1/2) range across a bandwidth from DC to several kHz. We provide a comprehensive account of the drive and selection coil geometries and their hardware realization, which enables field-free-line (FFL) operation compatible with optimal AM performance. Furthermore, we estimate the scanner's achievable field of view, spatial resolution, and sensitivity, based on the mechanical scanning of a Resovist sample through the field-free point or line.

Following three years of polarimetric monitoring of blazars by the RoboPol project, several fundamental traits of optical polarimetric rotations have been identified in these highly variable sources. The most significant finding is that the polarization characteristics of optical synchrotron emission seem directly correlated with gamma-ray activity. This paper examines the evidence supporting this link, alongside broader aspects of polarimetric behavior in blazars that are essential for advancing theoretical models of blazar emission.

This study addresses the challenge of inferring causal structures from observations across various experimental conditions, specifically when the targets of interventions remain unknown. We operate within a linear structural causal model featuring additive Gaussian noise, assuming interventions perturb target variables without altering the system's causal relationships. Since distinct models can yield identical distributions, creating competing causal explanations, we fully characterize these equivalence classes and establish identifiability results. These findings enable the development of a greedy algorithm, GnIES, which recovers the data-generating model's equivalence class without requiring knowledge of intervention targets. Furthermore, we introduce a new method for creating semi-synthetic datasets that maintain known causal ground truths while closely mimicking the distributional properties of real-world data. Utilizing this approach, we evaluate GnIES on synthetic, real, and semi-synthetic datasets. Despite relying on a strong Gaussian assumption, GnIES demonstrates robustness against various model violations and performs competitively in recovering causal structures across small to large sample sizes. We provide Python implementations of both GnIES and the semi-synthetic data generation procedure in the packages "gnies" and "sempler."

Partitura is a lightweight Python library designed for processing symbolic music data. It simplifies access to common music information retrieval features, including note arrays (sequences of timed, pitched events) and 2D piano roll matrices, alongside other score components like time and key signatures, performance instructions, and repeat structures. The library supports loading scores in MEI, MusicXML, Kern, and MIDI formats, as well as MIDI performances and score-to-performance alignments. Additionally, it offers music analysis tools such as automatic pitch spelling, key signature detection, and voice separation. As an open-source project, Partitura can be accessed at https://github.com/CPJKU/partitura/.

Attacks against millions of users of non-internet applications, such as SMS and USSD, are increasing. These systems often lack protection from standard multi-factor authentication (MFA) due to their specific interaction models and operational constraints. To mitigate this, we introduce a method that integrates blockchain with an MFA system grounded in blockchain transaction evidence and risk analysis. This approach constructs a user transaction profile over time to evaluate the risk level of each new transaction. When a transaction is identified as high risk, the system generates n-factor authentication layers utilizing historically endorsed blockchain transactions. Additionally, we present a demonstration of applying this approach to secure critical financial transactions within a blockchain-based asset financing platform.

The quantum switch functions as a higher-order operation that accepts two quantum processes as input and merges them into a coherent superposition of two distinct sequential orders. This paper presents an approach to the quantum switch utilizing categorical quantum mechanics techniques. Specifically, we model the switch as a sum of diagrams within the category of finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, or equivalently, as a sum of diagrams constructed via Selinger's CPM framework. This sum-of-diagrams perspective offers insight into the activation of classical capacity in completely depolarising channels (CDPCs) and facilitates extension to N-channel switches. We illustrate the utility of these partially diagrammatic methods by deriving a permutation condition for calculating the output of any N-channel switch involving CDPCs. Subsequently, we apply this condition to demonstrate that among all possible terms, the interference terms linked to cyclic permutations of the N channels represent the information-transmitting terms with the highest normalisation.

Nuclei exhibiting octupole deformation possess a non-zero intrinsic electric octupole moment, electric dipole moment (EDM), Schiff moment, and magnetic quadrupole moment (MQM) within their rotating intrinsic frame. However, in the laboratory frame, states with definite angular momentum forbid these moments due to parity (P) and time reversal (T) conservation, causing their expectation values to vanish as a result of nuclear rotation. Conversely, octupole-deformed nuclei feature rotational doublets of close opposite parity with identical spin, which are mixed by T,P-odd nuclear forces. This mixing aligns the nuclear axis with the nuclear spin, allowing all intrinsic-frame moments to manifest in the laboratory frame, provided the nuclear spin $I$ is sufficiently large. This mechanism significantly enhances T,P-violating nuclear moments, an effect also observed in nuclei with soft octupole vibrational modes. While Schiff moments have been previously calculated for such nuclei, this paper focuses on the magnetic quadrupole moment in isotopes with $I \geq 1$. The interaction between the nuclear MQM and electrons generates an atomic EDM and T,P-violating nuclear spin-molecular axis interaction constants for molecules in states with non-zero electron angular momentum. Measuring these constants offers a means to test CP-violation theories and search for axion dark matter in atomic, molecular, and solid-state experiments. Potential candidate nuclei include $^{153}\text{Eu}$, $^{161}\text{Dy}$, $^{221}\text{Fr}$, $^{223}\text{Fr}$, $^{223}\text{Ra}$, $^{223}\text{Rn}$, $^{225}\text{Ac}$, $^{227}\text{Ac}$, $^{229}\text{Th}$, $^{229}\text{Pa}$, $^{233}\text{U}$, and $^{235}\text{U}$. The study subsequently examines molecules containing these nuclei, specifically EuO, EuN$^+$, RaF, AcO, AcN$^+$, AcF$^+$, ThO, and ThF$^+$.

This paper investigates the formation of singularities in the geometric flow of complex curves defined by $z_t = -z_{xxx} + \frac{3}{2}\o z_{x} z_{xx}^2$, an equation originally derived by Goldstein and Petrich [Phys. Rev. Lett., 69 (1992), pp. 555--558] in the context of vortex patch dynamics for the incompressible 2D Euler equation. We demonstrate that a smooth solution to this flow can develop a finite-time singularity in the form of an arbitrary curve composed of two rotating logarithmic spirals. Furthermore, we present an exact construction of this solution using specific Painlevé II transcendents and derive its asymptotic expansion near the singularity.

Workloads characterized by low data reuse and irregular memory access patterns, such as those in graph processing and sparse linear algebra, struggle to scale effectively due to memory bottlenecks and inefficient core usage. Although existing techniques involving prefetching, decoupling, or pipelining can alleviate memory latency and boost core utilization, they cannot resolve the persistent issue of limited off-chip bandwidth. While Processing-in-Memory (PIM) approaches leveraging the Hybrid Memory Cube (HMC) address bandwidth constraints, they suffer from low core utilization caused by scheduling difficulties and synchronization overheads, and the high memory-per-core ratio inherent to HMC restricts strong scaling capabilities.

We present Dalorex, a hardware-software co-design that delivers high parallelism and energy efficiency, achieving strong scaling with over 16,000 cores for graph and sparse linear algebra tasks. Compared to previous PIM implementations using 256 cores, Dalorex enhances both performance and energy efficiency by two orders of magnitude through five key innovations: (1) a tile-based distributed-memory architecture ensuring equal data distribution per tile and strictly local memory operations; (2) a task-based parallel programming model that executes tasks on processing units co-located with the required data; (3) a network architecture optimized for irregular traffic by enforcing one-way communication and eliminating routing metadata from messages; (4) novel hardware for traffic-aware task scheduling to sustain high core utilization; and (5) a data placement strategy that enhances workload balance. This research introduces architectural and software advancements that offer unprecedented scalability for graph algorithms while remaining programmable for diverse application domains.

The GDMC AI settlement generation challenge is a PCG competition focused on developing algorithms capable of generating "interesting" Minecraft settlements tailored to specific maps. This paper compiles written reflections from participants, judges, organizers, and advisors regarding both the generated artifacts and the competition itself. Our objective is to present an edited, shareable collection of qualitative feedback and experiences that offer valuable insights into PCG and computational creativity—perspectives that might otherwise be lost if the competition's results were reduced solely to scalar performance metrics. Additionally, we examine organizational challenges within AI competitions and discuss the future trajectory of the GDMC event.

Image spam, or spam text hidden within images to bypass text-based filters, is the focus of this research. We address image spam detection using convolutional neural networks (CNNs), comparing our approach against other machine learning methods and prior studies. Our evaluation includes both real-world examples and challenging datasets resembling spam. By utilizing a novel feature set that combines raw image data with Canny edges, our CNN-based results demonstrate improvements over previous work.

Federated learning aggregates collaborative models from distributed nodes to learn from scattered data; however, traditional FedAvg, which relies on coordinate-based averaging, often overlooks parameter-specific random information, leading to structural feature misalignment. To address this, we introduce Fed2, a feature-aligned federated learning framework that establishes robust structure-feature alignment across collaborative models. Fed2 incorporates two key innovations: first, a feature-oriented model structure adaptation technique that ensures explicit feature allocation within various neural architectures, allowing collaborative models to initialize with matching structures and similar feature information from the outset. Second, during the federated learning process, we implement a feature-paired averaging scheme to maintain aligned feature distributions and prevent fusion conflicts, regardless of whether data is IID or non-IID. Consequently, Fed2 significantly improves federated learning convergence across diverse homogeneous and heterogeneous settings, delivering superior convergence speed, accuracy, and computational and communication efficiency.

This work investigates Convex Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs) featuring a concave objective and convex constraints within the state-action occupancy measure. We introduce a policy-based primal-dual algorithm that employs policy gradient ascent for the primal variable and projected sub-gradient descent for the dual variable. Although the problem lacks an additivity structure and exhibits nonconvex characteristics, we demonstrate global convergence by exploiting hidden convexity, proving an $\mathcal{O}\left(T^{-1/3}\right)$ convergence rate regarding both the optimality gap and constraint violation. When the objective is strongly concave in the occupancy measure, we establish an enhanced rate of $\mathcal{O}\left(T^{-1/2}\right)$. Furthermore, by incorporating a pessimistic term into the constraint, we show that zero constraint violation is attainable without compromising the convergence rate of the optimality gap. To our knowledge, this is the first study to provide non-asymptotic convergence guarantees for policy-based primal-dual methods applied to infinite-horizon discounted convex CMDPs.

High-dimensional photonic entanglement represents a promising avenue for quantum information processing that offers enhanced capacity and error protection. By encoding high-dimensional qudits into photon carrier frequencies, this method leverages straightforward generation, universal single-photon gates achieved through electro-optic modulation and wave shaping, and compatibility with fiber transmission for high-capacity communication. While recent landmark experiments have successfully demonstrated quantum interference among a few frequency modes, certifying massive-dimensional frequency entanglement has remained a significant challenge. This study reports a record-breaking certification of discretized frequency entanglement, introducing a novel, highly efficient, and nonlocally implementable certification approach that paves the way for utilizing this encoding in quantum communication.

We introduce a new category of graph neural networks grounded in the discretized Beltrami flow, a non-Euclidean diffusion partial differential equation. Our framework augments node features with positional encodings extracted from graph topology, which are then co-evolved via the Beltrami flow to enable simultaneous continuous feature learning and topological evolution. This approach generalizes numerous established graph neural networks and attains state-of-the-art performance across various benchmarks.

This work details a systematic examination of heavy-flavour production within the underlying event associated with a primary hard process in pp collisions at $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV, utilizing the PYTHIA 8 Monte Carlo event generator. We contrast outcomes derived from events triggered by the leading hadron against those selected via reconstructed jets. Our findings indicate that the kinematic properties of heavy-flavour fragmentation complicate the characterization of the underlying event; consequently, the conventional approach of using the leading charged final-state hadron as a trigger can obscure the link between the leading process and the associated heavy-flavour particle. Conversely, events triggered by light or heavy-flavour jets maintain this connection, offering more direct insights into the underlying heavy-flavour production mechanism, though they may introduce sensitivity to gluon radiation. The methodologies presented herein enable detailed verification of model calculations regarding light and heavy-flavour production in both jets and the underlying event.

This research addresses multi-agent computation under differential privacy constraints applied to agents' local data, specifically in the presence of eavesdroppers utilizing node-to-node communication. The study considers networks comprising both private and public channels. The private network is characterized as sparse and potentially disconnected, featuring encrypted and secure communications that protect both data and intermediate node states; conversely, the public network is connected, possibly dense, and permits open communication. Within this framework, we introduce a multi-gossip PPSC mechanism operating on the private network. In this mechanism, randomly selected node pairs iteratively update their states by shuffling values with added random noise while preserving summation consistency. We demonstrate that this approach can attain any specified differential privacy level with a defined probability. Furthermore, we integrate this mechanism into distributed computing workflows, proposing privacy-guarantee protocols for three fundamental tasks. These protocols employ an adaptive strategy that adjusts noise injection in PPSC steps for privacy and the frequency of standard computation steps for accuracy. For average consensus, we develop a PPSC-Gossip averaging algorithm that applies the multi-gossip PPSC mechanism for privacy encryption prior to executing an averaging consensus algorithm over the public network. Regarding network linear equations and distributed convex optimization, we construct two distinct distributed protocols that extend the PPSC-Gossip averaging consensus with additional projection or gradient descent steps, respectively. Finally, we prove that given specific privacy and accuracy requirements, all three proposed protocols can solve their respective problems with the desired precision while satisfying the required differential privacy standards.

Unlike traditional frame-based sensors that accumulate light to form images, event cameras detect illumination changes in a scene. This capability enables their use in scenarios involving rapid motion and complex lighting, where conventional sensors typically suffer from blur or exposure issues. Consequently, event cameras have become highly desirable for Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS). The growing popularity of neuromorphic sensors has spurred research into Event-based Optical Flow (EBOF). However, the emergence of high-definition neuromorphic sensors presents new challenges due to their larger pixel arrays and significantly higher event throughput. To address this, we introduce an optimized framework for real-time optical flow computation compatible with both low- and high-resolution event cameras. Our approach formulates a novel dense representation of sparse event flow called the "inverse exponential distance surface," which acts as an intermediate frame to leverage established, state-of-the-art frame-based optical flow algorithms. Evaluations on driving sequences at various resolutions demonstrate that our method often outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques while achieving superior frame rates: 250Hz at 346 x 260 pixels and 77Hz at 1280 x 720 pixels.

This paper addresses system identification in scenarios where steady-state (or DC) gain side-information is accessible. We propose a general nonparametric identification framework formulated as an infinite-dimensional constrained convex optimization problem within the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) of stable impulse responses. The optimization objective combines empirical loss with RKHS norm regularization, while the constraint enforces the incorporation of steady-state gain data. Our approach accommodates both discrete-time and continuous-time systems. We demonstrate that this program yields a unique solution, which can be derived by solving an equivalent finite-dimensional convex optimization problem. Furthermore, a closed-form solution exists when the empirical loss and regularization functions are quadratic and the side-information is exact. Finally, we conduct extensive numerical experiments to validate the efficiency of the proposed identification method.

Artificial intelligence (AI) serves as a potent instrument for executing numerous tasks, and this rapidly evolving technological field is gaining traction across diverse sectors, notably within the insurance industry. However, the capabilities of AI also introduce significant challenges, chief among them being the lack of transparency and explainability of algorithms, which affects both specialists and laypeople. This opacity casts doubt on an algorithm's utility and precision while complicating the evaluation of potential biases inherent in the data or the model itself. This paper examines the prevailing application of AI algorithms and the integration of explainable AI (XAI) methods within the Dutch insurance sector. Utilizing these insights, we have developed a checklist for insurance firms to ensure adherence to quality standards for XAI and to establish a robust basis for organizational collaboration. Furthermore, this checklist expands upon an existing framework created by SIVI, the Dutch standardization institute for digital cooperation and innovation in insurance.

Effective electromagnetic filtering is crucial for the coherent control, operation, and readout of superconducting quantum circuits operating at milliKelvin temperatures. While the suppression of spurious modes near a few GHz transition frequencies is well-established through on-chip and packaging design, higher-frequency noise photons—exceeding pair-breaking energies—induce decoherence and necessitate spectral engineering prior to reaching the packaged chip. External wires entering the refrigerator offer a direct conduit for these photons into the quantum circuit. This paper presents quantitative analysis and experimental data regarding noise photon flux through coaxial, filtered wiring, detailing coaxial cable attenuation at room temperature and estimating flux for standard wiring setups. Additionally, compact cryogenic microwave low-pass filters utilizing CR-110 and Esorb-230 absorptive dielectric materials are introduced, with experimental results provided across room and cryogenic temperatures up to 70 GHz. Filter cut-off frequencies, ranging from 1 to 10 GHz, are determined by filter length, while the roll-off characteristics depend on the material. Measurements of the relative dielectric permittivity and magnetic permeability for Esorb-230 within the 75 to 110 GHz pair-breaking range are reported, alongside calculated filter properties for this band. The study demonstrates that filters dramatically suppress noise photon flux, confirming their utility for experiments involving superconducting quantum systems.

Simulations in high energy density physics are computationally costly, primarily due to the requirement for generating non-local thermodynamic equilibrium opacities. While high-fidelity spectra can uncover new physical phenomena that lower-fidelity spectra miss, the simulation costs increase proportionally with the fidelity of the opacities employed. Although neural networks can replicate these spectra, their performance is constrained by the fidelity of the training data they require. This study demonstrates that high-fidelity spectra can be accurately reproduced with median errors between 3% and 4% using as few as 50 high-fidelity Krypton data samples, achieved by applying transfer learning to a neural network initially trained on a significantly larger dataset of low-fidelity data.

Wavelength shifting fibers are extensively employed to collect light from scintillation counters, enabling the connection of diverse scintillation planes to the relatively small photocathodes of photodetectors, particularly those of silicon photomultipliers. In October 2020, Kuraray introduced a new class of faster fibers. We compared this new fiber, YS-2, against the established Y-11 model. The YS-2 exhibited a decay time nearly half that of the Y-11, measuring approximately 4.0 ns compared to 7.4 ns. Concurrently, its light yield and attenuation length matched those of the Y-11, positioning the YS-2 as an excellent option for timing applications in scintillation detectors.

This study analyzes Anatoly Karpov's Queen sacrifices using Stockfish 14 NNUE, an AI chess engine, to assess their efficiency. For comparison, we also examine a dataset of Karpov's Rook and Knight sacrifices to determine if he maintains comparable accuracy across these piece types. Our research offers insights into human-AI interaction, specifically how humans can better interpret the strategies of opaque AI algorithms. Finally, we discuss the broader implications for the study of chess through the lens of computer engines.

In program evaluation, it is common for units to expect a new policy's implementation before it actually happens. This anticipatory behavior can cause unit outcomes to depend on their future treatment assignments. This paper utilizes a potential outcomes framework to examine treatment effects under anticipation. Beginning with a classical two-period difference-in-differences model, it offers partially identified sets along with straightforward estimation and inference strategies for causal parameters. The study also explores extensions involving covariates and longitudinal models, as well as scenarios featuring imperfect anticipation and nonlinear outcomes. Furthermore, the findings are illustrated through an analysis of an early retirement incentive program for teachers, which the target units were likely to anticipate, and its impact on student achievement. The empirical results highlight the risks of neglecting anticipation in policy evaluation.

To effectively serve users in millimeter-Wave (mmWave) networks, clustering is essential for determining beam count and orientation. Since user mobility necessitates maintaining current beam targeting, an online clustering approach is required. This mobility also creates fluctuating cluster patterns, causing dynamic traffic loads across beams, which in turn demands efficient resource allocation and beam management strategies to handle these changes. This study addresses the coexistence of Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication (URLLC) and enhanced Mobile BroadBand (eMBB) users in 5G mmWave environments by proposing a Quality-of-Service (QoS)-driven clustering and resource allocation framework. Specifically, the Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) algorithm is employed for online user clustering and beam selection, while an LSTM-based Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) method manages resource block allocation. The proposed approach is evaluated against a baseline utilizing K-means for clustering and priority-based proportional fairness for resource distribution. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme surpasses the baseline in latency, reliability, and throughput for both URLLC and eMBB users.

Problems involving multiple networks are common across numerous scientific and other fields. Specifically, network alignment—the task of identifying corresponding nodes across different networks—has broad applications in both social and natural sciences. Inspired by recent breakthroughs in node representation learning for single-graph tasks, we introduce REGAL (REpresentation learning-based Graph ALignment), a framework that utilizes automatically learned node representations to match nodes between different graphs. Within REGAL, we develop xNetMF, an elegant and principled node embedding formulation that uniquely extends to multi-network scenarios. Our findings demonstrate the effectiveness and potential of unsupervised, representation-learning-based network alignment regarding both speed and accuracy. REGAL achieves up to a 30x speedup in the representation learning phase compared to similar methods, improves average accuracy by 20% to 30% over existing network alignment techniques, and successfully scales to networks containing millions of nodes each.

For a fair coin flip, let $W = L_1L_2...L_N$ denote a binary sequence of length $N=2$ or $N=3$, where each $L_i$ is either Heads ($H$) or Tails ($T$). This paper derives second- and third-order linear recurrence relations along with their corresponding generating functions to analyze the probabilities $p_{W}(n)$ of observing the word $W$ for the first time after exactly $n$ coin tosses.

Open-domain conversational agents are gaining significant traction within the natural language processing field, yet enabling them to respond empathetically remains a major hurdle. Existing neural response generation techniques depend exclusively on end-to-end learning from vast conversation datasets, a strategy that often yields socially inappropriate replies due to insufficient high-quality training data. Conversely, recent studies highlight the potential of integrating dialogue act/intent modeling with neural response generation; this hybrid framework enhances response quality while increasing controllability and interpretability. A critical component of intent modeling is the creation of a comprehensive taxonomy. Drawing inspiration from this, we manually annotated 500 response intents based on a subset of a large empathetic dialogue corpus containing 25,000 dialogues, aiming to establish a large-scale taxonomy for empathetic responses. Additionally, leveraging lexical analysis and machine learning, we examined both speaker and listener utterances across the entire dataset, identifying response intents alongside 32 emotion categories. Finally, through information visualization, we summarized emotional dialogue exchange patterns and their temporal evolution. These findings uncover novel empathy dynamics inherent in human-human open-domain conversations, offering valuable heuristics for hybrid modeling approaches.

It is widely recognized that outliers emerge in the high-frequency region of the approximate spectrum for isogeometric analysis involving second-order elliptic operators. Recently, these outliers were successfully removed using a boundary penalty technique, which involves imposing additional conditions derived from the differential equation at the domain's boundary. This paper extends that concept to eliminate outliers within the superconvergent approximate spectrum of isogeometric analysis when employing optimally-blended quadrature rules. Numerical results demonstrate that the eigenvalue errors achieve a superconvergence rate of $h^{2p+2}$ and that the entire spectrum is free of outliers. Furthermore, the condition number and stiffness of the resulting algebraic system are substantially reduced. Several numerical examples illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

The development of preparation and analysis techniques for structured waves involving light, electrons, and atoms has progressed quickly. Although neutrons have established capabilities for material characterization and fundamental physics research, neutron science has struggled to adopt these methods because of limited transverse coherence lengths, inadequate spatial detector resolution, and low particle flux rates. In this work, we present methods compatible with current technology and demonstrate the successful experimental generation of neutron helical wavefronts possessing well-defined orbital angular momentum (OAM). Furthermore, we explore potential applications, including extensions to spin-orbit correlations and advanced material characterization approaches.
General considerations regarding the equivalence conjectures and an overview of several mathematical findings.

This article introduces an algorithmic framework designed to globally solve mixed optimization problems involving both continuous and categorical variables, where variable properties are drawn from a catalog. The approach accommodates catalogs of any size and properties of any dimension without requiring user modeling. Utilizing a tree search strategy akin to spatial branch and bound methods, the framework exhaustively explores the property ranges of categorical variables. It alternates between branching, constraint programming, and catalog lookup phases to eliminate inconsistent values, while a new catalog-based contractor ensures consistency between categorical properties and available catalog items. This yields an intuitive, exact, and easily implementable generic method, whose validity is demonstrated through a numerical example featuring a two-dimensional property space for a categorical variable.

We demonstrate that every closed, orientable surface $ S $ with negative Euler characteristic possesses a pair of finite-degree covers that are length isospectral over $ S $ but lack generic simple length isospectrality. Our approach begins by characterizing the conditions under which two finite-degree covers of a connected, orientable surface with negative Euler characteristic are isomorphic, specifically based on the curves that admit simple elevations. We also establish an effective version of this characterization, relaxing the requirements to include curves with explicitly bounded self-intersection numbers. Furthermore, we prove that for sufficiently large $ N $, the set of unmarked traces corresponding to simple closed curves in a generically selected representation into $ \mathrm{ SL }_{ N } \left( \mathbb{ R } \right) $ can distinguish between non-isomorphic pairs of covers. In the process, we construct hyperbolic surfaces $ X $ and $ Y $ that share the same complete unmarked length spectrum, yet for every integer $ k $, the sets of lengths associated with curves having at most $ k $ self-intersections are distinct.

Although violating the primordial null energy condition (NEC) is known to produce a blue-tilted gravitational wave background (GWB), its potential effects could be even more significant. We propose a scenario where, following an initial slow-roll inflation phase that respects the NEC (with Hubble parameter $H\simeq H_{inf1}$), the universe undergoes a period of NEC violation before entering a subsequent slow-roll inflation stage characterized by a much larger Hubble parameter ($H=H_{inf2}\gg H_{inf1}$). This model yields a primordial gravitational wave spectrum that remains nearly flat across both the cosmic microwave background scale and the frequency range $f\sim 1/{\rm yr}$, while exhibiting an amplitude consistent with recent NANOGrav observations. Furthermore, we note that in multi-stage inflation models where NEC violations occur intermittently, the stochastic GWB could develop a "Great Wall-like" spectral structure at the corresponding frequency bands.

Originating from the diffusion approximation of spiking neuron models, moment activation (MA) accurately models the nonlinear interactions of correlated neural variability. However, computing MA numerically is difficult because of numerous ill-conditioned Dawson-like functions. To address this, we derived asymptotic expansions for these functions, creating a robust and efficient numerical algorithm that calculates MA and its derivatives with high speed, accuracy, and reliability. Additionally, we present exact analytical solutions for MA under weak fluctuation conditions. Equipped with this efficient computational approach, MA becomes a powerful instrument for exploring the dynamics of correlated neural variability within large-scale spiking neural networks.

This paper details the findings from the NLP Community Metasurvey, conducted between May and June 2022. The survey gathered opinions on contentious topics such as industry influence, artificial general intelligence (AGI) concerns, and ethical considerations. Our findings quantify several debates: respondents are nearly evenly divided on the significance of AGI, whether language models truly comprehend language, and the necessity of linguistic structure and inductive bias for addressing NLP challenges. Furthermore, the survey included meta-questions asking participants to forecast the distribution of responses. This approach provides insight into the spectrum of beliefs among NLP researchers and reveals false sociological assumptions where community predictions diverge from actual outcomes. We identified such discrepancies across numerous issues. Specifically, the community significantly overestimates its confidence in the utility of benchmarks and the ability of scaling to resolve real-world problems, while underestimating its own conviction in the value of linguistic structure, inductive bias, and interdisciplinary research.

We examine the associated production of the CP-odd Higgs boson $A^0$ with a real photon $\gamma$ in $e^+e^-$ collisions. Given the coupling characteristics of $A^0$, the dominant contribution arises from top-quark triangle loop diagrams. We derive the timelike transition form factor that characterizes the $A^0$ production amplitude in these collisions. This timelike form factor is connected to the spacelike form factor pertinent to $A^0$ production in $e^-\gamma$ collisions. Furthermore, potential additional contributions from chargino-sneutrino and neutralino-selectron box diagrams are found to be negligible.

Recent years have seen significant advancements in causal inference and learning, with numerous methods developed to identify cause-effect pairs and determine causal directions in observational data. However, many of these approaches rely on simplifying assumptions, such as the absence of confounding, cycles, and selection bias, making bivariate causal discovery particularly challenging. Among the methods capable of addressing bivariate cases are those based on Additive Noise Models (ANMs). Despite their utility, the influence of varying noise levels on an ANM's ability to correctly identify causal direction has remained largely unexplored. This study addresses that gap through an empirical investigation focused on bivariate scenarios, where the objective is to determine whether variable X causes Y or vice versa given their joint distribution. Two specific techniques—Regression with Subsequent Independence Test and Identification using Conditional Variances—were evaluated across a comprehensive spectrum of ANMs. In these tests, additive noise levels were systematically varied from 1% to 10,000% relative to a fixed causal noise level. The experiments also incorporated diverse distribution types and both linear and non-linear ANMs. The findings indicate that these methods can fail to accurately capture the true causal direction at certain noise levels.

In today's information-driven society, personal data has emerged as a critical asset, fueling the growth of data markets that facilitate transactions between providers and consumers. However, these markets face significant privacy risks, necessitating protective measures that often compromise data utility. Consequently, an effective pricing mechanism for private data must account for privacy levels. This paper introduces a data federation model where data providers, typically holding less market power than consumers, unite into a coalition to trade data while simultaneously mitigating privacy threats through differential privacy. Furthermore, we propose a pricing technique for private data and a fair revenue-distribution mechanism tailored for this federation environment. The model incentivizes providers to collaborate with their federations, promoting a fair and efficient trading process. Experimental validation demonstrates that the proposed methods yield benefits for both data providers and consumers.

Investigating the existence of Hamiltonian cycles remains a fundamental issue in graph theory. By integrating toughness and spectral constraints, we re-examine Chvátal's conjecture, specifically asking for the spectral requirements that ensure a Hamiltonian cycle in $t$-tough graphs. We first address the case of 1-tough graphs: if the spectral radius $\rho(G)$ is at least $\rho(M_{n})$, then $G$ possesses a Hamiltonian cycle, unless $G$ is isomorphic to $M_{n}$, where $M_{n}=K_{1}\nabla K_{n-4}^{+3}$ and $K_{n-4}^{+3}$ denotes the graph formed by adding three independent edges between the sets $3K_{1}$ and $K_{n-4}$ in the disjoint union $3K_{1}\cup K_{n-4}$. While Brouwer's toughness theorem establishes that every connected $d$-regular graph satisfies $t(G)>\frac{d}{\lambda}-1$ (with $\lambda$ being the second largest absolute eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix), this paper extends the result spectrally. We provide specific spectral conditions for a graph to be 1-tough given a minimum degree $\delta$, as well as conditions for a graph to be $t$-tough.

The creation and dispersal of metals within the diffuse intergalactic medium (IGM) significantly impact galaxy formation theories and baryon (re)cycling mechanisms. Furthermore, the ratio of metal abundances in high versus low-ionization states is thought to reflect the Universe's reionization history. Yet, observations of IGM metallicity at redshifts around 4 remain scarce and inconsistent, while limited near-infrared sensitivity makes identifying individual metal absorbers extremely difficult. This study introduces a novel clustering method that detects these faint IGM absorbers by statistically averaging across all spectral pixels, specifically applied to the C IV forest. We simulate the IGM at z=4.5 using various models of inhomogeneous metal distribution and analyze the two-point correlation function (2PCF) via mock C IV forest skewers. The 2PCF reveals a distinct peak corresponding to the C IV doublet separation, with peak amplitude scaling quadratically with metallicity; enrichment morphology influences both the 2PCF's shape and magnitude. We also relate enrichment topology to metal mass- and volume-filling factors, illustrating their dependencies on topological variations. For models aligning with z~3 metal distributions, our approach constrains [C/H] to within 0.2 dex, log$\,M_{\rm{min}}$ to within 0.4 dex, and the filling factor $R$ to within 15%. Additionally, we demonstrate that strong absorbers from the circumgalactic medium can be readily identified and masked to isolate the underlying IGM signal. The auto-correlation of the metal-line forest offers a promising new method to precisely constrain both IGM metallicity and enrichment topology simultaneously at z>4, extending such measurements into the Epoch of Reionization.

We re-evaluate the gravitational capture of dark matter (DM) driven by long-range forces. We show that ignoring the thermal motion of target particles—an approximation often valid for short-range capture—leads to parametrically incorrect outcomes for long-range scenarios. When the scattering mediator's mass is negligible compared to the momentum transfer, accurately accounting for the thermal motion of target particles shifts the sensitivity to the mediator mass from logarithmic to quadratic, thereby significantly boosting the capture rate. We quantitatively analyze how this finite-temperature effect influences the DM population captured within the Sun across varying mediator masses. Our findings indicate that DM capture via light dark photons, such as in mirror DM models, can be dramatically enhanced, with self-capture reaching a geometric limit across much of the parameter space. While thermal corrections remain minor for visibly decaying dark photons within the Sun, they are likely crucial for understanding long-range DM capture in more massive objects like Population III stars. Furthermore, we present the first calculation of the long-range DM self-evaporation rate.

HEXME is a comprehensive dataset comprising tetrahedral meshes annotated with specific features, accompanied by a dedicated workflow for their creation. Its primary objective is to facilitate consistent and equitable assessment of hexahedral meshing algorithms and associated methods. These meshes were generated using Gmsh from 63 computer-aided design (CAD) models sourced from diverse databases. To underscore and categorize the diverse challenges inherent in hexahedral mesh generation, the CAD models are divided into three groups: simple, complex ("nasty"), and industrial. For every CAD model, three distinct types of tetrahedral meshes are provided. The process producing these 189 meshes is orchestrated via Snakemake, a contemporary workflow management system that enables a fully automated, scalable, and maintainable pipeline. Users can either download the entire dataset or select specific meshes through an online catalog. Anticipating advancements in hexahedral meshing techniques, the HEXME dataset was constructed with future evolution in mind. The HEXME workflow is publicly hosted on a GitHub repository, where external contributions and subsequent releases are welcomed and encouraged.

The Karlsruhe TRItium Neutrino experiment (KATRIN) is designed to determine the electron neutrino mass with a record-breaking sensitivity of 0.2 eV/c² by analyzing electrons from tritium beta decay. To manage the magnetic field within the main spectrometer, a mobile magnetic sensor unit was built and evaluated at the experiment's primary site. This unit travels along the inner rails of the low-field shaping coil support structures, which are positioned throughout the main spectrometer. Powered by a caterpillar drive, the device incorporates an electric motor, a battery pack, board electronics, two triaxial fluxgate sensors, and two inclination sensors. During operation, all pertinent data are recorded on board and subsequently transmitted to the master station once the unit reaches the docking station.

Utilizing the perturbative quantum chromodynamics (pQCD) framework alongside the quasi-two-body approximation, this study investigates the three-body decays of $B^{0}_{s} \rightarrow \psi(3686,3770)K\pi$. The analysis incorporates contributions from intermediate resonances including $\bar{K}^{*}_{0}(1430)^{0}$, $\bar{K}^{*}(892)^{0}$, $\bar{K}^{*}(1410)^{0}$, $\bar{K}^{*}(1680)^{0}$, and $\bar{K}^{*}_{2}(1430)^{0}$. We employed parameterized time-like form factors corresponding to the S, P, and D-wave distribution amplitudes of the $K\pi$ pair to model their interactions within the resonance region. Initially, the decays $B^{0}_{s} \rightarrow \psi(2S,1D)K^{-}\pi^{+}$ were calculated, followed by the determination of branching ratios for $B^{0}_{s} \rightarrow \psi(3686,3770)K^{-}\pi^{+}$ using the 2S-1D mixing scheme. Additionally, pQCD predictions for both $B^{0}_{s} \rightarrow \psi(2S,1D)K\pi$ and $B^{0}_{s} \rightarrow \psi(3686,3770)K\pi$ were derived using the narrow-width approximation via Clebsch-Gordan coefficients. Our results indicate that the $\bar{K}^{*}(892)^{0}$ resonance dominates the total decay, and the branching ratio and longitudinal polarization fraction for the $\psi(2S)\bar{K}^{*}(892)^{0}$ mode align well with existing experimental data within uncertainties. Furthermore, the theoretical predictions for $\psi(2S)$ and $\psi(3686)$ decay modes are nearly identical, suggesting they may be treated as the same meson state. Finally, the predicted pQCD branching ratios for $B^{0}_{s} \rightarrow \psi(3686,3770)K\pi$ are estimated to be in the range of $10^{-5}$ and $10^{-6}$, respectively, making them testable through ongoing experiments at LHCb and Belle II.

Model-based Reinforcement Learning (MBRL) utilizes a world model to approximate the true environment and derive an optimal policy, typically offering superior sample efficiency compared to model-free approaches. This study examines the robustness and generalization capabilities of controllers learned via MBRL when subjected to minor environmental perturbations. Drawing inspiration from the PILCO algorithm for probabilistic policy search, we demonstrate that constraining the likelihood noise within the Gaussian Process dynamics model acts as a regularizer for policy updates, resulting in more robust controllers. We validate the empirical advantages of this approach through a simulation benchmark.

Autoencoders typically employ an encoder to project data into a lower-dimensional latent space and a decoder to reconstruct the original data from that space. This architecture implicitly assumes the encoder approximates the decoder's inverse to ensure faithful bidirectional mapping, a process that can result in sub-optimal latent representations. In contrast, this study explores a decoder-only approach that utilizes gradient flow to encode samples directly into the latent space. By defining gradient flow relative to a specific decoder, we optimize the latent representation for each sample, thereby removing the reliance on approximate inversion via an encoder. We implement this gradient flow using Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) and the adjoint method to train the decoder. Our empirical results indicate that the computationally expensive integrals inherent to the adjoint method may be unnecessary. Furthermore, we introduce a second-order ODE variant that mimics Nesterov's accelerated gradient descent, achieving faster convergence per iteration. Since standard ODE solvers can be highly sensitive to integration step sizes due to ODE stiffness, we employ an adaptive solver that prioritizes loss minimization at each step. When evaluated against traditional autoencoding models, our proposed method, Gradient Flow Encoding (GFE), demonstrates significantly higher data efficiency, a critical advantage for applications constrained by limited data.

This study examines the early evolution of the Universe, focusing on preheating within the context of hybrid braneworld inflation by establishing constraints on the coupling constants $\lambda$ and $g$ to ensure the effective production of $\chi$-particles. By analyzing the epoch from when observable CMB scales crossed the horizon until the present, we express the reheating and preheating parameters—$N_{re}$, $T_{re}$, and $N_{pre}$—as functions of the scalar spectral index $n_{s}$. We demonstrate that, in contrast to reheating, the duration of preheating is independent of the equation of state parameter $\omega^{\ast}$. Applying the slow-roll approximation in the high-energy limit allows us to constrain the parameters of the D-term hybrid potential. Furthermore, we find that inflationary parameters, specifically the spectral index $n_{s}$, necessitate a bound of $\alpha \geq 1$ for the potential parameter $\alpha$ to align with $Planck$ data, whereas the tensor-to-scalar ratio $r$ remains consistent with observations for $\alpha \leq 1$ under high inflationary e-folds. We also propose investigating the impact of brane tension on the reheating temperature. Comparing our findings with recent CMB measurements, we analyze the preheating and reheating parameters in the Hybrid D-term inflation model for the range $0.8 \leq \alpha \leq 1.1$. Our results indicate that $T_{re}$ and $N_{re}$ require $\alpha \leq 1$, while compatibility with $Planck$ results for $N_{pre}$ demands the stricter condition $\alpha \leq 0.9$.

This paper presents the multi-layer quiver and demonstrates the construction of $(n+1)$-slice algebras of infinite type from an $n$-slice algebra of infinite type via bound quivers. Consequently, we construct these $(n+1)$-slice algebras both as matrix algebras and as tensor algebras over an $n$-slice algebra, establishing equivalences between their module categories and those of a diagram of a quiver of type $\widetilde{A}_{n+1}$.

This paper presents the first stable outcomes for predicting gender through eye movements, utilizing a dataset of facial images and a substantial cohort of 370 participants. For our purposes, stability encompasses two aspects: first, the ability to estimate the standard deviation (SD) of a single prediction experiment, which stands at approximately 4.1% and was determined by varying participant numbers; second, the capacity to report a mean accuracy with a minimal standard error (SEM). We achieved an accuracy of 65.2% with an SEM of 0.80% by repeatedly running experiments with randomly selected training and test sets. Our findings indicate that Random Forests and Logistic Regression are the top-performing classifiers. Furthermore, our results corroborate prior studies suggesting that females exhibit a bias toward the left eye of the stimuli.

Supervised machine learning models have been trained using diverse molecular descriptors to forecast infrared emission spectra of interstellar polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. This study demonstrates that feature importance analysis derived from the random forest algorithm can elucidate the physical relationships underlying specific emission features. By identifying shared molecular fragments responsible for distinct infrared bands, we analyzed astronomical correlations, thereby enhancing the current comprehension of long-standing spectral relationships. Furthermore, we introduce a method to quantify band correlations by assessing the similarity between feature importance arrays across different bands, resulting in a correlation map for emissions within the out-of-plane bending region. Finally, comparing predictions generated by various descriptor combinations highlights the robust predictive capability of extended-connectivity molecular fingerprints while indicating that integrating multiple descriptors of different types generally yields superior predictivity.

Acquiring time-lapse seismic data is a critical method for monitoring reservoir alterations caused by fluid injection, such as CO$_2$ injection. By conducting multiple surveys at identical locations, reservoir changes are identified through data comparison; however, this analysis can be distorted by near-surface seasonal velocity fluctuations, acquisition parameter inaccuracies, and inherent noise. A standard solution, known as cross-equalization, involves using non-changing data regions to create a matching filter applied across the entire dataset, including the reservoir. Similarly, we train a recurrent neural network on data excluding the reservoir area before inferring reservoir-related information. Unlike the matching filter, which relies on local information within a filter window, the recurrent neural network captures the temporal dependencies of the data. We validate this matching approach against conventional filters using various examples, beginning with trace matching, followed by testing on pre-stack 2D synthetic data. Furthermore, we assess improvements in the 4D signal by generating RTM images. Using normalized root mean square and predictability metrics to evaluate repeatability, our results demonstrate that this method outperforms the traditional matching filter in certain scenarios.

This study examines how incorporating author context influences the detection of textual sarcasm. We define author context as the embedded representations derived from a user's historical Twitter activity and propose neural architectures designed to extract these features. Our experiments utilize two tweet datasets: one annotated manually for sarcasm and another generated through tag-based distant supervision. While our approach achieves state-of-the-art results on the distant supervision dataset, it does not outperform existing methods on the manually labelled one, highlighting a distinction between sarcasm intended by the author (as captured by distant supervision) and sarcasm perceived by readers (as captured by manual labelling).

Langevin dynamics (LD) simulations have been employed to investigate the translocation dynamics of an active semi-flexible polymer entering a rigid two-dimensional circular cavity, along with the associated polymer packing behaviors. The findings indicate that the force exponent $\beta$, defined by the scaling relation $\langle \tau \rangle \propto F_{\textrm{sp}}^{\beta}$ (where $\langle \tau \rangle$ is the average translocation time and $F_{\textrm{sp}}$ is the self-propelling force), takes a value of $\beta = -1$ for small cavity radii ($R \ll R_{\textrm{g}}$). In contrast, for large cavity radii ($R \gg R_{\textrm{g}}$), the exponent approaches an asymptotic value of $\beta \approx -0.92$, with $R_{\textrm{g}}$ representing the gyration radius of the passive polymer in 2D free space. Furthermore, analysis using the turning number definition reveals that in the strong force limit and for small $R$, the polymer configuration at the conclusion of translocation is more regular compared to scenarios involving large $R$ or weak forces.

In holographic frameworks, reflected entropy corresponds to the area of the entanglement wedge cross section; we investigate this same duality within random tensor networks and confirm its validity. For a single random tensor, we examine crucial non-perturbative effects that smooth the discontinuity in reflected entropy across the Page transition. Summing these effects yields an analytical expression for the reflected entanglement spectrum, which aligns closely with numerical results. This approach suggests a method for the analytic continuation needed to compute reflected entropy and its Rényi extensions, addressing a previously noted issue with the order of limits. Applying this method to hyperbolic tensor networks produces results consistent with holographic predictions, revealing that random tensor networks possess the same non-trivial tripartite entanglement structure found in holographic states. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the reflected Rényi spectrum is non-flat, contrasting sharply with the typically flat Rényi spectra of such networks. We propose that the distinct contributions to the reflected entanglement spectrum can be organized into approximate superselection sectors, interpreted as an effective description of the canonically purified state as a superposition of different tensor network configurations. Each configuration arises from doubling and gluing various candidate entanglement wedges of the original network, with the superselection sectors labeled by the differing cross-sectional areas of these wedges.

This study presents the inaugural VLBA observations of 43 GHz v=1, J=1-0 SiO masers within the circumstellar envelope of the M-type semi-regular supergiant AH Sco, captured over two epochs spaced 12 days apart in March 2004. High-resolution VLBA imaging reveals that the SiO masers form a persistent elliptical ring with major and minor axes of approximately 18.5 and 15.8 mas, respectively, oriented at a position angle of 150°. Red-shifted masers are situated slightly nearer to the central star than their blue-shifted counterparts. The line-of-sight velocity structure indicates that features with higher velocities relative to the systemic velocity of -6.8 km/s are closer to the star, a pattern consistent with simple outflow or infall kinematics lacking rotational motion around AH Sco. Proper motion analysis of 59 matched features across the two epochs demonstrates that the SiO maser shell is contracting toward the star at a velocity of roughly 13 km/s. Given the distance to AH Sco of 2.26 kpc, our three-dimensional kinematic model suggests this inward motion is likely driven by the central star's gravity. Furthermore, the distance to AH Sco derived from the 3D model fitting, 2.26 ± 0.19 kpc, aligns well with its established kinematic distance of 2.0 kpc.

We present a quantum sensing approach for detecting dc magnetic fields that surpasses the sensitivity of standard $T_2^\ast$-limited magnetometry by over an order of magnitude. This achievement utilizes nitrogen-vacancy centers within a diamond rotated at frequencies comparable to the spin coherence time, with a detailed analysis of how magnetic sensitivity varies with rotation speed and measurement duration. The technique selectively up-converts the target dc field while maintaining the sensor's quantum coherence. These findings definitively enhance the sensitivity of quantum magnetometers to dc fields, offering a valuable addition to the quantum sensing toolkit.

We provide an exact solution for a class of fragmented Bose-Hubbard models, depicted as graphs where vertices represent condensates, utilizing the algebraic Bethe ansatz. Our findings demonstrate that these models share the same spectrum as a family of twisted models derived through a local U(1) gauge transformation.

We develop a systematic expansion method for solving the Fokker-Planck equation by extending the approach introduced in [J. Phys. A50, 325001 (2017)]. This framework yields a novel perturbative formula for calculating mean work, specifically designed for systems exhibiting eigenvalue degeneracy within the Fokker-Planck operator. The method facilitates an investigation into how geometrical symmetry influences the thermodynamic description of Brownian particles. To demonstrate the theory, we analyze the Fokker-Planck equation under a two-dimensional harmonic potential. We examine thermodynamic properties during both symmetric and asymmetric deformations of this potential; the former preserves rotational symmetry, while the latter breaks it. Optimal deformation paths are identified by minimizing the mean work. A comparison of these optimized processes reveals that the distinction between symmetric and asymmetric scenarios is most pronounced at a critical deformation time, which corresponds to the relaxation time of the Fokker-Planck equation. Furthermore, this critical time associated with mean work is found to be shorter than that for mean energy changes, a discrepancy attributed to hysteresis effects inherent in irreversible processes.

Clickbait articles frequently employ question-based or vague titles to lure readers into clicking for an explanation. We created a system to automatically extract the answer to these clickbait hooks directly from the article's text, sparing users the effort of reading through the content. This system fine-tunes both an extractive model (RoBERTa) and an abstractive one (T5) using datasets gathered from the 'StopClickbait' Facebook pages and Reddit's 'SavedYouAClick' subforum. Our results show that both models significantly improve after fine-tuning. While the extractive model achieves slightly higher ROUGE scores, the abstractive model performs marginally better in terms of BERT scores.

This paper posits that internal function sharing contributes to the degradation of out-of-distribution (o.o.d.) and systematic generalization in deep learning classification models. Under conditions of equivalent prediction, a model divides the input space into distinct regions demarcated by boundaries. Because function sharing favors the reuse of these boundaries, it results in fewer partitions for novel outputs, thereby creating a conflict with systematic generalization. We demonstrate this phenomenon across standard deep learning architectures, including fully connected, convolutional, residual networks, LSTMs, and (Vision) Transformers. We anticipate that this study offers fresh perspectives on systematic generalization and establishes a foundation for future research avenues.

This work surveys recent advancements in multiple polylogarithms, covering their associated Hopf algebra and symbol map, the formulation of single-valued variants, and an algorithm for determining fibration bases. We detail the implementation of these methods within the Mathematica package PolyLogTools, demonstrating its utility in analyzing the coproduct structure of polylogarithmic terms and calculating iterated parametric integrals relevant to low-loop-order Feynman integral computations.

Many practical scenarios involve choosing the optimal option from a limited set, where the best choice depends on specific contextual data. This study examines the contextual Ranking and Selection problem within a finite-alternative and finite-context framework, aiming to identify the superior alternative for every given context. We model the reward for each option using a distinct Gaussian process and derive the large deviations rate function for both the expected and worst-case probabilities of correct selection. We introduce the GP-C-OCBA sampling policy, which leverages the Gaussian process posterior to iteratively assign observations, thereby maximizing the rate function. We demonstrate its consistency and establish that it attains the optimal convergence rate under a non-informative prior assumption. Furthermore, numerical experiments indicate that our algorithm is highly competitive regarding sampling efficiency while incurring significantly lower computational costs.

DBSCAN* and HDBSCAN* are recognized density-based clustering methods; however, processing very large datasets is currently impractical, which restricts their application in real-world scenarios. By leveraging the geometry of Euclidean space, we demonstrate that DBSCAN* and HDBSCAN* clusters for a finite set $X \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ can be systematically constructed from carefully selected subsets of $X$. Since the size of these subsets is controllable, our findings enable the clustering of massive datasets. To validate this theoretical approach, we successfully clustered the Microsoft Building Footprint Database of the US, a task that standard implementations cannot handle.

Myasnikov et al. previously established that the knapsack problem is solvable in $\mathsf{NP}$ for graph groups, extending their earlier work on the problem for arbitrary finitely generated groups. This paper determines the precise computational complexity of the knapsack problem across all graph groups. Specifically, the problem is $\mathsf{TC}^0$-complete for complete graphs, $\mathsf{LogCFL}$-complete for non-complete transitive forests, and $\mathsf{NP}$-complete for all other graph groups.

We describe the recent enhancements to the TwinSol radioactive nuclear beam (RNB) facility at the University of Notre Dame. The upgraded TriSol system features an additional magnetic dipole to establish a second beamline and a third solenoid designed to minimize the radioactive beam's footprint on the target.

Using proton-proton collision data with an integrated luminosity of 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ gathered by the ATLAS detector at the LHC during 2015 and 2016 at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, inclusive and differential cross-sections for top-quark pair production accompanied by a photon have been measured. These analyses focus on single-lepton and dilepton final states within a defined fiducial region. Event selection criteria require exactly one photon, one or two leptons, a variable minimum number of jets depending on the channel, and at least one $b$-jet. Neural network techniques were employed to distinguish signal events from backgrounds. The resulting fiducial cross-sections are 521 $\pm$ 9(stat.) $\pm$ 41(sys.) fb for the single-lepton channel and 69 $\pm$ 3(stat.) $\pm$ 4(sys.) fb for the dilepton channel. Differential cross-sections were determined as functions of photon transverse momentum, photon absolute pseudorapidity, and the angular separation between the photon and the nearest lepton in both channels, as well as the azimuthal opening angle and absolute pseudorapidity difference between the two leptons in the dilepton channel. All findings align with theoretical predictions.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has become the leading machine translation technology today due to its end-to-end trainable flexibility; however, it continues to face difficulties in low-resource scenarios, particularly with distant language pairs. A potential solution involves leveraging available information from other modalities. This approach relies on the premise that although languages differ, speakers of both the source and target languages perceive the same visual content, meaning their visual representations align, which can aid the system. Integrating multimodal data allows NMT to enhance translation quality by resolving ambiguities regarding specific phrases or words. In this context, we participated in the English-Hindi multimodal translation task at the 8th Workshop on Asian Translation (WAT - 2021), achieving BLEU scores of 42.47 for the Evaluation subset and 37.50 for the Challenge subset.

Adversarial training enhances the robustness of deep neural networks by incorporating adversarial examples into the learning process. However, current approaches for creating NLP adversarial examples rely on costly sentence encoders and combinatorial search, making it difficult to apply vanilla adversarial training effectively to NLP models, leaving their potential benefits largely unexplored. To address this, we introduce Attacking to Training (A2T), a streamlined and enhanced vanilla adversarial training framework for NLP. A2T centers on a novel, cost-effective word substitution attack tailored specifically for vanilla training. We evaluated A2T by training BERT and RoBERTa models across the IMDB, Rotten Tomatoes, Yelp, and SNLI datasets. Empirical findings indicate that robust NLP models can be achieved using a significantly cheaper adversary. We demonstrate that vanilla adversarial training augmented with A2T not only boosts robustness against the specific attack used during training but also provides defense against various other word substitution attacks. Additionally, A2T improves standard accuracy, cross-domain generalization, and model interpretability. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/QData/Textattack-A2T.

At the high collision energies reached at the LHC, hard processes calculable via perturbative QCD become increasingly significant; however, particle production remains primarily driven by soft QCD interactions involving momentum transfers of a few GeV. These non-perturbative phenomena pose challenges to theoretical models and are addressed through phenomenological approaches. The ALICE collaboration has measured various observables targeting soft QCD across Run 1 and 2, including proton-proton and proton-lead collisions. These proceedings will present a selection of such results, emphasizing model comparisons and summarizing our understanding of soft QCD following nearly eight years of data collection.

Let $\mathcal{D}=\left(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{B} \right)$ denote a symmetric $2$-$(v,k,\lambda )$ design that possesses a flag-transitive, point-imprimitive automorphism group $G$ leaving a non-trivial partition $\Sigma$ of $\mathcal{P}$ invariant. According to Praeger and Zhou \cite{PZ}, there exists a constant $k_{0}$ such that for every block $B \in \mathcal{B}$ and partition set $\Delta \in \Sigma$, the intersection size $\left\vert B \cap \Delta \right \vert$ takes only the values $0$ or $k_{0}$. In this paper, we demonstrate that under the conditions $k>\lambda \left(\lambda-3 \right)/2$ and $k_{0} \geq 3$, the design $\mathcal{D}$ must be isomorphic to one of the established flag-transitive, point-imprimitive symmetric $2$-designs with parameters $(45,12,3)$ or $(96,20,4)$.

Identifying content, services, and applications within network traffic remains a significant area of research for network control systems. Although contemporary firewalls can decrypt packets, this approach conflicts with privacy concerns, making the identification of information within encrypted traffic a difficult challenge. Despite this, prior studies have demonstrated that machine learning can facilitate service and application detection. This process typically entails extracting high-level features from network packet data and training a robust classifier for traffic identification. We introduce a classification method utilizing an ensemble of deep learning architectures applied to packet data, payload content, and inter-arrival time sequences. To our knowledge, this marks the first application of such deep learning architectures to the Server Name Indication (SNI) classification problem. Our ensemble model outperforms existing state-of-the-art machine learning techniques, and the updated model is available on GitHub at: \url{https://github.com/niloofarbayat/NetworkClassification}.

This work investigates the performance and computational complexity of sequential decoding for polarization-adjusted convolutional (PAC) codes. Specifically, it provides a comparative analysis of PAC code performance and complexity against both 5G polar codes and conventional convolutional codes. Additionally, a novel approach for establishing bounds on the complexity of sequentially decoding PAC codes is introduced.

Network communication challenges such as coded caching and distributed computation are closely interconnected. While centralized coded caching aims to alleviate network congestion during peak periods in wireless systems, coded distributed computation investigates the trade-off between communication and computation in distributed environments. Inspired by research on rainbow $3$-term arithmetic progressions, this paper introduces a unified framework for constructing coded caching schemes. Leveraging the flexibility in selecting families and operations, this framework establishes connections between coded caching and various combinatorial structures. We demonstrate that any scheme derived from a placement delivery array (PDA) can be modeled as a rainbow scheme within this framework, and it encompasses numerous other established schemes. Furthermore, we introduce a novel coded caching scheme that achieves linear subpacketization and a near-constant rate by utilizing the only rainbow $3$-term arithmetic progressions set. Subsequently, we adapt the framework for distributed computing applications. We propose a new transmission strategy for the shuffle phase, demonstrating that in specific scenarios, it yields a lower communication load compared to schemes based on PDAs or resolvable designs with an equivalent number of files.

Let $H$ denote the standard Hadamard matrix of order two, and define $K = 2^{-1/2}H$. It is established that the complete weight enumerator $W$ of a binary self-dual code with length $n$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 1 for the Kronecker power $K^{[n]}$. For each integer $t$ within the range $[0, n]$, we define the $t$-th order derivative $W_{<t>}$ such that it resides in the eigenspace corresponding to eigenvalue 1 of the matrix $K^{[n-t]}$. While $W_{<0>} = W$ fully characterizes the code, higher-order derivatives like $W_{<t>}$ for large $t$ offer reduced code information but result in shorter lengths. We calculate the $(n-5)$-th derivative for the extended Golay code (length 24), the extended quadratic residue code (length 48), and the conjectured $[72,24,12]$ code, demonstrating that all three lie within the eigenspace of 1 for $K^{[5]}$. Utilizing these derivatives, we derive a novel balance equation concerning the count of codewords of specific weights containing a 1 at a chosen coordinate. As an application, we employ this equation to rule out certain candidates for weight enumerators of binary self-dual codes of length eight.

Recent advancements in the field prompt a re-assessment of how local-type non-Gaussianity influences the abundance of primordial black holes (PBHs), which in turn affects constraints on the primordial power spectrum. By applying peaks theory to the full non-linear compaction, we find that while the qualitative impact of non-Gaussianity remains consistent with prior studies, its magnitude is substantially reduced. Specifically, the local non-Gaussianity parameters $f_\mathrm{NL}^\mathrm{local}$ and $g_\mathrm{NL}^\mathrm{local}$ must be roughly one to two orders of magnitude larger than previously estimated to produce equivalent effects. This discovery weakens the dependence of PBH constraints on non-Gaussianity parameters and significantly relaxes the limits placed on these parameters (and/or PBH abundance) derived from the non-detection of dark matter isocurvature modes. Furthermore, our analysis of the correlation between curvature perturbation $\zeta$ and compaction $C$ reveals that while PBHs can form at rare peaks in $C$, these do not necessarily align with rare peaks in $\zeta$, thereby casting doubt on numerous existing calculations of PBH abundance.

Despite their immense capacity, very large deep learning models trained via gradient descent are surprisingly robust against memorization, yet paradoxically capable of fitting extensive datasets containing only noise. This work introduces techniques to train such models to memorize data that they would otherwise generalize. Our findings indicate that memorization is inherently more challenging than generalization, but the presence of noise facilitates memorization. Furthermore, expanding the dataset size amplifies the dataset's specific characteristics: while access to more samples simplifies overfitting on random data, it complicates it somewhat for natural images. Theoretically, we explore the deep learning bias toward generalization, demonstrating that it arises because gradient descent drives model parameters toward regions of maximal stability relative to the inputs.

The LUXE experiment is designed to investigate high-field QED phenomena through interactions between electrons, lasers, and photons, utilizing a 16.5 GeV electron beam from the European XFEL and a laser capable of up to 350 TW power. The study will focus on measuring electron and photon spectra in non-linear Compton scattering, with anticipated production rates exceeding $10^9$ events per 1 Hz bunch crossing. Simultaneously, the experiment will detect positrons generated via pair creation in either the two-step trident or Breit-Wheeler processes, expecting rates between $10^{-3}$ and $10^3$ per bunch crossing based on laser power and focal conditions. These measurements must be conducted amidst significant low-energy radiation backgrounds. To address these challenges, the setup employs Cherenkov detectors, scintillator screens, sapphire sensors, and lead-glass monitors for backscattering analysis. Positron spectra will be captured using a four-layer silicon-pixel tracker and a compact tungsten electromagnetic calorimeter equipped with GaAs sensors. The presentation will detail the experimental layout and its projected performance under such harsh radiation environments.

This paper presents recent findings from the Pierre Auger Collaboration, including measurements of the cosmic ray energy spectrum across a broad energy range ($10^{17.5}$ to beyond $10^{20}$ eV). It also details studies on cosmic-ray mass composition using the Observatory's fluorescence and surface detectors, along with observations of large-scale anisotropy in arrival directions above $8 \times 10^{18}$ eV and indications of anisotropy at intermediate angular scales above $4 \times 10^{19}$ eV. The discussion covers the astrophysical implications of these spectral and compositional results and concludes with an overview of the progress made in upgrading the Observatory to AugerPrime.

Blockchain-based Distributed Ledgers (DLs) offer the potential to democratize the financial sector, having found diverse applications in banking and real estate over the last ten years.
