Both methods were calibrated using genuine gravitational-wave events from the initial three observing runs of the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration—GW1501914, GW151226, GW170817, and GW190521—which represent diverse compact binary coalescence types. Our analysis reveals that the iterative rROF algorithm, when integrated into the cWB pipeline, successfully removes noise while maintaining the integrity of the waveform signals. As a result, the combined approach produces higher signal-to-noise ratios compared to the cWB pipeline operating without the rROF denoising step. Thus, incorporating the iterative rROF algorithm could enhance the pipeline's detectability and improve the inference of source characteristics.

This study examines a framework featuring general regressors and unobserved factors, proposing an estimator derived from iterated principal components. This method is demonstrated to be asymptotically normal and oracle efficient; furthermore, under specific conditions, it eliminates the common asymptotic incidental parameters bias. Notably, the requirements for achieving unbiasedness relax as factor trends intensify, meaning that sufficiently strong trending renders unbiasedness cost-free. Crucially, the approach requires no prior knowledge of the number of factors, their nature (deterministic versus stochastic), the integration order of the factors, or the integration order of the regressors. Consequently, there is no necessity to conduct pre-tests for unit roots or determine which deterministic terms to incorporate into the model.

Simulation platforms offer an abstract approach to mastering driving maneuvers such as lane changes, parking, and navigating intersections. However, these environments typically limit vehicle interactions to conservative behaviors, failing to replicate the high-risk situations encountered in real-world driving where other drivers may act unpredictably due to fatigue or inexperience. Since current simulations often neglect this variability during the training of navigation agents, this study focuses on systematically generating risk-prone scenarios characterized by heavy traffic and erratic driver actions to enhance model-free learning agents. We created multiple autonomous driving scenarios by developing custom iterations of the Markov Decision Process (MDP) within the highway-env simulation package. Using deep reinforcement learning, we trained agents to develop behavior policies capable of managing collisions and responding to randomized, risky driving patterns. By training these model-free agents with data from these hazardous scenarios and comparing their results against baseline agents, we aim to evaluate the impact of incorporating such perturbations into the training process. This analysis seeks to quantify the performance improvements gained from learning within these challenging environments.

To address the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, researchers are developing new strategies to forecast outbreak trends, aiming to mitigate or halt the spread. Traditional epidemiological models, such as the Susceptible-Infected-Recovered (SIR) framework and its derivatives, offer valuable insights into pandemic dynamics to inform control decisions; however, their reliance on mathematical assumptions often limits their accuracy in predicting real-world scenarios. Consequently, machine learning techniques are increasingly employed to analyze the complex patterns of virus transmission. This study introduces recurrent and convolutional neural network architectures—including vanilla LSTM, stacked LSTM, ED-LSTM, Bi-LSTM, CNN, and a hybrid CNN+LSTM model—to capture the intricate trends of the outbreak and forecast daily confirmed cases for the next 7, 14, and 21 days across India and four highly impacted states (Maharashtra, Kerala, Karnataka, and Tamil Nadu). Using Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) and Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) on testing data, the study evaluates the relative performance of these models. The findings indicate that the stacked LSTM and hybrid CNN+LSTM models outperformed the others.

Learning continuously with an expanding set of classes poses significant challenges, particularly when each instance appears only once, necessitating online learning. Traditional approaches relying on standard parameter optimization often fail in these scenarios or suffer from drawbacks such as non-differentiable elements or the need for memory buffers. To address this, we introduce a fully differentiable ensemble framework that enables efficient, end-to-end training of neural network ensembles. This method achieves state-of-the-art results without requiring a memory buffer and surpasses existing reference techniques. Furthermore, our experiments reveal a substantial performance boost for small ensembles, demonstrating that high classification accuracy can be attained even with a reduced number of classifiers.

Nanophononics offers the promise of information transfer similar to its photonic and electronic analogues, yet its implementation has been hindered by challenges in generating, manipulating, and detecting phonons, particularly at GHz frequencies. Current methods typically rely on piezoelectric materials driven by external radiofrequency sources, which are difficult to integrate with standard CMOS infrastructure, while non-piezoelectric approaches have suffered from low efficiency. This study investigates the optomechanical creation of coherent phonons within a suspended 2D silicon phononic crystal cavity featuring a guided mode near 6.8 GHz. By integrating an air-slot into the cavity, we convert the phononic waveguide into an optomechanical system that utilizes localized photonic modes arising from natural fabrication defects to transduce mechanical energy. This platform enables precise optical control over phonons and achieves coherent, self-sustained phonon generation through mechanical lasing at approximately 6.8 GHz. The capacity to produce high-frequency coherent mechanical oscillations in this straightforward, 2D CMOS-compatible architecture may represent a foundational step toward developing sources for phononic circuits and the coherent manipulation of various solid-state properties.

Identifying concealed common patterns within dynamic processes could revolutionize various research fields. This study introduces the Mapper-Coach network, a two-module feedforward neural architecture designed to extract hidden shared dynamics from time series. Using this method, we reconstructed an unobserved, continuous latent variable driving a chaotic logistic map by analyzing data from two simultaneously forced chaotic logistic maps. The network was trained via error-back propagation to forecast one observed time series based on its own history and the other observed series. We demonstrated that once the prediction task was mastered, the activity of the bottleneck neuron linking the mapper and coach modules exhibited a strong correlation with the latent shared input. Consequently, this approach offers a promising tool for uncovering hidden components in dynamical systems where direct experimental intervention is impossible.

We examine model-free multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) within environments characterized by off-beat actions, where every action possesses a fixed execution duration. During these durations, environmental changes are affected by but not synchronized with the action execution, a scenario common in numerous real-world applications. However, most existing MARL approaches assume immediate action execution following inference, an assumption that is frequently unrealistic and can result in catastrophic coordination failures when dealing with off-beat actions. To address this gap, we introduce an algorithmic framework for MARL designed specifically for off-beat actions. Furthermore, we propose LeGEM, a novel episodic memory mechanism for model-free MARL algorithms. LeGEM constructs agents' episodic memories by leveraging their individual experiences. It enhances multi-agent learning by tackling the challenging temporal credit assignment problem induced by off-beat actions through a new reward redistribution scheme, thereby mitigating issues related to non-Markovian rewards. We evaluate LeGEM across various multi-agent scenarios involving off-beat actions, including the Stag-Hunter Game, Quarry Game, Afforestation Game, and StarCraft II micromanagement tasks. Empirical findings demonstrate that LeGEM substantially improves multi-agent coordination, achieving state-of-the-art performance and superior sample efficiency.

The capacity of cells to restructure themselves in reaction to external cues is vital across fields such as tissue engineering and morphogenesis. While steric interactions can cause elongated cells to align locally, we demonstrate that anisotropy at the molecular level of the substrate can guide cell arrangement, leading to nematic order at the tissue scale. To rigorously study the transition from disorder to order, we created a high-throughput imaging system capable of tracking velocity and orientational correlations across thousands of cells over extended periods. We found that the formation of global, long-ranged order is driven by increased cell division along the substrate's nematic axis and the resulting extensile stresses, which remodel the cells' actomyosin networks. This research, linking cellular behavior to active dry nematics, offers new insights into how weakly interacting cell collectives remodel and organize. Furthermore, it facilitates data-driven identification of cell-cell interactions and suggests novel approaches for tissue engineering.

Biomedical entity linking involves mapping biomedical mentions, such as diseases and drugs, to standard entities within a specific knowledge base. A key challenge in this field is that a single entity often has numerous names, including synonyms, morphological variations, and different word orderings. Recently, BERT-based approaches have improved performance by providing rich representations of word sequences; however, their hundreds of millions of parameters and high computational demands restrict their use in resource-constrained settings. We introduce a lightweight neural approach for biomedical entity linking that requires only a fraction of the parameters and significantly fewer computing resources compared to BERT models. By employing a simple alignment layer with attention mechanisms to capture discrepancies between mention and entity names, our method demonstrates competitiveness with prior work on standard evaluation benchmarks.

The study examined low-energy dipole (LED) excitations in $^{20}$O using deformation($\beta$)-constraint antisymmetrized molecular dynamics combined with the generator coordinate method, applied via variation after $K$-projection. Two LED states were identified: the $1_1^-$ state, featuring a toroidal dipole (TD) mode with vortical nuclear current arising from a single-proton excitation on a weakly deformed structure, and the $1_2^-$ state, exhibiting a parity-asymmetric normal deformation linked to a low-energy $E1$ mode driven by surface neutron oscillations along a prolate shape. While the TD and $E1$ modes correspond to distinct $K^\pi$ components ($1^-$ and $0^-$, respectively) in deformed states, they couple within the $1_1^-$ and $1_2^-$ states of $^{20}$O due to $K$-mixing and shape fluctuations. Consequently, the transition strengths for both TD and $E1$ modes are distributed across these two states. Additionally, bands with cluster structures possessing $K^\pi=0^+$, $0^-$, and $1^-$ configurations were identified in the energy range above the LED states.

This paper addresses the design of a two-arm superiority cluster randomised controlled trial (RCT) featuring a continuous outcome, focusing on Bayesian inference via a linear mixed-effects model. Treatment efficacy is evaluated against a control group by examining the posterior distribution of the treatment effect. We formulate an assurance metric to determine sample size and evaluate it using a two-loop Monte Carlo sampling method. Our assessment investigates the impact of various prior distribution forms and the requisite number of Monte Carlo samples within both loops to ensure accurate assurance and sample size estimation, offering practical guidance on these parameters. We apply this methodology to determine sample size for a cluster RCT addressing post-stroke incontinence, comparing the results against traditional power calculations and assurance derived from Wald tests. Ultimately, the Bayesian design and analysis framework presented here demonstrates advantages, including greater robustness of the selected sample size to parameter mis-specification and the potential for reduced sample sizes when prior evidence suggests the treatment effect exceeds the minimal clinically important difference.

This paper establishes a robust uniqueness theorem for the Ricci flow on Euclidean space under specific constraints. Consider a Ricci flow solution $(\R^n,g_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$ with $n\geq 3$, where the initial metric $g_0$ is the standard Euclidean metric $g_E$. If either (1) $g_t$ remains uniformly lower equivalent to a fixed complete metric, or (2) $g_t$ adheres to a logarithmic lower bound on Ricci curvature, then it follows that $g_t$ is identical to $g_E$ for all $t\in[0,T]$. This result provides a partial resolution to a question posed by B-L.~Chen.

We demonstrate that summing the $n$th derivative of the Riemann zeta function over its non-trivial zeros yields a real value that is positive or negative on average when $n$ is odd or even, respectively. This result is established by providing a complete asymptotic expansion for these sums.

R-symmetry results in a unique SUSY framework characterized by a substantially altered colored sector, containing a Dirac gluino and a scalar color octet (sgluon). This work examines the effects of R-symmetry on squark production at the 13 TeV LHC. We analyze total cross sections and their next-to-leading order (NLO) corrections arising from all strongly interacting particles, investigating their reliance on the masses of the Dirac gluino and sgluon, as well as their systematic uncertainties for specific benchmark scenarios. Our findings indicate that while tree-level cross sections in the R-symmetric model are lower than those in the MSSM, the NLO K-factors are typically higher, ranging from ten to twenty percent. Additionally, we derive the necessary DREG $\to$ DRED transition counterterms and relevant on-shell renormalization constants. Real corrections are handled via the FKS subtraction method, with results validated against an independent calculation using the two-cut phase space slicing technique.

Although detailed chemical analyses of M dwarfs are limited, they are essential for understanding the formation environments and internal structures of their planetary systems. This study presents elemental abundances for 13 mid-to-late M dwarfs (2900 < Teff < 3500 K) identified through the Subaru/IRD planet search project. Utilizing high-resolution (~70,000) near-infrared spectra (970–1750 nm), we measured the abundances of Na, Mg, Si, K, Ca, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, and Sr via line-by-line analysis based on model atmospheres, achieving typical uncertainties between 0.2 dex for [Fe/H] and 0.3–0.4 dex for other elements. By combining radial velocities derived from these spectra with Gaia astrometry, we calculated Galactocentric space velocities (UVW). The resulting [Fe/H] values align with prior medium-resolution K-band estimates, revealing a broad metallicity range (-0.6 < [Fe/H] < +0.4). Individual element ratios [X/Fe] generally match solar values across all targets. While the [X/Fe] distributions resemble those of nearby FGK stars—mostly thin disk members—the most metal-poor target, GJ 699, may belong to the thick disk, a conclusion supported by its UVW velocities. These findings suggest that near-infrared spectra from M dwarf planet searches can effectively reveal trends in elemental abundances and Galactic stellar populations among nearby M dwarfs.

This study explores spherically symmetric wormhole solutions under tidal forces, utilizing techniques such as test particle orbital dynamics, ray-tracing, and microlensing. Theoretical predictions regarding test particle motion around tidal wormholes are derived using an effective potential normalized by $\mathcal{L}^2$. To generate ray-tracing images for both thin and thick accretion disks and relativistic jets, the open-source $\texttt{GYOTO}$ code was adapted with a Python interface. These methods were employed to investigate accretion flows near Schwarzschild-like and charged Reissner-Nordström (RS) wormholes, including the Damour-Solodukhin (DS) case where electromagnetic charge vanishes. Results indicate that the photon sphere exists for both disk types in Schwarzschild-like wormholes, even with zero tidal forces; however, as $\alpha \to \infty$, the radius $r_{\mathrm{ph}}$ approaches infinity, implying $\alpha$ must be small and positive to align with EHT data. Conversely, for RS wormholes, the photon sphere radius diminishes as $\Lambda \to \infty$, consistent with effective potential predictions. Beyond accretion disks, relativistic jets were also analyzed for both solutions. Furthermore, star bulge microlensing was used to estimate the wormhole shadow radius: for the Schild wormhole, $R_{\mathrm{Sh}}\approx r_0$ in the ZTF limit but increases linearly with $\alpha$, whereas the shadow radius of charged wormholes gradually decreases as the DS parameter $\Lambda$ grows.

The DART mission is scheduled to impact Dimorphos, the secondary body of the Didymos system, at the conclusion of 2022, thereby altering its orbital period. While most prior numerical simulations have simplified the DART spacecraft as a spherical projectile to model this event, this study investigates how alternative, simplified geometries influence the impact outcome. Utilizing the iSALE shock physics code in both two and three dimensions, we modeled vertical impacts of projectiles with mass and velocity matching the nominal DART parameters into porous basalt targets. Our findings indicate that the simple geometries examined here exert minimal influence on crater morphology and momentum enhancement. Specifically, two-dimensional projectile shapes with comparable impact surface areas alter crater radius and volume by less than 5%. In contrast, a more extreme three-dimensional geometry (a rod) produced an elliptical crater that was 50% shallower than one created by a spherical projectile of equivalent momentum. The momentum enhancement factor, or beta, remained within 7% for the 2D simulations and within 10% for the 3D simulations relative to the uniform spherical baseline. The most significant impact of projectile geometry appears in the ejection velocity as a function of launch position and angle for fast ejecta within the "coupling zone." These results are intended to guide the analysis of the ejecta cone by the LICIACube.

We frame stochastic thermodynamics as a statistical inference theory applied to experimentally recorded fluctuating time-series. In support of this, we present a general framework to quantify knowledge regarding a system's dynamical state across two distinct scales: a fine-grained, deterministic microscopic level and a coarse-grained, stochastic mesoscopic level. For generic model dynamics, we demonstrate that the mathematical expressions for fluctuating entropy changes central to Markovian stochastic thermodynamics arise naturally from this approach. Our conceptual contributions aim to (i) bridge entropy production and its fluctuation relations between deterministic and stochastic systems, and (ii) offer a complementary information-theoretic perspective on the concepts of entropy and entropy production within stochastic thermodynamics.

Rapid advancements in radio astronomy are revealing new avenues for investigating Dark Matter (DM) properties. The recent direct imaging of the supermassive black hole (SMBH) at the center of the M87 radio galaxy by the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) collaboration offers a promising method to search for new physics. This study demonstrates that such observations can detect synchrotron radiation signatures generated by DM annihilation within the SMBH's innermost region. Assuming a DM density spike profile, we calculate the flux density resulting from DM-annihilation-induced electrons and positrons and establish new constraints on the DM annihilation cross section by comparing these values with the EHT's integral flux density at 230 GHz. Our findings indicate that the parameter space accessible through EHT observations is largely complementary to other experiments. Specifically, for Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs), EHT data under the density spike assumption can exclude annihilation cross sections several orders of magnitude below the thermal production level. Future EHT observations could further enhance sensitivity in DM searches and offer a unique opportunity to examine the interactions between DM and SMBHs.

The Standard Model (SM) of particle physics, which integrates Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) and the unified electro-weak (EW) theories, successfully accounts for nearly all experimental findings in the micro-world and has correctly predicted the existence of previously unknown particles, most famously the Higgs scalar boson. Consequently, the SM is widely recognized as the definitive framework for fundamental particles and their interactions. Despite these achievements, the model faces significant limitations: it relies on numerous free parameters determined by experiment, fails to explain the universe's matter-antimatter asymmetry, and offers no account for gravity, dark matter, neutrino masses, or the specific number of particle generations. These gaps motivate the search for new physics beyond the Standard Model (BSM). Although BESIII operates at center-of-mass energies well below the frontier, identifying BSM phenomena remains a vital part of its mission. This paper outlines BESIII's strategies for detecting BSM signatures, including measuring rates of processes that are forbidden or highly suppressed in the SM, searching for exotic particles like dark photons, conducting precision tests of SM predictions, and investigating violations of $C$ and $CP$ symmetries in processes where the SM predicts negligible effects.

Although various pretrained Transformer-based language models have proven effective for text-driven brain encoding, current research has largely overlooked the potential of task-specific learned representations. This study investigates transfer learning from ten popular NLP tasks (comprising two syntactic and eight semantic tasks) to predict neural responses across two distinct datasets: Pereira, involving subjects reading sentences, and Narratives, involving subjects listening to spoken stories. By utilizing encoding models based on these task features to predict activity throughout the brain, we found that features derived from coreference resolution, named entity recognition (NER), and shallow syntax parsing account for greater variance in reading-related activity. Conversely, for listening-related activity, tasks such as paraphrase generation, summarization, and natural language inference demonstrated superior encoding performance. Across all ten task representations, the experiments yield three key cognitive insights: (i) the left hemisphere exhibits higher predictive brain activity compared to the right; (ii) the posterior medial cortex, temporo-parieto-occipital junction, and dorsal frontal lobe show stronger correlations than early auditory and auditory association cortices; and (iii) syntactic and semantic tasks respectively achieve robust predictive performance for reading and listening stimuli across various brain regions.

Reduced order models (ROMs) have served as a cornerstone of theoretical fluid mechanics for more than a hundred years. Early iterations included Galerkin models derived from the Orr-Sommerfeld stability equation and various vortex representations, notably the von K\'arm\'an vortex street. Later developments typically adhered to first principles, employing mathematical Galerkin approaches, weakly nonlinear stability theory, and two- and three-dimensional vortex frameworks. The field shifted with Aubry et al.'s [N. Aubry, P. Holmes, J. Lumley, and E. Stone, Journal of Fluid Mechanics, 192, 115-173 (1988)] introduction of data-driven proper orthogonal decomposition (POD). Initially, POD utilized available data to generate an optimal basis for classical Galerkin procedures. However, data's influence on ROMs extends far beyond this expansion technique. This paper demonstrates the transformative role of data-driven modeling within a key ROM domain: closures. These are correction terms appended to classical ROMs to account for discarded modes in under-resolved simulations. Using straightforward examples, we outline the principles behind classical ROMs, introduce modern ROM closures, and highlight how data-driven methods, artificial intelligence, and machine learning have reshaped standard ROM practices over the past twenty years. Finally, we present a vision for how advanced data-driven modeling will continue to redefine the field of reduced order modeling.

In deep learning, neural networks function as noisy conduits linking input data to its representations, a viewpoint that inherently connects the field to the quest for constructing information channels with peak transmission and representation efficiency. Although significant research focuses on optimizing network parameters to achieve optimal channel characteristics, this study investigates an often-neglected avenue: initializing neural networks to approximate optimal channels. Our theory, supported by experimental evidence, uncovers the fundamental mechanisms behind this phenomenon and reveals intrinsic links between statistical physics and deep learning. Contrary to conventional theories relying on the classic mean-field approximation to characterize neural networks as information channels, we provide analytic proof that this widely used simplification is invalid in this context. To address this limitation, we introduce a corrected mean-field framework capable of describing the limiting behaviors of information propagation without imposing strong assumptions on inputs. Leveraging this framework, we propose an analytic theory demonstrating that mutual information maximization between inputs and propagated signals occurs when neural networks are initialized at dynamic isometry—a state characterized by norm-preserving mappings. Experiments on real neural networks validate these theoretical predictions, confirming the theory's robustness against finite-size effects. Finally, by applying information bottleneck theory, we analyze our results to establish precise relationships among dynamic isometry, mutual information maximization, and optimal channel properties in deep learning.

Based on experimental data regarding the total $S=1$ transition cross-sections for the $^4$He$(\gamma,p)^3$H and $^4$He$(\gamma,n)^3$He reactions, this paper explores the potential for measuring $P$-state probabilities within the $^4$He nucleus. These $S=1$ transitions may arise from $^3P_0$ nuclear states, result from a spin-flip of the final-state particle system originating from $^1S_0$ or $^5D_0$ states, or stem from secondary effects. The analysis of the data indicates that, within statistical uncertainties, the ratio of $S=1$ transition cross-sections in collinear geometry to reaction cross-sections at a nucleon-exit angle of $\theta_N = 90^{\circ}$ remains independent of photon energy across the range $22 \le E_{\gamma} \le 100$ MeV. This finding supports the hypothesis that $S=1$ transitions originate from $^3P_0$ states in $^4$He. Calculated average magnitudes for $\nu_p$ and $\nu_n$ in this energy range are $0.01 \pm 0.002$ and $0.015 \pm 0.003$, respectively, with errors attributed solely to statistical variations.

Fonts carry deep semantic weight through their various glyph forms. Lacking typography expertise, manually choosing or designing a suitable font is an arduous process. To help users browse extensive font collections and generate novel styles, researchers have introduced font retrieval and style transfer techniques, highlighting a growing demand for high-quality font representations. Consequently, we introduce a new scheme for learning font representations that embeds stylistic features into a latent space. To ensure distinct differentiation between fonts, we propose a paired-glyph matching model that draws similar glyphs from the same font closer together in representation space while repelling those from different fonts. Experimental results on font retrieval using query glyphs demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods in generalization. Furthermore, we validate the advantages of transfer learning for downstream style transfer and generation tasks using our proposed method. The source code can be found at https://github.com/junhocho/paired-glyph-matching.

Accurately gauging demand elasticity to price changes is crucial for airlines seeking to optimize their pricing strategies. However, policies designed to maximize short-term revenue can sometimes exhibit insufficient price variation, which may degrade the accuracy of future demand forecasts. This challenge, referred to as the "earning while learning" problem, extends beyond the airline industry and has been a focus of recent academic and industrial research. A particularly promising approach identified in the literature integrates revenue maximization with demand model quality into a unified objective function. This method has demonstrated significant success in both simulations and real-world benchmarks. Despite its effectiveness, it requires adaptation to specific constraints inherent in airline revenue management (RM), such as the simultaneous pricing control required for multiple active flights on a single leg. This paper adapts the method to airline RM under the assumption of unconstrained capacity. We demonstrate that our new algorithm efficiently conducts price experimentation, generating higher revenue over long-term horizons compared to traditional methods that prioritize immediate revenue maximization alone.

Synergistic drug combinations hold immense promise for boosting therapeutic outcomes and minimizing adverse effects; however, predicting such combinations effectively remains an unsolved challenge due to the obscure causal disease signaling pathways involved. Although numerous deep learning (AI) models have been introduced to quantify drug synergy, a primary drawback of current methods is their lack of interpretability. This opacity renders AI conclusions difficult for human experts to understand, thereby restricting both the robustness of the findings and the practical deployment of these models in real-world human-AI healthcare settings. To address this, we propose an interpretable Graph Neural Network (GNN) designed to uncover the fundamental therapeutic targets and mechanisms of synergy (MoS) by extracting critical sub-molecular networks. Central to this approach is a novel graph pooling layer called Self-Attention based Node and Edge pool (SANEpool), which calculates the importance scores of nodes and edges by leveraging node features and graph topology. Consequently, the proposed GNN offers a structured framework for predicting and interpreting drug synergy based on identified pivotal sub-molecular networks. We evaluated SANEpool using molecular networks derived from 46 core cancer signaling pathways and drug combination data from the NCI ALMANAC screening dataset. Experimental findings demonstrate that: 1) SANEpool achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to other popular graph neural networks, and 2) the sub-molecular networks identified by SANEpool are both self-explanatory and highly salient for detecting synergistic drug combinations.

Considering a smooth, bounded domain $\mathcal{D}$ in $\mathbb{R}^N$ where $N\geq3$, this work investigates the existence and behavior of positive solutions to the following elliptic Neumann problem:
$$\begin{cases}-\Delta \upsilon+\upsilon=\upsilon^p,\,\quad \upsilon>0
\quad\textrm{in}\ \mathcal{D},\\[1mm] \frac{\partial
\upsilon}{\partial\nu}=0\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad \textrm{on}\
\partial\mathcal{D}, \end{cases}$$
where $p>1$ represents a sufficiently large exponent and $\nu$ is the outer unit normal to the boundary $\partial\mathcal{D}$. Through a constructive approach, we demonstrate that for appropriate domains $\mathcal{D}$, if $p$ is large enough, the problem admits a family of positive solutions characterized by $k$ boundary layers and $l$ interior layers (for any non-negative integers $k, l$ with $k+l\geq1$). These layers concentrate along $k+l$ distinct $(N-2)$-dimensional minimal submanifolds of $\partial\mathcal{D}$, or potentially collapse onto a single $(N-2)$-dimensional minimal submanifold as $p\rightarrow+\infty$.

The high integration density of Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (MAPS), which combine silicon sensors and readout electronics within a single device, enables the creation of extremely thin structures with a significantly reduced material budget. Thicknesses on the order of 50~$\mu$m, at which silicon chips become flexible, are now readily utilized in various applications. Furthermore, MAPS can be manufactured into wafer-sized sensors through a technique called stitching, allowing for the construction of detector elements large enough to cover entire tracker half-layers using single bent sensors. The ALICE ITS~3 project aims to develop a new vertex tracker based on truly cylindrical, wafer-scale sensors featuring a material budget of less than 0.05\% X/X$_{0}$ per layer and positioned as close as 18 mm from the interaction point. Research and development across all project aspects—including mechanical designs for bent wafer-scale devices, test beams of bent MAPS, and the design of stitched sensors—are advancing rapidly, targeting installation during the LHC Long Shutdown 3 (2025--2027). This contribution outlines the project's motivation, its R&D timeline, and highlights recent milestones, including full-scale engineering prototypes with dummy chips and small-scale, fully functional assemblies of bent MAPS.

A sidelobe-free pulse-compression technique has been developed by utilizing quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) alongside a complementary representation of a causal waveform. This approach investigates radio-frequency (RF) pulse envelopes featuring both unimodal shapes (such as rectangular, Gaussian, and Laplacian) and bimodal shapes (specifically Hermite-Gaussian). While the resulting compression gain remains modest (approximately 2), these compressible pulses can be generated and processed via phase-invariant correlation using systems with low complexity.

Currently, state-of-the-art single image super-resolution (SISR) techniques have achieved remarkable results through deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs). However, existing methods are constrained by fixed degradation assumptions, typically assuming bicubic downscaling of low-resolution (LR) images. In contrast, real-world LR images often undergo unknown degradation processes, such as bicubic, bilinear, nearest-neighbor, or actual physical degradation. Consequently, most current SR models struggle to efficiently handle multiple degradation types within a single architecture. To address this challenge of multi-domain image super-resolution, we introduce SR2*GAN, a novel and scalable deep Super-Resolution Residual StarGAN. This approach utilizes a single model to super-resolve LR images across various domains, employing a StarGAN-like topology with one generator and one discriminator. We validate the efficacy of our method through both quantitative and qualitative experiments, demonstrating its superiority over other state-of-the-art approaches.

Dark matter candidates known as feebly interacting massive particles (FIMPs) may have never reached thermal equilibrium with the cosmic plasma. Their present-day abundance is established through the freeze-in mechanism across a broad spectrum of masses, thereby greatly enlarging the parameter space accessible for experimental testing compared to alternative production scenarios. Nevertheless, directly probing the extremely weak couplings necessitated by freeze-in presents significant difficulties. We demonstrate that FIMPs can be investigated through Large Hadron Collider (LHC) searches for new physics manifested as mono-jet events accompanied by substantial missing energy. Specifically, we examine a $Z'$ portal framework where gluon annihilation generates FIMPs both in the early universe and at modern collider facilities. Data from LHC Run 3 mono-jet analyses could potentially reveal new physics attributed to FIMPs spanning a mass range from MeV to TeV.

This paper introduces the foundational framework of the Socio-physical Model of Activities (SOMA), which captures both the physical and social dimensions of daily tasks. While such activities appear effortless to humans, they present significant challenges for artificial agents. For instance, a natural language command often lacks the specific details required for execution. Humans overcome this by rapidly narrowing the search space through prior knowledge, such as a network of plans that outline how goals can be met at different levels of abstraction. Unlike approaches that enumerate fine-grained physical contexts, SOMA focuses on integrating socially constructed knowledge regarding the functions of actions in achieving various goals and the roles objects play within specific situations. Drawing on the human cognitive ability to generalize experiences into abstract knowledge applicable to new scenarios, we argue that a comprehensive solution requires modeling both physical and social contexts. SOMA achieves this by linking physical and social domains, establishing relationships between specific occurrences and their generalizations, a capability validated through multiple use cases.
We prove a convergence theorem for a specific form of stochastic gradient descent, resulting in a convergent version of the back-propagation algorithm.

A complete grasp of many-body quantum systems relies fundamentally on characterizing their entanglement structure, yet experimentally detecting such entanglement in spatially extended systems described by quantum fields remains a significant hurdle. We introduce a universal framework for verifying entanglement and validate it by uncovering correlations between separate subsystems within a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate. This approach leverages the simultaneous, spatially resolved measurement of a quantum field across two conjugate observables, enabling the experimental confirmation of quantum correlations across both local and non-local partitions. Furthermore, observing squeezing in Bogoliubov modes within a multi-mode context highlights the scheme's potential to enhance quantum simulations for investigating entanglement in spatially extended many-body systems.

Dendric shifts are characterized by specific combinatorial constraints governing the extensions of words within their languages. This class encompasses and extends prominent shift families, including Sturmian shifts, Arnoux-Rauzy shifts, and codings of interval exchange transformations. It is established that every minimal dendric shift admits a primitive $\mathcal{S}$-adic representation, where the morphisms in $\mathcal{S}$ act as positive tame automorphisms on the free group generated by the alphabet. This paper presents an $\mathcal{S}$-adic characterization of dendric shifts utilizing two finite graphs.

This study examines interactions among charged and uncharged branes across various dimensions within three non-supersymmetric string frameworks. These models encompass the $USp(32)$ and $U(32)$ orientifold projections of type IIB and type $0$B strings, alongside the $SO(16) \times SO(16)$ projection of the exceptional heterotic string. The derived ten-dimensional spectra are tachyon-free, and the associated brane configurations generate diverse and complex dynamics. We calculate static potentials for parallel brane stacks across three complementary domains: the probe regime (where one stack is parametrically heavier), the string-amplitude regime (where both stacks are light), and the holographic regime. Wherever direct comparison is feasible, qualitative agreement is observed despite the lack of supersymmetry. Furthermore, our analysis of charged branes demonstrates that the Weak Gravity Conjecture holds true through a unique mechanism involving the renormalization of the effective charge-to-tension ratio.

The origins and persistence of biological diversity have long been central to ecology and evolutionary theory. The competitive exclusion principle posits that the number of coexisting species is constrained by available resources or the degree of similarity in how species utilize those resources. However, natural systems, such as the vast diversity of unicellular organisms in the oceans, often contradict this principle. It has been established that mathematical models accounting for population fluctuations can result in violations of the exclusion principle. In this study, we utilize simple eco-evolutionary models to demonstrate that specific population dynamics, known as boom-bust cycles, enable the evolution of significantly higher diversity levels than those predicted by stable equilibrium dynamics. Boom-bust dynamics involve extended phases of near-exponential growth followed by population crashes driven by competition. When these ecological patterns are integrated into evolutionary models permitting adaptive diversification within continuous phenotype spaces, the desynchronization of boom-bust cycles among coexisting species facilitates the maintenance of high diversity.

This study introduces a new method for training Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) that leverages attention maps from a Teacher Network. This approach enhances the quality of generated images and enables weak object localization within them. Specifically, we generate images of HEp-2 cells captured via Indirect Immunofluorescence (IIF) to evaluate the network's capability for weakly supervised cell localization. First, we demonstrate that while GANs can efficiently learn the mapping between input and target distributions, the discriminator fails to identify regions of interest. Second, we propose a novel attention transfer mechanism that utilizes transfer learning to compel the discriminator to focus on these critical areas. Third, we show that this results in more realistic images, as the discriminator successfully learns to prioritize the areas of interest. Finally, the proposed method facilitates the generation of both images and attention maps, which are valuable for data annotation tasks such as object detection.

In their letter published in *Phys. Rev. Lett.* (2013), Haziot et al. describe a novel giant plasticity phenomenon in hcp Helium-4 quantum crystals, claiming that the material displays mechanical behaviors inconsistent with classical plasticity theory. Their study of high-quality crystals across varying temperatures and strain levels reveals that the shear modulus plateaus and dissipation approaches zero, with both metrics remaining independent of stress and strain; these observations are interpreted as evidence of reversible dissipation and quantum tunneling. In this Comment, we demonstrate that such signatures can be accounted for by a classical model of thermally activated dislocation glide, eliminating the necessity to invoke quantum tunneling or dissipationless motion. Previously, we introduced a dislocation glide model for solid Helium-4 that includes dissipation contributions arising from interactions with other dislocations, yielding qualitatively similar results (Zhou et al., *Philos. Mag. Lett.* 2012).
We calculate the area of an arbitrary d-sphere within a Snyder geometry.

Large-scale pre-trained language models have driven significant advancements in NLP, achieving state-of-the-art results across various text processing tasks through pre-training and fine-tuning. Data augmentation techniques have further enabled the creation of top-performing models for low-resource and zero-shot scenarios. Previous research has focused on developing single, massively multilingual machine translation models for zero-shot translation; while these models generate accurate translations, they frequently suffer from off-target language errors by outputting incorrect target languages. This study demonstrates that prompt-conditioned large models are immune to such language selection errors. Furthermore, we empirically validate the efficacy of combining self-supervised pre-training with data augmentation for achieving high performance in zero-shot multilingual machine translation.

This research investigates multilingual AMR parsing through the lens of knowledge distillation, aiming to enhance a multilingual parser by leveraging an existing English parser as a teacher. Our approach adheres to a strict multilingual framework, utilizing a single model to parse all languages, including English. We find that successful distillation hinges on noisy inputs paired with precise outputs. By combining this strategy with extensive pre-training, we developed an AMR parser that significantly outperforms all prior published results on four foreign languages—German, Spanish, Italian, and Chinese, achieving gains of up to 18.8 \textsc{Smatch} points on Chinese and an average of 11.3 \textsc{Smatch} points. Furthermore, our parser matches the performance of the latest state-of-the-art English-only model on English.

Both empirical research and everyday observations confirm that learning models often produce biased results. These models tend to mirror historical societal discrimination, disproportionately harming underrepresented groups. As robots increasingly rely on such models to perform ever-more-complex tasks, their learning processes—which depend heavily on human judgment—become vulnerable to biases rooted in human behavior. Since these models are trained on recorded, labeled data or demonstrations, the resulting robot decisions may reflect current social inequities, posing significant risks when robots interact with people in real-world settings. To address this, feminist frameworks offer vital insights into dismantling bias across various domains. Furthermore, feminism provides the tools to reshape social dynamics and stereotypes, promoting equality through diversity. Consequently, this work adopts a feminist perspective on robot learning, grounded in intersectional, community, decolonial, and pedagogical feminist theories within a broader feminist robotics approach. We present an initial discussion highlighting the importance of these perspectives to investigate, anticipate, and ultimately rectify biased robotic decision-making.

Consider a 3-fold flopping contraction $f\colon X\to\mathrm{Spec}\, R$, where $X$ possesses at worst Gorenstein terminal singularities and $R$ is a complete local ring. We characterize the space of Bridgeland stability conditions defined on two specific subcategories of the bounded derived category of $X$: the null subcategory $\mathscr{C}$, comprising complexes that push forward to zero under the derived map, and the affine subcategory $\mathscr{D}$, consisting of complexes supported on the exceptional locus. We demonstrate that any connected component of stability conditions on $\mathscr{C}$ corresponds to the universal cover of the complexified complement of a real hyperplane arrangement linked to $X$ through the Homological MMP. More broadly, we show that a connected component of normalized stability conditions on $\mathscr{D}$ forms a regular covering space of the infinite hyperplane arrangement detailed by Iyama and Wemyss [IW9]. Notably, neither arrangement is necessarily Coxeter. As a result, we provide the inaugural description of the Stringy Kähler Moduli Space (SKMS) for all smooth irreducible 3-fold flops. The finding is unexpected: we establish that the SKMS is invariably a sphere punctured by 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, or 14 points, contingent upon the curve length.

Linear projection techniques, including proper orthogonal decomposition, are standard for building reduced-order models of dynamical systems; however, many such systems are best represented by a *nonlinear* manifold in a lower-dimensional state space. While prior studies indicate that deep learning offers an efficient approach to nonlinear dimensionality reduction, these methods typically require training data and are often specific to individual problems \citep[see][]{carlberg_ca}. In this work, we employ randomized training data to develop and train convolutional autoencoders for performing nonlinear dimension reduction on the wave and Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equations. Furthermore, we introduce training strategies that do not rely on full-order model samples and apply the manifold least-squares Petrov-Galerkin projection method to construct reduced-order models for the heat, wave, and Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equations using the same autoencoder architecture.

Recently, clinical practice has adopted ultra-wide optical coherence tomography angiography (UW-OCTA) for screening diabetic retinopathy (DR) to identify early-stage indicators. However, creating a deep learning system for DR analysis using UW-OCTA images is challenging due to data acquisition difficulties and the lack of public datasets. Under these realistic constraints, models trained on limited data often yield suboptimal results. Consequently, to prevent ophthalmologists from being misled by erroneous model predictions, it is essential that models remain robust even when data is scarce. To address this practical challenge, we conducted a comprehensive empirical study covering DR analysis tasks such as lesion segmentation, image quality assessment, and DR grading. For each task, we implemented a robust training strategy utilizing ensemble learning, data augmentation, and semi-supervised learning. Additionally, we introduced a reliable pseudo-labeling method that filters out uncertain labels based on confidence scores to mitigate the adverse impact of noisy pseudo-labels. Leveraging these proposed approaches, we secured first place in the Diabetic Retinopathy Analysis Challenge.

We investigate BTZ black holes within the context of low-energy heterotic string theory (BTZ-Sen BH), a framework necessitating a non-trivial dilaton $\phi$ and a 3-form $H_{\mu\nu\rho}$ field. By employing the Hassan-Sen transformation with the BTZ black hole as the seed solution, we derive the corresponding solution in the string frame and examine several properties of these black hole configurations.

The study of metric geometries and Einstein's vacuum field equations employs generalized differential forms. Cartan's structure equations are extended and utilized within this framework. Specifically, every metric corresponds to a flat generalized connection. By adopting a fresh perspective, the text examines Einstein's vacuum equations alongside their Lorentzian four-metric solutions. It demonstrates that specific flat generalized connections and their associated geometries can represent these Ricci-flat metrics.

In Correlation Clustering, we are presented with a weighted graph $G$ where edges are categorized as "similar" or "dissimilar" by a binary classifier. The objective is to find a clustering that minimizes the total weight of disagreements, defined as the sum of weights for "similar" edges placed in different clusters and "dissimilar" edges placed within the same cluster. We investigate this problem under the condition that every "similar" edge $e$ has a weight $\mathbf{w}_e\in[\alpha \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{w}]$, while every "dissimilar" edge $e$ satisfies $\mathbf{w}_e\geq \alpha \mathbf{w}$ (with $\alpha\leq 1$ and $\mathbf{w}>0$ as a scaling factor). Under these constraints, we propose a $(3 + 2 \log_e (1/\alpha))$-approximation algorithm. This assumption effectively models scenarios involving asymmetric classification errors. Furthermore, we demonstrate an asymptotically matching Linear Programming integrality gap of $\Omega(\log 1/\alpha)$.

While GPT-3 and T5 illustrate that transformer capabilities scale with parameter size, non-parametric memory offers a more efficient path for knowledge-intensive tasks by enabling dramatic model growth with sub-linear increases in computational cost and GPU memory. Building on recent advancements like RAG and REALM, which integrate retrieval into conditional generation using neural initial retrieval from passage corpora, we introduce Re2G. This framework combines neural initial retrieval with reranking within a BART-based sequence-to-sequence architecture. Our reranking method uniquely allows for the merging of retrieval results from sources with incomparable scores, facilitating an ensemble of BM25 and neural retrieval. To achieve end-to-end training, we propose a novel knowledge distillation variant that trains the initial retriever, reranker, and generator using only ground truth labels for the target sequence output. Experiments across four diverse domains—zero-shot slot filling, question answering, fact-checking, and dialog—demonstrate significant improvements, yielding relative gains of 9% to 34% over the previous state-of-the-art on the KILT leaderboard. We have released our code as open source at https://github.com/IBM/kgi-slot-filling/tree/re2g.

Stochastic simulators serve as essential instruments across numerous scientific disciplines. Typically grounded in first principles, they generate sample sets whose distributions implicitly define probability measures to characterize phenomena of interest. Yet, these simulators often lack the necessary fidelity for specific scientific applications, requiring the development of ad-hoc adjustments to "calibrate" the simulation and guarantee that its outputs accurately reflect reality. This paper employs techniques from transportation theory to establish such corrections systematically. Specifically, we utilize a neural network to calculate the minimal alterations required for individual simulator samples so that the resulting distribution achieves proper calibration. We demonstrate the method and its advantages within the domain of experimental particle physics, where the demand for calibrated stochastic simulators is especially acute.

This article details a measurement of $
u_e$ interactions lacking pions in the final state, conducted via the MicroBooNE experiment, alongside an inquiry into the low-energy electromagnetic event excess reported by the MiniBooNE collaboration. The analysis utilizes an exclusive approach, examining channels with visible protons (1$e$N$p$0$\pi$) and those without (1$e$0$p$0$\pi$), based on $6.86	imes 10^{20}$ protons on target from the Fermilab Booster Neutrino Beam. Event reconstruction relies on the Pandora pattern recognition toolkit, supplemented by topological data from the MicroBooNE liquid argon time projection chamber. A goodness-of-fit test indicates that the data align with predictions using nominal flux and interaction models, yielding a combined $p$-value of 0.098. A model addressing the MiniBooNE low-energy excess is proposed to assess potential $
u_e$ contributions. The results suggest that any existing excess does not follow a simple scaling of the $
u_e$ flux component. While the combined channels do not definitively validate or reject the tested model, each channel individually disfavors the low-energy excess model at greater than 90% confidence level. Specifically, the most sensitive 1$e$N$p$0$\pi$ channel shows observations below the prediction, consistent with no excess. Conversely, the less sensitive 1$e$0$p$0$\pi$ channel exhibits low-energy observations above the prediction, though overall agreement persists across the full energy spectrum.

While large language models exhibit remarkable zero-shot capabilities, their substantial size often leads to high computational costs. Recently, semi-parametric language models have emerged as a promising solution by combining a smaller base model with an external retriever. However, it has remained uncertain whether these semi-parametric architectures can match the zero-shot generalization performance of fully-parametric models on downstream tasks. This study presents $\text{Zemi}$, a zero-shot semi-parametric language model. To our knowledge, $\text{Zemi}$ is the first semi-parametric model to achieve robust zero-shot performance across a broad spectrum of held-out unseen tasks. We developed $\text{Zemi}$ using a novel semi-parametric multitask prompted training framework, which yields significant gains over the parametric multitask training method introduced by T0. Specifically, we enhanced both multitask training and zero-shot evaluation by incorporating retrieval from a large-scale, task-agnostic unlabeled corpus. To effectively integrate multiple potentially noisy retrieved augmentations, we introduced a new $\text{augmentation fusion}$ module that utilizes a perceiver resampler and gated cross-attention. Notably, our $\text{Zemi}_\text{LARGE}$ surpasses T0-3B by 16% across all seven evaluation tasks while maintaining a model size 3.9 times smaller.

Hybrid Free-Space Optical (FSO) and Radio Frequency (RF) systems demand a robust switching mechanism to leverage the complementary strengths of both links and enhance overall capacity. However, environmental dynamics such as fog, dust, and sandstorms exacerbate the complexity of link switching. To mitigate these challenges, this study introduces Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) for optimizing link switching in hybrid FSO/RF environments. Specifically, we investigate two primary approaches: an Actor-Critic model (Actor/Critic-FSO/RF) and a Deep-Q Network (DQN-FSO/RF) designed to handle atmospheric turbulence. By defining specific states, actions, and reward functions, we formulate the switching problem. While the DQN-FSO/RF model frequently updates its policy through environmental interaction, this leads to substantial switching costs. To resolve this issue, we propose DQNEnsemble-FSO/RF, an ensemble consensus-based representation learning framework for deep reinforcement learning. This novel approach utilizes consensus-learned feature representations derived from asynchronous threads to update the deployed policy. Experimental findings demonstrate that DQNEnsemble-FSO/RF outperforms Actor/Critic-FSO/RF, DQN-FSO/RF, and MyOpic in terms of switching performance while significantly reducing switching costs.

Addressing a significant challenge in web search and question answering, this paper focuses on count queries, exemplified by "number of songs by John Lennon." Existing approaches typically respond with a solitary, often confusing figure or present a ranked list of text snippets containing varying counts. In contrast, our proposed methodology answers count queries through inference, contextualization, and explanatory evidence. Unlike prior systems, our approach derives final answers from multiple observations, accommodates semantic qualifiers within counts, and supplies evidence by listing representative instances. Extensive experiments across diverse queries demonstrate the advantages of this method. To encourage further research in this underexplored area, we have released an annotated dataset comprising 5,000 queries and 200,000 relevant text spans.

Halo morphology provides critical insights into cosmological and galaxy formation theories. By utilizing Minkowski Functionals (MFs), we characterize the actual shapes of haloes, capturing details that smooth density profiles often miss and extending beyond simple spherical or ellipsoidal symmetries. We apply semi-analytical models featuring NFW and $\alpha\beta\gamma$ profiles in both spherical and ellipsoidal configurations to interpret MFs in relation to inner and outer slopes, concentration, and sphericity. Furthermore, these same models replicate the density profiles of $N$-body haloes, demonstrating that their MFs distinctly diverge due to sensitivity to internal substructures. This underscores the utility of MFs at halo scales as a robust statistical tool for refining dark matter spatial modeling, which is essential for advancing future lensing, Sunyaev-Zel'dovich, and X-ray mass mapping efforts, as well as high-precision dark matter detection.

This article explores a specific variation of the notorious 15-puzzle and establishes a mathematical foundation for its unsolvability. By applying principles of permutations, bijectivity, and cycle transpositions, we demonstrate how to model the puzzle as a group and identify which configurations are reachable.

This study examines the relationship between shifts in the investor base and idiosyncratic volatility within cryptocurrency markets. Using changes in subreddit follower counts as a proxy for investor base fluctuations, the research demonstrates that these changes significantly elevate the idiosyncratic volatility of cryptocurrencies. This result remains robust across various volatility measures and is not explained by factors such as size, momentum, liquidity, or trading volume.

Recent advancements in deep learning have driven significant success in multi-image super-resolution using multi-temporal satellite data. This paper moves beyond traditional high-resolution image reconstruction to address a super-resolved inference challenge: semantic segmentation at a spatial resolution exceeding that of the sensing platform. Building on recent models that leverage temporal permutation invariance, we introduce a multi-resolution fusion module capable of deriving the rich semantic details required for segmentation. The proposed model recently secured victory in the AI4EO challenge on Enhanced Sentinel 2 Agriculture.

Although machine learning has proven effective across diverse domains, its viability for calculating distances to molecular clouds within the Galaxy remains uncertain. Typically, kinematic distances are used for this purpose, yet the inner Galaxy presents an ambiguity where both "Near" and "Far" distance solutions can be simultaneously derived. To address this, we developed a two-class inference model—distinguishing between "Near" and "Far" solutions—using a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), a deep learning architecture capable of extracting spatial features. Our study utilized a CO dataset from the Nobeyama 45-m radio telescope covering the first Galactic quadrant (l = 62-10 degrees, |b| < 1 degree). The model was trained using the three-dimensional distribution (position-position-velocity) of 12CO (J=1-0) emissions, with training labels for "Near" or "Far" classifications derived from the HII region catalog of the WISE infrared satellite. This approach yielded a CNN model achieving 76% accuracy on the training set. We applied this model to determine distances for molecular clouds identified by the CLUMPFIND algorithm. Our analysis revealed that the masses of molecular clouds located within 8.15 kpc, as detected in the 12CO data, adhere to a power-law distribution with an index of approximately -2.3 for masses exceeding 10^3 solar masses. Furthermore, we mapped the detailed distribution of molecular gas in the Galaxy as viewed from the Galactic North pole.

We provide a simpler proof of Brian Clarke's result, which states that the completion of the space of Riemannian metrics on a compact, orientable smooth manifold with respect to the $L^2$-distance is CAT$(0)$. Specifically, we demonstrate that this completion is isometric to the space of $L^2$-maps from a standard probability space to a fixed CAT$(0)$ space.

A significant issue in post hoc explainability is the absence of a shared foundational objective across different methods. For instance, some approaches are driven by function approximation, others by game-theoretic concepts, and still others by the pursuit of clear visualizations. This divergence in goals leads not only to an inconsistent theoretical understanding of explanations but also to the practical difficulty of determining which method to apply in specific scenarios.

This study addresses these challenges by unifying eight widely used post hoc explanation techniques (LIME, C-LIME, SHAP, Occlusion, Vanilla Gradients, Gradients x Input, SmoothGrad, and Integrated Gradients). We demonstrate that all these methods fundamentally perform local function approximation of the black-box model, with the only distinctions lying in the specific neighborhood and loss function employed for the approximation. This unification allows us to: (1) formulate a no free lunch theorem for explanation methods, proving that no single approach can achieve optimal performance across all neighborhoods, and (2) offer a principled framework for selecting methods based on their faithfulness to the black-box model. We empirically corroborate these theoretical findings using diverse real-world datasets, model architectures, and prediction tasks.

By integrating varied explanation methods into a unified framework, this work: (1) deepens the conceptual understanding of these techniques by exposing their common local function approximation goals, intrinsic properties, and interrelationships, and (2) facilitates practical application by providing a reasoned strategy for method selection and laying the groundwork for the development of future methods.

Recent advancements in runtime analysis of evolutionary algorithms have successfully connected algorithm performance to specific parameters, yet studies examining the influence of problem parameters remain scarce. The newly introduced W-model offers a robust framework for such investigations by generating pseudo-Boolean optimization problems with adjustable characteristics. This paper initiates theoretical research on the W-model by investigating how the property of neutrality affects the runtime of random local search. Neutrality induces plateaus in the search space by applying a majority vote to subsets of candidate solutions before evaluating the reduced-dimensional string using a low-level fitness function. We establish upper bounds for the expected runtime of random local search across the entire parameter spectrum of this MAJORITY problem. To achieve this, we present a theorem applicable to various optimization algorithms that correlates the runtime of MAJORITY with its symmetric counterpart, HASMAJORITY, where a sufficient majority is required to optimize the subset. Furthermore, we introduce generalized versions of classic drift theorems and Wald's equation, both of which we consider to be of independent interest.

In medical image analysis, the expense of gathering high-quality data and expert annotation creates significant barriers for many applications. Since most existing methods rely on supervised learning and require extensive labeled datasets to perform well, this paper introduces a self-supervised learning (SSL) alternative. Our approach learns spatial anatomical representations from frames within magnetic resonance (MR) video clips to diagnose knee conditions. A pretext model is employed to derive meaningful representations that are invariant to spatial context. The subsequent downstream task involves class-imbalanced multi-label classification. Experimental results demonstrate that features extracted by the pretext model achieve competitive performance in this task. Furthermore, the findings highlight the model's efficiency and reliability in representing minority classes without any specific strategies to address dataset imbalance. To our knowledge, this study is the first to validate the effectiveness and reliability of self-supervised learning algorithms for class-imbalanced multi-label classification on MR video data. The code for evaluating this work can be found at https://github.com/sadimanna/skid.

This study calculates dispersion interactions between heavy species (Zn$^+$, Cd$^+$, Hg$^+$, Pb$^+$, Zn, Cd, Hg, and Pb) and graphene or carbon nanotubes by determining van der Waals $C_3$ coefficients via established Lifshitz theory. These coefficients are formulated using the reflection properties of the nanomaterials, derived from the Dirac model. Furthermore, precise dynamic dipole polarizabilities at imaginary frequencies for the relevant atoms and ions—critical parameters—were computed using relativistic approaches, alongside a comparison of static dipole polarizabilities against existing literature values. The research investigates these interactions across various separation distances and radii for both graphene and carbon nanotubes, also examining the influence of the graphene wall's gap parameter. A comparative analysis of the interaction coefficients for both materials reveals that graphene is the superior candidate for adsorbing these toxic heavy elements.

Jiang et al. recently identified a potential short-lived transient in a single image, spatially linked to a galaxy at a redshift of approximately 11. While Jiang et al. and Kahn et al. propose a Gamma-Ray Burst (GRB) origin, Padmanabhan & Loeb suggest it may be a supernova shock breakout from a 300 solar mass Population III star. Although Jiang et al. dismissed the idea that the event was sunlight reflected off a satellite, we demonstrate that reflection from a high-orbit satellite or space debris offers a plausible explanation. Recent studies indicate that point-like satellite reflections brighter than magnitude 11 occur at a rate exceeding 10 per square degree per day near the equatorial plane. Although this rate drops by a factor of 5 to 50 at higher declinations, it remains significant, being roughly four orders of magnitude greater than the estimated rate for GRBs.

Estimating higher-order terms in the asymptotic perturbative series of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) is a challenging yet essential task for accurately assessing uncertainties in phenomenological studies. This study examines the Adler function and the scalar correlator, developing models for their Borel transforms that adhere to constraints imposed by the operator product expansion and the renormalization group. A key innovation is the use of the QCD coupling within the $C$-scheme, which offers specific benefits. The findings for the Adler function corroborate previous results derived directly in the $\overline{\rm MS}$ scheme, while the results for the scalar correlation function represent new contributions. The analysis reveals that the significantly larger perturbative corrections observed for the scalar correlator in the $\overline{\rm MS}$ scheme are primarily attributable to the choice of renormalization scheme; these can be substantially mitigated by adopting more suitable schemes, which are readily implemented in the $C$-scheme.

This paper introduces CS-Insights, an interactive web platform designed to examine computer science publications from DBLP across various dimensions. Its specialized interfaces enable users to uncover trends regarding research activity, productivity, accessibility, author output, venue statistics, key topics, and the influence of computer science on other disciplines. CS-Insights is openly accessible, and its modular design allows for straightforward adaptation to domains beyond computer science.

This work presents an asymptotic analysis of limit cycles within mathematical models describing oscillating chemical reactions. Following a concise overview of mathematical preliminaries regarding the biased Van der Pol oscillator, the study examines two-dimensional models of the Chlorine dioxide Iodine Malonic-Acid (CIMA) reaction, alongside both two- and three-dimensional versions of the Oregonator models for the Belousov-Zhabotinsky (BZ) reaction. Explicit analytical formulas are derived for the relaxation-oscillation periods of these systems, achieving accuracy within 5% of their corresponding numerical values. Furthermore, for the two-dimensional CIMA and Oregonator models, critical parameter values are determined that trigger canard explosions and implosions in their respective limit cycles.

Direct photons with transverse momenta below 5 GeV/$c$ have been measured at midrapidity for minimum bias and 0%--40% most central Cu+Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV. The $e^{+}e^{-}$ yield from quasi-real direct virtual photons was isolated as an excess above established hadronic contributions within the $e^{+}e^{-}$ mass spectrum. A significant enhancement of photons relative to the binary scaled $p$$+$$p$ baseline is evident for $p_T<4$ GeV/$c$ in the Cu+Cu dataset. The $p_T$ spectra align with Au+Au data for comparable participant numbers. The inverse slopes of the exponential fits applied to the residual excess (after subtracting the $p$$+$$p$ baseline) are 285$\pm$53(stat)$\pm$57(syst)~MeV/$c$ for minimum bias events and 333$\pm$72(stat)$\pm$45(syst)~MeV/$c$ for the 0%--40% most central events. Furthermore, the photon rapidity density, $dN/dy$, follows the same power-law dependence on charged particle multiplicity ($dN_{\rm ch}/d\eta$) as observed in Au+Au collisions at the same energy.

Free-energy landscapes for short peptides, particularly variants of the pH Low Insertion Peptide (pHLIP), have been constructed within the heterogeneous milieu of lipid bilayers and cell membranes. This construction incorporates dominant interactions and the conformational preferences of the peptide backbone. Our approach models broken internal hydrogen bonds along the polypeptide backbone as statistically interacting quasiparticles that are activated from a helical reference state. The preferred conformation is dictated by the local environment—spanning from polar to nonpolar conditions—specifically by the availability of external hydrogen bonds (from water molecules or lipid headgroups) to substitute for internal ones. Side-chain contributions are captured through residue-specific transfer free energies between polar and nonpolar settings. Consequently, the free-energy landscape responds to the pH level of the aqueous environment surrounding the membrane. At high pH, we identify descending free-energy pathways indicating a coexistence of peptides adsorbed on the membrane and those remaining in solution. Conversely, a decrease in pH increases the protonation of negatively charged residues, thereby enhancing the hydrophobicity of peptide segments near the C terminus. At low pH, we identify insertion pathways connecting the membrane-adsorbed state to a stable trans-membrane state where the C terminus has traversed the membrane.

The standard two-sided and one-sided matching problems, along with the closely related school choice problem, have been extensively examined from an axiomatic perspective. A limited set of algorithms currently dominates the existing literature: the Gale-Shapley algorithm for two-sided matching; (random) Serial Dictatorship and the Probabilistic Serial rule for one-sided matching; and Gale-Shapley and Boston mechanisms for school choice. The primary reason for the prevalence of these algorithms is their strong worst-case axiomatic performance regarding efficiency and strategyproofness. However, shifting the focus to fairness, social welfare, trade-offs between conflicting axioms, and average-case analysis reveals that these algorithms are not necessarily optimal.

This study explores new algorithms, several of which, to our knowledge, have not previously appeared in the literature. We provide a unified framework where algorithms for two-sided matching systematically generate those for one-sided matching. Beyond axiomatic properties, we examine agent welfare using both theoretical and computational methods. Our findings suggest that some of these new algorithms merit consideration for specific applications. Notably, when evaluating welfare under truthful preferences, certain new algorithms surpass the performance of classic ones.

This paper demonstrates that two specific properties of C*-algebras within the class $\mathcal{P}$—namely, (1) $\beta$-comparison, as defined by Kirchberg and R{\o}rdam, and (2) $n$-comparison, as defined by Winter—are preserved when inherited by simple unital C*-algebras that are asymptotically tracially in $\mathcal{P}$.

While numerous studies have long examined how developers debug, informing our understanding and driving the development of better tools, there remains limited knowledge regarding the typical progression of debugging in real-world contexts. This study aims to characterize debugging episodes from the initial encounter with a defect until its resolution. We analyzed the typical duration and frequency of these episodes, as well as the common activities involved. By observing professional developers during live-streamed programming sessions, we curated 15 sessions involving 11 developers across 30 hours. Systematically coding the debugging episodes and activities within these videos resulted in a dataset comprising 2,137 debugging activities and 1,407 programming activities. Our findings indicate that debugging is highly frequent, occurring on average once every eight minutes during programming work. Debugging episodes vary significantly in length, with most lasting only a few minutes while a minority extend beyond 100 minutes; however, the majority of debugging time is consumed by these longer episodes. We observed that no single activity dominates debugging time, and extended episodes often involve a wide variety of tasks. Furthermore, we found that the activities performed during debugging are remarkably similar to those during general programming, particularly regarding the frequency of code editing and browsing.

This paper examines the relationships within the ring of quasiautomorphic forms linked to triangle groups possessing a single cusp, building upon previous findings regarding Hecke groups. We demonstrate that the Eisenstein series corresponding to these groups obey identities analogous to those discovered by Ramanujan. These identities facilitate the derivation of a specific nonlinear differential equation for each triangle group. We prove that this equation is resolved by the weight-2 quasiautomorphic Eisenstein series associated with the group and its orbit under group transformations. The study concludes with an analysis of the Painlevé property exhibited by these nonlinear differential equations.

We introduce an energy-scale correspondence linking Mott and Kondo lattice physics, proposing a preliminary phase diagram for their correlated electron systems defined by two characteristic energy scales, $\omega^*$ and $\Omega$. These scales denote, respectively, the upper limit of a low-energy regime featuring well-established long-range coherence and the lower limit of localized spectral weight within energy space. Separating these boundaries is a crossover region characterized by emergent yet damped quasiparticle excitations. We contend that the existence of these distinct energy scales is a universal feature of lattice-based correlated electrons, reflecting an intrinsic two-stage mechanism in quasiparticle dynamics that establishes lattice coherence.
