Ultimately, these results, which apply to general quantum systems, establish a theoretical foundation for utilizing VQE with penalty terms to obtain symmetry-resolving energy spectra, thereby advancing the potential of near-term quantum computing.

Data-driven decision-making is crucial even in high-stakes domains such as healthcare and public policy. Deriving optimal policies from observed data necessitates a precise definition of the utility function, which is then maximized in expectation across a population. While researchers often rely on utilities based solely on observed outcomes, in many contexts the decision-maker's utility is better described by the joint set of potential outcomes under all possible actions. For instance, the Hippocratic principle of "do no harm" suggests that the cost of causing death to a patient who would have survived without intervention exceeds the cost of withholding life-saving treatment. This work examines optimal policy learning involving asymmetric utility functions of this nature. We demonstrate that such asymmetries render the social welfare function unidentifiable; consequently, we first establish partial identification. Leveraging statistical decision theory, we subsequently derive minimax decision rules by minimizing the maximum regret compared to alternative policies. We prove that minimax decision rules can be learned from observed data by solving intermediate classification tasks. Furthermore, we show that the finite sample regret of this approach is bounded by the misclassification rate of these intermediate classifiers. Finally, we apply this theoretical framework and methodology to the clinical decision regarding the use of right heart catheterization for patients suspected of having pulmonary hypertension.

This study investigates $H_{\infty}$ filtering for attitude estimation utilizing rotation matrices and vector measurements. By beginning with a storage function defined on the Special Orthogonal Group $SO(3)$, a dissipation inequality is formulated to derive a deterministic nonlinear $H_{\infty}$ filter. This filter adheres to a specified upper bound, $\gamma$, on the energy gain from external disturbances and initial estimation errors to the generalized estimation error. The findings are applicable to all estimation errors representing an angular deviation of less than $\pi/2$ radians within the axis-angle framework. Building upon prior work in nonlinear $H_{\infty}$ filtering with quaternions, this approach introduces a novel filter constructed directly on $SO(3)$. The proposed method utilizes the same innovation term as the Multiplicative Extended Kalman Filter (MEKF) and features a matrix gain updated via a Riccati-type equation. Distinct from the MEKF, it incorporates an additional tuning gain, $\gamma$, allowing for more aggressive behavior during transients. Simulations under various conditions compare the proposed filter against the continuous-time quaternion MEKF and the Geometric Approximate Minimum Energy (GAME) filter, demonstrating competitive performance. Specifically, the GAME filter exhibits superior transient performance, followed by the proposed $H_{\infty}$ filter and the quaternion MEKF, while all three achieve comparable steady-state performance. Consequently, the proposed filter can be viewed as a MEKF variant that improves transient response without significantly compromising steady-state noise rejection.

This paper introduces a highly precise continuous-time trajectory estimation framework designed for Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM), facilitating the effective fusion of high-frequency and asynchronous sensor data. We evaluate this framework using a 3D LiDAR-inertial system. The approach employs a non-rigid registration technique for continuous-time trajectory estimation while simultaneously correcting motion distortion in LiDAR scans. Furthermore, we present a two-state continuous-time trajectory correction method to efficiently address the computationally intractable global optimization challenges that arise during loop closures. We assess the accuracy of our method on both publicly available datasets and our own collected data. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses discrete-time approaches in accuracy, particularly under conditions of aggressive motion. Finally, we release our code at \url{https://github.com/APRIL-ZJU/clins} to support the research community.

We introduce 3DP3, a framework for inverse graphics that leverages inference within a structured generative model encompassing objects, scenes, and images. This system utilizes (i) voxel models to capture 3D object geometry, (ii) hierarchical scene graphs to break down scenes into individual objects and their contact points, and (iii) depth image likelihoods derived from real-time graphics. When provided with an observed RGB-D image, 3DP3's inference algorithm reconstructs the latent 3D scene, including object poses and a concise joint parametrization of these poses. This is achieved through rapid bottom-up pose proposals, innovative involutive MCMC updates to the scene graph structure, and optionally, neural object detectors and pose estimators. Our findings indicate that 3DP3 facilitates scene understanding that accounts for 3D shape, occlusion, and contact structures. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that 3DP3 surpasses deep learning baselines in 6DoF object pose estimation from real images and exhibits superior generalization to complex scenes involving novel viewpoints, intricate contacts, and partial observability.

Genetic and pharmacological perturbation experiments, including gene deletion and the monitoring of subsequent expression changes, serve as potent tools for investigating cellular signal transduction pathways. Nevertheless, automatically extracting conceptual knowledge about signaling systems from systematic perturbation-response data remains a significant challenge. This study examines a framework that integrates knowledge mining and data mining strategies to address this goal. The framework employs three automated processes: first, an ontology-driven knowledge mining method identifies functional modules among perturbation-responsive genes to uncover potential affected signals; second, a graph-based data mining technique searches for perturbations influencing a common signal within a specific functional module; and third, an analysis reveals the system's architecture by organizing signaling units into a hierarchy based on their relationships. When applied to a comprehensive dataset of yeast perturbation-response data, this framework successfully reconstructed numerous established signal transduction pathways, generated multiple hypotheses regarding the yeast signaling system, and automatically organized perturbed genes into a graph mirroring the system's architecture. Crucially, this approach elevates molecular findings from the gene level to a conceptual level, facilitating their translation into computable rules about yeast signaling. For instance, it can derive rules such as: "if genes involved in MAPK signaling are perturbed, genes involved in pheromone responses will be differentially expressed."

This paper demonstrates that the function $r\mapsto r^{-2}\{[\log(2\K(r)/\pi)]/\log((\arth r)/r)-3/4\}$ is strictly increasing on the interval $(0,1)$, mapping onto $(1/320,1/4)$. Consequently, for $r\in(0,1)$, the inequality $[(\arth r)/r]^{3/4+r^2/320}<2\K(r)/\pi<[(\arth r)/r]^{3/4+r^2/4}$ holds, with the coefficients in the exponents of both bounds being optimal. This result confirms a conjecture by Alzer and Qiu and provides tighter bounds for $\K(r)$ than their original proposal. Additionally, the study derives other analytic properties of complete elliptic integrals, including various alternative approximations for $\K(r)$.

We explore the semi-classical transverse confinement of waves utilizing an inhomogeneous gauge field. In this proposed framework, a temporally periodic perturbation is temporally shifted, with the resulting delay varying according to the transverse direction. We demonstrate that, driven by the Kapitza effect, an effective potential emerges, which is proportional to the square of the transverse gradient of the delay. From a physical perspective, this delay generates a transverse force that varies periodically, thereby inducing a phase shift through the local modulation of kinetic energy. Our findings are broadly applicable and relevant to diverse domains, including cold atoms and optics; consequently, we present a proof-of-concept experiment implemented via an optical setup employing fiber loops.

This study proposes an approximation method for a specific category of non-zero-sum stochastic differential games concerning investment and reinsurance strategies between two insurance firms. The analysis incorporates both proportional reinsurance and excess-of-loss reinsurance policies. By utilizing the Markov chain approximation technique alongside the dynamic programming principle, we construct numerical algorithms to determine the Nash equilibrium for the resulting nonlinear integro-differential Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs (HJI) equations. Additionally, we prove the convergence of the approximation sequences and the corresponding value functions, providing numerical examples to demonstrate the practical utility of the developed algorithms.

This study examines the phenomenological consequences of introducing new dark particles on the neutral pion decay. We first compute the contribution to the $\pi^0$ decay width and subsequently expand the theoretical framework by incorporating dark sector vector particles that interact via $\gamma^\mu$, $\sigma^{\mu\nu}$, and $\sigma^{\mu\nu}\gamma^5$ couplings. The total decay width for $\pi^0\rightarrow \gamma e^+ e^-$ is calculated, assuming the electron-positron pair originates from the decay of a dark meson. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of this model for current and prospective searches for new dark particles.

Following an analysis of Feynman diagrams for hadronic molecular states such as $\bar D^{(*)}\Sigma_c^{(*)}$, $\bar D^{(*)}\Lambda_c$, $D^{(*)}\bar K^{*}$, and $D^{(*)}\bar D^{(*)}$, we suggest a binding mechanism driven by the exchange of shared light quarks. This process mirrors the covalent bonding in chemical molecules, where electrons are shared. Employing QCD sum rules, we computed the relevant light-quark-exchange diagrams, yielding a model-independent conclusion: the interaction becomes attractive when the shared light quarks are totally antisymmetric, thereby satisfying the Pauli principle. We constructed a four-parameter toy model to formalize this framework and estimated the binding energies of several potential covalent hadronic molecules. A distinctive characteristic of this approach is that the binding energies for the $(I)J^P = (0)1^+$ $D\bar B^*/D^*\bar B$ molecules are significantly greater than those for the $(I)J^P = (0)1^+$ $DD^*/\bar B \bar B^*$ systems, whereas the $(I)J^P = (1/2)1/2^+$ $\bar D \Sigma_c/\bar D \Sigma_b/B \Sigma_c/B \Sigma_b$ molecules exhibit comparable binding energies.

Although the median-of-medians linear pivot selection algorithm guarantees a worst-case time complexity of $\mathrm{O}(n\ln n)$ for quicksort, it has frequently been regarded as too costly for practical use. This article demonstrates that quicksort employing this specific pivot selection method can indeed be made efficient.

While diagrammatic methods, ranging from Feynman diagrams to tensor networks, have significantly advanced quantum mechanics by visualizing mathematical operations and aiding interpretation, they often cannot be computed directly. This paper introduces the ZXH-calculus, a graphical framework extending the ZX-calculus, designed to represent and reason about many-body states entirely through diagrams. As a case study, we encode the 1D AKLT state—a symmetry-protected topological phase—into the ZXH-calculus by formulating representations for spins greater than 1/2. Leveraging the calculus's simplification rules, we demonstrate that this graphical representation naturally yields the AKLT matrix-product state form, confirms topologically protected edge states, and establishes a non-zero string order parameter. Beyond these established features, our approach analytically proves that the Berry phase for any finite-length 1D AKLT chain equals $\pi$. Furthermore, we offer an alternative derivation showing that the 2D AKLT state on a hexagonal lattice reduces to a graph state, highlighting its potential as a universal resource for quantum computing. Additionally, we construct 2D higher-order topological phases diagrammatically to illustrate a symmetry-breaking phase transition. Collectively, these findings establish the ZXH-calculus as a potent tool for fully graphical state representation and computation, promising more efficient many-body algorithms and offering fresh diagrammatic insights into quantum phase transitions.

This study presents a search for narrow vector resonances that decay into quark-antiquark pairs, utilizing data from proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV recorded by the CMS detector at the LHC. The dataset corresponds to an integrated luminosity of 35.9 inverse femtobarns. The analysis targets hypothetical resonances produced with high transverse momentum, causing their decay products to merge into a single jet exhibiting two-prong substructure. Potential signals are identified as peaks above a smoothly falling background in the jet invariant mass distribution, employing new jet substructure methods. No evidence for such a resonance was found within the 50–300 GeV mass range. Consequently, 95% confidence level upper limits on the production cross-section were established and displayed across a mass-coupling parameter space. These limits constrain simplified dark matter production models where a mediator couples quarks and dark matter particles via vector or axial-vector currents. Within this framework, the results represent the most sensitive constraints to date, marking the first extension of the search region to masses below 100 GeV.

Recent observations of the long-period comet C/2016 R2 (PanSTARRS) reveal an unusually high N2/CO abundance ratio, typically exceeding 0.05 and standing at least two to three times higher than that of 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko. Additionally, this comet exhibits a significant depletion in H2O relative to other comets. This study investigates the formation conditions of a generic comet matching these two distinctive characteristics. Initially, we considered a scenario where the comet formed from clathrates; however, this hypothesis failed to account for the observed low water content. Consequently, we explored an alternative model wherein the comet's building blocks agglomerated from pure condensate grains and pebbles, utilizing a disk model to simulate the radial transport of volatiles. Our results demonstrate that N2/CO ratios consistent with C/2016 R2 can be achieved in grains condensed near the CO and N2 icelines. Furthermore, grains forming near the CO iceline yield CO/H2O ratios exceeding 100 times the initial gas-phase value. If a comet assembled from such grains, it would exhibit N2/CO and CO/H2O ratios aligning with measurements from C/2016 R2's coma. This model suggests that C/2016 R2 originated in a colder environment than comets with standard compositions and also accounts for the anomalous makeup of the interstellar comet 2I/Borisov.

This study examines the prompt light curves (LCs) of long gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) sourced from the Swift/BAT catalog. Our objectives included characterizing power spectral densities (PSDs), detecting quasiperiodic oscillations (QPOs), and performing original analyses within the time domain. We employed Lomb-Scargle periodograms to analyze PSDs and utilized wavelet scalograms to search for QPOs. Additionally, we classified GRBs based on the Hurst exponent ($H$) and the $\mathcal{A}-\mathcal{T}$ plane. The resulting PSDs were grouped into three categories: a power law (PL) with index $\beta\in(0,2)$, a power law with significant Poisson noise (PLC) where $\beta\in(1,3)$, and a smoothly broken power law (SBPL) featuring Poisson noise and a high-frequency index $\beta_2\in(2,6)$. The SBPL category produces break time scales ranging from 1 to 100 seconds. Both PL and PLC models align generally with fully developed turbulence, indicated by $\beta=5/3$. For 93% of the GRBs analyzed, $H>0.5$, indicating the widespread presence of long-term memory. No convincing substructure was identified in the $\mathcal{A}-\mathcal{T}$ plane. Furthermore, we identified 34 new QPOs, including those with constant leading periods and several chirping signals. The detection of breaks and QPOs implies characteristic time scales that, in certain GRBs, may correspond to the dynamical properties of plasma trajectories within the accretion disks driving relativistic jets.

A universal entangler (UE) is defined as a unitary operation that transforms every pure product state into an entangled state. In bipartite systems composed of particles 1 and 2 within a Hilbert space $\mathbb{C}^{d_1}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{d_2}$, a UE is established to exist whenever $\min{(d_1,d_2)}\geq 3$, excluding the specific case where $(d_1,d_2) = (3,3)$. Although almost all unitaries function as UEs whenever one exists, verifying if a specific unitary qualifies is computationally challenging because it generally requires solving an NP-hard quadratic system of equations. This study investigates the existence and construction of UEs for bipartite bosonic and fermionic systems, where wave functions reside in the symmetric or antisymmetric subspaces of $\mathbb{C}^{d}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{d}$. Developing a theory for these systems demands distinct methodologies compared to those used for distinguishable particles, as the standard discussion of entanglement is complicated by (anti)-symmetrization effects that generate practically inaccessible "pseudo entanglement." We demonstrate that, contrary to the distinguishable particle scenario, UEs exist for bosonic and fermionic systems with symmetric (respectively, antisymmetric) subspaces of $\mathbb{C}^{d}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{d}$ if and only if $d\geq 3$ (respectively, $d\geq 8$). To establish this result, we utilize algebraic geometry to analyze the unique algebraic structures of these systems. Furthermore, leveraging the relatively simple coherent state representation of unentangled bosonic states, we provide explicit constructions for two bosonic UEs. This investigation offers new insights into the entanglement characteristics of identical particle systems, particularly highlighting the distinctions between the entanglement structures of bosonic, fermionic, and distinguishable particle systems.

We introduce Tails, an open-source deep-learning framework designed to identify and localize comets within Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) image data. The ZTF is a robotic optical time-domain survey currently operating at Palomar Observatory in California, USA. Utilizing a custom EfficientDet-based architecture, Tails can detect comets in single images nearly in real time, eliminating the need for the multiple epochs required by traditional methods. The system delivers state-of-the-art performance with a 99% recall rate, a 0.01% false positive rate, and a predicted position root mean square error of 1-2 pixels. We also report initial efficiency evaluation results from a production setting on ZTF Twilight survey data, which include the first AI-assisted discovery of a comet (C/2020 T2) and the recovery of another (P/2016 J3 = P/2021 A3).

Identifying community structures within social networks has garnered significant interest in sociology and behavioral sciences. These networks possess a dynamic character, evolving continuously over time, and often display a hierarchical organization driven by key individuals such as managers and decision-makers. Detecting and visualizing how these networks shift in response to societal events and individual roles remains a complex challenge. This paper addresses these challenges by introducing a system designed to analyze dynamic social networks, which relies on dynamic graph discretization and clustering techniques. The system facilitates the identification of significant structural changes in communities over time and uncovers hierarchies by pinpointing influential members. Empirical evaluations using two distinct datasets demonstrate that the proposed system effectively reveals insightful details regarding the social and hierarchical architectures inherent in these networks.

This research addresses the challenge of dividing a simple polygon $P$ into the fewest possible polygonal fragments, where each fragment adheres to a specific size constraint. We present algorithms for seven distinct definitions of "bounded size," including limits on area, perimeter, straight-line diameter, and geodesic diameter, as well as constraints requiring each piece to fit within a unit disk, an axis-aligned unit square, or an arbitrarily rotated unit square.

While a generalized version of the area-based partitioning problem has been previously explored, this study introduces a specific variant where, alongside polygon $P$, a set of positive real values $a_1,\ldots,a_k$ is provided such that their sum equals the total area of $P$. The objective is to partition $P$ into exactly $k$ pieces, $Q_1,\ldots,Q_k$, where the area of each $Q_i$ matches the corresponding $a_i$. Although such a partition is guaranteed to exist and a prior algorithm achieved an $O(nk)$ running time (with $n$ being the number of vertices of $P$), we introduce an algorithm with an optimal running time of $O(n+k)$. For polygons containing holes, our approach achieves a running time of $O(n\log n+k)$.

Regarding the other size-constrained problems, computing optimal partitions for simple polygons appears intractable, even under highly restricted conditions like when $P$ is a square. Consequently, we develop $O(1)$-approximation algorithms, ensuring that the number of pieces generated is at most a constant factor greater than the minimum required. Unlike existing methods that forbid Steiner points—requiring all vertices of the resulting pieces to coincide with vertices of $P$—our algorithms always produce valid partitions, even when no such partition exists under the strict vertex constraint. Moreover, we note that optimal partitions without Steiner points may necessitate $\Omega(n)$ pieces for polygons where a solution using only two pieces is achievable if Steiner points are permitted.

This paper aims to establish Ein--Lazarsfeld's conjecture regarding the asymptotic vanishing of syzygies for algebraic varieties. Combined with their earlier theorem on asymptotic nonvanishing, this work elucidates the comprehensive behavior of minimal free resolutions for the graded section rings of line bundles on projective varieties as the line bundles' positivity increases. Prior research by Raicu narrowed the problem to the specific case of products of three projective spaces, which is resolved in this study.

The $k$-gonal random group models are constructed as quotients of free groups with $n$ generators, where relations are cyclically reduced words of length $k$. As $k$ grows indefinitely, this framework converges toward the Gromov density model. This paper demonstrates that for any fixed $d_0 \in (0, 1)$, if $k$-gonal random groups exhibit Property (T) with overwhelming probability for densities $d > d_0$, then this property also holds for $nk$-gonal random groups for any natural number $n$. Specifically, this result implies that for densities exceeding $1/3$, groups within $3k$-gonal models satisfy Property (T) with probability approaching 1 as $n$ tends to infinity.

We present two main findings regarding computational complexity classes. First, we address a modified version of the random oracle hypothesis introduced by Bennett and Gill, who demonstrated that P ≠ NP relative to a randomly selected oracle with probability 1. Although this hypothesis was subsequently refuted in multiple ways—most notably in 1992 when IP was shown to equal PSPACE despite the classes being separated with probability 1—we introduce a novel definition of "large" based on the Ellentuck topology. Within this framework, we show that the collection of oracles separating NP and co-NP is not small, and we derive analogous results for the separation of PSPACE from PH and NP from BQP. Furthermore, we establish that this revised hypothesis serves as a sufficient condition for unrelativized relationships in these three specific instances. Second, we examine the descriptive complexity of the oracle classes responsible for these separations and pinpoint their precise location within the Borel hierarchy.

This research investigates linear perturbations around non-rotating black hole solutions within scalar-tensor frameworks, specifically Horndeski theories. We examine two specific models known to support hairy black hole solutions: the first is Einstein-scalar-Gauss-Bonnet theory, which features a Gauss-Bonnet term coupled to a scalar field and yields black hole solutions via a perturbative expansion based on a small parameter representing the deviation from general relativity. The second is 4-dimensional-Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet theory, interpretable as a compactification of higher-dimensional Lovelock theories, which allows for an exact black hole solution. We analyze both axial and polar perturbations for these solutions, reformulating their equations of motion into a first-order radial differential system. This approach facilitates the study of asymptotic behaviors at the horizon and infinity using a recently developed algorithm. Furthermore, for axial perturbations, we derive effective Schrödinger-like equations, providing explicit formulas for the potentials and propagation speeds. Our findings reveal that while perturbations in the Einstein-scalar-Gauss-Bonnet solution remain well-behaved, those in the 4-dimensional-Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet theory display unusual asymptotic characteristics near the horizon and at infinity, rendering the definition of ingoing and outgoing modes impossible. These results suggest that the perturbation dynamics in this theory differ significantly from general relativity and appear pathological.

Researchers have introduced learning-based pre-simulation models, which map IC layouts to their fabricated circuit shapes to predict fabrication-induced deformations. These models typically rely on pairwise learning, requiring extensive training data consisting of layout patterns paired with their corresponding post-fabrication shape images. However, gathering reference shape images for every layout clip is both costly and time-intensive. To mitigate this challenge, we present a deep learning framework for layout novelty detection that identifies unseen patterns which a pre-trained pre-simulation model struggles to predict accurately. Our approach employs a global-local novelty scoring mechanism utilizing two subnetworks: an autoencoder to capture global structural dissimilarities between input layouts and training data, and a pre-trained pre-simulation model to extract latent codes representing local fabrication deformations. By combining global dissimilarity with local deformation features enhanced by a self-attention mechanism, our system effectively detects novelties without requiring ground-truth circuit shapes for test samples. Leveraging these detected novelties, we develop two active-learning strategies to selectively fabricate a minimal set of representative layouts most valuable for updating the model. Experimental results confirm that our method is effective in detecting layout novelties and that our active-learning strategies successfully select representative novel layouts to maintain the pre-simulation model's performance.

A Coxeter link is formed by closing a product of two braids, where one component is a quasi-Coxeter element and the other consists of partial full twists. This category of links encompasses torus knots \(T_{n,k}\) and torus links \(T_{n,nk}\). We establish that the knot homology of a Coxeter link corresponds to the space of sections of a specific line bundle defined on a natural extension of the punctual locus within the flag Hilbert scheme of points in \(\mathbb{C}^2\).

Internet censors must constantly identify and block emerging proxy servers to bypass restrictions. This study examines the time lag between when a proxy becomes detectable and when it is successfully blocked, specifically focusing on obfuscated Tor bridges. Researchers measured this delay by testing bridge accessibility before and after their integration into the Tor Browser, conducting tests from locations in the U.S., China, and Iran over a five-month span. Results from China's national firewall show that blocking new bridges occurred with varying delays ranging from 2 to 36 days. Crucially, censorship only took effect following the release of updated end-user software, even though bridges might have been discoverable through other means earlier. Although the firewall eventually identified Tor Browser bridges, those appearing solely in Orbot, the mobile version of Tor, remained unblocked. These findings reveal that censors can act in counterintuitive ways, creating challenges for threat modeling while simultaneously offering new avenues for evasion.

This study employs gauge/string duality to examine Liouvillian integrability conditions for string sigma models, specifically within the recently introduced Arutyunov-Bassi-Lacroix (ABL) model [JHEP \textbf{03} (2021), 062]. Our findings complement earlier numerical investigations and Lax pair formulations by analyzing a winding string ansatz on the deformed torus $T^{\qty(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda)}_{k}$, which can be viewed as a system of coupled pendulums. Our analysis demonstrates that the associated sigma model is Liouvillian nonintegrable. Furthermore, we derive the \emph{generalized} decoupling limit and verify the analytic integrability of the resulting decoupled sector.

This paper primarily investigates cognitive exploitation within cache-enabled device-to-device (D2D) communication that operates under a multi-channel cellular network. D2D pairs establish direct links by sensing available cellular channels, thereby circumventing the base station (BS). The study incorporates dynamic service requirements and evaluates network performance using stochastic geometry. Initially, node locations are modeled as mutually independent Poisson Point Processes, followed by the formulation of the service queueing process. Subsequently, tier association and cognitive access protocols are developed. The analysis further elaborates on queue delay and length at both the BS and D2D transmitters, characterizing traffic dynamics of request arrivals and departures as a discrete-time multiserver queue with priorities. Additionally, the joint impacts of physical layer characteristics and content-centric features on system performance are examined to offer valuable insights.

Using first-principles calculations based on the plane-wave pseudopotential method and generalized gradient approximation, this study investigates how pressure influences the structural, elastic, electronic, and optical characteristics of the half-Heusler compounds ScPtSb and YPtSb, which crystallize in a cubic MgAgAs-type structure. Spin-orbit coupling was included in the computations, yielding equilibrium lattice parameters that align well with existing experimental and theoretical data. Mechanical stability and crystal rigidity were analyzed through elastic constants and associated metrics, including bulk and shear moduli, Debye temperature, Poisson's ratio, Young's modulus, and isotropic sound velocities. Electronic band structure results indicate that ScPtSb possesses an indirect $\Gamma-X$ band gap, while YPtSb exhibits a direct $\Gamma-\Gamma$ band gap. Additionally, the impact of pressure on various optical properties—specifically the dielectric function, absorption spectrum, refractive index, extinction coefficient, reflectivity, and energy-loss spectrum—was examined for both materials.

We analyze the collective excitation spectrum of quasi-two-dimensional binary Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) incorporating both spin-orbit (SO) and Rabi couplings. Employing Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) theory, we examine how the strengths of SO and Rabi couplings influence the dynamical stability of these coupled systems. By examining the eigenenergies of the BdG spectrum, we identify phonon, roton, and maxon modes under weak repulsive intra- and inter-species contact interactions. Notably, the depth of the roton mode's minimum exhibits a strong dependence on coupling strength. Our findings reveal that increasing SO coupling induces instability, whereas increasing Rabi coupling enhances stability. Furthermore, the eigenvectors of the BdG spectrum indicate that stable regimes are characterized by density-like modes, while unstable regimes feature spin-like modes. We construct a phase diagram mapping the stability regions within the plane of SO and Rabi coupling strengths. Finally, we validate our spectral observations with direct numerical simulations based on the coupled Gross-Pitaevskii equations.

Dynamic load balancing involves distributing balls into bins within a dynamic environment where both entities can be inserted or deleted. The objective is to minimize the maximum load per bin while simultaneously reducing the number of balls and bins affected during updates, all while maintaining an efficient, hashing-like mechanism to locate a ball given its ID.

Given a balancing parameter $c=1+\epsilon$ (where $0 < \epsilon < 1$), and current counts of $n$ balls and $m$ bins, the goal is to ensure no bin exceeds a load of $C = \lceil c n/m \rceil$, defined as the bin capacity. The proposed scheme allows locating a ball by inspecting $1+O(\log 1/\epsilon)$ bins on average. Upon inserting or deleting a ball, we expect to move $O(1/\epsilon)$ balls; for bin insertions or deletions, we expect to move $O(C/\epsilon)$ balls. These improvements represent a factor of $1/\epsilon$ better than previous bounds.

While these bounds are optimal when $C=O(1)$, superior performance is achievable for larger $C$. We define a function $f$ as follows: $f=\epsilon C$ if $C\leq \log 1/\epsilon$; $f=\epsilon\sqrt{C}\cdot \sqrt{\log(1/(\epsilon\sqrt{C}))}$ if $\log 1/\epsilon\leq C<\tfrac{1}{2\epsilon^2}$; and $f=C$ if $C\geq \tfrac{1}{2\epsilon^2}$. Under these conditions, we expect to move $O(1/f)$ balls when updating a ball and $O(C/f)$ balls when updating a bin.

To achieve the bounds for larger $C$, we first address a simpler probabilistic problem: placing $n$ balls into $m$ bins of capacity $C$ sequentially, where each ball selects a uniformly random non-full bin. We demonstrate that, in expectation and with high probability, the fraction of non-full bins is $\Theta(f)$. Consequently, the expected number of bins a new ball must visit to find an available slot is $\Theta(1/f)$. Notably, this same complexity holds for our more complex scheme accommodating dynamic additions and removals of both balls and bins.

We introduce a new optomechanical inertial sensor designed for low-frequency applications, featuring corresponding acceleration measurements. With a resonant frequency of 4.7 Hz, a mechanical quality factor of 476k, a 2.6-gram test mass, and a projected noise floor of approximately $5 \times 10^{-11} \, \text{m/s}^2/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ at 1 Hz, this device offers compelling advantages for future geodesy missions. Its compact size, minimal weight, low power requirements, and resilience to environmental factors like magnetic fields or drag make it highly suitable for such tasks. Furthermore, this paper provides an experimental demonstration of detecting low-frequency ground seismic noise through direct comparison with a commercial seismometer, alongside data analysis algorithms designed to identify, characterize, and correct various noise sources.

Accurately gauging uncertainty in the face of the unknown is fundamental to intelligent decision-making. Yet, machine learning models often fail to provide reliable uncertainty estimates, resulting in erroneous and overconfident predictions when they encounter classes not present during training. Although equipping classifiers with robust uncertainty assessments is crucial for real-world application, previous research has largely been confined to small datasets with minimal discrepancy between training and testing distributions. To address this limitation, we present UIMNET: a realistic, ImageNet-scale benchmark designed to evaluate predictive uncertainty in deep image classifiers. This framework includes implementations of eight state-of-the-art algorithms, six uncertainty metrics, four in-domain metrics, and three out-of-domain metrics, alongside a fully automated pipeline for training, calibration, ensembling, selection, and evaluation. As an open-source resource, all results are reproducible from a fixed repository commit. Adding new datasets, algorithms, or metrics requires only a few lines of code, with the hope that UIMNET serves as a catalyst for rigorous and reproducible uncertainty research. Our findings indicate that ensembles of Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) classifiers and single MIMO classifiers currently offer the best approaches for estimating uncertainty regarding both in-domain and out-of-domain classes.

HD 222925 holds the record for the highest number of trans-iron elements detected in any extragalactic star and offers the most comprehensive chemical inventory among r-process-enhanced, metal-poor stars. Although the abundance patterns of its heaviest elements align with scaled Solar r-process residuals, the newly measured lighter r-process elements show significant deviations from Solar counterparts. This study investigates whether a single astrophysical site could account for the full range of elements ($34\leq Z\leq 90$) found in HD 22225. We conclude that current nucleosynthesis models struggle to reproduce the patterns of these newly identified lighter elements. While the most probable explanation suggests these light r-process elements formed in rapidly expanding ejecta—such as dynamical ejecta from compact object mergers—their patterns can also be replicated using alternative nuclear mass models. This discrepancy highlights an urgent need for experimental nuclear data for elements with $46\lesssim Z\lesssim 52$. Regardless of the specific cause, the novel abundance profile of HD 222925, derived largely from space-based ultraviolet (UV) observations, demands a more profound understanding of both r-process astrophysical sites and nuclear physics. Future UV surveys of other r-process-enhanced stars are essential to determine if HD 222925 serves as a canonical template for the r-process at low metallicities.

Hypergraph neural networks (HNNs) that utilize neural architectures to encode hypergraphs offer a promising approach for modeling higher-order data relations and addressing associated prediction tasks. However, real-world higher-order relations are frequently characterized by complex patterns and high irregularity, making it difficult to design HNNs that can effectively represent these relations without sacrificing computational efficiency. Drawing inspiration from hypergraph diffusion algorithms, this study introduces ED-HNN, a novel HNN architecture that provably captures any continuous equivariant hypergraph diffusion operator capable of modeling diverse higher-order relations. By integrating star expansions of hypergraphs with standard message-passing neural networks, ED-HNN achieves efficient implementation. Furthermore, ED-HNN demonstrates superior performance in handling heterophilic hypergraphs and constructing deep architectures. Evaluated on nine real-world datasets for node classification, ED-HNN consistently outperforms the best existing baselines across all datasets, achieving over a 2% increase in prediction accuracy on four of them.

Current fair machine learning research focuses mainly on classification tasks involving discrimination. However, as algorithms are deployed in new settings, the resulting harms differ qualitatively from those traditionally examined. Existing metrics and definitions fail to capture these distinct forms of injustice; for instance, algorithmic collusion creates market unfairness that negatively impacts all consumers, rather than just specific protected groups. Drawing on this case study, I propose an ethical framework for fair machine learning in emerging domains. This approach links fairness metrics to specific normative principles, allowing them to address concerns beyond discrimination. I outline this framework, provide its philosophical justification, and apply it to algorithmic collusion, concluding with the proposal's limitations and potential directions for future research.

This research investigates the global behavior of the mean curvature flow applied to non-separating hypersurfaces $S$ within closed manifolds. Specifically, we demonstrate that if $S$ possesses non-vanishing mean curvature, its level set flow converges smoothly to an embedded minimal hypersurface $\Gamma$. A comparable result is established for the surgery-based flow in two dimensions. Leveraging these findings, we prove the existence of monotone incompressible isotopies in manifolds characterized by negative curvature. By integrating this outcome with min-max theory, we establish that quasi-Fuchsian and hyperbolic $3$-manifolds fibered over $\mathrm{S}^1$ admit smooth entire foliations where the leaves are either minimal or exhibit non-vanishing mean curvature. Furthermore, we confirm the presence of outermost minimal surfaces in quasi-Fuchsian ends and analyze their continuity relative to variations in the quasi-Fuchsian metric.

A mixed graph is defined as \emph{second kind hermitian integral} (or \emph{HS-integral}) when the eigenvalues of its second-kind Hermitian-adjacency matrix are integers. It is termed \emph{Eisenstein integral} if the eigenvalues of its (0, 1)-adjacency matrix consist of Eisenstein integers. This work characterizes the set $S$ such that a mixed circulant graph $\text{Circ}(\mathbb{Z}_n, S)$ is HS-integral. Additionally, it is demonstrated that a mixed circulant graph is Eisenstein integral if and only if it is HS-integral. Furthermore, the eigenvalues and HS-eigenvalues for certain oriented circulant graphs are formulated using the generalized Möbius function.

Current image retrieval research typically handles one or two query inputs, failing to generalize to multiple queries. This study addresses the more complex task of composing numerous multimodal queries for image retrieval. Our objective is to retrieve target images that encompass the semantic concepts defined by an arbitrary set of query images and/or texts. To achieve this, we introduce a novel Multimodal Probabilistic Composer (MPC) designed to learn embeddings that flexibly encode the semantics of diverse queries. Specifically, we represent input images and texts as probabilistic embeddings, which are then combined using a probabilistic composition rule to enable effective retrieval across multiple multimodal queries. We establish a new benchmark based on the MS-COCO dataset and evaluate our model across various configurations involving multiple image and/or text queries. Demonstrating that our approach requires no complex auxiliary components, we show that the probabilistic formulation significantly outperforms existing methods in multimodal image retrieval while effectively generalizing to queries with varying numbers of inputs across different visual and textual modalities. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/andreineculai/MPC.

Self-supervised representation learning addresses the challenge of recognition tasks that suffer from a scarcity of manually labeled data but possess abundant unlabeled data—a frequent situation in sound event research. This study investigates unsupervised contrastive learning as a mechanism for acquiring sound event representations. Specifically, we introduce a pretext task involving the contrast of differently augmented views of sound events, where these views are generated mainly by mixing training examples with unrelated backgrounds and applying additional data augmentations. Through ablation experiments, we dissect the primary components of our approach. We assess the learned representations via linear evaluation and two in-domain downstream sound event classification tasks: one utilizing limited manually labeled data and another employing noisy labeled data. Our findings indicate that unsupervised contrastive pre-training effectively reduces the impact of data scarcity and enhances robustness against label noise, thereby surpassing supervised baselines.

Fair machine learning research typically distinguishes between `group` and `individual` fairness metrics. While many technical studies assume these concepts are mutually exclusive and focus on minimizing the trade-offs between them, this paper contends that such a conflict stems from a misunderstanding. Drawing on theoretical insights from fair machine learning, as well as political and legal philosophy, the author argues that individual and group fairness are not inherently contradictory. First, the paper outlines egalitarian fairness frameworks that provide plausible motivations for both metrics, suggesting that no principled conflict exists. Second, it examines the concept of individual justice within legal philosophy and jurisprudence, demonstrating that while it appears similar to individual fairness in machine learning literature, it actually contradicts it. The conclusion is that the perceived tension is an artifact of applying fairness measures too broadly, rather than a clash of underlying principles. Practically, this issue can be resolved by carefully analyzing the specific sources of unfairness in a given deployment context and applying mitigation measures with rigorous justification.

Quantum circuits face strict constraints on qubit and gate counts when executed on quantum hardware. A viable strategy to satisfy both limits is leveraging uncomputation to exchange qubits for gates. We introduce Reqomp, an automated method for synthesizing correct and efficient ancilla uncomputation that adheres to hardware constraints. For any given circuit, Reqomp provides a spectrum of trade-offs between minimizing qubit usage and reducing gate counts. Our evaluation shows that Reqomp can lower the number of required ancilla qubits by as much as 96%. Furthermore, on 80% of our benchmarks, the method reduces ancilla qubits by at least 25% without increasing the gate count by more than 28%.

We present Halfedge Texturing (Htex), a GPU-optimized technique for applying textures to arbitrary polygon meshes without the need for explicit parameterization. This method leverages the observation that halfedges naturally define an intrinsic triangulation, with each halfedge uniquely spanning a triangle and maintaining direct adjacency data. Unlike prior parameterization-free approaches that assign a distinct texture to every mesh face, Htex allocates a square texture to each halfedge and its twin. We demonstrate that shifting from a face-based to a halfedge-based storage scheme yields two key advantages for high-performance texturing: first, it natively accommodates arbitrary polygon topologies without requiring specialized handling for non-quad faces; second, it enables a streamlined and efficient GPU implementation that generates continuous texturing across the entire mesh using only three texture fetches per halfedge. The efficacy of Htex is validated through real-time rendering of production-grade assets.

The topological charge (TC) of light rings (LRs) in a spacetime is defined as the difference between the count of stable and unstable LRs, remaining invariant under smooth deformations with fixed boundaries. Typically, asymptotically flat equilibrium black holes (BHs) possess a TC of -1. However, within Einstein-Maxwell theory, the Schwarzschild-Melvin black hole—a neutral BH situated in a strong magnetic field—exhibits a TC of 0. This property permits the existence of black holes devoid of light rings, resulting in distinctive phenomena such as panoramic shadows. This study examines the generalized Schwarzschild-Melvin solution within Einstein-Maxwell-dilaton theory by varying the dilaton coupling $a$. Our findings reveal that the TC undergoes a discontinuous shift from 0 to -1 exactly at the Kaluza-Klein limit ($a=\sqrt{3}$), where the empty Melvin solution represents a twisted Kaluza-Klein reduction of five-dimensional flat spacetime; thus, the dilaton coupling $a$ triggers a topological transition in the TC. We connect this qualitative shift to the Melvin asymptotics across different $a$ values and further analyze the shadows and lensing effects of the generalized Schwarzschild-Melvin solution for various $a$, linking these observations to the TC.

This paper investigates the existence of field theories in four spacetime dimensions, beyond standard supergravity, that possess symmetries including local spacetime translations and supersymmetries defined by transformations whose commutators yield infinitesimal local translations. Several new supersymmetric free field theories are identified as potential candidates for this class. The authors outline a method to extend these free theories into globally supersymmetric frameworks with the required properties, explicitly constructing one such class. These theories resemble globally supersymmetric Yang-Mills theories in flat spacetime but feature supersymmetries generated by transformations whose commutators produce infinitesimal general coordinate transformations with field-dependent gauge parameters.

This study examines the thermodynamics and weak cosmic censorship conjecture for charged anti-de Sitter black holes within the framework of massive gravity, using the absorption of scalar particles and fermions. By treating the cosmological constant as pressure with its conjugate volume, the first law of thermodynamics is upheld. However, the second law of thermodynamics is found to be violated in the extended phase space of extremal black holes. Furthermore, the validity of the weak cosmic censorship conjecture is assessed for both near-extremal and extremal cases by calculating the minimum values of the metric function $f$; the results indicate that the black holes retain their near-extremal and extremal states following particle absorption.

Adverse weather frequently impairs transportation system operations. Current approaches typically rely on sensor arrays or in-vehicle cameras to forecast weather, yet these methods incur incremental costs and offer limited scope. To guarantee the uninterrupted operation of all transportation services regardless of conditions, a robust detection system capable of classifying weather in the wild is essential. However, solving this problem is challenging due to the diverse nature of weather conditions and the lack of distinctive features across different scenarios. Existing solutions are often scene-specific and restricted to classifying only two weather categories. This paper introduces a novel open-source dataset named RFS, comprising images of three weather classes: rain, snow, and fog. Additionally, a new algorithm is proposed that employs super-pixel delimiting masks for data augmentation, achieving reasonable performance across ten Convolutional Neural Network architectures.

This study examines the precision with which two angles of the "flat" unitarity triangle, defined by $V_{ub}^* V_{us} + V_{cb}^* V_{cs} + V_{tb}^* V_{ts} =0$, can be directly measured at FCCee. We demonstrate that the uncertainties for the angles $\alpha_s = \arg(- V_{ub}^* V_{us} /V_{tb}^* V_{ts})$ and $\beta_s = \arg(-V_{tb}^* V_{ts} / V_{cb}^* V_{cs})$ are expected to be superior to $0.4^\circ$ and $0.035^\circ$, respectively. When these results are integrated with the measurement of the third angle, $\gamma_s = \arg(- V_{cb}^* V_{cs}/ V_{ub}^* V_{us})$, as detailed in a separate publication, they will enable a rigorous test of the CP sector's consistency within the Standard Model with exceptional accuracy.

This study examines momentum differences among charged hadrons in high-energy proton-proton collisions to investigate coherent particle production. The observed correlation patterns align with a model depicting a helical QCD string that fragments into a sequence of ground-state hadrons. A threshold momentum difference for adjacent charged hadron pairs is detected, matching theoretical predictions. Furthermore, low-mass hadron chains account for charge-combination-dependent two-particle correlations often ascribed to Bose-Einstein interference. The dataset comprises 190 inverse microbarns of minimum bias events from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV, gathered during the early low-luminosity phase of the LHC using the ATLAS detector.

Although planetary science and plasma physics are closely linked, there are limited advanced numerical tools capable of uniting these fields. The Menura code represents a significant advancement by enabling self-consistent modeling of this overlapping domain through a novel two-step approach, facilitating global simulations of the interaction between a fully turbulent solar wind and various solar system bodies. This paper presents the new code and its two-step global algorithm, demonstrating its capabilities with an initial case study of the interaction between a turbulent solar wind and a comet.

Conventional soft pneumatic gripping relies on pressurizing soft elastomeric structures, which constrains designs regarding size, mass, force capacity, and manufacturability. Conversely, fabric-based inflatable systems provide high stiffness-to-weight ratios for soft robotics but remain underexplored in terms of actuation. This work introduces a novel class of pneumatic soft grippers that utilizes the in-plane over-curvature of inextensible fabric flat balloons during inflation. The proposed star-shaped gripper contracts radially when pressurized, generating a gripping force whose magnitude is adjustable via pressure input. Initially, the kinematics and mechanics of a single V-shaped actuator are investigated through experiments, finite element simulations, and analytical modeling. These findings are then applied to predict the mechanical behavior of the full star configuration, optimize its geometry, and enhance both contraction and stiffness. Furthermore, stacking multiple stars within a rigid frame is shown to significantly increase gripping force. We anticipate that the flexibility, robustness, scalability, and ease of fabrication inherent to this approach will enable a new generation of lighter, larger actuators capable of producing higher forces to manipulate delicate and irregular objects while maintaining manageable complexity.

Room acoustic measurements play a vital role across various audio research domains, including physical modeling, speech enhancement, and virtual reality. This paper details the technical specifications and methodological decisions behind capturing a dataset of spatial room impulse responses (SRIRs) within a variable acoustics environment. The study employs two spherical microphone arrays: the mh Acoustics Eigenmike em32, which supports fourth-order Ambisonic capture, and the Zylia ZM-1, capable of third-order Ambisonic capture. The dataset comprises recordings from three source locations and seven receiver positions, repeated across five distinct room acoustic configurations with varying reverberation levels. Potential applications for this dataset include six degrees-of-freedom (6DoF) analysis and rendering, SRIR interpolation, and spatial dereverberation techniques.

A thirteen-year dataset from the Fermi Large Area Telescope (Fermi/LAT) concerning 4FGL J0824.9+3915 is examined to reassess whether 4C +39.23B, a compact steep-spectrum (CSS) source located near the flat-spectrum radio quasar 4C +39.23A within the $\gamma$-ray emitting zone of 4FGL J0824.9+3915, actually emits $\gamma$-rays. Our analysis reveals that the time-integrated $\gamma$-ray output of 4FGL J0824.9+3915 is overwhelmingly driven by 4C +39.23A, which exhibits significant variability at a 6.7$\sigma$ confidence level. The mean $\gamma$-ray flux in the 0.1--300 GeV range is $(1.60\pm 0.15)\times10^{-8}$ ph cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, with a power-law photon spectral index of $2.48\pm0.05$. Between MJD 57500 and 58500, 4FGL J0824.9+3915 entered a low state characterized by steady $\gamma$-ray flux. An analysis of Fermi/LAT data from this specific interval yielded Test Statistic (TS) values of approximately 5 for 4C +39.23A and 31 for 4C +39.23B, indicating that $\gamma$-ray emission during this period is dominated by the CSS source 4C +39.23B. The calculated average flux for 4C +39.23B in this window is $(9.40\pm4.10)\times 10^{-9}$ ph cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, with a spectral index $\Gamma_{\gamma}=2.45\pm0.17$. By modeling the spectral energy distribution (SED) of 4C +39.23B using a two-zone leptonic model to account for radiation from both its core and extended regions, we determined that its $\gamma$-ray emission originates from the core. The derived magnetic field strength and Doppler boosting factor for this core are 0.13 G and 6.5, respectively. When compared to other $\gamma$-ray emitting CSS sources and compact symmetric objects (CSOs) in the $\Gamma_{\gamma}-L_{\gamma}$ plane, 4C +39.23B aligns with the characteristics of CSSs.

Humans have an inherent capacity to recognize and distinguish unfamiliar instances by adapting their existing knowledge, all without compromising their performance on previously learned tasks. Drawing inspiration from this, we define and formulate a new, practical problem setting called Novel Class Discovery without Forgetting (NCDwF). This setting requires a machine learning model to progressively discover new categories from unlabeled data while retaining its proficiency on earlier classes. Our contributions include: 1) a technique to create pseudo-latent representations that serve as proxies for inaccessible labeled data, thus mitigating forgetting; 2) a mutual-information-based regularizer that improves the unsupervised identification of novel classes; and 3) a straightforward Known Class Identifier that facilitates generalized inference when test data includes both familiar and unfamiliar categories. We establish experimental protocols using CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-1000 to evaluate the trade-off between knowledge retention and new class discovery. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that current models suffer from catastrophic forgetting when identifying new categories, whereas our approach effectively balances these competing goals. We hope this work encourages further investigation into this newly defined practical problem.

By introducing a minor correction to the Maxwell field, we demonstrate that the resulting black hole solutions—identified as asymptotically Reissner–Nordström black holes—exhibit a reentrant phase transition and display novel phase behaviors. Furthermore, we establish that this slight nonlinear modification significantly impacts the phase structure of these solutions. This influence facilitates a new classification within the canonical ensemble of extended phase space, applicable when the nonlinearity parameter $\alpha$ satisfies $\alpha \lesseqqgtr 4q^{2}/7$. We analyze these three distinct classes to explore deviations from standard Reissner–Nordström solutions. Notably, we observe a reentrant phase transition for $\alpha < 4q^{2}/7$, whereas at the specific case of $\alpha = 4q^{2}/7$, no phase transition occurs below or at the critical point. In this final scenario, small and large black holes remain thermodynamically distinguishable at temperatures and pressures exceeding the critical values.

To facilitate comparison with other antenna systems, the voltage power spectral density recorded by the Solar Orbiter's Radio and Plasma Waves (RPW) receiver must be transformed into physical quantities dependent on the radiation's intrinsic properties. The primary objective of this study is to calibrate the RPW dipole antenna system, enabling the conversion of input voltage power spectral density into incoming flux density. This calibration utilizes space observations from the Thermal Noise Receiver (TNR) and the High Frequency Receiver (HFR). Additionally, Type III burst observations from the Wind spacecraft provide a reference radio flux density for cross-calibrating the RPW dipoles. By analyzing approximately ten months of HFR data in conjunction with TNR-HFR data prior to antenna deployment, we estimated the reference system noise of the TNR-HFR receivers. We successfully determined the effective length of the RPW dipoles and the reference system noise of the TNR-HFR in the space environment, where antennas and pre-amplifiers are immersed in the solar wind plasma. The derived effective length ($l_{eff}$) values align with ground-based simulations and measurements. Furthermore, an investigation of 35 Type III bursts simultaneously detected by Solar Orbiter and Wind revealed that while the scaling of decay time versus frequency remains consistent between the Waves and RPW instruments, the median values are higher for the Waves. This offers the first observational proof that Type III radio waves continue to experience density scattering even after propagating from the source through a medium with a plasma frequency significantly lower than their emission frequency.

Recent years have seen significant focus on deep learning for vision-based construction safety systems, particularly concerning personal protective equipment. Despite this interest, reliably linking workers to their hard hats remains an unresolved challenge. This article proposes a solution combining deep learning, object detection, head keypoint localization, and straightforward rule-based reasoning. Testing demonstrates that this approach outperforms prior methods relying on relative bounding box positions or direct detection of wearers versus non-wearers. The findings indicate that integrating novel deep learning techniques with interpretable rule-based systems yields a reliable solution capable of effectively replicating manual on-site supervision. This research advances the development of fully autonomous construction safety systems and highlights further potential for improvement in this domain.

This paper investigates nonconvex homogeneous quadratically constrained quadratic optimization problems with one or two constraints, labeled (QQ1) and (QQ2). The latter encompasses (QQ1), the trust region subproblem (TRS), and the ellipsoid-regularized total least squares problem as specific instances. While a necessary and sufficient condition for global optimality exists for (QQ2), we demonstrate that every local minimizer of (QQ1) is in fact globally optimal. In contrast to the TRS case, which allows at most one local non-global minimizer, (QQ2) can possess infinitely many such minimizers. At any local non-global minimizer of (QQ2), both the linearly independent constraint qualification and the strict complementary condition are satisfied, and the Lagrangian's Hessian exhibits exactly one negative eigenvalue. Our primary contribution establishes that the standard second-order sufficient optimality condition remains necessary for any strict local non-global minimizer of (QQ2). Finally, we explore applications and address the limitations regarding potential extensions of these results.

This study presents measurements of inclusive, prompt, and non-prompt ${\rm J}/\psi$ production in proton-lead (p-Pb) collisions at a nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}} = 5.02$ TeV. The ${\rm J}/\psi$ mesons are identified via their dielectron decay channel within the midrapidity region, extending down to a transverse momentum of $p_{\rm T} = 0$. The inclusive ${\rm J}/\psi$ nuclear modification factor, $R_{\rm pPb}$, is determined by contrasting the p-Pb results with a proton-proton reference measured at the identical center-of-mass energy. For transverse momenta exceeding 1.0 GeV/$c$, non-prompt ${\rm J}/\psi$ mesons, which arise from the decay of beauty hadrons, are statistically distinguished from promptly produced ${\rm J}/\psi$ mesons. These findings rely on data collected by the ALICE detector during the 2016 LHC p-Pb run, featuring an integrated luminosity of ${\cal L}_{\rm int} = 292 \pm 11 \; {\rm \mu b}^{-1}$, which represents a sixfold increase over previous publications. Consequently, the total uncertainties on the $p_{\rm T}$-integrated inclusive and non-prompt ${\rm J}/\psi$ cross sections have been reduced by factors of 1.7 and 2.2, respectively. The measured cross sections and $R_{\rm pPb}$ values are evaluated against theoretical models incorporating various combinations of cold nuclear matter effects. Furthermore, the ${\rm b\overline{b}}$ production cross section at midrapidity, $\mathrm{d}\sigma_{\rm b\overline{b}}/\mathrm{d}y$, as well as the total cross section extrapolated to full phase space, $\sigma_{\rm b\overline{b}}$, are derived from the non-prompt ${\rm J}/\psi$ production cross section.

Route selection in public transit has been a subject of study for some time, with path length or travel duration typically being the primary determinants. However, ticket cost also plays a significant role, as travelers generally favor cheaper options. This paper addresses the "cheapest ticket problem," which seeks the most economical route between two stations. The difficulty of solving this problem and the appropriate algorithms depend heavily on the fare structure; for instance, solutions are straightforward when prices scale with distance, but can become NP-complete under zone-based tariffs. Consequently, we examine the cheapest ticket problem across various distance-based and zone-based fare systems. Our approach involves mathematically modeling each structure, analyzing its key characteristics, and then either presenting a polynomial-time algorithm or demonstrating NP-completeness. Furthermore, we offer general findings regarding the combination of two fare structures, a scenario frequently encountered in real-world applications.

Simulating the geometry and visual properties of knitted fabrics remains difficult because of their intricate structures and complex light interactions. Existing surface-based approaches struggle to represent fine-grained knit details, whereas micro-appearance models, which explicitly store individual fibers, are costly to generate and render. Additionally, neither approach has successfully matched real photographs to simultaneously capture both light reflection and transmission. In this paper, we present an efficient method for generating knit models based on user-defined knitting patterns. Our approach stores individual knit plies with fiber-level detail, utilizing normal and tangent mapping. We assess our generated models across a diverse range of knitting patterns and qualitatively compare our renderings against photographs of real fabric samples.

This study examines phase noise in communication systems that utilize local oscillators for frequency and timing synchronization. We aim to bridge the gap between empirical measurements and analytical models for both free-running and phase-locked oscillators. Specifically, we introduce a closed-form expression for the power spectral density (PSD) of phase noise, defined by a limited set of parameters directly derived from oscillator measurements. Additionally, we present an analytical model for the oscillator's PSD. Moving to the discrete-time domain, we analyze the most prevalent discrete-time phase noise channel model in relation to these measurement parameters and system bandwidth. In this context, we demonstrate that the proposed PSD models yield analytical representations of the discrete-time phase noise signal, which are applicable for designing estimation and detection algorithms, evaluating system performance, or conducting rapid simulations.

Recent breakthroughs in machine learning have enabled the creation of artificial agents that achieve super-human proficiency across a wide range of complex tasks. However, acquiring these abilities typically requires millions of labeled examples—far exceeding the number of instances humans usually need to reach a comparable level of competence. Consequently, although current machine learning methods yield agents with superior performance, their learning efficiency per opportunity often lags significantly behind human learning rates. This study introduces a theoretical framework known as Decomposed Inductive Procedure Learning (DIPL), which illustrates how various forms of inductive symbolic learning can be integrated to develop agents that master educationally significant tasks, such as mathematical and scientific procedures, at a pace akin to human learners. Grounded in Marr's principles of computational, algorithmic, and implementation levels in cognitive modeling, we define six essential learning capacities required at the computational level to accurately simulate human learning. We show that agents constructed according to the DIPL theory can fulfill these capacities and provide both empirical and theoretical evidence that DIPL facilitates the development of agents demonstrating human-like learning performance.

Three primary biomarkers—beta-amyloid (A), pathologic tau (T), and neurodegeneration (N)—serve as validated indicators of Alzheimer's disease neuropathology. Although cerebrospinal fluid studies have extensively examined amyloid and tau levels, the spatial propagation patterns across the brain and their interactive mechanisms with neurodegeneration remain poorly understood. Consequently, this study aims to analyze the spatiotemporal relationships among ATN biomarkers using large-scale neuroimaging datasets. First, we model longitudinal transition trajectories to examine the timing of amyloid plaque formation, tau tangle accumulation, and neuronal loss. Second, we employ linear mixed-effects models to quantify regional pathological interactions and propagation dynamics for each ATN marker. Our analysis reveals a temporal delay between the accumulation of amyloid and the onset of tau pathology and neurodegeneration. Furthermore, amyloid propagation follows a diffusion pattern along the brain's topological network. Finally, our models demonstrate that the progression of pathological tau and neurodegeneration exhibits a strong regional association distinct from that of amyloid.

Stellar streams within the Galactic halo serve as valuable tools for understanding how galaxies such as the Milky Way assembled. While many recently discovered tidal streams have identified progenitor globular clusters or dwarf galaxies, the Orphan-Chenab (OC) stream remains an exception as a relatively narrow stream lacking a known parent. To identify the OC stream's origin, we combined astrometric data from the early third Gaia data release (Gaia EDR3) with radial velocities from the SDSS-IV APOGEE survey to identify up to 13 probable member stars. Using APOGEE, we analyzed the chemical compositions of these stars across $\alpha$ (O, Mg, Ca, Si, Ti, S), odd-Z (Al, K, V), Fe-peak (Fe, Ni, Mn, Co, Cr), and neutron capture (Ce) elemental groups. Our findings reveal that the OC stream stars do not form a mono-metallic population, exhibiting a median metallicity of -1.92 dex with a dispersion of 0.28 dex. Furthermore, the $\alpha$-elements appear depleted relative to typical Milky Way populations, and the [Mg/Al] ratio is inconsistent with second-generation stars found in globular clusters. These detailed chemical signatures strongly suggest that the OC stream's progenitor was a dwarf spheroidal galaxy with a mass of approximately $10^6$ M$_\odot$.

Hall-effect thrusters (HETs) are essential for contemporary near-Earth spacecraft propulsion and hold critical importance for upcoming deep-space missions. While modeling techniques for HETs are advancing quickly, current methods lack the precision needed to reliably forecast the parameters of newly designed thrusters, largely because HET plasma simulations are computationally expensive. An alternative strategy involves employing scaling techniques derived from existing experimental data. This paper introduces a novel scaling approach for HETs that utilizes neural networks and other advanced machine learning methods. The proposed model was constructed using a comprehensive database of HET parameters gathered from published literature. Its predictions are accurate within the operational parameter range covered by this dataset. During the design phase, the model assists developers in estimating the performance of new thrusters, while in experimental research, it enables the comparison of a thruster's achieved characteristics against those obtained by other developers. The study also includes a comparison with the current state-of-the-art HET scaling models.

It is widely acknowledged that neural network-based image classifiers are susceptible to being deceived by images containing minute perturbations designed by adversaries. While substantial research has focused on generating and defending against such adversarial attacks, a critical gap remains: how to reverse-engineer these perturbations from an adversarial image. This unexplored area introduces a novel adversarial learning paradigm known as Reverse Engineering of Deceptions (RED). Successful implementation of RED enables the estimation of adversarial perturbations and the recovery of original images. However, recovering these carefully crafted, tiny perturbations is challenging when optimizing a unilateral RED objective; for instance, standard image denoising methods may overfit to minimizing reconstruction error while failing to preserve the classification characteristics of the true adversarial perturbations. To address this, we formalize the RED problem and establish key principles essential for designing effective RED approaches. Specifically, we identify that prediction alignment and appropriate data augmentation via spatial transformations are critical criteria for achieving a generalizable RED method. By combining these principles with image denoising, we introduce a new framework called Class-Discriminative Denoising based RED (CDD-RED). Extensive experiments confirm the efficacy of CDD-RED across various evaluation metrics—including pixel-level, prediction-level, and attribution-level alignment—and against diverse attack generation techniques such as FGSM, PGD, CW, AutoAttack, and adaptive attacks.

The synthesis of heavy and superheavy elements has been analyzed by considering the roles of Coulomb interaction, mean fissility, mass asymmetry, and charge asymmetry parameters in relation to the deformation parameters of both projectile and target nuclei, consistent with experimental findings. These observations were categorized into four groups to evaluate various unsuccessful and planned reactions aimed at creating new superheavy elements with atomic numbers $Z=119$ and $120$. However, drawing definitive conclusions from these results is challenging due to significant discrepancies in evaporation residue cross-section data. This substantial deviation is attributed primarily to the arbitrary selection of excitation energy in the studied experiments. This complex issue can be effectively addressed through theoretical excitation function analyses utilizing advanced statistical models or the dinuclear system model, specifically by selecting an excitation energy that corresponds to the peak of the excitation function curve. We believe this approach will aid in predicting whether the estimated evaporation residue cross-sections for future planned reactions will be measurable within the detection limits of current facilities.

The proposed third-generation gravitational-wave detector, the Einstein Telescope, features a triangular configuration comprising three co-located interferometers. By summing the strain outputs from these interferometers, any gravitational-wave signal is cancelled, producing a signal-free stream referred to as the "null stream." This null stream resides within a fixed subspace of the Einstein Telescope's observation space where gravitational-wave signals cannot occur. In this study, we demonstrate the decomposition of the observation space into a signal space, which encompasses all potential gravitational-wave signals, and a null space, which contains the null stream. We show that Bayesian parameter estimation and model selection results derived from strain data within the signal space are identical to those obtained using the complete set of strain data. This finding implies that utilizing a subset of the strain data is sufficient to extract all source information, thereby reducing memory requirements and accelerating likelihood evaluations. Furthermore, we discuss how the presence of a fixed null space in the Einstein Telescope enables the unbiased estimation of noise properties within the signal-free subspace.

While extensive research on Convolutional Neural Networks has primarily addressed flat multi-class classification, real-world scenarios often involve naturally occurring hierarchical classification tasks where predicted classes are organized into a hierarchy. This paper introduces a novel architecture for hierarchical image classification that integrates a stack of deep linear layers with both cross-entropy loss and center loss. This proposed framework can be applied to any neural network model, simultaneously optimizing for local hierarchical class relationships and global information across the entire class hierarchy while penalizing violations of the class structure. Experimental results demonstrate that our hierarchical classifier offers significant advantages over traditional classification methods, making it suitable for various computer vision applications.

The stability of Landau Fermi liquid theory can be compromised when particle interactions become sufficiently strong, leading to a reconstructed ground state with a distribution distinct from the Fermi-step function. This phenomenon is examined in two specific scenarios: vector boson exchange and relativistic heavy-ion collisions. In the case of vector boson exchange, it is observed that even a relatively weak interaction strength can trigger ground-state rearrangement provided the fermion mass is large enough. Similarly, relativistic heavy-ion collisions can induce such rearrangements, thereby influencing the statistical properties of the collision system.

This paper examines space-like graphs defined on a domain $\Omega\subset M^{n}$ within the Lorentzian manifold $M^{n}\times\mathbb{R}$, equipped with the metric $-ds^{2}+\sigma$. In this setting, $M^{n}$ is a complete Riemannian $n$-manifold with metric $\sigma$, $\Omega$ possesses a piecewise smooth boundary, and $\mathbb{R}$ represents Euclidean 1-space. We establish a notable stability result concerning translating space-like graphs in $M^{n}\times\mathbb{R}$ subjected to a conformal transformation.
