The analysis involves reviewing popular keywords, synthesizing clusters into broad research topics, mapping the relationships between topics, and assessing shifts within the field.

**Results:** The research landscape is categorized into 16 high-level topics and 18 subtopics. Areas such as creation guidance, automated test generation, evolution and maintenance, and test oracles demonstrate particularly robust links to other topics, underscoring their multidisciplinary character. Emerging keywords include web and mobile applications, machine learning, energy consumption, and automated program repair and test generation, with new connections forming between web apps, test oracles, and machine learning across numerous topics. Conversely, random and requirements-based testing appear to be declining.

**Conclusions:** The findings, strategic advice, and mapped data provide deeper insight into the field and offer inspiration for exploring future challenges and connections.

Net bisimilarity serves as a behavioral equivalence for finite Petri nets that aligns with both structure-preserving bisimilarity and causal-net bisimilarity, yet offers a significantly more concise definition. This concept represents a smooth extension of standard bisimilarity as applied to Labeled Transition Systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that it admits a logical characterization via a specific modal logic known as NML (net modal logic), where two markings are net bisimilar precisely when they satisfy identical NML formulae.

We introduce a straightforward and broadly applicable analytical approximation that calculates the energy of covalent single and double bonds based on the nuclear charges of the involved atoms, utilizing only three parameters: $[{E_\text{AB} \approx a - b Z_\text{A} Z_\text{B} + c (Z_\text{A}^{7/3} + Z_\text{B}^{7/3})}]$. This functional form represents an alchemical decomposition of atomic energy between atoms A and B. Following calibration, the model yields reasonably accurate bond energy estimates for hydrogen-saturated diatomics formed by $p$-block elements within the same periodic table row ($2\le n\le 4$). Simple formulas allow for the determination of corresponding bond energy changes when atom B is substituted by C. Although our model differs in functional form and origin from Pauling's renowned electronegativity model, it achieves comparable simplicity and accuracy. Furthermore, analysis reveals that the model's response to variations in nuclear charge within covalent bonding is nearly linear, aligning with Hammett's equation.

This study examines Tchentzov's well-known projection density estimation to derive the exponential decay in the tail of the distribution for the natural normalized deviation. By adapting these estimations under the assumption of square integrability for the estimated function, we establish a recursive formulation that is more practical for applications. Despite this modification, the convergence speed remains identical to that of classical methods within the composite Hilbert space norm.

The effectiveness of vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communication relies heavily on the scheduling strategy employed. Although centralized network schedulers provide superior reliability, they are typically limited to regions with complete cellular coverage. Conversely, areas lacking cellular access traditionally rely on less efficient distributed radio resource management. To leverage the advantages of centralized scheduling for enhancing V2V reliability in cellular-deprived zones, we introduce VRLS (Vehicular Reinforcement Learning Scheduler). This centralized scheduler proactively allocates resources for out-of-coverage V2V interactions *before* vehicles exit the cellular network. By training within simulated vehicular settings, VRLS develops a robust and adaptable scheduling policy that removes the necessity for targeted retraining in intricate real-world scenarios. We assess VRLS performance across various mobility patterns, network loads, wireless channel conditions, and resource configurations. Results indicate that VRLS surpasses state-of-the-art distributed scheduling algorithms in cellular-free zones, cutting the packet error rate by half under heavy load and achieving near-maximum reliability in low-load situations.

This study explores the origins of cation ordering in double perovskites by integrating first-principles computations, machine learning (ML), and causal analysis. We constructed a broad compositional space by incorporating various oxidation states of A, A', B, and B' transition metal ions. A conventional framework utilizing traditional ML classification algorithms, specifically Random Forest (RF), alongside features such as geometry-driven metrics and key structural modes, achieves highly accurate predictions (~98%) of A-site cation ordering. The reliability of these ML models was assessed through decision path analysis, probabilistic confidence bounds, and the implementation of a direct non-Gaussian acyclic structural equation model to examine causality. Our findings indicate that structural modes are the most critical features for distinguishing between layered, columnar, and rock-salt ordering. Specifically, clear layered ordering is primarily driven by the charge difference between A and A' ions, which itself relies on the charge separation between B and B' ions. Leveraging insights from the ML models, we formulated functional relationships using these features to derive energy differences associated with clear layered ordering. Ultimately, our results identify the trilinear coupling between tilt, rotation, and A-site antiferroelectric displacement within the Landau free-energy expansion as the essential condition for the emergence of A-site cation ordering.

It is reasonable to anticipate that a comprehensive physical theory should be capable of consistently modeling agents as physical systems within that theory. In a 2018 publication, Frauchiger and Renner (FR) argued that when agents within quantum theory reason about each other's knowledge in a specific Wigner's friend scenario, they encounter a logical contradiction. Consequently, Renner frequently challenges researchers to define a set of reasoning rules suitable for programming quantum computers as agents that are (a) logically consistent, (b) applicable to any Wigner's friend scenario, (c) efficiently programmable, and (d) aligned with the temporal sequence of the protocol. This paper presents a general framework demonstrating that every logical Wigner's friend scenario (LWFS) can be represented as a single, temporally ordered quantum circuit, enabling agents in any LWFS to reason in a manner satisfying all four of these criteria. Notably, this resolution is achieved without altering classical logic, unitary quantum evolution, or the Born rule, while permitting agents' perspectives to remain fundamentally subjective. We provide a detailed analysis of the FR protocol, illustrating how the apparent paradox is resolved. We demonstrate that apparent logical contradictions in any LWFS stem solely from neglecting the selection of the Heisenberg cut in contexts where this choice is significant; accounting for this dependence invariably resolves the paradox. Our findings confirm that the universal applicability of quantum theory does not undermine multi-agent logical reasoning and we examine the implications for FR's no-go theorem. Furthermore, our formalism hints at a genuinely relational and operational description of Wigner's friend scenarios that remains consistent with both quantum theory and probability theory regarding measurement outcomes.

The integration of classical theory with the Deep Learning paradigm has propelled recent Reinforcement Learning advancements, resulting in significant AI breakthroughs and establishing Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) as a distinct research domain. This study examines contemporary DRL algorithms, emphasizing their theoretical underpinnings, practical constraints, and empirically observed characteristics.

This study establishes that the solution map for the Fokas_Olver_Rosenau_Qiao (FORQ) equation lacks uniform continuity with respect to initial data in Besov spaces. This finding generalizes earlier results demonstrating non-uniform continuity in Sobolev spaces (Nonlinear Anal., 2014) to the Besov setting and aligns with recent findings on the Novikov equation (J. Math. Fluid Mech., 2020), provided the additional term $(\partial_xu)^3$ in the FORQ equation is omitted.

Simplified Hartree-Fock calculations were performed for atoms ranging from helium to neon, employing orthonormalized basis functions for the 1s, 2s, and 2p orbitals that rely on three parameters. By utilizing Mathematica on the new Apple M1 processor, these computations complete in approximately 0.005 seconds of CPU time. This approach yields energies within 1% of the optimal Hartree-Fock results while requiring roughly an order of magnitude less computational effort.

The review examines the Solar Cycle, defined as an 11-year fluctuation in solar activity marked by changes in sunspot count and surface area. Various indicators associated with sunspots also exhibit variability, including the 10.7cm radio flux, total solar irradiance, magnetic fields, solar flares, coronal mass ejections, geomagnetic activity, galactic cosmic ray fluxes, and radioisotopes found in tree rings and ice cores. Distinctive features of individual cycles encompass their maxima and minima, duration, amplitude, shape, equatorward migration of active latitudes, hemispheric asymmetries, and active longitudes. Variability between cycles involves phenomena such as the Maunder Minimum, the Gleissberg Cycle, and the Gnevyshev-Ohl (even-odd) Rule, while short-term fluctuations include a 154-day periodicity, quasi-biennial variations, and double-peaked maxima. The discussion concludes by evaluating prediction methods for the solar cycle and providing a detailed analysis of cycles 23 and 24.

A graph $G$ is defined as $q$-Ramsey for a $q$-tuple of graphs $(H_1,\ldots,H_q)$, written as $G\to_q(H_1,\ldots,H_q)$, if any $q$-edge-coloring of $G$ yields a monochromatic copy of $H_i$ in color $i$ for at least one $i\in[q]$. The parameter $s_q(H_1,\ldots,H_q)$ represents the minimum degree of $G$ among all graphs that are minimally $q$-Ramsey for this tuple under subgraph inclusion. This parameter was first investigated in 1976 by Burr, Erd\H{o}s, and Lov\'asz, who established its exact values for pairs of cliques. While numerous researchers have focused on the symmetric case where $H_i\cong H$ for all $i\in [q]$ over the last twenty years, the asymmetric case remains underexplored. This paper advances the study of asymmetric tuples comprising cliques, cycles, and trees. Specifically, we compute $s_2(H_1,H_2)$ for pairs consisting of one clique and one tree, one clique and one cycle, or two distinct cycles. Furthermore, we extend these findings to multiple colors, deriving bounds for $s_q(C_\ell,\ldots,C_\ell,K_t,\ldots,K_t)$ based on the clique size $t$, the count of cycles, and the count of cliques. These bounds are proven to be tight up to logarithmic factors when any two of the three parameters are held constant.

We calculate the genus of the normalization for the curve defined by $H(x,y)=0$, where $H$ is the irreducible numerator of $f(x)-g(y)$ for any nonconstant $f,g \in C(x)$. Additionally, we establish a comparable formula in arbitrary characteristic provided $f$ and $g$ share no wildly ramified branch points, and we extend these results to fiber products of nonconstant morphisms $f:A\to D$ and $g:B\to D$, which may yield reducible curves.

The ability of remote entities to exchange signals is essential for numerous information-processing applications, a capability dictated by the underlying causal architecture and the intermediate mechanisms transmitting data between laboratories. This study constructs a comprehensive resource theory of causal connection applicable to all multi-party communication contexts, including both those with definite causal orders and those with indefinite orders. We define and analyze three distinct sets of free transformations acting on free processes, thereby establishing three separate resource theories of causal connection. Within the causally ordered framework, we pinpoint the most resourceful processes for bipartite and tripartite scenarios; however, in the general setting, our findings indicate the absence of a globally most valuable resource. We introduce signalling robustness as a resource monotone for causal connection and derive tight bounds for various relevant process sets. Furthermore, we present a resource theory of causal non-separability, demonstrating that, unlike causal connection, it is unique. Collectively, these results provide a versatile and thorough framework for quantifying and transforming general quantum processes, along with deeper insights into their multi-layered causal structures.

Approximate Bayesian deep learning offers a promising solution to key challenges in deploying deep learning within intelligent systems, such as reducing over-confident errors and enhancing robustness against out-of-distribution inputs. Nevertheless, the high computational demands of current approximate Bayesian inference techniques often render them unsuitable for intelligent IoT environments featuring low-power edge devices. This paper introduces various approximate Bayesian inference approaches for supervised deep learning, examining both the obstacles and possibilities of implementing these methods on existing edge hardware. Furthermore, we propose several strategies to reduce model storage needs and boost computational scalability, specifically through techniques like model pruning and distillation.

Soft grippers are increasingly popular due to their adaptability and dexterity, yet the inherent non-linearity and infinite dimensionality of soft robotics pose significant challenges for modeling and closed-loop control during grasping. While data-driven approaches have been suggested to address these issues, they typically depend on intensive offline simulation or pre-training, often failing to generalize to unseen environments or support real-time online control required for physical deployment. To overcome this, we introduce an online modeling and control algorithm based on Koopman operator theory, which dynamically updates the estimated system dynamics at every time step. These continuously refined models are integrated into an online Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework and implemented on soft multi-fingered grippers. We first evaluate our method's prediction accuracy against other model-extraction techniques across various datasets, followed by experimental validation using a soft 3-fingered gripper to grasp objects of diverse shapes and weights without prior knowledge. The results demonstrate a high success rate in grasping these varied objects. Sample demonstrations are available at https://youtu.be/i2hCMX7zSKQ.

The ongoing growth of galaxy clusters through the accretion of galaxies and groups is primarily evidenced by cluster substructure and ram pressure stripping observed in individual members. This study presents a multi-wavelength analysis of the Hydra I cluster core, utilizing high-resolution new MeerKAT HI and DECam Hα data. These observations provide definitive proof of ram pressure stripping affecting NGC 3312, NGC 3314a, and NGC 3314b, characterized by compressed HI contours, distinct HI tails, and active star formation within the stripped gas. Specifically, the stripped material from NGC 3312 and NGC 3314a constitutes 8% to 35% of their remaining disk gas, forms stars at a rate of approximately 0.5 M☉ yr⁻¹, and stretches 30–60 kpc beyond the main disk. While the stellar mass in these tails is roughly one-tenth of the HI mass, a fourth "ring" galaxy sharing the same velocity shows no HI signatures of stripping. Furthermore, by combining HI and stellar morphologies with a Beta model of the hot intracluster medium, we constrained the galaxies' true distances from the cluster center. Additionally, the chance alignment of NGC 3314b behind NGC 3314a resolved the positional degeneracy regarding whether the galaxies lie in front of or behind the cluster. The drag observed in the HI tails supports the preferred scenario that NGC 3312 and NGC 3314a belong to a foreground substructure moving toward us; this substructure has already passed pericenter and is currently in an "out-fall" phase from the cluster. Finally, the high residual HI content in these galaxies may indicate that the substructure or intragroup medium shields them from the most severe ram pressure effects, or that they are following more tangential orbits.

We present an open-source solver for the Lindblad master equation utilizing matrix product states and operators. Applying this tool, we investigate the dynamics of tens of interacting qubits with varying connectivity patterns, specifically examining a scenario where an edge qubit is continuously driven on resonance—a key operation for quantum devices. Due to this driving, induced excitations propagate across the qubits until the system stabilizes via incoherent terms. Our results show that with alternating-frequency qubits, where interactions with off-resonant neighbors appear weak, tunneling excitations generate significant correlations between distant qubits. Notably, certain two-qubit correlation functions increase with distance, contrary to the usual decay, and reach their maximum at the two edge qubits farthest apart.

Image datasets are frequently employed in both psychophysical studies and machine learning research. Most open-access collections feature realistic, natural objects. However, since standard machine learning models lack domain-specific knowledge about these objects, whereas humans can utilize prior experience, comparing artificial and natural learning processes remains difficult. In this work, we present DELAUNAY, a dataset containing abstract paintings and non-figurative artworks labeled with the artists' names. Serving as a bridge between natural imagery and artificial patterns, this resource is versatile and can be applied in various settings, such as examining the sample efficiency of both human subjects and artificial neural networks. Furthermore, we train a standard convolutional neural network on DELAUNAY to demonstrate several of its fascinating characteristics.

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) excel at modeling the complex distributions of high-dimensional data, such as images, making them valuable for unsupervised anomaly detection in medical imaging. However, discrepancies in training data, including image dimensionality and the presence of semantically meaningful features, prevent natural image GANs from functioning effectively in medical contexts without adaptation. This study adapts and evaluates three GAN architectures—DCGAN, styleGAN, and bigGAN—for modeling 3D healthy patches in pulmonary CT scans. To our knowledge, this is the first evaluation of these specific models for this task. Selected for their ubiquity and performance in natural image processing, these models were trained in various configurations and assessed using the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) score. Additionally, we conducted a human observer study to evaluate image quality, analyzed the networks' ability to capture 3D domain-specific features, and examined the structure of the latent spaces. The findings indicate that while 3D styleGAN generates realistic images with meaningful 3D structures, it suffers from mode collapse, limiting sample diversity unless addressed during training. In contrast, 3D DCGAN models offer greater image variability but produce lower-quality images. The 3D bigGAN models strike a balance, providing intermediate image quality while most accurately modeling the distribution of key semantic features. Ultimately, the results suggest that further development is needed to create a 3D GAN capable of effective patch-based lung CT anomaly detection, with recommendations for future research including testing alternative architectures and integrating position encoding.

Distributed data naturally occur in settings with multiple observation sources located at distinct sites. Directly aggregating this data is frequently restricted by constraints on bandwidth and storage, or by privacy regulations. This paper presents a novel robust distributed algorithm for fitting linear regressions, specifically designed to handle heavy-tailed and/or asymmetric errors with finite second moments. The method communicates only gradient information during each iteration, ensuring communication efficiency. Statistically, the resulting estimator attains the centralized nonasymptotic error bound equivalent to pooling all data and assuming a sub-Gaussian distribution. Under a finite $(2+\delta)$-th moment condition, we establish a Berry-Esseen bound for the distributed estimator, enabling the construction of robust confidence intervals. Numerical experiments demonstrate that, compared to existing distributed approaches, the proposed method achieves near-optimal accuracy with reduced variability and superior coverage through narrower confidence intervals.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have significantly accelerated semantic parsing research, leading to notable improvements in downstream applications such as web API interfaces and text-to-SQL generation. Nevertheless, despite sharing a strong connection with these areas, Question Answering over Knowledge Bases (KBQA) has lagged behind. We attribute this slower progress to two distinct challenges specific to KBQA: schema-level and fact-level complexity. This survey places KBQA within the wider context of semantic parsing literature and provides a detailed overview of how current approaches tackle these unique obstacles. We argue that, regardless of these specific hurdles, existing KBQA research has overlooked valuable insights from the broader semantic parsing field. By examining these gaps, we can identify the bottlenecks hindering current KBQA advancements and highlight promising future directions, especially in the era of pre-trained language models, to help KBQA catch up with semantic parsing.

Extending the methods introduced by Harel, Mousset, and Samotij, who resolved the upper tail problem for cliques, we determine the asymptotic behavior of the upper tail for induced 4-cycles in the binomial random graph $G_{n,p}$. Our analysis reveals a novel phenomenon within the theory of large deviations for subgraph counts: for a specific (substantial) interval of $p$, the upper tail of induced 4-cycles fails to conform to a naive mean-field approximation.

Real-time scattering simulations on Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices are hindered by accumulating circuit errors. To enhance the precision of these physics simulations, we employed Noisy Output eXtrapolation (NOX), a recent error mitigation technique, alongside application circuits. Testing these protocols on a Transverse Field Ising model yielded improved phase shift calculations compared to prior work. We executed proof-of-concept 4-qubit circuits across multiple IBM quantum hardware platforms. We introduced metrics demonstrating a 21% to 74% reduction in errors for circuit depths spanning 14 to 37 hard cycles, validating NOX's effectiveness across a wide spectrum of failure rates. Furthermore, observations on various cloud-accessible devices confirm that NOX delivers performance gains even when circuits are run in significantly time-separated batches. Lastly, we present a heuristic approach for deriving systematic error bars for mitigated results, comparing them against empirical errors and analyzing their impact on phase shift estimates.

We introduce SIBELIUS-DARK, a constrained simulation modeling the local volume out to 200~Mpc from the Milky Way. This represents the inaugural study of the \textit{Simulations Beyond The Local Universe} (SIBELIUS) initiative, designed to embed a Local Group-like system within its proper cosmic context. As a dark-matter-only simulation, it employs the GALFORM semi-analytic model to generate the galaxy population. Our results show that the large-scale structure arising from SIBELIUS constrained initial conditions aligns closely with observational data. Furthermore, the inferred galaxy population matches observations well, both statistically across the entire volume and individually for the most massive clusters. Specifically, $K$-band number counts across the full sky, as well as when separated by northern and southern Galactic hemispheres, are accurately reproduced. We observe that the local volume exhibits peculiarities within the broader $\Lambda$CDM framework, featuring an unusually high count of supermassive clusters and a large-scale underdensity of approximately 5\% relative to the cosmic mean. Nevertheless, although these anomalies are rare, their magnitude does not substantially undermine the $\Lambda$CDM model. To date, SIBELIUS-DARK stands as the most comprehensive constrained realization of the local volume; accompanying this publication, we publicly release the $z=0$ halo and galaxy catalogues, which we anticipate will benefit the broader astronomical community.

This case study analyzes and quantifies the consequences of failing to co-optimize energy and reserves under high wind energy penetration, with the methodology detailed in a companion paper, Part I. It compares two models: one incorporating co-optimization and one without. Drawing inspiration from the Spanish market, the modeling incorporates reserve representation, renewable incentives, and model calibration. A sensitivity analysis examines various configurations differing in generation capacity, ramping capabilities, and market parameters, including available wind, wind Feed-in Premiums, generator risk aversion, and reserve requirements. While the specific models and case study serve an illustrative purpose, the underlying methodology remains general.

Accurate and rapid dose estimation represents a critical bottleneck in treatment planning for microbeam radiation therapy (MRT). This study introduces a machine learning model utilizing a 3D U-Net architecture to address this challenge. The method separately forecasts the high-intensity synchrotron microbeams and the lower doses found in the valleys between them. To achieve this, we introduce the concept of "macro" peak and valley doses, which characterize these values as macroscopic quantities within larger voxels rather than at a microscopic level. The model is trained to replicate full Monte Carlo (MC) data, thereby automatically incorporating complex physical phenomena such as polarization. By adopting this macro dose distribution framework, single microbeam predictions can be superimposed onto a beam array field, making the approach promising for clinical treatment planning. Results demonstrate that this method overcomes a primary limitation in MRT by generating a complete microbeam irradiation field in under a minute while maintaining acceptable accuracy.

We establish asymptotic stability conditions for port-Hamiltonian systems through matrix criteria derived from established resolvent methods in $C_0$-semigroup theory. The proof relies on a recent characterization of exponential stability found in [Trostorff, Waurick, arXiv:2201.10367], which originates from structural insights into port-Hamiltonian systems presented in [Picard et al., arXiv:2106.10937, accepted in SIAM SICON]. These findings are then utilized to analyze the asymptotic stability of a network of vibrating strings.

Ferromagnetic semimetals with the formula Fe$_n$GeTe$_2$ (where n=3, 4, or 5) display symmetry-protected band crossings near the Fermi energy, resulting in unique transport characteristics driven by these topological features. Using first-principles calculations and a corresponding tight-binding Hamiltonian derived from fitting those parameters, we investigated these materials. When spin-orbit coupling is included for n=3 and n=5, significant Berry curvature concentrates along the nodal lines. We analyzed how the interplay between these topological nodal lines and magnetic moments influences the anomalous Hall conductivity ($\sigma_{xy}$) and anomalous Nernst conductivity ($\alpha_{xy}$). Our results show $\sigma_{xy}$ values of 150 S/cm for n=3, 295 S/cm for n=4, and 90 S/cm for n=5 at 0 K. At room temperature near the Fermi level, the anomalous Nernst conductivity ($\alpha_{xy}$) is measured as 0.55 A/Km for n=3, 0.80 A/Km for n=4, and 0.10 A/Km for n=5. Notably, our calculated zero-temperature AHC for Fe$_3$GeTe$_2$ (150 S/cm) and Fe$_5$GeTe$_2$ (90 S/cm) aligns with experimental data, and our room-temperature prediction for the ANC of Fe$_5$GeTe$_2$ (0.10 A/Km) closely matches reported experimental values.

Following the recent determination of the reactor mixing angle $\theta_{13}$ and the updated upper limit on $BR(\mu \to e \gamma)$ from the MEG experiment, we re-evaluate charged lepton flavor violations within the supersymmetric type II seesaw framework. This model predicts a robust correlation between $BR(\mu \to e \gamma)$ and $BR(\tau \to \mu \gamma)$, primarily driven by neutrino mixing angles, which can be precisely calculated once $\theta_{13}$ is known. We analyze various factors influencing this relationship and demonstrate that mSUGRA-like scenarios, characterized by universal slepton masses at the high scale, yield a ratio of $3.5 \lesssim BR(\tau \to \mu \gamma)/BR(\mu \to e \gamma) \lesssim 30$ for normally hierarchical neutrino masses. Any experimental observation deviating from this range would exclude minimal supersymmetric type II seesaw models. Furthermore, current MEG constraints severely restrict the light sparticle spectrum in mSUGRA if the seesaw scale falls between $10^{13}$ and $10^{15}$ GeV; however, these constraints can be alleviated in models where the triplet scalar soft mass is non-universal at the high scale, allowing for a relatively light sparticle spectrum.

The Mexico-UK Submillimetre Camera for Astronomy (MUSCAT) represents the second-generation large-format continuum camera designed for the 1.1 mm band on Mexico's 50-meter Large Millimeter Telescope (LMT). Its focal plane comprises 1,458 horn-coupled lumped-element kinetic inductance detectors (LEKIDs) split evenly into six channels across three silicon wafers. This paper details the preliminary laboratory characterization of the entire MUSCAT focal plane. Using the instrument's readout system, we conducted frequency sweeps to locate resonance frequencies and performed continuous timestream acquisitions to assess intrinsic noise and the 1/f knee. Subsequently, employing a re-imaging lens and a black body point source, we mapped the beam for each detector, yielding a mean Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM) of approximately 3.27 mm, which aligns closely with the anticipated 3.1 mm. Furthermore, by adjusting the intensity of a beam-filling black body source, we measured the responsivity and noise power spectral density (PSD) for every detector under a 300 K optical load to determine the noise equivalent power (NEP), confirming that most detectors are photon-noise limited. Finally, utilizing a Fourier Transform Spectrometer (FTS), we evaluated the instrument's spectral response, revealing a 1.0–1.2 mm bandwidth centered at 1.1 mm, as predicted.

Data structures like Bloom Filters accelerate network routing and measurement by maintaining a compressed set representation. While space-efficient, they allow for tunable, bounded one-sided errors known as false positives, where an absent element may incorrectly appear present. Recent efforts have aimed to dynamically adjust these filters to minimize false positives for frequently queried elements. An ideal "support optimal" filter would maintain a bounded false positive probability for new elements while ensuring that repeated queries to the same element generate negligible additional false positives. This paper introduces a novel Adaptive Cuckoo Filter that achieves support optimality (up to logarithmic factors) for storing sets of size $n$ across $n$ queries. The design is straightforward: correcting previous false positives requires only a basic cuckoo operation, eliminating the need for extra metadata or storage. As the first practical support-optimal data structure and the first filter capable of fixing false positives without additional space, our approach is validated through experiments on network traces, demonstrating superior performance over existing Adaptive Cuckoo Filters. Furthermore, we examine adversarial adaptivity, where an adversary exploits query results to maximize false positive rates. We establish a lower bound proving that a wide class of filters, including all current Adaptive Cuckoo Filters, can be compelled by such adversaries to accumulate a significant number of false positives.

We present an algorithm for constructing functional bases of absolute invariants under the rotation group for rank 2 tensors and vectors within Euclidean spaces of arbitrary dimensions. Building upon our previous findings regarding symmetric tensors, this work extends the results to include sets containing antisymmetric rank 2 tensors. Consequently, this approach enables the construction of functional bases for differential invariants of vector functions, specifically yielding first-order invariants of the Poincaré algebra (the invariance algebra associated with Maxwell equations for the vector potential).

Theoretical findings indicate that the number of degrees of freedom in quantum fields diminishes when examined at extremely short distances. This concept arises from black hole entropy studies and holographic theories within AdS geometries. It is anticipated that a complete theory of quantum gravity will explicitly detail how these degrees of freedom thin out at high energy scales. Currently, we lack a comprehensive framework explaining the mechanism of this thinning. While residual and potentially measurable effects might persist at larger length scales, such effects are likely significant only near the Planck scale, making observable instances in nature rare. One promising area for detection is cosmic inflation, which, in simplest models, involves a scalar inflaton field with a potential featuring a flat "slow-roll" region and a potential well. By calculating the impact of this degree of freedom thinning on the running of the spectral index for quantum fluctuations of the inflaton, we deduce that it results in a positive power of the wave-vector—contrasting with the usual $\sim -\epsilon$ negative power correction. The text concludes with remarks on the implications of these fluctuations for observational data or the lack thereof \cite{Martin}.

Although the prevalence of active galactic nuclei (AGN) within cosmic voids remains underexplored, studying them offers potential insights into how AGN activity depends on environment and how AGNs co-evolve with their hosts. This study analyzed the AGN fraction in one of the largest samples of optically selected cosmic voids from the SDSS Data Release 12, focusing on moderately bright and bright AGN across a redshift range of 0.2 to 0.7. Galaxies were categorized into inner and outer void regions based on the void's effective radius: those within 0.6 times the effective radius ($R_{\text{eff}}$) were classified as inner members, while those between 0.6 and 1.3 times $R_{\text{eff}}$ were considered outer void galaxies. Results indicate that for redshifts greater than 0.42, the average AGN fraction in inner voids (4.9 ± 0.7%) is significantly higher than in outer regions (3.1 ± 0.1%), demonstrating a clear environmental dependence. This trend was reinforced by dividing the data into narrower distance bins, which revealed a marked decline in AGN activity from the center toward the edges of voids at $z > 0.42$. Conversely, at lower redshifts ($z < 0.42$), the dependence on the environment was found to be very weak for two out of three distance bins. The observed higher AGN fractions in low-density regions near void centers compared to their outer counterparts at higher redshifts suggests that one-on-one galaxy interactions may occur more efficiently in voids, potentially because such interactions are suppressed in denser environments by higher velocity dispersions. Additionally, this could imply reduced ram pressure stripping in voids or point to intrinsic properties of the host galaxies or the void environment itself.

Chern numbers can be determined using a vortex field framework tied to the phase conventions of a wave function. In gapped bands, the Chern number corresponds directly to the total count of flux-carrying vortices. However, this approach becomes complicated when topological defects, such as Dirac cones, are present, especially if they do not possess a well-defined winding number. We propose a method to incorporate these defects into the vortex field framework by defining a winding number based on the phase behavior in reciprocal space as one encircles the defect's contact point. To handle cases where a specific winding number is absent, we employ a broader concept of winding vectors. We validate this approach by applying it to Dirac cones arising from bands in the Hofstadter model.

We introduce a proof-of-concept, differentiable biomechanical model grounded in deep learning that simulates realistic brain deformations. By utilizing prescribed maps of local atrophy and growth as inputs, the network learns to warp images in accordance with a Neo-Hookean tissue deformation model. Validated against longitudinal brain atrophy data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), the trained model demonstrates the ability to rapidly simulate novel brain deformations with minimal residuals. This approach holds promise for applications in data augmentation or for investigating various causal hypotheses regarding brain growth and atrophy.

We investigate cold collisions of $^{87}$Rb atoms within a static magnetic field and a single-frequency radio frequency (RF) field using multi-channel quantum defect theory combined with the Floquet method to solve the two-body time-dependent Schr\"odinger equation. Our findings demonstrate that RF fields can significantly alter the two-body scattering length via Feshbach resonances across both low and high static magnetic field regimes. These RF-induced resonances offer potential applications for quenching experiments and interaction control in spinor condensates. Furthermore, we show that, similar to photo-association, RF fields can effectively bind cold atoms into molecules at a practical rate.

This research introduces a data-driven approach to identifying cable damage by detecting deviations from normal force patterns using deep learning time series classification (TSC). The method leverages the implicit behavioral representation of cables found in their measured force series. Specifically, an LSTM-FCN model is employed, where segmented force data serves as input and cable identifiers act as class labels. The classifier is first trained and validated using data from intact stay cables, then evaluated against data from potentially damaged states. The system identifies the most likely damaged cable or pair by selecting the one with the lowest classification accuracy. Validated on an in-service cable-stayed bridge with actual damage, the study examined two scenarios: one using raw force time series and another using force ratios to account for distribution variations caused by damage. By integrating results from both scenarios, the method successfully identified a ruptured cable. Ultimately, this methodology offers a streamlined solution for cable damage detection that minimizes the need for data preprocessing and feature engineering, facilitating rapid and practical early warning capabilities.

We present the discovery of five new eclipsing AM CVn binaries—ultra-compact, helium-rich accreting systems featuring degenerate or semi-degenerate donors—with orbital periods of 61.5, 55.5, 53.3, 37.4, and 35.4 minutes. Identified by searching for deep eclipses in Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) light curves of white dwarfs selected via Gaia parallaxes, these systems were confirmed through phase-resolved spectroscopy and high-speed photometry. Spectra from the two longer-period systems (61.5 and 53.3 minutes) reveal numerous emission and absorption lines indicating the presence of N, O, Na, Mg, Si, Ca, K, and Zn; notably, K and Zn represent the first detection of these elements in AM CVn systems. Modeling the high-speed photometry allowed us to determine donor mass and radius, offering constraints on the systems' formation channels. We found that the average accreting white dwarf mass is approximately $0.8\,\mathrm{M_{\odot}}$, and white dwarfs in long-period systems are hotter than recent theoretical models predict. The donors exhibit high entropy and are roughly twice as massive as zero-entropy donors at the same orbital period. While the large donor radii suggest He-star progenitors, this conflicts with observed spectral features. The discovery of these five systems aligns with known AM CVn space density and ZTF recovery efficiency, suggesting that 1–4 additional eclipsing systems will be found as ZTF data collection continues. This expansion will enhance our understanding of the population but demands high-precision data to fully characterize both these new findings and future discoveries.

Sparse matrix formats are fundamental in computational science and machine learning, offering substantial compute time savings over dense representations for tasks involving local connectivity. Despite these benefits, their integration into major ML frameworks like PyTorch remains partial, lacking support for both GPU acceleration and automatic differentiation. This paper introduces a CUDA-accelerated, CSR-based sparse matrix wrapper for PyTorch that enables efficient basic matrix operations alongside full automatic differentiability. Furthermore, we demonstrate the utility of these sparse kernels in optimization problems, highlighting their ease of implementation and comparing their performance against dense equivalents.

We calculate intersection matrices for modular curves $X_0(p^r)$ where $r \in \{3,4\}$. Applying this, we derive an asymptotic formula for the Arakelov self-intersection number of the relative dualizing sheaf associated with Edixhoven's minimal regular model of $X_0(p^r)$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. This result aids in formulating an effective version of the Bogomolov conjecture regarding stable models of these modular curves and yields a bound on their stable Faltings heights.

This paper aims to demonstrate that numerous intriguing wavelets (or coherent states) emerge from group representations that are not square integrable or from vacuum vectors that are not admissible. This finding broadens the scope of standard wavelet constructions to include classic instances such as the Hardy space.

Keywords: Wavelets, coherent states, group representations, Hardy space, functional calculus, Berezin calculus, Radon transform, Moebius map, maximal function, affine group, special linear group, numerical range.

By applying an uncertainty relation for Rényi entropies of conjugate quantum observables, we derive a robust Heisenberg limit expressed as ${\rm RMSE} \geq f(\alpha)/(\langle N\rangle+\frac12)$. This inequality bounds the root mean square error in estimating a random optical phase shift relative to the average photon number, where the function $f(\alpha)$ reaches its maximum for non-Shannon entropies. Additionally, we establish simple yet powerful uncertainty relations connecting phase uncertainty to the photon number distribution, such as $\Delta\Phi\geq \max_n p_n$. These findings are substantially enhanced through upper and lower bounds on the Rényi mutual information of quantum communication channels, which relate to asymmetry and convolution. These improved bounds are utilized to estimate unitary shift parameters—like rotation angles and time—with prior information and to derive tight constraints on coherence measures. Furthermore, sharper Rényi entropic uncertainty relations are derived, including time-energy uncertainty relations for Hamiltonians with discrete spectra; in this context, almost-periodic Rényi entropies are introduced to address nonperiodic systems.

We introduce a quantum temporal imaging technique designed to restore the indistinguishability of signal and idler photons generated via type-II spontaneous parametric down-conversion using a pulsed broadband pump. Typically, these photons exhibit distinct spectral and temporal characteristics, which degrade their indistinguishability and consequently reduce the visibility of Hong-Ou-Mandel interference. By incorporating a time lens into one arm of the interferometer and selecting an appropriate magnification factor, we demonstrate the restoration of perfect indistinguishability between the photon pairs. This approach achieves 100% Hong-Ou-Mandel interference visibility under conditions of high focal group delay dispersion within the time lens.

Charts frequently incorporate visually striking elements and text captions designed to highlight specific data aspects. To investigate how readers synthesize information from both charts and captions, we conducted a crowdsourced study. Initially, participants identified visually prominent areas within a series of line charts. Subsequently, we created text captions based on these salient features and asked participants to summarize their key takeaways after viewing the combined chart-caption pairs. Our results indicate that when both the chart and caption highlight the same prominent feature, readers identify that doubly emphasized element as the primary takeaway. Conversely, when a caption describes a low-prominence feature while the chart highlights a more prominent one, readers rely on the visual chart and select the higher-prominence feature as their takeaway. Additionally, we discovered that external contextual information aids in conveying the caption's message more effectively. Based on these insights, we offer guidelines for creating effective chart-caption combinations.

Recently, multi-fluid models have been introduced to enhance the depiction of convection within weather and climate simulations. This approach is appealing because it relies on fundamental dynamics, thereby circumventing the invalid assumptions found in mass-flux convection schemes at current resolutions. Nevertheless, the optimal closure strategies for multi-fluid equations governing atmospheric convection remain unclear. This study develops a straightforward single-column model featuring two fluids—one rising and one falling—without incorporating additional sub-filter variability modeling. When applied to Rayleigh-Bénard convection, the model demonstrates that minimal closures suffice to predict the correct scaling of heat flux (Nu) across six orders of magnitude in buoyancy forcing (Ra). These findings indicate that even a rudimentary two-fluid model can effectively capture the primary coherent overturning structures of convection.

Anomaly detection in dynamic graphs has gained significant traction owing to its extensive utility in domains like cybersecurity, e-commerce, and social networks. While recent deep learning methods have surpassed shallow techniques, they still struggle with two primary hurdles: encoding unattributed nodes effectively and extracting discriminative knowledge from coupled spatial-temporal dynamics. To address these issues, we introduce TADDY, a novel Transformer-based framework for anomaly detection in dynamic graphs. TADDY employs a robust node encoding strategy to capture both structural and temporal roles within evolving graph streams and utilizes a dynamic graph transformer to learn informative representations from complex spatial-temporal patterns. Extensive experiments on six real-world datasets confirm that TADDY significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods.

This work initiates a broader initiative to automate skein theoretic reasoning. Specifically, we investigate skein theoretic invariants associated with planar trivalent graphs, which is equivalent to classifying trivalent categories. These categories are defined as nondegenerate pivotal tensor categories over $\mathbb C$ generated by a symmetric self-dual simple object $X$ and a rotationally invariant morphism mapping $1 \rightarrow X \otimes X \otimes X$. Our primary finding identifies that the sole trivalent categories satisfying the condition that $\dim \operatorname{Hom}(1, X^{\otimes n})$ does not exceed the sequence $1,0,1,1,4,11,40$ for $0 \leq n \leq 6$ are quantum $SO(3)$, quantum $G_2$, a one-parameter family of free products of specific Temperley-Lieb categories (termed ABA categories), and the $H3$ Haagerup fusion category. Furthermore, we establish analogous results for cases where the map $1 \rightarrow X^{\otimes 3}$ lacks rotational invariance and provide a comprehensive classification of nondegenerate braided trivalent categories where the dimensions of invariant spaces are bounded by $1,0,1,1,4$. The core methodologies employed include a novel strategy for deriving skein relations, amenable to automation via Gr\"obner bases, and evaluation algorithms utilizing the discharging method originally applied in the proof of the 4-color theorem.

This study introduces a real-time image reconstruction technique for scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM). The method utilizes an algorithm that calculates only the center of mass (COM) of the diffraction pattern for a single probe position at any given moment. Consequently, it updates the image output as each new position is scanned without needing to store intermediate diffraction data. Experimental results demonstrate clear features at high spatial frequencies, including atomic column locations. Furthermore, common post-processing steps, such as band-pass filtering, can be seamlessly incorporated into the real-time workflow. Compared to existing reconstruction approaches, this method delivers high-quality images with strong noise resilience while demanding minimal memory and computational resources. An efficient, interactive open-source implementation is also provided, supporting both frame-based and event-based camera or file inputs. This approach offers the desirable benefit of immediate feedback, familiar to operators from conventional high-angle annular dark field STEM, thereby enabling rapid decision-making and fine-tuning. This is particularly advantageous for beam-sensitive samples, allowing for the acquisition of optimal images at the lowest possible electron dose.

The solenoid scan is a widely used technique for measuring the thermal emittance of photocathodes in situ within rf photoinjectors. However, in many photoinjectors, the solenoid's fringe field overlaps with the gun's rf field, complicating the determination of the transfer matrix and consequently increasing the uncertainty of the thermal emittance measurement. This paper reviews two existing methods used to address this overlap problem and outlines their limitations. Additionally, we introduce a novel approach to eliminate measurement errors caused by solenoid-rf field overlap. This new method is rigorously validated through theoretical derivations, beam dynamics simulations, and experimental data derived from photoinjector configurations across three different groups. The results demonstrate that the measurement error associated with this new method is negligible for most photoinjector setups.

The phenomenon of quantum reflection, where wave packets bounce off downward potential steps or attractive potentials, has been investigated regarding bright matter-wave solitons, particularly focusing on trapping them atop a pedestal-shaped potential. Numerical simulations reveal that moving solitons can rebound from the potential's boundaries and remain trapped for extended periods. However, this shuttle-like motion involves shedding a portion of the soliton's matter with each reflection, thereby diminishing its norm. The study examines both single- and two-soliton setups and discusses the discontinuous jumps in the trajectories of colliding solitons. Furthermore, the time-delay observed during the step-like decay of the norm in two-soliton configurations is connected to these trajectory jumps. These findings hold potential significance for designing future experiments involving solitons in Bose-Einstein condensates.

The Berry curvature is fundamental to the magnetic transport properties of topological materials, yet its capacity to independently generate universal transport phenomena with distinct scaling laws remains uncertain. Utilizing the semiclassical Boltzmann formalism alongside symmetry analysis, this study demonstrates that a noncentrosymmetric distribution of Berry curvature typically yields linear magnetoresistivity and thermoelectric conductivity, both characterized by $B$-scaling. We investigate this topological linear magnetoresistivity in two-dimensional MnBi$_2$Te$_4$ flakes and three-dimensional spin-orbit-coupled electron gases, with the former aligning well with experimental data. Furthermore, we clarify the distinction between this mechanism and conventional anisotropic magnetoresistance. Our theoretical framework establishes a universal scenario for topological linear magnetoresistivity and thermoelectric conductivity, predicting these effects across diverse materials and offering a plausible explanation for recent observations of linear magnetoresistivity.

The Coronagraph Instrument (CGI) aboard the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is designed to showcase high-contrast technologies essential for visible-light exoplanet imaging and spectroscopy in space. By directly imaging Jupiter-sized planets and debris disks, CGI will provide crucial in-space data that serves as a vital precursor to future, larger missions aimed at directly imaging Earth-like planets within the habitable zones of nearby stars. This paper outlines the current instrument design and requirements, emphasizing the key hardware, algorithms, and operational procedures being demonstrated. Additionally, we detail several scientific opportunities for exoplanets and circumstellar disks made possible by these capabilities. A competitively selected Community Participation Program team will play a central role in this technology demonstration and may conduct further CGI observations beyond the initial tech demo, contingent upon the instrument's performance.

Astronomical surveys are producing data at an accelerating rate, creating a challenge for traditional spectroscopic analysis methods that are either labor-intensive or computationally demanding. In this context, machine learning—specifically unsupervised clustering—presents a promising alternative. The Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment (APOGEE) provides an extensive dataset of near-infrared stellar spectra ideal for evaluating these approaches. This study applies a $K$-means unsupervised classification scheme to the large APOGEE dataset to investigate the feasibility of categorizing data into discrete classes. Specifically, the $K$-means algorithm was utilized on 153,847 high-resolution spectra ($R\approx22,500$), with a discussion on the algorithm's strengths, weaknesses, and parameter selection. Results demonstrate that classification using normalized spectra effectively captures variations in stellar atmospheric parameters, chemical abundances, and rotational velocity. The method successfully distinguishes between bulge and halo populations, as well as separating dwarfs, sub-giants, red clump (RC), and red giant branch (RGB) stars. However, classification based on flux space fails to produce a clear organization in parameter space. Consequently, the absence of distinct groups in flux space makes the outcomes highly sensitive to initialization and hinders the efficiency of standard methods for determining the optimal number of clusters. This classification, along with extensive online resources linked to APOGEE Data Release 12 (DR12), is publicly accessible. Our detailed description of the APOGEE database can significantly aid in identifying specific target types for various applications. Ultimately, we observe a lack of obvious groupings in flux space and identify specific limitations of the $K$-means algorithm when handling such data.

This note examines planar lattices formed by their atoms. We establish that for a planar lattice $L$ generated by $n$ atoms, the left and right boundaries of $L$ contain at most $n+1$ elements each. Conversely, the size of $L$ can be unbounded. Specifically, for every $k > 1$, we construct a planar lattice $L$ generated by only $4$ atoms that contains more than $k$ elements.

Superconformal geometries in spacetime dimensions $D=3,4,5$, and $6$ are examined using local supertwistor bundles defined over standard superspace. These structures naturally support superconformal connections represented as matrix-valued one-forms. To align with the standard superspace formalism, it is demonstrated that appropriate gauge choices exist where the scale components of both the connection and curvature vanish; under these conditions, conformal and $S$-supersymmetry transformations are absorbed into super-Weyl transformations. By imposing constraints—typically setting the even covariant torsion two-form to zero—the number of component fields is reduced to match those of minimal off-shell conformal supergravity multiplets, with additional dimension-one constraints required for the maximal cases in $D=3$ and $D=4$. The topic is also analyzed from a minimal perspective involving only dimension-zero torsion. Finally, a novel class of supermanifolds known as local super Grassmannians is introduced, offering an alternative framework for superconformal theories.

We demonstrate that neural networks utilizing absolute value activations, governed by the path norm, and featuring logarithmic scaling of depth, width, and weights relative to $1/\varepsilon$ are capable of $\varepsilon$-approximating functions that are analytic within specific domains of $\mathbb{C}^d$.

Using the Wigner--Weyl formalism, we develop a quantum kinetic model that captures the phase-space dynamics of graphene electrons. To incorporate the quantum characteristics of the carriers, we apply the quantum Liouville equation to the density matrix. By linking the density matrix elements to the Wigner function, we derive its equation of motion, including the Coulomb interaction treated self-consistently via the Hartree approximation. We calculate the long-wavelength limit of the plasmon dispersion relation for both ungated and gated scenarios. Furthermore, as an application, we derive the corresponding fluid equations from first principles and examine the accurate value of the effective hydrodynamic mass of the carriers. This step is essential for formulating a proper fluid description of Dirac electrons, thereby facilitating a more comprehensive understanding of graphene plasmonics.

This paper aims to show two main points: first, that the framework of elliptic hypergeometric integrals (EHIs) can be expanded through insights from supersymmetric gauge theory, and second, that examining the hyperbolic limit of these extended EHIs reveals a complex structure with significant mathematical challenges relevant to supersymmetric quantum field theorists. Both points have previously been explored in the theoretical physics community; the first was established by Dolan and Osborn in 2008, while the second was addressed in the author's 2016 Ph.D. thesis, which incorporated key elements from Rains' 2006 work on the hyperbolic limits of specific EHI classes. This article provides a concise review of these advancements, including minor refinements and clarifications, primarily targeting mathematicians interested in EHIs. Specifically, we utilize a representation-theoretic formulation of supersymmetric gauge theory, enabling readers with no prior gauge theory background but familiarity with the representation theory of semi-simple Lie algebras to follow the discussion.

We present a high-resolution neutron diffraction study examining the interplay between structural and magnetic transitions in Ba$_{1-x}$K$_x$Fe$_2$As$_2$. Potassium doping suppresses both the tetragonal-to-orthorhombic and antiferromagnetic transitions, which vanish for $x \lesssim 0.3$. Distinct from Ba(Fe$_{1-x}$Co$_x$)$_2$As$_2$, these transitions remain first-order and coincide across the entire phase diagram, driven by a biquadratic coupling of the order parameters. Refined phase diagram analysis indicates that superconductivity begins at $x = 0.133$, with all three phases coexisting up to $x \gtrsim 0.24$.

Evolutionary multi-agent systems (EMASs) excel at addressing complex, multi-dimensional challenges, a capability validated theoretically through Markov-Chain analysis. Current research now aims to incorporate autonomous hybridization into EMAS. This paper introduces a hybrid variant of EMAS, detailing the selection and implementation of various hybrid operators and the rules governing the initiation of hybrid steps within the primary algorithm. These steps utilize established, efficient metaheuristics and integrate their outcomes into the main process. The proposed modifications are assessed using a suite of demanding continuous-optimization benchmarks.

Event attribution in the context of climate change aims to determine the influence of human-induced greenhouse gas emissions on extreme weather phenomena, ranging from individual occurrences to broader categories. A prevalent methodology involves comparing climate model outputs from factual scenarios (reflecting the real world) with counterfactual scenarios (imagining a world without anthropogenic emissions) to calculate the likelihood of specific events under both conditions. The attribution is subsequently expressed as the ratio of these probabilities. Although this approach has been widely applied over the past 15 years, the statistical techniques employed to estimate risk ratios using climate model ensembles have not fully utilized the broader statistical literature; in some instances, the bootstrap method has been applied and interpreted in non-standard manners. This paper introduces a rigorous frequentist statistical framework for assessing how sampling uncertainty impacts risk ratio estimation, proposes statistical methods previously unexplored in event attribution, and evaluates various approaches through statistical simulations. Our findings indicate that existing statistical methods not yet adopted in this field offer several advantages over the commonly used bootstrap technique, such as superior performance in repeated sampling and greater robustness when dealing with small estimated probabilities. Software implementing these methods is accessible via the `climextRemes` package for both R and Python. While our primary focus remains on frequentist methods, Bayesian approaches are likely to be especially valuable when addressing sources of uncertainty beyond sampling variability.

Gavruta defined $K$-frames for Hilbert spaces to analyze atomic systems relative to a bounded linear operator. Given the significant distinctions between $K$-frames and standard frames, this work investigates the weaving properties of $K$-frames. Two frames, $\{\phi_{i}\}_{i \in I}$ and $\{\psi_{i}\}_{i \in I}$, associated with a separable Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$, are considered woven if there exist positive constants $A \leq B$ such that for any subset $\sigma \subset I$, the combined family $\{\phi_{i}\}_{i \in \sigma} \cup \{\psi_{i}\}_{i \in \sigma^{c}}$ constitutes a frame for $\mathcal{H}$ with bounds $A$ and $B$. This paper establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for weaving $K$-frames in Hilbert spaces. Furthermore, it demonstrates the equivalence between woven $K$-frames and weakly woven $K$-frames, and finally provides sufficient conditions for Paley-Wiener type perturbations of woven $K$-frames.

The Minimum Common String Partition Problem (MCSP) involves receiving two strings and partitioning them into an identical set of substrings while minimizing the total count of those substrings. This combinatorial optimization challenge, which is NP-hard, finds applications in computational biology and is addressed by various exact and heuristic techniques, including Integer Linear Programming, Greedy methods, and Ant Colony Optimization. This paper presents the MCSP as a Dynamic Programming formulation and proposes an exact algorithm utilizing Decision Diagrams. Furthermore, we introduce a restricted Decision Diagram to generate heuristic solutions, comparing their runtime and solution quality against established methods on standard benchmark instances. Our approach demonstrates strong scalability, making it effective for solving large-scale MCSP instances heuristically.

Network Utility Maximization (NUM) focuses on assigning traffic rates to users to maximize aggregate utility within network resource limits. This paper introduces a novel NUM framework called Learning-NUM, designed for scenarios where utility functions are initially unknown and can only be observed after traffic delivery, introducing \textit{queueing delays} in feedback. The objective is to develop a policy that incrementally learns these utility functions while optimizing rate allocation and network scheduling/routing to maximize total utility over a finite horizon $T$. Beyond unknown utilities and stochastic constraints, a primary challenge involves unbounded queueing delays that depend on the policy's decisions. We first demonstrate that the expected total utility of the optimal dynamic policy is bounded by a static optimization solution. In the absence of feedback delay, we propose an algorithm leveraging gradient estimation and Max-Weight scheduling. To address feedback delay, we integrate the algorithm into a parallel-instance paradigm, yielding a policy with $\tilde{O}(T^{3/4})$-regret, representing the gap between the optimal dynamic utility and our policy's expected utility. Finally, to validate the practical utility of the Learning-NUM framework, we apply it to three domains: database queries, job scheduling, and video streaming. We further simulate the job scheduling scenario to assess the empirical performance of our proposed policy.

The compound 1T'-TaTe2 undergoes a fascinating first-order structural phase transition near 170 K. To uncover the origin of this transition, it is essential to investigate its electronic structure. We conducted a combined optical and ultrafast pump-probe investigation of the material spanning the transition temperature. The results demonstrate that the phase transition causes sharp alterations in both optical spectra and ultrafast electronic relaxation dynamics, indicating an abrupt reconstruction of the band structure. We argue that this transition is first-order and cannot be explained by conventional density-wave instabilities. These findings provide valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms driving the structural phase transition.

Tasks involving high dynamics, large accelerations, and precise trajectory tracking typically depend on accurate models or high-gain feedback. Although kinematic optimization offers an efficient method for representing and generating hitting trajectories online, learning to track such dynamic motions with imperfect models remains an unsolved challenge. Specifically, stability concerns within the iteration domain often hinder the successful application of model-based learning techniques. To address this, we introduce a novel adaptive Iterative Learning Control (ILC) algorithm designed for efficient execution via a recursive approach. Furthermore, we incorporate covariance estimates of model matrices to ensure caution during the learning process. We validate the proposed method through extensive simulations and on a robotic table tennis system, demonstrating optimized striking performance for two seven-degree-of-freedom anthropomorphic robot arms. Our results on the table tennis platform outperform high-gain PD control, model-free ILC (using simple PD feedback), and standard model-based ILC lacking cautious adaptation.

Unintentionally, identifiers within a software system's source code significantly influence the system's overall quality. Ambiguous or confusing naming conventions cause developers to misinterpret code behavior, extend comprehension time, and reduce productivity. Although renaming operations offer a solution to poor naming, the act of renaming constitutes rework and carries its own risk of introducing defects. This study seeks to investigate the motivations behind developers' choices in naming and renaming identifiers, as well as the decision-making processes involved. Based on these findings, we propose a linguistic model capable of generating identifier names that reflect their specific behaviors. To build this model, we first conducted multiple studies to identify the necessary input features. This paper presents the results of those completed studies and provides justification for pursuing further research in this area.

Drawing from biological principles, this work demonstrates how monocular visual sensing can offer a dependable signal for mobile robot navigation. Inspired by a seminal 1981 study by Lee and Reddish on diving seabirds that utilized the visual cue of time-to-contact, we introduce the closely related concept of time-to-transit, or tau. We show that steering laws derived from idealized monocular perceptions of tau can reliably and robustly guide a mobile vehicle through diverse environments, provided that walls and objects offer sufficient visual features. This paper makes two primary contributions: it establishes a simple yet robust theory for vision-based steering control and illustrates how this theory directs the implementation of visual navigation. These implementations are validated through ROS-Gazebo simulations and real-world experiments using a camera-equipped Jackal robot. To our knowledge, these experiments represent the first demonstration of visual navigation grounded in the concept of tau.

This study examines the function of a particular warped extra dimension in modeling higher-dimensional Lorentzian wormholes. The specific warping is inspired by the well-known non-static Witten bubble of nothing, although our resulting spacetimes are static and geometrically distinct. We interpret vacuum solutions in $D\geq 5$ dimensions, as well as non-asymptotically flat solutions featuring "perfectly normal" matter stress-energy, as potential Lorentzian wormholes. Furthermore, asymptotically flat wormholes in $D\geq 5$ requiring "exotic matter" appear to exist across all dimensions within this framework. The paper also revisits and discusses the wormhole-black hole correspondence through double Wick rotation. Finally, we briefly analyze geodesic motion and the behavior of geodesic congruences within a subclass of five-dimensional, warped, vacuum wormhole spacetimes to identify characteristic properties and specific signatures that could enhance our understanding of these geometries.

In any finite mixture of distinct normal distributions, precisely one component will dominate the right tail, completely overshadowing all other subpopulations in the extreme right region. While this characteristic is not exclusive to normal distributions, it is absent in other standard continuous, centrally symmetric, unimodal distributions like the Laplace, as well as in other bell-shaped distributions such as the Cauchy (Lorentz) distribution.

This historical overview examines low-energy pion-nucleon interactions, adopting a pedagogical style that addresses topics relevant to contemporary research. Key subjects include chiral effective field theory, the sigma term, the qualitative analysis of low-energy phase shifts, the physics of the $\Delta$ resonance, and isospin violation. The narrative emphasizes that low-energy pion-nucleon scattering connects directly to QCD through effective field theory. Furthermore, it highlights that modern investigations into the pion-nucleon sigma term and isospin violation necessitate an improved dataset for low-energy observations.

Building on recent proposals to link IceCube TeV and PeV neutrino events with gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) through neutrino Lorentz violation, we present a revised estimate of the GRB neutrino flux that significantly exceeds previous findings from the IceCube Collaboration. Of the 24 neutrino "shower" events detected above 60 TeV, 12 are attributed to GRBs, a figure that aligns closely with predictions from GRB fireball models. Furthermore, the analysis of track events yields consistent results regarding the association of high-energy cosmic neutrinos with GRBs under identical Lorentz violation conditions. After conducting a background estimation, we identify GRBs as a significant source for ultra-high energy IceCube neutrino events. This study supports the existence of Lorentz and CPT violations in neutrinos, suggesting new physics beyond the standard framework of relativity.

While Rydberg atom-based electric field sensing offers significant benefits compared to conventional antenna methods, it typically relies on a local oscillator (LO) for detecting low-field and phase-resolved signals. This study demonstrates the broad utility of closed-loop quantum interferometric approaches for Rydberg field sensing, effectively removing the requirement for an LO. We show that the phase and frequency defined within our quantum-interferometric framework serve as an internal reference, enabling full 360°-resolved phase sensitivity without an external LO. Furthermore, this internal reference can function similarly to a traditional LO for atom-based down-conversion to an intermediate frequency, facilitating lock-in phase detection; we validate this by successfully demodulating a four-phase-state signal transmitted via the atoms.

This study addresses the challenge of detecting anomalies as quickly as possible in networks where data samples lack labels. At an unspecified moment, an anomaly alters the data distribution of a specific, unknown sensor. Consequently, the data vectors received by the fusion center undergo an unknown and arbitrary reordering of their entries at each time step. The fusion center's objective is to identify this anomaly with the shortest possible delay while adhering to false alarm constraints. Because samples are unlabeled, traditional methods relying on local cumulative sum (CuSum) statistics become inapplicable. Key inquiries involve determining if detection remains feasible without label information, identifying the fundamental performance limits, and establishing methods to reach those limits. The analysis examines two scenarios involving static and dynamic anomalies, where the affected sensor may or may not vary over time. For both cases, practical algorithms are developed using principles of mixture likelihood ratios and/or maximum likelihood estimation. Theoretical characterizations of the average detection delays and false alarm rates for these algorithms are provided. Additionally, universal lower bounds on the average detection delay for a specified false alarm rate are derived, further validating the asymptotic optimality of the proposed algorithms.

This paper details an extension of standard statistical mechanics to investigate the thermodynamics of large-scale structure formation within nonlocal gravity. By deriving the grand partition function through a modified Yang-Lee theory, we establish thermodynamic properties consistent with a Bose-Einstein dark matter model and determine the associated gravitational phase transition.

We present a robust sample of nine massive quiescent galaxies at redshifts $z > 3$, identified through initial data from the JWST CEERS programme. Among these, three reside at $4 < z < 5$, offering the strongest evidence to date for quiescent galaxies existing significantly prior to $z=4$. These extreme systems possess stellar masses ranging from $\log_{10}(M_*/M_\odot) = 10.5$ to $11.3$ and accumulated the majority of their mass between $6 < z < 9$; notably, two objects appear to have reached $\log_{10}(M_*/M_\odot) > 10$ by $z \simeq 8$. Our derived number densities reveal that prior studies underestimated the abundance of quiescent galaxies at $3 < z < 4$ by a factor of $3-6$, a discrepancy attributed to the absence of ultra-deep imaging beyond $\lambda > 2\,\mu$m. This finding intensifies the tension between observational data and theoretical models, which have already struggled to match earlier estimates of quiescent galaxy densities at $z > 3$. Future wider-area JWST imaging surveys will expand such samples and enable searches for quiescent galaxies at $z > 5$. The reported galaxies are prime candidates for JWST NIRSpec spectroscopy, a tool essential for elucidating their physical properties and gaining deeper insights into the mechanisms that quenched star formation during the universe's first billion years.

Pretrained language models are known to encapsulate diverse forms of knowledge within their architectures. While traditional adaptation to new tasks typically relies solely on features from the final layer, we hypothesize that intermediate layer representations relevant to downstream objectives are underutilized due to their depth, leading to inefficiencies in sample and computational requirements. To address this, we introduce Depth-Wise Attention (DWAtt), a novel layer fusion technique designed to recover valuable signals from non-terminal layers. We evaluate DWAtt against a standard concatenation-based approach (Concat) and a deeper model baseline, ensuring all methods operate within comparable parameter limits. Our results indicate that both DWAtt and Concat achieve superior step and sample efficiency compared to the baseline, particularly in few-shot scenarios. Furthermore, DWAtt surpasses Concat when processing larger datasets. Specifically, on the CoNLL-03 Named Entity Recognition task, layer fusion methods yielded F1 score improvements ranging from 3.68% to 9.73% across various few-shot configurations. Overall, these layer fusion strategies demonstrate significant performance gains over the baseline across diverse training conditions, including variations in data volume, model architecture, and training constraints.

Recently, few-shot learning (FSL) has garnered significant interest. Among current methodologies, metric-based approaches train embedding networks to cluster similar samples while pushing dissimilar ones apart, yielding promising outcomes. FSL is defined by its ability to generalize to novel classes in image classification using only a handful of training images; however, this constraint complicates the learning of visual features capable of capturing appearance variations. Consequently, training may diverge from the correct direction because images within the same semantic class can exhibit distinct appearances, while images from different classes might look alike. We posit that FSL can be enhanced by incorporating additional semantic features to learn more discriminative representations.
