Accordingly, this study introduces a multi-task learning framework that treats label text semantics as an auxiliary task to bolster FSL performance. Our model leverages word-embeddings as semantic features to guide the embedding network and employs a semantic cross-attention module to integrate these features into the standard visual modality. Although the proposed approach is straightforward, it delivers excellent results. We applied this method to two existing metric-based FSL techniques, achieving substantial performance improvements. The source code for our model is available on GitHub.

Driven by applications in polymer-based data storage, we investigate the reconstruction of a string from a portion of its composition multiset. We provide a complete characterization of the string structures that resist unique reconstruction (modulo reversal) from their full set of prefix-suffix compositions. Utilizing this characterization, we demonstrate that for all $n \ge 6$, there exists at least one string of length $n$ that cannot be uniquely recovered up to reversal. Furthermore, for every $n \ge 6$, we explicitly define the set of all length $n$ strings that admit unique reconstruction up to reversal. As a corollary, we show that any binary string can be formed using Dyck and Catalan-Bertrand strings. For any specific string $\bm{s}$, we offer a procedure to explicitly generate the set of all strings sharing $\bm{s}$'s prefix-suffix composition multiset, along with a formula for the cardinality of this set. Applying this, we construct a composition code of maximal size and develop two distinct classes of composition codes capable of correcting composition missing errors and mass-reducing substitution errors, respectively. Additionally, we propose two new challenges: reconstructing a string from its composition multiset when at most a constant number of substring compositions are lost, and reconstructing a string given only the compositions of its substrings with length at most $r$. For both scenarios, we present appropriate codes under specific conditions.

Loop closure detection is a crucial technology for enabling long-term robot navigation in complex settings. This paper introduces a global descriptor called the Normal Distribution Descriptor (NDD) specifically for 3D point cloud loop closure detection. The descriptor encodes both the probability density score and entropy of a point cloud. We also propose a fast rotation alignment process and use the correlation coefficient to measure similarity between descriptors. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses state-of-the-art point cloud descriptors in both accuracy and efficiency. The source code is available and can be integrated into existing LiDAR odometry and mapping (LOAM) systems.

This paper investigates electromagnetic scattering, absorption, and performance limits for short-time modulated pulses interacting with a time-varying lossy layer positioned between vacuum and a perfect electric conductor. The layer's electrical properties—conductivity, permittivity, and permeability—are assumed to vary either abruptly or gradually over time. Numerical results demonstrate that a time-varying absorbing layer capable of temporally switching its permittivity and conductance can dissipate the power of both modulated ultra-wideband and quasi-monochromatic pulses beyond the constraints of the time-invariant Rozanov bound when integrated across the entire frequency spectrum. We propose and simulate a practical metamaterial implementation composed of a three-dimensional array of resistor-loaded dipoles, where effective media properties are achieved by switching only the dipole's load resistance. Additionally, we show that Rozanov's bound can be circumvented through both abrupt and more practical gradual soft switching, thereby addressing potential causality issues associated with abrupt transitions.

This study investigates the relationship between dark matter (DM) and neutrinoless double beta ($0
u eta eta$) decay within a scotogenic framework featuring a hybrid texture in the neutrino mass matrix. Distinctively, this model expresses all non-zero elements of the mass matrix as proportional to the effective Majorana mass $\left|M_{ee}ight|$, with the total neutrino mass scale determined by this same parameter. We have derived significant correlations linking the dark matter relic density ($\Omega h^2$) to both the DM mass $M_1$ and $\left|M_{ee}ight|$. Utilizing the experimentally measured value for DM relic density, we determine that the DM mass $M_1$ is approximately $\mathcal{O}$(1 TeV), placing it within the detection capabilities of collider experiments. Specifically, across all five hybrid textures, the upper limit on the DM mass $M_1$ ranges between 2.27 and 5.31 TeV. A notable characteristic of this model is the presence of a lower bound on $|M_{ee}|$ for all permissible hybrid textures, except for texture $T_5$, making them accessible to current and future $0
u eta eta$ decay searches. High-sensitivity experiments will be crucial in validating the model's theoretical predictions; for instance, failing to observe $0
u eta eta$ decay down to a sensitivity of $\mathcal{O}(0.03)$ eV would rule out the $T_3$ hybrid texture.

We introduce a recurrent network designed for 3D neuron reconstruction, which sequentially produces binary masks for each object in an image while maintaining spatio-temporal consistency. This consistency is modeled through two components: (i) a local mechanism that utilizes bi-directional recurrence to analyze non-occluding and temporally adjacent object relationships, and (ii) a non-local mechanism that employs skip connections to capture long-range dependencies across time. Our network is fully end-to-end trainable, mapping an input image directly to a sequence of object masks; unlike methods dependent on object boundaries, it yields results that do not require post-processing. We tested our approach on three neuron segmentation benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art results on the SNEMI3D challenge.

Data-free knowledge distillation (DFKD) has recently gained significant research interest due to its ability to compress models using solely synthetic data. However, despite promising outcomes, current state-of-the-art DFKD methods remain inefficient because data synthesis is time-consuming, rendering them unsuitable for large-scale applications. To address this, we present FastDFKD, an effective framework that accelerates DFKD by orders of magnitude. Our core innovation involves a novel strategy to reuse shared common features from training data to generate diverse data instances. Unlike previous approaches that optimize data sets independently, we propose learning a meta-synthesizer that utilizes these common features as an initialization for rapid data synthesis. Consequently, FastDFKD achieves data synthesis in just a few steps, markedly improving the efficiency of data-free training. Experiments conducted on CIFAR, NYUv2, and ImageNet demonstrate that FastDFKD accelerates the process by 10$\times$ to 100$\times$ while maintaining performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/zju-vipa/Fast-Datafree}.

Let $K$ denote a field and $R=K[x_1,\ldots, x_n]$ the polynomial ring over $K$ in $n$ variables. Given a simplicial complex $\Delta$ on $n$ vertices with associated Stanley-Reisner ideal $I=I_{\Delta}$, this paper establishes that when $I$ is matroidal, the properties of $\Delta$ being sequentially Cohen-Macaulay, shellable, and vertex decomposable are equivalent. Additionally, if $I$ is minimally generated by $u_1,\ldots,u_s$ where $s\leq 3$ or the union of supports of any pair of generators equals $\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$, then $\Delta$ is vertex decomposable. Finally, we demonstrate that for a monomial ideal $I$ of degree $2$, the conditions of being weakly polymatroidal, possessing linear quotients, and being vertex splittable are all equivalent.

The SAO/NASA Astrophysics Data System (ADS) has evolved alongside the Information Age, proactively tracking and addressing the requirements of its users. Today, virtually every professional astronomer relies on ADS daily, with many utilizing it throughout their entire careers. Beyond serving as an essential resource for professional scientists, the ADS has expanded into the public sphere as an instrument for science education. This paper examines and discusses key indicators of ADS's influence on research and access to scholarly literature. The ADS is supported by NASA Grant NNX09AB39G.
We provide criteria determining when a sequence of randomly selected orthogonal subspaces within a separable Hilbert space spans the entire space.

We introduce an alternative protocol that prepares critical states by exploiting critical speeding-up rather than the conventional critical slowing-down. Paradoxically, this acceleration is achieved by moving away from the critical point. We apply this method to the quantum Rabi model, its classical oscillator limit, and the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model. Following this, we examine the adiabatic speed-up protocol's utility in quantum metrology, contrasting its performance with that of critical quantum metrology. Our findings indicate that critical metrology using the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model fails to surpass the standard quantum limit. Furthermore, we argue that while critical protocols can occasionally exceed this limit, they represent a suboptimal strategy overall. In conclusion, although systems with phase transitions hold significant promise for quantum technologies, the critical point itself may not warrant the primary focus.

Violations of community norms can hinder constructive online communication and collaboration. As a defensive strategy, moderators frequently respond to such breaches by temporarily suspending offenders. However, these measures carry the risk of alienating members, creating a necessary tradeoff that makes it crucial to evaluate the effectiveness and specific contexts of this common moderation practice. This study introduces a computational framework designed to analyze the post-block behavior of Wikipedia users. Upon the expiration of a suspension, users may follow one of several paths: they might reform and comply with rules, recidivate, or leave the community entirely. Our findings indicate that these trajectories depend on both the individual's characteristics and their perception of whether the block was fair and justified. Leveraging these insights, we define a series of prediction tasks to forecast which path a user is likely to take following a first offense, demonstrating the feasibility of these approaches. Ultimately, this work advocates for a more nuanced moderation strategy by illuminating the underlying tradeoffs.

Although drones have been a subject of intense research for ten years, they remain absent from daily life. This article examines the underlying causes of this gap and proposes strategies to bridge it. Drawing on the principles of Technology Assessment (TA)—an interdisciplinary field dedicated to informing sound decisions regarding emerging technologies—we identify safety as the most pressing area needing advancement. Since Unmanned Aerial System Traffic Management (UTM) offers a systematic solution to safety concerns, we outline specific design requirements for wireless experts. Additionally, we provide implementation guidelines for various drone applications, incorporating public acceptance levels derived from current literature in the relevant domains.

We have numerically solved boost-invariant spin hydrodynamics equations restricted to first-order gradient terms, consistently incorporating the spin equation of state that links the spin density tensor to the spin chemical potential. Our results reveal both stable and unstable solutions depending on the specific form of the equation of state and the structure of the spin transport coefficients, observed within an evolution timeframe of 10 fm/c. These outcomes complement recent studies identifying stable and unstable modes in perturbed uniform spin systems using analogous hydrodynamic models.

The Asymptotic safe gravity framework proposes a specific behavior for the running Newtonian coupling constant, characterized by two free parameters, typically labeled $\omega$ and $\gamma$. This running constant allows for the derivation of novel metrics, including new black hole spacetimes. A fundamental condition for these metrics is that they must match the Schwarzschild solution at large radial distances. Additionally, by requiring the metric to align with the Donoghue quantum-corrected potential, we determine that the $\omega$ parameter must be negative. This leads to an unexplored black hole metric that naturally describes what are known as Planck stars.

Quantum physics laws provide enhanced security and performance for information processing; specifically, quantum sensing utilizes nonclassical resources to achieve measurement precision beyond classical capabilities, while quantum cryptography ensures the absolute secrecy of data. In this work, we introduce both the theoretical framework and experimental demonstration of entanglement-enhanced covert sensing. This paradigm simultaneously delivers high measurement accuracy and data integrity by hiding the probe signal within ambient noise, rendering the protocol's execution undetectable with high probability. We demonstrate that entanglement significantly improves phase estimation accuracy compared to classical protocols operating at equivalent levels of covertness. Furthermore, the implemented protocol approaches the fundamental quantum limit, achieved through a near-optimal entanglement source and quantum receiver. This research is poised to open new avenues for quantum information processing, offering unprecedented combinations of security and performance.

A number defined by the formula $x(x+1)/2$ for an integer $x$ is known as a triangular number. Let $N(a_1,\cdots,a_k;n)$ and $T(a_1,\cdots,a_k;n)$ represent the count of representations of $n$ as $\sum_{i=1}^k a_ix_i^2$ and $\sum_{i=1}^k a_i\frac{x_i(x_i+1)}{2}$, respectively. In \cite{4}, Z.-H. Sun proposed specific relationships connecting $T(a,b,c;n)$ with $N(a,b,c;8n+a+b+c)$. This paper demonstrates the validity of these conjectures through theta function identities and further identifies additional triplets $(a,b,c)$ that satisfy them.

This study introduces a weakly-supervised data augmentation method designed to enhance Named Entity Recognition (NER) within the complex field of biomedical entity extraction from scientific literature. Initially, a neural NER (NNER) model is trained on a limited set of fully labeled data. Subsequently, a reference collection of entity names (such as proteins from UniProt) is employed to detect entity mentions in an unlabeled corpus with high precision but lower recall. Next, the NNER model applies weak labels to this corpus. Finally, the model is retrained iteratively using an expanded dataset that combines the original seed, reference-set examples, and weakly-labeled instances, resulting in improved performance. Empirical results demonstrate that this augmented bootstrapping process significantly boosts NER effectiveness, and we analyze the factors influencing the method's success.

Research into temporal networks and the detection of dynamic communities has been a prominent focus over the past decade, yet the inherent complexity of the task has prevented a consensus. Static communities are already ill-defined, and introducing a temporal dimension further complicates their description. This article introduces a coherent approach for temporal clustering called the Best Combination of Local Communities (BCLC). Our method seeks to strike an optimal balance between two competing goals: accurately tracking short-term evolution through optimal partitions at each time step, and ensuring temporal smoothness by prioritizing historical continuity.

The unique characteristics of quantum mechanics distinguish machine learning (ML) applications in the quantum domain from their classical counterparts. ML facilitates knowledge discovery by continuously extracting information from quantum systems across various tasks. In this approach, models receive streaming quantum data for learning and decision-making, enabling immediate feedback to the system. We introduce a deep reinforcement learning framework designed for streaming data from a continuously measured qubit, accounting for detuning, dephasing, and relaxation. Additionally, we examine how the agent adjusts to different quantum noise patterns through transfer learning. This stream learning methodology enhances our comprehension of closed-loop quantum control, potentially paving the path for advanced quantum technologies.

We introduce a zeta function defined in relation to the twisted Grover matrix of a mixed digraph, providing both an exponential formulation and a determinant-based expression for it. Furthermore, we derive a trace formula concerning this twisted Grover matrix as a specific application.

Consider any word defined over a given alphabet. If the word is not empty, begin by selecting a position and outputting the character at that location. Next, repeat this process any number of times (including zero): either remain at the current character, move one step left (if valid), or move one step right (if valid), and then output the character currently being scanned. This process describes a traversal or "walk" across the input word. Let $u$ represent the infix of the input word formed by the visited positions, and let $w$ be the resulting output string (which is empty if the input word is empty). Since unvisited prefixes or suffixes of the input word have no impact on $w$, they can be disregarded, allowing us to state that $u$ generates $w$. The central question is: for a given word $w$, which words $u$ generate it? The result is unexpected. We define a word $u$ as a *primitive generator* of $w$ if $u$ generates $w$ and no shorter word can generate $u$. We demonstrate that, aside from certain degenerate cases, every word has exactly two primitive generators.

Forward-secure signatures ensure that signatures created prior to a private key compromise remain secure, providing robust protection for critical applications like audit logs, digital forensics, and financial systems. However, most current forward-secure schemes depend on classical computational hardness assumptions, rendering them vulnerable to quantum computers. While hash-based signatures (HBS), such as XMSS, provide post-quantum forward security, they suffer from high key generation costs, expensive signing operations, and large signature sizes as the number of signed messages grows, limiting them to a predefined message count. A significant challenge remains in developing efficient, practical, quantum-safe forward-secure signatures with scalable signing capabilities. This paper introduces FROG (Forward-secuRe pOst-quantum siGnature), a novel series of post-quantum signatures. Unlike HBS alternatives, FROG delivers highly efficient signatures with sub-linear key and signature sizes and supports practically unbounded signing. This is accomplished by applying MMM constructions to transform suitable post-quantum signatures into forward-secure variants. We evaluated this approach by transforming prominent schemes like Dilithium, WOTS, and BLISS. Experimental results show that FROG surpasses XMSS across most performance metrics, potentially for all cases when handling large volumes of messages. Additionally, we explore one-time variants of these base schemes to further optimize FROG's performance. Overall, FROG demonstrates superior performance compared to existing forward-secure alternatives, making it a strong candidate for standardization efforts in post-quantum forward-secure signatures.

Focused crawling seeks to maximize the discovery of web pages pertinent to a specific subject while filtering out unrelated content. Although Reinforcement Learning (RL) has previously been applied to optimize this process, this paper introduces TRES, a novel RL-driven framework for focused crawling. We formulate the crawling environment as a Markov Decision Process, enabling an RL agent to derive an effective crawling strategy. Initialized with a limited set of human-supplied keywords and a small, topic-relevant text corpus, TRES employs a keyword expansion procedure to guide the crawl and train a classifier that serves as the reward function. To circumvent the computational inefficiency of brute-force action selection, we introduce Tree-Frontier, a decision-tree-based algorithm that adaptively discretizes expansive state and action spaces to identify a select few representative actions. This approach allows the agent to likely choose near-optimal actions by greedily selecting the best representative option. Experimental results demonstrate that TRES significantly surpasses state-of-the-art methods in harvest rate (the proportion of relevant pages crawled), while Tree-Frontier reduces the number of actions requiring evaluation at each timestep by orders of magnitude.

This paper establishes that for a $C^\infty$-generic Finsler metric (including symmetric Finsler and Riemannian cases) on a closed surface $\Sigma$, a sequence of nondegenerate closed geodesics exists that are equidistributed across $\Sigma$. The proof relies on the volume property of spectral invariants within embedded contact homology, as developed by Cristofaro-Gardiner, Hutchings, and Ramos, alongside transversality arguments. These arguments draw inspiration from Irie's equidistribution result for three-dimensional Reeb flows and the analogous findings by Marques, Neves, and Song regarding embedded minimal hypersurfaces.

We explain how recent findings regarding exclusive-mode contributions to $a_\mu^{\rm LO,HVP}$—the leading-order hadronic vacuum polarization part of the muon's anomalous magnetic moment—can yield a data-driven dispersive calculation of $a_\mu^{\rm lqc;\, IL}$, the isospin-limit, light-quark-connected component, accurate up to minor electromagnetic corrections obtainable via lattice methods. This approach is significant given the availability of multiple lattice calculations for this specific quantity, emerging indications of a discrepancy between lattice and dispersive evaluations of $a_\mu^{\rm LO,HVP}$, and the need to identify the origin of such tension. Utilizing the $-0.93(58)\times 10^{-10}$ value from a recent BMW lattice study as the necessary electromagnetic correction, we determine $a_\mu^{\rm lqc;\, IL}$ to be $635.0(2.7)\times 10^{-10}$ when employing the results of Keshavarzi, Nomura, and Teubner, or $638.4(4.1)\times 10^{-10}$ when using those of Davier, H\"ocker, Malaescu, and Zhang.

A generalized pentagonal geometry, denoted PENT($k$,$r$,$w$), is a partial linear space where each line contains $k$ points, each point lies on $r$ lines, and the set of points non-collinear with any given point $x$ constitutes the point set of a Steiner system $S(2,k,w)$, with the system's blocks corresponding to the geometry's lines. When $w = k$, the structure is termed a pentagonal geometry, represented as PENT($k$,$r$). The deficiency graph of such a geometry features the geometry's points as vertices, with an edge connecting $x$ and $y$ if and only if they are non-collinear. Our main goal is to explore the construction of PENT($k$,$r$,$w$) geometries whose deficiency graphs possess a girth of 4. Furthermore, we introduce several new instances of PENT(5,$r$) featuring connected deficiency graphs. As a result, we demonstrate the existence of pentagonal geometries PENT(5,$r$) with deficiency graphs having a girth of at least 5 for all $r \ge 200,000$ where $r \equiv 0$ or $1 \pmod{5}$.

This Letter explores how time-dependent, short-ranged interactions influence the long-term expansion of Fermi gases. We demonstrate that the impact of these interactions is governed by their transformation under conformal mappings and establish a specific criterion for the relevance of time-dependent interactions in both strongly interacting and nearly scale-invariant non-interacting quantum gases. Furthermore, we show that interactions can be engineered to produce non-exponential thermalization dynamics in trapped Fermi gases. Complementing our symmetry-based analysis, hydrodynamic simulations confirm that the moment of inertia of the trapped gas adheres to a universal time-dependence dictated by the interplay between conformal symmetry and the time-dependent scattering length $a(t)$. These findings are likely applicable to the dynamics of other nearly scale-invariant systems governed by non-relativistic conformal symmetry.

Although the thermo-mechanical coupling governing graphene fracture under thermal gradients offers significant practical potential, its coupled non-equilibrium nature makes it difficult to investigate. We utilized non-equilibrium molecular dynamics to analyze graphene fracture by imposing a constant strain rate across various thermal gradients, utilizing distinct potential fields. Our findings indicate that for AIREBO and AIREBO-M potentials, fracture stresses do not strictly correlate positively with initial crack lengths. Instead, strain-hardening effects were detected in "REBO-based" models for small initial defects, interpreted as a blunting phenomenon in porous graphene. Furthermore, no clear relationship was established between temperature gradients and either fracture stresses or crack propagation dynamics. Quantized fracture mechanics served to validate our molecular dynamics results. We propose a novel perspective suggesting that transverse bond forces contribute to load sharing, explaining the nonlinear rise in fracture stress associated with shorter crack lengths. In "REBO-based" models, anomalous kinetic energy transport along crack tips was observed, attributed to the high interatomic attractions inherent in those potentials. Fracture behavior exhibited using machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIP) appeared more "brittle-like" but failed to capture post-fracture dynamic behaviors. Additionally, mechanical responses derived from MLIP showed no dependence on temperature gradients. Among the tested potentials, the dropout uncertainty neural network potential with a dropout rate of 0.2 yielded the most accurate temperature configuration for equilibration simulations. This study is anticipated to motivate further exploration of non-equilibrium dynamics in graphene, supporting practical applications across diverse engineering domains.

This work investigates the impact of supersymmetric frameworks featuring a $U(1)$ horizontal symmetry and exclusively spontaneous CP violation on lepton flavor observables, including $\mu \to e\gamma$ and the electron electric dipole moment. We demonstrate that incorporating horizontal symmetry alongside the absence of explicit CP violation can mitigate current experimental constraints. However, the presence of undetermined $\mathcal{O}(1)$ coefficients in these mass matrix models complicates the interpretation of flavor bounds. To address this ambiguity, we introduce a novel fine-tuning metric tailored for such scenarios, enabling an assessment of how naturally low-energy flavor observables arise from specific mass matrix structures. Applying this flavor-naturalness measure to our supersymmetric models, we quantify the extent of fine-tuning necessitated by lepton flavor constraints across different mass scales for sleptons, neutralinos, and charginos.

Intent-driven networks represent a pivotal advancement in the transition toward fully autonomous network and service management. By utilizing user-centric intents, operators can abstractly influence the design, provisioning, deployment, and assurance of network infrastructure and services, guided by service level agreements and minimum capability requirements. However, the concept of Intent-based Networking (IBN) introduces significant challenges regarding the contextual definition of intents, stakeholder roles, and the establishment of a generalized architecture. This review offers a comprehensive examination of current IBN state-of-the-art practices, covering intent description models, lifecycle management, the strategic significance of IBN, and a proposed generalized architectural framework, alongside an analysis of future prospects and hurdles. An analytical study was conducted on data from relevant research, with a primary focus on the interoperability between IBN and softwarized networking infrastructures based on NFV and SDN. The exploration of critical functions within IBN management and service model design employs various abstract modeling techniques to propose a converged architectural framework. Key findings highlight: 1) the benefits and role of IBN in enabling autonomous networking; 2) necessary improvements for integrating intents as fundamental policies in service modeling and network management; 3) the requirement for domain-agnostic abstract representation models for intents; and 4) the necessity of incorporating learning as a core function in autonomous networks. These insights lay the groundwork for further investigation and standardization efforts to establish IBN as a fundamental paradigm for network management in beyond 5G environments.

As cybercriminals rapidly create malicious tools powered by artificial intelligence (AI) to execute adaptive and stealthy attacks, new defensive strategies are urgently needed. While some cybersecurity experts speculate that AI could similarly enable proactive cyber defense measures, it remains uncertain whether this is realistic or merely hype. Last year, the Alan Turing Institute, advised by experts from the UK National Cyber Security Centre and Defence Science Technology Laboratory, released a research roadmap for AI-driven active cyber defense. This position paper updates that roadmap by focusing on two promising AI methodologies—reinforcement learning and causal inference—and explains how they could shift the balance of power back in favor of defenders.

As the demands and service requirements of next-generation wireless networks become increasingly diverse, it is projected that the existing frequency bands of mobile network operators (MNOs) will fail to meet the anticipated volume of traffic. Driven by spectrum scarcity, stakeholders are increasingly seeking practical solutions to maximize the efficiency of exclusively allocated bands through spectrum sharing mechanisms. However, the technical intricacies of these mechanisms pose significant design challenges, particularly regarding the need for coordination among multiple entities. To address this, the paper begins with a comprehensive review of recent literature on spectrum sharing methods, categorized by their operational frequency regimes: licensed bands (including Licensed Shared Access (LSA), Spectrum Access System (SAS), and Dynamic Spectrum Sharing (DSS)) and unlicensed bands (such as LTE-Unlicensed (LTE-U), Licensed Assisted Access (LAA), MulteFire, and New Radio-Unlicensed (NR-U)). Furthermore, to bridge the gap between standardization and vendor-specific implementations, we examine potential deployment scenarios and the necessary modifications to legacy cellular networks from the perspectives of telecom vendors and regulators. Additionally, we analyze the application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) techniques to enhance spectrum sharing mechanisms and enable fully autonomous sharing scenarios. The paper concludes by outlining open research challenges to guide future research endeavors.

Human interactions naturally flow between various subjects with ease, yet dialog system research frequently overlooks the capacity to actively and smoothly transition to new topics. This paper presents TIAGE, a novel benchmark designed for topic-shift awareness, built upon human annotations of these shifts. Leveraging TIAGE, we define three tasks to explore different aspects of modeling topic transitions in dialogue: detecting topic shifts, generating responses triggered by these shifts, and creating topic-aware dialogues. Experimental results indicate that the topic-shift signals within TIAGE effectively support response generation; however, systems still face significant challenges in determining the appropriate moment to switch topics. These findings suggest that further research is essential for advancing topic-shift aware dialog modeling.

We detail recent computations of proton gravitational form factors (GFFs) utilizing the soft-wall AdS/QCD framework within a light-front quark-diquark model. Specifically, we calculate the four GFFs: $A(Q^2)$, $B(Q^2)$, $C(Q^2)$, and $\bar{C}(Q^2)$. Additionally, we derive the pressure and shear distributions of quarks within the proton. Our results indicate that the GFFs $A(Q^2)$ and $B(Q^2)$ align well with lattice QCD findings, while the qualitative behavior of the $D$-term form factor matches data extracted from JLab's deeply virtual Compton scattering (DVCS) experiments, as well as predictions from both lattice QCD and various phenomenological models.

We utilize the characteristics of chain mapping transformations for bosonic environments to pinpoint a finite set of modes that encapsulate the environment's distinctive features or fingerprint. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the infinite number of remaining bath modes can be substituted with a universal Markovian closure, consisting of a limited group of damped modes following Lindblad-type dynamics, where the parameters remain independent of the specific spectral density. This Markovian closure achieves a quadratic acceleration compared to conventional chain mapping methods, renders memory usage independent of simulation duration, and retains all information regarding the fingerprint modes. We apply this Markovian closure to calculating both linear spectra and non-linear spectral responses, the latter serving as a significant, experimentally accessible witness of many-body coherence for which efficient, numerically exact calculations in realistic environments are currently unavailable.

Quantum simulation offers a method to investigate non-equilibrium many-body systems by mapping them onto controllable quantum platforms, thereby addressing computationally intractable challenges. In this work, we employ a programmable quantum processor comprising a chain of 10 superconducting qubits connected via tunable couplers to simulate the one-dimensional generalized Aubry-Andr\'e-Harper model across three distinct phases: extended, localized, and critical. We examine phase transitions and many-body dynamics under quasi-periodic modulations affecting both off-diagonal hopping coefficients and on-site potentials, which are regulated by adjusting coupling strengths and qubit frequencies, respectively. Our observations include spin transport behaviors for initial single- and multi-excitation states within various phases, alongside the characterization of phase transitions through the experimental measurement of participation entropy dynamics. These results illustrate that the newly developed tunable coupling architecture in superconducting processors significantly expands the scope of simulatable Hamiltonians and could catalyze further research into diverse quantum and topological phenomena.

We employ Friedrich's characterization of spatial infinity to investigate the asymptotic expansions of the Maxwell-scalar field system in the vicinity of spatial infinity. The primary aim of this study is to elucidate how the system's non-linearities influence the regularity of solutions and the structure of polyhomogeneous expansions at null infinity, specifically at the critical points where null infinity intersects with spatial infinity. Our analysis reveals that non-linear interactions cause both fields to exhibit greater singularity at the conformal boundary compared to the non-interacting case. Notably, we identify a novel class of logarithmic terms within the asymptotic expansions that are contingent upon the coupling constant between the Maxwell and scalar fields. Furthermore, we examine the consequences of these findings regarding the peeling properties of the fields at null infinity.

This study examines a spherical CdS/SiO$_2$ quantum dot (QD) heterosystem containing a central hydrogen-like impurity. The analysis incorporates an electron polarization trap at the interfaces, resulting from the dielectric permittivity mismatch between the QD and the matrix. It is established that surface electron states emerge for small QD radii. For various radii, the partial contributions of these surface states to electron energy—arising from interactions between the electron-ion and electron-polarization charges—have been quantified. Furthermore, the linear light absorption coefficient of noninteracting QDs was calculated, accounting for size dispersion. The findings demonstrate that surface states can be detected across different ranges of the electromagnetic spectrum.

Magnetic droplets are non-topological magnetodynamical solitons known for complex dynamic behaviors and their potential in generating microwave signals. In contrast, bubbles are internally static cylindrical magnetic domains maintained by external fields and magnetostatic forces. Originally, droplet theory described them as bubbles on the verge of collapse, stabilized by spin transfer torque, and noted their equivalence to bubbles at zero frequency. Without nanoscale lateral confinement, pinning, or an external field, such a nanobubble is inherently unstable and prone to collapse. This study demonstrates that dynamic droplets can be frozen into static nanobubbles by reducing the magnetic field. Although the bubble retains virtually the same resistance as the droplet, all low-frequency microwave noise vanishes. This transition is fully reversible; increasing the current can thaw the bubble back into a droplet. While droplets collapse without a sustaining current, the resulting bubble is highly stable, remaining intact for days without external drive. These electrical measurements are supported by direct observations via scanning transmission x-ray microscopy, which validates the analysis and confirms that pinning stabilizes the bubble.

The extension of the geometric phase to mixed states is termed the Uhlmann phase. While recent research has applied this concept to topological insulators—documenting an experimental critical temperature where the topological Uhlmann phase vanishes—the Uhlmann phase for a paradigmatic system like a spin-$j$ particle in a slowly rotating magnetic field remains unexplored. This study investigates that specific system within a thermal ensemble. We demonstrate that the Uhlmann phase corresponds to the argument of a complex-valued Chebyshev polynomial of the second kind with order $2j$. Consequently, the phase exhibits $2j$ singularities located at the polynomial's roots, which define critical temperatures marking topological order transitions. Using the argument principle from complex analysis, we characterize each topological order by a winding number; this number equals $2j$ for the ground state and decreases by one for every critical temperature crossed as the temperature rises. We anticipate that this work will motivate experimental validation of the thermal control of topological properties, extending previous findings made for spin-$1/2$ particles.

Min-Nets draw inspiration from end-stopped cortical cells by incorporating units that compute the minimum of two learned filters. When integrated into leading deep architectures like ResNet and DenseNet, these Min-Nets demonstrate superior performance on the Cifar-10 benchmark and exhibit enhanced robustness against JPEG compression artifacts. We contend that the minimum operation serves as the most straightforward method for executing an AND operation on filter pairs, thereby introducing a bias that aligns well with the statistical properties of natural images.

This study reports the inaugural simultaneous measurement of double-differential charged-current cross sections for muon neutrinos and antineutrinos, specifically those with no pions in the final state, on a hydrocarbon target at the off-axis near detector of the T2K experiment. The analysis utilizes datasets corresponding to $5.8\times10^{20}$ and $6.3\times10^{20}$ protons on target for neutrino and antineutrino modes, respectively, at a beam energy peak of 0.6 GeV. By computing the sum, difference, and asymmetry from the measured cross sections, the research aims to elucidate the nuclear effects governing these interactions. When comparing the extracted results against various Monte Carlo generators and theoretical models, the study highlights that the disparity between the neutrino and antineutrino cross sections offers significant sensitivity to these nuclear effects.

A spanning generalized caterpillar is defined as a spanning tree where every vertex with a degree exceeding two lies on a single path. This note establishes a connection between the existence of such trees and the independence and connectivity numbers of a graph. Additionally, it identifies an error in a theorem presented by L. Gargano et al. in their 2004 paper, "Spanning spiders and light-splitting switches," published in Discrete Math., and further explores the relationship between another theorem from that work and the existence of spanning generalized caterpillars.

We evaluate nine anisotropic hyperelastic constitutive models of the invariant and dispersion types by assessing their ability to fit experimental data from three distinct human soft tissues. To achieve this, we employed a hybrid multi-objective optimization strategy that combines a genetic algorithm for generating initial parameter guesses with a subsequent gradient-based search. These models were calibrated against uniaxial and biaxial tension test data obtained from tissues featuring varying fiber orientations, specifically aneurysmatic abdominal aorta, linea alba, and rectus sheath. Each model was then ranked using a normalized quality of fit metric, followed by an in-depth analysis of their individual fitting performance. This study offers a rigorous quantitative comparison of these anisotropic hyperelastic models, providing insights that can assist researchers in selecting the most appropriate constitutive model for specific applications involving soft tissue behavior.

This paper introduces the true stages machinery and demonstrates its utility within descriptive set theory. Leveraging this framework, we offer fresh proofs for the Hausdorff-Kuratowski and Wadge theorems concerning the structure of ${\mathbf \Delta}^0_\xi$, as well as for Louveau and Saint-Raymond's separation theorem and Louveau's separation theorem.

A method for measuring biological diversity involves analyzing the statistical distribution of specific traits within a taxonomic group or habitat. For motile microorganisms in fluid environments, propulsion is achieved through diverse shapes, forms, and swimming strategies. This study examines swimming speed variability in unicellular eukaryotes using existing data. The data naturally divides into two categories: flagellates (possessing few flagella) and ciliates (possessing tens or more). Although these groups differ in morphology and size, the swimming speed probability distributions for both are accurately modeled by log-normal distributions, with strong agreement extending to the fourth moment. When scaled by a characteristic speed specific to each dataset, the distributions collapse onto an apparently universal curve. These findings imply a universal mechanism by which abundant microorganisms populate ecological niches.

In medical imaging, deep convolutional neural networks (ConvNets) have proven highly effective for classification, segmentation, and registration due to their exceptional ability to extract image features. However, these applications typically rely on extensive manually annotated datasets, making them labor-intensive. Consequently, developing unsupervised semantic feature learning is crucial. Our work introduces a self-supervised approach where ConvNets are trained to identify geometric transformations applied to medical images. We mathematically define a specific set of these transformations, extend the model to three dimensions by distinguishing between spatial and temporal axes, and present a straightforward task for predicting these changes. Evaluations on cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) images across different modalities (bSSFP, T2, and LGE) yielded accuracies of 96.4%, 97.5%, and 96.4%, respectively. The associated code and models will be available at: https://github.com/gaoxin492/Geometric_Transformation_CMR.

We re-examine the proposal by Castin and Weiss [Phys. Rev. Lett. vol. 102, 010403 (2009]), which suggests generating a coherent superposition of a quantum matter-wave soliton located entirely on either side of a barrier via scattering. Their original model assumed perfectly elastic scattering, implying the soliton's center-of-mass kinetic energy remained below its chemical potential. In this work, we relax that constraint. Furthermore, we propose an interferometric method utilizing soliton interference to measure the coherence between the reflected and transmitted components. Through exact diagonalization, we numerically simulate a full interferometric cycle for a six-atom soliton. Our results demonstrate that interference fringes remain observable even when the soliton's center-of-mass kinetic energy exceeds the threshold required for its complete dissociation into individual atoms.

Delta-self-consistent field theory (delta-SCF) offers a straightforward and computationally efficient approach for determining excited states. By employing the maximum overlap method to direct the optimization process, delta-SCF yields excitation energies with accuracy comparable to, and occasionally surpassing, that of TDDFT. This study benchmarks delta-SCF against a broader collection of molecules, with a specific focus on its ability to predict transition dipole moments, which are critical for calculating spectral intensities. A notable limitation of delta-SCF regarding transition dipoles is their origin dependence, stemming from the nonorthogonality between the ground and excited states. We introduce and evaluate a basic correction for this issue utilizing symmetric orthogonalization of the states, applying the method to bacteriochlorophyll structures extracted from the photosynthetic antenna of purple bacteria.

Recent literature has introduced several multipoint root-ratio techniques designed to locate multiple zeros in univariate functions. These approaches are defined by their reliance on the $m$-th root of the ratio between two functions, where $m$ represents the known multiplicity of the target zero. While some of these methods appeared without clear derivation or motivation, this paper offers a straightforward and natural framework for constructing root-ratio multipoint iterative schemes based on existing methods for simple zeros. This approach enables the generation of numerous existing and novel root-ratio methods for multiple zeros. To illustrate the process, we derive four such methods and analyze their computational costs, specifically examining the CPU time required for extracting the $m$-th root. Our findings indicate that root-ratio methods are computationally inefficient and therefore impractical for real-world applications. Additionally, we discuss the broader necessity of employing multipoint methods with very high orders.

This paper presents key findings regarding the impulsive wave equation. First, we demonstrate the existence of a solution. Subsequently, we examine approximate controllability under impulse conditions, where the control function operates within a subdomain $\omega$ at a specific time instant $\tau \in (0, T)$. Finally, we investigate impulse observability.

We present the synthesis and magnetic characteristics of BaNa$_2$Cu(VO$_4$)$_2$, a quasi-one-dimensional spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ Heisenberg antiferromagnetic chain compound. This orthovanadate features a centrosymmetric $C2/c$ crystal structure in which magnetic Cu$^{2+}$ ions constitute spin chains organized into layers; the chain orientation rotates by 62$^\circ$ between successive layers. Alternatively, accounting for inter-chain interactions, the spin lattice can be modeled as anisotropic triangular layers. Despite this structural complexity, experimental data—including temperature-dependent magnetic susceptibility, heat capacity, ESR intensity, and NMR shifts—align well with a uniform spin-$1/2$ Heisenberg chain model featuring an intrachain coupling of $J/k_{\rm B} \simeq 5.6$ K. This value is consistently supported by the saturation field derived from magnetic isotherm measurements. Furthermore, the $^{51}$V NMR spin-lattice relaxation rate reflects the 1D nature in the intermediate temperature regime, while magnetic long-range order emerges below $T_{\rm N} \simeq 0.25$ K. The effective interchain coupling is estimated at $J_{\perp}/k_{\rm B} \simeq 0.1$ K. Band-structure calculations theoretically estimate exchange couplings that corroborate our experimental results, definitively confirming the compound's 1D character. Finally, we compare the spin lattice of BaNa$_2$Cu(VO$_4$)$_2$ with the chemically analogous but non-isostructural BaAg$_2$Cu(VO$_4)_2$.

In October 2019, "Nature" released a paper detailing an experimental project at Google that demonstrated quantum supremacy using a 53-qubit quantum computer. Starting in September 2019, the authors embarked on a long-term initiative to examine various statistical dimensions of this experiment. Specifically, they have been collecting pertinent data and information to reconstruct and verify the components of the 2019 supremacy study that rely on classical computations (excluding those requiring excessive processing power) and to subject this data to statistical analysis. As of August 2022, the data collection phase for our investigation into the 2019 Google experiment is nearly complete. This document outlines the available data and information regarding the 2019 experiment, along with some of our findings and future plans.

Two derivative Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity theories are known to describe the near-horizon dynamics of higher-dimensional, near-extremal black holes, which are governed by a Schwarzian action at the boundary of the near-horizon region. This boundary action's partition function accurately yields the statistical entropy of these black holes. In this paper, we investigate the thermodynamics of spherically symmetric, four-dimensional near-extremal black holes subject to arbitrary perturbative four-derivative corrections. We find that the near-horizon dynamics is still captured by a Jackiw-Teitelboim-like action, specifically one modified by the square of the Ricci scalar. Consequently, the theory is effectively described by a boundary Schwarzian action that undergoes appropriate modifications due to these higher-derivative interactions, leading to corresponding corrections in the near-extremal entropy and free energy.

We introduce an analogue of spin fields for the relativistic RNS-particle in four dimensions, designed to characterize Ramond-Ramond states as "two-particle" excitations along the world line. Within a natural representation space, we identify a differential whose cohomology aligns with the equations governing RR-fields. Subsequently, we explore the non-linear theory represented by deformations of this structure via background fields. Additionally, we construct a sigma model for this spin field, from which the RNS-formulation emerges upon applying appropriate constraints.

In principle, real-time time-dependent density functional theory (RT-TDDFT) can calculate the entire absorption spectrum of a many-electron system subjected to a narrow pulse, provided there is an accurate and efficient propagator for numerically integrating the time-dependent Kohn-Sham equation. While low-order propagators suffice for low-lying valence absorption spectra, they are inadequate for X-ray absorption spectra (XAS) even in systems composed solely of light elements, necessitating high-order propagators. Consequently, it is essential to maximize the time step and minimize the simulation duration to reduce computational costs. To address this, we introduce a robust AutoPST method that automatically determines the propagator (P), time step (S), and simulation time (T) for relativistic RT-TDDFT simulations of XAS.

Building on the work of Adcock, Carlsson, and Carlsson, we derive numerical invariants by calculating a multidimensional persistence module, following the approach outlined by Carlsson, Singh, and Zomorodian.

Radio Frequency Interference (RFI) remains a pervasive challenge in radio astronomy. When frequency channels are contaminated, valuable information is lost, and failure to adequately model this interference can result in substantial systematic errors. This paper introduces a novel RFI mitigation strategy employing a Bayesian framework, which simultaneously flags and manages corrupted data within a unified fitting procedure. To our knowledge, this represents a first-of-its-kind approach. The methodologies outlined here can be seamlessly integrated into a Bayesian data analysis pipeline with minimal coding effort. A practical usage example is available at \href{https://github.com/samleeney/Publications}{github.com/samleeney/publications}.

Let $R$ be a complete intersection ring and $M, N$ be $R$-modules. We demonstrate that if $\text{Ext}^i_R(M,N)$ vanishes for a specific sequence of consecutive integers beginning at $n$, then the complete intersection dimension of $M$ is bounded above by $n-1$. Furthermore, we provide an estimation for the complete intersection dimension of the dual of $M$, based on the vanishing properties of the cohomology modules $\text{Ext}^i_R(M,N)$.

Free electrons within large-scale structures scatter cosmic microwave background (CMB) photons, generating a linear polarization pattern that reflects the remote CMB temperature quadrupole observed in the electrons' rest frame; this phenomenon is identified as the polarized Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (pSZ) effect. When relativistic corrections are applied to this remote quadrupole field, they produce a non-blackbody polarization anisotropy proportional to the square of the transverse peculiar velocity field, known as the kinetic polarized Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (kpSZ) effect. This paper projects that upcoming CMB and galaxy surveys will be capable of detecting the kpSZ effect with statistical significance. Additionally, we propose a quadratic estimator for the squared peculiar velocity field utilizing both galaxy survey data and CMB polarization. Finally, we describe how the kpSZ effect serves as a tool for investigating cosmic birefringence and primordial non-Gaussianity, along with forecasts regarding the sensitivity of future experiments.

Superconductors' lowest-energy excitations lack electric charge because their wave functions possess an equal mixture of electron and hole characteristics. This intrinsic property makes them difficult to investigate using standard electrical measurements that depend on charge to produce a detectable signal. However, a quantum dot's capacity to function as a charge filter allows us to overcome this challenge and measure the quasiparticle charge within superconducting-semiconducting hybrid nanowire heterostructures. We present findings from a three-terminal circuit where an injection lead creates a non-equilibrium quasiparticle distribution, and the electron or hole fraction of these quasiparticles is identified via a quantum dot serving as a tunable energy and charge filter. These results confirm the chargeless nature of quasiparticles at the energy gap edge and demonstrate the full relaxation of injected charge and energy in a proximitized nanowire, thereby addressing unresolved questions from prior three-terminal studies.

Facial editing via pretrained StyleGAN generators has become a robust technique, offering disentangled manipulation of attributes like age, expression, and lighting. Nevertheless, this method is not directly applicable to video editing. We posit that the primary limitation is the absence of precise, disentangled control over face position, pose, and localized expressions. This study shows that such fine-grained control can be realized using pretrained StyleGAN by operating across multiple latent spaces—specifically positional, W+, and S spaces—and synthesizing optimization results from each. Leveraging this capability, we present Video2StyleGAN, a system that accepts a target image and driving video(s) to transfer local and global movements and expressions from the video onto the target's identity. We assess the method across various challenging scenarios, demonstrating significant performance gains compared to existing alternatives.

Conventional process mining relies on a single case concept to discover and analyze models, an assumption that often fails to reflect real-world scenarios where multiple case notions interact and influence one another within a process. Object-centric process mining addresses this by providing the necessary techniques and concepts to manage multiple case notions; although standardized event logs and novel discovery methods for this approach have emerged, a framework for evaluating model quality is currently absent. Such evaluation metrics are essential for advancing research in object-centric discovery and enabling objective quality assessments. This paper presents a formal definition of precision and fitness for object-centric Petri nets relative to object-centric event logs, accompanied by an illustrative example and an algorithm for computing these measures. We further discuss these notions using event logs containing various models. Our approach effectively generalizes quality measures to the object-centric domain by accounting for multiple case notions, their dependencies, and their interactions.

We examine random graphs drawn uniformly from structured families, including those that can be embedded on a specific surface. We refine and broaden previous findings regarding pendant occurrences, such as the count of leaves, and derive results on the asymptotic distribution of non-giant components under fairly general conditions.

Transporting microorganisms within fluids and driving fluid movement across cellular surfaces rely on long, slender structures known as motile cilia and flagella. Their transport capability stems from regular, oscillatory beating that breaks time-reversal symmetry. While top-down experiments and theoretical models have broadly characterized these organelles and suggested mechanisms for their complex dynamics, creating minimal systems that mimic ciliary beating and isolate the function of each component remains difficult. In this study, we present the bottom-up construction of a minimal synthetic axoneme, termed a "synthoneme," using biological components from natural sources: paired microtubules and cooperatively linked axonemal dynein motors. We demonstrate that when supplied with ATP, these microtubules exhibit rhythmic bending through the cyclic association and dissociation of dyneins. This simple yet unique beating synthoneme functions as a self-organized nanoscale biomolecular machine, offering new insights into the mechanisms governing ciliary beating.

A natural extension of Lehmer's conjecture, which posits that the Ramanujan $\tau$-function never equals zero, investigates whether any positive integer $n$ exists such that $\tau(n) = \alpha$ for a given integer $\alpha$. Recent research has ruled out many integers as potential values for the $\tau$-function by employing the theory of primitive divisors in Lucas numbers, calculating integer points on curves, and utilizing congruences for $\tau(n)$. By combining these approaches and findings, we establish that for any integer $\alpha$ where $0 < |\alpha| < 100$ and $\alpha$ is not in the set $T := \{2^k, -24, -48, -70, -90, 92, -96\}$, the equation $\tau(n) = \alpha$ has no solutions for $n > 1$. Furthermore, if $\alpha$ belongs to $T$ and $\tau(n) = \alpha$ holds, then $n$ must be square-free with a specific prime factorization. Lastly, we demonstrate that a robust version of the Atkin-Serre conjecture implies that $|\tau(n)| > 100$ for all $n > 2$.

This paper develops a spectral expansion for non-self-adjoint differential operators acting on vector function spaces, which are defined by ordinary differential expressions of arbitrary order with periodic matrix coefficients. The construction utilizes essential spectral singularities, singular quasimomenta, and series with parentheses.

Process execution generates event data within information systems, which can be analyzed using process mining methods. Conventional process mining requires each event to be linked to a single object, such as a specific customer; these events form a "case," representing a complete end-to-end process run. Cases in event logs are utilized to discover process models, identify bottlenecks, or build predictive models. However, events in real-world systems, like ERPs, often relate to multiple objects. The traditional linear case model is insufficient for this object-centric data, which possesses a graph-like structure. Attempting to adapt this data by flattening it into traditional cases distorts the information by losing details. Consequently, a new concept analogous to the traditional case is required to facilitate process mining tasks on object-centric data. This paper introduces "process executions" for object-centric process mining, defined as graph-based generalizations of traditional cases. We also present methods to extract these executions and determine equivalent process behaviors regarding specific attributes using graph isomorphism. Equivalent executions based on activity are termed "object-centric variants," a generalization of traditional process variants. We also offer a visualization technique for these variants and extensively evaluate the scalability and efficiency of our contribution. Finally, a case study demonstrates the most frequent object-centric variants found in a real-life event log.

We establish a pair of sharp reverse isoperimetric inequalities applicable to domains on surfaces with nonpositive curvature. First, metric disks centered at the vertex of a Euclidean cone with an angle of at least $2\pi$ possess the minimal area among all nonpositively curved disks sharing the same perimeter and total curvature. Second, geodesic triangles situated in a Euclidean (respectively, hyperbolic) cone with an angle of at least $2\pi$ achieve the minimal area among all nonpositively curved geodesic triangles (respectively, all geodesic triangles with curvature no greater than $-1$) that have identical side lengths and angles.

This paper extends the concept of the Taylor spectrum to modules over any Lie algebra, focusing specifically on finite-dimensional cases. We demonstrate that for nilpotent and semisimple Lie algebras, the spectrum consists precisely of the set of simple submodules. However, we show that this characterization fails for solvable Lie algebras and instead provide an exact description of the spectrum when considering Borel subalgebras of semisimple Lie algebras.

Standard numerical techniques typically yield uncontrollably high errors when solving ill-conditioned linear systems, unless specific conditions are met. These systems frequently emerge from discretizing operator equations involving numerous variables. This paper demonstrates that accuracy can be substantially enhanced by transforming the equation prior to discretization, a technique termed full operator preconditioning (FOP). While FOP shares characteristics with traditional preconditioning for iterative solvers, it applies transformations directly at the operator level. We illustrate that whereas traditional preconditioning usually fails to improve solution accuracy by merely reducing the condition number, FOP succeeds in doing so. Several areas of numerical analysis can be viewed as implicitly utilizing FOP; specifically, we highlight Chebyshev interpolation in polynomial approximation and Olver-Townsend's spectral method, both of which achieve significantly higher accuracy than naive formulations. Furthermore, we introduce an FOP-based preconditioner utilizing integration to solve fourth-order differential equations via the finite-element method, proving that the resulting linear systems remain well-conditioned irrespective of discretization scale, and demonstrating its error-mitigation potential across multiple examples. Ultimately, this research confirms that FOP can surpass the standard accuracy limits inherent to both direct and iterative methods.

A geometric graph is defined as a combinatorial structure equipped with geometric properties derived from its embedding in Euclidean space. Determining a significant metric for measuring similarity or dissimilarity in both the geometric and combinatorial aspects of these graphs remains a difficult challenge within pattern recognition. This study examines two distance measures for geometric graphs: geometric edit distance (GED) and geometric graph distance (GGD). GED operates on the principle of transforming one graph into another through editing, whereas GGD is inspired by inexact graph matching. For many years, both approaches have served effectively as similarity metrics for attributed graphs; however, when applied unmodified to geometric graphs, they fail to yield meaningful distances and may not even satisfy metric axioms. To address this, we have adapted their respective cost functions specifically for geometric contexts. In addition to analyzing the metric properties of GED and GGD, we compare the two approaches. Furthermore, we deepen the understanding of the computational complexity of GGD by demonstrating that calculating this distance is $\mathcal{NP}$-hard, even when restricted to planar graphs with arbitrary cost coefficients.

This review offers a clear overview of pivotal topics in Modern Cosmology, consistently employing accessible mathematical examples and analogies where possible. Beginning with the established Big Bang Cosmology (BBC), the text examines the mathematical singularities inherent in the theory and explores potential resolutions. Prior to introducing the inflationary paradigm through illustrative examples, it addresses the horizon and flatness problems of the traditional BBC model. The discussion then turns to the present epoch of cosmic acceleration; to unify an understanding of both acceleration phases, the study focuses on quintessential inflation. Finally, the reheating phase following inflation is analyzed using straightforward mathematics, specifically through gravitational particle production within the framework of $\alpha$-attractors applied to quintessential inflation.

Recent advancements in Click-While-Through Rate (CTR) prediction have achieved new heights by incorporating longer user behavior sequences. Among various approaches, two-stage methods remain the state-of-the-art (SOTA) for industrial use. These methods initially employ a retrieval model to truncate long behavior sequences before training a CTR model on the shortened data. However, because the retrieval and CTR models are trained independently, the subsequences retrieved for the CTR model often lack accuracy, ultimately hindering overall performance. To address this, we introduce an end-to-end paradigm for modeling long behavior sequences that delivers superior performance and significant cost-efficiency compared to existing solutions. Our contributions are three-fold: First, we develop ETA-Net, a hashing-based efficient target attention network that enables end-to-end user behavior retrieval using low-cost bitwise operations, reducing the complexity of standard target attention by orders of magnitude for sequential data. Second, we present a general system architecture suitable for industrial deployment; ETA-Net has been integrated into Taobao's recommender system, yielding a 1.8% lift in CTR and a 3.1% lift in Gross Merchandise Value (GMV) over SOTA two-stage methods. Third, extensive experiments on offline datasets and online A/B tests confirm that our model significantly outperforms existing CTR models in both prediction accuracy and cost-efficiency. Currently, ETA-Net supports the majority of Taobao's traffic, serving hundreds of millions of users with billions of items daily.

Artificial Neural Networks (NN) are extensively employed to tackle intricate challenges, ranging from medical diagnosis to facial recognition. Although they have achieved significant success, NNs suffer from well-documented drawbacks, including overfitting risks, a lack of interpretability (the inability to derive explicit algorithms from trained models), and substantial computational demands. Selecting an appropriate NN architecture for specific tasks can mitigate these issues: networks that are too sparse fail to train effectively, whereas overly complex ones yield unexplainable results and are prone to overfitting. Lowering the precision of NN parameters streamlines implementation, conserves computational resources, and enhances the transparency of the network's capabilities. This paper outlines fundamental challenges in NN simplification and presents controlled pruning techniques to address them. All described pruning methods are compatible within a unified framework. Specifically, these procedures identify the optimal network structure for each task, quantify the impact of individual input signals and parameters, and generate a detailed verbal explanation of the network's algorithms and skills. The proposed methods are demonstrated through a straightforward example: creating explicit algorithms to forecast outcomes of the US presidential election.

For any velocity field $\mathbf{v}$ within a finite, fixed spatial domain, we determine the nearest rigid-body velocity field $\mathbf{v}_{RB}$ using the $L^2$ norm. The derived deformation velocity component, defined as $\mathbf{v}_{d}=\mathbf{v-\mathbf{v}}_{RB}$, is both frame-indifferent and physically observable. Specifically, when $\mathbf{Q}_{\text{RB}}(t)$ represents the rotation tensor of the closest rigid-body frame, an observer in that frame perceives $\mathbf{v}$ as $\mathbf{Q}_{\text{RB}}^{T}\mathbf{v}_{d}$. Consequently, calculating momentum, energy, vorticity, enstrophy, and helicity from the deformation velocity $\mathbf{v}_{d}$ yields frame-indifferent results.

Learned index structures operate on the premise that a database index's input-output behavior resembles a prediction task, allowing it to be realized through machine learning models rather than conventional algorithms. While this fresh perspective on a long-standing issue has spurred significant advancements at the intersection of data structures and machine learning, the primary benefit of learned indexes—their adaptability to specific datasets via ML models—can also pose security risks. This work introduces the first investigation into poisoning attacks targeting learned index structures. The proposed attack method differs from prior research because the model relies on a cumulative distribution function (CDF); consequently, any alteration to the training data triggers cascading effects across multiple data points. We develop novel poisoning attacks against linear regression models trained on CDFs, which serve as fundamental components of these indexes. Furthermore, we extend these techniques to target the Recursive Model Index (RMI), a sophisticated two-stage architecture that surpasses traditional B-Trees in performance. Evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets across various model configurations demonstrate that our attacks can escalate the error in RMI by up to 300 times and the error in its second-stage models by up to 3,000 times.

Electromagnetic waves inherently generate a gravitational field, which manifests as a pp-wave for standard plane waves. This work provides the precise solution to the Einstein-Maxwell equations associated with this phenomenon and examines the behavior of both classical particles and quantum fields within this combined gravitational and electromagnetic environment.

We examine three independent pairs of Jaynes-Cummings systems, where two atoms exhibit correlation with one another while the third remains uncorrelated with the others. We analyze the conditions required for these three uncorrelated atoms to achieve genuine multipartite entanglement. Our results indicate that this process is unattainable if the cavities interacting with the uncorrelated atoms share classical correlations with any other cavity. However, we observe that the atomic states can become genuinely multipartite entangled if the cavity housing the uncorrelated atom is highly entangled with another cavity. This non-trivial finding offers a potential method for generating multipartite entangled atoms through Jaynes-Cummings interactions and can be implemented using existing experimental setups.

Phase-field modeling offers an effective yet computationally intensive approach for capturing mesoscale morphological and microstructural evolution in materials. Consequently, there is a critical need for rapid, generalizable surrogate models to mitigate the costs associated with demanding processes like material optimization and design. The inherent discontinuity arising from sharp phase boundaries complicates the training of these surrogates. To address this, we propose a framework combining a convolutional autoencoder with a DeepONet to learn the dynamic evolution of two-phase mixtures and significantly reduce time-to-solution for microstructure prediction. The convolutional autoencoder generates a compact, low-dimensional latent representation of microstructure data, which is then processed by the DeepONet. Comprising a branch net that encodes input functions at fixed sensor locations and a trunk net that encodes output function locations, the DeepONet learns mesoscale dynamics directly from this latent space. Finally, the autoencoder's decoder reconstructs the time-evolved microstructure based on the DeepONet's predictions. The resulting trained architecture can either replace high-fidelity phase-field solvers during interpolation or accelerate them during extrapolation.

Over the past decade, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have become the foundational architecture for deep learning in most computer vision applications, yet they are not always the optimal choice. For instance, mathematical morphology is often more effective for processing binary images. This study introduces a morphological neural network specifically designed for binary inputs and outputs. Inspired by CNN structures, we construct layers tailored for such images by substituting standard convolutions with erosions and dilations. We provide theoretical explanations regarding whether these learned networks function as true morphological operators. Additionally, we present encouraging experimental results demonstrating the learning of fundamental binary operators and have released our code publicly online.

Previous research demonstrated that nanopatterned monolayer graphene (NPG) achieves spectrally selective mid-infrared (mid-IR) thermal emission from 3 to 12 $\mu$m via localized surface plasmon (LSP) resonances within the graphene. In this study, we show that graphene decorated with metallic nanoparticles, such as silver nanocubes or nanospheres, also enables spectrally selective thermal emission; however, this mechanism relies on acoustic graphene plasmons (AGPs) confined between the graphene and the silver nanoparticle within a dielectric. Our finite-difference time domain (FDTD) simulations indicate that the emission wavelength can be electrically tuned via gate voltage to switch between two regimes: an atmospherically opaque range ($\lambda=5$ to $8$ $\mu$m) and an atmospherically transparent range ($\lambda=8$ to $12$ $\mu$m). This capability allows for electrical switching between radiative heat trapping and radiative cooling modes. These theoretical findings provide a foundation for developing graphene-based thermal management systems for smart textiles.

Social media has gained immense influence over policy-making in contemporary societies, particularly in the West, where 48% of Europeans engage with these platforms daily or nearly so. Platforms like Twitter facilitate citizen engagement by allowing users to track politicians, fostering active participation in political discourse. Conversely, politicians leverage Twitter to voice opinions, engage in debates, and advance their agendas to sway voter behavior. Prior research suggests that tweets with negative sentiment tend to be retweeted more often. This study examines whether this pattern holds across politicians from various nations by analyzing hundreds of thousands of tweets from Members of Parliament in Greece, Spain, and the United Kingdom, including devolved administrations. Using advanced pre-trained language models, we conducted sentiment analysis to systematically compare the characteristics of highly influential versus less popular tweets. Our findings confirm that negatively charged tweets by politicians spread more extensively, a trend that has intensified recently, revealing significant patterns at the intersection of sentiment and virality.

Let ${\mathcal C}$ denote the category of finite graphs. Lovász (1967) established that if the number of homomorphisms from any graph $X$ to $A$ equals the number from $X$ to $B$, then $A$ and $B$ are isomorphic. Pultr (1973) extended this result categorically using a comparable approach. Both of these proofs rely on the assumption that every object possesses a finite number of subobject isomorphism classes. However, Dawar, Jakl, and Reggio (2021), along with Reggio (2021), provided generalizations that do not require this condition. This paper presents another such assumption-free generalization featuring a more concise proof. Furthermore, specific categories are identified where the new theorem applies, yet the previous results do not.

For an odd prime $p$, let $\phi$ represent the quadratic character of the multiplicative group ${\mathbb F}_p^\times$, where ${\mathbb F}_p$ denotes the finite field containing $p$ elements. This paper presents evaluations of the hypergeometric functions ${}_2F_1\left(\begin{matrix} \phi\psi & \psi\\ & \phi \end{matrix};x\right)$, defined for $x \in {\mathbb F}_p$ with $x \neq 0, 1$, expressed in terms of Hecke characters associated with CM elliptic curves. These evaluations are derived for characters $\psi$ of ${\mathbb F}_p^\times$ possessing orders of $3$, $4$, $6$, $8$, and $12$.

This study examines limits on diverse new physics resonances using existing data from four-top-quark production events, analyzing both light and heavy candidates. Additionally, we compare the effects of full width versus the narrow width approximation.

The study investigates how spin waves interact with a stationary Bloch point. The topological complexity of the Bloch point influences spin wave propagation by imparting a gauge potential analogous to that generated by a magnetic monopole interacting with an electron.
