Studies indicate that this malware can propagate rapidly across devices with diverse processor architectures, highlighting the necessity for cross-architecture binary similarity comparison technology. This field aims to identify semantic similarities between binary code snippets. However, existing learning-based methods typically generate representations for individual code snippets and assess similarity using distance metrics, neglecting inter-binary semantic interactions. Furthermore, these approaches often depend on large-scale external code corpora for pre-training instruction embeddings, a process that is computationally expensive and prone to out-of-vocabulary (OOV) issues. To address these challenges, we introduce Inter-BIN, an interaction-driven system for cross-architecture IoT binary similarity comparison. Our core insight involves employing a co-attention mechanism to facilitate interactions between instruction sequences, enabling flexible soft alignment of semantically related instructions across different architectures. Additionally, we developed a lightweight instruction embedding method based on multi-feature fusion, which mitigates the computational burden and OOV problems inherent in previous techniques. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Inter-BIN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on cross-architecture binary similarity tasks across various input granularities. Moreover, we released CrossMal, an IoT malware function matching dataset derived from real network environments, comprising 1,878,437 cross-architecture reused function pairs. Results on CrossMal confirm that Inter-BIN is both practical and scalable for real-world binary similarity comparison collections.

We introduce a new approach for the interactive creation and visualization of massive molecular environments that can depict numerous biological cells at atomic resolution. This method specializes in procedurally generated scenes derived from specific building rules. While rendering large datasets typically demands either keeping the entire scene in core memory or utilizing out-of-core strategies to manage data loading during the render loop, we propose generating the scene procedurally on demand. Our core concept involves a positional and view-dependent strategy where only a subset of the atomic scene surrounding the camera resides in GPU memory at any moment. Atomic details are organized within a uniform spatial partitioning grid covering the whole scene; however, only grid cells potentially visible to the camera are populated. These details are filled via compute shaders and linked with acceleration structures to enable hardware ray-tracing on modern GPUs. For distant objects where atomic detail is imperceptible from the current viewpoint, we use triangle meshes mapped with seamless textures, which are generated by rendering the atomic geometry. The system operates through two coordinated pipelines—a construction pipeline and a rendering pipeline—working together to display molecular scenes at atomic resolution far exceeding the capacity of GPU memory to hold trillions of atoms. We validate this technique using models of the SARS-CoV-2 virus and red blood cells.

This paper presents a reinforcement learning method that employs a new topology-based information gain metric to guide the optimal viewpoint for a noisy 3D sensor. By integrating disjoint segments of an observed surface, this metric prioritizes high-detail features like holes and concave areas. Experimental findings demonstrate that the proposed approach facilitates the strategic placement of robotic sensors to maximize the informational value of their streaming point cloud data. Additionally, we have publicly released a labeled dataset of 3D objects, a CAD design for a custom robotic manipulator, and software tools for point cloud transformation, union, and registration to support the research community.

The CMS experiment at the LHC has compiled recent findings regarding top quark production in conjunction with a Z boson or photon, as well as the generation of four top quarks. These results rely on proton-proton collision data with an integrated luminosity reaching up to 138 fb$^{-1}$, gathered at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The reported measurements include the most accurate inclusive cross sections to date, the tightest constraints on models extending beyond the standard model, and initial differential analyses. In general, the data align well with standard model predictions.

Contemporary seismic imaging and monitoring depend heavily on dense, full-azimuth data sampling. However, the high expenses associated with acquiring such data necessitate sparser collection strategies, such as using distributed ocean bottom nodes, followed by wavefield reconstruction to generate dense surveys. Matrix factorization-based wavefield reconstruction has emerged as a cost-effective and scalable alternative to transform-based methods due to its computational simplicity. Although this approach can process full-azimuth data slice-by-slice across frequencies, its efficacy diminishes at higher frequencies where monochromatic data are poorly approximated by low-rank factorizations. To mitigate this, we introduce a recursive recovery technique utilizing weighted matrix factorizations, wherein lower-frequency recovered wavefields act as priors for higher-frequency reconstruction. To prevent overfitting, we further propose a limited-subspace recursively weighted matrix factorization method, constraining the dimensions of the row and column subspaces used to build the weight matrices. Application of this technique to data from the Gulf of Suez demonstrates that the proposed limited-subspace weighted recovery approach substantially enhances reconstruction quality.

Let $N(\sigma,T)$ represent the count of nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function possessing a real part exceeding $\sigma$ and an imaginary part ranging from $0$ to $T$. We establish explicit upper bounds for $N(\sigma,T)$, known as zero density estimates. In 1937, Ingham demonstrated the asymptotic relation $N(\sigma,T)=\mathcal{O} ( T^{\frac83(1-\sigma)} (\log T)^5 )$. Ramar\'{e} subsequently derived an explicit formulation of this estimate. We examine a generalization of the approach employed in these works, which produces an explicit bound of comparable form while enhancing the associated constants.

In system identification, uncertainties—stemming from either measurement data or computational processes—invariably accompany the phenomena under study. Interval data offers a robust method for representing information in complex scenarios where uncertainty, inaccuracy, or variability must be addressed. This research aims to derive interval parameters for a model that accounts for measurement uncertainties by employing the MQ estimator alongside neural networks. The primary goal is to apply this methodology to audiometric systems, specifically for the automatic detection of auditory responses, leveraging flexible computing concepts that provide solutions resilient to subjectivity, inaccuracy, and uncertainty. Consequently, a model featuring interval parameters was developed, enabling the evaluation of an infinite set of parameters within a defined limited range. Validation was conducted using two approaches: one predicting two steps ahead with the MQ estimator, and another utilizing a neural network representation with a five-step delay. Results demonstrate that interval parameters yield interval outputs that encompass the majority of validation data, thereby enhancing system reliability.

Extending a prior derivation of the local chiral projector for a two-dimensional superspace featuring eight real supercharges, we present the comprehensive density projection formula essential for locally supersymmetrical theories within this framework. We demonstrate that this result can be derived efficiently by employing techniques rooted in the Ectoplasmic construction of local measures in superspace.

Beginning with an error made by a student, we uncover a novel approach to simultaneously determine the eigenvectors of a $2\times2$ matrix with distinct eigenvalues through a single calculation. We explore the relationship with the Cayley-Hamilton theorem and extend this result to $3\times3$ matrices, presenting arguments accessible to advanced linear algebra students.

We introduce a technique for generating selective interactions within the Dicke-Stark model using time-dependent perturbation theory. By selecting an appropriate rotating frame, we observe that time-oscillating terms are functions of both atomic and photonic excitation counts. This allows Rabi oscillations between specific states to be achieved by tuning the frequency of the two-level system accordingly. Furthermore, this approach facilitates the study of second-order selective interactions. Leveraging these interactions, we can construct various quantum states, including Dicke states, superpositions of Dicke states, and GHZ states. Numerical simulations confirm that high-fidelity Dicke and Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states are attainable through optimal selection of the two-level system frequency and precise control of evolution time.

Cross-document event coreference resolution (CDCR) is an NLP task focused on identifying and clustering event mentions across multiple documents. Although CDCR is intended to enhance downstream multi-document applications, its practical benefits remain unproven despite recent advances in system development and corpora. A key observation is that all existing CDCR systems have been developed, trained, and evaluated exclusively on a single corpus, raising serious doubts about their generalizability—a critical requirement for real-world applications where domain and event magnitude often surpass curated datasets. To test this hypothesis, we established a unified evaluation framework using three corpora: ECB+, the Gun Violence Corpus, and the Football Coreference Corpus (the latter reannotated at the token level for analysis). We compared a corpus-independent, feature-based system against a recent neural system optimized for ECB+. While the feature-based system achieved lower absolute scores, it demonstrated more consistent performance across all datasets compared to the neural system, which performed erratically. Through model introspection, we discovered that the significance of features such as event actions and timestamps varies significantly between corpora. Further analysis revealed that several systems overfit to the specific structure of the ECB+ corpus. We conclude with recommendations for building generally applicable CDCR systems, emphasizing that evaluation across multiple corpora is essential. To support future research, we have publicly released our dataset, annotation guidelines, and system implementation.

This study introduces an empirical approach for conducting recentered influence function (RIF) regression, as developed by Firpo, Fortin, and Lemieux (2009), a technique useful for analyzing how covariates impact various statistics beyond the mean. In scenarios where the influence function is either inaccessible or computationally challenging, we recommend utilizing the \emph{sensitivity curve} (Tukey, 1977) as a practical substitute, although this can be computationally intensive with large datasets. The validity of this strategy stems from the fact that, under general conditions, the sensitivity curve converges in probability to the influence function. To enhance computational efficiency, we propose applying a non-parametric cubic splines method to a random subsample and subsequently interpolating the results for the remaining observations. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate favorable finite sample properties, and we apply the proposed estimator to analyze the polarization index defined by Duclos, Esteban, and Ray (2004).

We provide a concise overview of high-energy scattering within string theory, examine the thermal characteristics of strings, elucidate the link between these two areas, and demonstrate how they integrate with the string/black hole transition.

The generalization capability of deep-learning models relies heavily on richly labeled data, yet this reliance on large-scale annotated supervision is often prohibitive in real-world contexts due to the high costs of data collection and labeling. While various domain adaptation methods exist to address distribution discrepancies, most assume identical label sets across source and target domains. To address this limitation and tackle a more practical challenge, we frame the problem as partial domain adaptation, where the source label set is a superset of the target label set. Motivated by the premise that image styles are domain-specific, we propose a method that identifies outlier classes solely based on image content and trains a label classifier exclusively on the relationship between classes and content within source images. Furthermore, we prevent negative transfer from source-specific classes by converting soft class-level weights into two distinct clusters—representing outlier source classes (0) and shared classes (1)—through the maximization of between-cluster variance.

High-redshift active galactic nuclei (AGNs) serve as direct probes for investigating black hole activity in the early Universe, with radio sources featuring jets misaligned from our line of sight anticipated to be the most prevalent. This study presents high-resolution imaging of the z=4.57 AGN J2102+6015, derived from multi-epoch dual-frequency very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) data. The 8.4-GHz VLBI images expose two prominent structures oriented east-west and separated by approximately 10 milli-arcseconds (mas). Spectral index mapping indicates that both features exhibit flat or inverted spectra. Over a monitoring span of roughly 13 years, the distance between these two components remained virtually constant, establishing an upper limit on their separation speed at about 0.04 mas year$^{-1}$. While earlier research categorized J2102+6015 as a GHz-peaked spectrum quasar, our findings suggest it is more likely a young, compact symmetric object rather than a blazar-type core-jet source.

Reinforcement learning (RL) is now extensively used in robot control, yet it frequently suffers from low data efficiency. Although interactive feedback has proven to significantly accelerate RL, the various strategies available are mostly evaluated only in discrete grid worlds or small-scale optimal control settings. Consequently, the literature lacks agreement on the optimal feedback frequency or the most advantageous timing for feedback. To address these inconsistencies, this study isolates and quantifies the impact of feedback frequency within robotic tasks featuring continuous state and action spaces, specifically focusing on inverse kinematics learning for manipulator arms of varying complexity. Our findings reveal that previously contradictory observations arise from differences in task complexity and indicate that there is no single ideal feedback frequency; instead, the frequency should be adjusted as the agent's proficiency improves.

This study introduces novel approaches for characterizing the spectral-temporal distribution of individual photons. The proposed protocols leverage spectral filtering, frequency entanglement between a target photon and a reference photon, and a generalized Hong, Ou, and Mandel interferometer. By measuring coincidence probabilities across these various schemes, one can determine the chronocyclic Wigner function, the pseudo-Wigner distribution, and the spectrogram at the single-photon level.

As gravitational-wave detectors achieve greater sensitivity and longer observing durations, a wider array of signals from diverse sources is anticipated. Notably, long-lived gravitational-wave transients have garnered significant interest over the past decade. Since most long-duration signals lack precise theoretical models, detection relies on generic search algorithms that impose minimal assumptions regarding signal characteristics. However, the high computational expense of these searches limits their performance, resulting in sub-optimal sensitivity. To address this challenge, various detection algorithms have been developed. This paper introduces a novel data analysis pipeline designed to identify unmodeled long-lived transient gravitational-wave signals lasting between 10 and 1000 seconds, utilizing an excess cross-power statistic across a detector network. The pipeline incorporates several innovative features aimed at lowering computational costs and enhancing detection sensitivity for a broad spectrum of signal morphologies. Generalized to accommodate networks with any number of detectors, the method provides a stable framework for future enhancements. Comparisons against a prior implementation of a similar technique, using both simulated and real gravitational-wave data, demonstrate an overall improvement in detection efficiency dependent on signal morphology, alongside a reduction in computing time by at least a factor of ten.

We re-examine the classical challenge of constructing cryptographically secure hash functions with optimal efficiency. Traditionally, these functions are built by applying modes of operation to primitives with smaller domains. Prior research by Shrimpton and Stam (ICALP 2008), Rogaway and Steinberger (CRYPTO 2008), and Mennink and Preneel (CRYPTO 2012) demonstrated how to achieve optimally efficient $2n$-to-$n$-bit compression functions from non-compressing primitives, ensuring asymptotically optimal collision resistance against $2^{n/2-\epsilon}$ queries. However, creating optimally efficient and secure hash functions for domains larger than $2n$ bits remains an unsolved problem.

In this paper, we introduce a new efficiency concept called \textit{compactness}. This notion enables us to concentrate on hash functions that are asymptotically optimally collision resistant and to normalize their parameters based on Stam's CRYPTO 2008 bound to maximize efficiency. We subsequently present two tree-based modes of operation:

- Our first construction is an \underline{A}ugmented \underline{B}inary \underline{T}ree (ABR) mode. This design creates a $(2^{\ell}+2^{\ell-1} -1)n$-to-$n$-bit hash function that utilizes a total of $(2^{\ell}-1)$ calls to $2n$-to-$n$-bit compression functions for any $\ell\geq 2$. The ABR mode is optimally compact, offering asymptotically optimal ($2^{n/2-\epsilon}$-query) collision resistance in the ideal model. For a tree of height $\ell$, compared to a Merkle tree, the ABR mode processes an additional $(2^{\ell-1}-1)$ data blocks while performing the same number of internal compression function calls.

- Although the ABR mode provides collision resistance, it does not achieve indifferentiability from a random oracle within $2^{n/3}$ queries. The improved variant, $ABR^{+}$, compresses only one fewer data block than ABR for the same number of compression calls and additionally achieves indifferentiability up to $2^{n/2-\epsilon}$ queries.

Extracting data from line charts extends Optical Character Recognition (OCR) by aiming to retrieve the numerical values depicted in chart images. Recent approaches, such as ChartOCR, utilize multi-stage networks that integrate object detection with OCR models. However, most current datasets and models rely on "clean" screenshots, which differ significantly from real-world camera photos. Furthermore, generating new domain-specific datasets is often time-consuming due to the need for extensive labeling. Our primary contributions include a synthetic data generation framework and a one-stage model capable of simultaneously outputting text labels, mark coordinates, and perspective estimates. We compiled two evaluation datasets featuring real camera photos. Our results demonstrate that a model trained exclusively on synthetic data can be effectively applied to real photos without fine-tuning, making it viable for practical applications.

While Radio Environment Maps (REMs) significantly improve the performance of radio-equipped agents, their creation, particularly in three-dimensional settings, is often a demanding task. This project demonstrates an autonomous and scalable approach to generating a 3D indoor REM. Building on prior research from Project 1, it employs multiple drones to capture WiFi signals in a real-world environment; each drone visits 36 waypoints to collectively amass thousands of WiFi beacon samples. The report analyzes this dataset and concludes by suggesting machine-learning methods to estimate signal strength for known access points in areas the drones did not visit.

Exoplanet and brown dwarf atmospheres frequently exhibit disequilibrium chemistry. The advent of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) enables high-resolution spectral analysis of directly imaged exoplanets, facilitating detailed atmospheric characterization and systematic detection of chemical species that deviate from thermochemical equilibrium. By constraining the prevalence of disequilibrium chemistry across parameters like effective temperature and surface gravity, we can refine our understanding of the underlying atmospheric physics. This work contributes to the Sonora grid of atmosphere models series (Marley et al. 2021; Morley et al. in prep.), specifically presenting a cloud-free, solar metallicity grid for brown dwarfs and wide-orbit giant planets featuring disequilibrium key molecules such as CH4, H2O, CO, and NH3. The grid spans effective temperatures from 500 K to 1300 K, surface gravities from 3.0 to 5.5 (cgs), and eddy diffusion coefficients of log Kzz = 2, 4, and 7 (cgs). We analyze how these parameters influence temperature and compositional profiles, assess their impact on near-infrared colors, and evaluate the detectability of the specified molecules using JWST. Furthermore, we compare our models with existing MKO and Spitzer data of brown dwarfs to confirm the significance of disequilibrium chemistry in T dwarfs and discuss how these models aid in determining the vertical structure and chemical makeup of these atmospheres.

The excitonic insulator (EI) state represents a strongly correlated many-body ground state resulting from a band structure instability that favors exciton formation. We demonstrate that the flat valence and conduction bands found in a semiconducting diatomic Kagome lattice—specifically within a superatomic graphene lattice—can facilitate an intriguing triplet EI state. This conclusion is drawn from density functional theory (DFT) calculations augmented by many-body GW and Bethe-Salpeter Equation (BSE) methods. Our findings suggest that massive carriers within flat bands, characterized by highly localized electron and hole wavefunctions, markedly diminish screening and amplify exchange interactions. Consequently, this yields an exceptionally high triplet exciton binding energy of approximately 1.1 eV, which surpasses the GW band gap by roughly 0.2 eV, alongside a substantial singlet-triplet splitting of about 0.4 eV. These results further illuminate the complex physics of flat bands and broaden the range of potential EI materials.

As human-machine interaction via language grows, users increasingly engage with systems without realizing they are conversing with a machine, such as during phone calls or text-based chats. This study investigates strategies for system designers and researchers to enable their systems to disclose their non-human nature. We have gathered more than 2,500 expressions reflecting the intent of "Are you a robot?" and paired them with over 2,500 adversarially chosen utterances where simply confirming non-human status is inadequate or awkward. We evaluate classifiers designed to detect this intent, analyzing tradeoffs between precision, recall, and model complexity. These tools could be embedded in dialogue systems to prevent unintentional deception. Furthermore, we examine how a generative research model (Blender) and two commercial systems (Amazon Alexa and Google Assistant) respond to this query, revealing frequent failures in these systems to acknowledge their artificial identity. Finally, we define criteria for an effective response to this intent and conduct a user study to identify the most critical factors in how systems should answer.

Ensuring public safety and health is a critical application of automatic fall detection, yet conventional home camera systems often compromise user privacy. Thermal imaging offers a solution by obscuring facial details, thereby protecting individual privacy. Furthermore, the scarcity of fall events compared to routine daily activities creates a significant class imbalance challenge that complicates algorithm training. To address these issues, we propose formulating fall detection as an anomaly detection problem within an adversarial framework utilizing thermal imagery. Our approach introduces a novel adversarial network featuring dual-channel 3D convolutional autoencoders; one reconstructs thermal data sequences while the other processes optical flow inputs. We also implement a region-of-interest tracking method, a region-based difference constraint, and a joint discriminator to calculate reconstruction errors, where elevated errors signal a fall. Experimental results on a public thermal fall dataset demonstrate that our method outperforms standard baselines.

A novel approach, grounded in the concept of a rotationally stretched nucleus treated via quantum mechanics, has been applied to investigate deviations from the I(I+1) rule in even-even isotopes such as 62Sm, 64Gd, 66Dy, 68Er, 70Yb, 72Hf, 74W, and 76Os. This method yielded a new formula effectively describing the angular momentum dependence of the moment of inertia for even-even nuclei across the actinide and rare-earth regions within the range 2.9 < R < 3.3. Calculations performed using this quantized stretched model produced results that align reasonably well with experimental data for all spin values up to I = 16.

We introduce PlaneMVS, a new framework designed for reconstructing 3D planes from multiple input views with known camera poses. Unlike most existing learning-based approaches that rely on single-image regression and struggle with depth scale ambiguity, our method utilizes a multi-view stereo (MVS) pipeline to leverage multi-view geometry. We separate the reconstruction process into two components: a semantic plane detection branch, which builds upon single-view detection but with key modifications, and a plane MVS branch. This second branch employs slanted plane hypotheses instead of standard depth hypotheses to execute a plane sweeping strategy, ultimately learning pixel-level plane parameters and depth maps. We detail how these branches are trained in a balanced manner and propose a soft-pooling loss to align their outputs, allowing them to mutually enhance performance. Extensive evaluations on various indoor datasets demonstrate that PlaneMVS significantly surpasses state-of-the-art single-view methods in both detection and 3D geometry metrics. Furthermore, our approach outperforms several leading learning-based MVS methods by effectively utilizing learned plane priors. To our knowledge, this marks the first end-to-end MVS framework dedicated to 3D plane reconstruction.

Many critical domains, including machine learning and computer vision, rely on streaming applications that process input sequences over time. Determining optimal runtime performance configurations for these systems is difficult because ideal settings depend on variables such as input data, hardware platforms, temporal factors, and diverse user requirements. While previous research typically addresses this through offline profiling followed by model training, such methods incur significant overhead before execution and struggle with redeployment across different runtime environments. This paper introduces Sonic, a sampling-based online controller designed for long-running streaming applications that eliminates the need for pre-execution profiling. During each execution phase, Sonic strategically samples the configuration space using the initial portion of the run to identify optimal settings for the remainder, adhering to user-defined constrained optimization goals. To enhance sampling efficiency, the system combines machine learning regression with Bayesian optimization. Sonic is designed to be independent of specific applications, devices, inputs, performance metrics, or constraints. Evaluated on both traditional parallel benchmarks and deep learning inference tasks across various platforms, Sonic achieves runtime performance within 5.3% of the theoretical optimum. These results demonstrate that Sonic can rapidly identify near-optimal configurations under diverse runtime conditions without requiring prior knowledge.

In statistical mechanics, the trace of the thermal average of any energy-momentum tensor is given by $\langle T^{\mu}_{\;\;\mu}\rangle =T\partial P/\partial T-4P$. For QCD with massless fermions, the renormalization group formula $\langle T^{\mu}_{\;\;\mu}\rangle =\beta(g_{M})\partial P/\partial g_{M}$ necessitates that the pressure takes the form \begin{equation} P=T^{4}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \phi_{n}(g_{M})\big[\ln\big({M\over 4\pi
T}\big)\big]^{n},\end{equation} where the factor $4\pi$ is included for future convenience. For $n\ge 1$, the functions $\phi_{n}(g_{M})$ can be derived from $\phi_{0}(g_{M})$ via the recursion relation $n\,\phi_{n}(g_{M})=-\beta(g_{M})d\phi_{n-1}/dg_{M}$. This relation is validated against established perturbation theory results by employing the $(g_{M})^{2}, (g_{M})^{3}$, and $(g_{M})^{4}$ terms of $\phi_{0}(g_{M})$ to generate the corresponding known terms of order $(g_{M})^{4}, (g_{M})^{5}$, and $(g_{M})^{6}$ in $\phi_{1}(g_{M})$, as well as the $(g_{M})^{6}$ term in $\phi_{2}(g_{M})$. Summing this series yields the same result as setting $M=4\pi T$, which is expressed as $T^{4}\phi_{0}(g_{4\pi T})$.

This study investigates the Fractional Fourier Transform (FRFT) as a method for deriving probability density functions (PDFs) and their derivatives, with a primary focus on fitting stochastic models that adhere to the fundamental property of infinite divisibility. The analysis computes PDFs and evaluates distributional characteristics—including leptokurtosis, peakedness, and asymmetry—for both the Variance-Gamma (VG) model and the Compound Poisson model with Normal compounding. Additionally, the first and second derivatives of the VG model's PDF are calculated to construct the Fisher information matrix required for Maximum Likelihood estimation. Increasingly utilized as an alternative to the Classical Lognormal Model (CLM) for asset price modeling, the five-parameter VG model was estimated using the FRFT approach on daily SPY ETF data. Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) goodness-of-fit tests indicate that the VG model provides a superior fit to the empirical cumulative distribution compared to the CLM, with the FRFT-based estimation yielding the optimal VG model.

Entanglement serves as a critical resource within quantum information technology. In the realm of continuous-variable quantum optics, photon subtraction can enhance the entanglement of Gaussian light states, yet the degree of this increase for mixed states remains largely unclear. This study employs an entanglement metric derived from Rényi-2 entropy to demonstrate that single-photon subtraction boosts bipartite entanglement by at most log 2. This limit aligns with the maximum bipartite entanglement achievable using a single photon. Crucially, this upper bound applies universally to all Gaussian input states, irrespective of their mode count or purity.

Liquids equilibrated beneath a critical onset density exhibit comparable inherent states, whereas those above this threshold display significantly distinct states. Despite being documented in simulations more than two decades ago, the underlying physical cause of this memory effect remains debated, particularly due to its omission from mean-field theories, which has questioned its thermodynamic significance. Driven by a recent theoretical suggestion, we re-evaluate the onset phenomenon using simulations with a rapid hard-sphere jamming algorithm, confirming its robustness across both thermodynamic and dimensional scales. Notably, we also identify a second form of memory linked to a Gardner-like transition within the jamming algorithm.

It has been shown that the transport coefficients (specifically self-diffusion, shear viscosity, and thermal conductivity) of properly reduced Lennard-Jones fluids, when plotted along isotherms, display quasi-universal scaling with respect to the ratio of density to its value at the freezing point. This scaling behavior closely mirrors that observed in hard-sphere fluids. Furthermore, the Stokes-Einstein relation, excluding the hydrodynamic diameter, holds true within the dense fluid regime, where its lower density limit effectively delineates the boundary between gas-like and liquid-like behaviors.

The Dixmier-Moeglin Equivalence (DM-equivalence) refers to the condition where three distinct characteristics of prime ideals within a non-commutative algebra A are equivalent: (i) primitivity, (ii) rationality, and (iii) being locally closed under the Zariski topology on Spec(A). While this equivalence is known to hold in various significant algebras over a field, recent findings established that it also applies to the prime ideals of Leavitt path algebras associated with finite graphs. This note extends that inquiry to Leavitt path algebras $L$ derived from arbitrary directed graphs $E$. Our analysis demonstrates that locally closed prime ideals in $L$ satisfy notable equivalent conditions, specifically strong primitivity and complete irreducibility. The findings are supported by illustrative examples that highlight the results and their limitations.

To enable highly dynamic leaps in legged robots, managing rotational dynamics is crucial. This paper introduces a unified model designed to enhance jumping performance by approximating centroidal inertia for planning such movements. The model simplifies the robot into a single rigid body for the base and treats legs as point masses, referred to as the Lump Leg Single Rigid Body Model (LL-SRBM), applicable to both bipedal and quadrupedal systems. By incorporating leg dynamics, LL-SRBM offers a computationally efficient method for motion planners to adjust the robot's centroidal inertia across different leg configurations. Additionally, we present a new contact detection technique based on the norm of average spatial velocity. Upon detecting contact, the controller transitions to force control to ensure a soft landing. Experiments involving twisting and forward jumps on the bipedal robot SLIDER and the quadrupedal robot ANYmal confirm that actively modifying centroidal inertia improves jump performance. Furthermore, these trials demonstrate the generalization and robustness of the combined planning and control framework.

While analyzing nighttime artificial light colors affects various domains, existing data sources often suffer from low resolution or limited image availability for specific areas. To address this, we introduce crowdsourced streetlight photography as a viable alternative through "NightUp Castelldefels," a citizen science pilot designed to gather such data. By extracting colors from these images and comparing them against an official database, we demonstrate that untrained citizens can effectively classify streetlight colors using smartphone photos. Furthermore, comparing our results with those from established sources reveals that these methods provide complementary insights into regional nighttime lighting. This research establishes a new pathway for studying artificial light colors, enabling the accurate, large-scale, and cost-effective collection of data.

The robotics literature addresses optimal tracking through various robust and adaptive control methods, yet these approaches face implementation hurdles, including handling uncertain dynamics with complete or partial models, complexity and integrity issues in discrete-time settings, and scalability within complex coupled systems. To overcome these challenges, an online adaptive learning mechanism is proposed as a generalized solution for a specific class of tracking control problems. This method minimizes tracking errors and optimizes overall dynamic behavior using simultaneous linear feedback control. By employing reinforcement learning based on value iteration, the approach solves the underlying Bellman optimality equations. Consequently, control strategies are updated interactively in real time without needing prior knowledge of the system's dynamics. Adaptive critics are utilized to approximate optimal value functions and corresponding control strategies in real time. The efficacy of this proposed adaptive tracking mechanism is demonstrated via simulations controlling a flexible wing aircraft within an uncertain aerodynamic learning environment.

This study seeks to elucidate the remarkable efficacy of deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) through a theoretical examination of their generalization capabilities and by establishing optimization guarantees for gradient descent-based training methods. Specifically, considering a CNN architecture with $l$ convolutional layers and a single fully connected layer, we demonstrate that the generalization error is bounded by $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\dt\widetilde{\varrho}/n})$, where $\theta$ represents the degrees of freedom of the network parameters, and $\widetilde{\varrho}=\mathcal{O}(\log(\prod_{i=1}^{l}\rwi{i} (\ki{i}-\si{i}+1)/p)+\log(\rf))$ aggregates architectural parameters such as kernel size $\ki{i}$, stride $\si{i}$, pooling size $p$, and parameter magnitude $\rwi{i}$. To the best of our knowledge, this marks the first generalization bound relying solely on $\mathcal{O}(\log(\prod_{i=1}^{l+1}\rwi{i}))$, offering a significant improvement over previous bounds that included exponential terms like $\mathcal{O}(\prod_{i=1}^{l+1}\rwi{i})$. Additionally, we establish that for any gradient descent algorithm, an approximate stationary point derived from minimizing empirical risk also serves as an approximate stationary point for the population risk. This finding clarifies why gradient descent algorithms typically exhibit strong practical performance. Furthermore, we prove the one-to-one correspondence and convergence properties of non-degenerate stationary points between empirical and population risks. This implies that a local minimum found during empirical risk minimization remains close to a local minimum of the population risk, thereby ensuring robust generalization performance for CNNs.

Recent large-scale vision-language pre-training (VLP) using dual-stream architectures, such as CLIP, has demonstrated superior performance across various multimodal alignment tasks by leveraging vast amounts of image-text pairs. However, these models currently lack the capability for multimodal generation due to limitations in their text encoders. To address this, we introduce a method that enhances dual-stream VLP models by integrating a pre-trained language model (PLM) through vision-language knowledge distillation (VLKD), thereby enabling multimodal generation. VLKD offers significant advantages in data and computational efficiency compared to training from scratch. Experimental results indicate that the proposed model achieves strong zero-shot performance on multimodal generation tasks, including open-ended visual question answering and image captioning. For instance, it attains 44.5% zero-shot accuracy on the VQAv2 dataset, outperforming the previous state-of-the-art zero-shot model while utilizing $7\times$ fewer parameters. Additionally, the VLKD approach preserves the original PLM's textual language understanding and generation capabilities, ensuring the model remains versatile for both multimodal and unimodal applications.

This paper addresses solving discounted Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) with the requirement that the resulting policy must be stabilizing. Since practical MDP solutions often rely on policy approximation, we utilize recent advancements in applying Model Predictive Control (MPC) within Reinforcement Learning to embed stability constraints directly into the MPC-based policy. This approach inherently restricts the MDP solution space to stabilizing policies. Given that stability theory for MPC is most well-developed for undiscounted scenarios, we first demonstrate that stable discounted MDPs can be reformulated as undiscounted ones. This reformulation ensures that an MPC-based policy incorporating stability requirements yields the optimal policy for the discounted MDP when stable, and otherwise provides the best possible stabilizing policy.

Natural Language Processing has leveraged pre-trained language models to achieve state-of-the-art performance across various downstream applications, including sentiment analysis and author identification. This study investigates the application of such methods for text-based personality classification, specifically targeting the Myers-Briggs (MBTI) framework. We detail a series of experiments where the Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) model was fine-tuned to execute MBTI classification. Our primary results indicate that this approach substantially surpasses established text classification techniques relying on bag-of-words and static word embeddings across diverse evaluation settings, and it also exceeds prior efforts within this domain.

This study examines an ${\cal N}=1$ $SU(N_c)$ SQCD-like theory (along with its Seiberg dual featuring $SU(N_F-N_c)$ colors), containing $N_F$ light quark flavors ${\overline Q}_j, Q^i$ governed by a superpotential mass term $m_Q{\rm Tr}({\overline Q} Q)$ where $m_Q\ll\Lambda_Q$. Additionally, the model includes $N_F^2$ colorless but flavored fields $\Phi^j_i$ with a large mass scale $\mu_{\Phi}\gg\Lambda_Q$. The analysis focuses on the regime $N_c+1<N_F<3N_c/2$, where the UV-free direct $SU(N_c)$ theory becomes strongly coupled below the scale $\mu<\Lambda_Q$.

Mass spectra for this direct theory across various vacua and values of $\mu_{\Phi}\gg\Lambda_Q$ are computed using a dynamical framework proposed in [10]. This framework posits that quarks in such ${\cal N}=1$ SQCD-like theories exist in only two standard phases: the Higgs phase or the heavy quark (confined) phase. The results demonstrate that, due to strong power-like renormalization group evolution, the fields $\Phi^j_i$, which appear heavy and dynamically irrelevant at scales $\mu<\Lambda_Q$, can become light and relevant at lower energies. Consequently, two additional generations of light $\Phi$-particles emerge with pole masses $\mu_{2,3}^{\rm pole}(\Phi)\ll\Lambda_Q$.

When comparing the calculated mass spectra of this strongly coupled $SU(N_c)$ theory to those of its weakly coupled Seiberg dual $SU(N_F-N_c)$ variant at scales $\mu<\Lambda_Q$, a parametric difference is observed. It is noted that the dynamical scenario from [10] employed here passes all standard tests used to verify Seiberg's hypothesis regarding the equivalence of direct and dual theories. This discrepancy indicates that while these tests are necessary, they may not be sufficient to guarantee duality equivalence.

This work investigates complex-valued scaling, a distinctive symmetry inherent to complex-valued data and representations. While Deep Complex Networks (DCN) extend real-valued algebra into the complex domain without handling complex-valued scaling, SurReal employs a restrictive manifold perspective using a distance metric to achieve complex-scaling invariance, albeit at the cost of discarding rich complex-valued information. By treating complex-valued scaling as a co-domain transformation, we develop new equivariant and invariant neural network layer functions tailored for this specific operation. Additionally, we introduce novel complex-valued representations for RGB images, where complex-valued scaling corresponds to hue shifts or correlated variations across color channels. Experiments on MSTAR, CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and SVHN demonstrate that our co-domain symmetric (CDS) classifiers outperform DCN and SurReal by achieving higher accuracy, improved generalization, greater robustness to co-domain transformations, and reduced model bias and variance, all with significantly fewer parameters.

We introduce and analyze a runtime architecture that combines sensor data and classifiers with a logic-driven decision-making system within an e-Health framework designed for rehabilitating children with neuromotor disorders. In this scenario, children engage in rehabilitation tasks through games. The primary objective is to extract parameters reflecting the child's current cognitive and behavioral performance—such as engagement, attention, and task accuracy—from various sensors and classifiers (including eye trackers, motion sensors, and emotion recognition methods) to inform adaptive decisions. These decisions aim to enhance performance by deploying re-engagement stimuli when attention wanes or by adjusting game difficulty to maintain interest when the task becomes too easy. Complementing state-of-the-art emotion recognition and head pose estimation, we employ a runtime variant of the Epistemic Probabilistic Event Calculus, a dialect of probabilistic and epistemic logic programming. Specifically, the probabilistic aspect of this symbolic framework provides a natural interface for machine learning techniques. We provide an overview of the architecture and its components, illustrating its characteristics through a running example and experimental results. This work is under consideration for publication in *Theory and Practice of Logic Programming* (TPLP).

This paper addresses the question of whether the r-th inequality is violated by extremal curves in projective r-space, a problem originally posed by T. Kato and G. Martens. We demonstrate that the answer is negative in numerous instances. This conclusion is derived from a thorough examination of the geometry of these extremal curves and their canonical models. Consequently, we establish that specific curves on a Hirzebruch surface do not breach slope inequalities within a particular range.

Recent advancements in artificial intelligence highlight the significant potential of deep learning and deep reinforcement learning. However, these achievements remain largely task-specific, resulting in constrained progress regarding out-of-distribution generalization. Although it is hypothesized that appropriate inductive biases could resolve these issues, the concept itself often remains ill-defined, offering little practical direction. This paper proposes an alternative learning paradigm where representations are not derived from architectural biases but are instead learned within a target language possessing known semantics. The foundational principles of this approach are already present in mainstream AI, which has utilized various linguistic frameworks—from first-order logic fragments to probabilistic structural causal models—to encode representations. The primary challenge lies in automating the learning of representations that have historically been manually designed. In this framework, generalization stems directly from the semantics of the language employed. The objectives of this work are to clarify these concepts, situate them within a broader context emphasizing the critical role of target language design, and demonstrate their application in learning to act and plan. Following an introductory overview, the paper examines the learning of action representations, general policies, and subgoals (conceptualized as intrinsic rewards). While these tasks can be formulated as combinatorial problems, deep learning techniques remain applicable. Ultimately, learning over languages with defined semantics explains *what* needs to be learned, whereas neural network methods explain *how* it can be learned; the key opportunity lies in integrating these two perspectives.

This work introduces, for the first time, an active optical clock utilizing a highly charged Nd$^{9+}$ ion. Designed to achieve an ultra-narrow linewidth at the $\mu$Hz level, this clock surpasses current laser linewidth records by more than two orders of magnitude. By operating on a 605(90) nm superradiant transition between the $5p^2~4f$ ground state and a long-lived $5p~4f^2$ excited state, the system exhibits inherent immunity to cavity noise, ensuring high stability. Furthermore, the clock functions as a highly sensitive probe capable of detecting variations in the fine-structure constant with precision below the 10$^{-19}$ level. These findings are supported by sophisticated relativistic many-body calculations that accurately predict the relevant atomic properties.

Machine learning techniques commonly scan chemical space to identify promising molecules prior to expensive experimental synthesis, yet these approaches frequently depend on graph-based representations that overlook 3D structural details critical for assessing molecular stability. We introduce a reinforcement learning framework designed to generate molecules in Cartesian coordinates, enabling accurate quantum chemical stability predictions. To enhance sample efficiency, we employ imitation learning on the GDB-11 dataset to extract fundamental chemical rules, establishing a foundational model capable of handling various stoichiometries. Subsequently, we utilize multiple stoichiometry-conditioned instances of this model within a reinforcement learning environment. Our approach successfully identifies low-energy molecules within the database and generates novel isomers absent from the training data. Furthermore, applying the model to larger molecular structures demonstrates how reinforcement learning effectively refines the imitation learning baseline in regions distant from the original training distribution.

Utilizing multiple degrees of freedom, structured light has emerged as a potent method for employing complex light states in both foundational research and practical applications. In this work, we examine the light field of an ultrafast laser beam characterized by a polarization state dependent on wavelength, which we define as a spectral vector beam. We introduce a straightforward technique for generating and adjusting these structured beams and highlight their spectroscopic potential. By measuring polarization states with rapid photodetectors, one can monitor pulse-to-pulse variations in the frequency spectrum resulting from phenomena such as narrowband transmission or absorption. Our experiments achieved read-out speeds of approximately 6 MHz, a limit imposed by our current technical capacity for spectral modulation, though GHz rates are theoretically feasible. Furthermore, simulations utilizing a supercontinuum light source extend the spectral range beyond 1000 nm, opening possibilities for diverse applications demanding high-speed spectroscopic analysis.

Sea subsurface temperature, a critical factor influencing marine ecosystems, underwater dynamics, and heat exchange with the surface, is significantly impacted by global warming. Current research typically relies on either physics-based numerical models or data-driven approaches. Traditionally, these two domains—physics-driven modeling and data-driven machine learning—are viewed as distinct with divergent scientific paradigms for predicting sea subsurface temperatures. However, we argue that they are mutually complementary; physical models provide extrapolation capabilities beyond observed conditions, whereas data-driven methods offer flexibility in adapting to data and identifying unforeseen patterns. Integrating both approaches is promising and holds the potential to enhance predictive performance. This paper introduces a novel framework combining a generative adversarial network (GAN) with a numerical model for sea subsurface temperature prediction. Initially, the GAN learns the simplified physical relationships between surface and target subsurface temperatures within the numerical model. Subsequently, observational data are employed to calibrate the GAN's parameters for improved accuracy. The framework's efficacy is evaluated by predicting daily subsurface temperatures in the South China Sea, with extensive experiments confirming its superiority over existing state-of-the-art methods.

Deep Neural Networks typically rely on iterative gradient updates for training. However, gradient magnitudes are influenced by various elements, such as activation function choices and initialization strategies. Crucially, these magnitudes often vary significantly across layers, with some receiving much smaller updates than others. This disparity causes uneven training speeds among layers, ultimately delaying overall convergence. We provide an analytical explanation for this gradient disproportionality and propose a method to synchronize training speeds across all layers by scaling gradients relative to each trainable tensor's current value. Specifically, during every batch update, we ensure that the relative change in the L1-norm of tensors remains consistent across all network layers throughout the training process. Experiments on the MNIST dataset demonstrate that our approach effectively scales gradients, resulting in approximately equal relative changes in trainable tensors across layers. Furthermore, when evaluating test accuracy against training time, our method achieves faster convergence and higher final accuracy compared to other methods, given the same number of training steps.

Driven by the need to explore the connection between progesterone levels and days within the menstrual cycle in a longitudinal context, we introduce a multi-kink quantile regression model tailored for such data. This approach relaxes standard linearity assumptions by allowing distinct regression structures across different regions of the threshold covariate's domain. Initially, we develop the multi-kink quantile regression framework for longitudinal settings and present two estimation strategies for determining regression coefficients and kink point locations: a computationally efficient profile estimator assuming working independence, and an unbiased generalized estimation equation method that accounts for within-subject correlations. We establish the selection consistency regarding the number of kink points and the asymptotic normality of both estimators. Furthermore, we construct a rank score test utilizing partial subgradients to detect the presence of kink effects in longitudinal studies, deriving both the null and local alternative distributions for the test statistic. Simulation results indicate that the proposed methods exhibit excellent performance in finite samples. In an application to longitudinal progesterone data, we identified two kink points across various quantiles, revealing that progesterone levels remain stable prior to ovulation, rise sharply within five to six days post-ovulation, and subsequently stabilize or decrease slightly.

We introduce the Multivariate Quantile Function Forecaster (MQF$^2$), a global probabilistic forecasting technique built upon multivariate quantile functions, specifically designed to address multi-horizon prediction tasks. Existing methods generally fall into two categories: autoregressive models, which capture temporal dependencies but suffer from error accumulation over longer horizons, and sequence-to-sequence models, which avoid error accumulation yet often fail to model time-step dependencies effectively. MQF$^2$ merges the strengths of these approaches by generating direct predictions as multivariate quantile functions, defined as the gradient of a convex function parameterized via input-convex neural networks. This design ensures the quantile function remains monotonic with respect to input levels, thereby preventing quantile crossing. We offer two training strategies for MQF$^2$: energy score optimization and maximum likelihood estimation. Empirical evaluations on both real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate that our model achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods on single-time-step metrics while successfully capturing temporal dependency structures.

5G represents the fifth generation of wireless networking, characterized by features such as high bandwidth and data speeds. Its primary application scenarios encompass Enhanced Mobile Broadband (eMBB), massive Machine Type Communications (mMTC), and ultra-Reliable and Low-Latency Communications (uRLLC), with the potential to support a diverse array of applications. This paper presents a systematic mapping study of literature published from January 2012 to December 2019 focusing on 5G integration within smart cities. Based on an analysis of 32 selected studies, we summarize and examine the associated scenarios, architectures, technologies, challenges, and lessons learned. The key findings are as follows: (1) Research was distributed across 27 publication venues; 17 studies relied on academic simulations, 13 utilized demonstrations or toy examples, and only 2 reported industrial applications. Additionally, 16 studies incorporated assumptions regarding 5G network design or smart city scenarios. (2) Transportation emerged as the most frequently discussed smart city scenario, followed by public safety, healthcare, tourism, entertainment, and education. (3) Twenty-eight studies addressed the architecture of 5G-enabled smart cities, covering smart city frameworks (with 5G as a component), 5G network architectures within smart cities, and business models for 5G deployment. (4) The most cited 5G-related technologies include radio access technologies, network slicing, and edge computing. (5) Primary challenges identified involve complex contexts, stringent requirements, and network development issues. (6) Most lessons learned highlighted benefits pertaining to 5G itself or the proposed methods for smart cities. Overall, this work offers a reflective overview of the state of the art over the past eight years, aiming to benefit both researchers and practitioners in the field.

This paper introduces the systems developed by the University of Stuttgart and the University of Colorado Boulder for SIGMORPHON 2020 Task 2, which focused on unsupervised morphological paradigm completion (Kann et al., 2020). The objective of this task was to generate morphological paradigms for a given set of lemmas using only the lemmas and unlabeled text as input. Our proposed approach is a variation of the task's baseline, specifically experimenting with replacing the inflection generation module with both an LSTM sequence-to-sequence model and an LSTM pointer-generator network. Our pointer-generator system achieved the highest average score across all seven submitted systems and surpassed the official baseline, which was the overall leader, on Bulgarian and Kannada.

For the upcoming five years, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) will utilize the 4-meter Mayall Telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory, employing 10 spectrographs equipped with 5,000 fibers each, to execute the initial Stage-IV dark energy galaxy survey. Specifically, the DESI Bright Galaxy Survey (BGS) aims to create the most comprehensive map of the universe during the dark energy-dominated era (at $z < 0.6$), targeting over 10 million galaxies across 14,000 square degrees. This study introduces and validates the final BGS target selection and survey design. Drawing from Legacy Surveys, the BGS will observe a magnitude-limited sample ($r < 19.5$, designated BGS Bright), a color-selected fainter sample ($19.5 < r < 20.175$, designated BGS Faint) optimized for high redshift efficiency, and a smaller low-redshift quasar sample. To ensure uniform completeness, the survey will apply scaled exposure times and visit every point on the footprint three times. By combining pre-survey validation observations with realistic simulations, we confirm that BGS can successfully implement its strategy and maximize the use of "bright" time. Our analysis demonstrates that BGS targets exhibit less than 1% stellar contamination with densities largely independent of imaging properties. Furthermore, we verify that BGS Bright achieves fiber assignment efficiencies exceeding 80%, while both BGS Bright and Faint attain redshift success rates above 95%, regardless of observing conditions. Consequently, BGS fulfills the requirements for a wide array of scientific applications. It is poised to deliver the most precise measurements of Baryon Acoustic Oscillations and Redshift-Space Distortions at $z < 0.4$, enabling the exploration of new methods reliant on highly complete and dense galaxy samples, such as N-point statistics and multi-tracer techniques. Additionally, BGS serves as a potent instrument for investigating galaxy populations and the relationships between galaxies and dark matter.

Recently, there has been significant interest in solving time-dependent differential equations using neural networks, a method that learns the governing laws of solution evolution from data potentially contaminated with random noise. Unlike many other machine learning tasks, this domain often possesses substantial prior knowledge about the system, such as the exact conservation of physical quantities like energy or angular momentum in various dynamical systems. Consequently, when neural networks attempt to learn these conservation laws directly from data, they can only approximate them due to limitations in training duration and noise. This paper introduces an alternative strategy that leverages Noether's Theorem to embed conservation laws directly into the neural network's architecture. We show that this approach yields superior predictions for three distinct model systems: a non-relativistic particle moving within a three-dimensional Newtonian gravitational potential, a massive relativistic particle navigating the Schwarzschild metric, and a four-dimensional system comprising two interacting particles.

Metalenses are gaining significant attention for enabling complex optical capabilities within planar and compact systems, yet chromatic and off-axis aberrations persist as major hurdles. In this study, we experimentally examine the broadband performance of metalenses utilizing quadratic phase profiles. Our findings reveal that these devices not only support an arbitrarily wide field of view but also possess intrinsic tolerance against both longitudinal and transverse chromatic aberrations. Consequently, we present a single-layer silicon metalens capable of operating across a 140 nm bandwidth at both 1300 nm and 1550 nm telecommunication wavelengths, achieving a field of view of 86 degrees.

Algorithmic recourse aims to reverse adverse automated decisions, such as converting a loan denial into an approval, by proposing actionable modifications to specific features. Most existing approaches generate cost-effective recourse by assuming that features can be manipulated independently (IMF). To handle feature dependencies, researchers typically employ a causal recourse framework; however, the rigid assumptions inherent in causal models and structural equations often limit their effectiveness in complex domains where causal relationships are unclear. This study introduces \texttt{DEAR} (DisEntangling Algorithmic Recourse), a new and practical framework that bridges the divide between the IMF assumption and strong causal requirements. \texttt{DEAR} creates recourses by disentangling the latent representation of co-varying features from a selected subset of promising candidates, thereby addressing key practical goals. Empirical results on real-world datasets validate our theoretically grounded model and demonstrate the framework's capacity to deliver reliable, low-cost recourse even when feature dependencies exist.

The pre-saddle neutron multiplicity has been computed for various fission reactions triggered by both heavy ions and light particles. However, experimental methods cannot distinguish between neutrons emitted prior to the saddle point and those released between the saddle and scission points. In this study, the pre-saddle neutron multiplicity is determined by comparing experimental anisotropies with those forecasted by the standard saddle-point statistical model. The findings indicate that this multiplicity is influenced by the compound nucleus's stability and fission barrier height. Specifically, in heavy ion-induced fission, the number of pre-saddle neutrons declines as the compound nucleus's excitation energy rises, primarily because the transition time from the ground state to the saddle point shortens with higher excitation energy. Conversely, in fission induced by light particles, the pre-saddle neutron count increases with rising excitation energy.

We examine a non-negative sequence defined as $c_n = h(n) \cdot n^{\alpha-1} \cdot \rho^{-n}$, where $h$ is slowly varying, $\alpha>0$, $0<\rho<1$, and $n\in\mathbb{N}$. We analyze the coefficients of $G(x,y) = \prod_{k\ge1}(1-x^ky)^{-c_k}$, representing the bivariate generating function for multisets of combinatorial objects. Combining probabilistic techniques derived from the Boltzmann model with analytic saddle-point methods, we derive the asymptotic count of multisets of total size $n$ containing $N$ components—specifically, the coefficient of $x^ny^N$ in $G(x,y)$—as $n\to\infty$ across all values of $N$. These findings uncover a phase transition in the counting formula governed by the ratio $n/N$, illustrating a fundamental shift from a bivariate local limit theorem to an univariate one.

Significant advancements have recently occurred in reconstructing an object's 3D geometry from a single image, yet it is argued that existing approaches often rely on a simplistic "nearest-neighbor" tactic rather than truly comprehending the underlying shape. This paper rigorously demonstrates that many state-of-the-art methods suffer from two key flaws: discrepancies between coarse reconstructions and the input images, and a failure to generalize across different domains. To address this, we introduce REFINE, a post-processing mesh refinement module designed to be seamlessly integrated into any existing black-box reconstruction pipeline. During inference, REFINE optimizes a network for each specific mesh to enforce consistency between the generated geometry and the provided view. By combining this optimization with a new set of regularizing losses, we effectively bridge the domain gap and achieve state-of-the-art results. We contend that this novel paradigm represents a crucial step toward robust and accurate reconstructions, ensuring continued relevance as new reconstruction networks emerge.

Following the introduction of $Gaia$ astrometry, massive accreted systems in the Galaxy can now be identified by their distinctive dynamical signatures. Among these, the $Gaia$-Sausage-Enceladus (GSE) stands out as an early "building block," possessing a virial mass exceeding $10^{10}\,\mathrm{M_\odot}$ at the time of infall ($z\sim1-3$). To distinguish the progenitor population from background stars, we examined its chemical composition using up to 30 elemental abundances from the GALAH+ Survey Data Release 3 (DR3). To guide our selection of elements for chemically isolating accreted stars, we analyzed 4164 stars exhibiting low-$\alpha$ abundances and halo kinematics; these stars showed the greatest deviations from Milky Way stars in Mg, Si, Na, Al, Mn, Fe, Ni, and Cu abundances. Using Gaussian mixture models on various element combinations based on significance and detection rates, we identified the most populated and least contaminated component representing GSE, which consists of 1049 stars selected via [Na/Fe] versus [Mg/Mn] in GALAH+ DR3. We provide selection tables and report the chrono-chemodynamical properties (age, chemistry, and dynamics) of this group. By cross-referencing with a previously established clean dynamical selection for GSE stars ($30 < \sqrt{J_R~/~\mathrm{kpc\,km\,s^{-1}}} < 55$), we characterized an unprecedented 24 abundances for this structure using GALAH+ DR3. This chemical selection method avoids circular reasoning and allows for the characterization of GSE's dynamical properties, such as a mean $\sqrt{J_R~/~\mathrm{kpc\,km\,s^{-1}}}$ of $26_{-14}^{+9}$. We found that only $(29\pm1)\%$ of GSE stars fall within the clean dynamical selection region. Our methodology will enhance future investigations into accreted structures and their roles in the Milky Way's formation.

In Random Forests, proximity distances serve as a metric representation of data within the decision space. By examining how input variations correspond to the shifting positions of instances in this space, we can identify the independent impact of each feature on decision-making. For binary feature vectors, this methodology is completely defined. As input changes drive specific instances closer to either the in-group or out-group, the distinct contribution of each feature is revealed. This approach enables the calculation of individual feature roles in black-box decisions, facilitating the explanation of the decision process, the auditing of the classifier, and the post-hoc analysis of classification errors.

Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) astrometry is a proven method for reaching $\pm10~\mu$as parallax precision at frequencies exceeding 10~GHz. However, at lower frequencies, astrometric accuracy is primarily constrained by uncompensated interferometer delays caused by the ionosphere. Multiview is a new calibration approach that leverages observations of several quasars to precisely model and eliminate time-variable, direction-dependent delay variations. This study expands the Multiview technique by applying phase referencing to the target source (termed "inverse Multiview") and evaluates its efficacy. Observations conducted with a four-antenna VLBI array at 8.3~GHz demonstrate single-epoch astrometric accuracies approaching $20~\mu$as for target-reference quasar separations of up to approximately 7 degrees. This marks an improvement in astrometric precision of up to an order of magnitude relative to standard phase referencing.

We introduce Self-Imitation via Reduction (SIR), a new learning framework designed to address compositional reinforcement learning challenges. This approach relies on two fundamental concepts: task reduction and self-imitation. Task reduction simplifies difficult problems by actively transforming them into easier tasks that the RL agent can solve. Once the agent resolves the original complex task through this reduction, it inherently generates a solution trajectory to emulate. By repeatedly gathering and imitating these self-created demonstrations, the agent can gradually broaden the solved subspace across the entire task domain. Experimental results demonstrate that SIR substantially enhances and speeds up learning on various difficult sparse-reward continuous-control tasks featuring compositional structures. The code and accompanying videos can be found at https://sites.google.com/view/sir-compositional.

Segmenting commercial product portfolios into priority tiers known as ABCD analysis is a standard supply chain practice, where key planning parameters linked to this segmentation dictate strategic and execution priorities that ultimately influence supply chain performance. Because manual segmentation is impractical for extensive product assortments, an automated algorithm is required; consequently, we recommend that the design of such an ABCD algorithm receives careful scrutiny and propose three essential features that can be integrated to enhance its quality and commercial value.

Utilizing a two-mode framework, we demonstrate that rotating a double-well system—composed of a toroidal condensate featuring two diametrically opposed barriers—enables transitions into various coexistent regime arrays within the phase space. This setup mirrors the atomtronic equivalent of the direct-current superconducting quantum interference device. As the system rotates, the localized on-site functions experience a phase gradient, necessitating a phase difference across each junction to maintain velocity field quantization around the torus. We show that this induced phase significantly alters the relative magnitudes of different hopping parameters. Specifically, within a defined range of rotation frequencies, a hopping parameter typically neglected in static systems becomes the dominant factor governing dynamics. At the boundaries of this frequency interval, bifurcations in stationary points occur, drastically reshaping the phase space portrait of the macroscopic canonical conjugate variables' orbits. We further examine the resulting dynamics, which integrate $0$ and $\pi$ Josephson modes, and calculate the small-oscillation periods for these orbits across the frequency ranges where each mode persists. All model predictions are validated through Gross-Pitaevskii simulations.

We investigate the task of dividing a graph into a variable number of disjoint subgraphs that maximize total density. A partition's density is defined as the sum of individual subgraph densities, where each subgraph's density equals its average degree (the ratio of edges to vertices). This problem, termed Dense Graph Partition, is established as NP-hard for general graphs but admits polynomial-time solutions for trees and a 2-approximation algorithm. This study restricts Dense Graph Partition to specific sparse and dense graph classes. We demonstrate that the problem remains NP-hard on dense bipartite graphs and cubic graphs. Furthermore, for dense graphs with $n$ vertices, we show it is polynomial-time solvable when the minimum degree is $n-3$, yet NP-hard for $(n-4)$-regular graphs. Additionally, we establish a polynomial-time $4/3$-approximation for cubic graphs and an efficient polynomial-time approximation scheme for graphs with a minimum degree of $n-t$, where $t$ is any constant greater than or equal to 4.

We utilized the VULCAN laser facility to create a laser plasma X-ray source for photoionisation studies. By irradiating thin silver or tin foils mounted on parylene substrates with a nanosecond laser pulse of approximately ${10}^{15}$ W cm$^{-2}$ intensity, we recorded L-shell emissions between 3.3 and 4.4 keV from both the laser-irradiated and non-irradiated surfaces. Both experimental data and simulations demonstrate that silver produces significantly higher laser-to-X-ray conversion yields than tin, with simulations predicting yields roughly twice as high as those observed experimentally. While detailed angular measurements were not obtained in the experiments, simulations suggest the emission is nearly isotropic on the irradiated side but follows a near-cosine distribution on the non-irradiated side, a pattern consistent with prior experimental findings.

Quantum coherence, akin to entanglement, serves as a cornerstone resource in quantum information science. Recent years have witnessed significant advancements in developing a comprehensive resource theory of coherence, leading to the formulation of concepts such as block-coherence and POVM-based coherence. Despite these strides, unresolved challenges persist. Specifically, defining incoherent operations independently of incoherent states remains difficult, posing a substantial barrier to establishing a resource theory for dynamical coherence. This study addresses that limitation by proposing an alternative definition of incoherent operations derived from coherence measures, which we then use to quantify dynamical coherence. Furthermore, we apply this new definition to measure POVM-based dynamical coherence.

Using Subaru/MOIRCS for deep near-infrared imaging of the low-metallicity (${\rm [O/H]}=-0.7$ dex) H II region Sh 2-127 (S127), we identified two young clusters: S127A, containing 413 members in an extended region, and S127B, with 338 members in a compact region. The survey reached a limiting magnitude of $K=21.3$ mag (10$\sigma$), allowing detection of stars down to $\sim$0.2 $M_\odot$. These clusters are approximately ten times larger than previously studied young low-metallicity clusters and exceed the size of most young clusters in the solar neighborhood. Analysis of the K-band luminosity functions reveals very young ages of 0.5 Myr for S127A and 0.1–0.5 Myr for S127B. These ages align with the high extinction ($A_V\simeq20$ mag) caused by thick molecular clouds, the presence of a compact H II region, and class I source candidates. Furthermore, the initial mass function (IMF) of these low-metallicity clusters appears indistinguishable from that of the solar neighborhood. However, disk fractions of $28\% \pm 3\%$ for S127A and $40\% \pm 4\%$ for S127B are significantly lower than the $\sim$50$\%$–60% observed in similarly aged solar neighborhood clusters. The higher disk fraction in S127B compared to other studied low-metallicity clusters (<30%) is likely attributed to its youth. These findings suggest that while a substantial portion of very young stars in low-metallicity environments retain disks, these disks are rapidly dispersed. Overall, these results corroborate our prior studies, indicating that a solar-neighborhood-like IMF and low disk fractions are characteristic features of low-metallicity regions, irrespective of cluster scale.

The MultiWOZ dataset (Budzianowski et al., 2018) is commonly employed to benchmark the context-to-response capabilities of task-oriented dialogue systems. In this study, we uncover inconsistencies in the data preprocessing and reporting of three corpus-based metrics applied to this dataset, specifically the BLEU score and Inform & Success rates. We highlight several deficiencies within the MultiWOZ benchmark, including inadequate preprocessing, vague or incomplete evaluation metrics, and a rigid database structure. By re-evaluating seven end-to-end and six policy optimization models under fair and consistent conditions, we demonstrate that their previously reported scores are not directly comparable. To support future system comparisons, we release standalone, standardized evaluation scripts and provide fundamental recommendations for corpus-based benchmarking in subsequent research.
Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a semifinite von Neumann algebra endowed with an increasing sequence of semifinite von Neumann subalgebras $(\mathcal{M}_n)_{n\geq 1}$. For any $0

This manuscript details measurements of water-based liquid scintillators (WbLS), illustrating the separation of Cherenkov and scintillation components via the nanosecond-scale timing capabilities of a Large Area Picosecond Photodetector (LAPPD). Furthermore, the temporal profiles of three WbLS mixtures, distinguished by varying ratios of scintillating compounds, are analyzed, revealing enhanced sensitivity to the scintillator's rise time. Data were collected using both an LAPPD and a standard photomultiplier tube (PMT).

All samples were measured with an effective resolution on the order of 100 picoseconds, enabling the distinction between Cherenkov and scintillation light solely through photon arrival time selection. In all instances, the Cherenkov purity of the selected photons exceeded 60%, surpassing 80% for a mixture containing 1% scintillator.
